connections.hePhrase: קוּנְטְרֵס קְרָאתִיו צִדְקַת הַצַּדִּיק בִּשְׁנַת "צִדְקוֹת אָהֵב"
connections.quote: ‘The soul that sins is the one that will die. A son will not bear his father’s guilt, nor will a father bear his son’s guilt. The righteousness of the righteous person will remain his own, and the wickedness of the wicked person will remain his own.’

connections.hePhrase: קוּנְטְרֵס קְרָאתִיו צִדְקַת הַצַּדִּיק בִּשְׁנַת "צִדְקוֹת אָהֵב"
connections.quote: ‘For Hashem is righteous and loves righteous deeds; the upright will behold His face.’

connections.hePhrase: [א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן,
connections.quote: ‘This is how you shall eat it: with your belts fastened, your shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. Eat it in haste; it is a Pesach offering to Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: [א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן,
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 2:3
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 2:3
connections.quote: “Afterward, “to learn and to teach”: first one receives from his teachers, then still more from his colleagues, as is taught in Ta’anit 7a—this is “to learn”; and from his students more than from them all—this is “to teach.” These correspond to the passages “You shall love” and “And it shall be, if you listen,” as is taught in Berakhot 14b. Afterward, “to guard”: this is the reflection before an action comes into practice, from the expression “His father kept [the matter],” which signifies waiting. As is written in Asarah Ma’amarot, a mitzvah requires watchfulness and waiting so that one can prepare oneself, while the zealous act early lest death overtake them. This corresponds to “So that your days may be many.” After one has passed through all these levels, he should then be deliberate, for he is assured of “so that they may be many”: life will increase, and his desire will not cease after a time. At the beginning it is different. When a desire reaches him, he must act upon it promptly, lest the desire cease in the meantime. As we have written elsewhere concerning the Passover offering in Egypt, it is eaten in haste while one has not yet passed through the preceding levels.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek locates this transition within the sequence “to learn, to teach, to guard, to do, and to establish.” It explains how patient preparation can become appropriate once the earlier stages have steadied the desire. This gives a fuller account of the deliberation with which Tzidkat HaTzadik concludes.
connections.headline: Haste at the beginning and deliberation afterward

connections.hePhrase: [א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן,
connections.quote: “The first commandment was the eating of the paschal offerings: to eat sacred meat, so that holiness would enter every Israelite through it. The commandment given concerning it was: “This is how you shall eat it—your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand.” Why did they need this, when the eating took place at night and the departure from Egypt by day? Rather, this was the preparation of being ready to follow the LORD: “your following Me into the wilderness.” This is the meaning of “the right foot”: the work of this month is to be ready to follow the LORD, “to walk in His ways.” This is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, represented by the final letter heh, kingship.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik asks why the Israelites ate ready for travel although their departure would occur only later. Readiness itself was their first acceptance of Heaven’s rule. This gives substance to Tzidkat HaTzadik’s initial haste: the decisive moment is used to orient oneself toward following God, before the journey has been completed. It also helps explain why the urgency of the beginning need not dictate the pace of everything that follows.
connections.headline: Seizing the first awakening, then proceeding patiently

connections.hePhrase: [א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 25:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 25:1
connections.quote: “All this indicates that, in a situation where Israel clearly recognizes His blessed will, they no longer attend to any established order, but have the capacity to leap without proceeding through gradual stages, acting with great alacrity to do His blessed will. This is the meaning of: “The Passover offering that our ancestors would eat—for what reason? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over.” That is, why were they commanded to undertake such intense service? “Because the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over the houses of our ancestors in Egypt”: because the Holy One, blessed be He, also leapt over, and shone salvation upon us by a leap, in haste, before the appointed time. Therefore we too were commanded, and it was fixed in our hearts, to perform such service in a short time and with great alacrity.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why Pesach can require a leap past ordinary stages: clearly recognized Divine will calls forth swift service, answering the salvation that arrived by a leap. This illuminates why Rav Tzadok treats the awakening as an opportunity that can be lost through delay. Tzidkat HaTzadik supplies the further distinction in this pair: after the initial departure, service proceeds slowly and deliberately. The comparison does not turn every impulse into authorization to skip stages.
connections.headline: Seizing the first awakening, then proceeding patiently

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
connections.quote: ““You shall eat it in haste”: that one is eaten in haste, but no other [Paschal offering] is eaten in haste.”
connections.context: The discussion distinguishes the first Passover in Egypt from later Passovers. Rav Tzadok applies that distinction to spiritual beginnings: the first break with one’s former course calls for haste; the subsequent course can proceed deliberately.

connections.hePhrase: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ל״א:י״ד-ט״ז
connections.quote: “This condition is the condition of the Exodus from Egypt, of which it is said, ‘For the people fled.’ At first sight this is puzzling: why was it so? Had they told Pharaoh to release them forever, would he not have been compelled to release them? Rather, the evil in the souls of Israel was still at full strength in the left chamber, for their impurity did not cease until the giving of the Torah. Their aim and desire were only that their divine soul should leave the exile of the other side, which is the impurity of Egypt, and cleave to Him, blessed be He. As it is written, ‘Hashem, my strength, my stronghold, and my refuge in a day of distress,’ and so forth; ‘my stronghold and my refuge,’ and so forth; ‘He is a refuge for me,’ and so forth. Therefore, in the future, when Hashem removes the spirit of impurity from the earth, it is written, ‘You shall not go in flight, for Hashem goes before you,’ and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: [ב] בְּרָכוֹת לְרֹאשׁ צַדִּיק.
connections.quote: ‘Blessings rest upon the head of the righteous, but violence will cover the mouth of the wicked.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעִקַּר הַכֹּל: "דַּע אֶת אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ" – וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וְעָבְדֵהוּ",
connections.quote: ‘And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul. For Hashem searches every heart and understands every inclination of thought. If you seek Him, He will let you find Him; if you abandon Him, He will cast you off forever.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַבְּרָכָה לִפְנֵי כָּל מַעֲשֶׂה, לְיַחֵד כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לַהַשֵּׁם,
connections.quote: “At the beginning we bless, “Who brings bread forth from the earth,” as the Sages said in Berakhot: “Ha-motzi means ‘who brought forth.’” Blessing is also an expression of drawing forth: one draws to oneself the utterance of God’s mouth clothed within the food. As it is written, “For a person does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds from God’s mouth.” The blessed will that, from the creation of the world, brings into being and gives life to everything in the world is clothed within the bread and gives life to the person. Through the blessing, the person breaks through the garments and finds and draws forth to himself the blessed will that gives him life. Before eating, at the time of the blessing, the person gives to the food, for through the blessing the food is raised. But at the time of eating, the food is called the giver, because the person is nourished by it. After eating, the person prevails over the food, because the choice is then in his hands: according to the way he serves God with the strength of that eating, so will be the ascent of that food.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the present siman’s instruction to dedicate one’s deeds to Hashem through the blessing. Recognition before eating uncovers the divine will within the food, but the account continues afterward: the person chooses how to serve Hashem with the received strength. Knowing before Whom one blesses thus begins a relationship that governs the ensuing action; it is more than an acknowledgment that ends when the words of the blessing end.
connections.headline: A blessing redirects the life received from food toward its Giver

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם [רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן].
connections.quote: ‘Know Him in all your ways, and He will make your paths straight.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם [רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן].
connections.quote: “Someone who conducts himself according to medicine, but intends only that his body and limbs should be sound and that he should have children to perform his work and labor for his needs, is not following a good path. Rather, he should intend that his body be sound and strong so that his soul may be upright in knowing Hashem, for one cannot understand and contemplate wisdom while hungry or ill, or while one of his limbs is in pain. He should intend to have a son who may become wise and great in Israel. Thus, one who follows this path throughout his life serves Hashem continually, even while doing business and even during marital relations, because his intention in everything is to obtain what he needs so that his body will be sound for serving Hashem. Even while sleeping, if he sleeps deliberately so that his mind and body may rest, lest he become ill and be unable to serve Hashem because of his illness, his sleep is service of the Omnipresent, blessed be He. Concerning this, the Sages commanded, ‘Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.’ This is what Solomon said in his wisdom: ‘Know Him in all your ways, and He will make your paths straight.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַבְּרָכָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: הַשִּׁעוּר בָּהּ קָטָן שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ לְמִי מְבָרְכִין.
connections.quote: ‘The halakhah does not follow any of these teachings, but rather this statement of Rav Nachman: A minor who knows to Whom the blessing is addressed may be included in the zimmun. Abaye and Rava were sitting before Rabbah. Rabbah asked them: ‘To Whom do we recite the blessing?’ They answered: ‘To the Merciful One.’ ‘And where does the Merciful One dwell?’ Rava pointed toward the ceiling. Abaye went outside and pointed toward heaven. Rabbah told them: ‘Both of you will become Torah scholars.’ This is what people say: ‘Gourds are recognizable from their sap, as they first begin to form.’’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּשְׁאָר מִצְוֹת, אֵין הַשִּׁעוּר שֶׁיֵּדַע לְמִי מַנִּיחִין תְּפִלִּין וְכַיּוֹצֵא.
connections.quote: “A minor who knows how to wave the lulav: The Sages taught, a minor who knows how to wave is obligated in lulav; one who knows how to wrap himself is obligated in tzitzit; one who knows how to safeguard tefillin—his father obtains tefillin for him; one who knows how to speak—his father teaches him Torah and the recitation of Shema.”
connections.context: These age criteria concern the child’s capacity to perform or safeguard each mitzvah. They supply the contrast to the criterion cited just before this phrase: knowing to Whom a blessing is addressed.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַתְחָלַת הַכְּנִיסָה לַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם".
connections.quote: ‘Fear of Hashem is the beginning of wisdom; all who carry out His commands have sound understanding. His praise endures forever.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הוּא עַל יְדֵי "שִׁוִּיתִי הַשֵּׁם לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אֹרַח חַיִּים.
connections.quote: ‘I have kept Hashem before me always; with Him at my right hand, I will not falter.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הוּא עַל יְדֵי "שִׁוִּיתִי הַשֵּׁם לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אֹרַח חַיִּים.
connections.displayRef: Rema on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 1:1
connections.quote: ““I have set Hashem before me always” is a great principle of the Torah and of the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person’s sitting, movements, and affairs when alone at home are unlike his sitting, movements, and affairs before a great king. His speech and free expression as he wishes among his household and relatives are unlike his speech in the king’s presence. All the more so, when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills all the earth, stands over him and sees his deeds—as it is said, “Can a person hide in secret places and I not see him? declares Hashem”—fear and submission in awe of Hashem, and shame before Him, will immediately come upon him continually.”
connections.context: This is the Rema’s passage that Rav Tzadok explicitly cites. Awareness of standing before Hashem produces the awe that precedes action; it explains why the beginning of a blessing addresses Him directly as “You.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְנוּ בְּרָכוֹת שֶׁכֻּלָּן מַתְחִילִין בִּלְשׁוֹן נוֹכֵחַ,
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 2:5
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 2:5
connections.quote: “Therefore, in this world, ‘I am not read as I am written’ (Pesachim 50a): every blessing begins in direct address, ‘Blessed are You,’ and then becomes concealed, ‘Who has sanctified us.’ Only at the beginning do ‘his eyes look directly ahead,’ as written in Tanya, chapter 41, that an intention for its own sake suffices at the beginning. [Therefore, a blessing adjoining another blessing needs only the first opening (Berakhot 46a). Some blessings conclude with ‘Blessed,’ corresponding to ‘its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah,’ explained above in another connection; this is not the place to elaborate.]”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek explains the same change of grammatical person through the difference between an opening recognition and an enduring possession of the heart. Its preceding discussion describes that enduring possession as the completion of the stages of service. This gives the siman's moment of direct address a precise role: it begins and directs the act, even while the awareness is not yet continuously manifest. It also connects this to the initial intention discussed in Siman 5.
connections.headline: Recognition at the opening of a blessing

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עַל גּוֹזָלָיו יְרַחֵף" – נוֹגֵעַ וְאֵינוֹ נוֹגֵעַ, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
connections.quote: “Like an eagle that stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, spreading its wings to take up a fledgling and carry it upon its pinion.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עַל גּוֹזָלָיו יְרַחֵף" – נוֹגֵעַ וְאֵינוֹ נוֹגֵעַ, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
connections.quote: “‘Over its fledglings it hovers’: it does not press its weight upon them, but hovers over them—touching and not touching.”

connections.hePhrase: [ג] עִקַּר הַקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע: קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹל תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת, כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת יג.),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said: Why does the paragraph “Shema” precede “And it shall be, if you listen”? So that one first accepts the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, and afterward accepts the yoke of the commandments.”
connections.context: This Mishnah supplies the two acceptances that Rav Tzadok identifies as the substance of Shema.

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא בְּבֹקֶר וָעֶרֶב, אֶלָּא "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ", עַיֵּן שָׁם י"א עַמּוּד א'.
connections.quote: “Beit Shammai say: If so, let Scripture say “in the morning and in the evening.” Why does it say “when you lie down and when you rise”?”

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא בְּבֹקֶר וָעֶרֶב, אֶלָּא "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ", עַיֵּן שָׁם י"א עַמּוּד א'.
connections.quote: “Why, then, does it say “when you lie down and when you rise”? At the time when people lie down, and at the time when people rise.”
connections.context: The first quotation raises the wording question in Beit Shammai’s argument; the second gives Beit Hillel’s explanation of the times. Rav Tzadok draws attention to the Torah’s choice of human activity, lying down and rising, to define the obligation.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֵירוּבִין סה.): "אֲנַן פּוֹעֲלֵי דִּימָמָא", כְּפוֹעֲלִים הָעוֹשִׂים מְלָאכָה שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם לָאָדוֹן,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: We are daytime workers. Rav Acha bar Yaakov would borrow [from his daytime study allotment] and repay [at night].’

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִלּוּ בְּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן מְקַצֵּר בִּשְׁבִיל עֲבוֹדָתוֹ (בְּרָכוֹת טז.).
connections.quote: “But it was taught: Laborers working for an employer recite Shema and pray. They eat their bread and do not recite a blessing before it, but afterward they recite two blessings. How so? They recite the first blessing in its usual form; in the second they begin with the blessing for the land and include “Who builds Jerusalem” within the blessing for the land. When does this apply? When they work for wages. But if they work in exchange for their meal, or if the employer reclines at the meal with them, they recite the blessings in their usual form.”
connections.context: This is the Talmudic rule behind Rav Tzadok’s illustration of a laborer’s commitment to his employer’s work. Its concluding qualifications are part of the source. Rav Tzadok uses that commitment as a model for dedicating the day’s activity to Hashem.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַלַּיְלָה, עֵת שְׁכִיבָה וּמְנוּחָה, צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 11:2
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 11:2
connections.quote: ““To declare Your kindness in the morning.” When Abraham’s morning shines before a person—as in “one called to another,” translated “they receive from one another”—one explicitly recognizes “the kindness of God all day.” “Your faithfulness in the nights” means that when Abraham’s morning is concealed, a person does not recognize the connection. This concealment is called night: “One did not approach the other all night.” As the Midrash explains, when people become separated from one another it is called night, appearing as separation and interruption. Then the person’s only counsel is to hold to greater faith. This is “Your faithfulness in the nights.” Through faith, the whole of a person’s existence can be strengthened. In truth, a person’s essential existence corresponds to the faith established in his heart. As the Zohar says, “‘Her husband is known in the gates’—this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who becomes known according to what each measures within his heart, as much as each can cleave ….” According to the faith that each establishes in his heart, God dwells within him and gives him existence and endurance.”
connections.explanation: The Radziner passage explains the inward meaning of night: the connection is not apparent, so faith must carry the person’s existence and endurance. This clarifies why the present siman requires a separate acceptance for lying down and calls that inactive service a greater labor. The night’s avodah is not simply a second performance of the daytime task. It carries allegiance to Hashem into a condition in which ordinary conscious activity and visible reassurance have receded.
connections.headline: Accepting Heaven’s yoke at night preserves connection when it cannot be clearly seen

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁגַּם בְּשָׁכְבוֹ עַל מִטָּתוֹ יֵדַע לִפְנֵי מִי הוּא שׁוֹכֵב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אֹרַח חַיִּים.
connections.displayRef: Rema on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 1:1
connections.quote: “Even when going about privately and when lying upon his bed, he should know before Whom he lies. Immediately upon awakening from sleep, he should rise promptly to serve his Creator, blessed and exalted be He.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok quotes this clause almost word for word. It extends awareness of Hashem into the person’s private, inactive state, and then carries that awareness into the moment of rising.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בָּזֶה עַל פָּסוּק "וַיַּחֲלֹם יַעֲקֹב", שֶׁמֵּהַחֲלוֹמוֹת נִכָּר מַעֲלַת הָאָדָם,
connections.quote: ‘He dreamed, and there was a ladder standing on the earth, its top reaching toward heaven; and there were angels of God ascending and descending upon it.’

connections.hePhrase: אִם גַּם כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ עוֹשֶׂה כְּלוּם, רַעְיוֹנָיו רַק "וְהִנֵּה הַשֵּׁם נִצָּב עָלָיו".
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.linkedRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ספר בראשית, ויצא ו׳
connections.quote: ““The land upon which you lie, I shall give to you.” The meaning of this blessing is that even while lying down and sleeping, your thoughts will be clear and pure.”
connections.context: This teaching explains the same blessing of Yaakov in terms of the purity of his thoughts during sleep. It supplies the precise parallel to the teaching Rav Tzadok introduces with “I heard,” at the phrase describing Yaakov’s thoughts even when he is inactive.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נָתְנוּ בְּרָכָה הַיְּתֵרָה לְעַרְבִית, שֶׁהוּא "הַשְׁכִּיבֵנוּ לְשָׁלוֹם".
connections.quote: “In the morning one recites two blessings before it [Shema] and one after it; in the evening, two before it and two after it.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נָתְנוּ בְּרָכָה הַיְּתֵרָה לְעַרְבִית, שֶׁהוּא "הַשְׁכִּיבֵנוּ לְשָׁלוֹם".
connections.quote: “Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: [The blessings were set] because of “You shall meditate in it day and night” (Joshua 1:8), so that the meditation of the day and of the night should be equal. Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Because of “Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments” (Psalms 119:164).”
connections.context: Hashkiveinu is the second blessing after the evening Shema, the one the evening has beyond the morning. Rashi on the Mishnah (Berakhot 11a) cites this Yerushalmi for the count of seven blessings.

connections.hePhrase: וְשֶׁל עַרְבִית קוֹדֵם, כִּדְפָתַח בֵּיהּ תַּנָּא: "דִּקְרָא קָאֵי",
connections.quote: ‘The tanna bases his teaching on the verse that says, ‘When you lie down and when you rise.’ This is what he teaches: When is the time for the Shema recited on lying down? From the time the priests enter to eat their terumah.’

connections.hePhrase: דִּבְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא,
connections.quote: “He [Rabbi Zeira] said to him: Why do the goats go at the head [of the flock] and then the sheep? He [Rav Yehudah] said to him: Like the creation of the world—first darkness and then light.”

connections.hePhrase: דִּבְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא,
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:1-2
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:1–2
connections.quote: “Berakhot (2a): “He derives it from the creation of the world,” etc., see there. For with sacred offerings the night follows the day … even though at the creation of the world first there was darkness and then light (Shabbat 77b). … One might have thought that our acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven depends on us, so that the day would come first. Therefore he said “and he derives it,” etc.: as soon as a person has accepted the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, and it has become clear to him that Hashem is One, everything returns to its source.”

connections.hePhrase: דִּבְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Day of Pesach 15:2
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Day of Pesach 15:2
connections.quote: “Israel had to clarify the difference so that it could be seen explicitly: between Israel’s flock, a flock for a commandment, and Egypt’s flock, a flock of idolatry. A flock hints at the evening before the morning, as the Gemara asks: “Why do goats walk first and then sheep? Like the world’s creation: first darkness and then light, as it says, ‘There was evening and there was morning.’” My holy father explained that this is what the Sages meant in saying that Egypt’s idolatry was the flock. All their service was directed to the darkness preceding the light; they made that primordial darkness their object of fear, so that all their deeds would remain in darkness and they could receive every flow of good without any service, above their understanding. This is called darkness: proceeding without knowledge. Light is when a person proceeds with knowledge and reckoning. The Zohar says concerning this, “Flock was bound to flock”: outwardly, Israel too follow without knowledge or calculation, above their apprehension. They were even called “a hasty people, who put your mouth before your ears,” not calculating whether they would have the strength to bear it. Of this it says that Israel were bound in this for four hundred years, until the distinction would be explicitly clarified and separated from its knot. It would become apparent that Israel’s entire purpose in following beyond their apprehension was to reach the source at the root of His will, which is a light far higher than the light called light from the human side. Such following without knowledge and reckoning is called a flock of a commandment. Egypt’s flock, by contrast, is called idolatry: they do not wish to look at the light. They say that His will intentionally emanated evening before morning in order to conceal the light from human eyes, so that a person would always walk in darkness and not in light, with deeds in darkness. The Zohar speaks of the clarification’s not being easily untied because this is truly a very fine distinction; it is not easy to show the difference between flock and flock explicitly to human eyes.”
connections.explanation: Both passages invoke darkness preceding light, but Sod Yesharim explains why the direction of the response matters. Israel follows beyond present comprehension in order to reach the source of Hashem’s will; Egypt treats the preceding darkness as a place in which to avoid accountable service. This sharpens the present siman’s first acceptance of Heaven’s yoke: one begins faithfully without clarity so that clearer understanding and deed can follow, rather than making lack of understanding an end in itself.
connections.headline: Fidelity before understanding seeks a greater light rather than permanent obscurity

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז סוֹפוֹ לְקַיְּמָהּ בְּעֹשֶׁר וּנְהוֹרָא דִּימָמָא,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yonatan says: Whoever upholds the Torah in poverty will ultimately uphold it in wealth; and whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will ultimately neglect it in poverty.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok draws on the Mishnah’s “ultimately uphold it in wealth,” applying poverty and wealth here to obscurity and clear understanding. The Mishnah’s opposite clause is retained with the teaching.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ רֶגַע אֶחָד לֹא יָזוּז מִמֶּנּוּ הָעוֹל.
connections.quote:
“I found in Pesikta Zutarta, Parashat Ekev, concerning “Beware lest you forget”: this is one who casts off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, eating without prayer and without a blessing. It appears that forgetting is interpreted as casting off the yoke. Although blessings over enjoyment and the prohibition against eating before prayer are only rabbinic prohibitions, since Israel have already become accustomed to them, one who violates them does so through casting off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. Casting off the yoke is the subject of the warning against forgetting. Accordingly, this is a continual warning that there should be no moment in which he casts off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. This requires great mindfulness, so that the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven remains continually upon his heart, in addition to accepting the yoke in Shema morning and evening.

Sefer Yereim, section 11, explains this warning as requiring a person not to forget to accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven and recite Shema each day. According to the view that Shema is rabbinic, he explains that a person should continually remember his Creator and His commandments. His position is that accepting the yoke morning and evening suffices. Presumably the concluding word “continually” has the same meaning: he should remember this matter every day in the morning and evening, or at another time during the day and night. Someone who recites Shema and prays without any attention, because his heart is directed elsewhere, and who throughout the entire day never brings the remembrance of Hashem to his heart, has violated this warning according to his words.

Rabbeinu Yonah writes in Sha’arei Teshuvah, gate 3, section 27, that this is a warning to remember Hashem at all times, and the apparent meaning of his words is literally at every moment. Yet it seems that this interpretation would not be pleasing to the Master: one who forgot for a single moment would transgress a prohibition, and a person would thereby transgress countless prohibitions every day. As explained, not every person merits remaining constantly attached to Hashem, never departing entirely from remembrance of Him even while occupied with worldly affairs and the like.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes an enduring acceptance of Hashem’s authority from uninterrupted conscious contemplation. This discussion gives essential context to “not even for one moment should the yoke depart from him,” before the following teaching describes the exceptional level of constant attachment.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק: "אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם לֹא יַחְשֹׁב הַשֵּׁם לוֹ עָוֹן".
connections.quote: “I heard from my master, my grandfather, of blessed memory, concerning the verse ‘Fortunate is the person to whom Hashem does not reckon iniquity’: his thought is continually attached to the blessed Hashem. Therefore, when he falls away from that thought for a single moment and does not think of Hashem, he regards it as iniquity and sin. This is ‘Fortunate is the person who does not think of Hashem’: when he does not think of Hashem, ‘it is iniquity for him’—it is an iniquity in his eyes. This is a sign that his thought is continually attached to the blessed Hashem, and therefore fortunate is he.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק: "אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם לֹא יַחְשֹׁב הַשֵּׁם לוֹ עָוֹן".
connections.quote: ‘Fortunate is the person to whom Hashem does not reckon guilt, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ "בִּלְשְׁמָהּ" גַּבֵּי גֵּט, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּתַנְיָא פֶּרֶק מ"א,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים מ״א:כ״ה
connections.quote: “With this preparation of surrendering his soul to Hashem, he should begin the morning blessings: ‘Blessed are You…’ With this same preparation, he should begin his regular study session immediately after prayer. Likewise, before beginning to study in the middle of the day, he needs at least this preparation. As is known, for people at the intermediate spiritual level, the indispensable preparation for studying for its own sake takes place at the beginning of the study. This is like a bill of divorce or a Torah scroll, for which the proper intention is indispensable: it is enough to declare at the beginning of writing, ‘I am writing for the sake of the sanctity of a Torah scroll,’ or ‘for his sake and for hers,’ and so on.”

connections.hePhrase: [ו] קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שְׁלֵמָה אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת טו.):
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan also said: Someone who wishes to accept upon himself the complete yoke of Heaven’s kingship should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, recite the Shema, and pray. This is the complete acceptance of Heaven’s kingship. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Anyone who relieves himself, washes his hands, puts on tefillin, recites the Shema, and prays is regarded by Scripture as though he built an altar and offered a sacrifice upon it, as it is written: ‘I wash my hands in purity and circle Your altar, Hashem.’ Rava said to him: Does the Master not hold that it is as though he immersed? For it says erchatz, ‘I will bathe [in purity],’ and does not say architz, ‘I will wash [my hands].’’

connections.hePhrase: "נִפְנָה" – פֵּרוּשׁ: מִכָּל גִּלּוּלֵי תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמֻּתָּרוֹת אֲשֶׁר לֹא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם.
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of “tefillin require a clean body”: one should be completely clean of every desire for the affairs of this world. Bodily cleanliness in its plain sense also removes distracting thoughts. As the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter 3, halakhah 5, says, one keeps a distance from a child’s excrement because his thoughts are bad. The essential reason that removing excrement is called “your camp shall be holy” is the distracting and evil thoughts arising from it, for holiness is their opposite. Therefore the Sages said, “He should relieve himself and wash his hands,” and so forth: this is the complete acceptance of the yoke of Heaven. Even “he should relieve himself” is included in accepting that yoke. This is why the practice has become weak in our hands: it is difficult to attain this level, and none arose like Moses. At least during prayer a person should strive to attain it—to cleave entirely to Hashem with all his heart, soul, and resources. It is sufficient to wear tefillin then; throughout the rest of the day he should be satisfied with wrapping himself in tzitzit, so that he will at least remember to repel every distracting thought that confronts him.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok returns to the same Talmudic sequence and explicitly includes bodily preparation within accepting Heaven’s yoke. The closing practical qualification distinguishes the ideal of constant purity from the concentration sought during prayer.

connections.hePhrase: "וְנוֹטֵל יָדָיו" – שָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁזֶּה רְמִיזַת רְחִיצַת יָדַיִם עַל סִלּוּק נְגִיעוֹת.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Ki Tisa 1
connections.linkedRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Ki Tisa 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Ki Tisa 1
connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ספר שמות, כי תשא א׳
connections.quote: “‘They shall wash their hands and feet.’ The priests’ washing from the laver signifies the removal and elimination of personal bias. Washing indicates this, as it is written concerning the heifer whose neck is broken: ‘The elders shall wash,’ and so forth, ‘and say: Our hands did not shed,’ and so forth. They declare that they have no personal involvement or share in this deed. The priest who serves also needs washing: he must remove his personal bias and nullify his judgment and will before the will of the blessed Hashem, serving only in the way that Hashem desires. So too, our command to wash our hands in the morning and before a meal means that before beginning to attend to bodily needs, a person needs to pray to Hashem. If something of this world comes to him that is, Heaven forbid, contrary to Hashem’s will, he asks Hashem to take away and remove his desire for it. Even a permitted thing contains good and its opposite. If a person eats something permitted and afterward uses that strength to commit a transgression, it becomes apparent that he did not receive the good power contained in that thing. This is the purpose of washing: a prayer to Hashem that, in everything, he receive only the good power it contains. For a person may stipulate concerning an inheritance coming to him from elsewhere that he will not inherit it. For this reason, they established the recitation of the passage of the laver before prayer and before the passages of the offerings: that we should pray only for what Hashem desires.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר עוֹד: רוֹמֵז עַל הָרְחִיצָה מִמַּה שֶּׁכְּבָר נִתְלַכְלְכוּ כְּלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה מֵאוֹתָם הַטִּנּוּפוֹת, יִרְחָצֵם בְּמֵי הַדַּעַת וְטָהֵר.
connections.quote: “It is clear and evident that the laws of impurity and purity are decrees of Scripture. They are not matters decided by human reason; they belong among the statutes. Immersion from impurity likewise belongs among the statutes, for impurity is not mud or filth that water can remove. It is a decree of Scripture, and the matter depends on the heart’s intention. Therefore the Sages said: if one immersed without establishing the intended degree of purification, it is as though he had not immersed. Nevertheless, there is an allusion in this matter. Just as one who intends in his heart to purify himself becomes pure upon immersion, although nothing has changed in his body, so one who intends to purify his soul from the impurities of the soul—wicked thoughts and evil opinions—becomes pure once he resolves in his heart to separate from those counsels and brings his soul into the waters of knowledge. Scripture says: ‘I shall sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall become pure; from all your impurities and all your idols I shall purify you.’ May Hashem, in His abundant mercy, purify us from every sin, iniquity, and guilt. Amen.”

connections.hePhrase: "וּמַנִּיחַ תְּפִלִּין" – כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּיַעֲרוֹת דְּבַשׁ, שֶׁהוּא חוֹתַם שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם שֶׁנּוֹשֵׂא עָלָיו,
connections.quote: “We are the Lord’s servants, and the seal that the Master of all the earth has fastened upon us as a sign that we are His servants is tefillin and tzitzit. They are the seal of our Master in Heaven, our insignia from the Holy One, blessed be He. It is unfitting to walk without this seal, for they are the sign that we are His servants.”
connections.context: Ya’arot Devash compares these mitzvot to the mark by which a servant belongs to his master, drawing on the Gittin discussion of a slave’s insignia. This is the specific image Rav Tzadok invokes when he calls tefillin the seal of Heaven’s Name borne by its wearer.

connections.hePhrase: "וּמִתְפַּלֵּל" – [גַּם זֶה (הַתְּפִלָּה) מִכְּלַל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת (בְּרָכוֹת יד:)].
connections.quote: “‘And he puts on tefillin and prays.’ … Shema and prayer are bound up with tefillin … and prayer too, as we have said: ‘He recites Shema and prays—this is the Kingdom of Heaven.’”
connections.context: Tosafot is explaining why tefillin, unlike a tallit, belong to Shema and prayer; in passing they count prayer, like Shema, as accepting the Kingdom of Heaven.

connections.hePhrase: "וּמִתְפַּלֵּל" – [גַּם זֶה (הַתְּפִלָּה) מִכְּלַל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת (בְּרָכוֹת יד:)].
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef identifies the human task as humility and fear of Heaven that make room for divine Torah

connections.hePhrase: "וּמִתְפַּלֵּל" – [גַּם זֶה (הַתְּפִלָּה) מִכְּלַל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת (בְּרָכוֹת יד:)].
connections.quote: ““For this commandment that I command you today ... is not in Heaven ... nor beyond the sea ... for the matter is very close to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it.” My grandfather of blessed memory asked: the Zohar repeatedly says how exalted and precious the words of Torah are; this appears to place them in Heaven and beyond the sea! The explanation follows “Everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven.” How can one say “except,” when everything is in God’s hands? God established in this world that the vessel belongs to the person, and this is called fear of Heaven. What is the person’s vessel? Principally, that he lowers himself so that God’s majesty may rest upon him. Thus “The human being became a living soul” is translated “a speaking spirit.” The Zohar says that this spirit rises and speaks before the holy King, enters every gate, and none restrains it; therefore it is called a speaking spirit. When a person stands in prayer before God, God bestows words of Torah upon him. The words He bestows are indeed exalted and precious. The vessel the person establishes, however, is in the person’s hands. This is “The matter is very close to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it”: when a person lowers himself for God’s majesty to rest upon him, forming his vessel, God bestows upon him the exalted words of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef describes the person standing in prayer as a vessel made through lowering oneself before Hashem. This develops the progression here from removing personal bias and bearing the Master’s sign to direct encounter in prayer. The preparations do not manufacture the light by independent human power. They make the person receptive, so that accepting Heaven’s kingship is expressed not only in a declaration but in how he stands before its Source.
connections.headline: The preparations for prayer form a vessel for what Hashem bestows

connections.hePhrase: כִּי קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע אֵינוֹ לְנֹכַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תְּפִלָּה, כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י (בְּרָכוֹת כה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א),
connections.quote: “But for prayer: he must present himself as standing before the King and stand in awe. In the recitation of Shema, however, he is not speaking before the King.”
connections.context: Rashi explains why prayer imposes a stricter requirement here than Shema. Rav Tzadok uses his distinction between addressing the King and accepting His kingship.

connections.hePhrase: [ז] זְמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע תָּלֵי בִּזְמַן אֲכִילָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת, וְשָׁם בַּבָּרַיְתָא עַמּוּד ב'.
connections.quote: “From when does one recite Shema in the evening? From when the poor person comes in to eat his bread with salt, until he rises to leave his meal.”

connections.hePhrase: [ז] זְמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע תָּלֵי בִּזְמַן אֲכִילָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת, וְשָׁם בַּבָּרַיְתָא עַמּוּד ב'.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua says: From when the priests are purified to eat their terumah. … Rabbi Chanina says: From when the poor person comes in to eat his bread with salt. Rabbi Achai—and some say Rabbi Acha—says: From when most people come in to recline at their meal.”
connections.context: These different measures for the beginning of evening Shema are stated in terms of eating. That wording is the basis for Rav Tzadok’s connection between accepting Heaven’s yoke and sanctifying ordinary physical life.

connections.hePhrase: [ז] זְמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע תָּלֵי בִּזְמַן אֲכִילָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת, וְשָׁם בַּבָּרַיְתָא עַמּוּד ב'.

connections.quote: “The master said: ‘From the time the priests enter,’ and so forth. They raised a contradiction: ‘From the time the poor person,’ and so forth; ‘from the time the day becomes sanctified,’ and so forth; ‘from the time people enter to recline at a meal.’ This tanna refers to Scripture, explaining ‘when you lie down and when you rise,’ and asks: From when do we recite the Shema in the evening? Reciting the Shema means recognizing the light of Hashem’s abundant love. Thus, ‘From when do we recite the Shema in the evening?’ asks how a revelation of His light is found in the evening. He explains that we find the priests awaiting this time and attaining at that hour more than they attained in the sunlight. Necessarily, then, this hour contains a revelation of the light of abundant love for every soul of Israel, and reciting the Shema belongs to this time. The Gemara shows how each sage found a further sanctity at this hour. ‘The time people enter to recline’ means that on Passover there is additional sanctity at that hour; on Friday evenings, there is the sanctification of the day.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֲכִילָה הוּא קִיּוּם הַחַיִּים, וְכָךְ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם.
connections.quote: “The windpipe and the food pipe are next to one another: one brings out speech and voice, and the other brings in food. They are called “signs,” because the sign of life is in them. Through the windpipe a person draws life in his breath, without which he has no life; in the human being this also gives the power of speech, making him a speaking spirit. Eating through the food pipe sustains life. The root of an Israelite’s life depends solely upon recognizing his Master and that Hashem dwells within him: “You give life to them all.” The life he receives from eating likewise comes only from Hashem’s will that he eat and receive life from it. Thus it is written, “A person does not live by bread alone, but by everything that issues from Hashem’s mouth.” This means that bread alone, separated from Hashem, does not give life; the word of Hashem together with the bread is what gives life. Without this recognition it is not called life at all for an Israelite. Through this, eating is considered like an offering, and even more precious. As the Sages explain the verse “For Hashem your God arranged it before me”: if He arranged it for your offering, all the more so for your food. The table is like an altar, and one who fills the throats of Torah scholars with wine is like one offering libations, because they are Hashem’s sanctuary and altar, and are superior to a physical altar of stones. This, however, requires complete intention for the sake of Heaven: one must not eat to satisfy his desire, but because Hashem established within creation that food sustains life, and this is therefore His will.”
connections.context: This passage explains why eating and accepting Heaven’s yoke belong together: both express the recognition that life comes from Hashem. Its condition of complete intention for Heaven is part of the source and limits its comparison of eating to an offering.

connections.hePhrase: רַק מְתִינוּת קְצָת עַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה "נֵר הַשֵּׁם נִשְׁמַת אָדָם" מֵאִיר עֵינֵי שִׂכְלָם.
connections.quote: ‘A person’s soul is Hashem’s lamp, searching every chamber within.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם [רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן] סוֹף הִלְכוֹת שְׁמִטָּה וְיוֹבֵל, וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי בָּזֶה,

connections.quote: ‘This applies not only to the tribe of Levi, but to every person among all the inhabitants of the world whose spirit freely moves him, and whose understanding leads him, to set himself apart: to stand before Hashem, minister to Him, serve Him, and know Hashem; to walk uprightly, as God made him; and to cast off the yoke of the many calculations that human beings have sought. Such a person is sanctified as holy of holies. Hashem will be his portion and inheritance forever and for all eternity, and he will be granted what is sufficient for him in this world, just as the priests and Levites were granted their portion. Thus David, peace be upon him, says: ‘Hashem is my allotted portion and my cup; You uphold my lot’ (Psalms 16:5).’

connections.hePhrase: [ח] וּזְמַן הַהַכָנָה הַזּוֹ הַכֹּל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא אָדָם,
connections.quote:
“Among the practices that guide a person toward attaining this trait is preparation for divine service and the commandments. That is, one should not begin performing a commandment suddenly, before the mind is settled and able to reflect on what one is doing. Rather, one should prepare for it and ready the heart calmly until one enters into reflection.

Then one should consider what one is about to do and before Whom one is about to do it. For once one enters into this reflection, it is easy to cast off ulterior motives and establish in the heart the true and desired intention.

You see that the early pious ones would wait an hour before their prayer and then pray, so that they might direct their hearts toward the Omnipresent. Certainly they did not spend an hour idly. Rather, they directed and prepared their hearts for the prayer they were to offer, casting away foreign thoughts and filling themselves with the requisite awe and love. Scripture says: ‘If you prepare your heart and spread your hands toward Him’ (Job 11:13).”

connections.hePhrase: [ח] וּזְמַן הַהַכָנָה הַזּוֹ הַכֹּל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא אָדָם,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov describes human refinement reaching the point at which one asks Hashem to complete what effort alone cannot finish

connections.hePhrase: [ח] וּזְמַן הַהַכָנָה הַזּוֹ הַכֹּל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא אָדָם,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:1
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:1
connections.quote: ““A time of finding” points to an ultimate purpose: the purpose of all the affairs of this world, a world of uncertainty full of concealment, is that a person refine himself as far as his strength permits. After all this, he will need prayer, praying to Hashem, blessed be He, to bring matters to a good conclusion for him. For all the refinements a person achieves according to his strength and intellectual grasp count as nothing, since creation itself was originally brought into being from nothing. He therefore needs to pray to Hashem after all his refinements, surrendering his soul and all his resources to Him and recognizing that Hashem gives him the strength to accomplish—even in his service of Hashem and his own refinements.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why prayer is still needed after a person has refined himself to the extent of his ability. This clarifies the present siman’s account of preparation differing with the person and being difficult in concealment. Preparation is a real obligation of the person’s side, yet direct encounter is also a gift for which he prays. Its success cannot be measured only by the time or effort already invested.
connections.headline: Preparation reaches its purpose when it becomes prayer for divine completion

connections.hePhrase: וַחֲסִידִים הָיוּ שׁוֹהִים רַק שָׁעָה אַחַת לִתְפִלָּה, כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת ל:).
connections.quote: ‘Mishnah: One should stand to pray only with solemnity. The pious people of earlier generations would wait for an hour and then pray, so that they could direct their hearts toward their Father in Heaven. Even if the king greets him, he should not answer; even if a snake is coiled around his heel, he should not interrupt.’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּיּוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לְהַגִּיד בַּבֹּקֶר חַסְדֶּךָ" – אָז אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיד מִיָּד בַּבֹּקֶר מִתּוֹךְ אוֹר הַנִּכָּר.
connections.quote: ‘To proclaim Your kindness in the morning, and Your faithfulness through the nights.’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּלֵּילוֹת, רַק הָאֱמוּנָה בַּלֵּב וְלֹא הַהַגָּדָה, שֶׁהוּא הַהוֹצָאָה מִכֹּחַ אֶל הַפּוֹעַל עַל הֶעָבָר,
connections.quote: “As it is said, “Your faithfulness in the nights”: in the darkness of night, when Kedushah is not recited at night, there is darkness and an absence of clear recognition. Then the faith hidden in the heart of every person of Israel is drawn forth: there is a King, even though one is not standing before Him. Were one standing before Him, He would be like a master standing over his servant or a father over his son; here He is like a king seated in his palace. From this mode of apprehension, which the Zohar and the masters of the esoteric teaching call the “lower unification,” a concealed and lowly apprehension, comes the blessing and request “from His place”: that it increase and grow until He becomes recognizable and apprehensible to those below.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes belief in the King while His presence is concealed from the direct awareness of standing before Him. That distinction explains the present passage’s contrast between faith at night and the fuller encounter required for prayer.

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא הַקִּוּוּי עַל הֶעָתִיד כַּאֲשֶׁר "אָתָא בֹקֶר", גַּם בְּכָל הַלַּיְלָה כֻּלָּהּ.
connections.quote: “One calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said: The morning comes, and also the night.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית רְשׁוּת,
connections.quote: “As the one who said: The evening prayer is optional. For Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel: About the evening prayer, Rabban Gamliel says it is obligatory; Rabbi Yehoshua says it is optional.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְחַיֵּב בַּלַּיְלָה, דְּ"זֶה שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם" כְּתִיב, בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה.
connections.quote: “And God said further to Moses: Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: Hashem, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you; this is My name forever, and this is My remembrance for all generations.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְחַיֵּב בַּלַּיְלָה, דְּ"זֶה שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם" כְּתִיב, בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה.
connections.quote: “Rava thought to expound it [the Name] in his public lecture. A certain elder said to him: It is written le’alem [to conceal]. Rabbi Avina raised a contradiction: It is written, “This is My name le’alem,” and “this is My remembrance for all generations.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Not as I am written am I read.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק רְשׁוּת לְמִי שֶׁחֲנָנוֹ הַשֵּׁם לִהְיוֹת "לַיְלָה כַּיּוֹם יָאִיר" לוֹ.
connections.quote: “Even the darkness is not too dark for You; the night shines as the day; darkness and light are alike.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק הָאִידְּנָא, בְּעִקְּבוֹת דִּמְשִׁיחָא, קָרוֹב לְאוֹר הַיּוֹם, קִבְּלִינְהוּ לְחוֹבָה.
connections.quote: “As with the holiness of place, so with the holiness of time: just as holiness is established at that time for every generation afterward, there is also a radiance of holiness before it. Certainly the holiness and light that are destined to be revealed speedily in our days at the time of the end also shine beforehand on the appointed day prepared for them, which, according to what is written, is Rosh Chodesh Nisan. In every year that draws closer to redemption, more of this light is felt—the light of the true deliverance of all the souls of Israel, to perfect the world under the kingship of His blessed Name.”
connections.context: Here Rav Tzadok states the principle that a future revelation already casts light before its arrival. His immediate discussion concerns Rosh Chodesh Nisan; the shared principle illuminates why the present ois connects the later acceptance of evening prayer with approaching the light of redemption.

connections.hePhrase: כָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי מִדִּיּוּק לְשׁוֹן הַמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת: "לְהַרְחִיק מִן הָעֲבֵרָה".
connections.quote: “… If so, why did the Sages say “until midnight”? In order to distance a person from transgression.”
connections.context: The Sages set the earlier limit so that a person would not miss the mitzvah altogether; Rav Tzadok reads their word “transgression” as showing that failing to fulfill it is itself a sin.

connections.hePhrase: וּפָשׁוּט הוּא, שֶׁכֵּן מָצִינוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יז.):
connections.quote: ‘Who are the transgressors of Israel who sin with their bodies? Rav said: A head on which tefillin are not laid. As for the transgressors of the nations of the world who sin with their bodies, Rav said: Those who engage in forbidden sexual relations.’

connections.hePhrase: "פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן – קַרְקַפְתָּא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין",
connections.quote: “Thus it is not possible to speak of bodily transgressors of Israel who have no remedy: repentance remains possible. Even the transgressors of Israel are full of regret. Even if a person has not repented completely, one who sins only because of desire cannot fail to feel regret in his heart after the desire and appetite have passed. Although this is not complete repentance that reaches the place where penitents stand, he has nevertheless already left the category of bodily transgressors of Israel. Therefore this category is found only in “a head that does not put on tefillin,” because that is not driven by desire. The Sages also said “a head that does not,” rather than “someone who does not put them on”: a thought of regret may still pass through a person’s heart sometime in his life, for Hashem is the heart of Israel, and even Israel’s transgressors have attachment and desire for Hashem in the concealed depths of their hearts. “A head that does not,” however, means that the head itself has no connection to the holiness of tefillin: it has passed through all ten levels of evil up to the root and crown of impurity, until the mind within the head is wholly immersed in evil, without any good thought at all. Even so, the name Israel still remains upon him, for he is called one of the transgressors of Israel.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the force of the same Talmudic expression. The omission matters because tefillin embody the mind’s bond with Hashem; Rav Tzadok also preserves the significance of regret and the continuing possibility of repentance. It should not be read as classifying every isolated missed act as the extreme spiritual condition described here.

connections.hePhrase: [י] כָּל בִּנְיַן לִמּוּדוֹ יִהְיֶה עַל הַמִּקְרָא שֶׁצִּוָּה הַשֵּׁם,
connections.quote: “Since the light hidden and concealed within the performed mitzvah is not visible to human eyes, the act alone is insufficient: one must also learn the Torah of every mitzvah, so as to recognize its inward depth, the essential light hidden within the garment of the action. Therefore Torah study is itself one of the 613 mitzvot. The sages instituted blessings before and after Torah, for their purpose is to establish this light firmly in the heart. They likewise instituted saying before the Torah reading, “You were shown to know that the Lord is God,” indicating that this very Torah is the light hidden deep within the garments of the mitzvot. For this purpose Ezra also instituted that Israel should not pass three days without Torah. In Babylonia, Written Torah began to enter the clothing of Oral Torah. Therefore one must continually awaken, each time anew, the light hidden within this clothing, so as to recognize the light of Written Torah through all the garments.”
connections.explanation: The Radziner passage gives inward content to the present siman’s insistence that the Mishnah stands upon Scripture. Learning the details is a continual recovery of the divine light present in Written Torah and the mitzvah, rather than a detached exercise in ideas. Its account of Ezra’s institution explains why this recognition must be renewed: the light remains present through the garments, but the learner must keep uncovering and establishing it in the heart.
connections.headline: Oral Torah continually uncovers the light of Written Torah within its details

connections.hePhrase: לְאוֹרוֹיֵי דְּכָל מִשְׁנָתוֹ רַק אַקְּרָא קָאֵי,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the contribution for the sockets of the Mishkan. The Written Torah is the support of the Oral Torah; therefore the Talmud opens, “The tanna is referring to Scripture.” This means that Scripture is the foundation upon which the Mishnah stands. This is also the meaning of the sockets of the Mishkan: they are the foundation of the divine influx in its equal aspect, before it divides into the particular apprehensions of the hearts of Israel. This also comes from Israel’s collective preparation in equal measure through saying, “We shall do and we shall hear.” In this respect, “the wealthy shall not give more.” Upon this is built the body of the Mishkan—the dwelling of Hashem within the individual hearts of Israel.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok repeats the phrase “the tanna is referring to Scripture” and compares the Written Torah to the sockets supporting the Mishkan. This explains how individual understanding in Oral Torah rests upon the common foundation of the divine command.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִמְדֻמֶּה שֶׁכָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי גַּם כֵּן.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 2a:3
connections.linkedRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 2a:3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 2a:3
connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ליקוטי הש"ס, מסכת ברכות ב׳ א:ג׳
connections.quote: “In the Gemara: ‘What is the tanna referring to when he teaches “From when”?’ It answers: ‘The tanna refers to Scripture.’ Rabbi’s compilation of the Mishnah was not separated from the Written Torah by any division or distance. Just as the tannaim and amoraim of the Gemara studied the Mishnah, sought to understand its meaning, and explained it, so the compilation of the Mishnah was based on the Written Torah. When he studied the verse ‘when you lie down and when you rise,’ he immediately explained the time for reciting the Shema. In this way he arranged the entire Mishnah.”

connections.hePhrase: [יא] יָלְפִינַן מִבְּרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם דִּבְכָל דָּבָר הַלַּיְלָה קוֹדֵם לַיּוֹם כִּדְאִיתָא רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת.
connections.quote: ‘Alternatively, you may say that he derives it from the creation of the world, as it is written: ‘There was evening and there was morning, one day.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְ"כִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחֹשֶׁךְ" אֵדַע כִּי אַחַר כָּךְ "ה' אוֹר לִי".
connections.quote: ‘Do not rejoice over me, my enemy. Though I have fallen, I will rise; though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light for me.’

connections.hePhrase: וְ"כִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחֹשֶׁךְ" אֵדַע כִּי אַחַר כָּךְ "ה' אוֹר לִי".
connections.quote:
“One who trusts in Hashem must hope amid the gloom of distress, for the darkness will become the cause of light. As it is written: ‘Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; though I have fallen, I have risen; though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light for me’ (Micah 7:8). Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: ‘Had I not fallen, I would not have risen; had I not sat in darkness, there would have been no light for me.’

Every person, on a day of distress, should set the heart to understanding and to fasting, together with repentance and prayer, just as the community is obligated to fast and afflict itself in a time of distress, as our Sages instituted. This is a chosen fast and a day of favor. When Hashem’s chastisement comes upon a person who is pure and upright, it is a trial and serves to increase that person’s reward in the World to Come, as it is said: ‘To afflict you and to test you, to do you good in your latter end’ (Deuteronomy 8:16). Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: If a person scrutinized his deeds in a time of distress, searched and investigated, and found no sin in his hands, these are afflictions of love.”

connections.hePhrase: וְ"כִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחֹשֶׁךְ" אֵדַע כִּי אַחַר כָּךְ "ה' אוֹר לִי".
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the creation of the world: first darkness, and afterward light. The world was created in this way so that one could attain delight; that is possible only through darkness coming first. Thus it says, “When I sit in darkness”—precisely then—“Hashem is a light for me.” It also says, “He made darkness His hiding place”: the Holy One, blessed be He, conceals Himself within the darkness. The greater the darkness and concealment, the greater the light hidden within it, which one can attain through that darkness. Thus it says, “You shall seek Hashem from there”—precisely from there—and, “It is a time of distress … and from it he will be saved.” Scripture does not call bodily trouble alone “distress,” but that which truly constricts the soul as well. From that very place comes the soul’s deliverance.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the quoted verse as light discovered through the very concealment that preceded it. The passage concerns seeking Hashem from within the darkness.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ גַּם לִקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר].
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:1
connections.linkedRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:1
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:1
connections.heRef: דובר צדק, קונטרס דובר צדק, ברכות ג׳:א׳
connections.quote: “Berakhot 2a derives the order from the creation of the world. In sacred offerings, the night follows the day, just as the blessing mentions “forming light” before “creating darkness.” Although in the creation of the world darkness came first and then light, from Hashem’s perspective creation precedes formation. Creation is darkness to us, as the Zohar explains that light can be so great that it is dark to weak eyes; therefore “creates” is said of darkness. From our perspective, ascending from below to above, formation precedes creation. Thus with offerings, which bring atonement to one who has sinned and is deficient, day comes first. In Hashem’s governance of the whole creation, however, night comes first. One might have thought that our acceptance of the yoke of Heaven depends on us, and that day therefore comes first. The Gemara teaches that it is derived from creation: as soon as one accepts the yoke of Heaven and recognizes that Hashem is one, everything returns to its source. The end is rooted in the beginning, and the lower returns to become the upper, like the flash of lightning, as I have explained elsewhere.”
connections.context: This parallel expands the question raised here about the order of Shema. It distinguishes the person’s ascent toward holiness from the order of divine governance; it does not erase the differing day-and-night rules.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בְּרָכוֹת ח' עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְאוֹמֵר", דְּגַם בַּתּוֹרָה כֵּן.
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות ו׳ א:א׳
connections.quote: “Even when he studies at night, we do not say that the night belongs to the next day, requiring him to bless again. Although in other matters the day follows the night, in Torah study the night follows the day. … Thus the night’s study belongs to that same day, and the blessing he recited in the morning also exempts what he studies at night.”
connections.context: The subject is the morning blessing over Torah, which continues to cover that night’s study. The printed reference “8a” in Rav Tzadok’s text corresponds here to 6a in the current pagination of Rabbeinu Yonah on the Rif.

connections.hePhrase: [בְּמֵי הַדַּעַת הוּא תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין וּמַצְלֵי מֵעֲבֵירוֹת לְהַבָּא שֶׁהַמָּאוֹר מַחֲזִיר לְמוּטָב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רֵישׁ אֵיכָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כה) שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה: לָמַד דַּף אֶחָד יִלְמוֹד שְׁנֵי דַפִּים]
connections.quote: “If only they had forsaken Me but kept My Torah! Through occupying themselves with it, the light within it would have brought them back to the good.”
connections.context: This is the Midrash cited in Rav Tzadok’s preceding words about Torah’s light returning a person to the good. It addresses the future direction of the person; the neighboring Vayikra Rabbah note addresses repair of the past.

connections.hePhrase: [בְּמֵי הַדַּעַת הוּא תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין וּמַצְלֵי מֵעֲבֵירוֹת לְהַבָּא שֶׁהַמָּאוֹר מַחֲזִיר לְמוּטָב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רֵישׁ אֵיכָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כה) שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה: לָמַד דַּף אֶחָד יִלְמוֹד שְׁנֵי דַפִּים]
connections.quote: “Rav Huna said: If a person stumbled in a transgression and became liable to death at Heaven’s hand, what should he do and live? If he was accustomed to reading one page, let him read two pages; if he was accustomed to studying one chapter, let him study two. If he was not accustomed to reading or studying, what should he do and live? Let him become a communal administrator or a collector of charity, and he will live.”
connections.context: The Midrash prescribes additional Torah study, or active support of communal charity, as a response to past wrongdoing. Rav Tzadok distinguishes this reparative increase from Torah’s protection against future sin.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי קָרְבָּן וְדוּגְמָתוֹ תְּפִלָּה אוֹ תַּעֲנִית וּצְדָקָה.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 14:1
connections.linkedRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 14:1
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 14:1
connections.heRef: ספר ליקוטי מאמרים, חודשים ומועדים י״ד:א׳
connections.quote: “Kapparah also means reconciliation, as Rashi explains on the verse “He will appease His land and His people.” Korban, an offering, means drawing close. Of offerings it says, “It shall be accepted for him”: through the offerings, reconciliation and appeasement are achieved. Likewise, the prayers were instituted in place of the daily offerings, and we say, “He is appeased through supplication.” The essence of prayer is to become reconciled with Hashem. The first request for one’s needs is for understanding, so that one may know how to become reconciled with one’s Creator through repentance, which follows in the blessing “Return us.” For, as the Sages said, “If there is no understanding, how can there be discernment?” If one cannot distinguish between good and evil, how will one know to repent?”
connections.context: This passage explains why prayer stands alongside offerings in the work of kapparah: both express drawing close and seeking divine favor. The prayer’s request for understanding prepares the request for repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן כַּפָּרָה לֹא מְעַכֶּבֶת, דִּתְשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ הִרְהֵר בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר,
connections.quote: “And this teaches us that atonement does not hold him back, as it was taught: “And when the sun sets he shall be pure” (Leviticus 22:7)—the setting of his sun holds him back from eating terumah, but his atonement [offering] does not hold him back from eating terumah.”

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן כַּפָּרָה לֹא מְעַכֶּבֶת, דִּתְשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ הִרְהֵר בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר,
connections.quote: “[If he says:] “on condition that I am righteous,” even if he is completely wicked she is betrothed, for perhaps he contemplated repentance in his mind.”

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן כַּפָּרָה לֹא מְעַכֶּבֶת, דִּתְשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ הִרְהֵר בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר,
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef explains why the act of accepting teshuvah can already receive an answer from Hashem

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן כַּפָּרָה לֹא מְעַכֶּבֶת, דִּתְשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ הִרְהֵר בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר,
connections.quote: “God is without limit or end, whereas the human being is limited. When a person sins, he damages a relation to One without limit or end; how, then, can repentance coming from a limited person help? But God abounds in kindness. Therefore, when a person accepts upon himself to return in repentance, God raises his perception and shows him that he has a connection with God’s light. Repentance thereby becomes unlimited, while the sin lies only within his limited perception. Of this it says, “He remembered that they are flesh,” as explained elsewhere. This is the Talmud’s statement that Rabbi Zeira said, “Let us accept it upon ourselves, and afterward observe it,” and the verse, “He said to me: Do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard.” If we accept the fast upon ourselves, our words will immediately be heard. This is what the sages say here: one who fasts for part of a day recites the fast-day prayer. When he accepts repentance upon himself, even though he is limited, he prays Aneinu: God shows him that he has a connection with His light, so that repentance too becomes unlimited.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads Daniel’s prayer as heard from the first day he set his heart to return. Divine kindness connects the limited person’s beginning to a light beyond his measure. This illuminates the present siman’s distinction between present purification and atonement for the past. A genuine resolve can already establish the standing needed to accept Heaven’s yoke, while the deeper healing of what preceded remains a further task.
connections.headline: The first accepted resolve is real even while further repair remains

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לְקָדָשִׁים הָרוֹצֶה לְהִתְקַדֵּשׁ וְלִהְיוֹת קָדוֹשׁ צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן לְרַפֵּא אֶת הַקּוֹדֵם.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שלישי; אגרת התשובה ב׳:א׳-ג׳
connections.quote: “All this concerns atonement and forgiveness of the sin: when a person repents completely, his past violation of the King’s command is wholly forgiven. Not a thing or half a thing is mentioned against him on the day of judgment to punish him for it, Heaven forbid, in the World to Come, and he is entirely released from judgment in the World to Come. However, to be acceptable before Hashem, pleasing and beloved before Him as before the sin, so that his service brings satisfaction to his Maker, he needed to bring a burnt offering even for a minor positive commandment involving neither excision nor execution by the court. So our Sages expounded in the Sifra on the verse ‘It shall be accepted for him’; and so it is stated in the first chapter of Zevachim: a burnt offering atones for a positive commandment and is a gift after a person has repented and his punishment has been forgiven. It is like someone who offended a king, appeased him through advocates, and was pardoned: nevertheless, he sends a gift and tribute so that the king will consent to receive him. The expression ‘atones,’ and Scripture’s words ‘It shall be accepted for him, to atone for him,’ do not mean atonement for his soul, but atonement before Hashem, bringing satisfaction to his Maker, as stated there in the Gemara and as it is written, ‘It shall be unblemished to be accepted.’”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לְקָדָשִׁים הָרוֹצֶה לְהִתְקַדֵּשׁ וְלִהְיוֹת קָדוֹשׁ צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן לְרַפֵּא אֶת הַקּוֹדֵם.
connections.quote: “Through the power of his repentance, it lies within his ability to repair what came before through the power of Torah. For the essential repair of the past, for all sins, until he becomes as one who never sinned, is only through Torah. Concerning this particular sin, the Zohar states that repentance does not avail; its meaning is that repentance alone cannot completely repair the past in this matter, but can do so when joined with Torah.”
connections.context: The surrounding discussion concerns a Torah scholar’s repentance and, specifically, sins involving the covenant. Rav Tzadok interprets the Zohar as requiring repentance together with Torah for complete repair of the past; he is not denying the possibility of return.

connections.hePhrase: כָּךְ פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת בְּשֵׁם הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּבִמְנָחוֹת צ"ט עַמּוּד ב' עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “… If so, why do we recite it in the synagogue [before nightfall]? In order to stand in prayer out of words of Torah. And so it is taught in a baraita in the Yerushalmi, Berakhot.”
connections.context: Rashi treats the recitation of Shema as words of Torah; this is the point Rav Tzadok takes from him.

connections.hePhrase: כָּךְ פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת בְּשֵׁם הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּבִמְנָחוֹת צ"ט עַמּוּד ב' עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: Even if a person recited only Shema in the morning and evening, he has fulfilled “This Torah shall not depart [from your mouth].” … Rava said: It is a mitzvah to say this in the presence of unlearned people.”
connections.context: The passage supplies the minimal daily act of Torah study invoked by Rav Tzadok. His distinction is between Torah’s inherent continuing bond and an increased measure of study undertaken to repair wrongdoing.

connections.hePhrase: "וְלָרָשָׁע אָמַר אֱלֹהִים מַה לְּךָ לְסַפֵּר חֻקָּי",
connections.quote: ‘But to the wicked person God says: What claim have you to recount My statutes and take My covenant upon your lips?’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ שִׁינּוּי זְמַן עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם (פֶּרֶק ב מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה) בְּשִׁינּוּי הַשֵּׁם, כִּלְשׁוֹנוֹ: אֵינִי עוֹמֵד עַכְשָׁו בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן וּגְבוּל כָּעֵת שֶׁנִּטְמֵאתִי,
connections.quote: ‘Among the ways of repentance are these: the person returning should constantly cry out before Hashem with tears and supplications, give charity according to his ability, and distance himself greatly from the matter in which he sinned. He should change his name, as if to say, ‘I am someone else, not the person who committed those deeds,’ and change all his conduct for the better and toward the upright path. He should also leave his place for exile, for exile atones for sin by causing him to submit, become humble, and be lowly in spirit.’

connections.hePhrase: וְשִׁמְשָׁא מִמֵּילָא עָרְבָא עַל יְדֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כִּי אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: A person’s inclination overpowers him every day and seeks to kill him … and were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, he could not withstand it, as it is said: “Hashem will not leave him in his hand” (Psalms 37:33).”

connections.hePhrase: וְשִׁמְשָׁא מִמֵּילָא עָרְבָא עַל יְדֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כִּי אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי:
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:3
connections.linkedRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:3
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:3
connections.heRef: דובר צדק, קונטרס דובר צדק, ברכות ג׳:ג׳
connections.quote: “Atonement is required only for sacred offerings—that is, to enter farther within, for one who wishes to sanctify himself. For purification, immersion alone suffices; it represents the person’s own awakening. Sunset, however, happens of itself and is not in the person’s hands. It is the completion of the assistance given to one who comes to purify himself, for “were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him …” (Sukkah 52a).”
connections.context: Immersion and sunset represent two stages: the person’s initiative and the divine assistance that completes it. The distinct requirement of atonement for sacred offerings remains in place.
