connections.hePhrase: [יג] הַזְּמַן מוּרְכָּב מִיּוֹם וָלַיְלָה וְכֵן חַיֵּי הָאָדָם אוֹר וְחֹשֶׁךְ עוֹלֶה וְיוֹרֵד,
connections.quote: “Having explained the matter of love and aversion, we say that one who serves Hashem must recognize at the beginning of his service that love and aversion struggle with each other: sometimes one prevails, and sometimes the other. Therefore, at the beginning of his service he need not be alarmed if he grows weary of it. Such is the way of love at its beginning: it reaches a certain limit and stops, and afterward returns, gains strength, and renews itself like an eagle. If love weakens and aversion grows strong, he must not despair of the service, but know that after some days this will pass. If, however, he lacks understanding and does not recognize the delights in serving the Creator, the days of aversion will lengthen and the days of love diminish, and aversion will continue to grow. A thoughtful person must therefore accustom himself gradually at the beginning of his service, so that he does not become weary of it. When love enters his heart to perform a mitzvah, he should hasten to perform it. When he sees love diminishing and aversion beginning, some wisehearted people press themselves and do not permit themselves to cast off the task until the aversion passes. Foolish people cannot overcome their aversion: they grow weary of that practice and abandon it until it is lost to them. If they held on to part of it and did not abandon everything, it would not be lost. Therefore, when a thoughtful person sees aversion entering his heart and grows weary of the service, he should not abandon the whole practice or say, “I shall leave it all now and return to it afterward.” If he leaves it all, it will be lost to him; if he holds on to part of it, it will not be lost.”
connections.context: The passage supplies a practical response to alternating ascent and descent: build the practice gradually and preserve an actual part of it when enthusiasm weakens.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מַאֲמַר הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק "שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם".
connections.quote: ‘For a righteous person falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble into calamity.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מַאֲמַר הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק "שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם".
connections.quote: “A second approach: even faithful Jews who have attained a lofty level cannot remain at one level. Rather, they move through the mystery of ‘running and returning,’ and the mystery of ‘the righteous person falls seven times and rises,’ as written in the Tikkunim; see there. This is in order to raise the lesser levels, in the mystery of ‘the souls they made in Haran,’ and as it is written, ‘I have taken off my garment; how shall I put it on?’ And as was said of Abraham and Sarah: although they were old and advanced in days, the way of women returned; see there.”
connections.context: This is a parallel explanation of the righteous person’s descent and return in Toldot Yaakov Yosef. The quoted paragraph cites the Tikkunim; it does not itself attribute these words to the Baal Shem Tov. It helps explain the movement Rav Tzadok describes without serving as a direct quotation of the Baal Shem Tov’s teaching.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְנָם גַּם בְּעֵת הַחֹשֶׁךְ צָרִיךְ אוֹר הַלְּבָנָה אוֹ אוֹר כּוֹכָבִים דְּנַמֵּי אוֹר הוּא כִּדְאִיתָא רֵישׁ פְּסָחִים, וְלֹא שֶׁיְּהֵא חָשׁוּךְ לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.quote: ‘Rather, this teaches us that starlight is also called light. What practical difference does this make? It concerns someone who vows not to benefit from light. (As we learned:) Someone who vows not to benefit from light is forbidden to benefit from starlight.’

connections.hePhrase: [מִצְוָה, וְאוֹר תּוֹרָה "שֶׁמֶשׁ וּמָגֵן ה'", זֶהוּ תּוֹרָה לִשְׁמָהּ בִּבְהִירוּת הַכָּרַת שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, וְזֶהוּ "וְאֹהֲבָיו כְּצֵאת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ", וּ"מַצְדִּיקֵי הָרַבִּים כַּכּוֹכָבִים" שֶׁלּוֹמְדִים תּוֹרָה נִגְלֶה לָרַבִּים].
connections.quote: ‘So may all Your enemies perish, Hashem! But may those who love Him be like the sun coming forth in its might. And the land was quiet for forty years.’

connections.hePhrase: [מִצְוָה, וְאוֹר תּוֹרָה "שֶׁמֶשׁ וּמָגֵן ה'", זֶהוּ תּוֹרָה לִשְׁמָהּ בִּבְהִירוּת הַכָּרַת שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, וְזֶהוּ "וְאֹהֲבָיו כְּצֵאת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ", וּ"מַצְדִּיקֵי הָרַבִּים כַּכּוֹכָבִים" שֶׁלּוֹמְדִים תּוֹרָה נִגְלֶה לָרַבִּים].
connections.quote: ‘Those with understanding will shine like the radiance of the heavens, and those who lead the many to righteousness will be like the stars forever and ever.’

connections.hePhrase: וּפֵירוּשׁ "בְּבֵיתוֹ" – בְּחַדְרֵי לְבָבוֹ, אוֹר הַנֵּר יָפֶה לִבְדִיקָה,
connections.quote: “This is their meaning: one does not search by the light of a torch, but by a candle, which is suited to searching. Hashem concealed His light so that there are places in this world where His light is not recognizable; these are called ‘holes and cracks.’ Through his labor and service, called a candle, a person brings the honor of Heaven even there, as it is written, ‘The soul of a person is Hashem's candle’ (Proverbs 20:27). The righteous stand before the Shechinah like a candle before a torch. This is Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reasoning: the candle can be brought into holes and cracks. Hashem established His will that there should, as it were, be holes and cracks in this world: to human eyes, light and goodness seem absent there and the honor of Heaven seems deficient. This leaves a place for human labor, through which a person, serving Hashem with his own effort, illuminates those holes and cracks, fills them with the shining of his candle, and completes the work so that no breach remains and His honor is whole, without deficiency. This is the candle suited to searching. From the standpoint of the torch, however, there is no place for human service.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the candle, rather than the larger torch, suits the search of the heart. A place where the light is already seen as complete leaves no apparent deficiency for human work to address. The candle represents the person's deliberate effort to recognize and reveal holiness within the concealed particulars. This clarifies why the siman values a mitzvah's limited light precisely during darkness, while still requiring a search as far as one's ability reaches.
connections.headline: Why the smaller light serves the search

connections.hePhrase: [מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּיּוֹם אֵין מֵאִיר דִּשְׁרָגָא בְּטִיהֲרָא, וְעַיֵּין בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פְּסָחִים דִּבְיוֹם אַף בְּמָקוֹם חָשׁוּךְ אֵין מֵאִיר כָּל כָּךְ, בִּזְמַן שֶׁשֵּׁם שָׁמַיִם נִגְלֶה עַל כָּל פְּנֵי הָעוֹלָם קָטָן אֵין נֵר מִצְוָה חָשׁוּב לִכְלוּם],
connections.quote: “The moon said before Him: ‘Master of the universe, because I said something reasonable before You, must I make myself smaller?’ He said to her: ‘Go and rule by day and by night.’ She said to Him: ‘What advantage is there in that? What use is a lamp in broad daylight?’ He said to her: ‘Let Israel reckon days and years by you.’ She said to Him: ‘But they must also use the sun to reckon the seasons, as it is written: ‘They shall be for signs, for appointed times, and for days and years.’’ He said: ‘Let righteous people be called by your name: Jacob the Small, Samuel the Small, and David the Small.’”

connections.hePhrase: [מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּיּוֹם אֵין מֵאִיר דִּשְׁרָגָא בְּטִיהֲרָא, וְעַיֵּין בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פְּסָחִים דִּבְיוֹם אַף בְּמָקוֹם חָשׁוּךְ אֵין מֵאִיר כָּל כָּךְ, בִּזְמַן שֶׁשֵּׁם שָׁמַיִם נִגְלֶה עַל כָּל פְּנֵי הָעוֹלָם קָטָן אֵין נֵר מִצְוָה חָשׁוּב לִכְלוּם],
connections.quote: “It does not shine by day as it shines by night. Rav Huna said: When we were hiding in those vaults of the great study hall, they lit lamps for us. When the lamps were dim, we knew it was day; when they shone brightly, we knew it was night.”
connections.context: The Yerushalmi explains the contrast in the visibility of lamplight during day and night. Rav Tzadok uses that contrast for the light of a mitzvah and the greater light of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יָדוֹ יָכוֹל לִבְדּוֹק כָּל הַמִּינֵי חִימּוּץ מִסִּדְקֵי לְבָבוֹ עַד מָקוֹם שֶׁיָּדוֹ מַגַּעַת, וְהַשְּׁאָר מְבַטְּלוֹ בְּלִבּוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Avodat Yisrael, Sefer Vayikra, Shabbat HaGadol 11
connections.linkedRef: Avodat Yisrael, Sefer Vayikra, Shabbat HaGadol 11
connections.canonicalRef: Avodat Yisrael, Sefer Vayikra, Shabbat HaGadol 11
connections.heRef: עבודת ישראל, ספר ויקרא, לשבת הגדול י״א
connections.quote: “High crevices that a person’s hand cannot reach, and low crevices less than three handbreadths above the ground, do not require examination. The allusion appears to be this: a person should not say, “How can I examine all my sins and iniquities when I do not remember them all?” Therefore it says that high crevices that a person’s hand cannot reach—that is, those he does not remember—do not require examination. A person must examine and repent for the sins he does remember. Those he does not remember will then be nullified of themselves, for the Holy One, blessed be He, says: “If he remembered his earlier sins, he would certainly regret them and repent of them, just as he regrets and repents of those he remembers.””
connections.context: This homiletic reading distinguishes the faults one can identify and actively repair from those one cannot remember. Its conclusion depends on sincere regret and repentance for the faults that are known.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה אוֹר הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ מְטַהֵר זְמַן הַיּוֹם, וְהַשְׁלָמַת הַטָּהֳרָה כַּאֲשֶׁר אִיעֲרַב שִׁמְשָׁא כִּדְאִיתָא בְּרָכוֹת ב',
connections.quote: ‘Rabba bar Rav Sheila said: If so, the verse should say veyithar, ‘and he shall become pure.’ What, then, does vetaher mean? The day has cleared away, as people say: ‘The sun has set and the day has cleared away.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם לְטוֹבָה, כִּי הַמִּסְתַּכֵּל בַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ עֵינָיו כֵּהוֹת, וְגַם לִמְנוֹעַ תּוֹקֶף הַחֹם הַמַּזִּיק פְּעָמִים לָאָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּנָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא.
connections.quote:
“Another interpretation of “after the death”: Hashem told Moshe how their death occurred—“when they drew near before Hashem.” They approached the supernal light out of love of holiness, and through this they died. This is the mystery of the kiss through which the righteous die. Their death resembles that of the righteous, but with this distinction: for the righteous, the kiss approaches them; these men approached it. That is the meaning of “when they drew near before Hashem.”

The added vav in “and they died” alludes to the extraordinary love of these righteous men. Although they sensed that they were dying, they did not hold back from drawing near to the attachment, pleasantness, sweetness, friendship, affection, yearning, and delight, until their souls departed from them. Understand this.”
connections.context: This is Or HaChaim’s interpretation of Nadav and Avihu’s death through their approach to the supernal light. The quoted distinction between being approached and approaching explains why unbounded intensity can be dangerous.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם עִיקַּר טוֹבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בְּעִנְיָן זֶה עַל פָּסוּק "הַמְכַסֶּה שָׁמַיִם בְּעָבִים הַמֵּכִין לָאָרֶץ מָטָר",
connections.quote: ‘He covers the heavens with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow upon the mountains.’

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם עִיקַּר טוֹבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בְּעִנְיָן זֶה עַל פָּסוּק "הַמְכַסֶּה שָׁמַיִם בְּעָבִים הַמֵּכִין לָאָרֶץ מָטָר",
connections.quote: “The times of descent a person experiences, when he has no desire for light and divine service, are a preparation for a great ascent. This comes through the cry he cries when he considers his ways and sees his lowliness and descent. As it is written, ‘They journeyed from Refidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai’ (Exodus 19:2): the Sages' exposition of ‘Refidim’ is known—that their hands had weakened in words of Torah (Sanhedrin 106a). This was a preparation for the giving of the Torah, the ultimate strengthening of the hands in words of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Siman 151 returns to the very cloud-and-rain teaching quoted here, but spells out the human response: a person recognizes his decline and cries out. Its example of Refidim before Sinai explains preparation through renewed need for Torah. This adds a practical distinction to the cloud image without erasing the present siman's qualification that rain is beneficial in its proper season.
connections.headline: What makes a descent a preparation

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מוֹרִיד טִיפָּה חֲדָשָׁה לַגּוּף הַמַּצְמַחַת, אֲבָל הַמָּטָר עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ טוֹבָה אֶלָּא בִּזְמַנּוֹ.
connections.quote: “The meaning of the blessing for rain on this day is that rain supplies the vitality of created beings. On this day, after Yom Kippur and the festival of Sukkot, new vitality is absorbed in the hearts of the souls of Israel, so that all seven holy qualities may be absorbed in the heart through a renewed reception of words of Torah. This is the meaning of rain descending on this day: a drop of life is bestowed upon the heart. To this day the Sages alluded when they said, “Great is the day of rain,” as explained in Avodat Yisrael. One may say that their seven statements beginning “Great is the day of rain” correspond to the seven holy qualities bestowed as new vitality in the hearts of the souls of Israel.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s discourse concerns Shemini Atzeret. It explains the “new drop” as renewed life and a renewed reception of Torah within the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וּפְעָמִים שֶׁהֶעָנָן רָעָה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ תּוֹקֶף הַחֹם, וְהוּא בְּעֵת גְּמַר הַקְּצִירָה שֶׁהוּא גְּמַר הַמַּעֲשֶׂה דִּמְכוּנֶּה קְצִירָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא קַמָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר:
connections.quote: “So too, the completion of the deed is not in a person’s hands. As it says in the first chapter of Megillah, “To retain one’s learning requires assistance from Heaven,” and in Sanhedrin, “‘Hashem is with him’—the halakhah follows him in every case.” Every action that emerged through his wisdom and understanding was in accordance with halakhah and as it ought to be. This was only because Hashem was with him: bringing forth a good deed is solely in the hands of the Holy One, blessed be He. Without this, it is not called a true product.”
connections.context: This parallel explains “the completion of the deed”: a person’s preparation must reach an actual good result through Hashem’s assistance.

connections.hePhrase: [טו] מִצְוָה הוּא זְכוּת לָאָדָם שֶׁתִּזְדַּמֵּן לְיָדוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ "שְׂכַר מִצְוָה – מִצְוָה",
connections.quote: ‘Ben Azzai says: Run to a light mitzvah as you would to a weighty one, and flee from transgression. For one mitzvah draws another mitzvah after it, and one transgression draws another transgression after it. The reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah, and the recompense for a transgression is a transgression.’

connections.hePhrase: [טו] מִצְוָה הוּא זְכוּת לָאָדָם שֶׁתִּזְדַּמֵּן לְיָדוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ "שְׂכַר מִצְוָה – מִצְוָה",
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 20:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 20:1
connections.quote: ““As You desired and said to bless us”: all the desire awakened within a person comes from God’s will to bestow, as it is written, “You ... revealed to Your servant ... therefore Your servant found his heart to pray to You.” “Sanctify us through Your mitzvot”: holiness is desire and warmth. Thus we ask for desire and warmth in performing the mitzvah. When a mitzvah is performed coldly, without desire, it feels like a burden, as the Sages said, “Our leaders in Torah and our burdened ones in mitzvot”: the person feels that he bears their weight. When he performs the mitzvot with warmth and desire, however, he recognizes that the mitzvah bears him, like “the Ark bore its bearers.””
connections.explanation: The Radziner teaching develops the present siman’s description of a mitzvah as a gift. When the act is approached with desire and warmth, its sustaining power becomes perceptible: the mitzvah bears its bearer. This helps explain why Rav Tzadok stresses gratitude for an opportunity and alacrity in entering it. The invitation to act is already a form of divine generosity, while preparation makes the person able to receive it as such.
connections.headline: The privilege of a mitzvah is the support it gives the one who performs it

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּתּוֹסֶפְתָּא (פֵּאָה פֶּרֶק ג) בְּאוֹתוֹ שֶׁנִּזְדַּמְּנָה לְיָדוֹ מִצְוַת שִׁכְחָה הֵבִיא עוֹלָה,
connections.quote: “There was an incident involving a pious man who forgot a sheaf in his field. He said to his son, ‘Go and offer a bull as a burnt offering and a bull as a peace offering on my behalf.’ His son said to him, ‘Father, what led you to rejoice over this commandment more than over all the other commandments in the Torah?’ He replied, ‘The Omnipresent gave us all the commandments in the Torah to fulfill knowingly, but this one unknowingly. Had we done it intentionally before the Omnipresent, this commandment would not have come into our hands. Rather, Scripture says, “When you reap,” and so forth: Scripture assigns him a blessing. The argument follows all the more strongly: if one who did not intend to acquire merit nevertheless acquired it and is credited as meritorious, how much more so one who intended to acquire merit and acquired it! Similarly, “If a person sins and does,” and so forth, “he shall bring an unblemished ram,” and so forth. The argument follows all the more strongly: if one who did not intend to sin nevertheless sinned and is regarded as having sinned, how much more so one who intended to sin and sinned!’”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְסֻכָּה (כח:) דִּגְשָׁמִים בֶּחָג סִימָן רַע מָשָׁל וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Mishnah: Throughout all seven days, a person makes his sukkah his permanent dwelling and his house a temporary one. If rain falls, from what point may he leave? Once the porridge would be spoiled. They offered a parable: To what is this comparable? To a servant who came to mix a cup for his master, and his master poured a pitcher over his face.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְחוֹבוֹת הַלְּבָבוֹת: כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה לִשְׁלוֹחַ דּוֹרוֹן לְאוֹהֲבוֹ מַזְמִין לוֹ עָנִי.
connections.displayRef: Duties of the Heart, Fourth Treatise on Trust 4:73
connections.linkedRef: Duties of the Heart, Fourth Treatise on Trust 4:73
connections.canonicalRef: Duties of the Heart, Fourth Treatise on Trust 4:73
connections.heRef: חובות הלבבות, שער רביעי - שער הביטחון ד׳:ע״ג
connections.quote: “Likewise, if someone above him or below him asks him for something, he should seek to do it wholeheartedly and sincerely strive to complete it, if the opportunity is available and the person making the request deserves his efforts in that matter. He should then trust in God for its completion. If God completes it through him and makes him a means of benefiting another person, he should give thanks for this. If it is withheld from him and he does not have the opportunity to accomplish it, he should not blame himself; after personally making the effort, he should let his fellow know that he did not neglect it.”
connections.context: Chovos HaLevavos teaches gratitude for the opportunity to become a means of another person’s good, while distinguishing sincere effort from the outcome. The explicit image of the poor person as a gift is quoted separately from the Zohar at the end of this Hebrew phrase.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְחוֹבוֹת הַלְּבָבוֹת: כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה לִשְׁלוֹחַ דּוֹרוֹן לְאוֹהֲבוֹ מַזְמִין לוֹ עָנִי.
connections.quote: ““Take from among yourselves an offering to Hashem.” Rabbi Yehudah opened: “Is it not to share your bread with the hungry …?” Come and see: fortunate is a person’s portion when a poor person encounters him, for that poor person is a gift sent to him by the Holy One, blessed be He. Fortunate is the portion of one who receives that gift with a welcoming face.”
connections.context: The Zohar describes the encounter itself as Hashem’s gift and adds the requirement to welcome the person graciously.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַלָּשׁוֹן "זַכָּאִין לֶאֱכוֹל בִּתְרוּמָה" בִּבְרָכוֹת ב' עַמּוּד ב', דַּאֲכִילַת תְּרוּמָה מִצְוָה כִּדְאִיתָא פְּסָחִים (עג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א).
connections.quote: “A contradiction is raised: From when does one begin to recite the evening Shema? From the time people come in to eat their bread on Friday evenings; this is Rabbi Meir’s opinion. The Sages say: From the time the priests are entitled to eat their terumah. The indication of this time is the appearance of the stars. Although there is no proof of the matter, there is an allusion to it, as it is said: ‘We were engaged in the work, and half of them held spears, from the rising of dawn until the stars appeared.’ And it says: ‘The night was for us a watch, and the day was for work.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַלָּשׁוֹן "זַכָּאִין לֶאֱכוֹל בִּתְרוּמָה" בִּבְרָכוֹת ב' עַמּוּד ב', דַּאֲכִילַת תְּרוּמָה מִצְוָה כִּדְאִיתָא פְּסָחִים (עג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א).
connections.quote: “‘I give you your priesthood as a service bestowed as a gift, and the outsider who approaches shall be put to death.’ They treated eating terumah outside the Temple as equivalent to service in the Temple. ‘If he slaughtered it for those unable to eat it’: is this not obvious? Since the offering is invalid in that case, here he is liable! Because the latter clause teaches that he is exempt, the earlier clause teaches that he is liable.”

connections.hePhrase: וְתַנָּא דִידַן: "נִכְנָסִין", לְאוֹרוֹיֵי דְּכֹהֲנִים זְרִיזִים וּזְרִיזִים מַקְדִּימִין,
connections.quote: “The second counsel is deliberateness. The foundation of overpowering appetite is haste: a person wants to swallow and satisfy his desire quickly. As stated in Beitzah 25b, planting ‘cuts off the feet’ of butchers and those who have relations with menstruating women—the two principal desires mentioned, which arise from haste. The Sages said in Chullin 84a that the Torah teaches proper conduct: a person should eat meat only with preparation. At the beginning of Berakhot (2a–b), the Sages use ‘enters’ and ‘enter’ for every meal mentioned, teaching that eating requires an entrance and preparation. Even for a poor person's meal they say ‘enters’ (see Tosafot there, beginning ‘From the time,’ and my novellae there). Likewise, eating terumah and eating on Shabbat, which are mitzvah meals, are described as ‘entering’: they require preparation, rather than casual eating like a glutton who snatches and eats. As for ‘snatch and eat’ in Eruvin 54a, it appears that people differ: someone whose thoughts are already firmly attached to words of Torah may snatch and eat, like someone at a wedding feast whose main concern is the celebration and who eats incidentally. There is no concern or suspicion about his heart's appetite, and one can be confident that his thoughts are attached only to Torah and service.”
connections.explanation: The siman expressly refers the reader to Et HaOchel. There, the word ‘enter’ is explained as preparation even for an ordinary meal, and all the more for eating terumah or a Shabbat meal. This distinguishes promptly beginning the mitzvah's preparation from consuming its food impulsively. The quotation retains the closing qualification: the instruction to ‘snatch and eat’ concerns a person whose settled attention is already in Torah and service.
connections.headline: Alacrity begins with preparation

connections.hePhrase: וּמַאן דְּאָמַר "מְטוֹהָרִין", יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מִשָּׁעָה" הִקְשׁוּ עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ““From the time when the poor person enters to eat his bread with salt.” This is puzzling: when does the poor person himself pray? You have said that the time of his meal is the time of Shema, yet once the time of Shema arrives he may not begin a meal before praying, as the baraita teaches below: he recites Shema, prays, eats his bread, and recites the blessing; whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death. One may answer that the time for prayer is before the time of the meal. “When the poor person enters to eat” is not exact; it means a little earlier, so that while his meal is being prepared he recites Shema and prays.”
connections.context: This is the question and answer to which Rav Tzadok refers. He develops “entering” as preparation for the mitzvah; Tosafot identifies the interval while the meal is being prepared.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַבְּרָכָה שֶׁלִּפְנֵי אֲכִילָה שֶׁהוּא נוֹכַח וְנִסְתָּר,
connections.quote: “There is another reason for speaking of Him in the third person: He, blessed be He, is concealed and hidden from the apprehension of every being that apprehends. “Please save” addresses Him directly, to explain that although He is concealed and hidden, He is revealed and present in people’s hearts. This resembles the wording of the blessings: the Sages instituted “Blessed are You” as direct address, and “Who has sanctified us” in the third person. Here too, “Please save” is direct address, while “I and He” is in the third person—from wherever He is, for His place is unknown, as it says, “Blessed is the glory of Hashem from His place.” This is the meaning of “Your faithful ones shall bless You”: they bless in this manner, addressing the One who is revealed and concealed. It immediately continues, “They shall speak of the glory of Your kingdom,” and then, “To make known to human beings His mighty acts and the glorious splendor of His kingdom.””
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya explains the grammatical shift between direct address and the third person. Divine presence can be recognized in the heart while Hashem remains beyond complete apprehension.

connections.hePhrase: [טז] דְּבַר מִצְוָה שֶׁעוֹשֵׂהוּ מִפְּנֵי הַסָּפֵק חָל עָלָיו קְדוּשַׁת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּוַדַּאי כֵּיוָן שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַסָּפֵק, דּוּגְמַת יוֹם טוֹב שֵׁנִי.
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 3:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 3:1
connections.quote: “The reading of this passage on the second festival day in the Diaspora, which also arises on account of doubt, points to this as well. It teaches that through what Israel adds because of doubt, with generosity and willing hearts, they have a share even in the holiness of the first day. Its holiness is certain, like holiness rooted at the source; nevertheless, Israel acquires a share in it through the labor of their own hands.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim uses the same example of the second festival day to explain why service arising from doubt has positive spiritual content. The added observance gives Israel a share, through its own willing effort, in the first day's certain holiness. In the full discourse this follows the example of declaring a firstborn animal holy even though it is holy from birth. The comparison concerns the established observance named by the siman; it does not settle which blessing to recite in other doubtful cases.
connections.headline: A share in certain holiness through service amid doubt

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שַׁבָּת כ"ג עַמּוּד א' דִּמְבָרְכִין "אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו" אַסָּפֵק, חוּץ מִדְּמַאי דְּרוֹב עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְכוּלֵי [יְעוּיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי בָּזֶה לַהֲלָכָה בְּחִדּוּשַׁי].
connections.quote: “Abaye said: A definite enactment of the Sages requires a blessing; a doubtful enactment of the Sages does not require a blessing.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שַׁבָּת כ"ג עַמּוּד א' דִּמְבָרְכִין "אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו" אַסָּפֵק, חוּץ מִדְּמַאי דְּרוֹב עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְכוּלֵי [יְעוּיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי בָּזֶה לַהֲלָכָה בְּחִדּוּשַׁי].
connections.quote: “But the second festival day is a doubtful enactment of the Sages, and it requires a blessing! There, it is so that people will not treat it lightly. Rava said: Most unlearned people do separate tithes.”
connections.context: The discussion concerns why separating demai does not receive a blessing, and distinguishes it from the second festival day. These qualifications explain the issue of certainty in an obligation and its blessing that Rav Tzadok is considering.

connections.hePhrase: דּוּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בִּתְשׁוּבַת הָרַ"ן הוּבָא בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף יוֹרֶה דֵעָה סִימָן רכ"ח, דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁמִּסָּפֵק צָרִיךְ חָשׁוּב כְּוַדַּאי [יְעוּיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי בָּזֶה בְּחִדּוּשַׁי].
connections.quote: “The Ran wrote in responsum 50 concerning someone who swore on Friday morning not to be within the city of Perpignan on the coming Shabbat, and near sunset on Friday regretted his oath and sought its release: It appears to me that in such a case the vow is regarded as having taken effect, and a sage may release it. … Since by Torah law he is obligated to leave the city because of his vow, it is certainly regarded as a vow that has taken effect. … Even if the matter is doubtful, the reasoning inclines to the view that, since he is obligated by Torah law, the vow is regarded as having taken effect.”
connections.context: A sage can release a vow only after it has taken effect. The Ran’s ruling depends on the obligation created by a Torah-level doubt; he explicitly discusses whether stringent treatment of such a doubt is itself required by Torah law. Rav Tzadok cites this limited legal analogy for treating an existing obligation as operative despite its uncertain basis.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מַשְׁמָע לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא בְּרָכוֹת ב' עַמּוּד ב': "מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁקִּידֵּשׁ הַיּוֹם בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת", עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י דְּהַיְינוּ בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת וְקָרוּי קִידֵּשׁ הַיּוֹם בִּקְדוּשַׁת שַׁבָּת.
connections.quote: “From when does one begin reciting Shema in the evening? From when the day becomes sanctified on Friday evening; these are Rabbi Eliezer’s words.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מַשְׁמָע לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא בְּרָכוֹת ב' עַמּוּד ב': "מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁקִּידֵּשׁ הַיּוֹם בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת", עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י דְּהַיְינוּ בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת וְקָרוּי קִידֵּשׁ הַיּוֹם בִּקְדוּשַׁת שַׁבָּת.
connections.quote: ““From when the day becomes sanctified on Friday evening”: this is twilight, a doubt whether it is day or night. Since it is doubtful, the day becomes sanctified out of doubt.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies the proposed starting time with twilight and its doubtful status. This is why Rav Tzadok connects the passage to an obligation arising under uncertainty.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַל שְׁעַת בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת יֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם אַשַּׁבָּת "יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּקַדְּשִׁינְהוּ לְשַׁבָּת", אַף דִּקְבִיעָא וְקַיָּימָא, חוּמְרָא דְּסָפֵק הוּא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל],
connections.quote: “Shabbat, which is fixed and established—both in prayer and in Kiddush: “Who sanctifies Shabbat.” A festival, which Israel fixes by declaring months full and fixing the years: “Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons.””
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes Shabbat’s fixed sanctity from the festival calendar established by Israel. This is the distinction behind Rav Tzadok’s qualification that Israel’s contribution here concerns the doubtful twilight period.

connections.hePhrase: דְּכָל שֶׁבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מַחֲמִירִים עַל עַצְמָם לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ מִצְוָה – נַעֲשָׂה מִצְוָה וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ קְדוּשָּׁה:
connections.displayRef: Meshiv Tzedek, A Rebuttal Regarding Sitting in the Sukkah on Shemini Atzeret 150
connections.canonicalRef: Meshiv Tzedek, A Rebuttal Regarding Sitting in the Sukkah on Shemini Atzeret 150
connections.quote: “In truth, Maimonides already established in Sefer HaMitzvot, root 1, and at the beginning of chapter 1 of his Laws of Rebels, that every rabbinic obligation is a Torah obligation through the positive commandment “According to the teaching that they instruct you” and the prohibition “Do not turn aside.” This is explicit in the Gemara, Shabbat 23a: for this reason we bless, “Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us.” Thus we regard them as commandments that Hashem commanded us, and people rightly perform them simply as the mitzvah of Hashem, blessed be He. Even with a rabbinic obligation, those who perform it do so only because of Hashem’s commandment to heed the words of the Sages; without this, what would require them to heed the Sages? These are precisely the Rashba’s words: we rightly perform it as a mitzvah, and there is no prohibition of adding, for we were indeed commanded to act “according to” their instruction.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains why carrying out an established rabbinic enactment is itself obedience to Hashem. This provides his own fuller discussion of how the obligation gives the act the character of a mitzvah.

connections.hePhrase: [יז] זְמַן עֲבוֹדַת הַפּוֹעֵל רַק בַּיּוֹם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יֵצֵא אָדָם לְפָעֳלוֹ [וְלַעֲבֹדָתוֹ] עֲדֵי עָרֶב",
connections.quote: ‘A person goes out to his work, and to his labor until evening.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (סה.): "אֲנַן פּוֹעֲלֵי דִימָמָא", אֲבָל לֵילְיָא לְשֵׁינְתָא,
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda said: Night was created only for sleep. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Moonlight was created only for study.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (סה.): "אֲנַן פּוֹעֲלֵי דִימָמָא", אֲבָל לֵילְיָא לְשֵׁינְתָא,
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: We are workers of the daytime. Rav Acha bar Yaakov borrowed and repaid.”
connections.context: These are distinct sayings about the allocation of study and sleep. The “workers of the daytime” wording is essential to Rav Tzadok’s account of daytime service; “borrowed and repaid” is explained in the following note.

connections.hePhrase: רַק כִּי יָזֵיף בִּימָמָא פָּרַע בְּלֵילְיָא [וְעַיֵּין בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בְּרָכוֹת ח' עַמּוּד א' מַשְׁמָע דְּכֵן הֲלָכָה].
connections.quote: ““He borrowed and repaid”: He fixed for himself a certain number of chapters to study each day and normally studied by day. At times he was occupied with his livelihood by day, and he repaid his fixed study period at night.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק כִּי יָזֵיף בִּימָמָא פָּרַע בְּלֵילְיָא [וְעַיֵּין בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בְּרָכוֹת ח' עַמּוּד א' מַשְׁמָע דְּכֵן הֲלָכָה].
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות ו׳ א:א׳
connections.quote: “What we neglect of study by day is like a loan with us, and we repay it at night. Thus the night’s study belongs to that same day.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the Gemara’s metaphor; Rabbeinu Yonah applies it to the continuity of that day’s Torah obligation and blessing. The printed “8a” reference is the passage now numbered 6a on the Rif.

connections.hePhrase: רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם מָצָאנוּ גַּבֵּי מְלֶאכֶת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ (בְּרָכוֹת ב' עַמּוּד ב') סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּמַקְדְּמֵי וּמַחְשְׁכֵי גַּם בַּלַּיְלָה,
connections.quote: ‘If you say that it is already night once the sun has set, and that they simply worked late and started early, come and hear: ‘The night was for us a watch, and the day was for work.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שַׁבָּת פ"ט עַמּוּד ב' אָמְרִינַן: "דַּל פַּלְגָא דְּלֵילוֹתָא".
connections.quote: “‘Furthermore, how much have they sinned? How many years does a person live? Seventy years. Subtract the twenty for which You do not punish them, and fifty remain. Subtract twenty-five for the nights, and twenty-five remain. Subtract twelve and a half for prayer, eating, and attending to bodily needs, and twelve and a half remain. If You will bear all of them, well and good. If not, let half be upon me and half upon You. And if You say that all of them should be upon me, I have already offered myself before You.’ They begin to say, ‘For you are our father.’ Yitzchak tells them, ‘Instead of praising me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He,’ and with his eyes Yitzchak directs them toward the Holy One, blessed be He. At once they raise their eyes on high and say, ‘You, Hashem, are our Father; our Redeemer from of old is Your name.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דְּגַם בְּכָל עֲבוֹדַת ה' הַלַּיְלָה רַק לְמִשְׁמָר,
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:10
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:10
connections.quote: “During the first watch, up to its end, is the time when people go to lie down and have not yet lain down, since it is close to the light of day. For night is a time of sleep, meaning the absence of harm, as it says in Avodah Zarah 19b: “Might one give himself over to sleep?” [And in Shabbat 89b: “Subtract half for the nights.”] For in darkness it suffices to guard against harm. Nevertheless, sleep is not sufficient, as the conclusion in Avodah Zarah explains that this is not the ultimate purpose. Even at night, when it is not the time for most regular mitzvot such as tzitzit and tefillin, and even though the evening prayer is optional, one is nevertheless obligated in Shema. According to Rabbi Eliezer, this is during the first watch, while a little of the light of the nearby day still shines for him and the illuminating light has not yet faded and been forgotten entirely; he should accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven.”
connections.context: This parallel sets out the meaning and limit of night as a time of guarding: avoiding harm does not cancel the obligation to accept the yoke of Heaven through Shema.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, כז עַמּוּד א): "לְשָׁמְרָהּ" – זוֹ מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה,
connections.quote: ‘In this same way the Holy One, blessed be He, will act toward a person who was created from four elements. When he returns in repentance and engages in Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, takes him from there. Of them it is said: ‘From there it divides.’ He separates the person’s soul from their desire and places him in His garden, which is the Shekhinah: ‘to cultivate it’ through the positive commandments, and ‘to guard it’ through the negative commandments. If he merits guarding her, he will be head over the four elements. He becomes a river through which they are watered, and not through another; and they recognize that he is master and ruler over them.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֵירוּבִין צו.): דְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "הִשָּׁמֶר" וְכוּלֵי הוּא לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה,
connections.quote: “But then, what of that which we learned: The Pesach offering and circumcision are positive commandments? Must we say that this does not follow Rabbi Akiva? For if it followed Rabbi Akiva, since he interprets it as referring to the Pesach offering, there is a negative commandment as well, in accordance with Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ilai. For Rabbi Avin said in the name of Rabbi Ilai: Wherever ‘Be on guard,’ ‘lest,’ or ‘do not’ is said, it signifies a negative commandment!”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בְּשֵׁינָה דַּי, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט:): "יָכוֹל יְגָרֶה עַצְמוֹ בְּשֵׁינָה וְכוּלֵי", עַיֵּין שָׁם:
connections.quote: ‘‘Turn away from evil and do good,’ and so forth. Perhaps a person will say: ‘I have guarded my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit. I shall go and indulge in sleep.’ Therefore the verse says: ‘Turn away from evil and do good.’ ‘Good’ means Torah, as it is said: ‘For I have given you a good teaching; do not forsake My Torah.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַשְּׁכִיבָה מְיוּחֶדֶת לַלַּיְלָה שֶׁאֵינוֹ זְמַן פְּעוּלָה, אֲפִילּוּ אִי אִיכָּא אֱינָשֵׁי דִּבְזֶה סַגִּי, עַיֵּין ט' רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א' דְּגָנוּ בַּיּוֹם אֵינוֹ קָרוּי שְׁכִיבָה,
connections.quote: “Some teach Rav Acha bar Chanina’s statement concerning the following: It was taught, Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says in Rabbi Akiva’s name: Sometimes a person recites Shema twice during the day, once before sunrise and once after sunrise, and fulfills his obligation through them, once for the day and once for the night. This itself is difficult: You said that a person sometimes recites Shema twice during the day, implying that before sunrise is day; yet you then taught that he fulfills his obligation once for the day and once for the night, implying that it is night! No: it is actually day, and it is called “night” because some people are asleep at that time. Rabbi Acha, son of Rabbi Chanina, said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name: The halakhah follows Rabbi Shimon, who spoke in Rabbi Akiva’s name. Rabbi Zeira said: Provided that he does not say “Hashkivenu.” When Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef came, he said: This statement of Rabbi Acha, son of Rabbi Chanina, in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name was not stated explicitly but inferred. For two Sages became drunk at the wedding feast of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s son. They came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said: Rabbi Shimon is worthy of being relied upon in pressing circumstances.”
connections.context: This is the passage at the beginning of 9a to which Rav Tzadok refers. The source retains both qualifications: the blessing Hashkivenu is omitted, and reliance on this late nighttime recitation is limited to pressing circumstances. Rav Tzadok distinguishes that allowance from the ordinary designation of daytime as the time for rising and work.

connections.hePhrase: כֵּן מַשְׁמָע דְּהָעִיקָּר בַּלַּיְלָה מִלְּשׁוֹן "מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁקִּידֵּשׁ וְכוּלֵי" בִּבְרָכוֹת ב' עַמּוּד ב',
connections.quote: see note 118.
connections.context: The relevant formulation is the sanctification of the day. It is a different opinion from Rabbi Meir’s earlier measure of people beginning their Friday-night meal.

connections.hePhrase: דְּקָשֶׁה עַל זֶה קוּשְׁיַת הַגְּמָרָא שָׁם: מִכְּדִי וְכוּלֵי לֵימָא מִשְּׁעַת בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת לְפִי פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם,
connections.quote: “The Master said: “From when the priests enter to eat their terumah.” Since the priests eat terumah from the appearance of the stars, let it teach: “From the appearance of the stars”! It teaches another matter along the way: When do the priests eat terumah? From the appearance of the stars. It teaches us that bringing the atonement offering does not delay their permission to eat. As it was taught: “The sun shall set and he shall be pure”—sunset prevents him from eating terumah beforehand, but his atonement offering does not prevent him from eating terumah.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s question about choosing an indirect description of the time, together with its answer. Rav Tzadok applies the same question to the separate wording “from when the day becomes sanctified.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּקָשֶׁה עַל זֶה קוּשְׁיַת הַגְּמָרָא שָׁם: מִכְּדִי וְכוּלֵי לֵימָא מִשְּׁעַת בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת לְפִי פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם,
connections.quote: ““From when the day becomes sanctified on Friday evenings”: this is twilight, a doubt whether it is day or night. Since it is doubtful, the day becomes sanctified out of doubt.”
connections.context: This is the specific explanation of Rashi on which the preceding question depends: “the day becomes sanctified” designates doubtful twilight.

connections.hePhrase: [וְלוּלֵי פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּ"מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁקִּידֵּשׁ" הַיְינוּ תּוֹסֶפֶת שַׁבָּת, וְאִם כֵּן לָא קַשְׁיָא מִידֵי דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּנָפְקָא מִינַּהּ אַבֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי עַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא. וּלְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י צָרִיךְ לִדְחוֹק דְּתוֹסֶפֶת שַׁבָּת דְּרַבָּנָן וְהָכָא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא קָאָמַר, וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן],
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, according to Rabbeinu Hai Gaon of blessed memory, we learn that “the time when the day becomes sanctified” means the beginning of sunset, that is, the setting of the sun. If so, we should not explain it as the day becoming sanctified of itself, namely twilight, but as the time fit to be sanctified, which is the time suitable for adding from the weekday to the sacred.”
connections.context: The Rashba presents this interpretation specifically within Rabbeinu Hai Gaon’s account. It supplies a direct parallel to Rav Tzadok’s proposed reading of the phrase as the added time of Shabbat.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מַשְׁמָע עוֹד שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא: "וַהֲלֹא כֹּהֲנִים מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם הֵם טוֹבְלִים", מַשְׁמָע דְּאֵין סְבָרָא דְּיִהְיֶה זְמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע דִּשְׁכִיבָה אָז מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם
connections.quote: “The Master said: Rabbi Yehudah said to him, “But the priests immerse while it is still day!” Rabbi Yehudah has indeed spoken correctly to Rabbi Meir! Rabbi Meir replies to him as follows: Do you think that I refer to your twilight? I refer to Rabbi Yosei’s twilight. For Rabbi Yosei said: Twilight is like the blink of an eye; one period enters and the other departs, and it is impossible to determine its exact point.”
connections.context: The objection cited by Rav Tzadok is followed by this answer distinguishing Rabbi Yehudah’s twilight from Rabbi Yosei’s. Keeping the reply makes clear which discussion supplies the basis for Rav Tzadok’s inference about daytime and the time for lying down.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַיּוֹם לִמְלָאכָה, בְּעֵת הָאוֹר לֹא יֵשֵׁב בָּטֵל כְּיָשֵׁן:
connections.quote: ““And not to sleep”: The Ari said that after midday it is permitted to sleep, because the angel has already been awakened through the prayers and the shofar blasts. Bach writes that Maharam slept on Rosh Hashanah. One who sits idle is like one who is asleep.”
connections.context: The concluding phrase is the direct parallel to Rav Tzadok’s “idle like one who sleeps.” The Magen Avraham states it within the discussion of sleeping on Rosh Hashanah, while Rav Tzadok applies the comparison here to the opportunity for service during spiritual daylight.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק הָרוֹאֶה (בְּרָכוֹת נח.): "מַלְכוּתָא דִרְקִיעָא כְּמַלְכוּתָא דְאַרְעָא",
connections.quote: ‘A certain heretic said to him: ‘How do you know this?’ He replied: ‘Earthly kingship resembles heavenly kingship, as it is written: Go out and stand on the mountain before Hashem. Behold, Hashem was passing by, and a great, powerful wind was tearing apart mountains and shattering rocks before Hashem; Hashem was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake; Hashem was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake came fire; Hashem was not in the fire. After the fire came a faint sound of stillness.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת ג' עַמּוּד א': "אִיכָּא מִשְׁמוֹרוֹת בָּרָקִיעַ כִּי הֵיכִי דְּאִיכָּא (כֵּן הוּא גִּרְסַת הָרֹא"שׁ) בְּאַרְעָא",
connections.quote: “He does indeed hold that the night has three watches. What he teaches us is that there are watches in heaven and watches on earth. For it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says, ‘The night has three watches, and at each watch the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and roars like a lion, as it is said: “Hashem roars from on high, and from His holy dwelling He gives forth His voice; He roars mightily over His habitation.”’”

connections.hePhrase: וְרַשִּׁ"י שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ אַמַּלְאָכִים – לֹא יָדַעְתִּי לָמָּה לֵיהּ;
connections.quote: ““If he holds”: The tannaim disagree about this matter below. One opinion says that the night has three watches: it is divided into three parts according to the watches of the angels’ service and their song—the first for one group, the second for another group, and the third for a third group. Another opinion says that the night has four watches.”
connections.context: This is Rashi’s explanation that Rav Tzadok expressly examines. The quotation includes the competing count of four watches as well as the description of the angels’ service.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּאַרְעָא נִיכָּר חֲלוּקַּת הַזְּמַן לְכָל אָדָם כִּדְמַסַּיֵּים "חֲמוֹר וְכוּלֵי", כֵּן בָּרָקִיעַ נִיכָּר גַּם לְגַבֵּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֶגֶד לְמַטָּה.
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:16
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:16
connections.quote: “From every act of a person’s service below, the spiritual power of that service stands above as one of the heavenly host. This is what they said: an angel is created from every mitzvah. These are the watches in heaven, which follow “just as there are” [watches below]—this is the Rosh’s reading. For all the angels’ service comes only through human service, as it says in the chapter Gid HaNasheh, Chullin 91b: “The angels do not say ‘Holy’,” and so forth. Then they have permission and power [for they have no free choice; when they have no permission, they have no power] to say it—that is, to reveal and make this matter known, because Israel has already made it known. Their power above is created and revealed as an angel, a spiritual power standing and serving on high and revealing the power of this deed. This is the angels’ service and song, which come only through Israel, and these are their three watches. See the beginning of the commentary headed “If he holds.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel discussion explains the correspondence between service below and the angels’ watches above, and explicitly returns to the same comment of Rashi.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרֹא"שׁ שָׁם אַהָא דִּ"וְעַל כָּל מִשְׁמָר", לָכֵן רָאוּי לְכָל יְרֵא שָׁמַיִם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Gemara: ‘Until the end of the first watch’—these are Rabbi Eliezer’s words. We conclude that he holds that the night has three watches. He does not say ‘a third of the night’ because he teaches another matter along the way: there are watches in heaven just as there are watches on earth. For it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says that the night has three watches, and at each watch the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and roars like a lion, as it is said, ‘Hashem will roar from on high, and from His holy dwelling,’ and so forth, ‘He will roar mightily over His abode.’ It was also stated: Rav Shmuel bar Marta said in Rav’s name that the night has three watches, and at each watch the Holy One, blessed be He, says, ‘Woe to My children, for because of their sins I destroyed My house, burned My sanctuary, and exiled them among the nations of the world.’ Every person who fears Heaven should therefore grieve and be concerned at that hour and pour out supplications over the destruction of the Temple, as it is said, ‘Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת הוּא כְּפִי עִנְיַן הַזְּמַן, וּבַלַּיְלָה שֶׁהוּא רוֹמֵז זְמַן הַגָּלוּת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "שֹׁמֵר מַה מִּלַּיְלָה", הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יוֹשֵׁב וְשׁוֹאֵג וְכוּלֵי:
connections.quote: ‘An oracle concerning Dumah: Someone calls to me from Seir, ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’’

connections.hePhrase: סִימָן לַדָּבָר: מִשְׁמָר א' – חֲמוֹר נוֹעֵר:
connections.quote: “The signs for the matter are: in the first watch, a donkey brays; in the second, dogs cry out; in the third, a child nurses at his mother’s breasts and a woman speaks with her husband.”
connections.context: This is the complete sequence of signs that Rav Tzadok now interprets in terms of action, prayer, and Torah.

connections.hePhrase: הַחֹמֶר דּוּגְמַת חֲמוֹר, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ "עַם הַדּוֹמֶה לַחֲמוֹר" גַּם הוּא נוֹעֵר כַּחֲמוֹר לְמַשׂוֹי הַמִּצְווֹת בִּכְלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה.
connections.quote: “Rav said: Everyone agrees that a slave has no legally recognized genealogy, for it is written, “Stay here with the donkey”—a people comparable to a donkey. An objection was raised: “Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty slaves”! Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: It is like “a bull, the young of cattle.””
connections.context: The Gemara’s wordplay concerns a slave’s legal genealogy; its answer distinguishes a description of offspring from recognized lineage. Rav Tzadok draws on the image of the donkey here to describe the material body bearing the burden of mitzvot.

connections.hePhrase: הַחֹמֶר דּוּגְמַת חֲמוֹר, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ "עַם הַדּוֹמֶה לַחֲמוֹר" גַּם הוּא נוֹעֵר כַּחֲמוֹר לְמַשׂוֹי הַמִּצְווֹת בִּכְלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה.
connections.quote: “The school of Eliyahu taught: A person should always place himself toward words of Torah like an ox for the yoke and like a donkey for a burden.”
connections.context: This teaching supplies the image of willingly bearing a burden. Rav Tzadok applies it here to carrying the mitzvot through the bodily instruments of action.

connections.hePhrase: ב' – כְּלָבִים צוֹעֲקִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר: צָוְוחִין כְּכַלְבָּא, בִּתְפִלָּה
connections.quote: ““He turned this way and that and saw that there was no man.” Instead, “each turned to his own way,” to their own affairs and paths, “each to his own gain, from his quarter”—to the gain of this world, to possess this world. They are not of the side of those described as “men of valor, fearing God, men of truth, hating gain.” Instead, they all cry out in their prayers on Yom Kippur like dogs: “Give, give us food, forgiveness, atonement, and life; inscribe us for life.” They are bold of spirit like dogs, like the nations of the world who cry out to Him and have no shame. For there is no one who calls to Him in repentance so that the Shekhinah, who is far from the Holy One, blessed be He, should return to Him. They resemble dogs, as it says, “They mingled with the nations and learned their deeds”; they are the mixed multitude, for every kindness they perform they perform for themselves.”
connections.context: The surrounding passage rebukes prayer centered on personal benefit while neglecting the Shekhinah’s exile. Rav Tzadok draws on its image of crying out in prayer when describing the second watch.

connections.hePhrase: [וְהַכְּלָבִים עַזֵּי פָנִים, וְכֵן חוּצְפָּה בִּתְפִלָּה כְּלַפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא מַהֲנְיָא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית ח' עַמּוּד א'].
connections.quote: “If he prayed in a whisper and was not answered, what is his remedy? Let him go to the pious person of the generation, who will increase prayer on his behalf, as it says, “He commands it through entreaty”; entreaty means prayer.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְהַכְּלָבִים עַזֵּי פָנִים, וְכֵן חוּצְפָּה בִּתְפִלָּה כְּלַפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא מַהֲנְיָא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית ח' עַמּוּד א'].
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman said: Persistence can be effective even toward Heaven. At first it is written, “Do not go with them,” and afterward it is written, “Rise, go with them.””
connections.context: Taanit, the reference printed here, speaks of increasing entreaty after a prayer was unanswered. The explicit maxim about bold persistence appears in Sanhedrin, in the discussion of Balaam. Rav Tzadok applies the power of persistence to prayer; that application is his, not a quotation of Taanit’s wording.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנה:): "לֵית דְּעַנְיָא מִכַּלְבָּא" – עָנִי בְּדַעַת, וְאֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Hamnuna said: Learn from this that proper conduct is to throw a piece of meat to a dog. How much? Rav Mari said: A piece the size of its ear, and then drive it away with a stick. This applies in the countryside, but not in town, lest it become accustomed to following you. Rav Pappa said: No creature is poorer than a dog, and none is richer than a pig.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנה:): "לֵית דְּעַנְיָא מִכַּלְבָּא" – עָנִי בְּדַעַת, וְאֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה,
connections.quote: “Abaye said: We have a received teaching—there is no poverty except in knowledge. In the West they say: One who has this [knowledge] has everything; one who does not have this, what does he have? One who has acquired this, what does he lack? One who has not acquired this, what has he acquired?”
connections.context: This is the source of “poor in knowledge.” It explains the transition from the dog’s poverty to a person who lacks understanding and turns to prayer.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה לח): אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אֵין אָנוּ יוֹדְעִין וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “They said to Him: We are poor and have nothing with which to bring offerings. He said to them: I ask for words, as it is said, “Take words with you and return to the Lord,” and I will forgive all your sins. “Words” means words of Torah. They said to Him: We do not know [Torah]. He said to them: Weep and pray before Me, and I will accept you.”
connections.context: The Midrash moves from offerings to Torah and then to prayer, showing that poverty or lack of learning does not shut the way to returning to God. This is the particular sequence Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק עַרְבֵי פְסָחִים (פְּסָחִים קיב.): "מִמַּה שֶּׁהָעֵגֶל רוֹצֶה לִינַק", שֶׁתּוֹרָה נִמְשְׁלָה לְחָלָב.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Akiva gave Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai five instructions while he was confined in prison. Rabbi Shimon said to him: ‘My teacher, teach me Torah.’ He answered: ‘I will not teach you.’ Rabbi Shimon said: ‘If you do not teach me, I will tell my father Yochai and have you reported to the government.’ Rabbi Akiva said: ‘My son, more than the calf wants to nurse, the cow wants to give milk.’ Rabbi Shimon replied: ‘And who is in danger? Is it not the calf that is in danger?’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק עַרְבֵי פְסָחִים (פְּסָחִים קיב.): "מִמַּה שֶּׁהָעֵגֶל רוֹצֶה לִינַק", שֶׁתּוֹרָה נִמְשְׁלָה לְחָלָב.
connections.quote: ““Let her breasts satisfy you at all times”: Why are words of Torah compared to a breast? Just as this breast, whenever the child handles it, yields milk, so words of Torah, whenever a person studies them, yield flavor.”
connections.context: This is the direct comparison of Torah to nourishing milk. It explains the symbol of the nursing child beyond the already quoted teaching about a teacher’s desire to teach.

connections.hePhrase: וְאִשָּׁה וְכוּלֵי הַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת ס"ג עַמּוּד ב'.
connections.quote: ‘What practical difference does this make? It concerns reciting the Shema for someone who sleeps in a dark house and does not know when the time for reciting the Shema has arrived. Once a woman is talking with her husband and a baby is nursing at its mother’s breast, he should get up and recite it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאִשָּׁה וְכוּלֵי הַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת ס"ג עַמּוּד ב'.
connections.quote: ‘Rava said: Come and see how good a good wife is, and how bad a bad wife is. How good a good wife is, as it is written: ‘He who has found a wife has found good.’ If the verse speaks about her, how good a good wife is, for Scripture praises her. If the verse speaks about Torah, how good a good wife is, for Torah is compared to her. How bad a bad wife is, as it is written: ‘I find the woman more bitter than death.’ If the verse speaks about her, how bad a bad wife is, for Scripture condemns her. If the verse speaks about Gehinnom, how bad a bad wife is, for Gehinnom is compared to her.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק הָאִשָּׁה הִיא הַמֵּינֶקֶת וְהַיְינוּ גְּדוֹלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְתִינוֹקוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית רַבָּן מְקַבְּלִין מֵהֶם.
connections.quote: ““I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers.” Rabbi Yochanan said: “I am a wall”—this is Torah; “and my breasts are like towers”—these are Torah scholars. Rava said: “I am a wall”—this is the congregation of Israel; “and my breasts are like towers”—these are synagogues and houses of study.”
connections.context: Rabbi Yochanan’s reading supplies the identification of the nourishing breasts with Torah scholars. Rava’s alternative reading is retained as part of the source.

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם תּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה וּגְמִילוּת חֲסָדִים
connections.quote: “Shimon the Righteous was among the remaining members of the Great Assembly. He used to say: The world stands on three things—on Torah, on service, and on deeds of kindness.”
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s threefold formulation that Rav Tzadok identifies with the watches. His account of the night proceeds through the corresponding activities in the reverse order.

connections.hePhrase: [כא] אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא בַּעֲבוֹדַת ה' מְעוֹרֵר לְמַעְלָה דּוּגְמָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים.
connections.quote: “A person’s voice has an echo, as our Sages said in Shemot Rabbah, chapter 29. The voice of Torah and prayer rises above and pierces the heavens, as stated there in the section of Shelach; wherever it reaches, it produces a returning voice. The returning voice of prayer is like the accounts in Taanit and HaPoalim: he said, “Who makes the wind blow,” and the wind blew; “Who brings down rain,” and rain came. This is the returning voice of his prayer. The heavenly voice issuing from Hashem’s mouth is likewise so. Hashem’s speech is equivalent to action, as stated in the chapter Kol Kitvei, Shabbat 119b; immediately the wind blew and rain came through Hashem’s heavenly voice. Similarly, the statement in Berakhot 7a, “From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays?” means that through Israel’s prayers they bring forth a returning voice above.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the correspondence between service below and its response above through the image of an echo. In the sentences immediately preceding this selection, he applies the same principle to Hashem repeating the Torah taught by the sages.

connections.hePhrase: [כא] אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא בַּעֲבוֹדַת ה' מְעוֹרֵר לְמַעְלָה דּוּגְמָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 5
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 5
connections.quote: “and therefore Hashem arranged that the multiplication of humanity occur through the childbearing of father and mother, and He implanted natural compassion within the hearts of parents, so that even if their children transgress the will and command of their parents, and even if they act to provoke them, nevertheless He ingrained such compassion in the hearts of parents that despite all this they plead with Hashem not to punish their children, because it is the intrinsic nature of the cause to have compassion upon its effect, its mercy rising above all to cover over all transgressions. And this obligates, measure for measure, that Hashem, blessed be He, have compassion upon Israel even when they transgress His will, by the very law of measure for measure.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach places the principle of awakening from below within the structure of human family life. A parent's compassionate intercession for a disobedient child awakens corresponding compassion Above. This supplies a concrete ethical example for the siman's general principle, alongside its examples of Torah discussed below and spoken Above. The source presents the relation through measure-for-measure judgment.
connections.headline: Compassion as an awakening from below

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה טו:): אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר שִׁילָא לְאֵלִיָּהוּ וְכוּלֵי, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עַכְשָׁו אָמַר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
connections.quote: “Rabbah bar Sheila encountered Elijah and asked him: ‘What is the Holy One, blessed be He, doing?’ He replied: ‘He is relating teachings in the names of all the Sages, but He is not relating teachings in Rabbi Meir’s name.’ He asked him: ‘Why?’ ‘Because he learned teachings from Aher.’ He said to him: ‘Why should that prevent it? Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate: he ate its inside and threw away its peel.’ Elijah said to him: ‘Now He is saying: ‘My son Meir says: When a person suffers, what does the Shechinah say? My head aches; My arm aches. If the Holy One, blessed be He, suffers this way over the blood of the wicked, how much more so over the blood of the righteous that has been shed.’’”

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְעֵין זֶה בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּגִטִּין (ו:) בְּרַבִּי אֶבְיָתָר].
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Evyatar met Elijah and asked him: ‘What is the Holy One, blessed be He, doing?’ Elijah answered: ‘He is studying the matter of the concubine at Gibeah.’ ‘And what is He saying?’ Elijah replied: ‘My son Evyatar says this, and My son Yonatan says this.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "אִיכָּא מִשְׁמוֹרוֹת בָּרָקִיעַ כִּי הֵיכִי דְּאִיכָּא בְּאַרְעָא"
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:16
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:16
connections.quote: see note 140.
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s direct parallel explanation of the same wording, including his note that it follows the Rosh’s reading. The correspondence between earthly and heavenly watches expresses the effect of human service on the heavenly service.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם עַמּוּד ב' דִּלְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר – ד'].
connections.quote: ‘What is Rabbi’s reason? Rabbi Zerika said in the name of Rabbi Ami, who said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: One verse says, ‘At midnight I rise to thank You for Your righteous judgments,’ while another verse says, ‘My eyes have preceded the watches.’ How can these be reconciled? The night has four watches.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאוֹתָם הַיּוֹדְעֵי בִינָה לַעִתִּים יֵשׁ לָהֶם גַּם כֵּן לְחַלֵּק הַלַּיְלָה לְג' מִשְׁמוֹרוֹת וּזְמַנִּים, כָּל מִשְׁמָר הוּא זְמַן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
connections.quote: “Concerning “those who understand the times,” I heard that this means they recognized, at every time, how it differed from another time. Every time is different: Shabbat, a festival, Rosh Chodesh, and other seasons and occasions have their distinctions. Likewise every day differs from the next, as do morning and evening, as the Zohar says: the garments worn in the morning are not worn in the evening. One who possesses clear understanding knows and recognizes the changes of the times—in his heart, even without knowing the particular character of that time. Through this he knows what Israel should do, at “a time to act for Hashem.” This is possible only through the level described above, cleaving so closely to Hashem, “as a belt clings,” and so forth. As the Midrash says of twins, when one has a headache the other feels it: every change of time below has its counterpart above, and conversely. As I wrote elsewhere concerning the opening passage of Berakhot 3a, there are watches in heaven just as there are below—this is the Rosh’s reading—and a sign of the matter. Therefore one can sense the times. This comes through the heart’s understanding, for feeling belongs to the heart.”
connections.context: This passage directly explains the expression “those who understand the times.” Rav Tzadok connects the discernment of spiritual changes with the same teaching about the watches of the night.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן חֶשְׁכַּת הָאוֹר וְכֵן הוּא זְמַן הַגָּלוּת חָלוּק לְג' עִתִּים אֵלּוּ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר:
connections.quote: “The night is divided into three watches, as stated in the first chapter of Berakhot: it was taught that Rabbi Eliezer says the night has three watches, and at every watch the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and roars like a lion, as it is said, ‘Hashem will roar from on high; He will roar mightily over His abode.’ The signs are: in the first watch a donkey brays; in the second, dogs cry; in the third, an infant nurses from its mother and a wife speaks with her husband. One must ask why at every watch the Holy One, blessed be He, cries, ‘Woe to Me, for I have destroyed My house,’ and so forth. Know that night is darkness and resembles exile, in which Israel sits in darkness without light. Thus, when Israel was redeemed, it is written, ‘The Jews had light.’ Night is therefore a sign of exile. Just as night divides into three watches, exile divides into three parts, corresponding exactly to the watches of the night, which signify the three parts of exile. Therefore the blessed Hashem sits and cries at every watch, ‘Woe to Me, for I have destroyed My house,’ and so forth. At the beginning of exile, they placed a yoke upon Israel and made the exile exceedingly burdensome. Israel constantly bore a great yoke and burden, like a donkey bearing a heavy load. This was how they acted at the beginning of exile, under the Babylonian kingdom; such was its first part. The second part of exile was a generation of persecution, when decrees of death and apostasy were imposed upon them. This corresponds to the second watch, when dogs cry. Dogs crying is a sign of death, as the Sages said: when dogs cry, the angel of death has come to the city. So in the second part of exile they killed and put Jews to death. Therefore it says, ‘In the second watch, dogs cry,’ a sign of lamentation and death; over this too the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and roars like a lion. In the third part of exile there is no such persecution—may Hashem protect His people Israel from it—and the nations treat Israel as a husband treats a wife. For the nations are considered Israel’s husbands in exile, as it is said, ‘Lords other than You have ruled over us.’ When a wife finds no favor in her husband’s eyes, he divorces her. So the nations expel Israel when Israel finds no favor in their eyes. This is the principal feature of exile’s third part. Concerning it he said, ‘In the third watch, a wife speaks with her husband.’ He also said that in the third watch an infant nurses from its mother. Correspondingly, at the end of exile Israel, considered infants in Torah, nurse from their mother’s breasts—from the earlier sages, who are called their mother. This is because they were given no rest to settle in one place, but wandered from place to place, until, because of our many sins, Torah was entirely forgotten from Israel through the exile.”
connections.context: Maharal explicitly compares the three watches of night to three periods of exile. This is a parallel to Rav Tzadok’s threefold account; the passage gives Maharal’s own historical explanation of the watches, rather than supplying the identical interpretation of each stage in the reader.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן חֶשְׁכַּת הָאוֹר וְכֵן הוּא זְמַן הַגָּלוּת חָלוּק לְג' עִתִּים אֵלּוּ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר:
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:9
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:9
connections.quote: ““The night has three watches,” and so forth. Night means darkness and the absence of the light that comes through the Temple. As our Sages say in Menachot 86b—see also Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 31—concerning its windows, broad on the outside and narrow within: light goes forth from it to the world. This is the meaning of “He will roar over His abode,” and “Woe to the children.” It divides into three: beginning, middle, and end, for this is the division of every thing. There are also watches below for the service of Hashem even in a time of darkness. They are called “watches” because the time itself calls for this service, as it is written, “The night was for keeping watch,” and “The watchmen found me” at night. It is also said, “The watchman said: Morning comes”; and the prophet in exile said, “I will stand at my watch.” For then is the time to guard against robbers and harmful forces through the watchmen and those who keep the watches.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s own discussion explains why the darkness of exile has three stages and why each calls for a corresponding form of service. This adds his direct account alongside the existing quotation of Maharal’s historical interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר לִקּוּטֵי אֲמָרִים מֵהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד מִמֶּזְרִיטְשׁ זְצוֹקַ"ל, כִּי חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לַצַּדִּיק הוּא לְסִימָן לוֹ שֶׁיֵּדַע שֶׁאוֹתוֹ הַחִסָּרוֹן בַּשְּׁכִינָה כִּבְיָכוֹל, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵיאוּרוֹ.
connections.quote:
“When a person needs to ask the Creator, blessed be He, for something, he should think that his soul is, as it were, a limb of the Shekhinah, like a drop from the sea. He should pray on behalf of the Shekhinah, for that thing is lacking in the Shekhinah, and he should have faith that he is certainly bringing about an effect above for the Shekhinah. Only if he is properly attached to the Shekhinah will the abundance also be drawn upon him.

This is like a person who experiences joy and claps his hands even without intending to, because the joy spreads into the limb. So it is here: since he is, as it were, a limb of the Shekhinah, the abundance will also be drawn upon him. He should think that he is only a vessel, and that his thought and speech are worlds that extend forth. The world of speech, which is the Shekhinah, petitions the world of thought concerning these words. When he draws the light of the Creator, blessed be He, into his thought and speech, his request should be that abundance spread from the world of thought to the world of speech. It will also come into the matter he is speaking about, which he needs, and his request will be granted. This is the meaning of ‘Be found by us in our beseeching’: that He, blessed be He, should be found within those requests.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "עַם הַדּוֹמֶה לַחֲמוֹר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (צב:): "קַרְיָיךְ חַמְרָא וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: ‘Rava said to Rabbah bar Mari: What is the source of the Sages’ saying, ‘If your companion calls you a donkey, place a saddle on your back’? He answered: It is written: ‘He said: Hagar, Sarai’s maidservant, where have you come from, and where are you going? She said: I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא קַמָּא ס:): כְּלָבִים מְשַׂחֲקִים וְכוּלֵי כְּלָבִים בּוֹכִים וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: When dogs weep, the Angel of Death has come to the city. When dogs frolic, Elijah the prophet has come to the city. This applies when there is no female among them.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי יֵשׁ עַזּוּת דִּקְדוּשָׁה: "עַז כַּנָּמֵר"
connections.quote: “He began with “bold as a leopard” because this is a great principle in serving the blessed Creator. Sometimes a person wishes to perform a mitzvah but refrains because people mock him. He therefore warned you to show boldness before those who mock you, and not to refrain from performing the mitzvah. Similarly, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai said to his disciples: May it be His will that your fear of Heaven be like your fear of flesh and blood.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְלִישָׁנָא דְּאֶמְצָעִית דְּאֶמְצָעִיתָא, הַיְינוּ חֲצוֹת, עֵת רָצוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יְבָמוֹת ע"ב עַמּוּד א',
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: Throughout all forty years that Israel was in the wilderness, there was no day on which a north wind did not blow at midnight, as it is said: ‘At midnight, Hashem struck every firstborn,’ and so forth. What does this establish? It teaches us that a favorable time has significance.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הִנְנִי שֹׁלֵחַ לָכֶם אֵת אֵלִיָּה הַנָּבִיא לִפְנֵי בּוֹא יוֹם ה' וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ‘Behold, I am sending you Elijah the prophet before the coming of Hashem’s great and fearsome day.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מֵחֲצוֹת וְאֵילָךְ מַתְחִיל הַרְגָּשַׁת הַיּוֹם, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "מִשְׁמוּרָה וּפַלְגָא נַמֵּי הָוֵי מִשְׁמוֹרוֹת".
connections.quote: “It is well known that the Sages’ manner is to reckon everything before its midpoint as beginning, and after its midpoint as completed. This is like “a watch and a half are also called watches” in Berakhot 3b, and their statement in Yoma 38b, “Once most of a person’s years have passed without his sinning,” and so forth. This follows the principle that the majority is regarded as the whole.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the same phrase about a watch and a half by the principle that most of a period may count as the whole. It supplies the reasoning behind treating the post-midnight remainder as the later stage of the night.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הֵם מִתְעוֹרְרִים בְּסִיפּוּר דְּחִיבָּה: אִשָּׁה לְבַעְלָהּ
connections.quote: “The words of prayer are the words of the Congregation of Israel, like a wife speaking with her husband. This is called conversation, and it is the feminine counterpart to the masculine speech.”
connections.context: This parallel identifies the image of a wife speaking with her husband as Israel’s prayer to Hashem. Rav Tzadok’s distinction between “conversation” and “speech” explains the spiritual meaning of the third watch’s domestic scene.

connections.hePhrase: [דְּלָא תֵימָא דְּמַה דְּאִיכָּא דְּהוֹלְכִים לִשְׁכַּב יוֹעִיל כִּדְלָדִידַן אִיכָּא דְּגָנוּ, דְּאִם כֵּן כָּל הַלַּיְלָה נַמֵּי, עַיֵּין בְּרַשִׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת ט' עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וּבִלְבַד", דְּיֵשׁ שֶׁהוֹלְכִים אָז תְּחִלַּת שְׁכִיבָה],
connections.displayRef: Rashi on Berakhot 9a, s.v. Ve-vilvad shelo yomar hashkivenu
connections.quote: ““Provided that he does not say ‘Hashkivenu’”: One who recites the nighttime Shema in the early morning, close to dawn, should not say “Hashkivenu,” because this is no longer the time for beginning to lie down, but the time when lying down is ending.”

connections.hePhrase: [דְּלָא תֵימָא דְּמַה דְּאִיכָּא דְּהוֹלְכִים לִשְׁכַּב יוֹעִיל כִּדְלָדִידַן אִיכָּא דְּגָנוּ, דְּאִם כֵּן כָּל הַלַּיְלָה נַמֵּי, עַיֵּין בְּרַשִׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת ט' עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וּבִלְבַד", דְּיֵשׁ שֶׁהוֹלְכִים אָז תְּחִלַּת שְׁכִיבָה],
connections.quote: ““Provided that he does not say ‘Hashkivenu’”: Rashi explains that this refers to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s statement about one who reads before dawn. It appears to me that then it is certainly still a time of lying down, and one may say “Hashkivenu.” Moreover, the ruling should have referred to the statement immediately preceding it. The Sar of Coucy therefore explains that it refers to the immediately preceding case, before sunrise. For this reason it says that one may not say “Hashkivenu”: once dawn has already come, even before sunrise, it is no longer a time of lying down.”
connections.context: Tosafot preserves the distinction Rav Tzadok needs: before dawn can still be a time for beginning to lie down; after dawn, even before sunrise, the ruling about Hashkivenu is different. The quotation includes both the objection to Rashi and the alternative interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: עַיֵּין בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת
connections.displayRef: Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah on Rif, Berakhot 1a, s.v. Ad sof ha-ashmurah ha-rishonah
connections.quote: ““Until the end of the first watch”: this is one third of the night, for the night has three watches, as it is written, “In the middle watch.” Calling it “middle” implies that there is one before it and one after it. Rabbi Eliezer understands “when you lie down” to mean not the entire time that people lie in their beds, but the entire time that they go to bed. Some people delay going to bed until a third of the night has passed; it is therefore still called a time of lying down.”

connections.hePhrase: [רֶמֶז "אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר", צְעָקָה בִּתְפִלָּה עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב],
connections.quote: ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake. Listen! My beloved is knocking: ‘Open for me, my sister, my companion, my dove, my flawless one, for my head is filled with dew, my locks with the droplets of the night.’’

connections.hePhrase: [רֶמֶז "אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר", צְעָקָה בִּתְפִלָּה עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב],
connections.quote: “The Congregation of Israel declares with pride, “I am asleep, but my heart is awake.” Our Sages interpret “my heart” as the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, “The Rock of my heart,” and so forth.
