Although they are asleep with respect to the mitzvot and have no eyes—as in sleep, when the eyes are closed and the heart is immersed in imaginings—nevertheless, since the soul’s root is a portion of the Divine and the depths of the heart cleave to Hashem, even all the imaginings are attached to Hashem. Even at the point of deepest immersion in the imaginings of this world that conceal the absolute truth, a person retains the power to awaken to Hashem because the heart cleaves to the living God.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s explanation of the same verse. The heart’s underlying attachment to Hashem remains even during spiritual sleep, making an awakening in prayer possible.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ כְּדִבְרֵי הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת דֵּעוֹת דְּפָסַק כְּלִישָׁנָא בַּתְרָא כְּדַרְכּוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Day and night comprise twenty-four hours. It is enough for a person to sleep for a third of them, which is eight hours. These should be at the end of the night, so that eight hours extend from the beginning of his sleep until sunrise. Thus he will get up from his bed before the sun rises.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּתוֹסָפוֹת עֵירוּבִין ס"ה עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "אֶלָּא", יֵשׁ לוֹמַר לֵילֵי תְּקוּפַת תַּמּוּז הֵם ח' שָׁעוֹת בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: ““Only for sleep”: for example, the nights of the summer season.”
connections.context: Tosafot limits the saying about night being for sleep by giving the short summer nights as an example. Rav Tzadok uses that qualification in his calculation; Tosafot does not itself state the eight-hour figure.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שִׁילְהֵי תַּעֲנִית ל"א עַמּוּד א' דְּמִטַּ"וּ בְּאָב צָרִיךְ לְהוֹסִיף, וְהַיְינוּ מֵחֲצִי תְּקוּפַת תַּמּוּז, דְּמֵחֲצִי וּלְמַעְלָה מַתְחִיל לְהִתְגַּדֵּל הַלַּיְלָה.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Menashya said: They call it ‘the day of breaking the axe.’ From this point on, one who adds (to his Torah study) will have (life) added to him, while one who does not add will be gathered in. What does ‘gathered in’ mean? Rav Yosef said: His mother will bury him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין סֻכָּה כ"ו עַמּוּד ב'.
connections.quote: ‘Rav said: A person may not sleep during the day for longer than a horse sleeps. How long does a horse sleep? Sixty breaths. Abaye said: My teacher’s sleep was like Rav’s; Rav’s was like Rabbi’s; Rabbi’s was like David’s; David’s was like a horse’s; and a horse’s sleep is sixty breaths.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל כָּתַב דְּשִׁיתִּין נִשְׁמֵי – ו' שָׁעוֹת, עַיֵּין בְּמִקְדַּשׁ מֶלֶךְ וַיִּגַּשׁ ר"ז עַמּוּד א', וְיְעוּיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּחִדּוּשַׁי:
connections.displayRef: Peri Tzadik, The Fifteenth of Av 5:2
connections.canonicalRef: Peri Tzadik, The Fifteenth of Av 5:2
connections.quote: “This applies from the fifteenth of Av onward. Before that, the Gemara in Eruvin says, “Night was created only for sleep”; Tosafot writes, “such as the nights of the summer season.” Some say that the measure of sixty breaths is six hours. From the fifteenth of Av onward, when the night is longer than six hours, one must add nighttime to daytime study and learn at night as well. Concerning this it says, “Moonlight was created only for reviewing one’s learning.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok elsewhere connects the opinion that sixty breaths signifies six hours with the discussion of adding nighttime Torah study after the fifteenth of Av. His wording “some say” is retained. This is a parallel in his own work, not a replacement for the separate citation to Mikdash Melekh.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן תְּפִלָּה טוֹב בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין בְּנֵי אָדָם, כִּי הֵם מְבַלְבְּלִים אוֹתוֹ בִּפְנִיּוֹת וּמַחֲשֶׁבֶת חוּץ, וּשְׁאָר מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת בָּא עַל יְדֵי כֵּן,
connections.quote: “Then he enters the Holy of Holies, concerning which it is said, “No person shall be in the Tent of Meeting.” This means that he should have no distracting thought, for most distracting thoughts come from a person’s attachment to created beings: that is what occupies his thoughts. Were he alone in the world, together with the blessed Creator, all his thoughts would be solely of the Creator, blessed be His Name. For imaginings and distracting thoughts arise from the things that pass before him, as is known.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok later gives his own explanation of the same verse about entry into the holy place. It identifies the inward aim of solitude: attention directed to Hashem, free from the distracting thoughts arising from one’s surroundings.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּדֶגֶל מַחֲנֵה אֶפְרַיִם כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים עַל פָּסוּק "וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד בְּבֹאוֹ לְכַפֵּר בַּקֹּדֶשׁ".
connections.quote: “‘Arm men from among you for the army, that they may go against Midian,’ and so forth, ‘to execute Hashem’s vengeance upon Midian.’ One may explain this by allusion, following what I heard from my relative by marriage, the venerable, departed Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka, of blessed memory, concerning the verse ‘No man shall ascend with you on that entire mountain.’ When a person wishes to serve Hashem truly and wholeheartedly, he must think and imagine himself as though he alone exists in the world, without any ulterior consideration arising from another person. On this basis I explained, ‘No person shall be in the Tent of Meeting when he enters to atone in the holy place’; understand this. This is also the meaning of ‘Where there are no people, strive to be a man’: strive always to be as though in a place without people. This may also be hinted at here: ‘Arm yourselves’ can mean ‘remove’—remove people from yourselves, as in ‘No man shall ascend with you.’ Fight only Hashem’s battle against Midian, for no human purpose, Heaven forbid, but solely to execute Hashem’s vengeance upon Midian. Understand this.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּדֶגֶל מַחֲנֵה אֶפְרַיִם כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים עַל פָּסוּק "וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד בְּבֹאוֹ לְכַפֵּר בַּקֹּדֶשׁ".
connections.quote: ‘No one shall be in the Tent of Meeting from the time he enters to make atonement in the holy place until he comes out. He shall make atonement for himself, for his household, and for the entire congregation of Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְגַם בַּתּוֹרָה אָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים קיב.): "לֹא תִשְׁנֶה בְּגוֹבְהָהּ שֶׁל עִיר",
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: Rabbi Akiva gave his son Rabbi Yehoshua seven instructions: ‘My son, do not sit at the highest point of a town and study, and do not live in a town whose leaders are Torah scholars.’’

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים פא.): "הִזָּהֲרוּ בַּחֲבוּרָה" וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת –
connections.quote: ‘They sent word from there: ‘Guard against neglecting cleanliness. Be careful to study in a group. Take care with the children of the poor, for Torah will come from them, as it says: “Water will flow from his buckets (mi-dalav)”—Torah will come from his poor.’’

connections.hePhrase: רַק יְכַוֵּין הַכֹּל צֹרֶךְ גָּבוֹהַּ כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: “If so, there is a profound secret in this matter. On a plain reading, the dwelling of the Shechinah among Israel serves a human need, rather than a need above. Yet it is like the verse, “Israel, in whom I shall be glorified,” and Joshua’s words, “What will You do for Your great Name?””
connections.context: Discussing Hashem’s dwelling among Israel, Ramban distinguishes the apparent human benefit from the deeper concern for divine glory. This gives the background to “for the sake of Heaven” here: even requests for material needs are directed toward the revelation and honor of Hashem’s presence.

connections.hePhrase: [הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כֵּיצַד מְבָרְכִין (בְּרָכוֹת לה:)]
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa said: Whoever enjoys this world without a blessing is as though he robs the Holy One, blessed be He, and the community of Israel, as it is said, “One who robs his father and mother and says, ‘It is no transgression,’ is a companion to a destroyer.” “His father” refers to the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, “Is He not your Father who acquired you?” “His mother” refers to the community of Israel, as it is said, “Hear, my son, the instruction of your father, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.””
connections.context: This is the Talmudic identification used here for both the “father,” Hashem, and the “mother,” the community of Israel. It appears in the chapter Keitzad Mevarkhin, in the discussion of blessings over enjoyment.

connections.hePhrase: [כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כֵּיצַד מְבָרְכִין (דַּף לה:)],
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים נ״ב:ד׳
connections.quote: “Therefore it is metaphorically called “the mother of the children” and “the community of Israel,” for from this source the souls of Atzilut are emanated and the souls of Beriah are created, and so forth. All of them are only the extension of vitality and light from this source, which is called the Shekhinah, like light spreading from the sun.”
connections.context: Tanya explains the maternal image as the souls’ derivation from the Shekhinah. “Mother” is explicitly a metaphor for the spiritual source of their life.

connections.hePhrase: רַק לְהַרְגָּשַׁת עֵין בְּנֵי אָדָם אִשָּׁה מְסַפֶּרֶת קוֹדֶם.
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:5
connections.linkedRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:5
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:5
connections.heRef: דובר צדק, קונטרס דובר צדק, ברכות ג׳:ה׳
connections.quote: “At first the Gemara puts the infant before the woman, while at the end, concerning one who is sleeping, it puts the woman first. In the actual event, the infant comes first: his need awakens them from sleep. But another person first perceives the sound of the woman speaking. Understand the meaning of the analogy well: those who awaken are the people of Israel. Through their yearning, the teacher is raised to receive Torah from Hashem and convey it to them, even though human beings perceive and experience the order in the reverse way.”
connections.context: This parallel states the difference between the actual cause and the order perceived by an observer. The people’s desire to learn helps raise the teacher who then teaches them.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר תּוֹלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב יוֹסֵף עַל פָּסוּק "גָּמַר חָסִיד כִּי פַסּוּ אֱמוּנִים" בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי לֵיבּ פִּיסְטִינֶער, דְּהַאי קְרָא מֵרֵישֵׁיהּ לְסֵיפֵיהּ וּמִסֵּיפֵיהּ לְרֵישֵׁיהּ מִדְרַשׁ.
connections.quote: “It appears to me in accordance with what I explained about the passage in Arakhin: ‘I wonder whether there is anyone in this generation who knows how to rebuke’; see there. I heard from the departed Rabbi Yehudah Leib of Pistina an explanation of the verse ‘Save, Hashem, for the pious person has ceased, for the faithful have vanished from among mankind.’ The pious person has ceased because the faithful have vanished from mankind: one draws the other along, because of their unity. He was told in a dream that perhaps the meaning is the reverse: because the pious person has ceased, the faithful have vanished from mankind. His words are words from the mouth of a wise person, gracious words. Accordingly I explained the verse ‘Declare to My people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sins.’ Tell ‘My people,’ the Torah scholars, that their transgression caused the faithful to vanish from mankind. Tell ‘the house of Jacob,’ the ordinary people, that their sins caused the pious person to cease. Thus each should attribute the sin and deficiency to himself rather than to his fellow.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר תּוֹלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב יוֹסֵף עַל פָּסוּק "גָּמַר חָסִיד כִּי פַסּוּ אֱמוּנִים" בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי לֵיבּ פִּיסְטִינֶער, דְּהַאי קְרָא מֵרֵישֵׁיהּ לְסֵיפֵיהּ וּמִסֵּיפֵיהּ לְרֵישֵׁיהּ מִדְרַשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘Save us, Hashem, for the devout are gone; faithful people have vanished from among humankind.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֲרָכִין יז.): פַּרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר, דּוֹר לְפִי פַּרְנָס, וְהֵי קָדִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל:
connections.quote: ‘‘This is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face: Jacob, selah.’ Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and the Rabbis disagreed about this. One said: A generation reflects its leader. The other said: A leader reflects his generation.’

connections.hePhrase: [שִׁעְבּוּד וְכוּלֵי וּשְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה (בְּרָכוֹת יז.) שְׁקוּלִים, וְהַכֹּל אֶחָד],
connections.quote: “After he prayed, Rabbi Alexandri would say: Master of the worlds, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will. And what holds us back? The leaven in the dough and the subjugation to the kingdoms. May it be Your will that You save us from their hand, so that we may return to do the statutes of Your will with a whole heart.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּמָגֵן אַבְרָהָם רֵישׁ סִימָן א' בְּשֵׁם שְׁלָ"ה.
connections.quote: “‘So that he awakens the dawn.’ The Shelah writes of the secret of joining day and night through Torah or prayer, both in the morning and in the evening.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּמָגֵן אַבְרָהָם רֵישׁ סִימָן א' בְּשֵׁם שְׁלָ"ה.
connections.displayRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Chullin, Derekh Chayim 1:13
connections.linkedRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Chullin, Derekh Chayim 1:13
connections.canonicalRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Chullin, Derekh Chayim 1:13
connections.heRef: שני לוחות הברית, עשרת הדברות, מסכת חולין, דרך חיים א׳:י״ג
connections.quote: “The order of the night: First, one should join the entry of night to the departure of the day through serving Hashem, by performing a mitzvah or studying Torah. Likewise, one should join the departure of night to the entry of day. This is explained in the Zohar and alluded to in the verse “There was evening and there was morning, one day”: one should join evening and morning at both their entry and their departure, so that they form a single unity in the unity of the world’s Master. Our Sages already alluded to this in the blessings of Shema. Before “Hear, Israel, Hashem is our God, Hashem is one,” they instituted mention of the quality of day at night and of night by day: “Who forms light and creates darkness,” and “Who brings on evenings, who opens the gates in wisdom.” This excludes the heretical claim that the One who created day did not create night.”
connections.context: The existing Magen Avraham note cites the Shelah briefly. This is the fuller original passage: Torah or prayer at the transition joins both times in the recognition of one Creator.

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְדִיָלֵיף בְּהָרֹא"שׁ עַל סוֹף כָּל מִשְׁמָר מִזֶּה],
connections.quote: “… On each and every watch the Holy One, blessed be He, says: Woe to My children, for because of their sins I destroyed My house, burned My Sanctuary, and exiled them among the nations of the world. It is fitting for every God-fearing person to be pained and anxious at that hour, and to pour out supplications over the destruction of the Holy Temple, as it is said: “Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches” (Lamentations 2:19).”

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְמַשְׁמָע מִלְּשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא: סִימָנָא לְמַאי לִי? אוּרְתָּא! סִימָנָא לְמַאי לִי? יְמָמָא הוּא!
connections.quote: ‘What is Rabbi Eliezer counting? If he is counting the beginnings of the watches, why do I need a sign for the beginning of the first watch? It is nightfall! If he is counting the ends of the watches, why do I need a sign for the end of the last watch? It is daytime!’

connections.hePhrase: דְּקָשֶׁה, הָא מָצִינוּ בְּיוֹמָא (כח.) שֶׁטָּעוּ בִּמְאוֹר הַלְּבָנָה שֶׁהוּא אוֹר הַיּוֹם, וְכֵן מָצִינוּ לְהַלָּן (כז עַמּוּד ב) בְּיוֹם הַמְּעוּנָּן הִתְפַּלְּלוּ שֶׁל שַׁבָּת בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת, וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר צָרִיךְ סִימָנָא כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר.
connections.quote: “The appointed officer said to them: ‘Go out and see whether the time for slaughter has arrived.’ If it had arrived, the observer would say: ‘Daybreak!’ Matya ben Shmuel says: ‘Has the whole eastern horizon grown bright, as far as Hebron?’ And he answers: ‘Yes!’ Why was this necessary? Once the moonlight rose, and they thought the east had grown bright. They slaughtered the daily offering and then carried it out to the place of burning.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּקָשֶׁה, הָא מָצִינוּ בְּיוֹמָא (כח.) שֶׁטָּעוּ בִּמְאוֹר הַלְּבָנָה שֶׁהוּא אוֹר הַיּוֹם, וְכֵן מָצִינוּ לְהַלָּן (כז עַמּוּד ב) בְּיוֹם הַמְּעוּנָּן הִתְפַּלְּלוּ שֶׁל שַׁבָּת בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת, וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר צָרִיךְ סִימָנָא כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר.
connections.heRef: שיטה מקובצת על ברכות כ״ז ב:ז׳-ח׳
connections.quote:
““Can a mistaken acceptance be reversed? Avdan said: Once the heavens became covered with clouds. The people thought it had grown dark and recited the Shabbat prayer on Friday. [Editorial gloss: Our text reads, ‘the prayer for the departure of Shabbat on Shabbat.’] Afterward the clouds dispersed and the sun shone. They came and asked Rabbi, who said: Since they have prayed, they have prayed.” There is no greater mistake than this, since the sun subsequently shone, yet he still said that their prayer counted as prayer. They were, however, certainly permitted to perform work.

“A congregation is different, because we do not trouble them to pray again.” They were certainly permitted to perform work. One may ask: how could the questioner suppose that their prayer counted when the sun had shone? Everything stated above applies only after sunset; before that, acceptance is ineffective. Why did he not also raise this difficulty? One can answer that this indeed also troubled him, but the Talmud did not spell it out. The answer given resolves both points: a congregation is different, and an additional allowance is made for it.”
connections.context: Shita Mekubetzet preserves the wording used by Rav Tzadok—Shabbat prayer recited on Friday—and records the alternative wording in the usual Talmud text. The case supplies his example of clouds misleading people about the time; the source also retains the distinction between a mistaken communal prayer and the prohibition of work.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין צב.): "הֱוֵי קַבֵּל וְקַיֵּים, כִּדִתְנַן: בַּיִת אָפֵל וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Elazar also said: Always remain in obscurity, and you will endure. Rabbi Zeira said: We too learned this: One does not open windows in a dark house to inspect its plague. Learn it from here.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבַהֲדַיְיהוּ גַּם הוּא יוּכַל לְקַבֵּל, כַּיָּדוּעַ כַּאֲשֶׁר נִכְלָל נַפְשׁוֹ בְּנִשְׁמַת גְּדוֹלֵי הַדּוֹר הֵם מַעֲלִים אוֹתוֹ.
connections.heRef: יושר דברי אמת, קונטרס שני ל״ג:א׳
connections.quote: “The principal battle against the evil inclination takes place in the service of the heart, which is prayer. Throughout the day one cannot fight it in the same way, for the weapons are not in one’s hands. During prayer a person wraps himself in a tallit and is crowned with tefillin, the battle garments against the adversary. He girds himself with strength to subdue his inclination and prepare his soul with pure thought for its Creator, using a two-edged sword—the holy words of the offerings and the verses of praise. He takes a spear in his hand, the 248 words of Shema, until he overthrows many of the opposing forces. It then becomes easier to direct himself with proper thought in the silent prayer, so that thought and speech are one. Even if he cannot attain fear and love, his words of prayer can nevertheless ascend through his binding himself to others, saying, “I accept upon myself the positive commandment, ‘Love your fellow as yourself.’” He includes himself with complete love among the holy souls of the righteous of his generation whose appearance he knows, and pictures them before him in his mind at that time, as explained in Chesed LeAvraham. I indeed heard from the holy mouth of Rabbi Yechiel Michel, of blessed memory, that before each prayer he would say: “I bind myself to all Israel, both to those greater than I and to those smaller than I. The benefit of joining those greater than I is that through them my thought will ascend; the benefit of joining those smaller than I is that they will ascend through me.” This I heard from his holy mouth.”
connections.context: The binding described here accompanies an effort to unite one’s own thought and speech in prayer. It also runs in both directions: receiving help from those greater and helping those smaller. The existing note from the following section retains the parable and its requirement of some living intention.

connections.hePhrase: וְדַוְקָא כְּשֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לָצֵאת מִן הַבַּיִת אָפֵל, דְּלָא עָדִיף הַאי סִימָנָא מֵחֲזָקָה, דְּהֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא לְבָרוּרֵי מְבָרְרִינַן, וְיֵצֵא לַחוּץ לִרְאוֹת.
connections.quote: “Gloss: Some say that one may rely on the presumption only after the event; initially, one should not rely on a presumption where the matter can be verified. All this concerns other people who are not familiar with the slaughterer and do not know whether he is proficient. The slaughterer himself, however, may not slaughter—even if he knows the laws of slaughter and is learned in them—until he has slaughtered three times before a sage expert in those laws, who knows that he is practiced and capable and will not faint. Therefore, the custom is that no one slaughters unless he has received authorization before a sage. The sage does not authorize him until he knows that the person knows the laws of slaughter and is skilled in practice. Therefore, the custom is to rely initially on those who present themselves to slaughter, without examining them before or afterward, because those who engage in slaughter have already received authorization before a sage.”
connections.context: This is the Rema’s discussion of a slaughterer’s presumed qualifications. It supplies the principle about verification that Rav Tzadok uses in his analogy. The source’s qualification is retained: prior expert authorization can itself provide the basis for reliance.

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּיָכוֹל לָצֵאת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשַׁעַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִמְּשַׁל דַּחֲבוּרָה שֶׁנֶּחְלָה אֶחָד אוֹ שֶׁמֵּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם:
connections.heRef: יושר דברי אמת, קונטרס שני ל״ד:ב׳
connections.quote: “I heard a fine parable concerning this from the departed righteous Rabbi Yissachar Ber of our community, who related it in the name of his teacher, Rabbi Mendel. Suppose a company of many people are traveling on foot to a certain place, and one of them, Heaven forbid, falls ill. They must continue their journey. Surely they will not leave him there to perish; if he cannot walk, they will take him by the arms and lead him. But if, Heaven forbid, one of them dies, what use have they for a dead person? They will bury him there. The application is this: when speech is united with thought, even without fear and love, it is like a sick person who has a little life, and the righteous will assist it, as explained above. But without any thought at all, it is considered dead, Heaven forbid, and is thrown onto the refuse heap. He added: even if, Heaven forbid, this is its condition, such prayers still fulfill the King’s will when nothing else is possible, for the King also needs dogs and their sustenance is His responsibility. These are the wholly unfit prayers. Yet this is no reason for us to choose to provide the dogs’ portion; it is better for us to give nourishment to the King Himself, or at least to His close servants, the holy worlds.”
connections.context: Yosher Divrei Emet preserves the precise parable Rav Tzadok invokes: fellow travelers can help a sick member who still has life, while a dead member cannot continue with them. Here the application is to prayer with some accompanying thought, even when love and awe are lacking. This verifies the parable in this work; the title “Sha’ar HaTeshuvah” used in the main text is retained as Rav Tzadok’s reference.

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁשָּׁם אֵינוֹ מָדוֹר קָבוּעַ, כִּי "בַּיִת זוֹ אִשָּׁה" שֶׁהִיא הַלֵּב, וְהוּא נִשְׂרָף לְגַמְרֵי שֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ מָקוֹם מֵכִיל אַף לִפְרָקִים מַחֲשֶׁבֶת שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם שֶׁאוּלַי יָבוֹא הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה לַלֵּב],
connections.quote: “The Sages also said that the wicked are under the control of their hearts, while the righteous are otherwise. “They” signifies the complete human form, which bestows influence, while the heart receives it. As explained elsewhere, it is compared to a woman, as in “Every wisehearted woman.” The Sages also interpreted “He built” as referring to the additional understanding given to woman, and understanding is in the heart, as stated at the beginning of Tikkunei Zohar. It also says, “A woman who fears Hashem,” and, “Fear of Hashem is His treasury”; the Sages compare a woman to a treasury. Awe is in the heart, as stated in Yoma, and the woman represents yearning and desire, as in “Your desire shall be for your husband”; this too is in the heart, as in “His heart’s desire.” This is not the place to expand further. This is the meaning of “they are under the control of their hearts”: the earthly recipient is primary, and they follow it rather than the Giver. The righteous, however, do not follow matter but form. “You shall remember that He is the One who gives you strength”: in all the good things of this world, their primary concern is knowing the Giver, so that through them He grants them awareness of His divinity, as explained above.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the symbolic relation between the receiving heart and what gives it direction. The conclusion makes the point of the analogy explicit: the righteous attend to the divine Giver within the good they receive.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִתְשׁוּבָה לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קלד עַמּוּד א): מִתְּחִלָּה "בּוֹנֵה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם" וַהֲדַר "נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֵּס"
connections.quote: “So in the days to come, when the Holy One, blessed be He, will remember His people, the community of Israel, the Shekinah will return from exile first and proceed to her House, as the holy Temple will be built first. The Holy One, blessed be He, will then say to the Community of Israel: “Shake thyself from the dust, arise and sit down, O Jerusalem” (Is. 52, 2). She will enquire, “Whereto shall I go, since my House is destroyed, my Temple is burnt with fire?” The Holy One, blessed be He, will then rebuild the Temple first, restore the Holy of Holies, build the city of Jerusalem and then raise her from the dust. So Scripture says: “The Lord doth build up Jerusalem” first, and then, “He gathereth together the dispersed of Israel”, and afterwards, "Who healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds" (Ps. 147, 2, 3)-this being an allusion to the resurrection of the dead. Then will be fulfilled that which is written, "And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, etc." (Ezek. 36, 27). 'Blessed be the Lord for evermore!'”

connections.hePhrase: [וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּמַעֲשֵׂר שֵׁנִי (פֶּרֶק ה הֲלָכָה ב) דְּבִנְיַן הַבַּיִת עַל יְדֵי מַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said: This teaches that the Temple is destined to be built before the kingdom of the house of David, as it is written, “You drank the blood of grapes as wine.””
connections.context: The Yerushalmi infers an order between rebuilding the Temple and restoring Davidic kingship from a discussion of fourth-year vineyard produce. That order is the point Rav Tzadok cites; the agricultural rules alone do not explain his words.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דְּהֵיכָל קוֹדֵם בְּבִנְיָן לַבַּיִת, וְכֵן מִתְּחִלָּה הַמּוֹחַ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ב מֵהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה: "וְכֵיצַד הִיא הַדֶּרֶךְ וְכוּלֵי":
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות יסודי התורה ב׳:ב׳
connections.quote: “What is the way to love and fear Him? When a person contemplates His wondrous and great works and creations, and perceives from them His wisdom, which has no measure or limit, he immediately loves, praises, and glorifies Him, and longs intensely to know the great Name. As David said, “My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.” When he reflects on these same matters, he immediately draws back in awe and knows that he is a small, lowly, obscure creature, standing with slight and limited understanding before the One whose knowledge is perfect. As David said, “When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers … what is man that You remember him?” In accordance with these matters, I explain broad principles concerning the works of the Master of all worlds, so that they may provide an opening for one who understands to love Hashem. As the Sages said concerning love: through this you come to recognize the One who spoke and the world came into being.”
connections.context: This is the Rambam passage explicitly cited at the close of the ois. Contemplation gives rise to both love and awe, explaining why the repair of thought precedes the repair of the heart’s qualities.

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְמַשְׁמָע מֵאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁהִמְתִּין עַד שֶׁסִּיֵּים תְּפִלָּתוֹ וְלֹא מְנָעוֹ תֵּיכֶף.
connections.quote: “It was taught: Rabbi Yosei said: Once I was walking along the road, and I entered one of Jerusalem’s ruins to pray. Elijah, remembered for good, came and kept watch for me at the entrance (and waited for me) until I finished my prayer. After I finished my prayer, he said to me: ‘Peace to you, Rabbi.’ I said to him: ‘Peace to you, my rabbi and teacher.’ He said to me: ‘My son, why did you enter this ruin?’ I answered him: ‘To pray.’ He said to me: ‘You should have prayed on the road.’ I said to him: ‘I was afraid that travelers might interrupt me.’ He said to me: ‘You should have recited a short prayer.’”

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְמַשְׁמָע מֵאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁהִמְתִּין עַד שֶׁסִּיֵּים תְּפִלָּתוֹ וְלֹא מְנָעוֹ תֵּיכֶף.
connections.heRef: בן יהוידע על ברכות ג׳ א:ד׳
connections.quote: “There is, however, a difficulty: why repeat “he kept watch for me” and “he waited for me,” when shamar means waiting? It appears to me that if Rabbi Yosei had said only “he waited for me,” I would have thought that Eliyahu arrived after Rabbi Yosei was already standing in prayer, and therefore did not interrupt him but waited until he finished. Had he arrived before the prayer began, he would not have permitted him to pray there and would have brought him out at once. The repeated wording therefore teaches that Eliyahu came before he began to pray, yet did not stop him and allowed him to pray there. Why did Eliyahu not require him to recite the shortened prayer, instead of waiting while he prayed at his usual length? It appears that Eliyahu wanted Rabbi Yosei to remain there so that he would hear the heavenly voice and know how greatly the Holy One, blessed be He, grieves over Israel’s suffering. Eliyahu knew through holy inspiration the moment when the heavenly voice sounded each day, and allowed him to prolong his prayer until that time arrived and he would hear it.”
connections.context: Ben Yehoyada also reads the repeated wording as showing that Eliyahu arrived before the prayer. He then offers a particular explanation for the delay: enabling Rabbi Yosei to hear the heavenly voice. That explanation is retained alongside Rav Tzadok’s own tentative explanations, rather than being turned into an unrestricted rule.

connections.hePhrase: [לא] אֵין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְבַּלְבֵּל בָּאֶמְצַע, אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה שֶׁלֹּא יִתְבַּלְבֵּל בָּהּ.
connections.quote: see note 211. Elijah’s closing words there are the line this siman builds on: “You should have prayed a short prayer.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok applies the preference for a short, undisturbed prayer to other situations in which sustained concentration is not possible.

connections.hePhrase: [לא] אֵין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְבַּלְבֵּל בָּאֶמְצַע, אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה שֶׁלֹּא יִתְבַּלְבֵּל בָּהּ.
connections.quote: “He said to him, ‘You should have prayed a short prayer.’ For when goodness proceeds directly from Hashem, there is no suffering in that goodness, as it is written, ‘Evil does not dwell with You’ (Psalms 5:5), expounded in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Tazria): evil does not descend from Heaven. Only when goodness descends clothed in the garments of this world can it appear to a person that he suffers from that goodness. A person must therefore see that no one suffers because of his good fortune. When he is distracted and cannot clarify himself in this way, the counsel is to pray a short prayer. Concerning the short prayer, the Gemara later states (Berakhot 29b): ‘Others say: The needs of Your people are many, and their understanding is limited.’ The entire prayer concerns their limited understanding: they pray to Hashem to raise their perception. They will then receive the goodness from its source and have no suffering. When a person sees that he receives goodness from its source, he has no suffering. This is the counsel when a person is distracted: to pray that Hashem raise his perception to the source, so that he will have no suffering.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the same exchange with Eliyahu as a difficulty in clarifying one's request: under distraction, a person cannot adequately examine whether the desired benefit could burden someone else. The short prayer asks Hashem to raise the petitioner's understanding toward the source of the good. This gives positive content to the siman's preference for a short prayer that can be said with attention.
connections.headline: What to ask when attention is constrained

connections.hePhrase: כִּי טוֹב מְעַט בְּכַוָּנָה מֵהַרְבּוֹת בְּלֹא כַוָּנָה.
connections.quote: ‘A few supplications with focused intention are better than many without focused intention.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעוֹבְרֵי דְּרָכִים – דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, חָלָל שְׂמָאלִי שֶׁבַּלֵּב – יַפְסִיקוּהוּ מֵעֲבוֹדָתוֹ,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ט׳:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: “The dwelling place of the animal soul, which derives from kelipat nogah in every person of Israel, is in the heart, in the left chamber, which is full of blood; and it is written, “For the blood is the soul.” Therefore all desires, self-glorification, anger, and similar traits are in the heart. From the heart they spread throughout the body and also rise to the brain in the head, to think about them, dwell upon them, and devise ways of pursuing them—just as the blood has its source in the heart, spreads from the heart to all the limbs, and also rises to the brain in the head.”
connections.context: The “left chamber of the heart” is the spiritual description of the animal soul’s activity. It explains the inner source of the distractions that Rav Tzadok calls “passersby.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעוֹבְרֵי דְּרָכִים – דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, חָלָל שְׂמָאלִי שֶׁבַּלֵּב – יַפְסִיקוּהוּ מֵעֲבוֹדָתוֹ,
connections.heRef: יושר דברי אמת, קונטרס ראשון י״ט:א׳
connections.quote: “That is, those called “sons,” who possess a level of neshamah in addition to their nefesh and ruach, are bound in their thought to the blessed Creator. They may therefore go out even into the marketplace at times when they need to: because they are deeply bound to the blessed Creator, passersby will not interrupt their attachment. This is “sons go out with knots”—with attachment to the Creator in their thought. “Sons of kings” means those who have only nefesh and ruach, who are called sons of kings from the side of the kingdom of Heaven. They go out “with bells”: one must not go out idle, but, like a bell that rings and makes a sound, should continually sound forth words of Torah, prayer, and fear of the blessed God. One must not rely on attachment in thought, for passersby will interrupt it, Heaven forbid, since that attachment is weak. “And every person” means that all people are alike in this respect; scarcely anyone is to be found at the level of the “sons who go out with knots.” Rather, when the Sages spoke of “sons who go out with knots,” they spoke of what was usual—that is, of their own condition. They were speaking about themselves, not others. These are the master’s words.”
connections.context: The passage uses “passersby” for interruptions of inner attachment. It expressly qualifies the exceptional level at which silent attachment suffices: ordinary people should continue to voice words of Torah, prayer, and reverence.

connections.hePhrase: יִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה עַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּכַוָּנָה:
connections.quote: ““A short prayer”—Havineinu; it is explained below in the chapter Tefillat HaShachar, Berakhot 29a.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies the short prayer in this particular incident as Havineinu, the condensed form of the middle blessings of the Amidah.

connections.hePhrase: [לב] "אֵין נִכְנָסִים לַחָרְבָּה" – פֵּירוּשׁ: מָקוֹם פָּנוּי מִמּוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי אָדָם הָאֲמִתִּיִּים וּמְקוֹם מִצְוָה, רַק כָּל מַחֲשֶׁבֶת הָרְשׁוּת.
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: For three reasons one does not enter a ruin: because of suspicion, because of collapse, and because of harmful forces.”
connections.context: The Gemara’s warning concerns a literal ruined building. Rav Tzadok applies the image to a mind emptied of mitzvah and occupied by unregulated mundane thoughts; that application is his interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: מִפְּנֵי הַחֲשָׁד – שֶׁיַּחְשׁוֹד לְעַצְמוֹ שֶׁמָּא יֵשׁ אֵיזֶה תַּאֲוָה בַּדָּבָר.
connections.quote: “The essence of complete holiness is reaching this great level: to be able to make holy use of all one’s enjoyments, without intending one’s own benefit or bodily pleasure. Rabbenu HaKadosh said of himself, in Ketubot 104a, that he had not enjoyed [this world] even with his little finger. See Tosafot there: “Delicacies did not enter his body.” Yet Avodah Zarah 11a says that neither radish nor lettuce, and so forth, ever ceased from his table. See Tosafot, beginning “shelo”: these expand the intestines to accommodate many delicacies. In the comment beginning “tznon,” Tosafot raises the difficulty from Ketubot and gives a strained answer, for the expression “their table” implies that he too ate in this manner. Moreover, why would he provide so many delicacies for his household if he did not desire them and considered them inappropriate? And the passage compares him with Antoninus. Rather, the truth is as I received it, and later saw in a certain book: the statement is to be understood literally. Although his table was full of every worldly delicacy, he nevertheless derived no enjoyment from it at all. All his eating was in exceptional holiness, in accordance with his quality of being called “holy.” This is complete holiness: for all one’s actions and enjoyments to be for the sake of Heaven, without feeling any personal enjoyment at all.”
connections.context: This parallel defines the exceptional state in which ordinary pleasures are wholly directed toward Heaven. It clarifies why the ois warns a person to suspect that personal desire may still be present in an apparently permissible pursuit.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִפְּנֵי הַמַּפּוֹלֶת – דִּסְתָם חָרְבָּה רְעוּעָה שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קִיּוּם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שֶׁקֶר אֵין לוֹ רַגְלַיִם".
connections.quote: “Shin: sheker, falsehood. Tav: emet, truth. Why are the letters of sheker close together, while the letters of emet are far apart? Falsehood is common; truth is not common. And why does falsehood stand on one leg, while truth has a bricklike base? Truth stands; falsehood does not stand.”
connections.context: The saying is based on the positions and shapes of the Hebrew letters. “Falsehood has no legs” expresses the Gemara’s conclusion that falsehood cannot endure.

connections.hePhrase: אִם יָכוֹל [לְהִתְפַּלֵּל] בַּדֶּרֶךְ, הוּא דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ, פִּילוֹן מְפוּלָּשׁ לַעֲבוֹדַת ה',
connections.quote: “Another interpretation of “You shall take for yourselves”: This is what is written, “You will make known to me the path of life, fullness of joys.” David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Make known to me which gateway opens through to the life of the World to Come. Rabbi Yudan said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to David: If you need life, you need afflictions, as it is written, “The way of life is the rebukes of discipline.””
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the phrase “a gateway that opens through.” Rav Tzadok uses that image for a direct path into divine service.

connections.hePhrase: וּדְלָא קָאֵי בִּדְבָרָא, שֶׁהוּא מְקוֹמָן שֶׁל כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע:
connections.quote: ““Because of suspicion”: But should it not be prohibited because of collapse? In a new [ruin]. But should it not be prohibited because of harmful forces? When there are two people. If there are two, there is no suspicion either! When the two are dissolute. “Because of collapse”: But should it not be prohibited because of suspicion and harmful forces? When there are two upright people. “Because of harmful forces”: But should it not be prohibited because of suspicion and collapse? In a new ruin, with two upright people. If there are two, there are no harmful forces either! In their own place, we are concerned about them. Alternatively: It is indeed a case of one person, in a new ruin that stands in the open country. There is no suspicion there, because a woman is not commonly found in the open country; but there is concern about harmful forces.”
connections.context: The existing note quotes the three reasons. This continuation gives the qualifications that Rav Tzadok interprets here: a new ruin, two people, upright companions, and the location of harmful forces. The Gemara discusses a literal ruin; the inward application belongs to Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: [לג] אַף עַל גַּב דִּזְרִיזִים אֵין מַקְדִּימִין טְפֵי מִצַּפְרָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּפְסָחִים (ד.),
connections.quote: ‘If you say that the zealous perform commandments early, let us search in the morning. For it is written: ‘On the eighth day, the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised,’ and it was taught: The entire day is valid for circumcision, but the zealous perform commandments early, as it is said: ‘Abraham rose early in the morning.’’

connections.hePhrase: [לג] אַף עַל גַּב דִּזְרִיזִים אֵין מַקְדִּימִין טְפֵי מִצַּפְרָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּפְסָחִים (ד.),
connections.quote: ““Let us search in the morning”—for the zealous act early, as we find concerning circumcision and Avraham’s zeal: “Avraham rose early in the morning.” He did not wait until sunrise, but nevertheless he did not act earlier, at night.”
connections.context: Rashi makes explicit the limit that the ois takes as its starting point: ordinary zeal brings the act forward to the morning, without itself requiring action during the night.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בִּבְרָכוֹת [ב:] דִּלִמְלֶאכֶת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הָווּ מַחְשְׁכֵי וּמַקְדְּמֵי גַּם בַּלַּיְלָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “If you say that it is night from sunset and they were merely working late and rising early, come and hear: “The night was a watch for us, and the day was for work.””
connections.context: The discussion uses Nehemiah’s description of work from dawn until the stars appear to identify the day’s limits, and considers whether the workers had simply extended their work into the night. This is the objection Rav Tzadok refers to; its location is Berakhot 2b, not 3b.

connections.hePhrase: [לד] "כָּל הַלַּיְלָה אִיבְרִי לְשֵׁינְתָא" לְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר בְּעֵירוּבִין ס"ה עַמּוּד א',
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yehudah said: Night was created only for sleep. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Moonlight was created only for study. They said to Rabbi Zeira: ‘Your teachings are sharp.’ He answered: ‘They are from the daytime.’ Rav Chisda’s daughter said to Rav Chisda: ‘Does the Master not wish to sleep a little?’ He answered: ‘Days that are long [for sleep] and short [for Torah and mitzvot] will soon come, and we shall sleep a great deal.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת דְּהַיְינוּ לֵילֵי תְּקוּפַת תַּמּוּז.
connections.quote: see note 180.
connections.context: Tosafot limits the saying to the short summer nights. This qualification is the basis of Rav Tzadok’s next discussion of increasing nighttime study as the nights grow longer.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר דִּלְעוֹלָם הַהַתְחָלָה נִמְשָׁךְ עַד הַחֲצִי, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ רוּבּוֹ כְּכֻלּוֹ וּכְאִלּוּ כֻּלּוֹ עָבַר, וְהַלֵּילוֹת מַתְחִילִין לְהִתְגַּדֵּל.
connections.quote: “The way of our Sages, of blessed memory, is well known: in every matter they reckon up to the halfway point as a beginning, and after the halfway point as completed.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s parallel formulation of the principle introduced here by “as I wrote elsewhere.” It supplies the general rule without importing the surrounding discussion of stages of purification.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בַּמִּשְׁנָה רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת דִּזְמַן הַהַתְחָלָה לִישַׁן עַד סוֹף הָאַשְׁמוּרָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה,
connections.quote: “From when may one recite the Shema in the evening? From the time when the priests enter to eat their terumah until the end of the first watch: these are Rabbi Eliezer’s words. The Sages say: Until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: Until dawn. It happened that his sons returned from a feast and said to him: We have not recited the Shema. He said to them: If dawn has not risen, you are obligated to recite it. Not only this: in every case in which the Sages said “until midnight,” the mitzvah extends until dawn. The burning of sacrificial fats and limbs may be performed until dawn; and all offerings eaten for one day may be eaten until dawn. If so, why did the Sages say “until midnight”? To distance a person from transgression.”
connections.context: The Mishnah gives the three endpoints that the ois compares. Its final explanation distinguishes the underlying time limit from the Sages’ protective deadline.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וַחֲכָמִים מוֹדִים לָזֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות א׳ א:ב׳-ג׳
connections.quote: ““Until the end of the first watch”—that is, one third of the night. There are three watches in the night, as it is written, “at the middle watch”: calling it the middle implies that there is one before it and one after it. Rabbi Eliezer holds that “when you lie down” does not mean all the time people are lying in their beds, but all the time during which they go to lie down. Until a third of the night, some people delay going to bed, and it is still called the time of lying down. “The Sages say,” and so forth: The Sages and Rabban Gamliel disagree with Rabbi Eliezer about the end of the time. They interpret “when you lie down” as all the time people are lying in their beds. Even the Sages, who say “until midnight,” do not disagree with Rabban Gamliel about the interpretation of “when you lie down”: they agree that by Torah law its time extends throughout the night. Their disagreement concerns a safeguard. The Sages made a safeguard to distance a person from transgression; Rabban Gamliel did not require that safeguard. Nevertheless, both the Sages and Rabban Gamliel agree that, from the outset, one should recite it immediately at the appearance of the stars. This is evident from the passage below: “So that a person should not come from the field in the evening,” and so forth. Even when he comes from the field before its time, he should not say: Since the time for the Shema has not yet arrived, I will first eat and drink. Instead, he should read Scripture or study until the stars appear, then recite the Shema and pray, and afterward eat. Since we see that even when he arrives before its time they were concerned that he might become negligent, and required him to read or study so that he would pray immediately, we learn that everyone agrees that one should initially recite it as soon as the stars appear. They disagree only after the fact: the Sages hold that, even after the fact, he fulfills his obligation only until midnight, because of the safeguard; Rabban Gamliel holds that, after the fact, he fulfills it throughout the night.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah distinguishes the period when people begin going to bed from the full period when they remain asleep. The passage also preserves the separate requirement to recite the evening Shema promptly at nightfall.

connections.hePhrase: דְּהָא קַיְימָא לַן דְּאוֹמֵר "הַשְׁכִּיבֵנוּ", עַיֵּין לְעֵיל ט' עַמּוּד א' בְּרַשִּׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "בִּלְבַד",
connections.quote: ““Provided that he does not say Hashkivenu”—one who recites the nighttime Shema in the early morning, near dawn, should not say Hashkivenu, for it is no longer the time of beginning to lie down, but the time of finishing one’s sleep.”
connections.context: Rashi relates Hashkivenu to beginning to go to bed. Tosafot, cited alongside him, questions the timing of this restriction.

connections.hePhrase: דְּהָא קַיְימָא לַן דְּאוֹמֵר "הַשְׁכִּיבֵנוּ", עַיֵּין לְעֵיל ט' עַמּוּד א' בְּרַשִּׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "בִּלְבַד",
connections.quote: ““Provided that he does not say Hashkivenu”—Rashi explains that this refers to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s statement about someone who recites before dawn. It appears to me that at that time it is certainly still a time for lying down, and he may say Hashkivenu. Moreover, the statement should refer to the discussion immediately preceding it. The master of Coucy therefore explains that it refers to the case just discussed, before sunrise. That is why he says that one may not say Hashkivenu: it is no longer the time for lying down, because dawn has already risen, even though it is still before sunrise.”
connections.context: Tosafot distinguishes before dawn from the interval between dawn and sunrise. That distinction is needed for Rav Tzadok’s question about people who begin sleeping late in the night.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא ב' עַמּוּד ב' בָּזֶה מַחֲלוֹקֶת בַּהַתְחָלָה, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְאִי":
connections.quote: ““If you think that the poor person’s time is earlier, Rabbi Chanina is the same as Rabbi Eliezer”—one cannot say that the poor person’s time precedes the sanctification of the day, or that the sanctification of the day precedes the poor person’s time. It is not reasonable to distinguish so finely among the measures of the time for lying down, within which all these times fall.”
connections.context: Tosafot explains why the Gemara cannot resolve the disagreement by drawing still finer distinctions among nearby bedtimes. Rav Tzadok directs the reader to this constraint on defining the beginning of the sleeping period.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא עוֹד שְׁנֵי טְעָמִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם הַנָּפְקָא מִינַּהּ בָּהֶם].
connections.quote: see note 223.
connections.context: This supplies both the “other two reasons” and the practical differences among them to which Rav Tzadok explicitly refers. The conditions concern a literal ruined building.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בָּבָא קַמָּא כ"א עַמּוּד א' וּבְרַשִּׁ"י עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rav Sechora said in the name of Rav Huna, in the name of Rav: One who occupies another’s courtyard without his knowledge need not pay rent, because it is said, “Desolation strikes the gate.” … Rav Yosef said: A house that is inhabited remains settled.”
connections.context: The discussion identifies a benefit that a property owner receives when a house is occupied rather than left deserted. The saying about habitation, not merely the rent ruling, explains Rav Tzadok’s use of this passage.

connections.hePhrase: [וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא קַמָּא שָׁם דְּגַם בְּמַחֲזִיק בּוֹ תִּבְנָא וְצִיבֵי סַגִּי],
connections.heRef: רש"י על בבא קמא כ״א א:ח׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““He uses it”—the owner uses it for wood and straw, keeping his wood and straw inside, and this other person went and lived there. There is no concern about Shaia, since the house is in use. But the consideration that “a house that is inhabited remains settled” still applies: storage is not habitation, and the person who lived there did well and benefited the owner.”
connections.context: Rashi distinguishes storage, which prevents the destructive force associated with abandonment, from habitation, which also brings care for the building. Rav Tzadok’s statement that wood and straw suffice concerns the first of these benefits.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִיכָךְ אָמְרוּ שָׁם בְּבָבָא קַמָּא דִּמְקַלְקֵל גַּם כֵּן הַבִּנְיָן,
connections.heRef: רש"י על בבא קמא כ״א א:ז׳:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: ““As it is said, ‘Desolation strikes the gate’”—a harmful spirit named Shaia batters the gate of a house in which no people live; therefore the person who stayed in it benefited its owner. Another explanation: A house that is desolate and alone, without people, has its gate battered: harmful forces batter it. “A house that is inhabited remains settled”—a house occupied by people retains its settled condition, because those living inside see what it needs and repair it.”
connections.context: The two explanations distinguish destruction associated with abandonment from the ordinary maintenance supplied by inhabitants. Both explain why occupancy benefits the building itself.

connections.hePhrase: וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁזֶּה הִיפּוּךְ הַיִּשּׁוּב, הוּא גַּם כֵּן הָפְכִּי וּמַזִּיק לַבִּנְיָן שֶׁהוּא מִכְּלַל הַיִּשּׁוּב:
connections.quote: “This means that roads are presumed dangerous, as explained in the commentary on the chapters of Avot. The reason roads are presumed dangerous is that there is no human settlement there. Such a place is removed from the essential world, for the essential world is the settled world, and this lies outside settlement. Therefore destructive forces, which oppose the world, hold sway there, and there is reason to fear that forces outside the order of the world will prevail over a person. Thus the statement says: “One who walks on the road and has no escort.” Certainly, when he has an escort, other people accompany him; because a person is with him, it is considered as though he were within the settled world, and he is not called one who has separated from settlement. But someone without an escort and a connection to settlement—what should he do to gain that connection? He should engage in Torah, for Torah is the order that preserves the world, as explained. When he attaches himself to Torah, he has an escort and a connection to the order of the world. Preserving that order saves him from destructive forces, so that they do not prevail; such forces prevail only when a person separates from the world, as we have said. That is why all roads are presumed dangerous. But when he attaches himself to Torah, he has an escort into the world’s order, and therefore does not leave the settled world. This is a complete escort for a person. If connection to other people is considered an escort—because he is then not regarded as being alone, but connected to the creatures that make up the world—then all the more so when he attaches himself to Torah, which is the order of the whole world and in which everything is found. He has a complete escort, connects himself to the world, and is not separated from it so that destructive forces would prevail over him. This is clear.”
connections.context: Maharal explains the opposition between human settlement and destructive forces. The connection to Torah supplies the spiritual counterpart to the protection of a settled, inhabited place.

connections.hePhrase: [תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם ב' עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מְבָרֵךְ"].
connections.quote: “The blessing “May our eyes see” was instituted so that people would wait for their companions in the synagogue. This applied specifically to their synagogues, which stood in the fields and were exposed to harmful forces. In our synagogues, however, one need wait for one’s companions only at night.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok is examining Tosafot’s distinctions between an outlying synagogue and one in town, and between day and night. These are the exact distinctions missing from a quotation of the opening Gemara alone.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַהַמְתָּנָה סַגִּי כְּמַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם מ"ג עַמּוּד ב' דִּלִשְׁנַיִם אֵין מַזִּיק, וְכֵן אִיתָא שָׁם ג' עַמּוּד ב' דִּבִּתְרֵי לֵיכָּא,
connections.quote: “Rav Zutra bar Toviya also said in the name of Rav: A torch is like two people, and moonlight is like three. They asked: Is a torch like two including the person carrying it, or is a torch like two besides him? Come and hear: “Moonlight is like three.” If you say that this includes him, that is understandable. But if you say that it means three besides him, why would four be needed? Has not the Master said: To one person a harmful spirit appears and causes harm; to two it appears but does not cause harm; to three it does not appear at all? Rather, must we not conclude that a torch is like two including the person himself? Indeed, conclude this.”
connections.context: The discussion distinguishes appearance from actual harm: two people are protected from harm, while three are protected even from the spirit’s appearance. Rav Tzadok cites the rule about two people to explain why waiting for one’s fellow is sufficient.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם ו' עַמּוּד א' תּוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל", וְיְעוּיַּן שָׁם שֶׁסִּיְּמוּ: וּלְכָךְ בַּלַּיְלָה וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “‘One who prays and does not wait for his fellow—his prayer is torn up,’ and so forth. Rabbeinu Tam explained that this concerned their synagogues, which were in the fields; therefore one must wait at night. Ri would delay and prolong his prayer until everyone had left. If meanwhile someone entered the synagogue, he would study a book until they finished their prayers. It is proper for us too to observe this stringency.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבָרִי"ף אַהָא דִּשְׁנַיִם שֶׁנִּכְנְסוּ וְכוּלֵי מַשְׁמָע גַּם בִּזְמַנָּם דַּוְקָא בַּלַּיְלָה,
connections.quote: “The rabbis have explained this and established that it concerns the evening prayer. If he leaves the other person alone and departs, there is concern that the other may come into danger. He must therefore wait for his fellow until he finishes his prayer.”
connections.context: Rif expressly limits this application to the evening prayer. Rav Tzadok examines how that limitation relates to the distinctions between a synagogue in the fields and one in town.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּאֹרַח חַיִּים סִימָן צ' סָעִיף ט"ו יֵשׁ לְעַיֵּין,
connections.quote: ‘If a person remains alone praying in a synagogue in the fields, or even in a city synagogue when it is the evening prayer (which is prayed at night), his companion must wait for him until he finishes his prayer, so that he will not become distracted in his prayer. Some are stringent even during the day and in our synagogues within the city (Tur and Mordechai in the name of Ri, and Rabbeinu Yonah, first chapter of Berakhot). If, however, he prolongs his requests and supplications, his companion is not required to wait for him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דְּסָבְרֵי דִּ"יִתְבַּלְבֵּל" שַׁיָּיךְ גַּם בָּעִיר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, וְגַם זֶה דַּוְקָא בַּלַּיְלָה.
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות ג׳ א:י״א
connections.quote: ““The rabbis have explained this and established that it concerns the evening prayer,” and so forth. Rabbeinu Ḥananel wrote that in their days the synagogues were outside the city; consequently, leaving someone alone might expose him to danger from the harmful forces more commonly found there. It appears that this rule applies even to synagogues in the city, for it is common that when a person stands alone in prayer, his prayer becomes confused.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah adds a distinct concern: leaving a person alone can disturb his concentration even in town. Rav Tzadok asks whether this extension still presupposes Rif’s reference to the evening prayer.

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ עַל הַ"יֵּשׁ אוֹמְרִים" שֶׁבָּרַמָ"א נִרְשָׁם תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, מְבוֹאָר דִּלְתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה הוּא הַדִּין בַּיּוֹם, וְכֵן כָּתַב בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף לְהַתַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, אַךְ לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מִנַּיִן לוֹ.
connections.quote: ““Two people who entered a synagogue, and one finished his prayer before his fellow,” and so forth: this is discussed there, on Berakhot 5b. Rabbeinu Yonah wrote that the same applies when many people entered a synagogue, even if they did not enter together: of those remaining last, one must wait for the other. However, if someone entered alone at a time when he could not finish his prayer with them, his fellow need not wait for him. Since he saw that he could not finish with them and nevertheless entered, he showed that he entered on that understanding and is not afraid to remain alone. He further wrote: When we say that his fellow must wait for him, this applies specifically when he is not prolonging anything beyond his prayer. But if he prolongs petitions and other matters, his fellow is not required to wait for him in any circumstance. This concludes his words. What our author explained in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel was also written by Rabbeinu Yonah in his name, and Tosafot likewise wrote it in the name of Rabbeinu Tam. Rif wrote: “The rabbis explained this and established that it concerns the evening prayer; if he leaves him alone and departs, there is concern that he may come into danger.” Concerning the statement that Ri would wait even in our synagogues during the day: Tosafot’s words indicate that he did so as an additional stringency. Mordechai likewise wrote: “Ri was stringent even in our synagogues. He would prolong his prayer until everyone left; and if someone entered the synagogue in the meantime, he would study a book until that person finished his prayer. It is proper for us too to be stringent.” This concludes his words. Rabbeinu Yonah, however, wrote that this rule appears to apply even in synagogues within the city, because a person’s prayer commonly becomes unsettled when he stands alone in prayer.”
connections.context: Beit Yosef preserves the exceptions for a late arrival who knowingly remains alone and for someone prolonging additional petitions. He then distinguishes Ri’s daytime stringency from Rabbeinu Yonah’s rule for synagogues in town. Rav Tzadok questions whether the latter statement, which does not expressly mention daytime, establishes the same obligation by day.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בַּטּוּר מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב: "וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים דְּאַף בְּשֶׁלָּנוּ וְכוּלֵי", לִכְאוֹרָה הַךְ "יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים" דִּבְרֵי תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי.
connections.quote: “If two people enter the synagogue and one finishes his prayer before the other, hurries to leave and does not wait for his fellow, his prayer is not heard. If he waits, his reward is exceedingly great. Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained that this applied specifically in their days, when synagogues stood in the fields and harmful forces were common. Some say that even in our synagogues one must wait at night. Ri would wait even in our synagogues during the day.”
connections.context: The Tur places three formulations side by side: Rabbeinu Ḥananel’s explanation, the view requiring waiting at night in contemporary synagogues, and Ri’s daytime practice. These are the precise distinctions whose attribution Rav Tzadok investigates.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּטוּר וְשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ סִימָן רל"ו טַעַם אַחֵר, דְּהוּא בִּמְקוֹם תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית דְּגַם כְּשֶׁכֻּלָּם בְּיַחַד יְרֵאִים
connections.quote: “The custom to interrupt with verses, “May our eyes see,” and Kaddish arose because in earlier days their synagogues were in the fields, and they feared remaining there until the time of the evening prayer. They instituted these verses, which contain eighteen mentions of God’s name corresponding to the eighteen blessings of the evening prayer, and concluded with Kaddish. Now that they have resumed praying the evening prayer in synagogues, the original custom has not been abolished. Nevertheless, one must not interrupt with other matters. Some of the great authorities followed the practice of not reciting these verses.”
connections.context: Here the verses originally provide a shorter substitute for the evening Amidah because the congregation feared remaining outside. This differs from an explanation based on waiting for a late individual. The quotation preserves the later continuation of the custom and the practice of those who omitted the verses.

connections.hePhrase: [אוֹ דִּמְקוֹמָן שָׁאנֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל ג' עַמּוּד ב', אוֹ מִשּׁוּם חַיּוֹת וְלִסְטִים, עַיֵּין בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פִּרְקִין, וְעַיֵּין פְּסָחִים ב' עַמּוּד א' וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת, וְיוֹמָא כ"א עַמּוּד א'].
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: A person should always enter [a town] while it is light, and leave while it is light.”
connections.context: The maxim follows the verse about Joseph’s brothers being sent away at daybreak. Rav Tzadok cites it when considering dangers associated with being outside at night.

connections.hePhrase: [אוֹ דִּמְקוֹמָן שָׁאנֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל ג' עַמּוּד ב', אוֹ מִשּׁוּם חַיּוֹת וְלִסְטִים, עַיֵּין בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פִּרְקִין, וְעַיֵּין פְּסָחִים ב' עַמּוּד א' וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת, וְיוֹמָא כ"א עַמּוּד א'].
connections.quote: “One who sets out on a journey before the rooster’s call has his blood upon his own head. Rabbi Yoshiyah says: Until it calls a second time; some say: Until it calls a third time. Which rooster was meant? An average rooster.”
connections.context: This baraita warns against setting out before the normal approach of daylight. It supplies the travel-danger context in Rav Tzadok’s discussion, rather than the unrelated Temple-vessel miracle previously quoted.

connections.hePhrase: [רַק לִישַׁן יְחִידִי],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥanina said: It is forbidden to sleep alone in a house, and whoever sleeps alone in a house is seized by Lilith.”
connections.context: This is the specific warning about sleeping alone that Rav Tzadok distinguishes from merely entering or being alone in a sound building.

connections.hePhrase: [רַק בַּשָּׂדֶה בַּלַּיְלָה יֵשׁ לוֹמַר חֲשָׁשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פְּסָחִים ב' עַמּוּד א' עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת].
connections.quote: “The Ri explains that the chapter “HaKones” indicates that the reason is harmful forces. … The Rashba explains that two verses are needed: “The morning grew light” concerns another town, even where harmful forces need not be feared, as with Joseph’s brothers, who were eleven; the reason is pits. The verse “Do not go out” is needed for one’s own town, because of harmful forces.”
connections.context: Tosafot distinguishes risks of unfamiliar terrain from harmful forces, and unfamiliar towns from one’s own town. Rav Tzadok is weighing those distinctions in the case of people leaving a synagogue.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין אֹרַח חַיִּים סִימָן ג' סָעִיף י"א בַּהַגָּהָה, גַּם לְעִנְיַן בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא חָלוּק בֵּין בַּשָּׂדֶה לְבָעִיר.
connections.quote: ‘One should not wipe himself with a potsherd because of sorcery, nor with dry grasses, for one who wipes with something that fire can consume has his lower teeth fall out. Nor should he use a stone with which another person has wiped, because it brings a person to hemorrhoids. Gloss: Now that our privies are not in the fields, the custom is to wipe with a potsherd, and likewise with material that fire can consume; it causes no harm. Go and see what the people do (Chiddushei Agudah, chapter HaMotzi).’

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא לֹא מִקְרֵי חָרְבָּה דְּהוּא לְתַשְׁמִישׁ אָדָם, וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר שָׁאנֵי בֵּית הַכִּסֵּא דִּשְׁכִיחֵי מַזִּיקִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שִׁילְהֵי בְּרָכוֹת.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Tanḥum bar Ḥanilai said: Anyone who conducts himself modestly in the privy is saved from three things—from snakes, from scorpions and from harmful spirits. Some say that his dreams are also settled. There was a privy in Tiberias where even two people entering together during the day would be harmed. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi would enter individually and were not harmed. The rabbis asked them, “Are you not afraid?” They answered, “We have learned a received tradition: protection in the privy consists of modesty and silence; protection in suffering consists of silence and seeking mercy.””
connections.context: This is the passage at the end of Berakhot explicitly invoked here. Its account treats the particular place as dangerous even during the day and even for two people, and it also states the protective conduct of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi.

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ יֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא קַמָּא ס' עַמּוּד ב' דְּמַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת מַפְקִיד כֵּלָיו:
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: When there is a plague in a city, a person should not enter the synagogue alone, because the Angel of Death deposits his instruments there. This applies where children do not study and where ten people do not pray.’

connections.hePhrase: [לז] "אִשָּׁה בִּדְבָרָא לָא שְׁכִיחָא".
connections.quote: ‘In their own haunts, we are concerned about them. Alternatively, the case is indeed that of one person, in a recent ruin standing in the countryside. There is no concern there about suspicion, since a woman is not commonly found in the countryside, but there is a concern about harmful spirits.’

connections.hePhrase: שָׂדֶה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת לְאֹרֶךְ וָרֹחַב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כד, כז): "וְעַתְּדָהּ בַּשָּׂדֶה לָךְ",
connections.quote: ‘Prepare your work outside and make it ready for yourself in the field; afterward, build your house.’

connections.hePhrase: שָׂדֶה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת לְאֹרֶךְ וָרֹחַב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כד, כז): "וְעַתְּדָהּ בַּשָּׂדֶה לָךְ",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 24:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 24:1
connections.quote: ““Prepare your work outside, make it ready for yourself in the field, and afterward build your house.” “Prepare your work outside” means that initially a person must observe all the mitzvot in their plain meaning: to be very careful about every prohibition and turn away from evil. “Make it ready for yourself in the field”: a field signifies expansion, so that all the prohibitions extend for him into safeguards and all the stringencies of the Sages. It is known how far the words of God branch out: even a trace of anger is termed “You shall not murder,” and excessive conversation with a woman is an adjunct of “You shall not commit adultery.” Thus the Gemara in Eruvin 53b records Beruriah saying to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, “You should have said, ‘Which way to Lod?’” “Make it ready” conveys establishment and strengthening, for the boundaries and safeguards sustain the mitzvah itself. “Afterward build your house” means that after you have developed yourself in strength and firmness, you will be bounded on every side and permitted to expand into all your wishes without needing an additional safeguard. Rabbi Yose HaGelili therefore did not in fact transgress “Do not speak excessively,” because he had already attained completeness and did not need those safeguards.”
connections.context: This is the interpretation of “make it ready in the field” that Rav Tzadok says he heard. The order matters: observance and inwardly established safeguards precede the described freedom of action. The passage identifies its final example with Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s attained state.

connections.hePhrase: שָׂדֶה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת לְאֹרֶךְ וָרֹחַב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כד, כז): "וְעַתְּדָהּ בַּשָּׂדֶה לָךְ",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach distinguishes expansion in unholy desires from Yaakov's expansion in holiness

connections.hePhrase: שָׂדֶה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת לְאֹרֶךְ וָרֹחַב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כד, כז): "וְעַתְּדָהּ בַּשָּׂדֶה לָךְ",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 9
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 9
connections.quote: “‘See, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field,’ and so forth. A field alludes to an expansion of desires. Esav was therefore called ‘a man of the field,’ because he expanded into all kinds of evil cravings and desires. Yaakov our father, however, had an expansion in holiness. This is ‘like the fragrance of a field that Hashem has blessed’—the holy apple orchard.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explicitly interprets ‘field’ as an expansion of desire, then distinguishes Esav's field from Yaakov's field blessed by Hashem. This helps identify the kind of expansion intended by the siman: its claim that bodily desires are uncommon concerns the spiritual state under discussion. The word ‘field’ by itself does not always signify freedom from bodily desire. This is a conceptual comparison, rather than an identification of the unnamed teaching Rav Tzadok reports hearing.
connections.headline: The field's expansion takes its character from its direction

connections.hePhrase: [לח] "לַמֵּד לְשׁוֹנְךָ לוֹמַר אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ, שֶׁמָּא תִּתְבַּדֶּה וְתֵאָחֵז" (בְּרָכוֹת ד' עַמּוּד א').
connections.quote: ‘Since Moses knew, why did he need to say ‘around midnight’? Moses reasoned: Pharaoh’s astrologers might make a mistake and say, ‘Moses is a liar.’ As the Master said: Train your tongue to say, ‘I do not know,’ lest you be caught in a false statement.’

connections.hePhrase: וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר: אַף בִּדְבָרִים הַבְּרוּרִים בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה, כְּשֶׁבָּאִים לְגִלּוּי שֶׁהוּא הַלָּשׁוֹן הַמּוֹצִיא לַפּוֹעַל מַה שֶּׁבַּכֹּחַ בַּלֵּב – יִהְיוּ תְּלוּיִים בְּסָפֵק,
connections.quote: “‘Faces’ means disclosures: the sage shows the grounds for saying what he says. The forty-nine are known to be seven times seven, corresponding to the seven attributes of the structure of revelation. The fiftieth gate corresponds to understanding in the heart: one cannot disclose to another the heart's feeling, the inward taste one feels concerning a matter, for that taste cannot be explained and disclosed. This is as they said in Sanhedrin 35a, ‘The human heart forgets’: it cannot be disclosed in writing, nor can it be disclosed in speech. Rather, the impression in the heart clothes itself in speech. The force of the speech follows the feeling of the reason's taste in the heart, and the heart's feeling can be recognized in the speech; but the actual taste that one feels cannot be disclosed.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla distinguishes the reasons a sage can disclose from the inward taste of those reasons in the heart. Speech bears an impression of that understanding but does not reproduce it completely. This explains why the present siman demands a further clarification when a private conviction becomes public speech or action. The comparison preserves both sides: inward understanding has substance, while the speaker's certainty alone does not establish the matter for others.
connections.headline: The heart's understanding and its expression

connections.hePhrase: וּבִכְגוֹן זֶה: לִבָּא לְפוּמָא לָא גַּלְיָא:
connections.displayRef: Kohelet Rabbah 12:10, on the hidden time of redemption
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shaul of Naveh taught in the name of Rabbi Shimon: If someone asks you, “When is the appointed time of redemption?” tell him: It is written, “For a day of vengeance is in My heart.” Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: I gave you three identifying signs and specified them concerning Moshe’s burial place—“in the valley,” “in the land of Moav,” and “opposite Beit Peor.” Nevertheless, “no one knew his burial place.” The heart has not disclosed it to the mouth; to whom, then, could the mouth disclose it?”
connections.context: The Midrash uses this expression for what Hashem has kept undisclosed, in its discussion of the time of redemption and Moshe’s burial place. Rav Tzadok applies the expression here to the distinction between an inward conviction and what one can responsibly express to others.

connections.hePhrase: דְּלוּלֵי כֵן לֹא הָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ, שֶׁרַק לַבָּא לִטָּהֵר מְסַיְּעִין אוֹתוֹ, אֲבָל בְּבָא לִטָּמֵא אָמְרוּ: רַק פּוֹתְחִין לוֹ וְלֹא מְסַיְּעִין.
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: What is meant by the verse, “If it concerns scoffers, He lets them scoff; but to the humble He gives favor”? If someone comes to become impure, an opening is made for him; if someone comes to become pure, he is assisted.”
connections.context: The distinction between an opening and active assistance is the premise of Rav Tzadok’s discussion. He then cautions that apparent assistance in a particular action is not, by itself, proof that the action is right.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִיכָה שֶׁאָמַר (שׁוֹפְטִים יז, יג): "עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יֵיטִיב ה' לִי, כִּי הָיָה לִי הַלֵּוִי לְכֹהֵן",
connections.quote: ‘Micah said: Now I know that Hashem will do good for me, because the Levite has become my priest.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְשֵׁם זֶה בַּהֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא קֹדֶשׁ כִּדְאִיתָא בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת (לה:)],
connections.quote: “All the divine names stated in the account of Naboth are sacred; in the account of Micah they are profane. Rabbi Eliezer says: In Naboth they are sacred; in Micah, some are profane and some sacred. “El” is profane and the four-letter Name is sacred, except “all the days that the house of God was in Shiloh,” where “Elohim” is sacred.”
connections.context: The discussion distinguishes references to God from references to Micah’s idolatrous cult. Rav Tzadok’s argument concerns the status of divine names in that mixed account; the previous quotation about Lot did not address it.

connections.hePhrase: אָמְנָם רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כו) כִּי מִיכָה כָּפַר בְּ"אָנֹכִי",
connections.quote: “Another interpretation of “I am the Lord your God”: this teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, looked over the entire world, from its beginning to its end, and foresaw ten people who rebelled against Him. These are: Micah, Jeroboam, the son of the Israelite woman, the wood-gatherer, Absalom, Joab, Samson, Achan, the witnesses against Naboth, and Ahab. Against “I am the Lord your God,” Micah rebelled.”
connections.context: This is the explicit source for the statement that Micah rebelled against “Anokhi.” The midrash maps these figures onto the Ten Commandments; Rav Tzadok’s discussion focuses on the special significance of the first declaration.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאַרְתִּי שֶׁהוּא כְּפִירָה בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵיאוּרוֹ.
connections.quote: “But Micah rebelled against “I am,” which precedes “You shall have no other gods,” the prohibition of idolatry that is among the commandments. “I am,” however, was not expressed as a command at all.
