As is known, faith is not something to which a command can apply: if a person does not believe in his heart, what would a command accomplish? Israel are “believers, children of believers”; this is the root of Jewish identity present from birth in all the seed of Jacob. A simple declaration therefore suffices: “I am the Lord your God,” and the believing seed of Israel will believe it. Nevertheless, in this world, which is the world of choice, room for choice was granted even in this, so that a person can depart from the root of Jewish identity and deny the fundamental principle.”
connections.context: This develops the author’s reference to his explanation elsewhere: Micah’s fault is described as rejection of the root expressed by “Anokhi,” beyond the separate prohibition of idolatry. The continuation of this ois directs the reader toward prayer for transformation rather than confidence in one’s own origins.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אַטּוּ אֲנַן מִי יָדְעִינַן מֵהֵיכָא קָאָתֵינַן וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ קִדּוּשִׁין עא:),
connections.quote: ‘Ulla came to Pumbedita, to Rav Yehudah’s house. He saw that Rav Yitzchak, Rav Yehudah’s son, had grown up but had not married. He said to him: ‘Why has the Master not found a wife for his son?’ He answered: ‘Do I know from which family to find him a wife?’ He replied: ‘Do we ourselves know where we come from? Perhaps we descend from those of whom it is written: Women in Zion were violated, maidens in the cities of Judah.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה תְּפִלָּה וְתַחֲנוּנִים לְרַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם הַמּוֹעִילִים לַהֲפוֹךְ גַּם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:37
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:37
connections.quote: “This is found specifically in Israel, for in them there can be a completely new creation, bringing something into being from nothing, as it is said, “A people newly created shall praise the Lord.” As is known, “creation” everywhere denotes bringing something into being from nothing. It is like the verse, “Create in me a pure heart, O God”: this is Israel’s power in prayer—to effect even such a creation. Where there is a deficiency at the root, one can repair the root until a new purity is created in one’s heart, brought into being from nothing.”
connections.context: The parallel explicitly connects prayer to a change in the root itself, using the same verse and the same explanation of “creation.” It gives the affirmative answer to the concern raised earlier in the ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה תְּפִלָּה וְתַחֲנוּנִים לְרַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם הַמּוֹעִילִים לַהֲפוֹךְ גַּם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ,
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 5:8
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 5:8
connections.quote: “Thus, since he [Rabbi Akiva] was descended from converts, through his effort he became holy flesh and an Israelite soul. Previously he had been unlearned and said, ‘If only I had a Torah scholar,’ and so forth (Pesachim 49b): his natural starting point was not good. Only through effort did he merit the Oral Torah, which clarifies that the essential thing is to be of Israel's holy stock; through his effort he brought it about that he belonged to that holy stock. [Effort is effective even in this, and Hashem has many means, as stated in Taanit 25a: ‘Am I asking from someone who does not have it?’ The principal means is Torah, as the Midrash teaches in several places concerning Yitro and his descendants. A person can attain heavenly mercy so that ‘his flesh returns like the flesh of a young child’ (II Kings 5:14), like a convert who converts, who is considered a newborn child (Yevamot 22a), and return to holy flesh. This is as I wrote elsewhere on ‘Create in me a pure heart, God’ (Psalms 51:12): as is known, ‘creation’ everywhere denotes something from nothing. These matters contain great and substantial discussions, whose place is not here.]”
connections.explanation: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik also reads ‘Create in me a pure heart’ as creation from nothing. Its context is Rabbi Akiva's transformation through Torah and effort, followed by the images of a convert as newly born and flesh restored like a child's. This gives the siman's final remedy a concrete meaning: prayer for mercy can seek a renewed spiritual beginning, rather than treating one's present condition as an unchangeable verdict. The matching cross-reference is suggestive; it does not by itself prove which passage the author intended by ‘elsewhere.’
connections.headline: Creation reaches beyond an improved surface

connections.hePhrase: [כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי אֱלֹהִים וְגוֹמֵר", דִּבְרִיאָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם הַיְינוּ יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן כַּנּוֹדָע].
connections.quote: ‘Create a pure heart for me, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.’

connections.hePhrase: [כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי אֱלֹהִים וְגוֹמֵר", דִּבְרִיאָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם הַיְינוּ יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן כַּנּוֹדָע].
connections.quote: “The correct explanation is that it denotes bringing something into existence from nothing, for in the holy language we have no expression denoting this other than this word.”
connections.context: Ramban explains the word “creation” in the account of the earth opening to swallow Korah’s company. Rav Tzadok applies this meaning to the request, “Create in me a pure heart.”

connections.hePhrase: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.displayRef: Rambam asked how a person’s choice can be free if Hashem knows beforehand whether he will be righteous or wicked, and answered that His knowledge is not like ours (Hilchot Teshuvah 5:5; see note 282 below). Rav Tzadok holds that this admission is itself the true answer, and he explains it, after Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and the Ari’s Arba Me’ot Shekel Kesef, as two truths that stand in two different “places”: “In the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no grasp of His knowledge; choice exists only from the side of this world” (Takanat HaShavin 6). The place of knowledge is hidden in this world and will be revealed in the future, when the evil inclination is removed and choice falls away (Machshavot Charutz 8; Resisei Layla 50). Elsewhere he spells out that this is Rambam’s answer itself: for us two opposites cannot rest in one subject, but for Hashem they can (citing Maharal’s introduction to Gevurot Hashem); “for us there is choice, and for Hashem knowledge,” and when we merit such a revelation of Godliness that “the righteous will be called by the name of the Holy One” (Bava Batra 75b), we will see that there was no room for choice at all (Likkutei Maamarim, On Shimshon 17)

connections.hePhrase: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: Morris M. Faierstein, All Is in the Hands of Heaven: The Teachings of Rabbi Mordecai Joseph Leiner of Izbica (1989); Alan Brill, Thinking God: The Mysticism of Rabbi Zadok of Lublin (2002), chapter “Determinism and Sin in R. Zadok’s Thought,” pp. 169–88; R’ Uriel Eitam, “Ta’am HaBechirah HaChofshit,” lessons on the Mei HaShiloach and on R’ Tzadok (Yeshivat Har Etzion, 2023).

connections.hePhrase: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “Likewise, with all the transgressions that brought a person to return and to attain the level of a penitent—of which the Sages said that even the completely righteous cannot stand in that place—the distancing has become the cause of closeness.”

connections.hePhrase: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “This level comes through repentance out of love, with greater closeness after the distancing. As the Sages explained the impurity of a menstruant: it is so that she should become beloved to her husband. The deliberate sins thus become like merits, for they are what bring about the closeness.”
connections.context: These passages explain why the section begins with teshuvah and ends with transformed sins. The transformation is realized through repentance out of love: the earlier distance has led to deeper attachment. It is not a claim that a person may choose a transgression in advance and call it a mitzvah. The act of the scapegoat later in this section is a mitzvah because Hashem explicitly commands it.

connections.hePhrase: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “Then Elijah said the verse, “You have turned their heart backward.” Of this they said, “Elijah hurled words toward Heaven,” and they said that the Holy One, blessed be He, afterward acknowledged his argument, as it is written, “Whom I afflicted.” There it says, “Were it not for these three verses, their feet would have faltered.” At that moment there appeared to them something of the concealed light from the Ancient One. This is the meaning of “If your sins are like these years, ordered and coming since the six days of Creation, they shall become white as snow.” In the utterance of Creation it says “formless and void,” which alludes to the deeds of the wicked, as Bereishit Rabbah says. When, through repentance from love, one merits the revelation of this light, “they shall become white as snow”: his deliberate sins become like merits.”
connections.explanation: In Chanukah, Rav Tzadok returns to the very verses quoted in this siman and identifies the means of the revelation: repentance from love. This makes the siman’s language about divine will more precise. The light is disclosed through a repaired relationship with Hashem; it is not an inference a person can use beforehand to authorize a transgression. The siman’s own example of the goat sent to Azazel preserves that distinction: an explicit command makes that particular act a mitzvah.
connections.headline: Loving repentance reveals a meaning that could not guide the original choice

connections.hePhrase: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of “Yours is the dew of your youth”: it is the dew of Atika, the Ancient One. It corresponds to what they said (Shabbat 89b): “If your sins are like years”—like these years that have been ordered and have come from the six days of Creation until now—“they shall become white as snow.” Through repentance from love it becomes clear that in the utterance “Bereishit,” in which “And He said” does not appear and which signifies an understanding concealed from every conception, “formlessness and emptiness” had already been mentioned. These allude to the deeds of the wicked, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This was the intention: first darkness, then light, so that light should gain its advantage from within darkness. It corresponds to the Zohar’s statement (II, 184a), “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness.” Then “they shall become white as snow”: they become merits. This is the meaning of “Yours is the dew of your youth”: it was the blessed God’s intention that the forty-eight years should come first and that afterward Abraham our father should recognize his Creator. This is what they said: “Just as dew flies away, so your sins fly away.” It had been ordered from the utterance “Bereishit,” from Atika, and “they shall become white as snow,” becoming merits. “Just as dew is a sign of blessing for the world, so you are a sign of blessing for the world.””
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik supplies Abraham’s youth as a concrete setting for the difficult retrospective claim in Tzidkat HaTzadik. The first darkness becomes part of a greater light through repentance from love, and the image of dew places this recognition within Shabbat’s revelation. It illustrates the transformation after return while leaving intact the distinction between human choice and the illumination of Divine knowledge.
connections.headline: Repentance and the transformation of the past

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: Were it not for these three verses, the feet of Israel’s enemies [a euphemism for Israel] would have faltered.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “One is written, “And whom I have afflicted”; one is written, “Like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, house of Israel”; and one is written, “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.””
connections.context: These verses are presented as grounds for a plea of mercy: the human struggle takes place under God’s creative power. The passage is on 32a, continuing the preceding discussion; it does not erase responsibility for repentance.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘Answer me, Hashem, answer me, so that this people may know that You, Hashem, are God, and that You have turned their hearts backward.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “On that day, declares Hashem, I will gather the limping one; I will assemble the outcast and the one whom I afflicted.”
connections.context: Berakhot 32a reads the final words, “whom I afflicted,” as one of the three verses without which Israel would have no defense. Rav Tzadok cites that reading within his account of repentance and the retrospective disclosure of divine knowledge. The full Talmudic passage is quoted in the adjacent note; the verse here preserves the precise words on which that interpretation rests.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְטַעַם יְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה שֶׁבֵּיאַר הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שֶׁקֶל כֶּסֶף,
connections.quote: “One difficult question must be asked. We have seen in the books of Kabbalah that when God is engaged with Beriah [the realm of Creation], He does not know, whereas in Atzilut [the realm of Emanation] He knows. Thus it would seem that in Atzilut there is knowledge and compulsion. But this presents a difficulty concerning our Sages’ teaching on “Hashem said to Moses: Speak to the priests”: the first king who would arise over Israel would be pierced by a sword. He said to Him, “And to me You say, ‘Speak to the priests’?”—for Saul had killed Nob, the city of priests. It would follow that His knowledge compelled Saul, whether in Beriah or in Atzilut; in either case it compelled him.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, כָּל אֶחָד בְּמָקוֹם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ:
connections.quote: “You may ask: Does the Holy One, blessed be He, not know all that will happen? Before it happens, does He know that this person will be righteous or wicked, or does He not know? If He knows that the person will be righteous, it is impossible for him not to be righteous; and if you say that He knows he will be righteous but he may be wicked, then He does not know the matter clearly. Know that the answer to this question is longer than the earth and broader than the sea; many great principles and lofty mountains depend upon it. But you must know and understand what I say here. We have already explained in the second chapter of the Laws of the Foundations of the Torah that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not know through a knowledge external to Himself, as human beings and their knowledge are two things. Rather, He, exalted be His name, and His knowledge are one, and human understanding cannot grasp this matter fully. Just as a person cannot grasp and discover the truth of the Creator, as it is said, ‘A person cannot see Me and live,’ so a person cannot grasp and discover the Creator’s knowledge. This is what the prophet said: ‘My thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not My ways.’ Since this is so, we lack the power to know how the Holy One, blessed be He, knows all creatures and deeds. Nevertheless, we know without doubt that a person’s action lies in his own hands, and the Holy One, blessed be He, neither draws him nor decrees that he act in a particular way. We know this not only from received religion but also through clear rational proofs. Therefore prophecy says that a person is judged for his actions according to what he has done, whether good or evil. This is the principle upon which all the words of prophecy depend.”
connections.context: Rambam presents the coexistence of divine knowledge and human choice, while explaining that the nature of divine knowledge exceeds human understanding. This is a related formulation of the question Rav Tzadok addresses; it is not a quotation from the Ari or from Arba Meot Shekel Kesef mentioned in the surrounding discussion.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, כָּל אֶחָד בְּמָקוֹם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ:
connections.quote: “As is known concerning the secret of divine knowledge and free choice, over which Rambam found difficulty: he revealed there the culmination of his knowledge by saying that he did not know a solution, because our knowledge is not like His knowledge. This is the true answer to the question, unlike Raavad, who wrote that he had left it as a difficulty. Its secret is known in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and the Ari’s Arba Meot Shekel Kesef. The essence is that in the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no apprehension of His knowledge. Choice belongs to the standpoint of this world, for as long as a person remains attached to materiality and is not entirely attached to Him. He has not yet reached the ultimate perfection of choice, which is to cleave entirely to the living God. When he reaches that level, he apprehends the truth that there is no choice, and that it is not through his own righteousness and uprightness of heart. Pride arises from the lowliness and materiality within him; then Hashem is also exalted beyond him. If he recognized that Hashem is with him and that everything is from Him, there would be no place for pride. There, in the place of His greatness, is His humility. Thus humility is the greatness of a person whose soul cleaves to its source.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok here explicitly connects Rambam’s discussion to the Ari’s two-domain account. The sentence about not knowing a solution is Rav Tzadok’s characterization of Rambam; Rambam’s own full formulation is quoted in the adjacent note on Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:5. The end of the passage shows the spiritual consequence Rav Tzadok draws: humility and dependence on Hashem. This passage is in section 6, paragraph 4 in the linked source; the reader’s paragraph division places it in 6:5. It is quoted in both supplied commentaries.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִמְקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה שָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין מָקוֹם לַבְּחִירָה.
connections.quote: “The question of divine knowledge and free choice is well known. Zohar Chadash and the Ari’s Arba Meot Shekel Kesef resolve it according to the esoteric teaching. The root of the matter is that they occupy two different places. In the place of knowledge there truly is no room for choice; but this place is concealed in this world and will be revealed in the future, when the evil inclination is removed and choice is in fact annulled. As Shabbat 151b says, “Days in which there is no desire” are the days of the Messiah. Then it will also become clear concerning all Israel’s sins that they were ordered from the six days of Creation, as stated in the chapter Rabbi Akiva. This means that the knowledge will be revealed: everything was within His knowledge at the beginning of Creation. But this world is the place of choice.”
connections.context: Machshavot Charutz, section 8, provides a close verbal parallel. It explains the two “places” as different levels of disclosure. The present world remains the arena of choice; the later revelation of divine knowledge is the background for Rav Tzadok’s account of sins transformed through teshuvah.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא וְדַעְתּוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ הַכֹּל אֶחָד.
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות יסודי התורה ב׳:י׳
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, apprehends His own truth and knows it as it is. He does not know through a knowledge external to Himself, as we know. We and our knowledge are not one, but the Creator, blessed be He, His knowledge, and His life are one from every side, every aspect, and every form of unity. If He lived through a life or knew through a knowledge outside Himself, there would be many divinities—Him, His life, and His knowledge. This is not so; He is one from every side, every aspect, and every form of unity. Thus you say: He is the knower, He is the known, and He is knowledge itself—all are one. This is something that the mouth cannot express, the ear cannot hear, and the human heart cannot fully apprehend.”
connections.context: This is the precise Rambam passage invoked by the commentaries beside “He, His knowledge, and His will are all one.” Hilkhot Yesodei HaTorah 2:10 speaks explicitly of His knowledge and life; Rav Tzadok’s sentence also speaks of His will. Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:5 refers back to this chapter to explain why divine knowledge cannot be modeled on human knowledge. The additional word “will” is therefore identified as Rav Tzadok’s formulation, rather than silently inserted into Rambam’s quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצָה כֵּן, הֲרֵי הַכֹּל זְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “Therefore Yom Kippur is called “at every time,” because a person reaches that level—repentance, which comes from the understanding within the heart, as it says, “His heart will understand, and he will return.” Through this all the deeds are good, for even the deliberate sins have been transformed into merits. This is called “at every time,” without any limitation. There is no outward recognition of it in this world, as in the teaching in Kiddushin 49b: “On condition that I am righteous”—even a completely wicked person may have contemplated repentance in his heart. Its essence is a matter entrusted to the heart: whether he has reached such a depth that the Examiner of hearts can testify that he will never return to this matter again.”
connections.context: This passage is Dover Tzedek, Acharei Mot 4; the linked text catalogs it as Miscellany 4:9. It ties sins becoming merits to the inward depth of repentance and to Yom Kippur. It also specifies the decisive condition: a return so complete that the Examiner of hearts bears witness to it.

connections.hePhrase: וְזוֹכֶה לְכַפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה שֶׁבְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים,
connections.quote: “Therefore, according to Rabbi, the essence of the day atones without any human effort at all, because the illumination of that day is that everything is in the hands of Heaven. This is the question of knowledge and choice over which the earlier authorities were perplexed. Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, at its end, answers it; this is not the place to explain it. The substance is that they are not in one place: in the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice—and so forth. Yom Kippur is a radiance of the gate of freedom, from the place of Binah within Hashem’s knowledge, above the place of choice. From there there is no place for sin at all, since everything is ordered within His knowledge.”
connections.context: Resisei Layla 50:2 explicitly connects the same knowledge-and-choice distinction to Yom Kippur. Rav Tzadok is explaining Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi’s position in the dispute about the day’s atoning power; the qualification “according to Rabbi” is part of his text. The parallel illuminates “the complete atonement of Yom Kippur” here.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה סוֹד הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל,
connections.quote: “Rav Shmuel said: Although the sin-offering goat is described as belonging to Hashem, the goat sent away also belongs to Hashem. This is unnecessary, because the goat sent away is not a sacrificial offering, since it is not slaughtered. If you can understand the secret that follows the word Azazel, you will know its secret and the secret of its name, for it has companions in Scripture. I will reveal a little of the secret by a hint: when you are thirty-three, you will know it.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה סוֹד הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abraham hinted that you would know its secret when you reach the verse, “They shall no longer sacrifice their sacrifices to the se’irim.” The word is compound, and it has many companions.”
connections.context: Ramban reads Ibn Ezra’s “thirty-three” as a pointer from Leviticus 16:8 to Leviticus 17:7, the prohibition of sacrifices to the se’irim. That is why the apparent resemblance to prohibited worship must be explained. Ramban’s full answer—the act is performed solely to fulfill the Creator’s command, like giving a servant a portion at his master’s direction—is quoted at Rav Tzadok’s explicit Ramban reference below. Neither commentator presents an independently chosen offering to Azazel as permissible.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ פֵּירְשׁוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק מו),
connections.quote: “Samael said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “Master of all worlds, You have given me authority over all the nations of the world, but You do not give me authority over Israel?” He replied: “You have authority over them on Yom Kippur if they have sin; if they do not, you have no authority over them.” Therefore they give him a gift [literally, a bribe] on Yom Kippur so that he will not obstruct Israel or Israel’s offering, as it says, “One lot for Hashem and one lot for Azazel.””

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ פֵּירְשׁוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק מו),
connections.quote: “The lot of the Holy One, blessed be He, is a burnt offering, and the lot of Azazel is a sin-offering goat, with all Israel’s sins upon it, as it says, “The goat shall bear upon itself all their iniquities.” Samael saw that no sin was found in them on Yom Kippur and said before Him: “Master of the universe, You have one people on earth like the ministering angels in Heaven. Just as the ministering angels have no joints, so Israel stands on its feet on Yom Kippur; just as the angels have no eating or drinking, so Israel has no eating or drinking on Yom Kippur; just as the ministering angels are clean of every sin, so Israel is clean of every sin on Yom Kippur; just as peace prevails among the ministering angels, so peace prevails among Israel on Yom Kippur.” The Holy One, blessed be He, hears Israel’s pleas from their accuser and atones for the altar, the priests, and the entire congregation, from great to small, as it says, “He shall atone for the holy sanctuary.””
connections.context: The “gift” is given so that the accuser does not obstruct Israel’s offering; the Hebrew does not say that Israel should refrain from bringing its offering. The passage then turns the accuser into a witness to Israel’s purity. Ramban cites this Midrash in explaining that the goat is sent solely at Hashem’s command. That is the connection to Rav Tzadok’s contrast between an independently initiated act of worship and the commanded mitzvah. The continuation in 46:9 supplies the outcome of the gift described in 46:8. The printed Midrash’s description of Hashem’s lot as a “burnt offering” is retained as its wording; it is not a statement that the Torah classifies that goat as an olah.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בָּרַמְבַּ"ן פָּרָשַׁת אַחֲרֵי,
connections.quote: “The intention concerning the scapegoat is not, Heaven forbid, that it should be an offering from us to him. Rather, our intention is to fulfill the will of our Creator, who commanded us to do so. The analogy is someone who prepares a feast for a master, and the master tells the person preparing it, ‘Give one portion to such-and-such servant of mine.’ The person preparing the feast gives nothing of his own to that servant and does not act in his honor. Everything was given to the master; the master gives a portion to his servant, while this person keeps his command and does all that he commanded in the master’s honor. The master, in compassion for the host, wished all his servants to enjoy the feast, so that they would speak his praise and not his disparagement. This is the reason for the lots. Had the priest verbally consecrated the goats to Hashem and to Azazel, he would have been like someone worshipping him and making a vow in his name. Instead, he placed them before Hashem at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, for both are a gift to Hashem. He gives His servant the portion that comes to him from Hashem: He cast their lot and His hand apportioned it to them, as it is said, ‘The lot is cast into the lap, but all its judgment is from Hashem.’ Even after the lot, he would place the goat before Hashem, to declare that it belongs to Him and that in sending it we intend only to fulfill Hashem’s will, as it says, ‘It shall stand alive before Hashem, to atone over it and send it,’ and so forth. For this reason, we do not slaughter it at all.”

connections.hePhrase: [מא] "אָנֹכִי" קוֹדֵם לְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ",
connections.quote: “He explained that this was among Hashem's kindnesses. If the statement ‘You shall have no other gods,’ which signifies turning from evil, had preceded ‘I am,’ which signifies doing good, then someone not yet clean in turning from evil would have no place to perform any mitzvah, because he was not yet purified in turning from evil. Hashem's saying ‘I am’ first teaches that even if someone has, Heaven forbid, stumbled in something bad, repentance is not withheld from him, and he can perform mitzvot even while he is not yet clean in turning from evil.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef draws another consequence from the same order of commandments. If removal of evil were an absolute precondition for every positive act, someone not yet purified would have no beginning. Anokhi comes first as divine kindness that leaves repentance and mitzvot open even while repair remains incomplete. This complements the siman's account of faith leading to protection; it does not turn unfinished repair into permission to continue the wrongdoing.
connections.headline: The first commandment leaves a beginning for return

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת הַגְּמוּרָה בְּ"אָנֹכִי" מִצַּד אֱמוּנָה הַבְּרוּרָה בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא מָצוּי
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות יסודי התורה א׳:א׳
connections.quote: “The foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdoms is to know that there is a first existent. He brings every existent into being. All beings, from heaven and earth and everything between them, exist only through the truth of His existence.”
connections.context: Rambam begins the laws of the foundations of Torah with knowledge of Hashem’s existence. This supplies the original formulation behind the contemplation of “I am” and “He exists” at this point in the ois.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיֵּצֵא): עָשָׂה מִצְוָה אַחַת מוֹסְרִין לוֹ מַלְאָךְ אֶחָד לְשָׁמְרוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Meir said: If a person performs one mitzvah, one angel is assigned to him; if he performs two mitzvot, two angels are assigned to him; if he performs many mitzvot, many angels are assigned to him, as it is written, “For He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you.” Why? To guard him from harmful forces.”
connections.context: The Midrash’s subject is the protection assigned through mitzvot. Rav Tzadok then distinguishes the commandments heard directly from God, for which he describes God’s own protection.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"אָנֹכִי" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה" שָׁמְעוּ מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה,
connections.quote: “[“Torah” amounts to] six hundred and eleven; “I am [the Lord your God]” and “You shall have no other [gods]” we heard from the mouth of the Almighty.”
connections.context: The calculation of 613 commandments begins on 23b and continues here. These two commandments are distinguished as heard directly from God, which is the basis of Rav Tzadok’s contrast between angelic mediation and God’s own protection.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר אָמְרוּ כִּי מִמִּצְוָה נִבְרָא מַלְאָךְ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: One who performs one mitzvah acquires one advocate for himself; one who commits one transgression acquires one accuser for himself. Repentance and good deeds are like a shield against calamity.”
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s formulation of the advocate created through a mitzvah. The existing Tanchuma note describes an angel assigned to guard the person; this related source supplies the advocate-and-accuser formulation.

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי אִתְעָרוּתָא כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט מִתַּתָּא
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yassa said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, open for Me one opening of repentance like the point of a needle, and I will open for you openings through which wagons and carriages can enter.”
connections.context: The small opening is expressly an opening of repentance. Rav Tzadok uses the contrast between a minute human beginning and the much larger divine response.

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי אִתְעָרוּתָא כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט מִתַּתָּא
connections.quote: “The awakening from below must come first. Concerning this they said, “Open for Me like the point of a needle”: any amount of fear of Heaven is sufficient, and a corresponding measure of wisdom will then be imparted to his heart. Through that wisdom he will naturally gain more fear, and then more wisdom will come. The cycle continues until there are openings of the kind described there. The earlier teachers said: provided that the hole passes through from one side to the other. This means that there must be, from the depths of his heart, a complete awakening to abandon sin and leave all worldly concerns; even a single moment is sufficient.”
connections.context: The parallel explains the quality of the small opening: it must reach through the heart. Its final qualification requires a sincere abandonment of sin, even when the initial awakening lasts only a moment.

connections.hePhrase: נִפְתַּח אַחַר כָּךְ כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם:
connections.quote: “As soon as a person wishes to return, he is already “coming to be purified,” and the rule is to assist him, as stated in Yoma 38b. When he is assisted, a spirit of purity is naturally added to him, and he comes further toward purification. Then the assistance from above returns with greater strength, and he in turn comes further toward purification below. This continues in a cycle, until an opening like the point of a needle becomes like the entrance of a great hall, as our Sages said in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the growing opening as a succession of human beginnings and divine assistance. Later in that ois he asks why repentance sometimes remains incomplete and directs the person to seek heavenly mercy, with confidence joined to remorse.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "אַל תַּעַשׂ תְּפִלָּתְךָ קֶבַע אֶלָּא רַחֲמִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shimon says: Be careful about reciting the Shema and praying. When you pray, do not make your prayer a mere routine, but an appeal for mercy and supplication before the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said, ‘For He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abundant in kindness, and relents from calamity’ (Joel 2). And do not regard yourself as wicked.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא עַצְמוֹ מַאֲמָרָם שִׁילְהֵי מְנָחוֹת בְּקָרְבָּנוֹת [שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה דּוּגְמָתָן]:
connections.quote: “I did not tell you to offer sacrifices so that you would say, “I will do His will and He will do my will.” You do not offer sacrifices for My desire; you offer them for your own desire, as it is written, “For your acceptance you shall sacrifice it.””
connections.context: The passage rejects treating an offering as a transaction that obligates God to satisfy the worshipper. Rav Tzadok cites this distinction when discussing the intention underlying divine service.

connections.hePhrase: "שֶׁלֹּא תֹאמַר אֶעֱשֶׂה רְצוֹנוֹ וְכוּלֵי, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: 'לִרְצֹנְכֶם תִּזְבָּחוּהוּ'",
connections.quote: ‘When you slaughter a peace offering to Hashem, slaughter it so that it may be accepted on your behalf.’

connections.hePhrase: "שֶׁלֹּא תֹאמַר אֶעֱשֶׂה רְצוֹנוֹ וְכוּלֵי, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: 'לִרְצֹנְכֶם תִּזְבָּחוּהוּ'",
connections.quote: ““So that you would say: I will do His will”—by offering Him a sacrifice, and He will do my will, because He needs it and I can bribe Him. “You do not sacrifice for My desire”—that is, not for My benefit, for I do not wish to burden you to act against your will. “For your desire”—for your own need, to fulfill My commandments, so that through this there will be atonement for you.”
connections.context: Rashi explains all three parts of the saying: the mistaken attempt to bargain with God, God’s lack of need, and the benefit to the worshipper. These qualifications clarify the distinction Rav Tzadok applies to prayer.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְלֹא צִוִּיתִים וְגוֹמֵר עַל דִּבְרֵי עוֹלָה וָזָבַח", וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת.
connections.quote: ‘For on the day I brought your ancestors out of the land of Egypt, I neither spoke to them nor commanded them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים בְּטַעַם הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת.
connections.quote: “The meaning of the statement is what I have explained to you: He said that the primary intention was that you should apprehend Me and worship no one other than Me, “and I shall be your God, and you shall be My people.” This command to offer sacrifices and direct yourselves toward the House was given so that you would attain this principle. For its sake I transferred these forms of worship to My name, until the name of idolatry would be erased and the principle of My unity established.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנוֹדַע מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב מַהֲרַ"ם אַלְשַׁקַר סִימָן קי"ז דְּכֵן הוּא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ, וְכָתַב מָשָׁל וְכוּלֵי עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Pinchas said in the name of Rabbi Levi: A parable of a king’s son who became presumptuous and was accustomed to eating the flesh of animals that had died or were torn. The king said: Let him always be at my table, and he will be restrained of himself. So too, because Israel were passionately attached to idolatry in Egypt and brought their sacrifices to the goat-demons—as it is written, “They shall no longer sacrifice their sacrifices to the goat-demons”; these are demons, as it says, “They sacrificed to demons,” and the demons are called goat-demons, as it says, “Goat-demons shall dance there”—they offered their sacrifices on forbidden high places, and calamities came upon them. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let them always bring their sacrifices before Me in the Tent of Meeting; they will separate from idolatry and be saved. This is what is written: “Any man of the house of Israel,” and so forth.”
connections.context: This is the original Midrash’s parable of the king’s table. Its application is the redirection of Israel’s offerings away from idolatry and toward the Tent of Meeting.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל הָעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה – אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ נֶהֱנֶה וּמִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ קָרְבָּן כְּמוֹ אָדָם עַל יְדֵי מַאֲכָל;
connections.quote: “This is the secret of the matter: they used to worship other gods, namely the angels, offering sacrifices to them, and these were a pleasing aroma to them. This is like what is said: “My oil and My incense you placed before them; and My bread that I gave you—fine flour, oil, and honey with which I fed you—you placed before them as a pleasing aroma. And so it was, says the Lord God.””
connections.context: Ramban is discussing offerings directed to intermediate powers. In the continuation he explicitly forbids accepting them as gods or worshipping them, and explains that Israel’s intention in the commanded service must be to fulfill the Creator’s will.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֶיךָ תִכְסֹף", כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא תְּצַוֶּה ב),
connections.quote: ‘You would call, and I would answer You; You would yearn for the work of Your hands.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֶיךָ תִכְסֹף", כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא תְּצַוֶּה ב),
connections.quote: “You desire the work of Your hands. You sustain the whole world, yet command the sons of Kehat to carry Your glory. … You feed the whole world, yet command them to bring “My offering, My food.” You illuminate the whole world, yet command them to raise a continual lamp. By Your light we see light, yet You tell us to light lamps.”
connections.context: The Midrash lists services God requests even though He supplies the strength, food, and light. Rav Tzadok uses this paradox to explain the value of human participation in His service.

connections.hePhrase: רַק דְּמִזֶּה הוּא הַהֲנָאָה לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: מֵהָרָצוֹן וְהַחֵשֶׁק שֶׁלָּהֶם לְהַהֲנוֹתוֹ.
connections.quote: “A person should not set his final purpose and intention on a particular thing, such as restraining desires, studying Torah, engaging in service, or the like. Concerning this the prophet repeatedly cries out that sacrifices were not requested. The commentators ask: were they not in fact commanded? The meaning is that they made this alone the final purpose—to bring sacrifices and perform mitzvot—as it is written, ‘Their fear of Me became a commandment of people learned by rote’ (Isaiah 29:13); this was not commanded. As the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Shemini 8; Bereshit Rabbah 44:1): what difference does it make to the Holy One, blessed be He, whether one slaughters from the neck, and so forth? Rather, the purpose is to refine. The bare physical act is not the final purpose of the command; its purpose is what each mitzvah signifies and intends, in order to refine.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah directly addresses the apparent contradiction behind the siman's sacrificial analogy: the prophets speak of offerings as unrequested although the Torah commands them. The criticism concerns making the external act an isolated final purpose. Its intended refinement and relation to Hashem's will give the act its meaning. This clarifies the siman's emphasis on the desire to pray while preserving the distinction between that purpose and the existence of a commandment.
connections.headline: What the prophets reject in a mechanical offering

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לב.): "מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה הַבֵּן וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: It is like a man who had a son. He bathed him and anointed him with oil, gave him food and drink, hung a purse around his neck, and seated him at the entrance to a brothel. What could that son do to avoid sinning?’

connections.hePhrase: וּבָזֶה הוּא נֶחְשָׁב אֹנֶס גָּמוּר דְּרַחֲמָנָא פַּטְרֵיהּ.
connections.quote: “A certain man deposited his supporting documents in court and said: If I do not come within thirty days, let these documents be void. He was prevented by circumstances beyond his control and did not come. Rav Huna said: His documents are void. Rava said to him: He was under compulsion, and the Merciful One exempts one under compulsion, as it is written, “You shall do nothing to the young woman.” And if you say that a capital case is different, did we not learn: Vows prevented by circumstances beyond one’s control—one’s fellow imposed a vow that he should eat with him, but he or his son became ill, or a river prevented him—these are vows prevented by circumstances beyond one’s control!”
connections.context: This is the Talmudic formulation “the Merciful One exempts one under compulsion.” Its immediate discussion concerns court documents and vows. Rav Tzadok’s application to an overwhelming inner trial is followed by his express warning that a person cannot establish this claim about himself.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בְּהַסָּתַת הַיֵּצֶר בְּתוֹקֶף עָצוּם שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְנַצְּחוֹ, שַׁיָּיךְ אֹנֶס
connections.quote: “In the Gemara, Sukkah, before the statement “Draw it to the house of study,” it says that a person’s inclination overpowers him each day, and that without the Holy One’s help he cannot overcome it. This appears to show that even through Torah there is no remedy against the evil inclination without Hashem’s help. It concerns what the evil inclination provokes on its own, beyond what it was assigned. For this it is called wicked, as they derive from “The wicked watches the righteous”: in its wickedness it seeks to cause the person to stumble. Concerning the inclination implanted at creation, according to the measure of each individual soul, it says, “I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its remedy.” But against what the evil inclination adds on its own, a person has no strength to stand. The Holy One does not act unfairly, and “Hashem will not abandon him into its hand”—He helps him. Yet the Holy One does not help everyone in this way, but the one who looks to Him for it. This is through prayer, casting one’s burden upon Hashem.”
connections.context: This parallel distinguishes the inclination a person was created to confront from an added assault requiring divine help. Its conclusion directs the person toward prayer and reliance on Hashem; it does not authorize a person to certify his own conduct as unavoidable.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּכְתוּבּוֹת (נא:) גַּבֵּי תְּחִלָּתוֹ בְּאֹנֶס:
connections.quote: ‘This disagrees with Rava, for Rava said: Whenever intercourse began under compulsion and ended willingly—even if she says, ‘Leave him alone,’ and, had he not coupled with her, she would have hired him—she remains permitted to her husband. Why? Her inclination has taken hold of her.’

connections.hePhrase: מַאי טַעְמָא? יֵצֶר אַלְבְּשַׁהּ;
connections.quote: ““The inclination clothed her”—this too is compulsion, because at the beginning of intercourse, which was forced, the assailant clothed her in desire.”
connections.context: Rashi is explaining a case that began with rape: the desire that followed was itself imposed by the initial assault. Rav Tzadok cites this explanation as the specific basis for his analogy; the existing Gemara note supplies the surrounding case.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהָעִיד עַל עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, כִּי אוּלַי עֲדַיִן הָיָה לוֹ כֹּחַ לִכְפּוֹת הַיֵּצֶר
connections.quote: “What is someone who sees his way as straight to do? According to his own understanding, he is walking uprightly. Concerning this it says, “Hashem weighs hearts.” When a person’s heart is whole, Hashem does not cause him to err and be misled, and He does not act unfairly. Rather, it is the crookedness within the heart that causes the error.”
connections.context: The parallel places the problem of mistaken self-assessment in the heart’s sincerity. It supports the warning here that one’s own conviction does not by itself establish that a transgression was unavoidable.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהָעִיד עַל עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, כִּי אוּלַי עֲדַיִן הָיָה לוֹ כֹּחַ לִכְפּוֹת הַיֵּצֶר
connections.quote: “‘Their ear is uncircumcised, and they cannot listen’ (Jeremiah 6:10)—even if they wish to, so that they are like people under compulsion; for ‘Hashem's word has become a reproach to them; they do not desire it’ (there). This is like ‘its beginning was under compulsion and its end with willingness’ (Ketubot 51b): according to Shmuel's father, ‘the inclination clothed her.’ So too with the inclination to idolatry then, as Menashe said (Sanhedrin 102b): at the end, even the willingness is compulsion; the essential matter is the beginning. Or it may be understood according to the saying (Yerushalmi Chagigah 1:7), ‘Would that they abandoned Me but kept My Torah: its light would return them to the good,’ and as stated (Kiddushin 30b), ‘I created the evil inclination; I created Torah as its remedy.’”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah examines the same Talmudic case of initial compulsion followed by apparent willingness. It directs attention back to the beginning, then offers Torah's restoring light as another reading of the prophetic passage. This illuminates why the siman combines recognition of genuine compulsion with its explicit refusal to let a person certify that condition for himself. The parallel supplies a distinction to examine, rather than a ruling about any particular case.
connections.headline: The beginning matters when judging compulsion

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בָּזֶה מֵעִנְיַן זִמְרִי שֶׁטָּעָה בָּזֶה]:
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Matot 6
connections.linkedRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Matot 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Matot 6
connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ספר במדבר, מטות ו׳
connections.quote: “Their error was that they saw holiness in these souls. Thus Zimri argued, “Who permitted Jethro’s daughter to you?” His argument was that, just as Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, understood that Zipporah belonged with him, so he understood that Cozbi belonged with him. As the Ari of blessed memory said in the discourse on Abraham’s steps, she was a reincarnation of Dinah, and he was Shechem. There Phinehas saw his error and killed him, as explained there, for in this world the Holy One, blessed be He, did not choose this course.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אַדְּרַבָּא, הוּא כְּלִי מוּכָן לְתוֹקֶף אַהֲבַת וּתְשׁוּקַת דְּרִישַׁת הָאֱמֶת.
connections.quote: “Therefore, whoever is greater than his fellow has a greater evil inclination. That is why the righteous perceive it as a mountain: the evil inclination’s assault upon them is exceedingly powerful, corresponding to the powerful good inherent in their nature from birth.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אַדְּרַבָּא, הוּא כְּלִי מוּכָן לְתוֹקֶף אַהֲבַת וּתְשׁוּקַת דְּרִישַׁת הָאֱמֶת.
connections.quote: “The essence of a person is the desire in the heart, through which he has an advantage over the angels. This is called inclination: the good inclination and the evil inclination. When he strengthens his desire toward good, it is good; otherwise, the reverse. Our Sages said: Whoever is greater than his fellow has a greater inclination. For one person’s greatness over another is only according to the greatness of his desire for good, which is the power of inclination. The good inclination and the evil inclination stand opposite one another in the heart’s two chambers: according to the desire in his heart on the right for good, so it is on the left for evil. Therefore the evil inclination is also greater.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s direct explanation of the correspondence between strong desire for good and strong temptation. The opening makes the direction of the desire decisive; its strength alone does not establish virtue.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּחֲמוֹ הַהוּא סָבָא
connections.quote: ‘Abaye said: ‘If ‘the one who hates me’ [his way of referring to himself] had been there, he would not have been able to restrain himself.’ He went and leaned against the door bolt in distress. An elder came and taught him: ‘Whoever is greater than his fellow has an inclination greater than his fellow’s.’’

connections.hePhrase: [אֲשֶׁר הוּא אֵלִיָּהוּ לְדַעַת יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים בְּתוֹסָפוֹת פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּחֻלִּין (ו.), וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּכֵן הוּא הָאֱמֶת, וּדְקוּשְׁיַת תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם אֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]
connections.quote: “Some explain that wherever “a certain elder” is mentioned, he is Elijah. But this cannot be said of the incident concerning Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in the chapter “Bameh Madlikin.””
connections.context: Tosafot records the identification and immediately objects to making it a universal rule. Rav Tzadok explicitly adopts the identification in the present case while setting the objection aside for discussion elsewhere.

connections.hePhrase: [אֲשֶׁר הוּא אֵלִיָּהוּ לְדַעַת יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים בְּתוֹסָפוֹת פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּחֻלִּין (ו.), וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּכֵן הוּא הָאֱמֶת, וּדְקוּשְׁיַת תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם אֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]
connections.quote: “Although Tosafot wrote that this cannot be said of the incident concerning Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in Shabbat, that refers to the end of the incident: the elder who said that Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai had purified the cemetery, after which the account concludes that he directed his eyes at him, and so forth. But the elder who carried the bundles of myrtle could have been Eliyahu.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the two elders in the Shabbat narrative when discussing Tosafot’s objection. This supplies the precise qualification in his related discussion, while the existing Tosafot note remains unchanged.

connections.hePhrase: לְאַבַּיֵּי (בְּסֻכָּה נב.).
connections.quote: ““For it has acted greatly”: Abaye said: [The evil inclination] provokes Torah scholars more than everyone else.”
connections.context: This statement immediately precedes the story in which an elder reassures Abaye that the greater the person, the greater his inclination. The other note supplies that story; this note supplies Abaye’s own related statement.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ דִּלְעָתִיד לָבוֹא צַדִּיקִים נִדְמֶה לָהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע כְּהַר וּרְשָׁעִים כְּחוּט הַשַּׂעֲרָה,
connections.quote: “As Rabbi Yehudah expounded: In the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will bring the evil inclination and slaughter it before the righteous and before the wicked. To the righteous it appears like a high mountain; to the wicked it appears like a strand of hair. These weep and those weep. The righteous weep and say: How were we able to overcome such a high mountain? The wicked weep and say: How were we unable to overcome this strand of hair? Even the Holy One, blessed be He, marvels with them, as it is written: “Thus says Hashem of hosts: If it is wondrous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, it will also be wondrous in My eyes.””
connections.context: The full saying includes the tears of both groups and Hashem’s wonder. Rav Tzadok explains here how the mountain and the hair can both be true descriptions, corresponding to different strengths of desire.

connections.hePhrase: עַל זֶה אָמַר: "בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם",
connections.quote: “Creating the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace to the far and to the near, says the Lord; and I will heal him.”
connections.context: The promise of healing stands within Isaiah’s rebuke and consolation. Rav Tzadok reads the “far” and the “near” in relation to the possibility of return after severe wrongdoing.

connections.hePhrase: עַל זֶה אָמַר: "בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם",
connections.heRef: ספר ליקוטי מאמרים, עניין שמשון ט׳
connections.quote: “For the Holy One, blessed be He, found no vessel that could hold blessing other than peace, as explained above. The first vessels could not hold the light and the blessing of Hashem because they lacked peace. From the aspect of the encompassing light, He pursues peace, as explained above: He pursues it so that even one who has no peace will have peace. Therefore that light encompasses even the broken vessels, as explained above.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא קַבָּלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה, הֵיפֶךְ הַנֶּאֱמָר: "לָרְשָׁעִים אֵין שָׁלוֹם".
connections.quote: “Great is peace, for it was given to those who repent, as it is said: “Creating the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace to the far and to the near.” Great is peace, for it was given as the portion of the righteous, as it is said: “He shall enter peace; they shall rest upon their beds.” Great is peace, for it was not given as the portion of the wicked, as it is said: “There is no peace, says Hashem, for the wicked.””
connections.context: These three consecutive teachings join the same promises and rebuke from Isaiah 57 that Rav Tzadok reads together: peace for those who return, peace for the righteous, and the denial of peace to the wicked.

connections.hePhrase: וּתְחִלַּת אוֹתָהּ פָּרָשָׁה (יְשַׁעְיָה נז) בַּפָּסוּק "הַנֵּחָמִים בָּאֵלִים וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “You who inflame yourselves among the terebinths, beneath every leafy tree, who slaughter the children in the valleys, beneath the clefts of the rocks.”
connections.context: This is the verse whose words “slaughter the children” the Gemara interprets homiletically in the following note. The later promise of healing in the same chapter is central to Rav Tzadok’s argument.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ (נִדָּה יג.) עַל הַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Ami said: [One who emits seed in vain] is as though he shed blood, as it is written, “You who inflame yourselves among the terebinths … who slaughter the children.” Do not read “slaughterers,” but “squeezers.””
connections.context: The Gemara makes a wordplay between “slaughterers” and “squeezers,” connecting Isaiah 57:5 with wasted seed. Rav Tzadok cites this interpretation before turning to Isaiah’s language of healing.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמַר בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ריט עַמּוּד ב) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehuda said: There is no sin in the world that does not have repentance, except this one; and there is no sinner who does not see the face of the Divine Presence, except this one.”
connections.context: The Zohar is speaking about deliberately wasting seed. Rav Tzadok introduces its severe formulation as a difficulty to be understood alongside Isaiah’s promise of healing; the reader should not mistake the quoted difficulty for his conclusion that return is impossible.

connections.hePhrase: דְּיָדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר דְּשׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית נִקְרָא צַדִּיק, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה.
connections.quote: “Moreover, for this reason they are called righteous. From here we learn: whoever guards this covenant, upon which the world is sustained, is called righteous. From whom do we learn this? From Yosef. Because he guarded the covenant of the world, he merited being called righteous. Therefore: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.””
connections.context: This passage, on Zohar I 59b, supplies the identification used here: the one who guards the covenant is called a tzaddik. Yosef is its example, and the passage connects that title with inheritance of the land.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם קָרָא יְשַׁעְיָה לְיֵצֶר הָרָע "מִכְשׁוֹל", כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סֻכָּה נב.),
connections.quote: “Isaiah called it “a stumbling block,” as it is written, “Build up, build up, clear a way; remove the stumbling block from the way of My people.””
connections.context: The Gemara is listing names of the evil inclination. It identifies the “stumbling block” in Isaiah 57:14 with that inclination, completing the link between the verses Rav Tzadok discusses.

connections.hePhrase: [קָדוֹשׁ הוּא בִּמְקוֹם גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi said: Why was the passage of forbidden sexual relations placed next to the passage of “You shall be holy”? To teach you that wherever you find a boundary against forbidden sexual relations, you find holiness. This agrees with Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi’s teaching that whoever guards himself against forbidden sexual relations is called holy. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi brings proof from the Shunammite woman, as it is written: “She said to her husband: Behold, I know that he is a holy man of God.””
connections.context: The Midrash explicitly connects holiness with maintaining the boundaries against forbidden sexual relations. This is the saying invoked as Rav Tzadok reads “holy” in Isaiah’s promise to dwell with the broken and lowly in spirit.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵיךְ מַשִּׂיג זֶה? יָדוּעַ מַאֲמַר הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק "ה' צִלְּךָ":
connections.quote: ‘Hashem is your guardian; Hashem is your shade at your right hand.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵיךְ מַשִּׂיג זֶה? יָדוּעַ מַאֲמַר הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק "ה' צִלְּךָ":
connections.quote: “The meaning of “Hashem is your shadow” is known: He is like a shadow that does what the person does. Through an awakening below, an awakening is aroused above in all the actions a person performs; everything follows the intention of the heart, as is known.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok states the “shadow” teaching in his own Kedushat Shabbat. The point is the response above to the person’s inner intention and action; here he applies it to profound humility and renewal.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְבָמוֹת סב.) שֶׁיִּכְלוּ הַנְּשָׁמוֹת,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Huna said: He has fulfilled the commandment, on account of Rav Asi’s teaching. For Rav Asi said: The son of David will not come until all the souls in the Guf [the treasury of souls] have been exhausted, as it is said: ‘For the spirit from before Me grows faint,’ and so forth. Rabbi Yochanan said: He has not fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply. We require ‘He formed it to be inhabited,’ and that is absent here.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאֵין בָּזֶה שׁוּם עֵצָה, רַק שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרוֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו אָמַר "וּרְפָאתִיו", שֶׁכְּבָר נִרְפָּא:
connections.quote: “Concerning wasting seed, the Zohar says that repentance does not avail. This is because the drops of seed are drawn from the brain, and the person has damaged the drops of his brain. Repentance is in the heart, as it is written, “His heart will understand and he will return”; therefore it cannot repair wisdom, which is above it. Rather, Torah is needed, for it is the fallen fruit of the wisdom above, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah 17, and it too is in the brain. [It is called “being,” as is known; its numerical value equals that of keri, as I have written elsewhere.] A broken heart, becoming truly as nothing, belongs to keter, which, as is known, is higher still, and this avails. As it is written: “The face of Hashem is against evildoers”—this is that sin, which is called evil—“to cut off from the earth,” and so forth; as it says, “Your people are all righteous,” for inheritance of the land belongs only to the righteous, meaning the one who guards the covenant. It says, “They cried out,” and so forth: prayer is a remedy against being cut off from the earth. [Prayer is rooted in malkhut, the supernal land. His damage reached it, in the manner of “Hashem is your shadow”: exactly like a shadow, it does what he does, whether for good or, Heaven forbid, the reverse.] But to draw near to Hashem, the remedy is a broken heart: “And the crushed in spirit,” and so forth. Likewise, in the psalm “when he had come to Bathsheba,” which was composed concerning a breach of the covenant [which is present from birth, as it says, “For the inclination … from his youth”; therefore he asked, “Create in me a pure heart,” and creation is something new that now springs forth, being from nothing], it says, “For You do not desire a sacrifice,” and so forth [meaning repentance, in the sense of “Whoever sacrifices his inclination and confesses,” Sanhedrin 43b]: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit,” and so forth.”
connections.context: This complete parallel explains why the severe Zohar formulation does not mean that return is impossible. Rav Tzadok describes Torah, prayer, and a broken heart, and ends with David’s request for the creation of a pure heart. These are the same themes of humility, creation anew, and healing developed in the present ois.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הָעוֹבֵר עַל דִּבְרֵי סוֹפְרִים נִקְרָא רָשָׁע כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת כ.).
connections.quote: “‘A prohibition of holiness’ means the secondary forbidden relationships established by the Sages. Why does he call it ‘a prohibition of holiness’? Abaye said: ‘Whoever upholds the words of the Sages is called holy.’ Rava said to him: ‘And someone who does not uphold the words of the Sages is merely not called holy? Is he not also called wicked?’ Rather, Rava said: ‘Sanctify yourself in what is permitted to you.’”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עַל זֶה אָמְרוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים מַאֲמַר חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים פו:):
connections.quote: ‘They said to him: ‘Why did you call yourself Rav Huna?’ He answered: ‘That is the name by which I am known.’ ‘Why did you sit down when they told you to sit on the couch?’ He answered: ‘Do whatever the host tells you (except leave).’’

connections.hePhrase: כָּל מַה שֶּׁיֹּאמַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת עֲשֵׂה – חוּץ מִצֵּא.
connections.quote: “As we heard from our holy master, of blessed memory, on the verse, “The Rock of Israel spoke to me: a righteous one rules over man, ruling through the fear of God”: “Rock” denotes firmness. Hashem gives firmness to the penitent’s heart, as though He had spoken to him personally, enabling him to rule over a righteous man. This means that even concerning matters of which Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said in the holy Zohar that repentance is ineffective, Heaven forbid, the penitent has the power to annul that judgment and repair them. “Ruling through the fear of God” also includes what was spoken by the Holy One, blessed be He, as when a heavenly voice declared, “Return, wayward children, except Acher.” Nevertheless, he could have repaired himself through repentance, because this is Hashem’s will. As the Shelah and Reishit Chokhmah wrote, this is what the Sages hinted at: “Do everything the master of the house tells you, except ‘Leave.’””

connections.hePhrase: כָּל מַה שֶּׁיֹּאמַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת עֲשֵׂה – חוּץ מִצֵּא.
connections.quote: “The rule is that there is nothing that cannot be repaired through repentance. When the Zohar explains that it does not depend on repentance, this means that its repentance is difficult. Being shown that it does not depend on repentance is itself part of that difficulty. Nothing stands in the way of repentance. Even if you hear, “Return, wayward children, except so-and-so,” as in the case of Elisha Acher, pay no heed. After all, Elisha Acher was ultimately accepted even though he did not repent; all the more so, had he repented, it would have helped him still more. Rather, they closed the doors of repentance before him, and he needed to persist until the entrance opened. This is what the Sages meant: “Do whatever the householder tells you, except ‘Leave.’” The householder is the Holy One, blessed be He. Whatever He tells you to do of the mitzvot, do—except “Leave.” If He says to you, “Leave My house and do not enter,” as in Elisha Acher’s case, do not listen to Him; instead, enter through repentance. For this is the householder’s desire, but He is misleading you.”
connections.context: This is the original interpretation behind “except ‘Leave.’” The apparent rejection is itself a test of persistence: the passage expressly distinguishes difficult repentance from impossible repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קס עַמּוּד א) הִמְלִיץ כָּל עִנְיַן מְרַגְּלִים עַל הַתּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ‘‘But the people are strong’ (Numbers 13:28): one must be strong enough to take no account at all of worldly affairs, because one must have abundant wealth in order to devote oneself to Torah. Who can attain it? Indeed, ‘But the people who dwell in the land are strong’: anyone who wishes to attain it must be powerful in wealth, as it says: ‘A rich man answers harshly’ (Proverbs 18:23). ‘And the cities are great and fortified’: houses filled with every good thing, lacking nothing. Even with all this, ‘We also saw the descendants of the giant there’: a strong body is needed, mighty as a lion (being found there continually), because it exhausts a person’s strength to labor over what is forbidden and permitted, impure and pure, valid and invalid. Who can attain it? Furthermore, ‘Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev’ (Numbers 13:29). If a person says that despite all this he will attain it, ‘Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev’: this is the evil inclination, the prosecutor who accuses a person and is constantly present in the body. ‘And the Hittite and the Amorite,’ and so forth: how many accusers are there, so that a person cannot enter that world at all! Who can merit it, and who can enter it? With these words, ‘They discouraged the hearts of the children of Israel’ (Numbers 32:9), for they brought out a bad reputation concerning it, as it says: ‘They brought out a slanderous report of the land.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קס עַמּוּד א) הִמְלִיץ כָּל עִנְיַן מְרַגְּלִים עַל הַתּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ““Hebron”—this is Torah; one who occupies himself with it is called a companion. … “Hebron was built seven years”: these are the seventy aspects of Torah, seventy aspects, ten on each side.”
connections.context: The Zohar interprets the spies’ journey as an encounter with Torah. Calling Hebron “Torah” makes the allegorical setting explicit; Rav Tzadok then applies the spies’ discouragement and the response to it to spiritual effort.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה.): "חוּצְפָּתָא – מַלְכוּתָא בְּלָא תָּגָא"
connections.quote: ‘Rav Nachman said: Insolence is effective even toward Heaven. At first it is written, ‘You shall not go with them,’ but in the end it is written, ‘Arise, go with them.’ Rav Sheshet said: Insolence is kingship without a crown, as it is written: ‘Today I am weak, though anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are harder than I,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, כִּידוּעַ "מַלְכוּת" הוּא כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְ"כֶתֶר" הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים נ״ב:ג׳-ד׳
connections.quote: “This source is called “the revealed world,” “the Matron,” “the lower Mother,” and “Shekhinah,” from the expression “I shall dwell among them.” It is so called because this source is the beginning of the revelation of the light of the Infinite, which it draws down and illuminates into the worlds in a revealed manner. From this source, the particular light and vitality appropriate to each one is drawn forth, dwelling and clothing itself within them to give them life. Therefore it is metaphorically called “the mother of the children” and “Knesset Yisrael”: from this source the souls of Atzilut were emanated, the souls of Beriah were created, and so forth. All of them come only from the extension of vitality and light from this source called Shekhinah, like the extension of light from the sun.”
connections.context: Knesset Yisrael here names the shared spiritual source of Israel’s souls. This explains why the ois can speak of Israel collectively through a single feminine figure.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, כִּידוּעַ "מַלְכוּת" הוּא כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְ"כֶתֶר" הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 28
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 28
connections.quote: “Boldness means audacity: kingship without a crown, even though it is effective even toward Heaven. “Toward” means “against” in the holy tongue—that is, opposition; one who opposes the will of the blessed God can also accomplish something. Therefore Yosef too attained kingship through the intensity of his desire for it, as his brothers said to him, “Will you indeed reign over us?” His dreams likewise arose from his thoughts during the day. He attained it by the strength of his righteousness, and this is “kingship without a crown.” “Crown” means the beginning and hidden root of every complete structure of ten sefirot, as is known. It means an extension of kingship that has no root in its upper source, from whose power comes enduring existence. It exists only in the extension of the nine attributes revealed in this world, through the force of his righteousness, good deeds, and intense desire for it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the metaphor directly: the crown is the hidden root that gives rule enduring existence. This distinguishes power won by intense personal striving from power rooted in the divine will.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה מט:): "בְּעִקְּבוֹתָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא חוּצְפָּא יִסְגֵּא", שֶׁאָז הוּא הָעֵת לָזֶה
connections.quote: ‘In the footsteps of the Messiah, insolence will increase and prices will soar. The vine will yield its fruit, yet wine will be expensive. The kingdom will turn to heresy, and there will be no rebuke. The meeting house will become a place of prostitution; Galilee will be laid waste, and Gavlan will be desolate. People from the border regions will wander from city to city, and no one will show them favor.’

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְעָתִיד: "נְקֵבָה תְּסוֹבֵב גָּבֶר", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: (31:22 on Sefaria): “How long will you turn this way and that, wayward daughter? For Hashem has created something new on earth: a woman will encompass a man.”
connections.context: The words “a woman will encompass a man” close the verse that follows the summons to return. Rav Tzadok reads the reversal as a figure for initiative arising from below.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְעָתִיד: "נְקֵבָה תְּסוֹבֵב גָּבֶר", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: ““For Hashem has created a new thing in the land”: He will create a new thing after you have remained in exile for many days. What is the new thing? “A woman shall go about a man.” Ordinarily, the man seeks and goes about after the woman, as the Sages likewise said: The owner of a lost object searches for his lost object. Then the woman will go about after her husband. That is, the children of Israel will return to Hashem their God, and He will redeem them. Likewise, in Hoshea’s prophecy: “Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek Hashem their God and David their king, and they shall come trembling to Hashem and to His goodness in the latter days.””
connections.context: Radak identifies the woman’s initiative with Israel returning to God. His explanation supplies the prophetic meaning of the reversal of the ordinary pattern of seeking.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמַר לָהֶם מֹשֶׁה: "וְהִוא לֹא תִצְלָח",
connections.quote: ‘Moses said: Why are you transgressing Hashem’s command? This will not succeed.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֵין לְךָ שׁוּם מִדָּה וְכֹחַ שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ צַד טוֹב גַּם כֵּן,
connections.quote: “God made man upright, so that all of him should be good, even the turbidity and residue within him. The anger in the liver should be only the anger of the Sages, which is good on every side, and only where Hashem commands anger. These are the holy powers of severity, from whose side Torah proceeds; it therefore contains laws of judgment.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בָּהּ כְּפִי רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “But in perfecting one’s character, even when the traits are naturally implanted within him, he should not employ them merely because of his nature, but for the sake of Heaven, to act according to the will of the blessed God. When he acts harshly where God does not desire compassion, he is the truly compassionate person, for this is compassion toward truth: acting harshly toward them is “a benefit to them and a benefit to the world.” Through “I shall cut off the horns of the wicked,” “the horns of the righteous shall be raised,” and all abundance and blessing increase in the world through this.”
connections.context: This parallel states the ois’s governing principle in direct terms: a natural trait gains its proper value through the purpose for which it is used.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שָׁאוּל שֶׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ בַּעֲבוּר הָרַחְמָנוּת,
connections.quote: ““Do not be excessively righteous, and do not be overly wise”: Do not be more righteous than your Creator. This speaks of Shaul, as it is written, “Shaul came to the city of Amalek.” Rabbi Huna and Rabbi Benaya say: He began arguing against his Creator, saying: The Holy One, blessed be He, said, “Go and strike Amalek.” If the men sinned, what did the women sin? What did the children sin? What did the cattle, ox, and donkey sin? A heavenly voice went forth and said, “Do not be excessively righteous”—more than your Creator. The Sages say: He began arguing from the heifer whose neck is broken, saying: Scripture says, “They shall break the heifer’s neck there in the wadi.” He kills, yet she has her neck broken! If a human being sinned, what did the animal sin? A heavenly voice went forth and said, “Do not be excessively righteous.” Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: Whoever becomes compassionate where severity is called for will ultimately become cruel where compassion is called for. From where do we know that he became cruel where compassion was called for? It is stated, “He struck Nob, the city of the priests, by the sword.” Should Nob not have been treated at least like the offspring of Amalek? The Sages say: Whoever becomes compassionate where severity is called for will ultimately be struck by the attribute of judgment, as it is stated, “Shaul and his three sons died.””
connections.context: The Midrash contrasts compassion governed by the divine command with a personal impulse that can turn into cruelty elsewhere. Rav Tzadok uses this contrast to explain why even an attractive character trait needs to be directed toward God.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְגִטִּין (נו.): עַנְוְתָנוּתוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי זְכַרְיָה בֶּן אַבְקוּלַס הֶחֱרִיבָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: Rabbi Zecharyah ben Avkulas’s forbearance destroyed our House, burned our Sanctuary, and exiled us from our land.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְהֵיפֶךְ אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת סג.):
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: If a Torah scholar takes vengeance and bears a grudge like a snake, gird him around your waist. If an unlearned person is pious, do not live in his neighborhood.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְתַלְמִיד חָכָם – רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר אֲשֶׁר כָּל מְגַמּוֹתָיו רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ – אַדְּרַבָּה הוּא טוֹב מְאֹד,
