connections.quote: ““Nor did my fellow’s curse come upon my bed”—as with Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman, who, when going up to his bed, would say: May everyone who has distressed me be released and forgiven. As for the statement that any Torah scholar who does not take vengeance and bear a grudge like a snake is no Torah scholar: that concerns someone who sinned against him in matters of Heaven, and disciplining those who sin.”
connections.context: Ritva distinguishes forgiveness of personal injury from firmness in matters of Heaven. This is the qualification needed for the ois’s contrast between natural anger and anger directed toward a sacred purpose.

connections.hePhrase: עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): "טוֹב מְאֹד" – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע.
connections.quote: ““And behold, it was very good”—this is the evil inclination. Can the evil inclination be very good? Rather, without the evil inclination a person would not build a house, marry a wife, have children, or engage in business.”
connections.context: The Midrash points to the constructive activity that would cease without desire. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the energy of desire from its sinful use and discusses its eventual rectification.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּגַאֲוָה (בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּסוֹטָה ה.): בְּשַׁמְתָּא מַאן דְּלֵית בֵּיהּ.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Chiyya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav: A Torah scholar needs to have one eighth of an eighth [of pride]. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said: It crowns him like the awn on an ear of grain. Rava said: Under a ban is one who has [excessive] pride, and under a ban is one who lacks [even a little of] it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן הַנְּבִיאִים הָיוּ מְיַלְּלִים עַל אָבְדַן הָאֻמּוֹת: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב וְגוֹמֵר" וְכַיּוֹצֵא,
connections.quote: ‘My heart cries out for Moab. Her fugitives reach as far as Zoar, the strong heifer. They climb the ascent of Luchit weeping; on the road to Choronaim they raise a cry of ruin.’

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שִׁבְּחוּם עַל זֶה בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק).
connections.quote: “See the difference between the prophets of Israel and the prophets of the idolaters. The prophets of Israel warn Israel against transgressions, as it is stated, “You, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman,” and so forth. The prophet who arose from the nations made a breach through which to destroy creatures from the world. Moreover, all the prophets showed compassion toward Israel and toward the idolaters. Thus Yirmeyahu says, “My heart moans for Moab like flutes,” and likewise Yechezkel: “Son of man, raise a lament over Tyre.” But this cruel one arose to uproot an entire nation for nothing, without cause. Therefore the account of Bilam was written, to make known why the Holy One, blessed be He, removed the holy spirit from the idolaters: this one arose from among them, and see what he did.”
connections.context: The Midrash’s evidence includes Israel’s prophets mourning for Moab and Tyre. It therefore makes their compassion broader than concern for their own people, and contrasts this with Bilam’s destructive purpose.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְוַדַּאי לֹא חָסוּ עַל אִיבּוּד גּוּפָם, כִּי "בַּאֲבֹד רְשָׁעִים רִנָּה"
connections.quote: ‘When the righteous prosper, the city rejoices; when the wicked perish, there are shouts of joy.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְאוּלַי יִהְיֶה "לִבִּי" עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ה, ב): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה י:): הוּא אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ],
connections.quote: ““I am asleep, but my heart is awake; it is the sound of my beloved knocking: Open for me, my sister, my love, my faultless dove, for my head is filled with dew, my locks, drops of night” (Song of Songs 5:2). “I am asleep” – the congregation of Israel said before the Holy One blessed be He: Master of the universe, “I am asleep” regarding the mitzvot, “but my heart is awake” for acts of kindness. “I am asleep” regarding acts of charity, “but my heart is awake” to perform them. “I am asleep” regarding the offerings, “but my heart is awake” for reciting Shema and Amida. “I am asleep” regarding the Temple, “but my heart is awake,” in synagogues and study halls. “I am asleep” regarding the end [of days], “but my heart is awake” for the redemption. “I am asleep” regarding the redemption, but the heart of the Holy One blessed be He is awake to redeem me. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said: Where have we found that the Holy One blessed be He is called the heart of Israel? It is from this verse, as it is written: “But God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalms 73:26).”

connections.hePhrase: [וְאוּלַי יִהְיֶה "לִבִּי" עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ה, ב): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה י:): הוּא אֵינוֹ שָׂשׂ],
connections.quote: ‘Does the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoice at the downfall of the wicked? Is it not written: ‘As they went out before the armed force, they would say: Give thanks to Hashem, for His kindness is everlasting’? Rabbi Yochanan said: Why is ‘for He is good’ not said in this thanksgiving? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק יָדוּעַ: כָּל אֻמָּה הוּא כֹּחַ מְיוּחָד, ע' אֻמּוֹת וְע' כֹּחוֹת בַּנֶּפֶשׁ.
connections.quote: “The totality of good character traits consists of seven, each containing ten. Corresponding to them are the seventy souls who descended to Egypt, each one a distinct power in holiness. Opposite them are seventy nations, each one a distinct power in the realm of impurity, expressed in a particular evil trait; their roots are the seven nations of the Land of Israel.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok supplies the numerical structure behind the phrase “seventy nations and seventy powers of the soul”: seven root traits, each comprising ten aspects.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַיּוֹם הַהוּא יִגְדַּל הַמִּסְפֵּד בְּאָבְדַן הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב.),
connections.quote: “What is the reason for that mourning? Rabbi Dosa and the Sages disagree: One says it is for Messiah son of Joseph, who was killed; the other says it is for the evil inclination, which was killed.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבַיּוֹם הַהוּא יִגְדַּל הַמִּסְפֵּד בְּאָבְדַן הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב.),
connections.quote: “In the future the Holy One, blessed be He, brings the evil inclination and slaughters it before the righteous and the wicked. To the righteous it appears like a high mountain, and to the wicked like a strand of hair. Both weep.”
connections.context: The Gemara explicitly gives the interpretation that the mourning concerns the destruction of the evil inclination. Rav Tzadok explores what may be lost when the power that had driven struggle and achievement is removed.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "יָפָה שָׁעָה אַחַת בִּתְשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִכָּל חַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא", וְאָז יִהְיֶה בִּכְלָל.
connections.quote: “He used to say: One hour of repentance and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come; and one hour of contentment in the World to Come is better than all the life of this world.”
connections.context: The Mishnah preserves both sides of the comparison: this world offers the distinctive opportunity for repentance and action, while the World to Come offers a kind of contentment beyond earthly life.

connections.hePhrase: [עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנִּתְאוֹנֵן קֹהֶלֶת וְכֵן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת עַל הַיַּלְדוּת,
connections.quote: “It was taught: Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma says: Two [legs] are better than three [two legs and a staff]. Woe for the one thing that goes away and does not return! What is it? Rav Chisda said: Youth. When Rav Dimi came, he said: Youth is a crown of roses; old age is a crown of thorns.”
connections.context: The saying laments the physical powers of youth that cannot be recovered. The ois sets this physical decline beside the different trajectory of wisdom acquired through Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשָּׁנִינוּ: זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וְכוּלֵי דַּעְתָּן מִתְיַשֶּׁבֶת וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Akashya says: As the elders of the unlearned grow older, their minds become more confused, as it is stated, “He removes speech from the trusted, and takes away the judgment of elders.” But the elders of Torah are not so: as they grow older, their minds become more settled, as it is stated, “With the aged is wisdom, and with length of days is understanding.””
connections.context: The Mishnah gives the exact contrast cited here: the loss of physical youth need not entail a decline in the wisdom of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ה) מֵחֲשִׁיבוּת הַזְּקֵנִים, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת –
connections.quote: ““Moshe and Aharon went and gathered,” and so forth. Rabbi Akiva said: Why are Israel compared to a bird? Just as a bird flies only with its wings, so Israel can endure only through the elders. Great is the standing of the elders: if they are old, they are beloved before the Holy One, blessed be He; if they are young, their youth takes a secondary place. Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai taught: In several places we learned that the Holy One, blessed be He, accorded honor to the elders. At the burning bush, it is written, “Go and gather the elders of Israel.” At Sinai, it is written, “To Moshe He said: Ascend to Hashem,” and so forth. At the Tent of Meeting, it is written, “Moshe called Aharon and his sons,” and so forth. In the future as well, it is stated, “For Hashem of hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders there will be honor.””
connections.context: The Midrash presents the elders as indispensable to Israel’s endurance and traces their honor through successive revelations. Its reference to young elders shows that this standing is not simply a measure of physical age.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֹחַ בִּלְעָם בַּחֲצִיפוּת שֶׁלָּמְדוּ מִמֶּנּוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה.),
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman said: Bold persistence is effective even toward Heaven. At first it is written, “Do not go with them,” and afterward it is written, “Rise, go with them.” Rav Sheshet said: Boldness is kingship without a crown.”
connections.context: Both sayings occur in the discussion of Balaam’s persistence. Rav Tzadok considers how that force may be redirected toward holiness, while distinguishing it from Balaam’s use of it.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הָיָה רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם, דּוּגְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, קצג עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: “Moses had no equal among the upper crowns; Balaam had no equal among the lower crowns. This one was on the side of holiness, and that one on the side of the left.”
connections.context: The Zohar explains the comparison of Moses and Balaam by placing their powers on opposite spiritual sides. Rav Tzadok invokes the correspondence, not an equality of their moral standing.

connections.hePhrase: [מח] לֹא יִתְחַבֵּר עִם רְשָׁעִים, וַאֲפִילּוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach applies the same verse to avoiding an appearance of joining another's wrongful purpose

connections.hePhrase: [מח] לֹא יִתְחַבֵּר עִם רְשָׁעִים, וַאֲפִילּוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
connections.quote: “So too with King David, who went with Achish king of Gat (I Samuel 29–30) and did not wish to benefit from the spoil, for this too was contrary to proper judgment. Although he did not share their intention—his intention was for Heaven—it nevertheless says, ‘Do not walk in the way with them’ (Proverbs 1:15). That is: even when you are not inwardly going with them, refrain from them in such a way that others cannot mistakenly think you are going with them.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach applies ‘Do not walk in the way with them’ to David's association with Achish. Even an inward intention for Heaven does not remove the need to prevent others from reasonably reading the association as participation in their purpose. This adds a distinct outward dimension to the siman's warning about joining a wicked partner for an apparently good end. The full source also examines removing personal benefit, rather than treating intention alone as sufficient clarification.
connections.headline: Sincere intention does not remove the meaning of association

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הוּא מְפוֹרָשׁ בַּמְּכִילְתָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּהִתְחַבֶּרְךָ עִם אֲחַזְיָהוּ פָּרַץ ה' אֶת מַעֲשֶׂיךָ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב כ, לז),
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דַעֲמָלֵק ג׳:י׳
connections.quote: “As it is stated, “Because you associated with Achazyahu, Hashem has shattered your works.” From here the Sages said: A person should not associate with a wicked person, even in order to bring him close to Torah.”
connections.context: This supplies the Mekhilta’s actual inference, beyond the biblical verse already quoted in the existing note. It is the strong formulation that Rav Tzadok is explaining at the opening of this ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הוּא מְפוֹרָשׁ בַּמְּכִילְתָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּהִתְחַבֶּרְךָ עִם אֲחַזְיָהוּ פָּרַץ ה' אֶת מַעֲשֶׂיךָ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב כ, לז),
connections.quote: ‘Eliezer son of Dodavahu, from Mareshah, prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying: ‘Because you joined yourself to Ahaziah, Hashem has wrecked your undertakings.’ The ships were broken and could not sail to Tarshish.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "בְּנִי, אַל תֵּלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ אִתָּם" (מִשְׁלֵי א, טו),
connections.quote: ‘My son, do not walk on the road with them; keep your foot away from their path.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא לה:) גַּבֵּי יוֹסֵף: "לִהְיוֹת עִמָּהּ" – לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: ‘‘To lie beside her’—in this world; ‘to be with her’—in the World to Come. It follows that Hillel holds the poor accountable, Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom holds the wealthy accountable, and Joseph holds the wicked accountable.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא רַק קִבּוּל שָׂכָר וְלֹא עוֹנֶשׁ, דְּזֶה אֵין נִקְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא.
connections.quote: “There is also absence in the world. This is because deficiency adheres to created existence: existence is not absolutely complete, but absence adheres to the creation of the world. This is Gehinnom, which is the absence of created existence. Therefore, whoever is suited to destruction and absence comes to Gehinnom, where there is absence and deficiency of created existence. When the Holy One, blessed be He, brought the plague of darkness upon Egypt, He brought absence upon them, because absence and deficiency adhere to creation.”
connections.context: Maharal uses Gehinnom to describe privation—the loss or absence of created being. This clarifies the terminology Rav Tzadok uses when contrasting loss with the positive good of the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת יוֹסֵף נָשָׂא בִּתָּהּ וּמֵהֶם יָצָא שֵׁבֶט בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל וּמָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף.
connections.quote: “The Midrash says that she saw that he would marry her daughter, for Potiphar is Poti-phera. Elsewhere it is said that Asenath was Dinah’s daughter from Shechem. Certainly both are true, except that one who raises a child is regarded as having given birth to the child. They raised her, and therefore she is called their daughter; presumably they truly have a connection to her like that of a parent who gave birth. Thus Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him, is called the son of Bityah.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reconciles the two accounts of Asenath’s parentage through the significance of upbringing. He retains a real connection between the child and the people who raised her, which helps explain the reference to “her daughter.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיוֹסֵף רָאָה גַּם כֵּן זֶה שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה יֵצֵא שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת גְּדוֹלָה כָּזוֹ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: [The passages are adjacent] to place Tamar’s act beside the act of Potiphar’s wife. Just as this one acted for the sake of Heaven, so did that one. For Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: She saw in her astrology that she was destined to have a son from him, but she did not know whether it would be from herself or from her daughter. Thus it is written, “Those who announce by the months some of what will come upon you.” Rabbi Aivu said: “Some of what”—not all of what.”
connections.context: The Midrash speaks of Potiphar’s wife and her incomplete knowledge. Rav Tzadok develops the implications for Yosef; the original passage itself attributes the astrological vision to her.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה י:): יָצְתָה בַּת קוֹל "מִמֶּנִּי וְכוּלֵי", וּלְמִצְוָה יֵחָשֵׁב
connections.quote: ““She is more righteous than I”: How did he know? A heavenly voice went forth and said: From Me came forth these hidden matters.”
connections.context: The Gemara concerns Judah’s acknowledgment of Tamar. The heavenly voice attributes the concealed course of the events to God; Rav Tzadok applies that statement to the emergence of the Davidic line.

connections.hePhrase: [מט] כָּל אֶחָד יֵדַע שֶׁבַּמֶּה שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ תּוֹקְפוֹ בְּיוֹתֵר, הוּא כְּלִי מוּכָן לְאוֹתָם דְּבָרִים בְּיוֹתֵר לִהְיוֹת נְקִיִּים וְזַכִּים אֶצְלוֹ.
connections.quote: “Just as, from the subject a person most desires to study, he can understand that he has been reincarnated to complete that matter, so a person must know the root of his soul, from where it is drawn, and what he has come to repair and complete, as the Zohar on Song of Songs says concerning “Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” and so forth. To understand this, he should see which mitzvah his inclination most forcefully urges him to neglect, and strengthen himself to fulfill it. Certainly he has been reincarnated for that mitzvah. To prevent him from completing his task, his inclination opposes him and urges him to neglect it, so as to take him from the world empty-handed. Thus you find among the accomplished sages of the Talmud that, through their great wisdom, they perceived which mitzvah they had been reincarnated to fulfill, and held firmly to it more than to the other mitzvot. As it is said in Shabbat 118b, Rav Yosef asked Rav Yosef son of Rabba: In which mitzvah was your father especially careful? He answered: In the mitzvah of tzitzit, and so forth. Others were careful in other mitzvot, because through their wisdom they recognized what they had come to complete.”
connections.context: The source explicitly connects unusually strong resistance to a particular task of spiritual repair. Its parallel with a person’s preferred area of Torah study supplies the two ways of discerning that task.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כא) שֶׁבְּאֵבֶר שֶׁבּוֹ חָטָא, בּוֹ יַעֲשֶׂה מִצְווֹת;
connections.quote: ‘‘With this Aaron shall enter.’ This is what Scripture says: ‘For with strategies you shall wage war’ (Proverbs 24:6). Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Acha said in Rabbi Simon’s name: If you have made bundles of transgressions, make corresponding bundles of mitzvot. Against ‘haughty eyes’ (Proverbs 6:17), set ‘They shall be frontlets between your eyes’ (Deuteronomy 6:8). Against ‘a lying tongue’ (Proverbs 6:17), set ‘You shall teach them to your children’ (Deuteronomy 11:19). Against ‘hands that shed innocent blood’ (Proverbs 6:17), set ‘Bind them as a sign upon your hand’ (Deuteronomy 6:8). Against ‘a heart devising wicked thoughts’ (Proverbs 6:18), set ‘These words shall be’ (Deuteronomy 6:6). Against ‘feet that hurry to run to evil’ (Proverbs 6:18), run after the mitzvah of circumcision, which is between the knees. Against ‘a false witness who breathes lies’ (Proverbs 6:19), set ‘You are My witnesses, declares Hashem’ (Isaiah 43:12). Against ‘one who spreads strife among brothers’ (Proverbs 6:19), set ‘Seek peace and pursue it’ (Psalms 34:15). Rabbi Yochanan interpreted the verse in terms of helmsmen, for Rabbi Yochanan said: A person should always make himself a helmsman, planning how he can perform a mitzvah. Rabbi Benaah interpreted the verse in terms of Mishnah study, for Rabbi Benaah said: A person should always immerse himself in Mishnah study, so that if he becomes blocked, the Mishnayot will open a way for him—into Talmud if he seeks Talmud, or into aggadah if he seeks aggadah. Rabbi Elazar said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name: Mishnah is an iron pillar.’

connections.hePhrase: [כְּמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא פַּרְצוּפִים שָׁוִים, וּפַרְצוּף פָּנִים רוֹמֵז עַל צֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים דְּנֶפֶשׁ],
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: One who sees a multitude of Israel says: Blessed is the Knower of secrets, for their minds are not alike and their faces are not alike.”
connections.context: The Gemara pairs differences of understanding with differences of appearance. Rav Tzadok uses this as a basis for the distinct task belonging to each soul.

connections.hePhrase: כְּנוֹדָע מַאֲמַר הַקַּדְמוֹנִים עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת קיח:): "אֲבוּךְ בְּמַאי זָהִיר טְפֵי?".
connections.quote: “Rav Yosef said to Rav Yosef, the son of Rabba: ‘In what was your father especially careful?’ He answered: ‘In tzitzit. One day he was going up the stairs when a thread broke, and he did not come down until he had attached it.’ And Abaye said: ‘May I be credited for this: whenever I see a Torah scholar who has completed his tractate, I make a festive day for the scholars.’”

connections.hePhrase: כְּנוֹדָע מַאֲמַר הַקַּדְמוֹנִים עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת קיח:): "אֲבוּךְ בְּמַאי זָהִיר טְפֵי?".
connections.quote: “Therefore, according to the spark of a person’s soul, he is especially bound to fulfill the mitzvot of that part. For one who belongs to the aspect from the loins upward does not have the mitzvah of removing forbidden fat [as his particular task of rectification], since he does not need it. But if he eats it, he will certainly cause damage; nevertheless, he will not initially be reincarnated for this. Therefore the early masters, who knew where their spark depended, attached themselves to certain mitzvot more than to others. One who understands will understand. [Gloss—Tzemach: This is the meaning of their question: In what was your father especially careful?]”
connections.context: This passage discusses a soul’s particular work of rectification and the reason for reincarnation. It expressly retains the damage caused by transgression even when that mitzvah is not the soul’s primary task; the distinction does not exempt anyone from observing the mitzvah.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּזֶה אָמְרוּ (גִּטִּין מג.): אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbah bar Rav Huna then had a spokesman stand beside him and expounded: ‘And this stumbling block is under your hand’—a person does not arrive at an understanding of words of Torah unless he has first stumbled over them. Although they said that one who betroths half a woman has not effected a betrothal, the betrothal of a woman who is half a slave and half free is valid. Why? In the former case he left part out of his acquisition; in the latter he left nothing out of his acquisition.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּזֶה אָמְרוּ (גִּטִּין מג.): אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל,
connections.quote: “The moment of the inclination’s enticement between one spiritual level and another is the descent that the righteous undergo for the sake of ascent, as is known concerning “A righteous person falls seven times and rises.” This was the meaning of Rephidim after the splitting of the sea, when they were proceeding to the giving of the Torah, a higher level. When a person succeeds in overcoming it immediately, the descent is scarcely felt at all: he falls for only a moment and rises at once. There is only a momentary slackening; he immediately remembers, takes it to heart, and strengthens himself like a lion for Hashem’s service. The greater the subsequent ascent, however, the greater the preceding descent. For a great ascent the inclination grows stronger, one corresponding to the other, and the power that overcomes it is correspondingly greater.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּזֶה אָמְרוּ (גִּטִּין מג.): אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, then showed him the clarifications and suffering he would still need to undergo, and promised him concerning them, ‘I will guard you wherever you go and return you to this land.’ ‘I will return you’ is an expression of restoring a lost thing. For a person does not truly grasp words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them (Gittin 43a): through the stumbling that happens to a person, the words of Torah enter his heart with a greater desire than before. This is ‘I will return you’—an expression of teshuvah.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads Hashem's promise to return Yaakov as both the restoration of something lost and teshuvah. The same statement about learning through stumbling is explained through an increased desire that brings the Torah into the heart. This identifies a positive result of the repair described here: a deeper attachment to the very Torah in which one stumbled. The subject is the return from a stumbling that occurred, not an instruction to seek one.
connections.headline: What the stumbling can restore

connections.hePhrase: הֲלֹא תִרְאֶה: אָחָז חָתַם הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קג:) וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה מב) שֶׁמָּנַע תִּינוֹקוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית רַבָּן, אָמַר: אִם אֵין גְּדָיִים וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Ahaz suspended the service and sealed the Torah, as it is written, “Bind the testimony, seal the Torah among My disciples.””
connections.context: The statement describes Ahaz’s suppression of worship and Torah. Rav Tzadok contrasts that obstruction with the exceptional spread of Torah under Ahaz’s son Hezekiah.

connections.hePhrase: הֲלֹא תִרְאֶה: אָחָז חָתַם הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קג:) וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה מב) שֶׁמָּנַע תִּינוֹקוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית רַבָּן, אָמַר: אִם אֵין גְּדָיִים וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Ahaz said: If there are no kids, there will be no goats; if there are no goats, there will be no flock; if there is no flock, there will be no shepherd. Thus he reasoned: If there are no children, there will be no students; if there are no students, there will be no sages. … Rabbi Chunya son of Elazar said: Why was his name Ahaz? Because he seized the synagogues and study halls.”
connections.context: The Midrash explains Ahaz’s plan to end Torah learning by stopping children’s education. This gives the precise sense of Rav Tzadok’s compressed “if there are no kids, etc.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאִיתָא סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא קַמָּא וּפֶרֶק ב דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כ.), וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא עַם הָאָרֶץ בְּיָמָיו כִּדְאִיתָא בְּחֵלֶק (צד:) עַיֵּין שָׁם – מַמָּשׁ הַהִיפּוּךְ:
connections.quote: “They laid a Torah scroll on his bier and said: This one fulfilled what is written in this [scroll].”

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאִיתָא סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא קַמָּא וּפֶרֶק ב דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כ.), וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא עַם הָאָרֶץ בְּיָמָיו כִּדְאִיתָא בְּחֵלֶק (צד:) עַיֵּין שָׁם – מַמָּשׁ הַהִיפּוּךְ:
connections.quote: ““Grace is false”—this is the generation of Moses; “beauty is vain”—this is the generation of Joshua; “one who fears the Lord shall be praised”—this is the generation of Hezekiah.”
connections.context: The first source describes the honor given to Hezekiah; the second praises the stature of his generation. Together with Sanhedrin 94b, quoted separately, they support Rav Tzadok’s contrast between Ahaz and Hezekiah.

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאִיתָא סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא קַמָּא וּפֶרֶק ב דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כ.), וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא עַם הָאָרֶץ בְּיָמָיו כִּדְאִיתָא בְּחֵלֶק (צד:) עַיֵּין שָׁם – מַמָּשׁ הַהִיפּוּךְ:
connections.quote: ‘What did he do? He planted a sword at the entrance to the study house and said: Anyone who does not occupy himself with Torah shall be pierced with this sword. They searched from Dan to Beersheba and found no unlearned person; from Gevat to Antipras, they found no boy or girl, man or woman, who was not proficient in the laws of impurity and purity.’

connections.hePhrase: [נ] עַל כָּל מִינֵי יְשׁוּעוֹת שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָאָדָם יֵשׁ "בְּעִתָּהּ" וַ"אֲחִישֶׁנָּה": זָכוּ – "אֲחִישֶׁנָּה", לֹא זָכוּ – "בְּעִתָּהּ" (סַנְהֶדְרִין צח.).
connections.quote: ‘The smallest will become a thousand, and the least will become a mighty nation. I, Hashem, will hasten it in its time.’

connections.hePhrase: [נ] עַל כָּל מִינֵי יְשׁוּעוֹת שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָאָדָם יֵשׁ "בְּעִתָּהּ" וַ"אֲחִישֶׁנָּה": זָכוּ – "אֲחִישֶׁנָּה", לֹא זָכוּ – "בְּעִתָּהּ" (סַנְהֶדְרִין צח.).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Alexandri said: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi raised a contradiction. It is written, “In its time,” and it is written, “I shall hasten it.” If they merit it, “I shall hasten it”; if they do not merit it, “In its time.””
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes the appointed time from an earlier arrival brought by merit. This supplies the source for the ois’s discussion of “in its time, I shall hasten it.”

connections.hePhrase: וַ"אֲחִישֶׁנָּה" הַיְינוּ "טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ", שֶׁמַּקְדִּים רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה.
connections.quote: ‘Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear.’

connections.hePhrase: וַ"אֲחִישֶׁנָּה" הַיְינוּ "טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ", שֶׁמַּקְדִּים רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה.
connections.quote: ““After these events”—after what? Rava said: After the Holy One, blessed be He, had created a remedy for the blow. For Reish Lakish said: The Holy One, blessed be He, does not strike Israel unless He first creates a remedy for them, as it is stated, “When I would heal Israel, the sin of Ephraim is revealed.” But it is not so with the nations of the world: He strikes them and afterward creates a remedy for them, as it is stated, “Hashem will strike Egypt, striking and healing.””
connections.context: The saying is introduced through the order of events in Esther. Both the rule about Israel and the contrasting order for the nations are retained, so the quoted principle keeps its original scope.

connections.hePhrase: וַ"אֲחִישֶׁנָּה" הַיְינוּ "טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ", שֶׁמַּקְדִּים רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Chayei Sarah 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Chayei Sarah 4
connections.quote: “‘Yitzchak had come from coming,’ and so forth; ‘Yitzchak went out to converse,’ and so forth; ‘he saw, and behold,’ and so forth. Yitzchak was the root of all forms of fear in the world, even in refraining from action, as it is written, ‘He dwelt in the land of the Negev’—dried of every craving. Avraham our father recognized this quality in Yitzchak's soul and knew his great fear of taking any positive action, so he sent his servant to arrange a match for him. In truth, this was from Hashem, for the time had come for Yitzchak our father to marry. Yitzchak too began to awaken inwardly to ‘He did not create it for emptiness,’ and so forth. Yet because he feared taking practical action, he went out to converse in the field and pray that Hashem help him and bring him his match, for there is a person whose match comes to him (Moed Katan 18b). He was answered immediately in his prayer: ‘He raised his eyes,’ and so forth, for ‘Before they call, I answer.’”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach applies ‘Before they call, I answer’ to Yitzchak: Avraham has already sent his servant while Yitzchak is only now becoming inwardly ready to ask. His prayer and the arrival of the answer meet. This illustrates the siman's account of anticipatory help through an actual biblical narrative. The passage does not make the timing of an immediate answer a test of another petitioner's worth.
connections.headline: The answer already being prepared

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁרָמַז רָבָא לְרַב עִילִישׁ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קלג:) בַּמֶּה שֶׁקָּרָא עָלָיו "בְּעִתָּהּ אֲחִישֶׁנָּה",
connections.quote: “Rav Ilish, before Rava, thought to say that the second beneficiary also takes. Rava said to him: Is that how the judges of compromise judge?”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁרָמַז רָבָא לְרַב עִילִישׁ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קלג:) בַּמֶּה שֶׁקָּרָא עָלָיו "בְּעִתָּהּ אֲחִישֶׁנָּה",
connections.quote: “He was embarrassed. [Rava] applied to him the verse, “I am the Lord; in its time I will hasten it.””
connections.context: Rava corrected Rav Ilish before his proposed inheritance ruling was acted upon, then applied the verse to console him. The speaker is Rava, not Rav, as the opening of the exchange establishes.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁרָמַז רָבָא לְרַב עִילִישׁ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קלג:) בַּמֶּה שֶׁקָּרָא עָלָיו "בְּעִתָּהּ אֲחִישֶׁנָּה",
connections.heRef: רשב"ם על בבא בתרא קל״ג ב:ג׳:ב׳
connections.quote: ““He applied the verse to him”: Rava did so to console him: “I am Hashem; in its time I shall hasten it.” At the time when the righteous need salvation, the Holy One, blessed be He, provides it for them. So too with you: I know that no erroneous judgment has ever come about through you, for now the Holy One, blessed be He, arranged for me to be here before you reached a ruling, and you did not stumble.”
connections.context: Rashbam specifies that Rava arrived before Rav Ilish issued the ruling. This is the distinction the ois draws between beginning to make a mistake and allowing an erroneous judgment to take effect.

connections.hePhrase: [נא] כָּל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם בִּשְׁבִירַת הַיֵּצֶר בַּתַּאֲווֹת נִקְרָא חֵן וְיוֹפִי לְבַד, שֶׁהוּא שֶׁקֶר וָהֶבֶל שֶׁאֵינוֹ קִיּוּם לָעַד,
connections.quote: “For truth is that which endures forever, as it is said, “A truthful lip will be established forever.” As stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Sanhedrin, this is why it is the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He; see there.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok uses endurance as the measure of truth. This explains why a victory whose continuation is uncertain can be called “false” or “vain,” even though the effort at that moment has value.

connections.hePhrase: [נא] כָּל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם בִּשְׁבִירַת הַיֵּצֶר בַּתַּאֲווֹת נִקְרָא חֵן וְיוֹפִי לְבַד, שֶׁהוּא שֶׁקֶר וָהֶבֶל שֶׁאֵינוֹ קִיּוּם לָעַד,
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, God grants His help only to those who seek His help in prayer, as it is said, “The Lord is near to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth.” It resembles the community of Israel’s request, “Return us, Lord, to You,” and afterwards, “we shall return.””
connections.explanation: The Kislev passage supplies the practical content of the siman’s instruction to seek Hashem’s assistance: one asks for it in prayer. Its ordering of ‘Return us’ before ‘we shall return’ explains why Rav Tzadok distinguishes enduring reliance from an isolated act of self-mastery. The person still seeks and returns, but does not treat the strength needed for the next struggle as an acquired possession.
connections.headline: Prayer turns dependence on divine help into an act of avodah

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין כ.): "שֶׁקֶר הַחֵן" – זֶה יוֹסֵף
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: What is the meaning of ‘Grace is false, and beauty is fleeting’? ‘Grace is false’ refers to Joseph; ‘beauty is fleeting’ refers to Boaz. ‘One who fears Hashem shall be praised’ refers to Palti ben Layish.’

connections.hePhrase: [אֵינוֹ יוֹפִי גָּמוּר, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה לו:) שֶׁיָּצְאוּ טִפִּין, לָכֵן נִקְרָא שֶׁקֶר],
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Joseph was worthy of having twelve tribes descend from him, just as they descended from his father Jacob, as it is said: ‘These are the generations of Jacob: Joseph.’ However, his semen emerged from between the fingernails of his hands. Nevertheless, they descended from his brother Benjamin, and all were named in reference to him, as it is said: ‘The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הוּא נִקְרָא פַּלְטִיאֵל, שֶׁפְּלָטוֹ וְכוּלֵי, זָכָה לְסִיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא וְלֹא מֵהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ:
connections.quote: “It is written “Palti,” and it is written “Paltiel.” Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Palti was his name. Why was he called Paltiel? Because God delivered him from the transgression. What did he do? He planted a sword between himself and her and said, “Whoever engages in this act shall be pierced by this sword.” But is it not written, “Her husband went with her”? He became like a husband to her. But is it not written, “Walking and weeping”? He wept over the mitzvah that was leaving him. “As far as Baḥurim”: the two of them had remained like youths who had not experienced intercourse.”
connections.context: The passage supplies both details invoked here: Paltiel’s name signifies divine deliverance, and his tears were over the loss of the opportunity to refrain from sin. Rav Tzadok reads these together as evidence of the special assistance Palti received.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי יֵדַע שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא בַּעַל הַכֶּרֶם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא פג:), וְיוֹדֵעַ טִיבוֹ שֶׁל כֶּרֶם יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנּוּ, וּמְתַקֵּן צְרָכָיו בְּכָל עֵת וָרֶגַע.
connections.quote: ‘He sent word to him: ‘I am clearing the thorns from the vineyard.’ He sent back: ‘Let the owner of the vineyard come and clear away his thorns.’ One day a laundryman encountered him and called him ‘vinegar, son of wine.’ He said: ‘Since he is so brazen, it follows that he is wicked.’ He told them: ‘Arrest him.’ They arrested him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין צח.) אָמְרוּ שֶׁבֶּן דָּוִד אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיָּבוֹא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב, דְּיַעֲמִיד מֶלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: The son of David comes only in a generation that is entirely meritorious or entirely guilty.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין צח.) אָמְרוּ שֶׁבֶּן דָּוִד אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיָּבוֹא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב, דְּיַעֲמִיד מֶלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua said: If they do not repent, are they not redeemed? Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises over them a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman’s, and Israel repents and He brings them back to the good.”
connections.context: The passage answers how redemption can come when Israel has not yet repented: severe circumstances bring about repentance. Rav Tzadok sets this beside the saying that the generation of redemption may be wholly meritorious or wholly culpable.

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אֵיזֶה דּוֹר חָבִיב מִכָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת? זֶה דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁזָּכוּ לְקַבָּלַת תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “When he saw an upright person, he would seat two mockers beside him, and they would ask him, “Which generation was more beloved than all the generations?” He would answer them, “The generation of the wilderness.” They would say to him, “Did they not worship idols?” He would tell them, “Because they were beloved, they were not punished.” They would say to him, “Be quiet, for the king wants to do the same.” Moreover, they made one, whereas this king made two: “He placed one in Bethel, and the other he placed in Dan.””
connections.context: This is a report of Jeroboam’s mockers manipulating an upright person’s answer to promote idolatry. Rav Tzadok cites the identification of the wilderness generation as beloved; the surrounding exchange must not be read as the Talmud endorsing the mockers’ argument or granting permission to sin.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עַל דּוֹרוֹ שֶׁל שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמְרוּ (מוֹעֵד קָטָן ט.) שֶׁנִּתְבַּשְּׂרוּ לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁזָּכוּ לְבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Parnach said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: That year Israel did not observe Yom Kippur. They worried and said: Perhaps Israel has incurred destruction. A heavenly voice went forth and said to them: You are all destined for the life of the World to Come.”
connections.context: The setting is the dedication of Solomon’s Temple, whose celebration included eating on Yom Kippur. Their fear and the heavenly reassurance are both necessary to Rav Tzadok’s comparison.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב וְיִתְהַפְּכוּ לְדוֹר חָבִיב עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יְבִיאֵם לִתְשׁוּבָה,
connections.quote: “All the prophets commanded repentance, and Israel is redeemed only through repentance. The Torah has already promised that Israel will ultimately repent at the end of their exile and immediately be redeemed, as it is said: “When all these things come upon you,” and “You shall return to the Lord your God,” and “The Lord your God will restore,” and so forth.”
connections.context: Rambam joins the necessity of repentance to the promise that Israel will ultimately return. This is the basis for hope that even a guilty generation can be brought to repentance and redemption.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הִמְשִׁילוּם רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד.) לְאָסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי חִילְפֵי,
connections.quote: ‘‘Israel has sinned.’ Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is still Israel. Rabbi Abba said: This is what people say: A myrtle growing among nettles is still named myrtle, and myrtle is what they call it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַדְּרַבָּה, שׁוֹשַׁנָּה שֶׁבֵּין הַחוֹחִים חֲשׁוּבָה יוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קפט עַמּוּד ב)
connections.quote: ‘He opened and said: ‘Like a rose among the thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters’ (Song of Songs 2:2). The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to make Israel according to the pattern above, so that there would be one rose on earth corresponding to the upper pattern. A rose that gives off fragrance and is distinguished from all the other roses in the world is precisely the one that grows among thorns. This is the fitting way. Therefore He sowed seventy pairs, which were seventy souls, and brought them among the thorns. As soon as those pairs were there, those thorns put forth branches and leaves and ruled over the world. Then the rose blossomed among them.’

connections.hePhrase: וּתְשׁוּבָה אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד כִּדְמוּכָח בְּפֶרֶק ב דְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:),
connections.quote: ‘‘On condition that I am righteous’—even if he is completely wicked, she is betrothed, for perhaps he entertained a thought of repentance. ‘On condition that I am wicked’—even if he is completely righteous, she is betrothed, for perhaps he entertained a thought of idolatry.’

connections.hePhrase: וּתְשׁוּבָה אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד כִּדְמוּכָח בְּפֶרֶק ב דְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:),
connections.quote: “The essence of repentance is a resolve in the heart alone, for through this one is called completely righteous even if previously completely wicked, as explained in Kiddushin 49b. Even verbal confession, although it is a positive commandment of the Torah, “They shall confess,” is a separate mitzvah and does not prevent the repentance itself, whose essence is in the heart alone: regretting the past and resolving in one’s heart not to return to folly and not to sin again. Although this is not revealed to anyone—not even to the ministering angels, who do not know what is in the heart—it is revealed before Heaven, and the person is truly called completely righteous. This applies even if his sins have mounted exceedingly high: the statement there applies to every completely wicked person, even one who has transgressed the whole Torah. Beit Shmuel and Ḥelkat Meḥokek, in Even HaEzer [38], write that even if he stole and has not returned the stolen property, sincerely accepting in his heart that he will return it is effective.”
connections.context: The instantaneous change is sincere repentance: regret and a real commitment to cease sin and repair what is owed. The passage preserves confession as an independent mitzvah and requires a genuine intention to restore stolen property; it does not cancel those duties. The cross-reference is Even HaEzer 38: Beit Shmuel 38:55 and Chelkat Mechokek 38:44 discuss this point.

connections.hePhrase: וּתְשׁוּבָה אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד כִּדְמוּכָח בְּפֶרֶק ב דְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:),
connections.quote: “At the close of Yom Kippur we likewise say seven times, “YHVH is God.” After Israel has repented and the gate of freedom—Binah, the world to come—has been revealed, this unity is mentioned seven times; seven is the number of completeness. This follows “Then you will understand ... and find knowledge of God”: one attains the inward knowledge through which this particular unity is attained, as in “Know today.” Every year Chanukah is a time when anyone can merit to repair his deeds so that they are reckoned as merits. If he opens one opening of repentance, like the point of a needle, through an awakening from his side, God is ready to help him attain the full repentance that turns deliberate sins into merits.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah distinguishes the person’s tiny opening from the complete repentance that Hashem helps bring about. This clarifies how the present siman can join a change occurring in one instant with a generation’s eventual transformation. The initial turn is real and should not be postponed; its completion is received through continued return and divine assistance, culminating in the transformation of deliberate sins into merits.
connections.headline: A moment of return can open a process completed with divine help

connections.hePhrase: וְאָנוּ מְבַקְּשִׁים "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְגוֹמֵר", רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צוֹוֵחַ "שׁוּבוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה סוֹף אֵיכָה),
connections.quote: ““Return us, Lord, to You, and we shall return.” The community of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “Master of the world, it is for You to return us.” He said to them: “It is for you,” as it is said, “Return to Me and I shall return to you, says the Lord.” She said before Him: “Master of the world, it is for You,” as it is said, “Restore us, God of our salvation.” Therefore it is said, “Return us, Lord, to You, and we shall return.””
connections.context: This is the dialogue explicitly cited in the Hebrew. Israel asks God to initiate its return, while God calls on Israel to return to Him. Rav Tzadok applies this dialogue to the final generation’s need for divine assistance.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִרְצֶה, הֲרֵי בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד יִכְלוּ כָּל הַקּוֹצִים הַסּוֹבְבִים וְיִהְיֶה הַכֹּל כִּרְצוֹנוֹ,
connections.quote: “For in the end Israel is redeemed only through repentance, and they will prevail in their plea, “Return us to You,” so that even the awakening to repentance comes from Hashem. Likewise, for each individual soul of Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, helps it attain its perfection and taste the blessings of Jacob our father, peace be upon him: “I will guard you” and “I will bring you back.” These are the thoughts of repentance that enter the heart of themselves. Sometimes Hashem arranges circumstances that awaken a person to repentance, or something similar, so that ultimately our plea prevails: Hashem Himself also opens the needle’s-eye opening in the heart for complete repentance, in truth and with a whole heart.”

connections.hePhrase: [נג] דִּבּוּר שֶׁל חוֹל הַמּוּרְגָּל בְּפִי הָאָדָם וּמַרְגְּלָא בְּפוּמֵיהּ, הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ אֲפִילּוּ אֵצֶל אִישׁ הַהֲמוֹנִי מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל,
connections.quote: “The eighth day of Chanukah is called “Zot Chanukah.” Although this name is not mentioned among the early authorities, since it is used by most of Israel, it certainly has a place in words of Torah. We find something even greater: the Gemara cites “This is what people say,” and this becomes words of Torah in the Talmud. The root of the name is the passage read on that day, “This was the dedication of the altar”; presumably this has a connection to the holiness of the day.”
connections.explanation: Rav Tzadok applies the principle here to a name used by the Jewish people, even though that name is not recorded among the early authorities. He connects ‘Zot Chanukah’ to the day’s Torah reading and holiness. The example helps explain what it means to look for a soul’s Torah-root within habitual speech: one seeks the particular scriptural and spiritual content expressed by it, rather than dismissing it as merely commonplace.
connections.headline: An accepted name can disclose Torah within Israel’s ordinary speech

connections.hePhrase: וּבְפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (ז.) הַרְבֵּה: "הַהוּא דַּהֲוָה קָאָמַר וְאָזֵיל וְכוּלֵי, וַאֲמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: קְרָא כְּתִיב".
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 7
connections.linkedRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 7
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 7
connections.heRef: ספר ליקוטי מאמרים, ספר יהושע ז׳
connections.quote: “Every kind of wisdom expressed in popular sayings, provided it is true wisdom and truthful speech, is alluded to in the Torah. It is all present there in allusion and concealment. Later, over the course of the generations, it comes to light through the sages and interpreters of each generation and through all the individual souls, each of which brings forth a new insight for which it was specifically prepared.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (ז.) הַרְבֵּה: "הַהוּא דַּהֲוָה קָאָמַר וְאָזֵיל וְכוּלֵי, וַאֲמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: קְרָא כְּתִיב".
connections.quote: ‘There was a man who would go about saying: ‘A thief is not put to death for two or three thefts.’ Shmuel said to Rav Yehudah: It is written in Scripture: ‘Thus said Hashem: For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn it back.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לוֹ אֲחִיזָה בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מְיוּחֶדֶת כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: “All Israel also has a share in the Oral Torah, for even every unlearned Israelite possesses some matter of wisdom related to the Oral Torah, though it is completely concealed within him. Of the future it is said, “For they will all know,” meaning that their knowledge will emerge from concealment into revelation. Therefore the Zohar says that even an ordinary person’s words have substance, and sometimes a pearl is found in a poor person’s basket. In many places the Gemara says, “This is what people say,” and those words are Torah. At the beginning of Sanhedrin it records “A certain person used to say,” and these are words of Torah, as in many other places. Concerning this it says, “Who is wise? One who learns from every person,” for every person has some new matter of wisdom belonging specifically to the root of his soul, which can be learned from him. “You are called adam, but the nations of the world are not called adam”: only in each Israelite is there a particular matter of Oral Torah belonging to the root of his soul. An understanding person can learn it from him even if he himself knows nothing. But “those who seek the Lord understand everything”: from his conversations and speech about worldly matters they can grasp a matter of wisdom at the root of his soul that is concealed within it.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the specific Torah content Rav Tzadok seeks within ordinary habitual speech: a matter of wisdom belonging to that person’s soul-root. It is not a claim that every casual utterance, regardless of content, automatically becomes a Torah ruling.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי הַדִּבּוּר הוּא יְסוֹד הַנֶּפֶשׁ, תַּרְגּוּם "נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה" – "רוּחַ מְמַלְּלָא", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסִיקְתָּא: אֵין בֵּין צַדִּיקִים הַחַיִּים לַמֵּתִים אֶלָּא הַדִּבּוּר, זֶהוּ יְסוֹד הַחַיּוּת].
connections.quote: “The Lord God formed the human being from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and it became in the human being a speaking spirit.”
connections.context: Onkelos renders the verse’s “living soul” as “a speaking spirit.” Rav Tzadok cites this wording to connect a person’s speech with the expression of the soul.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי הַדִּבּוּר הוּא יְסוֹד הַנֶּפֶשׁ, תַּרְגּוּם "נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה" – "רוּחַ מְמַלְּלָא", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסִיקְתָּא: אֵין בֵּין צַדִּיקִים הַחַיִּים לַמֵּתִים אֶלָּא הַדִּבּוּר, זֶהוּ יְסוֹד הַחַיּוּת].
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: What does “They shall sing upon their beds” mean? That they praise the Holy One, blessed be He, there. Rabbi Ḥama son of Rabbi Yose said: The only difference between the living and the righteous dead is speech alone. They praise the Holy One, blessed be He, there, where their souls are bound in the bond of life, as it is written, “May my master’s soul be bound in the bond of life.” Therefore it says “They shall sing”: singing means praise, as it is written, “The sound of song and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.””
connections.context: The cited midrash speaks specifically about the righteous dead and their continuing praise. Rav Tzadok draws from its distinction the special role of spoken expression in embodied life.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִי הַאי גַּוְונָא בְּרֵישׁ פְּסָחִים: הַהוּא דַּהֲוָה אָמַר וְכוּלֵי, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ מִדָּן קָאָתֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם:
connections.quote: ‘There was a man who would say: ‘Judge my case.’ They said: This shows that he comes from Dan, as it is written: ‘Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel.’’

connections.hePhrase: [נד] (מִכְּתַב יַד קָדְשׁוֹ)
connections.displayRef: Tzvi Leshem, “From Tzidkas HaTzaddik to HaMalei to HaShalem: The Printing Stages of Tzidkas HaTzaddik” (Hebrew), The Librarians, National Library of Israel blog, 28 February 2018
connections.quote: The first edition (Lublin, 1902), prepared for the press by Rav Tzadok's son-in-law R' Baruch David HaKohen, left out whole sections, printing in their place notices such as “אות נד חסר,” and cut parts of Sections 102, 121 and 161 without notice. (The Lublin printing of 1913 still marks Sections 69, 74, 75, 103, 105, 146, 162 and 163 as missing.) R' Michael Mokotowski, a chasid of Rav Tzadok, travelled to Lublin and copied the omitted material from the author's manuscript into his copy of the book; his son, R' Avraham Eliyahu Kitov, printed it, marked (מכת"י), in Tzidkas HaTzaddik HaMalei (Jerusalem, 1968). Section 162, missing from that copy, was printed by R' Yehoshua Mondshine in Sifsei Tzaddikim 4 (1992), pp. 27–29, apparently from a four-page manuscript of the omissions bound into Gershom Scholem's copy of the first edition at the National Library of Israel.

connections.hePhrase: עִיקַּר הַיַּהֲדוּת – בִּקְרִיאַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:11
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:11
connections.quote: “The difference was only in the point within the heart. As the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 32:5), they were redeemed on account of four things. The intent of all four is that they distinguished themselves as a people of their own and called themselves ‘Israel.’ Even though no other distinguishing sign was visible, merely bearing the name and being set apart from the peoples by that name alone sufficed. [Therefore the book begins, ‘These are the names of the children of Israel’: this distinction of the name ‘children of Israel’ alone is the foundation of the Torah.] As the Sages stated at the beginning of the chapter Kelal Gadol (Shabbat 68b), even a child taken captive among the nations and a convert who converted among the nations is called someone who knew the fundamental principle of Shabbat and forgot it. So too with all Israel in Egypt then: because they were distinguished as a people of their own, although in practice ‘these worship idols,’ and so forth, they were considered to know the fundamental principle of Torah in the point within the heart. Knowledge of Torah lay hidden within them; it was merely forgotten and needed to be recalled.”
connections.explanation: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik develops the same name-of-Israel argument through the generation in Egypt and the same case of a captive child or convert. Its concluding description is significant: Torah knowledge is hidden in the heart, forgotten, and needs to be recalled. This helps explain what the siman means by the sufficiency of the name as a foundation of belonging, while the cited case itself continues to recognize obligations and the need to learn them.
connections.headline: The name preserves a beginning that calls for remembrance

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "זֶה יֹאמַר לַה' אָנִי, וְזֶה יִקְרָא בְשֵׁם יַעֲקֹב, וְזֶה יִכְתֹּב יָדוֹ לַה', וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּה" (יְשַׁעְיָה מד, ה).
connections.quote: ‘One will say, ‘I belong to Hashem’; another will call himself by Jacob’s name; another will write upon his hand, ‘For Hashem,’ and take the name Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כְּלָל גָּדוֹל (שַׁבָּת סח:) גֵּר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּיר בֵּין הָאֻמּוֹת, וּמֵבִיא חַטָּאת עַל הַחֵלֶב וְהַדָּם וְהַשַּׁבָּת וַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish both say: This applies specifically to someone who knew of Shabbat and later forgot; a child taken captive among non-Jews, or a convert who converted while living among non-Jews, is exempt. An objection was raised: They stated a broad rule about Shabbat: Anyone who forgets the very principle of Shabbat and performs many prohibited labors on many Shabbatot is liable for only one offering. What case does this describe? A child taken captive among non-Jews, or a convert who converted while living among non-Jews, who performs many prohibited labors on many Shabbatot is liable for only one sin offering. He is also liable for one offering for consuming blood, one for consuming forbidden fat, and one for idolatry. Monbaz exempts him.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כְּלָל גָּדוֹל (שַׁבָּת סח:) גֵּר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּיר בֵּין הָאֻמּוֹת, וּמֵבִיא חַטָּאת עַל הַחֵלֶב וְהַדָּם וְהַשַּׁבָּת וַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
connections.quote: “Rav and Shmuel both say: Even a child captured among gentiles, and a convert who converted among gentiles, is like one who knew [the law] and later forgot, and is liable.”
connections.context: The discussion treats a convert who never learned the laws of Shabbat. The following baraita and opposing opinion, cited in the neighboring note, debate the resulting liability. The point here is the recognized possibility of conversion without that knowledge.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִמְצָא שֶׁלֹּא יָדַע כְּלָל מִכָּל הַתּוֹרָה, וּבַמֶּה הוּא גֵּר לְהִתְחַיֵּיב חַטָּאת? רַק בִּקְרִיאַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּי.
connections.quote: “It is written, “All the families of the earth shall be blessed through you”: even someone from among the idolaters who wishes to enter Israel, circumcises himself, and accepts upon himself the yoke of the commandments will be called by the name of Israel and will be included in “Your people are all righteous.””

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הֲמָרַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַד, זֶה שָׁקוּל כְּכָל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ וּכְנֶגֶד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים, וְעַיֵּין בָּרַדְבַּ"ז מִזֶּה.
connections.quote: “Consequently, in the case before us I say that it follows all the more that he must suffer death rather than transgress. If concerning one Torah commandment they said that one must suffer death rather than transgress, how much more so one whom they coerce to abandon the entire religion, become one of the peoples of the land, and deny the whole Torah of Moses. There is another consideration: he must acknowledge that among them there was a person whose stature is higher than that of Moses our teacher, and this undermines the entire religion. Moreover, once he follows their religion he may transgress the grave prohibitions without realizing it.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "חֲבוּר עֲצַבִּים אֶפְרָיִם, הַנַּח לוֹ" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ד, יז),
connections.quote: ‘Ephraim is bound to idols; leave him alone.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֵם בְּחִיבּוּר אֻמָּה אַחַת וְלֹא נִתְפָּרְדוּ לְהִתְחַבֵּר עִם הַגּוֹיִם וְלִהְיוֹת בִּכְלָלָם:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar HaKappar said: Great is peace, for even when Israel themselves practice idolatry, if they form one united company, the attribute of judgment does not touch them, as it is said, “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him.””
connections.context: This is the midrashic reading of “joined” as the people’s joining together. Rav Tzadok uses it to explain the protective significance of their continuing bond as one people, while the conduct described remains idolatry.

connections.hePhrase: [נה] עִיקַּר הָעֲבֵירוֹת בָּאִים מֵחֲמַת הַשִּׁכְחָה, שֶׁהוּא בַּלֵּב כִּדְאִיתָא בִּמְגִילָּה (יח.),
connections.quote: “And how do we know that this remembrance means reading? Perhaps it means merely reflecting! That cannot be, for it is written: ‘Remember.’ Could this mean in the heart? When it says, ‘Do not forget,’ forgetting in the heart has already been addressed. How, then, do I fulfill ‘Remember’? With the mouth.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ זוֹכֵר בַּמּוֹחַ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵינוֹ זוֹכֵר בַּלֵּב;
connections.quote: “In any event, from what is written a person should reflect on how great the level of complete faith is and how much diligence is needed to root complete faith in his heart. Although every Israelite truly believes in the reality of His providence, blessed be He, and all the details of the principles of faith, it is nevertheless not yet rooted in the heart so as to be revealed through the powers of action that issue from the heart, such that this faith will never be forgotten.”
connections.context: The distinction is between accepting the truth intellectually and having it firmly present in the heart so that it governs action. This supplies Rav Tzadok’s fuller explanation of remembering in the mind while forgetting in the heart.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁהַיֵּצֶר מַעֲלִימוֹ מִלִּבּוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: “The point is that the evil inclination’s principal activity is to make a person forget, as it is said, “If you indeed forget,” and in many similar verses. The Gemara says that when the evil inclination is active, no one remembers the good inclination. The letters of “the darkness” are the letters of “forgetfulness.””

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁהַיֵּצֶר מַעֲלִימוֹ מִלִּבּוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: “Jeshurun grew fat and kicked—you grew fat, thick, and covered over. He abandoned the God who made him and spurned the Rock of his salvation.”
connections.context: The verse describes prosperity turning into forgetfulness and rebellion. Rav Tzadok uses it to explain why spiritual security can itself become a test.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְנָחוֹת מד.) בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּתַלְמִיד שֶׁזָּכַר עַל יְדֵי הַצִּיצִית,
connections.quote: “His four fringes came and struck him across the face. He slipped down and sat on the ground; she too slipped down and sat on the ground.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְנָחוֹת מד.) בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּתַלְמִיד שֶׁזָּכַר עַל יְדֵי הַצִּיצִית,
connections.quote: “There is one mitzvah that the Lord our God commanded us, called tzitzit. “I am the Lord your God” is written concerning it twice: I am the One who will exact punishment, and I am the One who will give reward. Now they appeared to me like four witnesses.”
connections.context: At the point when the man was about to sin, the tzitzit recalled the command and its accountability, and he withdrew. The original excerpt stopped before that decisive event.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם הָיָה מֵזִיד וְיוֹדֵעַ, רַק שֶׁעָמְדוּ הַצִּיצִית נֶגְדּוֹ, שֶׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ הַזְּכִירָה רַק מִן הַמּוֹחַ לַלֵּב.
connections.quote: “Concerning tzitzit it is explicitly stated, “You shall see it,” and “You shall not stray,” and so forth. The wording “You shall not stray” does not imply that the thought will be completely uprooted from the heart, but that one will have the strength to reject it. For as long as a person remembers the yoke of Heaven’s kingship, the yoke of Torah and the yoke of mitzvot that rest upon him, he can readily rebuke the inclination and reject every thought outside this. The inclination’s activity is only to make him forget this. As they said in Nedarim 32b, when the evil inclination is active no one remembers the good inclination, as it is said, “No person remembered,” and so forth. At that time the good thoughts of the unity of the Creator, blessed be He, are forgotten from the heart and are not recalled.”
connections.context: Tzitzit restores the awareness needed to reject the temptation. The passage carefully distinguishes gaining the power to dismiss a thought from having the thought’s root completely removed.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם הָיָה מֵזִיד וְיוֹדֵעַ, רַק שֶׁעָמְדוּ הַצִּיצִית נֶגְדּוֹ, שֶׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ הַזְּכִירָה רַק מִן הַמּוֹחַ לַלֵּב.
connections.quote: “The mitzvah of tzitzit points to this, as stated in Tanna Devei Eliyahu: tzitzit was given after the sin of the wood gatherer. Its words are: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe, ‘Why did this man profane Shabbat?’ Moshe said before Him, ‘Master of the world, I do not know.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said, ‘I will tell you. Throughout the six weekdays an Israelite has tefillin on his head and arm; he sees them and turns back from his deeds. But on Shabbat, when he has no tefillin, he therefore profaned Shabbat.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said, ‘Go and choose for them a mitzvah practiced also on Shabbat and festivals’—this is tzitzit, and so forth. This indicates why Hashem gave Israel tzitzit: it is true that at their root they are encompassed by His light. But because Hashem desires human service, He established the possibility of a person stepping outward and experiencing a concealed place. Through tzitzit one brings forth the precious from the worthless: the person serving Hashem brings it out of concealment and returns before Hashem. He then has a share in the service, and the service is called by his name.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef places the same Midrash about the wood gatherer within the dispute with Korach. Israel's connection to divine light at its root does not dispense with practical reminders: concealment makes conscious return through a mitzvah necessary. This develops the siman's distinction between already knowing the command in the mind and remembering it actively in the heart. The reminder awakens a present response, rather than supplying a previously unknown prohibition.
connections.headline: Why an inward connection still needs a visible reminder

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּנְדָרִים (ח.): נִשְׁבָּעִים לְקַיֵּים הַמִּצְווֹת,
connections.quote: “But is he not already bound by an oath from Mount Sinai? Rather, this teaches us that a person may urge himself on in this way. Rav Giddel also said in Rav’s name: One who says, ‘I shall rise early and study this chapter,’ or ‘I shall study this tractate,’ has made a great vow to the God of Israel. But he is already bound by an oath, and one oath does not take effect upon another oath! What is this teaching us—that it is permitted even merely to urge oneself on? That is already Rav Giddel’s first teaching!”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּמוּשְׁבָּע וְעוֹמֵד מֵהַר סִינַי – לְזָרוֹזֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ;
connections.quote: “Oaths, however, serve only to prohibit what is otherwise permitted. They do not apply at all to a matter already commanded: neither to violating a negative commandment nor to keeping it, nor to neglecting a positive commandment, such as “I swear that I will not make a sukkah” or “I will not put on tefillin.” They do not take effect even for fulfilling a positive commandment. If someone swears to fulfill the mitzvah and does not fulfill it, he incurs no liability on account of the oath—neither lashes nor an offering. It is simply permitted to stir oneself to action, as it is written, “I have sworn and shall uphold it, to keep Your righteous ordinances.””
connections.context: This is Ramban’s stated view of an oath to fulfill an existing mitzvah. It supplies the premise for Rav Tzadok’s question: if the oath adds no such liability, what does its power to motivate accomplish? The answer here concerns awakening the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה זֵּירוּז הוּא? אֲבָל הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ:
connections.quote: “One may add further: concerning someone who is not established as wicked, it is known that the evil inclination does not immediately entice him to a transgression. Rather, it makes him forget the severity of the prohibition and presents reasons why it is no transgression at all. This is why Nedarim 8a says that one may swear to fulfill the mitzvot. Vayikra Rabbah 23 and Midrash Ruth, on the verse “As the Lord lives,” say that Joseph, David and Boaz swore against their inclination. Although a person is already under oath from Mount Sinai, the inclination presents the act as permitted, so that he thinks he is not violating the oath at Sinai. Against this the new oath is effective.”
connections.context: Here Rav Tzadok explains the practical effect of the additional oath: it counters the inclination’s concealment and rationalization of a known prohibition. This develops the closing answer that the oath brings what is known into active awareness in the heart.

connections.hePhrase: [נו] הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נָתַן הַתּוֹרָה בְּעַל כָּרְחָם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Avdimi son of Chama son of Chasa said: This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, held the mountain over them like a vat and said: If you accept the Torah, well and good; if not, there will be your burial. … Rava said: Nevertheless, they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus.”
connections.context: The Gemara contrasts acceptance under the mountain’s compulsion with the later renewed acceptance. Rav Tzadok uses the first stage to describe an awakening imposed from above.

connections.hePhrase: [נו] הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נָתַן הַתּוֹרָה בְּעַל כָּרְחָם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
connections.quote: ““Israel His dominions”: dominion denotes rule without consent, as they explain “Will you reign over us, or will you indeed rule over us?” Likewise, “For kingship belongs to Hashem, and He rules over the nations”: among them Hashem is called a ruler. It is written, “Surely with a strong hand … I will reign over you,” and at the giving of the Torah He held the mountain over them like a vat. Nevertheless, it is written, “They gathered at Your feet.” This means that at their root Israel wanted to be compelled, and at the root this is the quality of kingship.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes compulsion as it appears outwardly from the inward root’s willing acceptance. That qualification explains how the imposed awakening discussed here can still belong to Israel’s bond with Hashem.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לֶעָתִיד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּיָד חֲזָקָה... אֶמְלוֹךְ עֲלֵיכֶם"
connections.quote: ‘As I live, declares the Lord Hashem, I will surely reign over you with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and wrath poured out.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה.) קְרָאוּהוּ "רִתְחָא",
connections.quote: ‘‘What has entered your minds will never happen: you say, “We will be like the nations, like the families of the lands, serving wood and stone.” As I live, declares Hashem God, surely with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will reign over you.’ Rav Nachman said: Let the Merciful One become as angry with us as that, and redeem us!’

connections.hePhrase: [וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה.) קְרָאוּהוּ "רִתְחָא",
connections.quote: ““All such wrath”—would that this anger should come upon us: “With fury poured out I will reign over you,” so that He would redeem us against our will and reign over us.”
connections.context: Rashi makes explicit why Rav Nachman welcomes the wrath described by the verse: it brings redemption and the renewal of Hashem’s rule. The existing Gemara note remains the surrounding source.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי אַתָּה אָבִינוּ" שֶׁיִּצְחָק הוּא הַגּוֹאֵל עַל יְדֵי מִדָּתוֹ].
connections.quote: see note 125.
connections.context: After Abraham and Jacob do not secure a favorable answer in the preceding dialogue, Isaac pleads on Israel’s behalf and then directs their praise to God. That role is the point Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צָרִיךְ כָּל אֶחָד לְיִסּוּרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרָכִין (טז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: “What is the least measure of suffering? Rabbi Elazar said: A garment was woven for him to wear, and it does not suit him. … They said something less than this: they intended to mix [his drink] with hot water and mixed it with cold, or with cold and mixed it with hot.”
connections.context: The Gemara includes small frustrations within the category of suffering. Rav Tzadok’s comparison depends on that broad scale, not only on exceptional calamity.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מְעוֹרֵר לְמַעְלָה לִמְשׁוֹל עָלָיו בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ כְּמוֹ אָדוֹן עַל עֶבֶד.
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 3:6
connections.linkedRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 3:6
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 3:6
connections.heRef: אור זרוע לצדיק, ענין גלות מצרים ג׳:ו׳
connections.quote: “Circumcision is the self-restraint that comes from fear, through the designation “Master,” with Hashem present before one’s eyes, as stated in the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chayim: the awareness that there is One who watches over us. Therefore the nations are called uncircumcised, but the house of Israel is not, as stated in Nedarim and as I explained above in section one. This is the level of a servant, as it is said, “If I am a master, where is My fear?” He may not deviate at all from his master’s will.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "מָה ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה", וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יַדְרִיכְךָ בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת בְּעַל כָּרְחֲךָ.
connections.quote: “And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, except to fear Hashem your God, to walk in all His ways, to love Him, and to serve Hashem your God with all your heart and all your soul; to keep Hashem’s commandments and statutes, which I command you today, for your good.”
connections.context: The complete sentence joins fear with walking in Hashem’s ways, love, service, and observance. Rav Tzadok develops the opening “except to fear” as the human awakening that draws divine guidance.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ מִצְוַת צִיצִית עַל זֶה, שֶׁהִיא לְיִרְאָה כַּנּוֹדָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף שְׁלַח דִּתְכֵלֶת הִיא יִרְאָה,
connections.quote: “Tekhelet is awe, and white indicates kindness and love, as is known. This is “You shall see it and remember all the commandments of Hashem.” Awe is the foundation of the prohibitions, and love is the foundation of the positive commandments. The testing of tekhelet with leaven, and so forth, as stated in Menachot 44a, means that through the strength of the inclination and the leaven in the dough its appearance does not depart, because of the depth of awe. We do not now possess such powerful awe; we use only white. For, as is known, from afar love is easier than awe, because from afar Hashem appears to us more in the aspect of love and attachment.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok interprets tekhelet and white as awe and love, and reads the dye test symbolically as resistance to temptation. His concluding statement describes the spiritual condition he is discussing; the passage supplies the symbolism behind this ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ מִצְוַת צִיצִית עַל זֶה, שֶׁהִיא לְיִרְאָה כַּנּוֹדָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף שְׁלַח דִּתְכֵלֶת הִיא יִרְאָה,
connections.quote: ““You shall not stray after your hearts”: it will keep other evil ways from you. Certainly, “you shall not stray,” and you shall not do evil. For this reason the blue color arises. This is tekhelet, which resembles the Throne of Glory. Just as the Throne of Glory causes a person to walk on a straight path and purifies him, so this tekhelet causes a person to walk on a straight path. Certainly all must stand in awe of this place, to walk uprightly.”
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s explanation near the end of Shelach: tekhelet recalls the Throne of Glory and awakens the awe that directs a person toward the straight path.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא זְכִירַת כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת אַף בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ, כְּעוֹבָדָא דִּמְנָחוֹת:
connections.quote: “There was a man who was careful about the mitzvah of tzitzit. He heard that there was a prostitute in the coastal cities who charged four hundred gold coins. He sent her four hundred gold coins and set a time with her. When his appointed time arrived, he came and sat at the entrance. Her maid entered and told her: The man who sent you four hundred gold coins has come and is sitting at the entrance. She said: Let him enter. He entered. She had prepared seven beds for him, six of silver and one of gold; between each was a silver ladder, and the uppermost was of gold. She went up and sat on the uppermost bed naked, and he too went up to sit naked opposite her. His four fringes came and struck him in the face. He slipped down and sat on the ground; she too slipped down and sat on the ground. She said: By the power of Rome, I will not let you go until you tell me what flaw you saw in me. He said: By the Temple service, I have never seen a woman as beautiful as you. But Hashem our God commanded us one mitzvah called tzitzit, and “I am Hashem your God” is written in it twice: I am the One who will exact punishment, and I am the One who will pay reward. Now they appeared to me like four witnesses.”
connections.context: This is the complete episode through the man’s explanation of his restraint. The fringes interrupt his intention and recall divine judgment, illustrating Rav Tzadok’s statement that tzitzit can awaken remembrance even against one’s immediate desire.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (יב:) דְּהַמִּתְבַּיֵּישׁ בָּהּ מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ, כִּי כְּבָר סָבַל עוֹנֶשׁ גֵּיהִנָּם.
