connections.quote: ‘Rabbah bar Chinena the Elder said in the name of Rav: Anyone who commits a transgression and feels ashamed of it is forgiven for all his iniquities, as it is said: ‘So that you may remember and be ashamed, and no longer have an opening of the mouth because of your humiliation, when I atone for you for everything you have done, declares Hashem God.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַפֵּרָעוֹן מִן הָעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁנִּפְרָעִים מִן הַצַּדִּיקִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
connections.quote: ““A faithful God, without injustice.” “A faithful God”: just as payment is exacted from the wicked in the world to come even for a minor transgression they commit, so payment is exacted from the righteous in this world for a minor transgression they commit. “Without injustice”: just as reward is paid to the righteous in the world to come even for a minor mitzvah they perform, so reward is paid to the wicked in this world even for a minor mitzvah they perform.”
connections.context: The saying retains both sides of the accounting: wrongdoing and good deeds, the righteous and the wicked, and this world and the world to come. Rav Tzadok applies the first part here to remorse over one’s sins.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּעָנְשֵׁי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַמָּשׁ יֵשׁ מִשְׁפָּטִים אֲחֵרִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מוֹעֵד קָטָן כח.): חַיֵּי, בָּנֵי וּמְזוֹנֵי לָא בִּזְכוּתָא תַּלְיָא מִלְּתָא אֶלָּא בְּמַזָּלָא.
connections.quote: ‘Rava said: Life, children, and sustenance do not depend on merit, but on mazal. For Rabbah and Rav Chisda were both righteous Sages: one would pray and rain would come, and the other would pray and rain would come…’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּעָנְשֵׁי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַמָּשׁ יֵשׁ מִשְׁפָּטִים אֲחֵרִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מוֹעֵד קָטָן כח.): חַיֵּי, בָּנֵי וּמְזוֹנֵי לָא בִּזְכוּתָא תַּלְיָא מִלְּתָא אֶלָּא בְּמַזָּלָא.
connections.quote: “In truth, this mazal is not one of the heavenly constellations known to astrologers. It is concerning their knowledge of the arrangement of the constellations that the Sages said, “There is no mazal for Israel.” For among the children of Israel everything follows His supreme judgment, blessed be His name, according to the quality of their souls.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי",
connections.quote: ‘Even when I walk through a valley of death’s shadow, I will fear no evil, for You are with me. Your rod and Your staff—they comfort me.’

connections.hePhrase: וַדַּאי לֹא חָשַׁב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּגֵיהִנָּם לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ד.) דְּקָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ חָסִיד עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ““Guard my soul, for I am pious.” David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, am I not pious? All the kings of east and west sleep until the third hour, while I rise at midnight to give thanks to You.”

connections.hePhrase: וַדַּאי לֹא חָשַׁב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּגֵיהִנָּם לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ד.) דְּקָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ חָסִיד עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, I am confident that You give the righteous good reward in the future, but I do not know whether I have a portion among them.”

connections.hePhrase: וַדַּאי לֹא חָשַׁב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּגֵיהִנָּם לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ד.) דְּקָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ חָסִיד עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “Lest sin cause [the promise not to be fulfilled].”
connections.context: The Gemara explains how David’s confidence can coexist with uncertainty about himself: future sin may intervene. The answer is needed for Rav Tzadok’s discussion of confidence without complacency.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים לֹא הָיָה פּוֹתֵחַ פִּיו לַשָּׂטָן חַס וְשָׁלוֹם אִם חָשַׁשׁ שֶׁמָּא יִגְרוֹם הַחֵטְא.
connections.quote: “Abaye said: A person should not speak in that way, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, and it was also taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei: A person should never open his mouth to the Accuser. Rav Yosef said: What verse supports this? It is written, “We almost became like Sodom.” What did the prophet answer them? “Hear the word of Hashem, officers of Sodom.””
connections.context: In its original setting Abaye objects to a mourner speaking as though further punishment were deserved. The rule and its scriptural example explain the expression Rav Tzadok uses when discussing David’s words.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי עַצְבוּת הַשְּׁכִינָה מִסְתַּלֶּקֶת וְיוּכַל לָבוֹא לִידֵי רַע כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: ““I praised joy”—the joy of a mitzvah. “What does joy accomplish?”—joy that is not of a mitzvah. This teaches that the Divine Presence rests neither through sadness, nor through laziness, laughter, frivolity, conversation, or idle words, but through the joy of a mitzvah, as it is written: “Now bring me a musician; and when the musician played, the hand of Hashem came upon him.” Rav Yehudah said: The same applies to a matter of halakhah. Rava said: The same applies to a good dream.”
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes the joy of a mitzvah from other forms of amusement and names sadness among the states through which the Divine Presence does not rest. This is the source of the premise that Rav Tzadok qualifies in the following lines.

connections.hePhrase: רַק מַדְרֵגַת קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא הַנִּקְרָא "אַתָּה", זֶהוּ עִמָּדִי גַּם בְּעֵת הָעַצְבוּת, שֶׁמִּצִּדּוֹ הוּא הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְכָךְ:
connections.quote: “Since the Temple was destroyed, we have only the lower level of the illumination of the face—that is, the radiance of the face. This is the Divine Presence that went into exile with them, the level of “I.” This means that He dwells within one’s heart: the very apprehension is itself what is apprehended, for the person apprehends that no place is empty of Him and that the whole earth is full of His glory. Glory is the radiance: the recognition that emerges from His lordship and the attribute of His kingship, which rules over all. Just as someone who has not seen a king knows him through his rule, so a person knows Hashem through the whole creation. Avraham our father saw a palace aflame, and so forth; our Sages said that no one called Him Master until Avraham came. The name of lordship indicates the glory and radiance, as is known. I also heard concerning “The owner of the palace looked out upon him”: “upon him” means that He told him, You yourself are also included in the owner of the palace. For the whole world sees this and their hearts are not stirred at all to apprehend that there is an owner of the palace and seek Him. Your very seeking also comes from Me, and your heart is the place of My Presence. This is the meaning of “I.” But seeing the King Himself is the apprehension of “You.” This is prayer, like standing before the King, which takes the place of the Temple sacrifices. Therefore our Sages said that one should direct one’s heart toward the Holy of Holies, where there is actual seeing of the face. This belongs to the one who has prevailed in battle through the two-edged sword of the Shema, which is complete unity now as before the world was created. Through it every evil thing and foreign thought is nullified, and then the person recognizes the One addressed as “You,” beyond recognition through creation and created beings.”
connections.context: This parallel defines the two terms used at the end of the present ois: “I” as the Divine Presence recognized within the heart and creation, and “You” as direct address to the King in prayer. Both paragraphs are retained so that the distinction is explained in Rav Tzadok’s own terms.

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַשְׁבָּ"א בְּנִדָּה (יד.) לְעִנְיַן גַּמָּלִין כֻּלָּם רְשָׁעִים, וּבְסוֹף קִדּוּשִׁין (פב.) אִיתָא רוּבָּם כְּשֵׁרִים, דִּלְגַבֵּי זֶה רְשָׁעִים וּלְגַבֵּי זֶה כְּשֵׁרִים]
connections.quote: ““The camel drivers are all wicked.” This means wicked in this matter; in other matters they are righteous, as we say in the chapter Ten Lineages: “The camel drivers are all righteous.””

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַשְׁבָּ"א בְּנִדָּה (יד.) לְעִנְיַן גַּמָּלִין כֻּלָּם רְשָׁעִים, וּבְסוֹף קִדּוּשִׁין (פב.) אִיתָא רוּבָּם כְּשֵׁרִים, דִּלְגַבֵּי זֶה רְשָׁעִים וּלְגַבֵּי זֶה כְּשֵׁרִים]
connections.quote: ‘Abba Guryan of Tzaydan says in the name of Abba Gurya: A man should not teach his son to be a donkey driver, camel driver, cart driver, sailor, shepherd, or shopkeeper, for these trades are trades of robbery. Rabbi Yehudah says in his name: Most donkey drivers are wicked; most camel drivers are upright; most sailors are pious. The best of physicians is destined for Gehinnom, and the most upright of butchers is a partner of Amalek.’

connections.hePhrase: לְעִנְיַן שֶׁעָלָיו הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר: "לֹא יְאֻנֶּה לַצַּדִּיק כָּל אָוֶן" (מִשְׁלֵי יב, כא) בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר.
connections.quote: ‘No wrongdoing will befall the righteous, but the wicked are filled with evil.’

connections.hePhrase: לְעִנְיַן שֶׁעָלָיו הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר: "לֹא יְאֻנֶּה לַצַּדִּיק כָּל אָוֶן" (מִשְׁלֵי יב, כא) בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר.
connections.quote: ““It shall not befall the righteous”—it will not occur: a transgression will not come his way without his knowledge.”
connections.context: Rashi understands the verse as protection from an unwitting transgression. Rav Tzadok applies that explanation to a particular matter in which a person is inwardly free of attachment.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְסוֹטָה (כח.): בִּזְמַן שֶׁאֵין הָאִישׁ מְנוּקֶּה מֵעָוֹן, אֵין הַמַּיִם בּוֹדְקִים אִשְׁתּוֹ
connections.quote: ‘Gemara: To whom does ‘him’ refer? If you say it refers to the husband, what has the husband done? And if you say that when he is guilty the water tests him, does the water test her when he himself is guilty? Was it not taught: ‘The man shall be free of guilt, and that woman shall bear her guilt’? When the man is free of guilt, the water tests his wife; when the man is not free of guilt, the water does not test his wife!’

connections.hePhrase: [וְלָכֵן תָּנֵי נָזִיר וְאַחַר כָּךְ סוֹטָה, עַיֵּין רֵישׁ סוֹטָה, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא תְּחִלָּה מְנוּקֶּה מֵעָוֹן],
connections.quote: “The tanna has just concluded Nazir; why does he now teach Sotah? In accordance with Rabbi, for it was taught: Rabbi says, Why was the passage of the nazir placed next to the passage of the sotah? To tell you that anyone who sees a sotah in her disgrace should abstain from wine. Then let him teach Sotah and afterward Nazir! Since he taught Ketubot, including the chapter concerning one who imposes a vow, he taught Nedarim. Since he taught Nedarim, he taught Nazir, which resembles vows. He then teaches Sotah, in accordance with Rabbi.”
connections.context: The Gemara gives its own explanation of the tractate sequence and the connection between sotah and abstention from wine. Rav Tzadok then draws an inward lesson from Nazir preceding Sotah: first one must purify oneself.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "כִּי כָשַׁלְתָּ בַּעֲוֹנֶךָ" – בָּאוּ לְךָ מִכְשׁוֹלִים בַּעֲוֹנֶךָ;
connections.quote: ““For you have stumbled”—stumbling blocks have come upon you because of your iniquities.”
connections.context: This is the original commentary’s formulation behind the words “stumbling blocks came upon you because of your iniquity.” It connects a stumbling with a fault that calls for return.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִן הַמִּכְשׁוֹלִים שֶׁאֵירַע לָאָדָם, יוּכַל לָדַעַת דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ נָקִי מֵהֶם עֲדַיִן בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ.
connections.quote: “These clarifications are very difficult and weighty for a person to undergo. They become ‘light’ in the World to Come, when Hashem will clarify all Israel's actions and illuminate them, showing that their actions had not been separated from His will, since in the depth of their hearts they intended them for Heaven. Even a person's good desire will not be lost; Hashem will join it to an act, as stated in Kiddushin 40a: if someone intended to perform a mitzvah and was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, Scripture credits him as though he performed it. Then it will become clear that even the obstruction occurred by His will. Since the person's whole aim, desire, and will were solely to fulfill His will, and God brought about the event preventing him, it follows that this too was for his benefit, refining him again and again. As the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Shemini): what difference does it make to the Holy One, blessed be He, whether one slaughters from the back of the neck or from the neck? Rather, it is to refine His creatures, as it is written, ‘Every word of Hashem is refined.’ All the concealments a person experienced—first thinking one order of service was good for him and afterward another—were only to refine him; he had never, Heaven forbid, been separated from His will.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef examines the nazir who is unexpectedly defiled and begins to fear that his whole original undertaking was mistaken. It distinguishes that painful present examination from Hashem's final clarification, when the sincere intention and even its obstruction are shown as part of refinement. This adds a necessary distinction to the siman's inward examination after a stumbling: the demand to repair is real, while a person cannot turn his present misgivings into a complete verdict about the whole history of his service.
connections.headline: Examination after a mishap and the final clarification

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה מא) עַל לוֹט: מִי שֶׁלָּהוּט וְכוּלֵי סוֹף וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““Lot raised his eyes and saw the entire plain of the Jordan, that it was all watered, before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt, as you come to Tzoar” (Genesis 13:10). “Lot raised his eyes and saw the entire plain of the Jordan” – Rabbi Naḥman bar Ḥanin said: Anyone who has a voracious appetite for sexual immorality will ultimately be fed from his own flesh and blood. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina said: This entire verse is comprised of expressions of sexual immorality. [“Lot raised his eyes”] – just as it says: “His master's wife raised her eyes [toward Joseph and she said: Lie with me]” (Genesis 39:7). “And saw the entire plain [kikar] of the Jordan, that it was all watered” – just as it says: “For due to a licentious woman, one is brought to a loaf [kikar] of bread” (Proverbs 6:26). “That it was all watered [mashke]” – just as it says: “He shall give the woman to drink [hishka] the bitter water that causes a curse” (Numbers 5:24). “Before the Lord destroyed [shaḥet]” – just as it says: “It was when he consorted with his brother's wife, he would spill [veshiḥet] on to the ground” (Genesis 38:9). “Like the garden of the Lord” – for trees; “like the land of Egypt” – for seeds. “Lot chose for himself all the plain of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed from the east, and each parted from his brother” (Genesis 13:11). “Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12). “And the men of Sodom were extremely wicked and sinful to the Lord” (Genesis 13:13). “Lot chose for himself” – Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra said: Like a person selecting his mother’s marriage contract. “Lot journeyed from the east [mikedem]” – he moved himself away from the One who preceded [kadmono] the world. He said: ‘I desire neither Abram nor his God.’ “Each parted from his brother. Abram lived [in the land of Canaan]” – Rabbi Meir says: You do not have among the cities any as evil as Sodom, as when a person is wicked, they refer to him as a person of Sodom. You do not have any among the peoples as tough as the Emorites, as when a person is tough, they refer to him as an Emorite. Rabbi Yosei said: You do not have among the cities any as beautiful as Sodom, as Lot circulated among all the cities of the plain and did not find a place as fine as Sodom, and these [the people of Sodom] were the most distinguished among them – “and the men of Sodom were extremely wicked and sinful to the Lord” (Genesis 13:13). “Wicked” – towards one another; “sinful” – through sexual immorality; “to the Lord” – through idolatry; “extremely” – through bloodshed.”

connections.hePhrase: [הוּא אַגּוֹנֵי וּמַצּוֹלֵי מִן הַחֵטְא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (כא.), וְזֶהוּ מַחֲזִיר לְמוּטָב]
connections.quote: “Rava said: Torah, while one is occupied with it, protects and rescues; when one is not occupied with it, it protects but does not rescue. A mitzvah, whether one is occupied with it or not, protects but does not rescue.”
connections.context: The sugya distinguishes protection from suffering from rescue from sin, and also distinguishes the time of study from other times. Those qualifications clarify Rav Tzadok’s reference to Torah’s protecting force.

connections.hePhrase: הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי מַיְמִינִים בָּהּ, שֶׁהוּא סַמָּא דְחַיֵּי, וְחַיִּים וְאוֹר הַכֹּל אֶחָד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי עִמְּךָ מְקוֹר חַיִּים, בְּאוֹרְךָ נִרְאֶה אוֹר".
connections.quote: ““Those who take it by the right hand”—they engage in it with all their strength and devote themselves to knowing its secret, like a person using the right hand, which is the principal one.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the metaphor of the right hand as wholehearted effort and the pursuit of Torah’s depth. This is the specific term Rav Tzadok uses here.

connections.hePhrase: הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי מַיְמִינִים בָּהּ, שֶׁהוּא סַמָּא דְחַיֵּי, וְחַיִּים וְאוֹר הַכֹּל אֶחָד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי עִמְּךָ מְקוֹר חַיִּים, בְּאוֹרְךָ נִרְאֶה אוֹר".
connections.quote: “This is what Rava said: For those who take it by the right hand, it is an elixir of life; for those who take it by the left hand, it is an elixir of death.”
connections.context: Both alternatives belong to the saying. Rav Tzadok invokes the first while explaining that the life-giving light of Torah depends on how a person engages with it.

connections.hePhrase: הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי מַיְמִינִים בָּהּ, שֶׁהוּא סַמָּא דְחַיֵּי, וְחַיִּים וְאוֹר הַכֹּל אֶחָד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי עִמְּךָ מְקוֹר חַיִּים, בְּאוֹרְךָ נִרְאֶה אוֹר".
connections.quote: ‘For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק הוּא בִּכְלַל "פִּטְטַיָּא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא" דְּאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (סוֹף בְּרָכוֹת) דְּטָבִין.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yonah said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Gezirah: All chatter is bad, but chatter about Torah is good.”
connections.context: The Yerushalmi explicitly gives value even to Torah conversation. Rav Tzadok uses this wording for an engagement whose words are holy even before the person attains Torah’s inward light.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָנוּ מְבָרְכִין "לַעֲסוֹק בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה" וְלֹא "בַּתּוֹרָה", דְּמַאן סָפֵין וּמַאן רָקֵיעַ לִהְיוֹת בָּטוּחַ שֶׁיַּעֲסוֹק בָּהּ;
connections.quote: “This is its wording: “Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the words of Torah.” The Ashkenazic wording is “to engage in the words of Torah.” “Please make the words of Your Torah sweet, Hashem our God, in our mouths and in the mouths of Your people, the house of Israel. May we and our descendants and the descendants of Your people, the house of Israel, all know Your name and study Your Torah. Blessed are You, Hashem, who teaches Torah to His people Israel.” Some conclude, “Blessed are You, Hashem, who gives the Torah.””
connections.context: The Tur records the wording Rav Tzadok explains and also records the other liturgical forms. The contrast between “the words of Your Torah” and “Your Torah” appears within the blessing itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא נִלְמָד מִצִּיוּוּי "וְדִבַּרְתָּ בָּם", שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּיוֹמָא (יט:): וְלֹא בִּדְבָרִים בְּטֵלִים;
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: ‘You shall speak of them’—these words are to be spoken aloud, whereas prayer is recited quietly. ‘You shall speak of them’—you have permission to speak of them, but not of other matters.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אוֹמְרִים אַחַר כָּךְ "וְהַעֲרֶב נָא וְגוֹמֵר", מְבַקְּשִׁים עַל עֵסֶק לִשְׁמָהּ עַל יְדֵי הַהַעֲרָבָה וּמִיתּוּק שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָתְךָ בְּפִינוּ,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
connections.quote: “This is also the meaning of the Gemara (Bava Metzia 44a): in his youth Rabbi taught his son Rabbi Shimon, ‘Silver acquires gold,’ and in his old age, ‘Gold acquires silver.’ In a person's youth there is great desire and longing for words of Torah, through which he acquires the gold: true words of Torah are called gold, while silver signifies desire and longing. In old age, however, a person must ask that his desire for words of Torah not depart, for all his powers of desire weaken. He therefore changed it to ‘Gold acquires silver’: this is a prayer to Hashem that words of Torah bring into his heart the desire for still more Torah. It is like a person already satisfied with food, who nevertheless desires to eat more when a good dish is brought before him. So it is with words of Torah. This is our daily prayer, ‘Hashem our God, please make the words of Your Torah sweet in our mouths’: that the Torah become sweet to us, so that we continually desire it more. This explains ‘You shall eat, eating and being satisfied’ (Joel 2:26): the doubled expression teaches that eating itself brings further desire. It is a parable for words of Torah, as explained.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the very prayer cited here through a reciprocal movement: desire acquires Torah, and Torah in turn renews desire. Its interpretation of silver and gold distinguishes the energy of beginning from the need to keep that energy alive after acquiring knowledge. This explains why the siman's prayer for sweetness is part of the transition toward learning for its own sake, rather than a request for pleasantness detached from further service.
connections.headline: Torah can renew the desire through which it is acquired

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ:) שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ:
connections.quote: “Rava raised a contradiction: It is written, ‘For Your kindness is great, reaching to the heavens,’ yet it is also written, ‘For Your kindness is great, above the heavens.’ How can both be true? The latter concerns service for its own sake, while the former concerns service for other motives. This accords with Rav Yehudah’s teaching, for Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name: A person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot, even for other motives, because practicing for other motives leads to practicing for their own sake.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ:) שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ:
connections.heRef: פרי צדיק, ראש חודש תמוז ג׳:ב׳
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, the counsel is, “Feed him,” for “you are heaping coals upon his head”: ultimately the words of Torah will benefit the person. Although the evil inclination supposes that it will draw nourishment from Torah studied for ulterior motives, a person should still always engage in it, for from study for ulterior motives one comes to study for its own sake. The Midrash says, “If only they had abandoned Me but kept My Torah, for through occupying themselves with it, the light within it would have brought them back to the good”—that is, they would come to study for its own sake, as explained concerning Rosh Chodesh Kislev. This is as we explained concerning the statements, “Bring water to meet the thirsty” and “Let everyone who is thirsty go to the water”: when the student is worthy, the teacher should go to him; otherwise, “Let everyone who is thirsty go to the water.” Although a teacher is not obliged to teach an unworthy student, Scripture counsels the student himself to go to the water, for from study for ulterior motives he will come to study for its own sake, and the light within it brings him back to the good.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ:) שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ:
connections.quote: “Torah acts upon the human heart, as it is said, “The light within it brings a person back to the good”; for this reason it is called Torah. But there are words of Torah that remain only on the lips, as stated in Sanhedrin concerning Doeg. Of this it says, “Why is there … when there is no heart?” This is called Torah chatter, which is also good, for it can bring a person to the Torah of truth, as it says that from study not for its own sake one comes to study for its own sake [as explained above in ois 59]—provided that sin does not cause an obstruction, as with Doeg.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok directly refers back to this ois and preserves an essential qualification: the movement from words on the lips to Torah in the heart can be obstructed by sin. The following lines in ois 133 explain the thirst and receptivity through which Torah enters the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן יֵשׁ לָאָדָם לִיזָּהֵר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא נָקִי בָּזֶה,
connections.quote: “It is possible to explain “Do not be a witness against your fellow without cause” as referring to testifying against him about transgressions in which you too are afflicted like him; for that reason he is called your fellow. The next words support this: “Do not say, As he has done to me, so I will do to him.” Although it is a mitzvah to expose those who sin against their souls and the hypocrites, a sinner must not publicize someone whose wickedness is like his own. For his intention in revealing the other’s secrets is not good, but to rejoice in his misfortune. Secondly, how can he fail to be ashamed to mention the disgrace of those deeds in another when he himself still holds to them? It is said, “I will visit the blood of Yizreel upon the house of Yehu.” Thus, although Yehu performed a mitzvah by destroying the house of Achav, he bore his guilt, because he too was greatly sinful.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah presents this as a possible interpretation and distinguishes appropriate exposure of hypocrisy from a sinner’s malicious disclosure of the same fault he still practices. Both the motive and the continuing personal fault are retained in the quoted explanation.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן יֵשׁ לָאָדָם לִיזָּהֵר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא נָקִי בָּזֶה,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of ‘When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof’: a person must see to it that no one falls to the ground through his service. Rather, he must make room for every creature; this is what the commandment of the parapet teaches.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef extends the parapet beyond physical construction to responsibility for the effects of one's avodah on another person. This sharpens Rav Tzadok's demand to correct oneself before correcting others: even an act presented as religious service needs a safeguard against causing another person's fall. The other's need for correction does not by itself justify the manner of rebuke.
connections.headline: A safeguard against harming others through one's own service

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּפָקַדְתִּי אֶת דְּמֵי יִזְרְעֶאל עַל בֵּית יֵהוּא", וְכֵן נֶאֱמַר גַּבֵּי בַּעְשָׁא, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י;
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said to him: ‘Name him Jezreel, for in a little while I will reckon with the house of Jehu for the bloodshed of Jezreel, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּפָקַדְתִּי אֶת דְּמֵי יִזְרְעֶאל עַל בֵּית יֵהוּא", וְכֵן נֶאֱמַר גַּבֵּי בַּעְשָׁא, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י;
connections.quote: ““The blood of Jezreel”: as the Targum explains, the blood of the house of Ahab, whom Jehu killed in Jezreel because they worshipped Baal. But he and his descendants subsequently followed their way and worshipped idolatry; therefore I account the blood of the house of Ahab against them as innocent blood.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּפָקַדְתִּי אֶת דְּמֵי יִזְרְעֶאל עַל בֵּית יֵהוּא", וְכֵן נֶאֱמַר גַּבֵּי בַּעְשָׁא, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י;
connections.quote: ““And because he struck him”: since he too followed in his sins, it follows that he should not have killed him; therefore he was punished for killing him. Similarly we find, “I will visit the blood of Yizreel upon the house of Yehu”: since they did not depart from Achav’s ways, they were punished for killing them.”
connections.context: This is the Rashi on Baasha expressly cited here. It adds the parallel to the existing Rashi on Hosea: participation in the same wrongdoing changes the account of the person who carries out punishment.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר: "הִתְקוֹשְׁשׁוּ וָקוֹשּׁוּ" – קְשׁוֹט עַצְמְךָ וְאַחַר כָּךְ קְשׁוֹט אֲחֵרִים (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא מְצִיעָא קז:), דִּבְלָאו הָכִי נֶעֱנָשׁ עַל כָּךְ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbah bar Rav Huna had a woodland on the riverbank. They said to him: ‘Let the Master cut it down!’ He answered: ‘Cut down those upstream and downstream, and afterward I will cut down mine.’ How could he act that way? Is it not written, ‘Gather yourselves and gather,’ and Reish Lakish said: ‘Set yourself right, and afterward set others right’!’

connections.hePhrase: [אִם לֹא שֶׁגַּם לוֹ יֵשׁ מִשְׁפָּט בָּזֶה שֶׁיְּקַבֵּל הָעוֹנֶשׁ עַל מַה שֶּׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ זֶה עַל יָדוֹ, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַכּוֹת (י:): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַזְמִינָם לְפוּנְדָּק זֶה וְכוּלֵי וְזֶה וְכוּלֵי].
connections.quote: “What is the verse speaking about? Two people who killed: one killed unintentionally and the other intentionally, and there are no witnesses to either killing. The Holy One, blessed be He, brings them together at one inn. The one who killed intentionally sits beneath a ladder; the one who killed unintentionally descends the ladder, falls upon him, and kills him. The one who killed intentionally is killed, and the one who killed unintentionally goes into exile.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה: כְּשֶׁאֵין הָאִישׁ מְנוּקֶּה מֵעָוֹן, אֵין הַמַּיִם בּוֹדְקִים אִשְׁתּוֹ:
connections.quote: “Was it not taught: “The man shall be clear of iniquity, and that woman shall bear her iniquity”? When the man is clear of iniquity, the water examines his wife; when the man is not clear of iniquity, the water does not examine his wife.”
connections.context: This is the baraita Rav Tzadok invokes at the conclusion. Its stated condition is the husband’s being clear of iniquity; he uses that condition in his discussion of the person through whom another is judged.

connections.hePhrase: [סא] הַכֹּהֲנִים נִקְרְאוּ קְדוֹשִׁים,
connections.quote: “for Aharon, peace be upon him, was separated from Israel "to sanctify him as most holy" (I Divrei HaYamim 23:13); within whom resided the ultimate manifestation of holiness and separation achievable in this world; wherefore he alone entered the Holy of Holies, the place concerning which it is written: "And there shall be no man in the tent of meeting when he goes in to make atonement" (Vayikra 16:17); which the Sages expounded in the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 1:5): "even the angels whose faces have the likeness of a man"; for there exists a holiness transcending the angels which they cannot reach, reserved for the righteous whose partition is set inside the ministering angels. And Israel is "one nation in the earth" (II Shmuel 7:23), all forming a single complete corporate stature; except that just as within the human body there are primary vital organs containing greater life-force, like the heart which is the wellspring of vitality; and so other organs exist in descending rungs: organs upon which life directly depends, like the brain and lungs; and organs upon which less vitality depends, like the liver, whose perforation does not render the animal a tereifah; removal does so if an olive-sized portion does not remain both at the gallbladder and at the place of the liver’s vital attachment (Chullin 46a); and organs whose complete removal does not impair life, but whose diseased condition does, such as the kidneys (Chullin 54a); and parts that do not touch vitality at all, yet their injury causes severe bodily pain and illness; and parts where injury causes only minor and brief pain, like bruises on the external surface of the body; and parts that feel no pain whatsoever, being like superfluities, such as fingernails and hair, possessing various descending rungs; yet all are an integral part of the complete stature, the fingernail being called a human fingernail, part of the person's body; all receiving vitality from the heart, whence flow the issues of life (Mishlei 4:23); and according to the vitality channeled from the heart, so is the life of all organs and the collective stature!”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim develops the comparison to a single body: Aharon's concentrated holiness serves a people whose different members receive life in different measures. This explains why the siman can affirm a real priestly root even where its outward expression is slight. Difference of function and degree need not mean a separate source of life.
connections.headline: Aharon's holiness within Israel's shared life

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיִּבָּדֵל אַהֲרֹן לְהַקְדִּישׁוֹ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כג, יג),
connections.quote: ‘The sons of Amram were Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to be consecrated as most holy, he and his sons forever, to offer incense before Hashem, to serve Him, and to bless in His Name forever.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְאֶת הַקָּדוֹשׁ וְהִקְרִיב אֵלָיו" (בַּמִּדְבָּר טז, ה).
connections.quote: ‘He spoke to Korah and all his assembly, saying: ‘In the morning Hashem will make known who belongs to Him and who is holy, and He will bring him near to Him. The one He chooses, He will bring near to Him.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן רִבָּה בָּהֶן הַכָּתוּב מִצְווֹת יְתֵירוֹת,
connections.quote: “Priests are different, because Scripture imposed additional mitzvot upon them, such as the Temple services and eating offerings of the highest sanctity, which do not apply to women. One might therefore have thought that a prohibition not applying to everyone, concerning a forbidden union, would likewise not apply to them [the women].”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן רִבָּה בָּהֶן הַכָּתוּב מִצְווֹת יְתֵירוֹת,
connections.quote: “Scripture imposed additional mitzvot upon the priests because Aharon was set apart to consecrate him as most holy. Correspondingly, his inclination is also distinct from the inclinations of other people’s thoughts, and he needs additional counsels to guard against it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains elsewhere why greater holiness is accompanied by additional obligations: the stronger spiritual capacity has its corresponding challenge and needs further remedies.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁמְּבָרְכִין: "אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ",
connections.quote: “It is well known that Israel’s holiness depends on the mitzvot. This is what the Sifrei says: “You shall sanctify yourselves”—this is the holiness of a mitzvah. The mitzvot through which we were commanded to sanctify ourselves are the commandments received through revelation, for these are the essence of holiness. It is concerning them that our Sages, the sages of truth, instituted the blessing, “Who sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us.” Because of these revealed commandments, Israel were called a holy nation at Sinai, as it is stated, “You shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.” A people is not called a holy nation through fulfilling the rational commandments, for even the idolaters, who are “a nation bereft of counsel, with no understanding,” occupy themselves with some of the rational commandments. Nor did the Sages institute a blessing over the rational commandments, for the essential blessing and holiness belong to the revealed commandments.”
connections.context: Rabbenu Bachya distinguishes commandments known through revelation from duties accessible to reason. His explanation connects the blessing “Who sanctified us with His mitzvot” directly with the holiness produced by observance.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וַעֲשִׂיתֶם אֶת כָּל מִצְוֹתָי וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים" (בַּמִּדְבָּר טו, מ).
connections.quote: ‘So that you remember and perform all My commandments, and be holy to your God.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ: כֹּהֲנִים זְרִיזִים בְּמַעֲשֶׂה – הִכְנִיס הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּהֶם מִדָּה זוֹ שֶׁל זְרִיזוּת בְּמַעֲשֶׂה כְּדֵי לְהַכְנִיס קְדוּשָּׁה בַּלֵּב.
connections.quote: “‘And one kindles the fire,’ and so forth. From where is this derived? Rav Huna said: ‘You shall not kindle a fire in any of your dwelling places.’ In any of your dwelling places you may not kindle it, but you may kindle it in the fire of the Chamber of the Hearth. Rav Hisda challenged this: If so, it should be permitted even on Shabbat itself! Rather, Rav Hisda said: The verse comes to permit the burning of sacrificial limbs and fats; and priests are diligent.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעִנְיַן הַקְּדוּשָּׁה הוּא הַבְדָּלָה מִכָּל עִנְיְנֵי חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק לִהְיוֹת עוֹבֵד ה'.
connections.quote: “Wherever you find restraint from forbidden relations and desire, there you find holiness. This is the meaning of holiness: separation from desires, being dedicated solely to Hashem. These are opposites: of one immersed in desire it is said, “One who separates himself seeks desire,” for he is separated from Hashem. In holiness, by contrast, he is dedicated to Heaven, just as the Sages explained a woman’s kiddushin as language of consecration, meaning that she belongs to her husband.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בַּכֹּהֲנִים: "לִי" (שְׁמוֹת כח, מא), שֶׁהוּא קַיָּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ב);
connections.quote: ‘‘Is he a son dear to Me?’ Wherever ‘to Me’ (li) is said, it never passes away, neither in this world nor in the World to Come. Of the priests it is written: ‘They shall serve Me as priests’ (Exodus 40:15). Of the Levites it is written: ‘The Levites shall be Mine’ (Numbers 8:14). Of Israel it is written: ‘For the children of Israel are Mine’ (Leviticus 25:55). Of the contribution it is written: ‘They shall take for Me’ (Exodus 25:2). Of the firstborn it is written: ‘For every firstborn is Mine’ (Numbers 3:13). Of the Sanhedrin it is written: ‘Gather for Me seventy men from the elders of Israel’ (Numbers 11:16). Of the Land of Israel: ‘For all the earth is Mine’ (Exodus 19:5). Of Jerusalem: ‘The city that I chose for Myself’ (I Kings 11:36). Of the kingdom of the house of David: ‘For I have seen among his sons a king for Me’ (I Samuel 16:1). Of the Sanctuary: ‘They shall make Me a sanctuary’ (Exodus 25:8). Of the altar: ‘An altar of earth you shall make for Me’ (Exodus 20:21). Of the offerings: ‘You shall take care to offer to Me’ (Numbers 28:2). Of the anointing oil: ‘This shall be sacred anointing oil for Me’ (Exodus 30:31). Thus, wherever ‘to Me’ is said, it does not pass away, neither in this world nor in the World to Come.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בַּכֹּהֲנִים: "לִי" (שְׁמוֹת כח, מא), שֶׁהוּא קַיָּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ב);
connections.quote: ‘You shall clothe Aaron your brother and his sons with him in them, anoint them, invest them in their office, and sanctify them, so that they may serve Me as priests.’

connections.hePhrase: "הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַה' יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב" (שְׁמוּאֵל א טז, ז),
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said to Samuel: ‘Do not look at his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. For it is not as a human being sees: a human being sees what is before the eyes, but Hashem sees into the heart.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְבָר הִבְטִיחַ: "אִם תָּפֵרוּ אֶת בְּרִיתִי הַיּוֹם וְגוֹמֵר" (יִרְמְיָה לג, כ) עַל בְּרִית הַכְּהֻנָּה:
connections.quote: “Thus says the Lord: If you can break My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night, so that day and night do not occur at their appointed time—”
connections.context: The prophet states an impossible condition: overturning the established succession of day and night. The next verse applies that condition to the permanence of Davidic kingship and the priesthood.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְבָר הִבְטִיחַ: "אִם תָּפֵרוּ אֶת בְּרִיתִי הַיּוֹם וְגוֹמֵר" (יִרְמְיָה לג, כ) עַל בְּרִית הַכְּהֻנָּה:
connections.quote: “—then My covenant with David My servant may also be broken, so that he has no son reigning upon his throne, and [My covenant] with the Levitical priests who minister to Me.”
connections.context: This is the part of the comparison that explicitly names the priesthood. Its omission left the earlier footnote unable to explain Rav Tzadok’s reference to the covenant of the priests.

connections.hePhrase: [סב] מַעֲלוֹת הַרְבֵּה יֵשׁ, וְכֻלָּם זָכוּ כְּבָר גְּדוֹלֵי הַדּוֹרוֹת וּנְטָלוּם וְזָכוּ לִבְנֵיהֶם אַחֲרֵיהֶם.
connections.quote: “Avraham our father’s faith was manifest in his heart through the intensity of his own effort; that is why he is called the first of the converts. Nevertheless, our Sages said at the beginning of Bereshit Rabbah, Toldot, that Avraham was called Israel: he merited becoming like a native-born Israelite, whose quality is present from birth. This was after the birth of Yitzchak, through whom “your offspring shall be called,” and who was circumcised at eight days. That is, he was good from birth and circumcised for the blessed God before he possessed any understanding at all; this came from Avraham’s power within him. It therefore became clear that, through his own effort, Avraham our father had changed at his root to be this way, as though he were so from birth. For offspring resemble what their parent is in essence and at the root.”
connections.context: This explains how a quality acquired through a forefather’s effort can become an inherited spiritual root. The surrounding passage distinguishes that inherited faith from its full expression in the heart, which still requires effort.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הַגֵּרִים אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לִזְכּוֹת לְמַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִזַּרְעוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב,
connections.quote: “for even converts joined to Israel are designated by Scripture: "and surname himself by the name of Israel" (Isaiah 44:5), expounded by our Sages as referring to sincere converts. And since the Holy Spirit declared "shall surname himself by the name of Israel," he is truly so designated, though not by natural biological lineage but through an acquired title earned through righteous actions. Nonetheless he is designated thus, and Ezekiel (47:23) foretells that the convert shall receive an inheritance within the tribe where he sojourns, subsumed within the tribe; and this is not its place.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek addresses the same expression, ‘by the name of Israel,’ and insists that Scripture's naming of converts is true; he also invokes their inclusion in a tribe's inheritance. This guards the present siman's terminology from being mistaken for a denial of the convert's actual inclusion in Israel. His distinction concerns the manner in which the name is received, through birth or subsequent attachment.
connections.headline: An acquired name that is nevertheless true

connections.hePhrase: רַק כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק לו) עַל פָּסוּק "וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּה" – אֵלּוּ גֵּרֵי הַצֶּדֶק,
connections.quote: ““This one will say, I am the Lord’s”—these are the completely righteous. “This one will call himself by the name of Jacob”—these are children of the wicked. “This one will write with his hand to the Lord”—these are wicked people who left their ways, changed, and repented. “And will call himself by the name of Israel”—these are converts from the nations.”
connections.context: The source reads Isaiah 44:5 as describing several ways of belonging to Israel and to God, including converts. This is the relevant classification behind Rav Tzadok’s point.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאוּר מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכג:): "אֵין עֲמָלֵק נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא בְּיַד זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף",
connections.quote: “Jacob our father saw that Esau’s descendants would be handed over only to Joseph’s descendants, as it is written, “The house of Jacob shall be fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau straw.””

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאוּר מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכג:): "אֵין עֲמָלֵק נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא בְּיַד זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף",
connections.quote: “They struck the surviving remnant of Amalek. … Rabba bar Sheila said: Yishi descended from Manasseh, as it is written, “The sons of Manasseh: Chefer and Yishi.””
connections.context: The Gemara speaks specifically of Joseph’s line and traces the fighters against Amalek to Manasseh. Joseph is Rachel’s son; Rav Tzadok places this relationship within his broader contrast of the tribes.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאוּר מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכג:): "אֵין עֲמָלֵק נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא בְּיַד זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף",
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:30
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:30
connections.quote: “But Israel’s obstinacy proceeds from wisdom, through knowledge that connects wisdom with what is below it and with the powers of action. A person is obstinate only for the honor of Heaven; on the contrary, this becomes the channel through which precious souls emerge from Israel. Therefore “Amalek falls only into the hands of Yosef’s descendants.” Amalek is the root of obstinacy, and the main object of his accusation is Israel’s desires, as the Sages said on the verse “who encountered you.” But his obstinacy opposes the will of the blessed God, while the obstinacy of Yosef’s descendants accords with the will of the blessed God.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the reference “as I wrote elsewhere.” The decisive contrast is the purpose of persistence: Yosef’s line turns it toward the divine will, while Amalek turns it against that will.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת כ.): "בְּזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף לָא שָׁלְטָא עֵינָא בִישָׁא",
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan would regularly go and sit at the entrances to the place of immersion. He said: When the daughters of Israel come up from immersion, they will look at me and have children as handsome as I am. The Sages asked him: Is the master not afraid of the evil eye? He answered: I come from Joseph’s descendants, over whom the evil eye has no power, as it is written: ‘Joseph is a fruitful son, a fruitful son by a spring (alei ayin).’ Rabbi Abbahu said: Do not read ‘alei ayin,’ but ‘olei ayin’—rising above the eye.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים", מִכָּל מָקוֹם עִיקָּרוֹ בְּזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף.
connections.quote: ‘Your people are all righteous; they will possess the land forever—a shoot of My planting, the work of My hands, through which I am glorified.’

connections.hePhrase: וְשֵׁם "חָסִיד" זָכָה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּנְטָלוֹ, וְכֵן זַרְעָא דְּדָוִד אַחֲרָיו, בֵּית דָּוִד לְבַד.
connections.quote: “Rather, it is in the manner said of Avraham our father: His two kidneys were like two springs, welling forth Torah. This comes only from being exceptionally pious, to the point that one does not need wisdom to awaken fear, as Rambam wrote at the beginning of chapter 2 of Hilkhot Yesodei HaTorah. Rather, he has reached the level at which “their hearts are in their control”: his heart is empty within him—the level of David the king, peace be upon him. For this reason he called himself “pious.” This is the definition of piety: that his heart is empty because he has slain the evil inclination, and he no longer desires any worldly desire, only what accords with the will of the blessed God. As it is written in the Zohar: “Who is pious? One who acts devotedly toward his Maker.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly connects David’s title hasid with a heart no longer ruled by self-directed desire. This gives the meaning of the title whose inheritance is discussed in the ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַהֲרֹן וְזַרְעוֹ אַחֲרָיו – לְשֵׁם "קָדוֹשׁ", עַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר רֵישׁ קֹרַח.
connections.quote: “As the Zohar says in Korach: The Levite is pure; the priest is holy. For the Levites come from the left side, which is the aspect of purity: to purify the “fool’s heart at his left” and empty it of evil. The priest is holy: to bring holiness into the “wise person’s heart at his right,” for the priest comes from lovingkindness on the right and is holy. The Levite comes from the left side, fear; and it is written, “The fear of Hashem is pure.” He is called pure because, through fear, he purifies the fool’s heart.”
connections.context: The parallel explains the difference in terms of inner work: purification removes evil, while holiness brings divine service into the heart. It adds the meaning of the distinction to the Zohar’s terminology.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַהֲרֹן וְזַרְעוֹ אַחֲרָיו – לְשֵׁם "קָדוֹשׁ", עַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר רֵישׁ קֹרַח.
connections.quote: “Therefore, “The man whom Hashem chooses—he is the holy one,” and not “the pure one.” There are two levels: holy and pure. The priest is holy; the Levite is pure. That is why “the holy one” is written.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כא) שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּנָּתֵן גְּדוּלָּתוֹ לְזַרְעוֹ וְלֹא נִתְּנוּ,
connections.quote: ‘‘Moses spoke to Hashem, saying: Let Hashem, the God of spirits, appoint’ (Numbers 27:15–16). Anyone who requests the needs of the community is as though he comes with force. ‘Let Hashem appoint’: Why did he see fit to request this after the order of inheritance? Rather, once the daughters of Zelophehad inherited from their father, Moses said: ‘This is the time to request what I need. If daughters inherit, it is fitting that my sons should inherit my honor.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: ‘One who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit’ (Proverbs 27:18). ‘Your sons sat by themselves and did not engage in Torah. Joshua served you a great deal and accorded you great honor. He would come early and stay late in your house of study. He arranged the benches and spread out the mats. Since he served you with all his strength, he is worthy to serve Israel; his reward is not to be lost. Take for yourself Joshua son of Nun’ (Numbers 27:18), to fulfill what is stated: ‘One who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין מְצוּיִים לִהְיוֹת בְּנֵיהֶם תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (פא.),
connections.quote: ‘Why is it uncommon for Torah scholars’ sons to become Torah scholars? Rav Yosef said: So that they will not say, ‘Torah is their inheritance.’ Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi says: So that they will not become arrogant toward the community. Mar Zutra says: Because they assert their power over the community. Rav Ashi says: Because they call people ‘donkeys.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:): כֶּתֶר תּוֹרָה מוּנָּח לַכֹּל.
connections.quote: “There are three crowns: that of the altar, that of the ark, and that of the table. Aaron merited and took that of the altar; David merited and took that of the table. That of the ark still lies available: whoever wishes to take it may come and take it. Lest you say it is lesser, Scripture says, “By me kings reign.””
connections.context: The altar and table correspond to priesthood and kingship; the ark’s crown is Torah and remains open to anyone who seeks it. That openness is the contrast Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:): כֶּתֶר תּוֹרָה מוּנָּח לַכֹּל.
connections.quote: “The crown of Torah, which stands above them all, is the level of “He”: the hidden depth to which all the seed of Israel are attached. That is why they all merited receiving the Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:): כֶּתֶר תּוֹרָה מוּנָּח לַכֹּל.
connections.quote: “From the aspect of the Oral Torah, a person bequeaths his power to his children, because the child derives from the father’s essence. Just as the offspring of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov are, from birth, from the womb, and from conception, offspring blessed by Hashem and holy offspring, so it should be with Torah: one who is the very essence of Torah, whose powers are all of this character, should be able to bequeath it to his children. Yet Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him, was the very essence of the Torah, which is called by his name, and he did not leave his crown to his children; rather, the crown of Torah lies available to everyone. For from the aspect of the Written Torah, which is Hashem’s Torah, he has no relationship with it that would make it exclusively his, so that he could bequeath it to his children. Only from the aspect of the Oral Torah, which is “his Torah,” would it be fitting for him to bequeath it; yet it is still not completely acquired, for “at first,” and so forth [it is called Hashem’s Torah]. Throughout a person’s life, the same beginning and end remain: at every level where he stands, he is at the end of what preceded it and at the beginning of what follows it. He always still needs labor and effort. With every teaching of Torah, he does not bless over the Torah at the beginning; only at the end does he recognize this, and it is then called “his Torah” retroactively.”
connections.context: The passage first raises the possibility of inheritance and then expressly limits it: Torah remains a continuing task of effort and acquisition. This explains why Moshe’s crown is open to all rather than secured for his biological descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא מֹשֶׁה "אָב בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי" (מְגִילָּה יג.),
connections.quote: ‘‘Father,’ ‘father,’ ‘father’—a father in Torah, a father in wisdom, a father in prophecy. ‘These are the sons of Bithiah, whom Mered took.’ Was his name Mered? Was his name not Caleb? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let Caleb, who rebelled against the spies’ counsel, come and marry Pharaoh’s daughter, who rebelled against the idols of her father’s house.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי תּוֹאַר "אָב" אַף לְשֶׁאֵין בָּנָיו, עַיֵּין בְּפֶרֶק ב דִּבְרָכוֹת (טז:) "אֵין קוֹרִין אָבוֹת וְכוּלֵי, אִי מֵרָחֵל וְכוּלֵי", עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Only three are called ‘patriarchs,’ and only four are called ‘matriarchs.’ What is the reason concerning the patriarchs? If it is because we do not know whether we descend from Reuven or from Shimon, then concerning the matriarchs, too, we do not know whether we descend from Rachel or from Leah! Rather, those up to this point possess the stature for this designation; those after them do not.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ עַל כָּל הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל: "אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים":
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abba said in the name of Shmuel: For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed. These said, “The law follows our view,” and those said, “The law follows our view.” A heavenly voice went forth and said: Both these and those are the words of the living God, and the law follows Beit Hillel. Since both these and those are the words of the living God, why did Beit Hillel merit having the law established according to their view? Because they were gentle and forbearing, and studied both their own words and the words of Beit Shammai. Moreover, they placed Beit Shammai’s words before their own.”
connections.context: The original passage preserves both the truth represented by the differing views and the practical decision in favor of Beit Hillel. Rav Tzadok explains how distinct spiritual qualities can give rise to those different views.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ עַל כָּל הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל: "אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים":
connections.quote: “Concerning a disagreement for the sake of Heaven, our Sages said: “Both these and those are the words of the living God.” Both are called “the city of our God” and the counsel of Hashem, for the blessed God created different views. Yet from this also emerged the disagreement of Korach and his congregation. The Zohar says that Korach was the beginning of disagreement in the manner of anger. The meaning is as follows: As is known, “the world is built through lovingkindness.” The beginning of creation comes from the attribute of lovingkindness associated with Avraham. This is God’s kindness in drawing forth abundance so that a creature should exist; from this aspect, the flow extends to every creature with the greatest possible perfection. If so, there could be no division into different creatures, for such division necessarily involves one lacking a quality that another has. Therefore, on the second day, the attribute of restriction was created: the left hand that pushes away, opposite the right hand that draws near. This produced distinctions: this creature’s attainment reaches this far, and that creature’s this far. From this came the attainment of Yitzchak our father, who followed Avraham, the first to attain knowledge that there is a Creator of the world. He was not satisfied with his father’s attainment, but sought an additional, distinct attainment. As is known, that is why “God of” is said separately concerning each of the forefathers: each attained something particular and distinct. Yitzchak introduced this recognition: there are different attainments and different paths to reaching God’s truth. Otherwise, one creature and one day of creation would have sufficed. Since God distinguished and formed different creatures, there must be different and distinct ways of praising Him, each true in itself and in its own place. This is the quality of the forefathers, among whom there is no actual disagreement: Avraham’s and Yitzchak’s qualities—love and fear—are both true together, and one must serve God through both. Each is true in itself and according to its level, like the upper and lower waters and the firmament separating them, each fully existing in its own place. But in the children afterward—that is, as these qualities spread—each already contained both qualities, though one quality predominated in one and the other in another. From this came disagreement: concerning the very same matter, one says this and another says that. For they are all also joined and united through their mutual inclusion; therefore they judge the same matter differently.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok connects differing judgments to differing proportions of shared spiritual qualities. The qualification “for the sake of Heaven” belongs to the source’s opening statement and is retained here.

connections.hePhrase: [סג] הַבָּנִים דּוֹמִים לָאֵם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (מט.): יִשָּׂא בַּת תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאִם וְכוּלֵי בָּנָיו תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים;
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: A person should always sell everything he possesses and marry the daughter of a Torah scholar, for if he dies or goes into exile, he is assured that his sons will be Torah scholars. He should not marry the daughter of an unlearned person, for if he dies or goes into exile, his sons will be unlearned.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "בֵּן כְּסִיל תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ" (מִשְׁלֵי י, א), וְלֹא אָבִיו.
connections.quote: ‘The proverbs of Solomon: A wise son gladdens his father, but a foolish son is his mother’s grief.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "בֵּן כְּסִיל תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ" (מִשְׁלֵי י, א), וְלֹא אָבִיו.
connections.quote: “The matter is explained by what is said in Eduyot: A father confers upon his son, among other things, wisdom; the influence of wisdom comes to the son from the father. The mother, who is not obligated in Torah study and is not obligated to teach her son Torah, brings fear of Hashem into the son, for she is called “a woman who fears Hashem.” This is what Scripture says: “A wise son gladdens his father, but a foolish son is his mother’s grief.” The son’s wisdom comes principally from the father, and the father rejoices. A foolish son means one who lacks fear of Heaven, as the Sages expounded: “Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to acquire wisdom, when he has no heart?”—those who engage in Torah but have no fear of Heaven. Because he lacks fear of Heaven, even though he studies Torah, he is nevertheless called a fool; for the essence of Torah is that it shows a person the way of Hashem. Since he lacks fear of Heaven, it is “a price in the hand of a fool.” Therefore it is written, “A foolish son”—who has no fear of Heaven—“is his mother’s grief,” because she did not instill fear of Heaven in him.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the specific reference to the mother’s grief through her role in instilling reverence. Later in the same passage Rav Tzadok also recognizes the mother’s share in the child’s Torah learning through helping him attend to it.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּנִדָּה (לא.): תָּלָה הַכָּתוּב הַזְּכָרִים בִּנְקֵבוֹת וּנְקֵבוֹת בִּזְכָרִים.
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: At first they would say: If the woman emits seed first, she bears a male; if the man emits seed first, she bears a female. The Sages did not explain the matter until Rabbi Tzadok came and explained it: ‘These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, and Dinah his daughter.’ Scripture attributes the males to the females, and the females to the males.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, מִצַּד הָרְגִילוּת הַבַּת אֵצֶל אִמָּהּ, הִיא דּוֹמָה גַּם כֵּן לְאִמָּהּ מִצַּד הַהֶרְגֵּל וְלֹא מִצַּד הַתּוֹלָדָה,
connections.quote: ““The young woman ran and told her mother’s household.” Rabbi Yochanan said: A woman ordinarily frequents her mother’s household. They objected to him: But is it not written, “She told her father”? He said to them: Her mother had died; whom else should she have told, if not her father?”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the background for the ois’s phrase “the daughter’s habitual presence with her mother.” It speaks about ordinary familiarity and includes the case in which the mother had died.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, מִצַּד הָרְגִילוּת הַבַּת אֵצֶל אִמָּהּ, הִיא דּוֹמָה גַּם כֵּן לְאִמָּהּ מִצַּד הַהֶרְגֵּל וְלֹא מִצַּד הַתּוֹלָדָה,
connections.quote: “On ‘Go forth from your land’ (Genesis 12:1): the Midrash teaches (Kohelet Rabbah on 7:1; Tanchuma, Vayakhel 1) that a person has three names. The first is the name others call him, meaning the character a person learns from others. This is ‘from your land’; corresponding to it is ‘I will make you a great nation’ (Genesis 12:2)—an entire nation from whom to learn, so that learning from others will itself be good and need not be abandoned. The second is the name his father calls him, as the Sages taught, ‘A father endows his son’ [Eduyot 2:9], and ‘a ewe follows a ewe’ (Ketubot 63a). This is ‘from your father's house’; corresponding to it is ‘I will make your name great,’ from Avram to Avraham, ‘a father of a multitude of nations’ (Genesis 17:5), so that he becomes a father to the whole world and the ancestral house is also good. The third is the name recorded at his birth: his inborn disposition, as in ‘one born under Mars’ (Shabbat 156a). This is ‘from your birthplace’; corresponding to it is ‘I will bless you’ within your inborn nature. One must depart from these influences, but the departure is not to the opposite extreme. Rather, it is ‘to the land that I will show you,’ to the place toward which the spirit of Hashem directs him. Sometimes Hashem's will is precisely in the quality that appears deficient, as is known.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah distinguishes the character learned from other people, what is received through one's family, and the disposition present at birth. This gives a fuller account of the siman's distinction between resemblance through upbringing and resemblance through origin. Its conclusion also qualifies the implications: departing from these influences does not mean mechanically choosing their opposite; their proper use depends on the direction Hashem shows a person. Citation correction: “A father endows his son” is in Mishnah Eduyot 2:9. The accompanying reference to Avot in the supplied Hebrew is mistaken; the corrected reference is shown in square brackets in the translation.
connections.headline: Distinguishing what is learned from what is inherited

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (כְּתוּבּוֹת סג.): "רְחֵילָא בָּתַר רְחֵילָא וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Her father heard that a great man had come to the town. He said, ‘I will go to him; perhaps he can release me from my vow.’ He came before him, and he asked him, ‘Would you have made your vow had you known that he would become a great man?’ He answered, ‘Not even if he had learned a single chapter, or even a single halakhah.’ He said to him, ‘I am that man.’ He fell on his face, kissed his feet, and gave him half his wealth. Rabbi Akiva’s daughter did the same for Ben Azzai. This is what people say: ‘A ewe follows a ewe; as the mother acts, so does her daughter.’”

connections.hePhrase: לְכָךְ הַנּוֹשֵׂא אִשָּׁה יִבְדּוֹק בְּאַחֶיהָ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קי.).
connections.quote: ‘Rava said: Someone who marries a woman should investigate her brothers, as it is said: ‘Aaron took Elisheva, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nachshon.’ Since it says ‘daughter of Amminadab,’ do I not already know that she is Nachshon’s sister? What does ‘sister of Nachshon’ teach? From here we learn that someone who marries a woman should investigate her brothers. It was taught: Most sons resemble their mother’s brothers.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מַה שֶּׁהוּא סָתוּם בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב שֶׁל הָאָבוֹת, מִתְגַּלֶּה לַפּוֹעַל בַּבָּנִים,
connections.quote: “As is known, the children reveal the depths of their fathers’ hearts that had been hidden even from the fathers themselves.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ קִבַּלְתִּי: כִּי הַבָּנִים – מַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב הָאָבוֹת:
connections.quote: “But it is known that the children clarify the fathers. As I heard, the depths of the fathers’ hearts and what is hidden within them are revealed in the children. It is also known that every clarification must come through its opposite. Therefore Avraham fathered Yitzchak: his desire was to clarify that Avraham’s lovingkindness was only for the sake of Heaven. The dross of Yishmael, who came from him, was not called his offspring; this was clarified when he fathered Yitzchak, who is called his offspring and in whom the depths of his heart are revealed. Yitzchak’s quality, on the contrary, was restriction and fear for the sake of Heaven. This clarified that the lovingkindness manifest in Avraham our father was also only for the sake of Heaven. He was not like the nations of the world, who are immersed in one quality and cannot change it; in his depths he also possessed the opposite quality, and if it were needed for the sake of Heaven, he would use it as well, as happened at the binding of Yitzchak.”
connections.context: This gives a developed instance of the teaching Rav Tzadok says he received: Yitzchak’s opposite quality reveals that Avraham’s kindness was a free devotion to God rather than an unchangeable temperament.

connections.hePhrase: [סד] פְּעָמִים שֶׁרוֹאֶה בְּבֵירוּר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְסַיְּיעוֹ וּמַסְכִּים עִם מַעֲשָׂיו, עִם כָּל זֶה אֵינוֹ רְאָיָה כִּי מַעֲשָׂיו יְשָׁרִים בֶּאֱמֶת,
connections.quote: “But one must not think, God forbid, that because everything comes from the blessed God, one may follow the way of one’s heart without any effort and rely on the blessed God’s help, as in “For You are with me.” Against this, the Tanchuma concludes: “The utterance of the Lord is refined; He is a shield for all who take refuge in Him.” This refers to someone who exerts and strengthens himself, on his own side, to subdue his inclination with all his power; desires to take refuge beneath His blessed wings; looks to God; and prays and pleads before the Holy One, blessed be He. He is then assured that God will not leave him in the inclination’s hand. “He is a shield for all who take refuge in Him”: the evil inclination will have no power over him at all. A shield means that He conceals him from his enemy so that it cannot approach him at all.”
connections.explanation: Lech Lecha explicitly rejects the inference that divine agency permits someone to follow whatever his heart desires. It describes reliance through resisting the inclination, seeking refuge in Hashem, and praying. Read alongside this siman’s warning about apparently confirming miracles, it directs attention back to the character of the person’s choice. Assistance and success are not substitutes for that examination; ‘It is not in heaven’ remains decisive in the siman’s halakhic example.
connections.headline: Reliance on Hashem requires examining and directing one’s own effort

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "מַדְרִיכֲךָ בְּדֶרֶךְ תֵּלֵךְ" (יְשַׁעְיָה מח, יז),
connections.quote: ‘Thus says Hashem, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: ‘I am Hashem your God, who teaches you for your benefit, who guides you on the path you shall take.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מַכּוֹת י:): בְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לֵילֵךְ – מוֹלִיכִין אוֹתוֹ
connections.quote: “Rabba bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Huna—and some say Rav Huna said it in the name of Rabbi Elazar: From the Torah, from the Prophets, and from the Writings we learn that a person is led along the path he wishes to take. From the Torah, as it is written: ‘You shall not go with them,’ and it is written: ‘Rise, go with them.’ From the Prophets, as it is written: ‘I am Hashem your God, who teaches you for your benefit, who guides you on the path you shall take.’ From the Writings, as it is written: ‘Toward scoffers He scoffs, but to the humble He gives favor.’”

connections.hePhrase: הֲלֹא תִרְאֶה בְּאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קיג.) שֶׁהָיָה קָשֶׁה לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ עֲצִירַת הַגְּשָׁמִים,
connections.quote: ‘‘The word of Hashem came to him, saying: Go from here, turn eastward, and hide in the brook Cherith.’ ‘The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning,’ and so forth. From where? Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: From Ahab’s slaughterhouse. ‘After a time the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.’ Once he saw that there was suffering in the world, it is written: ‘The word of Hashem came to him, saying: Arise, go to Zarephath.’’

connections.hePhrase: הֲלֹא תִרְאֶה בְּאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קיג.) שֶׁהָיָה קָשֶׁה לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ עֲצִירַת הַגְּשָׁמִים,
connections.quote: “When Eliyahu saw the death of the widow of Tzarfat's son, it touched his very life. The child's mother argued that Eliyahu was responsible: because he had come to lodge with her, the Holy One, blessed be He, compared her deeds with Eliyahu's, recalled her sin, and she was punished. This event therefore touched Eliyahu's very life. He understood from Hashem's bringing about such an event that His will was for him to pray that the whole generation repent, so that rain should come after the famine had become so severe. Hashem desired Eliyahu to pray for the whole generation's repentance, for He does not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from their ways and live. This is the Yerushalmi's meaning: when he revived the widow's son, the vow concerning dew and rain was released.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef follows the same drought narrative into the death of the widow's son. It reads Eliyahu's distress as a summons to pray for the generation's repentance and the return of rain. This supplies a particular corrective within the siman's example: the miraculous assistance that sustained Eliyahu did not end the need to discern what Hashem desired next. The source directs his strength toward the life and return of the people.
connections.headline: Eliyahu's crisis redirects his prayer

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן אָמַר לוֹ לְאֵלִיָּהוּ: "לֵךְ... וְנִסְתַּרְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר", וְעֲזָרוֹ לְהִסָּתֵר מִפְּנֵי אַחְאָב בְּדֶרֶךְ נֵס,
connections.quote: ‘Go from here, turn eastward, and hide at the Cherith stream, which faces the Jordan.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִוא" (דְּבָרִים ל, יב),
connections.quote: ‘It is not in heaven, so that you would say: ‘Who will go up to heaven for us, take it for us, and make us hear it, so that we may perform it?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעֲזָרוּ לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּדֶרֶךְ נֵס לְהַרְאוֹת שֶׁהַדִּין עִמּוֹ, לֹא סָמְכוּ עַל זֶה (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא נט:),
connections.quote: “He again said to them, “If the law follows my opinion, let Heaven prove it.” A heavenly voice came forth and said, “Why do you oppose Rabbi Eliezer, when the law follows his opinion in every matter?” Rabbi Yehoshua rose to his feet and said, “It is not in heaven!” What does “It is not in heaven” mean? Rabbi Yirmeyah said: The Torah has already been given at Mount Sinai. We do not heed a heavenly voice, for You already wrote in the Torah at Mount Sinai, “Incline after the majority.””

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעֲזָרוּ לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּדֶרֶךְ נֵס לְהַרְאוֹת שֶׁהַדִּין עִמּוֹ, לֹא סָמְכוּ עַל זֶה (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא נט:),
connections.heRef: תוספות הרא"ש על ברכות נ״ב א:א׳
connections.quote: ““It follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who says that we do not heed a heavenly voice.” This is difficult: Rabbi Yehoshua said this concerning the disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, and we too do not follow Rabbi Eliezer or the heavenly voice there. But here, concerning Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, we follow the heavenly voice; perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua agrees in this case as well. The answer is that Rabbi Yehoshua’s formulation—“We do not heed a heavenly voice,” because “It is not in heaven”—implies that a heavenly voice should be disregarded in every case. We, however, follow the heavenly voice in favor of Beit Hillel because Beit Hillel were the majority; a heavenly voice was needed because Beit Shammai were sharper. But the heavenly voice for Rabbi Eliezer came only in Rabbi Eliezer’s honor, and [following it] would contradict the verse “Incline after the majority.””
connections.context: Tosafot HaRosh distinguishes a heavenly voice that resolves a doubt while supporting the majority from the voice honoring Rabbi Eliezer against the majority. This provides a direct original-source explanation for the lack of practical authority of the latter voice.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁחָשְׁבוּ שֶׁהוּא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוּא רוֹצֶה לֵילֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ זֶה.
connections.heRef: רב נסים גאון על מסכת ברכות י״ט ב:א׳
connections.quote: “Concerning the statement that a heavenly voice went forth and said, “What have you against Rabbi Eliezer, whose view the law follows everywhere?” I have seen two answers. The first is that the heavenly voice did not say that the law followed him in this matter; it said “everywhere” without specification. It is possible that it meant everywhere except this case, or similar cases in which the law does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. Thus the words of the heavenly voice would remain correct and valid. The second is that its purpose was only to test the Sages: would they abandon the tradition in their possession and the teaching in their mouths because of a heavenly voice, or not? This resembles what is written, “For Hashem your God is testing you.” Through all this, the soundness of their tradition became known. This is what Rabbi Yehoshua said: “It is not in heaven.” That is, Hashem’s Torah is perfect and has already been given to us at Sinai; He made known that He does not replace a single word of it. Our Torah contains no deficiency or uncertainty that would require proof from heaven.”
connections.context: Rav Nissim presents testing the Sages as one of two explanations, both retained here. Rav Tzadok develops his own account of the divine assistance given to Rabbi Eliezer; the shared point is that a heavenly sign does not displace the Torah’s received rules of judgment.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה הָיְתָה גַּם כֵּן תְּלוּנַּת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל: "אַתֶּם הֲמִתֶּם אֶת עַם ה'" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יז, ו),
connections.quote: ‘On the next day, the whole assembly of the children of Israel complained against Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘You have put Hashem’s people to death.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה הָיְתָה גַּם כֵּן תְּלוּנַּת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל: "אַתֶּם הֲמִתֶּם אֶת עַם ה'" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יז, ו),
connections.quote: ““You have killed”—the meaning is: What proof did this provide that the tribe of Levi was chosen and that Aharon was chosen as High Priest? Perhaps through your prayer, or through wisdom that you possessed, you burned those who brought the offering.”
connections.context: Ibn Ezra explains the complaint as a challenge to what the miracle proved: the people imagined that Moshe and Aharon’s own spiritual power had brought about the deaths. This is the complaint Rav Tzadok develops.

connections.hePhrase: רַק: אַתֶּם רְצִיתֶם לֵילֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ זֶה וּזְכוּתְכֶם גָּדוֹל, וּלְכָךְ הֲמִתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר:
connections.quote: ““For it is not from my own heart.” This also explains the verse “You have killed the people of Hashem.” The principle is that sometimes a righteous person brings about something even though it was not decreed above; nevertheless, through his prayer, the righteous person accomplishes it. Sometimes the righteous person draws down an action from above that was decreed above. Here Israel suspected that Moshe our teacher and Aharon, through their righteousness, had accomplished this through their prayer. That is what they meant by “You have killed the people of Hashem.” Therefore Moshe our teacher said, “For it is not from my own heart”: this matter was decreed by the Holy One, blessed be He; we did not bring it about through our prayer.”
connections.context: Kedushat Levi distinguishes the people’s suspicion from Moshe’s answer. The note retains both, so that the explanation of their complaint is not mistaken for the source’s endorsement of it.

connections.hePhrase: כְּדִכְתִיב: "וּרְאֵה אִם דֶּרֶךְ עֹצֶב בִּי, וּנְחֵנִי בְּדֶרֶךְ עוֹלָם" (תְּהִלִּים קלט, כד),
connections.quote: ‘See whether there is a harmful way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּדִכְתִיב: "וּרְאֵה אִם דֶּרֶךְ עֹצֶב בִּי, וּנְחֵנִי בְּדֶרֶךְ עוֹלָם" (תְּהִלִּים קלט, כד),
connections.quote: ““A grievous way”—a way of rebellion, as in “They rebelled and grieved His holy spirit.” “And lead me”—if You see any rebellious way in me, put me to death immediately. This is “the way of the world,” as in “I am going the way of all the earth,” and “A person goes to his everlasting home.””
