connections.context: Radak reads “the way of the world” here as death, the way of all the earth. This is the reading of the verse needed to understand Rav Tzadok’s opening statement.

connections.hePhrase: כְּדִכְתִיב: "וּרְאֵה אִם דֶּרֶךְ עֹצֶב בִּי, וּנְחֵנִי בְּדֶרֶךְ עוֹלָם" (תְּהִלִּים קלט, כד),
connections.quote: “True clarification in prayer is as we find with King David, peace be upon him, when he said (Psalms 139:23–24): ‘Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my thoughts. See whether there is a grievous way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.’ This means: if my prayer is pure, and the good for which I pray will help me increase the honor of Heaven, then I entreat You to answer me and grant my request. But if it is revealed before You that the good for which I pray will turn me away from fearing You and from Your will, then I too do not desire the good You would bestow on me. This is like what the Gemara teaches (Ketubot 83a): a person may stipulate that he will not inherit an inheritance coming to him from another source. Hashem showed Avraham our father, peace be upon him, that He deals with him measure for measure: just as Avraham desires only such good as will increase the honor of Heaven, so Hashem desires the very life of Avraham our father, peace be upon him.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov develops the very Psalm cited here into a condition within prayer: the petitioner asks for the desired benefit insofar as it will increase the honor of Heaven, and relinquishes it if it would lead away from Hashem. This illuminates the inward submission expressed by nefilat apayim after articulated prayer. The surrender reaches one's own preferred outcome while preserving the reality of prayer and the preciousness of life, as the paragraph's conclusion about Avraham makes explicit.
connections.headline: Surrender within the request itself

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיָן זֶה אָמַר יוֹנָה: "טוֹב מוֹתִי מֵחַיָּי" (יוֹנָה ד, ג).
connections.quote: ‘Now, Hashem, please take my life from me, for my death is better than my life.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן נְפִילַת אַפַּיִם אַחַר כָּל תְּפִלָּה,
connections.quote: “To surrender one’s soul to Him and give Him one’s soul with the heart’s willing intention, when falling upon one’s face and saying, “To You, Hashem, I lift my soul”: one should direct one’s heart and will toward Him, to surrender one’s soul to Him with complete willingness.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן נְפִילַת אַפַּיִם אַחַר כָּל תְּפִלָּה,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the words spoken here, ‘God, God of the spirits of all flesh.’ As the holy Zohar says there, Moses and Aharon surrendered themselves to death: this surrender disclosed the truth concerning all Israel, whose root of vitality they receive from a high place above their sin; examine the Zohar there carefully. This is why ‘all flesh’ is mentioned here. As my holy grandfather explained, it alludes to ‘He remembered that they were flesh, a wind that passes and does not return.’ This is remembrance for good: Hashem has compassion on a person because he is only flesh. Moses mentioned this here in praying that Hashem awaken mercy from this place, so that none of the congregation be cast away.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the same Zohar passage as an appeal to the root of Israel's life that lies beyond its failure. This makes the direction of their surrender clear: it becomes a prayer that the congregation be preserved. Their willingness to relinquish their own standing is joined to compassion for others, rather than a claim of personal superiority over those who sinned.
connections.headline: Surrender that becomes a plea for the community

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רָמַ"ח אִישׁ "חָטְאוּ בְּנַפְשֹׁתָם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יז, ג),
connections.quote: ‘As for the firepans of these people who sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar. For they brought them before Hashem, and they became holy; they shall be a sign for the children of Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ: קֹרַח שֶׁפִּקֵּחַ הָיָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “This was Korah’s error: a garment entirely of tekhelet—the intensity of awe, with “I have set the Lord before me always” so utterly clear that it brings everything to annihilation—he wished to exempt from the thread of tzitzit that recalls all the commandments. For “the entire congregation is holy” to such a degree that within them is the Lord, who brings existence into being in the present just as He did in the past and will in the future. What room, then, is there for choice and service? So I heard.”

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ: קֹרַח שֶׁפִּקֵּחַ הָיָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “But Korach, who was astute, what led him to this foolishness? His eye misled him. He saw a great lineage arising from him: Shmuel, who is equal to Moshe and Aharon, as it is stated, “Moshe and Aharon among His priests, and Shmuel among those who call His name”; and twenty-four divisions arising from his descendants, all prophesying with the holy spirit, as it is stated, “All these were sons of Heman.” He said: Could such greatness be destined to arise from me, and I remain silent? But he did not see correctly: his sons repented, and these descendants arose from them. Moshe, however, did see. That is why Korach joined in, relying on the assurance he had heard from Moshe’s mouth that all would perish and one would survive: “The man whom Hashem chooses—he is the holy one.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains both Korach’s vision and the error in his inference. His descendants’ greatness came through his sons’ repentance; it did not guarantee that Korach himself would be chosen.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה) שֶׁהָיוּ בִּכְלָלָם הַשְּׁנֵים עָשָׂר נְשִׂיאִים,
connections.quote: “When Moshe said, “They shall put a thread of tekhelet on the corner fringe,” Korach immediately ordered two hundred and fifty garments of tekhelet to be made. The two hundred and fifty heads of Sanhedrin who rose against Moshe wrapped themselves in them, as it is stated, “They rose before Moshe, two hundred and fifty men from the children of Israel, leaders of the congregation, those summoned to assembly.” Korach arose and made them a feast, and they wrapped themselves in garments of tekhelet. Aharon’s sons came to take their priestly gifts, the breast and the thigh. They opposed them and said: Who commanded you to take this? Was it not Moshe? We will give nothing; God did not say this. They came and told Moshe. He went to appease them, and they immediately rose against him to confront him before Moshe. “Two hundred and fifty men from the children of Israel”—who were they? Elitzur son of Shedeur and his companions, “these men who were designated by name.” Although Scripture did not identify them openly, it gave their distinguishing signs, and from the verses you can recognize them. To what may this be compared? To a well-born man found stealing objects from a bathhouse. The owner did not want to expose him, so he began giving his distinguishing signs. When asked who had stolen his objects, he said: That well-born man, tall, with fine teeth, black hair, and a handsome nose. Once he gave the signs, they knew who he was. Here too, although Scripture left their identities unstated, it gave their signs, and you know who they were. Elsewhere it says, “These were those summoned from the congregation, the leaders of their ancestral tribes, heads of Israel’s thousands,” and “Moshe and Aharon took these men who were designated by name.” Here it says, “Leaders of the congregation, those summoned to assembly, men of renown,” and “They assembled against Moshe and Aharon.””
connections.context: This passage identifies the company both as heads of Sanhedrin and as Elitzur and his fellow tribal leaders. Its comparison of the two biblical descriptions supplies the basis for Rav Tzadok’s reference to the twelve princes.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הֵם חָטְאוּ בְּנַפְשׁוֹתָם, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּנָזִיר: "חָטָא עַל הַנָּפֶשׁ" – פֵּירוּשׁ מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ.
connections.quote: “Shmuel said: Anyone who observes a fast is called a sinner. He follows this tanna, as it was taught: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar the Great says: What does “He shall atone for him for having sinned against the soul” teach? Against what soul did this person sin? Rather, he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine. Is this not an argument from the lesser to the greater? If one who afflicted himself only by abstaining from wine is called a sinner, all the more so one who afflicts himself by abstaining from every kind of enjoyment. Rabbi Elazar says: He is called holy, as it is stated, “He shall be holy; he shall let the locks of his head grow.” If one who afflicted himself in only one respect is called holy, all the more so one who afflicts himself in every respect. But according to Shmuel, is he not called holy? That refers to the growth of his hair. And according to Rabbi Elazar, is he not called a sinner? That concerns one who rendered himself impure.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok draws on the interpretation of sinning “against the soul” as self-affliction. The original exchange also records the opposing description of the nazir as holy and explains how each view reads the other verse.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּדְעוּ כִּי לֶעָתִיד לֹא יְלַמְּדוּ אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ, וְיִהְיֶה מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ שֶׁ"כָּל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים",
connections.quote: (31:34 on Sefaria): “They will no longer teach, each his fellow and each his brother, saying, “Know the Lord,” for they will all know Me, from their smallest to their greatest, says the Lord; for I will forgive their iniquity and no longer remember their sin.”
connections.context: The promise is of direct, shared knowledge of God.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת לוּלֵי שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא הָיוּ עַל מַדְרֵגַת לֶעָתִיד, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ה.)],
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Come, let us be grateful to our fathers, for had they not sinned, we would not have come into the world, as it is said: ‘I said, you are godlike beings, and all of you are children of the Most High’ (Psalms 82:6). Once you corrupted your deeds: ‘Indeed, you shall die like men’ (Psalms 82:7).”
connections.context: Before the sin of the Golden Calf, Israel stood at the level of “godlike beings,” beyond death; the sin is what brought them down from it.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת לוּלֵי שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא הָיוּ עַל מַדְרֵגַת לֶעָתִיד, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ה.)],
connections.quote: “This was Korach’s error: at the giving of the Torah, it was indeed fitting that the true rectification should come about as it will in the future. This was his claim: “The entire congregation is holy”—they all heard at Sinai, “I am Hashem your God”—“and Hashem is among them.” That is, as it will be in the future, when the Holy One, blessed be He, sits among them and they surround Him in a circle. In a circle there are no differences of level; thus, “Why do you exalt yourselves above the congregation of Hashem?” This is indeed so when the attribute of Atika is revealed, as at the giving of the Torah, when “Hashem spoke with you face to face.” Likewise, the revelation at the splitting of the sea came from Atika, as the Zohar says, “It depends on Atika.” The Mekhilta and the Zohar say that a maidservant at the sea saw what Yechezkel did not see: she saw as did the greatest person in Israel. All were equal, for when the revelation depends on Atika, there are no differences of level. So too at the giving of the Torah: “Israel encamped there,” which Rashi explains as one person with one heart; there were no differences of level, as it is stated, “Hashem spoke with you face to face.” But afterward this level was lost, and this revelation will not come until the future, when the true rectification arrives.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the counterfactual in the ois: Sinai opened the possibility of the future level, but that level was subsequently lost. Korach’s error was to regard the complete future state as already continuously present.

connections.hePhrase: וּמֵרוֹב הִשְׁתּוֹקְקוּתָם לָזֶה, עַד שֶׁנִּתְרַצּוּ בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁאִם בֶּאֱמֶת אֵינָם בְּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ – אָז טוֹב מוֹתָם מֵחַיֵּיהֶם, וּמוּסְכָּמִים לָמוּת בֶּאֱמֶת
connections.quote: “This is what the Midrash Rabbah intimates: “Were they fools? Rather, they sinned against their own souls.” They thought and accepted upon themselves, in surrender of their souls, that if the incense should make clear that despite all this their souls were still not completely purified, then what need had they for life in this world? “And Korach, who was astute”—he was a great scholar in the wisdom of Torah and should have known that “there is no righteous person on earth” and that there are higher levels above higher levels in the chambers of Torah. “But his eye misled him,” because he possessed the holy spirit and saw a great lineage, and so it seemed to him that he would be the chosen one. This was clarified by “They descended alive to the underworld”: even in the underworld they remain in the fullness of their life in holiness. This resembles what was said of Adam: “Lest he stretch out his hand and take also from the Tree of Life, and eat and live forever.” As the Midrash Rabbah says, they remain alive and in existence until now; at that very moment it became clear to them that Moshe is true and his Torah is true. In the future they too are destined to ascend, as it is stated, “Hashem puts to death and brings to life; He brings down to the underworld and raises up.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel supplies the interpretation of their willingness to risk their lives, while retaining the error in their self-assessment and the distinction between Korach’s vision and its fulfillment.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶהוּ: קֹרַח שֶׁפִּקֵּחַ הָיָה – פֵּירוּשׁ, "פִּקֵּחַ" בְּכָל מָקוֹם בְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עָרוּם, כְּמוֹ "אִי פִּקֵּחַ הוּא וְכוּלֵי" (כְּתוּבּוֹת פח.), שֶׁטָּעַם מֵעֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ עוֹד].
connections.quote: “If he is astute, he brings her to a Torah-level oath. He pays her marriage settlement before one witness and joins the earlier witness to the later witness, treating the earlier money as a loan.”
connections.context: The case concerns a disputed payment of a marriage settlement and how a litigant may bring about the more stringent oath. Rav Tzadok refers to the phrase “if he is astute”; the surrounding legal case is supplied to identify that expression accurately.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר לְמֹשֶׁה וּלְאַהֲרֹן: "הִבָּדְלוּ וְגוֹמֵר", וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ: "הֵרֹמּוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Separate yourselves from the midst of this assembly, and I will consume them in an instant.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהִקְשָׁה הָרַמְבַּ"ן: וְכִי אֵין בְּיַד ה' לְהַצִּילָם וְהֵם תּוֹךְ הָעֵדָה?
connections.quote: ““Remove yourselves from this congregation”—I do not understand the reason for this verse and its counterpart above, “Separate yourselves from this congregation.” God has the power to kill many by plague around one righteous person, leaving that person alone alive, as occurred among the firstborn of Egypt. So too in every plague: three people sleep beneath one blanket, two die, and the one in the middle escapes. It appears that the wrath was going forth to kill the entire congregation as these sinners were killed, because they had followed them—through the opening of the earth’s mouth or the fire that came forth. These are encompassing blows, capable of killing everyone standing there together, unless a second miracle is performed for those who escape. Alternatively, the Holy One, blessed be He, said this in honor of the righteous: as long as they remained among them, He would not strike them. The purpose of these and similar statements is to make known that they need a plea for mercy and atonement, and Moshe is the one who hastens to do this immediately.”
connections.context: This is Ramban’s question, followed by his own two explanations and their practical purpose. Rav Tzadok takes up the question and offers the further explanation developed in this ois.

connections.hePhrase: [סו] תְּפִלָּה צָרִיךְ לְכָל דָּבָר, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּגְזַר מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: ““For He had not caused it to rain.” Why had He not caused it to rain? Because there was no human being to work the ground, and no one recognized the benefit of rain. When Adam came and knew that the world needed it, he prayed for it; the rain fell, and the trees and grasses grew.”
connections.context: Rashi presents a created benefit whose actual arrival awaits human recognition and prayer. This illustrates the opening claim that prayer remains necessary for something already provided for in the divine order.

connections.hePhrase: [סו] תְּפִלָּה צָרִיךְ לְכָל דָּבָר, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּגְזַר מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: see note 542.
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains Elijah's experience as a summons to pray for his generation's return. The rain is therefore connected with a change in the relationship between the people and Hashem. This illuminates why the promise cited here does not make Elijah's prayer redundant: the prayer itself belongs to the path by which the promised mercy is received.

connections.hePhrase: הֲלֹא תִרְאֶה בְּאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ה': "הֵרָאֵה אֶל אַחְאָב וְאֶתְּנָה מָטָר" (מְלָכִים א יח, א),
connections.quote: ‘After many days, the word of Hashem came to Elijah in the third year, saying: ‘Go, appear before Ahab, and I will give rain upon the face of the earth.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן נֶאֱמַר אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁעָלָה לְרֹאשׁ הַכַּרְמֶל "וַיִּגְהַר וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהִרְבָּה בִּתְפִלָּה עַד שֶׁבָּא גֶּשֶׁם.
connections.heRef: מצודת דוד על מלכים א י״ח:מ״ב:ב׳
connections.quote: ““He bent down toward the earth.” He prostrated himself on the ground; afterward he rose and placed his face between his knees to pray for rain. Although the Lord had told him, “I will give rain,” and so forth, he nevertheless prayed that it be given soon, while Ahab was still there. Because he was confident that his prayer would be accepted, he had already told Ahab, “There is the sound of abundant rain.””
connections.context: Metzudat David explicitly asks why Elijah prayed after the promise. His explanation concerns hastening the promised rain; Rav Tzadok uses Elijah’s conduct to establish the continuing place of prayer.

connections.hePhrase: וַחֲכָמִים דְּאָמְרוּ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (טז.) דִּגְזַר דִּין הוּא בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, לֹא פְּלִיגֵי אַאַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ סֵדֶר תְּפִלּוֹת בְּכָל יוֹם.
connections.quote: ‘For it was taught: Everything is judged on Rosh Hashanah, and its judgment is sealed on Yom Kippur; these are Rabbi Meir’s words. Rabbi Yehudah says: Everything is judged on Rosh Hashanah, but each judgment is sealed at its own time: on Pesach concerning grain; on Shavuot concerning the fruit of trees; on Sukkot concerning water. A person is judged on Rosh Hashanah, and his judgment is sealed on Yom Kippur.’

connections.hePhrase: וַחֲכָמִים דְּאָמְרוּ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (טז.) דִּגְזַר דִּין הוּא בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, לֹא פְּלִיגֵי אַאַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ סֵדֶר תְּפִלּוֹת בְּכָל יוֹם.
connections.heRef: תוספות על ראש השנה ט״ז א:י״ג:א׳
connections.quote: ““According to whom do we now pray for the sick and the weak? According to Rabbi Yosei.” If you ask: Even according to the Rabbis, do we not pray “Heal us” and the blessing over the years? Moreover, Rabbi Yehudah, who says here that a person is judged on Rosh Hashanah and that his decree is sealed on Yom Kippur, says in the first chapter of Shabbat that one visiting the sick says, “May the Omnipresent have mercy on you and on the sick of His people Israel.” Rabbeinu Tam answers that prayer that someone not become ill is indeed according to Rabbi Yosei alone, but prayer that someone recover is according to everyone: when people will become ill was decreed; when they will recover was not decreed. At the beginning of the chapter “One who vows from cooked food,” it explains Rav Yosef’s statement: “the sick” means those actually ill, while “the weak” means the scholars. Thus we pray that the sick recover, and that the weak—the scholars—not become ill. The prayer in the blessing over the years is as explained later in this chapter: if little rain was decreed, the Omnipresent should send it at the proper times. Another answer is that communal prayer is different, for the community’s decree can be torn up, as stated later. Rabbi Yehudah’s statement in Shabbat can likewise be explained this way, for it resembles communal prayer: together with the individual, one prays for all the sick.”
connections.context: Tosafot asks the same question about the established daily prayers. It offers two explanations, distinguishing prevention from recovery and distinguishing communal prayer. These are separate approaches to the difficulty that Rav Tzadok addresses here.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא: "כְּמַאן מְצַלֵּינַן הָאִידְנָא אַקְצִירֵי וּמָרִיעֵי? כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי" (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה טז.),
connections.quote: “Rav Yosef said: According to whom do we now pray for the sick and the weak? According to whom? According to Rabbi Yosei. Alternatively, you may say that this follows the Rabbis, in accordance with Rabbi Yitzchak. For Rabbi Yitzchak said: Crying out is beneficial for a person both before a decree and after a decree.”
connections.context: The full passage includes an alternative explanation that permits such prayer according to the Rabbis as well. Rav Tzadok develops the first answer, which names Rabbi Yosei. The earlier existing note quotes the annual judgment discussion; this is the separate passage that he now cites.

connections.hePhrase: [סז] בְּכָל מַדְרֵגָה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלֶה, יֵשׁ לוֹ לַחֲזוֹר וְלָשׁוּב עַל חֲטָאָיו,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים כ״ט:י״ג-י״ד
connections.quote: “Even though he has already repented properly, the essence of repentance is in the heart, and the heart has many levels and degrees. Everything depends on the person as he is, and on the time and place, as those who understand know. Therefore, now, at this moment, when he sees that the light of his soul does not rise within him, this indicates that today his repentance has not been accepted and his sins separate him, or that they wish to raise him to a higher repentance, from a still deeper place in his heart. Therefore David said, “My sin is before me always.””

connections.hePhrase: [סז] בְּכָל מַדְרֵגָה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלֶה, יֵשׁ לוֹ לַחֲזוֹר וְלָשׁוּב עַל חֲטָאָיו,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.quote: “This is why Hashem is called ‘the One who abundantly forgives’: forgiveness comes from His side, whereas from the human side there must be recognition of the sin and deficiency, as it says, ‘My sin is before me always’ (Psalms 51:5). Even though one confessed on this Yom Kippur, one confesses again on the next (Yoma 86b). For if a person decides for himself that there was no stumbling, but that everything was his own achievement, as do the nations around him, that itself is truly a stumbling. From the human side, one must recognize that a person has no independent power. The days when he walked in darkness, unaware that Hashem gives him the strength to act (Deuteronomy 8:18), were therefore sin and stumbling; then Hashem says that it was not a stumbling, as explained above.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim keeps together two statements that might appear to conflict: Hashem abundantly forgives, while the person continues to recognize his own failure. The distinction illuminates why a higher level can call forth renewed repentance without proving that the earlier repentance was rejected. The acknowledgment becomes more searching as the person's knowledge grows; the declaration that the past has been repaired remains a gift from Hashem rather than the person's self-exemption.
connections.headline: Accepted repentance and continuing recognition

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן "וְחַטָּאתִי נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ה),
connections.quote: ‘For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן "וְחַטָּאתִי נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ה),
connections.quote: “The eighteenth principle: that his sin remain before him always. It is fitting for the soul that has sinned to remember its transgressions always and not forget them with the passage of time. They should not be snatched away from his heart until the time of his passing, as it is said, “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is before me always.” This principle will be explained in the third gate.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah presents continued remembrance as a principle of repentance. Rav Tzadok explains why that remembrance can remain relevant even after repentance has been accepted: a higher spiritual level calls for renewed repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְנוֹדַע דִּבְרֵי הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל כִּי בְּגַן עֵדֶן, כָּל עֵת שֶׁמַּעֲלִין לְמַדְרֵגָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה, מוֹסִיפִין לְדַקְדֵּק עָלָיו בַּחֲטָאָיו וּלְהַעֲנִישׁוֹ עַל כָּל חֵטְא קָטָן, וְכֵן הוּא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: “After departing this world, the righteous person is prepared to rise through great levels in the World to Come, but not all at once. Immediately after his departure, he is punished to cleanse the more serious transgressions that he has, and then he is brought into one higher sphere. When his turn comes to ascend to a still higher sphere, he is again punished to cleanse sins lighter than the first ones, and then he rises to a second, higher level. Afterward he is punished again over fine points of the commandments that are like a hair’s breadth, in the mystery of “Around Him it storms exceedingly.” Then he is raised to the true sphere appropriate to him.”
connections.context: This is the Ari’s teaching to which the ois refers, recorded by Rabbi Chaim Vital. The passage describes successive purification before higher levels after death; Rav Tzadok extends that pattern to spiritual ascent during life.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ טַעַם "יְרִידָה לְצוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה" הַמְּבוֹאָר בַּסְּפָרִים,
connections.quote: “Sometimes a person falls from his level for a reason pertaining to himself, because the blessed God knows that he needs this. Sometimes the world causes a person to fall from his level. The descent serves an ascent, so that he may reach a great level, as it is written, “He will guide us unto death,” and it is written, “Abram descended to Egypt,” and “Abram ascended from Egypt.” Abram is the soul, and Egypt is the husks.”
connections.context: The teaching presents descent as a stage that can lead to a higher level. Rav Tzadok specifies the process here: renewed scrutiny, repentance, and the purification of remorse make the ascent possible.

connections.hePhrase: [סח] כָּל הָעֲבוֹדוֹת שֶׁבְּאֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף וְהַמִּצְווֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם הֵם רַק לְהַיְשִׁיר הַלֵּב,
connections.quote: “It is well known that all the limbs of the body follow the heart and the eyes, and the heart is the essential thing. If the heart is whole with the blessed God, everything is at peace; if the heart is deficient toward Him, everything is deficient. Our Sages expounded: “The Merciful One desires the heart.” They said in the Midrash: “My son, give Me your heart”—if you give Me your heart and your eyes, I know that you are Mine; if not, you are not Mine.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya locates the governing center of bodily conduct in the heart. This supplies a close formulation of the ois’s opening claim that the service performed through the limbs is directed toward the heart’s alignment with God.

connections.hePhrase: [סח] כָּל הָעֲבוֹדוֹת שֶׁבְּאֵבְרֵי הַגּוּף וְהַמִּצְווֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם הֵם רַק לְהַיְשִׁיר הַלֵּב,
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 3
connections.canonicalRef: Tiferet Yosef, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 3
connections.quote: “The 613 commandments are called in the holy Zohar (Yitro 82b) ‘613 counsels of the Torah.’ My holy father explained: toward what are they counsels? One cannot simply say that they are counsels toward love of Hashem, for love of Hashem is itself one of the 613 commandments. Fear of Hashem is likewise one of the 613 commandments. Rather, they are counsels by which a person's body is drawn after Hashem's will, so that there should be no inclination in his heart, Heaven forbid, contrary to Hashem's will.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks why all 613 commandments are called counsels: love and awe themselves are already included among the commandments, so neither alone explains what the complete set counsels a person toward. His answer is the alignment of the body and the will with Hashem's will. This deepens the siman's opening claim that bodily acts straighten the heart, and explains why the quiet inward attainment is the aim of their disciplined preparation.
connections.headline: What the commandments are counsels toward

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ‘My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, פב עַמּוּד ב) עַל תַּרְיַ"ג מִצְווֹת – תַּרְיַ"ג עֵיטִין.
connections.quote: “In many ways the Torah warns a person not to sin before his Master. In many ways it gives him counsel not to turn from His paths to the right or to the left. In many ways it gives him counsel how to return before his Master and be forgiven.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, פב עַמּוּד ב) עַל תַּרְיַ"ג מִצְווֹת – תַּרְיַ"ג עֵיטִין.
connections.quote: “We have learned: The Torah gives a person six hundred and thirteen kinds of counsel, so that he may be complete with his Master, for his Master wishes to benefit him in this world and in the World to Come.”
connections.context: The Zohar describes the commandments as counsel directing a person away from sin and toward restored closeness to God. This supplies Rav Tzadok’s compressed “613 counsels” and explains why he treats the deeds as directed toward the heart’s rectification.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְאַחַר הָרוּחַ רַעַשׁ – לֹא בָרַעַשׁ ה', וְאַחַר הָרַעַשׁ אֵשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א יט, יא–יב),
connections.quote: “A great and powerful wind tore the mountains and shattered rocks before the Lord; the Lord was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake.”
connections.context: Elijah is being shown a sequence of dramatic forces. Rav Tzadok compares this preliminary commotion to the activity that prepares the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְאַחַר הָרוּחַ רַעַשׁ – לֹא בָרַעַשׁ ה', וְאַחַר הָרַעַשׁ אֵשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א יט, יא–יב),
connections.quote: “After the earthquake came fire; the Lord was not in the fire. After the fire came a sound of fine stillness.”
connections.context: The quiet sound follows wind, earthquake, and fire. Rav Tzadok uses the contrast to distinguish the preparation from the inward end toward which it leads.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְאַחַר הָרוּחַ רַעַשׁ – לֹא בָרַעַשׁ ה', וְאַחַר הָרַעַשׁ אֵשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א יט, יא–יב),
connections.quote: “This is why we first say, ‘Rejoice, reapers of the field’: since this is only preparation for entering holiness, speech and sound are needed. Afterward comes ‘before the Master of worlds’: when one reaches the point of actually standing before Him, blessed be His name, then ‘it is not a matter of noise.’ The wind, earthquake, and fire that precede the still, thin voice are preparation for the root of unity and attachment to the one God.”
connections.explanation: In Nitzavim, Rav Tzadok applies the same sequence of wind, earthquake, fire, and stillness to entering Shabbos. The distinction is between preparation and attained closeness, not between worthwhile and worthless effort. It helps explain both halves of this siman: the initial struggle is necessary, while settled mastery is recognized by the heart's quieter attachment.
connections.headline: The noise prepares for a quieter attainment

connections.hePhrase: וּמַאן מַלְכֵי? רַבָּנָן, שֶׁהֵם הַמּוֹלְכִים עַל עַצְמָם, הַמּוֹשְׁלִים בְּיִצְרָם, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (עח:),
connections.quote: “Meanwhile, he came to them and said: “Peace to you, kings! Peace to you, kings!” They asked him: “From where do you know that the Sages are called kings?” He replied: “For it is written, ‘Through me kings reign,’ and so forth.””
connections.context: Geniva addresses Rav Huna and Rav Chisda as kings and supports that title with the verse spoken by wisdom. This is the source of the compressed “Who are the kings? The rabbis.” Rav Tzadok applies the title to their self-mastery.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַאן מַלְכֵי? רַבָּנָן, שֶׁהֵם הַמּוֹלְכִים עַל עַצְמָם, הַמּוֹשְׁלִים בְּיִצְרָם, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (עח:),
connections.quote: ‘‘The speakers in parables (ha-moshlim)’—these are the ones who rule over their inclination. ‘Come to Cheshbon’—come, let us calculate the world’s account: the cost of a mitzvah against its reward, and the gain from a transgression against its cost.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, "גּוּנְדָּא קַמַּיְיתָא חָלֵיף כִּי קָא אָוְושָׁא",
connections.quote: “The first troop passed. When there was a commotion, that heretic said to him, “The king has come.” Rav Sheshet replied, “He has not come.” The second troop passed. When there was a commotion, the heretic said, “Now the king is coming.” Rav Sheshet replied, “The king is not coming.” A third passed. When there was silence, Rav Sheshet said to him, “Now the king is certainly coming.””
connections.context: This is the procession itself, preceding the explanation already supplied in the existing Berakhot note. Rav Tzadok uses its sequence to distinguish the noisy preliminary struggle from the settled inward rule that follows.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ה.): לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז אָדָם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Levi bar Chama said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: A person should always stir his good inclination against his evil inclination, as it is said, ‘Be stirred, and do not sin.’ If he overcomes it, well and good. If not, he should engage in Torah, as it is said, ‘Speak within your hearts.’ If he overcomes it, well and good. If not, he should recite Shema, as it is said, ‘Upon your beds.’ If he overcomes it, well and good. If not, he should remind himself of the day of death, as it is said, ‘And be still, Selah.’”

connections.hePhrase: רַק כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "וְלִבִּי חָלַל בְּקִרְבִּי" (תְּהִלִּים קט, כב),
connections.quote: ‘For I am poor and needy, and my heart is wounded within me.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ט הֲלָכָה ה) שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ לְיֵצֶר הָרָע בְּתַעֲנִית
connections.quote: “Abraham our father made the evil inclination good, as it is written, “You found his heart faithful before You.” … David, however, could not withstand it and killed it in his heart. What is the source? “My heart is slain within me.””
connections.context: The Yerushalmi contrasts transforming the inclination with eliminating its force. That contrast explains Rav Tzadok’s reference to David; the source is the Jerusalem Talmud, not MishnahBerakhot 9:5.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ט הֲלָכָה ה) שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ לְיֵצֶר הָרָע בְּתַעֲנִית
connections.displayRef: Korban HaEdah on Jerusalem Talmud Sotah 5:5:5:4
connections.linkedRef: Korban HaEdah on Jerusalem Talmud Sotah 5:5:5:4
connections.canonicalRef: Korban HaEdah on Jerusalem Talmud Sotah 5:5:5:4
connections.heRef: קרבן העדה על תלמוד ירושלמי סוטה ה׳:ה׳:ה׳:ד׳
connections.quote: ““But David could not”—subdue his inclination to that degree, and he killed it at once. That is, he distanced himself from bodily desires through fasts and disciplines of self-denial.”
connections.context: The Yerushalmi passage already quoted in the existing note says that David killed the inclination in his heart. Korban HaEdah’s explanation of the parallel passage in Sotah explicitly supplies the fasts and self-denial mentioned here.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יְכוֹלָה הַכִּבְשָׂה לְהִתְקַיֵּם בֵּין הַזְּאֵבִים,
connections.quote: “The emperor Hadrian said to Rabbi Yehoshua: Great is the sheep that stands among seventy wolves. He replied: Great is the Shepherd who rescues it and breaks them before it, as it is written, “Every weapon formed against you shall not succeed.””
connections.context: The sheep is Israel and the saving Shepherd is God. Rav Tzadok develops his own explanation of how Israel endures among the nations; that explanation must be kept separate from the Midrash’s actual words.

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּיְקָא הַמִּתְחַבְּרִים לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
connections.quote: “The congregation of Israel likewise has this power to influence others; those outside the congregation of Israel are the nations of the world. This is like the seventy bulls offered on the festival corresponding to the seventy nations. It is also as will happen in the future, when Mashiach comes to give certain commandments and teach Torah to the nations of the world as well, as stated in Bereshit Rabbah 98: “Many peoples shall stream toward him,” and “Then I will turn to the peoples a pure language.” These are the feet that descend to death, to the place of the husks and evil—the powers of the nations—in order to draw out the holy sparks within them as well and return them to holiness. Through this power within the congregation of Israel, which seeks to return even the nations’ powers to holiness, the corresponding power in evil—for “God has made one opposite the other”—arouses in the nations the power and desire to decree forced apostasy, God forbid, upon Israel, to bring the congregation of Israel, God forbid, over to them instead. As long as the congregation of Israel is whole—that is, its intention in associating with the nations is solely for the sake of Heaven, to draw out the holy sparks in them, so that the thighs remain connected to the body—then, although “the wicked watches for the righteous,” and so forth, “the Lord will not abandon him into his hand.” But it is written, “Because you associated with Ahaziah,” and so forth. Even though his intention was initially for the sake of Heaven, one who works with something filthy becomes soiled, like someone clearing drains whose body cannot avoid becoming dirty with mud and excrement. This requires great alertness and strength to prevent any filth from adhering to him, and not everyone attains this.”
connections.context: This parallel explains both Israel’s power to influence other nations and the spiritual difficulty of association. Its image of the thighs joined to the body describes outward influence remaining rooted in inward truth. Against that background, the ois describes providence making even compromised association a means through which some good is transmitted.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדוֹר אַחְאָב הָיָה הַנִּצּוּחַ בְּנַעֲרֵי הַמְּדִינוֹת,
connections.quote: ‘Ahab said: ‘Through whom?’ He answered: ‘Thus said Hashem: Through the young attendants of the provincial governors.’ He said: ‘Who shall begin the battle?’ He answered: ‘You.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁהֵם בְּנֵי מַלְכֵי עַכּוּ״ם,
connections.quote: “They said: No one was as wealthy as Ahab son of Omri. Two hundred and thirty-two kings served him. They sought to rebel against him, so he sent for the son of each one and placed them under his authority in Jerusalem and Samaria. They had been idolaters, but when they came to Jerusalem and Samaria, they became truly God-fearing, as it is said, “He counted the youths of the governors of the provinces,” and so forth.”
connections.context: The Midrash identifies the youths as the sons of foreign rulers held under Ahab’s authority and explicitly describes the good they acquired in Israel. This is the missing source behind Rav Tzadok’s explanation of their role in the victory.

connections.hePhrase: "אִישׁ חֶרְמִי"
connections.quote: ‘He said to him: ‘Thus says Hashem: Because you released from your hand the man I had condemned to destruction, your life will be in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.’’

connections.hePhrase: כַּמָּה מְצוּדוֹת וַחֲרָמִים פֵּרַשְׂתִּי וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ““When Ben-hadad falls into your hand, do not have pity on him.” In the second statement He told him: “Know how many traps and nets I spread for him until he came into your hand. Now, if he is missing, ‘your life shall be in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.’””
connections.context: The Midrash interprets the doubled “he said” in the warning to Ahab. Its image of traps and nets provides the wording used here; Rav Tzadok explains the providential work behind that image in terms of the judgment permitting Israel’s victory.

connections.hePhrase: "אֵין עֲמָלֵק נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא בְּיַד זַרְעָהּ שֶׁל רָחֵל",
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said: “The seed of Amalek falls only at the hand of a son of Rachel.” Thus you find that at Rephidim it fell at Joshua’s hand, as it is said, “Joshua weakened Amalek.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: “This tribe is always prepared to exact retribution from Amalek.” From where is this learned? From what is completed in the Prophets: “From Ephraim, their root against Amalek; after you, Benjamin.””
connections.context: The Midrash links Joshua of Ephraim and Benjamin through their common descent from Rachel. The ois applies this pattern to Mordechai’s victory over Haman.

connections.hePhrase: זֶה נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹהִים",
connections.quote: ‘He encountered you on the way and struck at your rear, all the weakened stragglers behind you, while you were faint and weary; and he did not fear God.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים אֲנִי יָרֵא",
connections.quote: ‘On the third day Joseph said to them: ‘Do this and live, for I fear God.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים אֲנִי יָרֵא",
connections.quote: “Of this one it is written, “I fear God”; of that one it is written, “He did not fear God.” Into whose hand will the kingdom fall? Into the hand of the one anointed for battle, who comes from Joseph.”
connections.context: In this paragraph the Midrash contrasts Joseph with the kingdom of Edom and uses the verse about Amalek to characterize the opposing side. Rav Tzadok draws out the significance of fear of God for Joseph’s descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ "וְרַבִּים מֵעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ מִתְיַהֲדִים כִּי נָפַל פַּחַד מָרְדֳּכַי עֲלֵיהֶם",
connections.quote: “Many of the peoples of the land became Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ "וְרַבִּים מֵעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ מִתְיַהֲדִים כִּי נָפַל פַּחַד מָרְדֳּכַי עֲלֵיהֶם",
connections.quote: “All the provincial officials, satraps, governors, and royal administrators supported the Jews, for fear of Mordechai had fallen upon them.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok combines the language of two verses: 8:17 supplies the peoples becoming Jews, while 9:3 supplies the fear of Mordechai. His explanation connects the public change of allegiance to Mordechai’s influence.

connections.hePhrase: וְקִבְּלוּ יִרְאָה מִמֶּנּוּ,
connections.quote: “On Purim there was also a certain revelation of light to the nations, as it is written, “Many of the peoples of the land became Jews,” and it says, “The Jews had … honor.” Our Sages expounded: this refers to the head tefillin, for “all the peoples of the earth will see that the name [of the Lord] is called upon you.” This is the seeing that the Lord’s name is called upon Israel, as it is written, “For fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.” They attained no understanding of the revelation of His indwelling presence, blessed be He, for this was then deeply concealed, and the name of Heaven is not mentioned in the Megillah at all. There was no revelation and public manifestation of divinity to the nations, only a public manifestation of the greatness of the Jews—how they are watched over through a higher providence.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין ע.) עַל "וַיִּתְפְּרוּ עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה": בַּדָּבָר שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתְקָנוּ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Nechemiah says: It was a fig tree, for through the very thing by which they became corrupted they were repaired, as it is written, “They sewed fig leaves.””
connections.context: This opinion identifies the Tree of Knowledge with the fig tree. The fig leaves then supply the covering after the sin; Rav Tzadok generalizes this pattern of repair arising through the same medium as the failure.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין ע.) עַל "וַיִּתְפְּרוּ עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה": בַּדָּבָר שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתְקָנוּ.
connections.quote: ““Through the thing by which they became corrupted, they were repaired.” This is the way of the Holy One, blessed be He: with the very instrument with which He strikes, He heals—a miracle within a miracle. Thus, “He kindled a fire in Zion,” while it is written, “I will be for her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around.””
connections.context: Rashi explicitly generalizes the fig-leaf teaching already quoted in the existing note: the instrument associated with injury becomes the instrument of healing. This is the pattern Rav Tzadok extends to a person’s particular deficiency.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ב סוֹף הֲלָכָה ד): בַּיּוֹם שֶׁנֶּחְרַב הַבַּיִת נוֹלַד מָשִׁיחַ.
connections.quote: “A Jew was plowing when his cow lowed. An Arab passing by told him: “Unhitch your ox and your plow, for the Temple has been destroyed.” The cow lowed a second time. He told him: “Hitch up your ox and your plow, for the King Messiah has been born.””
connections.context: The Yerushalmi’s narrative places the birth of the redeemer alongside the destruction. Rav Tzadok invokes this conjunction as a pattern: the possibility of repair emerges at the point of the breakdown.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין צא:): מִנַּיִן לִתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים מִן הַתּוֹרָה
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: ‘I put to death and bring to life’—could this mean death for one person and life for another, as ordinarily happens in the world? Scripture says: ‘I wounded, and I will heal.’ Just as wounding and healing concern the same person, so death and life concern the same person. From here there is a reply to those who say that the resurrection of the dead is not taught by the Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: [רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל דָּבָר שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם יֵשׁ לוֹ שֹׁרֶשׁ בַּתּוֹרָה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דְּבֵיקוּת בִּמְקוֹר הַחַיִּים שֶׁהוּא אֲמִיתַּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ].
connections.quote: “This is Haman’s root in the Torah. That is, there is nothing that has no root in holiness, for without it the thing could have no existence in the world. All the worlds were created through the Torah, which is the pattern of all the work of creation, as our Sages said in Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 1. Every thing must therefore have a root in the Torah. Even every kind of evil has some root on the side of holiness; only because “God made this corresponding to that,” and willed that there be a tree of the knowledge of good and evil and the possibility for evil to appear in this world, what followed did follow.”
connections.context: The parallel supplies the meaning of “a root in Torah”: existence depends on a root in holiness even where its manifestation has become distorted. Rav Tzadok’s argument here turns to that root as the source from which restoration can arise.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ פָּרָה אֲדֻמָּה לְטַהֵר מִטֻּמְאַת מֵת,
connections.quote: “Therefore, when one draws from the mystery of wisdom, where no absence applies, he too recognizes that Israel's life cannot be utterly absent. This is why the purification of the red heifer is written before impurity from the dead. The meaning of its purification through ash follows the distinction explained in the holy Zohar between earth and ash: earth supports growth and produces fruit in the world, while ash produces no fruit. The ash's purification of the impure thus teaches that Israel's life cannot be utterly absent; rather, one stands and praises Hashem like the living.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef focuses on ash, which seems to have lost even the earth's capacity for growth, yet becomes the means of purification. He locates its meaning in divine wisdom, where the source of life exceeds what human perception can see. This develops the siman's example of the red heifer: the sign of loss itself can reveal a deeper source of restoration.
connections.headline: Why the substance of apparent loss becomes a means of purification

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה חֻקַּת): תָּבֹא אֵם וּתְקַנַּח צוֹאַת בְּנָהּ;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Aivu said: It is like the son of a maidservant who dirtied the king’s palace. The king said, “Let his mother come and clean up the filth.” So the Holy One, blessed be He, said: “Let the cow come and atone for the deed of the calf.””
connections.context: This is the original parable behind “Let the mother clean up her child’s filth.” The cow is related to the calf precisely as its mother; Rav Tzadok develops the idea of repair through the source from which the failure emerged.

connections.hePhrase: הָעֵגֶל הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַמִּיתָה, זֶהוּ צוֹאַת בְּנָהּ
connections.quote: “He follows this tanna, as it was taught: Rabbi Yosei says, “Israel received the Torah only so that the Angel of Death would not rule over them, as it is said, ‘I said: You are divine beings, and all of you sons of the Most High.’ You corrupted your deeds—‘But like Adam you shall die.’””
connections.context: The discussion associates the lost freedom from death with the sin after the giving of the Torah. It expressly identifies this as Rabbi Yosei’s view; this is the view underlying the statement that the calf is the root of death.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ נַעֲשָׂה גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי יָרָבְעָם שֶׁהוּא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף שֶׁיָּצָא מִזַּרְעוֹ מֵאֲבִיָּה (זֹהַר חָדָשׁ בָּלָק) שֶׁהָיָה מְעוּתָּד לֵהָרֵג,
connections.quote: “This Messiah is from the tribe of Ephraim and from the seed of Jeroboam son of Nebat, through the son of Abijah, who died in his youth. On the day that he died, a son was born to him and was taken from Jeroboam’s household to the wilderness. One hundred and seventy men went there, all righteous men of the tribe of Ephraim who had not participated in Jeroboam’s sin. From this son of Abijah this Messiah emerges.”
connections.context: The passage traces the Ephraimite Messiah’s line through a son born on the day of Abijah’s death and preserved away from Jeroboam’s household. This supplies the lineage compressed into the parenthetical reference to Zohar Chadash.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ נַעֲשָׂה גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי יָרָבְעָם שֶׁהוּא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף שֶׁיָּצָא מִזַּרְעוֹ מֵאֲבִיָּה (זֹהַר חָדָשׁ בָּלָק) שֶׁהָיָה מְעוּתָּד לֵהָרֵג,
connections.quote: “Messiah son of Joseph, who erases every trace of Amalek and will be entirely pure, is ultimately killed by Gog and Magog. Of him it is said, “They will look to Me concerning the one whom they pierced,” as our Sages said in Sukkah 52a. Its plain wording suggests that Israel pierced him. The meaning is that, on his own account, he certainly ought not to die at all. But because he has not become an angel like Elijah and remains joined to the other people of Israel, together forming the complete body of the congregation of Israel in that generation, and they have not been wholly cleansed, he must be killed to atone for Israel, as is known regarding the killing of the righteous and the mystery of the ten martyrs.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s fuller explanation explicitly describes this death as atonement connected to the generation, while the Messiah himself is entirely pure. That qualification clarifies the ois’s compressed statement that Messiah son of Joseph was destined to be killed.

connections.hePhrase: וְרַק מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד נֶאֱמַר: "חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ"]
connections.quote: ‘He asked You for life; You gave it to him—length of days forever and ever.’

connections.hePhrase: וְרַק מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד נֶאֱמַר: "חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ"]
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: To Messiah son of David, who is destined to be revealed speedily in our days, the Holy One, blessed be He, says, “Ask Me for something and I will give it to you,” as it is said, “I will relate the decree … today I have begotten you. Ask of Me, and I will give nations as your inheritance.” When he sees that Messiah son of Joseph has been killed, he says before Him, “Master of the world, I ask You only for life.” He answers him, “Life? Before you said this, David your father had already prophesied about you, as it is said, ‘He asked You for life; You gave it to him,’ and so forth.””
connections.context: This is the Talmudic passage applying the verse to Messiah son of David in relation to the death of Messiah son of Joseph. The existing note supplies the verse itself; this passage supplies its application in the ois.

connections.hePhrase: וּפָרָה הוּא הָאֵם [בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב] הַמּוֹלֶדֶת זֶה,
connections.quote: “The brain is wisdom; it is thought within. Understanding is the heart, and through it the heart understands.”
connections.context: Patach Eliyahu identifies Binah, understanding, with the heart. This explains the specific phrase “Binah in the heart” within the ois’s symbolism of the mother.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת י.): "יִתַּמּוּ חוֹטְאִים" – אֵין כְּתִיב אֶלָּא חַטָּאִים.
connections.quote: ‘There were some violent men in Rabbi Meir’s neighborhood who caused him much distress. Rabbi Meir prayed that they would die. His wife Beruriah said to him: ‘What is your reasoning? Is it because it is written, ‘Let sins cease’? Is it written ‘sinners’—chote’im? It is written ‘sins’—chatta’im.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ בְּרַע לַשָּׁמַיִם, אֲבָל רַע לַבְּרִיּוֹת עָנְשׁוֹ מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה, שֶׁמּוּתָּר לְבַקֵּשׁ רָעָתוֹ גַּם כֵּן;
connections.quote: “Rava said: Rav Idi explained to me: “Say of the righteous that he is good, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.” Is there a righteous person who is good and one who is not good? Rather, one who is good toward Heaven and toward people is a good righteous person; one who is good toward Heaven but bad toward people is a righteous person who is not good. Similarly: “Woe to the wicked who is bad, for the recompense of his hands shall be done to him.” Is there a wicked person who is bad and one who is not bad? Rather, one who is bad toward Heaven and toward people is a bad wicked person; one who is bad toward Heaven but is not bad toward people is a wicked person who is not bad.”
connections.context: This is the Talmudic distinction between conduct toward Heaven and conduct toward other people. Rav Tzadok applies that distinction here, then expressly limits personal judgment by noting Elisha’s punishment and the danger of self-interest.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בֶּאֱלִישָׁע שֶׁקִּלֵּל לַנְּעָרִים מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהֵם זִלְזְלוּהוּ לְפִי שֶׁרִפָּא לַמַּיִם וְעָשָׂה טוֹבָה לַבְּרִיּוֹת, וְהֵם חֲפֵצִים יוֹתֵר בְּרָעָתָם, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה מו: וְרַשִּׁ"י שָׁם), לָכֵן הָיָה רַשַּׁאי לְקַלְּלָם.
connections.quote: “They said to him: “Go up, for you have made the place bare for us.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בֶּאֱלִישָׁע שֶׁקִּלֵּל לַנְּעָרִים מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהֵם זִלְזְלוּהוּ לְפִי שֶׁרִפָּא לַמַּיִם וְעָשָׂה טוֹבָה לַבְּרִיּוֹת, וְהֵם חֲפֵצִים יוֹתֵר בְּרָעָתָם, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה מו: וְרַשִּׁ"י שָׁם), לָכֵן הָיָה רַשַּׁאי לְקַלְּלָם.
connections.quote: ““You have made the place bare for us”: When the water was bad, our livelihood was to bring water and sell it.”
connections.context: The youths’ insult concerned the income they lost when Elisha healed the water. Rashi supplies the motive that Rav Tzadok discusses: they resented a benefit to the town because it deprived them of their trade. The later notes give the Gemara’s criticism of Elisha’s response.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁקִּלֵּל אוֹיְבָיו בְּמִזְמוֹר ק"ט, פֵּירֵשׁ שָׁם בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיוּ מְרֵיעִים לוֹ,
connections.quote: “They surrounded me with words of hatred and fought against me without cause.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁקִּלֵּל אוֹיְבָיו בְּמִזְמוֹר ק"ט, פֵּירֵשׁ שָׁם בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיוּ מְרֵיעִים לוֹ,
connections.quote: “In return for my love they accuse me, but I am prayer.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁקִּלֵּל אוֹיְבָיו בְּמִזְמוֹר ק"ט, פֵּירֵשׁ שָׁם בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיוּ מְרֵיעִים לוֹ,
connections.quote: “They repay me evil for good and hatred for my love.”
connections.context: The opening of the psalm states the speaker’s grievance before the subsequent imprecations. These verses explain Rav Tzadok’s words “because they were harming him.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁקִּלֵּל אוֹיְבָיו בְּמִזְמוֹר ק"ט, פֵּירֵשׁ שָׁם בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיוּ מְרֵיעִים לוֹ,
connections.quote: ““For the conductor.” David composed this psalm while fleeing from Shaul, when many Israelites were speaking about him to Shaul. He said, “God of my praise, do not be silent”: that is, I glory in You, unlike those people who glory in their own understanding. I call to You not to remain silent at what the wicked are doing to me.”
connections.context: Radak places the psalm in the setting of David’s flight from Shaul and the reports being made against him. This explains the personal harm referred to in the Hebrew sentence.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמַר: "וַיֶּאֱהַב קְלָלָה וַתְּבוֹאֵהוּ" – מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאָהַב זֶה.
connections.quote: ‘He loved cursing, and it came upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it kept far from him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָמַר: "וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, ג), אֲבָל בְּלָאו הָכִי אֵין מְקַלֵּל לְאָדָם.
connections.quote: ‘I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse. Through you all the families of the earth will be blessed.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, גַּם בָּזֶה מָצִינוּ דֶּאֱלִישָׁע נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל זֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (מז.) וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קז:);
connections.quote: ; Sanhedrin 107b:16: “The Sages taught: Elisha suffered three illnesses: one because he incited bears against the children, one because he pushed Gehazi away with both hands, and one from which he died.”
connections.context: The first illness is expressly connected to the bears. This is Rav Tzadok’s counterweight to his preceding explanation of why Elisha cursed the youths: the Gemara nevertheless describes punishment for his response.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִלְּבַד זֶה גַּם כֵּן לֹא לְכָל אָדָם הוּתַּר, שֶׁהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בֶּאֱלִישָׁע (סוֹטָה שָׁם): "וַיַּרְאֵם" – רָאָה שֶׁאֵין וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: He saw that there was no moisture of a mitzvah in them. But perhaps there would be some in their offspring? Rabbi Elazar said: Neither in them nor in their offspring, to the end of all generations.”
connections.context: The Gemara describes a perception extending even to future descendants. This supplies the source for Rav Tzadok’s warning that an ordinary person, whose judgment may be distorted by self-interest, cannot assume Elisha’s authority.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁהַנְּגִיעָה מְעַוֶּורְתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “… If this happened to Elisha, who knew that they were wicked and that no righteous person would come from them, all the more so should another person not curse people.”
connections.context: Sefer Chasidim draws the explicit practical inference from Elisha’s punishment. The baraisa about Elisha’s illnesses is quoted in note 631; this passage adds the conclusion concerning other people.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר אָמַר פָּסוּק "וְלִבִּי חָלַל בְּקִרְבִּי" (תְּהִלִּים קט, כב), שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מִזֶּה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ לְיֵצֶר הָרָע,
connections.quote: ‘This is what Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: David was not suited to that deed, nor was Israel suited to that deed. David was not suited to that deed, as it is written: ‘My heart is slain within me.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר אָמַר פָּסוּק "וְלִבִּי חָלַל בְּקִרְבִּי" (תְּהִלִּים קט, כב), שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מִזֶּה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ לְיֵצֶר הָרָע,
connections.quote: see note 596.
connections.context: The preceding sentence describes Avraham as transforming the evil inclination into good. This sentence gives the contrasting description of David, explaining the reading of “my heart is empty within me” used here.

connections.hePhrase: וְקוֹדֶם מִזְמוֹר זֶה נֶאֱמַר מִזְמוֹר שֶׁבּוֹ פָּסוּק "לִי גִלְעָד וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קח, ט), שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ דָּרְשׁוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד:) שֶׁכֻּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: ‘Gilead is Mine, Manasseh is Mine, Ephraim is the stronghold of My head; Judah is My lawgiver.’

connections.hePhrase: וְקוֹדֶם מִזְמוֹר זֶה נֶאֱמַר מִזְמוֹר שֶׁבּוֹ פָּסוּק "לִי גִלְעָד וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קח, ט), שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ דָּרְשׁוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד:) שֶׁכֻּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “Those who interpreted the scriptural hints used to say: All of them come to the World to Come, as it is written, “Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is the strength of My head; Judah is My lawgiver.” “Gilead is Mine” refers to Ahab, who fell at Ramot Gilead; “Manasseh” is literal; “Ephraim” refers to Jeroboam, who came from Ephraim.”
connections.context: The teaching offers a different reading of the ultimate fate of figures listed in the preceding discussion as excluded from the World to Come. Rav Tzadok notices that the psalm containing these words stands immediately before the psalm of curses.

connections.hePhrase: וְקוֹדֶם מִזְמוֹר זֶה נֶאֱמַר מִזְמוֹר שֶׁבּוֹ פָּסוּק "לִי גִלְעָד וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קח, ט), שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ דָּרְשׁוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד:) שֶׁכֻּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: ““Gilead is Mine and Manasseh is Mine”—It is for Me to bear their iniquity so that they may merit.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the divine assurance underlying the interpretation of the psalm. This adds the meaning of the words to the Talmudic passage already quoted in the existing note.

connections.hePhrase: וְקוֹדֶם מִזְמוֹר זֶה נֶאֱמַר מִזְמוֹר שֶׁבּוֹ פָּסוּק "לִי גִלְעָד וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קח, ט), שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ דָּרְשׁוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד:) שֶׁכֻּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “How far does the protection arising from the righteous person's service extend in this world? Even concerning those four individuals of whom the ruling states that they have no share in the world to come, the Gemara nevertheless teaches (Sanhedrin 104b) that the interpreters of the remnant said they do have a share. The interpreters of the remnant are the righteous who take hold of the point of Israel and extend it, advocating that none be utterly cast away. They are called interpreters of the remnant because they expound the remaining impression in the heart, until through their service they can protect even those four individuals and bring them to the life of the world to come. Thus the day of rain is greater, for it includes both righteous and wicked, whereas resurrection is for the righteous, since then evil is entirely annulled.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the very interpreters of the remnant invoked at the close of this siman. Their favorable reading is an active attempt to take hold of the surviving good and enlarge it, rather than a denial that a serious judgment was stated. This clarifies the order Rav Tzadok requires: the heart must first contain a real concern for the other's possible restoration before it can claim to speak only for justice.
connections.headline: Seeking the surviving point of good

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ כְּעֵין שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יג:) מִמִּדַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּקְדִּים רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה.
connections.quote: ‘‘After these events.’ (After what?) Rava said: After the Holy One, blessed be He, had created the remedy for the blow.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בַּנְּבִיאִים שֶׁסִּפֵּר הַכָּתוּב כָּל הַמּוֹפְתִים שֶׁעָשָׂה אֵלִיָּהוּ וְשֶׁעָשָׂה אֱלִישָׁע, וְזוּלַת מִשְּׁאָר הַנְּבִיאִים לֹא נִזְכַּר מוֹפְתֵיהֶם.
connections.quote: “The matter is as my holy grandfather explained: there are two kinds of divine inspiration. One comes through a person's preparation: he prepares and disciplines himself for Hashem's will and thereby reaches divine inspiration. As the Midrash teaches, zeal leads to cleanliness, and so forth, and piety leads to divine inspiration. By preparing himself through all the stages enumerated by the Midrash, a person attains divine inspiration. This is called prophecy needed for the generations, for since it came through human preparation, it remains established for the whole world.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef distinguishes an isolated inspiration from a lasting path opened through human preparation. This helps explain the siman's question about recording miracles that served only a particular moment: what remains is not merely the report of a wonder, but an opening in avodas Hashem. The two discussions illuminate that lasting function without making every miracle identical with the prophecy discussed there.
connections.headline: What remains for later generations

connections.hePhrase: וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יד.): נְבוּאָה שֶׁהֻוצְרְכָה לְדוֹרוֹת נִכְתְּבָה, וְשֶׁלֹּא הֻוצְרְכָה לֹא נִכְתְּבָה;
connections.quote: ‘There were indeed many, as it was taught: Many prophets arose for Israel, twice as many as those who left Egypt. However, a prophecy needed for later generations was written down; one that was not needed was not written down.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יד.): נְבוּאָה שֶׁהֻוצְרְכָה לְדוֹרוֹת נִכְתְּבָה, וְשֶׁלֹּא הֻוצְרְכָה לֹא נִכְתְּבָה;
connections.quote: ““Prophecy needed for the generations”—to learn repentance or instruction; all of those forty-eight were needed.”
connections.context: Rashi specifies what makes a prophecy necessary for later generations: its teaching of repentance or instruction. This supports the ois’s inference that the recorded miracles continue to teach.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יד.): נְבוּאָה שֶׁהֻוצְרְכָה לְדוֹרוֹת נִכְתְּבָה, וְשֶׁלֹּא הֻוצְרְכָה לֹא נִכְתְּבָה;
connections.quote: “Jeremiah's prophecy was not heard in its own time, for he rebuked them for failing to listen, and calamity consequently came. Yet the Gemara teaches that the words of anyone who has fear of Heaven are heard. The explanation is that such a person becomes a vehicle for the attribute of kingship, which is fear, and ‘kingship is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah.’ These are ‘My words which I have placed in your mouth’; then ‘it shall not return to Me empty,’ and his words are heard. This is why the Gemara cites ‘The end of the matter: everything is heard.’ Even if it was not heard at the time, in the end events will turn so that it is heard. As the Sages said, ‘A prophecy needed for generations was written,’ and a time will come when it is heard.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains why Jeremiah's resisted words can still be called words that are heard: their effect unfolds through later hearers. This strengthens the siman's distinction between an event's short duration and the continuing gateway it opens. It explains the premise about what is preserved for generations, while the siman itself goes on to distinguish the particular powers of Torah and prayer.
connections.headline: A prophetic word can await its later hearers

connections.hePhrase: [דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל יְרִידַת הָאֵשׁ עַל יְדֵי חִדּוּשׁ תּוֹרָה שֶׁחִדֵּשׁ לְהַתִּיר הַבָּמָה],
connections.quote: ““Take care lest you offer your burnt offerings.” You are not permitted to do so after it [the Temple] has been built. But one can build an altar as Elijah did on Mount Carmel. From where did Elijah learn to do this on Mount Carmel? From what the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Yaakov: “A nation and an assembly of nations shall come from you.” A descendant of Binyamin would arise who would act before an assembly of nations: he would build an altar during the prohibition of private altars, and I would accept it.”
connections.context: The Midrash traces Elijah’s exceptional act on Mount Carmel to the words spoken to Yaakov. It begins with the prohibition of private altars; the passage concerns the particular prophetic act, rather than a general permission.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל מוֹפְתֵי אֱלִישָׁע עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (כז.): "וֶאֱלִישָׁע דַּעֲבַד בְּרַחֲמֵי",
connections.quote: ‘The one who says Torah relies on what is written: ‘Hashem desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify Torah and make it glorious.’ The one who says prayer relies on what is written: ‘Please recount the great things that Elisha did.’ What Elisha accomplished, he accomplished through prayer.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזָכָה לְפִי שְׁנַיִם מֵאֵלִיָּהוּ, כִּי יוֹתֵר יֵשׁ לִפְעוֹל עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה.
connections.quote: “Elisha too was a great man. You find that all the miracles Elijah performed, Elisha performed twice over, as it is stated: “Let there be a double portion of your spirit upon me.” Yet a time came when he knew nothing. When was this? When he saw the Shunammite woman coming to him, he said to Gehazi, “Run now to meet her,” and he did not know that the child had died. In the end he understood and said to Gehazi, “Let her be, for her soul is bitter, and Hashem has hidden it from me and has not told me.” You have learned that everything comes from the Holy One, blessed be He: if He wishes, people see; if He wishes, they hear. As it is written, “The hearing ear and the seeing eye—Hashem made them both.” Therefore it says, “Who commands the sun, and it does not shine.””
connections.context: The Midrash explicitly states that Elisha’s miracles were doubled. It also retains the essential qualification that prophetic knowledge and power depend entirely on God; Elisha was not independently all-knowing.

connections.hePhrase: וְזָכָה לְפִי שְׁנַיִם מֵאֵלִיָּהוּ, כִּי יוֹתֵר יֵשׁ לִפְעוֹל עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:9
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:9
connections.quote: “Shabbat corresponds to David the king, peace be upon him, as is known, and it is the level of prayer, called “temporal life,” for it is only for a time. Nevertheless it is life: the holiness of Shabbat is a temporary taste of eternal life. This taste of eternal life within the body in this world comes through prayer, the service of the heart. One draws eternal life into temporal life, so that even its moment is called vitality. They said: “One hour of repentance and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come.” This life of one hour of repentance and good deeds is David’s level, for he established the yoke of repentance, as our Sages said in Avodah Zarah. This is the aspect of the feminine, which is lacking: “Three things are never satisfied.” It has no satiety or contentment; its contentment and pleasure lie in longing—“your longing shall be for your husband”—in seeking completion. This is David’s level, as he said, “Seek His face always,” and many similar verses: one continually seeks and searches, for one never attains the satiety of finding. Rather, “Let the heart of those who seek Hashem rejoice”: there is joy in the seeking itself, and it is better for him than all the life of the World to Come. Then there will no longer be room for effort and petition, for “today is for performing them and tomorrow for receiving their reward.” That is the hour of contentment which is better than all the life of this world: one will have contentment and rest in exchange for having given pleasure to God in this world. This is through Torah, which “restores the soul”; its study contains pleasure and contentment. Therefore it is actual eternal life, for it is itself the vitality of the World to Come.”
connections.context: This parallel explains prayer’s distinctive power without reversing the ois’s concluding priority of Torah. It describes the value of present longing and effort alongside the lasting contentment associated with Torah.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, מַה שֶּׁעַל פִּי תּוֹרָה גָּדוֹל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּשַׁבָּת (י.): "מַנִּיחִים חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְעוֹסְקִים בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה", וְהַמַּעֲמִיק יָבִין:
connections.quote: “Rava saw Rav Hamnuna prolonging his prayer. He said, ‘They set aside eternal life and occupy themselves with the life of the moment.’ Rav Hamnuna, however, held that prayer has its own time and Torah has its own time. Rabbi Yirmeyah was sitting before Rabbi Zeira, and they were engaged in a teaching. It grew late for prayer, and Rabbi Yirmeyah was becoming impatient to leave. Rabbi Zeira applied this verse to him: ‘One who turns his ear away from hearing Torah—even his prayer is an abomination.’”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, מַה שֶּׁעַל פִּי תּוֹרָה גָּדוֹל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּשַׁבָּת (י.): "מַנִּיחִים חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְעוֹסְקִים בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה", וְהַמַּעֲמִיק יָבִין:
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:8
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:8
connections.quote: “The first is the vitality clothed in the body, to which death applies when the body dies. These lives have a limit in the measure of one’s days: throughout one’s life, one has this vitality of the soul flowing into the body. This is the life of this world, in which there is the effort of mitzvot and good deeds. There is also the soul’s eternal vitality in itself, apart from its clothing in the body. In itself it lacks nothing that would require the service of prayer; rather, the voice of Torah is “eternal life that He planted within us,” which is the occupation of the righteous in this world. The World to Come was created with the letter yod, the essence of wisdom, as is known; this world with the letter heh, the lower heh that alludes to prayer. The principal thing is certainly Torah, as it is said: “They leave eternal life and occupy themselves with temporal life!” Nevertheless, the view stated there that words of Torah have their own time and words of prayer their own time is also true. For “the beginning of wisdom is fear of Hashem,” and “if fear of Hashem is his treasure—yes.” The effort of temporal life prepares one to merit eternal life, as it is said: “Prepare yourself in the antechamber,” and “One who did not toil before Shabbat,” and so forth.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the terms “eternal life” and “temporal life,” while affirming the need for both Torah and prayer. The closing qualification makes prayer and fear of Heaven a preparation for Torah’s eternal life.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, מַה שֶּׁעַל פִּי תּוֹרָה גָּדוֹל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּשַׁבָּת (י.): "מַנִּיחִים חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְעוֹסְקִים בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה", וְהַמַּעֲמִיק יָבִין:
connections.quote: ““Eternal life”—Torah. Prayer concerns the needs of temporal life: healing, peace, and sustenance.”
connections.context: Rashi gives concrete examples of “temporal life.” The existing Gemara quotation also preserves Rav Hamnuna’s view that prayer and Torah each have their proper time.

connections.hePhrase: [עג] כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מְתַקֵּן מַה שֶּׁחָטָא, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַזְמִין לוֹ אוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק וְאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּהְיֶה תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל;
connections.quote: “The nineteenth principle is abandoning his sin when it presents itself to him and his desire is at its strongest. Our Sages of blessed memory said: Who is a penitent whose repentance reaches the Throne of Glory? One who is tested and emerges innocent at the same stage, in the same place, and with the same woman. This means that the sin presented itself to him while his inclination and physical vigor were as strong as at the first time when he sinned, yet he subdued his inclination and escaped the transgression out of fear of the Lord and dread of His majesty. If such an occasion has not presented itself to him, he should increase the fear of the Lord within himself day by day, throughout his life. When he renews the strength of that fear sufficiently to subdue his inclination and the force of its rule at the height of desire, surely He who searches hearts understands, and He who guards his soul knows, that if he were to face a test and encounter the same situation as before, he would save himself from his inclination. He thus stands before the Lord on the highest level of repentance.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah explains both the complete test of repentance and how repentance can reach its highest level when the same opportunity never returns. Rav Tzadok discusses providentially arranged encounters that reveal repair; this source does not require a person to seek out temptation.

connections.hePhrase: [עג] כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מְתַקֵּן מַה שֶּׁחָטָא, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַזְמִין לוֹ אוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק וְאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּהְיֶה תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל;
connections.quote: “And the essence of teshuvah is in the contemplation of the heart alone — for by it one is called a “complete tzaddik,” even if he was, beforehand, wholly wicked, as is explained in Kiddushin 49b.
