And even the verbal confession — though it is a positive Torah commandment, “and they shall confess” (Bamidbar 5:7) — that is a mitzvah in its own right, and it does not hold up the teshuvah, whose essence is in the heart alone: that he regrets the past, and resolves in his heart not to return again to his folly, and not to sin again. And although it is not revealed to any person — nor even to the ministering angels, who do not know what is in the heart — “before Heaven it is revealed”; and he is truly called a “complete tzaddik,” even if he multiplied transgressions to the utmost — for they said it there of “any wholly wicked man,” even one who transgressed the entire Torah. And in the Beis Shmuel and Chelkas Mechokek Even HaEzer §38 they wrote that even one who stole and did not return the theft — only that he accepted in his heart to return it — it avails to make him a “tzaddik”; and so it is implied in Berachos 5b in the case of the four hundred jars of wine of Rav Huna, that this acceptance suffices. And what they said in Sanhedrin 25b regarding the “return” of penitents breaking their dice and the like is with respect to his credibility to the public — for we are concerned lest he has not truly repented and is deceiving people, and so people need to see from him an actual act of teshuvah. And the “fences in the permitted” that they mentioned there are good counsels for the penitent, that his inclination not overpower him again in the future; and therefore he must fence himself even in the permitted, so as to distance himself from the prohibition in which he already stumbled — for the inclination, having already made itself a “nest” in his heart and become “master of the house,” can easily trip him, and so he needs extra fences.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin separates genuine inward teshuvah from the actions by which other people can safely restore their trust. That distinction explains the evidentiary role of the opportunities described here. They can disclose a repaired will without making an engineered encounter with temptation a requirement of repentance. The present siman explicitly forbids bringing oneself into an otherwise prohibited situation.
connections.headline: Inner return and the outward evidence of repair

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי וַדַּאי יֵשׁ דְּבָרִים שֶׁאָסוּר הָאָדָם לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי כָּךְ, כְּמוֹ בְּ"אוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה, בְּאוֹתוֹ וְכוּלֵי" יַעֲבוֹר עַל אִיסּוּר יִחוּד,
connections.quote: “One should not say: Rav Yehuda said, “With the same woman, in the same place, at the same stage”; I will fulfill this. For perhaps the woman will wish to join him, and he will incur sin. They did not say that a person should bring himself into a situation of transgression.”
connections.context: The source explicitly rejects deliberately recreating a temptation. This matches Rav Tzadok’s qualification that the encounter he describes is arranged by providence; the person does not arrange a forbidden situation.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כה.) בַּחֲזָרָתָן שֶׁל חָשׁוּד עַל טְרֵיפוֹת: שֶׁיַּחֲזִיר אֲבֵדָה וְכוּלֵי וְכַיּוֹצֵא עַיֵּין שָׁם;
connections.quote: ‘What, then, is his remedy? It is as Rav Idi bar Avin said, for Rav Idi bar Avin said: Someone suspected of selling tereifot has no remedy until he goes to a place where he is not known and either returns a valuable lost object or brings forward a valuable animal from his own property as a tereifah.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ בְּגֵיחֲזִי, שֶׁחֶטְאוֹ הָיָה שֶׁחָמַד לְמַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ:
connections.quote: “Gehazi too, whom Elisha chose to serve him and sent to revive the dead—presumably this was not without reason. He recognized that Gehazi was prepared for this, more than all his other disciples, the prophets of that generation.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the great spiritual potential underlying Gehazi’s appointment. The opening of the same passage states that the person’s choice remains in his own hands; potential does not remove responsibility for wrongdoing.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם קז:) דְּהַמְּצֹרָעִים הֵם גֵּיחֲזִי וּבָנָיו, וְלֹא חָמְדוּ לִשְׁתּוֹק וּלְהַרְבּוֹת בְּבִזָּה לְעַצְמָם כִּי חָשְׁשׁוּ לַחֵטְא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמְצָאָנוּ עָוֹן" (מְלָכִים ב ז, ט).
connections.quote: ““Four men were lepers at the entrance of the gate”: Rabbi Yochanan said: Gehazi and his three sons.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם קז:) דְּהַמְּצֹרָעִים הֵם גֵּיחֲזִי וּבָנָיו, וְלֹא חָמְדוּ לִשְׁתּוֹק וּלְהַרְבּוֹת בְּבִזָּה לְעַצְמָם כִּי חָשְׁשׁוּ לַחֵטְא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמְצָאָנוּ עָוֹן" (מְלָכִים ב ז, ט).
connections.quote: “They said to one another: “We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent. If we wait until the morning light, guilt will overtake us. Now let us go and tell the king’s house.””
connections.context: The Gemara identifies the men; the biblical verse records their decision to share the discovery of the abandoned enemy camp. Together they supply Rav Tzadok’s evidence that even Gehazi could turn from private gain toward responsibility to others.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם קז:) דְּהַמְּצֹרָעִים הֵם גֵּיחֲזִי וּבָנָיו, וְלֹא חָמְדוּ לִשְׁתּוֹק וּלְהַרְבּוֹת בְּבִזָּה לְעַצְמָם כִּי חָשְׁשׁוּ לַחֵטְא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמְצָאָנוּ עָוֹן" (מְלָכִים ב ז, ט).
connections.quote: “We read as the haftarah, “Four men were lepers.” The Gemara says that these were Gehazi and his three sons. Since it is written, “Upon you and your offspring forever,” this implies that his offspring were never healed. Nevertheless, this great salvation came about through them, and merit is brought about only through one who is meritorious. This proves that at their root they have a remedy, as the interpreters of scriptural hints said about all six who descend from Yaakov: they have a share in the World to Come. For everyone descended from Yaakov is bound at the root to the blessed God: “Your people are all righteous.””
connections.context: The parallel draws its conclusion from the salvation brought about through Gehazi and his sons. It distinguishes the lasting appearance of their affliction from the possibility of repair at the spiritual root.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ סִפֵּר מֵעִנְיַן הַחֲזָרַת נַחֲלָה לָאִשָּׁה עַל יָדוֹ, וְהוּא דָּבָר דְּמִמֵּילָא בָּא עַל יָדוֹ, הוּא סִימָן לִגְמַר תִּיקּוּנוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘While he was recounting to the king how (Elisha) had brought the dead man back to life, there was the woman whose son he had brought back to life, crying out to the king about her house and her field. Gehazi said: ‘My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha brought back to life.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז אַחַר כָּךְ הָלַךְ אֱלִישָׁע לַאֲרָם, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם): לְהַחֲזִיר גֵּיחֲזִי בִּתְשׁוּבָה;
connections.quote: “Gehazi—as it is written, “Elisha went to Damascus.” Where did he go? Rabbi Yochanan said: He went to bring Gehazi back in repentance, but he did not return. He said to him, “Return.” He answered him: “This is what I received from you: One who sins and causes the many to sin is not given the opportunity to repent.””
connections.context: The Gemara records both Elisha’s effort to draw Gehazi back and Gehazi’s refusal. Rav Tzadok expressly acknowledges that refusal later in the ois; it remains part of the source quotation.

connections.hePhrase: זָכָה לְמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּמִדּוֹת (פֶּרֶק ב): "יִתֵּן בְּלִבָּם וִיקָרְבוּךָ", שֶׁאַף אַחַר כָּל הַתִּיקּוּן צָרִיךְ לְהִתְקָרְבוּת אֱלִישָׁע.
connections.quote: “All who enter the Temple Mount enter by the right, go around, and leave by the left, except someone to whom something has happened, who goes around by the left. “Why do you go around by the left?” “Because I am a mourner.” “May He who dwells in this House comfort you.” “Because I am under a ban.” “May He who dwells in this House put it into their hearts to draw you near”—these are Rabbi Meir’s words. Rabbi Yosei said to him: You make it appear as though they treated him unjustly. Rather: “May He who dwells in this House put it into your heart to heed your colleagues’ words, and may they draw you near.””
connections.context: The phrase quoted in the ois is Rabbi Meir’s formulation. The Mishnah also records Rabbi Yosei’s qualification, which makes the person’s own response part of reconciliation.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מְנָאוּהוּ בְּאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא וְאָמְרוּ שֶׁלֹּא רָצָה לָשׁוּב,
connections.quote: “Three kings and four commoners have no share in the World to Come. The three kings are Yerovam, Achav, and Menashe. Rabbi Yehuda says: Menashe has a share in the World to Come, as it is stated, “He prayed to Him, and He was entreated by him and heard his supplication, and restored him to Jerusalem to his kingdom.” They said to him: He restored him to his kingdom, but did not restore him to the life of the World to Come. The four commoners are Bilam, Doeg, Achitofel, and Gehazi.”
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s list that Rav Tzadok acknowledges. Its dispute concerns Menashe; Gehazi appears in the list of four commoners. The following source gives the interpretation invoked at the end of the ois.

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל מָקוֹם דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת וְכוּלֵי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ:
connections.quote: “The interpreters of scriptural hints used to say: All of them come to the World to Come, as it is stated: “Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is the strength of My head; Judah is My lawgiver. Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I cast My shoe; over Philistia, shout in triumph.” “Gilead is Mine” is Achav, who fell at Ramot Gilead. “Manasseh” is literal. “Ephraim is the strength of My head” is Yerovam, who came from Ephraim. “Judah is My lawgiver” is Achitofel, who came from Judah. “Moab is My washbasin” is Gehazi, who was afflicted over the matter of washing. “Upon Edom I cast My shoe” is Doeg the Edomite. “Over Philistia, shout in triumph”—the ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, if David comes, who killed the Philistine and caused Your children to inherit Gat, what will You do for him? He said to them: It is for Me to make them friends with one another.”
connections.context: The original discussion continues across the page boundary into 105a, where Gehazi is named explicitly. The final exchange also explains the reconciliation with David alluded to in the parallel passages.

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל מָקוֹם דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת וְכוּלֵי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ:
connections.quote: “The meaning of “hints” is the imprint of the soul itself, revealed through the power of the agent within the action. Its interpreters are those who grasp the revelation and uncovering of the secret of Hashem within it. Through the revelation of the depth of the Israelite soul’s root and its attachment to the living God, they understand that it has no complete severance at the final end, when all the garments of choice, which are all garments of this world, fall away. From the essence of the soul as a portion of God above, each individual soul of Israel is wholly bound to the blessed God. This also brings atonement for the cutting off of the root, God forbid.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s explanation elsewhere of “interpreters of hints.” He distinguishes conduct and its consequences in this world from the final revelation of the soul’s underlying root.

connections.hePhrase: הָעֲבֵירוֹת בְּנֶפֶשׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי אֵינָם קִנְיַן עַצְמִי רַק מִקְרִי,
connections.quote: “As they said in Sanhedrin: “It is like a myrtle standing among reeds; it is still called a myrtle,” and so forth. They compared the sins surrounding a person to thorns surrounding a rose. They do not come from the person’s essence, but surround and encompass him on the side of his outward extension. From the essence of the Israelite soul, however, there is no sin at all. Differences in the levels of attachment are differences in the souls themselves, for in the upright arrangement there are degrees among souls.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains “incidental” through the image of thorns surrounding a plant. The selected passage distinguishes the soul’s essence from its outward conduct and also preserves the qualification that levels of attachment differ.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְהוּא יִפְדֶּה אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִכֹּל עֲוֹנֹתָיו".
connections.quote: ‘He will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "וְאֶתֵּן אָדָם תַּחְתֶּיךָ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Because you are precious in My eyes, you are honored and I love you; I will give people in your place and nations in exchange for your life.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן "וְנָשָׂא הַשָּׂעִיר עָלָיו אֶת עֲוֹנֹתָם",
connections.quote: ‘The goat shall bear upon itself all their iniquities to an isolated land, and he shall send the goat into the wilderness.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁנּוֹתֵן הָעֲווֹנוֹת עַל רֹאשׁ עֵשָׂו.
connections.quote: “Rather, “The goat shall bear upon itself”—this is Esav, as it is stated, “Esav my brother is a hairy man.” “All their iniquities”—the iniquities of the innocent one, as it is stated, “Yaakov was an innocent man.””
connections.context: Rabbi Yitzchak’s interpretation links se’ir, the goat, with se’ar, hair, and reads avonotam as “the iniquities of the tam.” This is the Midrashic source behind the ois’s allusion to Esav.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הַמִּצְווֹת הֵם קְדוּשַׁת הַגּוּף וְאֵין לָהֶם פִּדְיוֹן.
connections.quote: “The matter is that Hashem bound His love to Avraham our father in a place beyond the reach of human actions. As the holy Zohar teaches (Bereshit 22b), ‘He is One, without reckoning and without partnership’; this love endures forever. Of this love it is said, ‘Many waters cannot extinguish love’ (Song of Songs 8:7), for no action reaches that place so as to extinguish it. As the Midrash Tanchuma says (Tzav 8), ‘He chose Avraham’: after the Akeidah, the love and bond Hashem has with Avraham our father were revealed even apart from his good deeds, through the choice by which He chose him from birth, as it says, ‘Who chose Avram’ (Nehemiah 9:7).”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov develops the same verse about love that many waters cannot extinguish, locating the bond with Avraham in divine choice at a level beyond the reach of changing actions. This clarifies the root of the siman's analogy to intrinsic sanctity. The parallel explains the endurance of the bond; it does not cancel the siman's distinction between the person's true possession and the sins from which he still requires redemption.
connections.headline: The enduring root of the bond

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶת כָּל הוֹן בֵּיתוֹ בָּאַהֲבָה בּוֹז יָבוּזוּ לוֹ".
connections.quote: ‘Great waters cannot extinguish love, nor can rivers sweep it away. If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת רַב הַאי גָּאוֹן שֶׁהֵבִיא מַהֲרַ״ם אַלְשַׁקַּר בְּעִנְיַן אֶחָד שֶׁמָּכַר מִצְווֹתָיו דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.displayRef: Rav Hai Gaon, quoted in Responsa Maharam Alashkar 101
connections.quote: “Certainly, one who pays a teacher to teach what they need, and the teacher teaches them, receives great reward for this. The teacher himself sometimes receives reward and sometimes does not. Likewise, one who feeds a poor person or a sage so that he will bless him receives reward for this and benefits through that poor person’s or sage’s blessing. One who supports people fulfilling mitzvot so that they can fulfill them receives reward for this, as do they. Especially one who helps those occupied with Torah and mitzvot to free their hearts to engage in them receives reward; the reward he receives is for his own action. But one who persuades himself that he can acquire his fellow’s reward with money or as a gift deserves scorn and ridicule. No precious wealth or treasures enable a person to acquire his fellow’s reward. Thus it is written: “If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, they would utterly scorn him.” The Sages asked: What is meant by “they would utterly scorn him”? Ulla said: Not like Shimon, the brother of Azaryah, nor like Rabbi Yochanan of the house of the Nasi, but like Hillel and Shevna. For when Rav Dimi came, he said: Hillel and Shevna were brothers. One engaged in business and the other in Torah. He said to him, “Share with me and I will share with you.” A heavenly voice went forth and said: “If a man gave all the wealth of his house for love, they would utterly scorn him.””

connections.hePhrase: [וְעִנְיַן מְכִירַת הַבְּכוֹרָה דְּעֵשָׂו לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כִּמְכִירַת דָּבָר קְדוּשָׁה,
connections.quote: ““Your birthright”—Because the sacrificial service belonged to the firstborn, Yaakov said: This wicked person is not fit to offer sacrifices to the Holy One, blessed be He.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the connection between the birthright and offering sacrifices that the Hebrew assumes.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעִנְיַן מְכִירַת הַבְּכוֹרָה דְּעֵשָׂו לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כִּמְכִירַת דָּבָר קְדוּשָׁה,
connections.quote: “Yaakov was first in formation—that is, in the truth concealed in this world. But in the visible disclosure of this world, in birth, Esav appeared first, for the service is in deed and the power of action, and Esav is the root of the power of deeds. As long as Avraham our father himself was alive, clothed in a physical body in this world, there was also a physical garment of his level in Esav because of the mixture of good and evil in the bodily world. But at Avraham's passing, when his spiritual holiness remained without a physical garment in this world, Esav no longer had a connection with it, since all his power belongs to physical embodiment in this world. Through that embodiment he could extend his hooves and display himself as pure, for this world is a world of falsehood; this is not so from the standpoint of ‘truth to Yaakov’ (Micah 7:20). Only Yaakov therefore received the spiritual dimension, and then ‘Yaakov cooked a stew’ (Genesis 25:29).”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim expands the compressed exception about selling Esav's birthright. It distinguishes priority in visible birth from the inward priority of formation, and describes Esav's connection to Avraham as dependent on an outward bodily garment. This makes precise why the siman can treat that sale as effective without making intrinsic holiness generally saleable.
connections.headline: The visible birthright and its inward truth

connections.hePhrase: לְפִיכָךְ הוֹעִילָה מְכִירָה בְּדִמְיוֹן].
connections.quote: “He [Yitzchak] considered him [Esav] a vessel prepared for holiness, since he had been formed as a firstborn. Although the firstborn had not yet been sanctified, the forefathers fulfilled the whole Torah and he knew that the firstborn would be sanctified in the future. In truth, however, Yaakov took the birthright and the blessings from him, for everything truly belonged to Yaakov. The birthright came first, even though holiness follows blessing, because the birthright at that time was not holiness itself but a preparation for holiness. He had to take all this from Esav indirectly, because from the appearance of this world everything initially seemed to belong to Esav. For this is the order of the world: first darkness and then light, as they said at the beginning of Berakhot.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes a preparation for holiness from holiness already acquired in one’s essence. This explains how the earlier transfer of the birthright fits the ois’s argument about what can and cannot be sold.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ פּוֹרְעָנוּת הַבָּאָה לָעוֹלָם הוּא בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל (יְבָמוֹת סג.),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Elazar bar Avina said: Calamity comes upon the world only on account of Israel, as it says: ‘I cut off nations; their corner towers were laid waste; I devastated their streets.’ And it is written: ‘I said: If only you would fear Me and accept discipline.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה הוּא הַגָּלוּת שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל קוֹלְטִים אוֹתוֹ.
connections.quote: “All their association with the nations, in its deepest truth, is only to absorb holy sparks from them. As the Sages said: Israel went into exile only so that converts would be added to them. This does not mean only actual converts, but the additional absorption of the nations’ powers, returning them little by little to holiness, until the final time when everything returns to holiness. Although this is not yet revealed outwardly, in the inward heart this light is revealed and shines clearly, and nevertheless accomplishes its work.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the closing phrase about Israel’s gathering of good during exile. It explicitly extends “converts” beyond literal conversion and distinguishes hidden spiritual work from what is presently visible.

connections.hePhrase: [עו] בְּעֵת כִּשְׁלוֹן הָאָדָם, יֵדַע שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת הוּא הֲכָנָה לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר לְטוֹב;
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.quote: see note 577.
connections.context: The possibility described here depends on repentance. Rav Tzadok explicitly preserves the person’s recognition of sin and distinguishes it from the divine forgiveness that can transform the past.

connections.hePhrase: [עו] בְּעֵת כִּשְׁלוֹן הָאָדָם, יֵדַע שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת הוּא הֲכָנָה לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר לְטוֹב;
connections.quote: “It says, ‘The rain was upon the earth for forty days’: God brought it down in mercy, so that if they returned, it would be rain of blessing, as Rashi explains. This is Torah, for the Gemara says, ‘Water means Torah.’ But because they did not return and corrupted their ways, it became raging waters, and that generation was judged; afterward it says, ‘The Flood was forty days.’ In Tishrei, ‘There was light’ is Rosh Hashanah, as stated in Tikkunei Zohar; likewise the Midrash explains, ‘My light’ on Rosh Hashanah. The renewal in Torah begins then, for ‘Torah is light,’ and continues until Shemini Atzeret, the flowing wellspring of Torah. Then the light of Oral Torah and its innovations are established. From that time, forty days are given to receive this flow and renewal in Torah permanently. So too, concerning the rainy season, the first rain, yoreh, is in Mar Cheshvan. Yoreh ‘instructs’ people to plaster their roofs and so forth; it also alludes to instructing people to accept the yoke of Torah in truth.”
connections.explanation: The rain is first described as an act of mercy, capable of becoming blessing through return; only after the generation persists in corruption is it called a Flood. This gives the present siman’s ‘same matter’ a concrete meaning: the prepared influx is not itself evil, but its reception can turn toward destruction or Torah. Rav Tzadok then applies this to accepting the yoke of Torah in Mar Cheshvan. A promising spiritual moment calls for that response; its promise alone does not guarantee a good outcome.
connections.headline: The same prepared influx can become blessing or destructive waters

connections.hePhrase: כְּפִי גּוֹדֶל הַחֵטְא שֶׁהַיֵּצֶר מְסִיתוֹ, כָּךְ הוּא גּוֹדֶל הַטּוֹבָה שֶׁיּוּכַל לִקְלוֹט אָז,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 16
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 16
connections.quote: “Therefore Yehoshua, who was a vessel prepared to give the Land as an inheritance and to lead the generation that inherited it, presumably included within his soul all the holiness of the Land, since his soul included all the souls of the generation, as explained above. [This is why the Sages compared him to the face of the moon: it corresponds to the Oral Torah, which receives from the Written Torah, corresponding to the sun, as is known.] Moshe our teacher therefore feared especially for him. Since no one comes to understand words of Torah without stumbling, and since Moshe saw him attaining the fullest understanding of words of Torah, the greater the subsequent understanding, the greater the preceding stumbling. This is as explained above concerning the exiles. He therefore sought mercy for him in particular.”
connections.context: The parallel states the proportion directly. Its practical expression is Moshe’s prayer that Yehoshua be protected through the trial.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (פִּינְחָס רטז סוֹף עַמּוּד א), כִּי בְּעֵת הַמַּבּוּל הָיוּ רְאוּיִים לְקַבֵּל הַתּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “The Rabbis also explained that Moses was destined to receive the Torah in the generation of the Flood, but [did not] because they were wicked.”
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s explicit statement behind Rav Tzadok’s claim that the Flood generation contained a potential for receiving Torah. The relevant passage is 10:60, on the printed 216a–216b transition, beyond the previous range 10:48–58.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָיָה אָז מֹשֶׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין קלט:) עַל "בְּשַׁגַּם", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “The generation that departs is the generation that returns. One who departed lame returns lame; one who departed blind returns blind. … “For he too [beshagam] is flesh”: beshagam is Moses.”
connections.context: The same passage links recurrence of generations with Moses hidden in the Flood narrative. This supplies the surrounding framework of recurrence; the preceding note supplies the particular unrealized possibility of receiving Torah. The two notes quote distinct portions of the same source.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָיָה אָז מֹשֶׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין קלט:) עַל "בְּשַׁגַּם", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Where is Moses [hinted at] in the Torah? “For he too [beshagam] is flesh.””
connections.context: The letters of beshagam have the same numerical value, 345, as Moshe. In the same verse the lifespan of 120 years also recalls Moses. Rav Tzadok uses this allusion to describe Moses’ presence in potential within the Flood generation.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָיָה אָז מֹשֶׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין קלט:) עַל "בְּשַׁגַּם", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said: ‘My spirit shall not contend over man forever, since he too is flesh; his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּמַיִם הַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה, וְהֵם הֲפָכוּהוּ לַ"מַּיִם הַזֵּידוֹנִים";
connections.quote: ‘Then the raging waters would have passed over our lives.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא תַּכְלִית קִיּוּם הָעוֹלָם וְשֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ נִבְרָא, וְאִלְמָלֵא וְכוּלֵי, וְהֵם גָּרְמוּ אָבְדָנוֹ;
connections.quote: “Every thirty days Rav Sheshet would review his learning. He would stand leaning against the doorpost and say: “Rejoice, my soul; rejoice, my soul! For you I have studied Scripture; for you I have studied Mishnah.” Is that so? Did Rabbi Elazar not say: “Were it not for Torah, heaven and earth would not endure,” as it is stated, “If not for My covenant day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth”? At the outset, when a person acts, he acts for his own sake.”
connections.context: This supplies the phrase “were it not for it, etc.” The source places Torah’s sustaining of the world alongside the learner’s own benefit and explains why Rav Sheshet could speak of that personal benefit.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּעֵת הַחוּרְבָּן נוֹלַד מָשִׁיחַ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ב דִּבְרָכוֹת הֲלָכָה ד),
connections.quote: see note 613.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok places this narrative beside the potential for Torah in the generation of the Flood. Both illustrate his claim that a future remedy can be present within the moment of destruction.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אוֹתוֹ עֵת הָיָה מוּכָן, אִם זָכוּ, לְבִיאַת מָשִׁיחַ וּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הַנִּצְחִי וְקַיָּים לָעַד;
connections.quote: “There is a place prepared for distress, Heaven forbid, as our Sages say in chapter Chelek concerning Shechem: “A place,” and so forth. So too there is a time, as our Sages say there, “A time,” and as they say concerning an Israelite who has a lawsuit in Av. So too with a soul, as in what our Sages said about Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat and many other cases. But how can it be conceived that this was prepared for evil from the beginning of creation? Is it not written, “From the mouth of the Most High evils do not issue”? In truth, the Sages’ language brings healing: they said “prepared for punishment”—pur’anut, a term related to payment. But “the reward of a mitzvah is not in this world”; here there is only payment for transgressions, unless one merits tasting the fruit of his deeds in this world, or performs one of the mitzvot that bear fruit here. That time, place, and soul are prepared to receive payment for what has been earned. The reason that the reward of a mitzvah is not in this world is that the Holy One, blessed be He, gives His full measure, and this world cannot receive that great abundance of good at all. In that place, time, and soul where the blessed God’s payment and reward flow, the abundance of the flow becomes, Heaven forbid, harmful punishment—as is known concerning the mystery of the breaking of the vessels: their death comes through an excess of light. Thus our Sages said concerning “A person shall not see Me”: at the time of their death they do see. This is why our Sages said that the cherubim were found embracing, although Israel were not doing the Omnipresent’s will: the flow of light was then intensely abundant. That is why Yechezkel merited visions of God. One who truly merits receives the payment of good then; this is the meaning of Mashiach’s birth on the Ninth of Av.”
connections.context: This parallel explains how the same moment can contain destruction and the beginning of redemption. It distinguishes the abundant good from the recipient’s capacity to receive it.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אוֹתוֹ עֵת הָיָה מוּכָן, אִם זָכוּ, לְבִיאַת מָשִׁיחַ וּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הַנִּצְחִי וְקַיָּים לָעַד;
connections.quote: ““May the pleasantness of Hashem our God be upon us.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: In the past, because the Temple was built by flesh and blood, it was destroyed and I withdrew My Divine Presence. But in the future I will build it and cause My Divine Presence to dwell within it, and it will never be destroyed.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (מה.): אֲפִילּוּ נֶהֱוֵי כִּיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן לָא יָהֵיבְנָא לֵיהּ בְּרַתָּא.
connections.quote: ‘He said to him: ‘Even if he were like Joshua son of Nun, I would not give him my daughter.’ He replied: ‘If he were like Joshua son of Nun, then even if the Master did not give him his daughter, others would. As for this man, if the Master does not give him his daughter, others will not either.’’

connections.hePhrase: [וְהַפּוֹסְקִים הוֹכִיחוּ מִזֶּה דְּאָסוּר לוֹמַר "כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם", וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם טַעַם יֵשׁ בַּדָּבָר],
connections.displayRef: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 242:20
connections.linkedRef: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 242:20
connections.canonicalRef: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 242:20
connections.heRef: טורי זהב על שולחן ערוך יורה דעה רמ״ב:כ׳
connections.quote: ““Because of disrespect.” Beit Yosef wrote: It seems to me that this is why the Gemara says, “Even if Yehoshua son of Nun had said it, I would not obey him,” and does not say, “Even if Moshe had said it.” It appears that he understands the disrespect as directed toward Moshe our teacher: the speaker says, in effect, “If another person were like him,” which is impossible, for it is written, “There has not arisen one like Moshe.” In Maharshal’s work on chapter HaChovel, section 53, he cites the following: It is written in the responsa that if a person quarrels with his fellow and says, “I would not accept it from you even if you were like Moshe our teacher,” he is flogged because of the disrespect. [Maharshal continues:] This is a surprising ruling to me, for it is a customary expression and does not greatly disgrace Moshe our teacher. Moreover, ordinarily the speaker did not intend an insult, but merely expressed his refusal to accept forgiveness or appeasement in exaggerated terms. We therefore do not derive further rulings from such a novelty. Nevertheless, it is fitting to be stringent with him through a Monday–Thursday–Monday fast, so that he will take care with his speech. According to his explanation, someone who says “like Yehoshua” should likewise be flogged, for what difference would there be? But the explanation I gave in Beit Yosef’s name appears more correct, since he brings proof from the Gemara. So too in Yevamot: “Even if he were like Yehoshua son of Nun, I would not give him my daughter.””
connections.context: The Taz records Beit Yosef’s explanation, Maharshal’s different analysis, and his own preference for Beit Yosef. This is the authority behind Rav Tzadok’s reference to “the halakhic authorities”; the quoted discussion preserves the disagreement.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֶתֶר תּוֹרָה מוּנָּח לַכֹּל, וְאָמְרוּ (הוֹרָיוֹת יג.): "מַמְזֵר תַּלְמִיד חָכָם קוֹדֵם וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: see note 520.
connections.context: The Ark’s crown represents Torah. The source gives both elements used in the ois: that this crown remains available to everyone and that kingship itself is associated with Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֶתֶר תּוֹרָה מוּנָּח לַכֹּל, וְאָמְרוּ (הוֹרָיוֹת יג.): "מַמְזֵר תַּלְמִיד חָכָם קוֹדֵם וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘Mishnah: A Kohen takes precedence over a Levi; a Levi over an Israelite; an Israelite over a mamzer; a mamzer over a Natin; a Natin over a convert; and a convert over a freed slave. When does this apply? When they are all equal. But if the mamzer is a Torah scholar and the Kohen Gadol is unlearned, the mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over the unlearned Kohen Gadol.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קִבֵּל הָעֵרֶב רַב.
connections.quote: ““Go, descend, for your people have acted corruptly.” It does not say “the people,” but “your people.” Moshe said: Master of the world, how are they my people? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: They are your people. While they were still in Egypt, I told you, “I shall bring out My hosts, My people.” I told you not to mix a mixed multitude among them. But you, being humble and worthy, said to Me: Those who return are always accepted. I knew what they would ultimately do and told you no, but I fulfilled your wish. They are the ones who made the calf: they worshipped idols, made it, and caused My people to sin. See what is written: it does not say, “These are our gods,” but “These are your gods.” The converts who ascended with Moshe made it and told Israel, “These are your gods.” Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: “Go, descend, for your people have acted corruptly.””
connections.context: The Midrash supplies Moshe’s motive for accepting the mixed multitude and also relates the resulting failure at the calf. Rav Tzadok explains Moshe’s acceptance here through his connection to the crown of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת קא:): "מֹשֶׁה, שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרַתְּ" – הֲוָה יָהֵיב.
connections.quote: “Rav Safra said to him: “Moses, have you spoken well? We learned: from one to the other!””
connections.context: Rav Safra addresses another sage as “Moses” while challenging his interpretation of the rule for tied boats. The wording is interrogative in this exchange. Rav Tzadok’s point is the honorific identification of a Torah scholar with Moses, rather than the legal dispute about boats.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת קא:): "מֹשֶׁה, שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרַתְּ" – הֲוָה יָהֵיב.
connections.quote: ““Moshe”—that is, our teacher in his generation, as Moshe was in his generation.”
connections.context: Rashi explains precisely the sense in which the sage in the Gemara is addressed as “Moshe.” This supplies the interpretation used to distinguish the comparison in the ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא כב:): אֵין מַעֲמִידִין פַּרְנָס עַל הַצִּיבּוּר אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן קֻפָּה וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel: Why did the kingship of Saul’s house not continue? Because there was no blemish in him. For Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: A leader is appointed over the community only if a basket of creeping creatures hangs behind him, so that if he becomes conceited, they can tell him: ‘Turn around and look behind you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "בִּי מְלָכִים יִמְלֹכוּ", וְאַדְּרַבָּה, הַלָּלוּ רְאוּיִים יוֹתֵר לְכָךְ,
connections.quote: ‘Through me kings reign, and rulers decree justice.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים פא.): הִזָּהֲרוּ בִּבְנֵי עֲנִיִּים שֶׁמֵּהֶם תֵּצֵא תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ““Be attentive to the children of the poor”—make an effort to teach them Torah, for Torah will emerge from them: they have no other occupation, and, furthermore, they are humble in their own eyes.”
connections.context: The Ran identifies humility as one of the reasons for the saying. This explains the transition from the children of the poor to the image of broken vessels.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים פא.): הִזָּהֲרוּ בִּבְנֵי עֲנִיִּים שֶׁמֵּהֶם תֵּצֵא תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “It is taught in the name of the holy Ari that Moses our teacher was the root of the Written Torah, while Rabbi Akiva was the root of the Oral Torah. For this reason Rabbi Akiva came from Sisera and the wife of Heber the Kenite: within them were sparks belonging to the aspect of the Oral Torah, while Sisera was the husk surrounding this holiness.”
connections.explanation: In Ki Tavo, Rav Tzadok treats the tradition about Rabbi Akiva's ancestry as the emergence of Oral Torah from a place where its holiness had been enclosed. This gives a mechanism for the present siman's striking example of Torah in ‘broken vessels’: the apparent distance of the vessel does not determine the depth of the Torah hidden within it. The passage concerns a spiritual root and does not erase the distinctions in the siman's opening discussion.
connections.headline: Rabbi Akiva and the recovery of concealed Torah

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מְקוֹם הַתּוֹרָה דַּוְקָא בְּכֵלִים שְׁבוּרִים
connections.quote: “When they reached him [Rabbi Shimon], they found him sitting and studying Torah. He was saying: “A prayer of the poor person when he faints, and before Hashem he pours out his plea.” Every prayer of Israel is a prayer, but the poor person’s prayer is higher than them all. Why? Because it rises to the King’s throne of glory and becomes a crown upon His head. The Holy One, blessed be He, is indeed praised through that prayer. The poor person’s prayer is called “prayer.” “When he faints”: this wrapping is not the wrapping of a garment, for he has none. Rather, here it is written, “when he faints,” and elsewhere, “those who faint from hunger.” “Before Hashem he pours out his plea”—he complains before his Master, and this is pleasing before the Holy One, blessed be He, because through him the world is sustained when no other sustainers of the world are present. Woe to the one against whom that poor person complains to his Master, for the poor person is closer to the King than all others, as it is written, “When he cries to Me, I will hear, for I am gracious.” As for other people in the world, sometimes He hears and sometimes He does not. Why? Because the King dwells in these broken vessels, as it is written, “With the contrite and humble in spirit,” and “Hashem is close to the brokenhearted,” and “A broken and crushed heart, God, You will not despise.””
connections.context: The Zohar gives the image of the King dwelling in broken vessels within its teaching about the prayer of the poor and the brokenhearted. Rav Tzadok applies that image to the receptivity needed for Torah.

connections.hePhrase: [וִיסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, וְהוּא מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת גֵּרִים.
connections.quote: “That is why he was descended from converts: openly manifest love of Torah is found especially among converts. For the Holy One, blessed be He, brought the children of Israel out of slavery to freedom and made them a kingdom of priests. After all this He brought them before Mount Sinai—He drew them close and suspended the mountain over them like a barrel (Shabbat 88a). Even when they accepted it again out of love in the days of Ahasuerus, this arose from love for the miracle and deliverance. But a convert has left behind the ease of this world and the unrestricted pursuit of desires that he had among the nations. Of his own will he comes to restrain himself and to join Israel, who are afflicted, lowly, and hard pressed in this world. For “in your poverty he will fall to you,” and converts were not accepted in the days of David and Solomon, nor someone who converts out of love for some other thing (Yevamot 24b). Solely out of love for Torah he draws himself near and places himself under the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן רַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין יג:) שֶׁלֹּא יָכְלוּ חֲבֵירָיו לַעֲמוֹד עַל סוֹף דַּעְתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “[The Roman ruler] sent Nero Caesar against them. When he came, he shot an arrow toward the east, and it fell in Jerusalem; toward the west, and it fell in Jerusalem; toward the four directions of the heavens, and it fell in Jerusalem. He said to a child: Recite your verse to me. The child said: “I shall place My vengeance against Edom in the hand of My people Israel.” He said: The Holy One, blessed be He, wishes to destroy His house and to wipe His hands on that man [me]. He fled, went and converted, and Rabbi Meir descended from him.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s account connecting Rabbi Meir with a convert, which explains why he follows Rabbi Akiva in this series of examples.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן רַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין יג:) שֶׁלֹּא יָכְלוּ חֲבֵירָיו לַעֲמוֹד עַל סוֹף דַּעְתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Aha bar Hanina said: Before the One who spoke and the world came into being, it is revealed and known that no one in Rabbi Meir’s generation was his equal. Why, then, was the halakhah not established in accordance with his view? Because his colleagues could not grasp his reasoning to its full extent. He would declare an impure thing pure and offer grounds for it; he would declare a pure thing impure and offer grounds for it.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מִבְּנֵי קֵינִי חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה עָלוּ מֵעִיר הַתְּמָרִים, כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד.)]:
connections.quote: “The descendants of the Kenite, Moses’ father-in-law, went up from the City of Palms with the people of Judah to the wilderness of Judah south of Arad; they went and settled with the people.”
connections.context: This is the biblical sentence behind Rav Tzadok’s wording. The preceding Sanhedrin 104a note supplies the rabbinic interpretation of their move as study with Othniel’s descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מִבְּנֵי קֵינִי חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה עָלוּ מֵעִיר הַתְּמָרִים, כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד.)]:
connections.quote: ““From the City of Palms”—this is Jericho. Its fertile land was given to them to enjoy until the Temple would be built. Whoever’s territory would contain the Temple would take that land, so that all Israel would have a share in the Temple. It was given to Yitro’s descendants for four hundred and forty years. The scholars among them left it and went to Othniel son of Kenaz, who is Yavetz, in the wilderness of Yehudah south of Arad, to study Torah. “He settled with the people”—with the students who sat before him. He had asked the Holy One, blessed be He, to provide him with worthy students, as it is stated, “Yavetz called to the God of Israel,” and He provided him with these pious people.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the move from the City of Palms as leaving the fertile land of Jericho to study with Othniel. This supplies the Torah-learning content of the final example.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מִבְּנֵי קֵינִי חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה עָלוּ מֵעִיר הַתְּמָרִים, כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד.)]:
connections.quote: “‘And it brings those who are distant near’: this is learned from Yitro. Rabbi Yochanan said: As a reward for ‘Call him, and let him eat bread,’ his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, as it is said, ‘The families of scribes dwelling in Yabetz—the Tirathites, the Shimathites, and the Sucathites—these are the Kenites who came from Chammat, father of the house of Rechav.’ Elsewhere it is written, ‘The descendants of the Kenite, Moshe’s father-in-law, went up from the city of palms with the children of Yehudah to the wilderness of Yehudah south of Arad; he went and settled among the people.’”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן אַבְרָהָם שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ יִשְׁמָעֵאל וּבְנֵי קְטוּרָה, שֶׁיָּצָא הַפְּסֹלֶת עַל יְדֵיהֶם.
connections.quote: “Thus, when Avraham our father came into the world, dross emerged from him: Yishmael and all the sons of Keturah. When Yitzchak came into the world, dross emerged from him: Esav and all the chiefs of Edom. They became worse than the earlier ones. When Yaakov came, no dross emerged from him; rather, all his sons were born worthy, as it is stated, “Yaakov was a wholehearted man, dwelling in tents.” Through whom does the Omnipresent recognize His portion? Through Yaakov, as it is stated, “For Hashem’s portion is His people; Yaakov is the allotment of His inheritance,” and, “For Yah has chosen Yaakov for Himself.””
connections.context: This is the Midrashic source for the imagery of dross emerging through the earlier patriarchs’ offspring and for its completion in Yaakov.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאַבְרָהָם: "כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע",
connections.quote: ‘God said to Abraham: ‘Do not be distressed over the boy or over your maidservant. In everything that Sarah tells you, listen to her voice, for it is through Isaac that offspring shall be called yours.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאַבְרָהָם: "כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע",
connections.quote: “But the descendants of Yaakov our father can no longer change their name and uproot themselves from the root of Jewish identity. Even if their sins reach the heavens, one remains an Israelite in every respect, and the name Israel is not uprooted from him. This is the root in holiness within all Yaakov’s descendants, for his offspring are complete: there is no dross in the root that comes from him within all his subsequent descendants. Therefore this root of the name Israel, coming from Yaakov our father, remains forever. Esav, however, although born in holiness, still had the choice to uproot himself from this holiness inherited from his forefathers. Although the patriarchs merited that the root of their holiness should be fixed in all their descendants—for through their effort they transformed all their powers to holiness, no evil remained in them at all, and only good can emerge from a good root—they had not yet merited complete offspring until Yaakov. This means that their very essence should be transformed entirely, leaving no possibility of evil, so that their existence should be different from that of other human beings and they could beget only what resembled themselves. Just as a human being is not born from an animal, or an animal from a human being, so a gentile cannot be born from an Israelite, or an Israelite from a gentile. This began with Yaakov, who merited the name Israel for himself and his descendants. Avraham and Yitzchak had not yet had their essence transformed entirely until Yaakov’s birth. Then the promise “Through Yitzchak your offspring shall be called”—but not all of Yitzchak—was fulfilled, and Yishmael and Esav were excluded from being called the offspring of Avraham and Yitzchak. Avraham and Yitzchak were then also completed, so that their offspring were complete, because from then on only Yaakov’s descendants were called and reckoned their offspring.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the stages before and after Yaakov. The opening qualification is essential: the descendants of Yaakov retain the name Israel despite grave wrongdoing.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּיבָמוֹת (יז.): לֹא זָזוּ מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁעֲשָׂאוּם כְּגוֹיִם גְּמוּרִים,
connections.quote: ‘Some say: When I said this before Shmuel, he told me: They did not move from there until they had classified them as gentiles in all respects, as it is said: ‘They have betrayed Hashem, for they have borne foreign children.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּיבָמוֹת (יז.): לֹא זָזוּ מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁעֲשָׂאוּם כְּגוֹיִם גְּמוּרִים,
connections.quote: “His decree was fulfilled in the ten tribes who became assimilated among the nations, as they said in Yevamot: “They did not move from there until they made them complete gentiles.” However, he [Hoshea] was speaking about the sinners themselves, as was initially decreed that they should be called “not My people”; there [in the Gemara], however, the reference is to their offspring, as is proved from the verse “For they have begotten foreign children.” There, in Hoshea, Rashi explains this verse: because they married gentile women, whose child has the mother’s status. This is also what Shmuel’s first version there says. Both versions intended the same thing, except that each stated it in reference to a different verse.”
connections.context: In his fuller discussion, Rav Tzadok expressly limits the Talmudic statement to offspring of gentile mothers. He distinguishes this from Hoshea’s proposal concerning the sinners themselves; the passage does not describe the removal of Jewish identity from all sinners.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דִּבְרֵי רַמְבַּ"ן עַל פָּסוּק "שֹׁרֶשׁ פֹּרֶה רֹאשׁ", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “The father is the root, and the son is a shoot that grows from his roots. … “Bearing gall” hints that bitterness does not come from a sweet root: one whose heart is whole with the honored God and who has not entertained any thought of idolatry will not father one who acknowledges it. Do not challenge me from “he fathers a violent son,” for the matter is true and contains a great secret that I cannot explain.”
connections.context: Ramban interprets the root and its future growth as parent and descendants within the covenant. He expressly acknowledges the difficult counterexample in Ezekiel 18:10 and leaves its resolution unexplained. Rav Tzadok develops the connection between a parental root and its offspring; the verse alone does not state that interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר לְחִזְקִיָּהוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (י.): בַּהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ?
connections.quote: ‘He said to him: ‘What business have you with the Merciful One’s hidden matters? You must do what you have been commanded, and let the Holy One, blessed be He, do what is pleasing to Him.’ He answered: ‘Then give me your daughter now. Perhaps my merit and yours together will bring it about that worthy children will descend from me.’ He told him: ‘The decree against you has already been issued.’ He replied: ‘Son of Amoz, finish your prophecy and leave!’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר לְחִזְקִיָּהוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (י.): בַּהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ?
connections.quote: “A person may not set aside the positive commandment of procreation because he suspects that he or his partner will not produce worthy offspring—whether on the basis of something heard, reason, or experience. A person has no standing concerning the secrets of God, as they said: “Why involve yourself with the Merciful One’s hidden matters?” Nevertheless, in choosing a partner he should make the appropriate effort, so that he is seen to intend through the marriage to produce worthy children, as the Sages instructed concerning examining her brothers, marrying the daughter of a Torah scholar, and similar matters.”
connections.context: Meiri preserves both parts of the lesson: uncertainty about future children does not displace the mitzvah, and responsible effort in choosing a partner remains appropriate.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר לְחִזְקִיָּהוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (י.): בַּהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ?
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
connections.quote: “When Shem saw his disciple Avraham go to rescue Lot, he could not understand the act according to his own judgment. Seemingly he should not have helped him, since Ammon and Moab would emerge from him, troublesome neighbors of Jerusalem (Sanhedrin 96b), and Hashem had warned that they should not enter the congregation. Why, then, did Avraham risk his life to rescue him? But Shem knew Avraham as his disciple and recognized him as thoroughly righteous, so that surely no stumbling would come through him. He prayed to Hashem to illuminate his eyes and disclose the reason for Avraham's act. Thus it says, ‘He was a priest to God Most High’: when he brought out the bread and wine he was serving Hashem and praying that He illuminate his eyes to understand what lay beyond his own intellect and comprehension. Hashem then illuminated his eyes to show that nothing had been done through Avraham in vain. Although Ammon and Moab would emerge from Lot and were told not to enter (Lamentations 1:10), this restriction concerned the males; the females were permitted immediately. From them would emerge the kingship of David and Shlomo, the principal support of the kingship of the land of Israel and Jerusalem. Therefore he said, ‘Blessed is Avram to God Most High.’”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Shem's difficulty with Avraham's rescue of Lot: Ammon and Moab seemed to make the rescue an obstacle to Jerusalem's future. The answer appears through the permitted female lines from which David and Shlomo emerge. This is a close structural parallel to the siman's Menashe example: a visible failure in one generation does not disclose the whole future of the line. The qualification concerning male and female descendants is retained in the quotation.
connections.headline: A future good concealed within an unexpected rescue

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ "וַיִּקֹּד הָעָם וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ" בְּפָרָשַׁת בֹּא, וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: שָׂמְחוּ עַל בְּשׂוֹרַת הַבָּנִים;
connections.quote: ““The people bowed”: for the tidings of redemption, entry into the Land, and the children they would have.”
connections.context: Rashi includes future children among the good tidings for which the people gave thanks. Rav Tzadok singles out that element; the biblical verse alone does not spell it out.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיהוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (תַּנְחוּמָא תְּרוּמָה ט) מְפוֹרָשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “You must not say that the Sanctuary alone was precious to them, for the Temple was also precious. How do we know this? Solomon indicated it in his prayer: Moreover concerning the stranger that is not of Thy people Israel, when he shall come out of a far country for Thy name’s sake—for they shall hear of Thy great name, and of Thy mighty hand, and of Thine outstretched arm—when he shall come and pray toward this house, hear Thou in heaven Thy dwelling-place, and do according to all that the stranger calleth to Thee for; that all the peoples of the earth may know Thy name, to fear Thee, as doth Thy people Israel, and that they may know that Thy name is called upon this house which I have built (I Kings 8:41–43). However, when an Israelite prays before You in this Temple, Grant him all that his heart seeks, for You alone know what is in the heart of every man (ibid., v. 39). But if he should ask for children, and You know that they will provoke You to anger, do not give them to him. Similarly, if he desires property, and You know that in the future he will rebel against You because of it, do not give it to him, but for the non-Jew: Do according to all that the stranger calleth to Thee for, that all the people of the earth may know, etc. Israel, however, is aware of Thy name and Thy glory, and You can foresee at the beginning what will finally happen, for You are God, and whatever You desire, You can do.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיהוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (תַּנְחוּמָא תְּרוּמָה ט) מְפוֹרָשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “And although in Parashat Bo it says, “The people bowed and prostrated themselves,” and Rashi explains that this was over the news of children, while the question there is the wicked son’s “What is this service to you?”—there it is Hashem’s unsolicited promise. Evil does not issue from the Most High, and surely a chain of good will ultimately come from them. So too with Chizkiyahu: “Why concern yourself with the Merciful One’s hidden matters?” Although his son was wicked, to the point of being counted among those without a share in the World to Come, a great chain of righteous people later descended from him, and Mashiach will also be of his descendants. Thus what Hashem gives on His own is certainly good. When a person prays for children, he should pray for worthy children and Torah scholars, through whom the glory of Heaven will be increased, sanctified, and multiplied.”
connections.explanation: Poked Akarim returns to precisely the examples that close this siman. It distinguishes Hashem's unsolicited promise, which can include a hidden future chain of good, from the content of a person's prayer, which should ask for worthy children and increased kavod Shamayim. This supplies the distinction left unresolved here between rejoicing at the promise in Bo and Shlomo's prayer that an ultimately harmful request not be granted.
connections.headline: The distinction between a divine promise and one's own request

connections.hePhrase: [עט] עִנְיַן הַפְּגָם לְמַעְלָה עַל יְדֵי עֲווֹנוֹת הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁאָנוּ אוֹמְרִים שֶׁהַחַמָּה לוֹקָה;
connections.quote: “Alternatively: when the moon is eclipsed, the light is absent in the moon itself. This is an unfavorable sign for Israel, as it says, ‘I am with him in distress’ (Psalms 91:15), and when the Temple was destroyed the heavenly retinue was diminished. But an eclipse of the sun is an absence of light for those who see it, rather than in the sun. This is an unfavorable sign for the nations: the flow remains complete in its own place, but is lacking for them.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explicitly develops the same source-and-recipient distinction. Its alternative explanation treats the sun's eclipse as an absence of light for observers while the light remains complete at its source. This helps specify what the siman means by a blemish above: the intended disclosure and reception are impaired, and that impairment is described in relation to the source's purpose of giving light.
connections.headline: Diminished reception does not diminish the source

connections.hePhrase: [עט] עִנְיַן הַפְּגָם לְמַעְלָה עַל יְדֵי עֲווֹנוֹת הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁאָנוּ אוֹמְרִים שֶׁהַחַמָּה לוֹקָה;
connections.quote: “Spiritually, they are the light of Written Torah and Oral Torah, for ‘Torah is light.’ They are God’s luminaries and likewise correspond to the two luminaries just described. Written Torah is an intrinsic light from Him, containing no darkness. ‘Had Israel not sinned, they would have been given only the five books of Torah …,’ as Nedarim says; concerning this it says, ‘With much wisdom comes much vexation.’ At the giving of the Torah it says, ‘I said: you are divine beings.’ Avodah Zarah explains that they were free of the angel of death and would not die—and the angel of death is the evil inclination. They were like the future state, ‘They will no longer teach one another,’ and Written Torah, corresponding to sunlight, would have sufficed; the world to come is compared to day. Once they sinned, they returned to this world’s darkness, which is compared to night, and needed moonlight to illuminate from within darkness: Oral Torah, ‘the moon that receives from the sun,’ Written Torah. Oral Torah’s light is likewise a luminary God created. Although it consists of what scribes and Israel’s sages innovate, it only appears to the person that he discovers and innovates that light. In truth it comes from God, who illuminates that light in his heart.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah applies the sun and moon to Written and Oral Torah. The sages’ own discoveries are the form in which received light illuminates a darkened world. This develops the present siman’s distinction between the source of light and the condition of its reception: concealment need not mean that every illumination has ceased. Oral Torah is a specific expression of the continuing reflected light, and its apparent human authorship does not sever it from its divine source.
connections.headline: Oral Torah carries received divine light within concealment

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּכָל לַיְלָה הוּא לַקּוּת הַחַמָּה, שֶׁגַּם זֶה הוּא מִצַּד מָסָךְ הַמַּבְדִּיל, דּוּגְמַת לַקּוּתָהּ בַּיּוֹם.
connections.quote: “There are four kinds of impairment of the sun. First: every night, when the sun turns away from us. This corresponds to a head of the court who dies, so that his radiance departs, and who is not properly eulogized to draw forth some measure of that light, as the early authorities wrote concerning eulogies. Second: through a cloud, an intervening screen. This corresponds to a betrothed young woman who cries out with no one to save her: the increase of sexual immorality dulls the heart’s ability to receive light, as the Sages said, and as it is written, “All these abominations … and it became defiled.” A screen is thereby formed. Third: through the moon, which is closer to the sun, receives its influence, and is its brother in giving light, yet obstructs the light. This corresponds to two brothers whose blood is shed together in their dispute with one another. Fourth: through the spots visible to observers, which are a withdrawal of light within the luminary itself. This corresponds to intercourse between males, which the kabbalists wrote causes the withholding of the Divine Presence’s flow: measure for measure, the flow returns to the giver rather than to the Divine Presence that receives it, and light and flow are, as it were, absent from the Divine Presence.”
connections.context: This is the first complete set of correspondences in the parallel; Rav Tzadok then offers further mappings. It shows that he uses “impairment of the sun” broadly for several forms of obscured light, including ordinary night and an intervening screen.

connections.hePhrase: וְתַכְלִית הִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת הָאֲצִילוּת לְהַשְׁפִּיעַ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: “This is the revelation of the Divine Presence below: to impart great light within people’s hearts and also to receive from them. As is known, the dwelling of the Divine Presence below is a need on high; and as the Sages say, “Israel, as it were, sustain their Father in Heaven.” Every offering is described as a “pleasing fragrance,” and all the mitzvot likewise bring satisfaction before Him. It is stated, “You weaken the Rock who bore you”: through their sins they weaken, Heaven forbid, the power of the heavenly retinue. This is because “more than the calf wishes to nurse, the cow wishes to give milk.” Thus, although she gives, she also receives through giving, since she desires and longs to give. We likewise find that a woman can become betrothed through the benefit she receives by giving to an important person: she enjoys his acceptance, so that his receiving from her is considered her receiving, as stated in the first chapter of Kiddushin. This therefore does not contradict what is said elsewhere: “The mitzvot were given only to refine created beings. What difference does it make to the Holy One, blessed be He, whether one slaughters from the neck,” and so forth? Both are true. Since the blessed God wished thereby to refine created beings so that He could bestow every good upon them, He also receives benefit from them: it is a satisfaction before Him that He spoke and His will was done. Likewise, “If you are righteous, what do you give Him, and what does He take from your hand?” does not contradict this, for the same reason. Furthermore, as is known, service and the deeds of those below truly have no relation to the essence of the blessed Infinite. They relate only to His holy emanation, which is also His essence insofar as He emanated light apprehensible to those below. When it arose in His will to create beings, to reign over and guide them, and for them to recognize His kingship, He necessarily emanated light in measured attributes according to the recipients’ measure. All His names, and all the apprehensions of angels, seraphim, ofanim, prophets, and sages, relate only to the emanated attributes.”
connections.context: This parallel explains why giving can itself be described as receiving and why blocked reception can be termed a defect. It expressly distinguishes the divine attributes accessible to created beings from the infinite divine essence.

connections.hePhrase: אָז נֶחְשָׁב כִּבְיָכוֹל תְּשִׁישׁוּת לְפַמַלְיָא שֶׁל מַעְלָה;
connections.quote: ““They went without strength before the pursuer.” Rabbi Azaryah said in the name of Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon: When Israel do the Omnipresent’s will, they add strength to the might above, as it is stated, “Through God we shall do valiantly.” When Israel do not do the Omnipresent’s will, they weaken, as it were, the great power above, as it is written, “You weaken the Rock who bore you.” Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Levi son of Rabbi Tarfon: When Israel do the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, they add strength to the might above, as it is stated, “Now, let the power of Hashem be great.” When they do not do the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, they weaken, as it were, the great power above, and they too go without strength before the pursuer.”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the language of weakening the heavenly power and also its positive counterpart. Rav Tzadok explains that language through the relation between the light and its recipients.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן הַחוּרְבָּן דִּלְעֵילָא, וְגָלוּת הַדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה, וּמַדְרֵגוֹת בַּגָּלוּת עַצְמוֹ, וְהָבֵן כָּל זֶה.
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak: What is the meaning of “The Holy One is in your midst, and I shall not enter the city”? Is it because the Holy One is in your midst that He will not enter the city? He answered: Rabbi Yochanan said thus: The Holy One, blessed be He, said, “I shall not enter the Jerusalem above until I enter the Jerusalem below.” Is there a Jerusalem above? Yes, as it is written, “Jerusalem, built as a city joined together.””
connections.context: The source relates the heavenly Jerusalem to the earthly one. It supplies the background for Rav Tzadok’s language of destruction above accompanying the destruction below.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ: "רָאָה וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם",
connections.quote: ““He stood and measured the earth; He saw and released the nations.” What did He see? He saw the seven commandments that Noah’s descendants had accepted but had not kept. Since they had not kept them, He arose and released them.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ: "רָאָה וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם",
connections.quote: “Rather, this tells you that they do not receive reward as one who is commanded and performs, but as one who is not commanded and performs.”
connections.context: The Gemara rejects the idea that wrongdoing earns exemption or reward and explains “released” in terms of the level of reward. Rav Tzadok is invoking this rabbinic reading of Habakkuk 3:6, not the plain translation about making nations tremble.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מֵעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ מֹשֶׁה שֶׁלֹּא תִּשְׁרֶה שְׁכִינָה בְּעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, אֵין מְקַבְּלִים אוֹר כְּלָל וְאֵין כָּאן לַקּוּת:
connections.quote: “[Moshe] requested that the Divine Presence should not rest upon idolaters, and it was granted to him, as it is stated, “Let me and Your people be distinguished.””
connections.context: This is the Talmudic statement invoked in the closing sentence. Rav Tzadok develops its significance for the reception of divine light.

connections.hePhrase: [פ] תִּיקּוּן לְכַעַס – שִׁינּוּי מָקוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה גָּלוּת לְרוֹצֵחַ
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: Four things tear up a person’s decree: charity, crying out, a change of name, and a change of conduct. Charity—as it is written, “Charity rescues from death.” Crying out—as it is written, “They cried to Hashem in their distress, and He brought them out of their straits.” A change of name—as it is written, “Sarai your wife: you shall not call her name Sarai, for Sarah is her name,” and, “I will bless her and also give you a son through her.” A change of conduct—as it is written, “God saw their deeds,” and, “God relented concerning the harm He had said He would bring upon them, and did not do it.” Some say: a change of place as well, for it is written, “Hashem said to Avram: Go forth from your land,” and afterward, “I shall make you a great nation.” The other opinion holds that it was the merit of the Land of Israel that benefited him.”
connections.context: This is the Talmudic framework for the changes of place, conduct, and name developed in the ois. The source includes the alternative explanation of Avraham’s changed circumstances.

connections.hePhrase: [פ] תִּיקּוּן לְכַעַס – שִׁינּוּי מָקוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה גָּלוּת לְרוֹצֵחַ
connections.quote: “Moshe our teacher was also entirely clear of anger, without the slightest trace of it. Therefore, in this portion, when a slight appearance of displeasure was seen in him and he departed from his measure by a small amount, as it says, ‘Moshe became angry,’ the law of purifying Midian's vessels was concealed from him. He was thereby shown the need for care even in a very subtle matter, just as a vessel requires purification and immersion even after only a short time in gentile possession. In the incident of Zimri he was shown that a particular need can sometimes require precisely the use of anger and zeal. The law concerning the zealots was therefore concealed from him, since this act of zeal did not belong to his own task; Pinchas came and took what was fitting for him. For this reason, too, Moshe's burial was east of the Jordan in Gad's portion: ‘there the lawgiver's portion is concealed.’ The Sages teach (Makkot 9b) that three refuge cities were needed there because murderers were numerous in Gilead, the opposing husk of anger and zeal. Moshe, who was wholly pure in this respect, was buried there to subdue that opposing counterpart, as explained concerning his burial opposite Beit Peor.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik develops the same connection between Gilead, refuge cities, and anger through Moshe's burial there. It also distinguishes the specific task of Pinchas from Moshe's own exceptional purity, including the consequence of even a slight appearance of anger. That distinction helps explain why the siman's account of a holy root of severity cannot be used to justify Ahab's claim that his killing was therefore holy.
connections.headline: Gilead and the distinct uses of severity

connections.hePhrase: [פ] תִּיקּוּן לְכַעַס – שִׁינּוּי מָקוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה גָּלוּת לְרוֹצֵחַ
connections.quote: “For this protection comes only from the clarity of Moses our teacher, for whom it shone explicitly: “You were shown to know that Hashem is God; there is nothing besides Him.” As the Sages explained in the Midrash, Moses proclaimed the Holy One’s kingship even in the empty space of the world. From this grows protection for the unintentional killer: how could the axe split the air and kill this person, when in truth nothing, even in the air and the empty space of the world, happens by chance, Heaven forbid, but everything is under individual providence?”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim relates the cities of refuge to Moshe’s clarity that nothing lies outside divine providence, and concludes that this affords protection even to a very lowly soul. This helps explain why Rav Tzadok specifies a city of refuge rather than endless wandering: the change of place has a positive spiritual content. It is directed toward repair, rather than treating anger as an identity that can never change.
connections.headline: The city of refuge is a place of repair

connections.hePhrase: [וְהָיָה עִיר מִקְלָט וְלֹא נָע וָנָד לְעוֹלָם, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ פַּחַד יִצְחָק וּגְבוּרוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת שֶׁטּוֹב,
connections.quote: see note 352.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok expressly limits the “holy powers of severity” to their proper purpose. This clarifies the qualification “which are good” in the Hebrew phrase.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנָן דְּרָתַח (תַּעֲנִית ד.), וְזֶהוּ הָעִיר מִקְלָט.
connections.quote: ‘Rava said: When a young Torah scholar grows heated, it is the Torah that heats him, as it says: ‘Is not My word like fire, declares Hashem?’ Rav Ashi said: Any Torah scholar who is not hard as iron is not a Torah scholar, as it says: ‘And like a hammer that shatters rock.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן הַאי צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנָן דְּרָתַח (תַּעֲנִית ד.), וְזֶהוּ הָעִיר מִקְלָט.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: If a teacher goes into exile, his academy is exiled with him. Is that so? Did Rabbi Yochanan not say: From where do we know that words of Torah provide refuge? For it is stated, “Betzer in the wilderness,” and afterward, “This is the Torah.” There is no difficulty: one statement concerns the time when he is engaged in it, and the other the time when he is not engaged in it. Alternatively, what does “provide refuge” mean? From the Angel of Death. Thus Rav Chisda was sitting and studying in the academy, and the messenger of the Angel of Death could not approach him because his mouth never ceased its study. The messenger went up and sat upon the academy’s cedar tree; the cedar cracked, Rav Chisda fell silent, and the messenger was able to reach him.”
connections.context: The Gemara itself associates Torah with refuge, while preserving two explanations of its protection. Rav Tzadok’s association of the Torah scholar’s holy fervor with the city of refuge has this textual background.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְגִלְעָד וּשְׁכֶם דִּשְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים הִרְבּוּ עָרֵי מִקְלָט כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַכּוֹת (ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: “Three [cities] across the Jordan, and three in the Land of Israel? Abaye said: Murderers were common in Gilead.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְגִלְעָד וּשְׁכֶם דִּשְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים הִרְבּוּ עָרֵי מִקְלָט כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַכּוֹת (ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: “Abaye said: Murderers were also common in Shechem, as it is written, “Like bands lying in wait, a company of priests, they murder on the road to Shechem.””
connections.context: The discussion accounts for the placement and spacing of the cities of refuge. The first passage supplies Gilead; the continuation on the next page supplies Shechem, the second place named by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא;
connections.quote: “For the Holy One, blessed be He, does not act tyrannically toward His creatures.”
connections.context: The Gemara invokes this principle in explaining the further opportunity offered to the nations. Rav Tzadok applies it here to the corresponding possibility of repair where a particular failing is strong.

connections.hePhrase: וְגִלְעָד וּשְׁכֶם שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּנַחֲלַת יוֹסֵף, כִּי "לֹא תִרְצַח" וְ"לֹא תִנְאָף" שְׁנֵיהֶם הֲפָכִים כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 2
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 2
connections.quote: ““He sent out the raven, and it went out, going and returning,” and so forth. The raven alludes to anger. Noach wished that the trait of anger should not exist in the world, but the Holy One, blessed be He, showed him that, for the present, this trait is still needed in the world. Sometimes, when an evil desire comes upon a person, he can save himself from it by bringing himself into anger against it. This is the meaning of “going and returning until the waters dried”: until evil desires cease from the world, and then anger too will be abolished, for water signifies desire. A small hint of this began in the Temple, where there was a cubit-high deterrent against ravens, as stated in tractate Middot, chapter 4, mishnah 6.”
connections.context: The passage explains how anger and desire can oppose one another and why the corrective use of anger is temporary. It is a parallel teaching of the author’s teacher; it is not presented as the precise wording of the oral teaching about Gilead.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי: "שַׂעְרֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר מֵהַר גִּלְעָד" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ד, א), כִּידוּעַ שֵׂעָר הוּא הַדִּינִים וּגְבוּרוֹת שֶׁבָּאָדָם, וְהֵם קְדוֹשׁוֹת מֵהַר גִּלְעָד.
connections.quote: ‘You are beautiful, my companion; you are beautiful. Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Mount Gilead.’

connections.hePhrase: וְשֶׁזֶּהוּ מַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחְאָב: "הֲיָדַעְתֶּם כִּי לָנוּ רָמֹת גִּלְעָד" (מְלָכִים א כב, ג),
connections.quote: ‘The king of Israel said to his servants: ‘Do you know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, yet we sit still instead of taking it from the king of Aram?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְרָמוֹת בְּגִלְעָד הוּא עִיר מִקְלַט הָרוֹצֵחַ, לוֹמַר שֶׁהָיָה זֶה בִּקְדוּשָׁה, וְזֶהוּ "כִּי לָנוּ", אֲבָל לֹא הִצְלִיחַ.
connections.quote: “Thus the Sages said: “Ruddy”—[David] resembled Esav, and so forth; “this one kills with the approval of the Sanhedrin,” and so forth. This proceeds from wisdom, which is the fervor of the Sages. [As I heard concerning the verse “Do you know that Ramoth-gilead is ours?” in relation to “Your hair is like a flock [of goats streaming] from Mount Gilead”: hair signifies judgment and indicates anger and killing, as is known; but from Mount Gilead comes the good form of killing, in accordance with the blessed God’s will. This was Ahab’s purpose in seeking to capture Ramoth-gilead: through this he would know that his killing of the prophets had been forgiven, as it too had been killing in accordance with God’s will.
