That is why he did not succeed there.] Likewise, Yosef’s killing is to burn the house of Esav, pouring his wrath upon idolaters and not upon Israel, Heaven forbid. Therefore it is said, “He did not choose the tribe of Ephraim”—to endure forever, but only for a time. For this good form of killing is itself only temporary, while idolaters and evil remain. In the future, when everything is good, there will be no need for killing at all; desire, however, will remain even then, as explained above from Midrash HaNe’elam.”
connections.context: The parallel preserves Ahab’s unsuccessful attempt to establish that his actions had been justified. The surrounding passage distinguishes the Sanhedrin’s judgment from wrongdoing and confines the positive use of severity to the period in which evil remains.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בְּקַיִן: "נָע וָנָד תִּהְיֶה"
connections.quote: ‘When you work the soil, it will no longer give you its strength. You will be a restless wanderer on the earth.’

connections.hePhrase: וְתִיקּוּן לְתַאֲוָה – שִׁינּוּי מַעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁבָּא דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל הֵימֶנָּה, בָּזֶה נִתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם.
connections.quote: “What is the case of a repentant person? Rav Yehudah said: For example, the opportunity for a transgression came to him a first time and a second time, and he escaped it. Rav Yehudah indicated: with the same woman, at the same period, in the same place.”
connections.context: The original passage supplies the recurring test that Rav Tzadok calls a change of conduct: the person now withstands the kind of opportunity in which he previously failed.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁמּוֹעִיל לַחוֹלֶה, כִּי לִפְעָמִים אִידְּחֵי גַּבְרָא מִקַּמֵּי גַּבְרָא כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי אֵין מַלְכוּת נוֹגַעַת בַּחֲבֶרְתָּהּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman said to Rabbi Yitzchak: What does “It happened when Shmuel grew old” mean? Was Shmuel so old? He was only fifty-two, for a master said: Death at fifty-two years is the death of Shmuel of Ramah. He answered: Rabbi Yochanan said that old age came suddenly upon him. For it is written, “I regret that I made Shaul king.” Shmuel said before Him: Master of the world, You have equated me with Moshe and Aharon, as it is written, “Moshe and Aharon among His priests, and Shmuel among those who call His name.” Just as the work of Moshe’s and Aharon’s hands was not annulled during their lives, so may the work of my hands not be annulled during my life. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: What shall I do? If Shaul dies, Shmuel will not allow it. If Shmuel dies while young, people will speak against him. If neither Shaul nor Shmuel dies, David’s kingship has already arrived, and one reign does not overlap another’s even by a hair’s breadth. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I shall bring old age suddenly upon him. This is what is written: “Shaul was sitting in Givah beneath the tamarisk in Ramah.” What has Givah to do with Ramah? It teaches that what caused Shaul to remain in Givah for two and a half years was the prayer of Shmuel of Ramah. Is one person displaced before another? Yes, for Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: What does “Therefore I hewed through the prophets; I killed them by the words of My mouth” mean? It does not say “through their deeds,” but “by the words of My mouth.” Thus one person is displaced before another.”
connections.context: This is the narrative behind the two linked phrases in the ois: one person being displaced for another, and the exact boundary between reigns.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אָדָם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִקְרָא בֶּן מֶלֶךְ כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: “One whose loins ache may not anoint them with wine or vinegar, but may anoint them with oil, though not rose oil. Children of kings may anoint their wounds with rose oil, since that is their practice on weekdays. Rabbi Shimon says: All Israel are children of kings.”
connections.context: Rabbi Shimon uses this designation in the Mishnah’s discussion of anointing on Shabbat. Rav Tzadok draws upon the designation to extend the concept of kingship to each individual.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִגְזַר עָלָיו לִפְעָמִים, וְהַתִּיקּוּן לָזֶה שִׁינּוּי הַשֵּׁם, וְאֵינֶנּוּ הַאי גַּבְרָא כְּלָל:
connections.quote: see note 85.
connections.context: Rambam makes the meaning of the changed name explicit: it expresses the person’s transformed conduct and identity. He also explains the humbling effect of changing place, linking the end of the ois with its opening.

connections.hePhrase: [פא] פְּעָמִים נִגְזַר עַל אָדָם לָמוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם מִשּׁוּם "אֵין מַלְכוּת וְכוּלֵי", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם;
connections.quote: “He said to him: “You will die on Shabbat.” David asked: “May I die on the first day of the week?” He replied: “The time for the kingship of your son Solomon has already arrived, and one reign does not encroach upon another even by a hair’s breadth.””
connections.context: God’s answer to David supplies the rule abbreviated at the opening of the ois. Rav Tzadok then considers whether a predecessor can remain alive while willingly relinquishing the prominence that belongs to his successor.

connections.hePhrase: [פא] פְּעָמִים נִגְזַר עַל אָדָם לָמוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם מִשּׁוּם "אֵין מַלְכוּת וְכוּלֵי", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם;
connections.quote: “The counsel for this is the commandment of Hakhel. Men, women, and children were present, as the Gemara teaches (Chagigah 3a): the men come to learn, the women to hear; why do the children come? To give reward to those who bring them. Through Hakhel a person recognizes that even Israel's little children, who do not yet learn or hear, nevertheless have the power to give reward to those who bring them. No member of Israel can simply be treated as deficient. Thus ‘Moshe assembled’ is also written before the completion of the Mishkan, for there this recognition was explicit. As my holy grandfather explained in Mei HaShiloach (Volume I, Vayakhel, under ‘Vayakhel’), although one made the ark, another the curtain, and others the boards and hangings, afterward all recognized that the honor of Heaven coming through the maker of the ark also comes through the maker of the hangings. They recognized how each clarified the other. Once they recognized this, they became the vessel in which Hashem would rest His presence.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef supplies an account of the inward recognition that opposes envy: those making the ark and those making the curtains discover the honor of Heaven in one another's different tasks. This illuminates the disposition sought in the siman's succession argument. A person's own visible prominence can recede while the shared service continues through another; the source develops that relation through concrete complementary roles rather than merely advising a general feeling of goodwill.
connections.headline: Another person's task can complete the same service

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וָאֶתְחַנַּן וּמִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה וַיֵּלֶךְ, עַיֵּין שָׁם) בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
connections.quote: ““Until now it was your portion to serve before Me. Now your portion has passed, and the time has come for Joshua your disciple to serve.” Moses said before Him: “My Master, if I am to die because of Joshua, I will go and become his disciple.” He said to him: “If you wish to do this, go and do it.” … Joshua sat at the head, with Moses at his right and Aaron’s sons at his left, and Joshua expounded before Moses. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: When Joshua said, “Blessed is He who chooses the righteous,” the traditions of wisdom were taken from Moses and given to Joshua, and Moses did not know what Joshua was expounding. After Israel rose from the session, they said to Moses, “Explain the Torah to us.” He told them, “I do not know what to answer you.” Moses faltered and fell. At that moment he said: “Master of the worlds, until now I asked for life; now my soul is given to You.””
connections.context: The Tanchuma presents Moses’ proposal to live as Joshua’s student and the ensuing transfer of wisdom. This gives the narrative behind the reference here; Devarim Rabbah supplies the separate formulation about envy quoted next.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנִּסְתַּמּוּ מִמֶּנּוּ מַעְיְנוֹת הַחָכְמָה וְעָמַד לִפְנֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ,
connections.quote: ““I can no longer go out and come in.” Could it mean that his strength had failed? Scripture says, “His eye had not dimmed and his freshness had not departed.” What, then, does “I cannot” mean? I am not permitted: authority has been taken from me and given to Joshua. Another explanation: “To go out and come in” in words of Torah. This teaches that the traditions and wellsprings of wisdom were closed off from him.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the exact image of the closed wellsprings of wisdom. He distinguishes loss of authority or access to Torah wisdom from physical weakness.

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא אָמַר: מֵאָה מִיתוֹת וְלֹא קִנְאָה אַחַת
connections.quote: ““Call Joshua.” Moses said before Him: “Master of the world, let Joshua take my office, and let me remain alive.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: “Do for him as he does for you.” Moses immediately rose early and went to Joshua’s house. Joshua was afraid and said, “Moses, my teacher, come to me.” They went out to walk, and Moses walked at Joshua’s left. They entered the Tent of Meeting; the pillar of cloud descended and separated them. When the pillar of cloud withdrew, Moses went to Joshua and asked, “What did the divine utterance say to you?” Joshua replied: “When the divine utterance was revealed to you, did I know what it said to you?” At that moment Moses cried out: “A hundred deaths, but not one experience of envy!” Solomon explains it: “For love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as the grave”—the love Moses had for Joshua, and the envy Moses felt toward Joshua.”
connections.context: This is the Midrash’s full setting for “a hundred deaths, but not one envy.” Rav Tzadok takes its contrast between the transfer of leadership and the predecessor’s inner response as the starting point of his teaching.

connections.hePhrase: [אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה:) "בַּכֹּל מִתְקַנֵּא חוּץ וְכוּלֵי", זֶהוּ לְאַחַר מִיתָה כְּהָרְאָיָה דְּשָׁם],
connections.quote: “This differs from Rav Yosei bar Choni’s view, for Rav Yosei bar Choni said: A person can feel envy toward anyone except his own son and his student. The case of one’s son is learned from Solomon. As for one’s student, one may derive it from ‘Let a double portion of your spirit be upon me,’ or, alternatively, from ‘He laid his hands upon him and charged him.’”

connections.hePhrase: מִשּׁוּם דְּאַכַּתֵּי לָא עָבַר יַרְדְּנָא, כִּדְאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים (כב.) עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan was astonished: Is “The Lord will give you there an angry heart” not written concerning Babylonia? He answered: At that time…”

connections.hePhrase: מִשּׁוּם דְּאַכַּתֵּי לָא עָבַר יַרְדְּנָא, כִּדְאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים (כב.) עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “…we had not yet crossed the Jordan.”
connections.context: The exchange follows Ulla’s account of a fatal outburst of anger on his journey to the Land of Israel. The answer explains why the event could still be associated with the angry heart of exile: they had not yet crossed the Jordan.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמִּדַּבֵּק עַצְמוֹ בִּקְדוּשַׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הָאִידְנָא, שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שָׁם
connections.quote: “To annul the evil inclination, the merit of the Land of Israel was needed, as stated in Arakhin; that is why Moses did not annul it. In the Land of Israel, which is Israel’s root, the inclination of the angry heart does not have such great sway, for the angry heart is the very opposite of that root.”
connections.context: This parallel links the Land’s spiritual character with diminished dominion of anger. It helps explain why the ois makes attachment to the holiness of the Land relevant to overcoming envy.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמִּדַּבֵּק עַצְמוֹ בִּקְדוּשַׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הָאִידְנָא, שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שָׁם
connections.quote: “There is no member of Israel who does not have four cubits in the Land of Israel. Four cubits are the measure of the space belonging to a person wherever he is. This means that he recognizes that what belongs to him in this world is sanctified with the holiness of the Land. Its holiness comes from knowing that it is a land the blessed God gave to us and our ancestors, and that it did not come to us through our own power, the strength of our hand, or our efforts. This is the whole purpose of the Land’s holiness, as explained above. Every member of Israel has a portion in it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly explains the four cubits as a spiritual relation to one’s place and possessions: recognizing them as God’s gift. That explanation clarifies how the ois speaks of attachment to the Land even in the present.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמִּדַּבֵּק עַצְמוֹ בִּקְדוּשַׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הָאִידְנָא, שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שָׁם
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא בתרא מ״ד ב:ז׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““He never had land.” From here there is an answer to those who say that the practice of writing in authorizations, “I have given him four cubits in my courtyard,” even when the person has no land, rests on the claim that everyone has four cubits in the Land of Israel, since land cannot be acquired through robbery—or alternatively, that everyone has four cubits for his grave. For here it is evident that it is possible for a person to have no land.”
connections.context: Tosafot rejects the claim as a universal rule of actual landownership. The spiritual explanation in Dover Tzedek is therefore the relevant parallel for Rav Tzadok’s use of “four cubits” here; this passage should not be read as asserting a property right for every individual.

connections.hePhrase: [וְכֵן מְקוֹם רַגְלָיו בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, וְזֶהוּ "וְהִתְפַּלְלוּ אֵלֶיךָ דֶּרֶךְ אַרְצָם", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: “If one is standing outside the Land, one should direct one’s heart toward the Land of Israel, as it is said, “They shall pray to You toward their land.” If one is standing in the Land of Israel, one should direct one’s heart toward Jerusalem, as it is said, “They shall pray to the Lord toward the city You have chosen.” If one is standing in Jerusalem, one should direct one’s heart toward the Temple, as it is said, “They shall pray toward this house.” If one is standing in the Temple, one should direct one’s heart toward the Holy of Holies, as it is said, “They shall pray toward this place.” If one is standing in the Holy of Holies, one should direct one’s heart toward the place of the Ark-cover. If one is standing behind the place of the Ark-cover, one should view oneself as though standing before the Ark-cover. Thus, one standing in the east turns west; in the west, east; in the south, north; and in the north, south. All Israel therefore direct their hearts toward one place.”
connections.context: The baraita supplies both the verse about prayer toward the Land and the progression toward the Temple. Rav Tzadok relates that shared orientation to each person’s spiritual place in the Land and the Temple.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּגְלָה אֵלַי בַּחֲלוֹם (אוֹר לְיוֹם ב' רְאֵה כ"ה מְנַחֵם) פֵּירוּשׁ "לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “So that your days and the days of your children may be many on the land that the Lord swore to your ancestors to give them, like the days of the heavens above the earth.”
connections.context: The full verse joins the longevity of parents and children, life on the Land, and the enduring heavens. These are the three features Rav Tzadok brings together in the interpretation that follows.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (כח.) לְרַבִּי: יְהִי רָצוֹן שֶׁתַּגִּיעַ לַחֲצִי יָמַי, אֲבָל לְכוּלְּהוּ לָא, דְּהַבָּאִים אַחֲרֶיךָ בְּהֵמָה יִרְעוּ?
connections.quote: ‘As he took his leave, he said to him: ‘My teacher, bless me!’ He replied: ‘May it be His will that you reach half my years.’ ‘Not all of them?’ He answered: ‘Should those who come after you herd cattle?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכִי הַאי גַּוְונָא אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): אִלְמָלֵא אֲבוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁחָטְאוּ אָנוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בָּאנוּ לָעוֹלָם, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
connections.quote: “Do not say, “We would not have come into the world,” but rather, “as though we had not come into the world.””

connections.hePhrase: וְכִי הַאי גַּוְונָא אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): אִלְמָלֵא אֲבוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁחָטְאוּ אָנוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בָּאנוּ לָעוֹלָם, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
connections.heRef: רש"י על עבודה זרה ה׳ א:י״א:א׳
connections.quote: ““As though we had not come into the world”: because they would live forever, and as long as they existed, we would be considered insignificant.”
connections.context: The Gemara rejects the literal reading that later generations would never have been born. Its conclusion, explained by Rashi, is that the immortal earlier generation would overshadow its descendants. Rav Tzadok uses precisely the qualified wording “as though.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָאו דַּוְקָא רְצִיחָה מַמָּשׁ, אֶלָּא דּוּגְמָתוֹ: כְּגוֹן אַחְוָורֵי אַפֵּי שֶׁדִּמּוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא נח:) לִרְצִיחָה,
connections.quote: ‘A reciter taught before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Anyone who makes his fellow’s face pale in public [by humiliating him] is as though he sheds blood. He told him: You have spoken well, for we see the redness departing and pallor taking its place. Abaye said to Rav Dimi: What are they especially careful about in the West? He answered: Making a person’s face pale, for Rabbi Chanina said: Everyone descends to Gehinnom except three. Could you really mean everyone? Rather, say: All who descend to Gehinnom ascend again, except three who descend and do not ascend. These are: one who has relations with a married woman, one who humiliates his fellow in public, and one who gives his fellow an offensive nickname. Is giving an offensive nickname not the same as humiliating someone? This applies even when he is accustomed to that name.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן "הַנֵּחָמִים בָּאֵלִים" כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (נִדָּה יג.).
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Ami said: It is as though he sheds blood, as it is said: ‘Those who inflame themselves among the terebinths, beneath every leafy tree, who slaughter children in the wadis beneath the clefts of the rocks.’ Do not read shochatei, ‘those who slaughter,’ but sochatei, ‘those who squeeze out.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְלִפְעָמִים תְּפִלָּה מְכַפֶּרֶת מֶחֱצָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּקַיִן: "וַיֵּשֶׁב בְּאֶרֶץ נוֹד" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה י);
connections.quote: “Great is prayer before the Holy One, blessed be He. Rabbi Elazar said: Do you wish to know the power of prayer? If it does not accomplish the whole, it accomplishes half. Cain rose against his brother Abel and killed him, and the decree was issued: “You shall be restless and wandering in the land.” He immediately stood and confessed before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, “My iniquity is too great to bear.” He said before Him: “Master of the world, You bear the whole world, but You cannot bear my iniquity? You have written, ‘Bearing iniquity and passing over transgression’; forgive my iniquity, which is great.” He immediately found favor before the Holy One, blessed be He, and “restless,” half the decree, was withheld from him, as it is written, “He settled in the land of Nod.” From here you learn how great prayer is before the Holy One, blessed be He.”
connections.context: Unlike the formulation in Vayikra Rabbah quoted in the existing note, this parallel expressly introduces Cain’s confession as an illustration of the power of prayer to accomplish half. It directly illuminates the wording used here without changing the citation in Rav Tzadok’s text.

connections.hePhrase: וְלִפְעָמִים תְּפִלָּה מְכַפֶּרֶת מֶחֱצָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּקַיִן: "וַיֵּשֶׁב בְּאֶרֶץ נוֹד" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה י);
connections.displayRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 8:1
connections.canonicalRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 8:1
connections.quote: “But after Adam heard Cain tell him, “I repented and reached a compromise,” even though the Midrash says that Cain went out as one deceiving the divine mind, Adam said: “Such is the power of repentance”—that even verbal confession alone is effective, although the person has not yet abandoned the sin with the proper abandonment, to the point that the One who knows hidden things can testify about him, as explained above. This accords with the teaching in Taanit: “They enticed Him with their mouths and lied to Him with their tongues,” and so forth, and nevertheless, “He, being merciful, forgives iniquity.” “And I did not know!” Adam immediately stood and said, “A psalm, a song for the day of Shabbat”: there it says, “It is good to give thanks to the Lord,” without adding “and abandons,” as in “One who confesses and abandons will find mercy.” This is the power of Shabbat—that words alone can also be effective.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the benefit of an incomplete confession from the full abandonment of sin required for complete repentance. In this Shabbat teaching he reads Cain’s partial relief as evidence that the process can begin before its inner completion.

connections.hePhrase: וְלִפְעָמִים תְּפִלָּה מְכַפֶּרֶת מֶחֱצָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּקַיִן: "וַיֵּשֶׁב בְּאֶרֶץ נוֹד" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה י);
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehuda says: Repentance accomplishes half, and prayer accomplishes all. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: Repentance accomplishes all, and prayer accomplishes half. … According to Rabbi Yehuda, from whom do we learn that repentance accomplishes half? From Cain: a decree was issued against him, and when he repented half the decree was withheld. … “He dwelt in the land of Nod”: it does not say “restless and wandering,” but “in the land of Nod.””
connections.context: The Midrash distinguishes competing views about repentance and prayer. It expressly labels Cain’s response repentance and associates his confession to God with the mitigation of his sentence. Rav Tzadok draws on that episode when discussing the effect of prayer; the source does not itself phrase the Cain example as “prayer accomplishes half.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי "חֵן מָקוֹם עַל יוֹשְׁבָיו",
connections.quote: ‘‘The men of the city said to Elisha: Behold, the city’s situation is good, as my master sees,’ and so forth. But since the water was bad and the land caused miscarriage, what was good about it? Rabbi Chanin said: A place finds favor with its inhabitants. Rabbi Yochanan said: There are three kinds of favor: a place finds favor with its inhabitants, a wife finds favor with her husband, and a purchase finds favor with its buyer.’

connections.hePhrase: [הֲגַם שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּמְגִילָּה (ו:): "לֹא יָגַעְתָּ וּמָצָאתָ – אַל תַּאֲמֵן",
connections.quote: “If someone says to you, “I labored and did not find,” do not believe him; “I did not labor and found,” do not believe him; “I labored and found,” believe him.”
connections.context: The Gemara applies this maxim to sharpening one’s understanding of Torah, and then distinguishes preserving one’s learning, which requires help from Heaven. Rav Tzadok starts from the requirement of effort before examining what “finding” adds beyond the effort itself.

connections.hePhrase: הָא אַסְקֵיהּ שָׁם: הָנֵי מִילֵּי וְכוּלֵי, אֲבָל לְאוֹקְמֵי גִּירְסָא – סִיַּעְתָּא מִן שְׁמַיָּא;
connections.quote: “These words apply to Torah, but in business success is help from Heaven. Even concerning Torah, we said this only about sharpening one’s understanding; preserving one’s learning, however, depends on help from Heaven.”
connections.context: This is the qualification following the maxim quoted in the earlier note. Rav Tzadok focuses on its distinction between sharpening understanding through effort and maintaining one’s learning through divine assistance.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן "וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי ה'",
connections.quote: ‘But Noah found favor in the eyes of Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן "וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי ה'",
connections.quote: “Even Noah, who remained of them, was not worthy, but found favor in the eyes of the Lord, as it is said, “Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.””
connections.context: This neighboring interpretation distinguishes favor from earned worthiness. It explains the preceding point about finding grace; the other note gives the different wording about who does the finding.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן "וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי ה'",
connections.quote: “The meaning of the expression ‘you found’ is well known: a find comes unexpectedly (Sanhedrin 97a). The attainment afterward comes as a find, for a person attains something toward which he had not directed his labor at all. Before the attainment, he could not have labored toward an attainment of that kind. Rather, when someone labors in words of Torah, Hashem bestows and gives him wisdom to attain even what is above his own wisdom and comprehension. As the Gemara teaches (Bava Batra 12a): know that this is so, for a great scholar states a teaching, and it is found that a tradition given to Moshe at Sinai accords with him.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains why attainment after labor is still called a find: before attaining the insight, a person could not have aimed his effort at that unknown insight itself. This clarifies the siman's distinction between working and sitting in expectation of a windfall. The effort prepares a recipient; the particular disclosure remains a gift beyond what the recipient could previously describe or demand.
connections.headline: The find exceeds what effort could specify

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כט): הוּא מָצָא, אֲבָל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא מָצָא;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Simon said: The Holy One, blessed be He, found three things: Abraham, David, and Israel. … The colleagues objected: But it is written, “Noah found favor”! He said to them: Noah found; the Holy One, blessed be He, did not find.”
connections.context: The Midrash contrasts verses in which God is the one who “finds” with the wording in which Noah finds favor in God’s eyes. This is the exact distinction Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ כִּי פְּעָמִים אָדָם זוֹכֶה בְּלֹא שׁוּם יְגִיעָה שֶׁהוּא שָׁמוּר מִן הָעֲבֵירָה וְנִקְרָא צַדִּיק, וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת נֹחַ
connections.displayRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Noach, Torah Ohr 20
connections.linkedRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Noach, Torah Ohr 20
connections.canonicalRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Noach, Torah Ohr 20
connections.heRef: שני לוחות הברית, תורה שבכתב, נח, תורה אור כ׳
connections.quote: ““Noah found favor”: he found, but the Holy One, blessed be He, did not find. This means that Noah found from the Holy One, blessed be He, who was awakening him. But the Holy One, blessed be He, did not find this from Noah, for Noah had no awakening from below to above. This differs from Abraham, who said, “Before whom I walked”—meaning, my awakening preceded His. Likewise it is written, “You found his heart faithful before You.””
connections.context: Shelah explains the Midrash’s distinction in terms of who initiates the awakening. This illuminates Rav Tzadok’s description of Noah being protected through an unearned awakening from above.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁבָּזֶה מְיוּחָס גַּם כֵּן הַמְּצִיאָה לְמַעְלָה, כִּי יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁעֵגֶל וְכוּלֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ע"ט.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Akiva instructed Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in five matters when he was confined in prison. Rabbi Shimon said to him, “My teacher, teach me Torah.” He replied, “I will not teach you.” Rabbi Shimon said, “If you do not teach me, I will tell my father Yochai and have you handed over to the authorities.” Rabbi Akiva said: “My son, more than the calf wants to suckle, the cow wants to nurse.” Rabbi Shimon replied: “And who is in danger? Surely the calf is in danger.””
connections.context: The comparison originally expresses the teacher’s desire to teach, even while danger obstructs the lesson. Rav Tzadok applies that relation to God’s desire to impart His light and Israel’s desire to receive it.

connections.hePhrase: וּמְצִיאָה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין צז.) שֶׁאֵינָהּ בָּאָה אֶלָּא בְּהֶסַּח הַדַּעַת;
connections.quote: “Thus it is taught in Megillah 6b: “If one says, ‘I did not labor and I found,’ do not believe him.” Labor must come first, yet afterward it is still called “I found,” and a found object comes when one’s attention is diverted (Sanhedrin 97a). For Torah truly lies beyond human comprehension, and all a person’s toil and effort, which extend only as far as his own understanding, do not reach such a great attainment as the words of Torah, which are the wisdom of the blessed Lord. When he afterward attains it, he recognizes that it is a find that came when his attention was diverted, and that he did not reach it through his effort. Nevertheless, effort is also necessary: opening an opening the size of a needle’s point through an awakening from below. For the blessed Lord entrusts words of Torah only to those who long for them; of this it is said, “He gives wisdom to the wise.””

connections.hePhrase: וּמְצִיאָה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין צז.) שֶׁאֵינָהּ בָּאָה אֶלָּא בְּהֶסַּח הַדַּעַת;
connections.quote: ‘This is like Rabbi Zeira: when he found the Rabbis occupied with the matter, he would say to them: ‘Please, I ask you, do not delay him, for we have learned: Three things come when one is not thinking of them: the Messiah, a find, and a scorpion.’’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִי שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וּמְצַפֶּה לְכָךְ, לֹא יִמְצָא לְעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “The explanation is that things belonging to the order by which the world is governed arrive in an orderly way and with thought directed toward them, because they are close to the world. But things far from the world involve a diversion of attention: they are far from the world’s order, and therefore arrive only when attention is diverted. … The first is a find, which comes into one’s hand only by chance. This differs from a person’s other livelihood and sustenance, which follow the world’s order. A find does not follow that order; it happens by chance, and it is for good.”
connections.context: Maharal distinguishes an unexpected find from the ordinary course of earning a livelihood. This explains why “finding,” as used in the ois, cannot be produced simply by sitting and anticipating it.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מָצִינוּ בְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא יב:) שׂוֹכֵר פּוֹעֵל לִלְקוֹט מְצִיאוֹת,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Pappa said: The case is that he hired him to gather found objects. What sort of case is this? One in which floodwaters have left a marsh full of fish.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ יְהֵיב אַרְבַּע זוּזֵי לְסַפְּוָונָאֵי בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וְרַב גַּמְדָּא בִּנְדָרִים דַּף נ':
connections.quote: “And from a chest: once Rabbi Akiva gave four zuz to sailors and said to them, “Bring me something.” They found only a chest on the seashore and brought it to him. They said, “Let our master wait with this.” It turned out to be full of dinars. A ship had once sunk, and all its business funds had been placed in that chest; it was found on this occasion.”
connections.context: This is Rabbi Akiva’s episode, distinct from Rav Gamda’s monkey-and-pearls episode already quoted. The small payment prepared the way for the discovery, while the valuable contents remained unexpected. Rashi and Ran explain the Aramaic guvza here as a chest.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ יְהֵיב אַרְבַּע זוּזֵי לְסַפְּוָונָאֵי בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וְרַב גַּמְדָּא בִּנְדָרִים דַּף נ':
connections.quote: ‘Rav Gamda gave four zuz to sailors to bring him something with the money. They found nothing and brought him a monkey with it. The monkey slipped away and entered a crevice. They dug after it and found it lying on pearls, and they brought him all of them.’

connections.hePhrase: [פד] פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ "נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, כג), הַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, טו) – עַל יְדֵי צִדְקוּתוֹ,
connections.quote: “Much food is in the tilled field of the poor, yet there is what is swept away without justice.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reads the words nisppeh belo mishpat, “swept away without justice,” as a statement about a person’s fate and connects them with the righteous person who perishes in Ecclesiastes 7:15. The agricultural setting of the proverb and Rav Tzadok’s application are distinct.

connections.hePhrase: [פד] פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ "נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, כג), הַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, טו) – עַל יְדֵי צִדְקוּתוֹ,
connections.quote: ““Much food.” Much food comes into the world through the plowing of the poor, who plow a field of grain, yet the wealthy, who did not labor at it, eat it. Likewise, there is someone who is gathered away from the world without a sentence of death, for he did nothing for which he should be put to death, but is caught up in another’s sin.”
connections.context: Metzudat David reads the verse’s two parts as cases in which a person’s outcome does not correspond to his own visible labor or deed. Rav Tzadok’s discussion asks how such an appearance relates to the divine judgment concealed beneath it.

connections.hePhrase: [פד] פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ "נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, כג), הַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, טו) – עַל יְדֵי צִדְקוּתוֹ,
connections.quote: ‘In my fleeting days I have seen it all: a righteous person perishes in his righteousness, and a wicked person’s life is prolonged in his wickedness.’

connections.hePhrase: [פד] פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ "נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, כג), הַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, טו) – עַל יְדֵי צִדְקוּתוֹ,
connections.quote: ““All of this.” The word “there is” refers to something found on rare occasions. The meaning of “perishes through his righteousness” is that his righteousness brings about his loss, as with someone who fasts constantly. “Prolongs” means that he prolongs his days through his wickedness, eating, drinking, rejoicing, and providing pleasures for the body.”
connections.context: Ibn Ezra explicitly reads the phrase as “through his righteousness” and illustrates it with excessive fasting. Rav Tzadok applies that grammatical reading to another case: righteousness that becomes the occasion for another person’s envy.

connections.hePhrase: [פד] פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ "נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, כג), הַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "יֵשׁ צַדִּיק אֹבֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, טו) – עַל יְדֵי צִדְקוּתוֹ,
connections.quote: “For Mordechai himself, this was a repair for his participation in the feast. Presumably he had also been among those who bowed to the image, for he had already been exiled with Yechonyah (Esther 2:6) and was one of the Men of the Great Assembly; the Rambam writes that they were all included apart from Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah. When a Torah scholar has sinned, do not suspect him afterward, for he has certainly repented (Berakhot 19a). Yet repentance requires that the matter be occasioned for him and that he emerge from it without failure (Yoma 86b). Mordechai was presented with the matter of Haman and recognized that Hashem had placed it before him to repair the sin of the feast. He therefore devoted himself to it and repaired himself, becoming the one prepared for this redemption. Nevertheless, he brought some difficulty upon others: that act occasioned the decree, because it aroused prosecution against Israel. This resembles the widow's words to Eliyahu, ‘Have you come to remind me of my sin and cause my son's death?’ (I Kings 17:18) When one person is exceptionally righteous, the contrast can arouse prosecution against those with him who are not at that level.”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim develops the difficult distinction through Mordechai: an encounter could provide the occasion of his own repentance while also occasioning prosecution against others. This gives a concrete explanation of why the siman can describe a consequence as apparently unjust without denying hidden judgment. The originating siman's conclusion remains essential: motives can be hidden even from their owner, and its stated response is prayer for mercy.
connections.headline: A personal repair and its comparative effect

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ עָשָׂה אוֹתוֹ חָסִיד בְּתַעֲנִית (כד.) שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ עַל בִּתּוֹ שֶׁתָּשׁוּב לַעֲפָרָהּ שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשְׁלוּ בָּהּ בְּנֵי אָדָם;
connections.quote: ‘What was the incident involving his daughter? He had a beautiful daughter. One day he saw a man breaking an opening in a fence of branches and looking at her. He asked him: ‘What is this?’ The man replied: ‘My teacher, if I was not privileged to marry her, may I not at least be privileged to see her?’ He said to his daughter: ‘My daughter, you are causing people distress. Return to your dust, so that people will not stumble because of you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ בִּקְשָׁה אוֹתָהּ בְּתוּלָה דְּסוֹטָה (כב.) שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשְׁלוּ בָּהּ בְּנֵי אָדָם,
connections.quote: ‘Is that so? Did Rabbi Yochanan not say: ‘We learned fear of sin from a maiden, and the earning of reward from a widow’? Fear of sin from a maiden: Rabbi Yochanan heard a maiden who had fallen on her face and was saying: ‘Master of the universe, You created Gan Eden and You created Gehinnom; You created righteous people and You created wicked people. May it be Your will that people should not stumble into sin through me.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קמט:): כָּל שֶׁחֲבֵירוֹ נֶעֱנָשׁ עַל יָדוֹ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yaakov, the son of Yaakov’s daughter, also said: Anyone on whose account another person is punished is not admitted into the presence of the Holy One, blessed be He. From where is this learned? Could it be from what is written: ‘Hashem said: Who will entice Ahab, so that he goes up and falls at Ramot Gilead? One said this, and another said that. Then the spirit came forward, stood before Hashem, and said: I will entice him,’ and so on; ‘He said: I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets. He said: You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go out and do so’?”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ד הֲלָכָה ב, וְשָׁם הַגִּרְסָא: קִנְאָתֵינוּ עַל לֵב אָדָם, עַיֵּין שָׁם): "וְלֹא תַעֲלֶה קִנְאַת אָדָם עָלַי",
connections.quote: “May it be Your will … that hatred of us not arise in anyone’s heart, nor hatred of anyone arise in our hearts; that jealousy of us not arise in anyone’s heart, nor jealousy of anyone arise in our hearts. May Your Torah be our occupation all the days of our lives, and may our words be supplications before You.”
connections.context: This is Rabbi Elazar’s prayer after the Amidah. It asks to be spared both others’ jealousy and jealousy within oneself, matching the textual reading that Rav Tzadok explicitly notes.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"הַנִּסְתָּרֹת לַה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ", אֲבָל בַּנִּגְלוֹת הוּא שֶׁלֹּא בְּמִשְׁפָּט.
connections.quote: ‘The hidden things belong to Hashem our God; the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever, to carry out all the words of this Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי יֵשׁ נִסְתָּרוֹת שֶׁנִּסְתָּר גַּם לָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יוֹדֵעַ,
connections.quote: “Human thought also has several levels. There is a depth at the beginning of thought, from which all thoughts are drawn, that is closed off and hidden from the person. This is the concealed thought.”
connections.context: This parallel distinguishes the thought a person can observe from a deeper source that remains hidden even from that person. It directly explains the ois’s statement that some concealed matters escape one’s own awareness.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלַּת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנֶה כְּשֶׁנִּכְנַס לַתּוֹרָה, דְּשָׁם הוּא בְּיוֹתֵר כַּנּוֹדָע, דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם תִּיקּוּן הֶבֶל וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְקַן, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah would offer a short prayer on entering the study house and on leaving it. They asked him: “What occasion is there for this prayer?” He told them: “On entering I pray that no mishap occur through me; on leaving I give thanks for my portion.” The Sages taught: What does he say on entering? “May it be Your will, Lord my God, that no mishap occur through me; that I not stumble in a matter of law and have my colleagues rejoice over me; that I not call the impure pure or the pure impure; and that my colleagues not stumble in a matter of law and have me rejoice over them.””
connections.context: This is the prayer cited in the closing bracket. Following Rashi’s explanation, the request includes protection from the mutual harm of error and rejoicing at another scholar’s failure.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלַּת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנֶה כְּשֶׁנִּכְנַס לַתּוֹרָה, דְּשָׁם הוּא בְּיוֹתֵר כַּנּוֹדָע, דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם תִּיקּוּן הֶבֶל וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְקַן, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: ““And that I not stumble”—and have my colleagues rejoice over my failure. There would then be two evils occurring through me, because I would cause them to be punished.”
connections.context: Rashi explains why the prayer concerns more than the learner’s own mistake: another person’s pleasure in that mistake creates a second harm. This is the specific connection between the study-house prayer and the subject of this ois.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלַּת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנֶה כְּשֶׁנִּכְנַס לַתּוֹרָה, דְּשָׁם הוּא בְּיוֹתֵר כַּנּוֹדָע, דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם תִּיקּוּן הֶבֶל וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְקַן, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: ““She again bore his brother Abel.” … Here the reincarnation of the righteous is hinted at. The Holy One, blessed be He, showed him the course of his reincarnation in every generation: how it passed from one righteous person to another, up to six hundred thousand, until it reached the one of whom it is said, “In that he too is flesh.” “In that he too” refers to Abel; and the early sages explained that “in that he too” refers to Moses.”
connections.context: In its exposition of Abel’s birth, Tikkunei Zohar connects Abel with Moses through the verse containing beshagam. This supplies the kabbalistic identification presupposed by the phrase “Moses is the rectification of Abel”; its application to the repair of envy is developed here by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: [פה] כְּשֶׁאָדָם חוֹשֵׁב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה הַרְבֵּה בַּעֲבוֹדַת ה', יֵדַע שֶׁלֹּא נָגַע בָּהּ כְּלוּם,
connections.quote: “Jacob our father merited Torah through his smallness in his own eyes, as it says, ‘I am diminished by all the kindnesses …,’ and, ‘Jacob, for he is small.’ Words of Torah leave a high place and go to a low place. A sign of arrogance is poverty in Torah; and they said, ‘Words of Torah endure only in someone who makes himself like one who does not exist.’”
connections.explanation: The Chanukah passage uses the same saying about arrogance and poverty in Torah, but supplies its positive counterpart in Yaakov’s smallness in his own eyes. Humility makes the person a place where Torah can settle and endure. This helps explain why the present siman examines even unspoken pride: the obstacle is an inward sense of having already achieved enough, which prevents the honest recognition of bias and dependence described at the siman’s conclusion.
connections.headline: Humility makes room for Torah to remain with a person

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מט:): סִימָן לְגַסּוּת הָרוּחַ – עֲנִיּוּת דְּתוֹרָה;
connections.quote: ‘Is that so? Did the Master not say that a sign of arrogance is poverty? And poverty is found in Babylonia! What is meant by poverty? Poverty in Torah, as it is written: ‘We have a little sister, and she has no breasts.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: This is Elam, which merited learning but did not merit teaching.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "אִסְטִירָא בִּלְגִינָא קִישׁ קִישׁ קָרְיָא", מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כִּיס מָלֵא.
connections.quote: “Rav Chama said: What is meant by the verse, “Wisdom rests in the heart of one who understands, but among fools it makes itself known”? “Wisdom rests in the heart of one who understands” refers to a Torah scholar who is the son of a Torah scholar. “Among fools it makes itself known” refers to a Torah scholar who is the son of an unlearned man. Ulla said: This is what people say, “A coin in a jug cries, ‘Clink, clink.’””
connections.context: The Gemara applies the proverb to the conspicuous display of learning. Rav Tzadok extends the image to self-satisfaction about one’s spiritual achievements.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "אִסְטִירָא בִּלְגִינָא קִישׁ קִישׁ קָרְיָא", מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כִּיס מָלֵא.
connections.heRef: רש"י על בבא מציעא פ״ה ב:ב׳:ג׳-ד׳
connections.quote: ““A coin in a jug”—a single sela in a jug. “It cries, ‘Clink, clink’”—it rattles and makes a sound. If it were full of sela-coins, it would not make a sound.”
connections.context: Rashi gives the precise contrast assumed here: the lone coin rattles, while the full container is quiet. Rav Tzadok uses that contrast to test whether perceived spiritual abundance is real.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קצג עַמּוּד ב): סִימָן דְּלָא יָדַע כְּלוּם – שְׁבוּחֵי;
connections.quote: ‘Rather, in the book of King Solomon’s wisdom it says this: There are three signs. The sign of transgression is pallor. The sign of foolishness is much talk. The sign of knowing nothing is self-praise. This last one outweighs the others: he is a fool (suspect of every transgression); all these are in him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָאו דַּוְקָא שְׁבוּחֵי וְגַסּוּת בִּפְנֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת, רַק גַּם בֵּינוֹ לְבֵין עַצְמוֹ וּבְלִבּוֹ בִּלְבַד
connections.quote: “A person is also corrupted by the thought of pride even without exercising domination, as it is said: “Every haughty heart is an abomination to the Lord.””
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah distinguishes inward pride from the outward act of lording over other people. The harm therefore does not depend on public boasting, exactly as Rav Tzadok states here.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי עִיקַּר הַגַּאֲוָה בְּלִבּוֹ לְבַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "גְּבַהּ לֵב"] כְּשֶׁסָּבוּר כֵּן.
connections.quote: ‘Everyone whose heart is proud is an abomination to Hashem; hand to hand, he will not go unpunished.’

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיִן הִקְרִיב דָּבָר גָּרוּעַ וְחָשַׁב שֶׁעָשָׂה עֲבוֹדָה גְּדוֹלָה, שֶׁלְּכָךְ חָרָה לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַבֵּל.
connections.quote: ““Cain brought from the fruit of the ground”—what does this mean? From the leftovers of his food. The Rabbis say that it was flaxseed. “Abel also brought from the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions.””
connections.context: The Midrash contrasts Cain’s offering with Abel’s choice offering and records the alternative identification as flaxseed. Rav Tzadok asks how Cain could nevertheless regard his own offering as a great act of service.

connections.hePhrase: וְטָעוּת זֶה נִמְשָׁךְ מִצַּד שֶׁשּׁוֹכֵחַ עִנְיַן הַיֵּצֶר וְכֹחוֹ, וְחוֹשֵׁב שֶׁכָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹת לִבּוֹ רַק טוֹב וְאֵין לוֹ נְטִיָּה לְרָע;
connections.quote: “This is like what we explained concerning the teaching in Berakhot that the evil inclination resembles a fly and sits between the two openings of the heart. Sometimes the evil inclination turns toward “the heart of the wise at his right” and conceals itself as a teacher guiding the person for his benefit. The person then commits a transgression while imagining that he is performing a mitzvah.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the specific deception described here: a person can mistake an impulse of the inclination for a wholly good intention. It supplies the reason for examining the inner motives of an apparently good deed.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הוֹדִיעוֹ אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעִנְיַן הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע: "כִּי לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘If you do well, will there not be acceptance? But if you do not do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you can rule over it.’

connections.hePhrase: [פו] כָּל מַה שֶּׁהוּא מִקִּנְיַן הָאָדָם: אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו, עַבְדּוֹ וַאֲמָתוֹ, שׁוֹרוֹ וַחֲמוֹרוֹ, אָהֳלוֹ וְכַסְפּוֹ וּזְהָבוֹ וְכָל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ – הַכֹּל הוּא מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ,
connections.quote: “A person has these four parts: the first is the body, the second the soul, the third the intellect, and the fourth a person’s property. Although property is not the person himself, we have explained that property too enters into the definition of the person, because property is his livelihood; there are people whose property is dearer to them than their body. We have explained this several times.”

connections.hePhrase: [פו] כָּל מַה שֶּׁהוּא מִקִּנְיַן הָאָדָם: אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו, עַבְדּוֹ וַאֲמָתוֹ, שׁוֹרוֹ וַחֲמוֹרוֹ, אָהֳלוֹ וְכַסְפּוֹ וּזְהָבוֹ וְכָל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ – הַכֹּל הוּא מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 3
connections.quote: “‘God said, Let us make man.’ At first Hashem created all the creatures. Then the creatures understood and recognized their lack: they had no one to connect their life to Hashem. Through the human being all the things of this world are connected to Hashem, for he elevates everything. The inanimate gives its power to the growing, the growing to the living, and the living to the speaking human. When the human being serves Hashem with that strength, he elevates all the powers he received from this world, even the power of the inanimate. When the creatures perceived their lack, their collective power aroused the awakening above for the creation of humanity. ‘God said, Let us make man’ means that Hashem told all the creatures to contribute their powers and join in humanity's creation, so that the human being would have a share in all of them. When he needs something they can all assist him, since his harm also harms them, as in the generation of the Flood, and his good also benefits them.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach gives the mechanism behind the shared life described here: the human being receives powers from the inanimate, growing, and animal worlds, and through service returns them to Hashem. Its conclusion that the creatures share in the human being's good and harm makes the relation reciprocal. This helps explain why the siman treats one's associated creatures as an occasion for examining one's own service rather than as spiritually detached possessions.
connections.headline: A share in the creatures and their return to the source

connections.hePhrase: כִּי גַּם כָּל הַדּוֹמֵם, צוֹמֵחַ, חַי מְשׁוֹרָשִׁים בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ חַיּוּתָם מִמֶּנּוּ כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Every creature has particular letters through which it was created, and they are the root of its vitality and continued existence. The human being, who is called a “small world” because he includes the whole creation and the entire world, has all twenty-two letters. Therefore it is said of him, “In Our image, according to Our likeness.” The whole Book of Formation explains this: how everything—the world and the human being—was created through the twenty-two letters.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the shared root through the letters of creation: an individual creature embodies particular letters, while the human being includes the full alphabet.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי גַּם כָּל הַדּוֹמֵם, צוֹמֵחַ, חַי מְשׁוֹרָשִׁים בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ חַיּוּתָם מִמֶּנּוּ כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “It is known that the lower creatures have four divisions, one above another: the inanimate, the growing, the living, and the speaking. The inanimate are mountains and hills; this division has no soul at all, neither a vegetative soul nor a soul of movement, and certainly no intellectual soul. Above it is the growing: it has an advantage over the inanimate because it has a vegetative soul. Above the growing are the other living creatures, which have a soul of movement and a vegetative soul. Above the living creatures that do not speak is the human being, who includes them all through his vegetative soul and his soul of movement, and has an advantage over them all through his intellectual soul.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya defines the four traditional categories and explains how the human being includes the powers of the preceding levels. The next sentence traces their order in the creation account.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי גַּם כָּל הַדּוֹמֵם, צוֹמֵחַ, חַי מְשׁוֹרָשִׁים בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ חַיּוּתָם מִמֶּנּוּ כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “The nature of the human being has now been thoroughly explained: he includes all the worlds, both in their general structure and in their particulars. This is unlike all the other upper and lower creatures, for whatever is produced in any one world includes only the world in which it was created.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital gives the wider account of the human being as including the worlds. This addresses the ois’s statement that the other creatures are rooted in the human soul.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁקָּנוּי לוֹ הוּא שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ חַיּוּתָם מִמֶּנּוּ,
connections.quote: “According to the distance that his light and vitality extend into them, so are their character and their relation to him. Some are his possessions; some were in his hands for a time and he sold them; some were only borrowed or rented for a short time; some he saw with other people or looked at while passing through a place; some he never saw in his life but desired in his thoughts. There are countless such degrees. One who understands the matter can know and reflect upon how to repair all these. Their repair comes only by returning them to the source: to know that everything comes from the very vitality of the blessed God, who gives it life and sustains it; without this, it would be as though it did not exist.”
connections.context: The later ois distinguishes degrees of connection to objects and gives their common repair. It makes the present account of ownership part of a broader relationship to the source of life.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי וַדַּאי גַּם כֵּן שַׁיָּיךְ לָאָדָם, וּלְעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר: "וְגָר זְאֵב עִם כֶּבֶשׂ",
connections.quote: ‘A wolf shall dwell with a lamb, and a leopard shall lie down with a kid; a calf, a young lion, and a fattened beast shall be together, and a little child shall lead them.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי וַדַּאי גַּם כֵּן שַׁיָּיךְ לָאָדָם, וּלְעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר: "וְגָר זְאֵב עִם כֶּבֶשׂ",
connections.displayRef: Guide for the Perplexed III:11, Ibn Tibbon translation
connections.quote: “If there were wisdom whose relation to the human form was like that of the power of sight to the eye, all a person’s injuries to himself and to others would cease. Through knowledge of the truth, hatred and strife depart, and the harm people do to one another is abolished. This has already been promised: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,” “The cow and the bear,” and “The nursing child shall play.” It then gives the cause: the removal of hatred, quarrels, and domination will result from people’s knowledge at that time of the truth of God. It says: “They shall neither harm nor destroy throughout My holy mountain, for the earth shall be filled with knowledge of Hashem as the waters cover the sea.” Know this.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא שַׁמָּשׁ לָאָדָם (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין נט:).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says: What a pity for a great servant lost to the world! Had the serpent not been cursed, each person of Israel would have had two good serpents: one sent north and one south to bring precious stones and pearls. Moreover, a strap could have been fastened beneath its tail and it could bring earth for one’s garden and ruin.”
connections.context: The baraita imagines the serpent’s service had it not been cursed. This supplies Rav Tzadok’s comparison between the human being’s state and the creatures that serve him.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהוּא הָאָדָם, כָּךְ קִנְיָנָיו,
connections.quote: ““With all your resources,” however, is not within the power of human service alone, but comes through assistance from Heaven. Its meaning is that love of the blessed God should be established in all one’s property and possessions. It does not refer to one’s desire and longing for property, which is already included in “with all your heart,” but to the property itself. As is known, property belongs to the person; the person becomes so completely filled with love of the blessed God in all his depths that his possessions, which are his extension, are themselves filled with His love. This is like Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair’s donkey, which was stringent with itself about eating forbidden food. This concerns living creatures, and presumably the same applies to inanimate things, as in “A stone will cry out from the wall” in the future, when someone wishes to commit a transgression, as our Sages taught. This is the meaning of one’s utensils resting on Shabbat: then one is wholly for Hashem, including all one’s possessions. Similarly, our father Yaakov’s flocks numbered six hundred thousand, according to our Sages; the correspondence in number shows that they embodied the six hundred thousand souls of Israel. Certainly love of the blessed God was established in them too. The Zohar says that Yaakov’s intention with the rods concerned tefillin: the binding and attachment of his whole soul to the blessed God. Yaakov’s quality corresponds to “with all your resources”: binding his whole being and soul so completely that the possessions belonging to him are also included in this bond. Therefore this is not stated in “If you will indeed listen,” which addresses the many, for this level belongs only to individuals who merit it. The many cannot attain this level until the future, when He pours out His spirit upon all flesh.”
connections.context: This parallel describes holiness extending into possessions and preserves Rav Tzadok’s express limitation: in the present, this degree belongs to individuals who merit it; its general realization belongs to the future.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֻלִּין ז.): בְּהֶמְתָּן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא תַּקָּלָה עַל יָדָם – מֵחֲמוֹרוֹ דְּרַבִּי פִּינְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר;
connections.quote: “If the Holy One, blessed be He, does not bring a mishap through the animals of the righteous, all the more so through the righteous themselves.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֻלִּין ז.): בְּהֶמְתָּן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא תַּקָּלָה עַל יָדָם – מֵחֲמוֹרוֹ דְּרַבִּי פִּינְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר;
connections.quote: “He arrived at an inn. They set barley before his donkey, but it did not eat.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֻלִּין ז.): בְּהֶמְתָּן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא תַּקָּלָה עַל יָדָם – מֵחֲמוֹרוֹ דְּרַבִּי פִּינְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר;
connections.quote: “They beat it out; it did not eat. They picked it over; it did not eat. He said to them: “Perhaps it has not been tithed?” They tithed it, and it ate. He said: “This poor creature is going to do its Creator’s will, and you feed it untithed produce!””
connections.context: The maxim and the story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair’s donkey appear in the same discussion. The donkey’s refusal of untithed food is the specific illustration Rav Tzadok names.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּנֹחַ, כָּל הַמִּינִים שֶׁהָיוּ בַּתֵּבָה שֶׁהוּא זָנָם מִסְּתָמָא הָיוּ מִשָּׁרְשׁוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, לְכָךְ אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁלֹּא קִלְקְלוּ דַּרְכָּם.
connections.quote: ““From every clean animal take seven pairs for yourself, a man and his wife.” Do animals have marriage? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonatan’s name: From those with which no transgression had been committed. How did he know? Rav Chisda said: He passed them before the ark. Whatever the ark admitted was known to have had no transgression committed with it; whatever the ark did not admit was known to have had a transgression committed with it. Rabbi Abbahu said: From those that came by themselves.”
connections.context: The Gemara is the source for the qualification concerning the animals that entered the ark. Both explanations of how Noach identified them are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר "אֵשֶׁת חָבֵר כְּחָבֵר", וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: נִשֵּׂאת לְעַם הָאָרֶץ וְהָיְתָה וְכוּלֵי (בְּכוֹרוֹת ל סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: “The wife of a chaver is like a chaver. … The wife of a chaver who marries an am haaretz need not accept the practices of chaver status anew.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר "אֵשֶׁת חָבֵר כְּחָבֵר", וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: נִשֵּׂאת לְעַם הָאָרֶץ וְהָיְתָה וְכוּלֵי (בְּכוֹרוֹת ל סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Meir says: They too must accept them anew. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said in Rabbi Meir’s name: A woman married a chaver and tied his tefillin on his arm; afterward she married a tax collector and tied his tax seals on his arm.”
connections.context: The baraita first states the household’s assumed chaver status, then records a disagreement about retaining it after remarriage. Rav Tzadok invokes Rabbi Meir’s illustrative story for a spouse’s influence; the story should not be presented as an undisputed legal rule.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר הַבָּנִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ן עַל פָּסוּק "שֹׁרֶשׁ פֹּרֶה",
connections.quote: see note 716.
connections.context: The metaphor concerns the parent as root and descendants as its growth. Ramban acknowledges the apparent counterexample of a righteous parent’s violent son and says that its resolution involves a secret he does not explain. Rav Tzadok cites this interpretation for the influence of the parent upon the children.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ב דְּעֵדֻיּוֹת): הָאָב זוֹכֶה לַבֵּן.
connections.quote: ‘He used to say: A father benefits his son in beauty, strength, wealth, wisdom, and length of life, and in the count of generations before Him, which determines the appointed end. As it says: ‘He calls the generations from the beginning’ (Isaiah 41). Although it says, ‘They will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years’ (Genesis 15), it also says: ‘The fourth generation will return here’ (ibid.).’

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶהוּ "פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת וְגוֹמֵר", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין כז:) כְּשֶׁאוֹחֲזִין מַעֲשֵׂה וְכוּלֵי, וְהוּא עֲוֹן אָבוֹת מַמָּשׁ וְאֵינוֹ חוּץ מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין]
connections.quote: ‘Are children not punished for their fathers’ iniquity? But it is written: ‘Visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children’! That applies when they hold on to their fathers’ deeds.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאִדְרָא רַבָּא (קמב עַמּוּד ב): "סוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו", וְעַד דְּלָא אַסְכִּימוּ לָא נָחֲתִין דִּינִין לְעָלְמָא.
connections.quote: “It was taught: When severe judgments are aroused to descend upon the world, here it is written, “The secret of the Lord is for those who fear Him.””
connections.context: This is the wording present at Zohar III 142b. The further clause “until they assent, judgments do not descend” is Rav Tzadok’s explanation here, not wording found in this text of the Idra. The available text does not settle whether Rav Tzadok used another reading or supplied an interpretive expansion.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאִדְרָא רַבָּא (קמב עַמּוּד ב): "סוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו", וְעַד דְּלָא אַסְכִּימוּ לָא נָחֲתִין דִּינִין לְעָלְמָא.
connections.heRef: עבודת ישראל, ספר בראשית, נח ו׳
connections.quote: ““Noach entered because of the waters of the Flood.” Rashi explains: Noach too was of little faith; he believed and did not believe that the Flood would come, and did not enter until the water forced him. This is puzzling: could the righteous Noach, Heaven forbid, have lacked faith in his blessed Creator? We also know that he labored on the ark for one hundred and twenty years before the Flood and rebuked and warned his generation. Could he himself have been of little faith? The Sages’ words can be explained: it is the way of the righteous to sweeten judgments and seek the blessed God’s merciful favor toward His creatures. Even when it appears that the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees a decree, the righteous person increases prayer and holy thoughts until he draws mercy into the world. The Idra Rabba states: “The secret of Hashem is for those who fear Him; until they assent, judgments do not descend into the world.” Thus Noach the righteous, wishing to strengthen kindness and annul the decree of the Flood, did not allow the thought to spread in his heart that the King’s word had gone forth and could not be changed. He strengthened his thought instead: Hashem will return and relent, and His mercy will prevail over His attributes. Therefore the Sages called him, in their expressive language, “of little faith,” believing and not believing: he did not wish to believe, so as not to assent to the judgments. Only because he was alone in the world could he not save all his generation. He nevertheless did his part, and did not enter until the water forced him.”
connections.context: Avodat Yisrael records the same additional clause in an interpretation of Noach’s hope for mercy. This establishes an earlier parallel for the wording while preserving the limitation that Noach’s effort did not save his generation. The existing note on the available Idra text remains in place.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁהוּא בְּעִנְיָן אַחֵר הַדּוֹמֶה לוֹ, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁהָיָה בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּכִּבְשָׂה
connections.quote: “Hashem sent Natan to David. He came to him and said: “There were two men in one city, one rich and one poor. The rich man had very many sheep and cattle. The poor man had nothing but one small ewe that he had bought and raised. It grew up with him and his children, ate from his bread, drank from his cup, and lay in his bosom; it was like a daughter to him. A traveler came to the rich man. He spared his own sheep and cattle when preparing food for the guest who had come to him, and took the poor man’s ewe and prepared it for the man who had come.” David was very angry with the man and said to Natan: “As Hashem lives, the man who did this deserves death. He must repay the ewe fourfold, because he did this and had no compassion.” Natan said to David: “You are the man! Thus said Hashem, the God of Israel: I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from Shaul’s hand.””
connections.context: Natan first presents another person’s apparent case; David pronounces judgment before recognizing its application to himself. This is the biblical example explicitly named in the Hebrew.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיִרְמְיָה הָיָה בִּבְנֵי עֲנָתוֹת, וְגָלוּת עֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים הָיָה יְשַׁעְיָה בְּשֶׁבְנָא, וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בִּסְדוֹם הוּא בַּמֶּה שֶׁהִפְרִיד לוֹט מִקּוֹדֶם, וְכֵן הַכֹּל, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ].
connections.quote: “Therefore thus said Hashem concerning the men of Anatot who seek your life, saying, “Do not prophesy in Hashem’s name, or you will die by our hand”: Therefore thus said Hashem of hosts: “I am about to call them to account. The young men shall die by the sword; their sons and daughters shall die by famine. No remnant shall remain of them, for I shall bring calamity upon the men of Anatot in the year of their reckoning.””
connections.context: These verses identify the men of Anatot and their threat against Yirmiyahu. They supply the background to the first example in the bracketed sentence.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיִרְמְיָה הָיָה בִּבְנֵי עֲנָתוֹת, וְגָלוּת עֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים הָיָה יְשַׁעְיָה בְּשֶׁבְנָא, וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בִּסְדוֹם הוּא בַּמֶּה שֶׁהִפְרִיד לוֹט מִקּוֹדֶם, וְכֵן הַכֹּל, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ].
connections.quote: “They said: “Come, let us devise plans against Yirmiyahu, for instruction will not be lost from the priest, counsel from the wise, or a word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us pay no attention to any of his words.” “Attend to me, Hashem, and hear the voice of my opponents. Should evil be repaid for good? For they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath away from them. Therefore give their children over to famine and deliver them into the power of the sword; let their wives be bereaved and widowed, their men slain by death, and their young men struck by the sword in war. Let an outcry be heard from their houses when You suddenly bring a troop against them, for they have dug a pit to catch me and hidden snares for my feet. You, Hashem, know all their counsel against me for death. Do not atone for their iniquity, and do not erase their sin from before You. Let them stumble before You; deal with them at the time of Your anger.””
connections.context: The passage preserves both sides of Yirmiyahu’s prayer: his earlier intercession for their good and his later appeal after their plotting. It makes the tension raised by the ois explicit.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיִרְמְיָה הָיָה בִּבְנֵי עֲנָתוֹת, וְגָלוּת עֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים הָיָה יְשַׁעְיָה בְּשֶׁבְנָא, וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בִּסְדוֹם הוּא בַּמֶּה שֶׁהִפְרִיד לוֹט מִקּוֹדֶם, וְכֵן הַכֹּל, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ].
connections.quote: “What is a conspiracy of the wicked? Shevna taught thirteen myriads, while Chizkiyahu taught eleven myriads. When Sancheriv came and besieged Jerusalem, Shevna wrote a note and shot it out on an arrow: “Shevna and his company have made peace; Chizkiyahu and his company have not made peace.” This is as it is said: “For behold, the wicked bend the bow; they have readied their arrow on the string.” Chizkiyahu was afraid. He said: Perhaps, Heaven forbid, the Holy One’s judgment will incline after the majority; since the majority will be delivered into their hands, they too will be delivered. A prophet came and said to him: “Do not call a conspiracy everything that this people calls a conspiracy.” That is, it is a conspiracy of the wicked, and a conspiracy of the wicked does not enter the count.”
connections.context: This is the original account of Shevna, the siege of Jerusalem, and the prophet’s response to Chizkiyahu. Its stated setting is Jerusalem; the connection to the ten tribes in the ois is Rav Tzadok’s application.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיִרְמְיָה הָיָה בִּבְנֵי עֲנָתוֹת, וְגָלוּת עֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים הָיָה יְשַׁעְיָה בְּשֶׁבְנָא, וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ בִּסְדוֹם הוּא בַּמֶּה שֶׁהִפְרִיד לוֹט מִקּוֹדֶם, וְכֵן הַכֹּל, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ].
connections.quote: “Avram said to Lot: “Please let there be no strife between me and you, or between my herdsmen and yours, for we are kinsmen. Is not the whole land before you? Please separate from me. If you go left, I will go right; if you go right, I will go left.””
connections.context: This is the earlier separation of Lot mentioned in the ois. The request is framed as a way to end strife between relatives.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הַצַּדִּיק נִתְפָּס, וּ"בַהֲדֵי הוּצָא לָקֵי כְּרָבָא";
connections.quote: ‘Rava said to Rabba bar Mari: Where is the source for what people say: ‘Along with the thorn, the cabbage also gets struck’? He said to him: It is written: ‘Why do you contend with Me? You have all rebelled against Me, declares Hashem.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הַצַּדִּיק נִתְפָּס, וּ"בַהֲדֵי הוּצָא לָקֵי כְּרָבָא";
connections.quote: “Rabbi Guryon said—and some say Rav Yosef bar Shemaya: When there are righteous people in the generation, the righteous are seized on account of the generation. When there are no righteous people in the generation, the children of the study house are seized on account of the generation. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ze’iri said—and some say Rabbi Shimon ben Nezira: What is the verse? “If you do not know, fairest among women, go forth in the footsteps of the flock.” We interpret this as the kids taken as pledges for the shepherds.”
connections.context: The Gemara supplies the expression that the righteous bear the generation’s suffering. Both clauses of the teaching are included, together with its scriptural image.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ מִמֶּנּוּ מַתְחִיל כִּדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (צב.),
connections.quote: “One who submits judgment against his fellow [to Heaven] is punished first. … This applies when he has a case that can be judged on earth.”
connections.context: The rule concerns invoking heavenly judgment against another when an earthly court is available. Rav Tzadok draws on its order—judgment beginning with the complainant—to explain the need for care in condemning others.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ מִמֶּנּוּ מַתְחִיל כִּדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (צב.),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonatan’s name: Calamity comes to the world only when the wicked are in the world, and it begins with the righteous first, as it is said: “When fire goes forth and finds thorns.” When does fire go forth? When thorns are available to it. It begins with the righteous first, as it is said, “And a stack has been consumed”: it does not say, “It consumes a stack,” but “A stack has been consumed”—the stack has already been consumed. Rav Yosef taught: What is meant by “None of you shall go out from the door of his house until morning”? Once permission has been given to the destroyer, it does not distinguish between the righteous and the wicked. Moreover, it begins with the righteous first, as it is said: “I shall cut off from you the righteous and the wicked.””
connections.context: This is the separate Talmudic passage explicitly describing calamity as beginning with the righteous. The existing note concerning a person who invokes heavenly judgment against another is preserved with its own qualification.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן מִדָּה טוֹבָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל עַל חֲבֵירוֹ וְכוּלֵי נַעֲנֶה תְּחִלָּה.
connections.quote: “Anyone who asks for mercy for his fellow, while he himself needs that same thing, is answered first, as it is said, “The Lord restored Job’s fortunes when he prayed for his friends.””
connections.context: The condition “he himself needs that same thing” is part of the teaching. Rav Tzadok sets this beneficial order beside the preceding warning about invoking judgment against another.

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא הָיָה צַדִּיק שֶׁנִּיצּוֹל מִזֶּה לְגַמְרֵי רַק מָשִׁיחַ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ עוֹד:
connections.displayRef: Mekor Mayim Chayim on Baal Shem Tov, Bereshit 100:1
connections.linkedRef: Mekor Mayim Chayim on Baal Shem Tov, Bereshit 100:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mekor Mayim Chayim on Baal Shem Tov, Bereshit 100:1
connections.heRef: מקור מים חיים על בעל שם טוב, בראשית ק׳:א׳
connections.quote: “At the beginning of the new Midrash Pinchas it is written in the name of the righteous Rabbi Gedaliah of Linitz, who said in the name of his teacher, the righteous rebuker: Mashiach will offer a favorable defense of all Israel, even of the wicked, showing that they are in the right. Through the favorable defense he offers for them, they will return in repentance, and through this they will be redeemed, for they are redeemed through repentance. He would say: A small righteous person loves small sinners; a great righteous person loves great sinners; but Mashiach will love and offer a favorable defense even of utterly wicked people. Anyone who offers a favorable defense of all creatures has an aspect of Mashiach.”
connections.context: The recorded teaching connects Mashiach’s comprehensive defense of people with their return in repentance. The concluding condition—repentance leading to redemption—is part of the quotation. The attribution follows the transmission stated in the source.

connections.hePhrase: [פח] אֵין דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֲקַלְקַלּוֹת, רַק שֶׁבְּעֵינָיו הוּא יָשָׁר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִשְׁלֵי (כא, ב): "כָּל דֶּרֶךְ אִישׁ יָשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו";
connections.quote: “It appears to me that Israel’s intention in sending the scouts was that, as they went up, they would repair every harmful thing and subdue the heavenly princes through their righteousness. They would return and say, “The land is good,” and their speech would act so that no obstacle remained when Israel entered the land, allowing them to enter quietly and securely. This is Moshe’s rebuke: “You approached … let us send men”—righteous men, as Rashi explains that at that time they were worthy. “Let them explore the land for us”: through their righteousness they would dig as they went, repairing all the obstacles, bends, and accusations. The language of digging signifies that this must be done in concealment. “The road by which we shall ascend,” as Rashi explains, “There is no road without bends,” alludes to all these obstacles, accusations, and barriers. “And the cities to which we shall come” means that we could then enter the cities easily. Therefore it says, “The matter was good in my eyes,” for according to their intention the matter was good. “They turned” means that the scouts directed themselves toward this and set their hearts upon it. “They brought us back word and said, ‘The land is good.’” According to this explanation, we understand why he did not mention their evil report about the land: their failure was that they did not immediately trust the scouts’ statement, “The land is good.” Their intended purpose was that the scouts should come and say, “The land is good,” and they should not have turned to the other matters.”

connections.hePhrase: [פח] אֵין דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֲקַלְקַלּוֹת, רַק שֶׁבְּעֵינָיו הוּא יָשָׁר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִשְׁלֵי (כא, ב): "כָּל דֶּרֶךְ אִישׁ יָשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו";
connections.quote: ““The road by which we shall ascend”—There is no road that has no bends.”
connections.context: Rashi’s literal explanation supplies the wording that Rav Tzadok applies here to a person’s moral path.

connections.hePhrase: [פח] אֵין דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֲקַלְקַלּוֹת, רַק שֶׁבְּעֵינָיו הוּא יָשָׁר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִשְׁלֵי (כא, ב): "כָּל דֶּרֶךְ אִישׁ יָשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו";
connections.quote: ‘Every person’s way is right in his own eyes, but Hashem weighs hearts.’
