connections.hePhrase: [פח] אֵין דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֲקַלְקַלּוֹת, רַק שֶׁבְּעֵינָיו הוּא יָשָׁר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִשְׁלֵי (כא, ב): "כָּל דֶּרֶךְ אִישׁ יָשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו";
connections.quote: ““Right in his eyes”—because he does not see fault in himself. “And He weighs”—Hashem is within his heart and knows whether his way is straight or not.”
connections.context: Metzudat David explains both halves of the verse: the person’s self-favoring view and God’s knowledge of the heart.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה יב) עַל פָּסוּק "יִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּמֵישָׁרִים":
connections.quote: ““It goes smoothly”: In the end his wife says to him, “I saw [blood] like a red rose,” and he does not separate from her. Rabbi Asi said: If he is a Torah scholar, in the end he declares the impure pure and the pure impure.”
connections.context: The Midrash describes wine impairing restraint and judgment. Rav Tzadok uses the resulting appearance that everything is permitted to distinguish intoxicated confusion from a true perception of holiness.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה יב) עַל פָּסוּק "יִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּמֵישָׁרִים":
connections.quote: ‘Do not gaze at wine when it reddens, when it shows its color in the cup and flows smoothly.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַמִּתְהַלֵּךְ בְּמֵישָׁרִים כָּל הָעֲרָיוֹת דּוֹמוֹת עָלָיו כְּמִישׁוֹר (יוֹמָא עה.),
connections.quote: “‘When he sets his eye on the cup, he walks on level ground.’ Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi differed: One said, ‘To anyone who sets his eye on his cup, all forbidden sexual relationships appear like level ground.’ The other said, ‘To anyone who sets his eye on his cup, the entire world appears like level ground.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִי שֶׁבְּעֵינָיו הוּא יָשָׁר, מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה? וַהֲלֹא לְפִי דַעְתּוֹ הוֹלֵךְ בְּיֹשֶׁר!
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 4
connections.quote: “It is written (Proverbs 15:19), ‘The way of the lazy is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is paved.’ The way of the lazy means this: even if a person restrains himself from bad actions, bad thoughts, and bad desires, if he does so without love of Hashem but rather as a lazy person—for example, understanding that such things will not succeed for him in this world, or for another reason that is not love of Hashem—his way is like a hedge of thorns. The heart cannot be empty of thoughts and desires even for a moment. When thoughts of craving leave his heart, a thought of anger or the like enters it. All his ways are like a hedge of thorns: he will always need self-restraint and effort; before one thing leaves his heart, another improper thing enters. But ‘the path of the upright’ means turning away from everything because of love of Hashem. His path is paved toward the good, because when a bad thing leaves his heart, love of Hashem remains there, and consequently nothing else improper will enter his heart.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains why merely finding one’s conduct unobstructed is insufficient. Avoiding a bad desire for convenience can leave the heart available to another bad desire; love of Hashem changes what fills the space. This develops Rav Tzadok’s counsel to examine the heart when a path seems straight: the inward motive, rather than the feeling of ease, determines the character of the path.
connections.headline: What fills the heart after a desire is removed

connections.hePhrase: עַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְתֹכֵן לִבּוֹת ה'",
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות כ״א א:ח׳
connections.quote: ““So that they should direct their hearts to the Omnipresent.” Some explain that they put aside troubling thoughts and concentrate on reciting the prayer. This does not appear correct to my teacher, for then it should say “toward their prayer,” not “to the Omnipresent.” Below, when intention concerning the recitation is mentioned, it says that one who prays must direct his heart, giving as an indication, “You prepare their heart; You attend with Your ear.” Rather, the explanation is that they should intend that their heart be whole in the service of the Omnipresent and remove the pleasures and enjoyments of this world from their heart. When they purify their heart of this world’s vanities and direct their intention toward God’s greatness, their prayer will be desired and accepted. Of this intention it is said, “You prepare their heart; You attend with Your ear.” “You prepare their heart” is stated because the intention to purify the heart from transgressions and worldly pleasures requires assistance from the Omnipresent, as it is said, “Hashem prepares hearts,” and “Prepare their heart toward You.” Thus it asks: Help them and prepare their heart to be pure, so that You will attend to their prayer. Know that this is the principal explanation, since below it says, “An indication for the matter.” Why call it an indication when it would be a clear proof? Because the verse’s main subject is the intention to purify the heart, not the intention in reciting prayer; when it is cited concerning the recitation, it is called an indication.”
connections.context: The commentary explicitly reads ותוכן לבות in relation to divine help in purifying the heart. It also distinguishes inward preparation for service from concentration on the words of prayer.

connections.hePhrase: מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ שָׁלֵם אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁגֵּהוּ לְהַטְעוֹתוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא,
connections.quote: see note 739.
connections.context: The statement appears in the discussion of granting the nations an opportunity to perform the mitzvah of sukkah. Rav Tzadok uses its principle concerning divine fairness in his account of a sincere heart.

connections.hePhrase: מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ שָׁלֵם אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁגֵּהוּ לְהַטְעוֹתוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא,
connections.quote: “If someone asks: How can Scripture punish a thought without an act? Surely a person cannot control himself so that bad thoughts never arise in his heart; why punish what is beyond his control? I will explain the principle. The choice of deeds, for good or evil, is entrusted to the person, as it is written, “See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil … choose life.” The choice of thought is also entrusted to him after preparation: he is commanded to think a good thought and warned to turn his heart away from a bad thought, receiving reward for a good thought and punishment for a bad thought. When his reflections sometimes produce thoughts that are not good, and unworthy thoughts suddenly arise in his heart unintentionally, this is before preparation and is a sign of stumbling and sin: he has turned from the way and has not developed his soul through preparation. His repair and healing are to work at preparation—to direct his heart and thoughts toward the exalted God, subjecting and bending his thought to Him through good thought and worthy deeds. If a bad thought comes, he should rebuke it; if he does not rebuke it and it remains in his heart, he is punished. When he maintains this thought for a long time, preparing his heart to love the blessed God, draw near to Him, and walk in His ways, Hashem too will give good and reward his righteousness by preparing his heart so that he will not think of evil and only good will arise in his thought. Of this they said: “One who comes to purify himself is helped.” Many verses state this principle: “For Hashem searches all hearts and understands every formation of thoughts; if you seek Him, He will be found by you”; and “Hashem prepares hearts,” for the blessed God prepares a person’s heart and straightens his disposition when the person prepares his heart toward Him. Likewise, “You have heard the desire of the humble, Hashem; You prepare their heart; You attend with Your ear”; and “Hashem, God of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Israel our fathers, preserve this forever in the formation of Your people’s thoughts, and prepare their heart toward You.””
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya connects divine assistance with sustained preparation and the response to thoughts when they arise. The whole selected discussion is retained, including its question about involuntary thoughts and the distinction between their arrival and allowing them to remain. This is one explanation within his discussion; the following paragraph records additional interpretations.

connections.hePhrase: רַק עַקְמוּמִית שֶׁבַּלֵּב הוּא הַגּוֹרֵם הַטָּעוּת:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Alexandri said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name: Thunder was created only to straighten the crookedness in the heart, as it is said: “God has acted so that they should fear Him.””
connections.context: The Talmud uses the same image of crookedness in the heart and identifies reverence for God as its correction.

connections.hePhrase: [פט] דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּחֻלִּין (פט.) עַל פָּסוּק "הַאֻמְנָם אֵלֶם וְגוֹמֵר":
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: What does the verse mean, ‘Is it indeed silence? Speak righteousness; judge uprightly, sons of man’? What should a person’s craft be in this world? He should make himself like one who cannot speak. Could this apply even to words of Torah? The verse therefore says, ‘Speak righteousness.’ Could he then become arrogant? The verse therefore says, ‘Judge uprightly, sons of man.’”

connections.hePhrase: [פט] דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּחֻלִּין (פט.) עַל פָּסוּק "הַאֻמְנָם אֵלֶם וְגוֹמֵר":
connections.quote: ‘Is the justice you ought to speak truly silenced? Do you judge uprightly, you sons of man?’

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי שִׁילְהֵי סֻכָּה: "בֶּאֱמוּנָתָם – בְּאֻמָּנוּתָם, אֻמָּנוּת גְּדוֹלָה וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “Let them make them twenty-three divisions. This cannot be done, for it is written: “David and Shmuel the seer established them in their faithfulness”—read this as “in their craftsmanship.” Great craftsmanship was involved: no division received an ancestral field a second time before its fellow had received one. Rabbi Abbahu said: I calculated it; no division received an ancestral field a second time before its fellow had received one.”
connections.context: The discussion asks why the twenty-four priestly divisions cannot be reduced to twenty-three. Its carefully balanced arrangement is called “great craftsmanship,” supplying Rav Tzadok’s example of the word craft applied to demanding wisdom.

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן שֶׁלֹּא לְדַבֵּר כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “The meaning is: do not think that the separation of the tribe of Levi is an inborn statute, as though they were created like angels with no possibility of being otherwise. That would remove their choice. Rather, the description applies when Torah comes forth from a person's mouth. ‘Comes forth’ means almost of itself: his mouth has become so fully a sheath for words of Torah that Torah comes forth from it of itself, for his lips speak only Torah, even without a particular prior intention. This is like the teaching (Sukkah 21b), ‘Its leaf shall not wither’—even the ordinary conversation of Torah scholars. When his lips utter nothing detached from Torah, he is like the ministering angels, dedicated to Hashem's mission, all the thoughts of his heart in this world directed to that task. Otherwise, the opposite description applies.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains the same teaching about a scholar's ordinary conversation as Torah. It describes a mouth so devoted to Torah that even unplanned speech carries that direction, while expressly preserving the speaker's choice and the possibility of failing to live that role. This supplies the mechanism for the siman's second explanation: Torah heals and opens the tongue by changing the source from which its speech emerges.
connections.headline: When ordinary conversation is shaped by Torah

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרָכִין (טו:) וּבִדְבָרִים רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א) שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַרְפֵּא הַלָּשׁוֹן;
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: What is the remedy for someone who speaks lashon hara? If he is a Torah scholar, he should engage in Torah, as it says: ‘A healing for the tongue is a tree of life.’ ‘Tongue’ here means lashon hara, as it says: ‘Their tongue is a deadly arrow.’ And ‘tree’ means Torah, as it says: ‘It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it.’ If he is unlearned, he should humble himself, as it says: ‘But perversity in it is a breaking of the spirit.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרָכִין (טו:) וּבִדְבָרִים רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א) שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַרְפֵּא הַלָּשׁוֹן;
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said: See how precious the language of Torah is, for it heals the tongue. From where? “A healing tongue is a tree of life,” and the tree of life is Torah, as it is said, “It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it.””
connections.context: The Midrash proceeds to Moses, whose earlier difficulty speaking gives way to “These are the words” after he merits Torah. The relevant claim is Torah’s healing of speech, rather than the opening legal discussion about languages in which a scroll may be written.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרָכִין (טו:) וּבִדְבָרִים רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א) שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַרְפֵּא הַלָּשׁוֹן;
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:13
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:13
connections.quote: “This is the healing of a tongue that chatters excessively: through the Torah’s Tree of Life, the whole body becomes fire, as stated at the end of Chagigah from the verse, “Are not My words like fire, declares Hashem?” Through speaking words of Torah with vitality, the combination of letters at the root of one’s life becomes like this, so that one is wholly fire. It is said that fire purifies, for impurity has no place in fire at all. This heals the past as well, like heating with fire to remove absorbed forbidden matter. All one’s conversation becomes Torah, since it comes from the burning fire—that is, the vitality burning within.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains how Torah can heal habitual speech and its earlier damage. The comparison is to purification by fire, and the passage concludes with the transformation of ordinary conversation.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה: שֶׁמַּתִּיר הַלָּשׁוֹן, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא מַתִּירוֹ לְדַבֵּר הַכֹּל,
connections.quote: “The language of Torah also loosens the tongue. Know this: in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will bring forth excellent trees from the Garden of Eden. What is their excellence? They heal the tongue, as it is said: “Along the river, on its banks on either side, there shall grow…” How do we know that this is healing of the tongue? It says: “Its fruit shall be for food and its leaf for healing.” Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi offered two explanations: one said, “For loosening”; the other said that anyone who is mute and swallows some of it has his tongue healed and immediately polishes it with words of Torah. For it says “on this side and on that side,” and this expression refers to Torah, as it is said: “They were written on this side and on that side.” Rabbi Levi said: Why learn from elsewhere? Let us learn from the passage itself. Before Moshe merited Torah, it was written of him, “I am not a man of words.” Once he merited Torah, his tongue was healed and he began speaking words. From where? From what we have read in this passage: “These are the words that Moshe spoke.””
connections.context: This is the continuation of the Midrash beyond the portion already quoted in the existing footnote. It supplies the specific claim that Torah loosens the tongue and illustrates it through Moshe’s change from “not a man of words” to Devarim.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): עֲלֵיהוּ – אֲפִילּוּ שִׂיחַת חֻלִּין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “Why does it not say, ‘From Rabban Gamliel’s words’? It teaches us something in passing, in keeping with what Rav Acha bar Adda said—some report that Rav Acha bar Adda said it in the name of Rav Hamnuna, in Rav’s name: From where do we learn that even the ordinary conversation of Torah scholars requires study? From the verse, ‘And its leaf will not wither.’”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): עֲלֵיהוּ – אֲפִילּוּ שִׂיחַת חֻלִּין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “The righteous person is compared to a tree, as it is written, “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which gives its fruit in its season, and whose leaf does not wither.” A tree produces leaf and fruit; this is a natural property implanted in it on the third day by the utterance, “Let the earth sprout.” The leaf has a purpose, for its shade protects the fruit from the sun’s heat, while the fruit is the essential thing. So too, the righteous person has leaf and fruit. His leaf is his speech about ordinary matters—the affairs of this world, his instruction, and his accounts of events. These are greatly beneficial, just as the leaf that shelters with its shade is beneficial. This is what our Sages expounded: “His leaf does not wither”—even the ordinary conversation of Torah scholars requires study. His fruit is his speech in Torah and wisdom, which is the essential thing, just as fruit is the essential thing in a tree.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): עֲלֵיהוּ – אֲפִילּוּ שִׂיחַת חֻלִּין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “Our Sages said of Torah scholars that all their conversation is words of Torah. Since words of Torah are expressed in speech, all their speech becomes words of Torah. For wherever all a person’s thoughts are immersed, that immersion of thought is recognizable in every activity he undertakes, as is known. Similarly, the body’s eating and drinking, which resemble ordinary conversation, also become words of Torah and food and drink for the soul. Since through this the body is joined to the soul, and the body too derives benefit through a word of Torah, the body is then also included in holiness. Precisely through this comes holy inspiration; there is no room here to elaborate further.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains how an abiding immersion in Torah can shape ordinary speech and even bodily activity. The account includes the body’s participation in holiness and the resulting holy inspiration.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): עֲלֵיהוּ – אֲפִילּוּ שִׂיחַת חֻלִּין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “The school of Rav Anan taught: What is meant by “Riders on white donkeys, those who sit in judgment, and those who walk on the road—speak”? “Riders on donkeys” are Torah scholars who travel from city to city and from country to country to learn Torah. “White” means that they make it clear as midday. “Those who sit in judgment” are those who render a judgment true to its fullest truth. “Those who walk” are masters of Scripture. “On the road” are masters of Mishnah. “Speak” are masters of Talmud, all of whose conversation consists of words of Torah.”
connections.context: The Gemara states explicitly that the masters of Talmud have Torah in all their conversation. This is a separate source from the leaf-and-fruit exposition already quoted at this point.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ דְּמַיְיתֵי שָׁם: סְפָרִים נִכְתָּבִים בְּכָל לָשׁוֹן, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר אֲפִילּוּ שִׂיחַת חֻלִּין כַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא תּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ““These are the words.” A question of law: May a person of Israel write a Torah scroll in any language? The Sages taught: The difference between sacred books and tefillin and mezuzot is that the books may be written in any language. Rabban Gamliel says: Even for the books, they permitted writing only in Greek. What is Rabban Gamliel’s reason for allowing a Torah scroll to be written in Greek? Our teachers taught as follows. Bar Kappara said: It is written, “May God enlarge Yefet, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem”—the words of Shem are to be spoken in the languages of Yefet. Therefore they permitted writing in Greek.”
connections.context: The opening of this Midrash records both the general permission for sacred books and Rabban Gamliel’s narrower position. Neither part is present in the existing quotation from the middle of the same Midrash.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דִּבְרָכוֹת (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ט): פִּטְטַיָּא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא טָבִין
connections.quote: see note 478.
connections.context: This is the exact Yerushalmi formulation cited by Rav Tzadok. The following statement in the Yerushalmi concerns falsehood and is a separate teaching.

connections.hePhrase: [וּמַאן דְּאָמַר: אֶלָּא יְוָנִית, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר חָדָשׁ (יִתְרוֹ) דְּאִינּוּן קְרִיבִין לְאָרְחֵי מְהֵימְנוּתָא עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “Here is the mystery of the four kingdoms that surround everything. “A storm wind” is the kingdom of Babylon. “A great cloud” is the kingdom of Media. “A flashing fire” is the kingdom of Edom. “And brightness around it” is the kingdom of Greece: brightness surrounds them, but the brightness is not within them, for it is written “around.” For among all the kingdoms, none are as close to the path of faith as they are. Here too, among these shells, none is as close to the inner core as this one. Brightness surrounds it, but the brightness is not within it; rather, it comes out from the core and shines all around.”
connections.context: The Zohar Chadash identifies Greece with surrounding brightness. The quotation preserves its central qualification: the brightness surrounds this kingdom and does not originate within it.

connections.hePhrase: מִזֶּה זָכוּ לַלָּשׁוֹן, וּבְבָבָא קַמָּא (פג.) מְחַלְּקִים בֵּין לָשׁוֹן לְחָכְמָה עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ‘Why use the Syriac language? Use either the holy tongue or Greek! Rabbi Yosei also said: In Babylonia, why use Aramaic? Use either the holy tongue or Persian! They answered: The Greek language is one matter, and Greek wisdom is another.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ (בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית) דְּנֶחְשַׁךְ הָעוֹלָם בַּיּוֹם שֶׁנֶּעְתַּק הַתּוֹרָה לִיוָנִית וְשִׁנּוּ י"ג דְּבָרִים, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאַרְנוּם,
connections.quote: “On the eighth of Tevet, the Torah was written in Greek in the days of King Ptolemy, and there was darkness in the world for three days.”
connections.context: Shulchan Arukh records the tradition of darkness following the Greek translation, within its list of commemorative fast days. The date in this source is the eighth of Tevet.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ (בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית) דְּנֶחְשַׁךְ הָעוֹלָם בַּיּוֹם שֶׁנֶּעְתַּק הַתּוֹרָה לִיוָנִית וְשִׁנּוּ י"ג דְּבָרִים, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאַרְנוּם,
connections.quote: “There was also an incident involving King Ptolemy, who gathered seventy-two elders and placed them in seventy-two houses, without revealing why he had gathered them. He entered each one’s house and said: “Write for me the Torah of Moshe your teacher.” The Omnipresent placed counsel in each one’s heart, and their minds agreed upon one understanding, so that each wrote a Torah separately for him. They changed thirteen things in it. These are they: “God created in the beginning”; “God said: I shall make a human being in an image and likeness”; “He completed on the sixth day and rested on the seventh”; “Male and female He created him”; “Come, I shall descend and confuse there”; “She laughed among her relatives, saying”; “For in their anger they killed a man, and in their willfulness they uprooted a feeding trough”; “Moshe took his wife and sons and mounted them upon bearers of people”; “The dwelling of the children of Israel, who dwelt in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, was thirty years and four hundred years”; “Against the young men of the children of Israel He did not stretch out His hand”; “I have not taken one valuable thing from them”; “The short-legged one”; “Which Hashem your God allotted to give light to all the peoples under all the heavens”; “Which I did not command them to worship.””
connections.context: This source explicitly introduces “thirteen changes” and supplies the full transmitted list. The wording and list are preserved as transmitted, without deleting an item to reconcile the heading. The quoted phrases are the translation’s alterations, rather than quotations of the unaltered biblical wording.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ סְפָרִים נִכְתָּבִים בִּלְשׁוֹנָם, אֲבָל חָכְמָתָן שֶׁלָּהֶן בְּעַצְמָן אָסוּר לִלְמוֹד, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ]:
connections.quote: “Correspondingly, on the opposite side there are seven disciplines of wisdom. These, however, are permitted disciplines, and there is no prohibition in them; they are from the shell of nogah. As the Zohar Chadash says in Yitro, when enumerating the four shells: “Brightness around it” is the kingdom of Greece, which is surrounded by brightness, because among all the kingdoms none are as close to the path of faith as it is. This means that in Greek wisdom some attained an intellectual understanding of upright qualities. Yet “what wisdom have they,” since they are only from the shell of nogah: the brightness is not within them, but only around them, as stated in the Zohar Chadash.”
connections.context: This parallel preserves Rav Tzadok’s explicit qualification that the seven disciplines themselves are permitted. He then discusses Greek moral understanding through the Zohar’s distinction between inward light and surrounding brightness.

connections.hePhrase: [צ] הַתּוֹרָה הוּא מַפַּת הָעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א בַּמָּשָׁל דְּדִיפְתְּרָאוֹת וּפִנְקְסָאוֹת;
connections.quote: “When a human king builds a palace, he does not build it from his own knowledge but through an architect. The architect does not build it from his own knowledge but has plans and tablets, to know how to make its rooms and doors. So the Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world.”
connections.context: The architectural plans are the Midrash’s image for Torah’s relation to creation. This is the parable Rav Tzadok refers to when calling Torah the map of the world.

connections.hePhrase: [צ] הַתּוֹרָה הוּא מַפַּת הָעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א בַּמָּשָׁל דְּדִיפְתְּרָאוֹת וּפִנְקְסָאוֹת;
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 5
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 5
connections.quote: “To explain this, know that a “book” is the inscription of words of wisdom. It makes no difference whether they are inscribed on paper, parchment, or something else, just as the Torah existed before the world was created; see Midrash Konen, section one. When wisdom is inscribed in the mind, the mind too is a book of wisdom. When a person composes a book, this means revealing his wisdom to all, with his wisdom stored within it. Similarly, we find the blessed God’s wisdom revealed in the world, for He created the world with wisdom, as it says, “With wisdom He founded the earth”; as stated in Rosh Hashanah, “He created everything with His wisdom”; and in Targum Yonatan, “In the beginning” is rendered “With wisdom.” Creation reveals His wisdom and is therefore like a book on which all His wisdom is inscribed. It is called the blessed God’s book, as we learn at the beginning of Sefer Yetzirah that He engraved His world through three books. This is the book mentioned in Avot: “All your deeds are written in the book”; see Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance, chapter five, in the name of Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz. Concerning this, see Avodah Zarah: “Did Adam the first man have a book? This teaches that He showed him…” Bava Metzia mentions Adam’s book, which included all the souls; this is what is called Adam’s book. See Avodat Yisrael on Nitzavim concerning being written for life in the book; Raavad’s commentary at the beginning of Sefer Yetzirah concerning the opening of three books; and Shaarei HaYichudim, gate three, the end of chapter thirty-eight, concerning Adam’s book and Chanoch’s book. The Torah too is the pattern of all creation, as it is compared at the beginning of Bereshit Rabbah; therefore it too is called the book of His wisdom.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the image of Torah as the pattern of creation through the broader meaning of a book: the inscription and disclosure of wisdom. The selected unit also connects this image with the book containing the souls.

connections.hePhrase: [צ] הַתּוֹרָה הוּא מַפַּת הָעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א בַּמָּשָׁל דְּדִיפְתְּרָאוֹת וּפִנְקְסָאוֹת;
connections.quote: “The explanation is: although each soul encompasses all faculties, Hashem, desiring diverse souls, ordained that the composition and blend of faculties not be uniform across all souls; rather, one particular faculty predominates in that soul, coloring the perceptions of all other faculties: by way of example: to one He assigned the hardness of stone as dominant like a heart of stone or stiff-neckedness, to another the might of a lion, and the like. And although all faculties are present within him, their primary lens remains that dominant trait, wherefore perceptions diverge, just as a courageous person does not take the same pleasure in rest as a sluggard, and so throughout all details. For Hashem instituted a single order and statute for creation—the order of the Torah (Bereishit Rabbah 1:1), the blueprint of Genesis; and the architectural order decreeing that such-and-such creatures exist in the world must govern the arrangement of souls, which is the ordering of worlds; for corresponding to the diverse faculties within one world is the structure of different worlds, their variation depending upon them.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains how different souls can express one divine pattern: each contains the whole range of powers, but a particular power governs their arrangement. This supplies a conceptual basis for the siman’s claim that changes in souls, Torah, and the world correspond. Diversity does not require an independent blueprint for each generation; it can disclose a new arrangement within the Torah’s common order.
connections.headline: One Torah order, differently composed souls

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהֵם וְאוֹרַיְיתָא חַד כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי אוֹר הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא עַצְמוֹ אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּיֵשׁ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא אוֹתִיּוֹת לַתּוֹרָה]
connections.quote: “For we have learned: Three levels are interconnected with one another—the Holy One, blessed be He, Torah, and Israel. Each, level upon level, is concealed and revealed. The Holy One, blessed be He: level upon level, concealed and revealed. Torah likewise: concealed and revealed. Israel likewise: level upon level. This is as it is written: “He tells His words to Yaakov, His statutes and judgments to Israel.” There are two levels—Yaakov and Israel—one revealed and one concealed.”

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהֵם וְאוֹרַיְיתָא חַד כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי אוֹר הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא עַצְמוֹ אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּיֵשׁ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא אוֹתִיּוֹת לַתּוֹרָה]
connections.quote: “Every soul has its own particular lamp, the human soul. Torah too is a lamp: “Torah is light,” and “light means Torah,” as stated in Megillah. This is “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” Each person of Israel has a portion in Torah that is his own lamp. In the generation of the wilderness, the fundamental number was six hundred thousand souls, corresponding to the six hundred thousand letters of Torah, as is said: Yisrael forms the initials of “There are six hundred thousand letters in the Torah.” Although the numerical count does not match, each letter divides into sparks; this is the Written Torah. Subsequently, through the Torah insights in which the blessed God brings forth a new teaching every day, as stated in Bereshit Rabbah, the souls of Israel increase. This is what we ask: “Give us our portion in Your Torah,” for every person of Israel has a portion in Torah, which is his lamp—“The soul of man is Hashem’s lamp.””
connections.context: This parallel includes Rav Tzadok’s express qualification that the ordinary count of letters does not equal the stated number: the correspondence is through the letters’ division into sparks. It then connects new Torah teachings with the multiplication of souls.

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהֵם וְאוֹרַיְיתָא חַד כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי אוֹר הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא עַצְמוֹ אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּיֵשׁ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא אוֹתִיּוֹת לַתּוֹרָה]
connections.displayRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Korach, Torah Ohr 2
connections.linkedRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Korach, Torah Ohr 2
connections.canonicalRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Korach, Torah Ohr 2
connections.heRef: שני לוחות הברית, תורה שבכתב, קרח, תורה אור ב׳
connections.quote: “Know that the number of the children of Israel was six hundred thousand. The kabbalists said that these are six hundred thousand souls issuing from the six hundred thousand letters of the Torah, for the Torah’s spiritual reality is the souls of Israel. The generation that received the Torah comprised these six hundred thousand souls; the generations that came after them are all branches issuing from them.”
connections.context: Shelah states the correspondence between the founding generation, the letters of Torah, and the later generations as branches. He proceeds to ask how Levi is included and develops the distinction between general roots and their particulars; the selected quotation states the initial correspondence.

connections.hePhrase: כְּפִי הַהִתְחַדְּשׁוּת שֶׁבַּנְּפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל דּוֹר, כֵּן הִתְחַדְּשׁוּת הָעוֹלָם בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן,
connections.quote: “The way Torah is conducted within Israel is always the way He, blessed be He, conducts all the worlds; even the nations conduct themselves accordingly, one corresponding to the other. All their profusion of idolatry, magicians, and sorcerers existed while there was revelation of the Divine Presence and prophecy within Israel. Once that departed and Oral Torah began, Greek wisdom, which is human wisdom, also began among them.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (סג.): אֲפִילּוּ סְפִינוֹת וְכוּלֵי בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Elazar also said: What is the meaning of ‘All the families of the earth shall be blessed through you’? The Holy One, blessed be He, told Abraham: I have two good branches to graft into you: Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. ‘All the families of the earth’—even the families that dwell in the ground are blessed only on account of Israel. ‘All the nations of the earth’—even ships traveling from Gallia to Aspamia are blessed only on account of Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִשְׁתַּנּוֹת מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר, כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה, וְהַיְינוּ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁמִּתְחַדֵּשׁ בְּכָל דּוֹר חֲדָשׁוֹת עַל יְדֵי חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: “All the souls of the children of Israel have their root in Torah, for “Torah and Israel are one.” In the mystery of the souls of the wilderness generation—the generation of Moshe who received the Written Torah—their root is in the letters of the Written Torah, as is known. As for the other generations, which are branches spreading from that generation, it appears to me that their root is in the Oral Torah, the unfolding of the Written Torah. Nothing is absent from the hints of the Written Torah, but it is there in allusion and concealment. Similarly, the souls of all the other generations were stored and included in concealment in the wilderness generation, since they issued from them. According to the Oral Torah renewed in each generation, so are the souls of the children of Israel in that generation.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok offers the distinction between the soul-roots of the first generation and later generations as his own explanation—“it appears to me.” The quotation preserves that qualification and the inclusion of later generations within the original root.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִשְׁתַּנּוֹת מִדּוֹר לְדוֹר, כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה, וְהַיְינוּ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁמִּתְחַדֵּשׁ בְּכָל דּוֹר חֲדָשׁוֹת עַל יְדֵי חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 11:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 11:1
connections.quote: “‘When Pharaoh sent out the people, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, although it was near.’ It is written (Proverbs 10), ‘When the storm passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is an everlasting foundation.’ My holy grandfather explained that Hashem has a garment called storm, as it says, ‘Hashem's way is in storm and tempest.’ When Hashem governs the upper worlds through that garment, the righteous foundation of the world is likewise clothed in it here. Thus Eliyahu said in his generation, ‘I have been exceedingly zealous for Hashem, God of hosts, for Israel has forsaken Your covenant.’ Opposite the righteous person clothed in storm and tempest stands the contrary force with its storm of expansive assertion, as Ahab stood opposite Eliyahu. Afterward, when Hashem removes that garment from the order of His governance and begins to govern gently, Eliyahu is told (Zohar, Vayigash 209b) that the world cannot endure his manner among people. The storm and noise of the opposing force likewise quiet down, as the Sages said (Chagigah 5b), ‘When counsel is lost from the children, their wisdom decays.’ Whoever remains opposed to that new governance loses his standing entirely.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same concluding rabbinic proverb through Eliyahu and Ahab. A storm-like divine garment is expressed in the righteous figure and met by a corresponding storm of opposition; when the form of governance changes, neither response simply continues unchanged. This gives a concrete model of the siman's claim that the changing Torah and souls of a generation are reflected in the changing world around them.
connections.headline: The inward form of a generation and its outward counterpart

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל פִּיהֶם נִתְחַדֵּשׁ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיָנִים בָּעוֹלָם.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:37
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:37
connections.quote: “When a person of Israel develops something new in the wisdom of Torah, which is the blessed God’s wisdom, this wisdom spreads through all the worlds. In the physical world too, some matter of wisdom concerning this world is renewed correspondingly, drawn forth through this wisdom newly revealed in Hashem’s Torah and His service. The wise people of the nations of the world in that generation can receive it and develop it, and an observer will think that they originated it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok describes a spiritual relationship between new Torah insight and developments in worldly knowledge. This gives his fuller account of the connection asserted in the present ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל פִּיהֶם נִתְחַדֵּשׁ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיָנִים בָּעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “All the Oral Torah is hinted at in the Written Torah. Therefore whatever has already been revealed from the Oral Torah and is written down in the books of Israel’s sages has, for us, the character of Written Torah: these hints in the Written Torah have already been revealed and have become a fixed order of governance. The world’s entire governance according to Torah follows the Written Torah and its oral interpretation. Whatever is already revealed from the Oral Torah means that the governance too is already revealed in that form, just as the law is fixed and known to all. Every renewal in governance comes through the renewal of Oral Torah revealed to the hearts of Israel’s sages in that generation. According to those new insights are the renewals in governance, through the righteous person who rules in the fear of God—the true Torah scholar among Israel’s sages.”
connections.context: This passage distinguishes an established body of revealed teaching from new Oral Torah insight and explains how that distinction corresponds to established and renewed governance of the world.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (ה:): "אָבְדָה עֵצָה מִבָּנִים – נִסְרְחָה חָכְמָתָם", עַיֵּין שָׁם וּמוּבָן]:
connections.quote: ‘When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya was dying, the Sages asked him: ‘What will become of us in dealing with the heretics?’ He answered them: ‘Counsel has been lost from the children; their wisdom has decayed.’ Once counsel is lost from the children, the wisdom of the nations of the world decays.’

connections.hePhrase: [צא] כָּל קִנְיָנֵי הָאָדָם הוּא מֵחֶלְקֵי חַיּוּתוֹ הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט בַּבְּרוּאִים,
connections.quote: “Everything belonging to a person—his wife and children, his male and female servants, his ox and donkey, his tent, his silver and gold, and all that he has—comes from the root of his soul. For all inanimate things, plants, and animals are also rooted in the human soul, and the root of their life comes from it, as is known. What is acquired by him is that whose life is rooted in him. Ownerless possessions and all the beasts of the forest exist because he has not yet repaired the entire root of his life, for these certainly also relate to a person. Concerning the future it is said, “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb.” Likewise, before the sin the serpent served the human being. As the person is, so are his possessions, as it is stated concerning Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair’s donkey: the Holy One, blessed be He, does not bring a stumbling block through the animals of the righteous. Likewise, all the species in Noach’s ark, which he fed, presumably came from his root, as explained above. Therefore the Sages said that they had not corrupted their ways.”
connections.context: The earlier ois states the principle developed here and includes the case of creatures that are not presently someone’s property. Their present condition is distinguished from their future repair.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "בְּרֵאשִׁית" – בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Berekhiah said: Heaven and earth were created only for Israel’s merit, as it is written, “In the beginning God created.” “Beginning” refers to Israel, as it is stated, “Israel is holy to Hashem, the first of His produce.””
connections.context: This is the Midrashic derivation behind “for the sake of Israel.” The quoted sentence is Rabbi Berekhiah’s teaching within a passage that also relates creation to Yaakov and Moshe.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֵירוּבִין (יח:) מִשִּׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה: רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין]
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar said: During all those years that Adam was under ban, he fathered spirits, demons, and night spirits.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֵירוּבִין (יח:) מִשִּׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה: רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין]
connections.quote: “What we said concerned seminal emissions that occurred to him involuntarily.”
connections.context: The second sentence answers the objection that Adam had separated from his wife during those years. It supplies the specific connection to seed implied in Rav Tzadok’s allusion, and clarifies that this particular account concerns involuntary emissions.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה סוֹד מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כד): מִן הַכֹּל עָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְהִפָּרַע, אֲפִילּוּ מִן אֶבֶן וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “This is the common proverb that people use: even the stone over which people stumble, or with which they are stoned, and the peg used for those hanged on trees, are destined to give an accounting.”
connections.context: The original passage extends accountability even to instruments through which harm occurs. Rav Tzadok explains that image here through the human deeds from which their harmful condition arises.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְאָנֹכִי בָּרָאתִי מַשְׁחִית לְחַבֵּל",
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of “Evil pursues [sinners]”: the evil and the transgression themselves. For “the consequence of a transgression is a transgression,” and it itself is what punishes and exacts retribution.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s explicit interpretation of the verse quoted here: the consequence proceeds from the wrong itself. The selection is the complete statement of that principle, without detaching an accusation from the surrounding discussion of Rabbi’s mules.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְאָנֹכִי בָּרָאתִי מַשְׁחִית לְחַבֵּל",
connections.quote: ‘Evil pursues sinners, but good will be repaid to the righteous.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְאָנֹכִי בָּרָאתִי מַשְׁחִית לְחַבֵּל",
connections.quote: ‘See, it is I who created the smith, who blows into a coal fire and brings forth an instrument for his work; and it is I who created the destroyer to wreak destruction.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ו: אֵשׁ יוֹצְאָה מִגּוּפָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים וּמְלַהֶטֶת אוֹתָן],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai says: Neither the day nor Gehinnom, but a fire that issues from the bodies of the wicked and burns them. What is the reason? “You conceive chaff, you give birth to straw; your breath is a fire that consumes you.””
connections.context: This is one opinion in a discussion of the future judgment of the wicked. Rav Tzadok uses the image of punishment proceeding from the person’s own body; the other views concerning the sun and Gehinnom are not the sentence he cites.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַמֵּבִין עַל דָּבָר יוּכַל לָדַעַת וּלְהִתְבּוֹנֵן לְתַקֵּן כָּל אֵלֶּה,
connections.quote: “The order of these teachings has this meaning. As my grandfather, of blessed memory, said: whenever a person gives an acquisition over to Hashem, Hashem gives that acquisition back to the person with greater strength. Thus, ‘Bring an omer before Me on Pesach’: in this world Hashem placed garments from which a person receives the strength of his life. In truth, the principal life-giving power is the utterance of Hashem’s mouth contained in that garment. If a person takes the garment without recognizing that this utterance is primary, imagining instead that the garment gives him life, he not only fails to receive the utterance; the garment conceals it from him still further. Hashem therefore counsels us to take more than the garment itself, always recognizing the utterance within it. ‘Bring an omer before Me on Pesach’ teaches that at the very beginning of receiving a benefit, when its inward meaning is not yet recognized, it is still called animal food. A benefit whose inward meaning a person does not recognize is animal food. He should return that power to Hashem; this is what the omer offering signifies. Hashem promises that the grain in the fields will be blessed: He will give the person recognition of the benefit, so that he recognizes its inward meaning. This is called the grain in the fields—human food.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains what returning a possession to its source can mean while a person still uses it. Food is a garment through which life is received; the error is to treat that garment as an independent giver of life. The omer models receiving and returning the power in recognition of its Giver. This develops the siman’s account of livelihood as a place where one’s life is lodged, rather than reducing the connection to ownership alone.
connections.headline: Returning the power received through a possession

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתִּיקּוּן הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הַהֲשָׁבָה לַמָּקוֹר
connections.quote: “The commandment “Hear, Israel,” and so forth, concerns unity through hearing and faith. Once you have acknowledged His kingship over everything, no more is required: contemplation is not necessary, but rather accepting the yoke of Heaven’s kingship through faith, knowing that nothing is separate from Him or interposes before Him even after the world was created. But the commandment “You shall know,” and so forth, concerns contemplating this. This is the entire wisdom of the Work of Creation and the Work of the Chariot known to the masters of truth. The whole purpose of this wisdom is to demonstrate the truth of this unity: all creation, which appears separate from the Creator, has in truth no separation at all. This is the purpose of all creation—that all created beings recognize that they are not something separate from the Creator. This is the entire purpose of Torah and all the commandments: to purify the heart until it reaches this knowledge and apprehension through seeing and contemplation—that in every human activity, deed, and device, in everything whatsoever, nothing is separate from Him, blessed be He.”
connections.context: The parallel explains the act of returning to the source as recognition and contemplation of dependence on the Creator. It distinguishes accepting this in faith from attaining it through contemplation.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁיֵּדַע שֶׁהַכֹּל הוּא מֵעֶצֶם חַיּוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמְּחַיֵּיהוּ וּמְקַיְּימוֹ, זוּלַת זֶה הָיוּ כְּלֹא הָיָה
connections.displayRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 1:3-4
connections.linkedRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 1:3-4
connections.canonicalRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 1:3-4
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שני; שער היחוד והאמונה א׳:ג׳-ד׳
connections.quote: “It is written, “Forever, O Lord, Your word stands in the heavens.” The Baal Shem Tov, of blessed memory, explained: Your words, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters,” these words and letters stand and remain forever within the heavenly firmament and are forever clothed within all the firmaments to give them life, as it is written, “The word of our God will stand forever,” and “His words are living and enduring forever.” For if the letters were to depart for an instant, God forbid, and return to their source, all the heavens would become absolute nothingness and nonexistence; they would be as though they had never existed, exactly as before the utterance “Let there be a firmament.” The same applies to all creatures in all the higher and lower worlds. Even this physical earth, which is utterly inanimate: if the letters of the ten utterances through which the earth was created in the six days of Creation were to depart from it for an instant, God forbid, it would return to absolute nothingness and nonexistence, exactly as before the six days of Creation.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה סוֹד מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה עג שֶׁהָיָה לְיַעֲקֹב שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא עֶדְרֵי צֹאן,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Levi said: [Jacob had] six hundred thousand dogs. The Rabbis said: One million two hundred thousand. They do not disagree: the one who said six hundred thousand counts one dog for each flock; the one who said one million two hundred thousand counts two dogs for each flock.”
connections.context: The figure of six hundred thousand flocks follows from the number of dogs and dogs per flock in these two opinions. It is an inference from the Midrash’s explanation; a different estimate of Jacob’s flocks appears earlier in the same passage.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי נַפְשׁוֹ הָיְתָה כּוֹלֶלֶת שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נְפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל הַכְּלוּלָה כָּל אֶחָד מִפְּרָטֵי דּוֹרוֹתֵיהֶם,
connections.quote: “Yaakov encompasses the six hundred thousand souls of Israel. Therefore the Sages said in Bereshit Rabbah that he had six hundred thousand flocks of sheep: his property came from the portions of life. He rescued these from Lavan, for they were also rooted in him, since they issued from his daughters; but Yaakov rescued and separated the portion of life from him. After the birth of the tribes, which completed the form of the six hundred thousand souls, he saw the need “to provide for his own household,” to bring in property—that is, to repair all the particular portions of his soul.”
connections.context: This supplies Rav Tzadok’s own fuller explanation of the correspondence between Yaakov’s flocks and the souls included within him. The acquisition is described as a work of separation and repair.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָז עֲדַיִן נִקְרָא יַעֲקֹב שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת עַם הָאָרֶץ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק אֵלּוּ מְצִיאוֹת,
connections.quote: “What did they expound? As Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Ilai expounded: What is the meaning of “Tell My people their transgression, and the house of Yaakov their sins”? “Tell My people their transgression”—these are Torah scholars, whose inadvertent offenses are treated for them as deliberate ones. “And the house of Yaakov their sins”—these are the unlearned, whose deliberate offenses are treated for them as inadvertent ones. This is what we learned: Rabbi Yehudah says, “Be careful in study, for an error in study is counted as a deliberate offense.””
connections.context: This is the precise teaching behind the reference to the end of Elu Metziot. It uses “the house of Yaakov” for the unlearned and contrasts their responsibility with the greater responsibility of scholars.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם יִשְׂרָאֵל נִמְשְׁלוּ לְצֹאן, וְהָיָה קִנְיָנוֹ שֶׁנִּתְפַּרְנֵס מֵהֶם,
connections.quote: “This is what is then stated in Raaya Mehemna: the barley omer is animal food, and so forth, and of them it is said, “You are My flock, the flock of My pasture; you are human.” We find concerning Yaakov our father that he had six hundred thousand flocks of sheep, as the Midrash says: Reish Lakish says six hundred thousand; the Rabbis say one million two hundred thousand; they do not disagree, and so forth. The number six hundred thousand signifies the holiness of the congregation of Israel, which is six hundred thousand. Until the giving of the Torah, Israel were in the category of sheep—“the flock of My pasture.” They attained the holiness of the category of humanity—“you are called human”—only after the giving of the Torah, when they attained the beauty of Adam before the corruption. Although Yaakov himself truly possessed the very beauty of Adam, as stated in the holy Zohar, this concerned him personally: he was like Adam before the sin. But for his descendants he did not attain the level of “you are human” until after the giving of the Torah; before the giving of the Torah they were in the category of sheep. Although Yaakov our father said of himself, “The God who shepherds me,” considering himself also to be in the category of sheep—as the Midrash says, “There is no occupation more lowly than a shepherd,” and so forth—David said, “From the elders I gain understanding”: Yaakov called Him a shepherd, and so forth. The reason is that Yaakov considered himself to be in the category of sheep. In particular, the flocks that allude to his descendants really were in the category of sheep until the giving of the Torah, when they attained the level of “you are human.” For this reason we offer barley, animal food, in the omer. On Shavuot, the time when our Torah was given, when they had already merited being called human, with Adam’s beauty, the offering is “Eat of My bread”—the two loaves.”
connections.context: This parallel preserves an important distinction: Yaakov’s own attainment is not equated with that of his descendants before Sinai. It explains why the flocks can symbolize the collective stage before the giving of the Torah.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁלָּכֵן אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא קַמָּא צב:): בֵּירָא דִּשְׁתֵית מִנֵּיהּ מַיָּא לָא תִּשְׁדֵּי בֵּיהּ קָלָא,
connections.quote: ‘Rava asked Rabbah bar Mari: What is the source of the saying people use, ‘Do not throw a stone into a well from which you have drunk’? He answered: It is written: ‘Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother; and do not abhor an Egyptian, for you were a stranger in his land.’’

connections.hePhrase: [צב] לִפְעָמִים נִפְתָּח לָאָדָם מַדְרֵגוֹת, וְאִם הוּא רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ נֶעְלָם מִמֶּנּוּ וְהוּא חוֹזֵר לְסוּרוֹ לִהְיוֹת מְשׁוּקָּע בַּתַּאֲווֹת – יֵשׁ לוֹ לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן וְלִדְאוֹג פֶּן הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קח:) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁהִטְעִימָן מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא;
connections.quote: “Another explanation: Those seven days were when He gave them a foretaste of the World to Come, so that they would know the good they had denied themselves.”
connections.context: The taste is given before the Flood despite the generation’s coming destruction. Rav Tzadok therefore warns that a temporary spiritual opening, by itself, does not show that a person’s conduct has been repaired.

connections.hePhrase: [צב] לִפְעָמִים נִפְתָּח לָאָדָם מַדְרֵגוֹת, וְאִם הוּא רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ נֶעְלָם מִמֶּנּוּ וְהוּא חוֹזֵר לְסוּרוֹ לִהְיוֹת מְשׁוּקָּע בַּתַּאֲווֹת – יֵשׁ לוֹ לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן וְלִדְאוֹג פֶּן הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קח:) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁהִטְעִימָן מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא;
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 1:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 1:1
connections.quote: “Here, however, the expanded state came first. As the writings of the holy Ari teach, on this night the expanded consciousness preceded the constricted consciousness. The expanded state is like someone who understands a matter because he has a great intellect, without any labor at all. Yet, because it came without labor, he can easily forget it. This is unlike someone who understood a matter through labor: it becomes fixed in his heart so that he cannot forget it. Although this is called the constricted state, the matter is nevertheless fixed in his heart like a peg that will not move.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes the intensity of a revelation from its permanence. A person may grasp something through an extraordinary gift and still lose it; work makes the understanding fixed in the heart. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok treats the Flood generation’s taste of the world to come as an opening to repentance whose purpose was not fulfilled merely by experiencing it.
connections.headline: Gifted clarity and lasting acquisition

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק הָיָה קוֹרֵא שֶׁהָעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם הֲנָאָה וְחֶמְדָּה מֵעִנְיְנֵי תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק נֶהֱנִין מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה,
connections.quote: ‘Rav would often say: The World to Come is not like this world. In the World to Come there is no eating, drinking, procreation, business, jealousy, hatred, or rivalry. Rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah, as it says: ‘They beheld God, and they ate and drank.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר פְּתִיחַת אוֹר כָּזֶה הֲרֵי לֹא הָיוּ עוֹד בְּנֵי מַבּוּל, רַק עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁנִּפְתַּח לָהֶם לְשָׁעָה וְנֶעְלַם;
connections.quote: “In the heart there is a root of evil, as it is written, “For the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth”—that is, from its root; this concerns the sin of the generation of the Flood. Therefore repentance does not help for this, for it does not help a root of evil: evil does not become good. This refers to lower repentance. Rather, higher repentance is needed, from the World to Come, awakening from wisdom, which is the root of the root. There is no evil at all there in Israel, as it is said, “The soul You placed within me is pure.” For even the evil root has a root that is “very good,” as is known. [Therefore the Sages said that He gave the generation of the Flood a foretaste of the World to Come: this was to repair them as explained above, but it did not succeed.]”
connections.context: The qualification is essential: Rav Tzadok limits the statement that repentance does not help to lower repentance, then describes the higher repentance that reaches the root’s own good source. He also states that the offered taste did not accomplish this repair in the Flood generation.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא אֶחָד עִם הַדָּבָר אַחֵר דְּשָׁם דְּקָאָמַר: "זְמַן קָטָן אַחַר זְמַן גָּדוֹל", שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה זְמַן אוּלַי יָשׁוּבוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁפָּתַח לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹר כָּזֶה, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן הֶעְדֵּר הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הֶעֱלִימוֹ כְּרֶגַע וְחָזְרוּ לְתַאֲוָתָם.
connections.quote: “Another explanation: the Holy One, blessed be He, fixed a long period for them and afterward a short period.”
connections.context: This supplies the third interpretation used in the ois. It concerns the seven days mentioned immediately before the Flood; Rav Tzadok connects that final short extension with an opening for repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְאִידַךְ לִישָּׁנָא: שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי אֶבְלוֹ דִּמְתוּשֶׁלַח, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמִיתַת צַדִּיקִים מְכַפֶּרֶת כְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ (יוֹמָא מב.),
connections.quote: ““After the seven days, the waters of the Flood were upon the earth.” What was the nature of those seven days?”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִידַךְ לִישָּׁנָא: שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי אֶבְלוֹ דִּמְתוּשֶׁלַח, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמִיתַת צַדִּיקִים מְכַפֶּרֶת כְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ (יוֹמָא מב.),
connections.quote: “Rav said: These were the days of mourning for Methuselah, teaching that the eulogy of the righteous delays calamity.”
connections.context: The Gemara offers several explanations of the seven days before the Flood. This note supplies the mourning interpretation to which Rav Tzadok returns below; the neighboring note supplies the interpretation about a foretaste of the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: וְאִידַךְ לִישָּׁנָא: שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי אֶבְלוֹ דִּמְתוּשֶׁלַח, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמִיתַת צַדִּיקִים מְכַפֶּרֶת כְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ (יוֹמָא מב.),
connections.quote: “Why is Miriam’s death placed beside the passage of the red heifer? To tell you: Just as the red heifer atones, so the death of the righteous atones.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִידַךְ לִישָּׁנָא: שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי אֶבְלוֹ דִּמְתוּשֶׁלַח, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמִיתַת צַדִּיקִים מְכַפֶּרֶת כְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ (יוֹמָא מב.),
connections.quote: “Why does [Scripture] mention their death on Yom Kippur? To teach you that just as Yom Kippur atones for Israel, so the death of the righteous atones for Israel.”
connections.context: The Bavli compares the deaths of Miriam and Aaron with the red heifer and priestly garments; the Yerushalmi connects the deaths of Aaron’s sons with Yom Kippur. These are the actual sources for the atonement comparison. The printed Yoma 42b passage concerns the red-heifer rite and does not state this teaching.

connections.hePhrase: וְאִידַךְ לִישָּׁנָא: שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי אֶבְלוֹ דִּמְתוּשֶׁלַח, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמִיתַת צַדִּיקִים מְכַפֶּרֶת כְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ (יוֹמָא מב.),
connections.quote: “For the red heifer [the scarlet wool weighs] ten zuz; for the scapegoat, two sela; and for the person with tzaraat, one shekel. Rabbi Yochanan said: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta and the Rabbis disagree concerning the red heifer: one says a weight of ten, and one says a weight of one shekel. Your mnemonic is “One who brings much and one who brings little.” Rabbi Yirmeyah of Difti said to Ravina: They do not disagree concerning the red heifer; they disagree concerning the scapegoat. On that day Ravia bar Kisi died, and they established this mnemonic: “Ravia [bar] Kisi atones like the scapegoat.””
connections.context: The specific comparison with the scapegoat occurs on Yoma 42a, in this memorial mnemonic. This supplies the original wording alongside the existing note’s other parallels concerning the death of the righteous.

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן (שְׁבוּעוֹת יג.) גַּם בְּשָׂעִיר צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה,
connections.quote: “Could Yom Kippur atone for those who repent and those who do not repent? … Just as a sin offering and a guilt offering atone only for those who repent, so Yom Kippur atones only for those who repent.”

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן (שְׁבוּעוֹת יג.) גַּם בְּשָׂעִיר צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה,
connections.quote: “[One might argue that] it atones for those who repent and those who do not repent. The verse therefore says “but”—making a distinction.”

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לַן (שְׁבוּעוֹת יג.) גַּם בְּשָׂעִיר צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה,
connections.quote: “Who is the author of an anonymous Sifra? Rabbi Yehuda. And he says: Those who repent, yes; those who do not repent, no.”
connections.context: The discussion contrasts Rabbi Yehuda’s requirement of repentance with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s different position earlier on the page. Rav Tzadok invokes the former. The previous quotation presented the latter position, which would reverse his point.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הַחִלּוּק בָּזֶה: הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פּוֹתֵחַ הַפֶּתַח לִתְשׁוּבָה וּמֵאִיר אוֹרוֹ בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא קוֹדֶם וְכַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל;
connections.quote: “It is known what the Sages said concerning “Hashem is your shadow”: He is like the shadow that does what the body itself does. All His attributes are measure for measure; it is not without cause, but because they also turn their attention to Him. Yet the blessed God desires that awakening from below come first: “Return to Me and I shall return to you,” while we ask, “Bring us back to You, and we shall return.” For we have no strength to begin: You must first bring us back through awakening from above, and then we shall return. So it was in Egypt: through awakening from above, the blessed God sent them “I have surely taken notice,” and through this “they will listen to your voice”—they would immediately believe this declaration. By Moshe our teacher’s saying “I have surely taken notice,” he introduced into their hearts complete faith in the blessed God’s providence over them. They therefore listened specifically to his voice: through his voice he brought hearing into them, through that very voice and declaration of “I have surely taken notice,” which he placed within their hearts. As soon as this entered their hearts, they understood the truth that the blessed God was certainly taking notice of them. Once it was revealed in the depths of their hearts that He watches over them, and they believed this with complete faith, it was certainly fitting in judgment that He watch over them. The removal of providence and of God’s remembrance of a person occurs only when the person is also in concealment from God. But when a person remembers God and believes that God is with him and watches over all his affairs, God certainly remembers and watches over him too. In Egypt they had been utterly submerged in forgetfulness. They possessed this sign: the redeemer who spoke in the language of taking notice would introduce into their hearts the awareness and remembrance that there is a blessed Creator who directs, watches over, and can bring them out of Egypt. Through this, the corresponding attention above follows. There cannot be attention above without remembrance also entering their hearts. Sometimes the awakening above comes first, but afterward, in any event, there must be awakening below. This is the sign of the redeemer’s using the language of taking notice: they could immediately sense in their hearts whether that awareness arose within them too. So it was: “The people believed, and they heard that He had taken notice.” Through hearing that He had taken notice, faith entered their hearts.”
connections.context: The complete unit distinguishes the initiative from above from the response that must follow below. It explains why receiving an opening does not dispense with the person’s own return.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בְּאוֹתָם יְמֵי אֶבְלוֹ הָיָה כֵּן אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא מִקּוֹדֶם, אַחַר זְמַן גָּדוֹל שֶׁהָיָה קוֹדֶם לִהְיוֹת שׁוּבוּ וְכוּלֵי בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא:
connections.quote: “When they departed, what is written? “To go to the land of Canaan”—their desire was to go there. From this we learn that whoever awakens to become pure is assisted. Come and see that this is so: once it says “to go to the land of Canaan,” immediately “Hashem said to Avram: Go forth.” Before he first awakened, “Go forth” was not written. Come and see: what is above does not awaken until an awakening below first provides something upon which the awakening above can rest. The mystery of the matter is that the dark light does not unite with the white light until it first awakens. Once it first awakens, the white light immediately rests upon it. Therefore it is written, “God, do not be silent; do not be still and do not be quiet, God,” so that the white light never cease from the world. Likewise, “You who mention Hashem, give yourselves no rest,” in order to awaken below that upon which awakening above may rest. Thus, once a person first awakens, the awakening above then arises. Come and see: once it is written, “They went forth with them from Ur Kasdim,” immediately, “Hashem said to Avram,” and so forth.”
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s account of the ordinary sequence: human initiative followed by help from above. The ois contrasts that sequence with the exceptional prior opening given during the final days before the Flood.

connections.hePhrase: [צג] תְּחִלָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לָאָדָם, וְהָאָדָם אֵין רָגִיל בָּזֶה עֲדַיִן וְקָשֶׁה עָלָיו לְקַבְּלוֹ כְּיָתֵד קָבוּעַ בְּמָקוֹם נֶאֱמָן שֶׁלֹּא יִמּוֹט, וּמְאַבְּדוֹ;
connections.quote: “Shabbat 13b says: ‘Who wrote Megillat Ta’anit? They said: Chananyah ben Chizkiyah and his circle, who cherished the troubles.’ Apparently it should have said that they cherished the miracles; what have they to do with the troubles? Yet through the troubles and decrees they merited Torah’s illumination. As it says, ‘Your rod and Your staff comfort me’: precisely through the disciplinary rod, the support came to them with greater force. Pirkei Heikhalot says that although the Divine Presence did not dwell in the Second Temple, Torah’s splendor, preciousness, honor, and greatness were not given until the Second Temple. The intention is the Hasmonean period, when the illumination of Oral Torah began.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah explains the otherwise surprising expression ‘cherished the troubles’: the troubles became the setting in which greater Torah illumination was acquired. It invokes the same contrast between the Second Temple’s concealed Shechinah and its expanded Torah. The parallel clarifies the present siman’s movement from a light first bestowed and then lost to wisdom patiently sought in concealment. The gain is the Torah received through the renewed search, not difficulty considered in isolation.
connections.headline: Torah acquired through difficulty can exceed an earlier unearned illumination

connections.hePhrase: [צג] תְּחִלָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לָאָדָם, וְהָאָדָם אֵין רָגִיל בָּזֶה עֲדַיִן וְקָשֶׁה עָלָיו לְקַבְּלוֹ כְּיָתֵד קָבוּעַ בְּמָקוֹם נֶאֱמָן שֶׁלֹּא יִמּוֹט, וּמְאַבְּדוֹ;
connections.quote: “The meaning of a blessing after it is what remains permanently in a person’s heart after he engages in Torah. A blessing before it concerns the person’s drawing words of Torah into his heart. But the result of those words of Torah that he has drawn into himself should remain in his heart permanently, like a peg that will never move. That permanence is called the blessing after it.”
connections.explanation: The Ishbitz teaching defines permanence by what remains after the act of learning. That distinction illuminates the siman’s opening difficulty: receiving light does not yet make it a fixed possession. The comparison supplements the existing historical explanation of the Second Temple with a description of the inward result sought by the learner.
connections.headline: What remains after Torah study

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ הָאָדָם נוֹהֶה אַחֲרָיו וּמְבַקְּשׁוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר וּפוֹתֵחַ לוֹ, כְּטַעֲנַת "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְכוּלֵי", אִם לֹא בְּקֹשִׁי גָּדוֹל, כְּעִנְיַן "כְּשֶׁרָצִיתִי לֹא רָצִיתָ, עַכְשָׁו וְכוּלֵי" (בְּרָכוֹת ז.).
connections.quote: see note 416.
connections.context: The Midrash presents the petition as a dialogue about who must begin the return. This is the background to Rav Tzadok’s reference to the plea “Bring us back.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ הָאָדָם נוֹהֶה אַחֲרָיו וּמְבַקְּשׁוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר וּפוֹתֵחַ לוֹ, כְּטַעֲנַת "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְכוּלֵי", אִם לֹא בְּקֹשִׁי גָּדוֹל, כְּעִנְיַן "כְּשֶׁרָצִיתִי לֹא רָצִיתָ, עַכְשָׁו וְכוּלֵי" (בְּרָכוֹת ז.).
connections.quote: ‘‘He said: You cannot see My face.’ It was taught in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah: This is what the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: ‘When I wished, you did not wish. Now that you wish, I do not wish.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, הָיָה בִּכְפִיַּת הַר כְּגִיגִית, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הָדָר קִבְּלוּהָ בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ בְּרָצוֹן;
connections.quote: see note 444.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לֹא נַעֲשָׂה לָהֶם נֵס בִּימֵי עֶזְרָא כְּבִימֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן, שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא כִּדְאִיתָא בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (ד.), רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר חֵטְא הַקּוֹדֵם;
connections.quote: ‘‘Until Your people pass over, Hashem’ refers to the first entry; ‘until this people whom You acquired passes over’ refers to the second entry. From here the Sages said: Israel was worthy of having a miracle performed for them in Ezra’s days, just as one had been performed for them in the days of Joshua son of Nun, but sin prevented it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא שָׁרְתָה שְׁכִינָה בְּבַיִת שֵׁנִי.
connections.quote: “But was there fire in the Second Temple? Rav Shmuel bar Inya said: What is meant by the verse, ‘I shall take pleasure in it and be honored,’ where ve’ekkaved is written but ve’ekkavedah is read? Why is the letter hei missing? These are the five things that distinguished the First Temple from the Second Temple: the Ark, its cover, and the cherubim; the fire; the Shechinah; ruach hakodesh; and the Urim and Tummim. They answered: Yes, the fire was there, but it did not assist in the burning.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא שָׁרְתָה שְׁכִינָה בְּבַיִת שֵׁנִי.
connections.quote: “From the day the Divine Presence rested upon Mount Sinai at the giving of the Torah, it did not depart from Israel until the First Temple was destroyed. From the destruction of the First Temple, the Divine Presence did not rest among Israel, for in the Second Temple the Divine Presence did not rest. The intention is not to say that the Divine Presence did not rest in the Second Temple at all, for we find that it rests among twenty thousand, from what is written, “Return, Hashem, to the myriads of the thousands of Israel,” and, “The chariots of God are myriads, thousands upon thousands; Hashem is among them.” It need hardly be said that the Divine Presence rests among forty thousand. Moreover, Scripture testifies, “I shall be pleased with it and be glorified”—meaning: I shall cause the Glory, which is the Divine Presence, to rest in it. Rather, it did not rest there constantly as in the First Temple, because there were not six hundred thousand there: only forty thousand came up from Babylonia, as it is written, “The entire congregation together was forty thousand.” This is what the Sages expounded concerning “I shall be pleased with it and be glorified”: the written form of “be glorified” lacks the letter heh because five things were missing there—the Ark, the anointing oil, fire, the Divine Presence, and the Urim and Tummim. For this reason it says “be glorified,” to explain that the Glory, which is the Divine Presence, was there, but not Tiferet; this is the force of “be glorified,” excluding Tiferet. The missing heh, the last letter of the Name, indicates the absence of the Divine Presence, for it is among the five things that were missing. How was it absent, when Scripture says “I shall be glorified”? Rather, it did not rest there constantly as in the First Temple, but hovered over it. In the future, however, Israel will be numerous beyond counting. This is what is written: “The number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea.” It does not say, “The seed of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea,” but “the number”—meaning that those counted from twenty years of age and upward will be like the sand of the sea. Then Tiferet and the Glory will return. So Yeshayahu promised: “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of Hashem has shone upon you.” Understand this.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya expressly qualifies the statement that the Divine Presence did not rest in the Second Temple: he distinguishes its constant dwelling from its intermittent or hovering presence. The whole qualification is retained, together with his distinction between Glory and Tiferet.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אִיתָא בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר הֵיכָלוֹת שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּתְּנָה תּוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּל מַעֲלוֹתֶיהָ, עַיֵּין שָׁם י"ז מַעֲלוֹת דְּחָשֵׁיב, לֹא הָיוּ עַד הַבַּיִת שֵׁנִי, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא שָׁרְתָה בּוֹ שְׁכִינָה.
connections.quote: “As is stated explicitly in Sefer Heikhalot, the principal radiance and splendor of Torah were in the Second Temple period, even though the Divine Presence did not rest there. See there the many expressions of praise concerning that time, and how, because they longed for the blessed Lord to reveal the secrets of Torah to them, He promised them this. This is revelation through the wisdom of Oral Torah. They longed for it, to attain still greater understandings, even though it comes through concealment. Through this came the departure of prophecy: through the intensity of their longing for the revelation of Torah insights far above the attainment of the prophets, and for the mysteries of Oral Torah within their hearts in a concealed way, which is the quality of night. Prophecy, which was drawn from the prophecy of Moses our teacher, of blessed memory, departed. Therefore the prophets’ words, too, appeared in writing, like Written Torah, whose quality is day—that is, clear revelation, without darkness or concealment.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s parallel discussion in Machshavot Charutz. It confirms how he understands the Heikhalot tradition: the Second Temple period disclosed the splendor of Oral Torah despite the absence of overt revelation of the Divine Presence. The quotation is from Machshavot Charutz, not from Sefer Heikhalot itself, and does not enumerate the seventeen virtues mentioned in the reader.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אִיתָא בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר הֵיכָלוֹת שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּתְּנָה תּוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּל מַעֲלוֹתֶיהָ, עַיֵּין שָׁם י"ז מַעֲלוֹת דְּחָשֵׁיב, לֹא הָיוּ עַד הַבַּיִת שֵׁנִי, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא שָׁרְתָה בּוֹ שְׁכִינָה.
