connections.quote: “Rabbi Yishmael said: Thus said Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Eliezer the Great: From the day the Torah was given until the last Temple was built, the Torah was given, but its splendor, preciousness, greatness, honor, beauty, awe, dread, fear, wealth, majesty, exaltation, strength, might, and honor were not given until the last Temple was built; the Divine Presence did not rest in it.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין עוֹד שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁלֹּא הִנִּיחוּ אֶבֶן עַל אֶבֶן בְּבַיִת שֵׁנִי עַד שֶׁכָּפוּ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְגִלָּה לָהֶם רָזֵי כָּל דָּבָר, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yishmael said: Thus said Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Eliezer the Great: Our ancestors did not undertake to place one stone upon another in the Sanctuary until they compelled the King of the world and all His servants, who attended to them, and He revealed to them the secret of Torah—how they should perform it and how they should make use of it. Immediately the holy spirit appeared from the great passageway in the House of Hashem, for the Divine Presence had neither descended nor rested in the Holy of Holies because of the decree.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּכְפִיָּה זוֹ הוּא בִּיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ בְּפֶרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין (בְּרָכוֹת לב.) וּבְהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה נב:)].
connections.quote: “They said, ‘Since this is a time of favor, let us ask for mercy concerning the inclination toward sexual transgression.’ They asked for mercy, and it was delivered into their hands. He warned them, ‘Take care: if you kill it, the world will come to an end.’ They imprisoned it for three days, and when they sought a freshly laid egg throughout the Land of Israel, none could be found. They said, ‘What shall we do? If we kill it, the world will come to an end. Shall we ask for mercy concerning half of it? Heaven does not grant things by halves.’ They blinded its eyes and released it. This did help: it no longer aroused a person toward his close female relatives.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּכְפִיָּה זוֹ הוּא בִּיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ בְּפֶרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין (בְּרָכוֹת לב.) וּבְהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה נב:)].
connections.quote: ““They cried out to Hashem God with a great voice.” What did they say? Rav said, and some say Rabbi Yochanan: Woe, woe! This is the one that destroyed the Temple, burned its Sanctuary, killed all the righteous, exiled Israel from their land, and still dances among us. Did You give it to us for any reason other than that we should receive reward through it? We want neither it nor its reward! A note fell to them from heaven, on which “Truth” was written. Rav Chanina said: Learn from this that the seal of the Holy One, blessed be He, is truth. They observed a fast for three days and three nights, and it was handed over to them. It emerged like a fiery lion cub from the Holy of Holies. A prophet said to Israel: This is the inclination to idolatry, as it is stated, “He said: This is wickedness.” As they seized it, a hair slipped from its mane; it cried out, and its voice traveled four hundred parasangs. They said: What shall we do? Perhaps, Heaven forbid, they will have mercy on it from heaven. A prophet told them: Throw it into a lead pot and cover its mouth with lead, for lead absorbs sound, as it is stated, “He said: This is wickedness. He cast it into the ephah and cast the lead weight over its mouth.””
connections.context: This is the account of the cancellation of the inclination to idolatry. The existing note quotes the subsequent attempt to cancel sexual desire; the present passage supplies the earlier, distinct event to which the ois also alludes.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּכְפִיָּה זוֹ הוּא בִּיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ בְּפֶרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין (בְּרָכוֹת לב.) וּבְהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה נב:)].
connections.quote: see note 280.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּכְפִיָּה זוֹ הוּא בִּיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ בְּפֶרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין (בְּרָכוֹת לב.) וּבְהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה נב:)].
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: Were it not for these three verses, the feet of “the enemies of Israel” [a euphemism for Israel] would have collapsed. One is that it is written, “And whom I have caused harm”; another, “As clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, house of Israel”; and another, “I shall remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” Rav Pappa said: From here: “I shall place My spirit within you, and cause you to walk in My statutes.””
connections.context: This is the passage in the chapter Ein Omdin behind the reference to “whom I have caused harm.” The parallel in Sukkah 52b likewise cites these verses. The statement places human struggle alongside divine formation and help.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּכְפִיָּה זוֹ הוּא בִּיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ בְּפֶרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין (בְּרָכוֹת לב.) וּבְהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה נב:)].
connections.quote: “Rav Chana bar Acha said: They say in the school of Rav: There are four things that the Holy One, blessed be He, regrets having created: exile, the Chaldeans, the Ishmaelites, and the evil inclination. … The evil inclination, as it is written: “And whom I have harmed.””
connections.context: The Gemara reads “whom I have harmed” (Micah 4:6) as the evil inclination itself, the verse Rav Tzadok cites here.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה בְּהֶעְלֵם הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ אֵיכָה): "הַלְוַאי אוֹתִי עָזָבוּ וְתוֹרָתִי שָׁמָרוּ";
connections.displayRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.linkedRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6

connections.heRef: דרך ה', חלק רביעי, בתלמוד תורה ו׳
connections.quote: “Torah study in relation to the influences it brings: The second condition is rectifying one’s conduct. One who wishes to draw down an influence must be worthy and prepared to draw it down. But if he defiles himself through guilt and transgression, distances himself from his Creator, and strays after the powers of impurity and evil, it will certainly be said of him: “To the wicked, God said: What right have you to recount My statutes?” Likewise the Sages said: Whoever teaches an unworthy student is as though he throws a stone to Markulis. Such a person’s Torah will certainly draw down none of the influence we have described. Nevertheless, the Sages revealed a great secret to us: had the wicked not abandoned Torah study, they would ultimately have returned to the good. Although they cannot draw down any influence from before Him, as explained, the words of Torah themselves remain holy in their own right. Through persistent engagement with them, they will bring the student, time after time, a little awakening, like the faintest glimmer of illumination, which will eventually prevail over him and bring him back to the good. This is what the Sages wrote: “If only they had abandoned Me but kept My Torah, for its light brings them back to the good.” It is clear, however, that this does not concern someone who engages with it as mockery or jest, or to give it interpretations contrary to halakhah. Rather, he must engage with it at least as someone engages with other fields of wisdom.”
connections.context: Ramchal explains how continued study can gradually restore a person even when his conduct prevents the fuller influence of Torah. He explicitly excludes study undertaken as mockery or for distortion; that restriction is part of the quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה בְּהֶעְלֵם הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ אֵיכָה): "הַלְוַאי אוֹתִי עָזָבוּ וְתוֹרָתִי שָׁמָרוּ";
connections.quote: see note 74.
connections.context: This is the wording of the teaching at the opening of Eikhah Rabbah. It supplies the reason for the hope expressed in the ois: the Torah’s own light can bring its students back.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה בֶּאֱמֶת גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.): "חָכָם עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא":
connections.quote: “Through the wisdom of the Oral Torah, which brings human wisdom into Torah, Esav and also Amalek are overcome, for through this one is attached to Torah’s hidden root. As it is written in Bava Batra: “A sage is greater than a prophet”; see Ramban there, who explains that this is attainment through the holy spirit. This means a spirit from the higher holiness—higher wisdom—which influences lower wisdom. The fiftieth gate hidden from Moshe our teacher refers to his attainment through prophecy, which is like seeing with his own eyes. Concerning this, according to one opinion in Rosh Hashanah, they said: “Among prophets none arose, but among kings one arose.” This means attainment through the attribute of kingship, lower wisdom. Although this is a lesser mode of attainment, it has an advantage in being able to attain matters that are higher. As is known, the divine Rabbi Yitzchak [the Ari] revealed the place and root from which Moshe our teacher’s attainment came, and he revealed lofty secrets far above that root. But all his attainments were only through the holy spirit, which bears no comparison with prophetic vision—even the unclear mirror of the other prophets, and all the more so the prophecy of Moshe our teacher. Prophetic attainment is revealed attainment, and through revelation one can attain only what can be attained in this world. Concerning the attainment of the World to Come, “No eye has seen”—meaning the eyes of the prophets, who see with the eye. The sages’ attainment, by contrast, comes from concealment, and they can also attain the hidden root. Although it is said concerning this, “Do not investigate what is beyond you,” and so forth—for the root hidden from every creature’s eye is called “beyond,” the supreme wonder, where there is no permission to inquire at all—this means attaining it completely through wisdom. Nevertheless, they have a hold upon it because the root of their wisdom comes from there. Since it is the wisdom of their hearts that has become Torah, it is attached to its root.”
connections.context: The parallel distinguishes the range of wisdom’s subject matter from the clarity of prophetic vision. Its explicit qualification prevents the statement “a sage is greater” from being read as equating later inspiration with Moshe’s prophecy.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה בֶּאֱמֶת גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.): "חָכָם עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא":
connections.quote: “Amemar said: A sage is superior to a prophet, as it is said: ‘And let us bring a heart of wisdom’—ve’navi levav hokhmah, understood here as an allusion to a navi, a prophet, with a wise heart. Which is described in terms of which? You must say that the lesser is described in terms of the greater. Abaye said: You can see this from the fact that a great scholar states a teaching, and the same teaching is reported in the name of another great scholar. Rava said: What proves the point here? Perhaps the two share the same mazal! Rather, Rava said: You can see it from the fact that a great scholar states a teaching, and the same teaching is reported in the name of Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef. Rav Ashi said: What proves the point here? Perhaps, with regard to this matter, he shares Rabbi Akiva’s mazal!”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה בֶּאֱמֶת גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.): "חָכָם עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא":
connections.heRef: חידושי רמב"ן על בבא בתרא י״ב א:א׳
connections.quote: “Regarding the statement, “From the day the Temple was destroyed, although prophecy was taken from the prophets, it was not taken from the sages”: Rashi explained, “Although it was taken from prophets who are not sages.” This can be challenged, for in tractate Nedarim we say that the Holy One, blessed be He, causes His Presence to rest only upon someone wise, strong, and wealthy. Some answered that He causes His Presence to rest without interruption only upon a sage, but a prophet sent on a mission is different, such as the prophecy of Yonah son of Amittai on the mission to Nineveh. I am not satisfied with this. Rather, it means: although the prophecy of the prophets, which is appearance and vision, was removed, the prophecy of the sages, which comes by way of wisdom, was not removed. They know the truth through the holy spirit within them. For on a temporary occasion He causes His Presence to rest even upon pious people who are not sages; there we say, “From where do we know this? From Moshe,” and Moshe’s prophecy did not cease. This is the force of the expression “causes His Presence to rest.” Although the proof concerning wealth is also brought from Yonah, he was a prophet without interruption, but was sent only to Nineveh.”
connections.context: Ramban distinguishes prophetic appearance and vision from the sages’ knowledge of truth through the holy spirit. The quotation retains his objection to the alternative explanation and his distinction between continuous and occasional inspiration.

connections.hePhrase: [צד] פְּעָמִים מַשִּׂיג הָאָדָם הֶאָרָה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מַגִּיעַ לְיִרְאָה, וְהוּא פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם;
connections.quote: ““I have placed Hashem before me always” is a great principle of Torah and of the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person’s sitting, movements, and activities when he is alone in his house are not like his sitting, movements, and activities when he is before a great king. Nor are his speech and free expression when he is with his household and relatives like his speech in the king’s presence. All the more so when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, as it is stated, “Can a man hide in hidden places and I not see him? says Hashem.” Immediately fear and submission will come upon him in awe of the blessed God, and shame before Him always. [Guide of the Perplexed, Part III, chapter 52.]”
connections.context: Rema describes awareness of God’s presence as the immediate source of fear, submission, and shame. This gives the practical counterpart to the opening description of illumination leading to awe.

connections.hePhrase: [צד] פְּעָמִים מַשִּׂיג הָאָדָם הֶאָרָה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מַגִּיעַ לְיִרְאָה, וְהוּא פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם;
connections.quote: “These three kinds of repentance proceed from below upward. First a person has compassion on himself; this is easy for anyone to awaken on his own. Afterward he begins to feel awe before Hashem and the splendor of His majesty, and through this he sighs over his sins. Afterward he comes to love of Hashem and weeps before Him over what has already passed and is no longer.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla describes the movement that the siman compresses into a few lines: self-concern gives way to awe before Hashem, and awe can lead to love. The quoted sequence explains why the first alarming illumination is an opening that requires a response, rather than a condition in which the person is meant to remain.
connections.headline: The passage from awe to love

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ עַל יָדוֹ לְאַהֲבָה, הוּא פָּנִים שֶׁל רָצוֹן;
connections.quote: “Sometimes there is a face of wrath, as in “The face of Hashem dispersed them.” There is also a face of favor, as in “Shine Your face upon Your servant.” Everything depends upon the source from which it draws: when it draws from Chesed, there is a face of favor and mercy; when it draws from Gevurah, then, Heaven forbid, there is a face of wrath. In this way Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explained in Raaya Mehemna, Ki Tetze, page 282a: the faces of the sun are Gedulah and Gevurah; the faces of the moon are Netzach and Hod. Those on the right are of mercy, and those on the left are of wrath. Everything depends upon the influence reaching the sun or the moon.”
connections.context: The passage explains the same paired expressions within the symbolism of the sefirot. Favor and wrath describe differing influences, rather than two unrelated meanings of “face.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ, הוּא מְתַקֵּן הַזַּעַם שֶׁבַּפָּנִים וּמִתְהַפֵּךְ לְרָצוֹן, וּבָא אַחַר כָּךְ לְאַהֲבָה.
connections.quote: ““May Hashem lift His face toward you,” and so forth: may He remove His anger from you. “Lift” here means removal, as in “Pharaoh will lift your head,” and so forth. “His face”—these are faces of wrath, as in “I shall set My face against that person,” and so forth. That is: He will remove from you those faces of wrath that were fit to come upon you.”
connections.context: This is the Midrash’s opening interpretation of the priestly blessing. It explicitly reads the lifting of the face as the removal of the wrath that the person would otherwise encounter.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אִם מַדְחֶה אָז מִפָּנָיו עַל יְדֵי הוֹלֵלוּת וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת, אָז אֵין נִתְקַן חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, וְאָז הוּא "וְנָתַתִּי פָנַי בָּאִישׁ הַהוּא וְגוֹמֵר", רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן.
connections.quote: ‘I will set My face against that man and his family, and I will cut off from among their people both him and all who go astray after him, going astray after Molech.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי לְעוֹלָם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא פּוֹתֵחַ שַׁעַר לִתְשׁוּבָה, וּבִשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ אָדָם רוֹאֶה שְׁכִינָה, זֶה נִקְרָא פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם;
connections.quote: “Another explanation of “like Hashem our God”: This is what Scripture says, “As for me, may my prayer to You, Hashem, be at a time of favor.” Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa asked Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: What is the meaning of this verse? He answered: The gates of prayer are sometimes open and sometimes locked, but the gates of repentance are always open. He asked: From where is this known? For it is written, “With awesome deeds in righteousness You answer us, God of our salvation, the trust of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea.” Just as a ritual pool is sometimes open and sometimes locked, so the gates of prayer are sometimes open and sometimes locked; but as the sea is always open, so the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is always open to receive those who return. Rav Anan said: Even the gates of prayer are never locked, as it is written, “Like Hashem our God whenever we call to Him.” Calling means prayer, as it is stated, “Before they call, I shall answer.” Rabbi Chiya the Great said: It is written, “Hope to Hashem; be strong, and He will strengthen your heart; hope to Hashem.” Pray and pray again, for there is an hour when it will be granted to you. Another explanation of “As for me, may my prayer”: David said “a time of favor” because he was an individual. But the prayer of a congregation never returns empty. Thus: “Like Hashem our God whenever we call to Him.””
connections.context: The Midrash expressly states that the gates of repentance are always open. Its surrounding discussion also preserves the alternative opinion that the gates of prayer are never locked, and the distinction concerning communal prayer.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי לְעוֹלָם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא פּוֹתֵחַ שַׁעַר לִתְשׁוּבָה, וּבִשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ אָדָם רוֹאֶה שְׁכִינָה, זֶה נִקְרָא פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Dosa says: It is stated, “A human being cannot see Me and live.” During their lives they do not see, but at the time of their death they do see. Likewise it says, “Before Him all who go down to the dust shall bow, and he did not keep his soul alive.””
connections.context: Rabbi Dosa supplies the original teaching about seeing at the time of death. Rav Tzadok connects that encounter here with the continuing opening for repentance; that further connection is his explanation of the teaching.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמַר: "פָּנַי יֵלֵכוּ וַהֲנִחֹתִי לָךְ", כִּי יִרְאָה אֵינֶנָּה נִיחָא כַּנּוֹדָע:
connections.quote: ‘He said: ‘My Presence will go, and I will give you rest.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמַר: "פָּנַי יֵלֵכוּ וַהֲנִחֹתִי לָךְ", כִּי יִרְאָה אֵינֶנָּה נִיחָא כַּנּוֹדָע:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan also said in the name of Rabbi Yosei: From where do we know that one should not try to appease a person at the time of his anger? For it is written, “My face will go, and I shall give you rest.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: Wait for Me until the faces of wrath pass, and I shall give you rest.”
connections.context: The Gemara reads the verse as the passing of wrath followed by rest. Rav Tzadok uses that reading at the conclusion of the ois to explain the transition beyond the unrest of fear.

connections.hePhrase: [צה] בִּימֵי הַנְּעוּרִים רְתִיחַת הַתַּאֲוָה מִתְגַּבֶּרֶת, וְאָז מַרְבֶּה חֲטָאִים מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן, וְהֵם חַטֹּאת נְעוּרִים;
connections.quote: “I dreamed [while I was in Izbica] that certain matters concerning the root of my soul were being revealed to me. Among these matters, I was told that the generation of the Messiah would be the very same souls as the generation of the wilderness [and the Messiah is the soul of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, as mentioned in Raaya Mehemna, Zohar III, 246b]. They themselves are the same souls as the generation of the Flood [for Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was there too, as stated in the Zohar, III, 216b, and as they said in Chullin 139b: beshagam has the numerical value of Moshe]. At that time they corrupted their way. This sin is called in the books “the sin of youth,” as it is said of them, “for the inclination … from his youth.” They repaired this in the generation of the wilderness, when it was called “the kindness of youth” [as is known concerning the inward meaning of “a person’s desire is his kindness”], as it is written, “I remember for you the kindness of your youth.” The generation of the Messiah will embody “your youth is renewed like the eagle’s”: the same generation of youthful kindness will be renewed a second time. This is the substance of what I still remember.”
connections.explanation: Divrei Chalomot records the same sequence as a remembered dream, explicitly identifying the souls across the three generations. Tzidkat HaTzadik supplies the analysis of their work: youthful intensity first becomes corruption, then longing for Torah, and finally a good that transforms the intermingled evil. The parallel helps the reader distinguish the reported visionary setting from this siman’s explanation of the spiritual process. Neither passage describes the final renewal as a mere return to youthful innocence.
connections.headline: The three generations describe successive uses of the same youthful power

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה הָיָה בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו".
connections.quote: ‘Hashem smelled the pleasing aroma, and Hashem said in His heart: ‘I will not again curse the ground because of man, for the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; nor will I again strike down every living thing as I have done.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה הָיָה בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו".
connections.quote: “It is known that being called “evil” in the eyes of the blessed God concerns impairment of the covenant, as was said of Er: “Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem, [and Hashem put him to death],” and of King David concerning that incident: “I have done what is evil in Your eyes.” This is the root of evil in creation: the creation of the foreskin that covers the holy covenant. It is named only after the nations, as it is said, “All the nations are uncircumcised,” as we learn in Nedarim; this is the root of the nations’ evil in creation. For this reason the commandment of circumcision was given to Israel, who can remove that evil present from birth, because for them it is not at the root, but like thorns surrounding the rose and thorns around a myrtle. Although evil also has a hold upon that limb in Israel—this is the touching of the hollow of Yaakov’s thigh, where Esav’s angel had the power to accuse, since there is some root there of the little folly present from birth, concerning which they said, “Full of iniquity—even the most pious of the pious intends only his own pleasure”—concerning this it is said, “I shall remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” The Sages expounded: “A heart to bring forth flesh.” This will occur only in the future, through the blessed God’s removal of the heart of stone by slaughtering the evil inclination. Although Yaakov our father merited this even in this world, as they said concerning “Give me my wife”—“It was said only to establish descendants”—and therefore it is stated that he did not die, nevertheless, on account of his descendants, who are not like this, the hollow of his thigh was touched. But all this is only temporary, in this world, which resembles night: it is the world of falsehood, which lasts “only for a moment.” As soon as the sun shone upon him, he was healed of his limp. For in truth even the uncircumcised of Israel are called circumcised, since the foreskin is not at their root at all, and “what is destined to be cut is regarded as already cut.””
connections.context: The parallel explains why an inclination present from youth is nevertheless open to repair. It preserves the difference between Yaakov’s individual attainment, his descendants’ present struggle, and the complete removal of the inclination in the future.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כֵּן מְסַגֵּל טוֹב הַרְבֵּה מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הַטּוֹב וְחַשְׁקוּת לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְזֶה הָיָה דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְזָכַרְתִּי לָךְ חֶסֶד נְעוּרַיִךְ";
connections.quote: “Therefore the Zohar, Bereshit, page 52a, calls the good inclination “another serpent, of life.” For the inclination of the human heart means the desire within the heart, and every desire is called a serpent, because every desire may be for oneself and on one’s own account. Nevertheless, regarding Israel the Sages said in Rosh Hashanah that such a person is completely righteous even though he also intended his own benefit. It is therefore called “good” [the level of the righteous, as is known], and “of life” [for body and covenant are reckoned as one, and the body is called the tree of life]. Nevertheless, it is also called a serpent because it is not yet the choicest form. This is Yesod in a state of smallness, which is called a serpent, as the Ari wrote at the end of gate 21 of Peri Etz Chayim concerning the mystery of 160, because it draws from the rear aspect of the name Ehyeh; see there. The explanation is as stated in Pesachim: at first, when a person acts, he acts for himself. In a state of smallness a person does not yet have this additional understanding, to act without doing so for himself [from the root of the serpent’s incitement], for this still requires refinement. Yet this smallness too is attached to the blessed God’s very essence. It is the holy serpent that draws from the rear aspect of Ehyeh, for the Sages said concerning “You shall see My back”: this is the knot of the tefillin.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains that the same power of desire can operate as the good inclination even while mixed motives still require refinement. The positive designation does not erase the distinction between an initial stage and a more purified intention.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כֵּן מְסַגֵּל טוֹב הַרְבֵּה מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הַטּוֹב וְחַשְׁקוּת לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְזֶה הָיָה דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְזָכַרְתִּי לָךְ חֶסֶד נְעוּרַיִךְ";
connections.quote: “Love of Torah without the blessed God—that is, love of wisdom alone—is the generation of the Flood, concerning which the Zohar says that it was then fitting for the Torah to be given. For they loved Torah and wisdom greatly. This is the meaning of “the sons of God [came] to the daughters of man”: it is known that the feminine is desire and the masculine its fulfillment. Angels have wisdom and attainment, but they have no evil inclination or longing. As stated in Midrash HaNe’elam, even desire for words of Torah requires the evil inclination. A human being has desire but lacks attainment, and then they joined—this is not the place to explain it. But without the blessed God, sexual wrongdoing proceeds from this. The children of Israel, the seed of Avraham who loved Me, have love of the blessed God fixed within them from birth and from the womb. This is the root, corresponding to Keter, which is beyond human grasp. Chokhmah and Binah are love of Torah and of Israel, for Binah is the heart, and there lies the chief love of companions, as it is written, “So the human heart to another.” Every attribute is a complete structure; these are the first three within the attribute of Chesed, and afterward the lower seven are their extension into the powers. They are the powers of nefesh, ruach, and neshamah: the bond of Israel to one another is from nefesh; the bond to Torah is from ruach; and the bond to the blessed God is from neshamah, which is beneath the Throne of Glory. Therefore they said, “The soul You placed within me is pure,” for no corruption applies there, since it is a portion of the Divine. Love of the blessed God does not move away at all. Therefore they said, “If only they had abandoned Me but [kept] My Torah,” for the children of Israel cannot abandon Him, as it were, as in “With poured-out wrath I shall reign over you.” Even if a person greatly increases transgressions to provoke, the root of love of the blessed God, corresponding to Keter, the hidden root of thought, is not severed there at all, for “although he sinned, he is still Israel.” The First Temple’s destruction was for “their abandoning My Torah”; but through love of Torah, its light brings the hidden love of the blessed God into revelation.”
connections.context: The fuller discussion connects the Flood generation’s intensity with desire for Torah, while distinguishing love of wisdom alone from Torah’s disclosure of love of God. The enduring hidden root and the need to bring it into expression are both retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כֵּן מְסַגֵּל טוֹב הַרְבֵּה מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הַטּוֹב וְחַשְׁקוּת לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְזֶה הָיָה דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְזָכַרְתִּי לָךְ חֶסֶד נְעוּרַיִךְ";
connections.quote: ‘Go and proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem: Thus says Hashem: ‘I remember in your favor the kindness of your youth, your bridal love, how you followed Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם עַצְמָם אוֹתָם הַנְּפָשׁוֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר פִּינְחָס (רטז סוֹף עַמּוּד א, עַיֵּין שָׁם) דְּהָיוּ רְאוּיִים לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה בַּמַּבּוּל אִלּוּ זָכוּ, וְנִשְׁמַת מֹשֶׁה הָיְתָה שָׁם.
connections.quote: see note 683.
connections.context: The Zohar places the recurrence of generations and Moses’ unrealized reception of Torah together. This supplies both parts of Rav Tzadok’s statement about the same souls and Moses’ presence within that generation.

connections.hePhrase: וְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ, אָז יִהְיֶה פַּעַם שְׁלִישִׁית אוֹתוֹ דּוֹר, בְּסוֹד מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: "תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ כַּנֶּשֶׁר נְעוּרָיְכִי";
connections.quote: ‘Who satisfies your mouth with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (עב עַמּוּד ב) וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן יח): "כַּד תֶּחֱמֵי קַשְׁתָּא בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלֵי מְשִׁיחָא",
connections.quote: “Do not expect the footsteps of the Messiah until that rainbow is seen in the world adorned in bright colors and illuminating the world. Then expect the Messiah.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (עב עַמּוּד ב) וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן יח): "כַּד תֶּחֱמֵי קַשְׁתָּא בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלֵי מְשִׁיחָא",
connections.quote: ““I will see it to remember the everlasting covenant”: now it appears in dim colors, as a reminder that a Flood will not come. But at that time it will appear in bright colors, adorned like a bride for her husband.”
connections.context: The contrast is between the rainbow’s present reminder after the Flood and its future brightness as a sign of restoration. Rav Tzadok draws on that contrast in his account of the Flood generation’s future repair.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (עב עַמּוּד ב) וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן יח): "כַּד תֶּחֱמֵי קַשְׁתָּא בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלֵי מְשִׁיחָא",
connections.quote: “Let this be your sign: Until you see the rainbow in bright colors, do not expect the footsteps of the Messiah. As soon as it shines in bright colors, immediately: “I will see it to remember the everlasting covenant.””
connections.context: This is the parallel formulation in Tikkun 18. Its precise location is 36b:3 within the previously cited seven-page range. The sign concerns the transformation in the rainbow’s brightness.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (עב עַמּוּד ב) וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן יח): "כַּד תֶּחֱמֵי קַשְׁתָּא בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלֵי מְשִׁיחָא",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 5
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 5
connections.quote: “‘When I bring a cloud over the earth, the rainbow will appear in the cloud.’ A cloud means awe and concealment; a rainbow means strong confidence. Even amid the intensity of awe you will have great trust. This is what the Holy One promised Noach. Thus the holy Zohar says (Bereshit 72b): do not anticipate the footsteps of Mashiach until you see a rainbow in luminous colors. This means: when the assurance from Hashem is clear and explicit before your eyes, then anticipate the footsteps of Mashiach. This is why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (Ketubot 77b), ‘Was the rainbow seen in your days?’ He did not ask, ‘Did you see it?’ ‘Was seen’ implies sometimes, rather than constantly; for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai the rainbow was constant. Israel’s rainbow and strength are the passage of Shema Yisrael, which gives strength to the hearts of those who hope for His kindness.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads the cloud as concealment and the rainbow as the strength to trust within it. Its explanation of the rainbow’s luminous colors therefore clarifies the siman’s closing point: messianic illumination makes the assurance of the covenant apparent. The source’s contrast between occasional and constant perception also explains why the language concerns a revealed sign rather than confidence inferred from outward calm.
connections.headline: The luminous rainbow as visible assurance

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַקֶּשֶׁת הוּא אוֹת הַבְּרִית נֶגֶד עוֹנְשֵׁי חַטֹּאת נְעוּרִים,
connections.quote: ““And it shall be, when I bring a cloud”—a cloud of water, which was the principal element in the generation of the Flood; although there was a flood of fire and water, the principal element stated in Scripture is a flood of water. The Lord promised that there would no longer be a flood, such an overwhelming intensification of desire. This is the meaning of the rainbow appearing: restraint against desire, in the sense of “His bow remained firm.” This is why no rainbow appeared in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s generation: he was on the level of a chasid and did not need restraint, and he was then the foundation of the world, as is stated repeatedly in the Zohar. “Like the appearance of the rainbow in the cloud” is “the appearance of the glory of the Lord.” Glory refers only to Torah, which restrains a person. This is the Lord’s glory: when a person bends his nature and struggles for the sake of the Lord’s will. This is the appearance of the rainbow in the cloud.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ יִהְיֶה זֶה בְּאַנְפִּין נְהִירִין בְּהֶאָרַת פָּנִים, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר עֵינֵיהֶם לָדַעַת כִּי סָר עֲוֹנָם בָּזֶה,
connections.quote: “The rainbow is the aspect of a strong assurance, for the Holy One, blessed be He, made a covenant that all flesh would never again be cut off by the waters of the Flood. [From the author’s manuscript.] Certainly this is not without a reason, if judgment calls for annihilation, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not waive judgment. Rather, the rainbow, which is the appearance of the likeness of Hashem’s glory, awakens repentance. Therefore Tikkunei Zohar says: “When you see the rainbow in bright colors, look for the footsteps of the Messiah,” for Israel are redeemed only through repentance. “In bright colors” means that the awakening from above toward repentance will shine within the heart. Thus far. This means that even after all the corruptions in the world, repentance will avail, for “the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth.” This corresponds to Binah, the heart, as it is said, “His heart will understand, and he will return, and be healed.””
connections.context: The parallel explains the bright rainbow through an awakening to repentance in the heart. It explicitly preserves the condition of repentance and distinguishes the covenant’s promise from a simple waiver of judgment.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים וְגוֹמֵר", פֵּירוּשׁ שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית כַּנּוֹדָע:
connections.quote: “Come and see: all Israel have a share in the World to Come. Why? Because they guard the covenant upon which the world endures, as it is said, “Were it not for My covenant day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth.” Therefore Israel, who guard the covenant and accepted it, have a share in the World to Come. Moreover, for this reason they are called righteous. From here we learn that everyone who guards this covenant, upon which the world endures, is called righteous. From where do we know this? From Yosef: because he guarded the covenant of the world, he merited being called righteous. Therefore: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.””
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s explicit explanation of “righteous” as guarding the covenant. It supplies the meaning invoked by the ois’s closing words.

connections.hePhrase: [צו] מִי שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו, הוּא נִקְרָא "יְפֵה תֹאַר" בַּכָּתוּב, כְּעִנְיַן יוֹסֵף: "יְפֵה תֹאַר";
connections.quote: ‘He left everything he had in Joseph’s hands and took no interest in anything under his charge except the bread he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.’

connections.hePhrase: [צו] מִי שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו, הוּא נִקְרָא "יְפֵה תֹאַר" בַּכָּתוּב, כְּעִנְיַן יוֹסֵף: "יְפֵה תֹאַר";
connections.quote: “Joseph the righteous, who was guarded against sexual transgression and of whom it is written, “I fear God,” is the only man of whom the Torah writes that he was “beautiful in form and beautiful in appearance.” Beauty belongs primarily to women, as they said in the chapter HaPoalim, “Your beauty is for women.” This means “a woman who fears the Lord”; otherwise it is falsehood and vanity. Through being guarded against sexual transgression and fearing the Lord, the beauty associated with women extends also to men, for fear of the Lord belongs primarily to the feminine side, as is known.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s own parallel explains why the Torah’s description of Joseph signifies a spiritual quality. The claim concerns beauty as Scripture describes it, which is the particular wording under discussion here.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "שֶׁקֶר הַחֵן וְהֶבֶל הַיֹּפִי",
connections.quote: ‘Grace is false, and beauty is fleeting; a woman who fears Hashem is the one who shall be praised.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מָצִינוּ גַּם כֵּן בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים שֶׁהָיוּ נְקִיִּים מִזֶּה, כְּמוֹ עוֹג שֶׁפָּלַט מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, וּבְלֹא תֵּבָה כְּלָל;
connections.quote: “According to your reasoning, how could the ark proceed? Moreover, where did Og king of Bashan stand? Rather, a miracle was performed for them: the waters cooled at the sides of the ark.”
connections.context: The Gemara asks how survival was possible amid the hot Flood waters and answers that the water beside the ark was miraculously cooled. This supplies the original account behind Og’s survival outside the ark.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מָצִינוּ גַּם כֵּן בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים שֶׁהָיוּ נְקִיִּים מִזֶּה, כְּמוֹ עוֹג שֶׁפָּלַט מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, וּבְלֹא תֵּבָה כְּלָל;
connections.quote: “And except for Og king of Bashan, who sat on a wooden rung of one of the ark’s ladders and swore to Noah and his sons that he would be their servant forever. What did Noah do? He made a hole in the ark and passed him his food each day. He too remained, as it is said, “For only Og king of Bashan remained,” and so forth.”
connections.context: This account gives the physical detail behind “without an ark”: Og is outside the enclosed ark, while Noah still sustains him from it. It adds that detail to the Gemara’s brief account of the cooled water.

connections.hePhrase: וַדַּאי לֹא הָיָה נִיסָא לְשִׁקְרָא, רַק שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בֶּן מַבּוּל, דְּהַיְינוּ מַשְׁחִית זֶרַע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק כָּל הַיָּד (נִדָּה יג:),
connections.quote: “When he went out, that man said to him: “Would the Merciful One perform a miracle like this for a falsehood?” He replied: “Wicked man! Are they not called donkeys? For it is written, ‘Whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys.’””
connections.context: In the preceding narrative, Elijah appears as a witness to defend Rabbi Shila. The man challenges the apparent falsehood in Shila’s description; Shila answers by invoking Ezekiel’s scriptural imagery. Rav Tzadok borrows the question’s premise—that a miracle does not vindicate falsehood—for his argument about Og.

connections.hePhrase: וַדַּאי לֹא הָיָה נִיסָא לְשִׁקְרָא, רַק שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בֶּן מַבּוּל, דְּהַיְינוּ מַשְׁחִית זֶרַע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק כָּל הַיָּד (נִדָּה יג:),
connections.quote: ‘If it means intercourse between males, they are liable to stoning! Rather, if it means nonpenetrative intercourse [with emission of seed], they are liable to the punishment of the generation of the Flood!’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר אַגְּמָרָא דְּנִדָּה (סא.) שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן אֲחִיָּה בַּר שַׁמְחֲזַאי, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ
connections.quote: ‘‘Hashem said to Moses: Do not fear.’ Now, Sihon and Og were brothers, for the Master said: Sihon and Og were the sons of Achiyah son of Shamchazai. Why was Moses afraid of Og, and why was he not afraid of Sihon?’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר אַגְּמָרָא דְּנִדָּה (סא.) שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן אֲחִיָּה בַּר שַׁמְחֲזַאי, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ
connections.quote: “It is known what is written about Og escaping the generation of the Flood: this certainly was not for nothing, but because he was free of the sins of the generation of the Flood—end of quotation. It is also known what is written in the Zohar, volume III, at the beginning of 216b: the giving of the Torah was fit to occur in the generation of the Flood, and Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was present then too—beshagam has the numerical value of Moshe—had they merited it. Through their sin, however, the flow of Torah’s waters was changed into the waters of the Flood. Likewise, they said in Zevachim 116a that at the giving of the Torah the nations of the world gathered to Balaam. According to the statement in the chapter Chelek, Sanhedrin 106b, that Balaam was killed at the age of thirty-three, which was in the fortieth year after the Exodus, he was therefore born seven years after the giving of the Torah. We must say: just as the root of the soul of Moses our teacher is called “Moses,” as stated above concerning his presence in the generation of the Flood, and similarly the Talmud says, “Moses, you have spoken well,” addressing a Torah scholar of a generation who possesses some of Moses’ wisdom, so Balaam corresponds to the knowledge of the other side. The nations’ deliberation with their own understanding is called their gathering to Balaam. Similarly, they said in Sotah 11a that he was among Pharaoh’s advisers, according to which he lived for very many years; yet Sanhedrin 106b applies to him, “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days.” Sefer HaYashar writes that Pharaoh’s adviser was a different Balaam, this one’s grandfather, but the Sages’ wording does not suggest this. The same applies to their exposition in Sanhedrin 106a of “He saw the Kenite”: “You were with me in that counsel.” Rather, the meaning is as I have written: the root of the knowledge of the other side is called “Balaam,” whether clothed in a particular soul or present in Pharaoh’s own understanding. “Perhaps the Holy One, blessed be He, is bringing a Flood”: in accordance with their own condition, they took the flow of Torah’s waters coming into the world to be the waters of a Flood. If so, Og, who was saved from the Flood, necessarily had some connection with Torah.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s own extended discussion of the passage named here. In its continuation he speaks of Moses as the root of a soul present in different generations. The quotation supplies his connection between Og’s survival, the sins of that generation, and Torah; the Niddah quotation already present supplies Og’s ancestry.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ נִיתְּנָה אַרְצוֹ לַחֲצִי מַטֵּה מְנַשֶּׁה מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף, שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית].
connections.quote: “The rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to half the tribe of Manasseh—all the region of Argob, all that Bashan which is called the land of the Rephaim.”
connections.context: The verse establishes the transfer of Og’s territory to Manasseh. Rav Tzadok then gives his spiritual explanation for the connection between this land and Joseph’s descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִתְיָירֵא מֹשֶׁה מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי מֹשֶׁה הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין קלט:): "בְּשַׁגַּם" – בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא מֹשֶׁה, וְנֶאֱמַר עָלָיו: "כִּי מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ", שֶׁהָיָה אָז בַּמַּיִם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: From the answer to that righteous man you can know what was in his heart. He thought: “Perhaps the merit connected with Abraham our father will stand for him.” For it is said, “The fugitive came and told Abram the Hebrew,” and Rabbi Yochanan said: This is Og, who escaped the generation of the Flood.”
connections.context: The existing note quotes the Gemara’s question about Moses’ different reactions to Og and Sichon. This is its unquoted answer: Og’s service to Abraham. Rav Tzadok’s explanation through covenant purity develops a further spiritual reading of Moses’ fear.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִתְיָירֵא מֹשֶׁה מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי מֹשֶׁה הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין קלט:): "בְּשַׁגַּם" – בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא מֹשֶׁה, וְנֶאֱמַר עָלָיו: "כִּי מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ", שֶׁהָיָה אָז בַּמַּיִם.
connections.quote: see note 685.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִתְיָירֵא מֹשֶׁה מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי מֹשֶׁה הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין קלט:): "בְּשַׁגַּם" – בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא מֹשֶׁה, וְנֶאֱמַר עָלָיו: "כִּי מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ", שֶׁהָיָה אָז בַּמַּיִם.
connections.quote: “The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter; he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, “For I drew him out of the water.””
connections.context: In its narrative setting, Pharaoh’s daughter is explaining Moses’ name after his rescue from the Nile. Rav Tzadok reads the same water-language in connection with the preceding allusion to Moses and the Flood; that further connection is his interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כָּל עִיקַּר עִנְיַן מֹשֶׁה הָיָה לְתַקֵּן דָּבָר זֶה הַנִּקְרָא שְׁטוּת, שֶׁלְּכָךְ הָיָה פָּרוּשׁ מִן הָאִשָּׁה וְקָבוּר מוּל בֵּית פְּעוֹר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר;
connections.quote: “He separated from his wife—what did he expound? He reasoned by an inference from the lesser case to the greater: Israel, with whom the Divine Presence spoke for only one hour and for whom a time was fixed, were told by the Torah, “Be ready … do not approach a woman.” I, with whom the Divine Presence speaks at every hour, without setting a time—how much more so! How do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, agreed with him? For it is written, “Go, tell them: Return to your tents,” and afterward, “But you, stand here with Me.” Some say that the proof is “Mouth to mouth I speak with him.””
connections.context: The Gemara gives the particular basis for Moses’ separation: his continual readiness for prophecy, with divine approval. Rav Tzadok places that exceptional prophetic discipline within his account of Moses’ spiritual task.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כָּל עִיקַּר עִנְיַן מֹשֶׁה הָיָה לְתַקֵּן דָּבָר זֶה הַנִּקְרָא שְׁטוּת, שֶׁלְּכָךְ הָיָה פָּרוּשׁ מִן הָאִשָּׁה וְקָבוּר מוּל בֵּית פְּעוֹר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina said: Why was Moses buried beside Beth Peor? To atone for the deed of Peor.”
connections.context: This is the original rabbinic explanation of the location of Moses’ burial. Rav Tzadok connects the atonement for Peor with Moses’ opposition to the spiritual failing discussed here.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כָּל עִיקַּר עִנְיַן מֹשֶׁה הָיָה לְתַקֵּן דָּבָר זֶה הַנִּקְרָא שְׁטוּת, שֶׁלְּכָךְ הָיָה פָּרוּשׁ מִן הָאִשָּׁה וְקָבוּר מוּל בֵּית פְּעוֹר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר;
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:7
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:7
connections.quote: “Therefore he is the redeemer from Egypt, the nakedness of the land, the place of the harlot’s licentiousness. He testifies that among the children of Israel this power belongs to holiness, for holy daat—spiritual knowledge—is the very opposite of licentiousness. That is why he was buried opposite Beth Peor, after the episode at Shittim: he is its very opposite.”
connections.context: In the surrounding passage Rav Tzadok identifies Moses with the daat of Israel. His own explanation directly connects Moses’ work of redemption and his burial at Peor, supplying the fuller parallel indicated by “as I wrote elsewhere.”

connections.hePhrase: וְרָאָה זֶה נָקִי כָּל כָּךְ, נִתְיָירֵא מִמֶּנּוּ, עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: "אַל תִּירָא",
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said to Moses: ‘Do not fear him, for I have given him, all his people, and his land into your hand. You shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי קַיְימָא לַן בִּנְדָרִים (לא:): הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הָעֲרֵלִים אָסוּר בְּמוּלֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמוּתָּר בְּעַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרָא אֶלָּא עַל שְׁמָם, אֲפִילּוּ הֵם מוּלִים וְשׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית.
connections.quote: “If one says, “Benefit from the uncircumcised is forbidden to me,” he may benefit from uncircumcised Israelites, but may not benefit from circumcised members of the nations.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי קַיְימָא לַן בִּנְדָרִים (לא:): הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הָעֲרֵלִים אָסוּר בְּמוּלֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמוּתָּר בְּעַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרָא אֶלָּא עַל שְׁמָם, אֲפִילּוּ הֵם מוּלִים וְשׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית.
connections.quote: “For the term “uncircumcision” is applied to the nations, as it is said, “All the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised of heart.””
connections.context: The Mishnah interprets the categories used in a vow, rather than treating them solely as anatomical descriptions. Rav Tzadok uses that distinction in discussing covenantal identity.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי קַיְימָא לַן בִּנְדָרִים (לא:): הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הָעֲרֵלִים אָסוּר בְּמוּלֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמוּתָּר בְּעַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרָא אֶלָּא עַל שְׁמָם, אֲפִילּוּ הֵם מוּלִים וְשׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית.
connections.quote: “‘Gladness’ is circumcision, as it says, ‘I rejoice over Your utterance.’ Here too the matter is of this kind. Circumcision appears to a person as though he is repairing a lack that Hashem created in him. Yet did Hashem, Heaven forbid, create a lack? In truth, the holiness of circumcision is completely fixed in every soul of Israel even before he circumcises himself. As the Gemara says (Nedarim 31b): one who vows not to benefit from the uncircumcised may benefit from uncircumcised Israelites but may not benefit from circumcised gentiles; one who vows not to benefit from the circumcised may not benefit from uncircumcised Israelites but may benefit from circumcised gentiles. Uncircumcision is named only after the latter, as it says, ‘For all the nations are uncircumcised.’ Thus gentiles are called uncircumcised even when circumcised, and an Israelite is called circumcised even while uncircumcised. This proves that the holiness of circumcision is fixed and enduring in Israel even without their act of service. Yet a person cannot recognize that permanently present holiness except by first circumcising himself. Every person must therefore initially experience concealment, imagining that Hashem created a lack in him and that he repairs it through his service. Through this concealment every soul is obliged to circumcise himself. After he is circumcised, it is revealed retrospectively that the holiness of circumcision is permanently within him.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same vow-law proof while preserving a crucial qualification. Israel’s rooted relation to the covenant is not created by the physical act, yet the act remains necessary to disclose it. This helps explain the siman’s distinction between an outwardly unblemished appearance and belonging at the root of the covenant, without making the final assurance a reason to disregard the mitzvah.
connections.headline: A rooted covenant revealed through action

connections.hePhrase: [צז] תִּיקּוּן לְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה הוּא עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין ל:): בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי תוֹרָה תַּבְלִין;
connections.quote: ‘So the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its antidote. If you occupy yourselves with Torah, you will not be delivered into its hand, as it is said: ‘If you do well, will you not be lifted up?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קְרָאוֹ "רָע", וְהַיְינוּ בַּעֲוֹן דְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל דְּהַיְינוּ מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Avira expounded—and some say it was Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: The evil inclination has seven names. The Holy One, blessed be He, called it ‘evil,’ as it says: ‘For the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth.’ Moses called it ‘uncircumcised,’ as it says: ‘Circumcise the foreskin of your heart.’ David called it ‘impure,’ as it says: ‘Create a pure heart for me, God,’ implying that there is an impure one.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (יג.) דְּלֹא נִגְזַר עַל דָּגִים שֶׁבַּיָּם, הַיְינוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "וּרְדוּ בִּדְגַת הַיָּם"],
connections.quote: ‘It is written: ‘Therefore the land shall mourn, and everyone dwelling in it shall languish, along with the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens; even the fish of the sea shall be swept away,’ and so forth. Yet in the generation of the Flood, the decree was not imposed on the fish of the sea, as it is said: ‘Everything on dry land died’—but not the fish of the sea. Here, however, even the fish of the sea are included.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (יג.) דְּלֹא נִגְזַר עַל דָּגִים שֶׁבַּיָּם, הַיְינוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "וּרְדוּ בִּדְגַת הַיָּם"],
connections.quote: “Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel: What is meant by “You have made humankind like the fish of the sea, like creeping things without a ruler”? Why are human beings compared to the fish of the sea? To tell you: Just as fish in the sea die as soon as they come up onto dry land, so human beings die as soon as they separate from words of Torah and from the commandments.”
connections.context: The comparison with fish supplies Torah and mitzvot as the indispensable medium of life. Rav Tzadok applies that image here to Torah scholars, alongside the separate teaching that the fish were spared in the Flood.

connections.hePhrase: [וְאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (יג.) דְּלֹא נִגְזַר עַל דָּגִים שֶׁבַּיָּם, הַיְינוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "וּרְדוּ בִּדְגַת הַיָּם"],
connections.quote: “The blessing of Adam, which belongs to Israel—“you are called Adam”—is also “Be fruitful and multiply.” But it concludes, “Subdue it and rule over the fish,” and so forth. This is the principal purpose of their blessing of increase: to subdue all the earthliness and materiality of this world. Through this they rule over the living creatures whose life is material. For this a person was created, as they said, “If you have learned much Torah … for this you were created.” Torah is the pattern of all the work of Creation, and “Who are the kings? The Sages”: through their attainment in Torah, they rule over the whole creation.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s fuller interpretation of the verse “rule over the fish of the sea.” He makes mastery through Torah and the subordination of material desire the point of the blessing.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית (נז עַמּוּד א) וּבְרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד דְּנִקְרָא רַע, זֶה הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי";
connections.quote: “They committed every evil, but their guilt was not complete until they poured out blood upon the ground in vain—those who corrupted their way upon the earth. … Here it says, “only evil,” and there, “Er, Judah’s firstborn, was evil in the Lord’s eyes.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית (נז עַמּוּד א) וּבְרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד דְּנִקְרָא רַע, זֶה הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי";
connections.quote: “One is called “evil” only when he corrupts his way, defiles himself and the earth, and gives strength and power to the impure spirit called evil.”
connections.context: The passage distinguishes the designation ra, “evil,” from the more general rasha, “wicked.” This is the Zohar’s terminology that Rav Tzadok carries into his discussion of the evil inclination and its repair.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית (נז עַמּוּד א) וּבְרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד דְּנִקְרָא רַע, זֶה הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי";
connections.quote: “Some report it this way: Rabbi Ami said, “Anyone who brings himself into erotic thought is not admitted into the domain of the Holy One, blessed be He.” Here it is written, “What he did was evil in the eyes of the Lord,” and there it is written, “For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You.””
connections.context: This is the passage from the opening chapter Kol HaYad that connects the designation “evil” with exclusion from the divine presence. The passage concerns bringing oneself into such thoughts; Rav Tzadok discusses the separate case of an involuntary dream in the next sentence.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית (נז עַמּוּד א) וּבְרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד דְּנִקְרָא רַע, זֶה הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי";
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said: Elijah spoke forcefully toward Heaven, as it is said, “You have turned their heart backward.” Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yitzchak said: How do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, subsequently acknowledged Elijah’s words? For it is written, “And those whom I have afflicted.””
connections.context: The Gemara places the words from Micah 4:6 in the discussion of Elijah’s appeal about Israel’s wayward heart. Rav Tzadok uses that interpretation to discuss the divine creation of the inclination; the surrounding ois makes Torah its remedy.

connections.hePhrase: וְתַבְלִין הוּא לְמַתֵּק הַמַּאֲכָל, הַיְינוּ לַהֲפוֹךְ הָרַע לְטוֹב מְאֹד כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִמְתָּק.
connections.quote: see note 358.
connections.context: The Midrash identifies the productive energy within the evil inclination. Rav Tzadok’s further claim is that Torah can sweeten and direct that energy; the Midrash supplies the “very good” interpretation itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְתַבְלִין הוּא לְמַתֵּק הַמַּאֲכָל, הַיְינוּ לַהֲפוֹךְ הָרַע לְטוֹב מְאֹד כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִמְתָּק.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:7
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:7
connections.quote: “He draws all his desire and longing into words of Torah, and all his delight is there. Through this, the “heart of stone,” which signifies intense desire, melts away—the opposite of a “heart of flesh,” a heart directed toward bringing forth offspring.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the mechanism of Torah as seasoning: the energy of desire is directed into Torah. The contrast between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh connects that redirection with the proper creative purpose of the faculty.

connections.hePhrase: וְתַבְלִין הוּא לְמַתֵּק הַמַּאֲכָל, הַיְינוּ לַהֲפוֹךְ הָרַע לְטוֹב מְאֹד כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִמְתָּק.
connections.quote: “Why did the Sages say, “You might say their hope is lost …,” when nothing stands in the way of repentance? This initial possibility follows the holy Zohar’s statements that repentance for this blemish is difficult. It depends on the first blemish—the serpent’s instigation—being completely clarified, so that deliberate sins become merits. The death that the serpent brought into the world would then cease as a consequence. That clarification cannot occur in this world until the days of the Messiah, when we merit eternal life. This is the Messiah’s light: “He asked life of You; You gave him length of days forever and ever.” Then the Messiah will “smell and judge,” as Sanhedrin 93b says, because the quality of fragrance and purity will be completely perfected: “His sensing by scent is in the fear of the Lord.” Therefore they said, “Scripture says, ‘The mandrakes have given fragrance’: both these and those will in the future give fragrance.” Even one who has, Heaven forbid, blemished this always has hope and repair, by taking care to turn his heart and eyes away from evil thoughts and continually entering into the occupation of Torah. As Maimonides says at the end of the laws of forbidden intercourse, “Thoughts of forbidden relations grow strong only in a heart empty of wisdom.” Through occupation in Torah one merits holy sight, as it says, “Your eyes shall see your teachers.” The word Torah means that it instructs a person in the revelation of the glory of His blessed name. Through this one merits the fragrance of purity: “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.” Occupation in Torah is the consummation of repentance and the repair of the blemish mentioned above. The word yirah, fear, hints at repentance, as they expounded, “‘Happy is the man who fears the Lord’—happy is one who repents while still a man.” They likewise said, “The purpose of wisdom is repentance …,” for “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.” Through Torah study it is always possible for the blemish to be repaired even in this world, as it says, “Healing to all his flesh.” And “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever” refers to Torah, as the holy Zohar explains: it remains with a person forever, purifying him and refining his soul so that he merits a spirit of purity.”
connections.explanation: The Chanukah passage directly addresses the apparent loss of hope raised by the Zohar’s severe language. It distinguishes the complete removal of the serpent’s damage from the real purification that Torah can accomplish now. This expands the present siman’s comparison to atonement through Torah: a limitation on another form of repair does not close this path. Its practical description also explains the metaphor of seasoning—Torah enters and redirects the life of the heart rather than leaving the inclination untouched.
connections.headline: Torah’s power of repair remains available before the final restoration

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית וְנֹחַ: דְּלֵית מְסָאָבָא כְּמוֹהוּ.
connections.quote: “Come and see: Of all the sins through which a person becomes defiled in this world, this is the sin through which a person becomes most defiled in this world and in the world to come: one who pours out his seed to no purpose, brings forth seed in vain by hand or foot, and becomes defiled through it. As it is said, “For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You.””
connections.context: This explicit comparison occurs in Zohar I 188a, in Vayeshev. It supplies the wording about exceptional defilement used here. The ois immediately turns to purification through Torah and repentance; its existing Noach quotation preserves the exception for great repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית וְנֹחַ: דְּלֵית מְסָאָבָא כְּמוֹהוּ.
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Rosh Hashanah 1
connections.canonicalRef: Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Rosh Hashanah 1
connections.quote: “Rava said: through sacrifice and meal offering it is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah. Abaye said: it is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness. Thus the Talmud says (Megillah 31b) that on Rosh Hashanah we read ‘Hashem remembered Sarah’ and take the haftarah from Channah. Earlier it is written (I Samuel 2:27), ‘A man of God came to Eli,’ continuing through ‘all the increase of your house.’ The Sifrei identifies this man as Elkanah, Shmuel’s father. What did Shmuel add in his prophecy, when his father had already delivered that prophecy? He added its concluding words: ‘The sin of Eli’s house shall not be atoned through sacrifice and meal offering.’ The inference is: through sacrifice and meal offering it is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness. Even a decree accompanied by an oath therefore has a repair. Elkanah’s earlier prophecy had supplied no repair; Shmuel added that there is nothing in the world for which there is no repair. This is why we take the haftarah from Channah: even a decree accompanied by an oath has a repair.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef spells out the inference Rav Tzadok invokes. The added words about sacrifice in the prophecy concerning Eli’s house identify a limit on one means of atonement while opening another. This is the logical comparison behind the siman’s reading of the Zohar’s severe language; it does not erase the need for the actual repair described by the source.
connections.headline: A closed route of atonement and the possibility of repair

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה אָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק ב דִּבְרָכוֹת (טז.) דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַעֲלִין מִטֻּמְאָה לְטָהֳרָה.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: Why are tents placed next to streams, as it is written, ‘Like streams spreading out, like gardens beside a river, like tents He planted,’ and so on? To teach you that just as streams bring a person from impurity to purity, so tents (of Torah study) bring a person from the scale of guilt to the scale of merit.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (סב עַמּוּד א) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.): בְּזֶבַח אֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר, אֲבָל מִתְכַּפֵּר בַּתּוֹרָה; הָכָא נַמֵּי כֵּן;
connections.quote: “The earlier authorities already protested this, for nothing stands in the way of repentance. In the section Noach it says, “All a person’s sins … depend on repentance; but the sin of pouring out seed … your iniquity is stained … except through great repentance.” These three words, “except,” and so forth, are enclosed in brackets, because they are absent from older books and were added from another manuscript version. Reishit Chochmah, in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 17, writes that some manuscript versions read, “except through the power of mighty repentance.” This appears to contradict the wording in Vayechi, which closes the door to repentance altogether. But in Vayakhel too, after describing at length the damage done by impairing the covenant, it says, “These words apply when one has not performed complete repentance, repentance fit to cover all one’s deeds.” Yet we still need a reason for its treating repentance for this sin so stringently. As I have written, with regard to repentance it is less severe, according to all opinions, even than prohibitions punishable by lashes, and certainly than offenses carrying excision or judicial execution. We have already noted the teaching in Kiddushin 49b: there is no wicked person, whatever the transgression, who cannot be considered wholly righteous through a thought of repentance in the heart in a single moment. There it says simply “even a wholly wicked person,” implying every transgression in the world, with none excluded.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok himself examines the Zohar’s differing textual formulations and brings its explicit qualification about complete repentance. This fuller discussion explains why his language here about the apparent barrier to repentance leads into a path of repair through Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (סב עַמּוּד א) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.): בְּזֶבַח אֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר, אֲבָל מִתְכַּפֵּר בַּתּוֹרָה; הָכָא נַמֵּי כֵּן;
connections.quote: “All a person’s sins and corruptions depend upon repentance. But the sin of pouring seed upon the ground and corrupting his way damages him and damages the earth. … “Your iniquity is stained before Me” … except through great repentance.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (סב עַמּוּד א) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.): בְּזֶבַח אֵין מִתְכַּפֵּר, אֲבָל מִתְכַּפֵּר בַּתּוֹרָה; הָכָא נַמֵּי כֵּן;
connections.quote: “Rava said: It is not atoned through sacrifice or offering, but it is atoned through Torah. Abaye said: It is not atoned through sacrifice or offering, but it is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness.”
connections.context: The present text of Zohar I 62a includes the exception “except through great repentance.” Rav Tzadok explains the severity of the statement by distinguishing ordinary means of atonement from the deeper remedy of Torah. Rosh Hashanah makes a comparable distinction concerning the decree against Eli’s household; it does not discuss the same sin.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שִׁילְהֵי חֲגִיגָה: תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין אוֹר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֵט בָּהֶם.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: The fire of Gehinnom has no power over Torah scholars, as can be inferred from the salamandra: If one who anoints himself with the blood of a salamandra, a creature born of fire, is not subject to the power of fire, how much more so Torah scholars, whose whole bodies are fire, as it is written: ‘Is not My word like fire, declares Hashem’!’

connections.hePhrase: גֵּיהִנָּם גַּם כֵּן נִקְרָא "רָע", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת סא.) עַל פָּסוּק "לֹא יִנָּקֶה רָּע",
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: Someone who counts money to a woman from his hand into hers in order to gaze at her—even if he possesses Torah and good deeds like Moses our teacher—will not escape the judgment of Gehinnom. For it is said: ‘Hand to hand, the evil one will not go unpunished’—he will not escape the judgment of Gehinnom.’

connections.hePhrase: גֵּיהִנָּם גַּם כֵּן נִקְרָא "רָע", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת סא.) עַל פָּסוּק "לֹא יִנָּקֶה רָּע",
connections.quote: ‘Hand to hand, an evildoer will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous escape.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יט.) שֶׁהַכֹּל יוֹרֵד לָהּ עַל עִסְקֵי חִנָּם, הַיְינוּ שְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית;
connections.quote: ‘Are there no more? But there is ‘Gehinnom’! It is a deep valley, gei (in Gehinnom), to which everyone descends on account of hinnam [forbidden sexual relations]. But there is also ‘Tofteh,’ as it is written: ‘For Tofteh was prepared long ago’! That refers to the place into which everyone who is seduced—mitpatteh—by his inclination falls.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יט.) שֶׁהַכֹּל יוֹרֵד לָהּ עַל עִסְקֵי חִנָּם, הַיְינוּ שְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית;
connections.quote: ““On account of gratuitous affairs”—forbidden sexual relations.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the particular sense of iskei chinnam that connects the Gemara’s wordplay with Rav Tzadok’s discussion of guarding the covenant. The existing note retains the Gemara’s wording.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ גַּם כֵּן: "בָּרָאתָ גֵּיהִנָּם", שֶׁגַּם כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרָאוֹ כְּמוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע
connections.quote: “Rava said: Job sought to exempt the whole world from judgment. He said before Him: Master of the universe, You created the ox with split hooves and the donkey with closed hooves; You created the Garden of Eden and Gehinnom; You created the righteous and the wicked. Who can restrain You?”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ גַּם כֵּן: "בָּרָאתָ גֵּיהִנָּם", שֶׁגַּם כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרָאוֹ כְּמוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע
connections.quote: “What did Job’s companions answer him? “You undermine reverence and diminish prayer before God.” The Holy One, blessed be He, created the evil inclination, and He created Torah as its remedy.”
connections.context: The first statement is Job’s argument, which the Gemara follows with his companions’ response about Torah. Rav Tzadok invokes the created character of both the inclination and its remedy; the passage does not leave Job’s exemption from responsibility unchallenged.

connections.hePhrase: [צח] כָּל פָּסוּק שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ וְחַיּוּת שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ עִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ.
connections.quote: “All Israel’s miracles and deliverances are through the power of Torah. Miracles in Scripture are through the power of the very letters in which the miracle is written; those are the substance of Torah through which the miracle is drawn. This is also known concerning the operation of divine names: in the letters of the verse describing a miracle is alluded the name that effects that matter. As the Tikkunim say (Tikkun 69), the name ‘Hakhtav’ comes from the verse ‘The writing was the writing of God’ (Exodus 32:16), and ‘Hadoresh’ from ‘To know how to sustain the weary with a word’ (Isaiah 50:4), and similarly elsewhere. It is so at the plain level too, through the power of those words of Torah. Every word of Torah has pardes—plain meaning, allusion, exposition, and secret—as is known; through these four ways, too, those words of Torah have the power to effect the miracle. Miracles that were not given to be written occur through the power of Oral Torah. This began after the miracle of Esther.”
connections.explanation: Poked Akarim provides Rav Tzadok’s fuller formulation of the siman’s opening principle. The correspondence is more than a useful reminder: the letters recording the event are described as Torah through which its power is drawn. The distinction between written and Oral Torah also keeps the account from being reduced to a single technique involving written divine names.
connections.headline: The letters that record a miracle and the power they carry

connections.hePhrase: תֵּדַע בִּתְפִלִּין, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְהָיָה לְאוֹת וְגוֹמֵר", וְלֹא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ אֵיזֶה פָּרָשָׁה מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת לְאוֹת,
connections.quote: ‘It shall be a sign for you upon your hand and a reminder between your eyes, so that the Torah of Hashem may be in your mouth; for with a strong hand Hashem brought you out of Egypt.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַהֲלָכָה לִכְתּוֹב אוֹתָם הַפָּרָשִׁיּוֹת שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהֶם זֶה
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Tefillin, Mezuzah and the Torah Scroll 1:1
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Tefillin, Mezuzah and the Torah Scroll 1:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Tefillin, Mezuzah and the Torah Scroll 1:1
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות תפילין ומזוזה וספר תורה א׳:א׳
connections.quote: “These four passages—“Sanctify to Me” and “When the Lord brings you,” in the book of Exodus, and “Hear, O Israel” and “If you will indeed heed”—are written separately, covered with leather, and called tefillin. They are placed on the head and bound on the arm. Even the tip of one letter in these four passages prevents all of them from being valid under Torah law, until they are written completely and correctly.”
connections.context: Maimonides identifies the four passages that contain the commands concerning this sign. This supplies the halakhic fact on which Rav Tzadok builds his explanation of the passage’s own spiritual efficacy.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה סוֹד גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶּׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק יֵדְעוּן רָצוֹן" (מִשְׁלֵי י, לב),
connections.quote: ‘The lips of the righteous know what is pleasing, but the mouth of the wicked utters perversities.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה סוֹד גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶּׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק יֵדְעוּן רָצוֹן" (מִשְׁלֵי י, לב),
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 10:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 10:1
connections.quote: ““The lips of the righteous know what is pleasing.” This follows what the Sages said: “They compel him until he says, ‘I am willing.’” Through his speech he introduces willingness into his heart as well. This is “the lips of the righteous”: what he says only with his lips, because his heart is not yet clarified, helps him clarify his heart so that he wills it wholeheartedly. For example, when anger toward his fellow arises in his heart and he recognizes this as a failing, his first counsel is to speak kindly to his fellow. Even though this is not yet wholehearted, through it he works upon himself little by little, until he brings love into his heart in place of hatred.
