This is “know what is pleasing”: “know” means arranging. Through speech he arranges his will until he establishes it wholeheartedly in his heart. Similarly, “The sun knows its setting” means that it has order and regularity in its course, unlike the moon, whose path is sometimes longer, as stated in Rosh Hashanah.”
connections.context: This original teaching supplies the received interpretation mentioned here and gives its concrete example: speaking kindly can gradually replace anger with love. The existing Yisrael Kedoshim quotation gives the same general principle; this passage supplies the fuller formulation and example in Mei HaShiloach.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה סוֹד גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶּׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק יֵדְעוּן רָצוֹן" (מִשְׁלֵי י, לב),
connections.quote: “In Israel, even this is good, as they said: “They enticed Him with their mouths, and lied to Him with their tongues; their hearts were not firm with Him—but He, being merciful, forgives iniquity.” The Rambam’s explanation of “we compel him until he says, ‘I am willing’” is known: his heart’s refusal comes only from the evil inclination. Of this it says, “The lips of the righteous know favor.” I received the explanation that even when one sees that his heart does not yet want it, good speech with the mouth, called “the lips of the righteous,” helps teach and draw willingness into the heart as well. Yitzchak thought the same was true of Esav: since he saw him at least offering enticement with his mouth, he loved him in order to draw him toward his holy source.”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explicitly interprets the same verse, “The lips of the righteous know favor,” as speech that draws a good will into the heart. This makes the present siman’s counsel more intelligible: repeating a relevant verse is not merely reporting an intention already present. The words can help form the intention, while the distinction between Israel and Esav in the source prevents equating every outward profession with genuine inner repair.
connections.headline: Words can teach the heart to want

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל כָּתַב סְגֻלָּה לְמִי שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ מְסִיתוֹ לְאֵיזֶה עֲבֵירָה – לְדַבֵּר בְּפִיו כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים פָּסוּק הַלָּאו שֶׁל הָעֲבֵירָה, עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִשְׁתַּנֶּה הָרָצוֹן;
connections.quote: “6. If, Heaven forbid, an improper thought of sexual transgression comes to him, he should say several times, “Guard yourself from every evil thing,” and reflect on the Sages’ exposition of it: a person should not entertain such thoughts during the day and thereby come to a nocturnal emission. He should not allow the improper thought to remain in his mind, so as not to defile the higher intellect, Heaven forbid. 7. If, Heaven forbid, an improper sight happens to come before him—for example, an animal or bird mating, an exposed handbreadth of a woman in a place regarded as nakedness, the appearance of his wife during her menstrual impurity, or the like—he should immediately say the verse, “Do not stray after your heart,” and not defile his intellect, Heaven forbid.”

connections.hePhrase: [צט] סִימָן לִתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה – כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ זוֹכֵר כְּלָל הַחֵטְא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (נח:) שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמַר לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה: "זְכוֹר וְכוּלֵי";
connections.quote: ‘Mishnah: Just as there is wrongdoing in buying and selling, so there is wrongdoing through words. One must not ask someone, ‘How much is this item?’ when one has no intention of buying it. If someone has repented, one must not tell him, ‘Remember your former deeds.’ If he is the child of converts, one must not tell him, ‘Remember your ancestors’ deeds,’ as it is said: ‘Do not wrong a convert or oppress him.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל כֹּחוֹת הָאָדָם מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "מִי שָׂם פֶּה וְגוֹמֵר", וְכֵן כֹּחוֹת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה וְהַזְּכִירָה, וְאִם אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹפֵעַ לוֹ וּמַזְכִּיר לוֹ – אֵינוֹ זוֹכֵר.
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said to him: ‘Who gave a mouth to man, or who makes someone mute or deaf, sighted or blind? Is it not I, Hashem?’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק א: שֶׁעָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לוֹמַר: אֵינִי זוֹכֵר עֲווֹנוֹתָיו וְאֵין עוֹלִין עַל לִבִּי;
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, will sit in His great house of study, with the righteous sitting before Him, and say: The people of that generation practiced Torah in this way, and I dealt charitably with them in this way; that person practiced Torah in this way, and I dealt charitably with him in this way. But I do not remember his sins, and they do not arise in My heart.”
connections.context: The teaching describes God recalling a person’s Torah and the kindness shown to that person while leaving the sins out of that remembrance. These are the words Rav Tzadok links to divine knowledge and the heart of Israel.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: see note 363.
connections.context: The Midrash reads the wakeful heart as God’s continuing concern for Israel’s redemption. It explicitly supplies the identification “the heart of Israel,” which Rav Tzadok uses in the following inference.

connections.hePhrase: מִמֵּילָא גַּם עַל לִבּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם אֵינוֹ עוֹלֶה, וְזֶהוּ מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא.
connections.quote: ““All Israel have a portion in the world to come”: this means the hidden depths of their hearts, which are not disclosed even to the person himself. This is the root of their soul, a portion of God above, concerning which it was said that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel. This is the mystery of the world to come, corresponding to the heart, as is known. It is the portion in the world to come that all Israel possess, even sinners, for all sins arise from the material aspect and its manifestation in this world, and not from the depth of the pure soul, hidden in this world and revealed in the future. Then “the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun”: the light of the Congregation of Israel will shine and radiate like “the Lord is a sun and shield,” as it were. This follows what they said: “In the future Israel will be called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He”—that is, they will be included in their source. Concerning this they said at the end of the chapter Elu Ovrin that the divine name will be read as it is written: the inward light will be revealed without a concealing and covering garment. That garment is the source of the root of the Congregation of Israel in this world, in which there is concealment, and their cleaving to the living God is not fully revealed until the future, when the Holy One, blessed be He, renews His world. It will be that same world, yet entirely renewed. In this world it is sufficient to know that there is a world to come, and through this they have a portion, as stated at the beginning of the chapter Chelek: one who denies it has no portion.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok links the Midrash’s “heart of Israel” with the soul’s hidden depth and its future disclosure. That connection explains the progression here from the divine heart to “a foretaste of the world to come.” The quoted passage also retains his stated qualification concerning denial of the world to come.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ אָדָם לְעֹמֶק הַתְּשׁוּבָה כָּזֶה, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית שְׁלֵימוּת הַכַּפָּרָה, אֵינוֹ בְּנִיחָא;
connections.quote: “Conversely, if a person remembers his sin and fulfills ‘My sin is always before me’ (Psalms 51:5), then Hashem makes Himself forgetful and does not look at that sin at all.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov explicitly places the two directions together: the person keeps the sin before him, while Hashem puts it aside. This comparison helps read the siman’s final sentence alongside its description of completed forgiveness. Rav Tzadok describes the peace of complete repair, while the person’s chosen task remains honest remembrance and return; ordinary loss of memory is not itself the spiritual attainment described here.
connections.headline: Remembering one’s task while Hashem puts the sin aside

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הֶרֶב כַּבְּסֵנִי וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי פְשָׁעַי אֲנִי אֵדָע";
connections.quote: ‘Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me of my sin. For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הֶרֶב כַּבְּסֵנִי וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי פְשָׁעַי אֲנִי אֵדָע";
connections.quote: “He opened and said: “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.” How greatly must people guard themselves against their sins before the Holy One, blessed be He! For after a person sins, that sin is inscribed above and is not erased except through the strength of great repentance, as it is said, “Even if you wash with natron and use much soap, your iniquity is stained before Me.””
connections.context: This passage, at Zohar I 73b, connects David’s continuing awareness of his sin with the need for powerful repentance to erase its record. Rav Tzadok’s account of forgetting the sin develops the further consequence of complete cleansing.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָאָדָם מִצִּדּוֹ צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת חַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָּמִיד:
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.quote: see note 577.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok expressly maintains the two perspectives: the person continues to recognize his failings and dependence on God, while forgiveness belongs to God. His reference to renewed confession follows the view praised by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov in Yoma 86b.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָאָדָם מִצִּדּוֹ צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת חַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָּמִיד:
connections.quote: “Concerning “My sin is always before me,” the Midrash explains that the sins should be before his eyes and remembered in his heart, but he should not mention them with his mouth. The Jerusalem Talmud gives a further explanation: they should not be in your eyes as though you had not done them, but as though you had done them and they had been forgiven. We have already mentioned this among the principles of repentance. Nevertheless, he should ask for mercy all his life for the forgiveness of his earlier and later sins, and fear lest he has not fulfilled the requirements of repentance. … But he should not recount the earlier sins individually after repenting of them and confessing them on Yom Kippur, for he has already fulfilled the command of confession concerning them. He should trust that his confession has been accepted to the extent that confession is fit to atone. Still, he should pray all his days for the forgiveness of his sins, as we said. Specifying the sins is an obligation of confession, not of prayer.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah distinguishes continuing inner remembrance from repeating a spoken confession and combines that remembrance with trust in forgiveness. Rav Tzadok’s final sentence likewise keeps recollection of one’s failings within the person’s own work of repentance.

connections.hePhrase: אֲפִילּוּ הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה טֶרֶם נוֹצְרָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chaggai said in Rabbi Yitzchak’s name: “The Lord searches all hearts and understands every formation of thoughts.” Before a thought has been formed in a person’s heart, it is already revealed before You. Rabbi Yudan said in Rabbi Yitzchak’s name: Before a creature is created, its thought is already revealed before You.”
connections.context: The Midrash moves from God’s knowledge of creation to knowledge preceding even a thought’s formation. That is the exact extension Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה, אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה, הוּא זוֹכֶה שֶׁזְּדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשִׂין זְכִיּוֹת, כִּי גַּם זֶה הָיָה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ,
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for deliberate sins become like inadvertent sins, as it is said, “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity.” Iniquity is deliberate, yet it calls it a stumbling. Is that so? But Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for deliberate sins become like merits, as it is said, “When a wicked person turns from his wickedness and practices justice and righteousness, through them he shall live.” There is no difficulty: here it is repentance from love, and there it is repentance from fear.”
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes two effects: repentance from fear changes deliberate sins into inadvertent sins; repentance from love changes them into merits. This supplies the original qualification for the transformation discussed here after complete repentance.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:): "אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Why “like scarlet [kashanim]”? It should say “like scarlet [kashani]”! Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: Even if your sins are like the years [kashanim] arranged and coming from the six days of Creation until now, they will become white as snow.”
connections.context: The teaching reads shanim as “years,” linking the verse’s sins and their cleansing to the span of creation. Rav Tzadok draws on that reading in his discussion of what was already known at creation.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:): "אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘‘Come now, let us settle the matter,’ says Hashem. ‘If your sins are like scarlet, they will become white as snow; if they are red as crimson, they will be like wool.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיֵּשֶׁב ד) עַל פָּסוּק "נוֹרָא עֲלִילָה עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם",
connections.quote: “Adam said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, two thousand years before You created Your world, the Torah was with You. … It is written in it, “When a person dies in a tent.” Had You not prepared death for creatures, would You have written this? Rather, You have come to place the pretext upon me. This is “awesome in His dealings with humankind.””
connections.context: The Midrash puts the argument in Adam’s mouth after a parable of a husband who had prepared a divorce before finding his pretext. It illustrates the tension between the divine plan and the event that realizes it, which is the aspect Rav Tzadok invokes. It is not presented as an instruction to choose sin.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיֵּשֶׁב ד) עַל פָּסוּק "נוֹרָא עֲלִילָה עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם",
connections.quote: ‘Come and see the works of God, awesome in His deeds toward human beings.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיֵּשֶׁב ד) עַל פָּסוּק "נוֹרָא עֲלִילָה עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם",
connections.quote: “Therefore God gives the gentle warning, “Go and see the works of God”: direct your hearts toward the sacred, and do not err in this. His attributing these events to human actions is a matter of a pretext, for those divine purposes will in any case come to pass and will not turn aside, without thereby compelling people in the details of their individual actions. Similarly, the woman was not compelled to mix her husband’s cup with lukewarm or cold water because he intended to divorce her. Her mixing it lukewarm was only a pretext on his part: had that not occurred, another reason—or many others—would not have been lacking, and all those actions remained possible for her, as we explained.”
connections.context: Rabbi Yitzchak Arama is explaining the same Tanchuma parable quoted in the existing note. He distinguishes a divine purpose that will be fulfilled from the individual’s unforced choices. Rav Tzadok’s discussion of the past here likewise expressly follows complete repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ", רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר לְכָךְ נִטְּלָה מִמֶּנּוּ הַסַּיַּעְתָּא,
connections.quote: ‘Against You alone have I sinned, and I have done what is evil in Your eyes, so that You are justified in Your word and blameless when You judge.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ", רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר לְכָךְ נִטְּלָה מִמֶּנּוּ הַסַּיַּעְתָּא,
connections.quote: “Rava expounded: What is meant by “Against You alone have I sinned and done what is evil in Your eyes, so that You may be justified in Your words and prevail in Your judgment”? David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “It is revealed and known before You that, had I wished to subdue my inclination, I would have subdued it. But I said: Let people not say, ‘The servant defeated his Master.’””
connections.context: Rava presents this as David’s plea; the surrounding passage first warns a person not to bring himself into a trial and describes David’s failure after asking to be tested. Rav Tzadok interprets the plea here in terms of the withdrawal of divine assistance.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ", רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר לְכָךְ נִטְּלָה מִמֶּנּוּ הַסַּיַּעְתָּא,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Levi said: A person’s inclination grows stronger against him every day and seeks to kill him, as it is said, “The wicked watches the righteous and seeks to kill him.” If the Holy One, blessed be He, did not help him, he could not overcome it, as it is said, “God will not abandon him to its hand.””
connections.context: This teaching supplies the significance of the assistance mentioned here: overcoming the inclination requires God’s help. Rav Tzadok uses that dependence in his retrospective explanation of David’s failure.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יַלְקוּט שִׁמְעוֹנִי יְשַׁעְיָה רֶמֶז רצו): אֵלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘May Your priests clothe themselves in righteousness, and Your pious ones sing for joy.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יַלְקוּט שִׁמְעוֹנִי יְשַׁעְיָה רֶמֶז רצו): אֵלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ““Your priests shall be clothed in righteousness, and Your pious ones shall sing”: “Your priests” are the righteous of the nations, who are priests to the Holy One, blessed be He, in this world, such as Antoninus and his companions. “Your pious ones” are the wicked of Israel, who are called pious, as it is said, “Gather My pious ones to Me.” … When they enter, they fall on their faces, bow before Him, and bless and praise His name.”
connections.context: The Midrash describes those brought out of Gehinnom, healed, clothed, and admitted to behold God’s glory. Their praise after that restoration explains why the verse calls them “pious.” The correct remez is 429.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יַלְקוּט שִׁמְעוֹנִי יְשַׁעְיָה רֶמֶז רצו): אֵלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “King David, however, is ‘the man raised on high,’ who established the yoke of repentance: even the prior damage can be repaired so that the transgressions become merits. It will be clarified that this too was under God’s providence beforehand, as in ‘If your sins are like years’—like these years ordered and coming from the six days of Creation. It will become known that this was arranged before Him. This is turning darkness into light. This is the root of the light of Messiah son of David, which is eternal life: it will be clarified that all the damages were under God’s providence, and they will be repaired with greater force to become ‘very good,’ beyond someone righteous from the outset. The latter is the aspect of Messiah son of Joseph, who will not endure. This is ‘In the place where penitents stand, the completely righteous do not stand.’”
connections.explanation: Chanukah explains David’s ‘yoke of repentance’ as the power to repair prior damage and turn darkness itself into light. This illuminates why the present siman calls the restored sinners ‘Your pious ones’: their standing is disclosed through Hashem’s completed work of repentance, beyond how the deeds first appeared to human judgment. The comparison depends on complete repentance and retrospective clarification, both stated in this siman; it does not identify the unrepented deed with an act of piety.
connections.headline: David’s teshuvah repairs the past rather than merely beginning again

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יַלְקוּט שִׁמְעוֹנִי יְשַׁעְיָה רֶמֶז רצו): אֵלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Therefore they said in the Letters of Rabbi Akiva concerning the verse ‘Your pious ones shall sing’: these are the sinners of Israel who are destined to return. A sinner needs greater force of strength in conquering the inclination when he returns; therefore he is called ‘Your pious ones,’ meaning Hashem’s pious ones—those of exceptional piety. It is like ‘the trees of Hashem’ and ‘the cedars of Hashem’: wherever something is joined to Hashem’s name, it indicates its exceptional degree. Someone before whom an occasion for sin comes and who escapes it is called ‘mighty in strength’ (Kiddushin 40a). Through this he is assured of being guarded from then on, until he acquires through it the fixed name of a baal teshuvah.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin explains the same possessive expression through the returning sinner’s greater effort. Its context distinguishes a moment of sincere return from repentance that has become a settled identity. Read beside the siman, this keeps ‘Your pious ones’ tied to actual transformation after repentance, rather than treating the old sin as meritorious while it remains unrepaired.
connections.headline: Why the returning sinner is called Hashem’s chasid

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עַל פָּסוּק "אִסְפוּ לִי חֲסִידָי וְגוֹמֵר" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם).
connections.quote: ‘Gather My pious ones to Me, those who concluded My covenant over a sacrifice.’

connections.hePhrase: וְצַדִּיק וְחָסִיד הֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת בָּאָדָם בְּתוֹלָדָה, וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז.): "בָּרָאתָ צַדִּיקִים, בָּרָאתָ רְשָׁעִים",
connections.quote: “The conclusion is that one who fulfills the 613 commandments while the evil inclination remains within him and he overcomes it is called a tzaddik. When he fulfills them through the annulment of the evil inclination, indicating that he has acquired good character traits as an established nature, he is called a complete chasid.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital distinguishes overcoming the inclination from the settled acquisition of good character. His account concerns acquired character becoming natural; Rav Tzadok develops his own distinction here in terms of the roots of different dispositions, while retaining the teaching that righteousness and wickedness are not decreed at birth.

connections.hePhrase: וְצַדִּיק וְחָסִיד הֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת בָּאָדָם בְּתוֹלָדָה, וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז.): "בָּרָאתָ צַדִּיקִים, בָּרָאתָ רְשָׁעִים",
connections.quote: see note 995.
connections.context: The Gemara attributes the first claim to Job and immediately answers it with the possibility of Torah as a remedy. Rav Tzadok applies the creation-language to differing inborn dispositions; his present distinction between tzadik and chasid is his own development, not the Gemara’s stated conclusion.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּאִילּוּ "צַדִּיק וְרָשָׁע" לָא קָאָמַר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּנִדָּה (טז:);
connections.quote: ‘But ‘wicked or righteous’ is not said, in accordance with Rabbi Chanina. For Rabbi Chanina said: Everything is in Heaven’s hands except fear of Heaven, as it is said: ‘And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, except to fear,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: [קא] בְּמַעֲשֶׂה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם שֶׁלֹּא יֵצֵא מְעַט מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, כ);
connections.quote: ‘For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins.’

connections.hePhrase: [קא] בְּמַעֲשֶׂה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם שֶׁלֹּא יֵצֵא מְעַט מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, כ);
connections.quote: “Hillel was from the side of mercy, Abraham’s level, and Shammai from the side of judgment and might, Isaac’s level, as stated in Ra‘aya Mehemna. The Arizal likewise wrote that in the future the halakhah will follow Beit Shammai. This follows the Sages’ teaching that initially God intended to create the world with the attribute of judgment, and afterwards joined the attribute of mercy to judgment, as it says, “On the day the Lord God made.” There it also says “when they were created,” which is expounded as “through Abraham.” This is “The world is built through kindness.””
connections.explanation: Chanukah applies the same teaching about creation first arising in judgment to the schools of Hillel and Shammai. Mercy is joined to judgment so that the world can exist. This helps explain why the present siman does not treat practical kindness as a departure outside Torah: mercy itself belongs to Hashem’s revealed ways, even when practical life cannot sustain the original measure of strict judgment. The comparison concerns the structure Rav Tzadok describes; the quoted future teaching does not alter present halakhic rulings.
connections.headline: Mercy allows the divine order to enter the conditions of actual life

connections.hePhrase: [וְכַנּוֹדָע שֶׁבְּעוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה רִבּוּי הַקְּלִיפּוֹת בְּכָל הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: “The difference is that in Beriah the shell is less than the holiness, separate from it, and does not adhere to it. In Yetzirah the shell and holiness are evenly balanced and do not intermingle. In Asiyah the shell exceeds the holiness, and good and evil are intermingled in the aspect of the garments, but not in the aspect of the vessels or the essence, Heaven forbid. Understand this well and do not err.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital distinguishes the three worlds and locates the mixture in Asiyah. His qualification that the mixture concerns the garments, not the vessels or essence, is part of the source itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: בַּתְּחִלָּה עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה לִבְרוֹא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁבְּמַעֲשֶׂה הוּא יְצִיאָה מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין, אֲבָל בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה הוּא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין וְאֵין כָּאן יְצִיאָה.
connections.quote: ““Hashem God”: This is like a king who had empty cups. The king said: “If I put hot water into them, they will burst; cold water, they will crack.” What did the king do? He mixed hot water with cold and poured it into them, and they endured. Thus the Holy One, blessed be He, said: “If I create the world with the attribute of mercy, its sins will be many. With the attribute of judgment, how can the world endure? Rather, I shall create it with the attribute of judgment and the attribute of mercy—and may it endure.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains why both attributes are joined. It retains both sides of the argument: unbounded mercy allows sin to multiply, while judgment alone does not allow the world to endure.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: בַּתְּחִלָּה עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה לִבְרוֹא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁבְּמַעֲשֶׂה הוּא יְצִיאָה מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין, אֲבָל בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה הוּא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין וְאֵין כָּאן יְצִיאָה.
connections.quote: ““God created”: It does not say “Hashem created,” because initially it arose in thought to create it with the attribute of judgment. He saw that the world could not endure, so He gave precedence to the attribute of mercy and joined it to the attribute of judgment. This is what is written: “On the day that Hashem God made earth and heaven.””
connections.context: Rashi supplies the complete teaching alluded to here: the initial thought of judgment and the joining of mercy. Rav Tzadok develops the distinction between thought and actual conduct.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "צַדִּיק ה' בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יז) – פֵּירוּשׁ, "דְּרָכָיו" הֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יוֹדִיעַ דְּרָכָיו לְמֹשֶׁה", וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן מִתְנַהֵג עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “The Lord is righteous in all His ways, and pious in all His deeds.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok builds on the verse’s two different terms: tzaddik, righteous, and chasid, pious. He associates “ways” with the ordered standard of Torah and “deeds” with beneficence beyond that standard; a translation that makes both halves generic praise loses this distinction.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "צַדִּיק ה' בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יז) – פֵּירוּשׁ, "דְּרָכָיו" הֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יוֹדִיעַ דְּרָכָיו לְמֹשֶׁה", וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן מִתְנַהֵג עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: ‘The verses do not contradict one another. Here the subject is Torah, and Torah is referred to in the feminine, as it is written: ‘Hashem’s Torah is perfect, restoring the soul’; therefore it uses feminine language. There the subject is war, which it is a man’s way to wage and not a woman’s way to wage; therefore it uses masculine language.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "צַדִּיק ה' בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יז) – פֵּירוּשׁ, "דְּרָכָיו" הֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יוֹדִיעַ דְּרָכָיו לְמֹשֶׁה", וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן מִתְנַהֵג עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: ‘He made His ways known to Moses, His deeds to the children of Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "צַדִּיק ה' בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יז) – פֵּירוּשׁ, "דְּרָכָיו" הֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יוֹדִיעַ דְּרָכָיו לְמֹשֶׁה", וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן מִתְנַהֵג עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said: In the usual way of the world, a king of flesh and blood issues a decree. If he wishes to observe it, he observes it; if not, he ultimately has others observe it. But the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so: He issues a decree and observes it first. This is what is written: “You shall rise before the aged, honor the face of an elder, and fear your God; I am Hashem”—I am the One who first fulfilled the commandment of rising before an elder. “If you walk in My statutes.””
connections.context: The Midrash states that God first fulfills the command He gives. Rav Tzadok invokes the broader principle that divine conduct follows Torah.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְמַעֲשֶׂה הוּא "חָסִיד", דְּהַיְינוּ לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין כִּדְאִיתָא בְּשַׁבָּת (קכ. וּבְרַשִּׁ"י),
connections.quote: “‘And a cake of pressed figs,’ and so on. What place is there for a reckoning of payment? Have they not acquired ownerless property? Rav Chisda said: The teaching here describes a particularly pious practice. Rava said: Would pious people take payment for work on Shabbat? Rather, Rava said: We are dealing with a person who fears Heaven. He does not want to benefit from another’s property, but neither does he want to exert himself for nothing. This is what the teaching means: If they are discerning enough to know that payment of this kind is not payment for work on Shabbat, they settle accounts with him after Shabbat.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְמַעֲשֶׂה הוּא "חָסִיד", דְּהַיְינוּ לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין כִּדְאִיתָא בְּשַׁבָּת (קכ. וּבְרַשִּׁ"י),
connections.quote: “Alternatively, do not reverse the order: with Torah, of which “truth” is written—as it is written, “Acquire truth and do not sell it”—the Holy One, blessed be He, does not act beyond the strict measure of the law. With judgment, of which “truth” is not written, the Holy One, blessed be He, acts beyond the strict measure of the law.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s alternative resolution of its discussion about the times of divine Torah study and judgment. It distinguishes Torah’s truth from mercy exercised in judgment, which parallels the distinction made here.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְמַעֲשֶׂה הוּא "חָסִיד", דְּהַיְינוּ לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין כִּדְאִיתָא בְּשַׁבָּת (קכ. וּבְרַשִּׁ"י),
connections.quote: ““Do the pious take payment for Shabbat?” This is a question in astonishment: if they are pious, they should relinquish what is theirs in anything that has even a trace of transgression. Although this is not outright payment for Shabbat, because no agreement was made and they acquired it from ownerless property, nevertheless one is not called pious unless he relinquishes what is his.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the Gemara about rescuing property from a fire on Shabbat. He distinguishes an outright prohibition from the extra restraint associated with a chasid; the existing note already contains the underlying Gemara.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" וְגוֹמֵר.
connections.quote: “He said: I will cause all My goodness to pass before you, and I will proclaim the name of the Lord before you; I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will show compassion to whom I will show compassion.”
connections.context: The verse presents divine graciousness and compassion as expressions of God’s own will. Rav Tzadok notes that this freedom to bestow grace is itself stated in the Torah and therefore belongs to the divine order.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" וְגוֹמֵר.
connections.quote: “This disagrees with Rabbi Meir, for Rabbi Meir said: Two requests were granted to him and one was not granted to him, as it is said: “I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious”—even though he is not worthy; “and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy”—even though he is not worthy.”
connections.context: Rabbi Meir interprets God’s reply to Moshe as grace and mercy extending even to the unworthy. The quotation preserves the Gemara’s notice that this is a differing view within its discussion of Moshe’s requests.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם זֶה פָּסוּק בַּתּוֹרָה וְאֶחָד מִדְּרָכָיו שֶׁנּוֹדַע,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
connections.quote: “‘I have raised my hand to Hashem.’ Avraham did not want to benefit from the king of Sodom, although we find that he accepted from Pharaoh and Avimelech, because his going to rescue Lot required clarification. A good power was present in Lot, since Naamah the Ammonite and Ruth the Moabite descended from him; the remainder was evil, since Ammon and Moab descended from him, as explained. Avraham had to clarify that, in its depth, his intention was only to rescue those two good offspring (Bava Kamma 38b). Wherever a person needs clarification, the counsel is first to remove all his interests in personal benefit. Then Hashem will clarify that even what he did contrary to the rule was good, for ‘It is a time to act for Hashem; they have annulled Your Torah’ (Psalms 119:126).”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach applies the same verse about a time to act for Hashem to Avraham's refusal of benefit from Sodom. Its condition is essential: Avraham must first remove the personal interests that prevent clarification of his rescue of Lot. This gives a concrete discipline beside Rav Tzadok's concluding claim that the apparent exception belongs to Torah's order; the claim does not establish the purity of a person's own motives.
connections.headline: Personal interest and the need for clarification

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה' הֵפֵרוּ תּוֹרָתֶךָ" הוּא גַּם כֵּן הֲלָכָה קְבוּעָה;
connections.quote: ‘It is time to act for Hashem; they have annulled Your Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה' הֵפֵרוּ תּוֹרָתֶךָ" הוּא גַּם כֵּן הֲלָכָה קְבוּעָה;
connections.quote: ““And it says: It is a time to act for Hashem; they have set aside Your Torah”: At times, words of Torah are set aside in order to act for Hashem. Here too, one who intends to greet his fellow in peace is doing the will of the Omnipresent, as it is said, “Seek peace and pursue it”; it is permitted to set aside Torah and do something that appears forbidden.”
connections.context: Rashi is explaining the Mishnah’s particular enactment of greeting another person with God’s name. The example shows a permission recognized within Torah itself; it is not presented here as an unrestricted permission to disregard a commandment.

connections.hePhrase: [קב] מִי שֶׁמִּתְנַהֵג אֲפִילּוּ בְּכָל דִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת וְצָרְכֵי גּוּפָנִיִּים בִּקְדוּשָׁה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּמַכְנִיס בָּהֶם עַבְדוּת וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בֵּיצָה טז.) בְּהִלֵּל וְשַׁמַּאי – זֶהוּ נִקְרָא "חָסִיד",
connections.quote: ‘Hillel the Elder, however, had a different practice, for all his deeds were for the sake of Heaven, as it says: ‘Blessed is Hashem, day by day.’ It was likewise taught: Beit Shammai say: From the first day of your week, prepare for your Shabbat. Beit Hillel say: ‘Blessed is Hashem, day by day.’’

connections.hePhrase: [קב] מִי שֶׁמִּתְנַהֵג אֲפִילּוּ בְּכָל דִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת וְצָרְכֵי גּוּפָנִיִּים בִּקְדוּשָׁה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּמַכְנִיס בָּהֶם עַבְדוּת וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בֵּיצָה טז.) בְּהִלֵּל וְשַׁמַּאי – זֶהוּ נִקְרָא "חָסִיד",
connections.quote: “It was taught: They said of Shammai the Elder that all his days he ate in honor of Shabbat. If he found a fine animal, he would say, “This is for Shabbat.” If he found another finer than it, he would set aside the second and eat the first.”
connections.context: The existing note quotes Hillel’s practice. This preceding passage supplies Shammai’s distinct way of directing weekday eating toward Shabbat.

connections.hePhrase: [קב] מִי שֶׁמִּתְנַהֵג אֲפִילּוּ בְּכָל דִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת וְצָרְכֵי גּוּפָנִיִּים בִּקְדוּשָׁה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּמַכְנִיס בָּהֶם עַבְדוּת וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בֵּיצָה טז.) בְּהִלֵּל וְשַׁמַּאי – זֶהוּ נִקְרָא "חָסִיד",
connections.quote: “This is also what they said in Beitzah: “But Hillel the Elder had a different quality, for all his deeds were for the sake of Heaven.” This means that he did not set pleasure aside for Shabbat as Shammai did, because even on weekdays he ate in sacred purity: all his eating was in holiness and in the food’s spirituality, as on Shabbat. This is called “all his deeds were for the sake of Heaven.” As I wrote above, one who is like this does not need abstinence, because all his pleasures too are for the sake of Heaven and not for himself. This is “all his deeds”: even what appeared to be an act for his own pleasure was truly for the sake of Heaven. For one who is like this, all his permitted activities are holy, and he has no distinction between weekday and Shabbat.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains Hillel’s practice as sanctity reaching ordinary pleasure. The source repeatedly limits this account to a person whose pleasures are already entirely for the sake of Heaven.

connections.hePhrase: [קב] מִי שֶׁמִּתְנַהֵג אֲפִילּוּ בְּכָל דִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת וְצָרְכֵי גּוּפָנִיִּים בִּקְדוּשָׁה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּמַכְנִיס בָּהֶם עַבְדוּת וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בֵּיצָה טז.) בְּהִלֵּל וְשַׁמַּאי – זֶהוּ נִקְרָא "חָסִיד",
connections.quote: “Therefore the commandment is to bless over a cup of wine to gladden the heart, so that there is “joy for the upright of heart”: when one merits to empty evil from the fool’s heart and straighten the heart. The Talmud says: “What service is performed with joy and gladness of heart? This is song.” They said that song is recited only over wine, and so forth. “With gladness of heart” means the two hearts, as they expounded, “‘With all your heart’—with both your inclinations, the evil inclination and the good inclination.” This is a good heart: when one merits to straighten the heart so that it is one heart for good.”
connections.explanation: Lech Lecha explains ‘both inclinations’ through joy in a mitzvah: the heart’s powers become united toward good. This gives a concrete example of the present siman’s distinction between subduing a desire and bringing holiness into permitted bodily life. The example begins with removing evil and straightening the heart. It therefore does not erase the siman’s express requirement of repentance and atonement for what remains a sin; the desired end is a heart directed toward Hashem.
connections.headline: Serving with both inclinations means making one heart for good

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ" – בִּשְׁנֵי יְצָרֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘A person must bless for misfortune just as he blesses for good fortune, as it says: ‘You shall love Hashem your God with all your heart,’ and so on. ‘With all your heart’—with both your inclinations, the good inclination and the evil inclination. ‘With all your soul’—even if He takes your soul. ‘With all your might’—with all your wealth. Another interpretation: ‘With all your might’—whatever measure He measures out to you, give thanks to Him.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁצַּדִּיק הוּא הַכּוֹבֵשׁ יִצְרוֹ, אֲבָל זֶה מַכְנִיס קְדוּשָׁה גַּם בְּכָל חֶמְדּוֹת הַיֵּצֶר;
connections.quote: see note 1030.
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital distinguishes overcoming an opposing inclination from acquiring goodness as a settled disposition. This is a parallel definition of the two terms used here.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז נִקְרָא "טוֹב מְאֹד", שֶׁהוּא יוֹתֵר מִטּוֹב סְתָם;
connections.quote: see note 358.
connections.context: The Midrash itself asks how the evil inclination can be called “very good” and answers by identifying the human activities it motivates. Rav Tzadok discusses bringing holiness into those powers.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין אֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘This disagrees with Rabbi Abbahu, for Rabbi Abbahu said: In the place where those who repent stand, the completely righteous do not stand, as it is said: ‘Peace, peace, to the far and to the near’: first ‘to the far,’ and afterward ‘to the near.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין אֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים וְכוּלֵי.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 13
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 13
connections.quote: “It is known that there are two kinds of service: subduing and transforming. The first is the level of Yosef the righteous; the second is “the place where penitents stand,” where the bitter has been transformed into sweetness. The completely righteous cannot stand there, because they lack the power to transform it and stumble in it. “The place where penitents stand” means the very place of the sin that has been transformed into merit; for the completely righteous it is sin and deficiency. The Sefer HaYashar attributed to Rabbeinu Tam aptly writes that the completely righteous cannot stand there because it is evil; see there. In truth, the Gemara explicitly presents this as the penitents’ advantage. But both are true: the completely righteous cannot stand there because it is evil for them, while the penitents’ advantage is great because the bitter has been transformed into sweetness.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the statement through the difference between subduing and transforming. He preserves both the danger of the place of sin and the advantage of repentance that transforms it; the existing note supplies the Talmudic statement and its differing opinion.

connections.hePhrase: אַשְׁרֵי הַדּוֹר שֶׁהַנָּשִׂיא חוֹטֵא וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: ‘When (asher) a ruler sins’ (Leviticus 4:22). Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai said: Fortunate (ashrei) is the generation whose ruler brings an offering for his unwitting sin. If its ruler brings an offering, what need is there to speak of a commoner? And if he brings an offering for his unwitting sin, what need is there to speak of his deliberate sin?”
connections.context: The Gemara praises the generation whose ruler acknowledges his error and atones for it; Rav Tzadok cites it for the great man whose stumbling brings him to repentance.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ה.) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.
connections.quote: “This is what Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: What is the meaning of the verse ‘The utterance of David son of Yishai, and the utterance of the man raised on high (al)’ (II Samuel 23:1)? The utterance of David son of Yishai, who raised up the yoke (ullah) of repentance.”
connections.context: Just before this (4b–5a) the Gemara teaches that David was not fit for that sin, and that it happened to show that an individual who sins can repent.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת קיב:) עַל זֶה:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rava bar Zimuna: If the early ones were sons of angels, we are sons of men; and if the early ones were sons of men, we are like donkeys—and not like the donkey of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa or of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, but like ordinary donkeys.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנוֹדַע דִּבְנֵי אָדָם גְּדוֹלִים מִמַּלְאָכִים.
connections.quote: “The righteous are greater than the ministering angels, as it is said: ‘He answered and said: Lo, I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are unharmed; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods’ (Daniel 3:25).”
connections.context: The Gemara speaks of the righteous; Rav Tzadok applies it to the “human beings” of Shabbat 112b.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל צַדִּיק שֶׁאֵין יוֹצֵא מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין, גַּם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְנַהֵג עִמּוֹ כֵּן, וְ"לֹא יְאֻנֶּה לַצַּדִּיק" דַּיְיקָא "כָּל אָוֶן".
connections.quote: see note 468.
connections.context: Rashi reads the verse specifically in relation to an inadvertent transgression. The existing note already quotes the verse; this supplies the interpretation relevant to Rav Tzadok’s contrast.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכז:) בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּרָאָה קֶרִי "אוֹתוֹ חָסִיד"
connections.quote: “There was an incident involving a certain pious man who redeemed a young woman from captivity. When they reached an inn, he laid her down at his feet. The next day he went down, immersed, and taught his students.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכז:) בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּרָאָה קֶרִי "אוֹתוֹ חָסִיד"
connections.quote: “When I went down and immersed, what did you suspect of me? They said: Perhaps the exertion of the journey caused the Master an emission. He said: By the Temple service, that is what happened. Just as you judged me favorably, may the Omnipresent judge you favorably.”
connections.context: The second part supplies the essential point: the man is called pious even though he experienced an involuntary emission caused by travel. The earlier excerpt stopped before that explanation.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י, וּבְבִרְכַּת הַזֶּבַח בִּתְמוּרָה דִּיקְדֵּק לָמָּה פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם וְלֹא בִּבְרָכוֹת;
connections.quote: “Wherever we say “an incident involving a certain pious man,” it is either Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava or Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Ilai.”
connections.context: These are Rashi’s words identifying the unnamed chasid. Rav Tzadok then explains why making his greatness known can relieve the distress of someone who experienced an involuntary emission.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח:): אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן חָסִיד גָּדוֹל הָיָה וְכוּלֵי, בְּשִׁכְבַת זֶרַע דַּחֲזָא לְאוֹנְסוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Meir used to say: Adam the first man was a great chasid. When he saw that death had been decreed because of him, he fasted for one hundred and thirty years, separated from his wife for one hundred and thirty years, and wore belts of fig branches about his body for one hundred and thirty years.”

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח:): אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן חָסִיד גָּדוֹל הָיָה וְכוּלֵי, בְּשִׁכְבַת זֶרַע דַּחֲזָא לְאוֹנְסוֹ.
connections.quote: “When we made that statement, it concerned semen that he emitted involuntarily.”
connections.context: The Gemara reconciles Adam’s prolonged penitence with the earlier account of spirits being generated during those years by distinguishing involuntary emission from deliberate intercourse. That qualification is essential to Rav Tzadok’s discussion of the chasid.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל כִּי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּטִפֵּי קֶרִי הֵם יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלוֹת מֵהַיּוֹצְאִים מִזִּוּוּג,
connections.quote: “There is a distinction between these fifty or more drops mentioned above, from the five unions mentioned above, and all other souls. They possess a very great advantage over the others. All other souls come without an emission, through a union arising from the female’s awakening: she awakens toward the union and desires it, and afterward he too awakens. Since the male had no awakening of his own will but was awakened by her, the drops of the kindnesses and severities drawn forth in that union are not drawn from his faculty of knowledge itself, but from the kindnesses and severities that spread below into his six extremities, after becoming clothed and remaining there below. But the drops mentioned above are drawn forth without the female’s awakening, for they are drops of emission, as stated; they certainly emerge from the male’s awakening alone. The male desired to unite with his female counterpart but did not find her, because she was below in Beriah or a similar place, and then they emerged in vain. Since they come from the male’s awakening, they are certainly very great, drawn only from the faculty of knowledge itself, from the kindnesses and severities above, for that is the place where desire awakens. When they emerge from the foundation, they have not first descended and become clothed in the male’s six extremities; they merely passed through there and emerged from the foundation. Therefore the level of these souls is immeasurably greater than that of the other souls.”
connections.context: The Ari’s discussion concerns the particular fifty or more spiritual drops from five unions described earlier in this introduction. The quotation retains that scope and the distinction between the higher root in daat and the lower stages through which other souls descend. Rav Tzadok invokes the principle of higher roots here.

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת לא, ב) וּבְשַׁבָּת (עז).
connections.quote: ““Hannah was speaking upon her heart”: Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, concerning the matters of her heart. She said before Him: Master of the universe, of everything You created in a woman, You did not create one thing in vain: eyes to see, ears to hear, a nose to smell, a mouth to speak, hands to work, feet to walk, and breasts to nurse. Why did You place these breasts upon my heart? Was it not to nurse? Give me a son, and I will nurse him.”
connections.context: Hannah’s prayer argues from the purposeful creation of the body. Rav Tzadok cites that principle before discussing the possible purpose of an involuntary bodily event.

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת לא, ב) וּבְשַׁבָּת (עז).
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: Of everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He did not create even one thing without purpose. He created the snail for a wound; the fly for a hornet’s sting; the mosquito for a snake’s bite; the snake for skin sores; and the spider for a scorpion’s sting. How is the last remedy prepared? One brings a black spider and a white spider, boils them, and applies them to the affected person.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי נִקְרָא "לְאֹנְסוֹ" בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב, א) וְעֵירוּבִין (יח),
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman prepared a vessel holding nine kav. When Rav Dimi came, he said: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda Gelostera said that this was taught only of a sick person who experienced an emission involuntarily; a sick person who brought it about through intercourse requires forty se’ah.”
connections.context: The note is cited for the technical description “involuntarily,” as distinct from an emission following intercourse. Rav Tzadok draws on that distinction, rather than on the separate question of whether blessings may be contemplated silently.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי נִקְרָא "לְאֹנְסוֹ" בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב, א) וְעֵירוּבִין (יח),
connections.quote: “When we made that statement, it concerned semen that he emitted involuntarily.”
connections.context: This answers the objection that Adam had separated from his wife while undertaking penitence. The Gemara explicitly identifies the event as involuntary, which is the expression Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וְקַיְימָא לָן בְּכָל מָקוֹם "אֹנֶס רַחֲמָנָא פַּטְרֵיהּ",
connections.quote: “Rava said to him: He was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, and the Merciful One exempts a person under such compulsion, as it is written: “You shall do nothing to the young woman.” And if you would say that a capital case is different, did we not learn: Vows affected by circumstances beyond one’s control—if someone placed his fellow under a vow to eat with him, and he became ill, or his son became ill, or a river prevented him from coming, these are vows affected by circumstances beyond one’s control!”
connections.context: The Gemara applies the principle beyond the biblical capital case, giving illness and an impassable river as examples. It supplies the exact formula that Rav Tzadok quotes concerning an involuntary occurrence.

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּיֵשׁ לוֹ פְּעָמִים פִּדְיוֹן מִמִּיתָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז, ב).
connections.quote: “Six things are a favorable sign for a sick person: sneezing, perspiration, diarrhea, a seminal emission, sleep, and a dream. … A seminal emission, as it is written: “He shall see offspring; he shall prolong his days.””
connections.context: Within the Gemara’s discussion of signs associated with recovery, an emission is linked with prolonged life through Isaiah 53:10. This is the source for Rav Tzadok’s statement that the event can sometimes indicate deliverance from death.

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּיֵשׁ לוֹ פְּעָמִים פִּדְיוֹן מִמִּיתָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז, ב).
connections.quote: “He concluded, “He redeems,” because this can contain redemption and deliverance from death, as is known, and as our Sages said in Berakhot: it is a favorable sign for a sick person. This applies after the fact: when he has already experienced an emission, he should trust that it is certainly for the good. But beforehand he should ask that he not need this redemption. “You have already redeemed me … God of truth” means through the attribute of truth to which I was attached during the day. For desire is called falsehood, and this is called redemption through falsehood; there is also redemption through truth and words of Torah. Redemption occurs by giving a substitute, and this is like the principle that a part of the life is equivalent to the whole life.”
connections.context: The later ois makes the distinction explicit: trust in the good after an involuntary event, while praying beforehand not to need this form of deliverance. It also identifies a different redemption through truth and Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח, ב) שֶׁגַּם לְאֹנְסוֹ נִבְרְאוּ שֵׁדִין, רוּחוֹת, וְלִילִין,
connections.quote: see note 884.
connections.context: The statement and its concluding qualification belong together: the destructive beings are attributed here to involuntary emission. Rav Tzadok acknowledges that account before arguing that divine purpose can nevertheless be present.

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל מָקוֹם "כָּל דְּעָבֵיד רַחֲמָנָא לְטָב".
connections.quote: “Rav Huna said in the name of Rav, in the name of Rabbi Meir—and it was also taught in the name of Rabbi Akiva: A person should always accustom himself to say, “Whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good.””
connections.context: The following story of Rabbi Akiva illustrates this maxim: apparent losses ultimately save him from capture. Rav Tzadok cites the maxim itself as the principle governing the preceding discussion.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (ז) שֶׁהִמְשִׁילוּ הַשֵּׁדִין לְחֵפֶץ טוֹב אוֹ מַרְגָּלִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “These are the demons: the Holy One, blessed be He, created their souls, and when He came to create their bodies, Shabbat began and He did not create them. This teaches proper conduct: if a person has a fine object or pearl in hand on the eve of Shabbat near nightfall, we tell him to put it down, for the One who spoke and the world came into being was occupied with the creation of the world, yet when Shabbat began He did not create their bodies.”
connections.context: The Midrash portrays even these unfinished creatures as part of creation, while insisting that their completion yields to Shabbat. Rav Tzadok draws on the “fine object or pearl” comparison in considering the hidden purpose of what outwardly appears harmful.

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "יָקָר מֵחָכְמָה וּמִכָּבוֹד סִכְלוּת מְעָט",
connections.quote: “Dead flies make the perfumer’s oil foul and ferment; more weighty than wisdom and honor is a little folly.”
connections.context: In the verse’s immediate context, a little folly can outweigh and spoil much wisdom. Rav Tzadok reads yakar, “weighty” or “precious,” positively here: a small element of folly can serve a precious purpose within the larger divine plan. That interpretive turn is his exposition, not a claim that the verse’s ordinary contextual meaning praises folly.

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "יָקָר מֵחָכְמָה וּמִכָּבוֹד סִכְלוּת מְעָט",
connections.quote: “So too below: if folly were not present in the world, wisdom would not be present in the world. This is why, when the companions learned the mysteries of wisdom from Rav Hamnuna the Elder, he would arrange before them a chapter of foolish matters so that wisdom would benefit through it. This is what is written: “More precious than wisdom and honor is a little folly”—because it is the perfection of wisdom and the honor of wisdom. Therefore it is written: “My heart guiding with wisdom, and grasping folly.” Rabbi Yosi said: “Precious through wisdom and honor”—that is, the preciousness and beauty of wisdom and the preciousness of the glory above: what is it? “A little folly.” A little folly shows and reveals the preciousness of wisdom and the glory above more than all the ways of the world.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (מג.) דְּיָכוֹל לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת עַל יְדֵי יוֹסֵף שֵׁידָא אוֹתָם דְּבָרִים שֶׁמִּתְגַּלִּים בַּתּוֹרָה עַל יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ.
connections.quote: ‘Who said them? Was it not Elijah who said them? This would show that the laws of the Shabbat boundary do not apply above ten handbreadths! No; perhaps Yosef the demon said them.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְאֵלִיָּהוּ הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית,
connections.quote: “Eliyahu arose, fled from the Land of Israel, and escaped, as it is said: “He arose, ate, and drank.” There the Holy One, blessed be He, appeared to him and said: “What are you doing here, Eliyahu?” “I have been very zealous.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “You are always zealous. You were zealous at Shittim over forbidden relations, as it is said, ‘Pinchas son of Elazar son of Aharon the priest.’ And here you are zealous? By your life, Israel shall not perform a circumcision until you see it with your own eyes.” From here the Sages instituted that a seat of honor should be made for the angel of the covenant—Eliyahu of blessed memory being called the angel of the covenant—as it is said: “The angel of the covenant whom you desire, behold, he comes.” May the God of Israel hasten to bring the Messiah in our lifetime, to comfort us and renew our hearts, as it is said: “He shall turn the heart of the fathers toward the children.””
connections.context: This is the source identifying Eliyahu with the angel of the covenant and connecting him with every circumcision. The cited text is chapter 29 in this edition; chapter divisions differ in other editions.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים",
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abba opened and said: “Your people are all righteous.” The companions have explained this matter. Why is it written, “Your people are all righteous”? Are all Israel righteous? There are many guilty people among Israel, many sinners and wicked people who transgress the Torah’s commandments. Rather, the mystery of our teaching is this: Fortunate are Israel, who make a willing offering to the Holy One, blessed be He, offering their sons at eight days. When they are circumcised, they enter this good portion of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, “The righteous one is the foundation of the world.” Since they enter this portion of the righteous one, they are called righteous—certainly, all of them righteous. Therefore, “They shall inherit the land forever,” as it is written, “Open for me the gates of righteousness; I will enter them,” and, “This is the gate of Hashem; the righteous shall enter it”—those who have been circumcised and are called righteous.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרֵאת אֶלָּא עַל שֵׁם הָעַכּוּ״ם].
connections.quote: “Mishnah: “Benefit that I receive from the uncircumcised is forbidden to me”—he is permitted to receive benefit from uncircumcised Israelites and forbidden to receive benefit from circumcised members of the nations. “Benefit that I receive from the circumcised is forbidden to me”—he is forbidden to receive benefit from uncircumcised Israelites and permitted to receive benefit from circumcised members of the nations. For the designation “uncircumcision” is applied only to the nations, as it is said: “For all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised of heart.” And it says: “This uncircumcised Philistine.” And it says: “Lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.””
connections.context: The Mishnah is defining the meaning of terms in vows, giving both directions of the rule and the biblical examples. This supplies the specific rabbinic usage quoted by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין נִיכָּר בֵּינֵיהֶם אִם הוּא מִמַּדְרֵגַת גִּלּוּי אֵלִיָּהוּ אוֹ מִמַּדְרֵגַת יוֹסֵף שֵׁידָא,
connections.quote: “As it is taught in Netzach Yisrael by the Maharal of Prague concerning the statement in Eruvin 43a: “Those seven teachings that were said on Shabbat morning … was it not Elijah who said them? … Perhaps Joseph the demon said them.” If there had been an actual revelation of Elijah, visibly appearing to them, how could the Gemara have been uncertain through whom it came? Rather, the very appearance in the heart of a new understanding of Torah is an aspect of the revelation of Elijah. Discernment is needed here, however, because sometimes it comes from the opposite side, Joseph the demon.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מִשֵּׁידִין יְהוּדָאִין הַנִּזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר,
connections.quote: “Likewise, the King’s riders are the masters of Mishnah, who are like angels. Jewish demons serve them, marked with the sign of Shaddai—another reading: with the letter yod. There are also demons and harmful spirits from the side of impurity, called gentile demons. “God made this corresponding to that.” Therefore the masters of Mishnah said that there are three kinds of them: one kind is like the ministering angels, a second kind like human beings, and a third kind like animals. Among them are those learned in the Written and Oral Torah. He is called “Yosef the demon” because a demon fathered him. It was not for nothing that the masters of Mishnah said: “If the teacher resembles an angel of Hashem of hosts, seek Torah from his mouth.””

connections.hePhrase: דְּסוֹף אוֹתָן רוּחוֹת לִיתָקֵן לִהְיוֹת נְפָשׁוֹת יְקָרוֹת,
connections.quote: “Therefore the Peri Etz Chayim writes (Gate of the Festival of Matzot, chapter 1) that these spirits, demons, and lilin of Adam were the souls of the Egyptian exile, for they are truly aspects of Adam's soul, spirit, and higher soul. Similarly, he writes that the ten drops that came from Yosef were the souls of the ten martyrs. They certainly had previously been some power of spirits, demons, and lilin, but these were so holy that such holy souls were subsequently created from them. This appears to be the meaning of the foreign and Jewish spirits mentioned in the Raaya Mehemna (Pinchas 253a; Ki Tetzei 277a). From the drops of Israelites come Jewish spirits, and from those of gentiles, foreign ones. Even when that power is called spirits, demons, and lilin, there is within it a power of Jewish belonging and a holy spark that later enters a soul of Israel; through this it is repaired.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Shedim provides the fuller mystical account behind the siman's final sentence. The power described as a spirit still contains a spark that can later come into a soul of Israel and be repaired there. This explains why Rav Tzadok refuses to regard its existence as purposeless; it does not change his explicit distinction between an involuntary event and a deliberate act.
connections.headline: The holy spark within a power awaiting repair

connections.hePhrase: [קד] בְּכָל אָדָם יֵשׁ פְּסֹלֶת בַּתּוֹלָדָה מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ – עִרְבּוּבְיָא דְּטוֹב וָרָע,
connections.quote: “Know that after Adam sinned and ate from the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, his soul and body were each composed of good and evil. This is the impurity of the serpent that it placed in Chavah and Adam. Through the evil and impurity it placed in them, it brought illnesses, afflictions, and death upon their souls and bodies. This is what is written: “For on the day you eat of it, you shall surely die”—the death of the soul and the death of the body.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital describes the mixture in both soul and body as a result of Adam’s sin. It is the background to Rav Tzadok’s opening statement about inherited mixture.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמַר: "לֹא תְאֻנֶּה אֵלֶיךָ רָעָה" (תְּהִלִּים צא, י),
connections.quote: ‘No harm will happen to you, and no affliction will come near your tent.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קג.): חֲלוֹמוֹת רָעִים וְהִרְהוּרִים רָעִים,
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: ‘No evil shall befall you’—that bad dreams and bad thoughts should not terrify you. ‘Nor shall a plague approach your tent’—that you should have no son or pupil who openly goes astray—literally, ‘spoils his dish’—like Jesus the Nazarene. Up to this point his father blessed him; from here onward his mother blessed him: ‘For He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you upon their palms,’ and so forth. ‘You will tread upon the lion and the viper,’ and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכֹּל דָּבָר רָע" – שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: ‘Keep yourself from every evil thing’—a person should not entertain (sexual) thoughts by day and come to impurity at night.’

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכֹּל דָּבָר רָע" – שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘When you go out in a military camp against your enemies, keep yourself from every evil thing.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא "חֲלוֹמוֹת רָעִים", דְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה נִקְרָא "רַע" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּנִדָּה (יג:).
connections.quote: see note 980.
connections.context: The Gemara connects the language of evil with deliberate sexual misconduct and its thoughts. Rav Tzadok uses that terminology to explain why the troubling dream under discussion is called “evil”; the note must supply the word ra itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יז:): "וְלֹא כֶאֱלִישָׁע שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘‘There is no breach’—may our company not be like David’s company, from which Ahitophel emerged. ‘There is no departure’—may our company not be like Saul’s company, from which Doeg the Edomite emerged. ‘There is no outcry’—may our company not be like Elisha’s company, from which Gehazi emerged. ‘In our streets’—may we have no son or student who spoils his dish [goes astray] publicly, such as Jesus the Nazarene.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי אֱלִישָׁע לֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו כִּדְאִיתָא שָׁם (י:),
connections.quote: ‘‘He is holy.’ How did she know? Rav and Shmuel disagreed. One said: She never saw a fly pass over his table. The other said: She spread a linen sheet on his bed and never saw a seminal emission upon it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי אֱלִישָׁע לֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו כִּדְאִיתָא שָׁם (י:),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi said: Why did Scripture place the passage of forbidden relations next to the passage of holiness? To teach that anyone who separates himself from forbidden relations is called holy. Thus the Shunammite woman says to her husband: “Now I know that he is a holy man of God.” Rabbi Yonah said: He is holy, but his student is not holy. Rabbi Avin said: He did not look at her. The Rabbis said: He had never seen a drop of seminal emission in his life.”
connections.context: The existing Bavli quotation gives the Shunammite woman’s observations. This Yerushalmi passage supplies the explicit statement about Elisha’s entire life, while retaining the other explanation and the distinction between him and his student.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "רֵאשִׁית אוֹנִי" (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה).
connections.quote: “Why is “also” said of Avraham and Yitzchak, but “also” is not said of Yaakov? Because his bed was complete before Him. From Avraham came Yishmael and all the children of Keturah; from Yitzchak came Esav and all the chiefs of Edom. But Yaakov’s bed was complete: all his sons were righteous. This is what is written: “We are all sons of one man.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains the expression “his bed was complete” through the character of Yaakov’s children. This is a separate claim from the statement about his bodily purity that follows it in the Hebrew.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "רֵאשִׁית אוֹנִי" (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה).
connections.quote: ““Reuben, you are my firstborn”: You are a firstborn, and I am a firstborn. I was eighty-four years old and had not seen a drop of seminal emission, whereas you—“went and lay with Bilhah.””
connections.context: The Midrash places these words in Jacob’s rebuke to Reuben. Rav Tzadok cites the claim concerning Jacob’s bodily purity; the lengthy earlier quotation obscured it among many unrelated interpretations.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "רֵאשִׁית אוֹנִי" (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה).
connections.quote: “Abaye said: Was everyone like our father Yaakov, of whom it is written, “My strength and the first of my vigor,” who had never experienced a seminal emission in his life?”
connections.context: Abaye invokes Yaakov as an exceptional case when rejecting a proposal that assumes such purity in everyone. The earlier Midrash in the existing note is preserved; this supplies the Talmud’s explicit lifelong wording.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "רֵאשִׁית אוֹנִי" (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה).
connections.quote: “All the positive and negative commandments are helps and counsels from the One great in counsel, blessed be His name, to bring holiness upon a person from above. Therefore Avodah Zarah 20b says: ‘Guard yourself from every evil thing’ (Deuteronomy 23:10)—a person should not entertain sexual thoughts by day and thereby come to an emission at night. From here Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair said: Torah brings to watchfulness, watchfulness to diligence, and so on, until holiness. In our text holiness is last, although the passage concludes that piety is greater than them all. There is no contradiction: ‘greater’ concerns the soul's rank. With respect to a person's attainment while clothed in the body, holiness comes after all of them, because it is difficult for the body unless it has first been refined through the preceding stages. Although the principal vision proceeds from piety, it comes later in time, after the body too has been refined and reaches holiness. He learned this from ‘Guard yourself’: by guarding Torah's boundaries and sanctifying oneself from below, one is guarded from above against impurities during sleep, when the matter is outside one's control. This is the culmination of holiness: to be a holy person, beginning with Torah and being brought from stage to stage to holiness and holy inspiration.”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim distinguishes a high quality of the soul from holiness becoming settled in the body. The latter is described as the result of the preceding disciplines, reaching even the state of sleep where direct control is absent. This develops the siman's contrast between an isolated appearance of purity and Yaakov's complete purification through a life of discipline.
connections.headline: The soul’s holiness and its attainment in the body

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל נִקְיוֹנוֹ הָיָה עַל יְדֵי גָּלוּת וְיִסּוּרִים,
connections.quote: “This is why he later sought “to dwell in tranquility”—that is, in rest and cessation from all activity, like the holiness of Shabbat. But “the turmoil of Yosef sprang upon him”: on the side of his descendants, further refinement was still necessary. This is the touch upon the hollow of Yaakov’s thigh, meaning those who came from his loins, for all his powers were divided among his descendants as individual souls.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes Yaakov’s own attainment from the further refinement of his descendants. This explains why suffering associated with Yosef can remain after Yaakov’s personal purity has been described.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "כִּי מַלְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה לָּךְ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘For He will command His angels concerning you, to protect you along all your paths.’

connections.hePhrase: בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כא.) יָלֵיף בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה לְפָנֶיהָ מִקְּרָא דְּ"שֵׁם ה'", עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “What is the Torah basis for a blessing before Torah study? It is said, ‘When I proclaim the name of Hashem, ascribe greatness to our God.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: We derive a blessing after Torah study from the blessing after food by an a fortiori argument, and a blessing before food from the blessing before Torah study by an a fortiori argument. A blessing after Torah study is derived from the blessing after food as follows: food, which does not require a blessing beforehand, requires one afterward; Torah, which requires a blessing beforehand, should surely require one afterward. A blessing before food is derived from the blessing before Torah study as follows: Torah, which does not require a blessing afterward, requires one beforehand; food, which requires a blessing afterward, should surely require one beforehand.”

connections.hePhrase: בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כא.) יָלֵיף בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה לְפָנֶיהָ מִקְּרָא דְּ"שֵׁם ה'", עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ‘When I proclaim the name of Hashem, ascribe greatness to our God.’

connections.hePhrase: בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כא.) יָלֵיף בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה לְפָנֶיהָ מִקְּרָא דְּ"שֵׁם ה'", עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.heRef: חידושי אגדות על ברכות כ״א א:א׳
connections.quote: ““From where is the blessing over Torah derived?” I found it written that he understands the blessing over Torah in this way: “When I proclaim the name of Hashem”—that is, when I read the Torah, which is entirely names of the Holy One, blessed be He. For the whole Torah, in its letters, consists of the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, as is stated in the Midrashim. Understand this.”
connections.context: Maharsha connects the verse used for the blessing over Torah with the teaching that the Torah’s letters are divine names. The existing note already contains the Gemara’s derivation itself.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כֻּלָּהּ שְׁמוֹתָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
connections.heRef: רמב"ן על בראשית, פתיחה לפירוש התורה י״ד-ט״ו
connections.quote: “We also possess a true tradition that the entire Torah consists of the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, its words being divided into names in another manner. For example, you might consider the opening verse as divided into different words, such as “berosh yitbara Elohim,” and so throughout the Torah, apart from the permutations and numerical values of the names. Rabbi Shlomo has already written in his Talmudic commentary how the great name of seventy-two is formed from the three verses beginning “Vayissa,” “Vayavo,” and “Vayet.” For this reason, a Torah scroll with an error of one letter, whether added or missing, is invalid. This requires us to invalidate a Torah scroll that lacks one vav from the words “otam,” of which thirty-nine are written in full in the Torah, or that writes a vav in one of the other occurrences written defectively, and similarly in other cases, even though one might think it makes no difference. This led the great masters of Scripture to count every full and defective spelling throughout the Torah and Scripture and to compose books of the tradition, back to Ezra the scribe and prophet who worked on this, as they expounded from “They read in the book, in the Torah of God, distinctly, giving understanding, and they understood the reading.” It appears that the Torah written in black fire upon white fire was in the manner we have mentioned: the writing was continuous, without breaks between words. It could be read by the way of the names, and it could be read as we read it, concerning Torah and commandments.
