It was given to Moshe our teacher in the reading of the commandments, while its reading as names was transmitted to him orally. Likewise, the great name mentioned above is written continuously and divided into words of three letters and into many other divisions, according to the use made by those who possess the tradition.”
connections.context: Ramban explains both the reading through divine names and the normal reading of Torah and mitzvot. He expressly states that the latter was the written reading given to Moshe, while the reading of the names was transmitted orally; both parts of his explanation are retained.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָעֵצָה לְגָלוּת וְיִסּוּרִין: "הֱוֵי גוֹלֶה לִמְקוֹם תּוֹרָה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Nehorai says: Go into exile to a place of Torah. Do not say that it will follow you, for your companions will make it secure in your hands. ‘Do not rely on your own understanding’ (Proverbs 3).’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַמִּצְווֹת גַּם כֵּן נִקְרָא "עוֹל" בִּבְרָכוֹת (יז.) דּוּגְמַת יִסּוּרִין, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ““Our leaders bear burdens”: Rav and Shmuel—and some say Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar—disagreed. One said: “Our leaders” in Torah, and “bear burdens” in commandments. The other said: “Our leaders” in Torah and commandments, and “bear burdens” in suffering.”
connections.context: The two readings put commandments and suffering alongside one another as burdens borne by Torah leaders. This is the connection Rav Tzadok invokes; the Gemara does not use the literal word ol here.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַמִּצְווֹת גַּם כֵּן נִקְרָא "עוֹל" בִּבְרָכוֹת (יז.) דּוּגְמַת יִסּוּרִין, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Nechunya ben Hakanah says: Whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah has the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly occupation removed from him. Whoever casts off the yoke of Torah has the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly occupation placed upon him.”
connections.context: The Mishnah relates accepting Torah’s yoke to relief from other burdens and states the converse as well. It supplies the parallel behind the comparison of Torah’s burden with other forms of pressure.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַמִּצְווֹת גַּם כֵּן נִקְרָא "עוֹל" בִּבְרָכוֹת (יז.) דּוּגְמַת יִסּוּרִין, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “The matter is that we find “the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven,” followed by accepting “the yoke of mitzvot,” and likewise, “Our leaders are laden”: our leaders in Torah and laden with mitzvot. This shows that Torah and mitzvot are called a yoke and a burden upon a person. The difference, however, is that one bears the yoke of a human king only through compulsion and constraint, would wish to escape it, and cannot be happy in it. But among Israel, accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven and the yoke of Torah, although also called a yoke, is nevertheless done with joy, as we say, “They shall rejoice in Your kingship,” and as it is written, “Let Israel rejoice in its Maker; let the children of Zion exult in their King.” Likewise, it is written, “The precepts of Hashem are upright, gladdening the heart.” In its plain meaning this refers to mitzvot, while the Gemara expounds it concerning words of Torah. That is, although Torah and mitzvot are called a yoke, they gladden the human heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok qualifies the comparison with a burden: accepting Torah and mitzvot differs from forced service to a human ruler because it can be accompanied by joy. The selected passage contains the full distinction.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק אֵלּוּ מְצִיאוֹת, דְּשֵׁם יַעֲקֹב שׁוֹרֶשׁ לְעַם הָאָרֶץ וְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם:
connections.quote: ‘‘Declare to My people their transgression’—these are Torah scholars, whose inadvertent sins are counted as deliberate ones. ‘And to the house of Jacob their sins’—these are unlearned people, whose deliberate sins are counted as inadvertent ones. This is what we learned: Rabbi Yehuda says: Be careful in your study, for an error in study is counted as deliberate wrongdoing.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק אֵלּוּ מְצִיאוֹת, דְּשֵׁם יַעֲקֹב שׁוֹרֶשׁ לְעַם הָאָרֶץ וְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם:
connections.quote: ““Yaakov dwelt in the land where his father had sojourned … These are the generations of Yaakov: Yosef.” In these verses he is mentioned twice by the name Yaakov, and afterward twice by the name Israel: “Israel loved Yosef,” and “Israel said to Yosef: Are not your brothers shepherding in Shechem?” The matter is that the name Yaakov is applied to ordinary people, while the name Israel indicates Torah scholars, as they said: “Declare to My people their transgression”—these are Torah scholars; “and to the house of Yaakov their sins”—these are the unlearned.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok expressly applies the distinction between the names Yaakov and Israel to ordinary people and Torah scholars. The existing Talmudic note supplies the underlying exposition; this gives Rav Tzadok’s reading of the names in Vayeshev.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (נז, ב) מִקְּרָא דְּ"יִרְאֶה זֶרַע יַאֲרִיךְ יָמִים".
connections.quote: see note 1076.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (נז, ב) מִקְּרָא דְּ"יִרְאֶה זֶרַע יַאֲרִיךְ יָמִים".
connections.quote: ‘Hashem desired to crush him and made him ill. If his soul offers itself as reparation, he will see offspring and live long; the desire of Hashem will succeed through him.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא שִׁילְהֵי יוֹמָא,
connections.quote: “It was taught in Rabbi Yishmael’s school: A person who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur should be concerned throughout the entire year. If he lives out the year, he is assured a place in the World to Come. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: You can see this from the fact that the whole world is hungry, while he is satisfied. When Rav Dimi arrived, he said: Such a person will live long and have many children and grandchildren.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא זְמַן גְּמַר דִּין דְּחַיִּים וָמָוֶת לַבֵּינוֹנִים,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Kruspedai said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: Three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah: one of the completely wicked, one of the completely righteous, and one of those in between. The completely righteous are written and sealed immediately for life; the completely wicked are written and sealed immediately for death. Those in between remain suspended from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur: if they merit, they are written for life; if they do not merit, they are written for death.”
connections.context: The Gemara identifies Yom Kippur as the endpoint of the suspended judgment of the intermediate group. The complete three-part teaching and both possible outcomes are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּעִנְיַן מִקְצָת נֶפֶשׁ כְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ.
connections.quote: ““One by one, to find an account”: Rabbi Yitzchak said: Ordinarily, a person stumbles in a transgression for which he is liable to death at the hands of Heaven. Through what is atonement made for him? His ox dies, his hen is lost, his flask breaks, or he stumbles and injures his little finger, from which a drop of blood comes out. A part of the life is like the whole life, as it is said, “One by one, to find an account”: one offsets another, and the account is brought to its full reckoning. How exact is the reckoning? Rabbi Pinchas said: Down to one.”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the exact principle “a part of the life is like the whole life,” with its examples of limited loss or injury. Rav Tzadok applies this account of substitution to the occurrence discussed here.

connections.hePhrase: וּפְעָמִים הוּא לִמְחִילַת עֲווֹנוֹת, כִּדְאִיתָא (יוֹמָא פח, א) בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים שֶׁהוּא זְמַנּוֹ.
connections.quote: “A tanna taught before Rav Nachman: One who experiences an emission on Yom Kippur has his sins forgiven. But was it not taught: His sins are arranged? What does “arranged” mean? Arranged to be forgiven.”
connections.context: This is the distinct statement about forgiveness, immediately before the passage already quoted in the existing notes about concern during the year and surviving it. Those existing qualifications remain in place.

connections.hePhrase: דְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosi does not mean to say that Yom Kippur is Malkhut and that the ten days of repentance proceed from above downward. For it is already explained in the Zohar, the Tikkunim, and many places that Yom Kippur is in Binah. The five afflictions attest to this, and it is a foretaste of the World to Come, as our Sages said: “The World to Come has neither eating nor drinking,” and so on.”
connections.context: Rabbi Moshe Cordovero locates Yom Kippur in Binah and relates its five abstentions to the World to Come. The source also states which alternative identification it is rejecting. The existing connected Takanat HaShavin passage remains unchanged.

connections.hePhrase: וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים עִקָּרוֹ לְכַפָּרַת פְּגַם הַבְּרִית,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of Yom Kippur: ‘On this day He will atone for you, to purify you’ (Leviticus 16:30). Then there is an awakening of the understanding in the heart, which is the world to come, where there is neither eating nor drinking; then Israel's sin will be sought and not found. Then all Israel have a share in the world to come, as it says, ‘Your people are all righteous’ (Isaiah 60:21), as the Mishnah teaches at the beginning of Chelek (Sanhedrin 90a). ‘Righteous’ means one who guards the covenant. Those who transgressed in damaging the covenant were not excluded there from a share in the world to come, for in truth, from the depth of the heart that will then be revealed, they are all so. This revelation occurs on Yom Kippur as well: ‘The goat shall bear their iniquities with it to an isolated land’ (Leviticus 16:22), to Azazel.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin explains the siman's link between Yom Kippur, the world to come, and the designation ‘righteous’ as guarding the covenant. Its claim concerns what is disclosed from the depth of the heart. It should therefore be read alongside, rather than in place of, the siman's repeated qualification ‘sometimes’ and its instruction that the person remain concerned during the year.
connections.headline: The covenantal root disclosed on Yom Kippur

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּיוֹמָא ס"ז לְכַפֵּר עַל מַעֲשֵׂה עוּזָּא וַעֲזָאֵל,
connections.quote: ‘The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: ‘Azazel’—it atones for the deed of Uzza and Azael. The Sages taught: ‘You shall perform My judgments’ refers to matters that, had they not been written, reason would require that they be written. These are the prohibitions against idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, bloodshed, robbery, and blasphemy.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּיוֹמָא ס"ז לְכַפֵּר עַל מַעֲשֵׂה עוּזָּא וַעֲזָאֵל,
connections.quote: ““Uzza and Azael”: Destructive angels who descended to earth in the days of Naamah, the sister of Tuval Kayin. Of them it is said, “The sons of God saw the daughters of man.” That is, it atones for forbidden relations.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the names and the connection to atonement for forbidden relations. The passage is on Yoma 67b in the standard pagination; the Hebrew body and its inherited citation are preserved.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶן עוֹלָם הַבָּא נִקְרָא צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ חֵלֶק,
connections.quote: ‘Mishnah: All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it is said: ‘Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the shoot of My planting, the work of My hands, through which I am glorified.’ These have no share in the World to Come: one who says that the resurrection of the dead is not taught by the Torah, one who says that the Torah is not from Heaven, and a heretic.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית.
connections.quote: “From here we learn that whoever guards this covenant upon which the world stands is called righteous. From where do we learn this? From Yosef: because he guarded the covenant of the world, he merited being called righteous. Therefore, “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.””

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ, א): "עוֹלָם הָפוּךְ רָאִיתִי",
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: ‘These are people who are esteemed in this world but held in low regard in the World to Come.’ Thus Rav Yosef, the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, fell ill and his soul departed. When he returned, his father asked him: ‘What did you see?’ He answered: ‘I saw an inverted world: those above were below, and those below were above.’ His father said to him: ‘My son, you saw a clear world. And how are we there?’ He answered: ‘As we are here, so we are there.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּבִבְרָכוֹת (ה, א) דָּרְשׁוּ "חֵפֶץ ה'" דְּהַאי קְרָא אַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ‘If he accepts them, what is his reward? ‘He shall see offspring and prolong his days.’ Moreover, his learning remains with him, as it is said: ‘Hashem’s purpose shall prosper in his hand.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן נִדְרַשׁ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קפז, א).
connections.quote:
“It is written: “He created it not a waste, he formed it to be inhabited” (Is. 45, 18), that is, God made man for this purpose, and so dealt kindly with the world. Observe the Scriptural text: “And Abraham took another wife, and her name was Keturah” (Gen. 25, 1). Herein is an allusion to the soul which after death comes to earth to be built up as before.

Observe that of the body it is written: “And it pleased the Lord to crush him by disease; to see if his soul would offer itself in restitution, that he might see his seed, and prolong his days, and that the purpose of the Lord might prosper by his hand.” (Is. 53, 10). That is to say, if the soul desires to be rehabilitated then he must see seed, for the soul hovers round about and is ready to enter the seed of procreation, and thus “he will prolong his days, and the purpose of the Lord”, namely the Torah, “will prosper in his hand”.”

connections.hePhrase: [קו] "אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל" (גִּטִּין מג.),
connections.quote: ““And this stumbling block is under your hand”: He began his exposition in this way. Scripture says, “And this stumbling block is under your hand,” concerning the people of Jerusalem, among whom Torah had ceased. They would ask their fellows, “You have a garment; be our chief, and this stumbling block shall be under your hand.” That is: matters concealed like a garment belong to you, for you are knowledgeable in them; tell us, and become our chief. “And this stumbling block”—words of Torah whose truth a person does not grasp until he stumbles over them by issuing an erroneous ruling, is put to shame, and then pays attention and understands—are under your hand. I too stumbled in my ruling, and I retract it.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies the immediate meaning of the Gemara as learning from an erroneous ruling and correcting it. Rav Tzadok develops a further spiritual application here; the original explanation does not instruct a person to bring about a failure.

connections.hePhrase: [קו] "אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל" (גִּטִּין מג.),
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:1
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:1
connections.quote: “For a name everywhere denotes the essential inner purpose of that entity, and the essence of Moses is the Torah—termed "the gift of his portion," indicating the portion uniquely appertaining to him. And it is known from the teaching of the Arizal on the Talmudic idiom (Shabbat 101b), "Moses, you have spoken well," that Moses is the root of Da'at within every Torah scholar across all generations of Israel; for the soul of Moses comprehensively incorporates the entire reality of the Torah. And the Sages stated (Gittin 43a): "A person does not truly comprehend words of Torah unless he first stumbles over them," which is the mystery of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, falling into the Nile and being drawn out of it. And the explanation of this is known from the masters of esoteric truth, the early kabbalists: that the Torah descended into the exile of Egypt, and the Children of Israel were required to be exiled thither to redeem and extract it from there; see there at length.”
connections.explanation: Ohr Zarua places the teaching about stumbling before attainment within the story of Moshe being drawn from the Nile. Since Moshe embodies the root of Torah, the rescue becomes a model of Torah recovered from exile. This illuminates the siman’s movement from a fall to a newly recovered insight. The sequence describes the repair of a failure; it supplies no instruction to manufacture one.
connections.headline: Torah drawn out of the place of stumbling

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ע"ו מֵעִנְיַן דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל,
connections.quote: see note 967.
connections.context: The explanation “I drew him out” is the point of the name that Rav Tzadok cites. The earlier English quotation had accidentally incorporated an editorial etymological note into the verse.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ע"ו מֵעִנְיַן דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל,
connections.quote: “At the time of a person’s failure, he should know that at that same time a preparation for the good in that matter is present. If he merits it at that moment, he can rise to a very great level. The greatness of the sin toward which the inclination incites him corresponds to the greatness of the good he can then receive, if he turns this desire and longing toward the good. The good comes from that very matter, as the opposite of the evil. As the Zohar says in Pinchas, at the end of page 216a, at the time of the Flood they were fit to receive the Torah. Moshe was then present, as our Sages interpreted the word “beshegam” in Chullin 139b; see there. Water means Torah, but they turned it into “the raging waters.” Torah is the ultimate foundation of the world and the purpose for which it was created—“were it not,” and so forth—whereas they brought about its destruction. That same time was prepared, had they merited it, for precisely the opposite: the descent of the waters of Torah to sustain the world.”
connections.context: This is the earlier ois expressly cited here. It retains the decisive conditions: turning the desire toward good and meriting the prepared opportunity. The Flood generation’s failure is contrasted with the Torah they could have received.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת יד.): "וְשָׂבֵעַ יָלִין בַּל יִפָּקֶד רָע" – הַמַּשְׂבִּיעַ עַצְמוֹ מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, וּמִינַּהּ לְהֵיפֶךְ.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Acha son of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said to him: This is what Rabbi Chiya said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: Anyone who fills himself with words of Torah and then goes to sleep will not be given bad tidings, as it says: ‘He will sleep satisfied and will not be visited by evil.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר מֵעִנְיַן יוֹסֵף שֵׁידָא,
connections.quote: “Come and hear: Those seven teachings that were said on Shabbat morning before Rav Chisda in Sura were said toward evening on that Shabbat before Rava in Pumbedita. Who said them? Was it not Eliyahu who said them? Evidently the restriction on travelling beyond the Shabbat boundary does not apply above ten handbreadths! No; perhaps Yosef the demon said them.”
connections.context: This is the passage that connects Yosef the demon with words of Torah, which Rav Tzadok discusses above in Section 103.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דַּעֲווֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ זְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: see note 1016.
connections.context: The Gemara qualifies the transformation of sins into merits by repentance from love. Both statements and their reconciliation are included so that the claim is not presented without its condition.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִמַּיִם הַזֵּידוֹנִים נֶהְפַּךְ לְמֵי הַדַּעַת, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ הָעֲשׁוּקָה נִכְנְסָה לִקְדוּשָׁה וְנַעֲשָׂה מִמֶּנּוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה;
connections.quote: see note 41.
connections.context: Rambam supplies the expression “waters of knowledge” and explains its moral application through an actual resolution to abandon wrongful thoughts. He first distinguishes this allusion from the statutory laws of ritual purity.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ שֶׁנַּפְשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל הֵם עַצְמָן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְהִתְחַדְּשׁוּת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא הוֹלָדַת נְפָשׁוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת.
connections.quote: “The Torah is the map of the world, as stated at the beginning of Bereshit Rabbah, section 1, in the parable of plans and notebooks. Likewise Israel—for they and Torah are one, as is known, since the light of Israel’s souls is itself the light of Torah, and as it is written that Torah has six hundred thousand letters—are the map of the world in each generation. The renewal of the world in each period corresponds to the renewal within the souls of Israel in that generation, as stated in Yevamot 63a: even ships, and so forth, are for Israel’s sake. Just as souls change from generation to generation, so does Torah: that is, the Oral Torah, in which new teachings are renewed in each generation through the sages of Israel. Through every new teaching of the Oral Torah, new souls of Israel come to light, and through them new matters also arise in the world.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok states the connection directly in this earlier ois: new teachings of Oral Torah and the emergence of souls correspond to one another. This provides his own fuller explanation of the sentence here.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכז:): שָׁנָה לְתַלְמִידָיו – הוּא מַה שֶּׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ דַּיְיקָא אַחַר שֶׁטָּבַל מִקּוֹדֶם, שֶׁהוּא הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַתִּיקּוּן.
connections.quote: see note 1066.
connections.context: The account concerns the pious man who redeemed the captive girl. Rav Tzadok interprets the sequence of immersion followed by teaching; the previously quoted neighboring story concerned Rabbi Yehoshua and a different woman.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה שֶׁזֶּה עַצְמוֹ הָיָה מַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ מֵעִנְיַן לָדוּן לְכַף זְכוּת, אֲפִילּוּ בְּאֹפֶן זֶה שֶׁהַמַּעֲשֶׂה לִכְאוֹרָה מוֹרֶה בְּבֵירוּר לְחוֹב, וְלֹא יָדַע זֶה מִקּוֹדֶם,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 10
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 10
connections.quote: “‘You intended evil against me; God intended it for good.’ Here Hashem showed how the tribes could be brought into Egyptian exile. The principal cause was their beginning to separate, for when Israel are united nothing can rule over them. Yosef separated from the tribes in this way. While Yaakov was alive it was not clear who was greatest among the tribes: sometimes he drew one closer and sometimes another, according to what was right in his eyes then. Before his death, however, when he blessed them and told Yehudah, ‘Your father's sons will bow to you,’ everyone recognized Yehudah's superiority. Yosef therefore did not know how to act. If he seated Yehudah at the head, he himself was king, and a king may not be slighted. If he sat at the head himself, he knew that Yehudah was the head. He therefore sat apart. The brothers judged that he did so from hatred, and were punished with exile because they should have judged him favorably. Yosef too was held at fault for leaving them room to err: he should actually have sat at the head, since he was king then, while knowing in his heart that Yehudah was greater. Since the brothers erred about him, some trace of the matter was present in human eyes. A person should therefore always pray not to judge his fellow adversely, and that his fellow not judge him adversely. The brothers were punished for failing to judge him favorably.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies a concrete case of the good hidden beneath an apparently adverse act: Yosef sits apart because of a genuine conflict about precedence, and the brothers read it as hatred. The source holds both sides to a standard—the brothers should judge favorably, and Yosef should avoid leaving them room to err. This develops the siman's lesson without making hidden good intentions a reason to disregard the effect of one's conduct on others.
connections.headline: Favorable judgment and responsibility for appearances

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר שָׁם בְּתַלְמִיד שֶׁאֵינוֹ בָּדוּק וְדִבְּרָה תּוֹרָה לָשׁוֹן נְקִיָּה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה חָשׁוּד אֶצְלוֹ עַל זְנוּת;
connections.quote: “He said to them: “When I laid her at my feet, what did you suspect of me?” “We said: Perhaps there is among us a student whom the teacher has not vetted.””
connections.context: This is the intervening dialogue between the two parts of the episode already quoted in the existing note. The Gemara states the students’ favorable explanation; Rav Tzadok then interprets what the teacher’s uncertainty about a student implies.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵירְעוֹ מִפְּנֵי טֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ שֶׁהָיָה דְּבַר מִצְוָה, וַהֲרֵי "שׁוֹמֵר מִצְוָה לֹא יֵדַע דָּבָר רָע", וְזֶה נִקְרָא "רָע" כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “One who keeps a commandment will know no evil thing; a wise heart knows time and judgment.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reads “commandment” as mitzvah and “evil” in relation to the harmful spiritual event under discussion. This literal wording preserves those terms; the alternative translation “obeys orders” and “dangerous situation” obscures his reading.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁכָּל דָּבָר נִידּוֹן עַל שֵׁם סוֹפוֹ, וְאָז נִקְרָא "טוֹב מְאֹד";
connections.quote: see note 358.
connections.context: The Midrash explains “very good” through the constructive ends that human desire can serve. Rav Tzadok applies that pattern here to the good ultimately brought out of an initially troubling event.

connections.hePhrase: דְּאוֹתָהּ רִיבָה הִתְנַהֲגָה בְּדַרְכֵי גוֹיִם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן סוֹף פֶּרֶק ח,
connections.quote: “They said: All those days when you were confined in prison, you were hungry and thirsty. Now that you came out into the open, your body grew warm, and perhaps you experienced an emission. He said: Concerning the immersion of this young woman, what did you suspect? They said: All those days among the gentiles, she ate and drank from theirs; now you said to immerse her so that she would be purified. He said: By the Temple service, that is what happened. Since you judged me favorably, may the Omnipresent judge you favorably.”
connections.context: This is a parallel account of two pious men rescuing a captive woman; one of the men had also been imprisoned. Its explanation of the man’s immersion differs in detail from Shabbat 127b, where the cause is the exertion of travel. Rav Tzadok cites both accounts, and their different settings should remain clear.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קי:): שְׁבָקֵיהּ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לַחֲסִידוּתֵיהּ, מַאי חֲסִידוּתֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Akiva abandoned his usual piety, as it is written, “Return, faithless Israel, says the Lord; I will not turn My face against you, for I am pious, says the Lord; I will not bear a grudge forever.””

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קי:): שְׁבָקֵיהּ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לַחֲסִידוּתֵיהּ, מַאי חֲסִידוּתֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Akiva says: They come to the World to Come, as it is written, “The Lord protects the simple,” for in the coastal cities they call a child patya.”
connections.context: The surrounding Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva’s characteristic piety was and answers with his inclusive judgment concerning the minor children of the wicked. Rav Tzadok invokes that merciful stance in describing the chasid’s relation to others.

connections.hePhrase: [וִיעֻיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ק"ב],
connections.quote: “One who conducts himself with holiness even in all permitted matters and bodily needs—that is, whose deeds are all for the sake of Heaven, and who brings service and the will of the blessed God into them, in the manner the Sages described concerning Hillel and Shammai in Beitzah 16a—is called a chasid. This means that he does not merely take care to follow the strict line of the law. This is called “with all your heart”—with both your inclinations, and so forth. A righteous person subdues his inclination, but this person brings holiness into all the inclination’s desires as well. Then, measure for measure, the blessed God gives holiness to all that he does, and he merits bringing forth great holiness specifically from the evil inclination. It is then called “very good,” which is greater than simply good. Concerning this it is said: “In the place where penitents stand, completely righteous people cannot,” and so forth. The blessed God brings mishaps and stumbling blocks before him, and he needs repentance and atonement for this, for it is called sin; through this he brings the precious out of the worthless. But a righteous person who does not go beyond the line of the law is treated correspondingly by the blessed God, and “no iniquity will befall the righteous”—specifically the righteous. Therefore, in the account in Shabbat 127b of one who experienced an emission, they said “that chasid.””
connections.context: This is the ois explicitly cited here. Its distinction between a chasid and a righteous person is quoted together with the requirement of repentance and atonement; the eventual emergence of good does not remove that requirement.

connections.hePhrase: [זֶה נִקְרָא בְּלֹא דַעְתּוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "גַּם בְּלֹא דַעַת נֶפֶשׁ לֹא טוֹב",
connections.quote: ‘A soul without knowledge is also not good; one who rushes ahead with his feet goes astray.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קמט:): אֵין "לֹא טוֹב" אֶלָּא רָע, וְזֶה נִקְרָא רָע.
connections.quote: ‘Rather, the source is here: ‘Even for a righteous person, causing punishment is not good.’ ‘Not good’ means evil, and it is written: ‘For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You.’ You are righteous, Hashem, and evil shall not dwell in Your dwelling.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (ג.): אֵין אָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְנַס בּוֹ רוּחַ שְׁטוּת,
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly enters him, as it is said, “If any man’s wife strays”; shoteh is written.”
connections.context: The exposition links the verb for straying to folly. Rav Tzadok contrasts the loss of judgment involved in wrongdoing with the clarity restored through Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ אֵל אַחֵר שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קג עַמּוּד א): אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין,
connections.quote: “That river never ceases to increase, to multiply, and to produce fruit. The other god is castrated: it never has desire, does not multiply, and does not produce fruit; for were it to produce fruit, it would destroy the whole world.”
connections.context: The Zohar contrasts the holy river flowing from Eden with a destructive power lacking independent fruitfulness. Rav Tzadok relies on that contrast when distinguishing genuine spiritual offspring from the apparent products of evil.

connections.hePhrase: וּפֵירֵשׁ הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל שֶׁאֵין לוֹ דַּעַת כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “The drop drawn down through union comes from the faculty of Daat, for it mediates between and joins the male’s two faculties, Chokhmah and Binah. No union is possible except through Daat. Therefore union is called “knowing,” as in “Elkanah knew Channah his wife,” “The human knew Chavah his wife,” “No man had known her,” and many similar expressions. The reason is that without Daat there is no union at all. There, among the kelippot, even the male has no Daat, but only two faculties. They do not possess the third faculty, called Daat. Since that is so, it has no aspect of union; it resembles a eunuch who does not produce fruit.”
connections.context: This is the Ari’s explanation invoked by the author: the inability to produce the stated spiritual fruit is explained as the absence of the joining faculty of Daat. The passage is discussing the symbolic structure of the kelippot.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא סוֹד הַדַּעַת תִּיקּוּנוֹ,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים מ״ב:ב׳
connections.quote: “The matter is this: every single soul of the house of Israel contains an aspect of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him. He is one of the seven shepherds who draw life and divinity into the collective souls of Israel, for which reason they are called “shepherds.” Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, encompasses them all and is called the “faithful shepherd.” That is, he draws the quality of knowledge into all Israel, so that each person may know the Lord according to the attainment of his soul, its root above, and its nourishment from the root of Moses’ soul. That root is established in the supernal knowledge among the ten sefirot of Atzilut, which are united with their Emanator, blessed be He, for He and His knowledge are one, and “He is the knowledge.””

connections.hePhrase: וְרָצָה לְתַקֵּן זֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת צ"ו, וּ"מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ" הוּא בְּסוֹד הַמִּקְוֶוה].
connections.quote: “Therefore Moshe feared him, for Moshe too was present in the generation of the Flood, as our Sages said in Chullin 139b: “beshegam” has the numerical value of Moshe. It is said of him, “For I drew him out of the water,” for he was then in the water. The central matter of Moshe was to repair this thing called folly; therefore he separated from his wife and was buried opposite Beit Peor, as I have written elsewhere. When he saw how free this person was of it, he feared him, until the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, “Do not fear.” For we hold in Nedarim 31b that someone who vows to derive no benefit from the uncircumcised is forbidden to benefit from circumcised people of the idol-worshipping nations, but may benefit from uncircumcised Israelites. For the name “uncircumcised” applies to the former, even if they are circumcised and guard the covenant. “Your people are all righteous” and keepers of the covenant, even if they have caused damage.”
connections.context: In the cited earlier ois, the person Moshe fears is Og. The complete concluding unit explains Moshe’s relation to the Flood and to the repair of folly, then preserves the distinction with which the author answers that fear.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה הוּקְשׁוּ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז.), לְכָךְ גַּם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא מֵי הַדַּעַת מוֹעִיל כְּמוֹ כֵן.
connections.quote: “Just as streams raise a person from impurity to purity, so tents raise a person from the scale of guilt to the scale of merit.”
connections.context: The discussion links the ohalim, “tents,” and streams in Numbers 24:6; the tents are understood as places of Torah. Rav Tzadok uses the analogy between purification in water and the spiritual purification effected by Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה הוּקְשׁוּ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז.), לְכָךְ גַּם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא מֵי הַדַּעַת מוֹעִיל כְּמוֹ כֵן.
connections.quote: see note 41.
connections.context: Rambam’s “waters of knowledge” explains the expression used here for Torah’s purifying work. His analogy includes a sincere decision to withdraw from wrongful thoughts, while distinguishing the analogy from the statutory laws of immersion.

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ לָזֶה דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בִּדְחִילוּ,
connections.quote: “For Chokhmah and Binah are hidden in the mind and the heart, in love and fear. Torah without fear and love does not fly upward. [Another reading: “and through this eagle.”]”
connections.context: The source connects Torah’s ascent with both fear and love. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the element of fear here because it counters the state he is discussing.

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ לָזֶה דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בִּדְחִילוּ,
connections.quote: “The reason for immersion before words of Torah is explained in Berakhot there: one must learn with awe, fear, trembling, and perspiration. See Rashi there, under ‘From here,’ who says that the condition of a baal keri comes only from levity and an unrestrained state of mind. If immersion is required even for an involuntary event, that too must in some sense belong to this category. Yet Heaven forbid that the supremely holy should have even a moment of levity or an unrestrained mind while awake. Nevertheless, so long as they have not been completely freed from the serpent's effect, to become a heart of flesh as in the future and as Yaakov was, even an involuntary event in sleep was not free of bodily pleasure at that moment. This too is counted in that category and gives rise to powers of impurity, Heaven forbid. For this the Sages instituted immersion or washing with nine kav of water: through this one is purified from that spirit of impurity and unrestrained state of mind that proceeds from it, and can cleave to the light and holiness of Torah, which is a tree of life.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin explains the siman's pairing of water with awe in study. It explicitly discusses an involuntary event and rejects attributing frivolity to the holy person's waking conduct; its concern is the remaining bodily state and readiness for attachment to Torah. This preserves the difference between the account of purification and an accusation of a chosen offense.
connections.headline: Immersion and the inward attitude of study

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה הוּא הֵיפֶךְ, דְּאֵימָה וְיִרְאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב עַמּוּד א),
connections.quote: “Just as there, at Sinai, it was with awe, fear, trembling, and shaking, so here it must be with awe, fear, trembling, and shaking.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה הוּא הֵיפֶךְ, דְּאֵימָה וְיִרְאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב עַמּוּד א),
connections.quote: “All those who are ritually impure are permitted in Torah, for they too can be in awe and trembling; but a seminal emission comes only out of frivolity and an unrestrained state of mind.”
connections.context: The Gemara requires a Sinai-like disposition in Torah study. Rashi explains the contrast between that disposition and the state associated here with seminal emission. Rav Tzadok relies on this explanation, which was absent from the previous quotation; the discussion concerns the rationale of the restriction being expounded on this page.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא דּוּגְמַת שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קח:) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל: בְּרוֹתְחִין קִלְקְלוּ, בְּרוֹתְחִין נִידּוֹנוּ.
connections.quote: “It is taught: The waters of the Flood were harsh like semen, as it is said, “Ready for those whose foot slips.””
connections.context: This baraita introduces the bodily imagery that the next statement develops. The relevant passage is 108b, not 108a. Rav Tzadok is comparing the heat of the transgression with the corresponding form of judgment.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא דּוּגְמַת שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קח:) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל: בְּרוֹתְחִין קִלְקְלוּ, בְּרוֹתְחִין נִידּוֹנוּ.
connections.quote: “Rav Chisda said: They corrupted themselves through heat in their transgression, and through heat they were judged. Here it is written, “The waters subsided,” and there it is written, “The king’s anger subsided.””
connections.context: This is the exact measure-for-measure formulation Rav Tzadok quotes. The repeated verb links the subsiding Flood waters to the cooling of anger.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּתַקֵּן עַצְמוֹ קוֹדֶם, וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (עב:): תּוֹרָה בְּטָהֳרָה,
connections.quote: ‘‘The fear of Hashem is pure, enduring forever.’ Rabbi Chanina said: This refers to one who studies Torah in purity. What does that mean? He marries a woman and then studies Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרִינַן עֲלַהּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (כט:): הָא לַן וְהָא לְהוּ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: With millstones around his neck, can he engage in Torah?! The opinions do not conflict: one applies to us (in Babylonia), and the other to them (in the Land of Israel).’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרִינַן עֲלַהּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (כט:): הָא לַן וְהָא לְהוּ.
connections.quote: ““This is for us, and that is for them”: Rashi explains that the people of Babylonia would go to the Land of Israel to study the mishnayot of the Tannaim. Since they studied away from home, household needs did not rest upon them. A person should therefore marry, so that he would be without improper thoughts, and then study Torah. “That is for them” refers to the people of the Land of Israel, who studied in their own locality: if one married, all the needs of the household would fall upon him and interrupt his study. Rabbeinu Tam finds this difficult. It implies that Shmuel says to marry first in order to be without improper thoughts, and applies this to the people of Babylonia; but improper thoughts would still be present when they went away from home to study. Furthermore, how could he leave home to study after marrying, when he must provide sustenance for his wife and children? In the first chapter of Gittin, page 6b, Rabbi Evyatar sent the message that people coming from there to here fulfilled concerning themselves, “They gave the boy for a prostitute and sold the girl for wine”—meaning that their sons and daughters had to be pledged for their support. This indicates that they were not acting properly by going away from home to study. Rabbeinu Tam therefore explains the reverse: Rabbi Yochanan, who said, “With a millstone around his neck, shall he engage in Torah?” spoke about the people of Babylonia, who could not leave their wives and go to study Torah, and who were also poor. Shmuel, who said to marry first, spoke about the people of the Land of Israel, who could study in their own locality and who were also wealthy; it was preferable for such a person to marry and study Torah in purity. Sometimes people of the Land of Israel also went away to Babylonia to study, but most studied in their own locality.”
connections.context: Tosafot records two opposing assignments of “for us” and “for them.” Both explanations and Rabbeinu Tam’s stated reasons are retained, so the brief Talmudic phrase is not presented as having only one interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁהִתְחִילָה תּוֹרָה בְּבָבֶל, בִּטְּלוּהוּ לִטְבִילוּתָא,
connections.quote: “In matters of Torah, [the accepted practice follows] Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, for it was taught: Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira says that words of Torah do not receive impurity. When Zeiri came, he said: They abolished the immersion requirement. Some say: They abolished the washing requirement. The one who says they abolished immersion follows Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira. The one who says they abolished washing follows Rav Chisda, who would curse someone who went searching for water when it was time to pray.”
connections.context: This is the original report behind “they abolished immersion.” The Gemara preserves a second version concerning washing; the quotation distinguishes the two reports rather than silently omitting the variant.

connections.hePhrase: דְּזֶה מִקְרֵי רֵחַיִם בְּצַוָּארוֹ שָׁם בְּקִדּוּשִׁין, וּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה שָׁם בִּבְרָכוֹת,
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: A person who has had a seminal emission and has had nine kav of water poured over him is pure. Nachum of Gam Zo whispered this to Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva whispered it to Ben Azzai, and Ben Azzai went out and taught it to his students in the marketplace. Two amoraim in the West disagreed about this: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin and Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida. One transmitted “he taught it,” and one transmitted “he whispered it.” The one who transmitted “he taught it” explained that this was to prevent the interruption of Torah study and of procreation. The one who transmitted “he whispered it” explained that it was so that Torah scholars should not be constantly with their wives like roosters. Rabbi Yannai said: I have heard that they are lenient about it, and I have heard that they are stringent about it. Whoever is stringent about it for himself has his days and years prolonged.”
connections.context: The interruption of Torah is one side of an explicit dispute over publicizing the leniency. The opposite concern and Rabbi Yannai’s praise of voluntary stringency are retained with it.

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּקְרָא "בַּמַּחֲשַׁכִּים" בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.),
connections.quote: ‘What does ‘Babel’ mean? Rabbi Yochanan said: Blended with Scripture, blended with Mishnah, blended with Talmud. ‘He has made me dwell in darkness, like those long dead’—Rabbi Yirmeyah said: This is the Talmud of Babylonia.’

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּקְרָא "בַּמַּחֲשַׁכִּים" בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.),
connections.quote: “Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: The Holy One, blessed be He, did not write in the Torah “for the sake of these words,” “on account of these words,” or “because of these words,” but “by the mouth of these words.” This is the Oral Torah, which is difficult to learn and involves great hardship. It is likened to darkness, as it is stated: “The people who walk in darkness have seen a great light.” These are the masters of the Talmud, who have seen a great light, for the Holy One, blessed be He, illuminates their eyes concerning what is forbidden and permitted, impure and pure. In the future: “Those who love Him shall be like the sun going forth in its might.””
connections.context: The Midrash identifies the darkness with the demanding work of learning Oral Torah and the light with the clarity granted in that study. It supplies a direct source for the ois’s movement from darkness to an increase in Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן (כה.) שֶׁבָּבֶל גָּרְמָה לוֹ לְעִנְיַן הֶאָרַת גִּלּוּי שְׁכִינָה,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Abba began his eulogy for him: Our teacher was worthy of having the Divine Presence rest upon him, but Babylonia prevented it.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא רִבּוּי תּוֹרָה, וְהַכֹּל לְטוֹב, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ עוֹד:
connections.quote: “We say in Shabbat 77b that this is the order of the world’s creation: first darkness and afterward light. Since the blessed God established this order in natural matters, it is certainly the fundamental divine will, as it is written, “In the place where penitents stand,” and so forth. Although, Heaven forbid, one may not say, “I shall sin and repent,” and choose to act that way—because he is not enabled to repent—nevertheless, this order comes about of itself, for “there is no righteous person on earth,” and so forth. Even concerning Yosef the righteous, the Sages said in Sotah 36b that ten drops emerged, expounding “His arms were made supple,” and so forth. Even concerning Yishai, David’s father, who died through the serpent’s agency, the Sages said at the beginning of Vayikra Rabbah on Tazria, “He was filled with iniquity,” and so forth. Likewise, the foundation of the house of David and the Messiah in Peretz was preceded by Er and Onan—darkness. This is the order: “The people who walk in darkness have seen a great light,” greater than the light seen by one who does not walk in darkness. Wherever “darkness” is written, it means the obscuring of Torah’s light, and not merely this world’s troubles. Likewise, “A person does not grasp words of Torah unless he has stumbled” comes through this darkness, which is the serpent’s agency in the wicked Esav, who struck Yaakov’s thigh, as is known. As soon as a person has reached such a state, Heaven forbid, and returns and is healed, he rises to light—like the person upon whose head a spray of water fell, who said, and so forth: “He raises the needy from the refuse heap,” in Yoma 87a.”
connections.context: This fuller parallel expressly forbids choosing sin as a route to later repentance. Its account of light emerging from darkness is conditioned on returning and being healed, which preserves the meaning of the ois’s concluding hope.

connections.hePhrase: [קח] הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (סב עַמּוּד א) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה,
connections.quote: “Come and see: All a person’s sins, all the damage he has caused, depend upon repentance. But the sin of one who spills seed on the ground, corrupting his way and bringing forth seed upon the ground, damages him and damages the earth. Concerning him it is written, “Your iniquity is stained before Me,” and it is written, “For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil will not dwell with You”—except through abundant repentance. And it is written, “Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem, and Hashem put him to death.” This has already been explained.”
connections.context: The original Zohar passage on printed page 62a explicitly says “except through abundant repentance.” That qualification is retained. Rav Tzadok’s discussion explains the higher form of repair required; it should not be read as removing the possibility of repentance altogether.

connections.hePhrase: [קח] הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר נֹחַ (סב עַמּוּד א) דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה,
connections.quote: “Afterward it says, “Those who hate the righteous will be held guilty.” This refers specifically to someone who hates the aspect called “righteous”—one who does not take it to heart to regret this. But someone whose heart is broken within him over it, and who wishes to guard himself from now on, even though his heart is not yet refined, is described by “Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon those who fear Him, upon those who hope for His kindness.” One who fears and trembles over this, and hopes for God’s kindness that Heaven will help him improve his deeds from now on, has God’s eye upon him and will merit to repair the past. It is like what is said to Daniel: “From the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard.” Of this it says, “The Lord redeems the soul of His servants.” A servant is one who serves from fear, as in “If I am a master, where is My fear?” One who fears God and accepts from now on to become a servant of the King is described by “The Lord redeems,” even though he needs redemption, “and they shall not be held guilty.””
connections.explanation: Chanukah explains that the person’s heart need not already be purified for Hashem to attend to his return. Brokenness is joined there to wanting to guard oneself from now on, accepting service, and asking for assistance. This gives the present siman’s ‘broken heart’ a practical shape and explains why it can restore closeness beyond the limitation assigned to an ordinary form of repentance. The beginning is heard while the work of refining the heart is still ahead.
connections.headline: A contrite heart begins its return before it is fully refined

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא בַּלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּלְבָבוֹ יָבִין וְשָׁב",
connections.quote: ‘Make this people’s heart dull, make its ears heavy, and shut its eyes, lest it see with its eyes, hear with its ears, understand with its heart, turn back, and be healed.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק צָרִיךְ תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוּא נוֹבְלוֹת חָכְמָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה יז),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chanina bar Yitzchak said: There are three faint counterparts: sleep is a counterpart of death, a dream of prophecy, and Shabbat of the World to Come. Rabbi Avin adds two more: the sun is a counterpart of the light above, and Torah of the wisdom above.”
connections.context: Novlot expresses a diminished manifestation of a higher reality. The final phrase is the one Rav Tzadok needs: the Torah available below derives from a greater wisdom above.

connections.hePhrase: רַק צָרִיךְ תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוּא נוֹבְלוֹת חָכְמָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה יז),
connections.quote: see note 521.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the Midrash’s term through the image of a fallen leaf that still comes from the tree itself. The distinction is between the hidden divine knowledge and Torah as encountered within human choice.

connections.hePhrase: [וְנִקְרָא "יֵשׁ" כַּנּוֹדָע, בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא "קֶרִי", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בָּזֶה].
connections.quote: ““Those who taste it merit life” [the Shabbat prayer]—eternal life, as we have explained. These are the many worlds of each righteous person. “Righteous” means one who restrains himself from false desires and cleaves to truth, as with Yosef the righteous, because he restrained himself from desires. This is what the name “righteous” indicates everywhere in the holy tongue. He is the one who inherits yesh, for yesh means something substantial and existent, rather than false imagination, which is emptiness and nothingness. For the wicked person, the world of thought is a false imagining and does not qualify as yesh. [In the Ari’s Likkutei Shas it is stated that yesh has the same numerical value as keri: one who restrains himself from keri merits yesh; see there. This is clear, for keri is attachment to the world and its false, imagined desires, which is the opposite of substantial existence.]”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s fuller explanation of the numerical correspondence invoked here. Yesh and keri both equal 310, but the point of the parallel is the difference between spiritual substance and attachment to illusion.

connections.hePhrase: וְלֵב נִשְׁבָּר – לִהְיוֹת מַמָּשׁ כְּאַיִן, שֶׁהוּא בַּכֶּתֶר כַּנּוֹדָע שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה עוֹד,
connections.quote: “The hidden levels are the first three, corresponding to the two days of Rosh Hashanah. These form the stature of the head: Chokhmah in the mind, and Keter above the head, the depth of the beginning of thought, hidden from the person himself—the place where thought is born. Therefore it is called “being from nothingness,” and “Wisdom is found from nothingness,” as is known. The two days have one sanctity and are one long day, because nothingness cannot be grasped except through the being drawn from it. Yom Kippur corresponds to Binah in the heart: “His heart will understand, and he will return and be healed,” as is known. These repair the hidden matters: the beginning on Rosh Hashanah is repentance from fear, and the completion on Yom Kippur is repentance from love—higher repentance, repentance fit to cover all one’s deeds. The seven intervening days repair what is revealed in character traits and actions.”
connections.context: Within his account of the days of repentance, Rav Tzadok defines Keter as the hidden beginning from which thought emerges. The passage also distinguishes repentance from fear, higher repentance from love, and the repair of actual conduct.

connections.hePhrase: וְלֵב נִשְׁבָּר – לִהְיוֹת מַמָּשׁ כְּאַיִן, שֶׁהוּא בַּכֶּתֶר כַּנּוֹדָע שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה עוֹד,
connections.quote: “Repair also comes through crying out and prayer, as it says, “Hashem’s face is against those who do evil,” alluding to this blemish, which is called evil, as is known. And it is written, “They cried out, and Hashem heard”: crying out is effective. As the holy Zohar, volume II, 20a, states: “Crying out is greater than them all, for crying out is in the heart,” as it is written, “Their heart cried out,” and so forth. See there, where it concludes that it never returns empty. It therefore helps even for this blemish, from which repentance was withheld in the holy Zohar, volume I, 219b.”
connections.explanation: The Shvat passage follows the same verses from Tehillim as this siman and cites the Zohar’s distinction of a cry arising in the heart. This clarifies why the siman places heartfelt brokenness alongside prayer when discussing a blemish described so severely elsewhere. The connection is more specific than the general importance of prayer: both passages locate an available path of return in the heart’s own cry, even where the ordinary route appears blocked.
connections.headline: The cry of the heart reaches beyond words of ordinary prayer

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פְּנֵי ה' בְּעֹשֵׂי רָע", הוּא עָוֹן זֶה שֶׁנִּקְרָא כֵּן, "לְהַכְרִית מֵאֶרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Hashem’s face is set against evildoers, to cut off their remembrance from the earth.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ", שֶׁיְּרֻשַּׁת הָאָרֶץ הוּא רַק לַצַּדִּיק דְּהַיְינוּ שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית.
connections.quote: see note 954.
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly reads “righteous” as guarding the covenant and connects that designation with inheriting the land. This supplies the interpretation used here beyond the biblical verse already quoted.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמַר: "צָעֲקוּ וְגוֹמֵר" – תְּפִלָּה הוּא עֵצָה נֶגֶד לְהַכְרִית מֵאֶרֶץ
connections.quote: ‘They cried out, and Hashem heard; He rescued them from all their troubles.’

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה שָׁרְשָׁהּ בַּמַּלְכוּת שֶׁהִיא אֶרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה, וּפְגָמוֹ הִגִּיעַ לָהּ כְּעִנְיַן "ה' צִלְּךָ", מַמָּשׁ דּוּגְמַת הַצֵּל עוֹשֶׂה מַה שֶּׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה אִם לְטוֹב אִם לְהֵיפֶךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם];
connections.heRef: בעל שם טוב על התורה, קדושים כ״ג
connections.quote: “The holy Baal Shem Tov, of blessed memory, explained the verse “Hashem is your shadow” [Psalm 121]: the blessed God conducts Himself in accordance with your deeds, as it were, like your shadow. Whatever you do, the shadow also does. So it is, as it were, with the blessed God: a righteous person decrees, and the Holy One, blessed be He, fulfills it. [Vayechal Moshe, Psalm 121.]”
connections.context: The teaching explains the shadow as a correspondence between human action and the response above. Rav Tzadok applies that correspondence here to both improvement and damage.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לִהְיוֹת קָרוֹב לַה', הָעֵצָה – שְׁבִירוּת לֵב: "וְאֶת דַּכְּאֵי רוּחַ וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ‘Hashem is close to the brokenhearted, and He saves those whose spirit is crushed.’

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהוּא בַּתּוֹלָדָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי יֵצֶר וְגוֹמֵר מִנְּעֻרָיו", לְכָךְ בִּקֵּשׁ "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא", וּבְרִיאָה הוּא חֲדָשָׁה עַתָּה תִצְמַח יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן]
connections.quote: “For one who feels no desire in heart or mind for the service of Hashem, the counsel is: “Cast your burden upon Hashem.” Through his lowliness of mind in recognizing his lack, he awakens heavenly mercy, as it is written, “You have heard the desire of the humble, Hashem; You prepare their heart,” and so forth. This is the desire of the humble who recognize their lowliness and that they have no heart: the Holy One, blessed be He, prepares their heart. As is known, “Hashem is your shadow”: when a person is on the level of nothingness, he apprehends the blessed God likewise on the level of nothingness, and can draw forth and bring into being something from nothing, in the manner of “Create a pure heart.” This is wisdom in the mind; afterward comes something from something—will and desire in the heart. This means that the blessed God illuminates for him that there is nothing besides Him now, just as before the world was created; the whole earth is full of His glory. When this becomes clear before a person’s eyes, desires are immediately born in mind and heart. But first there must be “The nations have perished from His land”—meaning repentance for transgressions in deed, concerning which it is said, “Nations have entered Your inheritance.” For land, as is known, alludes to the body and the powers of action, while the nations are powers opposed to the will of the blessed God. Their removal comes through at least lower repentance, through which intentional sins become like inadvertent ones. Then the person attaches himself to the lowest of the ten levels of holiness taught in the first chapter of Kelim, the holiness of the land. It is known that everywhere the end is embedded in the beginning. Through this he can come to humility and the level of nothingness, the holiness of the Holy of Holies, as stated in Zohar II, page 121a. From there light goes forth into the world: “You prepare their heart,” in the sense that its light brings a person back to the good.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the request for a newly created heart through humility and recognition of one’s lack. It expressly requires prior repentance for wrongdoing in deed; that condition is included with the promise of renewed desire.

connections.hePhrase: "כִּי לֹא תַחְפֹּץ זֶבַח וְגוֹמֵר"
connections.quote: ‘For You do not desire a sacrifice, or I would give it; You do not favor a burnt offering.’

connections.hePhrase: [הַיְינוּ תְּשׁוּבָה, כְּעִנְיַן "כָּל הַזּוֹבֵחַ יִצְרוֹ וּמִתְוַדֶּה וְכוּלֵי" (סַנְהֶדְרִין מג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב)],
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Whoever slaughters his inclination and confesses concerning it is credited by Scripture as though he had honored the Holy One, blessed be He, in two worlds: this world and the World to Come. For it is written: ‘One who offers a thanksgiving sacrifice honors Me.’’

connections.hePhrase: "זִבְחֵי אֱלֹהִים – רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה, לֵב נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה אֱלֹהִים לֹא תִבְזֶה":
connections.quote: ‘The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken, crushed heart, God, You will not despise.’

connections.hePhrase: [קט] וּבְעִקְּבֵי מָשִׁיחַ מִתְגַּבֵּר מְאֹד עָוֹן זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה כִּי כִּמְעַט אֵין אָדָם בְּדוֹרוֹ שֶׁנִּיצּוֹל.
connections.quote: “Among the matters a penitent must repair is the sign of the covenant damaged through the emission of seed in vain, from which no person in our time escapes in his youth.”
connections.context: Reshit Chokhmah speaks about “our time,” meaning his own generation, and places the observation within the work required of a penitent. The verified electronic paragraph is 3:13; the printed subdivision cited elsewhere is chapter 3, item 10.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת שֶׁיָּצְאוּ עַד אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נוֹטְעוּ בְּזַרְעוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְבָמוֹת סג.) עַל פָּסוּק "וְנִבְרְכוּ בְךָ כָּל גּוֹיֵי הָאָרֶץ" – לְשׁוֹן הַבְרָכָה
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 22:1
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 22:1
connections.quote: “‘All the families of the earth shall be blessed through you’ (Genesis 12:3). ‘Venivrekhu’ is an expression like the Talmud's layering of a tree. This accords with the holy Ari (Gate of Verses, Shemot, under ‘A new king arose’): the generation of the dispersion was reincarnated in the generation of the wilderness, those who left Egypt. Because the dispersion generation sinned by building the tower with mortar and bricks, the Egyptians enslaved Israel with mortar and bricks in crushing labor. Thus ‘All the families of the earth shall be blessed through you’ means that they themselves will be layered and planted into your holiness.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov makes the siman's botanical interpretation of ‘venivrekhu’ explicit: souls are planted into Avraham's holiness. The historical allocation differs, however. This passage links the generation of the dispersion to the Egyptian exile and its bricks, whereas Rav Tzadok here associates Sodom with the Exodus and the dispersion with the later return from Shinar. The comparison supports the meaning of grafting while preserving the distinct schemes of repair.
connections.headline: Grafting souls and the different assignments of generations

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה נֶאֱמַר לְטַעַם עַל הַהוֹדָעָה מִסְּדוֹם שֶׁגַּם הֵם נִבְרְכוּ בוֹ וְהָיוּ צְרִיכִים הֲכָנָה יְתֵירָה לְשֶׁיְּתוּקְנוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל שֶׁהֵם הָיוּ יוֹצְאֵי מִצְרַיִם.
connections.quote: “The matter is this: Although the generation of the wilderness was being repaired and separated as good from evil, as mentioned, its original impurity did not entirely cease until they stood at Mount Sinai, as the Sages said. The secret is that the transgressions of Adam, and their own transgressions when reincarnated as the generation of the Flood, the generation of the Dispersion, and the people of Sodom, had not yet been repaired. Although they received their punishment in the Egyptian exile, they needed actively to return and fulfill the commandments they had transgressed. They therefore had to repair and fulfill them before the Torah was given at Mount Sinai. This is their meaning: Corresponding to the sin of the generation of the Dispersion, who denied the fundamental principle and worshipped idols as Adam also did, He gave them Shabbat and its laws at Marah, thereby repairing the sin of idolatry. This is the secret of the verse, “Happy is the person who does this, who keeps Shabbat from profaning it.” The Sages expounded that even an idolater like Enosh, who was in the generation of the Flood, is forgiven all his sins if he keeps Shabbat. For one who acknowledges idolatry is as though he denies the whole Torah; one who rejects idolatry is as though he acknowledges the whole Torah; and one who keeps Shabbat according to its laws is as though he fulfills the whole Torah. The denial of the fundamental principle is also repaired, because one who acknowledges Shabbat acknowledges the divine source above, who created the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Corresponding to the Flood generation’s sin of robbery, like Adam’s, He gave them the section Mishpatim, where all the laws of robbery and theft are written. Moreover, its first law, “When you acquire a Hebrew servant,” concerns a person sold by the court for his theft, who is not repaired until he is sold and afterward goes free. Accordingly, “Yosef was sold as a servant,” and all the Israelites were slaves to Egypt, to repair the sin of robbery; then they went free. Once they accepted this law of the Hebrew servant, it was counted as though it had been fulfilled through them, and their sin of robbery was forgiven. The emission of seed in vain had already been repaired by their being thrown into the Nile, as mentioned, and they were separated from evil. Corresponding to the people of Sodom’s sin of denying the laws of justice, like Adam’s, they were given the section “You shall discern from among all the people,” and the appointment of judges.”
connections.context: The original unit includes all three earlier generations in the wilderness generation and says that punishment alone did not complete the repair: positive observance was also required. Rav Tzadok’s later distribution among the Exodus, Ezra’s return, and the messianic generation is a further arrangement in this ois, rather than the exact distribution stated by this source.

connections.hePhrase: וְנוֹדַע דְּרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כג) עַל פָּסוּק "גּוֹי מִקֶּרֶב גּוֹי".
connections.quote: “Both these and those were uncircumcised; both grew a forelock; both wore mixed fabrics. If so, the attribute of justice would never have allowed Israel to be redeemed from Egypt. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Had the Holy One, blessed be He, not bound Himself by an oath, Israel would never have been redeemed.”
connections.context: The Midrash explains Israel’s redemption despite outward similarities to the Egyptians. Rav Tzadok uses that tension between external conduct and the deeper divine bond.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם יָדוּעַ דְּגָלוּת מִצְרַיִם הָיָה בַּעֲבוּר אַבְרָהָם, לְכָךְ הוּא הִתְפַּלֵּל עֲלֵיהֶם, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְקְנוּ בֶּעָתִיד].
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: Why was Avraham our father punished, and his descendants enslaved to Egypt for two hundred and ten years? Because he conscripted Torah scholars, as it is stated, “He mustered his trained men, those born in his house.” Shmuel said: Because he went too far in questioning the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is stated, “By what shall I know that I shall inherit it?” Rabbi Yochanan said: Because he kept people from entering beneath the wings of the Divine Presence, as it is stated, “Give me the persons, and take the possessions for yourself.””
connections.context: The Gemara gives three explanations for linking the Egyptian subjugation with Avraham. All three opinions are retained; the last concerns the people of Sodom whom he returned to their king.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא "אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם" – אַב מַמָּשׁ לְכָל הַגּוֹיִם.
connections.quote: ““For I have made you the father of a multitude of nations”: Avraham our father, of blessed memory, was the father of the world, like Adam, who was the father of a multitude of nations from whom all generations descend. Likewise, we find Avraham called “Adam,” as the Sages expounded “the great man among the giants”: this is Avraham. I have already alluded to this in the section Bereshit.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya makes the explicit comparison with Adam and calls Avraham the father of the world. Rav Tzadok develops this fatherhood here in relation to the souls planted in his descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי ב' אֲלָפִים הוּא סִבּוּב שָׁלֵם בַּבְּרִיאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: בְּבֵי"ת נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה דְּתוֹרָה קָדְמָה ב' אֲלָפִים שָׁנָה לָעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi expounded the account of Creation together with Bar Kappara: Why was the world created with the letter bet? To teach you that there are two worlds: this world and the World to Come.”
connections.context: The Midrash associates bet with two worlds. Rav Tzadok’s use of the number two for a two-thousand-year cycle is his interpretation in the present ois.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי ב' אֲלָפִים הוּא סִבּוּב שָׁלֵם בַּבְּרִיאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: בְּבֵי"ת נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה דְּתוֹרָה קָדְמָה ב' אֲלָפִים שָׁנָה לָעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “For Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Torah preceded the creation of the world by two thousand years. This is what is written: “I was beside Him as an amon,” and so forth. A day of the Holy One, blessed be He, is a thousand years, as it is written, “For a thousand years in Your eyes are like yesterday.” Thus, “Do you know this from of old,” and so forth: Torah knows what preceded the world’s creation. But you have no business expounding beyond “since a human was placed upon the earth.” Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Ben Sira: Do not expound what is greater than you; do not investigate what is stronger than you; do not seek to know what is beyond you; do not inquire into what is concealed from you. Contemplate what you have been permitted; you have no business with hidden matters.”
connections.context: The source gives the two-thousand-year statement and its comparison of divine days with a thousand years. Its accompanying restriction on speculative inquiry is retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי ב' אֲלָפִים הוּא סִבּוּב שָׁלֵם בַּבְּרִיאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: בְּבֵי"ת נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה דְּתוֹרָה קָדְמָה ב' אֲלָפִים שָׁנָה לָעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “The world and the body are material and destined to cease, including heaven and earth, as our Sages said in Bereshit Rabbah, section 42. But “year”—that is, the order of times—has no grasp in physical matter. Therefore Bereshit Rabbah says that an order of times existed before this. Likewise, as it says in Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 8, Torah preceded the world by two thousand years; this is an order of times. As soon as spiritual beings were created, time was created, for it is spiritual like them. [For even spiritual beings, insofar as they are created, have a time when they began to be created and an order of times.] Therefore time has no deficiency and never ceases, like the souls of the righteous and all spiritual created beings.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains elsewhere how an order of time can be spoken of before the physical world. The quotation preserves his distinction between created spiritual time and material bodies.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין צז.): ב' אֲלָפִים תֹּהוּ וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁבְּכָל חֵלֶק הָיוּ כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת הָרְאוּיוֹת לָצֵאת:
connections.quote: “The school of Eliyahu taught: The world is to exist for six thousand years: two thousand of desolation, two thousand of Torah, and two thousand of the days of the Messiah.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok uses these three eras to distinguish the historical emergence of different groups of souls. The neighboring discussion of a sabbatical millennium does not supply that threefold division.

connections.hePhrase: דְּתֹהוּ – עַד אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם;
connections.quote: ““Two thousand years were chaos”: Since Torah had not yet been given, the world was like chaos. From Adam until Avraham was fifty-two years old there were two thousand years, as the verses demonstrate. When the two thousand years were complete, Avraham engaged in Torah, as it is stated, “And the souls they had made in Charan,” which we translate, “whom they subjected to Torah in Charan.” In tractate Avodah Zarah, page 9a, we say that there is a received tradition that Avraham was then fifty-two years old.”
connections.context: Rashi locates the beginning of the Torah period at Avraham’s teaching in Charan, when he was fifty-two, rather than at his birth.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה ג' דּוֹרוֹת שֶׁקָּדְמוּ לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מָנוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “The generation of the Flood has no share in the World to Come and does not stand in judgment, as it is stated, “My spirit shall not judge the human forever”: neither judgment nor spirit. The generation of the Dispersion has no share in the World to Come, as it is stated, “Hashem scattered them from there over the face of all the earth”: “Hashem scattered them”—in this world; “and from there Hashem scattered them”—in the World to Come. The people of Sodom have no share in the World to Come, as it is stated, “The people of Sodom were evil and sinful against Hashem exceedingly”: “evil”—in this world; “sinful”—in the World to Come. But they do stand in judgment. Rabbi Nechemyah says: Neither these nor those stand in judgment, as it is stated, “Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.” “The wicked shall not rise in judgment”—this is the generation of the Flood; “nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous”—these are the people of Sodom. They said to him: They do not stand in the congregation of the righteous, but they do stand in the congregation of the wicked.”
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s actual list of the three generations invoked here. The dispute about Sodom’s standing in judgment is retained along with the statements concerning the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ תַּעֲנִית (ב.) דְּמַפְתֵּחַ שֶׁל עֲקָרוּת רַק בְּיָדוֹ],
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: Three keys are in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, and have not been entrusted to a messenger: the key of rain, the key of childbirth, and the key of the resurrection of the dead.’

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ תַּעֲנִית (ב.) דְּמַפְתֵּחַ שֶׁל עֲקָרוּת רַק בְּיָדוֹ],
connections.quote: ““Three keys were not entrusted to an agent”: One may ask: Do we not say in Sanhedrin, page 113, that the key to rain was entrusted to Eliyahu, and likewise the key to the resurrection of the dead, and likewise to Elisha, as it is written concerning Eliyahu, “As Hashem lives,” and so forth? It is also said in the later chapter, Taanit 23. The answer is that “they were not entrusted to an agent” does not mean that they were never entrusted, for the keys to resurrection and rain were indeed entrusted. Rather, they were not entrusted to an agent to be permanently appointed over them.”
connections.context: Tosafot qualifies the rule already quoted from the Gemara: it denies permanent delegated control, while acknowledging occasions when a key was entrusted to a prophet.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מִמֶּנִּי פֶּרְיְךָ נִמְצָא" (הוֹשֵׁעַ יד, ט);
connections.quote: ‘Ephraim will say: ‘What more have I to do with idols?’ I will answer him and watch over him. I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me.’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵל אַחֵר "אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין" כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר, וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ.): עֲבֵירָה אֵין לָהּ פֵּירוֹת.
connections.quote: see note 1159.
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s statement invoked by the author. Its final explanation—what would follow if that power produced fruit—is included with the contrast to the continually fruitful river.

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵל אַחֵר "אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין" כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר, וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ.): עֲבֵירָה אֵין לָהּ פֵּירוֹת.
connections.quote: “Merit has a principal and has fruits, as it says, “Say of the righteous that it is good.” A transgression has a principal but has no fruits, as it says, “Woe to the wicked; it is evil.””

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵל אַחֵר "אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין" כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר, וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ.): עֲבֵירָה אֵין לָהּ פֵּירוֹת.
connections.quote: “How, then, do I fulfill “They shall eat of the fruit of their way”? A transgression that produces fruits has fruits; one that does not produce fruits has none.”
connections.context: The first statement is the wording Rav Tzadok cites. The following qualification concerns wrongdoing that itself generates further consequences; including it keeps the general statement from being presented without its Talmudic limit.

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵל אַחֵר "אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין" כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר, וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ.): עֲבֵירָה אֵין לָהּ פֵּירוֹת.
connections.displayRef: Maharal, Chiddushei Aggadot, Kiddushin 40a (vol. II, p. 141)
connections.quote: “Fruit is what necessarily follows and proceeds from an existing thing, just as fruit comes from a tree. A transgression, which has no existence in its own right, cannot be said to produce fruit—unless the transgression itself produces fruit, as with desecrating the Name and similar cases in which others learn from the sinner and he has disciples who are his fruit. This is certainly a transgression that produces fruit, and this transgression does have fruit. A mitzvah, however, has fruit, for the mitzvah’s exalted rank and level are in the World to Come, and this world is the fruit of the World to Come. Therefore a mitzvah has fruit, whereas a transgression does not.”
