connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה גַּם רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין שֶׁנּוֹלָדִים מֵהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, הֵם נִקְרָאִים תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, נד עַמּוּד ב) עַל פָּסוּק "נִגְעֵי בְנֵי אָדָם".
connections.quote: “When a person is dreaming, female spirits come and play with him, become heated by him, and afterward give birth. These are called “the afflictions of human beings.””
connections.context: The Zohar applies II Samuel 7:14’s “afflictions of human beings” to offspring produced through these spirits. Rav Tzadok cites the attribution of offspring even in this troubling case before discussing the divine source of all life.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה גַּם רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין שֶׁנּוֹלָדִים מֵהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, הֵם נִקְרָאִים תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, נד עַמּוּד ב) עַל פָּסוּק "נִגְעֵי בְנֵי אָדָם".
connections.quote: ‘I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to Me. When he acts wrongly, I will chastise him with the rod of men and the blows of human beings.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה גַּם רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין שֶׁנּוֹלָדִים מֵהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, הֵם נִקְרָאִים תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, נד עַמּוּד ב) עַל פָּסוּק "נִגְעֵי בְנֵי אָדָם".
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yirmeyah ben Elazar also said: During all the years when Adam was under a ban, he fathered spirits, demons, and night spirits, as it is stated, “Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and fathered in his likeness, according to his image.” This implies that until then he had fathered what was not according to his image. They objected: Rabbi Meir used to say that Adam was a great chasid. When he saw that death had been decreed through him, he fasted for one hundred and thirty years, separated from his wife for one hundred and thirty years, and wore belts of fig leaves upon his flesh for one hundred and thirty years. The answer: When we spoke of that, we meant the seminal emissions that occurred to him involuntarily.”
connections.context: The Talmudic parallel identifies the births in question with involuntary emissions and expressly preserves Adam’s description as a great chasid. The existing Eruvin note concerns a different passage about giving money to a woman.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: "מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת" (אֵיכָה ג, לח), וְנֶאֱמַר: "לֹא יְגֻרְךָ רָע" (תְּהִלִּים ה, ה), וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּמַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא "רָע" יִהְיֶה מִמֶּנּוּ.
connections.quote: “From the mouth of the Most High do not come evils and good.”
connections.context: The biblical sentence is often read as a rhetorical question: do not both misfortune and good come from God? Rav Tzadok here invokes the non-interrogative wording “evils do not come,” distinguishing the divine source of vitality from its evil form. This quotation preserves the wording of his reading without presenting it as the only contextual translation.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: "מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת" (אֵיכָה ג, לח), וְנֶאֱמַר: "לֹא יְגֻרְךָ רָע" (תְּהִלִּים ה, ה), וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּמַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא "רָע" יִהְיֶה מִמֶּנּוּ.
connections.quote: ““I too”—I speak only in anger. “I”: what I built, I shall destroy; what I planted, I shall uproot. Thus it says, “What I built I am destroying, and what I planted I am uprooting.” “I shall do this”—this is harder for you than all else: My great Name will stand over you like a creditor. “To you”—this came about through your own hands. Evil never issues from before Me. Thus it says, “From the mouth of the Most High evil does not issue,” but rather good.”
connections.context: Sifra reads the verse in the noninterrogative sense used here. Its full unit places the resulting affliction in the context of divine judgment brought about by human conduct; the assurance about good is not detached from that context.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: "מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת" (אֵיכָה ג, לח), וְנֶאֱמַר: "לֹא יְגֻרְךָ רָע" (תְּהִלִּים ה, ה), וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּמַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא "רָע" יִהְיֶה מִמֶּנּוּ.
connections.quote: ‘For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil cannot dwell with You.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח:) וּבְסוֹטָה (ד:) דְּעַל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית לֹא יִנָּקֶה מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם.
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: Someone who counts out money to a woman from his hand into hers, or from her hand into his, in order to gaze at her—even if he is like Moses our teacher, who received the Torah from Mount Sinai—will not escape the judgment of Gehinnom. Of him Scripture says: ‘Hand to hand, the evil one will not go unpunished’: he will not escape the judgment of Gehinnom.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח:) וּבְסוֹטָה (ד:) דְּעַל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית לֹא יִנָּקֶה מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם.
connections.quote: “What does ‘Hand to hand, he will not go unpunished’ mean? Rav said: ‘Anyone who has relations with a married woman—even if, like Abraham our father, he established the Holy One, blessed be He, as Possessor of heaven and earth, as it is written of him, ‘I have raised my hand to Hashem, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth’—will not escape the judgment of Gehinnom.’”

connections.hePhrase: עַל זֶה אָמַר: "כִּי בָאֵשׁ ה' נִשְׁפָּט" (יְשַׁעְיָה סו, טז),
connections.quote: “For by fire the Lord will enter into judgment, and by His sword with all flesh; many will be those slain by the Lord.”
connections.context: The Hebrew names the Lord within the phrase “by fire the Lord enters into judgment.” Rav Tzadok focuses on the divine presence within that judgment, continuing his interpretation of “You are with me.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרַשׁ תְּהִלִּים א, יח): תֵּרֵד כָּל אוּמָּה וֵאלֹהֶיהָ וְכוּלֵי, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר הַנּוֹתֵן לָהּ כֹּחַ לַעֲשׂוֹת חַיִל.
connections.quote: “In the future the nations come to accuse Israel before the Holy One, blessed be He. … He says to them: If so, let every nation descend with its god. … Were the verse not written, it would be impossible to say it: “For by fire the Lord is judged.” It does not say “judges,” but “is judged.” This is what David said: “Even when I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil.””
connections.context: The Midrash links God’s accompaniment of Israel in judgment with Psalm 23; Rav Tzadok interprets this through the divine power that sustains every act.

connections.hePhrase: וְעָלֵינוּ נֶאֱמַר: "כִּי הוּא הַנֹּתֵן לְךָ כֹּחַ" (דְּבָרִים ח, יח), וְנֶאֱמַר: "כִּי גַם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ" (יְשַׁעְיָה כו, יב).
connections.quote: ‘Remember Hashem your God, for He is the One who gives you strength to gain wealth, in order to uphold His covenant, which He swore to your fathers, as it is this day.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעָלֵינוּ נֶאֱמַר: "כִּי הוּא הַנֹּתֵן לְךָ כֹּחַ" (דְּבָרִים ח, יח), וְנֶאֱמַר: "כִּי גַם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ" (יְשַׁעְיָה כו, יב).
connections.quote: “Lord, establish peace for us, for You have also accomplished all our deeds for us.”
connections.context: This is the reading Rav Tzadok invokes: the power to act ultimately comes from God. The verse’s wording is open to interpretation, but “requited all our misdeeds” does not convey the reading on which his argument rests.

connections.hePhrase: זֶהוּ "אַתָּה עִמָּדִי" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי שָׁם),
connections.quote: “The repair for one who emits seed in vain is engagement with Torah, as it is stated in Kiddushin 30b: “I created the evil inclination; I created Torah as its seasoning.” In Sukkah 52a they said that the Holy One, blessed be He, called it “evil,” meaning the sin of the Flood generation, the emission of seed in vain. [In Kiddushin 13a they said that the decree did not apply to the fish in the sea—meaning Torah scholars, as I have written elsewhere on the verse “Rule over the fish of the sea.”] As stated in Zohar, Bereshit, page 57a, and at the beginning of the chapter Kol HaYad, it is called evil. The Holy One, blessed be He, created this evil inclination, as it is written, “And whom I caused to suffer.” Therefore this can also occur in a dream, when it is evident that it is not a person’s action. A seasoning sweetens the food: that is, it turns the evil into “very good,” as our Sages said in Bereshit Rabbah, section 9, “This is the evil inclination,” which is sweetened through words of Torah. Zohar, Bereshit and Noach, says that there is no impurity like it. Yet in the second chapter of Berakhot, page 16a, they said that words of Torah raise a person from impurity to purity. The statement in Zohar, Noach, page 62a, that repentance does not avail is like what they said in Rosh Hashanah 18a: sacrifice does not atone, but Torah does atone. The same applies here. As our Sages said at the end of Chagigah, the fire of Gehinnom does not rule over Torah scholars. Gehinnom too is called “evil,” as stated in Berakhot 61a on the verse “Evil shall not go unpunished.” This is like what is said in Eruvin 19a, that everyone goes down there for matters of “chinnam,” meaning guarding the covenant. This too is the meaning of “You created Gehinnom”: the blessed God created it, just as He created the evil inclination. [There they also say, “You created righteous people.” A righteous person everywhere means one who guards the covenant; he too is so from the beginning of creation, as I wrote in the preceding ois, for this can also be found among the wicked and among the idol-worshipping nations.] Concerning this it is said, “Even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for You are with me.” “Evil” is the level just described, and “You” means that You created it.”
connections.context: The earlier parallel explicitly interprets “You are with me” through God’s creation of the inclination and Gehinnom, while placing the repair in engagement with Torah. The author’s original parenthetical references are preserved as they stand.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (יג:): נְהַר דִּינוּר מִזֵּיעָתָן שֶׁל חַיּוֹת יוֹרֵד עַל רֹאשׁ רְשָׁעִים בְּגֵיהִנָּם.
connections.quote: “From where does it flow? From the sweat of the living creatures. And where does it pour out? Rav Zutra bar Toviyya said in the name of Rav: ‘Upon the heads of the wicked in Gehinnom, as it is stated: ‘Behold, the storm of Hashem has gone forth in fury, a whirling storm; it will whirl upon the heads of the wicked.’’ Rav Aha bar Yaakov said: ‘Upon those who were cut off, as it is stated: ‘Who were cut off before their time; a river was poured over their foundation.’’ It was taught: Rabbi Shimon the Pious said: ‘These are the nine hundred and seventy-four generations that were decreed to be created before the world was created, but were not created. The Holy One, blessed be He, arose and planted them in every generation, and they are the brazen-faced people of each generation.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִית יִרְאָה רָעָה שֶׁהִיא רְצוּעָה לְאַלְקָאָה בִישַׁיָּא;
connections.quote: “Fear is divided into three kinds. Two of them do not have the proper foundation, and one is the foundation of fear. A person may fear the Holy One, blessed be He, so that his children will live and not die, or because he fears punishment affecting his body or possessions, and therefore fears Him continually. It follows that he does not make the fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, the primary matter. Another person fears the Holy One, blessed be He, because he fears punishment in that world and the punishment of Gehinnom. These two are not the foundation and root of fear. The fear that is fundamental is for a person to fear his Master because He is great and sovereign, the source and root of all worlds, and all are considered as nothing before Him, as it is stated, “All the inhabitants of the earth are considered as nothing.” He should place his will in that place called fear. Rabbi Shimon wept and said: Woe if I speak, and woe if I do not speak. If I speak, the wicked will know how to serve their Master. If I do not speak, the companions will lose this teaching. In the place where holy fear rests, below it there is an evil fear that lashes, strikes, and accuses; it is a strap for striking the wicked. Whoever fears because of the punishment of lashes and accusation, as described, does not have that fear of Hashem resting upon him which is called “the fear of Hashem leads to life.” What rests upon him instead? That evil fear. It follows that the strap, evil fear, rests upon him, and not the fear of Hashem. Therefore the place called fear of Hashem is called “the beginning of knowledge.” This commandment is included here; it is the root and foundation of all the other commandments of Torah. One who guards this fear guards everything; one who does not guard fear does not guard the commandments of Torah, for this is the gateway to everything.”
connections.context: The full distinction places fear of bodily or future punishment alongside the higher fear of God’s greatness. This gives the original context for the “strap” and for the ois’s transition to awe of exaltation.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי "כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי" נִתְהַפֵּךְ לְיִרְאַת ה' וְיִרְאַת הָרוֹמְמוּת הַמְּבִיאָה אַדְּרַבָּה לְשִׂמְחָה,
connections.quote: “The second kind is awe of exaltation: a person keeps away from sins and does not commit them because of the great honor of His blessed Name. How could lowly and despicable flesh and blood begin, or dare in its heart, to do something against the will of the Creator, blessed and exalted be His Name? This fear is not so easy to acquire. It is born only through knowledge and understanding, by contemplating His exaltation and the human being’s lowliness—matters that arise from an understanding and discerning mind. This is the fear we placed as the second part of one of the divisions of piety described earlier. Through it a person feels shame and trembles when standing before his Creator to pray or perform any service. This is the praiseworthy fear for which the pious of all generations were praised, and of which Moshe says, “To fear this honored and awesome Name, Hashem your God.” The fear we are now explaining, fear of sin, is a part of that awe of exaltation and also a kind in its own right. It means that a person is continually fearful and concerned about his deeds, lest some trace of sin be mixed into them, or something small or great be present that does not accord with the greatness of His honor and the exaltation of His Name. You can see the close relationship between this fear and the awe of exaltation: the aim of both is to do nothing against His exalted honor. The difference, through which it is considered a distinct kind and called by a different name, is that awe of exaltation occurs at the time of an act, service, or encounter with a transgression. When a person stands praying or serving, he feels shame and humiliation, quakes and trembles before His exalted honor; or when a transgression presents itself and he knows it is a transgression, he refrains from it so as not to act defiantly before His glory, Heaven forbid. Fear of sin, however, is at every time and every hour: at every moment he fears lest he stumble and do something, however slight, against the honor of His blessed Name. It is therefore called fear of sin, for its essence is fear that sin may enter and become mixed into his deeds through negligence, laxity, or unawareness, in whatever way. Concerning this it is stated, “Happy is the person who fears always,” which the Sages interpreted as referring to words of Torah. Even when he sees no stumbling block before his eyes, his heart must be anxious lest one be hidden at his feet and he fail to guard against it.”
connections.context: Ramchal defines awe of exaltation through recognition of God’s greatness and distinguishes it from the continual watchfulness called fear of sin. The ois’s subsequent teaching about joy is supplied by its existing Tanna DeBei Eliyahu quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי "כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי" נִתְהַפֵּךְ לְיִרְאַת ה' וְיִרְאַת הָרוֹמְמוּת הַמְּבִיאָה אַדְּרַבָּה לְשִׂמְחָה,
connections.quote: “Love reaches its perfection when it is mixed with awe. As Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 3, says: ‘I rejoiced from within my fear, and feared from within my joy.’ At the beginning of Berakhot's chapter Ein Omdin (30b), it says, ‘Rejoice with trembling’ (Psalms 2:11). This is service for the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shekhinah, as I explained elsewhere.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explicitly defines the perfection of love by its union with awe and quotes the same tradition about rejoicing through fear. This clarifies the siman's transformation: recognizing ‘You are with me’ redirects the fear toward Hashem and His greatness, allowing awe and joy to coexist. The outcome remains reverence that restrains sin, as the siman's last verse states.
connections.headline: Awe united with love and joy

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה" (תְּהִלִּים ב, יא);
connections.quote: “David the king further said: I feared through my joy and rejoiced through my fear, and my love rose above them all. Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, made a covenant with me that I would be proficient in Scripture, Mishnah, laws, and aggadot.”
connections.context: The teaching describes joy and awe strengthening each other. Rav Tzadok cites this union to distinguish holy awe from a fear that merely crushes or distances a person.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה" (תְּהִלִּים ב, יא);
connections.quote: “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling.”
connections.context: The conjunction of rejoicing and trembling is essential: Rav Tzadok describes awe that brings joy, rather than anxiety that excludes it.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַיִּרְאָה מֵסִיר עָוֹן זֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יְרָא אֶת ה' וְסוּר מֵרָע" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ז),
connections.quote: ‘Do not consider yourself wise. Fear Hashem and turn away from evil.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק ג דִּנְדָרִים (כ.) עַל פָּסוּק "וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ":
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: ‘So that His fear may be upon your faces’—this is shame. ‘So that you do not sin’—this teaches that shame leads to fear of sin. From here they said: Being bashful is a favorable sign in a person. Others say: Anyone who feels shame will not readily sin. Someone who has no shame of face—one can be certain that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק ג דִּנְדָרִים (כ.) עַל פָּסוּק "וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ":
connections.quote: ‘Moses said to the people: ‘Do not fear, for God has come to test you and so that awe of Him will be before you, keeping you from sin.’’

connections.hePhrase: [קיא] בְּעִקְּבָתָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא הָעִיקָּר הוּא רַק לְהוֹצִיא יָקָר מִזּוֹלֵל,
connections.quote: ‘Therefore Hashem says: If you return, I will restore you; you will stand before Me. If you bring forth what is precious from what is base, you will be as My mouth. They will turn toward you, but you must not turn toward them.’

connections.hePhrase: [קיא] בְּעִקְּבָתָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא הָעִיקָּר הוּא רַק לְהוֹצִיא יָקָר מִזּוֹלֵל,
connections.quote: “At the completion of action, there is in truth no evil here, for the end of everything is for good, and He “devises means so that no banished one is banished from Him” (II Samuel 14:14). There is therefore no truly evil body at all. This is the secret of the saying, “Falsehood has no legs” (Shabbat 104a), and of the statements in Berakhot 6a and in HaNizakin (Gittin 68b) that the feet of demons are like those of roosters; this is not the place to elaborate. This came about through Shabbat, which is the repair of Adam. As our Sages said, Adam recited the psalm for Shabbat, when his repentance was accepted. So too, at the end of everything, repair will return to its source. The Holy One, blessed be He, does not allow evil to reach completion; therefore no creature is wholly evil, but everything is a mixture of good and evil. As stated in Shabbat 77b, everything has some benefit. Likewise, in the future everything will be repaired, and no creature will be missing from the world: “The wolf will dwell with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6), and “The serpent—dust shall be its food” (Isaiah 65:25).”
connections.explanation: Sichat Shedim describes the final repair as a return to the source, drawing on Adam’s repentance and Shabbat. This illuminates the present siman’s ‘inverted world’: the lowest point can become the beginning of a renewed ascent because its created power is recovered for good. Both accounts place the complete transformation at the end of repair. Tzidkat HaTzadik explicitly names repentance as the way of extracting the precious from the vile.
connections.headline: The final repair restores created powers to their source

connections.hePhrase: וְרַק בִּמְקוֹם יֵצֶר הָרָע וְתִגְבֹּורֶת עֲווֹנוֹת מִשָּׁם יִקָּחֲךָ דַּיְיקָא עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה,
connections.displayRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 4:1
connections.canonicalRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 4:1
connections.quote: “But for the sin to be completely repaired, so that it is reckoned as merits, the section Nitzavim says, “You shall return to the Lord your God and heed His voice,” and “Even if your outcasts are at the end of the heavens, from there He will gather you, and from there”—specifically—“He will take you.” Even from the greatest distance, from the end of the heavens, specifically from there He will gather and take you. This follows what the Gemara says about “through them he shall live”: the sins become merits, and he receives reward for them. Here too, the gathering and taking will occur specifically through the sins that become merits through his repentance. This is when the repentance reaches “to the Lord your God”: through the bitterness of his great repentance, he comes especially close to the blessed God.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly interprets “from there He will take you” through the transformation brought about by repentance. This supplies his fuller explanation of the precise words used here; the distance itself is repaired through returning to God.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (צח.): בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: The son of David comes only in a generation that is entirely worthy or entirely guilty. In a generation that is entirely worthy—as it is written: ‘Your people are all righteous; they will inherit the land forever.’ In a generation that is entirely guilty—as it is written: ‘He saw that there was no man and was astonished that there was no intercessor,’ and it is written: ‘For My own sake I will act.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא שֶׁהֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: What is the meaning of ‘The utterance of David son of Jesse, the utterance of the man raised on high’? The utterance of David son of Jesse, who established the yoke of repentance.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל "רַגְלֶיהָ יֹרְדוֹת וְכוּלֵי" רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן;
connections.quote: ‘Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold of Sheol.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְעִקְבֵי מָשִׁיחַ הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִן הָרַגְלִין, וְשָׁם תִּגְבֹּורֶת הָרָע וְהַיֵּצֶר.
connections.quote: “Since the Temple was destroyed, this has been His work, until He completes the gathering of all the souls that fell among the shells of the man of wickedness and became mixed within him, from his head to his feet. Until He finishes gathering even those that fell as far as the feet, the Messiah is not revealed and Israel is not redeemed. This is explained in our discussion of the Zohar, Pekudei: “When feet reach feet, then it is written, ‘His feet shall stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives.’” Yet the Divine Presence gathers them only through the deeds and prayers of those below, in the mystery of “Give strength to God.” According to the quality of the deeds below is the quality of the extraction of those souls and sparks. If all Israel returned in complete repentance, His Divine Presence would have the power to bring all the souls out of there in a single moment.”
connections.context: The Ari’s teaching, recorded by Rabbi Chaim Vital, identifies the final gathering with the souls at the feet. The passage expressly connects that gathering to human deeds, prayer, and complete repentance, which is the work Rav Tzadok specifies here.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט): "טוֹב מְאֹד" – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע.
connections.quote: see note 358.
connections.context: The Midrash locates a constructive motive within the inclination that can also lead astray. Rav Tzadok’s point is the hidden purpose of that force, as expressed in the words “very good.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מָשִׁיחַ עַצְמוֹ נוֹלַד מִמָּקוֹם כָּזֶה,
connections.quote: “There the soul of King David, peace be upon him, was hidden, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah: “I found David My servant”—where did I find him? In Sodom. For “one opposite the other”: in one power’s rule over another, the strength of the surrounding shell corresponds to the strength of the holiness. Therefore, “Whoever is greater than his fellow has a greater inclination.” The holy spark of King David’s soul—he who is the principal victorious warrior, of whom “My heart is hollow within me” is interpreted to mean that he killed the evil inclination, and who will also slaughter it in the future—was submerged in the depths of evil, where the inclination was at its greatest strength. No person would have imagined that any holy spark or any holiness could be present there, amid the utmost defilement of bodily desire. It is therefore described as a “finding,” like a discovery that comes unexpectedly. Before Sodom was overturned through the side of might and the fire of Isaac that had begun to be revealed in the world, it was impossible for this to be revealed: that even in a place of such intense desire, holiness is present. Only after that strength of evil was overturned and weakened did a little holiness begin to appear in the intention of Lot’s daughters for the sake of Heaven. Even this was not yet without defilement; nevertheless, some intention to preserve the human species was revealed in her words, “There is no man in the land to come to us,” an intention for the sake of Heaven. This was the beginning of the revelation of King David’s holy light, which illuminates this truth: “Even darkness does not darken for You,” and “Even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for You are with me.” His sovereignty rules over all, holiness is present everywhere, and the soul of an Israelite is attached to that holy spark—“You who cleave to the Lord your God”—and cannot become separated from it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s own extended parallel explains the hidden root of David’s soul in Sodom and its emergence through Lot’s daughters. He retains both sides of the episode: an intention directed toward Heaven had begun to appear, while the act was still not free of defilement.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם וַיֵּרָא עַל בְּנוֹת לוֹט וְלוֹט, שֶׁהֵם שׁוֹרֶשׁ כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וּמִשָּׁם נִצְמַח שׁוֹרֶשׁ בֶּן דָּוִד.
connections.quote: “Midrash HaNe’elam: “Lot went up from Tzoar.” Rabbi Abbahu said: Come and see what is written about the evil inclination. Know that it is never abolished from human beings until the time of which it is written, “I will remove the heart of stone.” Although it sees people judged in Gehinnom, it returns to human beings. This is “Lot went up from Tzoar”: from the suffering of Gehinnom it rises to entice people. Rabbi Yehudah said: There are three governing faculties in a person: the governance of intellect and wisdom, which is the power of the holy soul; the governance of desire, which desires every kind of evil desire; and the governance that directs human beings and sustains the body, called the bodily soul. Rav Dimi said: This is the sustaining power. Rabbi Yehudah said: Come and see: the evil inclination rules only over the latter two powers. The desiring soul continually pursues the evil inclination, as implied by “The elder said to the younger: Our father is old.” The desiring soul stirs the other and entices it, together with the body, to cleave to the evil inclination. It says, “Come, let us give our father wine to drink and lie with him”: what do we have in the world to come? Let us pursue the evil inclination and the longing for this world’s pleasures. What do they do? Both agree to cleave to it. Thus it is written, “They gave their father wine to drink”: they fatten themselves with eating and drinking to stir the evil inclination.”
connections.context: This is the actual Midrash HaNe’elam allegory cited here: Lot represents the inclination, and his two daughters represent desire and the bodily faculty. The passage’s opening also specifies the eventual removal of the heart of stone. The emergence of David’s line from Lot is supplied by the separate lineage sources.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם וַיֵּרָא עַל בְּנוֹת לוֹט וְלוֹט, שֶׁהֵם שׁוֹרֶשׁ כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וּמִשָּׁם נִצְמַח שׁוֹרֶשׁ בֶּן דָּוִד.
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “What arose in your mind did not arise in My mind. I have two good young birds to bring forth from them: Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite.””
connections.context: God’s answer to Moses explains why Moab and Ammon were spared: Ruth and Naamah would emerge from them. This supplies the rabbinic source for the two lines of ancestry through which Rav Tzadok connects Lot’s descendants with the house of David.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אָז: שֶׁיִּתְהַפֵּךְ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרַע לְטוֹב, שֶׁזֶּה שְׁחִיטַת הַיֵּצֶר שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.).
connections.quote: see note 324.
connections.context: The Gemara describes the future removal of the evil inclination. Rav Tzadok interprets its slaughter as the transformation of evil’s root into good; that explanation is his interpretation of the image.

connections.hePhrase: בְּסוֹד הַחַיּוֹת: "רָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב כְּמַרְאֵה הַבָּזָק",
connections.quote: “The living creatures ran and returned, like the appearance of a flash of lightning.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok draws on the paired movements ratzo and shov—running forth and returning. This wording retains the two actions that structure his interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁמִּמָּקוֹם שֶׁפּוֹסֵק, מִשָּׁם חוֹזֵר וּמַתְחִיל לְהָאִיר,
connections.quote: “The meaning is as known in the mystery of “running and returning like the appearance of lightning,” seen by those who behold the Chariot: where they go, there they return. At the place where the light ends, it returns, and the end becomes a beginning, turning back again, so that the last of all the levels attaches to the beginning and the deepest origin and is called the head of all the levels. For the beginning of everything is the blessed God, and complete cleaving to Him is the deepest origin of the unfolding of created beings.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s explicit explanation of the image of running and returning. It supplies the link here between the light reaching its endpoint and that endpoint becoming a new head or beginning.

connections.hePhrase: [קיב] תַּאֲוַת הַיֵּצֶר שֶׁל הָאָדָם הוּא מִתֹּקֶף הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ בְּעֵת הֶרְיוֹנוֹ,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 52:10
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 52:10
connections.quote: “Therefore, although a person has sins that come from birth, as it is written (Psalms 51:7), ‘In sin my mother conceived me,’ and a person cannot clarify himself of those sins, Hashem in His abundant kindness and goodness suspends judgment concerning a person’s sin and judges him as he is now, in the present. As long as it is possible to turn the matter toward a person’s merit, that he did not act defiantly, He suspends judgment concerning his sins. Likewise, we see how many precious words of Torah come into being from this imaginary and temporal world; those words of Torah are eternal, standing at the height of the world forever.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov invokes the same verse about conception while distinguishing an inherited deficiency from a defiant act committed in the present. This qualification helps read the siman’s parent-and-child account as a description of transmitted conditions and shared repair, without making ancestry a substitute for judging the person’s present action.
connections.headline: Inherited deficiency and a present deliberate act

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּמִּזְמוֹר כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא וְכוּלֵי: "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ז),
connections.quote: ‘Indeed, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּמִּזְמוֹר כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא וְכוּלֵי: "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ז),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said: Even if he were the most pious of the pious, it is impossible that he should not have some aspect of sin. David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “Master of the worlds, did my father Jesse intend to bring me into being? Did he not intend his own pleasure? Know that this is so: after they have fulfilled their needs, this one turns his face one way and that one turns her face the other way, while You gather every drop that is there.” This is what David said, “For my father and mother abandoned me, but the Lord gathered me in,” and “In sin my mother conceived me.””
connections.context: The Midrash reads David’s verse through the parents’ bodily intention and God’s care in forming the child, even when the parent is pious. Rav Tzadok develops the passage into his account of transmitted desire and the shared work of repair; the existing Beit Yaakov note retains the distinction between an inherited condition and a deliberate present action.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם וַיֵּרָא (קיב עַמּוּד א) שֶׁהַמְּקַדֵּשׁ עַצְמוֹ בִּשְׁעַת תַּשְׁמִישׁ לָא מִסְתָּפוּ בָּנָיו מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע.
connections.quote: “When Rav Yosef went down to Babylon, he saw young men going in and out among beautiful women without sinning. He asked: Are these not afraid of the evil inclination? They replied: We do not come from a bad source; we were formed from holiness. For Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: A person must sanctify himself at the time of marital intimacy, and holy, worthy children come from him, who do not fear the evil inclination, as it is said, “Sanctify yourselves and be holy.””
connections.context: This is the actual Midrash HaNe’elam passage about the spiritual effect of the parents’ sanctification on their children. The previous quotation concerning Abraham’s description of Sarah as his sister belonged to a different passage. The precise structural reference avoids confusing the ordinary Zohar section with its Midrash HaNe’elam pagination.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בַּת כֹּהֵן שֶׁזִּנְתָה – "אֶת אָבִיהָ הִיא מְחַלֶּלֶת" (וַיִּקְרָא כא, ט), וַאֲפִילּוּ הוּא בְּגַן עֵדֶן דָּנִין אוֹתוֹ עַל דָּבָר זֶה.
connections.quote: ‘If a priest’s daughter profanes herself through sexual immorality, she profanes her father; she shall be burned in fire.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִרְאָה לְיוֹסֵף דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו שֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא.
connections.quote: ‘‘She seized him by his garment, saying,’ and so forth. At that moment, the image of his father came and appeared to him in the window. He said to him: ‘Joseph! Your brothers are destined to have their names written on the stones of the ephod, with you among them. Do you want your name erased from among theirs and to be called a companion of prostitutes? For it is written: One who keeps company with prostitutes loses wealth.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בְּעֵת הַמִּילָה שֶׁהוּא תִּיקּוּן הַבְּרִית וְהַתַּאֲוָה, אוֹמְרִים: "יִשְׂמַח אָבִיךָ וְאִמֶּךָ וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי כג, כה).
connections.quote: “They explained the reason for circumcision: it places a reminder upon the organ of desire, which is the source of much turmoil and sin, so that it will be used only for a commandment and for what is permitted.”
connections.context: Ramban records the covenantal sign as a reminder directing desire toward its permitted purpose. This supplies an original explanation for Rav Tzadok’s description of circumcision here as a repair of the covenant and of desire.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בְּעֵת הַמִּילָה שֶׁהוּא תִּיקּוּן הַבְּרִית וְהַתַּאֲוָה, אוֹמְרִים: "יִשְׂמַח אָבִיךָ וְאִמֶּךָ וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי כג, כה).
connections.quote: ‘Let your father and mother rejoice; let the one who bore you be glad.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה בִּכְלַל "הָאָב זוֹכֶה לִבְנוֹ בְּחָכְמָה",
connections.quote: “As it is written, “The wise inherit honor”—like an inheritance that does not cease, as our Sages said in Bava Metzia 85a: wherever a person is a Torah scholar, and his son, and so forth, it does not cease. “He, his son, and his grandson” means that his wisdom is complete, for a father endows his son with wisdom, as taught at the end of the second chapter of Eduyot, because the son is drawn from the drops of his father’s mind. When wisdom is merely outward speech and is not truly in his depths—when he is wise only in appearance—his wisdom is incomplete, and his son is not a Torah scholar. This is the meaning of their not having recited the blessing over Torah first, as taught in Nedarim 81a: the blessing before Torah is the recognition that wisdom comes from the blessed Lord. Without this, it is merely an illusion and apparent wisdom, not true wisdom. There are two depths in “from the depths,” the hidden mind and heart; the second depth is revealed in the grandson. When wisdom is complete in all its depths, it no longer ceases, and honor is his inheritance.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֵין אָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְנַס בּוֹ רוּחַ שְׁטוּת:
connections.quote: ‘Reish Lakish said: A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of foolishness enters him, as it says: ‘If any man’s wife goes astray (tisteh).’ It is written tishteh (evoking foolishness).’

connections.hePhrase: [קיג] "פְּרִי צַדִּיק – עֵץ חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי יא, ל),
connections.quote: ‘The fruit of a righteous person is a tree of life, and a wise person wins souls.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פה.) גַּבֵּי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, אַף שֶׁהָיָה נִרְאֶה לֹא כֵן.
connections.quote: ‘He applied this verse to him: ‘The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and one who wins souls is wise.’ ‘The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life’ refers to Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. ‘One who wins souls is wise’ refers to Rabbi Shimon ben Issi ben Lakonia.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְעֵץ חַיִּים הַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוּא אֶחָד עִם הַנְּפָשׁוֹת].
connections.quote: “She is a tree of life to those who hold fast to her, and those who support her are fortunate.”
connections.context: The verse describes wisdom as a tree of life. Rav Tzadok applies that scriptural description to Torah and then connects Torah’s root with the souls he is discussing.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל: דְּרוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין שֶׁהוֹלִיד אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן הָיוּ דּוֹר שִׁעְבּוּד מִצְרַיִם.
connections.quote: “It follows that all those demons and spirits created during the 130 years when Adam separated from Eve, as is known, were all exalted holy souls from the aspect of daat. They became mixed among the shells and required many reincarnations to refine and purify them until their impurity was removed. Therefore you find that the nation of Israel did not come into being until Jacob and afterward: most of the souls were mixed among the shells and were progressively refined, reincarnating from generation to generation. Their repair did not begin until Jacob, the chosen of the patriarchs, who repaired Adam. Then the repair of his children—the aforementioned souls—also began, and they continued to be refined in the Egyptian exile until Israel left Egypt.”
connections.context: This is the Ari’s teaching in Sha’ar HaPesukim, recorded by Rabbi Chaim Vital. It gives the precise connection named here between the spirits associated with Adam’s separation and the souls undergoing refinement in Egypt.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן י' טִפִּין שֶׁיָּצְאוּ מִיּוֹסֵף הֵם עֲשָׂרָה הֲרוּגֵי מַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: “It was taught: Joseph was fit to have twelve tribes issue from him, just as they issued from his father Jacob, as it is said, “These are the generations of Jacob: Joseph.” But his seed issued from between his fingernails. Nevertheless, they issued from his brother Benjamin, and all were named in reference to him, as it is said, “The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Ashbel,” and so forth.”
connections.context: The Gemara supplies the account of Joseph’s lost potential for twelve tribes and its continuation through Benjamin. The identification with the ten martyrs belongs to the separate teaching in Tikkunei Zohar, rather than to this Talmudic passage itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן י' טִפִּין שֶׁיָּצְאוּ מִיּוֹסֵף הֵם עֲשָׂרָה הֲרוּגֵי מַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: “With this yod Joseph sinned, as it is written, “His bow remained firm, and the arms of his hands were made supple.” What does “were made supple” mean? A drop, which is yod, was cast among the ten fingers and divided into ten sparks cast from the bow, which is the covenant. Where were they cast? Into the ten martyrs of the kingdom. He said to him: “But I heard that the ten martyrs were Jacob’s sons.” He replied: “Heaven forbid! Rather, they were in their likeness.””
connections.context: Tikkunei Zohar, in Tikkun 69, gives the specific identification of Joseph’s ten sparks with the ten martyrs. The quotation also retains its own distinction between this account and the statement that they were Jacob’s sons.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לָזֶה "וְלֹקֵחַ נְפָשׁוֹת חָכָם" (מִשְׁלֵי יא, ל), דִּבְחָכְמָה אִתְבְּרִירוּ וְלוֹקְחָם מִן הָרָע.
connections.quote: “This is the aspect of “higher wisdom” and the “concealed mind” of Arich Anpin. Concerning it, the holy Zohar says in many places, “Through wisdom they are refined,” and “darkness is transformed into light.” This means the world of repair, which was refined and repaired through the concealed mind of Arich Anpin from the world of chaos and the breaking of the vessels that fell into Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, and so forth, as is known.”
connections.context: In explaining the purifying power of the red heifer, Iggeret HaKodesh identifies the formula “through wisdom they are refined” with the transformation of darkness into light. This supplies the background of the formula Rav Tzadok applies here to recovering souls from evil.

connections.hePhrase: וְלִפְעָמִים הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ, שֶׁנִּקְרָא גַּם כֵּן לוֹקֵחַ נְפָשׁוֹת בְּמִשְׁפָּט בְּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן לְאָבֵל.
connections.quote: “He takes souls in judgment, rules His world, and acts within it as He wills, for all His ways are just. We are His people and servants, and in everything we are obliged to thank Him and bless Him. He who repairs the breaches of Israel—may He repair this breach for us and for this mourner, for life and peace.”
connections.context: This wording appears in the Rema’s gloss to the fourth blessing of Grace after Meals in a mourner’s home. It is the liturgical phrase Rav Tzadok interprets here when he connects God’s taking a soul in judgment with the repair of other souls.

connections.hePhrase: [וְלִפְעָמִים הוּא עַל אוֹתוֹ דֶּרֶךְ דִּבְגְמָרָא שָׁם דְּקָרוּ לֵיהּ "רַבִּי",
connections.quote: “Rabbi came to the place of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon and asked: “Does that righteous man have a son?” They answered: “He has a son, and every prostitute who is hired for two hires him for eight.” He brought him, ordained him with the title Rabbi, and entrusted him to Rabbi Shimon son of Isi son of Lakonya, his mother’s brother. Every day he would say: “I am going back to my town.” His teacher said to him: “They have made you a sage, spread a golden cloak over you, and call you Rabbi, and you say, ‘I am going back to my town’?” He answered: “I swear, I have abandoned that.” When he grew in stature, he came and sat in Rabbi’s academy. Rabbi heard his voice and said: “This voice resembles the voice of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.” They told him: “He is his son.””
connections.context: The existing note gives the Gemara’s interpretation of the verse “the fruit of the righteous.” This is the preceding narrative that explains how the title Rabbi and his uncle’s teaching helped bring the son back to Torah.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "מֵאַרְיָא בִּישָׁא גּוּרְיָא טָבָא לָא נָפֵיק".
connections.quote: “Concerning him, Nebuchadnezzar said: “From a bad dog a good pup does not come forth.””
connections.context: Seder Olam records the proverb in Nebuchadnezzar’s account of Jehoiachin. Its animal is a dog; Rav Tzadok uses the corresponding lion-and-cub wording here in his argument that the son’s eventual greatness reveals a good root. The author’s wording is preserved.

connections.hePhrase: וְתֵדַע, דְּאָמְרוּ שָׁם: "לֹא שֶׁזֶּה גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “When he died, they brought him to his father’s cave. A snake was coiled around the cave. They said to it: “Snake, snake, open your mouth, and let a son enter beside his father.” It did not open for them. The people thought that this meant one was greater than the other. A heavenly voice came forth and said: “It is not because one is greater than the other, but because this one experienced the suffering of the cave and this one did not experience the suffering of the cave.””
connections.context: The heavenly voice explicitly rejects a difference in greatness and gives the father’s suffering in the cave as the reason for the distinction in burial. Rav Tzadok relies on that rejection of unequal greatness in his reading of the son’s eventual stature.

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי לִמּוּד תּוֹרָתוֹ, כָּל דִּבּוּר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה מוֹצִיא אוֹתָם הַשַּׁיָּיכִים לוֹ,
connections.quote: “They said that the purpose of engaging in Torah is to refine the sparks of holiness that fell or were forcibly taken from holiness, and to restore them in complete unity to their former state. These are of two kinds. The first consists of the sparks of holiness that descended in the world of chaos, for a reason known to Him; what is understood by those who possess knowledge suffices as a sound explanation. The second consists of the oppressed souls that the man of wickedness seized from Adam through his sin, when he took great spoil, as is known concerning the vast number of souls he seized. Nothing commands him to disgorge what he swallowed except engagement in Torah. Through it one accomplishes the essential work: raising the holy sparks that fell before the world of repair, making Samael disgorge what he swallowed, and shattering and dissolving his power until he vomits out the wealth he swallowed. This is what the Sages said: “If [the evil inclination] encounters you”—if it is stone, it dissolves, and if it is iron, it shatters.”
connections.context: Or HaChaim explicitly distinguishes the fallen sparks of the world of chaos from the souls seized through Adam’s sin, and identifies Torah study as the means of recovering both. This supplies the fuller original account behind Rav Tzadok’s description of each Torah utterance bringing out the souls associated with its speaker.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פְּתִיחַת אֵיכָה): "הַמָּאוֹר שֶׁבָּהּ מַחֲזִירוֹ לְמוּטָב".
connections.quote: see note 74.
connections.context: This is the Midrash Rav Tzadok cites for Torah’s power to restore its own student. His following sentences distinguish the states in which that restorative power becomes immediately effective from those in which a person is still held captive by evil.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בָּזֶה יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת, שֶׁלִּפְעָמִים כְּשֶׁהִיא בְּעֹמֶק רַע רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁנֶּחְבְּשָׁה וְנִשְׁקְעָה שָׁם,
connections.displayRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.linkedRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.canonicalRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.heRef: דרך ה', חלק רביעי, בתלמוד תורה ו׳
connections.quote: see note 925.
connections.context: Ramchal distinguishes the immediate divine influence that requires worthy conduct from Torah’s intrinsic holiness, which can gradually awaken repentance even in a sinner. He expressly limits this latter claim to serious study, excluding mockery and deliberate distortion. This clarifies the distinction between Torah’s restorative power and the impediments Rav Tzadok describes here.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "אֵין חָבוּשׁ מַתִּיר עַצְמוֹ" (בְּרָכוֹת ה:),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan fell ill. Rabbi Chanina entered to visit him and asked: Are sufferings dear to you? He answered: Neither they nor their reward. He said: Give me your hand. He gave him his hand, and he raised him up.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "אֵין חָבוּשׁ מַתִּיר עַצְמוֹ" (בְּרָכוֹת ה:),
connections.quote: “A prisoner does not release himself from prison.”
connections.context: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan, who could help another sufferer, needed another sage to help him. The maxim answers that one’s own involvement in suffering can make outside help necessary; this is the point Rav Tzadok applies.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:): לֹא זָכָה – נַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘This is the Torah that Moses placed (sam)’? If one merits it, it becomes a life-giving drug (sam) for him; if he does not merit it, it becomes a deadly drug for him. This is what Rava said: For one who is skilled in it, it is a life-giving drug; for one who is not skilled in it, it is a deadly drug.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:): לֹא זָכָה – נַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, the body’s and heart’s power to sin comes through the wisdom within them. As it says (Hosea 14:10), ‘Transgressors stumble through them,’ and the Sages said (Shabbat 88b) that for those who turn it to the left, it becomes a potion of death. Through wisdom itself a person stumbles and dies, for without it the body could not sin so greatly. One cannot speak falsehood unless one says something true at the beginning. That is, something wholly imaginary is nothing, just as an animal has no sin because it has no wisdom and is entirely imagination. What is wholly imagination has no place for sin; only someone who first has a foundation of truth can afterward say something false. This is clear to one who understands.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains why Torah’s power does not guarantee a good immediate result. Wisdom can give the heart and body greater power to pursue a wrong direction; falsehood itself can become persuasive through the truth it initially borrows. This clarifies the siman’s warning that a learner’s unresolved captivity can draw other souls downward, even though eventual repair remains possible.
connections.headline: When wisdom supplies power to a wrong direction

connections.hePhrase: אַף דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לַסּוֹף כְּשֶׁיְּתַקֵּן הוּא מַרְוִיחַ, דְּעוֹלֶה וְעוֹלִים עִמּוֹ;
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ל״ט:י״ט-כ׳
connections.quote: “When one studies truly not for its own sake, with some ulterior motive for one’s own honor—for example, to become a Torah scholar and the like—that motive, which comes from kelipat nogah, clothes itself in one’s Torah. The Torah is then temporarily in exile within the shell, until one repents, bringing healing to the world. When one returns to the Lord, one’s Torah returns together with oneself. Therefore our Sages said, “A person should always occupy himself [with Torah and commandments], for from doing so not for its own sake he comes to do so for its own sake”—certainly so, for he will certainly eventually repent, whether in this incarnation or another, since “no banished one shall remain banished from Him.””
connections.context: Tanya describes the Torah studied with an explicit motive of personal honor as temporarily sharing its student’s exile, then returning together with the penitent. The qualification “until one repents” supplies the sequence Rav Tzadok states here: the person is repaired, and the Torah and the souls associated with it rise with him.

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ לְפִי שָׁעָה נֶאֱמַר עַל זֶה: "וּפֹשְׁעִים יִכָּשְׁלוּ בָם" (הוֹשֵׁעַ יד, י) דַּיְיקָא, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָרַע מִתְגַּבֵּר.
connections.quote: ‘Who is wise and will understand these things, discerning and will know them? For the paths of Hashem are straight: the righteous walk in them, while transgressors stumble in them.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַעֲשֶׂה דְּתַלְמִיד אֶחָד בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ זוּטָא (סוֹף פֶּרֶק כב) שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהַצִּיל עַצְמוֹ בְּתוֹרָתוֹ, רַק הִצִּיל נֶפֶשׁ הָאִשָּׁה
connections.quote: “There was a student of Rabbi Akiva who sat at the head of twenty-four thousand students. Once he went to the prostitutes’ market, saw a prostitute, and loved her. He kept sending a messenger between himself and her until evening. At evening she went up to the roof and saw that student sitting at the head of the students like an army commander, with Gabriel standing at his right. She immediately said to herself: “Woe to that woman, against whom all the punishments of Gehinnom will gather! Will this woman afflict a great man like this, who resembles an angel? When she dies and departs from this world, she will inherit Gehinnom. But if she does not receive him, she saves both him and herself from the judgment of Gehinnom.” When he came to her, she said: “My son, why are you losing the life of the world to come for an hour’s pleasure in this world?” His desire did not cool. She said: “My son, the place you desire is more filthy and unclean than all the other parts of the body, and no creature can bear its smell.” His desire still did not cool until she took hold of his nose and placed it at that place. When he smelled it, it became repulsive to him, and he never married. A heavenly voice went forth and said: “That woman and that man are destined for life in the world to come.””

connections.hePhrase: וְעִמְקֵי רַע נִקְרָא רַע בְּתַאֲווֹת רָעוֹת, וְכָל סֵפֶר מִשְׁלֵי מָלֵא מִזֶּה, וְנֶאֱמַר: "שׁוּחָה עֲמֻקָּה זוֹנָה" (מִשְׁלֵי כג, כז).
connections.quote: ‘For a prostitute is a deep pit, and a foreign woman is a narrow well.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח:): אֲפִילּוּ דּוֹמֶה לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁקִּבֵּל תּוֹרָה מֵהַר סִינַי, לֹא יִנָּקֶה מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם;
connections.quote: “One who counts money for a woman from his hand into her hand in order to gaze at her—even if he resembles Moses our teacher, who received Torah from Mount Sinai—will not be exempt from the judgment of Gehenna, as it says, “Hand to hand, the evil one will not go unpunished.””
connections.context: His point is that Torah attainment does not by itself remove the consequences of deliberate sexual wrongdoing.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אַחֵר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ "וְלָרָשָׁע וְגוֹמֵר", נִיצּוֹל עַל יְדֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר שֶׁלָּמַד תּוֹרָה מִמֶּנּוּ, וְהוּא תִּיקֵּן וְהִצִּיל נַפְשׁוֹ מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם:
connections.quote: “When Acher died, they said: Let him neither be judged nor enter the World to Come—let him not be judged because he studied Torah, and let him not enter the World to Come because he sinned. Rabbi Meir said: Better that he be judged and enter the World to Come. When shall I die and make smoke rise from his grave? When Rabbi Meir died, smoke rose from Acher’s grave.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אַחֵר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ "וְלָרָשָׁע וְגוֹמֵר", נִיצּוֹל עַל יְדֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר שֶׁלָּמַד תּוֹרָה מִמֶּנּוּ, וְהוּא תִּיקֵּן וְהִצִּיל נַפְשׁוֹ מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: Is it a feat to burn one’s teacher? There was one among us, and we could not save him? If I take him by the hand, who could take him from me? He said: When shall I die and extinguish the smoke from his grave? When Rabbi Yochanan died, the smoke ceased.”
connections.context: Rabbi Meir begins Acher’s passage toward the World to Come by enabling judgment; Rabbi Yochanan is credited with ending that punishment. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the saving bond created by a student’s Torah, while the full narrative distinguishes the two sages’ roles.

connections.hePhrase: [קטו] כְּשֶׁמְּחַדֵּשׁ דָּבָר בַּתּוֹרָה, צָרִיךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה מִצַּד שׁוּם נְגִיעָה בַּלֵּב שֶׁרוֹצֶה כָּךְ, אוֹ לְהִתְפָּאֲרוּת, אוֹ לַחְלוֹק עַל דִּבְרֵי זוּלָתוֹ וְכַיּוֹצֵא,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 19:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 19:1
connections.quote: “Concerning words of Torah, however, the Midrash concludes: lest you say that after a person gives his learning to another it no longer returns to him, Scripture says, ‘There they return to go.’ At the completion of every transmission there must be a little forgetting in the giver. This forgetting is the completion through which a new birth occurs, for every birth must first have forgetting before the birth can come from it. So too in transmitting Torah, when it moves from thought into speech, a person cannot always maintain a clearly illuminated awareness that he is only a conduit. Because he then forgets that he is only a conduit, he acquires a personal interest and wants to maintain his own statement, as the Talmud says, a person is inclined to maintain his statement. Thus the Midrash says: after a person gives his learning to another, when a little forgetting at the completion of transmission is unavoidable, lest you think those words of Torah are lost from him and remain in the isolated detail, Scripture says, ‘There they return to go.’ Since a person cannot avoid that little forgetting at the completion, they return to him; they do not, Heaven forbid, remain in the isolated detail.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim describes a subtler form of attachment to one’s teaching: forgetting for a moment that one is a conduit and therefore wanting to defend one’s own words. It also describes the teaching returning rather than remaining trapped in that private claim. This is a qualified comparison with Rav Tzadok’s distinction: a passing lapse during transmission is not identified with deliberately deriving an argument from envy or personal interest, but it too requires the teacher to relinquish ownership of the truth.
connections.headline: A teaching held as private property or returned to its source

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז אֲפִילּוּ טוֹעֶה נִקְרָא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְדִבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים,
connections.quote: see note 525.
connections.context: The Gemara recognizes both schools’ words as Torah while still deciding the practical law. Its explanation emphasizes Hillel’s humility and willingness to study the other view first—the qualities opposed to the self-interest and desire to defeat others that Rav Tzadok excludes here.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כְּשֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַנְּגִיעָה, אָז אֵינוֹ נִקְרָא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּלָל,
connections.displayRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 5
connections.linkedRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 5
connections.canonicalRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 5
connections.heRef: דרך ה', חלק רביעי, בתלמוד תורה ה׳
connections.quote: “The conditions that must accompany study are reverence during the study itself and the correction of conduct at all times. For all the power of Torah lies in His having attached His precious influence to it, so that speaking its words and understanding them draw down that great influence. Without this, speaking of it would be like speaking of other matters or books of learning, and understanding it would be like understanding other subjects of the natural world. These provide only knowledge of the particular subject; they impart no intrinsic excellence or elevation to the soul of the reader, speaker, or thinker, and no repair to creation as a whole. This influence, however, is divine, and is the highest and most exalted of the influences that reach created beings from Him. A person should therefore fear and tremble when engaged in such a matter: he approaches his God and occupies himself with drawing that great light from Him. He must be humbled by his human lowliness and tremble before His exaltedness. He should rejoice greatly in the good portion he has merited, but with trembling. This includes not sitting frivolously or treating either its words or its books disrespectfully, and knowing before Whom one stands and works. When one does this, one’s study truly becomes what it should be: the influence described is drawn down through it, divine excellence becomes rooted within oneself, and repair and illumination extend to all creation. But if this condition is absent, the illumination is not drawn down through one’s study. One’s words are merely like other human speech, one’s reading like reading a letter, and one’s thoughts like thoughts about worldly affairs. Indeed, one incurs guilt for approaching the holy without reverence and behaving frivolously before one’s Creator while speaking before Him and engaging with His holiness. The excellence of the study and the degree of influence it draws down correspond to the degree of reverence, honor, and care invested in it.”
connections.context: Ramchal distinguishes the divine effect of Torah study from the acquisition of information alone, and connects that effect with reverence and worthy conduct. This supplies an original parallel for Rav Tzadok’s distinction between words that function as Torah and words governed by the speaker’s own agenda.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיָרָבְעָם: "הַחֹדֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר בָּדָא מִלִּבּוֹ" (מְלָכִים א יב, לג),
connections.quote: ‘He went up onto the altar he had made in Bethel, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the month he had devised in his own heart. He made a festival for the children of Israel and went up onto the altar to burn offerings.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְוַדַּאי הוּא דָּרַשׁ לָהֶם אֵיזֶה דְּרָשׁ וְלִמּוּד שֶׁחַג הָאָסִיף הוּא בְּחֶשְׁוָן,
connections.quote: ““In the eighth month”: He expounded to them that this was the month of ingathering and that it was fitting for the festival to be held in it.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the specific interpretive argument behind Jeroboam’s choice of month. The existing verse note gives the statement that he devised it from his heart; this original explanation shows how his decision was presented as a Torah interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דּוֹאֵג עָשָׂה הַכֹּל עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה בְּדַעְתּוֹ, כִּי רֹאשׁ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין הָיָה,
connections.quote: ““Chief of the herdsmen”: Head of the court.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies Doeg’s position as judicial leadership. This is the original explanation for Rav Tzadok’s reference to him as head of the Sanhedrin; the position itself does not validate the decisions that Rav Tzadok goes on to criticize.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הוֹרָה "עַמּוֹנִי – וְאֲפִילּוּ עַמּוֹנִית" עַל פִּי הֲלָכָה שֶׁבְּדַעְתּוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי אִשְׁתִּיתוּ נֶגְדּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יְבָמוֹת עז.),
connections.quote: “Doeg put all these objections to them, and they fell silent. He was about to have David publicly declared disqualified. At once, the matter of ‘Amasa, the son of a man named Yitra the Israelite, who had relations with Avigal daughter of Nachash’ arose. Elsewhere it is written, ‘Yeter the Ishmaelite.’ Rava said: This teaches that he girded his sword like an Ishmaelite and declared: ‘Whoever refuses to accept this ruling will be pierced by the sword. This is the tradition I received from the court of Shmuel of Ramah: “An Ammonite” means an Ammonite man, not an Ammonite woman; “a Moabite” means a Moabite man, not a Moabite woman.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִמֵּילָא אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דָּוִד מֶלֶךְ וְהוּא מִפְּסוּלֵי קָהָל, וְדָנוֹ לְמוֹרֵד בַּמַּלְכוּת, וְכֵן לַאֲחִימֶלֶךְ.
connections.quote: “Nachman son of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani [said]: He [Doeg] said to Saul, “Does David still have a marriage? Is he not a rebel against the monarchy and regarded as dead? Now release his wife and make him a condemned man, as though he were dead, so that his blood is permitted and his wife is permitted.” Saul then gave Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish on Doeg’s word. As for bloodshed: it is written, “The king’s servants would not stretch out their hands against the priests of the Lord.” But Doeg killed them, as it is said, “Doeg the Edomite turned and struck the priests of the Lord.””
connections.context: The Midrash presents Doeg’s legal reasoning as a pretext for forbidden relations and bloodshed. It directly supplies Rav Tzadok’s account of treating David as a rebel and attacking the priests who assisted him; the reasoning is reported as Doeg’s wrongdoing, not endorsed as a valid ruling.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁאוּל, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה סָבוּר גַּם כֵּן כֵּן, הוּא הָיָה בְּטָעוּת וְנִקְרָא בֶּאֱמֶת בְּחִיר ה'.
connections.quote: “The Sages said: The proof is from here: “We shall hang them before the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the Lord.” A heavenly voice went forth and said, “The chosen of the Lord.””
connections.context: In the surrounding discussion the Gemara seeks evidence that Saul had been forgiven from Heaven. It identifies “the chosen of the Lord” as a heavenly declaration. This supplies the rabbinic basis for Rav Tzadok’s description of Saul while preserving the distinction between forgiveness and approval of every action.

connections.hePhrase: [וְאֵין בְּכֹחַ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כָּאֵלּוּ לְהוֹצִיא נְפָשׁוֹת כְּלָל, כְּעִנְיַן "אֵל אַחֵר אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין".
connections.quote: see note 1159.
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s contrast between the ever-fruitful river of holiness and the barren “other god” (Zohar II, 103a). Rav Tzadok applies its image here to teachings driven by self-interest, which lack the power to bring souls out of captivity.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה טו:) וּבְפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:): מִי זוּטַר וְכוּלֵי, אֶלָּא רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ami said: Doeg and Ahithophel raised three hundred questions about a tower suspended in the air. Yet we learned that three kings and four commoners have no share in the World to Come. What, then, will become of us? He said to him: Sharp one, there was mire in their hearts.”
connections.context: The question asks why exceptional Torah knowledge did not save Doeg and Ahithophel. The answer distinguishes intellectual achievement from the inward state of the heart, the distinction Rav Tzadok is making.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה טו:) וּבְפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:): מִי זוּטַר וְכוּלֵי, אֶלָּא רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי,
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda would take off his shoes and rain would come, whereas we cry out and no one pays attention to us. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, seeks the heart, as it is written: ‘Hashem sees into the heart.’ Rav Mesharshiya said: ‘Doeg and Ahithophel did not understand what they studied.’ Mar Zutra challenged this: ‘Of such a person it is written, ‘Where is the one who counts? Where is the one who weighs? Where is the one who counts the towers?’ Yet you say they did not understand what they studied?’ Rather, their study did not lead them to the halakha, as it is written: ‘The secret of Hashem is for those who fear Him.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁהַחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ יִהְיֶה מְחֻבֶּרֶת עִם הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב יַחַד, וְהַחָכְמָה יִהְיֶה יוֹצֵאת מִן הַלֵּב,
connections.quote: “Wisdom is in the thought of the mind, and understanding is the will and feeling of the heart, as is known from “Patach Eliyahu.” This is what lies within a person’s power, as it is written, “What does the Lord your God ask of you, except to fear”—which is in the heart, as stated in Yoma 72b. Likewise, in chapter Chelek, Sanhedrin 106b: “The Merciful One desires the heart”; and in Chronicles: “The Lord searches all hearts,” as I have explained at length elsewhere. Therefore, “understanding” denotes what a person originates, “wisdom” what one receives from others, and “knowledge” their union—that is, when the wisdom of the mind wells up from the heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s own explanation supplies the meanings of the terms in this sentence: wisdom in the mind, understanding as the heart’s will and feeling, and knowledge as their union. The connection is therefore a matter of the person’s inward will as well as intellectual understanding.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עַל יְדֵי הַדַּעַת הַמְּחַבֵּר חָכְמָה וּבִינָה,
connections.quote: “Knowledge is the joining of mind and heart: one desires only what one understands intellectually to be good and proper to do, and thinks only of what one wills. This is a person whose heart is under his control. With the wicked, by contrast, “they are under their hearts’ control.” That is, even though one knows that something is not good, one’s heart desires it and one cannot turn away from that desire. This is called lacking knowledge.”
connections.context: This parallel gives the practical meaning of the union Rav Tzadok describes: the heart’s desire and the mind’s judgment are brought into agreement under the person’s control. Merely knowing that something is wrong, while remaining governed by the desire for it, is the opposite condition.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה א): תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ דֵּעָה וְכוּלֵי]:
connections.quote: ‘Another interpretation: ‘He called to Moses, and Hashem spoke.’ From here they said: A Torah scholar who lacks judgment—a carcass is better than he is. Know that this is so: go and learn from Moses, the father of wisdom and the father of the prophets, who brought Israel out of Egypt. Through him many miracles were performed in Egypt and awesome deeds at the Sea of Reeds. He ascended to the highest heavens, brought Torah down from heaven, and worked on the construction of the Mishkan. Yet he did not enter the innermost place until He called him, as it is said, ‘He called to Moses, and He spoke’ (Leviticus 1:1). Elsewhere it says, ‘Hashem saw that he turned aside to see,’ and so forth (Exodus 3:4). At the bush, there was a separation between His calling to him and His speaking; in the Tent of Meeting there is no separation here. What is the case at the bush like? It is like a king of flesh and blood who became angry with his servant and ordered him imprisoned. When he gives instructions to the messenger, he gives them only from outside. But in the Tent of Meeting, when he is pleased with his children and his household is happy, he gives instructions to the messenger only from within, as if seating him between his knees, with a hand like a father’s upon his son. Therefore it says, ‘He called to Moses.’’

connections.hePhrase: [קטז] עַל יְדֵי הַטָּעֻיּוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁטּוֹעֶה וְאַחַר כָּךְ עוֹמֵד עַל הָאֱמֶת, שֶׁזֶּה קָרָא יְשַׁעְיָה "מַכְשֵׁלָה" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֲגִיגָה (יד.) דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ‘When a man takes hold of his brother in his father’s house, saying, ‘You have a cloak; become our leader, and let this ruin be under your hand.’’

connections.hePhrase: [קטז] עַל יְדֵי הַטָּעֻיּוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁטּוֹעֶה וְאַחַר כָּךְ עוֹמֵד עַל הָאֱמֶת, שֶׁזֶּה קָרָא יְשַׁעְיָה "מַכְשֵׁלָה" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֲגִיגָה (יד.) דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ““And this stumbling block”: What is “this stumbling block”? Matters that people do not fully understand unless they have stumbled over them—“are under your hand.””
connections.context: The Gemara interprets Isaiah 3:6 as referring to difficult matters of Torah whose meaning becomes clear through an earlier mistake. Rav Tzadok extends this pattern to the acquisition of Torah through the recognition and correction of failure.

connections.hePhrase: [קטז] עַל יְדֵי הַטָּעֻיּוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁטּוֹעֶה וְאַחַר כָּךְ עוֹמֵד עַל הָאֱמֶת, שֶׁזֶּה קָרָא יְשַׁעְיָה "מַכְשֵׁלָה" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֲגִיגָה (יד.) דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ““Unless he has stumbled over them”: When a student errs in a teaching a first and a second time, he applies his mind to understanding that teaching.”
connections.context: Rashi explains how an error can lead to clearer understanding: the student responds by giving the teaching closer attention. The existing note already quotes the Gemara itself.

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי זֶה לוֹקֵחַ אוֹתָם נְפָשׁוֹת דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה שֶׁבָּאִים מִצַּד יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ יְשַׁעְיָה "מִכְשׁוֹל" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.),
connections.quote: ‘He will say: ‘Build up, build up! Clear a road! Remove the obstacle from the path of My people.’’

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי זֶה לוֹקֵחַ אוֹתָם נְפָשׁוֹת דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה שֶׁבָּאִים מִצַּד יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ יְשַׁעְיָה "מִכְשׁוֹל" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.),
connections.quote: ‘Isaiah called it a ‘stumbling block,’ as it is said: ‘Build up, build up; clear a way; remove the stumbling block from My people’s path.’ Ezekiel called it a ‘stone,’ as it is said: ‘I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.’ Joel called it the ‘northern one’—tzefoni—as it is said: ‘I will remove the northern one far from you.’ The Sages taught: ‘I will remove the northern one far from you’ refers to the evil inclination, which lies hidden—tzafun—in a person’s heart.’

connections.hePhrase: [וּ"מִדֶּרֶךְ עַמִּי", וְ"דֶרֶךְ" בְּכָל מָקוֹם רוֹמֵז עַל "דֶּרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא.) "מִבְּלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ", וְכֵן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין].
connections.quote: ‘The path of an eagle in the heavens, the path of a snake upon a rock, the path of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman.’

connections.hePhrase: [וּ"מִדֶּרֶךְ עַמִּי", וְ"דֶרֶךְ" בְּכָל מָקוֹם רוֹמֵז עַל "דֶּרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא.) "מִבְּלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ", וְכֵן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין].
connections.quote: ““When you sit in your house”—excluding one occupied with a mitzvah; “when you walk on the way”—excluding a bridegroom. From here they said: One who marries a virgin is exempt, and one who marries a widow is obligated.”
connections.context: This is the derivation of exemption from Shema through involvement in a mitzvah. The subsequent discussion distinguishes concern arising from a mitzvah from ordinary anxiety. Rav Tzadok cites the former principle.

connections.hePhrase: [וּ"מִדֶּרֶךְ עַמִּי", וְ"דֶרֶךְ" בְּכָל מָקוֹם רוֹמֵז עַל "דֶּרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא.) "מִבְּלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ", וְכֵן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ קִדּוּשִׁין].
connections.quote: “The verses do not contradict one another: here, where the subject is Torah, and Torah is called by a feminine expression—as it is written, “The Torah of Hashem is perfect, restoring the soul”—it uses the feminine form. There, where the subject is warfare, and it is the way of a man to wage war while it is not the way of a woman to wage war, it uses the masculine form.”
connections.context: The Gemara explains why the word “way” takes different grammatical genders in different settings. This is the discussion at the beginning of Kiddushin to which Rav Tzadok refers.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְוַדַּאי אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹבֵר עַל לָאו דְּ"לִפְנֵי עִוֵּר לֹא תִתֵּן מִכְשֹׁל"
connections.quote: see note 1041.
connections.context: The Midrash gives the principle that God first fulfills His own command. Rav Tzadok applies that principle to the prohibition against placing a stumbling block.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (כט.) פְּלוּגְתָּא אִי נִתְקָל פּוֹשֵׁעַ, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּאַרְנוּ דְּכָל אֶחָד דִּבֵּר כְּפִי שָׁרְשׁוֹ, רַבִּי מֵאִיר לְשִׁיטָתוֹ בְּגִטִּין נב. וְהוֹרָיוֹת יג: דְּדִבְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת לֹא מַעֲלִין וְלֹא מוֹרִידִין, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: “They disagree about the moment of falling—whether one who stumbles is negligent. One master holds that one who stumbles is negligent, and the other holds that one who stumbles is not negligent.”
connections.context: The legal discussion concerns liability for damage caused by a fall. Rav Tzadok invokes the category “one who stumbles is negligent”; the Gemara presents that classification as a dispute, not an unqualified rule for every accidental act.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (כט.) פְּלוּגְתָּא אִי נִתְקָל פּוֹשֵׁעַ, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּאַרְנוּ דְּכָל אֶחָד דִּבֵּר כְּפִי שָׁרְשׁוֹ, רַבִּי מֵאִיר לְשִׁיטָתוֹ בְּגִטִּין נב. וְהוֹרָיוֹת יג: דְּדִבְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת לֹא מַעֲלִין וְלֹא מוֹרִידִין, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא קמא כ״ז ב:ג׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““And Shmuel said: They taught this concerning darkness”: The later disagreement about whether one who stumbles is negligent concerns someone who stumbles by himself, without stumbling over anything. Here, however, he stumbled because of an obstacle and was not required to look carefully, so he acted under compulsion. Although above we include an accidental injury like an intentional one in the liability of a person who causes damage, from “wound for wound,” the Merciful One did not include a case of complete compulsion.”
connections.context: Tosafot distinguishes stumbling on one’s own from encountering an obstacle one was not required to anticipate. This supplies the limits of the legal comparison; it does not characterize every stumble in the same way.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (כט.) פְּלוּגְתָּא אִי נִתְקָל פּוֹשֵׁעַ, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּאַרְנוּ דְּכָל אֶחָד דִּבֵּר כְּפִי שָׁרְשׁוֹ, רַבִּי מֵאִיר לְשִׁיטָתוֹ בְּגִטִּין נב. וְהוֹרָיוֹת יג: דְּדִבְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת לֹא מַעֲלִין וְלֹא מוֹרִידִין, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: ‘There was a guardian in Rabbi Meir’s neighborhood who was selling land and buying slaves, and Rabbi Meir would not allow him to do so.
