Rabbi Meir was shown in a dream: ‘I seek to destroy, and you seek to build?’ Even so, he paid no attention. He said: The words of dreams neither raise nor lower anything.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (כט.) פְּלוּגְתָּא אִי נִתְקָל פּוֹשֵׁעַ, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּאַרְנוּ דְּכָל אֶחָד דִּבֵּר כְּפִי שָׁרְשׁוֹ, רַבִּי מֵאִיר לְשִׁיטָתוֹ בְּגִטִּין נב. וְהוֹרָיוֹת יג: דְּדִבְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת לֹא מַעֲלִין וְלֹא מוֹרִידִין, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: ‘Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said to them: Let us admit them, but penalize them by not citing teachings in their names. They designated Rabbi Meir as ‘Others’ and Rabbi Natan as ‘Some say.’ They were shown in their dreams: Go and appease Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rabbi Natan went; Rabbi Meir did not go, saying: The words of dreams neither raise nor lower anything. When Rabbi Natan went, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said to him: Granted that your father’s golden belt [his rank] helped you become head of the court, did it also make you Nasi?’

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (כט.) פְּלוּגְתָּא אִי נִתְקָל פּוֹשֵׁעַ, וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּאַרְנוּ דְּכָל אֶחָד דִּבֵּר כְּפִי שָׁרְשׁוֹ, רַבִּי מֵאִיר לְשִׁיטָתוֹ בְּגִטִּין נב. וְהוֹרָיוֹת יג: דְּדִבְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת לֹא מַעֲלִין וְלֹא מוֹרִידִין, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 2:21
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 2:21
connections.quote: “For every created intellect and understanding has an end and a boundary: “Thus far shall you come.” His understanding, however, had no boundary or thing that limited it, so that one could say: “Thus far extends his intellect; a thing like this he can no longer declare pure through the breadth of his understanding.” “Standing” means that one stands and has no further place to go, as one who stands at a boundary. Therefore they said that, in his case, they could not reach the end of his understanding, because it had no boundary. For this reason the halakhah does not follow him, as mentioned above, concerning the rule that one does not put vitriol into the ink.”
connections.context: In his discussion of Rabbi Meir, Rav Tzadok relates the breadth of his understanding to the statement that his colleagues could not reach its end. The passage also retains the practical qualification that the halakhah does not follow his position.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הוּא כְּדֵי לַעֲמוֹד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְהוֹצִיא יָקָר מִזּוֹלֵל.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
connections.quote: see note 27.
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains what is gained through the return after a stumbling: Torah enters the heart with greater desire than before. The interpretation of ‘I will return you’ as both returning a lost thing and teshuvah gives a concrete image for the siman’s raising of the stumbling through the later discovery of truth. The direction is toward correction, rather than seeking an error for its own sake.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁגַּם בָּהּ נֶאֱרַע מַכְשֵׁלָה וְהַעֲמָדָה עַל הָאֱמֶת אַחַר כָּךְ דַּיְיקָא עַל יְדֵי זֶה, כִּי אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד וְכוּלֵי בְּעִנְיָן אַחֵר, עַל יְדֵי זֶה הֶעֱלָה הַמִּכְשׁוֹל.
connections.quote: see note 1136.
connections.context: Rashi explains the use of the verse when a sage publicly corrects an earlier ruling. His account adds the concrete sequence of error, attention, understanding, and retraction.

connections.hePhrase: כַּנּוֹדָע דִּבְרִית הַלָּשׁוֹן וּבְרִית הַמָּעוֹר מְכֻוָּונוֹת, דִּלְכָךְ בַּתּוֹרָה מְתַקְּנִים חֵטְא הַמָּעוֹר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת צ"ז וְק"ז;
connections.quote: “Ten sefirot of nothingness, corresponding to the ten fingers: five opposite five, with the covenant of the One aligned in the middle, in the circumcision of the tongue and the circumcision of the organ.”
connections.context: Sefer Yetzirah supplies the formulation linking the covenant of speech with the bodily covenant. Rav Tzadok invokes their correspondence here.

connections.hePhrase: כַּנּוֹדָע דִּבְרִית הַלָּשׁוֹן וּבְרִית הַמָּעוֹר מְכֻוָּונוֹת, דִּלְכָךְ בַּתּוֹרָה מְתַקְּנִים חֵטְא הַמָּעוֹר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת צ"ז וְק"ז;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: What remedy is there for those who speak maliciously? If he is a Torah scholar, he should engage in Torah, as it is said, “A healing tongue is a tree of life.” “Tongue” here means malicious speech, as it is said, “Their tongue is a sharpened arrow”; and “tree” means Torah, as it is said, “It is a tree of life to those who grasp it.” If he is unlearned, he should humble his spirit, as it is said, “And perverseness in it is a breaking of the spirit.” Rabbi Acha son of Rabbi Chanina says: Once he has spoken, he has no remedy, for David has already cut him off through the holy spirit, as it is said, “May Hashem cut off all smooth lips, the tongue speaking great things.” Rather, what remedy will keep him from coming to malicious speech? If he is a Torah scholar, he should engage in Torah; if he is unlearned, he should humble his spirit, as it is said, “And perverseness in it is a breaking of the spirit.””
connections.context: The Gemara connects Torah with the healing of speech. Both opinions are retained: Rabbi Chama speaks of a remedy, while Rabbi Acha places the teaching in the context of preventing the offense.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם: "פִּיו הִכְשִׁילוֹ",
connections.quote: ““You too”: His mouth caused him to stumble—“you too” will ultimately leave disappointed, just as the first messengers did.”
connections.context: Rashi uses the exact expression “his mouth caused him to stumble” in explaining Bilaam’s words to Balak’s second delegation.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְגִטִּין (נז.): אַכְשְׁלֵיהּ פּוּמֵיהּ לְבַר דְּרוֹמָא,
connections.quote: ‘Bar Daroma’s mouth caused him to stumble, and he said: ‘You, God, have surely abandoned us, and You, God, do not go out with our armies.’ But David said this too! David was speaking in astonishment.’

connections.hePhrase: "מִכְשׁוֹל", כִּי הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמֵה' מַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן" (מִשְׁלֵי טז, א), וּמִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ בַּפֶּה מַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְדַבֵּר כְּלָל כַּנּוֹדָע בְּכָל מָקוֹם.
connections.quote: ‘The arrangements of the heart belong to a person, but the tongue’s answer comes from Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבָזֶה נִכְשַׁל יְשַׁעְיָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי אִישׁ טְמֵא שְׂפָתַיִם אָנֹכִי" (יְשַׁעְיָה ו, ה),
connections.quote: ‘I said: ‘Woe to me, for I am undone! I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips, yet my eyes have seen the King, Hashem of hosts.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (מט:): כִּי מְטָא לַהֲדֵי פּוּמָא וְכוּלֵי, בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁדִּבֵּר רַע עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
connections.quote: ‘Isaiah said: ‘I know that he will not accept what I tell him; if I tell him, I will make him a deliberate sinner.’ He uttered a divine Name and was swallowed into a cedar tree. They brought the cedar and sawed it. When the saw reached the place of his mouth, he died, because he had said: ‘I dwell among a people of impure lips.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְנָם בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לֹא נִכְשַׁל רַק לְשָׁעָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְבְּעוּ דְּבָרָיו בַּסֵּפֶר וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי נְבוּאָה מִפִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “That is, what he said, “And I dwell among a people of unclean lips,” was spoken by the mouth of Hashem, for these words were according to His will. This is the meaning of “Your iniquity has departed.” Although Isaiah’s intention was to describe Israel as unclean of lips, and this was like speaking maliciously of Israel, the words written among the Prophets are words of Torah, truly spoken by the mouth of Hashem. They teach merit concerning Israel: their sin is only from the lips outward, like the statement, “Doeg’s Torah was only from the lips outward.” This was a merit for Israel, that their impurity and sin were only from the lips outward. Similarly, the Midrash says that in two places Israel acted toward the Holy One, blessed be He: at Sinai they acted with their mouths and not their hearts, as it is said, “They enticed Him with their mouths.” Since they went wrong shortly after saying, “We shall do and we shall hear,” their statement was only outward, in their mouths and not their hearts. In Babylonia they acted with their hearts and not their mouths: their sin there was only from the lips outward, while their hearts were bound to Hashem. This is the meaning of “They acted only outwardly.” Here too, the words taught merit concerning Israel: they were merely a people of unclean lips, outwardly, while their hearts were pure and bound at their root to Hashem. This was the intention from Hashem’s side. But Isaiah, for his part, intended to accuse Israel with these words. This resembles one who intended to take pork but actually took lamb, who still requires atonement and forgiveness. Concerning this it says, “Your sin shall be atoned.” See also Yevamot 49b.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the favorable divine meaning of the recorded prophecy from Isaiah’s own intention to criticize. The passage expressly retains the need for atonement for that intention.

connections.hePhrase: רַק טָעוּת לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, לְכָךְ הָיָה עָנְשׁוֹ עַל יְדֵי מְנַשֶּׁה שֶׁטָּעַן נֶגְדּוֹ שֶׁנִּכְשַׁל בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת לֹא נִכְשַׁל:
connections.quote: “Manasseh said to Isaiah: Moses your teacher said, “No person may see Me and live,” but you said, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne.” Moses your teacher said, “Who is like the Lord our God whenever we call to Him,” but you said, “Seek the Lord when He is to be found.” Moses your teacher said, “I shall fill the number of your days,” but you said, “I shall add fifteen years to your days.””
connections.context: These are Manasseh’s charges, not the Gemara’s conclusion. The continuation resolves the apparent contradictions. Rav Tzadok cites the tragic use of a mistaken Torah argument in Isaiah’s execution.

connections.hePhrase: רַק טָעוּת לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, לְכָךְ הָיָה עָנְשׁוֹ עַל יְדֵי מְנַשֶּׁה שֶׁטָּעַן נֶגְדּוֹ שֶׁנִּכְשַׁל בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת לֹא נִכְשַׁל:
connections.quote: ““I saw Hashem”: As it was taught, all the prophets looked through a dim glass, while Moshe our teacher looked through a clear glass. “Seek Hashem when He may be found”: One statement concerns an individual, the other a community. When can an individual find Him? Rav Nachman said in Rabbah bar Avuhah’s name: These are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. “I shall fulfill the number of your days”: This is a dispute among the tannaim. It was taught: “I shall fulfill the number of your days”—these are the years allotted to a generation. If one merits, they complete them for him; if he does not merit, they deduct from them. These are Rabbi Akiva’s words. The Sages say: If he merits, they add to them; if he does not merit, they deduct from them. They said to Rabbi Akiva: But it says, “I shall add fifteen years to your days”! He replied: They added years that were already his. Know this, for a prophet had already prophesied, “A son shall be born to the house of David, Yoshiyahu by name,” when Menashe had not yet been born. And the Rabbis? Does it say “from Chizkiyahu”? It says “to the house of David”: he might be born from Chizkiyahu or from someone else.”
connections.context: The existing note quotes Menashe’s accusations against Isaiah. This continuation gives the Gemara’s resolutions of all three apparent contradictions and preserves both opinions in the dispute about allotted years.

connections.hePhrase: [קיז] כָּל מִי שֶׁנָּקִי מֵחֲטָאֵי הַתַּאֲוָה, צָרִיךְ שְׁמִירָה יְתֵירָה בְּעִנְיְנֵי כַּעַס וּרְצִיחָה שֶׁהוּא עָלוּל לָהֶם,
connections.quote: “Even if someone is found completely pure from his childhood—which must mean that by the nature of his birth he has no deficiency of desire—opposite it he has a deficiency in anger, for these are the two opposing inclinations in a person. This is “the flame of the turning sword,” of which the Zohar and the Tikkunim say that it turns “at times to life, at times to death.” That is, one who is entirely free of desires cannot lack a root of anger. There is, however, “the anger of the scholars,” which is good in all its aspects, as the Zohar states. Similarly, our Sages said that “Torah makes him seethe,” for “My words are like fire”; these are words of the living God, and there is life and added vitality in this. Nevertheless, one free of desires cannot escape every deficiency of anger, for otherwise he would live forever. Hashem did not desire this until the end, when death will be swallowed forever, and He created the evil inclination “to guard the way to the Tree of Life.” Moshe our teacher, the teacher of Israel, demonstrates this: he was buried opposite Peor, which alludes to desires, and he stood entirely against them. Nevertheless, our Sages said, “He too died for his sin”: saying “Listen, rebels” and striking the rock belonged to anger and indignation that did not accord with Hashem’s revealed will.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok develops the opening warning at length, including the distinction between anger arising from Torah and a remaining deficiency in anger. The existing Taanit note’s instruction to cultivate gentleness remains in place.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִידוּעַ דְּ"לֹא תִרְצַח" וְ"לֹא תִנְאָף" הֵם שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים, וְהֵם יָמִין וּשְׂמֹאל בָּרָע
connections.quote: “Jealousy and desire, which correspond to “You shall not murder” and “You shall not commit adultery,” robbery and forbidden relations, are the father and mother of all bad traits. Therefore the generation of the Flood brought destruction upon the entire world, for these are the roots of everything.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok identifies the two prohibitions with the two basic roots of bad traits. This is a parallel formulation of the contrast in the Hebrew.

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל יָרָבְעָם בֶּן נְבָט שֶׁנִּקְרָא אֶפְרָתִי – דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו, וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ צְרוּעָה – הַיְסוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ כַּעַס].
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Shoftim 15
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Shoftim 15
connections.quote: “As we find concerning Achiyah the Shilonite anointing Yeravam as king: Achiyah was from Shiloh, from the tribe of Yosef, and Yeravam too is described as an Ephraimite, for he was especially refined and careful concerning “You shall not commit adultery,” which is Yosef’s inheritance. Among Yehudah this was not found in the same way, for of Shlomo it says, “He formed a marriage alliance,” while of King David it says, “The son of an Ephraimite man.” Therefore he was very pleased to anoint him. Afterward, when Yeravam sinned through the two golden calves, Achiyah prayed to Hashem concerning this error. Hashem then showed him that this love had been directed only toward Aviyah son of Yeravam, in whom something good was found. Therefore, from the time he anointed Yeravam until the statement that “the child died” by Hashem’s word, Achiyah is not called a prophet or a Shilonite, but simply Achiyah. In that statement it says, “According to the word of Hashem by the hand of Achiyah the Shilonite, the prophet,” for Hashem set matters right through this. Understand.”
connections.context: Mei HaShiloach relates Yeravam’s designation as an Ephraimite to Yosef’s quality, while retaining the account of Yeravam’s later sin and Achiyah’s recognition of his error.

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל יָרָבְעָם בֶּן נְבָט שֶׁנִּקְרָא אֶפְרָתִי – דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו, וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ צְרוּעָה – הַיְסוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ כַּעַס].
connections.quote: “I heard an explanation of the verse, “His mother’s name was Tzeruah”: the impurity of tzaraat comes from the trait of anger, and Yeravam’s root, through his mother, was in the trait of anger; this was his deficiency. This is also correct according to what I wrote: pride is drawn from anger and the force of evil that wishes to prevail over everyone.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok records the same received interpretation of Tzeruah found in this ois and explains its relation to pride. The quotation preserves his wording “I heard.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל זַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף הֵם שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית כַּנּוֹדָע, וּרְצִיחָה שְׁכִיחָה שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַכּוֹת (י.): בְּגִלְעָד שְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים, בִּשְׁכֶם שְׁכִיחָא רוֹצְחִים.
connections.quote: ““Gilead is a city of workers of iniquity, tracked with blood”: Rabbi Elazar said, They would lie in wait to kill people.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל זַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף הֵם שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית כַּנּוֹדָע, וּרְצִיחָה שְׁכִיחָה שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַכּוֹת (י.): בְּגִלְעָד שְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים, בִּשְׁכֶם שְׁכִיחָא רוֹצְחִים.
connections.quote: “Abaye said: In Shechem too, murderers were common, as it is written, “Like bands lying in wait for a man, a company of priests—they murder on the way to Shechem.””
connections.context: The passage explains the geographical arrangement of cities of refuge. Rav Tzadok explicitly cites both Gilead and Shechem, and both statements are therefore supplied.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פד.) שֶׁסִּפְּרוּ מִשּׁוּפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, וְיָדוּעַ שׁוּפְרֵיהּ וְיוֹפִי הַתֹּאַר בְּכָל מָקוֹם הוּא עַל שְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת צ"ו,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: I remain from the beautiful people of Jerusalem. Whoever wishes to see Rabbi Yochanan’s beauty should take a silver cup fresh from the furnace, fill it with the seeds of a red pomegranate, surround its rim with a wreath of red roses, and set it between sunlight and shade. Those glints of light are something like Rabbi Yochanan’s beauty.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ נֶאֱמַר עָלָיו דְּאָתֵי מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף,
connections.quote: “The Rabbis said to him: “Is the Master not afraid of the evil eye?” He replied: “I come from the descendants of Yosef, over whom the evil eye has no power, as it is written, ‘Yosef is a fruitful son, a fruitful son beside the spring.’” Rabbi Abbahu said: Do not read “beside the eye,” but “above the eye.” Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Chanina derived it from here: “Let them multiply like fish in the midst of the land.” Just as water covers the fish in the sea and the eye has no power over them, so the eye has no power over the descendants of Yosef.”
connections.context: This is Rabbi Yochanan’s statement about his descent from Yosef, followed by the two explanations of protection from the evil eye. The existing note quotes the preceding description of his beauty.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ הָעִנְיָן שֶׁאֵירַע לוֹ מֵרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
connections.quote: “One day Rabbi Yochanan was bathing in the Jordan. Reish Lakish saw him and jumped into the Jordan after him. Rabbi Yochanan said: “Your strength should be for Torah.” Reish Lakish replied: “Your beauty should be for women.” Rabbi Yochanan said: “If you repent, I shall give you my sister, who is more beautiful than I.” He accepted. He wished to return to fetch his clothes but could not return. Rabbi Yochanan taught him Scripture and Mishnah and made him a great man. One day they disagreed in the study hall: from when do a sword, knife, dagger, spear, hand sickle, and harvesting sickle become susceptible to impurity? From the completion of their manufacture. When is their manufacture complete? Rabbi Yochanan says: when one tempers them in the furnace. Reish Lakish says: when one polishes them in water. Rabbi Yochanan said to him: “A robber knows his robbery.” He replied: “What have you benefited me? There they called me master, and here they call me master!” Rabbi Yochanan said: “I benefited you by bringing you under the wings of the Divine Presence.” Rabbi Yochanan was distressed, and Reish Lakish became ill. His sister came weeping and said: “Act for the sake of my children!” He replied: “Leave your orphans; I shall keep them alive.” “Act for the sake of my widowhood!” He replied: “And let your widows trust in Me.” Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish died, and Rabbi Yochanan grieved greatly after him. The Rabbis said: “Who should go to console him? Let Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat go, for his teachings are sharp.””
connections.context: The Gemara gives the full sequence from Reish Lakish’s return to Torah to the dispute and its consequences. The existing connected Mei HaShiloach note discusses the following exchange about his twenty-four questions; that note is preserved.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם גּוּף הַהַעֲנָשָׁה שֶׁהָיָה רָגִיל בָּהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (קיז.) עִם רַב כַּהֲנָא, דָּבָר זֶה הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְמִי שֶׁהוּא בַּטֶּבַע כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת (קנו.): מָר נַמֵּי עָנֵישׁ וְקָטֵיל.
connections.quote: “He saw that Rav Kahana’s lips were parted and thought he was laughing at him. Rabbi Yochanan became distressed, and Rav Kahana died. The next day Rabbi Yochanan said to the rabbis: Did you see how that Babylonian behaved? They said to him: That was his natural appearance.”
connections.context: The narrative attributes the death to Rabbi Yochanan’s mistaken impression that Rav Kahana was mocking him. The continuation describes his going to the burial cave and reviving him. Rav Tzadok cites the unintended consequence of the initial mistake.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם גּוּף הַהַעֲנָשָׁה שֶׁהָיָה רָגִיל בָּהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (קיז.) עִם רַב כַּהֲנָא, דָּבָר זֶה הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְמִי שֶׁהוּא בַּטֶּבַע כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת (קנו.): מָר נַמֵּי עָנֵישׁ וְקָטֵיל.
connections.quote: “One born under Mars will be a person who spills blood. Rav Ashi said: Either a bloodletter, a thief, a slaughterer, or a circumciser. Rabba said: I was born under Mars. Abaye said: The Master too punishes and kills.”
connections.context: This passage illustrates different expressions of one natural disposition. Abaye’s reply is addressed to Rabba; Rav Tzadok applies the same category to Rabbi Yochanan’s punitive power in the preceding account.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּרִתְחָא דְּרַבָּנָן הוּא טָב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפב עַמּוּד ב) וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּתַעֲנִית (ד.) דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא מְרַתְּחָא לֵיהּ,
connections.quote: “If you ask about the anger of the rabbis: their anger is good in every respect, for we learned that Torah is fire, and Torah makes him burn, as it is written, “Are not My words like fire?” The rabbis’ anger is in matters of Torah; their anger is to give honor to Torah, and all is for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He.”
connections.context: The Zohar qualifies the praise by its object and purpose: matters of Torah and divine service. It is not a blanket endorsement of personal anger. Rav Tzadok discusses the fiery spiritual power that can underlie it.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּרִתְחָא דְּרַבָּנָן הוּא טָב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפב עַמּוּד ב) וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּתַעֲנִית (ד.) דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא מְרַתְּחָא לֵיהּ,
connections.quote: “Rava said: When a Torah scholar burns with anger, it is Torah that makes him burn, as it is said, “Are not My words like fire, says the Lord?””

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּרִתְחָא דְּרַבָּנָן הוּא טָב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפב עַמּוּד ב) וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּתַעֲנִית (ד.) דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא מְרַתְּחָא לֵיהּ,
connections.quote: “Ravina said: Even so, a person must teach himself gentleness, as it is said, “Remove anger from your heart.””
connections.context: The first statement identifies the fiery force of Torah; the continuation preserves the requirement to cultivate gentleness. Together they give the context for Rav Tzadok’s discussion of scholarly anger and its dangers.

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה דְּשָׁם לֹא הִצְלִיחַ רִתְחֵיהּ, וּמַאי סְלֵיק בֵּיהּ.
connections.quote: “He went about tearing his clothes, weeping and saying: “Where are you, son of Lakish? Where are you, son of Lakish?” He kept crying out until he lost his reason. The Rabbis prayed for mercy for him, and he died.”
connections.context: This is the end of the narrative alluded to by “what became of him.” It follows Rabbi Yochanan’s lament that Rabbi Elazar could not replace Reish Lakish as his partner in Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִי שֶׁקָּרָא לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ "לִסְטָאָה", דְּהַיְינוּ רוֹצֵחַ, וּלְפִי שֶׁאָסוּר לְהַזְכִּיר לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה מַעֲשָׂיו הָרִאשׁוֹנִים,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 9
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 9
connections.quote: “I will make him a help meet for him. He explained the matter: for such is the will of the Creator, blessed be He, that help and support should flourish for a person from that which opposes him, namely like a disciple to his master, as we find (Bava Metzia 84a) regarding Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish facing Rabbi Yochanan, who would raise twenty-four difficulties against him and he would resolve them with twenty-four solutions, and the teaching was consequently broadened and clarified, and not like Rabbi Elazar who merely told him: 'there is a Baraita that supports you'; for through a person seeing the challenges raised against him, he then fortifies his words with further proofs and his positions emerge thoroughly to light.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads Reish Lakish’s objections to Rabbi Yochanan as the model of “a help opposite him”: the challenge made the teaching clearer in a way that simple agreement could not. This supplies the positive side of Rav Tzadok’s warning about their quarrel. The person who seems to obstruct one’s Torah may be contributing precisely the scrutiny it needs, so personal anger can destroy an indispensable form of help.
connections.headline: The opposing colleague can be the essential helper

connections.hePhrase: לְכָךְ הוּא גַּם כֵּן נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ עִנְיָן כָּזֶה עַצְמוֹ עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁחֲבֵירוֹ נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל יָדוֹ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא מִזֶּה הַגְּרָם מִיתָה לְעַצְמוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁגָּרַם לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
connections.quote: see note 791.
connections.context: The Gemara states the consequence of another person being punished through someone. Rav Tzadok invokes that concern in explaining Rabbi Yochanan’s experience.

connections.hePhrase: [וְנִרְאֶה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָצָה לִמְחוֹל, כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁקָּרַב קִצּוֹ וְחָשַׁב דְּנִדְחֶה מִפְּנֵי גַּבְרָא, וּבְוַדַּאי רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ יִמְלוֹךְ תַּחְתָּיו, וְסָבַר חַיָּיו קוֹדְמִין, וּבָזֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ לִמְחוֹל כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בְּיוֹמָא פז:,
connections.quote: “Is one person displaced before another? Yes, for Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: What is the meaning of “Therefore I have hewn through the prophets; I have slain them with the words of My mouth”? It does not say “through their deeds,” but “with the words of My mouth.” Thus one person may be displaced before another.”
connections.context: This question and answer conclude the Gemara’s discussion of Shmuel, Shaul, and the arrival of David’s kingship. They supply the expression used in Rav Tzadok’s proposed explanation.

connections.hePhrase: [וְנִרְאֶה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָצָה לִמְחוֹל, כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁקָּרַב קִצּוֹ וְחָשַׁב דְּנִדְחֶה מִפְּנֵי גַּבְרָא, וּבְוַדַּאי רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ יִמְלוֹךְ תַּחְתָּיו, וְסָבַר חַיָּיו קוֹדְמִין, וּבָזֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ לִמְחוֹל כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בְּיוֹמָא פז:,
connections.quote: “And Rabbi Yochanan, what does he do with “Your brother shall live with you”? He needs it for the following teaching: Two people were traveling on a road, and one had a flask of water. If both drink, both will die; if one drinks, he will reach an inhabited place. Ben Petura taught: Better that both drink and die, rather than one witness his fellow’s death. Until Rabbi Akiva came and taught: “Your brother shall live with you”—your life takes precedence over your fellow’s life.”
connections.context: The source of “his own life takes precedence” is a concrete case of insufficient water. Both Ben Petura’s view and Rabbi Akiva’s conclusion are retained; Rav Tzadok then considers how Rabbi Yochanan may have understood his own situation.

connections.hePhrase: [וְנִרְאֶה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָצָה לִמְחוֹל, כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁקָּרַב קִצּוֹ וְחָשַׁב דְּנִדְחֶה מִפְּנֵי גַּבְרָא, וּבְוַדַּאי רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ יִמְלוֹךְ תַּחְתָּיו, וְסָבַר חַיָּיו קוֹדְמִין, וּבָזֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ לִמְחוֹל כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בְּיוֹמָא פז:,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chanina saw in a dream that Rav was being hung upon a palm tree, and he had a tradition that one seen in a dream hanging upon a palm tree would become head. He said: It follows that he must become head; I will not be appeased, so that he will go and study Torah in Babylon.”
connections.context: The sage in this passage is Rabbi Chanina, and the person seeking his forgiveness is Rav. Rav Tzadok draws on the concern that another scholar’s ascent may displace the incumbent. The name “Rav Huna” in the reader’s main sentence is not the name in this Talmudic account.

connections.hePhrase: [וְנִרְאֶה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָצָה לִמְחוֹל, כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁקָּרַב קִצּוֹ וְחָשַׁב דְּנִדְחֶה מִפְּנֵי גַּבְרָא, וּבְוַדַּאי רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ יִמְלוֹךְ תַּחְתָּיו, וְסָבַר חַיָּיו קוֹדְמִין, וּבָזֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ לִמְחוֹל כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בְּיוֹמָא פז:,
connections.quote: ““He saw a dream concerning Rav”: He saw a dream that Rav had been suspended from a palm tree, which is a sign of elevation and greatness. Rabbi Chanina was the head of the academy, as Rabbi said at his death, “Chanina bar Chama shall sit at the head.” When he saw this dream concerning Rav, he feared that he would die, because one reign does not encroach upon another. He said: “I shall drive him away from here, and he will flee from me to Babylonia. There he will become the head, and we shall not be displaced into death on his account.””
connections.context: Rashi explains the fear underlying Rabbi Chanina’s conduct in the Yoma narrative. The existing note contains the Gemara; this supplies Rashi’s explicit connection between succession and fear of death.

connections.hePhrase: אָז יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ גַּם בְּשִׂיחַת חוּלִין לְתַקֵּן נְפָשׁוֹת, שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “One whose concerns, thoughts, and reflections are all immersed in words of Torah merits that all his conversation is Torah. As it is said, “Converse”—these are the masters of Talmud, whose entire conversation is words of Torah. The masters of Talmud are those entirely immersed in Torah. Of them the Tanchuma says that there is great distress and loss of sleep, and it is compared to darkness, as it is said, “The people walking in darkness saw a great light”—these are the masters of Talmud; see there. Similarly, Sanhedrin says, “He has seated me in dark places”—this is the Babylonian Talmud. For Talmud is the examination of the depths of Torah, which is “deep; who can find it?” Rashi likewise explains that this was said because of its depth. Since one must deepen his thoughts in it, all his conversation thereby becomes words of Torah, for a person is wherever his thought is engaged and attached, as is known. “Conversation” means a light utterance that leaves his mouth without deliberate intention, as Chagigah says concerning “what is his conversation”: Rav said, even the extra conversation between husband and wife.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains how sustained immersion in Torah can shape even spontaneous speech. The existing Eruvin quotation is preserved; this gives his fuller explanation of its meaning.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:) שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: see note 861.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok treats this praise as referring to a person whose whole inner life has become Torah, so that even ordinary conversation expresses it. The maxim appears on 54b.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:) שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה;
connections.quote: see note 861.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ס): יָפָה שִׂיחָתָן שֶׁל עַבְדֵי אָבוֹת מִתּוֹרָתָן שֶׁל בָּנִים
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said: More beautiful is the conversation of the servants of the patriarchs’ households than the Torah of their descendants. Eliezer’s account occupies two or three pages, and it is stated and repeated; the creeping animal is a substantial matter of Torah, yet its blood is made impure like its flesh only by an additional word in Scripture.”
connections.context: The Midrash compares the Torah’s extensive telling of Eliezer’s conversation with its brevity in conveying a legal rule. Rav Tzadok uses that valuation to explain how ordinary speech can express Torah.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ס): יָפָה שִׂיחָתָן שֶׁל עַבְדֵי אָבוֹת מִתּוֹרָתָן שֶׁל בָּנִים
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said: More beautiful is the washing of the feet of the servants of the patriarchs’ households than the Torah of their descendants, for even their foot-washing must be written, while the creeping animal is a substantial matter of Torah and its blood is made impure like its flesh only by an additional word in Scripture.”
connections.context: This is the companion statement in the same section: even an ordinary bodily act associated with the patriarchs’ servants is narrated explicitly. It extends the preceding comparison from conversation to action.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ס): יָפָה שִׂיחָתָן שֶׁל עַבְדֵי אָבוֹת מִתּוֹרָתָן שֶׁל בָּנִים
connections.quote: “Afterward the holy Zohar (132a) says: come and see how many hidden supernal secrets there are in Torah. When David looked and knew how many wonders issue from Torah, he began, ‘Uncover my eyes, that I may behold wonders from Your Torah.’ The Zohar gives this introduction to Eliezer’s mission to bring Rivkah because it prepared the birth of Yaakov’s soul, the attribute of Torah. The principal wonder—‘wonders from Your Torah’—is that through this we merit ‘He will open our heart in His Torah.’ It says that this passage contains supernal secrets, as the Midrash says (Bereishit Rabbah 60:8), ‘The conversation of the servants of the patriarchal households is more beautiful than the Torah of their children.’ Certainly no letter in Torah is superfluous, Heaven forbid. Rather, in this passage of Eliezer’s conversation are secrets and many hidden treasures, to bring Yaakov’s soul out from the forces of Lavan and Betuel; through these words of Torah we merit the opening of the heart to Torah.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains why Eliezer’s ordinary account can be treated as Torah with power to draw forth a soul. His mission prepares the birth of Yaakov, the attribute of Torah, by taking Rivkah from the surrounding forces of Lavan and Betuel. Reading that narrative is then connected with the learner’s own heart opening to Torah. This develops the siman’s transition from a story to the repair and birth of souls.
connections.headline: The narrative that prepares a soul and opens the heart

connections.hePhrase: [וְלֹא הָיְתָה מַעֲלַת אֱלִיעֶזֶר רַק מַעֲלַת אַבְרָהָם, לְכָךְ קְרָאוֹ עַבְדֵי אָבוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא כח:): דַּמֶּשֶׂק – דּוֹלֶה וּמַשְׁקֶה מִתּוֹרַת רַבּוֹ, כִּי מַה שֶּׁקָּנָה עֶבֶד קָנָה רַבּוֹ, וְכָל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ הַכֹּל נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת רַבּוֹ].
connections.quote: ‘Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, was an elder who sat in the academy, as it is said: ‘Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his household, who ruled over all that he had.’ Rabbi Elazar said: He ruled over his master’s Torah. ‘He is Damesek Eliezer’: Rabbi Elazar said: He draws—doleh—and gives others to drink—mashkeh—from his master’s Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְלֹא הָיְתָה מַעֲלַת אֱלִיעֶזֶר רַק מַעֲלַת אַבְרָהָם, לְכָךְ קְרָאוֹ עַבְדֵי אָבוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא כח:): דַּמֶּשֶׂק – דּוֹלֶה וּמַשְׁקֶה מִתּוֹרַת רַבּוֹ, כִּי מַה שֶּׁקָּנָה עֶבֶד קָנָה רַבּוֹ, וְכָל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ הַכֹּל נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת רַבּוֹ].
connections.quote: ““He forgot what his master told him”: “Mine”?! Whatever a servant acquires, his master acquires! Abaye said: He goes to a shepherd with whom his master regularly deals, who wishes to make a proper arrangement for his master, and the shepherd transfers one of the animals to him on condition that his master has no right in it.”
connections.context: The Gemara states the ownership principle invoked here, then explains the special condition needed in its particular case. Rav Tzadok applies the principle figuratively to Eliezer’s Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זֶה בְּסֻכָּה (שָׁם) בְּשִׂיחַת רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל בְּסֻכָּתוֹ,
connections.quote: “One who sleeps beneath a bed in a sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation. Rabbi Yehudah said: We used to sleep beneath a bed in the presence of the elders, and they said nothing to us. Rabbi Shimon said: There was an incident involving Tavi, Rabban Gamliel’s servant, who slept beneath the bed. Rabban Gamliel said to the elders: “Have you seen Tavi my servant? He is a Torah scholar and knows that servants are exempt from the sukkah; therefore he sleeps beneath the bed.” In the course of this we learned that one who sleeps beneath a bed has not fulfilled his obligation.”
connections.context: This is the actual conversation about Tavi from which the Gemara draws its teaching about the conversation of Torah scholars. Rabbi Yehudah’s differing report is also retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זֶה בְּסֻכָּה (שָׁם) בְּשִׂיחַת רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל בְּסֻכָּתוֹ,
connections.quote: “I received a tradition that all statements in the Gemara, although on the plain reading they appear to have been brought in incidentally, in truth have a complete connection to the place where they were established, and that is their principal, proper place.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok records the principle behind drawing meaning from the placement of the conversation specifically in the discussion of sukkah. His description of it as a received tradition is preserved.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה מִזֶּה דִּבְסֻכָּה, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֵם בְּצִלָּא דִּמְהֵימְנוּתָא, זוֹכִים לִהְיוֹת כֵּן;
connections.quote: “Returning to the matter: this is what the Zohar alludes to by “one who is from the stock and root of Israel.” That is, one who is assured that the root of his birth is in holiness dwells in the shade of faith without fear at all. He can trust and take refuge in Him through faith beyond understanding, because he is attached to the root. Therefore he need fear no evil, and he inherits freedom for himself and his children forever. Israel as a whole are called the children of Israel: they are attached by their birth to the root, in the inner point of their hearts, beyond understanding. This is like our Sages’ statement: “It is revealed and known before You that our desire is to do Your will; only the yeast in the dough prevents us.” This is revealed through the mitzvah of sukkah, through which we gain this trust in the shade of faith. From it joy flows to us during this festival, the season of our rejoicing, as we explained concerning “Avraham made a great feast.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the sukkah’s “shade of faith” through the inner attachment to holiness and the desire to do God’s will. The selected closing passage retains the condition with which he introduces the explanation.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה מִזֶּה דִּבְסֻכָּה, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֵם בְּצִלָּא דִּמְהֵימְנוּתָא, זוֹכִים לִהְיוֹת כֵּן;
connections.quote: “Therefore it is written, “Every native among Israel shall dwell in sukkot”: everyone who comes from Israel’s holy root and stock shall dwell in sukkot beneath the shade of faith. One who is not from Israel’s holy stock and root does not sit in them and removes himself from beneath the shade of faith. It is written, “Canaan, in whose hand are deceitful scales”—this is Eliezer, Avraham’s servant. Come and see: it is written, “Cursed is Canaan.” Because this Canaan merited serving Avraham, once he served him he dwelled beneath the shade of faith and merited leaving that curse. Moreover, blessing is written of him: “He said: Come, blessed of Hashem.” What does this teach? Whoever dwells beneath the shade of faith inherits freedom for himself and his children forever and is blessed with a supernal blessing. Whoever removes himself from the shade of faith inherits exile for himself and his children, as it is written, “He fought against Israel and took captives from them.””

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם קְרָאוּ לְשִׂיחַת חוּלִין "עָלֵהוּ", וּמָצִינוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין ק.): "וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה" – לְהַתִּיר פֶּה עֲקָרוֹת,
connections.quote: ‘What does ‘its leaf shall be for healing’ mean? Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi and Rav Chisda differed: One said, to open the upper mouth [of those unable to speak]; the other said, to open the lower mouth [the womb of those unable to conceive].’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהַתִּיר פֶּה אִלְּמִים הוּא גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן – עֵץ חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, ד), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה דְּבָרִים רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א:
connections.quote: ‘A healing tongue is a tree of life, but crookedness in it breaks the spirit.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהַתִּיר פֶּה אִלְּמִים הוּא גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן – עֵץ חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, ד), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה דְּבָרִים רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Levi said: Why should we learn it from elsewhere? Let us learn it from this very passage. Before Moses attained Torah, it is written of him, “I am not a man of words.” Once he attained Torah, his tongue was healed and he began to speak words, as we read: “These are the words that Moses spoke.””
connections.context: The Midrash calls Torah a healing for the tongue and illustrates it with Moses. This gives the context for Rav Tzadok’s discussion of speech transformed through Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהַתִּיר פֶּה אִלְּמִים הוּא גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן – עֵץ חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, ד), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה דְּבָרִים רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א:
connections.quote: see note 855.
connections.context: The existing note contains Rabbi Levi’s concluding example of Moshe. This preceding portion explains the tree, the leaf, and the healing of the tongue, supplying the argument to which Rav Tzadok refers.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה חַיִּים וְקַיָּימִים וְשָׁם יֵשׁ הַחַיּוּת לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר,
connections.quote: “A person must know, in all his activities and deeds, that he is not the one who acts. Everything occurs through a higher power, and all his activities come from Hashem, as in “You have also performed all our deeds for us.” Without this he has no power to do anything; it is only through Hashem’s active power, drawn into him from the ten utterances of Creation. These stand living and enduring forever, supplying the powers of activity, each thing on its day, according to the activity of the things during the days of Creation.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok describes the enduring vitality of the divine utterances as the source of activity in the world. It is a parallel explanation of the living power he finds in words of Torah here.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים סוֹף תִּיקּוּן נ"ה: כִּי מִפָּסוּק "וְהַמִּכְתָּב מִכְתַּב אֱלֹהִים הוּא" יָצָא שֵׁם הַכּוֹתֵב,
connections.quote: “The name of the writer: “The writing was the writing of God.” … The name of the expounder: “The Lord God gave me a tongue of those taught, to know how to sustain the weary with a word.””
connections.context: The end of Tikkun 55 distinguishes divine-name configurations associated with writing and with oral exposition. Rav Tzadok invokes that distinction for the written and spoken forms of Torah. The earlier English gave an explanatory paraphrase about upper and lower Eden as though it were the source’s quotation; the quoted wording here is the actual relevant text.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים סוֹף תִּיקּוּן נ"ה: כִּי מִפָּסוּק "וְהַמִּכְתָּב מִכְתַּב אֱלֹהִים הוּא" יָצָא שֵׁם הַכּוֹתֵב,
connections.quote: ‘The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved upon the tablets.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִפָּסוּק "ה' אֱלֹהִים נָתַן לִי לְשׁוֹן לִמּוּדִים וְגוֹמֵר" – שֵׁם הַדּוֹרֵשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘The Lord Hashem has given me a trained tongue, so that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word. Morning after morning He awakens; He awakens my ear to listen as those who are taught.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְסֵפֶר עֲבוֹדַת יִשְׂרָאֵל פָּרָשַׁת חַיֵּי מִפָּסוּק "וָאָבֹא הַיּוֹם אֶל הָעָיִן", שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: הַיּוֹם יָצָאתִי וְהַיּוֹם בָּאתִי, יוֹצֵא שֵׁם לִקְפִיצַת הָאָרֶץ.
connections.quote: ‘I came today to the spring and said: ‘Hashem, God of my master Abraham, if You will please grant success to the journey on which I am going…’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְסֵפֶר עֲבוֹדַת יִשְׂרָאֵל פָּרָשַׁת חַיֵּי מִפָּסוּק "וָאָבֹא הַיּוֹם אֶל הָעָיִן", שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: הַיּוֹם יָצָאתִי וְהַיּוֹם בָּאתִי, יוֹצֵא שֵׁם לִקְפִיצַת הָאָרֶץ.
connections.displayRef: Avodat Yisrael, Sefer Bereshit, Chayei Sara 3
connections.linkedRef: Avodat Yisrael, Sefer Bereshit, Chayei Sara 3
connections.canonicalRef: Avodat Yisrael, Sefer Bereshit, Chayei Sara 3
connections.heRef: עבודת ישראל, ספר בראשית, חיי שרה ג׳
connections.quote: “In the name of the Baal Shem Tov, of blessed memory, concerning the verse, “I came today to the spring”: Rashi explains, “I left today and arrived today; from here we learn that the earth contracted for him.” Rabbi Acha said: The conversation of the servants of the patriarchs is more beautiful than the Torah of their children; see there. From this very verse emerges a name for the contraction of the earth. This is the meaning of “I left today and arrived today; from here we learn that it contracted”: from here itself, from these words in this statement. Understand. This is the meaning of “The conversation of the servants of the patriarchs is more beautiful,” for in their conversation they allude to wondrous secrets, with unifications for the contraction of the earth, which the children cannot accomplish even through their Torah.”
connections.context: Avodat Yisrael gives the teaching expressly cited in the Hebrew, including Rashi’s words and the explanation of “from here” as referring to the wording of the verse itself. The source’s attribution to the Baal Shem Tov is retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן יָדוּעַ מִפָּסוּק שֶׁל הַכָּאַת סַנְוֵרִים יוֹצֵא שֵׁם לִפְעוֹל כֵּן.
connections.quote: ‘They struck the men at the entrance of the house with blindness, from the youngest to the oldest, and they wore themselves out trying to find the entrance.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ה:): "יְהַב לֵיהּ יְדָא וְאוֹקְמֵיהּ", דְּרָאשֵׁי תֵּיבוֹת יְ'הַב לֵ'יהּ יְ'דָא הוּא שֵׁם הַפּוֹעֵל כֵּן.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba fell ill. Rabbi Yochanan came to him and asked: ‘Are sufferings dear to you?’ He answered: ‘Neither they nor their reward.’ He said: ‘Give me your hand.’ He gave him his hand, and Rabbi Yochanan raised him up.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ה:): "יְהַב לֵיהּ יְדָא וְאוֹקְמֵיהּ", דְּרָאשֵׁי תֵּיבוֹת יְ'הַב לֵ'יהּ יְ'דָא הוּא שֵׁם הַפּוֹעֵל כֵּן.
connections.quote: “I have already informed you, concerning “The ox knows its owner,” that by the name Y-L-Y, the second name of the seventy-twofold name, Moshe our teacher raised Yosef’s coffin; its reason was explained there. This name also has the property of raising a sick person from his illness. It is therefore alluded to in the initial letters of “He gave him his hand,” whose initials are Y-L-Y, and thereby “he raised him.” Therefore he should say to the sick person, “Give me your hand.” The sick person then gives his hand, and the person raising him says, “He gave him his hand and raised him,” intending the name indicated by these initial letters.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַרְבֵּה בְּסֵפֶר שִׁמּוּשׁ תְּהִלִּים וּשְׁאָרֵי, כִּי כָּל שֵׁם הוּא כְּמוֹ מַפְתֵּחַ לְאוֹתוֹ חֶדֶר.
connections.quote: “The true boundary and the tradition of the covenant are these: one who wishes to attain his needs through the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, should exert all his strength in Torah to understand the meaning of each of the holy names mentioned in Torah, such as Ehyeh, Yah, the four-letter name, Adonai, El, Eloah, Elohim, Shaddai, and Tzevaot. A person should know and understand that each of these names is like a key to every matter that a person needs in any respect in the world. When he contemplates these names, he will find all Torah and mitzvot dependent upon them. When he knows the meaning of each name, he will recognize the greatness of the One who spoke and the world came into being. He will fear and revere Him, and long, yearn, and desire to cleave to Him through knowing His names. Then he will be close to Hashem and his prayer will be accepted. Concerning this it is said, “I shall raise him high because he knows My name; he will call to Me and I shall answer him.” Scripture does not say, “because he mentions My name,” but “because he knows My name.” Knowledge is the essential thing, followed by “he will call to Me and I shall answer him”: when he needs something and directs his intention toward the name upon which that need depends, then “I shall answer him.””
connections.context: Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla explicitly compares the names to keys. His explanation makes knowledge, Torah, reverence, and attachment to God central, fitting Rav Tzadok’s closing emphasis on the work of mind and heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁפָּעַל אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר, הוּא שֶׁמָּצָא וְעָמַד עַל אוֹתוֹ מַפְתֵּחַ וּמְסָרוֹ לָרַבִּים שֶׁנָּהַג בּוֹ טוֹבַת עַיִן,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Chanina said: Torah was given only to Moshe and his descendants, as it is said, “Write for yourself” and “Carve for yourself”: just as the discarded stone is yours, so the writing is yours. Moshe acted generously with it and gave it to Israel. Of him Scripture says, “One with a generous eye shall be blessed.” Rav Chisda objected: “Hashem commanded me at that time to teach you”! He commanded me, and I taught you. “See, I have taught you statutes and laws as Hashem my God commanded me”! He commanded me, and I taught you. “Now write this song for yourselves”! That concerns the song alone. But it says, “So that this song may be a witness for Me among the children of Israel”! Rather, the statement concerns analytical reasoning alone.”
connections.context: The Gemara supplies the model of generously sharing a personal attainment. Its final qualification is retained: the special gift in question is analytical understanding, rather than the Torah being withheld from Israel.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"אִם רֵיק הוּא – מִכֶּם", לָמָּה? שֶׁאֵין אַתֶּם יְגֵיעִים וְכוּלֵי
connections.quote: ““For it is not an empty matter for you”: If it is empty, that is from you. Why? Because you do not labor in it. “For it is your life”: When is it your life? When you labor in it.”
connections.context: The Yerushalmi explains that a perceived lack of meaning calls for deeper effort in Torah. Rav Tzadok cites this as the basis for seeking the teaching contained even in what initially seems empty.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִידוּעַ הַמָּשָׁל עַל זֶה מִמִּי שֶׁגּוֹרֵף בִּיבִין
connections.quote: “As long as the community of Israel is whole—that is, their intention in joining with the nations is solely for the sake of Heaven, to bring out the holy sparks within them, so that the thighs remain joined to the body—then although “the wicked watches for the righteous,” “Hashem will not abandon him into his hand.” Yet it is indeed said, “Because you joined with Achazyahu…” Although his intention at the outset was for the sake of Heaven, one who deals with something filthy becomes soiled, like someone who cleans sewers, whose body cannot avoid becoming dirty with mud and excrement. This requires great vigilance and strength, so as not to allow any filth to adhere to him, and not everyone merits it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok gives the same image and explains both the protection associated with a wholly pure intention and the vigilance needed when engaging with what requires repair.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבָזֶה יוּבַן צַחוּת לְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וָאֵרָא): נוֹחַ הָיָה לִשְׁלֹמֹה לִהְיוֹת גּוֹרֵף בִּיבִין וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם בַּמִּדְרָשׁ
connections.quote: “Of Shlomo, who contemplated nullifying a letter of Torah, what is written? “The words of Agur son of Yakeh”: he gathered words of Torah and then cast them up. “The utterance of the man to Itiel”: this command of the Holy One, blessed be He, “He shall not multiply wives,” was given only because “his heart shall not turn away.” “To Itiel”: he said, “God is with me, and I am able.” What is written of him? “When Shlomo grew old, his wives turned his heart.” Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said: It would have been better for Shlomo to clean sewers than to have this verse written about him. Therefore Shlomo said of himself, “I turned to consider wisdom and knowledge, madness and folly.” Shlomo said: What I thought was being wiser than the words of Torah, imagining that I understood Torah’s reasoning—that understanding and that knowledge were madness and folly.”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the exact comparison cited here and places it in the account of Shlomo’s reasoning about the prohibition against multiplying wives.

connections.hePhrase: [אֲבָל בַּגְּמָרָא דְּשַׁבָּת נ"ו עַמּוּד ב' אִיתָא שַׁמָּשׁ לְדָבָר אַחֵר, וְהַכֹּל אֶחָד, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: It would have been better for that righteous man to be an attendant to idolatry than to have it written of him: ‘He did what was evil in the eyes of Hashem.’ Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: When Solomon married Pharaoh’s daughter, she brought him a thousand kinds of music and told him: ‘This is what they do for such-and-such an idol, and this is what they do for such-and-such an idol.’ He did not protest against her.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת כָּל מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדוֹ לִמְחוֹת וְכוּלֵי, וְנִדְבַּק בּוֹ הַכֹּל].
connections.quote: “But it is written, “Shlomo did what was evil in the eyes of Hashem”! Rather, because he could have protested against his wives and did not protest, Scripture accounts it to him as though he had sinned.”
connections.context: This is the preceding explanation in Shabbat of Shlomo’s failure to protest. The existing note contains the following statement about serving another deity; it remains unchanged.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לִרְאִיַּת קֶרִי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכז:) בְּאוֹתוֹ חָסִיד מִפְּנֵי טֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ לִפְדּוֹת אוֹתָהּ רִיבָה,
connections.quote: ‘When I went down and immersed, what did you suspect me of? They answered: We thought that perhaps the exertion of the journey had caused our teacher a seminal emission. He told them: By the Temple service, that is what happened! Just as you judged me favorably, may the Omnipresent judge you favorably.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּאִיתָא בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן (פֶּרֶק ח) שֶׁהִטְבִּיל לָרִיבָה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאָכְלָה אִיסּוּרִים, וְהָיָה מְזַכֶּה לְחַיָּיבַיָּא;
connections.quote: see note 1151.

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֱלִישָׁע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ עָלָיו סַנְהֶדְרִין (קז:) שֶׁהָיָה מַדְחֶה בִּשְׁתֵּי יָדַיִם, נֶאֱמַר עָלָיו בִּבְרָכוֹת (י:) שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו.
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Always let the left hand push away and the right hand draw near, unlike Elisha, who pushed Gehazi away with both hands, and unlike Yehoshua ben Perahya, who pushed Jesus the Nazarene away with both hands. Concerning Gehazi, it is written: ‘Naaman said: Please take two talents. He urged him, and he bound up two talents of silver,’ and so forth. ‘Elisha said to him: Where have you been, Gehazi? He said: Your servant has not gone anywhere. He said to him: Did my heart not go along when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Is this a time to take silver and to take garments, olive groves, vineyards, sheep, cattle, male servants, and female servants?’ Did he take all of that? He took only silver and garments!”

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֱלִישָׁע, שֶׁאָמְרוּ עָלָיו סַנְהֶדְרִין (קז:) שֶׁהָיָה מַדְחֶה בִּשְׁתֵּי יָדַיִם, נֶאֱמַר עָלָיו בִּבְרָכוֹת (י:) שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו.
connections.quote: see note 1099.
connections.context: The existing Bavli quotation records what the Shunammite woman observed. The Yerushalmi adds the explicit statement about Elisha’s whole life and preserves the alternative explanation of his holiness.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ שָׁם בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין דְּאֵין לִהְיוֹת כֶּאֱלִישָׁע, רַק הַקֵּירוּב יוֹתֵר בְּחֹזֶק מִן הַדִּחוּי, שֶׁהוּא בַּיָּמִין.
connections.heRef: יד רמה על סנהדרין ק״ז ב:ב׳
connections.quote: “The Rabbis taught: Always let the left hand push away one who ought to be pushed away, and the right hand draw near—that is, let the measure of drawing near be greater than the measure of pushing away; not like Elisha, who pushed Gechazi away with both hands.”
connections.context: Yad Ramah states explicitly that drawing near should outweigh rejection. This is the explanation of the stronger right hand used in the Hebrew.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ שָׁם דְּגַם הַיֵּצֶר כֵּן יִהְיֶה: שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה וְיָמִין מְקָרֶבֶת,
connections.quote: ““The inclination”: His desire. If he distances it from himself entirely, he diminishes the settlement of the world. If he draws it close entirely, he comes to a prohibition, for he cannot restrain his inclination from a transgression.”
connections.context: Rashi explains why this teaching calls for both restraint and closeness. Both dangers are retained, rather than turning the passage into an unqualified instruction in either direction.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ שָׁם דְּגַם הַיֵּצֶר כֵּן יִהְיֶה: שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה וְיָמִין מְקָרֶבֶת,
connections.quote: “It was taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: With the inclination, a child, and a woman, let the left hand push away and the right hand draw near.”
connections.context: This is the following baraita to which Rav Tzadok refers when applying the teaching to the inclination. The existing note contains the earlier account of Elisha and Gechazi.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ שָׁם דְּגַם הַיֵּצֶר כֵּן יִהְיֶה: שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה וְיָמִין מְקָרֶבֶת,
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:21
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:21
connections.quote: “Concerning this they said (Sotah 47a): with the inclination and the other cases, let the left hand push away and the right hand draw near. One may explain that the right draws near so that the left will push away; this is ‘very good.’ I heard that the Sages compared the inclination to leaven in the dough (Berakhot 17a), and leaven improves the dough. It is taught (Berakhot 34a) concerning leaven that a little of it is beneficial.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek interprets the two hands as a coordinated response rather than competing alternatives: the right draws near so that the left can effectively restrain. Its image of a little leaven being beneficial helps explain why Rav Tzadok distinguishes complete subduing from transformation and relates the appropriate response to the person’s level. The source does not dispense with the need for restraint.
connections.headline: Approach that makes restraint possible

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ט): "טוֹב מְאֹד" – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע,
connections.quote: see note 358.
connections.context: The Midrash asks its own question about calling the evil inclination “very good” and explains the constructive activities it motivates. The existing Tanya note supplies the subsequent distinction between subduing and transforming.

connections.hePhrase: יָדוּעַ דְּהַכֹּל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא אָדָם, וְיֵשׁ מִדָּתוֹ לְאַכְפַּיָּא וְלִהְיוֹת דּוֹחֶה לְגַמְרֵי, וְיֵשׁ מִדָּתוֹ לְאַהְפָּכָא:
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים כ״ז:ח׳-י׳
connections.quote: “There are two kinds of gratification before Him, blessed be He, on high. One comes from the complete elimination of the other side and the transformation of bitterness into sweetness and darkness into light, through the righteous. The second comes when the other side is subdued while it is still strong and powerful, raising itself like an eagle, and from there the Lord brings it down through the awakening from below brought about by the intermediate person. This is what Scripture says, “Make me delicacies, such as I love.” “Delicacies” is plural: two kinds of gratification. It is the Shekhinah speaking to her children, the collective Israel, as explained in the Tikkunim. By analogy, among physical delicacies there are two kinds: one consists of pleasant, sweet foods; the other of pungent or sour things that have been seasoned and prepared so well that they become delicacies that restore the soul. This is what Scripture says, “The Lord has made everything for His purpose, even the wicked for the day of evil.” It means that he should return from his wickedness and make his evil into day and light above, when the other side is subdued and the glory of the Holy One, blessed be He, is exalted on high.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְיָדוּעַ דְּעֵר הוּא נִיצוֹץ מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁיָּרַד פַּעַם רִאשׁוֹן לָעוֹלָם וּבָא לְתַקֵּן עָוֹן דְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, עַיֵּין מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ק"ט וְקי"א],
connections.quote: “It is known from the Ari that in him the soul of Mashiach was first revealed in this world; this is the meaning of Yehudah’s firstborn and the first of his strength. This is also alluded to in the wording of Bereshit Rabbah mentioned above, on “Yehudah went down”: He was occupied in creating the light of Mashiach. This was when Yehudah married Bat Shua, although Mashiach does not descend from her. Rather, Er’s birth was the first creation of Mashiach’s light in this world. Although he did not endure and died, its creation and the revelation of its light had already begun. But the power of evil inherent in creation and birth gained control over him. This is the sin of the generation of the Flood, for they too were prepared to receive Torah had they merited it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the allusion to Er as the first appearance of Mashiach’s light and its connection to the generation of the Flood. This is his own exposition of the Ari’s teaching, rather than a claim to quote an independently located passage of the Ari.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הִנִּיחָה תּוֹרָה דָּבָר זֶה לִלְמוֹד דָּבָר זֶה מִמִּצְוֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ דְּ"וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ", כְּמוֹ דְּמִיעֲטֵיהּ אֵשֶׁת חֲבֵירוֹ, הָכָא נַמֵּי כָּל שֶׁלֹּא בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh.”
connections.context: The “one flesh” union supplies the image for Rav Tzadok’s account of marital attachment. Editorial notes embedded in the earlier quotation have been removed.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הִנִּיחָה תּוֹרָה דָּבָר זֶה לִלְמוֹד דָּבָר זֶה מִמִּצְוֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ דְּ"וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ", כְּמוֹ דְּמִיעֲטֵיהּ אֵשֶׁת חֲבֵירוֹ, הָכָא נַמֵּי כָּל שֶׁלֹּא בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ.
connections.quote: ““And he shall cleave”—but not to a male. “To his wife”—but not to his fellow’s wife. “And they shall become one flesh”—those who become one flesh; this excludes an animal or a beast, with which they do not become one flesh.”
connections.context: This is the original derashah about the marital verse from which Rav Tzadok develops his further inference. The quoted Gemara itself concerns the specific exclusions it lists.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבָזֶה יוּבַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כב.) דְּבַעַל קֶרִי שׁוֹנֶה בְּהִלְכוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: ‘An incident occurred with Rabbi Yehuda, who had a seminal emission and was walking along the river. His students said to him: ‘Our teacher, teach us one chapter in the laws of proper conduct.’ He went down, immersed, and taught them. They said: ‘Our teacher, did you not teach us that a person in that state may teach the laws of proper conduct?’ He answered: ‘Although I am lenient for others, I am stringent with myself.’’

connections.hePhrase: [וּבָזֶה יוּבַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כב.) דְּבַעַל קֶרִי שׁוֹנֶה בְּהִלְכוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: “Akavya ben Mahalalel says: Whoever takes four matters to heart will no longer sin: from where he comes, where he is going, what he is destined to become, and who his Judge is. From where does he come? From a place of darkness. Where does he go? To a place of darkness and gloom. What is he destined to become? Dust, maggots, and worms. Who is his Judge? The King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.”
connections.context: This supplies the four reflections to which Rashi refers. The text of Avot DeRabbi Natan attributes them to Akavya ben Mahalalel; Rashi identifies the chapter by Ben Azzai, so the distinct attributions are retained.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבָזֶה יוּבַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כב.) דְּבַעַל קֶרִי שׁוֹנֶה בְּהִלְכוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: “The ways of Torah scholars are to be humble and lowly in spirit, diligent, accomplished, patient under insult, and beloved by everyone; humble toward the members of his household, fearful of sin, and assessing a person according to his deeds. He says: “I have no desire for all that is in this world, for this world is not mine.” He sits and studies, soiling his clothing at the feet of Torah scholars. No one sees anything evil in him. He asks about the matter at hand and answers according to the halakhah.”
connections.context: This is the opening teaching identified by Rashi as an example of the laws of derekh eretz. It makes the ethical content concrete: humility, restraint, and conduct toward others accompany study.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבָזֶה יוּבַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כב.) דְּבַעַל קֶרִי שׁוֹנֶה בְּהִלְכוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: ““The laws of derekh eretz”: Such as “The ways of Torah scholars,” which is a baraita, and the chapter of Ben Azzai, “One who takes four matters to heart.””
connections.context: Rashi identifies the kind of ethical teaching meant by the Gemara’s exception for a baal keri. The existing note quotes the Gemara; this explains what may be studied.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה, וּבְתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק א נִקְרָא דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ "דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים" עַיֵּין שָׁם
connections.quote: ““To guard the way”—this is proper conduct. “The Tree of Life”—this teaches that proper conduct preceded the Tree of Life. The Tree of Life is none other than Torah, as it is said, “It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it.””
connections.context: The exposition reads Genesis 3:24 in sequence: the “way” of proper human conduct comes before the “Tree of Life” of Torah. This is the exact basis for Rav Tzadok’s description of derekh eretz as the approach to Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה, וּבְתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק א נִקְרָא דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ "דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים" עַיֵּין שָׁם
connections.quote: “For Rabbi Yishmael son of Rav Nachman said: Derekh eretz preceded Torah by twenty-six generations. This is what is written: “To guard the way of the Tree of Life.” “The way”—this is derekh eretz; afterward, “the Tree of Life”—this is Torah.”
connections.context: The Midrash expressly states the order of derekh eretz and Torah and derives it from the wording of the verse. The existing Tanna DeBei Eliyahu quotation is preserved as a separate source.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה, וּבְתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק א נִקְרָא דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ "דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים" עַיֵּין שָׁם
connections.quote: “Since Torah was apportioned to the whole congregation of Yaakov, even the lowest soul, a true Torah scholar must recognize from the garment of derekh eretz he sees in an unlearned person the precious depth of the Torah point within him. This is why the man seized Rabbi Yannai and said, ‘My inheritance is with you’: it is not written ‘the congregation of Yannai,’ but ‘the congregation of Yaakov.’ Hashem apportioned Torah to all the souls of Israel, so that even the lowest soul of Israel is not completely devoid of Torah, Heaven forbid. In the Torah point within each one, he is distinguished and elevated above all Israel. Thus the man seized Rabbi Yannai and said, ‘My inheritance is with you.’ That is: although I myself do not recognize the words of Torah in the depth of my heart because I am unlearned, you, Rabbi Yannai, are a Torah scholar. You should have discerned from my derekh eretz the precious Torah point within me from which all that conduct branches. These true words awakened Rabbi Yannai; he immediately acknowledged them, regretted his act, and said, ‘You have all this derekh eretz, and I called you a dog.’”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why derekh eretz can stand before Torah without being detached from it. In the story of Rabbi Yannai, the guest's conduct expresses a Torah point he cannot yet identify through formal learning. The scholar is challenged to recognize it. This develops the siman's image of a path toward the tree of life: preparation can already carry the inward relation to what it prepares one to receive.
connections.headline: Derekh eretz and the Torah point already in the person

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ "חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ".
connections.quote: see note 622.

connections.hePhrase: הִתְחִילוּ הַטִּיפֵּי קֶרִי דַּחֲזָא לְאוֹנְסוֹ לָצֵאת מִמֶּנּוּ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yirmeyah ben Elazar said: All those years that Adam the first man was under the ban, he fathered spirits, demons and night-demons. … They objected: Rabbi Meir used to say: Adam the first man was a great chasid. When he saw that death had been decreed because of him, he fasted for one hundred and thirty years and separated from his wife for one hundred and thirty years. … When that was said, it was about semen that he emitted involuntarily.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל.
connections.quote: “Know that the Israelites of the generation of the bondage in Egypt were the aspect of those sparks of emission (keri) that Adam the first man emitted during those one hundred and thirty years before Shet was born, as our Sages said. … So it is with souls: through Adam’s sin good became mixed with evil, especially in these sparks of keri that he fathered during the one hundred and thirty years.”
connections.context: These are the years after the sin in which, according to Eruvin 18b, Adam separated from his wife.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קז:), עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י.
connections.quote: see note 1396.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קז:), עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִּׁ"י.
connections.quote: see note 1395.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה לְעָוֹן זֶה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah said: There is no sin in the world that has no repentance except this one, and there are no wicked who do not see the face of the Shechinah except this one, as it is written: ‘Evil shall not sojourn with You’ (Psalms 5:5)—at all.”
connections.context: “This one” is the man who emits his seed in vain, whom the Zohar has just called “evil” like Er (Genesis 38:7).

connections.hePhrase: אִם כֵּן הָיָה מַגִּיעַ לְעֵץ הַחַיִּים וְחַי לְעוֹלָם,
connections.quote: “Hashem God said: Behold, man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil; and now, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.”
connections.context: Two verses later the cherubim are set “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24), the guarding with which this passage opens.

connections.hePhrase: [קכב] קַיְימָא לַן בְּשַׁבָּת (עא.) שֶׁהַחַטָּאת הַבָּא לְכַפֵּר הַחֵטְא גּוֹרֵר אוֹתוֹ חֵטְא גַּם פַּעַם אַחֵר שֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם.
connections.quote: “One act of reaping draws in the other act of reaping, and one act of grinding draws in the other act of grinding. But if he became aware of the reaping done with knowledge that it was Shabbat but without awareness of the prohibited labors, that reaping draws in the other reaping and the grinding that accompanied it, while the corresponding grinding retains its separate obligation.”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם אִיתָא בְּלֹא יוֹדֵעַ דְּחַיָּיב אָשָׁם תָּלוּי, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְכַּפֵּר בְּחַטָּאת עַל זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן (פֶּרֶק ל),
connections.quote: “If a person sinned and then knew that he had sinned, he brings a sin-offering worth a sela, or a tenth of an ephah worth a pundion; if it is doubtful whether he sinned or did not sin, he brings a guilt-offering worth two selaim.”
connections.context: Rabbi Meir contrasts the offerings for a known inadvertent sin and for doubt about whether one sinned. The higher stated value of the provisional guilt-offering is the feature Rav Tzadok invokes when explaining why uncertain wrongdoing requires a different kind of repair.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם אִיתָא בְּלֹא יוֹדֵעַ דְּחַיָּיב אָשָׁם תָּלוּי, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְכַּפֵּר בְּחַטָּאת עַל זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן (פֶּרֶק ל),
connections.quote: “This was the meaning of the scapegoat, which the Zohar describes as a collective asham talui. An asham talui comes for what is not known, to protect the person from suffering until he knows and brings a sin offering. Likewise, acts that can be clarified only from Hashem's side, because their repair is wholly outside human understanding, require an asham talui; this was the scapegoat. It therefore had to remain alive until the blood of its fellow was applied. As long as it was possible to clarify from it actions that could be included in the goat whose lot was for Hashem, transforming deliberate sins into merits, they did not send it away. They delayed sending it into the wilderness until no more could be gathered from it and turned into merits through service. Then they sent it to Azazel, into the wilderness.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives a conceptual account of the uncertainty that Rav Tzadok mentions through the asham talui. Some actions can still be clarified through human service; other matters remain beyond a person's present understanding. The scapegoat waits while the first kind of work is still possible. This clarifies why lack of knowledge need not mean abandonment of repair, while keeping this explanation distinct from the siman's particular inference about one atonement drawing others with it.
connections.headline: Atonement while the matter is not yet fully known

connections.hePhrase: וְנִזְכַּר הָעִנְיָן גַּם כֵּן בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת, כִּי הֶחְמִירָה תּוֹרָה בְּסָפֵק דְּאָשָׁם תָּלוּי חָמִיר מֵחַטָּאת, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה הַטַּעַם: כִּי הַיְּדִיעָה שֶׁנּוֹדַע לוֹ מְכַפֶּרֶת מִקְצָת מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא מִתְחָרֵט, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות א׳ ב:ד׳
connections.quote: “The reason why they were more stringent about a doubtful transgression than a certain one, my master the Rav says, is that concerning a certain transgression a person takes the sin to heart, worries about it, regrets it, and returns in complete repentance. But concerning a doubt he devises arguments and says, “Perhaps that piece I ate was permitted.” He does not set his heart on returning, and therefore they were more stringent with him.”
connections.context: This is the exact explanation from the disciples of Rabbeinu Yonah cited in the Hebrew: knowledge of the offense prompts regret, whereas uncertainty can become an excuse to avoid repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ריט עַמּוּד ב), אִם שָׁב עַל עֲוֹן קֶרִי וּמִתְכַּפֵּר וּמוֹצִיא אוֹתָן טִפִּין הָעֲשׁוּקִים, מִמֵּילָא בִּגְרִירָה מוֹצִיא גַּם כֵּן טִפֵּי דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בְּהָקִיץ.
connections.quote: see note 330.
connections.context: The surrounding Zohar discusses deliberate destruction of seed. Rav Tzadok takes the severity of this statement seriously and then explains the exceptional depth of repair through which even this failure can be addressed. The quotation is the problem his discussion engages, not a direction to abandon repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּךְ גַּם כֵּן יִסַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עִנְיַן הַקֶּרִי בַּטֶּבַע, כִּי הוּא "חֹשֵׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח" (שְׁמוּאֵל ב יד, יד), וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יְתוּקַּן;
connections.quote: “For we must surely die, and are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered. Yet God does not take away a soul; He devises plans so that the banished one will not remain banished from Him.”
connections.context: These are the woman of Tekoa’s words to David concerning Absalom. Rav Tzadok applies the second half as an assurance that divine providence prepares a way of return. The interpretation requires God to be the One who devises the plans.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה סוֹד גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא פו:): עָבַר וְשָׁנָה הֻתְּרָה לוֹ, סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ? אֶלָּא וְכוּלֵי. וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁשָּׁב עַל הַהֶיתֵּרִים דְּאַחַר כָּךְ, מִמֵּילָא נִתְכַּפְּרוּ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ],
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: All the more is he praiseworthy, as it is said: ‘For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.’ How, then, do I understand ‘Like a dog returning to its vomit,’ and so forth? As Rav Huna said, for Rav Huna said: Once a person commits a transgression and repeats it, it becomes permitted to him. Can you really mean that it becomes permitted to him? Rather, say: It becomes like something permitted in his eyes.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה סוֹד גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא פו:): עָבַר וְשָׁנָה הֻתְּרָה לוֹ, סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ? אֶלָּא וְכוּלֵי. וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁשָּׁב עַל הַהֶיתֵּרִים דְּאַחַר כָּךְ, מִמֵּילָא נִתְכַּפְּרוּ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ],
