connections.quote: “This is what we wished to explain in the teaching “It becomes like something permitted to him.” When Hashem sees that he has transgressed and repeated it, and that there is no further expectation that he will overcome his inclination because the fire of desire for that thing has already burned within him, Hashem then implanted in him that the thing should become like something permitted. He no longer feels distant from it, as though he were not commanded concerning it at all, and has “bread in his basket.” Through this, perhaps the desire will not intensify so much, and it will become possible for him not to stumble over that matter again. Understand this.”
connections.context: Arvei Nachal reads this habituation as a possible opening for eventual restraint. The passage describes how the offense appears to the habitual sinner; it does not say that the prohibition has ceased to apply.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְתַקֵּן אֲחֵרִים הַחוֹטְאִים, דִּיחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם):
connections.quote: “Rabbi Meir used to say: Great is repentance, for on account of one individual who repents, the whole world is forgiven, as it is said: “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away from him.” It does not say “from them,” but “from him.””
connections.context: The contrast between the plural recipients and singular penitent is the source for Rav Tzadok’s claim that an individual’s repentance can have consequences for the whole community.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְתַקֵּן אֲחֵרִים הַחוֹטְאִים, דִּיחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם):
connections.quote: “When one individual repents, he and the whole world are forgiven, as our Sages teach in Yoma 86b. How is forgiveness possible? Only because he also awakens thoughts of repentance in their hearts. Not everyone who wishes to make himself that individual can do so, for this has not yet occurred; only Mashiach son of David will be such a person. His soul must include all souls, for otherwise his thoughts of repentance cannot give rise to thoughts of repentance in those whose souls have no connection with his. His thoughts of repentance must also encompass every part of his soul. One who encompasses the whole world possesses all the kinds of powers found in the whole world; if he repents in only one power, he awakens repentance only in those connected with that power.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok himself explains the scope and limits of another person’s repentance benefiting others: it awakens their own return, according to the souls and powers connected with the penitent.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּנִדָּה (יג.) דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה;
connections.quote: ‘Why such severity? Because he emits seed in vain, for Rabbi Yochanan said: Anyone who emits seed in vain is liable to death, as it is said: ‘What he did was evil in the eyes of Hashem, and He put him to death as well.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (מז:) בְּחַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין דְּמִיתָתָם כַּפָּרָתָם;
connections.quote: “If you suppose that once they have been executed they have atonement, let them be buried in their ancestral graves! We require death and burial.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (מז:) בְּחַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין דְּמִיתָתָם כַּפָּרָתָם;
connections.quote: “We also require the decomposition of the flesh. This is also precise from the teaching: Once the flesh has decomposed, they gather the bones and bury them in their proper place.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (מז:) בְּחַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין דְּמִיתָתָם כַּפָּרָתָם;
connections.quote: “Rav Ashi said: When does atonement occur? When they experience a little of the suffering of the grave.”
connections.context: The discussion does come to recognize atonement for those executed by the court, while distinguishing death itself from the further stages of burial and the grave. The previous note quoted only the preliminary objection denying atonement, leaving the reader with the opposite impression from the continuation Rav Tzadok is using.

connections.hePhrase: כַּנּוֹדָע שֶׁהָעוֹנֶשׁ הוּא כְּדֵי לְהִתְכַּפֵּר.
connections.quote: ““For every prohibition preceded by a positive commandment, one receives lashes”: This teaches that even according to the view that one does not receive lashes for a prohibition remedied by a positive commandment—as it is taught concerning “You shall not leave over” and “You shall burn what remains”—Scripture gives a positive command after the prohibition to say that one does not receive lashes for it. Scripture assigned the positive command as the penalty and repair of the prohibition: “Do not do this; if you have done it, do this and be exempt.” Rabbi Yochanan teaches that this applies to a positive command that follows the prohibition and can be fulfilled only after violating it. But a positive command that precedes the prohibition and can be fulfilled before violating it is not a remedy that detaches the prohibition from its penalty; even if one fulfills it after the violation, one has not been exempted from lashes.”
connections.context: Rashi expressly uses “penalty” together with “repair,” illustrating the corrective meaning emphasized here. His legal distinction is retained: not every later positive deed exempts a person from the penalty of an earlier violation.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ פְּעָמִים נִגְזַר עַל הָאָדָם בִּשְׁבִיל הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ בָּנִים וְכַיּוֹצֵא, שֶׁהוּא מֵאַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים שֶׁנִּקְרָא מִיתָה בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.).
connections.quote: ‘But according to the first tanna as well, is it not written, ‘Yet you will die like Adam’? What does ‘death’ mean here? Poverty. For the master said: Four are regarded as dead: a poor person, a blind person, a person afflicted with tzaraat, and one who has no children.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁמֵּמִית עַצְמוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן מִיתָה כִּדְרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת סג:) עַל פָּסוּק "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל",
connections.quote: ‘Another interpretation: ‘Be attentive and hear, Israel’—hasket—means: Break yourselves, kattetū, over words of Torah. This is as Reish Lakish said, for Reish Lakish said: From where do we know that words of Torah endure only in someone who puts himself to death for their sake? It is said: ‘This is the Torah: when a person dies in a tent.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁמֵּמִית עַצְמוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן מִיתָה כִּדְרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת סג:) עַל פָּסוּק "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל",
connections.quote: ‘This is the law: When a person dies in a tent, everyone who enters the tent and everything in the tent shall be impure for seven days.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁמֵּמִית עַצְמוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן מִיתָה כִּדְרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת סג:) עַל פָּסוּק "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל",
connections.quote: “They also said concerning this: “Torah endures only in one who puts himself to death for Torah,” as it is said, “A person who dies in a tent.” We explained that a human being, being physical, is not suited to the intellectual level until he entirely sets aside the concern of his body, so that his body has no importance in his eyes. He puts his body to death and sets himself aside for the sake of intellectual Torah, and then is suited to intellectual Torah. This is as it says here: “Reduce your business and engage in Torah”—he reduces his affairs, which are his needs in this world, for the sake of intellectual Torah, and then is suited to Torah.”
connections.context: Maharal explains the expression through subordinating bodily concerns and reducing worldly business for study. His final sentence supplies the concrete meaning of the metaphor in this passage.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁמֵּמִית עַצְמוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן מִיתָה כִּדְרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת סג:) עַל פָּסוּק "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל",
connections.quote: “Afterward comes the portion of Parah, to purify the impure through an awakening of holiness from the person's own side and effort. Through this, the impurity of death is purified by the dew of Torah that gives him life (Ketubot 111b), through his “putting himself to death” over words of Torah. For it is written, ‘A person who dies in a tent’ (Numbers 19:14; Berakhot 63b; Shabbat 83b), and Scripture compares tents to streams (Numbers 24:6; Berakhot 16a), which likewise raise a person from impurity to purity.”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim places the figurative dying in Torah within an expressly life-giving sequence. Personal effort in Torah is described as the dew that revives and the water that purifies. This supplies the positive mechanism of the siman’s image: the exertion of study becomes the path to renewed life and purity.
connections.headline: Torah labor as a purification that gives life

connections.hePhrase: [וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (תָּמִיד לב.): מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיִחְיֶה? יָמִית עַצְמוֹ].
connections.quote: ‘He asked them: ‘What should a person do to live?’ They answered: ‘Let him put himself to death [through self-denial].’ ‘What should a person do to die?’ ‘Let him give himself life [through self-indulgence].’ He asked them: ‘What should a person do to be accepted by other people?’ They answered: ‘Let him hate kingship and authority.’ He said to them: ‘My advice is better than yours: Let him love kingship and authority, and do good for people.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיתָה נִקְרָא "דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אָנֹכִי הֹלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ כָּל הָאָרֶץ" (מְלָכִים א ב, ב);
connections.quote: ‘I am going the way of all the earth. Be strong, and become a man.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ב): טוֹב תּוֹרָה עִם דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ,
connections.quote: ‘Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, says: Torah study together with work is fitting, for the exertion of both makes sin forgotten. Any Torah study unaccompanied by work will eventually cease and lead to sin. All who labor for the community should labor with them for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of their ancestors assists them, and their righteousness endures forever. As for you, I credit you with abundant reward as though you had accomplished it.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִבְרָכוֹת (לה:): הַנְהֵג בָּהֶן מִנְהַג דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְכוּלֵי, וְאִם לָאו אֵין מִתְקַיֵּים;
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: What does ‘You shall gather your grain’ teach? Since it is said, ‘This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth,’ one might understand the words literally. Therefore Scripture says, ‘You shall gather your grain’: Conduct yourself with the ordinary ways of earning a living alongside Torah; these are Rabbi Yishmael’s words.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דִּבְּרוּ עָלָיו לָשׁוֹן הָרָע עַל זֶה שֶׁחֲשָׁבוּהוּ לִמְבַטֵּל מִצְוָה, כֵּיוָן דְּאִשְׁתּוֹ לֹא מָחֲלָה;
connections.quote: “How did Miriam know that Moshe had separated from his wife? Rabbi Natan says: Miriam was beside Tzipporah when Moshe was told, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.” When Tzipporah heard, she said, “Woe to the wives of these men.” From when had Moshe separated from marital relations? When the Holy One, blessed be He, told Moshe at Sinai, before the giving of Torah, to sanctify the people, he told them, “For three days do not approach a woman.” They separated from their wives, and Moshe separated from his wife. After the giving of Torah, the Holy One told him, “Go, say to them: Return to your tents; but you stand here with Me”—and do not return to marital relations. When Tzipporah said, “Woe to their wives,” she meant that they would be required for prophecy and would separate from their wives, as her husband had separated from her. Through this Miriam learned of it and told Aharon. If Miriam, who did not intend to disparage Moshe, was punished, how much more will a person who disparages his fellow and speaks maliciously be afflicted with tzaraat.”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies Tzipporah’s words and explains how Miriam learned of Moshe’s separation. It also preserves the conclusion that Miriam was punished despite not intending to disparage him.

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם נֶעֶנְשׁוּ וְנֶאֱמַר: "אֲשֶׁר נוֹאַלְנוּ וַאֲשֶׁר חָטָאנוּ", דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הִסְכִּים עַל יָדוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שַׁבָּת פז.),
connections.quote: ‘Aaron said to Moses: ‘Please, my lord, do not lay upon us the sin in which we acted foolishly and sinned.’’

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם נֶעֶנְשׁוּ וְנֶאֱמַר: "אֲשֶׁר נוֹאַלְנוּ וַאֲשֶׁר חָטָאנוּ", דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הִסְכִּים עַל יָדוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שַׁבָּת פז.),
connections.quote: see note 968.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּעֵין עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ דְּהִיא גְּדוֹלָה גַּם כֵּן.
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: A transgression for its proper purpose is greater than a mitzvah performed for an ulterior purpose. But did Rav Yehudah not say in Rav’s name: A person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even for an ulterior purpose, for from acting for an ulterior purpose he comes to act for their proper purpose? Rather, say: It is like a mitzvah performed for an ulterior purpose. For it is written, “Blessed above women shall be Yael, wife of Chever the Kenite; above women in the tent shall she be blessed.” Who are the women in the tent? Sarah, Rivkah, Rachel, and Leah.”
connections.context: The Gemara qualifies its initial comparison. Its conclusion says “like,” rather than leaving the opening claim of superiority unqualified.

connections.hePhrase: וְחָשֵׁיב שָׁם שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים, וְדִמָּה זֶה לִשְׁבִירַת לוּחוֹת דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ.
connections.quote: “He broke the Tablets—what did he expound? He said: If concerning the Paschal offering, which is one of the six hundred and thirteen commandments, the Torah says, “No foreigner shall eat of it,” then here the whole Torah is present and Israel are apostates—how much more so. From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, agreed with him? From “which you broke”; Reish Lakish said: “Well done for breaking them.””
connections.context: This is the specific reasoning for breaking the Tablets that accompanies the discussion of Moshe’s separation from his wife. The existing footnote about that separation is preserved.

connections.hePhrase: וְלִפְעָמִים עַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל גַּם כֵּן לְתַקֵּן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "רְאֵה חַיִּים עִם אִשָּׁה", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: ‘Enjoy life with the woman you love throughout all the days of your fleeting life that He has given you under the sun, throughout all your fleeting days. For this is your portion in life and in the labor at which you toil under the sun.’

connections.hePhrase: כַּנִּרְאֶה מִדִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹסָפוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין (נט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּחִדּוּשַׁי;
connections.quote: “One can answer that it also involves refraining from an act: one who is commanded concerning procreation is commanded not to destroy seed.”
connections.context: Tosafot explain why procreation can figure in a discussion of prohibitions: its positive duty also implies a restraint against wasting seed. This is the linkage Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל לָאו הַבָּא מִכְּלַל עֲשֵׂה – הָעֲשֵׂה הוּא תִּיקּוּן הַלָּאו.
connections.quote: “The mitzvah of eating matzah gives holiness to eating. Every mitzvah, particularly one over which we bless ‘Who sanctified us through His commandments and commanded us,’ adds holiness to a person, especially to the organ and power through which it is performed. As the Sages said in Vayikra Rabbah (21:5): ‘If you have made bundles of transgressions, make corresponding bundles of mitzvot,’ continuing with the example of the hands and the other faculties.”
connections.explanation: Et HaOchel states the general principle behind the siman's inference: a mitzvah adds holiness especially to the organ and power through which it is performed. Its use of the same bundles-of-mitzvot teaching explains how the corresponding positive act can repair a damaged faculty. Rav Tzadok's explicit qualification here remains decisive: the proposed increase is in holiness and quality, within human ability.
connections.headline: A mitzvah sanctifies the faculty through which it is performed

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִיהוּ יֵשׁ לוֹמַר נַמֵּי "יָשַׁב וְלֹא עָבַר עֲבֵירָה" כִּדְרַב חֲנִינָא בַּר פַּפָּא שֶׁנִּזְדַּמְּנָה לְיָדוֹ, מִקְרֵי גַּם כֵּן מִצְוָה כִּדְאִיתָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (לט:)].
connections.quote: ‘Rav Tovi bar Rav Kisna raised a contradiction before Rava: We learned, ‘Anyone who performs one mitzvah is treated well.’ If he performs one, yes; if he does not, no. But this contradicts the teaching: If a person sits and does not commit a transgression, he is rewarded as though he performed a mitzvah! He answered: There the case is one in which an opportunity to transgress came to him and he escaped it.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב.): שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִין וְכוּלֵי, וְאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת: "אַל תַּרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה" כַּנּוֹדָע;
connections.quote: “According to the version that he taught it openly, he did so to prevent neglect of Torah study and of procreation. According to the version that he whispered it, it was so that Torah scholars would not be with their wives as often as roosters.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב.): שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִין וְכוּלֵי, וְאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת: "אַל תַּרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה" כַּנּוֹדָע;
connections.quote: “Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem says: Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household. Do not speak excessively with a woman. They said this concerning one’s own wife; how much more concerning one’s fellow’s wife. Hence the Sages said: Whenever a man speaks excessively with a woman, he brings harm upon himself, neglects words of Torah, and ultimately inherits Gehinnom.”
connections.context: This supplies the Mishnah’s complete statement that Rav Tzadok invokes when explaining why his counsel concerns the quality of holiness rather than simply increasing the frequency of an act.

connections.hePhrase: [דְּאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא, וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא" – דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ)],
connections.quote: see note 739.
connections.context: The first sentence is the principle Rav Tzadok cites in qualifying holiness by a person’s actual capacity. In the Gemara it introduces the opportunity to fulfill the mitzvah of sukkah.

connections.hePhrase: [דְּאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא, וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא" – דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ)],
connections.quote: see note 1259.
connections.context: This is the passage expressly cited about even the most pious person. Rav Tzadok uses its recognition of human limitation to explain “according to the person’s capacity.”

connections.hePhrase: אָז "ה' צִלְּךָ", גַּם כֵּן דּוּגְמָתוֹ שׁוֹפֵעַ לָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה
connections.quote: see note 334.
connections.context: Tzilcha literally denotes your shade or shadow. Rav Tzadok draws an analogy with a shadow that corresponds to one’s movements, describing a divine response corresponding to a person’s sanctification below.

connections.hePhrase: אָז "ה' צִלְּךָ", גַּם כֵּן דּוּגְמָתוֹ שׁוֹפֵעַ לָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה
connections.heRef: בעל שם טוב על התורה, קדושים כ״ג:א׳
connections.quote: “The holy Baal Shem Tov explained the verse “Hashem is your shadow”: Hashem conducts Himself according to your deeds, as it were, like your shadow. Whatever you do, the shadow does as well. So too, Hashem, as it were: a righteous person decrees and the Holy One, blessed be He, fulfills it.”
connections.context: The original teaching explains the shadow analogy used here: an action below is answered by a corresponding divine action above.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר: "וְרוּחַ קָדְשְׁךָ אַל תִּקַּח מִמֶּנִּי, הָשִׁיבָה לִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יג–יד):
connections.quote: “Do not cast me away from before You, and do not take Your holy spirit from me.”
connections.context: David asks that the divine spirit not be withdrawn. The next verse, quoted in the following note, adds the restoration of joy and a willing spirit.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר: "וְרוּחַ קָדְשְׁךָ אַל תִּקַּח מִמֶּנִּי, הָשִׁיבָה לִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יג–יד):
connections.quote: “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit.”
connections.context: This completes the words abbreviated in the main text as “restore to me, etc.” Nedivah is a willing or generous spirit, a significant expression in Rav Tzadok’s discussion of freely renewed good action.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר: "וְרוּחַ קָדְשְׁךָ אַל תִּקַּח מִמֶּנִּי, הָשִׁיבָה לִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יג–יד):
connections.quote: ““Restore to me the joy of Your salvation”: The holy spirit that departed from me.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies David’s request for restored joy with the return of the holy spirit, directly explaining Rav Tzadok’s concluding description of what returns to the heart.

connections.hePhrase: [קכה] צְדָקָה לַעֲנִיִּים גַּם כֵּן מוֹעִיל לְתַקֵּן עָוֹן הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
connections.quote: “There he also wrote, on folio 121a, another rectification: the wealthy person should increase his charity to forty small coins, and the poor person should give no fewer than four small coins to the four corners of the city, beginning at the southeast corner, in accordance with the rule governing the direction in which one turns. This is the attribute of kindness associated with Avraham. Corresponding to his own conduct, he becomes a wanderer, moves about, and exerts himself in the sweat of a mitzvah by going from place to place through the four corners and directions of the city, as much as he can bear. These correspond to the four exiles into which Israel was exiled. His intention in walking in the city’s four directions should be to gather Israel’s dispersed and bring into holiness his holy sparks that descended into the kelipot through wasted seed. The charity must be given secretly, like a mikveh of forty seah whose contents are unseen, and he should give it to those who labor in Torah. Of him it is said, “He removes the first offense first,” for this rectifies the blemish of the covenant for everything he blemished that week. He will not need another rectification or fasts, for this order is a wondrous and complete rectification.”

connections.hePhrase: [קכה] צְדָקָה לַעֲנִיִּים גַּם כֵּן מוֹעִיל לְתַקֵּן עָוֹן הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 5:2
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 5:2
connections.quote: “For sometimes a person fulfills the commandment of charity, giving a gift from his hand to a poor person. If the poor person uses this strength to fulfill the will of Hashem, blessed be He, the commandment will then be vindicated, and “the work of charity shall be peace.” But if, Heaven forbid, he gives to an unworthy poor person, who uses that strength to act contrary to the will of Hashem, blessed be He, he will thereby be helping those who transgress His will. This is termed “burial,” for the matter is hidden and stored away in concealment, and its ultimate outcome is unknown. For this, every devout person should pray to Hashem, blessed be He, to help him perform the commandment, so that he encounters a worthy poor person and can fulfill His commandments completely. For through his own grasp, a person cannot clarify his conduct in this matter, because this world is full of uncertainty.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov poses the exact difficulty that concludes this siman: the giver cannot know completely how the recipient will use the strength provided. He therefore joins the mitzvah to prayer for a fitting recipient and a good outcome. This deepens the siman’s appeal to divine help without turning uncertainty into a reason to abandon charity.
connections.headline: Praying for charity to reach its proper purpose

connections.hePhrase: וּבִכְלָל לְכָל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה מוֹעִיל צְדָקָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב דְּ"תַּצִּיל מִמָּוֶת" (מִשְׁלֵי י, ב), וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יא.).
connections.quote: ‘Treasures gained through wickedness will not help, but righteousness rescues from death.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִכְלָל לְכָל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה מוֹעִיל צְדָקָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב דְּ"תַּצִּיל מִמָּוֶת" (מִשְׁלֵי י, ב), וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יא.).
connections.quote: “It was taught: They said of Binyamin the Righteous that he was in charge of a charity fund. Once, during years of drought, a woman came before him and said to him: ‘Rabbi, provide for me!’ He said to her: ‘By the Temple service, the charity fund has nothing!’ She said to him: ‘Rabbi, if you do not provide for me, a woman and her seven sons will die!’ He arose and provided for her from his own funds. Some time later he became ill and was near death. The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the universe, You said: Whoever sustains a single life from Israel is as though he had sustained an entire world. Should Binyamin the Righteous, who kept a woman and her seven sons alive, die after these few years?’ Immediately his sentence was torn up. It was taught: Twenty-two years were added to his life.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבִכְלָל לְכָל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה מוֹעִיל צְדָקָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב דְּ"תַּצִּיל מִמָּוֶת" (מִשְׁלֵי י, ב), וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יא.).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said: Rabbi Yochanan raised a contradiction. It is written, “Wealth will not avail on a day of wrath, but charity saves from death,” and it is written, “Treasures of wickedness will not avail, but charity saves from death.” Why these two statements about charity? One saves a person from an unusual death, and one saves him from the judgment of Gehinnom. Which saves him from the judgment of Gehinnom? The verse in which “wrath” is written, for it is written, “That day is a day of wrath.” Which saves him from an unusual death? He gives it without knowing to whom he gives it, and the recipient receives it without knowing from whom he receives it. Giving without knowing to whom excludes the practice of Mar Ukva; receiving without knowing from whom excludes the practice of Rabbi Abba. What, then, should he do? Give to the charity fund. An objection was raised: What should a person do so that he will have male children? Rabbi Eliezer says: He should distribute his money to the poor. Rabbi Yehoshua says: He should gladden his wife for the marital mitzvah. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: A person should not give a coin to a charity purse unless someone like Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon is appointed over it. When we said to give to the fund, we meant one over which someone like Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon is appointed.”
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes the two forms of deliverance and the manner of giving associated with one of them. Its immediate qualification is retained: an anonymous charity fund must have a trustworthy administrator. The existing note about Binyamin the righteous supplies a separate narrative example.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיִרְמְיָה שֶׁקִּלֵּל לְאַנְשֵׁי עֲנָתוֹת: "וְיִהְיוּ מֻכְשָׁלִים לְפָנֶיךָ, בְּעֵת אַפְּךָ עֲשֵׂה בָהֶם" (יִרְמְיָה יח, כג) – הַכְשִׁילֵם בִּבְנֵי אָדָם שֶׁאֵינָם מְהֻגָּנִים, כִּדְאִיתָא סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא קַמָּא (טז:).
connections.quote: ‘You, Hashem, know all their plans to put me to death. Do not atone for their iniquity, and do not erase their sin from before You. Let them stumble before You; deal with them at the time of Your anger.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיִרְמְיָה שֶׁקִּלֵּל לְאַנְשֵׁי עֲנָתוֹת: "וְיִהְיוּ מֻכְשָׁלִים לְפָנֶיךָ, בְּעֵת אַפְּךָ עֲשֵׂה בָהֶם" (יִרְמְיָה יח, כג) – הַכְשִׁילֵם בִּבְנֵי אָדָם שֶׁאֵינָם מְהֻגָּנִים, כִּדְאִיתָא סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא קַמָּא (טז:).
connections.quote: ‘Rava expounded: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘Let them be made to stumble before You; act against them in the time of Your anger’? Jeremiah said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the world, even when they give charity, make them stumble by giving to unworthy people, so that they will receive no reward for it.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הֵם הֶחֱטִיאוּ לְיִרְמְיָה בְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה כַּנּוֹדָע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סִימָן א בְּחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק סָעִיף קָטָן ח)
connections.quote: “There is room to doubt: If a woman conceived in a bath, has the father fulfilled procreation, and is the child considered his son in every respect? In the collected writings of Maharil it is found that Ben Sira was the son of Jeremiah, who had bathed in a bath; for Sira has the numerical value of Yirmiyahu.”
connections.context: Chelkat Mechokek 1:8 records this traditional account while discussing legal parentage. The note supports the Ben Sira tradition; it does not itself recount the coercion by the people of Anathoth mentioned by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בֶּן סִירָא הָיָה כָּלוּל טוֹב וָרָע כִּדְאִיתָא בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין ק:) דְּהוּא מִסְּפָרִים חִיצוֹנִים, וּמִילְּתָא מַעֲלָיוּתָא דְּאִית בֵּיהּ דָּרְשִׁינַן עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yosef said: We expound the fine sayings that are in it: ‘A good wife is a good gift; she is given into the bosom of one who fears God. A bad wife is a plague of tzaraat to her husband.’ What is his remedy? ‘He should send her away from his house and be healed of his tzaraat. A beautiful wife—fortunate is her husband; the number of his days is doubled.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (צב:) קְרָאוּהוּ "כְּתוּבִים",
connections.quote: “Repeated in the Writings, as it is written: “Every bird dwells with its kind, and a human being with one like himself.””
connections.context: The Gemara includes this saying in a series of witnesses to the tendency of like to associate with like. The saying is from Ben Sira; the Gemara’s use of “Writings” here is the feature Rav Tzadok is discussing.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (צב:) קְרָאוּהוּ "כְּתוּבִים",
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא קמא צ״ב ב:י״ב:ג׳
connections.quote: ““Repeated a third time in the Writings”: “Every winged bird dwells with its own kind” is not a verse anywhere in Scripture. Perhaps it is in the book of Ben Sira, as is “Cherish her and she will exalt you, and seat you among nobles.””
connections.context: Tosafot addresses the very designation “Writings” used in this passage and proposes Ben Sira as its source. The word “perhaps” is preserved; this comment does not identify the line as a biblical verse.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה דָּבָר זֶה אֵין בְּיַד הָאָדָם לֵידַע כְּלָל, עַיֵּין בִּכְתוּבּוֹת (סח.) וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּסֻכָּה (מט:): שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר כָּל הַבָּא לִקְפּוֹץ קוֹפֵץ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: "מַה יָּקָר חַסְדְּךָ" (תְּהִלִּים לו, ח).
connections.quote: “This is what Rabbi Elazar said: Come, let us acknowledge a debt to the impostors; were it not for them, we would be sinning every day, as it is said: “He will cry out against you to the Lord, and there will be sin in you.””
connections.context: This follows an account of a supposed pauper whose household discusses expensive tablecloths. The existence of fraudulent claimants mitigates the judgment of those who fail to give. Rav Tzadok cites this particular teaching, not the separate comparison of withholding charity to idolatry.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה דָּבָר זֶה אֵין בְּיַד הָאָדָם לֵידַע כְּלָל, עַיֵּין בִּכְתוּבּוֹת (סח.) וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּסֻכָּה (מט:): שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר כָּל הַבָּא לִקְפּוֹץ קוֹפֵץ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: "מַה יָּקָר חַסְדְּךָ" (תְּהִלִּים לו, ח).
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Elazar also said: Anyone who performs righteousness and justice is as though he filled the entire world with kindness, as it is said: ‘He loves righteousness and justice; Hashem’s kindness fills the earth.’ Perhaps you will say that anyone who wishes to leap in can do so. Scripture says: ‘How precious is Your kindness, God’ (‘Hashem’s kindness fills the earth’), and so forth. Could the same be true even of one who fears Heaven? Scripture says: ‘Hashem’s kindness is from eternity to eternity upon those who fear Him.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה דָּבָר זֶה אֵין בְּיַד הָאָדָם לֵידַע כְּלָל, עַיֵּין בִּכְתוּבּוֹת (סח.) וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּסֻכָּה (מט:): שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר כָּל הַבָּא לִקְפּוֹץ קוֹפֵץ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: "מַה יָּקָר חַסְדְּךָ" (תְּהִלִּים לו, ח).
connections.quote: ‘How precious is Your kindness, God! Human beings take refuge in the shadow of Your wings.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה סא) דָּרְשׁוּ פָּסוּק "וְלָעֶרֶב אַל תַּנַּח יָדֶךָ, כִּי אֵינְךָ יוֹדֵעַ אֵי זֶה יִכְשָׁר" (קֹהֶלֶת יא, ו) עַל נְתִינַת צְדָקָה, שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ אֵיזֶה יִכְשָׁר;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua said: If a poor person comes to you in the morning, give to him; in the evening, give to him. For you do not know concerning which of them the Holy One, blessed be He, records merit for you—this one or that one—or whether both are equally good.”
connections.context: This interpretation of Ecclesiastes 11:6 addresses uncertainty about the recipient and the merit of giving. Rav Tzadok cites it as a reason to continue giving rather than assume one can always identify the worthy recipient.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה סא) דָּרְשׁוּ פָּסוּק "וְלָעֶרֶב אַל תַּנַּח יָדֶךָ, כִּי אֵינְךָ יוֹדֵעַ אֵי זֶה יִכְשָׁר" (קֹהֶלֶת יא, ו) עַל נְתִינַת צְדָקָה, שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ אֵיזֶה יִכְשָׁר;
connections.quote: ‘Sow your seed in the morning, and do not let your hand rest in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, this one or that one, or whether both will be equally good.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא "לוֹקֵחַ נְפָשׁוֹת", וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, ה) שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ עֲשָׂאָם, וְנֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
connections.quote: “And the souls that they had made in Haran.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא "לוֹקֵחַ נְפָשׁוֹת", וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, ה) שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ עֲשָׂאָם, וְנֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
connections.quote: “These are the converts whom they converted. If so, why does it say “that they made”? To teach you that whoever brings an idolater near and converts him is as though he created him. … Abraham converted the men, and Sarah converted the women.”
connections.context: The Midrash, rather than the verse alone, supplies the statement “as though he created them.” Rav Tzadok applies this spiritual begetting to restoring souls through bringing others near.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא "לוֹקֵחַ נְפָשׁוֹת", וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, ה) שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ עֲשָׂאָם, וְנֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
connections.quote: ““Every living creature”: A living thing that is eaten whole, such as small fish that have reached their full growth.”
connections.context: This explains the literal food-related sense of the Gemara’s phrase “every nefesh restores the nefesh.” Rav Tzadok applies its wording to a soul restoring another soul; that application is distinct from the original dietary context.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא "לוֹקֵחַ נְפָשׁוֹת", וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, ה) שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ עֲשָׂאָם, וְנֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Whoever teaches his fellow’s son Torah, Scripture accounts it to him as though he had made him, as it is said, “The souls that they made in Charan.” Rabbi Elazar says: As though he had made the words of Torah, as it is said, “You shall keep the words of this covenant and do them.” Rava said: As though he had made himself, as it is said, “And you shall do them”—read it as “yourselves.””
connections.context: The existing Midrash quotation concerns bringing converts near. This Talmudic passage expressly extends the image of spiritual creation to teaching another person Torah and records its further interpretations.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין ע:): בַּדָּבָר שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתְקָנוּ;
connections.quote: see note 611.
connections.context: Among the opinions identifying the tree of knowledge, Rabbi Nechemya identifies it with the fig because its leaves supplied Adam and Eve’s covering. Rav Tzadok draws a general pattern of repair from the same area in which a person failed.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת כְּעִנְיַן "שְׂכַר מִצְוָה – מִצְוָה", דְּגַם בָּזֶה הוּא מְזַכֶּה לְחַיָּיבַיָּא עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה.
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על פרקי אבות ד׳:ב׳:ג׳
connections.quote: ““The reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah”: This is another reason, beyond the natural explanation. It means that the Holy One, blessed be He, has not placed good and evil in a person’s hands, but only the choice, as it is said, “Choose life.” After he chooses one path, if he walks in the good, Hashem is with him. When he performs one mitzvah, it assists him to perform another, for by himself he does not even have the power to do good. Concerning this it says, “The reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression.” Heaven forbid that this is its entire reward; if so, what reward would he have? That is not so, for its reward remains for the World to Come. Rather, it means that the fruit of a mitzvah is a mitzvah: he enjoys its fruits in this world when it helps him perform other mitzvot. Thus the principal grows and remains for the World to Come. This is “Say of the righteous that it is good, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.””
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah distinguishes the additional mitzvah enabled in this world from the enduring reward in the World to Come. This explains the expression Rav Tzadok uses for a further opportunity to restore souls.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר: "אֲלַמְּדָה פֹשְׁעִים דְּרָכֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, טו),
connections.quote: ‘I will teach transgressors Your paths, and sinners will return to You.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְחַיָּיב לְזַכּוֹת אֶת הַחַיָּיב, וְאָמְרוּ: "יָבוֹא טָהוֹר וִיכַפֵּר עַל הַטָּהוֹר", וְאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת לב.): "מְגַלְגְּלִין זְכוּת עַל יְדֵי זַכַּאי".
connections.quote: “The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: Thus the attribute of justice requires: It is better that one who is acquitted come and atone for the liable, rather than that one who is liable come and atone for another who is liable.”
connections.context: The High Priest first obtains atonement for himself and then seeks atonement for his fellow priests. The actual contrast is zakkai and chayyav, “acquitted” and “liable”; Rav Tzadok’s wording, “the pure … for the pure,” gives the sense; the Gemara’s own words are “let one who is acquitted come and atone for one who is liable.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְחַיָּיב לְזַכּוֹת אֶת הַחַיָּיב, וְאָמְרוּ: "יָבוֹא טָהוֹר וִיכַפֵּר עַל הַטָּהוֹר", וְאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת לב.): "מְגַלְגְּלִין זְכוּת עַל יְדֵי זַכַּאי".
connections.quote: “Merit is brought about through one who is meritorious, and liability through one who is liable.”
connections.context: The maxim concludes an account in which Providence brings together two people answerable for different wrongs. Rav Tzadok uses the general principle that a deed’s human agent is not spiritually incidental.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד: הַמְשַׂחֲקִין בַּתִּינוֹקוֹת וּמְקַבְּלֵי גֵּרִים, זֶה בָּא מִזֶּה, כִּי הֵם גַּם כֵּן אוֹתָם נְפָשׁוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Converts and those who “play with children” delay the Messiah. … But what does “those who play with children” mean?”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד: הַמְשַׂחֲקִין בַּתִּינוֹקוֹת וּמְקַבְּלֵי גֵּרִים, זֶה בָּא מִזֶּה, כִּי הֵם גַּם כֵּן אוֹתָם נְפָשׁוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: “Rather, it means those who marry girls who are not yet capable of bearing children. For Rabbi Yosei said: The son of David does not come until all the souls in the Guf have been exhausted, as it is said, “For the spirit before Me will be enwrapped, and the souls I have made.””
connections.context: The quotation must include the Gemara’s final explanation of its ambiguous expression: the point here is the postponement of births, connected with the teaching about souls awaiting embodiment. Earlier proposed interpretations are rejected in the intervening discussion.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד: הַמְשַׂחֲקִין בַּתִּינוֹקוֹת וּמְקַבְּלֵי גֵּרִים, זֶה בָּא מִזֶּה, כִּי הֵם גַּם כֵּן אוֹתָם נְפָשׁוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: “So too, relations with a pregnant or nursing wife are permitted and are not called wasted seed, Heaven forbid. Although they do not serve physical generation, they serve spiritual generation: through the couple’s good intention, the supernal Bridegroom and Bride are united, as through other acts of mitzvot. This is the secret of Avraham and Sarah generating souls for converts, as our Sages explained. Through their intention, the Bridegroom and Bride were united and generated holy souls for those converts, in the mystery of the supernal generation explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance. This is “The souls that they made in Charan.””
connections.context: Pardes Rimmonim expressly distinguishes physical and spiritual generation and discusses permitted marital relations. This is the original kabbalistic explanation adduced for the closing allusion to the souls of converts.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כָּל הַיָּד: הַמְשַׂחֲקִין בַּתִּינוֹקוֹת וּמְקַבְּלֵי גֵּרִים, זֶה בָּא מִזֶּה, כִּי הֵם גַּם כֵּן אוֹתָם נְפָשׁוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: ““Evil after evil will come upon those who receive converts”: Ri says that this applies where they persuade them to convert or receive them immediately. But if they make an earnest effort to convert, we must accept them. We find that Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov were punished for not receiving Timna when she came to convert; she went and became the concubine of Eliphaz son of Esav, and Amalek, who afflicted Israel, descended from her, as is stated in the aggadah of Chelek. Yehoshua also accepted Rachav the harlot, and Naamah and Rut the Moabite were accepted. At the beginning of “With What May One Kindle,” Hillel converted the man who said, “Convert me on condition that you make me High Priest,” and the one who said, “On condition that you teach me the entire Torah.” Although they were not making an earnest effort to convert, Hillel knew that in the end they would become genuine converts, as indeed happened.”
connections.context: Tosafot’s parallel discussion supplies an essential qualification to the expression “those who receive converts”: it does not reject the acceptance of sincere converts, whom the comment explicitly says must be received.

connections.hePhrase: [קכז] סִימָן לִתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה וְשֶׁנִּתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ עַל עָוֹן זֶה דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה וּבִכְלָל קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית, הוּא כַּאֲשֶׁר נִפְתְּחוּ לְפָנָיו מַרְאוֹת הָאֱלֹהִים;
connections.quote: “… the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.”

connections.hePhrase: רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁרוֹאֶה וּמַכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִכְחוֹ, שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה נִקְרָא אֵצֶל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם "רוּחַ קָדְשְׁךָ" וּ"שְׂשׂוֹן יִשְׁעֶךָ";
connections.quote: “Cast me not away from Your presence, and take not Your holy spirit from me. Restore unto me the joy of Your salvation, and let a willing spirit uphold me.”

connections.hePhrase: רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁרוֹאֶה וּמַכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִכְחוֹ, שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה נִקְרָא אֵצֶל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם "רוּחַ קָדְשְׁךָ" וּ"שְׂשׂוֹן יִשְׁעֶךָ";
connections.quote: “The principal difference appears to be that the earlier revelation was for speech; this does not require circumcision, and there were prophets among the nations as well. Here it says ‘He appeared’ without recording any speech afterward to explain its purpose. The Sages therefore explained it as visiting the sick. But the plain meaning appears to be that, until then, revelation had occurred only for a prophetic message, occasionally, when Avraham prepared himself. Now he had become whole, his body always ready for it. ‘He appeared to him’ means that He now appeared to be with him continually. Thus, at the last speech before circumcision at the end of Lech Lecha, it says, ‘He finished speaking with him, and God ascended from Avraham’ (Genesis 17:22). This is a model for all the earlier speeches: the revelation was only during the speech and departed immediately afterward. Scripture states it here to explain the difference between seeing before circumcision and seeing afterward. The latter was not for a speech or another particular purpose and did not depart at all, for his body had already been sanctified to be a dwelling for the Shekhinah in his heart continually, as with Israel. Concerning ‘My heart is awake,’ Shir HaShirim Rabbah asks: from where is it known that the Holy One is the heart of Israel? From ‘The Rock of my heart.’”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik asks why circumcision is said to make revelation possible when Avraham had already received revelations before it. Its answer distinguishes an appearance for a particular prophetic message from the body becoming an enduring dwelling for the Shekhinah. This develops the siman's own definition of seeing as recognizing Hashem before oneself, read with its requirement of a lasting return.
connections.headline: An occasional revelation and an enduring dwelling

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּרָא עַל פָּסוּק "מִבְּשָׂרִי אֶחֱזֶה אֱלוֹהַּ" (אִיּוֹב יט, כו), דִּלִשְׁמִירַת בְּרִית בָּשָׂר תֵּיכֶף מַגִּיעַ מַחֲזֶה: "וַיֵּרָא וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ‘After my skin has been torn away in this way, from my flesh I will behold God.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּרָא עַל פָּסוּק "מִבְּשָׂרִי אֶחֱזֶה אֱלוֹהַּ" (אִיּוֹב יט, כו), דִּלִשְׁמִירַת בְּרִית בָּשָׂר תֵּיכֶף מַגִּיעַ מַחֲזֶה: "וַיֵּרָא וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: “The Lord appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּרָא עַל פָּסוּק "מִבְּשָׂרִי אֶחֱזֶה אֱלוֹהַּ" (אִיּוֹב יט, כו), דִּלִשְׁמִירַת בְּרִית בָּשָׂר תֵּיכֶף מַגִּיעַ מַחֲזֶה: "וַיֵּרָא וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ““From my flesh I shall behold God”: Had I not done this, on what basis would the Holy One, blessed be He, have appeared to me? “The Lord appeared to him.””
connections.context: The Midrash places these words in Abraham’s mouth after his circumcision. It explicitly connects the covenant in the flesh with the divine appearance that follows; the biblical verse alone did not explain that connection.

connections.hePhrase: וְהִנֵּה בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר חַיֵּי שָׂרָה (קכט סוֹף עַמּוּד א) דִּבְשַׁעְתָּא חֲדָא בְּרִגְעָא חֲדָא זוֹכֶה לְכָל הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת
connections.quote: “Fortunate are the masters of repentance, for in one hour, in one day, in one moment, they draw near to the Holy One, blessed be He. This is not so even for the completely righteous, who draw near to the Holy One, blessed be He, over many years. Avraham did not enter those supernal days until he was old, as has been said. So too David, of whom it is written, “King David was old, advanced in days.” But the master of repentance immediately enters and cleaves to the Holy One, blessed be He.”
connections.context: This is the passage cited as Zohar I, 129a. Its complete paragraph contrasts the penitent’s immediate approach with the righteous person’s long progression; the link uses the verified chapter-and-paragraph reference.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה עִיקָּרוֹ עַל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה מֵעָוֹן קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית כִּדְאִיתָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.) עַל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא;
connections.quote: “He said: The matter depends only on me. He placed his head between his knees and cried until his soul departed. A heavenly voice went forth and said: Rabbi Elazar ben Durdayya is destined for the life of the World to Come.”

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה עִיקָּרוֹ עַל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה מֵעָוֹן קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית כִּדְאִיתָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.) עַל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא;
connections.quote: “Rabbi wept and said: Some acquire their world over many years, and some acquire their world in one hour. Rabbi also said: It is not enough that penitents are accepted; they are even called “Rabbi.””
connections.context: Elazar ben Durdayya’s complete repentance overturns the earlier claim that he could not return. Rav Tzadok invokes precisely this accepted repentance and the concentrated spiritual transformation at the end of his life.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְלָאו הָכִי סְתָם תְּשׁוּבָה בְּעָוֹן זֶה כִּדְמַשְׁמָע בְּפֶרֶק יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים (יוֹמָא פו:): הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה? מַחֲוֵי וְכוּלֵי בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה.
connections.quote: ‘What defines a person who has repented? Rav Yehudah said: Someone to whom an opportunity to transgress comes a first and a second time, and who escapes it. Rav Yehudah indicated: With the same woman, at the same stage, in the same place.’

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהוּא שֶׁלְּעוֹלָם לֹא יַחֲזוֹר לְדָבָר זֶה אֲפִילּוּ יַעֲבוֹר עָלָיו מָה, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּעִיד עָלָיו יוֹצֵר בְּרֵאשִׁית עַל כָּךְ כִּלְשׁוֹן הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁהִגִּיעַ תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ לְכָךְ],
connections.quote: “What is repentance? The sinner must abandon his sin, remove it from his thoughts, and resolve in his heart never to do it again, as it is said, “Let the wicked abandon his way.” He must likewise regret what has passed, as it is said, “After I returned, I regretted.” The Knower of hidden things must bear witness concerning him that he will never return to this sin, as it is said, “We will no longer say, ‘Our god,’ to the work of our hands.” He must confess with his lips and state these matters that he has resolved in his heart.”
connections.context: This is Rambam’s cited definition. It retains abandoning the deed, regret, firm resolve, and spoken confession rather than isolating the phrase about the Knower of hidden things.

connections.hePhrase: [וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם שֶׁמֵּת תֵּיכֶף, הָא אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לד) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי וְגוֹמֵר": הָא בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ רוֹאֶה,
connections.quote: “When the soul leaves the body, its cry goes from one end of the world to the other, yet the sound is not heard. And the soul does not leave the body until it sees the Shechinah, as it is said: ‘For man shall not see Me and live’ (Exodus 33:20).”

connections.hePhrase: [וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם שֶׁמֵּת תֵּיכֶף, הָא אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לד) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי וְגוֹמֵר": הָא בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ רוֹאֶה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Dosa says: It is written, ‘No person may see Me and live.’ In their lifetime they do not see, but they see at the time of their death, as it also says, ‘Before Him shall kneel all who descend to the dust, whose soul He did not keep alive.’”
connections.context: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer is the source Rav Tzadok names; Bamidbar Rabbah gives the same reading of the verse in so many words: man does not see Hashem in life, but sees Him at death.

connections.hePhrase: [וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם שֶׁמֵּת תֵּיכֶף, הָא אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לד) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי וְגוֹמֵר": הָא בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ רוֹאֶה,
connections.quote: ‘He said: ‘You cannot see My face, for a human being cannot see Me and live.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְדִין אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת לֹא בָּטְלוּ, כִּי מִמִּיתַת בֵּית דִּין לָא מַהֲנֵי כֹּפֶר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לֹא תִקְחוּ כֹפֶר וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “Moreover, you shall take no ransom for the life of a murderer who is guilty of death; he shall surely be put to death.”

connections.hePhrase: וְדִין אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת לֹא בָּטְלוּ, כִּי מִמִּיתַת בֵּית דִּין לָא מַהֲנֵי כֹּפֶר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לֹא תִקְחוּ כֹפֶר וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “Did Rav Yosef not say, and Rabbi Chiyya likewise teach: From the day the Temple was destroyed, although the Sanhedrin ceased, the four forms of execution did not cease? Did they not cease? They certainly ceased! Rather, the judgment corresponding to the four forms of execution did not cease. One liable to stoning either falls from a roof or is trampled by an animal. One liable to burning either falls into a fire or is bitten by a snake. One liable to execution by the sword is either handed over to the government or attacked by bandits. One liable to strangulation either drowns in a river or dies from an illness that constricts the throat.”
connections.context: The Gemara carefully distinguishes the actual cessation of court-imposed executions from its aggadic teaching about corresponding divine judgments. Rav Tzadok invokes that distinction in his exposition of Elazar ben Durdayya’s death.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָמְרוּ: "יָפָה שָׁעָה אַחַת בִּתְשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: see note 367.
connections.context: The Mishnah distinguishes the unique opportunity to act and repent here from the contentment of the World to Come. Both halves are retained because Rav Tzadok’s explanation of Rabbi’s weeping depends on what is lost when earthly service ends.

connections.hePhrase: [קכח] כְּשֶׁאָדָם עוֹשֶׂה עֲבֵירָה כְּעִנְיַן "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קכו) וּ"בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו), מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה עַל הָעֲבֵירָה שֶׁעָשָׂה,
connections.quote: “So the holy Zohar says (Shemini 35b): when the Holy One wished to create the world, Torah said before Him, ‘This person whom You are about to create is destined to sin before You.’ The Holy One replied, ‘Was I called long-suffering for nothing?’ The Midrash (Devarim Rabbah, Vaetchanan 2) compares prayer to a mikveh and repentance to the sea. A mikveh is sometimes open and sometimes closed; so too prayer is sometimes open and sometimes closed. Repentance is like the sea: just as the sea is always open, the Holy One's hand is always open to receive those who return. All this teaches that even if a person, Heaven forbid, has stumbled in a bad act, repentance is not withheld from him. This is the meaning of ‘Know Him in all your ways,’ upon which the substance of Torah depends. As Rava concludes, ‘Even in a matter of transgression’: the person should not despair after stumbling in sin, because repentance is always available. This is the general principle of the substance of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef gives an explicit reading of the same rabbinic phrase, ‘even in a matter of transgression’: a person must not despair after stumbling, because return remains open. It is a useful qualification beside the siman's insistence that a higher purpose does not remove the need for repair. The possibility of continuing mitzvot before complete purification supplies a route back, rather than a justification for repeating the failure.
connections.headline: Knowing Hashem after a failure

connections.hePhrase: וּכְאוֹתָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לא:): דְּמִתְעַנִּין תַּעֲנִית חֲלוֹם בְּשַׁבָּת וְצָרִיךְ לְמֵיתַב תַּעֲנִיתָא לְתַעֲנִיתֵיהּ;
connections.quote: ‘What is his remedy? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Let him observe a fast for his fast.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְאוֹתָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לא:): דְּמִתְעַנִּין תַּעֲנִית חֲלוֹם בְּשַׁבָּת וְצָרִיךְ לְמֵיתַב תַּעֲנִיתָא לְתַעֲנִיתֵיהּ;
connections.quote: ““Whoever sits in a fast on Shabbat”: Rabbeinu Chananel explains that this means a fast for a dream, and this is also found in Midrash Tehillim. When one observes a fast for a dream on Shabbat, Halakhot Gedolot explains that he says “Answer us” in “My God, guard my tongue”; he may even establish it as a separate blessing, since it is not within the Eighteen Blessings.”
connections.context: Tosafot identifies the exceptional fast under discussion as a dream fast. This supplies the qualification behind the existing Gemara quotation about another fast to atone for fasting on Shabbat.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כו:): סָבְרִי מִצְוָה קָעָבְדִי, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם צְרִיכָה כַּפָּרָה;
connections.quote: ‘Rav Pappa said to him: ‘But are they not wicked?’ They believe that they are performing a mitzvah. ‘But we place them under a ban!’ They believe that the Rabbis are bringing them atonement.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּשְׁבִירַת הַלּוּחוֹת, וְגָרַם עַל יְדֵי זֶה שִׁכְחַת הַתּוֹרָה כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין נד.): אִלְמָלֵא וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Eliezer also said: What is the meaning of ‘engraved upon the tablets’? Had the first tablets not been broken, Torah would not have been forgotten from Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִסְכִּים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל יָדוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִקְרֵי עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
connections.quote: “Moses did three things on his own understanding, and the Holy One, blessed be He, agreed with him: he added one day on his own understanding, he separated from his wife, and he broke the Tablets.”

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִסְכִּים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל יָדוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִקְרֵי עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
connections.quote: “And from where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, agreed with him? For it is said: ‘[the first Tablets] which you broke’ (Exodus 34:1), and Reish Lakish said: Well done that you broke them.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ סָבַל גַּם הוּא כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת וָאֶתְחַנַּן) שֶׁנִּיטְּלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ מָסוֹרוֹת הַחָכְמָה וְהָיָה יְהוֹשֻׁעַ יוֹשֵׁב וְדוֹרֵשׁ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: see note 751.
connections.context: This is the cited account of the withdrawal of Moshe’s traditions of wisdom. The Midrash relates it to his acceptance of death; Rav Tzadok supplies the additional connection to the breaking of the Tablets.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אֶסְתֵּר, דְּנִיטְּלָה מִמֶּנָּה רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כְּשֶׁהִגִּיעָה לְבֵית הַצְּלָמִים (מְגִילָּה טו:), הוּא לְעוֹנֶשׁ אַעֲבֵירָה אַף עַל גַּב דְּמִצְוָה רַבָּה קָעָבְדָא
connections.quote: ‘‘She stood in the inner courtyard of the king’s house.’ Rabbi Levi said: When she reached the chamber of idols, the Shechinah departed from her. She said: ‘My God, my God, why have You abandoned me?! Do You perhaps judge an inadvertent act as though it were deliberate, and an act under compulsion as though it were willing?’’

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה סוֹד שֶׁאָמְרָה: שֶׁמָּא בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁקְּרָאתִיו "כֶּלֶב", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: “Or perhaps it is because I called him a “dog,” as it is said, “Save my soul from the sword, my only one from the power of the dog.” She then called him a “lion,” as it is said, “Save me from the lion’s mouth.””
connections.context: This is the immediate continuation omitted from the existing quotation about Esther’s loss of the Divine Presence. It supplies both the “dog” phrase discussed here and her subsequent change to “lion.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, אַף דִּזְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ זְכִיּוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ סִגּוּפִים וְתַעֲנִיּוֹת לְכַפָּרָה, מִשּׁוּם דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים לֹא עֲדִיפֵי מֵעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ.
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for through it willful sins become for him like merits, as it is said: ‘And when the wicked man turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he shall live by them’ (Ezekiel 33:19).”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (נ.): כָּל הָאוֹמֵר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וַתְּרָן וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chanina said: Whoever says that the Holy One, blessed be He, simply waives accountability—his life will be waived, as it is said: “The Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice.””
connections.context: The statement rejects the idea that wrongdoing has no reckoning. Rav Tzadok distinguishes that from repair through repentance and from a reckoning whose purpose and measure are hidden from the person experiencing it.

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָזֶה עֵצוֹת רַבּוֹת בְּרַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יז:) בִּגְזַר דִּין דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה בִּירִידַת גְּשָׁמִים: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיוּ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘They raised an objection: ‘The eyes of Hashem your God are upon it’—sometimes for good, sometimes for harm. How can it be for good? Suppose Israel were completely wicked on Rosh Hashanah, and only a little rain was allotted to them, but afterward they repented. It is impossible to add to the rain, since the decree has already been issued. Instead, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings it down at the proper times, upon the land that needs it, all according to the land’s needs.’

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם יֵשׁ חִלּוּפִין בִּדְבָרִים הַדּוֹמִים זֶה לָזֶה, וְעַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית יִסּוּרִין שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּעֵרָכִין (טז:).
connections.quote: see note 450.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם פְּעָמִים הוּא שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק ג) דְּנִפְרָעִין שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ
connections.quote: “Everything is given against a pledge, and a net is spread over all the living. The shop is open, the shopkeeper extends credit, the ledger is open, and the hand writes. Whoever wishes to borrow may come and borrow. The collectors make their rounds continually each day, and exact payment from a person knowingly and unknowingly. They have on what to rely; the judgment is true judgment, and everything is prepared for the feast.”
connections.context: “Knowingly and unknowingly” is the precise expression Rav Tzadok invokes. The Mishnah presents life as credit for which an account is ultimately collected; his discussion applies that image to a person’s unrecognized payment through suffering.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם עַל יְדֵי הַמְּרִירוּת בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ – זֶה מַמָּשׁ עוֹנְשֵׁי גֵיהִנָּם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר:
connections.quote: “The anguish a person feels over transgressions he committed is itself the suffering of Gehinnom for that transgression. Therefore they said at the end of the first chapter of Berakhot 12b that one who is ashamed of it is forgiven, for he has already undergone the punishment of Gehinnom. For one who merits it, Heaven continually brings his transgressions to mind, and he feels bitterness over them until he undergoes in this world the measure of Gehinnom due him for them. This is the reckoning for transgressions exacted from the righteous in this world. Actual worldly afflictions follow other judgments, as our Sages teach in Moed Katan 28a: life, children, and sustenance depend on mazal rather than merit.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s earlier passage supplies the “elsewhere” reference. Its final qualification is included: remorse and the circumstances of worldly life are not treated as one identical reckoning.

connections.hePhrase: [קכט] מִיָּד שֶׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב, הֲרֵי הוּא "בָּא לִטָּהֵר", וְהַמִּשְׁפָּט לְסַיֵּיעַ אוֹתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (לח:);
connections.quote: ‘Reish Lakish said: What is the meaning of ‘If it concerns scoffers, He scoffs, but to the humble He gives favor’? When someone comes to become impure, an opening is made for him; when someone comes to become pure, he is helped. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: It is like a man selling naphtha and balsam. When a customer comes to measure out naphtha, the seller tells him: ‘Measure it for yourself.’ When a customer comes to measure out balsam, he tells him: ‘Wait for me until I measure it with you, so that both you and I will be perfumed.’’

connections.hePhrase: [קכט] מִיָּד שֶׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב, הֲרֵי הוּא "בָּא לִטָּהֵר", וְהַמִּשְׁפָּט לְסַיֵּיעַ אוֹתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (לח:);
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 5:6
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 5:6
connections.quote: “Different is Israel: Hashem bestows upon them little by little as they are able to bear, so that they recognize and know Who is the One giving them wealth and strength, and at every hour and moment they return anew before the Master, Hashem God of Israel, that He channel unto them a renewed influx, and "before they call, Hashem will answer" (Isaiah 65:24); and this influx endures for all eternity, and unto them too it is accounted as an active share and acquisition, as written of them: "For Hashem's portion is His people", because Hashem bestows upon them with an exceedingly generous eye, so that it be credited to them that through the labor of their hands—namely through their prayer—they acquired this.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov describes help given gradually, in a measure the recipient can bear, so that the person repeatedly recognizes its Giver and turns to Him anew. This clarifies the ascending movement described here: assistance does not end human participation, but creates the capacity for a further movement toward Hashem. The resulting attainment can still be credited to the person’s prayer and effort.
connections.headline: Receiving fresh help at each step

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ חוֹזֵר חָלִילָה, עַד שֶׁמִּפֶּתַח כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט נַעֲשָׂה כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב).
connections.quote: see note 296.
connections.context: The Midrash promises a greatly enlarged opening in response to a small beginning of repentance. Rav Tzadok describes repeated openings becoming a great entrance; the source’s own wording is “wagons and carriages.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמֵאַיִן בָּא שֶׁפְּעָמִים אָדָם רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב וְאֵין נִגְמָר, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִין חֲרָטוֹת רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן?
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים י״א:ו׳
connections.quote: “There is a person in whom evil predominates more strongly, and all three garments of evil are clothed in him, causing him to commit more serious transgressions and at more frequent intervals. Yet in between he regrets them, and thoughts of repentance arise from the good within his soul, which grows somewhat stronger in the interval. But it does not gain enough strength to overcome the evil so that he abandons his sins entirely and becomes one who “confesses and forsakes.” Concerning this our Sages said, “The wicked are full of regrets.” These are most of the wicked, who still have an element of good within their souls.”
connections.context: Tanya explains how real regret can recur without yet becoming lasting abandonment of the sin. This is distinct from the existing quotation from Iggeret HaTeshuvah 11 about trust and joy after seeking forgiveness.

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם בְּזֹהַר חָדָשׁ סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית, כִּי בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב, אָז הוּא הַקִּטְרוּג הַגָּדוֹל מִיֵּצֶר;
connections.quote: ““It happened one day that the sons of God came,” and so forth. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: He is Satan, he is the evil inclination, he is the angel of death. Rabbi Yehudah said: That day was Rosh Hashanah, a day on which every person should return to the good. Thus you see: the evil inclination’s way is to bring an accusation precisely when a person wishes to return to the good.”
connections.context: This is the passage expressly cited from Midrash HaNeelam in Zohar Chadash, Bereishit. It supplies the timing of the accusation; Rav Tzadok explains what the accusation contests.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ זְמַן הַקִּטְרוּג בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה [שֶׁנִּקְרָא "בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ" וְעֵת רָצוֹן], עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Seek Hashem while He may be found; call upon Him while He is near.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ זְמַן הַקִּטְרוּג בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה [שֶׁנִּקְרָא "בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ" וְעֵת רָצוֹן], עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rav Shmuel bar Inya said in Rav’s name: From where do we know that a decree concerning a community is not sealed? Is it not sealed? But it is written, “Your iniquity is marked before Me.” Rather, even though it is sealed, it is torn up, as it is said, “Like Hashem our God whenever we call to Him.” But is it not written, “Seek Hashem when He is to be found”? That concerns an individual; this concerns a community. When does it apply to an individual? Rabbah bar Avuha said: These are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.”
connections.context: The Gemara identifies the special period meant by “when He is to be found.” Its distinction between an individual and a community is retained, so the special time does not imply that communal prayer is confined to those days.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה נֶגְדּוֹ הוּא הַשִּׂמְחָה וְהַבְּטִיחוּת בַּלֵּב, שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרוֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו יְקַבְּלוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵימָה לְפָנָיו;
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שלישי; אגרת התשובה י״א:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: “As for having humility in his heart—the lower repentance mentioned above—and joy in the Lord, both together: this has already been discussed in Likkutei Amarim at the end of chapter 34, as the holy Zohar says, “Joy is lodged in my heart on this side.” Added to this are faith and trust, so that his heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord: He desires kindness, is gracious and compassionate, and abundantly forgives immediately when one asks Him for pardon and forgiveness—“In Your abundant compassion, erase my transgressions”; “Wash me, purify me”; “Erase all my sins”—without any doubt or shadow of doubt whatsoever. Thus, in every Amidah, immediately after asking “Forgive us,” we bless: “Blessed are You, Lord, gracious One who abundantly forgives.” Yet the rule is to be lenient in a case of doubt concerning blessings, because of the concern for a blessing in vain. Rather, there is no doubt here at all, since we have asked, “Forgive us,” “Pardon us.” Had we not returned to sin, we would have been redeemed immediately, as we bless, “Blessed are You, Lord, Redeemer of Israel.””

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה מַמָּשׁ דּוּגְמַת תַּשְׁרַ"ת שֶׁעוֹשִׂין בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: “Therefore two sounds were required, before it and after it, in a blast of joy: to awaken Hashem's joy toward His children through His attributes of kindness and compassion, to hear the voice of their Torah of kindness and the voice of prayer, which is mercy. Through these they are called His children. It is part of the nature of creation that a father has compassion on his son and accepts his return.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla explains why the broken cry is surrounded by notes of joy: they awaken the Father's kindness and compassion toward His children. The comparison develops the siman's instruction to hold both confidence and inward bitterness together. Joy here concerns the relation that makes return possible, while the broken sound still gives expression to the work of repentance.
connections.headline: Why joy surrounds the broken sound

connections.hePhrase: דְּהַתְּקִיעוֹת הֵם לְשִׂמְחָה, וּשְׁבָרִים-תְּרוּעָה הַיְינוּ גְּנוֹחֵי גָּנַח וִילּוֹלֵי יִילֵיל כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה,
connections.quote: “The measure of a teruah is like three short cries. But was it not taught: The measure of a teruah is like three shevarim? Abaye said: On this they certainly disagree. For it is written, “It shall be a day of teruah for you,” and we translate it, “It shall be a day of crying for you.” Concerning Sisera’s mother it is written, “Through the window she looked out, and Sisera’s mother cried.” One master holds that this means groaning; the other holds that it means wailing.”
connections.context: This supplies the original distinction between groaning and wailing behind the shevarim–teruah imagery. Rav Tzadok places those broken sounds between the joyful, unbroken blasts.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְעַרְבֵּב הַשָּׂטָן.
connections.heRef: רש"י על ראש השנה ט״ז ב:א׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““To confound”: So that he will not accuse; when he hears Israel cherishing the mitzvot, his words are stopped up.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the Gemara’s statement about repeating the shofar blasts to confound Satan. It identifies the positive element that silences the accusation: Israel’s affection for the mitzvah.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר: "מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד בְּבוֹא אֵלָיו נָתָן וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, א–ב),
connections.quote: “For the leader. A psalm of David.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok attends to the designation “psalm” even in a composition prompted by rebuke and repentance. The next note gives the historical setting stated in the heading.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר: "מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד בְּבוֹא אֵלָיו נָתָן וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, א–ב),
connections.quote: “When Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had come to Bathsheba.”
connections.context: This is the second verse of the heading. It ties the psalm to Nathan’s rebuke after the Bathsheba episode, the setting for the discussion of confidence and repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּדִמְעָתִי עַרְשִׂי וְגוֹמֵר", וְתֵיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ: "כִּי שָׁמַע ה' קוֹל בִּכְיִי וְגוֹמֵר", וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת.
connections.quote: “I am weary with my sighing; every night I make my bed swim; with my tears I dissolve my couch.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּדִמְעָתִי עַרְשִׂי וְגוֹמֵר", וְתֵיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ: "כִּי שָׁמַע ה' קוֹל בִּכְיִי וְגוֹמֵר", וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת.
connections.quote: “Depart from me, all workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping.”
connections.context: The first verse supplies David’s tears; the later verse states that they were heard. Both parts are needed for Rav Tzadok’s transition from weeping to its effect.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (כט.): טָבָא לָא הָוֵי בִּישָׁא, אִם לֹא בְּרַע מֵעִיקָּרוֹ;
connections.quote: “Abaye said: We have a tradition that a good person does not become bad.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (כט.): טָבָא לָא הָוֵי בִּישָׁא, אִם לֹא בְּרַע מֵעִיקָּרוֹ;
connections.quote: “That refers to one who was wicked originally; but one who was righteous originally does not.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (כט.): טָבָא לָא הָוֵי בִּישָׁא, אִם לֹא בְּרַע מֵעִיקָּרוֹ;
connections.quote: “Rava would say to you: Even one who was righteous originally may turn back.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok uses Abaye’s formulation concerning someone good from his root. The Talmud records Rava’s disagreement, so the formulation should be identified as Abaye’s position rather than presented as the only position in the discussion.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּחֲגִיגָה (טו:): טִינָא הָיְתָה בְּלִבָּם;
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Ami said: Doeg and Ahitophel asked three hundred questions about a tower suspended in the air. Yet we learned: Three kings and four ordinary individuals have no share in the World to Come. What, then, will become of us? He said to him: ‘Sharp one! There was mire in their hearts.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת מח.): בּוּצִינָא מִקַּטְפֵיהּ יְדִיעַ.
connections.quote: see note 13.

connections.hePhrase: [דְּזֶהוּ בְּסוֹד הַיְדִיעָה וְהַבְּחִירָה שֶׁנִּתְקַשּׁוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים],
connections.quote: see note 282.
connections.context: Rambam states the problem Rav Tzadok alludes to and retains both conclusions: divine knowledge exceeds human comprehension, and human choice and accountability remain certain. Rav Tzadok’s further account of time is his own exposition.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי לִבָּא לְפוּמָא לָא גַּלְיָא.
connections.quote: “Kohelet sought to understand when the end would come, as it is said, “Do not awaken or arouse love until it desires.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: I have already written it in the Book of the Upright: “For the day of vengeance is in My heart.” Rabbi Shaul of Naveh taught in Rabbi Shimon’s name: If someone asks you when the end of the redemption will come, tell him that it is written, “For the day of vengeance is in My heart.” Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name: I gave you three signs and marked them for you concerning Moshe’s burial—“in the valley,” “in the land of Moav,” “opposite Beit Peor”—and nevertheless “no one knows his grave.” The heart has not revealed it to the mouth; to whom, then, could the mouth reveal it?”
connections.context: The Midrash uses the expression about a hidden divine matter, the end of redemption, and illustrates concealment with Moshe’s burial. Rav Tzadok applies this language to the hidden root of a person.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמַר אִידָךְ דִּמְרַפֶּה יְדֵי בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה, וְלָכֵן לֹא גִּלּוּ זֶה רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּפֵירוּשׁ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: Whoever says that Menashe has no share in the World to Come weakens the hands of penitents. For a tanna taught before Rabbi Yochanan: Menashe repented for thirty-three years, as it is written, “Menashe was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem,” and he made an asherah “as Achav king of Israel had done.” How long did Achav reign? Twenty-two years. How long did Menashe reign? Fifty-five. Subtract twenty-two, and thirty-three remain. Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s name: What is meant by “He heard him and tunneled toward him”? It should have said “He was entreated by him.” This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, made something like a tunnel in heaven to receive him in repentance, because of the attribute of justice.”
