connections.context: The complete selected unit gives both Rabbi Yochanan’s objection to discouraging penitents and the teaching about a hidden opening for Menashe. It supports the distinction Rav Tzadok draws between judgment as perceived by creatures and God’s acceptance.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים יָכוֹל לְהִתְקָרֵב, וַאֲפִילּוּ עוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּכֹהֵן גָּדוֹל (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.),
connections.quote: ‘Is that really so? But it was taught: Rabbi Meir used to say: From where do we know that even a gentile who engages in Torah is like a High Priest? Scripture says: ‘Which a person shall do and live by them.’ It does not say ‘priests,’ ‘Levites,’ or ‘Israelites,’ but ‘a person.’ You have thus learned that even a gentile who engages in Torah is like a High Priest.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים יָכוֹל לְהִתְקָרֵב, וַאֲפִילּוּ עוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּכֹהֵן גָּדוֹל (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.),
connections.quote: “Although it is true that every soul of Israel has a bond and connection in the divine root above the reach of its service, without repentance and service it is impossible to reach that higher root: the person's capacity would be annulled before arriving there. My holy grandfather compared this to a very wealthy person traveling in the wilderness far from home. Though he has great wealth and property at home, if he lacks food on the road he certainly will not reach his home, for he will die of hunger first. Through repentance and service, however, one can reach the illumination of the higher union that no sin or iniquity touches. When a person gives his entire understanding over to Hashem's will on this day, even what occurred with him earlier without awareness is clarified retrospectively as having been His will as well.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim places the higher connection and the required human path in the same complete thought. The wealthy traveler may own abundant resources at home, yet without provisions he will not reach them. So the deeper root and its retrospective clarification do not exempt a person from repentance and service. This develops the siman's insistence on chosen return alongside divine knowledge beyond time.
connections.headline: The higher root is reached through return and work

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל הַתּוֹרָה מָלֵא מִזֶּה, וְנֶאֱמַר: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא וְגוֹמֵר", וּבְרִיאָה הוּא יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן,
connections.quote: see note 273.
connections.context: Ramban is explaining the word beriah, “creation,” in the account of Korach. Rav Tzadok applies that meaning to David’s request that God create a pure heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל הַתּוֹרָה מָלֵא מִזֶּה, וְנֶאֱמַר: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא וְגוֹמֵר", וּבְרִיאָה הוּא יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן,
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 4:9
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 4:9
connections.quote: “This is the convert's claim in Shabbat's chapter Bameh Madlikin (31a), and Shammai's strictness in distancing him. Shammai is the level of awe, from which come strength and strictness, the level of Yitzchak, with whom Israel begins as explained above; therefore he distanced the converts there. From the side of awe, its complete attainment is the opposite of that request, as explained above. Hillel's humility brought them near, like Moshe, who was exceedingly humble (Numbers 12:3) and therefore brought near the mixed multitude and argued concerning Michah, as explained above. Avraham too was humble, as Berakhot 6b teaches that the humble person is Avraham's disciple; therefore he is the father of converts, as taught in Bikkurim [Jerusalem Talmud 1:4:5]. Humility is measuring one's deficiency against Hashem's greatness, leaving no place for superiority over the convert who comes with his staff and bag. The One who said [that oil should burn] can say that vinegar should burn as well (Taanit 25a), and can place light in vinegar too, like ‘Create a pure heart for me, God’ (Psalms 51:12). Creation is something from nothing; this is not the place to explain further.”
connections.explanation: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik applies the same new-heart principle to Hillel's receiving converts. Humility measures one's own deficiency against Hashem's greatness and leaves no basis for contempt toward the person arriving from outside. This gives a practical consequence to the siman's warning that the root is hidden from every creature: the human task remains welcome, prayer, repentance and good deeds, rather than a verdict about an allegedly fixed inner nature. Citation clarification: the teaching that Avraham is father of converts is Rabbi Yehudah’s teaching in Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 1:4:5, adopted there in practice. Mishnah Bikkurim 1:4 gives the initial contrary position. The square brackets distinguish the corrected location from the wording of the supplied Hebrew.
connections.headline: A new heart and humility toward the convert

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ (יַלְקוּט שִׁמְעוֹנִי יְחֶזְקֵאל שנח): שָׁאֲלוּ לַחָכְמָה וְכוּלֵי, לַתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, לַנְּבוּאָה וְכוּלֵי, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָמַר: יַעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה;
connections.quote: “They asked Wisdom: What is the sinner’s punishment? It answered: “Evil pursues sinners.” They asked Prophecy: What is the sinner’s punishment? It answered: “The soul that sins shall die.” They asked Torah: What is the sinner’s punishment? It answered: Let him bring a guilt offering and be atoned for. They asked the Holy One, blessed be He: What is the sinner’s punishment? He answered: Let him repent and be atoned for. This is “Good and upright is the Lord; therefore He guides sinners in the way.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok contrasts the judgments expressed through wisdom, prophecy, and Torah with the possibility of repentance disclosed by God. This is Yalkut Shimoni on Ezekiel 18, remez 358.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה הָיָה טַעֲנַת הָעָם בִּיחֶזְקֵאל בְּפָרָשַׁת "וּבְשׁוּב צַדִּיק וְגוֹמֵר וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע וְגוֹמֵר": "וַאֲמַרְתֶּם לֹא יִתָּכֵן דֶּרֶךְ ה'" (יְחֶזְקֵאל יח, כה);
connections.quote: ‘Yet you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ Listen, please, house of Israel: Is My way not just? Is it not your ways that are unjust?’

connections.hePhrase: [וַאֲפִילּוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁמָּנוּ שָׁם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם תִּיקּוּן עַל יְדֵי דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קד:)].
connections.quote: see note 638.
connections.context: “All of them” refers to the figures discussed in the surrounding passage as excluded from the World to Come. The interpreters find a different prospect through allusions in the psalm. Rav Tzadok explicitly invokes this interpretive approach when speaking of their eventual repair.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה נִתְגַּלָּה לָרִאשׁוֹנָה בְּבֵיאוּר גָּמוּר עַל יְדֵי בִּלְעָם, שֶׁכָּל פָּרָשָׁתוֹ הוּא עַל עִנְיַן מַעֲלָה זוֹ שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל:
connections.quote: “The double expression of ascent may also be explained as a promise to his descendants: He will redeem them after the exile and bring them up to the Land of Israel. After they are settled in the Land of Israel, where the principal fulfillment of Torah and mitzvot takes place, He promises them another ascent—the World to Come reserved for his descendants. This alludes to what our Sages said: All Israel have a share in the World to Come. This is also the statement of Bilaam, Israel’s accuser, who acknowledged it against his will and saw it in prophecy, saying, “Let my soul die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his.” He alluded to Israel alone, among the nations of the world, being the inheritors of Gan Eden; with this he connects “It is a people that dwells alone.” This is why He used the word Anokhi: through the merit of the Torah that his descendants would receive, the Divine Presence would be with them in the Egyptian exile, and they would merit these two ascents, which benefit body and soul in the two worlds.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya explicitly connects Israel’s future share with Bilaam’s unwilling prophetic acknowledgment. He reads the double ascent promised to Yaakov as both national redemption and the ascent of the soul; this supplies an earlier source for the connection developed here.

connections.hePhrase: וְעִם כָּל מַעֲלָתוֹ שֶׁהָיָה נְבִיא אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְדוּגְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
connections.quote: ““No prophet arose again in Israel like Moshe”: In Israel none arose, but among the nations of the world one arose. Who was this? Bilaam son of Beor. Yet there is a difference between Moshe’s prophecy and Bilaam’s prophecy. Moshe did not know who was speaking with him, whereas Bilaam knew who was speaking with him, as it is said, “The utterance of one who hears the sayings of God.” Moshe did not know when He would speak with him until He spoke with him, whereas Bilaam knew when He would speak with him, as it is said, “Who knows the knowledge of the Most High.” He spoke with Moshe only while Moshe stood, as it is said, “But you, stand here with Me”; He spoke with Bilaam when Bilaam was fallen, as it is said, “Who beholds a vision of the Almighty, fallen and with eyes uncovered.” To what may this be compared? To the king’s cook, who knows how much the king spends on his table.”
connections.context: The cited comparison comes from Sifrei on the end of the Torah. The full selected paragraph preserves its differences and its concluding analogy; the opening comparison should not be detached from that qualification.

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ יוֹסִיף מַעֲלוֹת זֶה עַל גַּבֵּי זֶה, וְכֵן אָמַר: "אֶת שִׁבְעַת הַמִּזְבְּחֹת עָרַכְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר" בַּעֲבוֹדָה –
connections.quote: “And God met Balaam, and he said to Him: I have prepared the seven altars, and I have offered up a bull and a ram on each altar.”

connections.hePhrase: אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם וְאַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד.
connections.quote: “And he saw Amalek, and took up his parable and said: Amalek was the first of the nations, but his end shall come to destruction.”

connections.hePhrase: וְדַיְיקָא עַל יְדֵי הַהֵיפֶךְ מִתְגַּלֶּה מַעֲלָה זוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן: אֵין שְׁבָחָהּ שֶׁל מַטְרוֹנִיתָא וְכוּלֵי (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה פָּרָשַׁת עֵקֶב)].
connections.quote: ““You shall be blessed above all the peoples.” Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said: A noblewoman’s praise is not when she is praised by her female relatives, but when she is praised by her rivals.”
connections.context: This is the exact Midrash in Ekev behind the image of the matron praised by her rivals. Rav Tzadok applies that image to the force of a blessing spoken by Israel’s adversary.

connections.hePhrase: וּקְרָאוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א): "מַחֲלִיק לָשׁוֹן", שֶׁהֶחֱלִיק וְכוּלֵי וְנָפְלוּ עַל יָדוֹ;
connections.quote: ““One who rebukes”—this is Moses. … “Than one who smooths his tongue”—this is Balaam, who smoothed his prophecies; their hearts grew proud, and they fell at Shittim.”
connections.context: The Midrash contrasts Moses’ beneficial rebuke with Balaam’s flattering speech. Rav Tzadok needs the connection between flattering words, pride, and Israel’s subsequent fall at Shittim.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה:): מִבִּרְכָתוֹ אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ מַה הָיָה בְּלִבּוֹ, וְנֶאֱמַר: "וַיַּהֲפֹךְ ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ לְּךָ אֶת הַקְּלָלָה לִבְרָכָה";
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: From the blessing of that wicked man you learn what was in his heart. He sought to say that they should have no synagogues or houses of study—“How good are your tents, Jacob”; that the Divine Presence should not rest upon them—“your dwelling places, Israel.””
connections.context: The Gemara reads Balaam’s spoken blessings as reversals of his intended curses. Rav Tzadok uses this contrast between outward blessing and inward intent; the next verse cited in his text supplies the divine reversal.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה:): מִבִּרְכָתוֹ אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ מַה הָיָה בְּלִבּוֹ, וְנֶאֱמַר: "וַיַּהֲפֹךְ ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ לְּךָ אֶת הַקְּלָלָה לִבְרָכָה";
connections.quote: ‘Hashem your God was unwilling to listen to Balaam. Hashem your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because Hashem your God loves you.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, סג עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ לְהַכְנִיס עַיִן הָרָע.
connections.quote: ‘There is a person through whom curses are destined to be fulfilled: wherever he directs his gaze, he brings curses, blight, and terror. Such was Balaam, who was called ‘evil-eyed’: he was suited to every evil and was not suited to good. Even when he blessed, his blessing was no blessing and did not endure. When he cursed, however, his curse against anyone was fulfilled, even in a single moment. Therefore it is written: ‘Open of eye’ (Numbers 24:3). Wherever his eye held sway became cursed. Come and see what is written: ‘He turned his face toward the wilderness’ (Numbers 24:1), so that he might arouse from that side the power ruling there, and it would bring an accusation against Israel. What is written of the priests? ‘One with a good eye shall be blessed’ (Proverbs 22:9), for he is suited to this, and blessing rests in his gaze. Therefore we learned: A person should turn aside even from a hundred roads rather than encounter someone who has an evil eye.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא לֹא הוֹדִיעָם זֶה, רַק הֶחֱלִיק לָשׁוֹן כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּבְטְחוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה וְיֶחֶטְאוּ וְיִשְׁתַּנֶּה הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the exposition, “Do not trust in an intimate companion”: If the evil inclination tells you, “Sin, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive you,” do not believe it. “An intimate companion” means the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, “You are the intimate companion of my youth.” Why is the blessed God called an aluf here? The evil inclination tempts a person by saying that God will afterward clarify that the person’s deed was bound at its root to God and that deliberate sins will become merits. Even when He was an aluf—a king without a crown—He was nevertheless “the intimate companion of my youth.” This is how Bilaam magnified Israel on this basis. Thus the Midrash expounds: “One who smooths his tongue”—this is Bilaam, who flattered them through his prophecies, so that their hearts became proud and they fell at Shittim. He made it seem easy to them by saying that God would clarify all Israel’s deeds for the good, and through this they fell at Shittim. Concerning this it says, “Do not believe in a friend”—the evil inclination—and “Do not trust in an intimate companion,” that God will clarify Israel’s deed. That applies only after the deed, when one repents out of love, so that it becomes a merit. But one who relies on this, Heaven forbid—one who says, “I will sin and repent”—is not given assistance to repent.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel exposition makes the qualification explicit: the eventual clarification of a deed through repentance out of love is no permission to sin in advance. This directly explains the danger of Bilaam’s flattering speech.

connections.hePhrase: [וְגַם כִּי כָּל הַשָּׂגוֹת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מֵעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא דּוּגְמַת מַשִּׂיג בַּחֲלוֹם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּשׁוּב ה' וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “A Song of Ascents. When Hashem brought back the captivity of Zion, we were like dreamers.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נה.): חֶלְמָא טָבָא חֶדְוָותֵיהּ מִסְתַּיֵּיהּ, וְכָל יָמָיו שֶׁל דָּוִד לֹא רָאָה חֲלוֹם טוֹב,
connections.quote: “Rav Chisda said: For a bad dream, its sadness is sufficient; for a good dream, its joy is sufficient. Rav Yosef said: A good dream—even for me, its gladness dissipates it.”
connections.context: The immediate sorrow or joy can itself supply the dream’s effect. Rav Tzadok applies this principle to the distinction between felt satisfaction in this world and the enduring value of the act itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נה.): חֶלְמָא טָבָא חֶדְוָותֵיהּ מִסְתַּיֵּיהּ, וְכָל יָמָיו שֶׁל דָּוִד לֹא רָאָה חֲלוֹם טוֹב,
connections.quote: ‘It was likewise taught: Throughout David’s life he never saw a good dream, and throughout Achitophel’s life he never saw a bad dream. But is it not written, ‘No harm will happen to you’? Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba: This means that neither bad dreams nor bad thoughts will frighten you. ‘And no affliction will come near your tent’—you will not find your wife in a state of doubtful niddah when you return from a journey. Rather, [the good person] does not see [a bad dream] himself; others see it about him.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ מַזְכִּירִים בַּהֲטָבַת חֲלוֹם הֲפוֹךְ קִלְלַת בִּלְעָם] –
connections.quote: “Master of the universe, I am Yours and my dreams are Yours … And just as You turned the curse of Balaam the wicked into a blessing, so turn all my dreams for me for good.”
connections.context: This is the prayer said during the Priestly Blessing by one who saw a dream and does not know what it means.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בִּקְשׁוּ לְדוּנוֹ לְאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֲבָל לֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָם,
connections.quote: “Who enumerated them? Rav Ashi said: The Men of the Great Assembly enumerated them. Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name: They sought to enumerate one more. His father’s likeness came and prostrated itself before them, but they paid no heed. Fire came from heaven and licked their benches, but they paid no heed. A heavenly voice came forth and said to them: “Have you seen a man skilled in his work? He shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before obscure men.” One who put My house before his own house—and moreover built My house in seven years and his own in thirteen—“shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before obscure men.” They paid no heed. A heavenly voice came forth and said: “Should He repay according to your judgment, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I,” and so forth.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies the additional person as Shlomo and the father as David. The passage supplies the attempted inclusion and its rejection; Rav Tzadok’s further explanation that Bilaam stands in Shlomo’s place is his interpretation, not an explicit statement of this Gemara.

connections.hePhrase: [קלב] בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָעִיקָּר הוּא טָהֳרַת הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:): רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי.
connections.quote: “Rav Yehudah would remove his shoes, and rain would come; we cry out, and no one pays heed to us. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the heart, as it is written, “Hashem sees into the heart.””
connections.context: In the preceding discussion Rava contrasts the extent of Torah learning in his generation with Rav Yehudah’s generation. This conclusion supplies the statement about the heart that opens the section; removing shoes belongs to the context of a fast and prayer for rain.

connections.hePhrase: [קלב] בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָעִיקָּר הוּא טָהֳרַת הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:): רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:8
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:8
connections.quote: “And the primary focus is certainly Torah, as rebuked in Shabbat (10a): "They abandon eternal life to engage in transient life!"; yet the statement there is also true: there is a time for Torah, and there is a time for prayer; for in truth: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem" Psalms 111:10, and "if the fear of Hashem is his treasure, yes" (Shabbat 31b), the labor of transient prayer serving as the essential preparation to merit eternal life, as in Avot (4:16): "Prepare yourself in the vestibule," and "he who did not toil on Friday, what shall he eat on the Sabbath?"”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim preserves both sides of the relationship: Torah is eternal life, yet the effort of prayer and yirah remains its necessary preparation. Its reference to preparing in the antechamber explains the siman’s image of the missing outer key. Intellectual attainment alone does not perform the heart’s work of preparing to enter.
connections.headline: The preparation that makes lasting wisdom accessible

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ (מְנָחוֹת כט:): "כִּי בְּיָהּ ה' צוּר עוֹלָמִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה כו, ד) – בְּיוֹ"ד נִבְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא וּבְהֵ"א עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: ‘Trust in Hashem forever, for Yah, Hashem, is the Rock of all ages.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ (מְנָחוֹת כט:): "כִּי בְּיָהּ ה' צוּר עוֹלָמִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה כו, ד) – בְּיוֹ"ד נִבְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא וּבְהֵ"א עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ilai expounded: These are the two worlds that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, one with heh and one with yod. I do not yet know whether the World to Come was with yod and this world with heh, or this world with yod and the World to Come with heh.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ (מְנָחוֹת כט:): "כִּי בְּיָהּ ה' צוּר עוֹלָמִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה כו, ד) – בְּיוֹ"ד נִבְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא וּבְהֵ"א עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: “When it says, “These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created,” do not read behibare’am, but beheh bera’am—with heh He created them.”
connections.context: The derivation assigns heh to this world and therefore yod to the World to Come. The previous quotation stopped before the interpretation of the letters that Rav Tzadok actually cites.

connections.hePhrase: [וְאָמְרוּ: הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כִּפְרוֹזְדּוֹר, וּמִי שֶׁלֹּא הִתְקִין עַצְמוֹ בּוֹ אֵין יָכוֹל לִכְנוֹס לִטְרַקְלִין,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yaakov says: This world is like an entrance hall before the World to Come. Prepare yourself in the entrance hall so that you may enter the reception chamber.’

connections.hePhrase: הוּא כְּאוֹתָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת לא:): מָשָׁל לְמִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדוֹ מַפְתְּחוֹת הַפְּנִימִיּוֹת וְהַחִיצוֹנוֹת לֹא מָסְרוּ לוֹ, בְּהֵי עָיֵיל?
connections.quote: “Like a treasurer to whom the inner keys were handed, but the outer keys were not handed—with what will he enter?”
connections.context: Rabba bar Rav Huna compares someone who has Torah but lacks fear of Heaven to this treasurer. His statement begins at the end of 31a and continues on 31b. Rav Tzadok uses the parable to distinguish possessing the inner content from having the means to enter it.

connections.hePhrase: עַיֵּין יוֹמָא (עב:) שֶׁלָּמְדוּ זֶה מִפָּסוּק "וְלֵב אָיִן"].
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonatan’s name: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘Why is there a price in the fool’s hand to acquire wisdom, when he has no heart’? Woe to Torah scholars (spoken of euphemistically as ‘their enemies’) who engage in Torah but have no fear of Heaven.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ שַׁבָּת, שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:),
connections.quote: “Three things are a foretaste of the World to Come: Shabbat, the sun, and bodily use.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ שַׁבָּת, שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:),
connections.quote: “What kind of use? If you say marital intercourse, that weakens the body! Rather, the use of the bodily openings.”
connections.context: Shabbat’s inclusion is the point Rav Tzadok cites. The second quotation prevents the ambiguous word tashmish in the list from being mistaken for marital intercourse; the Gemara itself rejects that interpretation here.

connections.hePhrase: רַק צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה עִלָּאָה מֵעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי הַמִּתְעוֹרֵר מִן הַחָכְמָה, שֶׁהוּא הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ לַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ,
connections.quote: “Although this teaching says without qualification that there is no repentance for it, we must explain this matter, for we hold that there is nothing for which repentance is unavailable: the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted even Menashe. Why, then, should this transgression differ from the others? It seems to me that the meaning is that the matter does not depend on lower repentance, as with other people who cause a blemish, whose initial return is through lower repentance—turning away from evil—and who are immediately accepted. This also follows from the adjacent wording: “There is no sinner who does not behold the face of the Divine Presence except this one.” The reason is that this sin affects both the Tzaddik and the Divine Presence, as explained; because the Divine Presence is his accuser, he is not accepted through that repentance. In this way we understand the verse, “The face of Hashem is against evildoers, to cut off their remembrance from the earth. They cried out, and Hashem heard.” The evildoers are those who emit seed in vain, who are cut off from the land of life because the blemish affects it. But they cried out and returned in repentance, and Hashem heard and saved them from all their troubles. The Zohar explains: Rabbi Yehudah said, Great is crying out, for it tears up a person’s decree for all his days. Rabbi Yitzchak says, Great is crying out, for it has power over the supernal attribute of judgment. Rabbi Yosei says, Great is crying out, for it has power in this world and the World to Come; through crying out one inherits this world and the World to Come, as it is written, “They cried out to Hashem in their trouble; He delivered them from their distress.” Thus crying out is above lower repentance according to all these explanations, and therefore “Hashem heard.” The meaning is that his repentance is difficult, until he reaches higher repentance.”
connections.context: Reshit Chokhmah expressly rejects an absolute denial of repentance and explains the severe Zoharic statement through the distinction between lower and higher repentance. “Tzaddik” here names the kabbalistic attribute of Yesod. This is the qualification behind Rav Tzadok’s discussion of reaching the root.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם אֵין רַע כְּלָל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה",
connections.quote: “When one awakens, one says: “My God, the soul You placed within me is pure. You formed it within me; You breathed it into me; You preserve it within me; You will take it from me and restore it within me in the future. As long as the soul is within me, I give thanks before You, Hashem my God and the God of my ancestors, Master of all worlds, Lord of all souls. Blessed are You, Hashem, who restores souls to dead bodies.””
connections.context: This is the morning blessing alluded to by “the soul You placed within me is pure.” Its full wording locates the soul’s purity in God’s creation, preservation, and eventual restoration of it.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי גַּם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ רַע שָׁרְשׁוֹ "טוֹב מְאֹד" כַּנּוֹדָע
connections.quote: “It is to return in repentance, for nothing is as important as repentance, since it repairs every blemish. Just as Binah sweetens all judgments and removes their bitterness, so a person should repent and repair every blemish. One who thinks of repentance throughout his days causes Binah to illuminate all his days; all his days are thus in repentance, that is, he includes himself in Binah, which is repentance, and his lifetime is crowned with the mystery of higher repentance. See that repentance contains the root of all things that exist, in the mystery of the Jubilee. The root of the external forces—the river of fire, included in holiness through the powers of judgment—is rooted there. From there it spreads and is called the spreading of fierce anger. Through the mystery of “Hashem smelled the pleasing aroma,” that expansion returns to its source, judgments are sweetened, anger is quieted, and Hashem relents concerning the calamity. A person likewise effects this mystery through repentance. Repentance also benefits evil: Do not say that repentance benefits only the holy part of a person: the evil part within him is also sweetened, in the likeness of this attribute. Know this, for Kayin was evil and came from the serpent, yet it was said to him, “If you do well, will you not be lifted up?” Do not think that because you come from the side of evil there is no repair for you; that is false. If you do well and root yourself in repentance, you can ascend there through the good rooted there, for every supernal bitterness has a sweet root, and one can enter through that root and make oneself good.”
connections.context: Tomer Devorah explains repentance through Binah and the return of harsh forces to their sweet root. Its explicit statement that the evil part itself can be repaired clarifies the phrase “the root of the root,” without declaring a person beyond repentance.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קח:) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל שֶׁהִטְעִימָן מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, הַיְינוּ כְּדֵי לְתַקְּנָם כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא הוֹעִיל]:
connections.quote: see note 898.
connections.context: This explains the seven-day delay before the Flood. Rav Tzadok reads the taste of the World to Come as an opportunity for repair that the generation did not use.

connections.hePhrase: [קלג] הַתּוֹרָה הִיא פּוֹעֶלֶת בְּלֵב הָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (אֵיכָה רַבָּתִי, פְּתִיחְתָּא ב): הַמָּאוֹר שֶׁבָּהּ מַחֲזִירוֹ לְמוּטָב, וְעַל שֵׁם כָּךְ נִקְרָא תּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: see note 74.
connections.context: This is the source of “the light within it brings one back to the good.” The immediate continuation about study not for its own sake is included because Rav Tzadok explains how preliminary engagement can lead to Torah that enters the heart.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל יֵשׁ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהֵם מִן הַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (קו:) עַל דּוֹאֵג,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yitzchak also said: What is the meaning of ‘To the wicked, God said: What business have you recounting My statutes’? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Doeg the wicked: ‘What business have you recounting My statutes? When you reach the passage about murderers and the passage about those who speak lashon hara, what do you expound in them?’ ‘You have taken My covenant upon your mouth.’ Rabbi Ami said: Doeg’s Torah was only from the lips outward.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר בְּיַד כְּסִיל לִקְנוֹת חָכְמָה וְלֶב אָיִן" (מִשְׁלֵי יז, טז),
connections.quote: ‘Why is there money in the hand of a fool to purchase wisdom, when he has no understanding?’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא "פִּטְטַיָּא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא", דְּגַם כֵּן טָבִין לְהָבִיא הָאָדָם לִידֵי תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ:) שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ וְכוּלֵי [כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת נ"ט], אִם אֵין הַחֵטְא גּוֹרֵם כִּבְדוֹאֵג.
connections.quote: see note 478.
connections.context: This is the Yerushalmi’s formulation of pittetaya de’oraita. Its paired saying distinguishes Torah conversation from falsehood in Torah; Rav Tzadok develops the value of the former even before the learner attains inward engagement. The terse generalization about falsehood is quoted as the passage’s wording, not as a general permission to deceive.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵיזֶה נִכְנָס לַלֵּב? כַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא צָמֵא וּמִשְׁתּוֹקֵק מְאֹד,
connections.quote: “My holy grandfather explained that a heart signifies inwardness. The principal thing in every matter is its inward content and the utterance of Hashem's mouth within it. Even the inward content of the 613 commandments is Torah, as the Zohar says (Shemini 35b), through Torah the Holy One created the world. The purpose of every matter is words of Torah. Thus the verse says (Proverbs 17:16), ‘Why is there a price in a fool's hand to acquire wisdom, when there is no heart?’ The fool does not want the inward content of the matter and is at rest with the garment itself. Israel, however, do not rest in any garment of this world; in every matter they want its inward content, and do not want things in which they do not see Heaven's honor. Even their intention in worldly benefit and pleasure is to be able to serve Hashem with that strength. Their whole aim is to fulfill His will. Hashem therefore says that all their worldly benefits are included in His will, since they serve Him with that strength.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same verse about a fool possessing the price of wisdom but lacking a heart. The defect is satisfaction with the garment while not wanting its inward content. This clarifies the positive side of Rav Tzadok's thirst: the learner feels that outward possession alone has not yet given him what he needs, and seeks the divine life within what he learns.
connections.headline: Wanting what lies within the garment

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וָאֹכְלָה וַתְּהִי בְפִי כִּדְבַשׁ לְמָתוֹק" (יְחֶזְקֵאל ג, ג), שֶׁהוּא כְּעִנְיַן: "וְתוֹרָתְךָ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָי" (תְּהִלִּים מ, ט), פֵּירוּשׁ נִבְלָעָה בְּכָל הָאֵבָרִים.
connections.quote: ‘He said to me: ‘Son of man, feed your belly and fill your innards with this scroll that I am giving you.’ I ate it, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וָאֹכְלָה וַתְּהִי בְפִי כִּדְבַשׁ לְמָתוֹק" (יְחֶזְקֵאל ג, ג), שֶׁהוּא כְּעִנְיַן: "וְתוֹרָתְךָ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָי" (תְּהִלִּים מ, ט), פֵּירוּשׁ נִבְלָעָה בְּכָל הָאֵבָרִים.
connections.quote: ‘I desire to do Your will, my God; Your Torah is within my innermost being.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וָאֹכְלָה וַתְּהִי בְפִי כִּדְבַשׁ לְמָתוֹק" (יְחֶזְקֵאל ג, ג), שֶׁהוּא כְּעִנְיַן: "וְתוֹרָתְךָ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָי" (תְּהִלִּים מ, ט), פֵּירוּשׁ נִבְלָעָה בְּכָל הָאֵבָרִים.
connections.quote: “This is what David meant when he said, “I desire to do Your will, my God, and Your Torah is within my innards.” Through the abundance of his attachment to the Master of masters, blessed be His name forever, even the heart was transformed to act as the soul acts: desire and longing arose within it to do His will. He was not among those who desire things distant from holiness and must restrain them by refusing consent; rather, of himself he desired His will, rejecting those things that the heart naturally desires and longs for. This is why he precisely said “I desire,” for the sensory desire had ceased. Elsewhere he said, “My heart is slain within me.” “Your Torah is within my innards” means that his longing for holy service was so great that, when studying Hashem’s Torah, he felt as though he were eating and filling his innards with natural nourishment.”
connections.context: Or HaChaim directly explains the same verse as the heart’s transformed desire and the felt nourishment of Torah. This supplies the original commentary behind Rav Tzadok’s image of Torah being absorbed inwardly.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ זוּטָא (פֶּרֶק יד): אֵין דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִבְלָעִים בְּלֵב הָאָדָם אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁהוּא עָיֵיף לָהֶם.
connections.quote: “The beginning and end of all matters are fear of Heaven and good deeds. A person should not read Scripture and study Mishnah while lacking fear of Heaven, as it is said, “The beginning of wisdom is fear of Hashem; good understanding belongs to all who practice them,” and, “The end of the matter, all having been heard: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man.” Who makes himself poor? One who indulges excessively in eating, drinking, and sleeping, as it is said, “The drunkard and glutton will become poor, and drowsiness will clothe one in rags,” and, “Do not love sleep, lest you become poor; open your eyes and be satisfied with bread.” Bread and wine mean words of Torah, as it is said, “Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed,” and, “The Lord God has given me a learned tongue, to know how to sustain the weary with a word; morning by morning He awakens my ear to hear like the learned.” You have thus learned that words of Torah are absorbed into a person’s heart only in one who is weary for them.”
connections.context: The source connects Torah’s inward absorption with fear of Heaven and sustained effort. Rav Tzadok explains “weary for them” as the learner’s thirsty recognition of what he lacks; the wording quoted here supplies the source and its surrounding argument.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת לא.): אִי יִרְאַת ה' הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ – אִין, וְאִי לָא – לָא;
connections.quote: “Rava said: When a person is brought in for judgment, he is asked: ‘Did you conduct business honestly? Did you set fixed times for Torah study? Did you engage in procreation? Did you look forward to salvation? Did you reason deeply in wisdom? Did you understand one thing from another?’ Even so, if fear of Hashem is his storehouse, then yes; if not, then no. This is like a man who told his agent: ‘Take a kor of wheat up to the upper story for me.’ He went and took it up. The man asked him: ‘Did you mix a kav of homton, preservative earth, into it for me?’ He answered: ‘No.’ The man said: ‘It would have been better had you not taken it up.’”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, הַיִּרְאָה הוּא הַרְגָּשַׁת הַחִסָּרוֹן, שֶׁמִּזֶּה יַגִּיעַ הַיִּרְאָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עֵקֶב עֲנָוָה יִרְאַת ה'" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ד), וְהִיא הָאוֹצָר לְקַבֵּל בָּהּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: ‘The reward of humility is fear of Hashem, wealth, honor, and life.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַצִּמָּאוֹן הוּא בַּלֵּב מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם (תּוֹלְדוֹת קלח עַמּוּד א) דְּאִלְמָלֵא יֵצֶר הָרָע חֶדְוָותָא דִּשְׁמַעְתָּא לָא לֶהֱוֵי.
connections.quote: “The evil inclination is as necessary to the world as rain is to the world. Were it not for the evil inclination, there would be no joy in Torah learning. But it will no longer be debased as before, so as to sin through it. This is what is written: “They shall not do evil or destroy on all My holy mountain.””
connections.context: Midrash HaNe’elam, ZoharI 138a, discusses the future transformation of the inclination. Its energetic desire remains useful for the joy of Torah, while its capacity to lead to sin is removed. This is exactly the distinction Rav Tzadok uses.

connections.hePhrase: [קלד] פְּעָמִים נִדְמֶה לָאָדָם שֶׁכְּבָר שָׁב וְנִמְחֲלוּ חֲטָאָיו, וְאַחַר זְמַן חוֹזֵר וּמִתְעוֹרֵר לְהִתְמַרְמֵר עַל חֲטָאָיו וּמַרְגִּישׁ שֶׁשְּׁנֵי הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת אֵינָם דִּמְיוֹן.
connections.quote: “The quality of all the Patriarchs was exertion in the service of the blessed God, as stated in Sanhedrin 96a: “When I pay the reward of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who ran before Me like horses,” and so on. This was especially true of Abraham our father, whose occupation was the holiness of positive commandments, rooted in love and alacrity. As they said in Chullin 16a, “The verse teaches us Abraham’s alacrity.” He never became still or rested from exerting himself in action in the service of the blessed God. This is what was said to him: “Go for yourself”—to set your own level right, as stated in the holy Zohar. He was to keep moving from level to level in his quality of love. This corresponds to reaching the passage “You shall love.””
connections.explanation: Lech Lecha describes Avraham’s service as movement that does not become stationary, with each level calling for further action rooted in love. This supplies the positive setting for the renewed teshuvah described here. The return of an awareness of sin can reflect a higher measure of understanding, rather than prove that the earlier forgiveness was unreal. The present siman explicitly affirms both experiences as true; the parallel explains why growth itself generates a new task.
connections.headline: Continuing ascent brings a new measure of responsibility

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, דְּקַיְימָא לַן (יוֹמָא פו:): עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהִתְוַדָּה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים זֶה, חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Transgressions confessed on this Yom Kippur should not be confessed on another Yom Kippur. If one repeated them, one must confess them on another Yom Kippur.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, דְּקַיְימָא לַן (יוֹמָא פו:): עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהִתְוַדָּה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים זֶה, חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: All the more is such a person praiseworthy, as it is said: “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is before me always.””
connections.context: The first view opposes repeating a confession for sins not repeated; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov praises it. Rav Tzadok relies on the latter view. Quoting only the first view reverses the point he cites.

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ בַּעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהַהֲלָכָה דְּלֹא זָז מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁמּוֹחֲלִין לוֹ, וַהֲרֵי גַּם זֶה אֱמֶת.
connections.quote: “If one transgressed a positive commandment and repented, he does not move from there before he is forgiven, as it is said, “Return, wayward children.””
connections.context: This is the precise category to which the quoted rule of immediate forgiveness applies. The Gemara goes on to distinguish other categories of atonement; Rav Tzadok’s point is that renewed repentance can still be meaningful even where forgiveness has already occurred.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְפִי מַעֲלַת הָאָדָם וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ, כָּךְ הוּא תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Sidduro Shel Shabbat, Part II, Derush 3, Chapter 3, item 5
connections.quote: “You thus learn that there is a further level of higher repentance above them all, which does not require a prior state of distance from Him, blessed be He. Rather, each and every day, as a person becomes increasingly aware of the greatness of the Creator of all and of his obligation to serve Him, he should repent and regret the earlier days that passed with less service than he now renders.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל זֶה נִתְאוֹנֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קוֹדֶם פְּטִירָתוֹ: "לֹא אוּכַל עוֹד וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בַּמֵּתִים חָפְשִׁי", וְנִקְרָא "נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ",
connections.quote: ‘He said to them: ‘I am a hundred and twenty years old today. I can no longer go out and come in, and Hashem has said to me: You shall not cross this Jordan.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל זֶה נִתְאוֹנֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קוֹדֶם פְּטִירָתוֹ: "לֹא אוּכַל עוֹד וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בַּמֵּתִים חָפְשִׁי", וְנִקְרָא "נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ",
connections.quote: “Free among the dead, like the slain who lie in the grave, whom You remember no more, and who are cut off from Your hand.”
connections.context: Chofshi can mean free or released. Rav Tzadok invokes its rabbinic sense of release from the obligations and work of this life. The translation “abandoned” alone does not make that wordplay visible.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל זֶה נִתְאוֹנֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קוֹדֶם פְּטִירָתוֹ: "לֹא אוּכַל עוֹד וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בַּמֵּתִים חָפְשִׁי", וְנִקְרָא "נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ",
connections.quote: “There is no difficulty. When David said, “The dead do not praise God,” this is what he meant: A person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot before he dies, for once he dies he ceases from Torah and mitzvot, and the Holy One, blessed be He, has no praise through him. This is what Rabbi Yochanan said: What is meant by “Free among the dead”? Once a person dies, he becomes free from Torah and mitzvot.”
connections.context: The existing Psalm quotation supplies the words “free among the dead.” This Gemara supplies the rabbinic interpretation that Rav Tzadok invokes: this life is the opportunity for active Torah and mitzvot.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין נָח לְעוֹלָם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין הוּא מַרְגִּישׁ.
connections.quote: “This is the difference between the resurrection of the dead and the World to Come. The World to Come is rest from toil: one reaches the utmost level to which one can go, and no further, as they said, “One who did not toil,” and as they said in Berakhot 17a, “The righteous sit”—meaning that they do not proceed to a further level. “And their crowns”: those that they prepared in this world, royal crowns, for the World to Come is the level of kingship, the level of David, peace be upon him, as stated above in section 60. “Upon their heads”: the head is the level of kingship, as in “the heads of the thousands of Israel,” and “David came to the summit,” as explained elsewhere. But in the resurrection of the dead, which is Isaac’s level, as stated there, there is still progression through levels according to what a person is prepared for. That is why they are in bodies, for in the spiritual state there is no progression, as it is written, “I shall give you walkers among these who stand.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנב.): זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּזְקִינִין וְכוּלֵי, זִקְנֵי עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rav said: Barzillai the Gileadite was not speaking truthfully, for there was a maidservant in Rabbi’s household who was ninety-two years old and could still taste the food in a pot. Rava said: Barzillai the Gileadite had been steeped in sexual immorality, and old age overtakes anyone steeped in sexual immorality. It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei says: As Torah scholars grow older, their wisdom increases, as it is said, ‘With the aged is wisdom, and with length of days, understanding.’ As people unlearned in Torah grow older, their foolishness increases, as it is said, ‘He removes speech from the trusted and takes discernment from the elders.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ כְּשֶׁעָלָה אַחֵר לַמַּדְרֵגוֹת, אָז נִתְגַּלָּה הַטִּינָא שֶׁהָיְתָה בְּלִבּוֹ בְּיַלְדוּת;
connections.quote: “Shmuel found Rav Yehudah leaning on a door bolt and weeping. He said to him, “Sharp one, why are you weeping?” He replied, “Is it a small matter, what is written concerning the Sages: ‘Where is the scribe, where is the one who weighs, where is the one who counts the towers?’ ‘Where is the scribe’—they counted all the letters in the Torah. ‘Where is the one who weighs’—they weighed the Torah’s arguments from lesser to greater. ‘Where is the one who counts the towers’—they studied three hundred laws concerning a tower that floats in the air. Rabbi Ami said that Doeg and Achitophel asked three hundred questions concerning a tower that floats in the air. Yet we learned that three kings and four ordinary people have no share in the World to Come. What, then, will become of us?” He said to him, “Sharp one, there was a hidden flaw in their hearts.” What of Acher? Greek song never ceased from his mouth. They said of Acher that when he rose from the study hall, many books of heretics would fall from his lap.”
connections.context: The phrase about a hidden flaw is first applied to Doeg and Achitophel, followed by the question about Acher. Rav Tzadok’s inference about Acher’s earlier repentance and the flaw becoming evident at a higher level is his own explanation, beyond the Gemara’s reported details.

connections.hePhrase: [קלה] מִי שֶׁמַּרְגִּישׁ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם חֵשֶׁק בְּלֵב וּמוֹחַ לַעֲבוֹדַת ה', אָז הָעֵצָה: "הַשְׁלֵךְ עַל ה' יְהָבְךָ" (תְּהִלִּים נה, כג).
connections.quote: ‘Cast your burden upon Hashem, and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous person totter.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "תַּאֲוַת עֲנָוִים שָׁמַעְתָּ ה' תָּכִין לִבָּם וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם י, יז), שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה הוּא תַּאֲוַת הָעֲנָוִים וּמַכִּירִים שִׁפְלוּתָם שֶׁלֵּב אָיִן – הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵכִין לִבָּם;
connections.quote: ‘Hashem, You have heard the longing of the humble; You will steady their heart and incline Your ear.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "תַּאֲוַת עֲנָוִים שָׁמַעְתָּ ה' תָּכִין לִבָּם וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם י, יז), שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה הוּא תַּאֲוַת הָעֲנָוִים וּמַכִּירִים שִׁפְלוּתָם שֶׁלֵּב אָיִן – הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵכִין לִבָּם;
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 21:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 21:1
connections.quote: “‘Grant us, Hashem our God, the blessing of Your appointed times.’ Every festival has its particular blessing. On this festival the principal blessing is the receptive vessel that Hashem builds in Israel's heart to receive all good. Therefore we pray ‘Grant us’: that Hashem arrange within us this vessel to receive every good at its time, when He too is occupied in bestowing it upon us. This is like ‘Prepare their heart; incline Your ear’ (Psalms 10:17): Hashem gives the vessel together with the good. That is the principal matter of this festival. ‘As You desired and promised to bless us’ means that on the festival Hashem stands in great favor toward creation. ‘Sanctify us through Your commandments’ means that all the benefits should be for us only the joy of a mitzvah, through which it will be easier to serve Hashem. ‘Give us our portion in Your Torah’ means that He open the mitzvah's inward content, and it will shine like Torah, as in a mitzvah at its time, as the Gemara teaches (Kiddushin 33). ‘Purify our heart to serve You in truth’ means removing all the barriers from the heart's inner point, leaving only service of You in truth.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim makes explicit what the siman means by Hashem preparing the heart: He gives both the good and the vessel through which it can be received at its proper time. The rest of the passage identifies that vessel with joy in a mitzvah, inward Torah and a purified heart. This develops the prayer for desire while preserving Rav Tzadok's prior requirement to turn away from wrongful deeds.
connections.headline: Receiving the vessel together with the gift

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ "ה' צִלְּךָ", כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּמַדְרֵגַת "אַיִן", מַשִּׂיג מַעֲלַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן בְּמַדְרֵגַת "אַיִן",
connections.heRef: בעל שם טוב על התורה, קדושים כ״ג:א׳
connections.quote: see note 1456.
connections.context: The teaching attributed to the Baal Shem Tov supplies the meaning of “Hashem is your shadow.” Rav Tzadok applies that correspondence to humility and the perception of ayin.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לוֹ שֶׁאֵין זוּלָתוֹ כְּלָל עַכְשָׁו כְּעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ,
connections.displayRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 7:10
connections.linkedRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 7:10
connections.canonicalRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 7:10
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שני; שער היחוד והאמונה ז׳:י׳
connections.quote: “From what has been explained, we can understand the verse, “I, Hashem, have not changed”: there is no change at all. Just as He was alone before the creation of the world, so He is alone after it was created. This is what we say, “You are He before the world was created; You are He,” and so forth—with no change in His essence or in His knowledge. By knowing Himself He knows all created things, for everything comes from Him and is null in its existence before Him. As Rambam wrote: “He is the knower, He is the known, and He is knowledge itself—all one. This is something the mouth cannot express, the ear cannot hear, nor the human heart fully comprehend.””
connections.context: This passage in Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah states the before-and-after-creation comparison expressly and grounds it in divine unity. Its qualification about the limits of human comprehension is retained.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת מִקּוֹדֶם "אָבְדוּ גוֹיִם מֵאַרְצוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים י, טז)
connections.quote: ‘Hashem is King forever and ever; the nations have vanished from His land.’

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, תְּשׁוּבָה עַל הָעֲבֵירוֹת בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "בָּאוּ גוֹיִם בְּנַחֲלָתֶךָ" (שָׁם עט, א),
connections.quote: ‘A psalm of Asaph. God, nations have entered Your inheritance. They have defiled Your holy sanctuary and made Jerusalem into heaps of ruins.’

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲבִידָתָם הוּא עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה עַל כָּל פָּנִים, שֶׁזְּדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כִּשְׁגָגוֹת,
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for through it willful sins become for him like unwitting transgressions, as it is said: ‘Return, O Israel, to Hashem your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity’ (Hosea 14:2).”
connections.context: The Gemara sets this beside Reish Lakish’s other saying, that willful sins become like merits, and explains: they become like merits when one repents out of love, and like unwitting sins when one repents out of fear.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז מִתְדַּבֵּק בַּמַּדְרֵגָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה מִמַּדְרֵגַת עֶשֶׂר קְדוּשׁוֹת דִּתְנַן בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּכֵלִים, שֶׁהִיא קְדוּשַׁת הָאָרֶץ.
connections.quote: “There are ten degrees of holiness. The Land of Israel is holier than all other lands. What is its holiness? From it the omer offering, first fruits, and the two loaves are brought, whereas they are not brought from other lands. Walled towns are holier than it, for those afflicted with tzaraat are sent out of them, and a corpse may be carried around within them as long as desired; once it has gone out, it is not brought back. Within the wall of Jerusalem is holier than these, for offerings of lesser sanctity and the second tithe are eaten there. The Temple Mount is holier than it, for men and women with an abnormal discharge, menstruating women, and women after childbirth may not enter there. The Cheil is holier than it, for non-Jews and those impure through contact with the dead may not enter there. The Women’s Courtyard is holier than it, for one who has immersed that day but awaits sunset may not enter there, though entry does not incur a sin offering. The Israelites’ Courtyard is holier than it, for one who still lacks the offering that completes purification may not enter there, and entry in the relevant state of impurity incurs a sin offering. The Priests’ Courtyard is holier than it, for Israelites enter only when needed for laying hands on an offering, slaughtering, or waving. Between the Entrance Hall and the altar is holier than it, for priests with bodily blemishes or untrimmed hair may not enter there. The Sanctuary is holier than it, for one who has not washed his hands and feet may not enter there. The Holy of Holies is holier than these, for only the High Priest enters there, on Yom Kippur, at the time of the service. Rabbi Yosei said: In five respects the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar is equal to the Sanctuary: priests with blemishes, untrimmed hair, those who have drunk wine, and those who have not washed their hands and feet may not enter there, and people withdraw from between the Entrance Hall and the altar during the burning of incense.”
connections.context: The Mishnah supplies the ascending degrees from the holiness of the Land to the Holy of Holies. Its concrete distinctions and Rabbi Yosei’s qualification are retained; Rav Tzadok uses this hierarchy as an analogy for the movement from action to the highest root.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ כִּי בְּכָל מָקוֹם נָעוּץ סוֹפָהּ בִּתְחִלָּתָהּ,
connections.quote: “Ten sefirot of belimah: Their end is embedded in their beginning, and their beginning in their end, like a flame bound to a coal. For the Master is one, and He has no second; before one, what can you count?”
connections.context: This is the source of “their end is embedded in their beginning.” The image of a flame bound to a coal and the conclusion about divine unity supply the context for Rav Tzadok’s movement from the lowest degree of holiness to the highest.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לָבוֹא לַעֲנָוָה וּמַדְרֵגַת "אַיִן", שֶׁהִיא קְדוּשַׁת הַקֹּדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קכא עַמּוּד א),
connections.quote: “It is written, “And wisdom—from where is it found?” Torah issues from wisdom, from the place called Holy; wisdom issues from the place called Holy of Holies.”
connections.context: The Zohar begins with me’ayin, “from where,” in Job 28:12. Rav Tzadok reads ayin as the level of self-nullification or nothingness above articulated wisdom and relates it to the Holy of Holies. The previous excerpt omitted that essential opening and also carried an erroneous incidental Leviticus citation.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִשָּׁם אוֹרָה יוֹצְאָה לָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהוּא "תָּכִין לִבָּם", כְּעִנְיַן הַמָּאוֹר מַחֲזִירוֹ לְמוּטָב:
connections.quote: “The Ark: Rabbi Chiyya the Great and Rabbi Yannai—one said that from there light goes forth to the world; the other said that from there a curse goes forth to the world.”
connections.context: The Yerushalmi gives these two explanations of the word aron, “Ark,” in its discussion of the place toward which prayer is directed. Rav Tzadok invokes the explanation about light and applies it to the heart’s illumination; the original wording refers to the Ark.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ז:): וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁזּוֹכֶה בַּדִּין, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מָרוֹם מִשְׁפָּטֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים י, ה),
connections.quote: ‘Is that so?! Rabbi Yitzchak said: If you see a wicked person whose fortunes are smiling upon him, do not provoke him, as it says: ‘His ways prosper at all times.’ Moreover, he wins in judgment, as it says: ‘Your judgments are far above, beyond his sight.’ Moreover, he sees his enemies defeated, as it says: ‘He blows upon all his foes.’’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ז:): וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁזּוֹכֶה בַּדִּין, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מָרוֹם מִשְׁפָּטֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים י, ה),
connections.quote: ‘His ways prosper at all times; Your judgments are high above him, beyond his sight. He snorts at all his foes.’

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִזְכּוֹת אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי מִצְווֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (לב.),
connections.quote: “These are a person’s advocates: repentance and good deeds. Even if nine hundred and ninety-nine argue for his guilt and one argues in his favor, he is saved, as it is said, ‘If there is an angel on his behalf, an advocate, one among a thousand, to declare a person’s uprightness, then He is gracious to him and says: Redeem him from descending to the pit,’ and so forth. Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, says: Even if within that one angel there are nine hundred and ninety-nine arguments for guilt and one in his favor, he is saved, as it is said, ‘An advocate, one among a thousand.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִזְכּוֹת אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי מִצְווֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (לב.),
connections.quote: ““These are the advocates”: What a person does below that is pleasing to the court above—repentance and good deeds.”
connections.context: Rashi makes the connection between deeds performed below and the heavenly judgment explicit. The existing note already quotes the Gemara’s identification of a person’s advocates.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה סוֹף פֶּרֶק כ): שְׂכָרוֹ שֶׁל אַשּׁוּר שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ סַנְחֵרִיב;
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, brought Sennacherib into the world only as a reward to Ashur, who was an upright man and was of Abraham our father’s counsel.”
connections.context: The chapter lists the antecedent merits through which several later rulers came to power. Rav Tzadok cites Ashur’s reward to show how an outwardly destructive historical power can arise through a divine accounting of an earlier merit.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה סוֹף פֶּרֶק כ): שְׂכָרוֹ שֶׁל אַשּׁוּר שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ סַנְחֵרִיב;
connections.quote: ““From that land”: When Ashur saw his children listening to Nimrod and rebelling against God by building the tower, he departed from among them.”
connections.context: Rashi identifies the departure of Ashur as withdrawal from the tower’s rebellion. This supplies the biblical episode behind the existing account of his reward.

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי כְּבָר הָיָה אַשּׁוּר אָז בְּעוֹלַם הָאֱמֶת, וּמַה שָּׂכָר הוּא לוֹ טוֹבַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהָיָה לְסַנְחֵרִיב, שֶׁיָּדַע שָׁם שֶׁזֶּה הֶבֶל וְשֶׁקֶר?
connections.quote: “But Ashur refused this because he denied every kind of divinity. Tanna Devei Eliyahu states that, as a reward for separating from them, Sennacherib descended from him. For this was also Sennacherib’s power: the quality of heresy, as he said, “Which among all the gods of the lands have delivered … that He should deliver Jerusalem …?” All the nations call Him the God of gods.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok elsewhere interprets Ashur’s separation as having an inward ambiguity: its outward rejection of the tower could coexist with denial of divinity. This is his interpretive account of Ashur and Sennacherib, illuminating why apparent merit need not reveal an act’s final spiritual meaning.

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם בְּכַבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא אֵיךְ מִדַּת מִשְׁפָּטָיו, אֲבָל עַל כָּל פָּנִים הָיָה כָּךְ, כִּי לוּלֵי כֵן אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁהָיָה נַעֲשָׂה בָּעוֹלָם כֵּן.
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, in this world there are wicked people to whom things happen as though they had performed the deeds of the righteous, and the reverse. Our Sages said in Berakhot 7b of a wicked person whose hour favors him, “Your judgments are far above, out of his sight.” How can this be, when all His judgments are true? In truth, every person has both merit and guilt. As they said, even the transgressors of Israel are full of mitzvot; and “there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.” Concerning the weighing of merits and sins, Maimonides has already written in the Laws of Repentance that they are weighed only in the knowledge of the blessed Lord. This is certain, for we have no knowledge of it at all. Although our Sages said in many places that one thing is greater than another, they spoke in general terms according to the judgment of Torah. But the judgment above concerns individual souls, and no soul is like another.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת שָׁם): "אַל תְּקַנֵּא בְּעֹשֵׂי עַוְלָה" (תְּהִלִּים לז, א) – לִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹהֶם, וּמֵאַיִן יָבוֹא זֶה?
connections.quote: ““Do not contend with evildoers”—to become like evildoers; “do not envy those who do wrong”—to become like those who do wrong.”
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes resisting wickedness from envying or imitating the wicked. Rav Tzadok cites the latter warning, not the neighboring discussion of a prosperous wicked person’s success in judgment.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת שָׁם): "אַל תְּקַנֵּא בְּעֹשֵׂי עַוְלָה" (תְּהִלִּים לז, א) – לִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹהֶם, וּמֵאַיִן יָבוֹא זֶה?
connections.quote: “Of David. Do not contend with evildoers; do not envy those who do wrong.”
connections.context: The second phrase is the one expounded in Berakhot 7b: do not desire to become like those who do wrong. Rav Tzadok asks how even their apparent success might provoke such envy.

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ לָזֶה מְבִינוּת גְּדוֹלָה אֵיזֶה דָּבָר הוּא רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ יִתְגַּלֶּה לְמַפְרֵעַ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה כֵן כְּלָל
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:34
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:34
connections.quote: “Even Avraham's statement (Genesis 17:18), ‘If only Yishmael would live before You,’ corresponds to ‘Do not bear false witness against your fellow.’ ‘Your fellow’ means the Holy One, as the Zohar teaches (Beshalach 55b). Hashem had promised him (Genesis 17:16), ‘I will bless her and also give you a son from her.’ Why then did he say, ‘If only Yishmael would live before You,’ which appears like false testimony? Hashem told him not to say so: rather, what I have counseled will stand, ‘Sarah your wife will bear you a son.’ Hashem illuminated this statement for him until he himself afterward sent Yishmael out of his house. Yet, because Yishmael was righteous at that time, Hashem showed him not to fix his gaze on what would occur with him later. ‘As he is there,’ he is righteous and must not be judged adversely, as taught in the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16b) and the Midrash.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov distinguishes Avraham's present view of Yishmael from the later outcome: Hashem directs attention to how he stands now. This is a qualified comparison with the siman's account of temporary success and final disclosure. It cautions against treating the visible present as proof of a permanent spiritual state, while also refusing to condemn a person now on the basis of a supposed knowledge of his future.
connections.headline: Present judgment and the later outcome

connections.hePhrase: [וְאַדְּרַבָּה, כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת הֵם הֵיפֶךְ עַל דֶּרֶךְ: בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה מְהַפְּכִין וְכוּלֵי, וְכֵן רְשָׁעִים מְהַפְּכִין מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for through it willful sins become for him like merits, as it is said: ‘And when the wicked man turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he shall live by them’ (Ezekiel 33:19).”

connections.hePhrase: [וְאַדְּרַבָּה, כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת הֵם הֵיפֶךְ עַל דֶּרֶךְ: בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה מְהַפְּכִין וְכוּלֵי, וְכֵן רְשָׁעִים מְהַפְּכִין מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Woe to the wicked, who turn the attribute of mercy into the attribute of judgment. Wherever the name Hashem is stated, it is the attribute of mercy: “Hashem, Hashem, God, merciful and gracious.” Yet it is written, “Hashem saw that human wickedness was great on the earth”; “Hashem regretted that He had made humankind”; and “Hashem said: I shall wipe out.” Fortunate are the righteous, who turn the attribute of judgment into the attribute of mercy. Wherever Elohim is stated, it is the attribute of judgment: “You shall not curse the judges,” and “The case of both shall come before the judges.” Yet it is written, “God heard their groaning, and God remembered His covenant”; “God remembered Rachel”; and “God remembered Noah.””
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the reversal of the two divine attributes that Rav Tzadok invokes. Both directions are retained, together with the verses used to identify the attributes.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחֶסֶד לְאֻמִּים חַטָּאת" (מִשְׁלֵי יד, לד), עַיֵּין בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (י:) דִּלְפִי שָׁעָה חַטָּאת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת לָהֶם],
connections.quote: “Righteousness exalts a nation, but the kindness of the peoples is sin.”
connections.context: This renders chesed as “kindness,” the rabbinic reading employed in Bava Batra 10b and in Rav Tzadok’s discussion. In its contextual biblical sense the same word can be read as “disgrace”; that alternative reading does not convey the exposition being cited here.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחֶסֶד לְאֻמִּים חַטָּאת" (מִשְׁלֵי יד, לד), עַיֵּין בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (י:) דִּלְפִי שָׁעָה חַטָּאת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת לָהֶם],
connections.quote: “It was taught: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said to his students, ‘My children, what does Scripture mean when it says, “Charity exalts a nation, but the kindness of peoples is sin”?’ Rabbi Eliezer answered: ‘“Charity exalts a nation” refers to Israel, as it is written, “Who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth?” “But the kindness of peoples is sin” means that every act of charity and kindness performed by the nations of the world is a sin for them, because they do it only to magnify themselves through it, as it is said, “So that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.”’”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחֶסֶד לְאֻמִּים חַטָּאת" (מִשְׁלֵי יד, לד), עַיֵּין בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (י:) דִּלְפִי שָׁעָה חַטָּאת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת לָהֶם],
connections.quote: “Rabban Gamliel said: We still need the Modaite. Rabbi Eliezer of Modi’in says: “Righteousness exalts a nation”—this is Israel, as it is written, “Who is like Your people, Israel, one nation?” “The kindness of nations is sin”—all the charity and kindness that the nations perform is sin for them, for they do it only to reproach us through it, as it is said, “Hashem came and did as He had spoken, because you sinned against Hashem and did not listen to His voice, and this thing befell you.””
connections.context: This is Rabbi Eliezer of Modi’in’s distinct interpretation within the discussion. It explains Rav Tzadok’s phrase that the deed can appear to be an accusation against Israel. The existing note quotes Rabbi Eliezer’s different interpretation concerning self-aggrandizement; the two opinions remain distinct.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחֶסֶד לְאֻמִּים חַטָּאת" (מִשְׁלֵי יד, לד), עַיֵּין בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (י:) דִּלְפִי שָׁעָה חַטָּאת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת לָהֶם],
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא בתרא י׳ ב:י״א:א׳
connections.quote: ““Hashem came and did as He had spoken, because you sinned”: At that time he performed an act of charity by being zealous for the Holy One, blessed be He. Alternatively, it was by releasing Jeremiah from his chains, as it is written there.”
connections.context: Tosafot identifies the apparent act of charity in Nebuzaradan’s speech, preserving both explanations. This makes the Gemara’s example intelligible without treating the reproach itself as an unqualified model of kindness.

connections.hePhrase: [קלז] כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם רוֹאֶה שֶׁכָּל הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת טוֹבוֹת וּרְצוֹנוֹת טוֹבוֹת שֶׁנּוֹפְלִים בְּלִבּוֹ וּמוֹחוֹ הוּא רַק לְרֶגַע וּמִיָּד מִתְעַלְּמִים מִמֶּנּוּ, וְדוֹאֵג שֶׁמָּא הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כְּעִנְיַן פּוֹשְׁעִים מְלֵאִים חֲרָטוֹת
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים י״א:ו׳
connections.quote: see note 1522.
connections.context: Tanya explains the recurring regret mentioned at the opening of this ois. It distinguishes the presence of good and the beginning of repentance from the further strength needed actually to abandon the sin.

connections.hePhrase: הָעֵצָה לָזֶה: "הַשְׁלֵךְ עַל ה' יְהָבְךָ וְהוּא יְכַלְכְּלֶךָ, לֹא יִתֵּן לְעוֹלָם מוֹט לַצַּדִּיק" (תְּהִלִּים נה, כג),
connections.quote: ““Cast”: David said to his soul: Cast your burden upon Hashem, and so it will be, for He will bear your burden. That is, trust in Him that He will lighten your burden from you, and so it will be, for He will not forever leave the righteous person tottering.”
connections.context: Metzudat David reads the verse as David addressing his own soul. His explanation gives both the burden and the assurance that the righteous person’s instability will not last forever.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים", רַק שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּמִתְמוֹטֵט חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּעֵת הַהֶעְלֵם.
connections.quote: “Your people shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.”

connections.hePhrase: וְ"הַשְׁלֵךְ וְכוּלֵי" הַיְינוּ שֶׁגַּם זֶה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְנִמְצָא כְּאִלּוּ הַמַּשָּׂא מוּטֶּלֶת עָלָיו, שֶׁמֵּאַחַר שֶׁאַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה כֵּן, וּמִמֵּילָא הַמִּשְׁפָּט עַל זֶה דְּ"הוּא יְכַלְכְּלֶךָ".
connections.quote: “This is the measure, as the Sages said (Niddah 70b): he should increase his business activity and seek mercy, and so on. He asks for mercy that Hashem grant him success through the natural course, for one without the other is insufficient; the Holy One does not perform a miracle for falsehood.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah develops the same casting-burden verse while requiring both natural action and prayer for success. This qualifies the siman's dependence on help from above: casting the burden concerns recognition of the source and relief of distress, while Torah, prayer and chosen effort remain the means through which the person responds.
connections.headline: Trust accompanied by prayer and effort

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כו:): דְּלָא הֲווֹ יָדְעֵי רַבָּנָן מַאי "יְהָבְךָ",
connections.quote: “The Sages did not know the meaning of “Cast your yehav upon the Lord, and He will sustain you.” Rabba bar bar Chana said: One day I was walking with an Arab, carrying a load, and he said to me: Take your yehav and throw it onto my camel.”
connections.context: The ordinary use of yehav for a carried load explains the psalm’s image of entrusting one’s burden to God. Rav Tzadok further expounds what a person can surrender in this way.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה כְּעִנְיַן: כָּל הַמְּשַׁתֵּף שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם [וְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם נִקְרָא "אַגַּמְלָאֵי" – גָּמָל שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ] בְּצַעֲרוֹ כּוֹפְלִין לוֹ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת סג.),
connections.quote: ‘Rav Huna bar Berechyah said in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar: Anyone who joins the name of Heaven to his distress has his livelihood doubled, as it is said: ‘Shaddai shall be with you in your distress, and silver shall be doubled for you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה כְּעִנְיַן: כָּל הַמְּשַׁתֵּף שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם [וְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם נִקְרָא "אַגַּמְלָאֵי" – גָּמָל שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ] בְּצַעֲרוֹ כּוֹפְלִין לוֹ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת סג.),
connections.quote: ““One who associates the name of Heaven with his distress”: He blesses over the misfortune, “The true Judge”; alternatively, he asks mercy of Him.”
connections.context: Rashi preserves two concrete meanings of sharing the divine name in distress: acknowledging God’s judgment and asking Him for mercy. Both belong to the teaching already quoted from the Gemara.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַשִּׁתּוּף הַיְינוּ שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמַכְנִיס אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר, וּמִמֵּילָא הֵקֵל מִמֶּנּוּ:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Meir said: When a person suffers, what expression does the Divine Presence use? “My head is heavy with pain; My arm is heavy with pain.” If the Omnipresent thus suffers over the blood of the wicked that is shed, how much more over the blood of the righteous.”
connections.context: The Mishnah describes divine participation in human suffering, even in the setting of punishment. It gives a source for the idea that a person’s burden is not separate from the Divine Presence.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא: "אֱוִיל שְׂפָתַיִם יִלָּבֵט" (מִשְׁלֵי י, ח), כְּמוֹ שֶׁמַּשְׁמָע מִמַּה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּסוֹטָה (מז:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְעָם לֹא יָבִין יִלָּבֵט", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ‘One who is wise of heart accepts commandments, but a babbling fool will come to grief.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא: "אֱוִיל שְׂפָתַיִם יִלָּבֵט" (מִשְׁלֵי י, ח), כְּמוֹ שֶׁמַּשְׁמָע מִמַּה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּסוֹטָה (מז:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְעָם לֹא יָבִין יִלָּבֵט", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “What is “A people without understanding will be cast down”? Rabbi Elazar said: The prophet told Israel, If you are exacting with yourselves, the waters examine your wives; if not, the waters do not examine your wives.”
connections.context: The passage concerns moral self-scrutiny as a condition for the sotah waters’ operation. Rav Tzadok uses the common word yillavet to explain why thoughtless speech and a lack of self-examination lead to failure.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא: "אֱוִיל שְׂפָתַיִם יִלָּבֵט" (מִשְׁלֵי י, ח), כְּמוֹ שֶׁמַּשְׁמָע מִמַּה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּסוֹטָה (מז:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְעָם לֹא יָבִין יִלָּבֵט", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “I will not punish your daughters when they commit harlotry, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery; for they themselves go aside with harlots and sacrifice with prostitutes, and a people that does not understand shall fall.”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, "חֲלוֹם" נִקְרָא עוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּשׁוּב ה' אֶת שִׁיבַת צִיּוֹן הָיִינוּ כְּחֹלְמִים", וְהוּא עוֹלַם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֵירוּבִין כב.): "הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם וְלֹא לְמָחָר וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘A song of ascents. When Hashem restored the captivity of Zion, we were like people dreaming.’

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, "חֲלוֹם" נִקְרָא עוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּשׁוּב ה' אֶת שִׁיבַת צִיּוֹן הָיִינוּ כְּחֹלְמִים", וְהוּא עוֹלַם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֵירוּבִין כב.): "הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם וְלֹא לְמָחָר וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘This is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of ‘which I command you today to do’? ‘Today to do them’—not tomorrow to do them. ‘Today to do them’—tomorrow to receive their reward.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדָבָר זֶה לֹא רָאָה מֵעוֹלָם דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם טוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁחָשַׁק מְאֹד לִבְנוֹת הַבַּיִת וְנֶאֱמַר: "רַק אַתָּה לֹא תִבְנֶה וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א ח, יט).
connections.quote: ‘But you shall not build the House. Rather, your son who comes forth from your loins—he shall build the House for My name.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדָבָר זֶה לֹא רָאָה מֵעוֹלָם דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם טוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁחָשַׁק מְאֹד לִבְנוֹת הַבַּיִת וְנֶאֱמַר: "רַק אַתָּה לֹא תִבְנֶה וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א ח, יט).
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the Talmud's statement that He caused His Shekhinah to dwell in Shiloh and the other places. In Shiloh and Gilgal He caused His presence to dwell from His side without Israel's prior suffering; concerning this it says, ‘Zion said, He has forsaken me,’ and ‘Even these may be forgotten’—their holiness ceased. See Aggadat Bereishit, chapter 71, cited in Sidrei Taharot, Kelim 72. The eternal Temple is different: there His presence dwelled through David's suffering and labor, and he prayed for it with self-giving, until Hashem said to him (I Kings 8:19), ‘Your son who will come from your loins will build the house for My name.’ Concerning this the verse says, ‘I will not forget you.’ Through the suffering associated with that holiness it is fixed; all the prayers and offerings were there. Although sin concealed this light, He promises us that through our prayer that He return to dwell in Jerusalem, He will certainly rebuild Jerusalem and return His presence as before to the eternal Temple. This is what we say here: like a woman in her period who awaits her return to her former permitted state, Jerusalem too will have a repair.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef identifies David's suffering, effort and prayer as the basis for the Temple's enduring holiness. His son builds it, and later sin conceals its light, yet neither fact erases what David's work established. This develops Rav Tzadok's distinction between a visible lack of completion and an inward desire that truly brought the work into being.
connections.headline: David’s labor and the Temple’s enduring holiness

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת דָּוִד הָיָה נֶגֶד הַמַּעֲשֶׂה כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: “The king Messiah is David himself, as is known. David, however, was the beginning of the endeavor from the side of the final deed, while the Messiah is the completion of the whole stature as it exists in the original thought. Reaching the root of that original thought itself is the World to Come. The days of the Messiah precede the World to Come: they are the end of this world, from which one reaches the World to Come, and the greatest perfection a person can attain in this world. “God made the human being upright.” Had Adam not sinned, he would himself have been David, the final deed of Creation; through his endeavor to reach the greatest perfection possible for him, he could afterward also have reached the level of the Messiah. As is known, he includes these two souls, hinted at by the initials of his name, Adam: Adam, David, Messiah.”
