connections.context: Rav Tzadok sets David within the movement from action toward the completion of the divine intention. The full paragraph distinguishes the beginning of the endeavor, the messianic completion within this world, and the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת ל.): בְּחַיֶּיךָ אֵינִי מוֹדִיעַ, בְּחַיֵּי שְׁלֹמֹה בִנְךָ אֲנִי מוֹדִיעַ;
connections.quote: ‘Another interpretation of ‘And I praised,’ and so forth, is as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘Show me a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see and be ashamed’? David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the universe, forgive me for that sin.’ He said to him: ‘You are forgiven.’ He said to Him: ‘Show me a sign during my lifetime.’ He answered: ‘During your lifetime I will not make it known; during the lifetime of Solomon your son I will make it known.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת ל.): בְּחַיֶּיךָ אֵינִי מוֹדִיעַ, בְּחַיֵּי שְׁלֹמֹה בִנְךָ אֲנִי מוֹדִיעַ;
connections.quote: “When Solomon built the Temple, he sought to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies. The gates clung to one another. Solomon uttered twenty-four songs of prayer and was not answered. He began, “Lift up your heads, gates; be uplifted, everlasting entrances, and let the King of glory enter.” They ran after him to swallow him, saying, “Who is this King of glory?” He said to them, “Hashem, mighty and powerful.” He again said, “Lift up your heads, gates; lift yourselves, everlasting entrances, and let the King of glory enter. Who is this King of glory? Hashem of hosts—He is the King of glory, forever,” and was not answered. When he said, “Hashem God, do not turn away the face of Your anointed; remember the kindnesses of David Your servant,” he was immediately answered. At that moment the faces of all David’s enemies became black like the bottom of a pot, and all the people, all Israel, knew that the Holy One, blessed be He, had forgiven him that sin. Did Solomon not speak well when he said, “I praise the dead who have already died”?”
connections.context: The existing note gives God’s promise that David’s forgiveness would be disclosed in Solomon’s lifetime. This continuation tells how that disclosure occurred at the completion of the Temple.

connections.hePhrase: וְסוֹף שֶׁנִּקְרָא הַבַּיִת עַל שֵׁם דָּוִד כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב),
connections.quote: “Solomon built the Temple. Yet because David devoted himself to the Temple that was built, the Holy One, blessed be He, did not withhold his reward, but had it written in his name: “A psalm, a song for the dedication of the House, of David.” It does not say “of Solomon,” but “of David.””
connections.context: The Midrash’s principle is that devoted effort is credited even when another person completes the work. Rav Tzadok uses the Temple’s attribution to David to explain the enduring force of David’s desire to build it.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה הָיָה דּוֹאֵג כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak also said: What is the meaning of “But to the wicked God says: What have you to do with recounting My statutes”? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to wicked Doeg: “What have you to do with recounting My statutes? When you reach the passage about murderers and the passage about speakers of slander, how do you expound them?” “And you carry My covenant upon your mouth.” Rabbi Ami said: Doeg’s Torah was only from the lips outward.”
connections.context: This is the precise passage cited about Doeg. Its questions about murder and slander show why verbal mastery, without inward obedience, does not establish the truth of a person’s service.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הָיָה לְפִי שָׁעָה נִרְאֶה כִּמְצַלִּיחַ בְּמַעֲשָׂיו, שֶׁעָלָיו אָמַר דָּוִד: "אַל תִּתְחַר בַּמַּצְלִיחַ דַּרְכּוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ז), וְיָדוּעַ "דַּרְכּוֹ" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דֶּרֶךְ ה'],
connections.quote: ‘Be still before Hashem and wait patiently for Him. Do not be provoked by one whose way prospers, by a man who carries out schemes.’

connections.hePhrase: [קלט] כָּל הַפְּעֻלּוֹת וְהָעֲבוֹדוֹת נִיכָּרִים רַק בַּסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנג.): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא? "וְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמַעְנָה דָבָר מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כא);
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar asked Rav: ‘Who is destined for the World to Come?’ He answered: ‘Your ears will hear a word behind you, saying: This is the way; walk in it, when you turn right and when you turn left.’ Rabbi Hanina said: ‘Anyone with whom our teachers are pleased.’ ‘The mourners go about in the street’: The people of Galilee say, ‘Do deeds (that will be recounted) before your bier.’ The people of Judea say, ‘Do deeds (that will be recounted) after your bier.’ They do not disagree: each speaks according to the practice of his own place.”

connections.hePhrase: [קלט] כָּל הַפְּעֻלּוֹת וְהָעֲבוֹדוֹת נִיכָּרִים רַק בַּסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנג.): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא? "וְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמַעְנָה דָבָר מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כא);
connections.quote: ‘Your ears will hear a word from behind you saying, ‘This is the path; walk in it,’ whether you turn right or turn left.’

connections.hePhrase: [קלט] כָּל הַפְּעֻלּוֹת וְהָעֲבוֹדוֹת נִיכָּרִים רַק בַּסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנג.): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא? "וְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמַעְנָה דָבָר מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כא);
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef, Ha'azinu and Shabbat Shuvah 6
connections.canonicalRef: Tiferet Yosef, Ha'azinu and Shabbat Shuvah 6
connections.quote: “‘May my teaching drop like rain; may my utterance flow like dew.’ My holy grandfather explained ya'arof as related to the back of the neck: some words of Torah hold a person from behind his neck and do not let him turn from Hashem's will. If a person clearly recognized direct light from Hashem and stood face to face before Him, there would be no place for service; he would recognize explicitly that departing from His will by a hair's breadth is departing from life. Because Hashem desires to benefit His creatures, He concealed this light, and a person does not stand so directly face to face. He must break through the concealment, recognize Hashem's light explicitly, and stand face to face again. Thus, when receiving prophecy, the prophet said, ‘Thus says Hashem,’ standing face to face and recognizing His will explicitly. The Talmud says (Megillah 32a): from where is it known that one may make use of a heavenly echo? From ‘Your ears will hear a word from behind you’ (Isaiah 30:21). When the person is in concealment, he must recognize Hashem's light from behind: he must attend to the words of Torah that hold him within the concealment so he does not turn from His will. This is called a heavenly echo. Those words of Torah that hold him within concealment are called ‘May my teaching drop like rain.’ When he breaks through the concealment and stands face to face before Hashem's light, this signifies ‘May my utterance flow like dew.’”
connections.explanation: Rav Tzadok emphasizes the end at which an action becomes known; Tiferet Yosef reads the same ‘word from behind you’ as Torah holding a person to Hashem's will while clarity is absent. The readings are complementary rather than identical. The second explains how to continue the effort and hope required by the siman without pretending to know the final verdict.
connections.headline: Guidance while the final result is still concealed

connections.hePhrase: [קלט] כָּל הַפְּעֻלּוֹת וְהָעֲבוֹדוֹת נִיכָּרִים רַק בַּסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנג.): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא? "וְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמַעְנָה דָבָר מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כא);
connections.quote: “Meaning: even though their forefathers had to rely on faith alone during the dark, as in "and Your faithfulness in the nights" (Psalms 92:3), before the morning light broke, they too believe in the dark, continually renewing their faith. For even regarding faith itself one needs faith, casting all upon "Cast your burden upon Hashem," constantly yearning for salvation: "Wait for Hashem; be strong, and let your heart take courage; yea, wait for Hashem" (Psalms 27:14). They hope and strengthen themselves through their longing to merit the light, and though it has not yet appeared, they hope anew and never fall from their faith.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek describes a person hoping, gaining strength through hope, and hoping again while the expected light remains concealed. This develops the siman’s concluding instruction to strengthen prayer: waiting for the end is not passive suspension of choice. The repeated return to Hashem is the form that effort takes when the outcome cannot yet be known.
connections.headline: Hope that continues before the answer is visible

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּדְמֶה צַדִּיק וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ אוֹמְרִים לוֹ "צַדִּיק אַתָּה" – הֱיֵה וְכוּלֵי (נִדָּה ל:),
connections.quote: ‘What oath do they make him swear? ‘Be righteous and do not be wicked. Even if the whole world tells you, “You are righteous,” regard yourself as though you were wicked. Know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is pure, His servants are pure, and the soul He has placed within you is pure. If you preserve it in purity, well and good; if not, I will take it from you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאִם בַּסּוֹף יֹאמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלֹּא הִצְלִיחַ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, אָז כָּל מִקּוֹדֶם נִקְרָא שֶׁקֶר וְכָזָב, לְשׁוֹן הֶפְסֵק, כְּמוֹ "יְכַזְּבוּ מֵימָיו" (יְשַׁעְיָה נח, יא).
connections.quote: ‘Hashem will guide you continually, satisfy your soul in parched places, and strengthen your bones. You will be like a well-watered garden and like a spring whose waters do not fail.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה – זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ זְכִיּוֹת, וְגַם מִקּוֹדֶם הִצְלִיחַ.
connections.quote: see note 1016.
connections.context: The Gemara gives the transformation of deliberate sins into merits cited here and explicitly distinguishes it from repentance motivated by fear. The condition of repentance from love is therefore retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים נד:): שִׁבְעָה דְּבָרִים מְכֻסִּים מִבְּנֵי אָדָם וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: Seven things are hidden from human beings: the day of death, the day of consolation, the depth of judgment, what is in another person’s heart, how a person will earn a profit, when the kingdom of the house of David will return, and when the guilty kingdom will come to an end.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "מְכֻסִּים מִבְּנֵי אָדָם" – הַיְינוּ אַף מִמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבִּבְנֵי אָדָם
connections.quote: ““The matter that is too difficult for you”: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: “You judge a difficult case? By your life, I shall make known to you that you do not judge a difficult case. I shall bring before you a case that your student’s student can understand, while you cannot understand it.” Which was this? The case of the daughters of Tzelofchad, as it is said, “Moshe brought their case before Hashem.””
connections.context: This is the Moshe passage immediately preceding the Samuel passage in the existing note. It supplies the source’s own example of knowledge withheld even from Moshe, without repeating the account about Samuel.

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סִפְרֵי דְּבָרִים פִּסְקָא יז) בִּשְׁמוּאֵל: "אַל תַּבֵּט אֶל מַרְאֵהוּ", לְפִי שֶׁאָמַר: "אָנֹכִי הָרֹאֶה"],
connections.quote: “Samuel answered Saul, “I am the seer.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Are you the seer? I will let you know that you do not see! … When he saw Eliab, he said, “Surely the Lord’s anointed is before Him.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Did you not say, “I am the seer”? “Do not look at his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him.””
connections.context: The Sifrei explicitly connects Samuel’s self-description as “the seer” with his mistaken judgment of Eliab. The biblical verse alone did not supply that connection, which is essential to Rav Tzadok’s warning about certainty in one’s own perception.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הָעֵצָה מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: "וְקֹוֵי ה' הֵמָּה יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ט), וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַחוֹסֶה בִי יִנְחַל אֶרֶץ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נז, יג), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יב:): נַחֲלָה אֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק.
connections.quote: ‘For evildoers will be cut off, but those who wait for Hashem—they will inherit the land.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק הָעֵצָה מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: "וְקֹוֵי ה' הֵמָּה יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ט), וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַחוֹסֶה בִי יִנְחַל אֶרֶץ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נז, יג), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יב:): נַחֲלָה אֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק.
connections.quote: ‘When you cry out, let what you have gathered rescue you. The wind will carry all of them away; a breath will take them. But the one who takes refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק הָעֵצָה מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: "וְקֹוֵי ה' הֵמָּה יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ט), וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַחוֹסֶה בִי יִנְחַל אֶרֶץ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נז, יג), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יב:): נַחֲלָה אֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק.
connections.quote: ‘Or perhaps even the first tithe should cease? Scripture therefore says: ‘Speak to the Levites and say to them: When you take from the children of Israel the tithe that I have given you from them as your inheritance.’ Scripture compares it to an inheritance: just as an inheritance has no interruption, so the first tithe has no interruption.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ תְּפִלָּה וְרַחֲמִים, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא קִיוּוּי לַה', כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קַוֵּה אֶל ה' חֲזַק וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה'" (תְּהִלִּים כז, יד), וְלָמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): תְּפִלָּה צְרִיכָה חִזּוּק.
connections.quote: ‘Wait for Hashem. Be strong, and let your heart be courageous; wait for Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ תְּפִלָּה וְרַחֲמִים, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא קִיוּוּי לַה', כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קַוֵּה אֶל ה' חֲזַק וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה'" (תְּהִלִּים כז, יד), וְלָמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): תְּפִלָּה צְרִיכָה חִזּוּק.
connections.quote: ‘What is the source regarding prayer? It is said: ‘Hope in Hashem; be strong and let your heart take courage, and hope in Hashem.’ What is the source regarding worldly activity? It is said: ‘Be strong, and let us strengthen ourselves for our people,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ תְּפִלָּה וְרַחֲמִים, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא קִיוּוּי לַה', כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קַוֵּה אֶל ה' חֲזַק וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה'" (תְּהִלִּים כז, יד), וְלָמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): תְּפִלָּה צְרִיכָה חִזּוּק.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: If a person sees that he prayed and was not answered, he should pray again, as it is said, “Hope to Hashem; be strong and let your heart take courage, and hope to Hashem.””
connections.context: This earlier statement in the same discussion explains the repeated “hope” as renewed prayer after an unanswered prayer. It complements the existing quotation about prayer requiring strength.

connections.hePhrase: [קמ] כָּל זְמַן שֶׁאֵין הָאָדָם בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, כָּל מַה שֶּׁמְּדַמֶּה לוֹ, יֵדַע שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּעִנְיַן "הָאֹמְרִים לָרַע טוֹב וְלַטּוֹב רָע" (יְשַׁעְיָה ה, כ),
connections.quote: ‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness into light and light into darkness, who make bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter.’

connections.hePhrase: [קמ] כָּל זְמַן שֶׁאֵין הָאָדָם בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, כָּל מַה שֶּׁמְּדַמֶּה לוֹ, יֵדַע שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּעִנְיַן "הָאֹמְרִים לָרַע טוֹב וְלַטּוֹב רָע" (יְשַׁעְיָה ה, כ),
connections.quote: “Those whose bodies are ill taste the bitter as sweet and the sweet as bitter. Some of the sick desire and crave foods unfit to eat, such as earth and charcoal, and hate good foods such as bread and meat, all according to the severity of the illness. Similarly, people whose souls are ill desire and love bad character traits, hate the good way, and are sluggish about following it; it is very burdensome to them, according to their illness. Of such people Isaiah says, “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness into light and light into darkness, bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter.” Of them it says, “Those who abandon upright paths to walk in ways of darkness.” What is the remedy for those whose souls are ill? They should go to the sages, who are physicians of souls, and they will heal their illness through the character traits they teach them, until they bring them back to the good way. Of those who recognize their bad traits but do not go to the sages to heal them, Solomon says, “Fools despise wisdom and instruction.””
connections.context: Rambam explains the same verse through a comparison between distorted taste and distorted moral judgment. His remedy—learning better traits from the sages—is part of the full teaching, rather than leaving the problem without a path of correction.

connections.hePhrase: רַק מִי שֶׁהֵאִיר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֵינָיו בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה דִּכְתִיב בָּהּ "אֱמֶת" כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד:), עַל יָדָהּ יָכוֹל לָבוֹא עַל הָאֱמֶת,
connections.quote: ‘Alternatively, you may say: Do not reverse the statements. Regarding Torah, where ‘truth’ is written—as it is written, ‘Acquire truth and do not sell it’—the Holy One, blessed be He, does not go beyond the strict line of justice. Regarding judgment, where ‘truth’ is not written, the Holy One, blessed be He, goes beyond the strict line of justice.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כו:): עֵצָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ דְּבַר ה' – הִיא תָקוּם.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbah said: If they study Torah for its own sake, [such worry] has no effect, as it is said: ‘Many are the thoughts in a person’s heart, but Hashem’s counsel shall stand.’ Counsel that contains the word of Hashem shall stand forever.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בְּלָאו הָכִי, מַחֲשָׁבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לְבַטֵּל, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַסּוֹף מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁחָשַׁב.
connections.quote: ““Thought”: Anxiety of the heart about a person’s livelihood. “Has an effect”: It causes him to forget his learning. “He frustrates the thoughts of the cunning”: He gives them sustenance and removes thoughts from their hearts that would not allow them to accomplish Torah wisdom. Another interpretation: Thought that a person thinks, “I shall do such and such; such and such will succeed for me,” has the effect of disrupting the matter, so that his plan is not fulfilled, even concerning Torah—for example, saying, “By a particular day I shall finish studying such and such tractates.” “He frustrates the thoughts of the cunning”: Their plans do not succeed, even concerning Torah wisdom.”
connections.context: Rashi records two readings: worry that impairs learning, and confident planning whose projected outcome is frustrated. Rav Tzadok’s explanation here follows the second; neither the first interpretation nor the Gemara’s existing qualification about study for its own sake is suppressed.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד" (מִשְׁלֵי יב, יט), וְאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפח עַמּוּד ב): כּוֹנַנְתָּ לֹא כְּתִיב אֶלָּא "תִּכּוֹן".
connections.quote: ‘Truthful speech stands forever; a lying tongue lasts only a moment.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד" (מִשְׁלֵי יב, יט), וְאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפח עַמּוּד ב): כּוֹנַנְתָּ לֹא כְּתִיב אֶלָּא "תִּכּוֹן".
connections.quote: “If the verse had said, “The lip of truth has been established forever,” it would be as you say. But it says only “shall be established”: the lip of truth is destined to be established, unlike its present state. Now the lip of falsehood stands, while the lip of truth lies in the dust. When truth rises to its standing and springs from the earth, then “the lip of truth shall be established forever.””
connections.context: The Zohar answers an objection drawn from the present apparent success of falsehood. Its emphasis is the future tense of tikkon, which allows Rav Tzadok to distinguish present concealment from future establishment.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נז:): חֲלוֹם אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בִּנְבוּאָה, וְכֵן שַׁבָּת אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “Five, six, and ten—a mnemonic. Five things are one-sixtieth: fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and a dream. Fire is one-sixtieth of Gehinnom; honey, one-sixtieth of manna; Shabbat, one-sixtieth of the World to Come; sleep, one-sixtieth of death; and a dream, one-sixtieth of prophecy.”
connections.context: This is the complete fivefold comparison containing both examples cited by Rav Tzadok: the dream’s relation to prophecy and Shabbat’s relation to the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נה:): הַחֲלוֹמוֹת הוֹלְכִים אַחַר הַפֶּה
connections.quote: “Rabbi Bizna bar Zavda said in Rabbi Akiva’s name, who said in Rabbi Panda’s name, who said in Rav Nachum’s name, who said in Rabbi Birayim’s name, in the name of a certain elder—Rabbi Bena’ah: There were twenty-four interpreters of dreams in Jerusalem. Once I dreamed a dream and went to all of them. What one interpreted for me another did not, and all of their interpretations came true for me, fulfilling the saying, “All dreams follow the mouth.” Is “All dreams follow the mouth” a verse? Yes, in accordance with Rabbi Elazar’s teaching: From where do we know that all dreams follow the mouth? As it is said, “As he interpreted for us, so it happened.” Rava said: This applies when he interprets it in keeping with the dream, as it is said, “He interpreted for each according to his dream.””
connections.context: The discussion gives both the principle and its express limit: the interpretation must correspond to the dream. Rav Tzadok applies dream interpretation as an analogy for the clarifying work of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נה:): הַחֲלוֹמוֹת הוֹלְכִים אַחַר הַפֶּה
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
connections.quote: “‘You hear a dream to interpret it.’ All the matters of this world are like a dream requiring interpretation, and as a person interprets it, so it is established with him. The person who understands in everything that all is only from Hashem and that all lives through the utterance of His mouth understands the meaning in every matter and reaches true life. With bread, for example, the principal life-giving element within it is the utterance of Hashem's mouth. Someone who eats simply like an animal receives from the bread only the life of this world. Someone who understands that Hashem's utterance gives life attains enduring life. For the letters of lechem, bread, are those of chalom, dream: it requires interpretation. So it is with all pleasures, for all the pleasures and benefits in the world are likened to bread.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach develops the siman's dream analogy through an ordinary act: eating bread. Receiving only the outward food gives temporal life, while recognizing Hashem's utterance within it connects the act to enduring life. This helps explain why Rav Tzadok locates the power of interpretation in Torah and in the person's attachment to truth, rather than in an arbitrary favorable statement about events.
connections.headline: Interpreting the world through the life within it

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה יָכוֹל לְבָרֵר כָּל מַעֲשִׂים שֶׁעָשָׂה יִהְיֶה לְטוֹב,
connections.quote: “For truth is also mixed into imagination, as with a dream, which is imagination yet contains both straw and grain. “They are clarified through wisdom”—meaning through Torah. This resembles Shmuel, who once said, “Dreams speak vanity,” and on another occasion took the dream favorably, for all dreams follow the mouth: “Kingship is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah.” These are the words of the sages and their mouths, as it is written, “Speak”—these are the masters of Talmud, whose entire conversation is Torah; this is not the place to elaborate. Therefore it is said, “Educate a youth according to his way.” Through Torah he can select the truth from within it and remove the scheming and imagination.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok develops the dream analogy into the distinction between mixed imagination and truth clarified through Torah. The excerpt gives the original account of how the “mouth” is associated with the sages and the Oral Torah.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "תַּכְלִית הַיְּדִיעָה שֶׁלֹּא נֵדַע".
connections.quote: “The utmost of what we know of You is that we do not know You.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "תַּכְלִית הַיְּדִיעָה שֶׁלֹּא נֵדַע".
connections.quote: “Avraham our father illuminated this light: although it is an understanding concealed from every thought, nevertheless, by apprehending that there is a concealed light here, we have already reached the ultimate knowledge—that we do not know. This was the beginning of Avraham our father’s apprehension, at the beginning of the light’s dawning: to apprehend that there is a concealed reality. He attained this through his great endeavor, without ceasing day or night.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the expression “the ultimate knowledge is that we do not know” as recognition of a hidden divine reality. This directly illuminates why awareness of concealment can itself be a form of illumination.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה נִקְרָא "עֲנָוָה", וְהוּא מַדְרֵגָה הַיּוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: “Piety is greater than them all, as it is said, “Then You spoke in a vision to Your pious ones.” This disagrees with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Humility is greater than them all, as it is said, “The spirit of Hashem God is upon me, because Hashem has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble.” It does not say “the pious,” but “the humble.” Thus you learn that humility is greater than them all.”
connections.context: The statement about humility is Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s view. The quotation retains the preceding preference for piety so that the Talmud’s explicit disagreement is not turned into a unanimous ranking.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וַעֲנָוִים יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (תְּהִלִּים לז, יא) – פֵּירוּשׁ, יְרֻשָּׁה אֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכט:),
connections.quote: ‘The humble will inherit the land and delight in abundant peace.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וַעֲנָוִים יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (תְּהִלִּים לז, יא) – פֵּירוּשׁ, יְרֻשָּׁה אֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכט:),
connections.quote: ‘But Rav Acha, son of Rav Avya, sent the following teaching: According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, if someone says, ‘My property is yours, and after you it shall go to so-and-so,’ and the first recipient is eligible to inherit him, the second recipient has no claim in place of the first. For this is language of inheritance, not of a gift, and inheritance has no interruption!’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם: "לֹא כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים לד, ז), שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ לְמַעֲלוֹתָיו שׁוּם הֶפְסֵק,
connections.quote: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than any man on the face of the earth.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם: "לֹא כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים לד, ז), שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ לְמַעֲלוֹתָיו שׁוּם הֶפְסֵק,
connections.quote: ‘Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died. His eye had not grown dim, and his vigor had not departed.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם: "לֹא כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים לד, ז), שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ לְמַעֲלוֹתָיו שׁוּם הֶפְסֵק,
connections.quote: ““Nor had his freshness departed”: His moisture. Since an old person normally becomes increasingly dry and loses his moisture, Scripture testifies here about Moshe that his moisture had not departed from him. We find the word lecho written with an added heh. Consider that when the prophet was born, Scripture added a heh, and now, at his death, it also added one. This explains that the Divine Presence remained attached to him throughout his existence, even after his death.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya reads the unusual spelling as a sign of the Divine Presence’s continuing attachment to Moshe. This supplies the source’s own explanation of continuity even after death.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר (הוֹשֵׁעַ ו, ד): "מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה לָּךְ וְגוֹמֵר, וְחַסְדְּכֶם כַּעֲנַן בֹּקֶר וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁפּוֹסֵק מִיָּד הַחֵשֶׁק,
connections.quote: ‘What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your loyalty is like a morning cloud, like dew that vanishes early.’

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, כִּי מִמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת וּרְצוֹנוֹת הַטּוֹבוֹת שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל נִבְנֶה קוֹמַת הַנָּבִיא וַחֲכַם הַדּוֹר,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
connections.quote: “It is known that the leader of a generation has a soul encompassing all the souls of that generation, as the Sages said (Arakhin 17a), a leader according to the generation, and a generation according to the leader. Every generation is a particular arrangement of the souls of that generation—that is, parts of Hashem's wisdom, as explained. The gathering of all those wisdoms is itself also one soul. Souls divide into details and further details according to the order Hashem arranged, and their totality is itself a distinct soul, different from the details taken alone. The father's soul includes the souls of all his children; Adam included the souls of all the generations, and their totality was Adam's distinct soul. Likewise, the leader's soul includes all the generation's souls, as a king is the whole nation. He can therefore lead them all, because his wisdom includes all their wisdom, and likewise his understanding and all his spiritual powers.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim explains the siman's statement that the generation's thoughts and desires build the stature of its leader. Their gathering is itself described as a distinct soul, with the leader including their wisdom and powers. This makes the relation reciprocal rather than a claim about popularity, and clarifies why the siman discusses the generation's brief illumination and its leader together.
connections.headline: The leader and the generation’s combined soul

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ: אֵיזֶה דוֹר חָבִיב וְכוּלֵי? דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, וְהָיָה אָז פַּרְנָס מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֹא קָם וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ‘No prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses, whom Hashem knew face to face.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ: אֵיזֶה דוֹר חָבִיב וְכוּלֵי? דּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, וְהָיָה אָז פַּרְנָס מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֹא קָם וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: see note 408.
connections.context: The Yerushalmi reports an exchange used by Yeravam’s scoffers to lure an upright person toward idolatry. Rav Tzadok draws on that person’s immediate identification of the wilderness generation as beloved; the scoffers’ attempted justification of idolatry is part of the reported provocation, not the teaching to adopt.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (תַּעֲנִית ה:): "בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם" לֹא נֶאֱמַר, אֶלָּא "בְּאִמְרֵי פִי" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ו, ה)
connections.quote: ‘Can one person be displaced to make way for another? Yes, for Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: What is the meaning of ‘Therefore I hewed down the prophets; I slew them by the utterances of My mouth’? It does not say ‘by their deeds,’ but ‘by the words of My mouth.’ Thus, one person can be displaced to make way for another.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (תַּעֲנִית ה:): "בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם" לֹא נֶאֱמַר, אֶלָּא "בְּאִמְרֵי פִי" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ו, ה)
connections.quote: ‘Therefore I hewed down the prophets; I slew them by the utterances of My mouth. How, then, could your judgment come forth into the light?’

connections.hePhrase: [קמב] אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבְּעִנְיְנֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין לָאָדָם לִסְמוֹךְ עַל נֵס כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת לב.), בְּעִנְיְנֵי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא יִסְמוֹךְ אַף עַל נֵס.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yannai would inspect a crossing and then cross it. Rabbi Yannai followed his own teaching: A person should never stand in a dangerous place expecting a miracle to be performed for him, for perhaps no miracle will be performed. Even if a miracle is performed for him, it is deducted from his merits. Rabbi Chanin said: What verse teaches this? ‘I have become small through all the kindnesses and all the faithfulness.’ On a day when a strong south wind was blowing, Rabbi Zeira would not go out among the palm trees.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "בְּטַח בַּה' וַעֲשֵׂה טוֹב וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ג), וְלֹא יָחוּשׁ שֶׁחַס וְשָׁלוֹם הַמַּעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים לָרִיק;
connections.quote: ‘Trust in Hashem and do good; dwell in the land and find your nourishment in faithfulness.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "בְּטַח בַּה' וַעֲשֵׂה טוֹב וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ג), וְלֹא יָחוּשׁ שֶׁחַס וְשָׁלוֹם הַמַּעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים לָרִיק;
connections.quote: “Emunah is related to ‘as a nurse carries the infant.’ As the Tikkunei Zohar explains (introduction, 2a), ‘the father of faith, which is understanding.’ One should not hasten the time or press the hour, but wait in faith. Then this kindness will be revealed, and he will recognize it within his understanding too. ‘Tend faith’ means to guard the matter until it is also revealed in one's understanding. The term faith applies only to what is not explicit in one's understanding: what is already explicit needs no faith. What is not explicit requires faith—guarding the matter well until it emerges into explicit revelation before human eyes.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same ‘trust in Hashem’ passage through a definition of faith: holding to what has not yet become clear without forcing its time. This qualifies the siman's permission to hope for an unexpected spiritual rescue. The hope accompanies its stated first response of doing good and prayer; it is not a timetable imposed on the rescue.
connections.headline: Faith that does not force the time

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (תּוֹלְדוֹת קמב עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "עָז לוֹ בָךְ" (שָׁם פד, ו) – הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיָן זֶה, שֶׁ"מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם", שֶׁיַּעַזְרֶנּוּ וִיהַפֵּךְ לִבּוֹ לְטוֹב, עַל זֶה יוּכַל לִסְמוֹךְ וְלֹא כַּחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ‘Rather, a person should not be so assured as to say, ‘The Holy One, blessed be He, will save me,’ or ‘He will do such and such for me.’ He should instead place his reliance upon the Holy One, blessed be He, to help him when he strives to fulfill the Torah’s commandments and to walk a path of truth. For when a person comes to purify himself, he is certainly helped. In this he should rely upon the Holy One, blessed be He, that He will help him; he should rely upon Him and place his reliance upon no other. This is why it says, ‘Whose strength is in You.’ ‘Paths are in their hearts’—he should make his heart fitting, without any other thought, like a road properly laid out for passage wherever it is needed; so too here.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (תּוֹלְדוֹת קמב עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "עָז לוֹ בָךְ" (שָׁם פד, ו) – הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיָן זֶה, שֶׁ"מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם", שֶׁיַּעַזְרֶנּוּ וִיהַפֵּךְ לִבּוֹ לְטוֹב, עַל זֶה יוּכַל לִסְמוֹךְ וְלֹא כַּחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Happy is the person whose strength is in You; highways are in their hearts.”
connections.context: The unusual expression “highways in their hearts” is the wording interpreted by the preceding Zohar passage. Rav Tzadok understands those inner paths as the heart’s direction toward good and its reliance on divine assistance.

connections.hePhrase: וּ"מְסִלּוֹת" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵינוֹ הַדֶּרֶךְ כְּבוּשָׁה, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לַעֲשׂוֹת מְסִלָּה מִן הַצַּד בִּלְבָבָם לְטוֹבָה.
connections.quote: “Therefore he does not succeed by entering through the lower opening, which is “the gate of the Lord through which the righteous enter,” merely restraining himself because the thing is forbidden. He must raise himself to a higher level, the upper opening: not doing anything that does not give satisfaction and fulfill the will of the blessed Lord. Even if it has become like something permitted to him, he nevertheless recognizes that it is at least not the fulfillment of the blessed Lord’s will. When he takes to heart whether it is the blessed Lord’s will, what desire the blessed Lord has in this, and that he does not wish to do anything that is not His will, he thereby escapes every kind of enticement by the inclination, even in the strongest trial. This accords with the well-known account of what happened to one of the outstanding holy men of the generation before ours. This is the gate through which penitents enter, which is a higher place. It is the lower opening in the first heh of the divine name, while in the final heh it is the upper opening; the lower opening is the gate open to the righteous.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: כָּל נֵס הוּא יֵשׁ מִיֵּשׁ וְלֹא בַּאֲתַר רֵיקַנְיָא, וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא מִקּוֹדֶם.
connections.quote: “Through an awakening below there is an awakening above, for there is no awakening above until there is an awakening below. And the blessings from above are found only in something that has substance, and not in what is empty. From where do we learn this? From the wife of Obadiah, to whom Elisha said: ‘Tell me, what do you have in the house?’ (II Kings 4:2), for the blessings from above do not rest on an empty table, nor in an empty place.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: כָּל נֵס הוּא יֵשׁ מִיֵּשׁ וְלֹא בַּאֲתַר רֵיקַנְיָא, וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא מִקּוֹדֶם.
connections.quote: ““A border of gold around it”: A sign of the crown of kingship, for the table signifies wealth and greatness, as people speak of “the table of kings”—Rashi’s explanation. This is indeed so, for this is the secret of the table: since the world came into existence, the blessing of Hashem does not create something from nothing; the world follows its customary order, as it is written, “God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good.” But when the root of something is present, the blessing rests upon it and increases it. Thus Elisha said, “Tell me what you have in the house,” and the blessing rested on a small vessel of oil and filled all the vessels. With Eliyahu, “The jar of flour did not come to an end, and the flask of oil did not diminish.” Likewise, the blessing rests on the table through the showbread, and from it abundance comes to all Israel. Therefore they said that any priest who received a portion the size of a bean would eat and be satisfied.”
connections.context: Ramban explains the usual pattern in which miraculous abundance grows from an existing thing. Rav Tzadok first invokes this pattern and then distinguishes a further level of renewal from nothing.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי וְגוֹמֵר", וּכִשְׁאֵלָתֵנוּ: "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְגוֹמֵר";
connections.quote: see note 272.
connections.context: The verse asks God to create the heart anew and renew the spirit. These exact verbs matter for Rav Tzadok’s account of divine transformation of the heart. This is David’s prayer in Psalm 51; the reader’s expanded phrase “as Shammai said” does not identify the source correctly.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי וְגוֹמֵר", וּכִשְׁאֵלָתֵנוּ: "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ וְגוֹמֵר";
connections.quote: “Turn us to You, Hashem, and we shall return; renew our days as of old.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַנִּסִּים הַנֶּעְלָמִים בְּדֶרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע כְּמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: "וְעַל נִסֶּיךָ וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “This is what Rabbi Elazar said: What is the meaning of “He alone performs great wonders, and blessed be His glorious name forever”? Even the person for whom a miracle occurs does not recognize his miracle.”
connections.context: The Gemara explicitly allows for a miracle hidden even from its beneficiary. This provides the original formulation behind the discussion of concealed miracles.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הַבַּת קוֹל שֶׁיּוֹצֵאת בְּכָל יוֹם: "שׁוּבוּ וְכוּלֵי", וְהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם גָּדוֹל.
connections.quote: “How much must a person look into and know the service of his Master! For every single day a herald calls out and says: ‘How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?’ (Proverbs 1:22); ‘Return, wayward children, I will heal your backslidings’ (Jeremiah 3:22). Yet no one inclines his ear; the Torah proclaims before them, and no one pays heed.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הַבַּת קוֹל שֶׁיּוֹצֵאת בְּכָל יוֹם: "שׁוּבוּ וְכוּלֵי", וְהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם גָּדוֹל.
connections.displayRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 21:1
connections.canonicalRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 21:1
connections.quote: “The assistance comes through the heavenly voice, “Return, wayward children,” which was heard even by Acher, as stated in Chagigah. What benefit does the heavenly voice provide? This follows what the Baal Shem Tov said about the teaching that every day a heavenly voice goes out from Mount Chorev, saying, “Woe to the creatures for the insult to Torah.” What benefit is there in the voice if its sound is not heard? He said that from it comes an awakening within Israel’s heart toward Torah. Likewise, from the heavenly voice, “Return, wayward children,” thoughts of repentance awaken in a Jewish heart; the person simply does not pay attention and supposes them to be ordinary thoughts of his own heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains how the daily call can work without being audibly heard: it is experienced as an inward awakening. The passage attributes this explanation of the heavenly voice to the Baal Shem Tov.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ: "גּוֹל עַל ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים לז, ה) – אַחַר "וּבְטַח וְגוֹמֵר" יָבוֹא לְמַדְרֵגָה שְׁנִיָּה שֶׁ"הוּא יַעֲשֶׂה": הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ יַעֲשֶׂה הַכֹּל
connections.quote: “Roll your way onto the Lord; trust in Him, and He will act.”
connections.context: “Roll your way onto” expresses entrusting one’s course to God. Rav Tzadok attends to the progression from trust to “He will act,” and also expounds the word al, “onto” or “upon,” in the following phrase.

connections.hePhrase: [פֵּירוּשׁ "עַל" – בְּסָמוּךְ, גַּם "עַל" מַמָּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: "כֶּתֶר יִתְּנוּ וְגוֹמֵר", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כא): מִתְּפִלָּתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל],
connections.quote: “After all the congregations finish all their prayers, the angel appointed over prayers takes all the prayers that they prayed in all the congregations, makes them into crowns, and places them on the head of the Holy One, blessed be He. … The Holy One, blessed be He, crowns Himself with the prayers of Israel.”
connections.context: The Midrash describes Israel’s prayers as crowns placed above. Rav Tzadok invokes that image when expounding al, “upon,” in entrusting one’s way to God.

connections.hePhrase: וּפְלוּגְתָּא אֵיזֶה גָּדוֹל, וְיָדוּעַ דְּאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abba said in the name of Shmuel: For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed. These said, ‘The halakhah is in accordance with us,’ and those said, ‘The halakhah is in accordance with us.’ A heavenly voice went forth and said: Both these and those are the words of the living God, and the halakhah is in accordance with Beit Hillel.”

connections.hePhrase: וּפְלוּגְתָּא אֵיזֶה גָּדוֹל, וְיָדוּעַ דְּאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: All the prophets prophesied only concerning penitents, but as for the wholly righteous, “No eye has seen, God, apart from You.” This disagrees with Rabbi Abbahu, for Rabbi Abbahu said: In the place where penitents stand, the wholly righteous do not stand, as it is said, “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near”—the far first, and then the near. Rabbi Yochanan interprets it as follows: “The far” is one who was always far from transgression; “the near” is one who was near transgression and has now become far from it.”
connections.context: The Gemara preserves both rankings and their different readings of “far” and “near.” This is the disagreement Rav Tzadok cites before saying that both are words of the living God.

connections.hePhrase: [קמג] כְּשֶׁמַּתְחִיל הָאָדָם לִכְנוֹס לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לוֹ מְאֹד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ יָאִיר מֵבִין פְּתָיִים" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קל).
connections.quote: “The opening of Your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple.”
connections.context: Petach means opening. Rav Tzadok takes that word as the beginning of a person’s entrance into Torah, when an initial illumination grants understanding before sustained effort.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַפְּתִיחָה יָאִיר מְאֹד, שֶׁזֶּה "מֵבִין פְּתָיִים", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ג) דְּקוֹרִין לְיָנוֹקָא פַּתְיָא;
connections.quote: ““A simple person believes every word”: What is peti? A youth, for in Arabia they call a youth patya. … When the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself to Moses, Moses was a novice in prophecy.”
connections.context: The Midrash connects peti with youth and describes Moses as a beginner who must be approached gently. Rav Tzadok invokes this sense of petayim in describing the illumination granted at the beginning of spiritual life.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ מִסְתַּלֵּק, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק זֶה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג): זֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: בְּרֵאשִׁית וְכוּלֵי וַיְהִי אוֹר, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אוֹר שֶׁבָּרָא וְכוּלֵי גְּנָזוֹ;
connections.quote: ““The opening of Your words gives light”: From the opening of Your mouth there was light for us—“God said: Let there be light.””

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ מִסְתַּלֵּק, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק זֶה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג): זֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: בְּרֵאשִׁית וְכוּלֵי וַיְהִי אוֹר, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אוֹר שֶׁבָּרָא וְכוּלֵי גְּנָזוֹ;
connections.quote: “Where is that light? It was hidden away, and it is prepared for the righteous in the future.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok combines two statements from chapter 3: the initial opening brings light, and that original light is subsequently hidden. Both are necessary for his account of illumination followed by concealment.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נֶאֱמַר: "אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי אֱלֹהִים אַתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים פב, ו), שֶׁהָיָה אָז "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ", וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסְתַּלֵּק עַד לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר.
connections.quote: ‘I said: You are divine beings, and all of you are children of the Most High.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נֶאֱמַר: "אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי אֱלֹהִים אַתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים פב, ו), שֶׁהָיָה אָז "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ", וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסְתַּלֵּק עַד לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר.
connections.quote: ““You are divine beings”: Angels. When I gave you the Torah, I gave it to you on the condition that the angel of death would no longer rule over you.”
connections.context: Rashi connects the verse explicitly to the giving of Torah. It supplies the interpretation used here, rather than leaving the reader with the verse’s general reference to divine beings.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה – תְּפִלָּה, כִּידוּעַ דְּהַתְחָלָה הוּא מַדְרֵגַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְהוּא "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ",
connections.quote: “When Hashem gives a person illumination of understanding in the light of Torah, without the person having endured or labored for those words of Torah, then if he turns his attention away even for a moment, Scripture says (Proverbs 23:5), ‘Will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone.’ As the Jerusalem Talmud says at the end of Berakhot in the name of the Scroll of the Pious: if you leave it one day, it leaves you two. But Torah that comes through labor, for which the person has endured, becomes fixed in his heart and will not let him turn away. As it says (Deuteronomy 32:2), ‘May my teaching drop like rain’: my holy grandfather explained that Torah for which a person labors holds him from behind his neck and will not let him turn away, like someone holding his fellow so he cannot leave. If the person nevertheless turns away from Torah that came through labor, he can reawaken it through much prayer and regain his former illumination. Through the endurance and labor he devoted to it, it became fixed in his heart, and he can reawaken the Torah repeatedly through prayer.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef adds a distinction to the siman's account of first light and prayer. A gift can be lost when attention moves away; Torah acquired through effort becomes fixed enough to be awakened again through prayer. This explains a way in which the plea to preserve the first desire works together with the learner's subsequent labor.
connections.headline: Prayer that reawakens Torah acquired through effort

connections.hePhrase: וְהַסּוֹף שֶׁחוֹזֵר לְהָאִיר הוּא דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמָשִׁיחַ, וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה" (שָׁם קט, ד).
connections.quote: “In return for my love they accuse me, but I am prayer.”
connections.context: The striking phrase va’ani tefillah is the one Rav Tzadok cites to identify David with prayer. A contextual translation as “I stand judgment” does not convey the prayer interpretation being used here.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַסּוֹף שֶׁחוֹזֵר לְהָאִיר הוּא דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמָשִׁיחַ, וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה" (שָׁם קט, ד).
connections.quote: “The statement “Be a blessing” resembles King David’s statement “I am prayer”: he himself is the very essence of prayer, drawn from the source of His kingship and lordship, as it is written, “My Lord, open my lips.” This is the realm of speech, as is known and as is written in the Tikkunim. When one accepts His lordship with complete truth, one becomes a vehicle for that attribute and is included in it. This is King David, who is the final deed in particular; therefore the prayer distinctive to the poor belongs to him.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains David’s identification with prayer through acceptance of divine lordship and the dependence expressed by the poor. This develops the brief “I am prayer” citation without repeating the existing Mei HaShiloach passage about preserving desire.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּעֵת בִּנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ" בְּאוֹר גָּדוֹל וְהִתְנַדְּבוּ בְּלֵב שָׁלֵם, פָּתַח בִּתְפִלָּה: "שָׁמְרָה זֹּאת לְעוֹלָם לְיֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבוֹת לְבַב עַמֶּךָ וְהָכֵן לְבָבָם אֵלֶיךָ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יח), שֶׁלֹּא יִסְתַּלֵּק וְיִגָּנֵז
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Psalms 69:1
connections.linkedRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Psalms 69:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Psalms 69:1
connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ליקוטים מכתובים, ספר תהלים ס״ט:א׳
connections.quote: ““But as for me, may my prayer be to You, Lord, at a time of favor.” Sometimes a person feels within himself a great longing and desire to seek the Lord and His strength. At that time he must exert himself in prayer and ask the blessed Lord that this desire remain fixed within him forever. Thus King David, peace be upon him, asked the blessed Lord, when he perceived Israel’s generous-heartedness toward the Temple, “Preserve this forever as the inclination of the thoughts [of Your people’s heart]” (I Chronicles 29:18)—that it never be severed from them. This is the meaning of “A time of favor is significant,” stated in the Gemara (Yevamot 72a).”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּעֵת בִּנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן "פֵּתַח דְּבָרֶיךָ" בְּאוֹר גָּדוֹל וְהִתְנַדְּבוּ בְּלֵב שָׁלֵם, פָּתַח בִּתְפִלָּה: "שָׁמְרָה זֹּאת לְעוֹלָם לְיֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבוֹת לְבַב עַמֶּךָ וְהָכֵן לְבָבָם אֵלֶיךָ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יח), שֶׁלֹּא יִסְתַּלֵּק וְיִגָּנֵז
connections.quote: “Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel our fathers, preserve this forever in the inclination of the thoughts of Your people’s heart, and direct their heart toward You.”
connections.context: David asks that the people’s generous disposition in preparing for the Temple be preserved. Rav Tzadok therefore cites this as prayer that the first illumination remain alive, rather than merely be credited as a past merit.

connections.hePhrase: [דְּזָכָה דִּקְדֻשָּׁה רִאשׁוֹנָה קִדְּשָׁה לִשְׁעָתָהּ וְקִדְּשָׁה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָרַב בִּקְדֻשָּׁתוֹ עוֹמֵד, כִּי קְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ נִשְׁאֲרָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לְעוֹלָם]
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות בית הבחירה ו׳:ט״ז
connections.quote: “Why do I say that, for the Temple and Jerusalem, the first sanctification also sanctified them for the future, while for the holiness of the rest of the Land of Israel concerning the sabbatical year, tithes, and similar matters, it did not sanctify for the future? Because the holiness of the Temple and Jerusalem is due to the Divine Presence, and the Divine Presence is not nullified. It is said, “I shall desolate your sanctuaries,” and the Sages said: Even when they are desolate, they remain in their holiness.”
connections.context: Rambam’s explanation expressly concerns the Temple and Jerusalem, whose holiness depends on the Divine Presence. The quotation retains his distinction from the first sanctification of the rest of the land, so that the enduring holiness is not generalized beyond the source’s scope.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְמִי שֶׁתְּפִלָּתוֹ מִצְוַת אֲנָשִׁים מְלֻמָּדָה, גַּם הָעֲנִיָּה כָּךְ שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַרְגִּישׁ רַק בְּהֶרְגֵּל;
connections.quote: “And Hashem said: Because this people draws near with its mouth and honors Me with its lips, but has removed its heart far from Me, and their fear of Me is a commandment of men learned by rote.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין שׁוּם תְּפִלָּה מֵאִישׁ יִשְׂרְאֵלִי שֶׁלֹּא יֵעָנֶה, רַק עַל כָּל תְּפִלָּה יֵשׁ עֲנִיָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קָרוֹב ה' לְכָל קֹרְאָיו לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת", וְנֶאֱמַר: "תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב" – הַיְינוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל],
connections.quote: “Hashem is near to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין שׁוּם תְּפִלָּה מֵאִישׁ יִשְׂרְאֵלִי שֶׁלֹּא יֵעָנֶה, רַק עַל כָּל תְּפִלָּה יֵשׁ עֲנִיָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קָרוֹב ה' לְכָל קֹרְאָיו לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת", וְנֶאֱמַר: "תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב" – הַיְינוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל],
connections.quote: “You will give truth to Jacob, lovingkindness to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers from the days of old.”

connections.hePhrase: [קמד] בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁהוּא הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁל אָדָם, שָׁם הוּא כָּל הָאָדָם;
connections.quote: “This may be explained by way of allusion, according to what is known from my grandfather, of blessed memory: in the place where a person’s thought is, there he is entirely. The same applies to speech and action: at whatever level and in whatever world he is present, there he is bound entirely to that world.”
connections.context: Degel Machaneh Ephraim transmits the teaching in his grandfather the Baal Shem Tov’s name. This supplies the original attribution and extends the formulation from thought to speech and action.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עִיקַּר הָאָדָם אֵינוֹ הַגּוּף רַק הַנֶּפֶשׁ, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֵינָהּ דָּבָר רַק כֹּחַ הַמְּחַשֵּׁב וּמְהַרְהֵר וְהָרוֹצֶה שֶׁבָּאָדָם.
connections.quote: “It is known to those of understanding that the human body is not the person himself as far as the body is concerned, for it is called the person’s flesh, as it is written, “You clothed me with skin and flesh, and covered me with bones and sinews.” It is also written, “It shall not be poured upon a person’s flesh.” The person is thus the inward being, while the body is a garment in which the intellectual soul, which is the person himself, is clothed while in this world. After death that garment is removed, and he is clothed in a pure, clean, spiritual garment, as it is written, “Remove the filthy garments,” and “Clothe you in fine garments.” This is called the garment of the sages.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital distinguishes the inward person from the body that clothes the soul. This is the metaphysical account underlying Rav Tzadok’s statement that the person’s essential identity is the soul.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָקוֹם שֶׁמַּחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אֲדוּקָה, כָּךְ הוּא כָּל צוּרַת הָאָדָם בְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת.
connections.quote: “A thought of this kind, upon which the heart's principal point of life depends, is the essence of the person—not the other outer thoughts, which are garments of the inward and principal thought. Almost no person is completely pure even in thought's outer garment, belonging to Hashem alone so that no other thought rises in his mind for even one moment throughout his life.”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz makes an explicit distinction relevant to ‘where his thought is attached.’ The thought carrying the heart's central life defines the person at depth; other thoughts can be outer garments. It also acknowledges how difficult it is to be entirely free of a momentary other thought. This helps read the siman's language of attachment with precision while preserving the task of directing thought toward Torah.
connections.headline: The thought that holds the heart’s life

connections.hePhrase: תֵּדַע, שֶׁכֹּחַ הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבָּאָדָם בְּעֵת הַזִּוּוּג פּוֹעֵל בַּוָּלָד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בַּכְּבָשִׂים דְּיַעֲקֹב, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא נָשׂא ז) מִלֵּידַת בֵּן לָבָן לְכוּשִׁיִּים
connections.quote: “An Arab king asked Rabbi Akiva: I am black and my wife is black, but she bore me a white son. I will kill her, for she has been unfaithful to me. He asked him: Are the images in your house black or white? He answered: White. He said: When you were with her, she set her eyes on the white images and bore a child like them. If you wonder at this, learn from Jacob’s sheep, which conceived from the rods, as it is said, “The sheep conceived at the rods.” The Arab king acknowledged the explanation and praised Rabbi Akiva.”
connections.context: This is the Midrashic narrative Rav Tzadok invokes for the effect of the image held in mind at conception; it explicitly links its example to Jacob’s sheep. The relevant source is this story at the end of Nasso 7, rather than the preceding laws of the suspected adulteress.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): "תַּמָּתִי" – תְּאוֹמָתִי וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yannai said: “My perfect one”—My twin; as it were, I am not greater than she, and she is not greater than I. Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in the name of Rabbi Levi: “My twin”—just as, if one of two twins has a headache, the other feels it, so the Holy One, blessed be He, says, “I am with him in distress.””
connections.context: The Midrash reads tamati as te’omati, “My twin.” Rav Tzadok uses this image of corresponding experience to discuss the bond between Israel and God. The analogy concerns that bond and should not be mistaken for a literal bodily identity.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (שָׁם סוֹף פֶּרֶק ג): לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ וְכוּלֵי, וְאָמְרוּ: שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת מִתּוֹךְ גְּרוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: ““With the crown with which his mother crowned him”: Rabbi Yochanan said: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai asked Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosi, “Have you perhaps heard from your father the meaning of ‘With the crown with which his mother crowned him’?” He replied, “Yes.” He asked, “How?” He replied: “It is like a king who had an only daughter whom he loved exceedingly and called ‘my daughter.’ He did not cease loving her until he called her ‘my sister,’ and did not cease loving her until he called her ‘my mother.’ So the Holy One, blessed be He, loved Israel exceedingly and called them ‘My daughter,’ as it is written, ‘Hear, daughter, and see.’ He did not cease loving them until He called them ‘My sister,’ as it is said, ‘Open to Me, My sister, My companion.’ He did not cease loving them until He called them ‘My mother,’ as it is said, ‘Listen to Me, My people, and My nation, give ear to Me’—the written form can be read ‘My mother.’” Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai stood and kissed him on his head, saying, “Had I come only to hear this explanation from your mouth, it would have been enough.””
connections.context: The Midrash’s parable is the source of “He did not cease loving her.” It explains the progression of terms—daughter, sister, and mother—as expressions of divine affection.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (שָׁם סוֹף פֶּרֶק ג): לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ וְכוּלֵי, וְאָמְרוּ: שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת מִתּוֹךְ גְּרוֹנוֹ.
וְאָמְרוּ (שָׁם סוֹף פֶּרֶק ג): לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ וְכוּלֵי, וְאָמְרוּ: שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת מִתּוֹךְ גְּרוֹנוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:2
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:2
connections.quote: “Moshe our teacher had this power: all his speech revealed his essential vitality, for he belongs to the mystery of knowledge, which joins wisdom and understanding, the father and mother. This is the revelation of the covenant of the tongue. Therefore he is called “the husband of the Matron,” for kingship is the mouth, and he has the power to impart to the mouth. Therefore he said, “This is the word,” for his speech was the actual word of Hashem: “The Divine Presence speaks from his throat.” He spoke from his essential vitality, meaning the letters of his soul: the combinations of his soul at that time corresponded to the words he spoke. All the vitality of his soul was gathered within his speech, which he spoke with his whole strength; thus the letters of his soul actually became that combination.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the expression about the Divine Presence speaking through Moshe as speech gathering the whole vitality of the soul. This gives the original development of the connection between inward life and spoken words.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַדָּבֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁמְּחַשֵּׁב בָּהּ תָּמִיד, כָּל אֵבָרָיו כֵּן,
connections.quote: “However, one can say that from the statement "they are not consumed" there is no difficulty: for that phrase "has no dominion," rather than stating "they do not enter at all," makes it clear that they enter, only that the fire does not dominate them; and so they stated in Menachos 100a that Topheth was prepared even for a king who is a Torah scholar; and if so, perforce it does not mean that the fire has no effect at all such that he feels no burning, for if so, for what purpose do they enter and why was it prepared for him? And they also related in Chagigah 15b regarding Acher, that Rabbi Meir caused smoke to ascend from his grave to judge him, showing that the fire held dominion over him even though he was a Torah scholar; and initially when the heavenly court ruled not to judge him on account of his Torah, that meant not to bring him into Gehinnom at all, for since they judged that he would have no share in the World to Come, they gave him the reward of his Torah—which the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold—that he should not be judged or suffer in the agony of Gehinnom; while Rabbi Meir said that he should be judged so that he might ultimately enter the World to Come; yet in any event we see that the fire dominated him even though his entire body was fire!”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin asks explicitly why a scholar whose body is fire can nevertheless undergo judgment, and uses Acher as the difficult example. This qualifies the siman’s account of thought shaping the whole person. Torah’s formative presence is not an automatic exemption from the consequences of misconduct; Rav Tzadok distinguishes entry into judgment from what judgment can ultimately destroy.
connections.headline: Being formed by Torah does not remove accountability

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹף חֲגִיגָה כז.): תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין אוֹר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֶטֶת בָּהֶן, שֶׁכָּל גּוּפָן אֵשׁ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ" (יִרְמְיָה כג, כט).
connections.quote: ‘Is not My word like fire, declares Hashem, and like a hammer that shatters rock?’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת יח:): רְשָׁעִים בְּחַיֵּיהֶם קְרוּיִים מֵתִים, לְפִי שֶׁדְּבוּקָה מַחֲשַׁבְתָּם בְּמָקוֹם הַנִּקְרָא מִיתָה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין קַיָּים לָעַד.
connections.quote: ‘‘The dead know nothing’—these are the wicked, who are called ‘dead’ during their lifetimes, as it is said: ‘And you, slain wicked one, prince of Israel.’ Alternatively, the source is here: ‘On the testimony of two witnesses or on the testimony of three witnesses, the dead man shall be put to death.’ But he is alive! Rather, he was already dead from the outset.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשִׁילְהֵי כְּתוּבּוֹת (קיא:): עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְכוּלֵי מָצָאתִי לָהֶם תַּקָּנָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁמִּצַּד הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם נַעֲשֶׂה כְּמוֹ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם:
connections.quote: “Whoever marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, conducts business on behalf of Torah scholars, or benefits Torah scholars from his property—the verse accounts it to him as though he cleaves to the Divine Presence.”
connections.context: This is the answer to Rabbi Elazar’s question about how people without Torah learning can cleave to God and share in the life associated with Torah. Rav Tzadok stresses their inward attachment to the scholar; the Gemara describes concrete forms of that attachment.

connections.hePhrase: רַק בַּחֲלָבִים וַעֲרָיוֹת שֶׁכֵּן נֶהֱנֶה, וּבַהֲנָאַת אָדָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִתְכַּוֵּין בְּהֶעְלֵם כָּל שֶׁהוּא עַל כָּל פָּנִים, שֶׁבְּטֶבַע הָאָדָם מַרְגִּישׁ בַּהֲנָאָתוֹ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ בְּעַצְמוֹ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ זוֹכֵר.
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman said in Shmuel’s name: One who acts without intending the particular act in the cases of forbidden fats and forbidden relations is liable, because he derives pleasure. One who acts in this manner on Shabbat is exempt, for the Torah prohibited considered labor.”
connections.context: The Gemara states the contrast Rav Tzadok invokes. The liability concerns the sin-offering discussion, and the Shabbat exemption depends on the requirement of considered labor; it does not make every unintended action equivalent.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה", וּלְכָךְ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.),
connections.quote: ‘The Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to a deed, as it is said: ‘If I have seen iniquity in my heart, Hashem will not listen.’ How, then, do I understand ‘Behold, I am bringing evil upon this people, the fruit of their thoughts’? A thought that produces fruit, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins to the deed; a thought that produces no fruit, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join to a deed.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה", וּלְכָךְ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.),
connections.quote: see note 1577.
connections.context: This is the original Talmudic text of the morning prayer. It connects the soul’s purity with its divine source, preservation, and eventual restoration.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל מַחֲשָׁבוֹת רָעוֹת הוּא מֵרוּחַ שְׁטוּת, שֶׁהוּא דִּמְיוֹן הַמִּתְדַּמֶּה לְחָכְמָה כְּקוֹף בִּפְנֵי אָדָם כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: see note 1158.
connections.context: Reish Lakish relates going astray to folly through the wording of the sotah passage. This supplies the direct source for Rav Tzadok’s account of an evil thought as a distortion of understanding.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת, דְּשָׁם מַחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה מִצְטָרֶפֶת שֶׁהוּא בֶּאֱמֶת.
connections.quote: “Our Sages said that the Holy One, blessed be He, joins a good thought to a deed. It seems to me that this means joining it to some deed that was performed without thought, when at another time he has the thought without the deed. Above, beyond time, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins the good thought with the good deed as though everything occurred together. For this reason, the intention need not necessarily be present at the very time of performing the mitzvah, the prayer, or a similar act. Although it is certainly best for his intention to be proper at the time of the act, there is nevertheless a remedy even for someone who did not then intend it: if afterward he merits a proper intention in a holy thought, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins and connects it to the deed and speech, so that they are regarded as having occurred together.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok offers his own interpretation of joining a good thought to a deed. He expressly retains the priority of proper intention at the time of action, while explaining how later intention can repair an earlier deficiency.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּלֹא מַחֲשָׁבָה הוּא בְּעוֹלַם עֲשִׂיָּה, וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי אִישׁ יָרֵא אֶת ה' בְּמִצְוֹתָיו חָפֵץ מְאֹד" (תְּהִלִּים קיב, א),
connections.quote: ‘Hallelujah! Fortunate is the person who fears Hashem and takes great delight in His commandments.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ח.): דְּ"טוֹב לָךְ" לֹא כְּתִיב,
connections.quote: “One who enjoys the labor of his hands is greater than one who fears Heaven. Of one who fears Heaven it is written, “Happy is the person who fears the Lord”; of one who enjoys the labor of his hands it is written, “When you eat the labor of your hands, happy are you and good is yours”—happy in this world, and good in the World to Come. Of one who fears Heaven, “good is yours” is not written.”
connections.context: The teaching compares the scriptural descriptions of two virtues. Rav Tzadok interprets the contrast in terms of fear, inward attainment, and the pleasure of one’s spiritual labor. The Gemara itself does not say that the God-fearing person “sits idly by.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ "אַשְׁרֶיךָ" – בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, "וְטוֹב לָךְ" – לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהוּא בְּיוֹ"ד עַל שֵׁם הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י עַל פָּסוּק "אָז יָשִׁיר".
connections.quote: ““Then Moshe would sing”: Then, when he saw the miracle, the thought arose in his heart to sing a song. Similarly, “Then Yehoshua would speak,” and “He would make a house for Pharaoh’s daughter”—he thought in his heart to make it for her. Here too, “would sing”: his heart told him to sing, and so he did—“They said: I shall sing to Hashem.” Similarly, when Yehoshua saw the miracle, his heart told him to speak, and so he did—“He said before the eyes of Israel.” Likewise, the song of the well begins, “Then Israel would sing,” and afterward spells it out: “Rise up, well; sing to it.” “Then Solomon would build a high place”—the Sages of Israel explained that he sought to build it but did not build it. We have learned that the yod is stated on account of the thought. This resolves the plain meaning.”
connections.context: Rashi’s grammatical explanation is the one expressly cited by Rav Tzadok: the future-form yod can express the thought preceding an act. This selected unit is Rashi’s plain-meaning interpretation; he separately proceeds to discuss the rabbinic allusion to resurrection.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מא.): לְאָדָם טוֹב מַטְעִימִין לוֹ מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “A good person is given a taste of the fruit of his deeds.”
connections.context: The statement is on 41a, continuing Bar Kappara’s teaching from the preceding page. Rav Tzadok interprets this taste as a present experience of the goodness generated through one’s spiritual work.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא בָּא אַחֲרֵי הַיְגִיעַ כַּפַּיִם בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, אַחַר כָּךְ מְהַנִּים אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “It is known that the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah itself: one merits that very matter. Thus Torah scholars have no rest in the world to come, as it says, ‘They go from strength to strength’ (Berakhot 64a). Through their engagement in Torah in this world, they merit delighting in Torah in the world to come. Likewise, through the mitzvah meal they observe in this world, they merit the feast of the righteous in the future, which is the culmination of holy delight, as explained in the holy books. As the Sages said: through fulfilling the mitzvah of sukkah one merits sitting in the sukkah of Leviathan's skin.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains the continuity between a person's embodied service and the good tasted afterward. Torah and the mitzvah meal become the very forms of future delight, rather than a reward detached from the service. This develops the siman's final distinction between the deed alone and enjoyment that makes its inward life perceptible.
connections.headline: The mitzvah itself as the future delight

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ שְׂכָרוֹ רַק "אַשְׁרֵי",
connections.quote: “A Song of Ascents. Happy is everyone who fears Hashem, who walks in His ways. When you eat the labor of your hands, happy shall you be, and it shall be well with you.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא פד.):
connections.quote: ‘One day Rabbi Yochanan was bathing in the Jordan. Reish Lakish saw him and leapt into the Jordan after him. Rabbi Yochanan said to him: ‘Your strength belongs to Torah!’ He replied: ‘Your beauty belongs to women!’ Rabbi Yochanan said to him: ‘If you turn back, I will give you my sister, who is more beautiful than I am.’ He accepted this upon himself. He wanted to return to fetch his belongings, but he could no longer make his way back.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "שְׁחוֹרָה אֲנִי וְנָאוָה",
connections.quote: ‘I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like Solomon’s curtains.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לַחָכְמָה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (תַּעֲנִית ז:):
connections.quote: “But there are beautiful people who are learned!”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לַחָכְמָה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (תַּעֲנִית ז:):
connections.quote: “Had they been ugly, they would have been more learned.”
connections.context: The question and reply conclude Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya’s exchange with Caesar’s daughter about fine wisdom in an unattractive vessel. The comparison with wine preserved in humble earthenware serves the surrounding teaching about humility; the reply does not deny the existence of beautiful Torah scholars.

connections.hePhrase: "אַדְּרַבָּא, אִי הֲווֹ סְנוּ – טְפֵי הֲווֹ גְּמִירֵי".
connections.quote: ““If they were unattractive”: those handsome men who are scholars. “They would have learned more”: because a handsome man cannot humble his own mind, and comes to forgetfulness.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the remark through humility and the retention of learning. His first comment expressly refers to handsome men who already are scholars; that qualification belongs with the sharp formulation that follows.

connections.hePhrase: בַּר פְּלוּגְתֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר שֶׁהָיוּ בָּנָיו יְפֵיפִין בְּיוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים (כ:),
connections.quote: “Why are your children exceptionally beautiful? She said to them: He does not have relations with me at the beginning of the night or at its end, but at midnight. When he does, he uncovers a handbreadth and covers a handbreadth, and he seems like one compelled by a demon.”
connections.context: The question is addressed to Imma Shalom about Rabbi Eliezer. The passage describes his restraint; “like one compelled by a demon” is a comparison, which Rav Tzadok interprets symbolically.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָאָב זוֹכֶה לַבֵּן.
connections.quote: see note 822.
connections.context: This is the Mishnah behind “the father benefits the son.” Its list expressly includes beauty and wisdom, the two qualities under discussion.

connections.hePhrase: לְהוֹרוֹת בָּזֶה עִנְיַן תַּלְמִיד חָכָם דַּהֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה לְגַבֵּי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר דְּשַׁמּוּתִי כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: ““He is shammuti”: they placed him under a ban, as we say in the chapter HaZahav. The Jerusalem Talmud explains “shammuti” to mean that he was among Shammai’s disciples.”
connections.context: Rashi preserves two explanations of the designation applied to Rabbi Eliezer. The second supplies the connection with Shammai; the first prevents treating that connection as the word’s only received explanation.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רעז.)
connections.quote: “The soul is yod, the Hebrew maidservant. Through it, that demon becomes Shaddai, guarding that soul; through it he returns in repentance, blesses the Holy One every day, sanctifies Him, and unites Him in the recitation of Shema.”
connections.context: Ra’aya Meheimna, ZoharIII 277a, connects shed with Shaddai by the addition of yod. Rav Tzadok refers to this symbolic transformation, not to the unrelated greeting between sages previously quoted.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּקֵּשׁ עַל רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר שֶׁיֵּצֵא מֵחֲלָצָיו,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said in Rabbi Chanina’s name: When Moshe ascended on high, he heard the voice of the Holy One, blessed be He, sitting and studying the passage of the red cow, and stating a law in the name of the one who said it: “Rabbi Eliezer says: a calf is one year old, and a cow two years old.” Moshe said before Him: “Master of the worlds, may it be Your will that he descend from me.” He replied: “By your life, he does descend from you.” This is what is written, “The name of the one was Eliezer”: the name of that distinguished one.”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the otherwise unquoted account of Moshe’s request. It connects Rabbi Eliezer’s teaching about the red cow with the name of Moshe’s son Eliezer.
