connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "מוּל בֵּית פְּעוֹר",
connections.quote: ‘He buried him in the valley, in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor. To this day, no one knows his burial place.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "מוּל בֵּית פְּעוֹר",
connections.quote: ““Opposite Beth Peor”: his grave had been prepared there from the six days of Creation to atone for the deed of Peor. This is one of the things created at twilight on the eve of Shabbat.”
connections.context: Rashi makes the relation between the burial place and Peor explicit. This supplies the traditional explanation behind the verse’s role in Rav Tzadok’s account of Moshe.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן ס) עַל פָּסוּק "רָאִיתִי עֲבָדִים וְגוֹמֵר וְשָׂרִים",
connections.quote: “Good within, with an inferior garment—this is “poor and riding upon a donkey.” Evil within, with a beautiful garment outside—of this it is said, “I have seen servants upon horses.” Everything is known through a person’s deeds—who is within. … Fools look at the body, which is a garment; the righteous at good deeds.”
connections.context: Tikkun 60 contrasts inward character with outward appearance. Rav Tzadok cites the image of servants on horses to explain why bodily beauty need not reveal inner spiritual worth.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן ס) עַל פָּסוּק "רָאִיתִי עֲבָדִים וְגוֹמֵר וְשָׂרִים",
connections.quote: ‘I have seen slaves on horses, while princes walk on the ground like slaves.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּיֵשׁ נְפָשׁוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת בְּגוּפִים מְכֹעָרִים,
connections.quote: “Ashur and Egypt are alluded to in ‘I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth’ (Ecclesiastes 10:7). My holy father explained: servants on horses indicate very beautiful and clean garments, while there is a deficiency at the root. As the Tikkunei Zohar says (Tikkun 60), evil within and a beautiful garment outside—of this it says, ‘I have seen servants on horses.’ Princes walking like servants on the earth indicate coarse and darkened garments, while at their root there is no deficiency.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same verse about servants on horses and princes walking on the ground. Its contrast concerns the relation between outward garment and root: an attractive appearance can conceal a deficiency, while a coarse appearance can conceal a root without that deficiency. This explains the siman's distinction without making bodily appearance alone a reliable measure of a person's inward quality.
connections.headline: The garment’s appearance and the soul’s root

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא סו:):
connections.quote: ‘A wise woman asked Rabbi Eliezer: Since their acts in the affair of the calf were alike, why were their deaths not alike? He answered her: A woman’s wisdom is only in the spindle, as Scripture says: ‘Every woman wise of heart spun with her hands.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נִדָּה מה:):
connections.quote: “Rav Chisda said: What is Rabbi’s reason? As it is written, “The Lord God built the side.” This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave greater understanding to a woman than to a man.”
connections.context: The discussion concerns the ages at which a girl’s and a boy’s vows are effective. The exposition associates vayiven, “He built,” with binah, understanding; this is the distinction Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וּמוֹחַ וְלֵב הֵם עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
connections.quote: “The apprehension of the Oral Torah is principally in the wisdom of the mind. Nevertheless, its foundation too depends upon the heart; otherwise it is called, “Why is there a price in a fool’s hand to acquire wisdom, when there is no heart?” The exposition in Yoma applies this to one who has Torah but lacks fear of Heaven: his Torah and wisdom are only like the price with which to buy, without his actually acquiring, for he is in truth a fool. As Devarim Rabbah teaches, all Torah and wisdom are placed in the heart of one who has fear of Heaven. This is “Fear of Hashem is his treasure”: the storehouse that holds wisdom, and this is in the heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s fuller treatment qualifies the distinction between mind and heart. Even the Oral Torah, whose apprehension he locates principally in the mind, requires the heart and fear of Heaven if wisdom is to become a real acquisition.

connections.hePhrase: [קמז] עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה אָדָם זוֹכֶה לְבָנִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי כֵן יְבֹרַךְ גָּבֶר יְרֵא ה'" (תְּהִלִּים קכח, ד).
connections.quote: “Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children like olive saplings around your table.”

connections.hePhrase: [קמז] עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה אָדָם זוֹכֶה לְבָנִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי כֵן יְבֹרַךְ גָּבֶר יְרֵא ה'" (תְּהִלִּים קכח, ד).
connections.quote: “Behold, so shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed.”
connections.context: “So shall he be blessed” points back to the household and children in the preceding verse. Including that verse makes the connection between fear of God and children explicit.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם שֵׁם הַגְּבוּרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר וְכוּלֵי" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, א).
connections.quote: ‘Ben Zoma says: Who is wise? Someone who learns from every person, as it says: ‘From all my teachers I have gained understanding, for Your testimonies are my meditation’ (Psalms 119). Who is mighty? Someone who masters his inclination, as it says: ‘One who is slow to anger is better than a mighty warrior, and one who rules his own spirit is better than one who captures a city’ (Proverbs 16). Who is wealthy? Someone who rejoices in his portion, as it says: ‘When you eat the labor of your hands, you are fortunate, and it is good for you’ (Psalms 128). ‘You are fortunate’ refers to this world; ‘it is good for you’ refers to the World to Come. Who is honored? Someone who honors other people, as it says: ‘Those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be held in contempt’ (I Samuel 2).’

connections.hePhrase: אָז זוֹכֶה לִשְׂכַר פְּרִי הַבֶּטֶן.
connections.quote: “Behold, children are a heritage from Hashem; the fruit of the womb is a reward.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁ"הַגֶּפֶן פֹּרִיָּה" עוֹשָׂה פֵּירוֹת זֵיתִים,
connections.quote: see note 1785.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי שֶׁמֶן הוּא חָכְמָה וְגֶפֶן יִרְאָה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְ"רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה יִרְאַת ה'" (שָׁם קיא, י), וְ"אִי יִרְאַת ה' אוֹצָרוֹ – אִין וְכוּלֵי" (שַׁבָּת לא.).
connections.quote: “… wisdom and knowledge; the fear of Hashem is his treasure.”

connections.hePhrase: וְ"יַיִן יְשַׂמַּח לֵבָב" (תְּהִלִּים קד, טו), כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי;
connections.quote: ‘Wine gladdens the human heart, oil makes the face shine, and bread sustains the human heart.’

connections.hePhrase: וְ"יַיִן יְשַׂמַּח לֵבָב" (תְּהִלִּים קד, טו), כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי;
connections.displayRef: Peri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 4:1
connections.linkedRef: Peri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 4:1
connections.canonicalRef: Peri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 4:1
connections.heRef: פרי צדיק, קונטרס עמלה של תורה ד׳:א׳
connections.quote: “Every fear of something arises when one fears that some harm will befall him, and he wishes and desires not to have that fear, because being afraid causes him pain. The fear of the Lord is different. It is taught in Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 3: “I feared through my joy, and I rejoiced through my fear.” Joy in the Lord brings one to fear Him because of His exaltedness, blessed be He, which one recognizes through that joy, as it is written, “Rejoice with trembling.” Likewise, from the fear that comes through sensing the light of His revealed indwelling presence within one’s heart, as stated above, one comes to joy.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁזֶּהוּ כַּוָּנַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ד:) עַל "אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא? זֶה הַסּוֹמֵךְ גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
connections.quote: ‘The Master said: He recites the Shema and prays. This supports Rabbi Yochanan, for Rabbi Yochanan said: Who belongs to the World to Come? One who places the blessing of redemption immediately before the evening prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: The prayers were instituted in the middle [between the morning and evening recitations of the Shema].’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בְּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמִסְפָּר אֶת רֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כג, י), שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַכְנִיס עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, מִמֵּילָא אֵין לָחוּשׁ.
connections.quote: “Who can count the dust of Jacob, or number the offspring of Israel? May my soul die the death of the upright, and may my end be like theirs.”
connections.context: Rova is rendered here as offspring in keeping with the rabbinic reading developed in Niddah 31a, which Rav Tzadok cites below. The verse is Balaam’s blessing. This preserves the procreative sense needed by the argument and removes stray editorial text.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בְּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמִסְפָּר אֶת רֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כג, י), שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַכְנִיס עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, מִמֵּילָא אֵין לָחוּשׁ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abbahu expounded: What is meant by the verse, “Who has counted the dust of Jacob, and numbered the unions of Israel?” It teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and counts the unions of Israel, awaiting when the drop from which a righteous person is formed will come.”
connections.context: This is the opening exposition of the passage whose continuation about Balaam is already quoted below. It supplies the precise source for divine concern with the future righteous person.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם;
connections.quote: ‘It was also taught this way: Blood is transformed and becomes milk; these are Rabbi Meir’s words. Rabbi Yosei says: Her limbs are loosened, and her blood does not return to its former state until twenty-four months have passed. Rabbi Ilai said: What is Rabbi Meir’s reason? It is written: ‘Who can bring something pure from something impure? Is it not the One?’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם;
connections.quote: “Who can bring a pure thing from an impure one? Is it not the One?”
connections.context: In the contextual biblical reading, the final words can mean “not one.” Niddah 9a reads them rhetorically as referring to the One God, who brings purity out of impurity. Rav Tzadok explicitly uses that rabbinic reading here.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם;
connections.quote: “It is written (Job 14:4), ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ This means being able to see purity in the very form of the garment that previously appeared to show its opposite, without the garment itself changing. This is possible only when illumination shines from the highest place, called One, indicating One beyond reckoning: illumination from the higher will that is removed from all garments and free of all forms.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same question, ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ Its point is the disclosure of purity within the very garment that previously seemed impure, rather than merely replacing that garment. This develops why Rav Tzadok links the paradox to divine unity and why Bilaam's view of the outward act alone misses the source of its holiness.
connections.headline: Purity within the same garment

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם;
connections.quote: “This corresponds to “from your father’s house,” for it says, “Indeed, in iniquity I was formed.” The Midrash teaches: even the most pious of the pious cannot be without one aspect of iniquity—that is, he is not entirely free of his own enjoyment. This comes from the serpent’s counsel. Shabbat 55b says that Scripture explicitly identifies Jesse, David’s father, as having died through the serpent’s counsel. Concerning him, the Midrash expounds “in iniquity” as a full spelling. The Messiah son of David will repair even the serpent’s counsel and draw true life into the world, as it says, “He asked You for life; You gave it to him.” He will be the final culmination that repairs everything in the world, and “He will swallow up death forever.””
connections.explanation: The Lech Lecha passage develops the same example of Yishai and identifies the serpent’s remaining trace with an inability to be entirely free of self-enjoyment. This clarifies the present siman’s claim that holiness can be found within bodily life despite its inherited mixture. The final removal of that root belongs to Mashiach ben David. The siman’s present avodah is therefore awe, restraint, and directing the bodily power toward Hashem’s will, rather than assuming that any remaining mixture makes holiness impossible.
connections.headline: The remaining trace of the serpent differs from deliberate impurity

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ יד, ה): בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא וְכוּלֵי, וְהוּא יִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ;
connections.quote: see note 1259.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok combines two sources: the Midrash’s statement about the personal pleasure involved in conception, and the Talmud’s identification of Jesse as free of the personal sin that would account for his death. Supplying both makes the apparent tension in his example intelligible.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יח): "הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי" – רָאָה אוֹתָן עֲסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said: It is to inform you through what failing that wicked one leapt upon them: because it saw them engaged in marital relations and desired her.”
connections.context: The Midrash explains why the serpent’s appearance follows the description of Adam and Eve’s nakedness. The act of seeing and the desire it awakens are the elements Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹלַד לָהֶם הַבּוּשָׁה בָּזוֹ וְיָדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם, דִּלְמִצְוָה אֵין בּוּשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיַעֲקֹב (תַּעֲנִית ה:) [דְּלֹא מֵת, שֶׁהוּא תִּיקֵּן זֶה].
connections.quote: “After he had eaten, he said to him: Thus said Rabbi Yochanan: Jacob our father did not die. He said to him: Was it for nothing that the eulogizers eulogized him, the embalmers embalmed him, and the buriers buried him? He said to him: I am expounding a verse: ‘Therefore do not fear, O Jacob My servant, says Hashem, and do not be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from afar, and your seed from the land of their captivity’ (Jeremiah 30:10). The verse likens him to his seed: just as his seed is alive, so too he is alive.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹלַד לָהֶם הַבּוּשָׁה בָּזוֹ וְיָדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם, דִּלְמִצְוָה אֵין בּוּשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיַעֲקֹב (תַּעֲנִית ה:) [דְּלֹא מֵת, שֶׁהוּא תִּיקֵּן זֶה].
connections.quote: ‘The eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loin coverings.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹלַד לָהֶם הַבּוּשָׁה בָּזוֹ וְיָדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם, דִּלְמִצְוָה אֵין בּוּשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיַעֲקֹב (תַּעֲנִית ה:) [דְּלֹא מֵת, שֶׁהוּא תִּיקֵּן זֶה].
connections.quote: ““My days have been fulfilled”: the days of which my mother spoke to me. Another explanation of “my days have been fulfilled”: I am already eighty-four years old; when shall I establish the twelve tribes? This is why he said, “And I shall come to her.” Would not even the most frivolous person refrain from speaking so? Rather, he said it in order to beget offspring.”
connections.context: Rashi explains Jacob’s direct language by his purpose of bringing forth the tribes. This is the textual basis for Rav Tzadok’s distinction between that intention and the shame associated with a different intention.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ: שִׁדְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם לְאַחַר שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים נַעֲשֶׂה נָחָשׁ וְכוּלֵי (בָּבָא קַמָּא טז.)
connections.quote: ‘For it was taught: A male hyena becomes a bat after seven years; a bat becomes an arpad after seven years; an arpad becomes a nettle after seven years; a nettle becomes a thorn after seven years; a thorn becomes a demon after seven years. A person’s spine becomes a snake after seven years. This applies to someone who did not bow during Modim.’

connections.hePhrase: [דְּשִׁדְרָה הוּא מַהֲלַךְ הַזֶּרַע מִן הַמּוֹחַ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְשֶׁבַע שָׁנִים הוּא סֵדֶר שָׁלֵם, וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זְמַן זֶה לְעִיבּוּרוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ בִּבְכוֹרוֹת (ח.), וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘An ef’eh viper first conceives at seventy years, and its counterpart among trees is the carob. From the time this carob is planted until its fruit fully develops is seventy years, and the fruit’s development from flowering lasts three years. A snake’s gestation is seven years, and for that wicked creature we have found no counterpart. Some say: Mokhesasim figs.’

connections.hePhrase: וְ"לֹא כָרַע בְּמוֹדִים" הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם יִרְאָה, כִּי הַכְּרִיעָה הוּא מִפְּנֵי הַיִּרְאָה וּבוּשָׁה.
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא קמא ט״ז א:כ״ב:א׳
connections.quote: ““Provided that he did not bow at Modim”: because it is a mitzvah to bow, and when one straightens up one straightens like a serpent, as we find concerning Rav Sheshet in Berakhot. Measure for measure, he becomes a serpent; this is his punishment, for becoming a serpent is a disgrace to him. A marginal comment: Some explain this by the Midrash’s statement that there is a bone in a person’s spine from which he will be formed in the future. That bone is so strong and hard that fire cannot burn it; now, when that bone becomes a serpent, he will not live in the future. But it is unreasonable to say that so great a punishment would come for this sin, for all Israel have a share in the World to Come.”
connections.context: Tosafot connects the image with the movement of bowing and rising, then records and rejects an interpretation that would deprive the person of future life. The rejection is retained so the image is not made to assert that consequence.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת עט.): שְׁלֹשָׁה סִימָנִים וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (כ.): בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי].
connections.quote: “He said: ‘This nation has three distinguishing traits: they are compassionate, bashful, and performers of kindness. Compassionate, as it is written: ‘He will give you compassion, have compassion on you, and multiply you.’ Bashful, as it is written: ‘So that His fear may be upon your faces.’ Performers of kindness, as it is written: ‘So that he will command his children and his household,’ and so on. Whoever possesses these three traits is fit to join this nation.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת עט.): שְׁלֹשָׁה סִימָנִים וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (כ.): בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי].
connections.quote: ““So that His fear shall be upon your faces”—this is shame. “So that you do not sin”—this teaches that shame leads to fear of sin. … One who lacks shamefacedness—it is known that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai.”
connections.context: This is the saying about shame and Sinai invoked alongside the three characteristics in Yevamot 79a. The note had instead quoted advice about vows and social company.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בִּלְעָם שֶׁהָיָה מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ רַע לֹא הֶאֱמִין בָּזֶה, וְאָמַר: מִי שֶׁהוּא טָהוֹר וְקָדוֹשׁ וְכוּלֵי (נִדָּה לא.), כִּי לֹא יָדַע כְּלָל שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן קְדוּשָׁה וְטָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא.
connections.quote: “For this matter the eye of the wicked Balaam was blinded. He said: ‘Would One who is pure and holy, whose servants are pure and holy, look upon such a thing?’ Immediately his eye was blinded, as it is written: ‘The utterance of the man whose eye is closed.’ This is what Rabbi Yohanan said: ‘What is meant by ‘He lay with her that night’? It teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, assisted in that act, as it is stated: ‘Issachar is a strong-boned donkey,’ chamor garem—a donkey brought about, garam, Issachar.’”

connections.hePhrase: רַק בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁדְּבֵקִים בִּיחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה' אֶחָד" (דְּבָרִים ו, ד):
connections.quote: ‘Hear, Israel: Hashem is our God; Hashem is one.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:) עַל דּוֹאֵג, דְּמִתְּחִלָּה בִּקֵּשׁ דָּוִד עָלָיו שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי, וְאַחַר כָּךְ דְּלָא לֵימְרוּ שְׁמַעְתָּא בֵּי מִדְרְשָׁא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzhak also said: ‘What is meant by ‘God too will tear you down forever’? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to David: ‘Let Doeg come into the World to Come.’ David said before Him: ‘God too will tear you down forever.’ What is meant by ‘He will snatch you up and pluck you from the tent, and uproot you from the land of the living, Selah’? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: ‘Let a teaching be stated in his name in the study hall.’ David said before Him: ‘He will snatch you up and pluck you from the tent.’ ‘Let him have sons who are Torah scholars.’ ‘And uproot you from the land of the living, Selah.’’”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּאַחֵר, מִתְּחִלָּה בְּחַיֵּי רַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמְרוּ שֶׁהָיָה מִשְׁפָּטוֹ דְּלָא לֵיתֵי לְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר שְׁמוּעוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ,
connections.quote: see note 1293.
connections.context: This supplies the first stage of the account, before the passage about Rabbi Yochanan that is already quoted. The Gemara distinguishes the protection due to Torah, the consequence of sin, and Rabbi Meir’s hope for eventual entry into the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּאַחֵר, מִתְּחִלָּה בְּחַיֵּי רַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמְרוּ שֶׁהָיָה מִשְׁפָּטוֹ דְּלָא לֵיתֵי לְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר שְׁמוּעוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ,
connections.quote: “How did Rabbi Meir learn Torah from Acher’s mouth? Did not Rabbah bar bar Chana say in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: What is meant by “For a priest’s lips should guard knowledge, and Torah should be sought from his mouth, for he is an angel of Hashem of hosts”? If the teacher resembles an angel of Hashem of hosts, seek Torah from his mouth; otherwise, do not seek Torah from his mouth. Reish Lakish said: Rabbi Meir found a verse and expounded it: “Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and set your heart to My knowledge.” It does not say “to their knowledge,” but “to My knowledge.” Rav Chanina derived it from here: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.” Do the verses contradict one another? There is no difficulty: one concerns a mature student, the other an immature student. When Rav Dimi came, he said: They say in the West, “Rabbi Meir ate the date and cast the pit away.” Rava expounded: What is meant by “I went down to the nut garden to see the greenery of the valley”? Why are Torah scholars compared to a nut? To tell you: just as, although a nut is soiled with mud and filth, what is inside it is not made repulsive, so too, although a Torah scholar has gone astray, his Torah is not made repulsive.”
connections.context: The Gemara itself asks how Rabbi Meir could learn from Acher. Its answer preserves the distinction between a mature student able to separate the teaching from the teacher’s errors and an immature student; the nut analogy follows that qualification.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם "אֲחֵרִים" הַיְינוּ מַה שֶּׁלָּמַד מֵאַחֵר.
connections.displayRef: Sefer Yuchasin (R. Avraham Zacuto), Ma’amar 1, in the name of the early authorities

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ עֲדַיִן הָיָה בְּגֵיהִנָּם עַד זְמַן רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּדְאִיתָא בַּחֲגִיגָה (טו:), וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי רַבִּי שֶׁסִּידֵּר הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת קָבַע שְׁמוּעָה בִּשְׁמוֹ בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק ד, כ), לְפִי שֶׁשְּׁמוּעוֹתָיו הֵם תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Is it a great feat to burn one’s teacher? There was one among us, and we cannot save him? If I take him by the hand, who will wrest him from me?’ He said: ‘When will I die and extinguish the smoke from his grave?’ When Rabbi Yochanan died, the smoke ceased from Acher’s grave. A eulogist began his eulogy: ‘Even the gatekeeper could not stand before you, our teacher!’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ עֲדַיִן הָיָה בְּגֵיהִנָּם עַד זְמַן רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּדְאִיתָא בַּחֲגִיגָה (טו:), וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי רַבִּי שֶׁסִּידֵּר הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת קָבַע שְׁמוּעָה בִּשְׁמוֹ בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק ד, כ), לְפִי שֶׁשְּׁמוּעוֹתָיו הֵם תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘Elisha ben Avuyah says: What is someone who learns as a child like? Ink written on fresh paper. What is someone who learns in old age like? Ink written on paper that has been erased. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah of Kfar HaBavli says: What is someone who learns from the young like? Someone who eats unripe grapes and drinks wine straight from the press. What is someone who learns from the old like? Someone who eats ripe grapes and drinks aged wine. Rabbi says: Do not look at the jar, but at what is inside it. There is a new jar filled with old wine, and an old jar that does not contain even new wine.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (שָׁם) בְּתוֹרָתוֹ שֶׁל דּוֹאֵג "מִן הַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ", פֵּירוּשׁ וְאֵין נִבְלָע בַּלֵּב לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ;
connections.quote: see note 1659.
connections.context: The source gives concrete force to “from the lips outward”: the learner can expound the prohibitions of murder and evil speech without allowing those teachings to govern his conduct.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִדְאִיתָא הָתָם: רְבוּתָא לְמִיבְעֵי בָּעֲיָא וְכוּלֵי, אֶלָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּא בָּעֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi said: Doeg and Achitophel posed four hundred questions concerning a tower suspended in the air, and not one was resolved for them. Rava said: Is it a great achievement to pose questions? In Rav Yehuda’s time, all his study was in Nezikin, whereas we study extensively even in Uktzin. When Rav Yehuda reached “a woman who presses vegetables in a pot”—or, some say, “olives pressed with their leaves are pure”—he said, “I see here the difficult discussions of Rav and Shmuel.” Yet we study Uktzin in thirteen academies. But Rav Yehuda would remove his shoes and rain would come, while we cry out and no one pays attention to us. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the heart, as it is written, “Hashem sees into the heart.””
connections.context: The quotation retains Rava’s comparison of learning with answered prayer, which explains the conclusion that Hashem desires the heart. Rav Tzadok then reads the questions themselves as questions that must also be alive within the learner’s service of Hashem.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַשָּׂגַת הָאָדָם וְחָכְמָתוֹ הוּא עֶצֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁמָתוֹ וְחַיּוּתוֹ,
connections.quote: “Each of the other members of Israel has some secret of His wisdom hidden in the root of his soul, of which he himself is unaware; it is the root of his life, as it is written, “Wisdom gives life to its possessor.” Through this, each has a distinction over all Israel, because of the portion of divinity from above at his soul’s root, in which there is a secret hidden from all Israel. This is why the chapter HaRoeh says that their minds are not alike and their faces do not resemble one another. The difference in a person’s outward form follows the difference in each one’s understanding, for the human face is in the image of God, and this comes from the soul, the portion of divinity. “A person’s wisdom illuminates his face”: according to the point of wisdom and understanding within each person, which is unlike that of his fellow, the light of his face is likewise different.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok develops the connection between an individual soul, its distinctive wisdom, and its face. The passage includes hidden wisdom even in a person who does not yet recognize it within himself.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נח.) שֶׁאֵין בְּנֵי אָדָם דּוֹמִין זֶה לָזֶה בְּפַרְצוּפֵיהֶן;
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: One who sees a multitude of Israel says: ‘Blessed ... is the Knower of secrets,’ for their minds are not alike and their faces are not alike. Ben Zoma saw a multitude upon a step on the Temple Mount and said: ‘Blessed ... is the Knower of secrets, and blessed ... is He who created all these to serve me.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַפַּרְצוּף הוּא מֵעִיד עַל פְּנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב כַּנּוֹדָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (יִתְרוֹ ע עַמּוּד א) מֵחָכְמַת הַפַּרְצוּף, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר פָּנָיו" (קֹהֶלֶת ח, א),
connections.quote: ““This is the book of the generations of man”: concerning forms, the mysteries of human forms, to recognize in a person’s features the form of his hidden traits—in the hair, the forehead, the eyes, the face, the lips, the lines of the hands, and the ears. Through these seven, people are recognized.”
connections.context: This is the introduction to the Zohar’s exposition of outward features as signs of inner character. It supplies the specific teaching about the face that Rav Tzadok cites; the previous note quoted only the earlier discussion of Adam being shown future generations.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַפַּרְצוּף הוּא מֵעִיד עַל פְּנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב כַּנּוֹדָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (יִתְרוֹ ע עַמּוּד א) מֵחָכְמַת הַפַּרְצוּף, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר פָּנָיו" (קֹהֶלֶת ח, א),
connections.quote: ‘Who is like the wise person, and who knows the meaning of a matter? A person’s wisdom lights up his face, and the sternness of his face is changed.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב) עַל פָּסוּק "הֹלֵךְ הָאָדָם אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת יב, ה), שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ;
connections.quote: “Does a person see his fellow in the World to Come? Does not every righteous person have a world of his own, as it is said, “For the person goes to the house of his world”? It does not say “their worlds,” but “his world.””
connections.context: In the narrative, Rabbi Shimon’s wife challenges the promise that Rabbi could make up a deficiency in her husband’s future reward. The individual “world” is the point Rav Tzadok invokes in discussing each soul’s distinct completion.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב) עַל פָּסוּק "הֹלֵךְ הָאָדָם אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת יב, ה), שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ;
connections.quote: “For a person goes to the house of his world, and the mourners go about in the street.”
connections.context: The contextual sense is a person’s final or enduring abode. Rav Tzadok follows the Midrash’s attention to the singular olamo, “his world,” to explain an individual soul’s own domain of completion.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הַנִּקְרָא אֶצְלָם בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר (שַׁבָּת קנב.): כָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ מָדוֹר לְפִי כְּבוֹדוֹ,
connections.quote: ‘‘For a person is going to his eternal home.’ Rabbi Yitzchak said: This teaches that every righteous person is given a dwelling according to his honor. It is like a king who enters a city together with his servants. When they enter, they all enter through one gate. When they lodge, each is given a dwelling according to his honor.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (רֵישׁ תִּיקּוּן סט) דְּעוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר עוֹלָם קָטָן שֶׁלּוֹ.
connections.quote: “We have certainly heard that every righteous person has a world of his own: this is a person’s body, which is called a small world. Therefore He said, “If you wish, I will destroy the world”—and bring him in another reincarnation, and perhaps he would fall in an hour of sustenance.”
connections.context: Tikkun 69 interprets the Talmudic offer to recreate a person’s world as a reference to that person’s own microcosm. Rav Tzadok cites the explicit identification of “his own world” with the individual human being.

connections.hePhrase: וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד כּוֹלֵל כָּל כֹּחוֹת הָעוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית א, כו),
connections.quote: ‘God said: Let Us make humankind in Our image, according to Our likeness. Let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, the livestock, all the earth, and every creeping creature that creeps upon the earth.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִשְׁלֵימוּתוֹ, זֶה נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.): יֵשׁ קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi wept and said: Some acquire their world over many years, and some acquire their world in a single hour. Rabbi also said: It is not enough that those who repent are accepted; they are even called ‘Rabbi.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי יֵשׁ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג וְאֵינוֹ כָּךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז הַשָּׂגָתוֹ רַק בִּרְאִיָּה לְבַד.
connections.quote: “This accords with what I heard from our holy teacher, of righteous and holy memory, concerning the seventh day of Passover. It is said in the Mekhilta, Beshallach, and elsewhere, “A maidservant at the sea saw what Ezekiel did not see.” He said that then they attained only seeing, but not acquisition, until the month of Sivan, the time of the giving of the Torah, when they attained acquisition as well. This is the meaning of the Gemara at the beginning of Bava Metzia: “I might have thought: What does ‘I found it’ mean? ‘I saw it’ … and one acquires through seeing alone.” This is only the Gemara’s initial supposition, and is not the actual conclusion.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַתְחָלַת כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּרוֹקֵחַ: אֵין חֹזֶק כַּחֲסִידוּת בִּתְחִלָּתוֹ, אֲבָל הוּא רַק בִּרְאִיָּה;
connections.displayRef: Sefer HaRokeach, Hilkhot Chasidut, at the opening of the book
connections.quote: “There is no strength like piety at its beginning.”

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ בְּקִנְיָן וְנִבְלָע בַּלֵּב כָּל מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז נִקְרָא "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ".
connections.quote: “The beginning of light emerging from darkness must come with force. As is known, this is the meaning of “There is no strength like piety at its beginning.” Afterwards it becomes concealed, and one must reach it through effort from within the concealment. “A righteous person falls seven times and rises,” until he reaches a complete stature in the perfection of all the levels. Then the first light returns and is revealed to him, to be fixed in the heart as an acquisition that will no longer be hidden or disappear.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s own fuller explanation of the initial strength of devotion. It supplies the sequence from first illumination, through concealment and effort, to a quality firmly acquired in the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ בְּקִנְיָן וְנִבְלָע בַּלֵּב כָּל מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז נִקְרָא "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ".
connections.quote: “Just as Torah is initially ‘Hashem's Torah’ and afterward the person's Torah, so the soul begins with ‘He breathed into his nostrils,’ from Hashem, as we say, ‘The soul You gave me.’ At the end it is called the house of his own world, belonging to him: the soul is called by his name because through his effort he merited it. Thus the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 35), ‘As though you made yourselves,’ concerning ‘You shall perform them’ (Leviticus 26:3): through performing Torah and mitzvot one merits this.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the transition from receiving a soul to calling its completed world one's own. The initial gift comes from Hashem; through Torah and mitzvot it becomes attributed to the person who has worked for it. This clarifies the siman's contrast between an insight that is only seen and a perfection that has become a settled acquisition.
connections.headline: The given soul becomes one’s own world

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עוֹד מַה לְּהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא הַפְּרוֹזְדּוֹר וְעוֹלַם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה וְהַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, וְהוּא לֹא יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ יוֹתֵר מֵעוֹלָמוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ.
connections.quote: see note 1570.
connections.context: The complete Mishnah states the purpose of the antechamber: preparation through the life of action. This is the source of Rav Tzadok’s description of this world as the place of effort.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בְּעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁאָז הָיָה הַבְלָעַת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בְּקִנְיָן [אַחַר שֶׁקָּדְמָה הָרְאִיָּה בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף: "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי"] כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְשִׁירָה ג׳:י׳
connections.quote: “‘This is my God, and I will glorify Him’ (Exodus 15:2). Rabbi Eliezer says: From where can you say that a maidservant saw at the sea what Isaiah and Ezekiel did not see? For it is said: ‘And by the hand of the prophets I am imagined’ (Hosea 12:11), and ‘The heavens were opened and I saw visions of God’ (Ezekiel 1:1).”

connections.hePhrase: אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת פח:): שֶׁיָּצְתָה נִשְׁמָתָם וְהוֹרִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא טַל שֶׁל תְּחִיָּה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also said: With every utterance that came from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, the souls of Israel departed, as it is said, ‘My soul went out when He spoke.’ Since their souls departed at the first utterance, how did they receive the second? He brought down the dew with which He will revive the dead, and revived them, as it is said, ‘You poured down a generous rain, O God; when Your inheritance was weary, You restored it.’ Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also said: With every utterance that came from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, Israel retreated twelve mil, and the ministering angels gently led them back, as it is said, ‘Angels of hosts flee, flee.’ Read not yiddodun, ‘flee,’ but yedaddun, ‘lead along.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי לִי כָל בְּכוֹר בְּיוֹם הַכֹּתִי כָל בְּכוֹר בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר ג, יג).
connections.quote: ‘For every firstborn is Mine. On the day I struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated to Myself every firstborn in Israel, human and animal alike. They shall be Mine; I am Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְכָל קַרְנֵי רְשָׁעִים אֲגַדֵּעַ, תְּרוֹמַמְנָה קַרְנוֹת צַדִּיק" (תְּהִלִּים עה, יא) – בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁזֶּה נִגְדָּע, זֶה נִתְרוֹמֵם;
connections.quote: ‘I will cut off all the horns of the wicked; the horns of the righteous will be raised high.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "אִמָּלְאָה הָחֳרָבָה" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כו, ב), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה ו.): קֵיסָרִי וִירוּשָׁלַיִם וְכוּלֵי, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם בְּמַדְרֵגָה אַחַת בְּמַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: ‘Son of man, because Tyre said about Jerusalem: ‘Aha! The gateway of the peoples is broken; it has turned toward me. I shall be filled, now that she lies in ruins’…’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "אִמָּלְאָה הָחֳרָבָה" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כו, ב), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה ו.): קֵיסָרִי וִירוּשָׁלַיִם וְכוּלֵי, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם בְּמַדְרֵגָה אַחַת בְּמַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: ‘Caesarea and Jerusalem: If someone tells you that both have been destroyed, do not believe it. If he says that both are settled, do not believe it. If Caesarea is destroyed and Jerusalem settled, or Jerusalem destroyed and Caesarea settled, believe it, as it says: ‘I shall be filled; she lies in ruins.’ If one is full, the other is ruined; if the other is full, the first is ruined.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל אוּמָּה יֵשׁ לָהּ כֹּחַ מַה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי שְׁקָלִים א, א): אָפְיָהּ שֶׁל אוּמָּה זוֹ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abba bar Acha said: You cannot fathom the character of this nation: they are asked for the Calf and they give; they are asked for the Tabernacle and they give.”
connections.context: The saying is about Israel; Rav Tzadok borrows its expression for the particular power that each nation has.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ יִרְמְיָה קוֹנֵן עַל אָבְדַן אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב כַּחֲלִלִים יֶהֱמֶה" (יִרְמְיָה מח, לו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבַמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק כ, א),
connections.quote: “Therefore my heart sounds for Moab like flutes, and my heart sounds like flutes for the people of Kir-heres; therefore the abundance they made has perished.”
connections.context: Jeremiah also mourns Moab’s destruction, but his wording differs from Isaiah’s “my heart cries out for Moab.” Together the passages support the prophetic grief under discussion.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ יִרְמְיָה קוֹנֵן עַל אָבְדַן אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב כַּחֲלִלִים יֶהֱמֶה" (יִרְמְיָה מח, לו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבַמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק כ, א),
connections.quote: see note 361.
connections.context: The Midrash contrasts the compassion of Jeremiah and Ezekiel with Balaam’s attempt to destroy Israel. It explicitly includes compassion for other nations, supplying the original source behind the lament discussed here.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ יִרְמְיָה קוֹנֵן עַל אָבְדַן אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב כַּחֲלִלִים יֶהֱמֶה" (יִרְמְיָה מח, לו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבַמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק כ, א),
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 10:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 10:1
connections.quote: “The matter is like what we find when a prophet foretold a nation's calamity: he lamented, as it says (Isaiah 15:5), ‘My heart cries out for Moav,’ and in chapter 16, ‘My innards sound like a harp for Moav, and my inward parts for Kir Cheres.’ He grieved over the nation's loss, because through this its inclination was annulled, and the power of service corresponding to that particular matter was thereby diminished. Yet in Egypt, although it says (Deuteronomy 17:16), ‘You shall not return by this way again’—even residence in Egypt was forbidden, alluding even to the inanimate—and the Sages said that it was made like a deep place without fish (Berakhot 9b), some points nevertheless remained there that would still enter holiness, to be gathered by Israel from a distance. Of them it says (Psalms 68:32), ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’ As Pesachim 118b teaches: Egypt will bring a gift to Mashiach. He thinks he should not accept it, but the Holy One tells him to accept it, for they provided lodging for His children in Egypt. Immediately, ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim expressly explains the prophet's lament over another nation's fall: the corresponding field of human service becomes smaller when its opposing inclination disappears. Its Egypt example adds that some good remains to be gathered from a distance afterward. This develops the siman's reciprocal powers while preserving the reason for lament and the possibility of later collection.
connections.headline: The prophet’s lament and the good still to be gathered

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ בְּאָבְדַן סְדוֹם שֶׁהָיוּ אַבִּירֵי לֵב הָרְחוֹקִים מִצְּדָקָה, נִתְבַּשֵּׂר לֵידַת יִצְחָק שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן גִּבּוֹר הַלֵּב כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Listen to Me, you stout-hearted, who are far from righteousness.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ בְּאָבְדַן סְדוֹם שֶׁהָיוּ אַבִּירֵי לֵב הָרְחוֹקִים מִצְּדָקָה, נִתְבַּשֵּׂר לֵידַת יִצְחָק שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן גִּבּוֹר הַלֵּב כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “With the announcement of Isaac’s birth, through which the holy attribute of strength would come into the world, it followed of itself that when this one rises, that one falls. For Sodom is the refuse within the attribute of strength and the evil within it: being cruel to other people. Therefore He rained sulfur and fire upon them, which belong to the attribute of strength.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ יְחֶזְקֵאל שֶׁנְּבוּאָתוֹ חָכְמָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (נז:): יְצַפֶּה לְחָכְמָה, אָמַר כַּמָּה פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת עַל חוּרְבַּן מִצְרַיִם, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה תְּרוֹמַמְנָה קַרְנוֹת חָכְמַת הָאֱמֶת.
connections.quote: ‘There are three prophets: One who sees the Book of Kings should expect greatness. One who sees Ezekiel should expect wisdom; Isaiah, consolation; Jeremiah, he should be concerned about calamity.’

connections.hePhrase: [צוֹר לְשׁוֹן צַיָּיר וְצָר צוּרָה; וּמָלֵא וָא"ו שֶׁהוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (רֵישׁ וַיִּקְרָא ב.), לְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַסְּקוּ בְּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וְהָיָה לִפְעֻלָּתָם אֲחִיזָה בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “What is written concerning Rahab? “Give me a true sign”—this is the letter vav, which is called the sign of truth. If you say that the other letters are not truth: certainly they are, but this letter is called the sign of truth.”
connections.context: The verified Zohar passage establishes vav as the sign of truth. Rav Tzadok himself applies that symbolism to the full spelling of Tzor and its role in the Temple’s building. The Zohar quotation should not be expanded into a claim that it explicitly discusses Hiram and Tyre.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל "צָר" חָסֵר [לְשׁוֹן צַר וְצוֹרֵר] בְּמַלְכוּת רְבִיעִית הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה סא),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said: Every Tzor written in Scripture in full refers to the city of Tyre; when written defectively, it refers to Rome.”
connections.context: The distinction is the presence or absence of vav in the spelling. Rav Tzadok combines this Midrashic distinction with the Zohar’s symbolism of vav as truth in the preceding note.

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהֶם "וְהַיָּדַיִם יְדֵי עֵשָׂו" שֶׁגַּם כֵּן כֹּחָם בִּפְעֻלַּת יָדָם וְנֶחְסְרָה הַוָּא"ו, וְעַיֵּין בְּלִקּוּטֵי תּוֹרָה מֵהָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל שֶׁבְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁיֶּחְסַר אוֹת מֵהַשֵּׁם יוֹרֶה עַל הַטֻּמְאָה]
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Torah of the Arizal, Parashat Chayei Sarah

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁאָז הָיְתָה הַתְחָלָתָהּ, וּלְכָךְ אָבְדַן צוֹר הָיָה בְּיוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְשָׂכָר לֹא הָיָה וְגוֹמֵר" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כט, יח), שֶׁנֶּאֱבַד גַּם כָּל שְׁלָלָהּ, וְהַיְינוּ כְּפִי תֹּקֶף הָרוֹמְמוּת הָרְאוּיָה לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּהַתְחָלָתָהּ.
connections.quote: “There in Babylon the expansion of the words of the Oral Torah began. Our Sages said, “I raised up many more righteous people in its desolation than when it was inhabited,” and, “I decreed many decrees upon myself and upheld them, more than You decreed upon me.” All of this came through the Men of the Great Assembly who were in Babylon.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok describes the beginning here as the expansion of the Oral Torah in Babylon. This gives the intended setting for “then was its beginning,” without making it a claim that oral teaching first existed only at that time.

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁאָז הָיְתָה הַתְחָלָתָהּ, וּלְכָךְ אָבְדַן צוֹר הָיָה בְּיוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְשָׂכָר לֹא הָיָה וְגוֹמֵר" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כט, יח), שֶׁנֶּאֱבַד גַּם כָּל שְׁלָלָהּ, וְהַיְינוּ כְּפִי תֹּקֶף הָרוֹמְמוּת הָרְאוּיָה לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּהַתְחָלָתָהּ.
connections.quote: ‘Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, made his army labor heavily against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army received any reward from Tyre for the work he had done against her.’

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁאָז הָיְתָה הַתְחָלָתָהּ, וּלְכָךְ אָבְדַן צוֹר הָיָה בְּיוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְשָׂכָר לֹא הָיָה וְגוֹמֵר" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כט, יח), שֶׁנֶּאֱבַד גַּם כָּל שְׁלָלָהּ, וְהַיְינוּ כְּפִי תֹּקֶף הָרוֹמְמוּת הָרְאוּיָה לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּהַתְחָלָתָהּ.
connections.quote: ““And there was no reward for him”: after they had plundered its spoil, the sea rose and swept it away from them, for it had been decreed that the city and its spoil should perish in the sea.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the traditional explanation of why the conquest yielded no reward. This is the source for the detail that even Tyre’s spoil was lost.

connections.hePhrase: וְקִבֵּל נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר שְׂכַר עֲבוֹדָתוֹ מִצּוֹר בְּמִצְרַיִם, כִּי מִשָּׁם נִצְמַח].
connections.quote: “Therefore, thus says the Lord Hashem: I am giving the land of Egypt to Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon. He shall carry off its abundance, plunder its spoil, and seize its booty, and it shall be wages for his army. As the recompense for the labor he performed, I have given him the land of Egypt, because they acted for Me—declares the Lord Hashem.”
connections.context: These are the next two verses after the already quoted verse about the lack of wages from Tyre. They expressly identify Egypt as the army’s recompense.

connections.hePhrase: [קנא] עִתּוֹת הַיְּרִידָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם חֵשֶׁק לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – זֶהוּ הֲכָנָה לַעֲלִיָּה גְּדוֹלָה,
connections.quote: see note 388.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok develops the same Rephidim example elsewhere: a lapse can precede a higher attainment, while its constructive turn depends on promptly recognizing it and renewing one’s effort. The passage explains the preparation described here; it does not recommend seeking a lapse.

connections.hePhrase: [קנא] עִתּוֹת הַיְּרִידָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם חֵשֶׁק לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – זֶהוּ הֲכָנָה לַעֲלִיָּה גְּדוֹלָה,
connections.quote: “It also teaches us how to attain such desire. Of this it says, “They journeyed from Rephidim”: this self-abandonment is not so difficult. As soon as they departed Rephidim, which signifies weakening their hands in Torah, and set their hearts to rouse themselves and seek Hashem’s will, the one who comes to purify himself is helped. When he opens an opening as small as a needle’s point, the Holy One opens entrances through which wagons and carriages can pass. They can therefore immediately reach the wilderness of Sinai, the self-abandonment needed to receive Torah.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik returns to the same journey from Rephidim to Sinai and identifies its active turning point: they set their hearts to seek Hashem’s will. This explains the condition within the present siman. Weakness does not improve a person by itself; the recognition of it and the renewed movement for divine help can open a greater readiness for Torah.
connections.headline: The departure from weakness begins the ascent

connections.hePhrase: [קנא] עִתּוֹת הַיְּרִידָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם חֵשֶׁק לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – זֶהוּ הֲכָנָה לַעֲלִיָּה גְּדוֹלָה,
connections.quote: ““They journeyed from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai.” The Gemara explains Rephidim as their weakening themselves from Torah. Through this failure before the giving of the Torah, Hashem showed them that the different failures sometimes found in Israel can all be repaired through Torah. We see that there are teachings a person cannot attain without first stumbling, as the Gemara says of “this stumbling block is under your hand”: a person does not grasp words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them. Hashem thus showed them that through Torah they could repair everything.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same journey as disclosure that Torah can repair earlier failures. Its full discussion also identifies the error of imagining that divine favor makes human service unnecessary. Read beside the siman's explicit crying out, the parallel describes how a failure becomes the occasion for return and greater reception, rather than recommending weakness or delay as a spiritual technique.
connections.headline: The weakness is repaired through the return to Torah

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרְפִידִים וַיָּבֹאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינַי" (שְׁמוֹת יט, ב), וְיָדוּעַ דְּרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.) עַל "רְפִידִים" – שֶׁרָפוּ יְדֵיהֶם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה;
connections.quote: ‘They set out from Rephidim, came to the wilderness of Sinai, and camped in the wilderness. Israel camped there, facing the mountain.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרְפִידִים וַיָּבֹאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינַי" (שְׁמוֹת יט, ב), וְיָדוּעַ דְּרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.) עַל "רְפִידִים" – שֶׁרָפוּ יְדֵיהֶם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה;
connections.quote: ‘What does the name ‘Rephidim’ mean? Rabbi Eliezer says: Its name was Rephidim. Rabbi Yehoshua says: They weakened their commitment to words of Torah, as it is said: ‘Fathers did not turn toward their sons because their hands were weak.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַנְּשִׂאִם הֵבִיאוּ אֵת אַבְנֵי הַשֹּׁהַם" (שָׁם לה, כז), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב, טז): "נְשִׂאִם" חָסֵר, לְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַצְּלוּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘The leaders brought the onyx stones and the stones to be set in the ephod and the breastplate.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַנְּשִׂאִם הֵבִיאוּ אֵת אַבְנֵי הַשֹּׁהַם" (שָׁם לה, כז), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב, טז): "נְשִׂאִם" חָסֵר, לְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַצְּלוּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Why did the princes hasten to offer first, when in the work of the Tabernacle they had been sluggish and brought the onyx stones and setting stones only at the end? … They said: Let the people bring what they bring, and we will make up what is lacking. All Israel rejoiced in the work of the Tabernacle and brought every gift joyfully and promptly.”
connections.context: The Midrash supplies the reason for their initial delay. Rav Tzadok contrasts that hesitation with the prompt movement toward Torah and sacred service. The next note supplies the Midrash’s specific interpretation of the missing letter.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַנְּשִׂאִם הֵבִיאוּ אֵת אַבְנֵי הַשֹּׁהַם" (שָׁם לה, כז), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב, טז): "נְשִׂאִם" חָסֵר, לְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַצְּלוּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said: My children who acted promptly shall be recorded as having brought more than enough. From the princes, who delayed, He removed one letter of their name: “the princes” is written without a yud. When the Tabernacle was completed, they came first and brought an offering promptly.”
connections.context: The missing yud marks their earlier hesitation; their later promptness shows its repair. This is the precise deficient-spelling teaching cited by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַגְּמָרָא (יוֹמָא עה.): נְשִׂיאִים מַמָּשׁ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘‘They continued bringing him a freewill offering morning by morning.’ What does ‘morning by morning’ mean? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: From something that descended for them morning by morning. This teaches that precious stones and pearls descended for Israel together with the manna. ‘The nesi’im brought the onyx stones’: It was taught: Actual nesi’im—clouds—as it also says: ‘Clouds and wind, but no rain.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַמָּשָׁל בִּנְשִׂיאִים – שֶׁהוּא חֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי הָעוֹלָם, וּמִמֶּנָּה הָאוֹרָה יֵצֵא לְכָל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם.
connections.quote: ““Light” here means rain, as it says: “He scatters His cloud’s light.””
connections.context: The Gemara interprets the word “light” in a verse about clouds as rain. This supplies the textual association behind Rav Tzadok’s image of a dark cloud producing the light of beneficial rain.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק: "הַמְכַסֶּה שָׁמַיִם בְּעָבִים", וְאַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי זֶה "הַמֵּכִין לָאָרֶץ מָטָר" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, ח).
connections.quote: “Even during the day there are sometimes clouds that obstruct the light without making it dark. They are beneficial, because one who looks at the sun damages his eyesight, and they also prevent the intensity of the heat that sometimes harms a person, as we find concerning Nadav and Avihu. Their principal benefit is also as I heard explained concerning the verse, “Who covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth”: through this He brings a fresh drop into the body that causes growth. Yet rain itself is beneficial only at its proper time. Sometimes the cloud is harmful, when the full heat is needed—at the completion of the harvest, which is the completion of action, called harvesting, as stated at the end of the first chapter of Bava Kamma, as I explained elsewhere.”
connections.context: This earlier passage preserves Rav Tzadok’s parallel account of the teaching he “heard.” It also supplies his qualification: the value of cloud and rain depends on their proper time and purpose.

connections.hePhrase: [קנב] כְּפִי הִתְרַחֲקוּת הָאָדָם מִן הָרַע, וְהַיְינוּ מִכָּל חֲמוּדוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּתְשׁוּקוֹת דִּלְגַרְמֵיהּ, כָּךְ הוּא מִתְקָרֵב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּמַשִּׂיג אוֹרוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “And nonetheless there is required for this also the holiness of Joseph: to be guarded in his spirit holding fast to his stronghold in the fear of Hashem, guarding the Covenant, whereby is achieved the connection and unification of the Holy One and His Shechinah, which is the union of Truth and Faith through the agency of Joseph; for it is impossible for the light of Truth to enter the heart and experience "Hashem is my light" when the heart is brimming with physical lusts. And through the holiness of Joseph one can merit the holiness of Jacob, the dimension of Truth.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah describes guarding the covenant and holding fast to fear of Hashem as the preparation through which the light of truth can enter the heart. This develops the vessel described in the present siman: a heart occupied by self-directed desires is unavailable for that illumination. The parallel gives the process a particular form, while this siman explains its continuing movement—an act of awe opens reception of wisdom, and the wisdom received deepens awe in turn.
connections.headline: Guarding the heart prepares a vessel for the light of truth

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ... וְהָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים פ, ד).
connections.quote: “O God, restore us; cause Your face to shine, and we shall be saved.”
connections.context: The two requests occur together: restoration and the shining of God’s face. Rav Tzadok uses that pairing for the movement between a person’s return and illumination bestowed from above.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: כְּפִי הַשָּׂגָתוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ מִתְרַחֵק מֵעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אָנֹכִי" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ".
connections.quote: “I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before Me.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז).
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says: If there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; if there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour. He used to say: To what can someone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds be compared? To a tree with many branches and few roots: the wind comes, uproots it, and topples it facedown, as it is said: ‘He shall be like a shrub in the desert and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land that is uninhabited’ (Jeremiah 17). But to what can someone whose deeds exceed his wisdom be compared? To a tree with few branches and many roots: even if all the winds in the world come and blow against it, they cannot move it from its place, as it is said: ‘He shall be like a tree planted beside water, sending its roots toward a stream. It does not notice when heat comes; its leaves remain fresh. In a year of drought it is not anxious, and it does not cease producing fruit’ (ibid.).’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז).
connections.quote: “Through the completion of fear, wisdom and Torah too become complete, for the two depend on one another: “Without fear there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no fear.” Shabbat therefore compares fear to outer keys and Torah to inner keys, apparently reversing its other image of gate and dwelling. Both are true. At the beginning Torah must be fixed in the heart as the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov, acquired within each Jew. By entering this gate of Torah through an opening like a needle's point, one can then enter service with fear in the heart, the purpose of “Hashem asks of you.””
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explicitly asks why fear is called the outer key to Torah while elsewhere Torah is called the gate into fear. Its answer distinguishes the inherited Torah that permits entry from the fuller wisdom received through developed fear. This gives the siman's repeated movement a concrete structure: an initial opening does not exhaust either fear or wisdom, and each prepares a deeper reception of the other.
connections.headline: The apparently reversed metaphors describe successive entries

connections.hePhrase: חָכְמָה הוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְיִרְאָה הוּא מִן הַחֵטְא, וְהָא בְּלָא הָא לָא סַגִּי.
connections.quote: “The fear we are now explaining—fear of sin—is both a part of the awe of God’s majesty discussed above and, in a sense, a category of its own. Its meaning is that a person should always be apprehensive and concerned about his actions, lest some trace of sin become mixed into them, or lest there be something small or great that does not accord with the greatness of His blessed honor and the exaltedness of His name.”
connections.context: Ramchal defines fear of sin as concern that one’s conduct remain fitting for God’s honor. This clarifies Rav Tzadok’s distinction between apprehending God through wisdom and turning away from sin through fear.

connections.hePhrase: וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָא "אוֹצָר" וּכְלִי קִבּוּל, שֶׁהַלֵּב מִתְפַּנֶּה מִכָּל מִינֵי תְּשׁוּקוֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת, וּמִמֵּילָא הוּא כְּלִי פָּנוּי לְקַבֵּל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “The faithfulness of your times shall be a store of salvation, wisdom and knowledge; the fear of Hashem is his treasure.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: יָצָא דָּבָר שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת – נִכְנַס דָּבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה, יָצָא דָּבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה – נִכְנַס שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת.
connections.quote: “Just as, when you hold a cup full of oil and a drop of water falls into it, a corresponding drop of oil comes out, so too, if a word of Torah enters the heart, a corresponding word of frivolity leaves it. If a word of frivolity enters the heart, a corresponding word of Torah leaves it.”
connections.context: This is the original midrash behind the reciprocal displacement described in the paragraph. Its full comparison explains why filling the heart with Torah and removing frivolity are inseparable processes.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כְּשֶׁהַלֵּב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, מִמֵּילָא הוּא מוּכָן לְקַבֵּל כָּל מִינֵי תַּאֲווֹת, כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה פָּנוּי לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות איסורי ביאה כ״ב:כ״א
connections.quote: “Greater than all this, they said, is that a person should direct himself and his thoughts to words of Torah and broaden his understanding in wisdom, for thoughts of sexual transgression prevail only in a heart empty of wisdom. Of wisdom it says: “A beloved doe, a graceful mountain goat; let her breasts satisfy you at all times; be constantly absorbed in her love.””
connections.context: Rambam’s concluding counsel identifies positive occupation with Torah as the remedy for the empty heart. This supports the precise point here that merely clearing the heart, without filling it with Torah, leaves room for desire.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַיִּרְאָה הִיא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹאֵל מִבְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְעַתָּה... מָה ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה" (דְּבָרִים י, יב),
connections.quote: ‘And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, except to fear Hashem your God, to walk in all His ways, to love Him, and to serve Hashem your God with all your heart and all your soul?’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחָכְמָה מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין" (דָּנִיֵּאל ב, כא), וְנֶאֱמַר: "כִּי ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ו).
connections.quote: ‘He changes times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes kings. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who possess understanding.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחָכְמָה מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין" (דָּנִיֵּאל ב, כא), וְנֶאֱמַר: "כִּי ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ו).
connections.quote: ‘For Hashem gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת מִקּוֹדֶם,
connections.quote: “Come and see: the movement above is not aroused until there is first an awakening below upon which the movement above can rest. The mystery of the matter is that the black light does not join the white light until it first stirs; as soon as it first stirs, the white light immediately rests upon it.”
connections.context: The Zohar states the principle of an initial awakening below through the image of the dark and bright parts of a flame. In its context, Abraham first begins his departure toward Canaan and then receives the divine call. This is the principle named in Rav Tzadok’s clause.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ קַדְמוֹנִים: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נֶקֶב מְפוּלָּשׁ מֵעֵבֶר לְעֵבֶר,
connections.quote: “The letter he represents assistance from Heaven: “A person sanctifies himself a little from below; the Holy One, blessed be He, sanctifies him greatly and from above.” This is impossible without the help of the blessed God. Holiness means a boundary against sexual wrongdoing and separation from all the inclination’s imaginings; becoming entirely clean is impossible unless the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him. Nevertheless, the person must at least begin a little from below, like the point of a needle, provided that the hole goes all the way through from one side to the other—that is, that it penetrates to the depths of the heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok himself explains the image of a hole that passes all the way through: the initial movement may be small, but it must reach the heart’s depths. The preceding sentences retain the complementary requirement of divine help.

connections.hePhrase: [קנג] הָעָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם עַל עֲווֹנוֹתָיו הוּא תְּמוּרַת יִסּוּרִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (וַיַּקְהֵל ריב עַמּוּד א) מִמָּשִׁיחַ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “When they tell the Messiah of Israel’s suffering in exile and of the sinners among them who do not attend to knowing their Master, he raises his voice and weeps over those sinners. Thus it is written: “He was wounded because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities.””

connections.hePhrase: [קנג] הָעָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם עַל עֲווֹנוֹתָיו הוּא תְּמוּרַת יִסּוּרִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (וַיַּקְהֵל ריב עַמּוּד א) מִמָּשִׁיחַ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “In the Garden of Eden there is a palace called the Palace of the Afflicted. The Messiah enters that palace and calls all illnesses, all pains, and all Israel’s sufferings to come upon him; and they all come upon him. Were he not to lighten Israel’s burden and take it upon himself, no person could bear Israel’s sufferings for the punishments of the Torah.”
connections.context: The preceding paragraph describes the Messiah’s grief over sin, and the next describes his bearing of suffering. Rav Tzadok applies this pattern to the point of Messiah present within a person: sincere anguish over wrongdoing can take the place of suffering. That inward application is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: [קנג] הָעָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם עַל עֲווֹנוֹתָיו הוּא תְּמוּרַת יִסּוּרִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (וַיַּקְהֵל ריב עַמּוּד א) מִמָּשִׁיחַ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “He should continually sigh in the bitterness of his heart, as we explained in the first gate on repentance, and put the abundance of that bitterness in place of suffering. As it says, “A person’s spirit sustains his illness, but a broken spirit—who can bear it?” The meaning is that when the body falls ill, the soul bears its illness; this is the sense of “Who can endure the day of His coming?” It helps and supports the body by speaking to its heart and consoling it so that it can accept and endure. But when the soul is ill and broken by sorrow and anxiety, who will console the soul, and who will bear and support it? Thus anxiety and bitterness of heart are heavier than bodily illness: the soul supports the body in illness, but when the soul is ill and broken by grief, the body does not support it.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah supplies an earlier statement that sincere remorse can take the place of suffering. His explanation concerns the spiritual weight of repentance’s sorrow, the point with which Rav Tzadok opens this section.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דְּנֶפֶשׁ מַנְהִיג הַדּוֹר הוּא הַכּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת הַפְּרָטִיּוֹת שֶׁבַּדּוֹר.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
connections.quote: see note 1701.
connections.context: This passage explains Rav Tzadok’s technical use of an “inclusive soul.” The leader’s relation to his generation is illustrated through the father, Adam, and the king; that structure underlies the present account of the Messiah’s inclusive soul.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶפֶשׁ מָשִׁיחַ הוּא כְּלַל נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת אַחַר הַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
connections.quote: see note 1655.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the Messiah’s completion of the human task within this world from the still higher attainment of the World to Come. This provides context for “after their completion” in the present paragraph.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְאוֹתוֹ נְקֻדָּה הוּא סוֹבֵל צַעַר עַל עֲווֹנוֹת, כְּטַעַם "מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נג, ה), וּמֵקֵל בָּזֶה הָעֳנָשִׁים דְּיִסּוּרִין.
connections.quote: ‘But he was wounded because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities. The chastisement for our well-being was upon him, and through his wound healing came to us.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם דִּמְקַבְּלָם בְּגַן עֵדֶן, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר עַל זֶה מִכֹּחַ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם (רי עַמּוּד א) דִּרְקִיעַ שֶׁעַל הַגַּן עֵדֶן נַעֲשֶׂה מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “The dew descends only from the letters inscribed and engraved in that firmament, because those letters encompass the Torah. That firmament is the mystery of the Torah, for it is made from the Torah’s fire and water.”
connections.context: This is the cited Zoharic description of the firmament over Eden. The selected conclusion identifies its letters and its fire and water with Torah; the preceding discussion describes souls being purified and healed through the dew of these letters.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הַצַּעַר וְהָעָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בִּנְקֻדַּת הַלֵּב מֵעֲווֹנוֹתָיו, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְעוֹרֵר תֹּקֶף נְקֻדַּת מָשִׁיחַ הַגְּנוּזָה בּוֹ וּמֵאִיר לוֹ.
connections.quote: “But the serpent's counsel, from which the root of “the first of the nations” extends, is a root of that root and is present even in the hidden part of the heart. It is effaced through visitation, which belongs to hidden thought; its effacement comes through suffering and grief in the heart over the sin. This is “I shall visit their sin upon them”: He brings it into their hearts to feel deep bitterness over the root of the heart's inclination toward it. This is through burning the heifer to ashes, which purifies contact with the dead, meaning contact with the fundamental source of impurity, the serpent's counsel. Now, when we have neither the heifer's ashes nor the practical performance of the mitzvah, “we shall render the bulls with our lips”: reading the passage gradually brings this into the heart. It comes before Pesach to merit through it the resurrection of the dead that will take place at Pesach, which is why we read the prophecy of the dry bones on Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach.”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz distinguishes repair of an openly expressed fault from the gradual repair of its hidden root. The latter involves sorrow in the heart and Torah that gradually makes a person aware of that root, in preparation for renewed life. This explains why the present siman places the significance of remorse in the point directed toward ultimate completion. The comparison concerns the spiritually productive movement of teshuvah described by these texts; the paragraph does not equate every experience of distress with completed repair.
connections.headline: Remorse and the gradual repair of the hidden root

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם (ריא עַמּוּד ב) דִּמְאוֹר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם בָּא לְגַן עֵדֶן,
connections.quote: “Before that soul has been purified in fire, those messengers call to them and say, “Here they are.” When it has been purified, those appointed over it leave that place with it and bring it to the entrance of the Garden of Eden, where those messengers are. They say to them, “Here they are: these are the souls that have been purified.” Then they bring that soul into the Garden of Eden. How broken it is from that breaking caused by purification in Gehinnom! That breaking comes from the lower fire. Although it descends from above, once it reaches the earth below it is a fire that is not subtle; the soul is punished by it and broken. Then the Holy One, blessed be He, brings forth the sun shining from those four gates that illuminate the firmament over the Garden. It reaches that soul, and the soul is healed. Thus it is written: “For you who fear My name, a sun of righteousness will shine, with healing in its wings.””
connections.context: These consecutive Zohar paragraphs supply the sequence used here: purification by the lower fire, entrance into Eden, and healing by the sun. They also explicitly distinguish the fire’s heavenly origin from the coarse form it takes below.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֲגִיגָה יג:): נְהַר דִּינוּר מִזֵּיעָתָן שֶׁל חַיּוֹת מִתֹּקֶף הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁלָּהֶם, וְיוֹרֵד עַל רֹאשׁ רְשָׁעִים,
connections.quote: “A river of fire flowed and came forth from before Him; thousands upon thousands served Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him; the court sat, and the books were opened.”
connections.context: The Gemara’s “nehar dinur” is the river of fire of this verse.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְלַבְּנִים, וְזוֹכִים יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי דַּיְיקָא לְשֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם:
connections.quote: “For you who fear My name, a sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings; you shall go out and leap like calves from the stall.”
connections.context: The verse contrasts those who fear God’s name with the wicked in the preceding verse. Rav Tzadok links that fear with the healing and refinement symbolized by the sun.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְלַבְּנִים, וְזוֹכִים יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי דַּיְיקָא לְשֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם:
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 1
connections.quote: “‘Hashem appeared to him in the terebinths of Mamre, while he sat at the entrance of the tent in the heat of the day.’ It is written (Malachi 3:20), ‘For you who fear My name, a sun of righteousness will shine, with healing in its wings.’ ‘Those who fear My name’ are those who have a grasp of Torah and Hashem, which brings them true awe. Hashem promises that the sun of righteousness will shine for them—that is, clarified words of Torah. ‘Healing in its wings’ means confidence and strength in Hashem and Torah, like wings, which are a strong support for winged creatures.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the siman's closing sun-and-healing verse as a promise of clarified Torah and confidence in Hashem. The wings support the person as a bird's wings support it. This supplies a positive description of the movement from the fire of awe toward delight and strength, without identifying the pain itself as the final attainment.
connections.headline: The healing wings of confidence

connections.hePhrase: [קנד] כְּשֵׁם שֶׁצָּרִיךְ אָדָם לְהַאֲמִין בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ צָרִיךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לְהַאֲמִין בְּעַצְמוֹ.
connections.quote: “And our Sages taught (Shabbat 87a) that Hashem told Moses: "More power to you for breaking them", for in truth the broken fragments of the tablets repose side by side within the Ark, matching the rabbinic warning (Berakhot 8b): "Be mindful of an elder who has forgotten his learning through lapse of memory", for both are equal in sanctity, except that in the manifest realm one is broken while the other remains whole, whereas their place within the Ark is identical.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek develops the same approval of Moshe’s breaking the tablets by emphasizing that broken and whole tablets share the Ark’s holiness. This supports the siman’s demand to believe that one’s life matters to Hashem. A visible break does not prove the disappearance of the underlying kedushah; the account calls for renewed fidelity rather than declaring that every present action is right.
connections.headline: The broken tablets still belong in the Ark

connections.hePhrase: [קנד] כְּשֵׁם שֶׁצָּרִיךְ אָדָם לְהַאֲמִין בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ צָרִיךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לְהַאֲמִין בְּעַצְמוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Shemot 3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Shemot 3
