connections.quote: “You should have understood: the hearts of human beings are in My hand, to turn according to My will. If I sent you, you should have trusted that I would place it in their hearts to be compelled to hear you.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach places Moshe's uncertainty about Israel's belief within his divine commission: the One who sends him can also turn hearts. Its surrounding argument questions Moshe's wish to possess an independent power of compulsion. This illuminates the siman's qualification of believing in oneself: the confidence is that one has a real place in Hashem's concern and service, while its power remains received from Him.
connections.headline: The sender also works within the hearers

connections.hePhrase: רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֵסֶק עִמּוֹ, וְשֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ פּוֹעֵל בָּטֵל "שֶׁבִּן לַיְלָה" וְכוּלֵי (יוֹנָה ד, י), וּכְחַיְתוֹ שָׂדֶה שֶׁלְּאַחַר מִיתָתָם נֶאֶבְדוּ וְאֵינָם.
connections.heRef: רש"י על בבא מציעא ס״ח א:י״ד:ב׳
connections.quote: ““Like an idle worker”—this means how much a person would be willing to receive in order to sit idle.”

connections.hePhrase: רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֵסֶק עִמּוֹ, וְשֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ פּוֹעֵל בָּטֵל "שֶׁבִּן לַיְלָה" וְכוּלֵי (יוֹנָה ד, י), וּכְחַיְתוֹ שָׂדֶה שֶׁלְּאַחַר מִיתָתָם נֶאֶבְדוּ וְאֵינָם.
connections.quote: “Hashem said: You cared about the plant for which you did not labor and which you did not grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night.”

connections.hePhrase: רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֵסֶק עִמּוֹ, וְשֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ פּוֹעֵל בָּטֵל "שֶׁבִּן לַיְלָה" וְכוּלֵי (יוֹנָה ד, י), וּכְחַיְתוֹ שָׂדֶה שֶׁלְּאַחַר מִיתָתָם נֶאֶבְדוּ וְאֵינָם.
connections.quote: “For a thousand years in Your eyes are like yesterday when it has passed, and like a watch in the night.”
connections.context: These sources clarify two images in this sentence. A po’el batel is paid for remaining idle; Rav Tzadok says that a person’s service of Hashem has real purpose. The overnight image recalls Jonah’s short-lived plant. Even a long human lifetime can appear like a passing night before Hashem, as Psalm 90 says. Rav Tzadok nevertheless insists that a person’s work and the moments of his life have lasting significance.

connections.hePhrase: רַק צָרִיךְ לְהַאֲמִין כִּי נַפְשׁוֹ מִמְּקוֹר הַחַיִּים יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְעַנֵּג וּמִשְׁתַּעֲשֵׁעַ בָּהּ כְּשֶׁעוֹשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: “Hashem knows the days of the whole-hearted, and their inheritance shall endure forever.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק צָרִיךְ לְהַאֲמִין כִּי נַפְשׁוֹ מִמְּקוֹר הַחַיִּים יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְעַנֵּג וּמִשְׁתַּעֲשֵׁעַ בָּהּ כְּשֶׁעוֹשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: ““What makes you see that your blood is redder?” That is: What is your reasoning for permitting the act because “he shall live by them,” rather than die by them? The reason is that the lives of Israel are dearer before the Omnipresent than the commandments. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let the commandment be set aside and let this person live. But now, when an Israelite is being killed and the commandment is also set aside, why should it be preferable before the Omnipresent to transgress His commandment? Why should your blood be dearer to Him than the blood of your fellow Israelite?”
connections.context: Psalm 37:18 and Rashi’s explanation illuminate why a person must believe that his soul and every moment of his life matter to Hashem. Rashi’s setting is the preservation of life: a commandment is ordinarily set aside to save life, while killing another person cannot be justified by claiming that one’s own life is more valuable. This illustrates the preciousness of life; Rav Tzadok’s further point is that Hashem takes delight in the soul’s fulfillment of His will.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ: "וַיַּאֲמִינוּ בַּה' וּבְמֹשֶׁה עַבְדּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת יד, לא)
connections.quote: ‘Israel saw the great hand that Hashem had exercised against Egypt. The people feared Hashem, and they believed in Hashem and in Moses, His servant.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ: "וַיַּאֲמִינוּ בַּה' וּבְמֹשֶׁה עַבְדּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת יד, לא)
connections.quote: “But in truth, although a person possesses choice, nevertheless, “Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him, he could not overcome it.” It is like a person who presents a riddle to his son and first supplies all the necessary premises, until he almost tells him the riddle’s answer, so that the son will understand and it will be credited to him. This is how Hashem conducts Himself with a person.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ: "וַיַּאֲמִינוּ בַּה' וּבְמֹשֶׁה עַבְדּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת יד, לא)
connections.quote: “This is what Moses meant when he said that they would therefore not believe him: they felt that they themselves possessed no merit through which they could deserve redemption. Hashem answered him that they were believers, children of believers—children of Abraham, who believed in Me, that I can send illumination into a person’s heart even when he possesses none of his own. This was their faith in Egypt, as it says, “The people believed.” So it was: Hashem sent them illumination and abundant love and brought them out from there. But Hashem’s true desire was that they should also experience an awakening from themselves, without an awakening from above.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ: "וַיַּאֲמִינוּ בַּה' וּבְמֹשֶׁה עַבְדּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת יד, לא)
connections.quote: “Afterward it says, “They believed in Hashem and in Moses His servant.” Moses comprised all the souls of the six hundred thousand of Israel. As the Mekhilta teaches concerning “The children of Israel were fruitful and multiplied,” six hundred thousand were born in one womb—and who was this? Moses. For Moses our teacher comprised all the souls of Israel. This explains the Gemara’s question, “Is fear such a small matter?” and its answer, “Yes, for Moses it is a small matter”: for Moses, the source of Israel’s souls, it was easy for them to reach the quality of fear. This is “They believed in Hashem and in Moses His servant”: since they believed that Moses was Hashem’s servant and that they were branches of him, through this they attained complete faith. This is what they attained at the splitting of the sea.”
connections.context: Peri Tzadik, Pesach 45, develops this extended parallel. The first two excerpts explain why a person’s lack of merit does not sever his relation to Hashem: divine assistance can illuminate his heart while still allowing his own response to count as his achievement. The final excerpt explains the same verse used here: believing in Moses includes recognizing the worth and spiritual capacity of the souls comprised within him. The three excerpts are selected passages from the same discourse; intervening material develops the stages of faith before the sea split.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, "מֹשֶׁה" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּלַל שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּדּוֹר הַהוּא, הֶאֱמִינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בָּהֶם
connections.quote: “Jacob our father was always at the point of unity. He is the collective whole of the children of Israel, for he was not a private individual. Therefore his image is engraved beneath the Throne of Glory, and therefore the aspect of unity was always present with him.”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, "מֹשֶׁה" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּלַל שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּדּוֹר הַהוּא, הֶאֱמִינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בָּהֶם
connections.quote: “For King David, peace be upon him, was not a private individual. It is taught that he has nothing of his own; through this self-nullification he had the power to awaken all the hearts of the children of Israel. As our Sages explained his request, “Let me dwell in Your tent forever”: his words should make an impression in the mouths of all Israel, through his psalms in the Book of Psalms.”
connections.context: Sefat Emet describes Jacob and David as figures whose spiritual identity embraces the people as a whole. These passages provide parallels to Rav Tzadok’s statement that Moses encompasses the souls of his generation. The quoted passages concern Jacob and David; Rav Tzadok applies the same collective principle here to Moses. The original references are Vayetzei, 5642, and Hanukkah, 5644; the linked digital subdivisions are 10:3 and 13:6.

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן בְּמֹשֶׁה, אֲשֶׁר הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵם, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:) שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד הַדִּבּוּר לְמֹשֶׁה.
connections.quote: “Just as, in the dimension of place, there is the Foundation Stone from which the world was founded, and it is the root of the entire world, so in the dimension of soul there is one soul that includes the entire generation: the leader of the generation, as is known; likewise, there is one that includes all generations. In the dimension of time there is a time that includes all the days: the Sabbath day.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן בְּמֹשֶׁה, אֲשֶׁר הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵם, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:) שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד הַדִּבּוּר לְמֹשֶׁה.
connections.quote: “The explanation is that, as is known, Moses’ prophecy consisted in his apprehending all the powers of the souls of all Israel. As is known, the Torah’s six hundred thousand letters correspond to the number of the children of Israel: the powers of their souls are the letters of the Torah. In accordance with their deeds, so was the prophecy of Moses our teacher, as our Sages said: As long as they were under censure, speech was not granted uniquely to Moses. This is the meaning of “Moses on the inside, Jacob on the outside.” Jacob denotes the collective souls of Israel: he is their father by birth. All the souls of the children are included in the father’s mind, for they issued from him, and outwardly it is evident that he is their father. Moses our teacher is likewise called a father, as our Sages said [he is called “my father” three times, corresponding to the three patriarchs], because he is Israel’s teacher. The students are called children. This is “on the inside,” within their souls.”
connections.context: Ois 172 supplies the general model of the generation’s souls being included in its leader. Dover Tzedek applies that model directly to Moses’ prophecy and to the Talmudic statement quoted here. The latter is printed as Dover Tzedek, Acharei Mot 4; the digital catalog places the passage in Miscellany 4:11. The correspondence with the Torah’s letters is Rav Tzadok’s mystical formulation.

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן בְּמֹשֶׁה, אֲשֶׁר הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵם, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:) שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד הַדִּבּוּר לְמֹשֶׁה.
connections.quote: “Rav Dimi bar Yosef said in Rav Nachman’s name: The day on which those destined to die in the wilderness had finished dying.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן בְּמֹשֶׁה, אֲשֶׁר הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵם, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:) שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד הַדִּבּוּר לְמֹשֶׁה.
connections.quote: “There was no speech with Moses, as it says, “When all the men of war had finished dying from among the people,” and adjacent to it is written, “Hashem spoke to me, saying”—to me the speech was directed.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן בְּמֹשֶׁה, אֲשֶׁר הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵם, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:) שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד הַדִּבּוּר לְמֹשֶׁה.
connections.heRef: רשב"ם על בבא בתרא קכ״א ב:א׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““There was no speech with Moses”: mouth to mouth as at first. But if they required a communication, as in the episode of Korach, which followed the spies, He would speak through an angel or through the Urim and Tummim. Alternatively, He spoke with him only when required for a matter they needed.”
connections.context: The discussion explains one reason for the joy of the fifteenth of Av. The sentence begins at the end of 121a and continues on 121b: until the wilderness generation’s deaths ended, Moses lacked the former mode of divine speech. Rashbam qualifies this as the loss of ordinary direct communication, not the claim that no necessary divine message reached Moses during those years. This is the connection between Israel’s condition and Moses’ prophecy used here.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, כִּי בְּכָל חֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חָטָא גַּם כֵּן מֹשֶׁה שֶׁהוּא כְּלָלוּתָם:
connections.quote: ““The children of Israel—I am their atonement”: out of his love for them he would say, “I am their atonement.” That is, all the punishment that ought to come upon them I accept upon myself, in order to atone for them.”
connections.context: This is Bartenura’s explanation of Rabbi Yishmael’s words in Mishnah Negaim 2:1. Takanat HaShavin 10:4 cites this willingness to bear Israel’s punishment when explaining how the leader is bound to the whole generation. It therefore clarifies the responsibility contained in Rav Tzadok’s statement here that Moses includes them all. The Mishnah’s surrounding subject is the assessment of skin lesions; the subsequent words about being intermediate between two extremes describe skin complexion, not a middle level of moral standing.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, כִּי בְּכָל חֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חָטָא גַּם כֵּן מֹשֶׁה שֶׁהוּא כְּלָלוּתָם:
connections.quote: “Such is Hashem’s way: He sweetens bitterness through bitterness. As our Sages said concerning “He cast it,” and so forth, “and the waters became sweet”: it was a bitter oleander tree, but this was done at Hashem’s command and in accordance with His will. Through it both this bitterness and the earlier bitterness were sweetened.
connections.context: The continuation explains how the leader’s identification with the people includes accepting their suffering. Esther’s “If I perish” is interpreted as self-sacrifice on their behalf, and Moses’s rebuke is interpreted as bearing the generation’s punishment. Thus “the head of the generation is the generation” supplies the precise parallel to Rav Tzadok’s words “Moses, who encompasses them.” The passage also makes the divine command and will explicit in its opening example of bitter wood sweetening the water. The excerpt ends after the complete explanation of Esther’s personal loss; the later discussion of her descendants is a separate continuation.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ בָּעֵגֶל הָיָה חֵטְא מֹשֶׁה בִּשְׁבִירַת הַלּוּחוֹת, וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא דָּבָר תָּמוּהַּ וְזָר מְאֹד אֲפִילּוּ לִקְרוֹעַ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה בַּחֲמָתוֹ וּלְהַשְׁלִיכָהּ לָאָרֶץ מִכְּתַב יַד סוֹפֵר דְּעָלְמָא, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן הַלּוּחוֹת מִכְּתַב ה'.
connections.quote: see note 1375.
connections.context: Exodus 32:16 explains the force of Rav Tzadok’s comparison: even destroying an ordinary handwritten Torah scroll would be extraordinary, and these tablets were themselves God’s work and bore His writing. The reason Moses broke them and the divine approval are supplied in the existing note on Shabbat 87a.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַמָּשׁ חֵטְא דְּעֵגֶל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר,
connections.quote: “Every sin of the generation must have some trace of itself in the head of the generation as well, for all Israel form one complete body, and the head of the generation includes the entire generation: the leader corresponds to his generation, as is known. Thus Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, broke the Tablets in connection with Israel’s sin of the Calf. This too was a sin in a corresponding form, but he intended it for the sake of Heaven. When He later said to him, “Well done for breaking them,” he thereby brought about forgiveness and atonement for Israel as well, because it became clear that their sin, too, had been something akin to a transgression for the sake of Heaven.
connections.context: This is the extended parallel behind “as I wrote elsewhere.” Rav Tzadok moves from Moses and the Tablets to Elijah, Yael, and Esther, while retaining repentance, punishment, and atonement as integral parts of the discussion. His argument distinguishes an act’s outward form from its true intention and from the retrospective disclosure of its role. Elijah’s exceptional act is explicitly commanded by Hashem, and Esther’s action is described as contrary to her true will and undertaken to save Israel. The paragraph itself states that even complete repentance out of love does not remove every need for atonement. The kabbalistic account of Dinah and Cozbi is quoted as Rav Tzadok’s interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ: "יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ", יָדַע כִּי גַּם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): "בּוֹאוּ וְנַחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: see note 1445.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ: "יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ", יָדַע כִּי גַּם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): "בּוֹאוּ וְנַחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Come, let us be grateful to our ancestors, for had they not sinned, we would not have come into the world. As it says, “I said: You are divine beings, all of you children of the Most High.” You ruined your deeds—“Yet you shall die like a human being.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ: "יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ", יָדַע כִּי גַּם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): "בּוֹאוּ וְנַחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “Do not say, “We would not have come into the world,” but rather, “We would have been as though we had not come into the world.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ: "יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ", יָדַע כִּי גַּם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): "בּוֹאוּ וְנַחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ וְכוּלֵי".
connections.heRef: רש"י על עבודה זרה ה׳ א:י״א:א׳
connections.quote: ““As though we had not come into the world”: because they would live forever, and as long as they endure, we are of no importance.”
connections.context: The Gemara tests the first wording and revises it: later generations would still be born, but their standing would be eclipsed by ancestors who lived forever. Rashi states this explanation explicitly. This resolved reading clarifies Rav Tzadok’s comparison with divine approval of Moses’ breaking the tablets.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְקִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה אָמַר: "הֲצֹאן וּבָקָר יִשָּׁחֵט לָהֶם וּמָצָא לָהֶם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יא, כב), וְכֵן בְּמֵי מְרִיבָה;
connections.quote: “Would flocks and herds be slaughtered for them and suffice for them? Or would all the fish of the sea be gathered for them and suffice for them?”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְקִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה אָמַר: "הֲצֹאן וּבָקָר יִשָּׁחֵט לָהֶם וּמָצָא לָהֶם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יא, כב), וְכֵן בְּמֵי מְרִיבָה;
connections.quote: “This is one of four matters that Rabbi Akiva expounded and Rabbi Shimon did not expound as he did. Rabbi Akiva says: “Six hundred thousand men on foot,” and You have said, “I will give them meat, and they shall eat for a month”; “would flocks and herds”—everything is according to its plain meaning: Who can provide enough for them? ... Which is more severe, this or “Listen, you rebels”? But because he did not say this publicly, Scripture spared him and did not exact punishment from him; the incident at Meribah was public, so Scripture did not spare him. Rabbi Shimon says: Heaven forbid! This did not enter that righteous man’s mind. Could someone of whom it is written, “He is faithful in all My house,” say that the Omnipresent cannot provide enough for us? Rather, he said: Six hundred thousand men on foot, and You say, “I will give them meat for a month,” and afterward You will kill so great a nation? Would flocks and herds be slaughtered for them so that they may be killed, and this meal suffice them forever? Is this to Your praise? Does one say to a donkey, “Take a kor of barley, and we shall cut off your head”? The Holy One, blessed be He, answered him: If I do not give it, they will say My power is limited. Is it good in your eyes that Hashem’s power be limited in their eyes? Let them and a hundred like them perish, but let My power not be limited before them even for a single moment.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְקִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה אָמַר: "הֲצֹאן וּבָקָר יִשָּׁחֵט לָהֶם וּמָצָא לָהֶם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יא, כב), וְכֵן בְּמֵי מְרִיבָה;
connections.quote: “Hashem said to Moses and Aaron: Because you did not believe in Me, to sanctify Me before the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this congregation into the land that I have given them.”
connections.context: Rashi on Numbers 11:22 preserves two readings of the meat request. Rabbi Akiva understands Moses’ words as questioning the provision, while Rabbi Shimon rejects that reading and understands Moses as protesting the sequence of feeding and then punishment. Rashi’s preservation of the disagreement matters: Rav Tzadok’s reference to a corresponding failure in Moses accords with the first approach, while his connection between the leader and the people is his larger interpretation. Numbers 20:12 supplies the explicitly named Meribah example.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַמְרַגְּלִים הָיָה חֶטְאוֹ הַשְּׁלִיחוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שְׁלַח לְךָ" – לְדַעְתְּךָ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ בְּכֻלָּם] –
connections.quote: ““Send men for yourself”: Reish Lakish said, “Send for yourself”—at your own discretion. Does a person select a bad portion for himself? This is the meaning of “The matter was good in my eyes.” Reish Lakish said: “In my eyes,” but not in the eyes of the Omnipresent.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבַמְרַגְּלִים הָיָה חֶטְאוֹ הַשְּׁלִיחוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שְׁלַח לְךָ" – לְדַעְתְּךָ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ בְּכֻלָּם] –
connections.quote: ““Send for yourself”: At your own discretion. I am not commanding you; if you wish, send them. For Israel came and said, “Let us send men before us,” as it says, “All of you approached me.” Moses consulted the Divine Presence. He said: I told them that it is good, as it says, “I will bring you up from the affliction of Egypt.” By their lives, I shall give them room to err through the spies’ words, so that they will not inherit it.”
connections.context: Sotah 34b and Rashi on Numbers 13:2 distinguish permission to send the spies from a command to do so. This supplies the basis for Rav Tzadok’s identifying Moses’ own initiative as the aspect of the episode that corresponded to the people’s failure.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (בְּשַׁלַּח סא עַמּוּד א) דְּנֶצַח וָהוֹד לְבוּשֵׁי מַלְכָּא, וְהֵם תְּרֵין בַּדֵּי עֲרָבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים,
connections.quote: “If he guards it, he is called mighty, and the Holy One, blessed be He, clothes him in His garments. What are the garments of the Holy One, blessed be He? Hod and Netzach, as it is written, “You are clothed in splendor and majesty.” … Then a person cleaves properly to the holy King.”
connections.context: The passage is interpreting the guarding of the holy covenant. Its identification of Netzach and Hod as the King’s garments is the clause Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (בְּשַׁלַּח סא עַמּוּד א) דְּנֶצַח וָהוֹד לְבוּשֵׁי מַלְכָּא, וְהֵם תְּרֵין בַּדֵּי עֲרָבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים,
connections.quote: “The lulav in the right hand includes six species: three myrtle branches—Gedulah, Gevurah, and Tiferet. … The two willow branches are Netzach and Hod, resembling the two lips. The lulav is Yesod, resembling the spine. … The etrog is Malkhut, resembling the heart.”
connections.context: This passage in Raaya Meheimna identifies the willow branches with Netzach and Hod. It supplies the separate symbolism invoked after the Zohar’s garment image; the earlier Beshalach quotation did not explain the two willows.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (בְּשַׁלַּח סא עַמּוּד א) דְּנֶצַח וָהוֹד לְבוּשֵׁי מַלְכָּא, וְהֵם תְּרֵין בַּדֵּי עֲרָבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים,
connections.quote: “So too with the matzah: through it the invitation is made for the seven days of Pesach; and the invitation for the seven days of Sukkot is made with seven species: the lulav, the etrog, three myrtles and two willow branches.”
connections.context: This passage of the Ra’aya Mehemna counts the two willow branches among the seven species that correspond to the seven days of Sukkot.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (בְּשַׁלַּח סא עַמּוּד א) דְּנֶצַח וָהוֹד לְבוּשֵׁי מַלְכָּא, וְהֵם תְּרֵין בַּדֵּי עֲרָבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא וּבַתִּיקּוּנִים,
connections.quote: “The three myrtles allude to the three Patriarchs, the two willow branches to the two true prophets, the lulav to ‘The righteous one shall flourish like the palm’ (Psalms 92:13); the etrog alludes to the Shechinah, and the sukkah to the Mother who shelters over them.”
connections.context: The “two true prophets” are the sefirot of Netzach and Hod.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשַׁת אֱמוֹר: עֲרָבָה לֹא טַעַם וְלֹא רֵיחַ, כָּךְ וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ““And willows of the brook”—these are Israel. Just as the willow has neither taste nor fragrance, so among Israel there are people who have neither Torah nor good deeds. What does the Holy One, blessed be He, do with them? Destroying them is impossible. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, says: Let them all be bound together in one bundle, and they will atone for one another. If you do this, at that time I am exalted, as it is written, “Who builds His upper chambers in heaven.” When is He exalted? When they are made into one bundle, as it says, “And establishes His bundle upon the earth.” Therefore Moses instructs Israel: “You shall take for yourselves on the first day.””
connections.context: The full willow interpretation adds the conclusion essential to the image: the four species are bound together and benefit one another. Rav Tzadok applies this relation within a person, between Torah activity and the ordinary activities that support it.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הִמְשִׁילוּ בְּחֻלִּין (צב.) עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים לְעַלְיָא וְאִתְכַּלְיָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: This nation is compared to a vine. Its branches are the householders; its clusters are the Torah scholars; its leaves are the unlearned; and its tendrils are the empty ones among Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הִמְשִׁילוּ בְּחֻלִּין (צב.) עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים לְעַלְיָא וְאִתְכַּלְיָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12:1
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12:1
connections.quote: “Although “leaves” are everywhere expounded as what is not the principal object, as Sukkah expounds “its leaf does not wither” to include even ordinary conversation, and Chullin identifies leaves and grape clusters with ordinary people and Torah scholars, it also says that without the leaves the clusters could not endure: in grape clusters the leaves protect. This concerns what lies ahead. The principal thing is certainly Torah scholars and effort in Torah with intention for the sake of Heaven, while action is the leaves: ordinary people are those who perform mitzvot and good deeds. So too within the individual: when a person engages in mitzvot and good deeds, this sustains his wisdom, as Avot teaches, while the principal fruit is wisdom.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim explicitly applies the scholars/common people and leaves/fruit images within one person. In that discussion, mitzvah action protects the wisdom cultivated through deliberate effort. Here Rav Tzadok places ordinary worldly work around Torah and mitzvos together, then changes the meaning of clothing again at higher levels. The comparison helps keep the imagery relational: it describes what sustains or clothes what at a particular level, rather than assigning one fixed meaning to “leaf” throughout all the teachings.
connections.headline: Leaves and fruit describe a relationship

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הִמְשִׁילוּ בְּחֻלִּין (צב.) עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים לְעַלְיָא וְאִתְכַּלְיָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: see note 853.
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains the same leaf verse through speech that has become an expression of Torah even when unplanned. It stresses that this is an attained direction of choice, rather than something automatic in a person's status. This makes the siman's garment image concrete: permitted activity can support and reveal the Torah within, while its different discussion of Rashbi remains an exceptional attained state.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סֻכָּה כא:) עַל "וְעָלֵהוּ לֹא יִבּוֹל" (תְּהִלִּים א, ג) – אֲפִילּוּ שִׂיחַת חוּלִין וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁהֵם עַלְיָא לְאִתְכַּלְיָא דְּהַיְינוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “He shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that brings forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf does not wither; and in all that he does he prospers.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִלְמָלֵא עַלְיָא וְכוּלֵי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה:): הַנְהֵג בָּהֶן וְכוּלֵי, בְּמָטוּתָא מִינַּיְיכוּ וְכוּלֵי, וְהַרְבֵּה וְכוּלֵי וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ, דְּאִלְמָלֵא וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““You shall gather your grain”: conduct yourself in the ordinary way of the world alongside [Torah study]; these are Rabbi Yishmael’s words.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִלְמָלֵא עַלְיָא וְכוּלֵי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה:): הַנְהֵג בָּהֶן וְכוּלֵי, בְּמָטוּתָא מִינַּיְיכוּ וְכוּלֵי, וְהַרְבֵּה וְכוּלֵי וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ, דְּאִלְמָלֵא וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rava said to the Sages: I ask you, during Nisan and Tishrei do not appear before me, so that you will not be troubled about your sustenance throughout the year.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִלְמָלֵא עַלְיָא וְכוּלֵי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה:): הַנְהֵג בָּהֶן וְכוּלֵי, בְּמָטוּתָא מִינַּיְיכוּ וְכוּלֵי, וְהַרְבֵּה וְכוּלֵי וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ, דְּאִלְמָלֵא וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Abaye said: Many acted according to Rabbi Yishmael and succeeded; according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, and did not succeed.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok abbreviates all three sayings: ordinary work alongside study, seasonal labor that protects the rest of the year, and the experience of those who attempted the more demanding alternative. Together they explain his comparison of worldly support to leaves protecting the fruit of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קיג.): מָאנֵי מְכַבְּדוּתָא, (וְשָׁם קמה:): וּבְלָא מָתָא תּוֹתְבָאי.
connections.quote: ““And you shall honor it”: your Shabbat clothing should not be like your weekday clothing. As Rabbi Yochanan would call his clothes “those that honor me.””

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קיג.): מָאנֵי מְכַבְּדוּתָא, (וְשָׁם קמה:): וּבְלָא מָתָא תּוֹתְבָאי.
connections.quote: “Why are the Torah scholars in Babylonia distinguished by their clothing? Because they are not in their home place. As people say: In my town, my name; away from my town, my clothes.”
connections.context: The first passage connects clothing with honor; the second says that clothing communicates standing where a person is not already known. Rav Tzadok uses both to explain the role of the spiritual garment.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קיג.): מָאנֵי מְכַבְּדוּתָא, (וְשָׁם קמה:): וּבְלָא מָתָא תּוֹתְבָאי.
connections.quote: “Every kind of suffering proceeds from the lack of a place, as the Talmud asks (Shabbat 145b): why are Babylonian Torah scholars distinguished by their clothing? Because they are not in their own place. As people say: in my own city, my name; outside it, my garment. Someone away from his place must distinguish himself through many boundaries, because opponents continually confront and press him, requiring extensive clarification. Concerning this Hashem promised, ‘I will establish a place for My people Israel.’ Israel's principal place is as the Midrash says: the Holy One is the place of the world, while His world is not His place. When He illuminates this recognition for Israel, that He is the world's place, they recognize that nowhere in the world is outside His protection.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same saying about name and garment through the lack of a settled place. Away from that place, outward boundaries answer the opposition confronting the person; recognizing Hashem as the world's place supplies a deeper protection. This develops the siman's hierarchy of garments and its contrast with being at home, where the person's own name expresses him.
connections.headline: Outward distinctions away from one’s own place

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בְּגַן עֵדֶן הַלְּבוּשׁ מִפְּעֻלַּת הַתּוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (וַיַּקְהֵל רי עַמּוּד א),
connections.quote: ‘Fortunate is the portion of one who merits those garments we have described, in which the righteous are clothed in the Garden of Eden (below). These come from the good deeds that a person does in this world through the commandments of the Torah. Through them, the soul stands in the lower Garden of Eden, clothed in these precious garments.’

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַגּוּף נִקְרָא גּוּף הָאָדָם וְהַלְּבוּשׁ הוּא הַמַּלְבִּישׁ אֶת הַגּוּף, וּלְאַחַר מִיתָה אָז גּוּף הָאָדָם נִקְרָא הַנְּשָׁמָה וְהַגּוּף נִקְרָא רַק לְבוּשׁ.
connections.quote: see note 1741.
connections.context: Rabbi Chaim Vital explicitly distinguishes the inner person from the body that clothes the soul. This supplies the conceptual background for Rav Tzadok’s changing use of “body” and “garment” at different levels.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּרַשְׁבִּ"י בִּבְרָכוֹת שָׁם דְּלֵית לֵיהּ הַנְהֵג בָּהֶן מִדַּת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ,
connections.quote: “There is likewise a difference among the souls of Torah scholars. Some are consecrated from birth to belong entirely to God, like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions, whose Torah was their occupation. They were exempt from prayer, which is called temporal life, because all their occupation was with eternal life. They did not turn their attention at all to their livelihood, and a carob tree and a spring of water were created for them. Yet not everyone merits this, as they said: Many acted like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and did not succeed. We have already discussed the Gemara’s statement that when Israel do not fulfill God’s will, they perform their own work, as it says, “You shall gather your grain.” Maharsha asks: Surely this passage says, “If you diligently obey My commandments”; how can they be called people who do not fulfill God’s will? The explanation is that God’s original thought and will at Creation, when He made the human being upright, was that the person should be free for His service. This is called God’s will. But the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal oppressively with His creatures, and therefore did not explicitly command this. Accordingly, when they left the cave, saw people plowing and harvesting, and punished them for leaving eternal life and occupying themselves with temporal life, a heavenly voice said, “Have you come out to destroy My world?”—because most of the public cannot maintain this way of life.”
connections.context: This parallel explains Rabbi Shimon’s exceptional level and preserves Rav Tzadok’s explicit qualification that most people cannot follow it. Ordinary work remains necessary for the many, as the existing Berakhot quotation in this section also states.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (לג:) שֶׁהֶעֱנִישׁ לְהָעוֹסְקִים בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
connections.quote: “They emerged and saw people plowing and sowing. They said: They abandon eternal life and occupy themselves with temporary life! Wherever they directed their eyes was immediately burned. A heavenly voice came forth and said: Have you come out to destroy My world? Return to your cave! … When they came out again, wherever Rabbi Elazar struck, Rabbi Shimon healed.”
connections.context: This is the episode Rav Tzadok invokes concerning their initial reaction to ordinary labor. The heavenly rebuke and Rabbi Shimon’s subsequent healing are part of the same account and limit how the initial reaction is understood.

connections.hePhrase: וְעוֹד לְמַעְלָה הַלְּבוּשׁ כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (שָׁם עַמּוּד ב) מִן הַכַּוָּנוֹת שֶׁבַּלֵּב וּרְצוֹנוֹת לְתוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם;
connections.quote: “When the soul ascends through that opening of the firmament above, other precious, higher garments are prepared for it, made from the heart’s desire and intention in Torah and prayer. When that desire ascends above, the one who is crowned is crowned through it, while a portion remains for that person; from it garments of light are made in which the soul is clothed so as to ascend above. Although it has been explained that garments depend on deeds, these depend only on the spirit’s desire, as stated, so that it may stand among the holy spiritual angels. This is the clarification of the matter. The Holy Lamp learned this from Elijah: the garments below, in the earthly Garden, come from deeds; the garments above come from desire and the spirit’s intention in the heart.”
connections.context: This paragraph immediately follows the lower-Eden garment discussion already quoted in the existing note. It supplies the additional distinction needed here: higher garments arise from inward desire and intention, while the lower garments arise from deeds.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל "בְּמָתַאי" – זֶה יִהְיֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהוּא שְׁנַת הַיּוֹבֵל (כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר):
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon said further: On this account we have learned that the Sabbath is a likeness of the World to Come, and so it surely is. And for this reason the Sabbatical year and the Jubilee are a likeness, one of the other; and so it is with the Sabbath and the World to Come.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל "בְּמָתַאי" – זֶה יִהְיֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהוּא שְׁנַת הַיּוֹבֵל (כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר):
connections.quote: “But in the World to Come, which is the world of the Jubilee, … the prayer leader does not discharge him of his obligation, because there he has no redemption through others.”
connections.context: The Zohar pairs the Sabbatical year with the Sabbath and the Jubilee with the World to Come.

connections.hePhrase: "תָּשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ אֶל אֲחֻזָּתוֹ" (וַיִּקְרָא כה, יג), שָׁם יִהְיֶה שְׁמַאי – הַשֵּׁם מוֹרֶה עַל הָעֶצֶם, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּפִי עֶצֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹר מַחְצַב הַנְּשָׁמוֹת.
connections.quote: ‘In this Jubilee year, each of you shall return to his ancestral holding.’

connections.hePhrase: "תָּשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ אֶל אֲחֻזָּתוֹ" (וַיִּקְרָא כה, יג), שָׁם יִהְיֶה שְׁמַאי – הַשֵּׁם מוֹרֶה עַל הָעֶצֶם, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּפִי עֶצֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹר מַחְצַב הַנְּשָׁמוֹת.
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the portion Mishpatim, the completion of the rectification of Shovavim, in the passage “When you acquire a Hebrew servant.” As we said, it indicates that all the souls of Israel have a rectification. One who has not caused so much damage “shall go free in the seventh,” as the Midrash says: Just as I created the world in six days and rested on the seventh, so he shall serve you six years and go free. Even if he caused greater damage and reached the utmost distance, as it then says, “But if he shall expressly say, I love …”—being so coarsened by his desire for the maidservant and her offspring, to whom he has no connection except satisfying his desire, and not wishing to repent—he too has a rectification through the supernal Jubilee. Thus it says of the Jubilee, “You shall return, each man to his holding, and each man to his family you shall return.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reads the Jubilee’s return to one’s holding as the ultimate restoration of souls, including a person still far from repentance. This explains why the present passage identifies the final return with the soul’s own root.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז יִהְיוּ עֲרוּמִּים כְּקוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא בְּלִי לְבוּשׁ,
connections.quote: ““They were both naked,” and so forth. The reason is that beforehand they were devoid of the aspect of evil and were wholly holy. Their lower face was therefore like their upper face, for it is the aspect of evil that became attached to the human being that distinguishes the lower part of the person: there evil acquired its place.”
connections.context: Or HaChaim explains the absence of shame before the sin through the absence of evil from the person. This clarifies Rav Tzadok’s comparison between the final state and the unclothed state before the sin.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַלְּבוּשׁ נַעֲשָׂה רַק עַל יְדֵי יְדִיעָה דְּטוֹב וָרָע וְעַל יְדֵי הַבְּחִירָה וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם, שֶׁהוּא הַטֹּרַח דְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת;
connections.quote: “They said before Him: Master of the universe, give it to us anew and we will perform it. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: Fools of the world! Whoever labored on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat; whoever did not labor on the eve of Shabbat—from where will he eat on Shabbat?”
connections.context: In the Gemara, the nations ask for a new opportunity to perform the Torah after the time of reward has arrived. The Friday-and-Shabbat analogy supplies the image of present preparation and subsequent enjoyment used here.

connections.hePhrase: [וְגַם בְּמֵזִיד נִקְרָא כֵּן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קו.) עַל פָּסוּק "וַתִּקְרֶאןָ" – רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר: שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ כֻּלָּם וְכוּלֵי]
connections.quote: ““They called the people to the sacrifices of their gods”: Rabbi Eliezer says that naked women encountered them. Rabbi Yehoshua says that they all became men who had experienced a seminal emission.”
connections.context: The wordplay connects “they called,” vatikrena, with keri. It is the use of that terminology for the sinful encounter that Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: [וְגַם בְּמֵזִיד נִקְרָא כֵּן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קו.) עַל פָּסוּק "וַתִּקְרֶאןָ" – רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר: שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ כֻּלָּם וְכוּלֵי]
connections.quote: ‘The women invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods. The people ate and bowed down to their gods.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְגַם בְּמֵזִיד נִקְרָא כֵּן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קו.) עַל פָּסוּק "וַתִּקְרֶאןָ" – רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר: שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ כֻּלָּם וְכוּלֵי]
connections.quote: “In the Torah it is called a “nocturnal occurrence” even when intentional. This is called an “occurrence” because even the most pious person, and so forth. Anything done for one’s own pleasure is called an “occurrence,” for the blessed God is the Master of order, and whatever is not intended for the blessed God alone is called an “occurrence.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the particular sense of mikreh used here: an act directed toward private pleasure appears detached from divine order. The abbreviated reference to the most pious person alludes to the Vayikra Rabbah passage concerning Jesse discussed in the following section.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת עִיקַּר הַכֹּל, וְכָל תַּרְיַ"ג מִצְווֹת הַתּוֹרָה הֵם רַק עֵיטִין לְהַגִּיעַ לִידִיעָה זוֹ שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “In many ways the Torah admonishes a person not to sin before his Master. In many ways it gives him counsel not to turn from his paths to the right or to the left. In many ways it gives him counsel on how to return before his Master and be forgiven. For we learned: the Torah gives a person six hundred and thirteen kinds of counsel, so that he may be whole with his Master, because his Master desires to benefit him in this world and in the World to Come.”
connections.context: This is the original description of the 613 commandments as counsels. Its context includes both avoiding wrongdoing and returning after wrongdoing; Rav Tzadok identifies their unifying aim as recognition of divine providence.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל הָעֲבֵירוֹת נִקְרָא בַּתּוֹכָחָה "אִם תֵּלְכוּ עִמִּי קֶרִי" (וַיִּקְרָא כו, כא) – לְשׁוֹן מִקְרֶה, כִּי הָעֲבֵירוֹת הֵם יְצִיאָה מִן הַסֵּדֶר וְאֵין לָהֶם סֵדֶר
connections.quote: ‘If you walk with Me only casually and refuse to listen to Me, I will add seven more blows upon you, corresponding to your sins.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל הָעֲבֵירוֹת נִקְרָא בַּתּוֹכָחָה "אִם תֵּלְכוּ עִמִּי קֶרִי" (וַיִּקְרָא כו, כא) – לְשׁוֹן מִקְרֶה, כִּי הָעֲבֵירוֹת הֵם יְצִיאָה מִן הַסֵּדֶר וְאֵין לָהֶם סֵדֶר
connections.quote: “We are not to believe that this is chance or an accidental occurrence. This is the meaning of “If you walk with Me by chance”: when I bring these troubles upon you to punish you, if you regard them as chance, I shall add more of that same chance—as you conceive it—with greater force and severity. This is the meaning of “You walk with Me by chance, and I shall walk with you in the fury of chance.” For their belief that it is chance causes them to persist in their corrupt opinions and unjust deeds and not repent of them.”
connections.context: Rambam explains the repeated language of keri in the rebuke as interpreting events as mere chance. The conclusion is essential: that interpretation obstructs repentance. The quotation uses the public-domain Hebrew translation by Ibn Tibbon.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כָּל הָעֳנָשִׁים נִקְרָא שָׁם "חֲמַת קֶרִי" (וַיִּקְרָא כו, כח).
connections.quote: “Then I will walk with you in a fury of keri, and I Myself will chastise you seven times for your sins.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁמַּאֲמִין שֶׁאֵין מִקְרֶה, מַמְתִּיק כָּל הַדִּינִים וּמְתַקֵּן כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 23
connections.quote: see note 577.
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim addresses the boundary within this teaching directly. The forgiving disclosure comes from Hashem; the human response still recognizes sin, deficiency and dependence on Him. This supplies a necessary companion to the siman's retrospective account of providence. The claim is not converted into a prior authorization to transgress or a self-issued verdict that no return is needed.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁמַּאֲמִין שֶׁאֵין מִקְרֶה, מַמְתִּיק כָּל הַדִּינִים וּמְתַקֵּן כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת,
connections.quote: “The essence of repentance is that Hashem illuminate a person's eyes until deliberate sins become merits: he recognizes and understands that all he sinned was also within Hashem's will, as the Sages teach in Berakhot concerning three verses, including “You turned their hearts backward” and “whom I afflicted.” This is the matter of knowledge and choice explained by the Ari at the end of Four Hundred Shekels of Silver: both are true, each in its own place. Where choice operates there is no place for knowledge, and where knowledge operates there is in truth no place for choice. When a person attains this immense light, all his deliberate sins cease to be outside the depth of Hashem's knowledge, and He, His knowledge and His will are all one. Since Hashem willed it so, all is merit, and he attains the complete atonement of Yom Kippur. This is the secret of the scapegoat: if a person performed this act on his own, he would be committing outright idolatry, the prohibition “You shall have no other gods,” the foundation of all negative commandments and all departures from Hashem's will. But because sending the goat is Hashem's will and command, it becomes a mitzvah rather than a transgression. The Sages explain this in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer, chapter 46; see Ramban on Acharei. We give a portion to Azazel, the evil, because Hashem commanded that it be given, and thus the transgression becomes a mitzvah.”
connections.explanation: Siman 40 is an especially precise counterpart to the retrospective claim here. It states explicitly that knowledge and choice are both true in their respective places, then uses the scapegoat to distinguish a commanded act from the same act undertaken independently. Read together, these passages describe the illumination of teshuvah without making the human standpoint of choice disappear or converting an uncommanded act into a mitzvah by personal assertion.
connections.headline: Knowledge and choice each have their place

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁמַּאֲמִין שֶׁאֵין מִקְרֶה, מַמְתִּיק כָּל הַדִּינִים וּמְתַקֵּן כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת,
connections.quote: “In Ashur, by contrast, the belief that everything is in Heaven's hands is only in the manner of Scripture's ‘which He allotted to them.’ They take strength from the fact that everything is in Heaven's hands so that they may expand into the flood of their desires. From this power called Ashur, deficiencies of this kind also branch into Israel: the entire deficiency is at the root, while nothing deficient is visible in the body's outward garment. Of this it says, ‘Those lost in the land of Ashur shall come.’”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes Israel's acknowledgment that everything is in Heaven's hands from taking that acknowledgment as encouragement to pursue one's desires. It places the latter fault at the root even when an outwardly fine garment hides it. This is an essential qualification when reading the siman's retrospective restoration of order. The same source later describes the great shofar bringing even those called lost back into recognition and repair.
connections.headline: Providence and the misuse of assurance

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אִם כֵּן עַל כָּרְחֲךָ כֻּלָּם לֹא הָיוּ יוֹצְאִים מִן הַסֵּדֶר, וְהָיָה מְסוּדָּר כָּךְ וְלֹא בְּמִקְרֶה, וְאִם כֵּן אֵינוֹ עֲבֵירָה,
connections.quote: “Even the wicked of Israel commit their wrongs only in accordance with the blessed God’s will, as will be clarified in the future [after repentance from love], when the sins will be like those years that have proceeded in order since the six days of Creation. So too all the sins were arranged from the six days of Creation, when the blessed God willed that Israel should perform them.”
connections.context: This parallel explicitly places the retrospective clarification after repentance from love. That qualification accompanies Rav Tzadok’s account of the eventual discovery of order and is retained in the quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כז): אִם יֹאמְרוּ לְךָ: אִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא אָדָם הָיָה חַי לְעוֹלָם? אֱמוֹר לָהֶם: הֲרֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “If a person says to you: Had the first Adam not sinned and eaten from that tree, he would have lived and endured forever, say to him: Elijah already existed—he did not sin, and he lives and endures forever.”
connections.context: Elijah is the Midrash’s example that life without death is possible. Rav Tzadok uses this example in his account of the source of mortality and its correction.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵלִיָּהוּ נִקְרָא "מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית" כַּנּוֹדָע
connections.quote: ““The lord”—this is the King Messiah, and he is the angel of the covenant. Alternatively, “the angel of the covenant” refers to Elijah. Thus the aggadah says that Elijah was zealous for the covenant of circumcision, which the kingdom of Ephraim prevented them from observing, as it says: “I have been very zealous for the Lord, God of Israel, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant.” He said to him: You were zealous at Shittim, and here you are zealous for circumcision. By your life, Israel will not perform circumcision without your seeing it with your own eyes. From this they established a seat of honor for Elijah, who is called the angel of the covenant, as it says: “The angel of the covenant whom you desire—behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts.””
connections.context: Radak records the interpretation identifying Elijah as the angel of the covenant and connects it to his presence at circumcisions. His alternative identification with the Messiah is preserved.

connections.hePhrase: [וּלְכָךְ אָמְרָה לוֹ אוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה: בָּאתָ אֵלַי בִּתְשַׁמִּישׁ הַמִּטָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפִרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לג;
connections.quote: “"He and she" (indicate that it was) by the merit of Elijah that they had to eat. After (a period of) days, the son of the woman fell sick and died, as it is said, "And it came to pass after these things that the son of the woman fell sick" (1 Kings 17:17). The woman said to him (Elijah): Thou didst come unto me for coition, and thou wilt bring my sin to remembrance against me, and my son is dead. Now take away all that which thou hast brought to me, and give me my son. Elijah, may he be remembered for good, arose and prayed before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said before Him: Sovereign of all the worlds ! Is it not enough (to endure) all the evils which have befallen me, but also this woman; for I know that out of sorrow for her son has she spoken of a matter which has not occurred, which she has brought against me to vex me. Now let all the generations learn that there is a resurrection of the dead, and restore the soul of this lad within him; and He was entreated of him, as it is said, "And the Lord hearkened unto the voice of Elijah" (1 Kings 17:22). Another Scripture text says, "And Elijah || took the child… See, thy son liveth" (1 Kings 17:23).”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְמֹשֶׁה: "וּמַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (בַּמִּדְבָּר טז, ג), וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה עָנָו וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם יב, ג).
connections.quote: “They assembled against Moses and against Aaron and said to them: You take too much upon yourselves! For the whole congregation, all of them, are holy, and Hashem is among them; why then do you lift yourselves up above the assembly of Hashem?”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְמֹשֶׁה: "וּמַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (בַּמִּדְבָּר טז, ג), וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה עָנָו וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם יב, ג).
connections.quote: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than any person on the face of the earth.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יח): אוֹתוֹ תִּינוֹק – מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף;
connections.quote: “Once our teachers and other Sages were sitting in the study hall and disputing where Elijah came from. One said from Rachel’s descendants, and another said from Leah’s descendants. While they were disputing, I came and stood before them and said: My teachers, I come only from Rachel’s descendants. They said: Give proof for your words. I said: Is it not written in the genealogy of Benjamin’s tribe, “Ya’aresheyah, Elijah, and Zichri, the sons of Yeroham”? They said to me: Are you not a priest? Did you not say to the widow, “First make me a small cake from it and bring it to me; afterward make for yourself and your son”? I said: That child was the son of Joseph. I gave a sign to the world that I descend first to Babylonia, and afterward the son of David will come.”
connections.context: This supplies the previously unquoted Seder Eliyahu passage behind the identification of the widow’s child with the Joseph figure. The text says “son of Joseph” and then speaks of the future son of David; Rav Tzadok reads that sequence messianically.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיתָתוֹ נִקְרָא: "וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר דָּקָרוּ" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.),
connections.quote: “I will pour upon the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication. They shall look toward Me concerning the one whom they pierced, and mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, grieving bitterly as for a firstborn.”
connections.context: The adjacent Sukkah passage applies this mourning to the slain Messiah son of Joseph according to one opinion. The verse note supplies the actual “whom they pierced” wording Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיתָתוֹ נִקְרָא: "וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר דָּקָרוּ" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.),
connections.quote: ‘According to the one who says that the mourning is for Messiah son of Joseph, who was killed, it is understandable that it is written: ‘They will look toward Me concerning the one they pierced, and mourn for him as one mourns for an only child.’ But according to the one who says that it is for the evil inclination, which was killed, should they mourn? They should rejoice! Why did they weep?’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיתָתוֹ נִקְרָא: "וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר דָּקָרוּ" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.),
connections.quote: “When the time comes for death to be swallowed up forever and the matter of killing to depart from the world, the corresponding holy power of killing in Yosef must also depart. Therefore he too will be killed and depart from the world. The sunlight of Yosef and his power of holy killing against Esav will then depart, for that matter will no longer exist in the world. Then the light of Mashiach ben David will shine, and he will revive Mashiach ben Yosef. “New faces have come here”: after resurrection he becomes a new creature, without the self-exaltation associated with his previously described level. Therefore he will no longer envy Yehudah and will acknowledge Mashiach ben David. Thus it says, “They shall look toward Me concerning the one whom they pierced”: the killing of Mashiach ben Yosef is attributed to Israel. All Israel's striving is to repair the serpent's counsel and have death swallowed up; through this the death reaches ben Yosef, like the death of the evil inclination mentioned there and above. In this way they have pierced him indirectly.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek expands the very interpretation signaled here by “as I have written elsewhere.” Yosef's role in opposing a destructive force belongs to the period when that force is present. Its cessation and renewal under Mashiach ben David are therefore connected to the removal of death itself. This supplies context for the deliberately compressed association of the deaths of Mashiach ben Yosef and the evil inclination, rather than treating the two expressions as an unexplained verbal equivalence.
connections.headline: The two messianic roles and the removal of death

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין נְקִיִּים בָּזֶה, עַל יָדָם מַגִּיעַ מִיתָתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר,
connections.quote: see note 620.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains his statement that the Messiah son of Joseph suffers because of the generation’s unfinished rectification. The passage also explicitly reconciles the two interpretations of the mourning in Sukkah.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרָה: "מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָ... לְהַזְכִּיר אֶת עֲוֹנִי", וְהוּא הֶחֱיָהוּ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: ‘She said to Elijah: What have I to do with you, man of God? Have you come to me to bring my iniquity to remembrance and to put my son to death?’

connections.hePhrase: וְיִשַׁי מֵת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ (שַׁבָּת נה:) וְנִקְרָא "נָחָשׁ" בַּכָּתוּב (שְׁמוּאֵל ב יז, כה), רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁרַק דָּבָר זֶה הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ נָחָשׁ,
connections.quote: “Four died through the counsel of the serpent: Benjamin son of Jacob, Amram the father of Moses, Jesse the father of David, and Kilab son of David. All of them are known by tradition, except Jesse the father of David, about whom a verse is explicit.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיִשַׁי מֵת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ (שַׁבָּת נה:) וְנִקְרָא "נָחָשׁ" בַּכָּתוּב (שְׁמוּאֵל ב יז, כה), רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁרַק דָּבָר זֶה הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ נָחָשׁ,
connections.quote: ‘Absalom placed Amasa over the army in Joab’s place. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had relations with Abigail daughter of Nahash, the sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עָלָיו (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ) עַל פָּסוּק "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי",
connections.quote: see note 1258.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עָלָיו (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ) עַל פָּסוּק "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי",
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said: Even the most pious of the pious cannot be without some aspect of iniquity. David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, did my father Jesse intend to bring me into being? He intended his own pleasure. … But You gather in every drop. This is what David said: “For my father and mother have forsaken me, but the Lord gathers me in.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains David’s verse in terms of the parents’ intention in conception and God’s part in bringing the child into being. This, rather than the verse alone, is the specific teaching about Jesse that Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן בִּישַׁעְיָה: "מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ נָחָשׁ יֵצֵא צֶפַע וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה יד, כט) עַל מָשִׁיחַ.
connections.quote: ‘Do not rejoice, all of Philistia, because the rod that struck you has been broken. For from the serpent’s root a viper will come forth, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן בִּישַׁעְיָה: "מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ נָחָשׁ יֵצֵא צֶפַע וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה יד, כט) עַל מָשִׁיחַ.
connections.quote: “Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, because the rule that subjugated you has been broken. For from the descendants of Jesse the Messiah will emerge, and his deeds against you will be like a flying serpent.”
connections.context: The Targum explicitly reads the serpent imagery of Isaiah’s verse as Jesse’s messianic descendant. It supplies the identification that the paragraph assumes.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רַק עַל יְדֵי תִּיקּוּן הַקִּלְקוּל יִהְיֶה הַחַיִּים, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תָּמִיד לב.): מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיִחְיֶה? יָמִית עַצְמוֹ.
connections.quote: “How hard death is for someone who has not separated worldly desires from his soul until death separates them! Our Sages said in Derekh Eretz: Do you wish not to die? Die before you die. The explanation is that one who wants the day of death to lead to everlasting life should take to heart that he must eventually leave the earth and abandon the body’s desires, and will finally reject and forsake them. Let him forsake them while alive and use this earthly life only for the service of the exalted Creator. Then his day of death will lead to life without interruption.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah explicitly interprets “die before you die” as relinquishing attachment to bodily desires while continuing to live in divine service. This clarifies the spiritual language of death and life used in this discussion.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רַק עַל יְדֵי תִּיקּוּן הַקִּלְקוּל יִהְיֶה הַחַיִּים, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תָּמִיד לב.): מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיִחְיֶה? יָמִית עַצְמוֹ.
connections.quote: “Since Hashem's name was sanctified through King David's consequences and the greatness of his repentance, that act is truly considered a sanctification of Hashem, rather than a desecration. Nevertheless, he does not need death to complete the cleansing; on the contrary, through this he merits enduring life. In every passage of Torah one infers the affirmative from the negative: if desecration of the Name requires death for atonement, the good measure is greater, and sanctification of Hashem gives life.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin explains the positive counterpart of the siman's atonement language. Through David's repentance and its consequences, the Name is sanctified; the former desecration becomes part of that sanctification. The source therefore speaks of gaining enduring life. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok locates the life of the Davidic repair in transformed failure rather than in an untouched outward record alone.
connections.headline: Repair as a sanctification that gives life

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ דְּאִילָנָא דְּמוֹתָא נִקְרָא הָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בַּמִּדְבָּר קיט עַמּוּד א, בְּהַעֲלוֹתְךָ קנה עַמּוּד ב,
connections.quote: “When night enters, the Tree of Death rules in the world, and the Tree of Life ascends higher and higher. When the Tree of Death alone rules in the world, all the inhabitants of the world taste the taste of death.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ דְּאִילָנָא דְּמוֹתָא נִקְרָא הָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בַּמִּדְבָּר קיט עַמּוּד א, בְּהַעֲלוֹתְךָ קנה עַמּוּד ב,
connections.quote: “People give it the deposit of their souls, and it takes all their souls. … Since they were handed over to it as a deposit, it returns all the deposits to their owners.”
connections.context: The Zohar is discussing the soul’s nightly deposit and return. Rav Tzadok reads this Tree of Death symbolism together with the feminine realm described in the next citation; the paragraph previously quoted concerned people awakening at night and omitted the defining image.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ דְּאִילָנָא דְּמוֹתָא נִקְרָא הָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר בַּמִּדְבָּר קיט עַמּוּד א, בְּהַעֲלוֹתְךָ קנה עַמּוּד ב,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yitzchak said: Why does Moses, in this utterance, address what is above in the feminine (as weak), as it is written: ‘If this is how You treat me’? At, the feminine ‘you,’ is written; it should have said attah, the masculine ‘you.’ Rather, he was speaking to the place in which death dwells, and that place is feminine. Therefore he said: ‘Please kill me outright,’ and this is the Tree of Death. We have already established that death does not dwell in the Tree of Life. Therefore he turned toward the Tree of Death and said at, not attah, and this was how he needed to speak.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית מַגִּיעַ הַקִּלְקוּל בָּזֶה כַּנּוֹדָע בְּטַעַם "ה' צִלְּךָ" (תְּהִלִּים קכא, ה),
connections.quote: see note 335.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok states the shadow analogy directly elsewhere and includes its inward qualification: the response follows the heart’s intention. This explains the brief reference to “The Lord is your shadow” here.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם יְכֻפַּר הֶעָוֹן הַזֶּה לָכֶם עַד תְּמֻתוּן" (יְשַׁעְיָה כב, יד) בְּג' חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah said: There is no sin in the world that has no repentance except this one, and there is no wicked person who will not see the face of the Shechinah except this one.”
connections.context: “This one” is the man who wastes his seed, whom the preceding lines of the Zohar call “evil” like Er (Genesis 38:7).

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם יְכֻפַּר הֶעָוֹן הַזֶּה לָכֶם עַד תְּמֻתוּן" (יְשַׁעְיָה כב, יד) בְּג' חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ,
connections.quote: ‘Hashem of hosts revealed this in my hearing: This iniquity will certainly not be atoned for you until you die, says the Lord, Hashem of hosts.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם יְכֻפַּר הֶעָוֹן הַזֶּה לָכֶם עַד תְּמֻתוּן" (יְשַׁעְיָה כב, יד) בְּג' חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ,
connections.quote: “Have you heard the four divisions of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael would expound? He replied: They are three, and repentance accompanies each.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם יְכֻפַּר הֶעָוֹן הַזֶּה לָכֶם עַד תְּמֻתוּן" (יְשַׁעְיָה כב, יד) בְּג' חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ,
connections.quote: “But one who has desecrated the Name: repentance cannot by itself suspend, Yom Kippur cannot by itself atone, and suffering cannot by itself cleanse. Rather, all of them suspend, and death completes the cleansing, as it says, “This iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die.””
connections.context: The last category is the one Rav Tzadok is discussing. The source includes repentance, Yom Kippur, and suffering before death completes atonement; it does not say that repentance has no role.

connections.hePhrase: דִּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית נִקְרָא קִדּוּשׁ ה' בְּסוֹטָה (י:): יוֹסֵף שֶׁקִּדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְכוּלֵי
connections.quote: ‘‘Judah recognized them and said: She is more righteous than I.’ This is what Rav Chanin bar Bizna said in Rabbi Shimon Chasida’s name: Joseph, who sanctified the name of Heaven in private, merited having one letter from the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, added to his name, as it is written: ‘He established it as a testimony in Yehosef.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִדְרָשׁ מִכְּלַל הֵן – לָאו.
connections.quote: “‘And you shall teach them to your sons’ (Deuteronomy 11:19)… If you teach them to your sons, ‘that your days may be multiplied and the days of your sons’ (Deuteronomy 11:21); and if not, that your days may be shortened. For thus are words of Torah expounded: from the positive, the negative, and from the negative, the positive.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִדְרָשׁ מִכְּלַל הֵן – לָאו.
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְבַחֹדֶשׁ ח׳:ח׳
connections.quote: “‘Honor your father and your mother’: if you honor them, ‘that your days may be long’; if not, your days will be shortened. For words of Torah are expounded from the positive, the negative, and from the negative, the positive.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בַּמִּדְבָּר (קכא עַמּוּד א): שֶׁיִּמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ לְמִיתָה בְּלֹא רַמִיָּה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “A person should regard himself as though he has departed from the world, for he entrusts his soul to this place of death. Therefore it has no letter vav, for vav is the Tree of Life, while this is the Tree of Death. This teaches the mystery that there are sins not atoned for until a person departs from the world, as it is written, “This sin will not be atoned for you until you die.” This person truly gives himself over to death and hands his soul over to that place—not as a deposit, as at night, but as one who has truly departed from the world. This rectification requires the heart’s intention; then the Holy One, blessed be He, has compassion on him and atones for his sins. Fortunate is the person who knows how to seek His favor and serve his Master with desire and intention of heart. Woe to one who comes to seek his Master’s favor with a distant heart and without willingness, as it says, “They enticed Him with their mouths and lied to Him with their tongues, but their heart was not steadfast with Him.” He says, “To You, Lord, I lift my soul,” while all his words come from a distant heart. He brings upon himself departure from the world before his time when that tree awakens in the world to execute judgment. Therefore a person must attach his soul and will to his Master and not approach Him with a false intention, for it says, “One who speaks falsehood will not stand before My eyes.” What does “will not stand” mean? When he prepares himself for this while his heart is distant from the Holy One, blessed be He, a voice goes out and says, “He will not stand before My eyes.” This person seeks to set himself in order; “he will not stand”—I do not desire that he should do so. All the more if he comes to unify the holy name without unifying it properly.”
connections.context: The setting is the inward intention of nefilat apayim after the Amidah, not a physical act of dying. These consecutive paragraphs preserve both the devotional image and the Zohar’s warning against insincere intention, which Rav Tzadok emphasizes immediately afterward.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בַּמִּדְבָּר (קכא עַמּוּד א): שֶׁיִּמְסוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ לְמִיתָה בְּלֹא רַמִיָּה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “But one who has truly clarified himself without any deceit, to the full extent of his ability—if an unclarified act should then come before him, Hashem will not reckon it to him as deliberate sin, for he certainly directed himself toward the depth of Hashem's will.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef interprets the same Zohar passage through the responsibility to clarify oneself to the limit of one's ability. The surrounding discussion warns that believing one has done everything is not sufficient if further clarification remains possible. This explains why the siman rejects an acceptance secretly adopted merely as a device for obtaining life: the condition concerns the reality of the heart's service, rather than the wording of a declaration.
connections.headline: Sincerity is measured by the work actually available

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (ח:) מִקְּרָא דְּדָנִיֵּאל, דְּקַבָּלַת הַלֵּב בֶּאֱמֶת הָוֵי כְּמַעֲשֶׂה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה לְחַיִּים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
connections.quote: ‘They said to him: ‘What is your source for this?’ He answered: It is written: ‘He said to me: Do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: אַל יִפְתַּח פִּיו לַשָּׂטָן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפָרָשַׁת בְּהַעֲלֹתְךָ שָׁם גַּבֵּי מֹשֶׁה.
connections.quote: “Abaye said: A person should not say this, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said—and it was likewise taught in Rabbi Yosei’s name: A person should never open his mouth to the Accuser.”
connections.context: The preceding discussion concerns language spoken by a mourner that invites further punishment. This is the source of the caution against speech that supplies an accusation, cited here after the warning about insincere declarations.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל, שֶׁמַּחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ וְקַבָּלָתוֹ עַל עַצְמוֹ כְּמַעֲשֶׂה, וְהוּא אַחַר כָּךְ כְּאִלּוּ בָּא בְּגִלְגּוּל שֵׁנִי לְזֶה הָעוֹלָם, וְהוּא יֵדַע מַה שֶּׁקִּלְקֵל בְּגִלְגּוּלוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹן וְיָכוֹל לְתַקְּנוֹ בְּגִלְגּוּל זֶה.
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 33:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 33:1
connections.quote: “Therefore, after the sin, Moshe was not at ease with the governance of an angel. An angel cannot recognize how a person's life from Hashem was not interrupted even during the sin. This resembles the teaching of the Zohar Chadash on Vayetzei: after a person surrenders all his life in Nefilas Apayim, Hashem returns his life through a narrow path hidden even from the heavenly host. So too after a person sins and repents, only Hashem Himself can show the repair: that this person's connection was never interrupted, even during the sin, as the Sages teach, “I am Hashem after a person sins and repents.” From the angel's standpoint, however, the connection is interrupted during the sin and no repair is available from that standpoint. Therefore Moshe was not at ease after the sin with the governance of an angel, and prayed, “See, You say to me…””
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim makes the same prayer comparison and explains what lies behind the renewed life: a connection sustained by Hashem even where an angel cannot perceive its continuity through the sin. This adds a precise dimension to the siman's image of beginning again with knowledge of what requires repair. The cited passage is about the inward act of Nefilas Apayim and the divine restoration that makes teshuvah possible.
connections.headline: Life restored through a bond hidden even from angels

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן מִזְמוֹר דְּ"אֵלֶיךָ ה' נַפְשִׁי אֶשָּׂא" (תְּהִלִּים כה, א) מְסַיֵּים בִּנְפִילַת אַפַּיִם: "וְהוּא יִפְדֶּה אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִכֹּל עֲוֹנֹתָיו" (שָׁם קל, ח)
connections.quote: “Of David. To You, Lord, I lift my soul.”
connections.context: The Hebrew “I lift my soul” supplies the image of surrender used in Rav Tzadok’s explanation of falling on one’s face in prayer. The following verse from Psalm 130 is a liturgical conclusion cited separately, not the last verse of Psalm 25.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה דִּמְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ לְמִיתָה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהוּא כְּלֹא נֶחְשָׁב בְּעֵינֵי עַצְמוֹ, עַל יְדֵי זֶה דָּבוּק בְּאוֹתָהּ מַדְרֵגָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא "הוּא" כַּנּוֹדָע].
connections.quote: “This matter of the deepest origin of thought is not clarified in this world, as is known. That deepest origin is called “nothing,” whereas thought is called “something,” since a person’s thought—what he is thinking—is already a perceptible entity. It is something from nothing: from the deepest origin, hidden from the person’s eye and seemingly nonexistent. For this reason it is also called “He,” as is known. It is said, “On that day Israel’s iniquity will be sought and will be absent.” In this world there are sins, for one cannot become purified at that level; only “on that day,” meaning that there is a day [indicating clarification of a matter] called “that day,” when the hidden gate called “He,” which indicates the concealed, will open.”
connections.context: This parallel explains why the pronoun “He” denotes a concealed level and how Rav Tzadok connects it with the future removal of sin. Its explicit distinction between present concealment and future revelation is retained.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, אָמַר דָּבָר זֶה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonatan’s name: What is meant by “The declaration of David son of Jesse, the declaration of the man raised on high”? It is the declaration of David son of Jesse, who established the yoke of repentance.”
connections.context: This is the original interpretation of David as the figure who established the path of repentance. It accounts for the title Rav Tzadok uses before discussing David’s prayer.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רָאשֵׁי הַיְצָרִים הֵם שְׁנַיִם: דַּעֲבֵירָה וּדְעַבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) וּבְשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה, וּמִשְּׁנֵיהֶם מִי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.);
connections.quote: “A likeness of a fiery lion cub emerged from the Holy of Holies. The prophet said to Israel: This is the inclination for idolatry.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רָאשֵׁי הַיְצָרִים הֵם שְׁנַיִם: דַּעֲבֵירָה וּדְעַבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) וּבְשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה, וּמִשְּׁנֵיהֶם מִי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.);
connections.quote: “They said: Since it is a favorable time, let us seek mercy concerning the inclination for sexual transgression. They sought mercy, and it was delivered into their hands.”
connections.context: The narrative treats these as two distinct inclinations, which is the distinction Rav Tzadok cites. It goes on to explain why the second could not simply be destroyed without ending reproduction.
