connections.hePhrase: כִּי רָאשֵׁי הַיְצָרִים הֵם שְׁנַיִם: דַּעֲבֵירָה וּדְעַבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) וּבְשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה, וּמִשְּׁנֵיהֶם מִי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.);
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chunya said in the name of Rabbi Dosa bar Tevet: The Holy One, blessed be He, created two inclinations in His world: the inclination toward idolatry and the inclination toward sexual immorality. The inclination toward idolatry has already been uprooted, while the inclination toward sexual immorality remains. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Whoever can withstand sexual immorality, I account it to him as though he had withstood both.”
connections.context: This is the second original source, alongside the existing Yoma quotation, for the two principal inclinations named in the section. It explicitly distinguishes the uprooted inclination from the one that remains.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רָאשֵׁי הַיְצָרִים הֵם שְׁנַיִם: דַּעֲבֵירָה וּדְעַבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) וּבְשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה, וּמִשְּׁנֵיהֶם מִי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.);
connections.quote: ““None who come to her return, nor attain the paths of life”: if they do return, they do not attain the paths of life.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רָאשֵׁי הַיְצָרִים הֵם שְׁנַיִם: דַּעֲבֵירָה וּדְעַבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט:) וּבְשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה, וּמִשְּׁנֵיהֶם מִי שֶׁפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.);
connections.quote: “He said: The matter depends only on me. He placed his head between his knees and cried aloud until his soul departed. A heavenly voice said: Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya is destined for life in the World to Come. … There too, because he was so strongly attached to it, it was like heresy.”
connections.context: The first statement concerns return from heresy; the story of Elazar ben Durdaya extends it to an exceptionally entrenched sexual transgression. The Gemara states that qualification explicitly. Rav Tzadok is drawing on these two cases, not asserting that every penitent dies.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי שְׁנֵי הַיְצָרִים הַנִּזְכָּרִים הֵם שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת שֶׁהֵם הָפְכִיִּים זֶה לָזֶה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְיוֹסֵף עָמַד בְּנִסָּיוֹן דַּעֲבֵירָה וְלֹא דָּוִד.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 13
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 13
connections.quote: “The two faces were present in the Chariot, as is known. Corresponding to them, in the external chariot of “one opposite the other,” the lion’s face is the inclination toward sexual transgression—to do whatever the heart desires—and the ox’s face is accepting a yoke, the alien service of the inclination toward idolatry.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the opposition between these inclinations through the lion and ox: unrestrained self-directed desire and submission to an alien authority. This gives the conceptual content of the “opposite extremes” mentioned here.

connections.hePhrase: רַק דְּמִיּוֹסֵף יָצָא יָרָבְעָם שֶׁהוּא יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְתַקֵּן רַק עַל יְדֵי בִּיטּוּלוֹ מִן הָעוֹלָם לְגַמְרֵי עַל יְדֵי אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה בְּטַעֲנַת "לָא הוּא וְלָא אַגְרֵיהּ".
connections.quote: “Did You give it to us for any purpose other than receiving reward through it? We want neither it nor its reward!”
connections.context: The plea here concerns the inclination for idolatry, blamed for the destruction of the Temple and exile. It precedes the separate attempt to suppress sexual desire; the earlier quotation belonged to that second discussion.

connections.hePhrase: רַק דְּמִיּוֹסֵף יָצָא יָרָבְעָם שֶׁהוּא יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְתַקֵּן רַק עַל יְדֵי בִּיטּוּלוֹ מִן הָעוֹלָם לְגַמְרֵי עַל יְדֵי אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה בְּטַעֲנַת "לָא הוּא וְלָא אַגְרֵיהּ".
connections.quote: “Sin caused this to be hidden through the request of the Great Assembly. Seeing the greatness of the sins, they said, “We want neither it nor its reward,” and abolished the impulse to idolatry; the Midrash places this in the days of Mordechai and Esther. By subduing that impulse, the opposite of recognizing Hashem, they had attained revelation of the Shechinah. Even when they followed it, nature was disrupted against them measure for measure: saying “Hashem does not see,” they were shown that He sees all their acts. But when the impulse was abolished, prophecy and the Shechinah's open presence withdrew as well, because the setting through which they attained that revelation was gone. All was then concealed. Esther, at the end of the Babylonian exile, therefore marks the end of the open miracles given to be written; thereafter the miracles were hidden and were not given to be written.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet develops what was included in “neither it nor its reward.” Overcoming the impulse toward idolatry had been a setting for open recognition of the Shechinah; when the impulse was abolished, that form of prophecy and open miracle also receded. This makes the siman's contrast of the two impulses more precise: their histories and place in the world differ, so removing one cannot simply be made the model for removing the other.
connections.headline: The removal of the impulse had a corresponding cost

connections.hePhrase: [וּפִינְחָס זֶה אֵלִיָּהוּ מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית, וּבָא מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף שֶׁפִּטְפֵּט בְּיִצְרוֹ;
connections.heRef: רש"י על בבא מציעא קי״ד ב:ב׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““Is the Master not a priest?”—for there is an opinion that Elijah is Phinehas. Of Elijah it is written, “I have been very zealous,” and likewise of Phinehas, “When he was zealous with My zeal.””
connections.context: Rashi explicitly records the identification of Elijah with Phinehas and the common language of zeal behind it. He presents it as an opinion, a qualification preserved here.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שְׁבָטִים בִּזּוּהוּ: מִזַּרְעָא דְּיִתְרוֹ שֶׁפִּטֵּם וְכוּלֵי – יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל;
connections.quote: “Did Phinehas not descend from Jethro? Is it not written, “Eleazar son of Aaron took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife”? Does this not mean that he descended from Jethro, who fattened calves for idolatry? No: it means that he descended from Joseph, who struggled against his inclination. But did the tribes not disparage him, saying: Have you seen this son of Puti, whose maternal ancestor fattened calves for idolatry—should he kill a prince of an Israelite tribe? Rather, if his mother’s father descended from Joseph, his mother’s mother descended from Jethro; and if his mother’s father descended from Jethro, his mother’s mother descended from Joseph. This is also precise in the wording “from the daughters of Putiel,” indicating two. Conclude from it that this is so.”
connections.context: The complete discussion concludes that both lines of descent were present. This is essential to Rav Tzadok’s treatment of the two inclinations and prevents the first proposed answer, Joseph alone, from being mistaken for the Gemara’s conclusion.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הוּא מָסַר נַפְשׁוֹ לְמִיתָה בְּזִמְרִי, שֶׁאִלְמָלֵי נֶהֱפַךְ זִמְרִי וַהֲרָגוֹ וְכוּלֵי כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין פב.),
connections.quote: ‘Moreover, if Zimri had withdrawn [from the act] and Pinchas had killed him, Pinchas would be executed for killing him. If Zimri had turned and killed Pinchas, Zimri would not be executed for killing him, for Pinchas was a pursuer.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן זָכָה לִבְרִית שָׁלוֹם בְּאֵלִיָּהוּ דְּחַי לְעוֹלָם]:
connections.quote: ““My covenant of peace”—peace from the angel of death, as in “He makes peace in His heights,” for destruction occurs only through the opposition of contrary forces. This was indeed fulfilled in Phinehas, who lived far longer than the other men of his generation, until he served in the sanctuary at Shiloh at the time of the concubine at Gibeah. That was undoubtedly after the deaths of Joshua and the elders who outlived Joshua. All the more so if he was still living in Jephthah’s time, when Jephthah wrote to the Ammonite king that Israel had dwelt in Heshbon and its towns for three hundred years; our Sages related that Phinehas then refused to go to Jephthah to release his vow. And all the more according to the opinion that Elijah is Phinehas, who is still alive and enduring.”
connections.context: Sforno interprets the covenant of peace as protection from the opposing forces that cause mortality. His explanation includes both Phinehas’s exceptional longevity and the opinion identifying him with Elijah.

connections.hePhrase: [קנט] יָחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא פו:);
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabbi Meir used to say: Great is repentance, for on account of one individual who repents, the entire world is forgiven, as it is said: ‘I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away from him.’ It does not say ‘from them,’ but ‘from him.’’

connections.hePhrase: רַק מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד הוּא יִהְיֶה כֵּן, כִּי צָרִיךְ שֶׁתִּהְיֶה נַפְשׁוֹ כּוֹלֶלֶת מִכָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת,
connections.quote: “Because all the souls together constitute one complete stature—the stature of Adam, within whom the souls of all his descendants were included, as the Midrash explains the verse “Where were you when I founded the earth”—even someone who returns to God with all his heart cannot rectify himself completely as long as all Israel have not returned as he has, so that the entire stature is rectified. As long as a single spark of that stature has not been fully rectified, its deficiency causes a deficiency in the whole stature.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the shared spiritual structure underlying the claim that one individual’s repentance can reach others. It retains the limitation that full rectification requires the whole stature.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן כּוֹלֵל כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת, שֶׁהֲרֵי הוּא רֶגֶל ד' שֶׁבַּמֶּרְכָּבָה, וְהֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה רַק בַּעֲוֹן תַּאֲוָה לְבַד.
connections.quote: “‘Only in your fathers’ (Deuteronomy 10:15): three, yet the Chariot has four. From where do we learn the fourth? As it is written, ‘He chose their seed after them’ (ibid.). What does this imply? To include with them King David, who is the fourth, to be set in place in the holy Chariot… Rabbi Yitzchak said: Just as the Patriarchs merited to be crowned in the holy Chariot, so David merited to be set in place as the fourth support of the Chariot.”

connections.hePhrase: [כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁנִּקְרָא אֶפְרָתִי, שֶׁפֵּירוּשׁ שֵׁם זֶה: מִי שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו, וְלָכֵן מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי אֲחִיָּה הַשִּׁילֹנִי שֶׁזֶּהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּשִׁילֹה יֵשׁ לוֹ יַחַס עִם שֵׁבֶט אֶפְרָיִם],
connections.quote: “And Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephrathite from Zeredah, whose mother’s name was Zeruah, a widow, a servant of Solomon, he too lifted up his hand against the king.”

connections.hePhrase: [כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁנִּקְרָא אֶפְרָתִי, שֶׁפֵּירוּשׁ שֵׁם זֶה: מִי שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו, וְלָכֵן מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי אֲחִיָּה הַשִּׁילֹנִי שֶׁזֶּהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּשִׁילֹה יֵשׁ לוֹ יַחַס עִם שֵׁבֶט אֶפְרָיִם],
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Shoftim 15
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Shoftim 15
connections.quote: see note 1337.
connections.context: This is a direct Ishbitz parallel for Jeroboam’s refinement, his attraction for Ahijah, and the meaning attached to “Ephratite.” The continuation concerning Jeroboam’s idolatry and Ahijah’s mistaken judgment is included, preserving the distinction between a particular spiritual strength and a person’s overall course.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כּוֹלֵל רַק הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, אֶלָּא שֶׁדּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר כֻּלּוֹ דּוֹר דֵּעָה וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים].
connections.quote: “‘And Darda’ (I Chronicles 2:6): this is the generation [dor] of the wilderness, which was entirely knowledge [de’ah].”

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כּוֹלֵל רַק הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, אֶלָּא שֶׁדּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר כֻּלּוֹ דּוֹר דֵּעָה וְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים].
connections.quote: “The Ari’s teaching concerning the statement in Shabbat and elsewhere, “Moses, you have spoken well,” is known: every Sage of the generation is called Moses. The straightforward meaning is that he is like Moses our teacher in his generation and stands in his place. The Zohar in Ekev states that Moses our teacher shines in every generation. This means within the Sage of the generation, who heads the congregation of Israel in that generation as Moses our teacher did; it is Moses himself whose light shines in him.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the continuity of Moses’s soul and light within the Sages of later generations. This provides the background for the present limitation of Moses’s inclusive role to the Torah scholars.

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁאָר יְחִידִים שֶׁשָּׁבִים יֵשׁ לָהֶם יְכוֹלֶת לְהָשִׁיב רַק הַנְּפָשׁוֹת הַתְּלוּיִים בָּהֶם [וּבְאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ שֶׁשָּׁבִים],
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, Yosi ben Yoezer’s words entered his heart, and he carried out upon himself the four court-imposed deaths; within a short time he preceded Yosi to the Garden of Eden. So too Yosef Meshita: although he had previously rebelled and entered the Sanctuary, afterwards he would not consent to enter again, even at the cost of his life, and sanctified the divine Name. This is ‘the fragrance of his garments,’ expounded as ‘the fragrance of his betrayers,’ as in Sanhedrin 37a. From the fragrance of his previous betrayal he was elevated with still greater force, for the inner heart was revealed: at Israel’s root they are bound to holiness. This is the meaning of ‘It is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will; what prevents us is the leaven in the dough.’ This applies even to the most disreputable person, as they had been beforehand.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah retells the encounter cited in this siman and explains its inward result: beneath the previous betrayal, a heart bound to holiness was revealed. This gives content to the siman’s claim that the tzaddik awakens a connected soul rather than mechanically transferring forgiveness. The other person’s own will turns and becomes manifest. The limits of such influence remain explicit here: a particular person awakens the souls and faculties connected to his own return, and the universal completion is reserved for Mashiach.
connections.headline: A word of teshuvah can awaken the hidden will of another soul

connections.hePhrase: כְּאוֹתוֹ תַלְמִיד בִּמְנָחוֹת (מד.) שֶׁעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ עוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה שֶׁהָיְתָה שַׁיָּיכֶת לוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי נַעֲשֵׂית אַחַר כָּךְ אִשְׁתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “She came to Rabbi Chiyya’s study hall and said: Rabbi, instruct them to make me a convert. He said: My daughter, perhaps you have set your eyes on one of the students? She took out the document from her hand and gave it to him. He said to her: Go and acquire what is yours.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּאוֹתוֹ תַלְמִיד בִּמְנָחוֹת (מד.) שֶׁעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ עוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה שֶׁהָיְתָה שַׁיָּיכֶת לוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי נַעֲשֵׂית אַחַר כָּךְ אִשְׁתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “Those same bedclothes which she had spread for him in a forbidden manner, she spread for him in a permitted manner.”
connections.context: The man’s withdrawal from sin leads the woman to seek conversion, and the story concludes with their permitted union. These are the events Rav Tzadok uses to illustrate how one person’s repentance can awaken another’s.

connections.hePhrase: כְּאוֹתוֹ תַלְמִיד בִּמְנָחוֹת (מד.) שֶׁעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ עוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה שֶׁהָיְתָה שַׁיָּיכֶת לוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי נַעֲשֵׂית אַחַר כָּךְ אִשְׁתּוֹ.
connections.quote: “That student in Menachot needed his tzitzit to strike him and restrain him. This was the revelation of Israel’s hidden treasures, showing that they have no such union with a gentile, because he had already become somewhat entangled in the thorns surrounding the myrtle. She too had become deeply immersed in prostitution, and her conversion could occur only through this circumstance: that she would arrange the bedding for a prohibited encounter, until the hidden root of complete Jewish identity awoke within him. Through this he drew forth the spark of good concealed within her, so that the desire to convert awoke in her, and he merited that she should arrange the bedding for him permissibly.”
connections.context: This interpretation of the Menachot story explains the mechanism invoked here: his return awakens the hidden good in the woman, leading to her conversion and their subsequent permitted marriage. It supplements the existing quotation of the Talmudic narrative.

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהוּא עוֹנֶשׁ הַמַּגִּיעַ לִזְנוּת – אַנְדְּרָלָמוּסְיָא, רַק שֶׁשָּׁבוּ]
connections.quote: “Rabbi Simlai said: Wherever you find licentiousness, indiscriminate destruction comes to the world and kills good and wicked alike.”

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי מְסִירַת נַפְשׁוֹ לְמִיתָה, וְעוֹרְרָם שֶׁשָּׁבוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ גַּבֵּי מִלְחֶמֶת מִדְיָן.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak expounded the verse about the war with Midian. You find that when Israel went out to the war with Midian, they would go in to a woman in pairs: one would blacken her face and the other would take off her earrings. She would say to them: Are we not creatures of the Holy One, blessed be He, that you do this to us? And Israel would answer them: Is it not enough for you that we have taken our punishment because of you?”
connections.context: In the war that followed the sin of Peor, the soldiers guarded themselves from that very sin; this is the repentance Rav Tzadok refers to.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה סה) בְּעוּבָדָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן יוֹעֶזֶר אִישׁ צְרֵידָה, שֶׁרַק כְּשֶׁהוֹלִיכוּהוּ לַצְּלָב, אָז עוֹרֵר בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבֶן אֲחוֹתוֹ.
connections.quote: “Yakum of Tzerorot was the nephew of Rabbi Yosei ben Yoezer of Tzeredah. He was riding a horse on Shabbat and went before the beam on which his uncle was to be hanged. He said to him: Look at the horse on which my master has mounted me, and look at the horse on which your Master has mounted you. He replied: If this is what He gives those who anger Him, how much more will He give those who do His will! He said: Has anyone done His will more than you? He replied: If this is how He treats those who do His will, how much more those who anger Him! The words entered him like the venom of a serpent.”
connections.context: This is the exchange that awakens Yakum’s repentance as his uncle is being led to execution. The narrative illustrates Rav Tzadok’s point about a soul’s influence at the moment of self-sacrifice; the quotation ends with the inward change itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן נָפְלוּ עַל פְּנֵיהֶם בְּעֵת מַחֲלוֹקֶת קֹרַח, שֶׁרָאוּ שֶׁנִּגְזַר עֲלֵיהֶם מִיתָה וּמָסְרוּ נַפְשָׁם לְמִיתָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר, וּכְדֵי לְהַעֲלוֹתָם בִּתְשׁוּבָה;
connections.quote: ““They fell upon their faces and said: God, God of the spirits of all flesh.” Come and see: Moses and Aaron gave themselves over to death. In what manner? As it is written, “They fell upon their faces and said: God, God of the spirits.” “Spirits” is written without a vav, and therefore it is the Tree of Death. Wherever there is falling upon the face, it is directed to that place.”
connections.context: The Zohar reads Moses and Aaron’s falling upon their faces during Korach’s rebellion as the devotional surrender discussed in the preceding sections. This is the exact original passage underlying the reference here.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּמִדָּה שֶׁאָדָם מוֹדֵד מוֹדְדִין לוֹ, וּבְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁרוֹצֶה לֵילֵךְ מוֹלִיכִין אוֹתוֹ:
connections.quote: “With the measure that a person measures, they measure for him.”
connections.context: The Mishnah states the rule of corresponding measure. Rav Tzadok applies it here to people who separate themselves from Moses and therefore no longer receive the awakening flowing through his soul.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּמִדָּה שֶׁאָדָם מוֹדֵד מוֹדְדִין לוֹ, וּבְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁרוֹצֶה לֵילֵךְ מוֹלִיכִין אוֹתוֹ:
connections.quote: see note 540.
connections.context: The Gemara’s statement and its three textual supports explain the second principle in Rav Tzadok’s closing sentence: the chosen direction itself shapes the help or permission a person receives.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ: "מֹשֵׁל מַקְשִׁיב עַל דְּבַר שָׁקֶר, כָּל מְשָׁרְתָיו רְשָׁעִים" (מִשְׁלֵי כט, יב), וְאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): הָא עַל דְּבַר אֱמֶת וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘When a ruler pays attention to falsehood, all his attendants become wicked.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ: "מֹשֵׁל מַקְשִׁיב עַל דְּבַר שָׁקֶר, כָּל מְשָׁרְתָיו רְשָׁעִים" (מִשְׁלֵי כט, יב), וְאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): הָא עַל דְּבַר אֱמֶת וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “That cannot enter your mind. From “A ruler who listens to falsehood—all his servants are wicked,” it follows that one who listens to truth has righteous servants.”
connections.context: The Gemara uses the positive converse to distinguish Jehoshaphat’s servants from Ahab’s. Rav Tzadok cites this inference to describe the influence of a ruler or spiritual head.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה עֹבַדְיָה גַּם כֵּן מִמְּשָׁרְתֵי אַחְאָב, לְפִי שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קב:): אַחְאָב וַתְּרָן בְּמָמוֹנוֹ הָיָה, וּלְכָךְ עֹבַדְיָה עַל הַבַּיִת, שֶׁבָּזֶה הָיָה כִּשְׁרוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rav Nahman said: ‘Ahab was evenly balanced, as it is stated: ‘Hashem said: Who will entice Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? One said this, and another said that.’’ Rabbi Yosef challenged this: ‘Of him it is written, ‘There was none like Ahab, who sold himself to do what was evil in the eyes of Hashem, whom Jezebel his wife incited.’ And we learned: Every day she weighed out gold shekels for idolatry. Yet you say that he was evenly balanced?’ Rather, Ahab was generous with his money, and because he benefited Torah scholars from his possessions, half was atoned for on his behalf.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִצַּד הַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ בְּוַתְּרָנוּת הָיָה עֹבַדְיָה.
connections.quote: “Who was this? Obadiah, who was wealthy and served as administrator to Ahab king of Israel, as it says, “Ahab summoned Obadiah, who was over the household.” He was exceedingly wealthy and spent all his money on charity, sustaining the prophets, as it says, “I hid a hundred of the Lord’s prophets, fifty men in each cave, and sustained them with bread and water.””
connections.context: Rabbeinu Bahya identifies Obadiah’s particular excellence as the material support of prophets. That is the point Rav Tzadok matches to Ahab’s own generosity in explaining why this righteous servant belonged to his household.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כָּל הַחֲפָצִים, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר הַמַּאֲכָלִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם, הוּא מֵהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כֹּחַ נַפְשׁוֹ וְחַיּוּתוֹ בָּהֶם, וּמִזֶּה הוּא חַיּוּתָם כַּיָּדוּעַ.
connections.quote: “Property belongs to a person: even when it is lost, it must be returned when he has an identifying mark or recognizes it, indicating a relation, recognition and testimony that it is his. Everything lives through Hashem's word, and the person's own life presumably has a relation to the life within the possession. There are four levels in the lower world—inanimate, plant, animal and speaking human—with the upper realms as a fifth. Likewise there are four elements—fire, air, water and earth—with heaven as a fifth substance. Likewise there are four soul levels: nefesh, ruach, neshamah and the soul of the soul, chayah, with yechidah as the fifth, as explained elsewhere. A person contains the inanimate, plant, animal and speaking levels; the inanimate power is the power of the nefesh, and so forth. There is certainly a difference between the inanimate power in an inanimate thing and the corresponding power within a person; nevertheless they have a bond and relation.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah begins from the marks by which a lost possession is recognized as belonging to a person and develops the relation through the divine life sustaining each. It explicitly distinguishes an inanimate power in an object from the corresponding power in a human being. This clarifies the siman's extension of a person's faculties into possessions and food: relation and correspondence are intended, without making the levels identical.
connections.headline: Possessions and the person have related powers of life

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כָּל הַחֲפָצִים, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר הַמַּאֲכָלִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם, הוּא מֵהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כֹּחַ נַפְשׁוֹ וְחַיּוּתוֹ בָּהֶם, וּמִזֶּה הוּא חַיּוּתָם כַּיָּדוּעַ.
connections.quote: ““Complete in his wealth” corresponds to “with all your might,” which Berakhot expounds as a person whose money is dearer to him than his body. How can there be someone whose money is dearer than his body to whom one says, “You shall love…”? In fact, Chullin says this of the righteous: their money is dearer to them than their bodies because they do not reach out to take what belongs to others. We likewise find concerning Abba Chilkiyah in Taanit that he said, “This heals, while this does not heal.” The reason is that their property is only what Hashem gives them, and they know that it belongs to the essential root of their life; therefore it is dear to them, as explained in teaching 6.”
connections.explanation: Vayishlach directly explains why a righteous person's money can be dearer than his body: he recognizes it as what Hashem has given him, belonging to the root of his life. This illuminates the particular claim about possessions as extensions of a soul. It does not make every possession or every use of it holy automatically; the present siman explicitly differentiates the good and bad powers of a mixed person.
connections.headline: Why possessions can belong to the root of a person's life

connections.hePhrase: וּמִמָּקוֹם שֶׁהוּא טוֹב, כָּךְ כָּל כֵּלָיו הַמִּתְפַּשְּׁטִים מֵאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ, וְכֵן הַמַּאֲכָלִים שֶׁמֵּאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ יֵשׁ בָּהֶם קְדוּשָּׁה גְּדוֹלָה.
connections.quote: “They established three meals for this, for food sustains life. Through eating in accordance with the blessed God’s will, these influences enter the heart: since God established food to sustain human life, it certainly contains a life-giving power. This applies even to weekday food, as they said in Bava Kamma: I did not tell you this last night because I had not eaten ox meat. They said in the Mekhilta: Torah was given only to those who ate manna. That is the bread eaten by the ministering angels; it contains immense spiritual vitality, and through it one merits much Torah. Presumably all the Torah scholars who occupy themselves with Torah, to whom Torah is given, are eaters of manna, as it says: Whoever accepts the yoke of Torah has the yoke of government and ordinary work removed from him. His livelihood resembles manna and certainly contains that holiness, bringing vitality from the truth of the blessed God into his heart, through which he apprehends Torah from the truth of His wisdom.”
connections.context: This later passage develops the connection between food, vitality, and apprehension of Torah, beginning with the three Shabbat meals and then extending the principle to weekday eating. It explains the spiritual sense of nourishment used here.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "עַל כֵּן לֹא יֹאכְלוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית לב, לג), שֶׁמֵּאַחַר שֶׁהַמַּלְאָךְ יָכֹל לוֹ שָׁם, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ דְּיֵשׁ שָׁם חִסָּרוֹן בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ
connections.quote: ‘Therefore, to this day the children of Israel do not eat the displaced sinew that is upon the hip socket, because he touched Jacob’s hip socket at the displaced sinew.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְהַיְינוּ בַּתַּאֲוָה דְּשָׁם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד וְכוּלֵי],
connections.quote: “The holiness of the Land is that a person has a God, as stated in Ketubot, while sexual immorality causes this to be forgotten. As the Zohar on Vayishlach explains concerning gid hanasheh, its name denotes forgetting, and its meaning is damage to the covenant. As they said in Sotah: “He made the eye above as though it did not see,” in contrast to what is written of the Land of Israel: “The eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok connects the sciatic nerve’s name with forgetting divine presence and with damage to the covenant. This supplies a direct parallel to the spiritual deficiency he associates with that part of Jacob’s body.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אֵין לֶאֱכוֹל גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה, דִּמְקוֹם חַיּוּתוֹ מִגִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה דְּאָדָם, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מד עַמּוּד ב): נֶפֶשׁ מְשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, כִּי יֵשׁ שָׁם חַיּוּת מֵאוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר.
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: Spleen is good for the teeth but harmful to the intestines. Leeks are harmful to the teeth but good for the intestines. Every raw vegetable makes the complexion pale; every undergrown animal diminishes one’s strength; every whole creature restores vitality; and every part near the seat of life restores vitality. Cabbage is for nourishment, and beet greens are for healing. Woe to the house through which the turnip passes.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְטַעַם דָּם – כִּי "הַדָּם הוּא הַנָּפֶשׁ" (דְּבָרִים יב, כג), שֶׁעִיקַּר חֵטְא בַּנֶּפֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא" (וַיִּקְרָא ד, ב) כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.
connections.quote: ‘Only be resolute about not eating the blood, for the blood is the life; you must not eat the life together with the flesh.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְטַעַם דָּם – כִּי "הַדָּם הוּא הַנָּפֶשׁ" (דְּבָרִים יב, כג), שֶׁעִיקַּר חֵטְא בַּנֶּפֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא" (וַיִּקְרָא ד, ב) כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.
connections.quote: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying: When a soul sins in error against any of the commandments of Hashem concerning things that are not to be done, and does one of them.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְטַעַם דָּם – כִּי "הַדָּם הוּא הַנָּפֶשׁ" (דְּבָרִים יב, כג), שֶׁעִיקַּר חֵטְא בַּנֶּפֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא" (וַיִּקְרָא ד, ב) כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.
connections.quote: ““When a soul sins inadvertently”: Because thought belongs to the soul, and it is the soul that errs, “soul” is mentioned here. The reason for offerings on behalf of the soul that errs is that all sins produce a disgrace in the soul and constitute a blemish in it. It cannot receive the presence of its Maker unless it is pure of every sin. Otherwise even the foolish among the nations would merit coming before Him. Therefore the soul that sins inadvertently brings an offering, so that it may merit drawing near to the God who gave it. For this reason too, “soul” is mentioned.”
connections.context: Ramban directly explains why the Torah assigns sin to the nefesh and why an offering repairs that soul’s blemish. This is the background for the section’s connection between the soul, sin, and the prohibition of blood.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עִיקַּר הַחֵטְא כְּעִנְיַן "שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים לב, טו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָצָא מֵחֵלֶב עֵינֵמוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים עג, ז) וּבְכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת, וְלָכֵן אָסוּר חֵלֶב, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: see note 437.
connections.context: The verse connects material fullness with spiritual rebellion. Rav Tzadok draws on the language of fatness when discussing forbidden fat and the soul’s failings.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עִיקַּר הַחֵטְא כְּעִנְיַן "שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים לב, טו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָצָא מֵחֵלֶב עֵינֵמוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים עג, ז) וּבְכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת, וְלָכֵן אָסוּר חֵלֶב, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: ‘Their eyes bulge from fat; what they obtain exceeds their hearts’ imaginings.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עִיקַּר הַחֵטְא כְּעִנְיַן "שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים לב, טו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָצָא מֵחֵלֶב עֵינֵמוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים עג, ז) וּבְכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת, וְלָכֵן אָסוּר חֵלֶב, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ]:
connections.quote: ““You grew fat, thick, covered over”: You, Jeshurun—the community of those who grasp Torah and engage in contemplation—turned toward bodily pleasures, and through this grew too thick to understand the subtlety of truth, as it says: “These too have erred through wine and strayed through strong drink, priest and prophet.””
connections.context: Sforno interprets the verse’s thickening as the loss of refined understanding through indulgence. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok associates the language of fatness with spiritual failure.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי ע' כֹּחוֹת בַּנֶּפֶשׁ נֶגֶד ע' אֻמּוֹת בָּרָע כַּיָּדוּעַ],
connections.quote: “In every evil power there is, in truth, also good. The seventy souls of the house of Israel correspond to the seventy nations: they comprise the good in the seventy powers of the soul, while the idolaters comprise the evil. By bringing out the words of Torah hidden within it and drawing what it has swallowed out of its mouth, the illusion is thereby nullified, and this is victory over that nation.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok gives the correspondence between seventy nations and seventy powers of the soul. His distinction between the good and evil manifestations of a power explains why its correction need not mean its destruction.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיָּד שֶׁלָּקָה, הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מַכּוֹת כג.)
connections.quote: “Mishnah: All those liable to karet, the penalty of being cut off, who have received lashes are released from that liability, as it is said, ‘And your brother is degraded before your eyes’: once he has received lashes, he is again your brother. These are the words of Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel. Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel also said: If a person who commits one transgression loses his life on its account, how much more should a person who performs one mitzvah be granted his life! Rabbi Shimon says: This is learned from the very same passage, for it is said, ‘The souls that do these things shall be cut off,’ and so on, and ‘Which a person shall do and live by them.’ Thus, one who refrains from committing a transgression is given a reward like one who performs a mitzvah.”

connections.hePhrase: [וַאֲפִילּוּ רַק כְּפָתוּהוּ וְכוּלֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַכּוֹת (שָׁם),
connections.quote: “When Yosef was thrown into the pit of snakes and scorpions and did not kill them, he knew that they had been brought before him to kill him and that a miracle had occurred. He then sensed that he needed clarification concerning two things: his report that his brothers looked at the daughters of the land, and that they were suspected of eating a limb from a living animal. For these matters the snakes and scorpions came before him. The snake is the root of damage to the covenant, the serpent's counsel that introduced the appetite for eating into Adam. It was therefore punished with “dust is the snake's bread,” losing the taste of that appetite. The scorpion certainly kills, as Berakhot 33a says, “For a scorpion he interrupts.” It corresponds to the damage of bloodshed extending through Kayin and to the fault of a limb from a living animal. The nations too guard against this because it is great cruelty, besides the prohibition commanded to the descendants of Noach. Nevuchadnezzar was therefore ashamed when he ate a live hare, as in Nedarim 65a. When the snakes and scorpions came before Yosef, he sensed his need for clarification concerning the evil report, and he certainly repented for these two faults.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah applies the same Shabbat passage to Yosef in the pit. It describes how the encounter awakened his own need to clarify the reports he had made about his brothers, followed by repentance. This provides a concrete example of the siman's movement from fear to the repair and strengthening of a particular faculty, rather than stopping at the fear itself.
connections.headline: Yosef turns the encounter toward his own repair

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכא:) בְּנָחָשׁ שֶׁהָיָה רוֹדֵף אַחֲרָיו, כִּי בָּזֶה יָצָא יְדֵי עוֹנְשׁוֹ וְיִסּוּרִין שֶׁלּוֹ בַּפַּחַד שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁיִּשְּׁכֶנּוּ;
connections.quote: “If snakes or scorpions encountered a person and he killed them, it is known that they were brought before him to be killed. If he did not kill them, it is known that they were brought to kill him and a miracle was performed for him from Heaven. Ulla—and some say Rabba bar bar Chana in Rabbi Yochanan’s name—said: This concerns creatures hissing at him.”
connections.context: The passage concerns a real danger from which the person was saved. Rav Tzadok explains the fear itself as taking the place of the threatened suffering. The teaching is an anonymous baraita; the main text’s expanded “Shammai” is not the attribution in the Gemara.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁחָסוּ עָלָיו וּפְדָאוּהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַפַּחַד, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נה.): חֶלְמָא בִּישָׁא וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: see note 1562. The same passage continues: “Rav Chisda said: A bad dream is harder than lashes, as it is said, ‘God has so made it that people should fear before Him’ (Ecclesiastes 3:14); and Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: This refers to a bad dream.”
connections.context: The fright of a bad dream is itself a kind of suffering; this is why Rav Tzadok treats the terror as having taken the place of the punishment.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כְּשֶׁשָּׁב בֶּאֱמֶת, אָז כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא כְּחוֹלְמִים (תְּהִלִּים קכו, א)];
connections.quote: “This may also be hinted at in the verse, “When the Lord brings back the captivity of Zion, we were like dreamers.” That is, in the future we shall see plainly that all the forms of rebuke were like a dream, as the Gemara says: “For a bad dream, its sadness suffices.” This is the purpose of the rebukes: they were spoken only to frighten and sadden a person’s heart so that he will improve his way from now on; then they will all turn to good.”
connections.context: This parallel joins the same dream passage to the purpose of rebuke. It explicitly retains the condition of improving one’s conduct, which is also present here in the words “when one truly repents.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז אוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר וְכֹחַ מְתוּקָּן, וְנֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, שֶׁאוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר יֵשׁ בּוֹ תִּיקּוּן, אֶלָּא שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהוֹסִיף וּלְחַזְּקוֹ.
connections.quote: “Of all the powers planted in every Jewish soul, one should not think that a power is wholly evil and must be reversed into its opposite. There is no trait or power that does not also have a good aspect; one must only use it according to the will of the blessed God. If it is not according to His will, even good traits are evil.”
connections.context: This explains what it means to strengthen a power after its correction: the power itself can serve good when directed according to God’s will. The qualification about even good traits being misused prevents reading the passage as unconditional approval of a trait.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז "בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב, א) – דַּיְיקָא בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם הוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ:
connections.quote: “The number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. In the place where it was said to them, “You are not My people,” it shall be said to them, “Children of the living God.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok emphasizes “in the place”: the very point that seemed to express rejection can become the point where the restored bond is revealed. The verse’s movement from “not My people” to “children of the living God” is the basis of that interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז "בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב, א) – דַּיְיקָא בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם הוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ:
connections.quote: “But one can say that this matter depends upon the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Meir in Kiddushin 36a: and then I merited to find in the Responsa of the Rashba Part I, §124 and §212 who likewise cited for this issue this dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah, and that the halachah follows Rabbi Meir because his textual proofs are more precise, see there, and it brought me great joy; for Rabbi Meir holds that in all circumstances they are termed "children of the Living God" (Hoshea 2:1); but Rabbi Yehudah says: when they do not conduct themselves as children, they are not termed "children." And at the beginning of the formation of the Israelite nation, at the start of the mission to redeem them from Egypt, it is stated in Parashas Shemos: "Israel is My son, My firstborn; send forth My son that he may serve Me" (Shemos 4:22–23); it is clear that the collective of Israel are His children, blessed be He, and that for this reason He brought them forth to be His people and serve Him because they are His children;”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin locates that verse within the dispute concerning whether Israel remains called Hashem’s children when conduct is deficient, and records the support for Rabbi Meir’s view. This explains the depth of the siman’s concluding reversal: the recognition of repair can uncover an enduring relationship, rather than create a wholly unrelated identity after punishment.
connections.headline: The enduring root beneath the language of rejection

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז "בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב, א) – דַּיְיקָא בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם הוּא מַמָּשׁ לְהֵיפֶךְ:
connections.quote: “This was fixed here in the census of the wilderness generation. Through their service they illuminated that no unfolding in the world lies outside words of Torah. It was thereby established for all later generations that even in the greatest concealment, it cannot be that a person has no way to return to Hashem's light: a path back always remains, although he himself recognizes no connection. Nevertheless, Israel retains the cry, ‘What will You do for Your great name?’ On his own account he is ready to accept all the suffering; what he lacks is, ‘What will You do for Your great name?’ Since Hashem established in this world that Heaven's honor is, as it were, incomplete and Israel completes it through service, he therefore cries that Heaven's honor is incomplete. From this very cry he has a way to return to Hashem's light.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef develops the same verse in Hosea by distinguishing consciously asking Hashem to fill one's lack from concealment so deep that no connection is felt. Even there, the cry that Heaven's honor remains incomplete is itself a way back. This explains the siman's insistence that the very place called ‘not My people’ becomes the place of renewed sonship.
connections.headline: The cry that remains in concealment

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (נב.)
connections.quote: “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav: From where do we know that the idol of a Jew requires interment (genizah)? As it is said: ‘You shall not plant for yourself an asherah of any kind of tree beside the altar’ (Deuteronomy 16:21)—just as the altar requires interment, so too the asherah requires interment.”

connections.hePhrase: כַּנּוֹדָע עַל פָּסוּק "וּמַלְכוּתוֹ בַּכֹּל מָשָׁלָה",
connections.quote: “Hashem has established His throne in the heavens, and His kingdom rules over all.”

connections.hePhrase: אַגְּמָרָא (נִדָּה יג:) מְשַׂחֲקִים בְּתִינוֹקוֹת וּמְקַבְּלֵי גֵּרִים,
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Converts and those who play with children delay the Messiah. … What are those who play with children? … Rather, those who marry minor girls who are not yet able to bear children, for Rabbi Yosei said: The son of David will not come until all the souls in the guf are finished, as it is said: ‘For the spirit that enwraps itself is from Me, and the souls that I have made’ (Isaiah 57:16).”

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל עֲבֵירָה נַעֲשָׂה מַלְאָךְ רַע כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה,
connections.quote: see note 295.
connections.context: The Mishnah supplies the original statement that a deed gives rise to an advocate or accuser. Rav Tzadok develops its spiritual meaning and explains how the result of the transgression can itself become an impetus to repentance.

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל עֲבֵירָה נַעֲשָׂה מַלְאָךְ רַע כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה,
connections.quote: “Repentance resembles a sage's release that uproots the matter retroactively, and the bad angel made by the transgression is entirely nullified. When repentance comes from love, sins become merits: the angel is not nullified but transformed to good. These are the levels of transformation and subduing. Fear establishes a boundary in the heart against evil; love turns the bitter—the person's impulse and desire—sweet, by drawing it to the study house and Torah. In this way the evil impulse becomes “very good,” since the desire for Torah comes through it. Torah seasons the impulse so that it becomes good.”
connections.explanation: Siman 242 supplies the distinction implicit in this opening: repentance can nullify the angel, while return from love transforms the desire itself toward Torah. It later explains “repentance that covers all his deeds” as the general return from love. Together the passages describe an actual change in the person and the power produced by the act; the emergence of remorse is the beginning of that work, rather than its automatic completion.
connections.headline: The angel's awakening can lead to a transformation

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הַמַּלְאָךְ שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה עַל יָדוֹ
connections.quote: “A person’s commandments and good deeds—and certainly words of Torah—bring good thoughts into his heart; transgressions bring the opposite, as our Sages say, “One commandment draws another, and a transgression, and so forth.” The meaning of this drawing is that an angel is created from every commandment: that is, a spiritual power. As the Zohar states, no deed or speech of a person, good or evil, is lost. Through this good angel, which belongs to him, was born of his action, and dwells near him—for the angel is spiritual, like human thought—a thought falls into his heart to perform other commandments.”
connections.context: Here Rav Tzadok defines “angel” as a spiritual power produced by an action and explains its influence on later thought. This supplies the mechanism assumed in the present discussion; the already connected passage from section 242 concerns the subsequent nullification or transformation of that power.

connections.hePhrase: [וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ב:): "רָאָה וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם" (חֲבַקּוּק ג, ו) – שֶׁהִתִּיר לָהֶם, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוֹלְכִים לַאֲבַדּוֹן],
connections.quote: see note 730.
connections.context: The Gemara questions a reading that would reward disobedience and explains the release in terms of losing the status and reward of commanded performance. It does not treat violation as a beneficial exemption. That conclusion supplies needed context for Rav Tzadok’s use of “released them.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים חֲרָטוֹת",
connections.quote: “There is no wicked person to whom thoughts of repentance do not come before he commits the transgression, except that his inclination entices him, and afterward he regrets it. And so they said: ‘The wicked are full of regrets.’”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים חֲרָטוֹת",
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים י״א:ו׳
connections.quote: see note 1522.
connections.context: Tanya records the saying about being full of regrets while carefully distinguishing remorse from actually abandoning the sin. That distinction helps explain why an awakening toward repentance can be present even before the person has completed repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה מַרְבֶּה מַזִּיקִים רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ מִזֹּהַר,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: From the time Cain killed Abel, Adam separated from his wife. Two female spirits would come and couple with him, and he begot spirits and demons that roam the world… Even now, when a man is in his dream, female spirits come…, are heated by him, and afterward give birth; and these are called ‘the plagues of the sons of men’ (II Samuel 7:14).”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה מַרְבֶּה מַזִּיקִים רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ מִזֹּהַר,
connections.quote: “When a man is in his dream and has no control over his body…, at times impure female spirits come and draw near to him…, are heated by him, and afterward give birth to spirits and harmful beings (mazikin).”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה מַרְבֶּה מַזִּיקִים רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת כַּיָּדוּעַ מִזֹּהַר,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ז׳:י״ב-ט״ז
connections.quote: “But the vitality in drops of semen emitted in vain, although it descended and became included in the three impure shells, rises from there through proper repentance and intense intention in the bedtime Shema, as is known from the Ari. This is hinted at in the Gemara: “Whoever recites the Shema upon his bed is as though he holds a two-edged sword,” and so forth—to slay the bodies of the external forces that have become a garment for the vitality in the drops, so that the vitality rises from them, as is known to those versed in the hidden wisdom. Therefore the transgression of seed emitted in vain is not listed in the Torah among forbidden relations, although it is more severe than they are in the magnitude and abundance of the impurity and shells it generates and greatly multiplies. In forbidden relations, however, one adds strength and vitality to an especially impure shell, from which one cannot raise the vitality through repentance—[gloss: because it has been absorbed into the foundation of the female aspect of the shell, which receives and absorbs vitality from holiness; in seed emitted in vain there is no such female aspect, but only its powers and armies clothing the vitality in the drops, as is known to those versed in the hidden wisdom]—unless one repents with such great love that deliberate sins become merits. This explains our Sages’ statement, “What is a crooked thing that cannot be repaired? One who has relations with a forbidden partner and fathers a mamzer”: then, even if he performs repentance of that magnitude, he cannot raise that vitality to holiness, because it has already descended into this world and become clothed in a body of flesh and blood.”
connections.context: This is the full distinction behind the comparison of harmful spiritual forces. Tanya differentiates their quantity from the way vitality becomes bound to them, and it specifies different conditions of repentance. The statement concerns the recovery of that vitality, not a denial of the person’s ability to repent.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל תּוֹרָה הוּא קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא עַצְמוֹ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ].
connections.quote: “Because it is a precious supernal treasure—His very name—the whole Torah is hidden and revealed in the mystery of His name. Therefore Israel has two levels, hidden and revealed. For we learned: three levels are bound to one another—the Holy One, blessed be He, the Torah, and Israel. Each has level upon level, hidden and revealed. The Holy One, blessed be He, has level upon level, hidden and revealed; the Torah likewise has hidden and revealed; Israel likewise has level upon level. This is what is written: “He declares His words to Jacob, His statutes and judgments to Israel.” There are two levels, Jacob and Israel: one revealed and one hidden.”
connections.context: The Zohar binds God, Torah, and Israel together and speaks of Torah as His name. It supplies the background to Rav Tzadok’s identification of Torah with the Holy One, while retaining the distinction between hidden and revealed levels.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה הוּא לִתְשׁוּבָה גְּדוֹלָה,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim distinguishes the exact Zohar formula from thought displacing thought

connections.hePhrase: וְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה הוּא לִתְשׁוּבָה גְּדוֹלָה,
connections.quote: “Therefore the repair is through intention in the recitation of Shema: the unification in which one unifies the whole world and all it contains as Hashem's unity. Hashem is thereby recognized as the One who acts and the master of the deed, and the deed too is repaired. This is called in the Zohar “teshuvah fit to cover all his deeds”: it covers and overspreads all the acts he did, declaring that they are not his acts but Hashem's act. This is not like other teshuvah, which displaces a thought and makes the sins like inadvertent acts, merits, or a transgression for Heaven's sake. Rather, this covers and overspreads them all until they are not revealed at all, since they are unified in Hashem's unity.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim quotes the same Zohar expression and explains the particular force of “covering.” In the surrounding argument, ordinary remorse displaces the earlier thought, while this further account addresses the deed through the unity proclaimed in Shema. This clarifies why the siman introduces “great teshuvah” at this exact point rather than using the phrase as a general adjective for strong remorse.
connections.headline: What it means for teshuvah to cover the deeds

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, ריד, ב),
connections.quote: ‘These words apply when he has not performed complete repentance—repentance fit to cover all his deeds. Even so, it is better for him not to be placed in a coffin, for as long as the body remains intact, the soul is judged and does not enter its place. The exceptions are those lofty, holy, pious ones who are worthy of ascending in their bodies. Fortunate is their portion in this world and in the World to Come.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן "מַאן מַלְכֵי? רַבָּנָן".
connections.quote: see note 591.
connections.context: This is the original discussion identifying Torah scholars as kings, the expression used here to explain how an aspect of kingship remains available through the sages.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל שְׁלֵימוּת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁהוּא הַכָּרַת הַחִסָּרוֹן,
connections.quote: “The essence of kingship is attained through exceptionally great awe, as they said: “Once the king bows, he does not straighten again”—because of the abundance of awe and fear. Through this he becomes a chariot for the attribute of kingship, of which it is said, “It is awe, and awe rests within it,” as the Zohar states. Then he recognizes his lowliness: that he has nothing from his own effort except what the blessed God has granted him, like Abraham, Moses, Aaron, and David. For the attribute of kingship signifies that it has nothing of its own. He then merits clarification in all the attributes up to the crown, as the passage Patach Eliyahu says, “The supernal crown is the crown of kingship”: by crowning the blessed God through his lowliness, he merits clarification in the attribute of the supernal crown.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains why the completion of kingship depends on recognizing one’s lack. The recognition is that all attainment is received from God, and this humility connects the final attribute of kingship with its highest source.

connections.hePhrase: הַנְּפָשׁוֹת כֻּלָּם קֶשֶׁר אֶחָד, כְּעִנְיַן "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ",
connections.quote: “For the Lord’s portion is His people; Jacob is the allotment of His inheritance.”
connections.context: The Hebrew word for “allotment,” chevel, also means a cord. Rav Tzadok develops that image into a single cord joining all souls; the cord image is his reading of the verse’s wording.

connections.hePhrase: הַנְּפָשׁוֹת כֻּלָּם קֶשֶׁר אֶחָד, כְּעִנְיַן "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ",
connections.quote: “But regarding the sinners of Israel, "Let sins cease" is written (Tehillim 104:35), and not "sinners," as they expounded in Berachos 10a; for the root of all the souls of Israel is cleaved unto the Living God, for "the portion of Hashem is His people" (Devarim 32:9); and as they stated in Kiddushin 36a that even when they lack faith and worship idols, where it is said of them "you are not My people" (Hoshea 1:9), appearing outwardly as if they are not His people; in truth they remain the portion of Hashem, believers the descendants of believers, as they stated in Shabbos 97a; and the seed of Yaakov whose bed is complete have in their hearts nothing other than the One, as they stated in Pesachim 56a. For Hoshea designated them "not My people" because when told to prophesy he said: "Exchange them for another nation," as related in Pesachim 87a; because he presumed that it was possible to sever the name of Israel and the root of Judaism through the multitude of sins, God forbid; until the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "They are My children, the descendants of My beloved ones, Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov," commanding him to plead for mercy to annul the decrees brought about through him, as they related ibid. 87b; for when the leading tzaddik of the generation below consents to the prosecuting Attribute of Judgment, the pleas of the Attribute of Mercy are sealed and judgment is decreed, and from the perspective of strict justice it was indeed so; but through the awakening of the Attribute of Mercy he perceived that "in the place where it was said unto them: 'You are not My people,' it shall be said unto them: 'You are the sons of the living God'" (Hoshea 2:1); that when sins cease, the wicked are no more, and the holy root remains. For all their sins stem merely from the brambles and thorns that encircle the myrtle and the rose (Vayikra Rabbah 23:3);”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin reads the same verses in Hoshea as an apparent loss of relationship that cannot eradicate the soul’s root in Hashem. Its distinction between the sin and the sinner explains what the rope image preserves through stretching and division. It also directs the desired outcome toward the removal of sin and recovery of the good root, rather than treating the sin as a model to imitate.
connections.headline: What the unbreakable bond preserves

connections.hePhrase: וְאִם אֶחָד מוֹשֵׁךְ לְמַעְלָה הַכֹּל נִמְשָׁךְ לְמַעְלָה, וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ,
connections.quote: “All Jewish souls form one bond. When one Jewish soul becomes wholly bound to Him, all are consequently drawn with it, like someone pulling the end of a rope, which draws the whole rope along. “Jacob is the rope of His inheritance”: one end is bound above to the form of Jacob engraved upon the Throne of Glory, and its lower end consists of the souls of the lowest sinners of Israel. It continues thus from level to level. Yom Kippur awakens the individual who repents to enter “unto the Lord,” into the Holy of Holies; the whole rope is consequently drawn with him in an awakening of repentance and an ascent above, each according to his measure and level, and atonement is drawn to them too. Rabbi and the Sages disagree whether it atones even for those who do not repent: that concerns complete atonement, beyond what is fitting through the individual who repents. In the latter matter all agree that there is forgiveness for the whole world; but this depends on the strength of his repentance—that is, the strength with which he draws the rope upward.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s extended use of the same rope image. He makes the effect on others proportionate to the penitent’s spiritual influence and distinguishes that effect from the separate dispute about unconditional atonement.

connections.hePhrase: עַל דֶּרֶךְ "וְחוֹטֶא אֶחָד יְאַבֵּד טוֹבָה הַרְבֵּה".
connections.quote: “Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok stresses the effect that one person can have on the whole. The following Kiddushin passage applies the verse to one action tipping the balance of the individual and the world.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁכָּל הָעוֹלָם מֶחֱצָה עַל מֶחֱצָה, כִּדְאִיתָא בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּקִדּוּשִׁין,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says: Since the world is judged according to the majority of its deeds, and an individual is judged according to the majority of his deeds, if he performs one mitzvah, fortunate is he, for he has tipped himself and the whole world toward the side of merit. If he commits one transgression, woe to him, for he has tipped himself and the whole world toward the side of guilt, as it is said: ‘One sinner,’ and so forth. Because of this one sin that he committed, much good was lost to him and to the whole world.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הַמְּשִׁיכָה בַּחֶבֶל, הַחֶבֶל מִתְפַּקֵּעַ וּמִתְאָרֵךְ,
connections.quote: “Because Hashem's desire to benefit was present in the creation of every individual of Israel, He placed before each one a particular matter whose completion, as He presents it to us, requires that person's service. “There shall be a number” means that each has a particular task through which he must complete the revealed divine honor. From Hashem's own side nothing is lacking; the arrangement comes from His desire to benefit the creatures. The particular matter placed before this person must be completed by him and no other. Thus each soul is important to Hashem. But in the totality, “it shall not be measured or counted”: all particulars are included in His unity, and His honor is complete even without human service.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same Hosea verse by distinguishing the countless whole from the significance of each counted individual. Each has a particular service that another cannot perform in his place. This gives a complementary explanation of the siman's division of the one rope into particular souls: the common root and the importance of individual work coexist. Its eventual inclusion in unity does not cancel that work.
connections.headline: The division into persons preserves each person's task

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁנִּתְרַבּוּ נְפָשׁוֹת – וְלֹא שֶׁנִּתְרַבּוּ, רַק שֶׁנֶּחְלְקוּ אֶחָד לִשְׁנַיִם.
connections.quote: “This is our father Jacob, peace be upon him, the complete human being who existed in this world: his offspring were whole, and he did not die, for “just as his descendants are alive,” and so forth, as they said in Taanit 5b. That is, the stature of the congregation of Israel—the descendants of our father Jacob in every generation—is itself the stature of our father Jacob, only differentiated and divided into many individual souls.”
connections.context: This parallel states the distinction made here between creating additional spiritual substance and dividing an already inclusive soul into individual descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (דַּף ה.):
connections.quote: see note 1916.
connections.context: The Gemara challenges the initial literal reading about descendants and corrects it to “as though.” Rav Tzadok explicitly uses that correction when he explains later souls as included in their source; the original footnote stopped before it.

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא כְּמִי שֶׁלֹּא בָּאנוּ לָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהָיוּ נִכְלָלִים בִּמְקוֹרָם.
connections.quote: “For they said in Avodah Zarah 5a: “Had Israel not sinned, we would not have come into the world”; the conclusion is, “as though we had not come into the world.” That is, all Jewish souls are rooted in the Torah, and as the Oral Torah is renewed in the hearts of Israel’s sages in each generation, so are the souls renewed in each generation. Had our ancestors merited that everything be revealed to all Israel within the Written Torah, so that they all grasped every renewal of the future generations, there would have been no place for the renewal of souls. Although souls would still have emerged into actuality in the world, it would have been “as though we had not come,” because everything would already have been included in the ancestors, openly actualized for all, with nothing new.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok interprets the same Talmudic passage cited in the existing note. He preserves the Gemara’s correction from “not born” to “as though not born” and explains it as the absence of an independent new contribution.

connections.hePhrase: פָּסוּק "וְהָיָה מִסְפַּר בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּחוֹל הַיָּם וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: see note 2048.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁיִּכְלוּ כָּל הַנְּשָׁמוֹת,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Assi said: The son of David will not come until all the souls in the repository called Guf are exhausted, as it is written, “For the spirit before Me will enwrap, and the souls that I have made.””
connections.context: This is the original statement behind “when all the souls are exhausted.” Rav Tzadok gives its meaning through the rope image: the unfolding of the souls reaches its completion.

connections.hePhrase: אָז יִמְשׁוֹךְ כִּבְיָכוֹל גַּם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָהֶם,
connections.quote: “A kingship verse, such as “As I live, declares the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured fury I shall reign over you”: although Rav Nachman said, “Let the Holy One, blessed be He, display anger of this kind toward us and redeem us,” since it is spoken in anger, we do not mention anger at the beginning of the year.”
connections.context: The Gemara recognizes even compulsory divine kingship as a means of deliverance, while excluding this angry wording from the Rosh Hashanah kingship verses. That retained liturgical qualification keeps the quotation in its original setting.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז יַכִּירוּ כֻּלָּם וְגוֹמֵר, וּמָלֵא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ.
connections.quote: “And one called to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is Hashem of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory.”

connections.hePhrase: "וְעָמְדוּ רַגְלָיו בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא עַל הַר הַזֵּיתִים וְגוֹמֵר וּבָא ה' אֱלֹהַי כָּל קְדֹשִׁים עִמָּךְ",
connections.quote: “On that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem. The Mount of Olives will split through its middle, from east to west, forming a very great valley. Half of the mountain will shift northward and the other half southward. You will flee through the valley of My mountains, for the valley between the mountains will reach Atzal. You will flee as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah. Then Hashem, my God, will come—all the holy ones with You.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר גַּם בְּפָרָשַׁת תּוֹכָחוֹת וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת בַּחֲטָאִים לְשׁוֹן "וְהָיָה" שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֶלָּא שִׂמְחָה,
connections.quote: “And it shall be (vehayah), if you will not listen to the voice of Hashem your God, to observe to do all His commandments and His statutes which I command you this day, that all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר גַּם בְּפָרָשַׁת תּוֹכָחוֹת וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת בַּחֲטָאִים לְשׁוֹן "וְהָיָה" שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֶלָּא שִׂמְחָה,
connections.quote: “And it shall be (vehayah) that as Hashem rejoiced over you to do you good and to multiply you, so Hashem will rejoice over you to cause you to perish and to destroy you.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה מב),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman distinguished: Wherever “vayehi” is stated, it denotes distress; “vehayah” denotes joy. … They challenged him: “And it was [vehayah] when Jerusalem was captured”! He replied: That too was joy, for on that day Israel received atonement for their sins. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: Israel received great atonement for their iniquities on the day the Temple was destroyed, as it says, “Your iniquity is completed, daughter of Zion.””
connections.context: The Midrash itself addresses an apparent exception: vehayah is used even at Jerusalem’s capture, because of the atonement associated with it. This is the relevant basis for Rav Tzadok’s use of the term in passages of rebuke.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי צֵירוּף "וְהָיָה" הַבָּנִים קוֹדְמִים לָאָבוֹת, כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: “For it has only been weakened, and it separates the letters of the Name [between yod-heh and vav-heh], so that the union of the revealed powers of action with the hidden powers of mind and heart, which cleave to the supernal root, is not revealed in this world. To erase Amalek, the arrangement “vav-heh-yod-heh” is made, in which the children precede the parents (vav-heh-yod-heh). This is Moses raising his hands—the powers of action—upward to the place of the supernal crown. Through this arrangement there is also rest from enemies, and therefore it signifies joy.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the ordering of the divine Name invoked here. The lower, active powers rise above their usual position and reunite with their hidden source; this is why the arrangement vehayah signifies joy.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עַל יְדֵי הָעֲבֵירוֹת כִּבְיָכוֹל "נִצְּחוּנִי בָּנַי" לַעֲבוֹר עַל רְצוֹנִי,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua stood up and said: ‘It is not in heaven!’ What does ‘It is not in heaven’ mean? Rabbi Yirmeya said: The Torah has already been given from Mount Sinai. We pay no heed to a heavenly voice, for You already wrote in the Torah at Mount Sinai: ‘Incline after the majority.’ Rabbi Natan met Elijah and asked him: ‘What was the Holy One, blessed be He, doing at that moment?’ He answered: ‘He was smiling and saying: ‘My children have prevailed against Me! My children have prevailed against Me!’’’
connections.context: In the Gemara, “My children have triumphed over Me” refers to the sages deciding law by the Torah’s own rule of majority, despite a heavenly voice. Rav Tzadok borrows that language for his further interpretation here; the Gemara itself is describing the exercise of legitimate Torah judgment.

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמַּאֲמִין בְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁזְּדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: see note 1016.

connections.hePhrase: [וּמַאן דִּפְלִיג, הַיְינוּ בְּעִנְיַן הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבִיאִים, דְּמָר יָלֵיף מִקְּרָא דִּ"לָרָחוֹק וְלַקָּרוֹב" שֶׁהוּא בַּנְּבִיאִים, וּלְדַעְתּוֹ אֵינוֹ כֵן מִצַּד הַנְּבוּאָה.
connections.quote: see note 325.
connections.context: The discussion in Berakhot uses the order “the far and the near” to compare penitents and the completely righteous. Rav Tzadok is examining that prophetic wording and the limits of what prophecy reveals.

connections.hePhrase: דְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר – "עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה", שֶׁזֶּהוּ רַק מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: ‘From ages past, people have neither heard nor listened; no eye apart from Yours, O God, has seen what He will do for one who waits for Him.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר – "עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה", שֶׁזֶּהוּ רַק מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “For a penitent merits this in one hour, in one instant, as they said in the Zohar, Chayei Sarah. Hence, “In the place where penitents stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand,” for they are closer to the King. It appears that this is what Bereshit Rabbah means: “‘Darkness’ is the deeds of the wicked … I do not know which He desires more,” and so forth. How could one suppose that He desires wicked deeds? The meaning concerns the created order, for “God made the human being upright.” Although He created the wicked and the evil inclination, He created Torah as its remedy, to be “a lamp for my feet, Your word, and a light for my path”; for “though I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light,” and “though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for You are with me.” Although in the end they become closer, because the penitent raises holy sparks from low places of life and turns darkness into light, one might suppose that the blessed God desires this more. Of this they said, “God saw the light, that it was good”: nevertheless, His principal desire and will is for the righteous person, “for it is good.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the height attained through repentance from God’s primary desire for righteous conduct. That distinction explains the different perspectives on the righteous person and the penitent without treating sin as an aim.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל תְּשׁוּבָה שַׁיָּיכוּת לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק הוּא כְּטַעַם: לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ אִמִּי, שֶׁגְּדוֹלָה מִמֶּנּוּ, וְעוֹד דְּבָרִים בְּגוֹ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמָם].
connections.quote: see note 1746.
connections.context: This is the original parable alluded to by “He did not cease cherishing her until He called her My mother.” The successive titles express increasing divine affection for Israel, providing the image that Rav Tzadok interprets in terms of repentance.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל תְּשׁוּבָה שַׁיָּיכוּת לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק הוּא כְּטַעַם: לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ אִמִּי, שֶׁגְּדוֹלָה מִמֶּנּוּ, וְעוֹד דְּבָרִים בְּגוֹ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמָם].
connections.quote: “Although it is known that the attribute of kingship is the last, the eighth counted from understanding in the heart, and is the crown of the foundation when it is only a point—when it expands into a complete stature, the stature of the feminine, of this they said in Shir HaShirim Rabbah that He cherishes her so much that He calls her “My daughter,” “My sister,” and “My mother.” The congregation of Israel, whose souls are a portion of God above—for one who breathes breathes from within himself—and are emanated from His holy emanation, which He emanated when He willed that there be room for the creation of worlds, is the last level of the emanated levels: the level capable of clothing itself in the bodily garment of this world, so that His Presence may dwell below, in this physical world. This is the purpose and end of the whole unfolding of emanation: He desired His light to be revealed also among those below, and this is the whole intention of creation. Therefore, although they are the end of all creation, they are also its beginning and principal purpose, for “the end of the deed is first in thought,” and Israel arose in thought. This is “You formed me behind and before”: once they reach their completion and the intention of all creation is fulfilled through the human being, he is before and at the head of everything, for this was the initial intention in creating the world. This is His calling her “My mother”: she is the source that gives birth to the unfolding of all six directions of emanation. For the depth of the end is itself the depth of the beginning, in the mystery of “their end is embedded in their beginning”; the whole unfolding of emanation was to attain the purpose, the building of the stature of the congregation of Israel and the dwelling of the Presence below, and this is the root of the unfolding’s beginning.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok gives the mystical interpretation of the daughter-sister-mother parable. The final recipient is called “mother” when the completion of creation discloses that it was the initial purpose; the quotation retains the stages on which this reversal depends.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה נִקְרָא עָלְמָא דְּאִתְכַּסְיָא, וְאֵינוֹ נִגְלֶה לִבְנֵי אָדָם הַיְקָרוּת וְהַיּוֹפִי שֶׁבָּהּ.
connections.quote: “People said, “The elder for the elder,” because outwardly it seemed as though she resembled him, Heaven forbid. In truth, Esav's deeds were hateful to her. In this she rose above Rachel, whose children are Esav's accusers because they are good while he is evil. If a person sins, he can outwardly appear like Esav. But for Leah, the root of his deeds is hateful: hatred is the heart's rejection of the thing, even if outward action does not appear so. The root within the heart is different. Therefore “one who denies idolatry is called a Jew”: this is the root of Judah from Leah, whose heart has no belief in idolatry or any power opposed to Hashem.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin distinguishes the public claim “the elder for the elder” from Leah's inward rejection of Esav's ways. That distinction explains how the siman uses apparent ugliness and hidden fruitfulness: the inner relation of the returning heart is not fully legible from its outward position. The comparison develops this particular symbolism, rather than making visible failure itself a virtue.
connections.headline: Leah's inward will differs from her outward association

connections.hePhrase: וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כט, לא), וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר הַטַּעַם.
connections.quote: “The Lord saw that Leah was unloved, and He opened her womb; Rachel was barren.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כט, לא), וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר הַטַּעַם.
connections.quote: “Why was she unloved? Are children of an unloved woman not lacking? Yet we see that all those excellent children came from Leah. Rather, Jubilee is always the concealed world, and all its matters are not revealed; therefore its workings were concealed from Jacob.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כט, לא), וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר הַטַּעַם.
connections.quote: ““He” is the upper world, which is always concealed. Jacob’s desire did not cleave to what was concealed, but to what was revealed.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כט, לא), וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר הַטַּעַם.
connections.quote: “‘Hashem saw that Leah was hated’: from here [we learn] that a man shuns the nakedness of his mother, and a man may be alone with his mother anywhere without concern… And all this was hidden from Jacob, for the upper world is not revealed at all.”
connections.context: The Zohar identifies Leah with the concealed upper world and Rachel with the revealed lower world. This is the explanation Rav Tzadok asks the reader to consult; he then develops it in his comparison of repentance and the completely righteous.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכג.) שֶׁהָיוּ אוֹמְרִים: הַגְּדוֹלָה לַגָּדוֹל וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Rav said: Her eyes were indeed literally tender, and this was not to her discredit but to her praise.
