For at the crossroads she would hear people saying: Rebecca has two sons, and Laban has two daughters; the elder daughter is for the elder son, and the younger daughter for the younger son.’

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ לְפִי הַנִּגְלֶה שַׁיָּיכֶת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְחֵלֶק עֵשָׂו, וְהָיְתָה בּוֹכָה – זֶהוּ סוֹד הַתְּשׁוּבָה.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 7
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 7
connections.quote: “This is also why Lavan gave his daughters names according to the nature he recognized in each. The name Rachel indicates that she held jealousy and the wish to prevail in her heart without expressing them with her lips, as it says (Isaiah 53:7), ‘Like a ewe silent before her shearers.’ Her jealousy was for Heaven, as it says, ‘Rachel was jealous of her sister.’ The name Leah derives from weariness: she was continually weary and thirsty for Hashem's salvations.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads Leah's name as continual weariness and thirst for Hashem's salvation. That supplies a further description of the inward yearning expressed by her tears here. Its contrast with Rachel keeps the source's qualification: Rachel's jealousy was for Heaven. The comparison concerns inward traits and yearning, without making every difference between the sisters identical across the two works.
connections.headline: Leah's continual thirst for salvation

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן רָחֵל: "יְפַת תֹּאַר וִיפַת מַרְאֶה", שֶׁהַכֹּל אוֹמְרִים: הַקְּטַנָּה לַקָּטָן, כִּי בְּעָלְמָא דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא יֵשׁ בָּהּ יֹפִי מַעֲשִׂים.
connections.quote: “Leah’s eyes were tender, but Rachel was of beautiful form and fair to look upon.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הִיא אִמּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (זוּטָא פֶּרֶק ה) דְּאֵין לְךָ מִדָּה טוֹבָה וְדָבָר טוֹב בָּא לִבְנֵי אָדָם אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי עֲנִיּוּת – פֵּירוּשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, surveyed all the qualities in the world and found no quality better for Israel than poverty. Through Israel’s poverty they fear the Lord: when they have no bread to eat, clothing to wear, or oil with which to anoint themselves, they seek mercy from the One who brings all things into being. For through poverty they fear the Lord; acts of righteousness come only through poverty, deeds of kindness come only through poverty, a person becomes God-fearing only through poverty, and a person learns words of Torah only through poverty, as it is written, “He raises the poor from the dust”—it does not say, “He raises the rich from the dust”—“for the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s,” and so forth. “Pillars” means Torah scholars, as it is written, “Every distressed man gathered to him.””
connections.context: The original passage speaks about material poverty prompting dependence on God. Rav Tzadok then reads it in relation to poverty of Torah knowledge, which opens a person to learning and correction. The distinction between the source’s plain setting and his interpretation is preserved.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הִיא אִמּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (זוּטָא פֶּרֶק ה) דְּאֵין לְךָ מִדָּה טוֹבָה וְדָבָר טוֹב בָּא לִבְנֵי אָדָם אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי עֲנִיּוּת – פֵּירוּשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: see note 149.
connections.context: This is the Talmudic basis for reading poverty as a lack of understanding. It clarifies Rav Tzadok’s brief qualification “that is, in words of Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין אִשָּׁה אֶלָּא לְבָנִים, וְהַתּוֹלָדוֹת רַק מִלֵּאָה
connections.quote: “The women of distinguished lineage among them would say, “Young man,” and so forth. The Sages taught: What would the beautiful women among them say? “Set your eyes on beauty, for a wife is for beauty.” What would the women of distinguished lineage say? “Set your eyes on family, for a wife is for children.” What would the unattractive women among them say? “Make your choice for the sake of Heaven, provided that you adorn us with gold ornaments.””
connections.context: This is the source of the phrase about children used here. In the original festival scene it is one group’s appeal alongside other groups’ appeals. Rav Tzadok draws on the phrase for the contrast between Rachel’s beauty and Leah’s descendants.

connections.hePhrase: [וְגָרַם עַד "וַתְּקַנֵּא רָחֵל וְגוֹמֵר", לְפִי שֶׁזֶּה עִיקָּר.
connections.quote: ‘Rachel saw that she had borne no children to Jacob, and Rachel became jealous of her sister. She said to Jacob: Give me children, or I am dead.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל כָּךְ כֹּחַ הַקִּנְאָה שֶׁהוֹעִיל, שֶׁאָז עָמְדָה לֵאָה מִלֶּדֶת, דְּפָרָשַׁת "וַתְּקַנֵּא וְגוֹמֵר" נֶאֱמַר שָׁם עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ““Rachel envied her sister”: She did not envy her until she had borne a fourth son, for now she had taken more than the share of the twelve tribes that was due to her.”
connections.context: Chizkuni notices the placement of Rachel’s envy after Leah’s fourth son. This supports the textual sequence on which Rav Tzadok builds his further interpretation; Chizkuni himself does not say that the envy caused Leah’s subsequent pause in childbirth.

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא יָלְדָה עַד שֶׁאָמַר לָהּ רָחֵל: "לָכֵן יִשְׁכַּב וְגוֹמֵר", וְסִילְּקָה קִנְאָתָהּ.
connections.quote: “She said to her: Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband, that you would also take my son’s mandrakes? And Rachel said: Therefore he shall lie with you tonight in return for your son’s mandrakes.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, נֶאֱמַר: "וְסָרָה קִנְאַת אֶפְרַיִם וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה יא, יג) – זַרְעָא דְּרָחֵל, וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּצַדִּיק כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: ‘Ephraim’s jealousy will depart, and Judah’s enemies will be cut off. Ephraim will not be jealous of Judah, and Judah will not show hostility toward Ephraim.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, נֶאֱמַר: "וְסָרָה קִנְאַת אֶפְרַיִם וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה יא, יג) – זַרְעָא דְּרָחֵל, וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּצַדִּיק כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.quote: “Then “Ephraim will not envy Judah, and Judah,” and so forth. For their warfare principally comes from the deficiencies in each, with each thinking that the other is wicked. As is known, Joseph brought a bad report about the tribes, while they hated him for the slander and arrogance in pursuing honor and rule that they saw in him. This is what drove Jeroboam from the world, as is stated explicitly in Scripture. Such a thing is no part of the order of creation—that there should be warfare and hatred in the world. Scripture warns, “Love your fellow as yourself,” and “Do not hate your brother,” and so forth.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains the rivalry between Joseph’s and Judah’s descendants through their judgments of one another. Its promised removal concerns the overcoming of that hostility, and the passage explicitly rejects hatred as the purpose of creation.

connections.hePhrase: [קסה] הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל כָּל אֶחָד מַדְרֵגָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
connections.quote: see note 2077.
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the individual number of each soul through the particular service assigned to that person, while the whole is included in divine unity beyond number. This gives content to the siman's claim that two souls are not interchangeable. The quotation supports that first claim; it is not offered as proof of the later, more specific account of assistance from earlier generations.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים שָׁוִים מַמָּשׁ, דְּאִם כֵּן מַה צֹּרֶךְ לִשְׁנַיִם
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda said in Rav’s name: Of everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He did not create a single thing in vain.”
connections.context: This is the general Talmudic principle behind the argument that no soul is superfluous. Rav Tzadok applies the principle to the distinctive contribution of each soul.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת קוֹמָה אַחַת שְׁלֵימָה, וְכֵן כָּל נֶפֶשׁ פְּרָטִית קוֹמָה שְׁלֵימָה,
connections.quote: “Every vessel apprehends according to what it is; likewise a person apprehends the blessed God according to what he is. It is known that the body’s organs are a garment for the soul’s organs. That is, just as we see the body divided into organs, so the soul that spreads through those organs and gives them life is also divided into organs; the soul’s vitality in the head is not like its vitality in the foot, for example. The soul therefore also has a division of levels, generally the three levels in the human stature: the head, the body, and the feet below the body. Through what does a person apprehend the blessed God? Through the soul. Apprehension is consequently divided into levels as well: the apprehension through the part of the soul called the head and brain is not like that through the part called the foot. Likewise, the whole congregation of Israel is one complete stature: there are souls who are the heads of the generation, eyes of the congregation, counterparts of the heart, counterparts of the feet, and similarly all the organs. One person’s apprehension is unlike another’s, according to his level and position in the stature of the whole congregation of Israel.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the relation between the complete individual and the collective stature. The anatomical terms describe different modes of spiritual apprehension, providing the framework for the stages described here.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת הוֹלְכִים מִמַּעְלָה לְמַטָּה, וְאָנוּ הַיּוֹם בְּעִקְּבוֹת מָשִׁיחַ מִן הָעִקְבִיִּים,
connections.quote: see note 1248.
connections.context: The Arizal’s account describes the final gathering as reaching the feet. It also insists that the gathering depends on human deeds, prayer, and repentance; those conditions are included here so that the image is not read as an automatic process requiring no effort.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת הוֹלְכִים מִמַּעְלָה לְמַטָּה, וְאָנוּ הַיּוֹם בְּעִקְּבוֹת מָשִׁיחַ מִן הָעִקְבִיִּים,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 26:5
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 26:5
connections.quote: “In every generation a person must see himself as though he left Egypt. Anything in which he is so immersed that he thinks escape from the habit impossible is called Egyptian bondage. He must work so that no fixed natural habit rules him; to the extent he is freed from it, he finds enduring freedom in his heart. How can he bring himself out? By fixing in his heart that Torah stands above the things of this world. One who accepts Torah's yoke is freed from the yoke of government and ordinary worldly occupation. As Torah becomes fixed in him, he rises above worldly habits. This must be through action and speech, for speech completes the matter, so that it is settled even in the final garment, without deliberate awareness. As the Yerushalmi says, “I am grateful to my head: when I reach Modim, it bows of its own accord.” That is, the body follows His will even without conscious direction.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives concrete meaning to the siman's work of departing from habit. The habit that seems impossible to leave is a personal Egypt; Torah is impressed through speech and action until even bodily response follows it. This illuminates why a later generation's apparently small task can still require real effort. Its explanation of habit does not replace the siman's separate account of aid from earlier souls.
connections.headline: What leaving a habit means

connections.hePhrase: עִיקָּר בַּעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁאָדָם דָּשׁ בַּעֲקֵבָיו וּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית, וְכֵן הַמִּצְווֹת וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לָצֵאת מִן הַהֶרְגֵּל],
connections.quote: “This is what Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: What is meant by “The iniquity of my heels surrounds me”? Transgressions that a person treads under his heels in this world surround him on the day of judgment.”
connections.context: The Gemara supplies the expression about sins trodden underfoot. It refers to neglected transgressions and complements the existing note about exceeding one’s habits in positive service.

connections.hePhrase: עִיקָּר בַּעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁאָדָם דָּשׁ בַּעֲקֵבָיו וּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית, וְכֵן הַמִּצְווֹת וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לָצֵאת מִן הַהֶרְגֵּל],
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ט״ו:ט׳-י״א
connections.quote: “Through this one can understand the Gemara’s statement that “one who serves God” means someone who reviews his chapter one hundred and one times, while “one who has not served Him” means someone who reviews his chapter only one hundred times. This is because in their days it was customary to review every chapter one hundred times, as the Gemara there illustrates with the market of donkey drivers: they are hired for ten parasangs at one zuz, but for eleven parasangs at two zuz, because this exceeds their usual distance. Therefore this one hundred and first repetition, beyond the habit in which he was trained from his youth, is equal to all the others and surpasses them in excellence and strength, so that he is called “one who serves God.” For to change the nature of habit, he must awaken love of the Lord by contemplating the Lord’s greatness in his mind, in order to rule over the nature in the left chamber, filled with the blood of the animal soul that comes from kelippah, from which this nature derives. This is complete service for the intermediate person. Alternatively, he may awaken the hidden love in his heart in order to rule through it over the nature in the left chamber. This too is called service: to struggle with nature and the inclination by awakening the hidden love in his heart.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁכְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לַמַּדְרֵגָה שֶׁל כָּל אֶחָד [בַּקּוֹמָה הַכְּלָלִית], הוּא בָּא וּמְסַיְּיעוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בְּסוֹד הָעִבּוּר.
connections.quote: “Through this you will also understand the matter well known in our Sages’ words: the spirits or souls of the righteous come and enter a person in the mystery called ibbur, to assist him in serving the blessed God. As written in the manuscript Midrash HaNe’elam concerning “one who comes to purify himself is assisted,” Rabbi Natan says: The souls of the righteous come and assist him. So too, in the Zohar’s introduction to Bereishit, Rav Hamnuna the Elder came to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Abba in the appearance of a donkey driver, and so forth. There is no doubt that the spirits and souls of the righteous are stored and bound in the bond of life, each at its fitting root with the Lord their God, and they do not descend from their place at all. Rather, those earlier spirits that remained below, at every aspect and level in Yetzirah, and did not ascend above as explained, descend and enter a person to assist him. The principal spirit, the highest of all that he acquired through his deeds, remains forever bound in the bond of life and does not move from there; likewise for the levels of neshamah, chayah, and yechidah.”
connections.context: This is the original explanation of assistance through ibbur. Its qualification is essential: the highest attained soul remains in its place, while lower enduring aspects provide the assistance described here.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת שֶׁל מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ כְּבָר נִשְׁאַר בָּעוֹלָם
connections.quote: “As is known, every Jewish soul has a particular power in holiness, and the number of generations that have passed corresponds to the number of powers of holiness and words of Torah revealed in the world. Therefore in every generation holiness continues to be revealed more, although the generations diminish, as is known, because what was revealed to the earlier ones has already been revealed—as in the familiar parable of a dwarf upon a giant. In words of Torah this is through the books. Certainly, too, the holiness of all the Jewish souls that reached completion is already revealed in the world—that is, in the hearts of the children of Israel. What requires no exertion, so that one performs a good act or thinks a good thought without deliberate intention and effort, is due to that power of holiness having already been revealed in the world. Every deed, action, and thought comes from a particular power and a particular holiness, with divisions into thousands upon thousands and myriads upon myriads, as numerous as the souls.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s own later explanation identifies the enduring help of earlier generations with holiness already revealed in books and in human hearts. It clarifies the statement here that their power of effort remains in the world.

connections.hePhrase: [עַל יְדֵי הַהֶבְלָא דְּגַרְמֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר],
connections.quote: “That voice is made up of spirit and soul and the breath of the bones…, and it roams in the air… When it reaches the place it enters, it sits like a dead thing. All the sorcerers and diviners know these places through their sorcery; they bend down to the ground and hear this voice, in which the spirit, the soul and the breath of the bones are joined, and they tell the matter.”
connections.context: The Zohar is speaking of the voice a person gives out when his soul leaves his body, which is never lost (Sh'lach 28:217); the “breath of the bones” is part of what remains of him in this world.

connections.hePhrase: [עַל יְדֵי הַהֶבְלָא דְּגַרְמֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר],
connections.quote: “Thus the breath rising from the spiritual soul builds the physical body [through the seed of man and woman, as with every fruit of the earth, where the earth brings forth the body of the tree], including all the soul’s powers. After maturity one attains the soul itself; but this breath is immediately the principal vitality and formation of the body during gestation and infancy—see Peri Etz Chayim. [This is the mystery of its root in the name Elohim, which is said throughout the work of creation: all creation is through the mystery of contraction, as is known, by which the physical can come into being from the spiritual. This is the mystery of the breath, the essence of the work of creation; this is not the place to elaborate.] Therefore it remains forever attached to the body, for it is the body’s essential power. Only the soul itself rises above—that is, the mature consciousness from the upper realms and from the soul itself. The breath pertains only to the formation of the body and therefore always remains in the body, below in the world.”
connections.context: This is Rav Tzadok’s explanation of the enduring “breath of the bones.” He distinguishes the soul that ascends from the formative vitality that remains connected to the body, the distinction assumed in this section.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה סוֹד מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טו.): לֹא עָלָה עֶזְרָא מִבָּבֶל עַד שֶׁיִּחֵס עַצְמוֹ].
connections.quote: ‘This supports Rav, for Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name: Ezra did not go up from Babylonia until he had recorded his own genealogy, and then he went up. Who completed (the book of Chronicles)? Nechemiah son of Chacaliah.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל כָּךְ מַכְבִּיד עָלֵינוּ הַיֵּצֶר אוֹתָהּ יְגִיעָה מוּעֶטֶת בְּדוֹרֵנוּ כְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הַמְּרֻבָּה שֶׁלָּהֶם:
connections.quote: “Once I asked my teacher of blessed memory how he could tell me that my soul was so elevated, as stated above, when even the least of the earlier generations was righteous and pious, and I do not reach his heel. He told me: Know that the greatness of the soul does not depend on a person’s deeds alone, but on the time and that generation. A very small deed in this generation is equivalent to several great commandments in other generations, because in these generations the shell grows exceedingly strong, without limit, unlike the earlier generations. Had I lived in the earlier generations, my deeds and wisdom would have been extraordinary compared with several of the earlier righteous ones. As our Sages said of Noah, “He was complete in his generations”: had he lived in generations of righteous people, he would have been more righteous. Therefore I should not grieve over this at all, for without doubt my soul has a great advantage over several of the earlier righteous ones from the time of the Tannaim and Amoraim.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chayim Vital records the Ari’s answer to his concern about the lesser apparent attainments of later generations. The answer measures effort against the strength of the obstacles in that generation, directly explaining the final qualification here.

connections.hePhrase: [קסו] כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ עוֹל תּוֹרָה וְנִכְנָס תַּחַת עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, צָרִיךְ קַבָּלָה בַּלֵּב וְהַסְכָּמָה גְּמוּרָה לַעֲזוֹב כָּל חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמִּתְנַגְּדִים לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “Words of Torah, moreover, intrinsically gladden the heart, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:19): "Wisdom strengthens the wise," imbuing him with strength and fortitude, and therefore they taught (Yoma 72b): "If he did not merit, it becomes a potion of death, etc.," because wisdom can engender levity and arrogance within him, and he is termed 'wise to do evil,' Heaven forbid. And this applies to that severe form of study not for its own sake of which our Sages of blessed memory said (Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:2): "'It would have been better for him had his afterbirth turned over, etc.';" whereas for standard learning not for its own sake, concerning which they said (Pesachim 50b): "'A person should always engage in Torah even not for its own sake...'", it certainly does not engender levity at any rate. However, when Torah study is conducted purely for Heaven's sake, the mark is quite the opposite: it brings forth reverence and meticulous care, as they stated (Kiddushin 40b): "Great is study, for it leads directly to action."”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla distinguishes ordinary shelo lishmah from study that produces irreverence, and describes lishmah by its increase of yirah and care in action. This gives a criterion for the tension examined here: a person may begin while the heart is still mixed, but must not turn Torah’s strength into indifference toward serving Hashem. The direction of the learning matters as well as its starting motive.
connections.headline: Imperfect motives differ from contempt for avodah

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר (יוֹמָא עב:): לֹא זָכָה – נַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי, כִּי גַּם תּוֹרָה אֵין לוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יְבָמוֹת קט:).
connections.quote: ‘That too is obvious! Rather, he does not have even (the reward of) Torah. Why? Rav Pappa said: Scripture says, ‘You shall learn them and do them’—whoever is involved in doing is included in learning; whoever is not involved in doing is not included in learning.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּעֵשָׂו: "וַיַּרְא עֵשָׂו כִּי רָעוֹת בְּנוֹת כְּנָעַן וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, ח–ט),
connections.quote: ‘Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing to his father Isaac. Esau went to Ishmael and took Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham and sister of Nebaioth, as a wife in addition to his other wives.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה סז): כּוֹב עַל כּוֹב, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ““Esav saw that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing”; “Esav went to Yishmael.” Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: He resolved to convert. “Machalat”—the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave all his sins. “Basemat”—his disposition became pleasing to Him. Rabbi Elazar said: Had he sent away the first wives, that would have been good. But “in addition to his wives”—pain upon pain. Another explanation: a thorn upon a thorn, an addition to an already full house.”
connections.context: This Midrash supplies the image of adding a thorn upon a thorn. Its preceding favorable interpretation of Esav’s intention is retained, followed by Rabbi Elazar’s criticism that the earlier wives were not sent away. Rav Tzadok uses that criticism to explain why accepting Torah must be joined to abandoning incompatible desires.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר בַּתּוֹרָה "אָנֹכִי" קוֹדֵם לְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ",
connections.quote: “I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before Me.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר בַּתּוֹרָה "אָנֹכִי" קוֹדֵם לְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 5
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 5
connections.quote: “In reason, a person ought not to attain the precious declaration ‘I am Hashem your God’ before his heart has been purified through ‘You shall have no other gods,’ for first one must turn from evil and afterward do good. But Hashem, in His great mercy, placed ‘I am’ before ‘You shall have no other gods.’ Otherwise no person in the world could attain the declaration ‘I am’: who can say that he has purified his heart in every prohibition? Of this King David said (Psalms 138:2), ‘You have magnified Your word above all Your name.’ An utterance here is a whisper: Hashem will afterward clarify that Israel's heart is clean. Therefore he says, ‘I will thank Your name’—the goodness and greatness You showed us by first giving us the declaration ‘I am,’ so that afterward He would clarify within our heart the declaration ‘You shall have no other gods.’”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach poses the same apparent reversal of the normal order of turning from evil before doing good. The first encounter with Anokhi makes the subsequent purification possible. This explains the siman's encouragement to begin Torah with mixed motives while intending to leave the desires opposed to it. It does not support retaining those desires as Esav retained his earlier wives.
connections.headline: The opening that enables purification

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת הִקְשָׁה מַה שֶּׁמָּצִינוּ בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת שֶׁכָּל הָעוֹסֵק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ נוֹחַ לוֹ וְכוּלֵי, וְשֶׁנֶּהֶפְכָה וְכוּלֵי, וְלֹא זָכָה נַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “‘A good understanding have all who do them’ (Psalms 111:10): it does not say ‘who do,’ but ‘who do them’: those who do them for their own sake, and not those who do them not for their own sake. And whoever does them not for their own sake, it would have been better for him had he not been created.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת הִקְשָׁה מַה שֶּׁמָּצִינוּ בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת שֶׁכָּל הָעוֹסֵק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ נוֹחַ לוֹ וְכוּלֵי, וְשֶׁנֶּהֶפְכָה וְכוּלֵי, וְלֹא זָכָה נַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: One who learns not in order to practice, it would have been better for him had his afterbirth been turned over on his face and he had never come out into the world.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת הִקְשָׁה מַה שֶּׁמָּצִינוּ בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת שֶׁכָּל הָעוֹסֵק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ נוֹחַ לוֹ וְכוּלֵי, וְשֶׁנֶּהֶפְכָה וְכוּלֵי, וְלֹא זָכָה נַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““Here it concerns those who act not for its own sake, in accordance with Rav Yehudah”: This is difficult, for Rav himself said in the second chapter of Berakhot that anyone who engages in Torah not for its own sake would have been better off not being created. Ri explains that there it concerns someone who studies to exalt himself, provoke others, and defeat his fellows in halakhic argument, without studying in order to practice. Here, however, it resembles the earlier case of one who is lowly yet rewarded: he does not work all week, nor on the eve of Shabbat. He intends no evil, but acts from laziness; even so, “Your kindness is great, up to the heavens.””
connections.context: Tosafot distinguishes malicious, self-aggrandizing study from an imperfect motive without an evil purpose. The complete comment supplies the question Rav Tzadok cites and Tosafot’s own answer; Rav Tzadok then develops his further explanation of accepting Torah despite the danger of an unpurified heart.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת: וְכָל הָעוֹסֵק וְכוּלֵי, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ דְּשֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ נוֹחַ וְכוּלֵי וְנַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “The expression “it would have been better not to have been created” was said about creation as a whole: they concluded that it would have been better for a person not to have been created. Creation's purpose is the person like Yaakov who acts for the Holy One's sake; for him it is good to have been created. Nevertheless, the Gemara rightly says always to engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, because from this he comes to acting for their own sake, and then it is good for him to have been created. This resolves Tosafot's question concerning that expression in Berakhot. Their distinction remains necessary for the other expressions elsewhere in the Talmud.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains the force of continuing despite an imperfect beginning through the eventual movement toward lishmah. It also says that other severe formulations still require Tosafot's distinction, so the warnings are not simply dissolved. This complements the existing note's practical criterion of growing fear and care: the siman's acceptance of study now is joined to the commitment to let Torah change the heart.
connections.headline: The imperfect beginning is directed toward lishmah

connections.hePhrase: בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה יִשְׁגֶּה, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ הַסַּכָּנָה וְהָרָע שֶׁבְּתוֹכָהּ,
connections.quote: ‘A beloved doe, a graceful mountain goat—let her breasts satisfy you at every time; remain always enraptured by her love.’

connections.hePhrase: בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה יִשְׁגֶּה, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ הַסַּכָּנָה וְהָרָע שֶׁבְּתוֹכָהּ,
connections.quote: ““Be constantly carried away by its love”: Out of love for it, make yourself seem erring and foolish, leaving your business and running to hear a matter of halakhah.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the rabbinic reading of the verse already quoted in the reader: love of Torah moves a person to set aside ordinary calculations and attend to learning. Rav Tzadok applies that devotion to continuing Torah study while working toward purity of motive.

connections.hePhrase: [קסז] בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מוּתָּר אָדָם לִפְחוֹד, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (ס.);
connections.quote: ‘Yehuda bar Natan was walking behind Rav Hamnuna and sighed. Rav Hamnuna said to him: ‘Does this man wish to bring suffering upon himself? For it is written: ‘The fear that I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has come to me.’’ But is it not written: ‘Fortunate is the person who is always afraid’? That verse concerns words of Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: [קסז] בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מוּתָּר אָדָם לִפְחוֹד, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (ס.);
connections.quote: ““It is written concerning words of Torah”: “Happy is the person who is always afraid”—lest he forget it; this causes him constantly to review and study it again.”
connections.context: The existing Gemara gives the exception permitting fear concerning Torah. Rashi explains it as fear of forgetting that prompts review; Rav Tzadok develops a further inward application concerning the spiritual effect of one’s study.

connections.hePhrase: [קסז] בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מוּתָּר אָדָם לִפְחוֹד, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (ס.);
connections.quote: “The Gemara expounds “Why is there a price in the hand of a fool?” concerning those who engage in Torah but have no awe of Heaven. The anger of the sages is to stir against the evil inclination so that one will not be a fool. This comes through awe, Isaac’s fear, holy fire; its waste is Esau—anger, the evil inclination’s fire. This is according to the Geonim’s reading.”
connections.explanation: Kislev distinguishes the fire of holy awe from its waste, anger, even while discussing the intensity of the sages. This sharpens the present siman’s explanation of why fear can sweeten learning that is not yet wholly lishmah. Awe governs the direction of the energy released by Torah and gathers it toward service. It is therefore compatible with Torah’s strength and joy, while checking the misuse of those powers that the siman fears.
connections.headline: Awe distinguishes holy intensity from the inclination’s fire

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "הַאי מַאן דִּמְבַעִית – מַזָּלֵיהּ חָזֵי" (מְגִילָּה ג.),
connections.quote: ‘Ravina said: Learn from this that when a person becomes frightened, although he himself does not see, his mazal sees. What is his remedy? He should recite the Shema. If he is standing in a filthy place, he should move four cubits from his place. If he cannot, he should say this: ‘The goat at the slaughterhouse is fatter than I am.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּ"פִקּוּדֵי ה' יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (תְּהִלִּים יט, ט), וְ"הַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט), וְכֵן בִּשְׁאָר פְּסוּקִים שֶׁנּוֹתֶנֶת עֹז וְחֶדְוָה שֶׁהוּא הִפּוּךְ הַפַּחַד.
connections.quote: ‘Hashem’s precepts are upright, gladdening the heart; Hashem’s commandment is pure, giving light to the eyes.’

connections.hePhrase: וּ"פִקּוּדֵי ה' יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (תְּהִלִּים יט, ט), וְ"הַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט), וְכֵן בִּשְׁאָר פְּסוּקִים שֶׁנּוֹתֶנֶת עֹז וְחֶדְוָה שֶׁהוּא הִפּוּךְ הַפַּחַד.
connections.quote: ‘Wisdom gives the wise person more strength than ten rulers who were in the city.’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַלִּשְׁמָהּ אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת בִּתְמִידוּת, דְּלִשְׁמָהּ הַיְינוּ דְּבֵיקוּת,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ה׳:י״ב
connections.quote: ““For its own sake” means in order to bind one’s soul to Hashem through understanding Torah, each person according to his intellect, as written in Pri Etz Chaim.”
connections.context: Tanya states the understanding of lishmah as attachment through understanding Torah. It supplies a parallel definition for Rav Tzadok’s discussion; the claim here that such an elevated state cannot be continuous is Rav Tzadok’s own development.

connections.hePhrase: וְשִׁעוּרוֹ כְּעוֹנַת תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֶחָד בְּשַׁבָּת, שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לָבוֹא לִדְבֵיקוּת רַק בְּשַׁבָּת,
connections.quote: “When is the conjugal time of Torah scholars? Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name: From one Shabbat eve to the next. “Who gives his fruit in its season”: Rav Yehudah said—and some say Rav Huna, and some say Rav Nachman—this refers to one who has intercourse from one Shabbat eve to the next.”
connections.context: The Gemara’s literal subject is the marital obligation of Torah scholars. Rav Tzadok uses its weekly rhythm as an analogy for the special times of attachment that cannot be sustained continuously.

connections.hePhrase: אוֹ הַטַּיָּילִין [פֵּירוּשׁ הַמְטַיְּילִים בַּפַּרְדֵּ"ס הַיָּדוּעַ] אֶחָד בַּיּוֹם לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר.
connections.quote: “The conjugal duty stated in the Torah: men of leisure (tayalin), every day; laborers, twice a week; donkey drivers, once a week; camel drivers, once in thirty days; sailors, once in six months.”

connections.hePhrase: אוֹ הַטַּיָּילִין [פֵּירוּשׁ הַמְטַיְּילִים בַּפַּרְדֵּ"ס הַיָּדוּעַ] אֶחָד בַּיּוֹם לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר.
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Four entered the Pardes, and they are: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher and Rabbi Akiva.”

connections.hePhrase: אוֹ הַטַּיָּילִין [פֵּירוּשׁ הַמְטַיְּילִים בַּפַּרְדֵּ"ס הַיָּדוּעַ] אֶחָד בַּיּוֹם לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said: From here we learn the conjugal obligation stated in the Torah: those of leisure, every day; laborers, twice a week; sailors, once every six months.”
connections.context: This is the Midrashic list behind “tayalim every day.” Its plain subject is the different marital schedules of occupations; the reading of tayalim as those who journey in the spiritual Pardes is Rav Tzadok’s further interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַפַּחַד דִּמְפַכְּחָא לֵיהּ, שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "אִי יִרְאַת ה' אוֹצָרוֹ – אִין וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: see note 1590.
connections.context: The full analogy explains why fear functions as an otzar, a treasury that preserves the value of one’s accomplishments. Rav Tzadok applies it here to fear that restrains the otherwise unbounded expansion produced by learning.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם מְפַחֵד תָּמִיד" (מִשְׁלֵי כח, יד) – פֵּירוּשׁ עַל עִסְקוֹ הַתְּמִידוּת,
connections.quote: ‘Fortunate is the person who is always fearful, but one who hardens his heart will fall into calamity.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ח.): "אַשְׁרֶיךָ" – בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דִּלְשׁוֹן אִישּׁוּר מַשְׁמָע מֵאֲחֵרִים [מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן לְשׁוֹן "וְטוֹב לָךְ"],
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chiyya bar Ami said in the name of Ulla: One who benefits from his own labor is greater than one who fears Heaven. Concerning one who fears Heaven, it is written: ‘Fortunate is the man who fears Hashem.’ Concerning one who benefits from his own labor, it is written: ‘When you eat the labor of your hands, fortunate are you, and it is good for you.’ ‘Fortunate are you’—in this world; ‘and it is good for you’—in the World to Come. Concerning one who fears Heaven, however, ‘and it is good for you’ is not written.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דִּבְעוֹלָם הַבָּא כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב).
connections.quote: see note 1830.
connections.context: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta’s wife refuses a miraculous gift taken from their future reward. When Rabbi offers to replace any shortfall from his own portion, she invokes each person’s own world. Rav Tzadok uses that individuality to explain why seeking other people’s approval belongs to this world.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ כְּלָל בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ, וְכִדְאָמְרוּ בִּזְבָחִים (ב:): סְתָמָא לִשְׁמָן קָיְימָא.
connections.quote: ‘And he answered: Sacrificial animals, without any specific intention, stand designated for their own sacrificial purpose; a woman, without any specific intention, does not stand designated for divorce.’
connections.context: The Gemara’s literal subject is offerings: an offering made without a contrary intention is presumed to retain its proper sacrificial purpose. Rav Tzadok applies that pattern to Torah study whose purpose has not been explicitly formulated.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִי שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם יֵשׁ דִּבּוּרִים דְּלָשׁוֹן הָרָע וְגַם כֵּן מִתְגַּבְּרִים, וְיוּכְלוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְדַבֵּר "חֵץ שָׁחוּט לְשׁוֹנָם" עָלָיו
connections.quote: “Their tongue is a sharpened arrow; it speaks deceit. With his mouth one speaks peace to his neighbor, but inwardly he lays an ambush for him.”

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁזֶּה עִנְיַן דָּוִד שֶׁהוּא סוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, הָיוּ דוֹרוֹ בַּעֲלֵי דִּלְטוֹרְיָא וְדִבְּרוּ לָשׁוֹן הָרָע עָלָיו],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosei of Milḥaya and Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in Rabbi Levi’s name: We find that children in David’s days, before they had tasted sin, knew how to expound the Torah in forty-nine ways toward impurity and forty-nine ways toward purity. David prayed for them, as he says, “You, Hashem, will preserve them”—You, Hashem, preserve their Torah within their hearts; “You will guard them from this generation forever”—from that generation liable to destruction. After all this praise, they went out to war and fell, because informers were among them. This is what David said: “My soul is among lions”—Avner and Amasa, who were lions in Torah; “I lie among those aflame”—Doeg and Achitophel, who burned with eagerness for evil speech; “men whose teeth are spear and arrows”—the people of Keilah, of whom it is written, “Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me into his hand?” “And their tongue a sharp sword”—the Ziphites, of whom it is written, “When the Ziphites came and said to Shaul.” At that time David said: What is the Divine Presence doing on earth? “Be exalted above the heavens, God”—remove Your Presence from among them. But Achav’s generation were all idolaters, and because there were no informers among them, they went out to war and were victorious.”
connections.context: This is the Midrashic source for the combination of great Torah knowledge and informers in David’s generation. Its contrast with Achav’s generation emphasizes the destructive force of informing; Rav Tzadok’s explanation through an expanded power of speech is his interpretation of this juxtaposition.

connections.hePhrase: [קסח] הַפְּחָדִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם הוּא מִן הַחֲטָאִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ס.), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פָּחֲדוּ בְצִיּוֹן חַטָּאִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה לג, יד);
connections.quote: ‘A student was walking behind Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, in the marketplace of Zion. Rabbi Yishmael saw that he was afraid and said to him: ‘You are a sinner, for it is written: Sinners in Zion are afraid.’ He answered: ‘But it is written: Fortunate is the person who is always afraid!’ He replied: ‘That verse concerns words of Torah.’’

connections.hePhrase: [קסח] הַפְּחָדִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם הוּא מִן הַחֲטָאִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ס.), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פָּחֲדוּ בְצִיּוֹן חַטָּאִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה לג, יד);
connections.quote: ‘The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless. Who among us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting flames?’

connections.hePhrase: [קסח] הַפְּחָדִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם הוּא מִן הַחֲטָאִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ס.), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פָּחֲדוּ בְצִיּוֹן חַטָּאִים" (יְשַׁעְיָה לג, יד);
connections.quote: “The scoffers say that this fear is foolishness and does not come from Avraham’s holy source, for fear born from love is true yirah; rather, they say it comes from Avimelech, who was also afraid. As it says, “I said: surely there is no fear of God”—implying that the truth was otherwise, as indeed it was, since he did not need to send them away. But it was a fear of melancholy, like “The sinners in Zion were afraid,” as the Sages said [Berakhot 60a]: “You are a sinner”; and, in explaining the verse that praises constant fear, “That refers to matters of Torah.” This is Yitzchak’s level, which is Torah, as I heard concerning the Sages’ expression “Moshe from the mouth of Gevurah”: the fear that comes from words of Torah is good.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah contrasts the fear associated with Avimelech with Yitzchak’s yirah, born from love and directed by Torah. This makes the distinction at the end of the siman more precise. The point is not to call every frightening feeling a spiritual attainment, but to identify the fear whose movement is toward Hashem and can itself be joined to joy. Citation correction: the quoted exchange is in Berakhot 60a. The reference to HaNizakin in the supplied Hebrew has been corrected here. The answer about Torah responds to the verse praising constant fear; it does not describe the student’s sinful fear as Torah study.
connections.headline: The source and direction of fear matter

connections.hePhrase: וְהַפְּחָדִים הֵם מַמָּשׁ יִסּוּרֵי גֵיהִנָּם, עַיֵּין רַאֲבַ"ד עַל סֵפֶר יְצִירָה בְּעִנְיַן יִסּוּרֵי גֵיהִנָּם.
connections.displayRef: Ra'avad on Sefer Yetzirah, Introduction, The Fifty Gates of Understanding 2:3:1-2
connections.linkedRef: Ra'avad on Sefer Yetzirah, Introduction, The Fifty Gates of Understanding 2:3:1-2
connections.canonicalRef: Ra'avad on Sefer Yetzirah, Introduction, The Fifty Gates of Understanding 2:3:1-2
connections.heRef: פירוש הראב"ד על ספר יצירה, הקדמה, חמשים שערי בינה ב׳:ג׳:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: “The heat of illness becomes material for the heat of elemental fire. When the soul departs from the sick person’s body, it reaches the element of fire through the imaginative faculty, which received its impression from the pain and heat of the illness. That elemental fire adheres to this soul, adding heat to its heat, until the fire descending from the river of fire reaches it and rests upon that fire. Further, the storm of Hashem—fury and whirling anguish—descends upon it, resting on the head of the wicked. The same applies to one who dies from cold: judgments and punishments from snow and hail attach to him, “for the day of battle and war.””
connections.context: The introduction printed under Raavad’s name describes postmortem pain through the impressions carried by the imaginative faculty and their encounter with spiritual judgment. Rav Tzadok invokes this account in explaining fear and suffering; the source is a metaphysical account of the soul, not a claim that bodily illness is merely imaginary.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא הַמְתָּקַת הַדִּינִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם ה. וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, קנג סוֹף עַמּוּד א): מַה מֶּלַח מְמַתֶּקֶת הַבָּשָׂר, אַף יִסּוּרִין מְמַתְּקִין הָעֲווֹנוֹת.
connections.quote: ““Covenant” is said of salt, and “covenant” is said of suffering. Just as the covenant of salt sweetens the meat, so the covenant of suffering cleanses all a person’s sins.”
connections.context: This is the Talmudic comparison of suffering to salt cited by Rav Tzadok. His following Zohar reference develops the associated language of sweetening.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא הַמְתָּקַת הַדִּינִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם ה. וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, קנג סוֹף עַמּוּד א): מַה מֶּלַח מְמַתֶּקֶת הַבָּשָׂר, אַף יִסּוּרִין מְמַתְּקִין הָעֲווֹנוֹת.
connections.quote: “As salt sweetens meat, so through the mysteries revealed by you all those difficulties and disputes will be sweetened, and the bitter waters of the Oral Torah will become sweet waters of Torah. Through these mysteries revealed by you, your sufferings will become sweet, and all your troubles will return to being like dreams that have passed. The letters of chalom, “dream,” rearranged are melach, “salt,” which sweetens meat; suffering also sweetens, as they have explained.”
connections.context: The passage addresses the Faithful Shepherd and joins Torah’s difficult disputes, suffering, salt, and dreams. This supplies the specific connection Rav Tzadok draws between receiving the meaning of suffering and its sweetening.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֲטָאִים וְהַדִּינִים וְהַיִּסּוּרִים הַכֹּל דָּבָר אֶחָד, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז.): יוֹרֵד וּמַסִּית, עוֹלֶה וּמַקְטְרִיג, יוֹרֵד וְנוֹטֵל נְשָׁמָה.
connections.quote: “It was taught in a baraita: He descends and leads a person astray, then ascends and arouses anger; he receives permission and takes the soul. ‘The Satan answered Hashem and said: Skin for skin! Everything a person has he will give for his life. But stretch out Your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse You to Your face. Hashem said to the Satan: He is in your hand, but preserve his life. The Satan went out from before Hashem and struck Iyov,’ and so forth. Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Satan’s distress was greater than Iyov’s. It is like a servant whose master told him, ‘Break the barrel, but preserve its wine.’”

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נ): אֵין מַלְאָךְ אֶחָד עוֹשֶׂה שְׁתֵּי שְׁלִיחוּת, הַיְינוּ דְּהַמַּלְאָךְ נִקְרָא כֹּחַ אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר
connections.quote: ““He acts through one, and who can respond to Him? His soul desires and He performs” (Job 23:13) – it is taught: One angel does not perform two missions, and two angels do not perform one mission. Yet you say: “[The] two [angels came to Sodom]”? The explanation is that Mikhael gave his tidings and departed, Gavriel was dispatched to overturn Sodom, and Refael, to rescue Lot. “The two angels came to Sodom” – here it says “angels,” but elsewhere, it characterizes them as “people” (Genesis 18:2). The explanation is that there, when the Divine Presence was over them, they were characterized as “people.” Once the Divine Presence departed from over them, they assumed the manifestation of angels. Rabbi Tanḥuma said that Rabbi Levi said: To Abraham, whose power was great, they appeared in the image of men; to Lot, whose strength was inferior, they appeared in the image of angels. Rabbi Ḥanina said: Before they performed their mission, they are characterized as people; after performing their mission, as angels. Rabbi Tanḥuma said: This is analogous to one who assumed a position of local government from the king. Until he reached his seat of authority, he walked about as a commoner. Once he reached the seat of his authority, he walked about as a nobleman. So, until they performed their mission, they are characterized as people, after performing their mission, they are characterized as angels.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, וְיַצִּיבָא מִילְּתָא גַּם מִטַּעַם חַכְמֵי הָאֱמֶת בְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר],
connections.quote: “The Sages of blessed memory have already explained, to one who is wise, that every bodily power is an “angel,” all the more so the powers spread throughout the world, and that each power has one particular operation and does not have two operations. In Bereshit Rabbah: “It was taught: One angel does not perform two missions, and two angels do not perform one mission.” Such is the nature of all the powers.”
connections.context: Rambam explicitly connects the Midrash’s one-mission principle with distinct powers and their operations. This is the philosophical source named here for understanding a malakh as a power; the quotation follows Ibn Tibbon’s Hebrew translation.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְעוֹלַם הַמַּלְאָכִים נִקְרָא "חֲטָאִים", כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה א, ו): מַתִּישׁ כֹּחַ פַּמַלְיָא שֶׁל מַעְלָה;
connections.quote: see note 728.
connections.context: The qualification “as it were” is part of the Midrash. Rav Tzadok uses this teaching about human conduct and heavenly strength to explain the language of weakening the heavenly retinue.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, אָז נַעֲשֶׂה הַמְתָּקַת הַדִּינִים בְּשָׁרְשָׁם,
connections.displayRef: Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on Rosh Hashanah 7:1:7
connections.linkedRef: Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on Rosh Hashanah 7:1:7
connections.canonicalRef: Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on Rosh Hashanah 7:1:7
connections.heRef: שער הכוונות, דרושי ראש השנה ז׳:א׳:ז׳
connections.quote: “Keep this general principle in mind: all subduing, nullifying, and sweetening of judgments takes place only through their actual root. For the supernal powers of severity and judgments are always sweetened and made gentle; therefore they themselves subdue the harsh judgments, make them gentle, and sweeten them. Do not be surprised, then, by what we shall explain with God’s help: how through the roots and sources of judgment we make judgment gentle and sweeten it.”
connections.context: This passage in the shofar intentions states the kabbalistic principle that judgments are sweetened through their own root. Rav Tzadok applies that principle to repentance and fear that return to the inward root.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, אָז נַעֲשֶׂה הַמְתָּקַת הַדִּינִים בְּשָׁרְשָׁם,
connections.quote: “After them comes “remember the day of death”: this means asking for help from Hashem when a person sees that he has labored without finding the needed result, so as to awaken heavenly mercy and assistance. It comes through remembering the soul's separation from the body and ascent to unite with its source. As is known from the Baal Shem Tov, the sweetening of judgments is through the surrender of the soul to its source, where the gate of freedom is found.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek explains remembrance of mortality as requesting divine aid after effort has not yet achieved its purpose. Its conclusion explicitly defines sweetening through the soul's return to its source. This helps distinguish the siman's inner movement of repentance from merely being frightened: the direction of the heart is toward its source and the mercy sought there.
connections.headline: Sweetening at the root turns toward divine aid

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּעֶזְרָא שֶׁהָעָם רָעֲדוּ מְאֹד עַל הָעֲבֵירָה, וְלֹא שֶׁמְּפַחֵד מִפְּנֵי מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא – זֶהוּ "אַשְׁרֵי";
connections.quote: ‘All the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. All the people sat in the open square of the House of God, trembling because of the matter and because of the rains.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): אֲנִי שָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי;
connections.quote: see note 1236.
connections.context: David’s statement combines joy and awe rather than treating either as the absence of the other. That is the example Rav Tzadok uses for fear that reaches a person inwardly.

connections.hePhrase: [קסט] כַּאֲשֶׁר נוֹפֵל עַל אָדָם פַּחַד מֵאֵיזֶה דָבָר, אָז תֵּיכֶף יְבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים לְהִנָּצֵל מִזֶּה,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 1
connections.quote: “That night Yosef's cry grew: “Return, Hashem—until when?” Immediately he attained deliverance. Concerning this it says, “Hashem, God of my deliverance… I cried at night before You.” Such is the Holy One's way: before He gives deliverance, He places a cry in the person's heart, so that it may be called “the labor of your hands.””
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Yosef's cry intensifying immediately before his deliverance, and explains that Hashem places such a cry in the heart so the gift may become the fruit of the person's own work. This supplies a concrete counterpart to the siman's call to turn an awakening into prayer before the matter fully emerges. The comparison concerns the sequence of awakening and response; it does not replace the siman's distinct explanation of Elul.
connections.headline: The prayer is awakened before the gift

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד:): לְעוֹלָם יַקְדִּים אָדָם תְּפִלָּה לַצָּרָה;
connections.quote: “‘Have you set out your plea before distress?’ Rabbi Elazar said: A person should always pray before trouble comes. Had Abraham not prayed between Bethel and Ai before the trouble came, not one survivor or escapee would have remained among Israel, referred to here euphemistically as ‘the enemies of Israel.’ Reish Lakish said: Anyone who exerts himself in prayer below has no adversaries above. Rabbi Yochanan said: A person should always seek mercy that all will strengthen him and that he will have no adversaries above.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד:): לְעוֹלָם יַקְדִּים אָדָם תְּפִלָּה לַצָּרָה;
connections.quote: “Every distress that Hashem sends a person in this world, Heaven forbid, is for this: to awaken him to prayer. As the Sages said (Shemot Rabbah 21) concerning ‘Pharaoh drew near’: it is like a noblewoman whose voice the king wished to hear. They also said (Yevamot 64a), ‘Why were the patriarchs infertile? Because the Holy One desires the prayers of the righteous.’ Of this they said (Sanhedrin 44b), ‘A person should always precede [trouble with prayer], as it says, “Will your cry set you beyond distress?”’ He should awaken himself to prayer earlier and not need trouble to awaken him, Heaven forbid. All the exiles and sufferings serve this: to elevate all the affairs of this world to the world's heights through prayer, so that the night shines like day.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla develops the same instruction to pray before trouble. Feeling the lack awakens the voice of prayer; praying earlier means that a crisis need not perform that awakening. This explains the siman's practical first step when fear arises, before its discussion of Elul and judgment at the root.
connections.headline: Awakening prayer before trouble

connections.hePhrase: כִּי יֵשׁ דִּינָא קַשְׁיָא רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַמְתִּיק אַחַר צֵאתוֹ לַאֲוִיר הָעוֹלָם, רַק צָרִיךְ לְהַמְתִּיקוֹ בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ בְּעוֹדוֹ בְּבֶטֶן אִמּוֹ.
connections.quote: “Come and see: there is harsh judgment (dina kashya) and there is soft judgment. Harsh judgment is strong and soft judgment is weak; and when this soft judgment draws from the harsh judgment, it is strengthened and becomes strong.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַזָּל הוּא הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ כַּיָּדוּעַ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, וּמַזָּלֵיהּ חָזֵי מַה שֶּׁהוּא בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ עֲדַיִן וּמִיבְעִית.
connections.quote: see note 459.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel discussion distinguishes the mazal of the soul from astrological constellations and traces it beyond the world of angels. It clarifies why the present section speaks of a person’s root perceiving what has not yet become manifest below.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה עִנְיַן יְמֵי אֱלוּל שֶׁהוּא ל' יוֹם לִפְנֵי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, שׁוֹאֲלִין וְדוֹרְשִׁין בְּעִנְיָנוֹ, דְּל' יוֹם מִקּוֹדֶם הוּא זְמַן הַהֲכָנָה.
connections.quote: “What is the significance of these thirty days? As it was taught: One asks about and expounds the laws of Passover thirty days before Passover. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Two weeks.”
connections.context: This is the thirty-day preparation principle to which Rav Tzadok alludes. The Gemara’s stated setting is preparation for Passover, and its alternative opinion is retained; applying the thirty-day pattern to Elul and Rosh Hashanah is the interpretation developed here.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה נִקְרָא "הַיּוֹם הֲרַת עוֹלָם", שֶׁהוּא הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁעָלָה לִבְרוֹא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין, דְּהַיְינוּ סוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁהוּא עֵת קֵץ וְעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Shofar 5
connections.quote: “We say on Rosh Hashanah, “Today is the world’s conception.” The Sages disagreed whether the world was created in Tishrei or in Nisan. How could they disagree over what occurred, and how could “These and those are the words of the living God” apply to such a disagreement? The answer is that there are conception and birth: one speaks of one thing and the other of another, and they do not disagree. Conception took place in Tishrei; the letters of Tishrei are also the letters of reishit, “beginning.” Birth took place in Nisan, since miracles are needed to emerge from the womb at birth. Nisan likewise suggests nes, “miracle,” and redemption occurred in it through a miracle. It is known that the entire exodus from Egypt is described in terms of birth: “I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood.” So too here it says, “Today is the world’s conception,” using the language of pregnancy, rather than saying, “The world was created,” for in Tishrei there was conception. Here it speaks of the human being, although the world itself was created on the twenty-fifth of Elul; from the human being the world may be understood.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאָז יִהְיֶה יִצְחָק רֹאשׁ הַהַנְהָגָה כַּנּוֹדָע, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כָּל מִינֵי טוֹבָה בְּדִין, זֶה הָיָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה.
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Passover 7:19
connections.linkedRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Passover 7:19
connections.canonicalRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Passover 7:19
connections.heRef: פרי עץ חיים, שער חג המצות ז׳:י״ט
connections.quote: “And this is what we say in Tractate Shabbat, that Israel will say to Isaac (for Abraham is the aspect of silver: ‘[Abraham] knew us not’), ‘For you are our father’ (Isaiah 63:16): the supernal Gevurah joined with Imma Ila’ah will be our redemption… Now Imma Ila’ah is revealed in Isaac, harsh judgment, and through it they will go out.”
connections.context: In the teaching of the Arizal the final redemption comes through Isaac’s attribute of judgment; this is the sense in which Isaac will head the governance.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה דְּחֹדֶשׁ אֱלוּל בְּיוֹ"ד, כִּידוּעַ דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּמְנָחוֹת (כט:) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי בְּיָהּ ה' וְגוֹמֵר": עוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּהֵ"א,
connections.quote: see note 1569.
connections.context: The Gemara’s answer assigns heh to this world and therefore yud to the World to Come. Sefer Yetzirah supplies the separate association of yud with Elul. The two sources together explain the main text’s connection; Sefer Yetzirah section numbering varies between recensions.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל יָדוּעַ דְּהַזְּמַנִּים יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא דִּמְקַדְּשֵׁי לְהוּ, וְהֵם קִדְּשׁוּ לֶאֱלוּל בִּקְדוּשָּׁה זוֹ כִּי רָצוּ לְהַמְתִּיק בְּשָׁרְשָׁן, וּלְכָךְ אֱלוּל בְּיוֹ"ד, וְהוּא עַל שֵׁם הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: ““Who sanctifies Israel and the appointed times”—it is Israel who sanctifies the appointed times. “Who sanctifies Israel and the new moons”—it is Israel who sanctifies the new moons.”
connections.context: The Gemara explains the blessing’s wording through Israel’s role in sanctifying the calendar. Rav Tzadok invokes that role in explaining the spiritual correspondence of months and letters; that further correspondence is his application.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדִשְׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְבָמוֹת סד.): מִפְּנֵי מָה הָיוּ אִמָּהוֹת עֲקוּרוֹת וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: Why were our ancestors unable to have children? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the prayer of the righteous. Rabbi Yitzchak said: Why is the prayer of the righteous compared to a pitchfork? Just as a pitchfork turns grain from one place to another, so the prayer of the righteous turns the Holy One’s attributes from anger to compassion.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok emphasizes the first explanation: the withholding itself creates an opening for the desired prayer. The second saying describes prayer’s change from severity to mercy.

connections.hePhrase: אוֹ רוֹאֶה אַחֵר מְעוּנֶּה בְּאוֹתוֹ דָבָר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים עָלָיו כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא נַעֲנֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פַּחַד פָּחַדְתִּי וַיֶּאֱתָיֵנִי" (אִיּוֹב ג, כה).
connections.quote: ‘For a fear that I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded comes to me.’

connections.hePhrase: אוֹ רוֹאֶה אַחֵר מְעוּנֶּה בְּאוֹתוֹ דָבָר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים עָלָיו כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא נַעֲנֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פַּחַד פָּחַדְתִּי וַיֶּאֱתָיֵנִי" (אִיּוֹב ג, כה).
connections.quote: “Rava said to Rabbah bar Mari: From where comes this statement of the Sages, that anyone who asks for mercy for another while he himself needs the same thing is answered first? He replied: It is written, “Hashem restored Iyov’s fortunes when he prayed for his friend.” He said to him: You cite that passage, but I cite this: “Avraham prayed to God, and God healed Avimelekh, his wife, and his maidservants,” and it is written, “Hashem attended to Sarah as He had said”—as Avraham had said concerning Avimelekh.”
connections.context: The source expressly includes the condition that the person praying needs the same thing. Both proofs are retained. Rav Tzadok uses it to explain how encountering another person’s distress can itself become an invitation to prayer and a channel of help.

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאָמְרוּ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ל וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רטז עַמּוּד ב) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל שֶׁהָיוּ מְעוּתָּדִים לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה אִלּוּ זָכוּ, וְכֵן בְּכָל דּוֹר וּבְכָל אָדָם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Acha said: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to give them four things—Torah, suffering, sacrificial service, and prayer—but they did not want them. … “They said to God: Depart from us”—this is suffering; “We do not desire knowledge of Your ways”—this is Torah.”
connections.context: The Midrash is discussing the generation of the Flood and its refusal of these gifts. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the pairing of Torah and suffering before proceeding to the two forms of service.

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאָמְרוּ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ל וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רטז עַמּוּד ב) בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל שֶׁהָיוּ מְעוּתָּדִים לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה אִלּוּ זָכוּ, וְכֵן בְּכָל דּוֹר וּבְכָל אָדָם.
connections.quote: see note 683.
connections.context: The Zohar identifies the generation’s lost opportunity with Torah and Moses. The description of lofty intellectual power in the former footnote was an explanation, not a quotation from this passage.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סו): צַדִּיקִים תְּחִלָּתָן יִסּוּרִין וְסוֹפָן שַׁלְוָה,
connections.quote: ““Peoples will serve you, and nations will prostrate themselves to you. Be a lord to your brethren, and your mother’s sons will prostrate themselves to you. Cursed be one who curses you, and blessed be one who blesses you” (Genesis 27:29). “Peoples will serve you” – these are the seventy nations. “And nations will prostrate themselves to you” – these are the descendants of Ishmael and the sons of Ketura, in whose regard it is written: “Ashurim, Letushim, and Leumim” (Genesis 25:3). “Be a lord to your brethren” – this is Esau and his chieftains. “And your mother’s sons will prostrate themselves to you” – here it says: “And your mother’s sons will prostrate themselves to you,” but elsewhere it says: “And your father’s sons will prostrate themselves to you” (Genesis 49:8). It is that Jacob, because he took four wives, Leah, Rachel, Zilpa, and Bilha, he says: “Your father’s sons.” Isaac took Rebecca, he said: “Your mother’s sons.” “Cursed be one who curses you…” – and elsewhere it says: “Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed” (Numbers 24:9). It is that Bilam, because he was a hater, began with a blessing and concluded with a curse. Yitzḥak, who was a lover, opened with a curse and concluded with a blessing. Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Rabbi Ḥiyya said: The wicked, because their beginning is tranquility and their end is suffering, they begin with blessing and end with curse. The righteous, because their beginning is suffering and their end is tranquility, they begin with curse and end with blessing: “Cursed be one who curses you, and blessed be one who blesses you.””

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ בְּכָל דָּבָר וְכָל מִדָּה טוֹבָה וְעִנְיָן טוֹב, תְּחִלַּת הַכְּנִיסָה בּוֹ הוּא בְּצַעַר, כְּטַעַם כָּל הַתְחָלוֹת קָשׁוֹת
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְבַחֹדֶשׁ ב׳:ט׳
connections.quote: “‘And now’ (Exodus 19:5): accept it upon yourselves now, for all beginnings are difficult.”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ בְּכָל דָּבָר וְכָל מִדָּה טוֹבָה וְעִנְיָן טוֹב, תְּחִלַּת הַכְּנִיסָה בּוֹ הוּא בְּצַעַר, כְּטַעַם כָּל הַתְחָלוֹת קָשׁוֹת
connections.quote: ““And now”: If you accept upon yourselves now, it will become pleasant for you from this point onward, for all beginnings are difficult.”
connections.context: Rashi, citing the Mekhilta, places “all beginnings are difficult” within acceptance of the covenant at Sinai. The continuation promising subsequent pleasantness supplies the transition from initial difficulty to enduring good used here.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (ה.): ג' מַתָּנוֹת טוֹבוֹת וְכוּלֵי, וּכִבְרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם: בְּרֵישָׁא וְכוּלֵי (שַׁבָּת עז:).
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says: The Holy One, blessed be He, gave Israel three good gifts, and He gave all of them only through suffering. These are they: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come. From where do we know this concerning Torah? For it is said: ‘Fortunate is the man whom You chastise, Yah, and whom You teach from Your Torah.’’
connections.context: The speaker in the Gemara is Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come are the three gifts obtained through suffering. The main text’s expanded name “Shammai” is not the attribution in this source.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (ה.): ג' מַתָּנוֹת טוֹבוֹת וְכוּלֵי, וּכִבְרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם: בְּרֵישָׁא וְכוּלֵי (שַׁבָּת עז:).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Zeira found Rav Yehudah standing at the entrance to his father-in-law’s house and saw that he was in a cheerful mood: if he asked him about anything in the world, he would answer him. He asked, ‘Why do goats walk at the front, followed by sheep?’ He answered, ‘It is like the creation of the world: first darkness, then light.’ ‘Why are these covered behind, while those are exposed?’ ‘Those from which we obtain clothing are covered, and those from which we do not obtain clothing are exposed.’ ‘Why does a camel have a short tail?’ ‘Because it eats thornbushes.’ ‘Why does an ox have a long tail?’ ‘Because it lives among the marsh reeds and needs to flick away gnats.’”

connections.hePhrase: לְפִי שֶׁהָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה רוּבּוֹ רַע כַּיָּדוּעַ, וּלְכָךְ כָּל דָּבָר שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ, רוֹאֶה הוּא מִקּוֹדֶם כֹּחַ הָרָע שֶׁבּוֹ וּמִצְטַעֵר, וְעַל יְדֵי הַצַּעַר מַמְתִּיקוֹ וּמִיָּד סוֹפוֹ שַׁלְוָה.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ז׳:א׳-ג׳
connections.quote: “However, the vital animal soul in Israel that comes from the kelippah and is clothed in human blood, as explained above; the souls of pure animals, beasts, birds, and fish permitted for eating; the existence and vitality of all inanimate things and plants permitted for eating; and the existence and vitality of every deed, speech, and thought in worldly affairs containing no forbidden aspect—not a root or branch of the 365 prohibitions and their biblical or rabbinic extensions—but performed without intent for Heaven, rather from bodily will, desire, and appetite, even when truly needed for the body’s existence and life, if the intention is not for Heaven in order to serve Hashem with one’s body: all these deeds, speech, and thoughts are no better than the vital animal soul itself. All alike flow and are drawn from the second level among the kelippot and the other side: the fourth kelippah, called kelippat nogah. In this world, called the World of Action, it is almost entirely evil, with only a little good mixed within it; from that good come the good qualities in Israel’s animal soul, as explained above. It is an intermediate level between the three entirely impure kelippot and the level and degree of holiness. Therefore it is sometimes included among the three impure kelippot, as written in Etz Chaim, Gate 49, at the beginning of chapter 4, in the Zohar’s name; and sometimes it is included and rises into the level and degree of holiness—that is, when the good mixed within it is separated from the evil, prevails, ascends, and is included in holiness.”
connections.context: Tanya gives the kabbalistic setting for the description of predominating evil in the World of Action. The selected unit retains the crucial qualification: nogah is a mixture whose good can be clarified and elevated into holiness. This is not an assertion that every person or every act is evil.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן תְּלָתָא דְּפוּרְעָנוּתָא וְשֶׁבַע דְּנֶחָמָתָא שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, שֶׁהֵם ג' רִאשׁוֹנוֹת וְז' תַּחְתּוֹנוֹת, שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה חָלוּק לְג' וְהַסּוֹף לְז' כַּיָּדוּעַ.
connections.quote: “The reason is that we follow the Pesikta in reciting three haftarot of calamity before the Ninth of Av: “The words of Yirmeyahu,” “Hear the word of Hashem,” and “The vision of Yeshayahu.” After the Ninth of Av come seven of consolation and two of repentance: “Comfort, comfort,” “Zion said,” “Afflicted, storm-tossed” by itself, “I, I,” “Sing, barren one,” “Arise, shine,” “I will greatly rejoice,” “Seek,” and “Return.” Therefore we place “Afflicted, storm-tossed” before “Sing, barren one,” for consolations proceed by becoming ever greater.”
connections.context: Tosafot supplies the liturgical sequence of three haftarot of calamity and seven of consolation, together with the explanation that the consolations increase in strength. Rav Tzadok interprets that sequence as an image of passing from constriction to expanded good.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְחָלַת כָּל פְּעֻלָּה הוּא מִצַּד הֶכְרֵחַ הַפּוֹעֵל שֶׁחָסֵר לְאוֹתָהּ פְּעֻלָּה, אִם כֵּן הַהַתְחָלָה מִצַּד הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וְדָחוּק לְכָךְ,
connections.quote: “Matzah brings the sense of poverty into the soul, which stands awaiting heavenly mercy like a poor person at the door. Afterward the Pesach offering is meat: Chullin interprets “when Hashem expands…” as wealth and expansion of boundaries, and so the soul's vitality expands in the heart. This is why the account of the Exodus must take the form of questions and answers: “When your son asks you…,” and even a wise person asks himself. The question is the state of poverty; afterward, “Hashem answered me with expansiveness” is the abundant response born from that poverty.”
connections.explanation: Et HaOchel interprets the same verse through the Seder's ordered movement: matzah makes need felt, the Pesach offering expresses expansion, and the answer emerges from a real question. This makes precise the siman's statement that the beginning of an action arises from a lack and that comfort is an answer to that lack. The source illustrates the movement within a mitzvah practice rather than asserting that any particular distress proves which benefit must follow.
connections.headline: From the lack expressed in a question to the expansive answer

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְחָלַת כָּל פְּעֻלָּה הוּא מִצַּד הֶכְרֵחַ הַפּוֹעֵל שֶׁחָסֵר לְאוֹתָהּ פְּעֻלָּה, אִם כֵּן הַהַתְחָלָה מִצַּד הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וְדָחוּק לְכָךְ,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 25:4
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 25:4
connections.quote: ““My strength and song is Yah”: strength indicates firmness, and song indicates limitation. Israel's strength comes from Hashem's limiting the greatness of His light. Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 21, page 63) says that with the name Yah He created the hidden worlds, and with Vav-He He created this world and the World to Come. Hashem limited His light and placed within this world a form in which completion requires Israel's service. Through this limitation there is a bond and unity with Israel. Concerning it the verse says, “From narrowness I called Yah; Yah answered me in breadth.” Through the limitation Israel sees its connection with Hashem, and there is no greater breadth than this. Therefore it says, “He became my deliverance”: all deliverances flow to Israel through this connection.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim interprets the same verse of calling from narrowness and being answered in breadth. Divine concealment gives Israel an actual part in the service; recognizing the connection made possible through that limitation is itself the breadth. This develops the siman's account of the good within a painful beginning without reducing its pattern to the outward pain alone.
connections.headline: The breadth disclosed through the narrowness

connections.hePhrase: וּ"מִן הַמֵּצַר קָרָאתִי יָּהּ" (תְּהִלִּים קיח, ה), שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ הַצַּעַר זוֹעֵק לַה', וְעוֹנֵהוּ בַּמֶּרְחָב,
connections.quote: “From constriction I called to the Lord; the Lord answered me with spaciousness.”
connections.context: The contrast between constriction, metzar, and spaciousness, merchav, is essential to Rav Tzadok’s explanation of the answer to prayer.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא נֶחָמָה, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁמִּתְנַחֵם עַל צַעַר הֶעָבָר, שֶׁרוֹאֶה שֶׁאֵין צַעַר, כְּעִנְיַן "וְנַסְתֶּם וְאֵין רֹדֵף" (וַיִּקְרָא כו, יז).
connections.quote: ‘I will set My face against you, and you will be defeated before your enemies. Those who hate you will rule over you, and you will flee when no one is pursuing you.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּקִלְלַת "וְלֹא תַאֲמִין בְּחַיֶּיךָ" (דְּבָרִים כח, סו), הוֹדִיעֲךָ שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בְּקַלְקָלָה הֵם קְרוּיִים חַיִּים, וְלֹא כִּרְשָׁעִים שֶׁבְּחַיֵּיהֶם קְרוּיִים מֵתִים.
connections.quote: ‘Your life will hang in suspense before you. You will be afraid night and day, and you will have no assurance of your life.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּקִלְלַת "וְלֹא תַאֲמִין בְּחַיֶּיךָ" (דְּבָרִים כח, סו), הוֹדִיעֲךָ שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בְּקַלְקָלָה הֵם קְרוּיִים חַיִּים, וְלֹא כִּרְשָׁעִים שֶׁבְּחַיֵּיהֶם קְרוּיִים מֵתִים.
connections.quote: “‘For the living know that they will die’ (Ecclesiastes 9:5): these are the righteous, who even in their death are called living… ‘And the dead know nothing’ (ibid.): these are the wicked, who even in their lifetime are called dead, as it is said: ‘And you, slain and wicked one, prince of Israel’ (Ezekiel 21:30).”

connections.hePhrase: [קעא] יֵשׁ מָקוֹם מוּכָן לְצַעַר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קב.): בִּשְׁכֶם מָקוֹם וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘‘Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.’ It was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei: It is a place marked out for calamity. In Shechem Dinah was violated; in Shechem Joseph’s brothers sold him; in Shechem the kingdom of the house of David was divided.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן זְמַן, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם): עֵת וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כט:): בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּאִית לֵיהּ דִּינָא וְכוּלֵי בְּאָב וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “It was taught in Rabbi Yosei’s name: It was a time prepared for calamity.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן זְמַן, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם): עֵת וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כט:): בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּאִית לֵיהּ דִּינָא וְכוּלֵי בְּאָב וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Rav Pappa said: Therefore, a Jew who has litigation with a gentile should avoid it in Av, when his fortune is unfavorable, and make himself available in Adar, when his fortune is favorable.”
connections.context: Sanhedrin supplies the general expression “a time prepared for calamity”; Taanit gives the particular comparison of Av and Adar. Rav Tzadok is asking how such a distinction in time can be reconciled with the goodness of creation.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בַּנֶּפֶשׁ, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם כה.) בְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פְּדָת וְטוּבָא.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was in very straitened circumstances. He underwent bloodletting and had nothing to eat afterward. He took a clove of garlic and put it in his mouth; his heart grew faint and he fell asleep. The Sages came to inquire after him. They saw him weeping and laughing, and a flash of fire emerged from his forehead. When he awoke, they asked him, “Why were you weeping and laughing?” He told them: “The Holy One, blessed be He, was sitting with me, and I said to Him, ‘How long must I suffer in this world?’ He said to me, ‘Elazar, My son, would you like Me to overturn the world from its beginning? Perhaps you would then be born at a time of sustenance.’ I said before Him, ‘All that—and only perhaps?’ I asked Him, ‘Have I already lived longer than I have yet to live?’ He said to me, ‘You have already lived longer.’ I said before Him, ‘If so, I do not want it.’””
connections.context: This is the specific story cited for hardship associated with a person’s original circumstances.
