The selected narrative retains both the uncertainty of a different birth and Rabbi Elazar’s eventual refusal; Rav Tzadok’s explanation of such hardship as an excess of divine bestowal is his interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵיךְ יְצוּיַּר זֶה שֶׁמּוּכָן מִתְּחִלַּת בְּרִיאָה לְרַע חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, וַהֲלֹא "מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת" (אֵיכָה ג, לח)?
connections.quote: see note 1221 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The verse is often translated as a rhetorical question. Rav Tzadok quotes its negative wording as a statement about evil not proceeding from the divine source. The Midrash also reads the wording negatively, in its discussion of human action and its consequences; Rav Tzadok develops his own explanation of the goodness at creation’s root.

connections.hePhrase: רַק דִּשְׂכַר מִצְוָה בְּהַאי עָלְמָא לֵיכָּא (קִדּוּשִׁין לט:), רַק פֵּירָעוֹן הָעֲבֵירוֹת, אִם לֹא שֶׁזָּכָה לִטְעוֹם מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אוֹ מֵאוֹתָן מִצְווֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם פֵּירוֹת.
connections.quote: ‘Abaye said: The Mishnah refers to preparing a good day or a bad day for a person [in the World to Come]. Rava said: Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Yaakov’s, for he said: There is no reward for a mitzvah in this world.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק דִּשְׂכַר מִצְוָה בְּהַאי עָלְמָא לֵיכָּא (קִדּוּשִׁין לט:), רַק פֵּירָעוֹן הָעֲבֵירוֹת, אִם לֹא שֶׁזָּכָה לִטְעוֹם מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אוֹ מֵאוֹתָן מִצְווֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם פֵּירוֹת.
connections.quote: “These are the things whose fruits a person eats in this world, while the principal remains for him in the World to Come: honoring father and mother, acts of kindness, and making peace between one person and another; and Torah study is equal to them all.”
connections.context: The Mishnah supplies the qualification concerning mitzvot that yield “fruits” in this world while their principal reward remains for the World to Come. It complements the existing source for the general statement about reward.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה דִּשְׂכַר מִצְוָה בְּהַאי עָלְמָא לֵיכָּא, הַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נוֹתֵן מְלֹא עָמְסוֹ וְכוּלֵי (סַנְהֶדְרִין ק.), וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְקַבֵּל רוֹב טוֹבָה הַהוּא כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “Rav Dimi said: The Holy One, blessed be He, will give each righteous person His full handful, as it says, “Blessed is the Lord, day by day, who loads us with benefit.” Abaye asked him: Can one say so? Is it not written, “Who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand, and measured the heavens with a span”?”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה דִּשְׂכַר מִצְוָה בְּהַאי עָלְמָא לֵיכָּא, הַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נוֹתֵן מְלֹא עָמְסוֹ וְכוּלֵי (סַנְהֶדְרִין ק.), וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְקַבֵּל רוֹב טוֹבָה הַהוּא כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, gives the wicked strength to receive their punishment, so He gives the righteous strength to receive their good.”
connections.context: The question concerns the human capacity to receive a divine measure of good. The answer continues on 100b: God supplies the capacity to receive it. This explains Rav Tzadok’s contrast between present bodily limits and future reward.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ בְּסוֹד שְׁבִירָתָן שֶׁל כֵּלִים זוֹהִי מִיתָתָן עַל יְדֵי רִבּוּי הָאוֹר;
connections.quote: “When the supreme Emanator saw that these vessels had shattered because the light was great and they could not bear it, it arose in His will to repair all the worlds in such a way that they could bear this light. This takes place through the spreading out of the light and their distance from the supreme Emanator, so that the lights arrive more concealed. In this way the worlds will endure and have the strength to bear the light.”
connections.context: Etz Chaim explicitly describes the vessels’ shattering through their inability to bear the great light, followed by repair through a form of reception they can sustain. This supplies the kabbalistic model behind Rav Tzadok’s language; its application to suffering in particular places, times, and souls is his own development.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא נד:) שֶׁמָּצְאוּ כְּרוּבִים מְעוֹרִים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ עוֹשִׂין רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם;
connections.quote: ‘Like a man joined to his companion. Reish Lakish said: When the nations entered the Sanctuary, they saw the cherubim embracing one another. They took them out to the marketplace and said: ‘These Israelites, whose blessing is a blessing and whose curse is a curse—do they occupy themselves with such things?’ Immediately they treated them with contempt, as it is said: ‘All who honored her have despised her, for they have seen her nakedness.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָז הָיָה תֹּקֶף רִבּוּי שֶׁפַע הָאוֹר, וּלְכָךְ זָכָה יְחֶזְקֵאל לְמַרְאוֹת אֱלֹהִים.
connections.quote: “For I heard from my holy master, teacher, and rabbi, of righteous and holy memory, that when they went into exile in Babylonia, everyone went with a bitter soul, while Ezekiel went with great joy. This was because Ezekiel sensed the light of holiness that the Holy One, blessed be He, would cause to shine upon Israel in Babylonia, more than when they dwelt upon their own land. So it was: there was revealed to Ezekiel what had not been revealed to any other prophet or seer, as it is taught in the holy Zohar, volume II, 2b: “When they went down to Babylonia, the heavens opened, and the holy spirit rested upon Ezekiel. He saw what he saw and said to Israel: Your Master is here, and all the hosts of Heaven and the chariot, which has come to dwell among you.… When Israel saw this, they rejoiced … and were not concerned about their exile at all, for they knew that the Holy One, blessed be He, had not abandoned them, and that the Shekhinah was there with them.””

connections.hePhrase: וּמִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה בֶּאֱמֶת, מְקַבֵּל פֵּירָעוֹן הַטּוֹבָה אָז, שֶׁזֶּה עִנְיַן לֵידַת מָשִׁיחַ בְּטִשְׁעָה בְּאָב.
connections.quote: see note 613 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Yerushalmi’s aggadah joins the destruction of the Temple to the birth of the Messiah. The complete source unit includes the child’s later disappearance and Rabbi Bun’s scriptural conclusion; Rav Tzadok reads the juxtaposition as hidden good present within the time of destruction.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יא): לַכֹּל נָתַתָּ בֶּן זוּג, שֶׁלְּכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ זוּג, דְּהַיְינוּ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ דָּבָר שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ נֶגְדּוֹ וְזֶהוּ לְעֵזֶר לוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai taught: Shabbat said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, each has a partner, but I have no partner. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to her: The congregation of Israel is your partner. When Israel stood before Mount Sinai, He said to them: Remember what I said to Shabbat—that the congregation of Israel is your partner. This is “Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it.””
connections.context: The source personifies Shabbat as seeking a partner and assigns Israel that role. Rav Tzadok uses that union in explaining the sanctity of time.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יא): לַכֹּל נָתַתָּ בֶּן זוּג, שֶׁלְּכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ זוּג, דְּהַיְינוּ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ דָּבָר שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ נֶגְדּוֹ וְזֶהוּ לְעֵזֶר לוֹ.
connections.quote: “Hashem God said: It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make him a helper corresponding to him (ezer kenegdo).”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְלַאכְתּוֹ הוּא מִיּוֹם שֶׁנִּבְרָא הָעוֹלָם כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח): לְזַוֵּוג זִוּוּגִים אֵלּוּ שֶׁל מָקוֹם וּזְמַן וְנֶפֶשׁ כָּל אֶחָד בְּהֶפְכָּן;
connections.quote: “A noblewoman asked Rabbi Yosei ben Chalafta: In how many days did the Holy One create His world? He said: In six days. She said: What has He been doing from that time until now? He said: The Holy One sits and makes matches—the daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so, the wife of so-and-so to so-and-so, the property of so-and-so to so-and-so.”
connections.context: The Midrash uses matchmaking to describe the continuing arrangement of particular connections within creation. Rav Tzadok applies that pattern to the joining of sanctified persons and times.

connections.hePhrase: דְּיֵשׁ מָקוֹם מוּכָן לְהֵיפֶךְ מַמָּשׁ, שֶׁלֹּא לְקַבֵּל שׁוּם שְׂכַר מַעֲשִׂים, רַק לִבְטוֹחַ בְּבַעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁנֶּאֱמָן לְשַׁלֵּם שָׂכָר, וּבְזִוּוּגָם מִתְמַתְּקִים יַחַד.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar says: Be diligent in the study of Torah… Know before whom you toil; and your Employer is faithful to pay you the reward of your work.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ נֶגֶד כ"ב יָמִים שֶׁבֵּין הַמְּצָרִים הֵם מֵרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה עַד שְׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת
connections.heRef: חידושי אגדות על בכורות ח׳ ב:ד׳
connections.quote: “Further, “They brought two eggs and said to him: Which is from the hen”—this follows what was said in our passage: a hen produces after twenty-one days, and its counterpart among trees is the almond. We say that Yirmeyahu alluded to this in “I see an almond rod”: the twenty-one days from the seventeenth of Tammuz to the Ninth of Av. They alluded to these days by a black hen, on account of exile. There are also twenty-one days of forgiveness and joy, from the first festival day of Rosh Hashanah to the twenty-first of Tishrei, Hoshana Rabbah, the day on which the sealing is completed, as found in the Midrashim. To these they alluded by a white hen, on account of the whitening of sins. Thus they said: The two eggs produced by the two hens are both white, and one cannot recognize which came from the black hen and which from the white. Likewise, you have no distinguishing sign, for one fate befalls them all: calamities and good things have equal numbers of days, twenty-one, and there is no ground for your hope. He answered by the corresponding example of black goats: these are the two goats Israel brought on Yom Kippur. The white one represents the goat for Hashem, and the black one the goat for Azazel. The cheese produced from both is white, for the goat sent to Azazel also whitened Israel’s sins, as it says, “The goat shall bear”; and as they said, they tied a crimson thread to the scapegoat, and when it reached the wilderness it turned white. So too with the two hens: both produced after twenty-one days, and both produced white eggs. These two periods of twenty-one days likewise have equal results in whitening: just as the twenty-one days from Rosh Hashanah to Hoshana Rabbah produce the whitening and atonement of sins, so the twenty-one days of calamity from the seventeenth of Tammuz to the Ninth of Av produced the whitening of sins, for troubles and sufferings atone, as they said, “Exile atones.””
connections.context: Maharsha gives a related correspondence between the Three Weeks and the season of repentance and rejoicing, interpreting both as periods of cleansing. His count is twenty-one days ending at Hoshana Rabbah; Rav Tzadok here develops the correspondence through the inclusive twenty-two-day span ending at Shemini Atzeret.

connections.hePhrase: [וְשִׂמְחַת תּוֹרָה הוּא נֶגֶד י' בְּאָב, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אִלּוּ הֲוַאי הָתָם וְכוּלֵי (תַּעֲנִית כט.),
connections.quote: “On the ninth, toward nightfall, they set fire to it, and it kept burning the whole day, as it is said: ‘Woe to us, for the day has declined, for the shadows of evening are lengthening’ (Jeremiah 6:4). And this is what Rabbi Yochanan said: Had I been in that generation, I would have fixed it only on the tenth, because most of the Sanctuary burned on that day. And the Rabbis held that the beginning of the calamity takes precedence.”
connections.context: The fire began near the end of the ninth and burned through the tenth; this is why Rabbi Yochanan would have fixed the fast on the tenth of Av.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דְּטַעַם סֻכָּה הוּא הַחִסָּיוֹן בַּה' וְהַבִּטָּחוֹן בּוֹ.
connections.quote: “The mitzvah of sukkah is the quality of trust in Hashem, blessed be He. As our Sages said, “Leave your permanent dwelling”: do not trust in wealth and possessions, but trust in Hashem. Therefore it is the time of our rejoicing, for there is no joy like the joy of one who truly trusts in Hashem, as explained in Chovot HaLevavot. Therefore prayers and Hoshanot were instituted on this festival: to know that all the blessings of the year depend only on Hashem’s help, and not to trust in gathering all the produce into one’s house. As it is written, “Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him.” The water libation alludes to this: pouring out the heart like water before Him, blessed be He. Surely this is implanted in the hearts of Israel: whenever they need deliverance, they trust in Him. Therefore Hashem shelters them during these days, as it is written, “One who trusts in Hashem—kindness will surround him.””
connections.context: Sefat Emet’s Sukkot teaching for 5645 explains the sukkah as trust, including its practical contrast with relying on stored wealth and harvest. This supplies a distinct original exposition of the trust Rav Tzadok associates with the festival.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶגֶד ט' בְּאָב הוּא שְׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא פִּינְחָס טז): פַּר אֶחָד וְכוּלֵי, אֲנִי וְאַתֶּם, כְּמוֹ לֶעָתִיד "ה' בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ וְגוֹמֵר", מַמָּשׁ הֵיפֶךְ ט' בְּאָב.
connections.quote: “A king made a feast for seven days and invited all the people of the city. When the seven days of feasting had passed, he said to his friend: We have fulfilled our obligations to all the people of the city. Let you and I manage with whatever is available—with a pound of meat, a pound of fish, or vegetables. So the Holy One said to Israel: All the offerings you brought in the seven days of the festival were for the nations of the world. But on the eighth day, you and I will manage with whatever you find—with one bull and one ram.”
connections.context: The private meal after the public feast represents Shemini Atzeret’s particular bond between God and Israel. Rav Tzadok contrasts that closeness with the separation experienced on the ninth of Av.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶגֶד ט' בְּאָב הוּא שְׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא פִּינְחָס טז): פַּר אֶחָד וְכוּלֵי, אֲנִי וְאַתֶּם, כְּמוֹ לֶעָתִיד "ה' בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ וְגוֹמֵר", מַמָּשׁ הֵיפֶךְ ט' בְּאָב.
connections.quote: “You shall offer a burnt offering, a fire offering of pleasing aroma to Hashem: one bull, one ram, seven yearling lambs without blemish.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶגֶד ט' בְּאָב הוּא שְׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא פִּינְחָס טז): פַּר אֶחָד וְכוּלֵי, אֲנִי וְאַתֶּם, כְּמוֹ לֶעָתִיד "ה' בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ וְגוֹמֵר", מַמָּשׁ הֵיפֶךְ ט' בְּאָב.
connections.quote: ‘Hashem alone guided him; no foreign god was with Him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכ"ב יָמִים הֵם נֶגֶד כ"ב אוֹתִיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁפָּגְמוּ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּאֵיכָה רַבָּתִי,
connections.quote: “Why was the Scroll of Lamentations composed alphabetically? Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Nechemyah, and the Sages discussed this. Rabbi Yehudah says: Because it is written, “All Israel transgressed Your Torah,” which is written from alef to tav; therefore this scroll was written in alphabetical sequences, one corresponding to the other.”
connections.context: This is the Midrashic explanation of the alphabetical form of Eikhah invoked here. Rav Tzadok applies its alef-to-tav correspondence to the twenty-two days and letters.

connections.hePhrase: דִּלְכָךְ בְּי"ז בְּתַמּוּז נִשְׁתַּבְּרוּ לוּחוֹת וְנִשְׂרְפָה הַתּוֹרָה, וְהוּא נֶגֶד אוֹת א' שֶׁמַּתְחִיל בּוֹ אוֹתִיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “Five things befell our fathers on the seventeenth of Tammuz and five on the Ninth of Av. On the seventeenth of Tammuz the Tablets were broken, the daily offering ceased, the city was breached, Apostemos burned the Torah, and an idol was set up in the Sanctuary.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְאוֹתוֹ זְמַן יוֹרֵד שֶׁפַע דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה, רַק שֶׁהוּא בִּרְאִיָּה כְּטַעַם מַרְאוֹת יְחֶזְקֵאל.
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of “between the narrow straits”: there is a boundary on either side, so the concealment cannot extend before it or beyond Tisha B'Av. Repair and completion take place precisely within those concealed days. We see that after the Temple's destruction, Oral Torah began to spread and multiply through the Tannaim and Amoraim who arose afterward. The Midrash likewise says that Oral Torah is principally disclosed through pain and toil, and concerning them it says, “The people walking in darkness saw a great light.””
connections.explanation: Matot develops the same twenty-two-day and alphabet structure by pointing to the expansion of Oral Torah through the Tannaim and Amoraim after the destruction. This supplies a concrete counterpart to the siman's movement from a powerful vision toward acquired Torah. The comparison concerns the capacity to receive and develop the light within concealment; it does not make the destruction itself the desired final state.
connections.headline: Concealment prepares a fuller reception of Torah

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:): הָרוֹאֶה יְחֶזְקֵאל יְצַפֶּה לְחָכְמָה, שֶׁזֶּהוּ דּוּגְמַת פֶּסַח "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי",
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְשִׁירָה ג׳:י׳
connections.quote: ““This is my God.” Rabbi Eliezer says: From where do you say that a maidservant at the sea saw what Yeshayahu and Yechezkel did not see? As it is said, “Through the prophets I use likenesses,” and, “The heavens opened, and I saw visions of God.””
connections.context: The Mekhilta supplies the precise comparison between revelation at the sea and prophetic visions. Rav Tzadok uses this comparison in distinguishing an initial vision from the later acquisition of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: [קעב] כְּמוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּמָקוֹם "אֶבֶן שְׁתִיָּה" שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ הֻשְׁתַּת הָעוֹלָם וְהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל הָעוֹלָם,
connections.quote: ““It was called Shetiyah.” It was taught: Because from it the world was founded. Our Mishnah follows the view that the world was created from Zion. For it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says: The world was created from its center, as it is said, “When the dust is poured into a solid mass and the clods cling together.” Rabbi Yehoshua says: The world was created from its sides, as it is said, “For to the snow He says: Become earth; and to the rain shower and the showers of His mighty rain.” Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha said: The Holy One, blessed be He, cast a stone into the sea, and from it the world was founded, as it is said, “On what were its foundations sunk, or who cast its cornerstone?” The Sages say: It was created from Zion, as it is said, “A psalm of Asaf: God, God, Hashem,” and it says, “From Zion, the perfection of beauty”—from it the beauty of the world was perfected.”
connections.context: This is the explicit source for the Foundation Stone. The competing explanations are retained, and the Gemara identifies creation from Zion as the view followed by the Mishnah. Rav Tzadok uses that view as the model for a root that includes a whole realm.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ בְּנֶפֶשׁ יֵשׁ נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת שֶׁכּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל הַדּוֹר וְהוּא פַּרְנַס הַדּוֹר כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְכֵן הַכּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10
connections.quote: see note 1701 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s fuller discussion explains what it means for one soul to include a generation, and explicitly connects the model to parents, Adam, and kingship. The statement describes the spiritual structure he is presenting; it is not an empirical ranking of every historical ruler.

connections.hePhrase: [וְכָל אֶחָד מֵאֵלּוּ חָלוּק לִשְׁנַיִם: בְּמָקוֹם יֵשׁ מִזְבֵּחַ וְקֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים, וּבִזְמַן שַׁבָּת וְיוֹם טוֹב, וּבִנְפָשׁוֹת מֶלֶךְ וְכֹהֵן גָּדוֹל;
connections.quote: ““From the earth”: Rabbi Berechyah and Rabbi Chelbo said in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: He was created from the place of his atonement, as it says, “An altar of earth you shall make for Me.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I will create him from the place of his atonement; would that he endure!”
connections.context: The Midrash relates Adam’s creation to the site of the altar and atonement. It provides the distinct altar side of Rav Tzadok’s pairing of the altar with the Holy of Holies.

connections.hePhrase: קְדֻשַּׁת כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל קְבִיעָא וְקַיָּימָא, שֶׁנִּבְדַּל אַהֲרֹן לְהַקְדִּישׁוֹ וְגוֹמֵר,
connections.quote: see note 494 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the verse quoted in shortened form. Its explicit inclusion of Aharon’s sons and the enduring priestly service supplies the textual basis for the established priestly sanctity discussed here.

connections.hePhrase: וּקְדֻשַּׁת מֶלֶךְ עַל יְדֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "תָּשִׂים עָלֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘You shall surely appoint over yourself a king whom Hashem your God chooses. You shall appoint a king from among your brothers; you may not place over yourself a foreign man who is not your brother.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד וְכוּלֵי (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:)].
connections.quote: see note 1910 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The sentence crosses the page boundary. Rav Tzadok uses the dependence of Moses’ communication on the people’s condition to illustrate the relationship between a leader and the whole community.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַמְתָּקַת הַמְּקוֹמוֹת הוּא עַל יְדֵי "וְהִתְפַּלְלוּ אֵלֶיךָ דֶּרֶךְ אַרְצָם" (מְלָכִים א ח, מח) וְדֶרֶךְ בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ,
connections.quote: ‘And they return to You with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies who took them captive, and pray to You toward their land, which You gave to their fathers, the city You chose, and the house I built for Your name.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדִשְׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ח.): כָּל זְמַן שֶׁשִּׁמְעִי בֶן גֵּרָא קַיָּים לֹא וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chiyya bar Ammi also said in Ulla’s name: A person should always live in the place where his teacher lives, for as long as Shimei son of Gera was alive, Solomon did not marry Pharaoh’s daughter.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל הוּא הָיָה נוֹשֵׂא עֲווֹנוֹת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
connections.quote: “Moses and Aaron embody netzach and hod. Moses corresponds to netzach, on the right side, as Abraham made His divinity known so that He would be called God of the earth; Moses likewise brought the Divine Presence down to earth. He is the King’s attendant. Aaron embodies hod, on the left side, and is the Matron’s attendant: he atones for and adorns the Matron, the Congregation of Israel, so that she finds favor in God’s eyes. The entire sacrificial service and the holiness of Yom Kippur operate through Aaron the priest. Yet the Zohar also says that the priest comes from kindness. This follows “For the priest’s lips preserve knowledge”: knowledge joins right and left, wisdom and understanding, mind and heart.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah spells out the imagery used here: Moshe makes the divine presence known below, while Aharon atones for and adorns the congregation so that it can find favor. This makes the siman’s two functions intelligible rather than treating king and High Priest as interchangeable encompassing figures. Its closing qualification also matters: the priest’s knowledge joins right and left, so the roles remain distinct without becoming disconnected powers.
connections.headline: Moshe reveals the King’s light; Aharon prepares Israel to receive it

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁמֵּסִיר כָּל מִינֵי כִּיעוּר וּמְיַפֶּה בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל מִינֵי יוֹפִי, כְּעִנְיַן אַהֲרֹן שׁוֹשְׁבִינָא דְּמַטְרוֹנִיתָא
connections.quote: “Come and see: What is the difference between Moshe and Aharon? Which of them is higher? Moshe is higher. Moshe is the attendant of the King; Aharon is the attendant of the Queen. It is like a king who had an exalted queen. What did he do? He gave her an attendant to prepare her and attend to the affairs of the household. Therefore, when this attendant enters before the king, he enters only with the queen. This is what is written: “With this shall Aharon enter.” Moshe is the attendant of the King; therefore he was invited as a guest, and afterward, “Hashem spoke to him.” Aharon is the attendant of the Queen, and all his affairs are to reconcile the King with the Queen, so that the King is reconciled with her. Therefore, because he is her attendant, he established his dwelling with her, to prepare the household and attend continually to its affairs. Accordingly he was appointed after the pattern above and called High Priest. From where do we know this? As it is written, “You are a priest forever, according to My word, Malki-Tzedek.””
connections.context: The original Zohar passage gives the household parable and explains Aharon’s work of preparation and reconciliation. It adds that explanation to the terminology already used in the connected source, and clarifies the distinction Rav Tzadok draws between the two forms of spiritual leadership.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִפְרָט זֶה בְּהַשָּׂגוֹת אוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הַהַמְשָׁכָה לְכָל הַשָּׁנָה הוּא מֵהָרְגָלִים שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהֶם: "יֵרָאֶה וְגוֹמֵר אֶת פְּנֵי וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת לד, כג):
connections.quote: “Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the face of the Master, Hashem, the God of Israel.”
connections.context: The words “et penei” quoted here are from this verse; Exodus 23:17 reads “el penei.”

connections.hePhrase: [קעג] כָּל הַדְּבָרִים הַטִּבְעִיִּים הֵם עוֹשִׂים רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כֹּל פָּעַל ה' לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי טז, ד) – לְקִילּוּסוֹ,
connections.quote: ‘Hashem has made everything for His sake, even the wicked for the day of evil.’

connections.hePhrase: [קעג] כָּל הַדְּבָרִים הַטִּבְעִיִּים הֵם עוֹשִׂים רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כֹּל פָּעַל ה' לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי טז, ד) – לְקִילּוּסוֹ,
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef, Ha'azinu and Shabbat Shuvah 11
connections.canonicalRef: Tiferet Yosef, Ha'azinu and Shabbat Shuvah 11
connections.quote: ““When the Most High apportioned nations… He set the boundaries of peoples according to the number of Israel, for Hashem's portion is His people.” Hashem grants great powers to the nations too, and precious powers are found in all kinds of creatures. The Gemara interprets “He teaches us from the beasts of the earth and makes us wise from the birds”: had Torah not been given, we would learn modesty from the cat, avoidance of theft from the ant, fidelity from the dove and proper conduct from the rooster. Great powers can likewise sometimes be found among the nations exceeding Israel's, for Israel is described as “the fewest of all peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7); all the more are great powers found among the heavenly hosts. Yet the principal point is “Hashem's portion is His people; Yaakov is the rope of His inheritance”: the whole is directed toward Israel.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same verse about learning from animals by naming distinct virtues in different creatures. Their particular powers may exceed a person's present achievement in that respect. This clarifies the siman's move from natural action to chosen learning: a person recognizes the lesson and brings it into his own service, while the siman itself supplies the conditions of necessary bodily life and sanctifying the Name.
connections.headline: Each creature can supply a particular lesson

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ז.): בְּגִינַאי נַהֲרָא, אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן קוֹנִי – מַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּטִבְעוֹ כָּךְ
connections.quote: ‘He said to it: ‘Ginnai, divide your waters for me so that I can cross through you!’ It answered: ‘You are going to carry out your Creator’s will, and I am going to carry out my Creator’s will. You may carry it out, or you may not; I certainly carry it out.’ He told it: ‘If you do not divide, I decree that water will never pass through you again.’ It divided for him.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִלְבַד מַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּהֶכְרֵחַ, כְּגוֹן אֲכִילָה לְרַעֲבוֹן,
connections.quote: “After the giving of Torah they knew that Hashem's will includes what a person needs. As Chullin 7a says of the river Ginai, ‘I am going to fulfill my Creator's will’: the nature implanted in it is its Creator's will, like a mitzvah. Likewise, what a person naturally needs for eating and drinking is the Creator's will and a mitzvah. They knew this through Torah's gift, called a complete gift: this gift belongs to them from their hidden root. Such is Torah's way—bread with salt and measured water, only what is necessary. Through this their hidden root became known to them. They still remained uncertain concerning the expansion and surplus of desires. This applies only to the fruits of the land, through mitzvot: when a person performs a mitzvah with bread or food, Heaven's name rests upon that expansion itself, in the manner of the land of Israel. As I wrote elsewhere, this is the secret of the blessing over enjoyment that the Sages instituted before every enjoyment; this is not the place to explain it. Through this their hidden root became known to them in this too.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek uses the same encounter with the river to explain why meeting a genuine natural need can fulfill the Creator's will. It then explicitly distinguishes surplus desire, which requires a further clarification through mitzvot. This keeps the siman's restriction to what is necessary beside its broad statement about natural service.
connections.headline: Natural necessity and surplus desire

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּזִוּוּג עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם כְּשֶׁמּוֹצֵא וְכוּלֵי, דְּהַטֶּבַע תּוֹבְעוֹ לְכָךְ,
connections.quote: “He should have intercourse only when he finds his body exceptionally healthy and strong, and he has a strong involuntary erection; he diverts his attention to something else, yet the erection remains as before; he feels heaviness from his loins downward, as though the cords of the testicles were being drawn, and his flesh is hot. Such a person needs intercourse, and intercourse is a remedy for him.”
connections.context: This is the passage Rav Tzadok abbreviates as “when he finds.” It belongs to Rambam’s historical regimen of bodily health and supplies the particular case of bodily necessity intended by the citation.

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בִּיהוּדָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה פה) רֶמֶז לַמַּלְאָךְ הַמְמוּנֶּה וְכוּלֵי, וְעַיֵּין בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים (פֶּרֶק ו מֵחֵלֶק ב);
connections.quote: ““Judah saw her and thought her to be a harlot, because she covered her face” (Genesis 38:15). “Judah saw her” – Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Zavda said: A person must be very careful regarding his wife’s sister and his female relatives, that he not stumble with one of them. From whom do you derive it? From Judah – “Judah saw her…” Why? It is “because she covered her face” while she was still in her father-in-law’s house. “He turned to her by the road, and he said: Please, let me consort with you, for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said: What will you give me that you would consort with me” (Genesis 38:16)? Another matter: “Judah saw her” – he did not pay attention to her. When she covered her face, he said: Were she a harlot, would she have covered her face? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: He sought to pass, but the Holy One blessed be He dispatched to him the angel that is responsible for desire. He said to him: ‘Judah, where are you going? From where will kings be produced, from where will the prominent ones be produced?’ “He turned to her by the road” – despite himself, against his will.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בִּיהוּדָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה פה) רֶמֶז לַמַּלְאָךְ הַמְמוּנֶּה וְכוּלֵי, וְעַיֵּין בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים (פֶּרֶק ו מֵחֵלֶק ב);
connections.quote: “In the section concerning Judah and Tamar, it says: “Rabbi Yochanan said: He sought to pass by, but the Holy One, blessed be He, appointed for him an angel in charge of desire”—meaning the power of sexual arousal. Thus it calls this power too an angel. … Every power that God, exalted be He, appoints over a thing is an angel appointed over that thing.”
connections.context: Maimonides expressly interprets the angel in the Judah and Tamar Midrash as a natural faculty. This is the explanation Rav Tzadok directs the reader to consult, after citing the Midrash itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְלִהְיוֹת מְכַוֵּין לְכָךְ רַק בִּשְׁבִיל רְצוֹן קוֹנוֹ שֶׁבְּרָאוֹ כֵּן,
connections.quote: see note 12 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rambam explicitly connects necessary bodily activity with intention for divine service, extending the principle even to sleep. This supplies a parallel original formulation of the intention Rav Tzadok requires here.

connections.hePhrase: זֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (כ:): דּוֹמֶה לְמִי שֶׁכְּפָאוֹ וְכוּלֵי, וְזֶהוּ רְצוֹן קוֹנוֹ].
connections.quote: ‘But they raised a contradiction: They asked Imma Shalom: Why are your children exceptionally beautiful? She told them: He is not intimate with me at the beginning of the night or at the end of the night, but only at midnight. When he is intimate, he uncovers a handbreadth and covers a handbreadth, and he is like someone compelled by a demon.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר פִּינְחָס (רכב עַמּוּד ב) וּבְפֶרֶק שִׁירָה, דִּצְפַרְדֵּעַ אָמְרָה לְדָוִד שֶׁהִיא מְקַלֶּסֶת יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “He too opened and said: “Hashem, my heart was not proud, nor were my eyes raised.” David said this verse when he was walking along a riverbank, saying: “Master of the world, is there a person in the world who gives thanks and praises his Master as I do?” A frog appeared before him and said: “David, do not be proud, for I have done more than you: I gave my body for my Master’s command, as it is written, ‘The river shall swarm with frogs,’ as has been explained. Moreover, I praise and sing day and night without ceasing.” At that moment David said: “Hashem, my heart was not proud, nor were my eyes raised.””
connections.context: The Zohar’s complete exchange joins the frog’s continual praise to its surrender of its body at God’s command. Both elements are needed for Rav Tzadok’s progression from natural activity to learning self-sacrifice from the frogs of Egypt.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ דְּמַה שֶּׁצּוֹוַחַת בְּקוֹלָהּ, כֵּיוָן דְּהַכֹּל לְמַעֲנֵהוּ – לְקִילּוּסוֹ (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים קמח), הֲרֵי פְּעֻלָּתָהּ תְּמִידִית לְקִילּוּס לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, created the human being only for His glory. So it says, “The Lord has made everything for His purpose.” He created them to praise Him, and they praised Him, as it says, “The heavens declare.” Just as the heavens and all within them praise Him, so the earth and all within it praise Him.”
connections.context: Shocher Tov is another name for Midrash Tehillim. This passage interprets “for His purpose” as praise, which is the connection Rav Tzadok invokes when describing the frog’s ongoing natural activity.

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ הָאָדָם לִלְמוֹד מֵהֶם, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (נג:): דַּחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה לָמְדוּ קַל וָחֹמֶר מִצְּפַרְדְּעִים;
connections.quote: “Come and hear: Todos of Rome also expounded this teaching: What led Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah to surrender themselves to the fiery furnace for the sanctification of the Name? They drew an a fortiori inference about themselves from the frogs. Frogs are not commanded to sanctify the Name, yet it is written of them, ‘They will come up into your house,’ and so forth, ‘and into your ovens and your kneading troughs.’ When are kneading troughs found beside an oven? You must say: when the oven is hot. How much more must we do so, since we are commanded to sanctify the Name!”

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ הָאָדָם לִלְמוֹד מֵהֶם, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (נג:): דַּחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה לָמְדוּ קַל וָחֹמֶר מִצְּפַרְדְּעִים;
connections.quote: “Its relation to circumcision follows the verses: “The Lord did not give you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear,” and “I led you,” and “You did not eat bread or drink wine and strong drink.” Once He gave them a heart to know, they merited eyes to see: to see only the blessed God and to learn from all creatures for His service. This resembles the saying in Eruvin: “‘Who teaches us from the beasts of the earth’—had Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty,” and so forth. Likewise in Berakhot: one who sees bread and says, “How beautiful is this bread; blessed is the Omnipresent who created it.” They also merited “ears to hear”: from everything they heard, they would learn for the service of the blessed God, as in “Your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying: This is the way; walk in it,” as we have explained.”
connections.explanation: Lech Lecha describes a heart that learns service from what the eyes see and the ears hear, and cites the same teaching about learning from animals. This explains how the present siman moves from a creature’s natural action to a person’s chosen avodah. The creature is a lesson to be understood, not a replacement for judgment. This siman accordingly distinguishes ordinary preservation of the body from the particular circumstances of sanctifying Hashem’s Name.
connections.headline: A knowing heart learns avodah from the creatures it encounters

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מַלְּפֵנוּ מִבַּהֲמוֹת אָרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר" (אִיּוֹב לה, יא), שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ בִּפְעֻלָּתֵנוּ הַבְּחִירִית לְמֵידִין מֵהֶם:
connections.quote: ‘He teaches us more than the animals of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens.’
connections.context: The verse can be translated comparatively, “more than the beasts.” Rav Tzadok develops the Hebrew prefix mi- as “from”: people can learn from the behavior of animals and apply the lesson through their own free choice. Compare Eruvin 100b:29, where Rabbi Yochanan describes learning modesty from a cat and avoidance of theft from an ant.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מַלְּפֵנוּ מִבַּהֲמוֹת אָרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר" (אִיּוֹב לה, יא), שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ בִּפְעֻלָּתֵנוּ הַבְּחִירִית לְמֵידִין מֵהֶם:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chiyya said: What is meant by ‘Who teaches us by the beasts of the earth and makes us wise by the birds of the heavens’? ‘Who teaches us by the beasts’: this is the mule, which kneels when it urinates; ‘and makes us wise by the birds of the heavens’: this is the rooster, which first appeases and then mates. Rabbi Yochanan said: Had the Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, [the prohibition of] theft from the ant, and [of] forbidden relations from the dove…”

connections.hePhrase: [קעד] עַל יְדֵי קִלְקוּל וּפְגַם הַבְּרִית נֶעְלָם אוֹר תּוֹרָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק" (תְּהִלִּים צז, יא) דַּיְיקָא, וּכְתִיב: "כִּי נֵר מִצְוָה וְתוֹרָה אוֹר" (מִשְׁלֵי ו, כג).
connections.quote: “Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright of heart.”
connections.context: The verse pairs the righteous with light and the upright of heart with joy. The translation preserves “joy” and “heart,” both of which matter for Rav Tzadok’s interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: [קעד] עַל יְדֵי קִלְקוּל וּפְגַם הַבְּרִית נֶעְלָם אוֹר תּוֹרָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק" (תְּהִלִּים צז, יא) דַּיְיקָא, וּכְתִיב: "כִּי נֵר מִצְוָה וְתוֹרָה אוֹר" (מִשְׁלֵי ו, כג).
connections.quote: ‘For a mitzvah is a lamp, Torah is light, and corrective rebukes are a path of life.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁבְּמִצְרַיִם – זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה: הֵם שְׁטוּפֵי זִמָּה, הָיָה לָהֶם חֹשֶׁךְ, וּלְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹר בְּמוֹשְׁבֹתָם, דְּ"עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים".
connections.quote: “No one saw his brother, and no one rose from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁבְּמִצְרַיִם – זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה: הֵם שְׁטוּפֵי זִמָּה, הָיָה לָהֶם חֹשֶׁךְ, וּלְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹר בְּמוֹשְׁבֹתָם, דְּ"עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים".
connections.quote: “Your people shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I glory.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת שׁוֹבָבִי"ם, מִתְּחִלַּת גָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם עַד אַחַר מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, מְיוּחָד לְתִיקּוּן הַבְּרִית.
connections.quote: “The matter of the well-known Shovavim: that is, there is an ancient custom throughout Israel to fast forty consecutive days, from the first day of the portion Shemot until the portion Terumah and part of Tetzaveh. They gave these days the sign “Return, wayward children”—the initials of Shemot, Vaera, Bo, Beshalach, Yitro, and Mishpatim. The main fasting during these forty days was instituted for the transgression of a seminal emission, and these days are more suited to fasting for this than all other days of the year. The reason becomes clear from what we explained concerning the exile in Egypt with mortar and bricks. There it was explained that those enslaved in the Egyptian exile were the sparks of souls that emerged from Adam during the 130 years in which he separated from his wife and generated demons and spirits through drops of seminal emission. All these were rectified in that Egyptian exile. Therefore, during the reading of these portions there is a special quality for accepting the repentance of one who fasts during them for this transgression. They begin with Shemot because that portion begins the enslavement, and end with Mishpatim for the reason explained there concerning the proximity of “When you acquire a Hebrew slave” to the giving of the Torah: then those sparks completed their rectification in the matter of “When you acquire a Hebrew slave”; see there.”
connections.context: This historical kabbalistic account explains the association of the Shovavim portions with rectification through the Egyptian exile. The work describes a penitential custom and then explains the six-portion sequence; Rav Tzadok draws on the latter connection here.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא בְּחֹדֶשׁ שְׁבָט שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְּאוֹת הַצַּדִּי"ק כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה
connections.quote: “He made the letter tzadi king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Aquarius in the world, Shevat in the year, and the stomach in the soul.”
connections.context: This is the explicit letter–month correspondence cited by Rav Tzadok. The passage is numbered 5:2 in this recension; other recensions divide the chapter into smaller units.

connections.hePhrase: [וְטֵי"ת מִתְחַלֵּף בְּצַדִּי"ק בַּאֲרַמִּי לָרוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּהַגָּהוֹת הֶעָרוּךְ, וְהוּא כְּטַעַם: אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב, דְּהַפּוֹגֵם נִקְרָא רַע כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר].
connections.quote: “Say of the righteous one that it is good, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְטֵי"ת מִתְחַלֵּף בְּצַדִּי"ק בַּאֲרַמִּי לָרוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּהַגָּהוֹת הֶעָרוּךְ, וְהוּא כְּטַעַם: אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב, דְּהַפּוֹגֵם נִקְרָא רַע כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר].
connections.quote: “But none is called evil except one who corrupts his way, defiles himself and defiles the earth, and gives power and strength to the impure spirit, which is called evil… And therefore, once he has defiled himself, he is called evil.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְטֵי"ת מִתְחַלֵּף בְּצַדִּי"ק בַּאֲרַמִּי לָרוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּהַגָּהוֹת הֶעָרוּךְ, וְהוּא כְּטַעַם: אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב, דְּהַפּוֹגֵם נִקְרָא רַע כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר].
connections.quote: “For we have learned: whoever emits his seed in vain is called evil and does not see the face of the Shechinah, as it is written, ‘Evil shall not dwell with You’ (Psalms 5:5), and it is written, ‘And Er, the firstborn of Judah, was evil’ (Genesis 38:7).”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרִינַן בְּשַׁבָּת (עז:): דְּכָךְ הוּא סֵדֶר בְּרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם – בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא;
connections.quote: see note 2200 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The comparison begins with the animals’ usual dark and light coloring. Rav Tzadok takes the creation pattern itself—darkness preceding light—as the model for the spiritual sequence he is describing.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרִינַן בְּשַׁבָּת (עז:): דְּכָךְ הוּא סֵדֶר בְּרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם – בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא;
connections.quote: “This is through the first light, which was hidden for the righteous, the light called good. It is attained through Torah’s light, as Israel merit to be ‘those occupied with Your Torah,’ for every Israelite has some occupation in Torah; and to be righteous, for ‘the righteous are destined for light,’ as it says, ‘Light is sown for the righteous’; and to be pure, for ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever,’ and, ‘The fear of the Lord is wisdom.’ Of someone occupied in Torah without fear of Heaven, the Sages said, ‘Why is there a price in the fool’s hand …?’—those who occupy themselves with Torah but lack fear of Heaven. This is the root of the dedication established for the first light that Israel merit, as God illuminates for Israel: ‘The Lord is God, and He illuminated for us.’ For this we make a dedication.”
connections.explanation: The present siman specifies that its darkness is a loss of Torah’s light, and that return leads back to that light. Chanukah develops the positive side: the concealed first light is received through Torah joined to fear of Heaven. This keeps the promised renewal connected to an actual form of service rather than to a change of feeling alone. The present siman’s rejection of choosing sin in order to repent remains essential to its account of darkness preceding light.
connections.headline: Emerging from darkness means receiving Torah together with awe

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם דְּחָלִילָה לוֹמַר "אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב" וְלַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן בִּבְחִירָתוֹ, מִשּׁוּם דְּאֵין מַסְפִּיקִין;
connections.quote: “One who says, “I will sin and repent; I will sin and repent,” is not afforded the opportunity to repent. “I will sin, and Yom Kippur will atone”—Yom Kippur does not atone.”
connections.context: The Mishnah supplies the essential restriction: the possibility of repentance does not justify deliberately planning a sin. Rav Tzadok expressly preserves that restriction before discussing how failures that have already occurred may be repaired.

connections.hePhrase: אֲפִילּוּ יוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה לו:) דְּיָצְאוּ י' טִפִּין עַל פָּסוּק "וַיָּפֹזּוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Immediately, ‘his bow remained firm.’ Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Meir’s name: His bow returned to its firmness. ‘The arms of his hands became agile’—he drove his hands into the ground, and his semen came out from between the nails of his hands.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲפִילּוּ יוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה לו:) דְּיָצְאוּ י' טִפִּין עַל פָּסוּק "וַיָּפֹזּוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘His bow remained firm, and the arms of his hands grew strong through the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob; from there he became the shepherd of the family of Israel.’

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ יִשַׁי אֲבִי דָוִד שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ) "בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “An objection was raised: Four died because of the serpent’s counsel, and these are they: Binyamin son of Yaakov, Amram father of Moshe, Yishai father of David, and Kilav son of David.”
connections.context: The Gemara lists Yishai among those whose death is attributed to the primordial serpent’s counsel rather than to a personal transgression. That premise is necessary for Rav Tzadok’s comparison with the Midrash about the mixed motives of human conception.

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ יִשַׁי אֲבִי דָוִד שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ) "בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: see note 1259 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the Midrash cited at the opening of Tazria. Its concern is the distinction between parental pleasure and God’s sustaining work in conception; Rav Tzadok uses it alongside Yishai’s exceptional righteousness to describe an inherited human mixture rather than a specific accusation of prohibited conduct.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן יְסוֹד בִּנְיַן בֵּית דָּוִד וּמָשִׁיחַ בְּפֶרֶץ, הָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם עֵר וְאוֹנָן – חֲשׁוֹכָא.
connections.quote: “Er and Onan themselves were reincarnated in Peretz and Zerach, the sons of their father Yehudah.”
connections.context: This is the explicit kabbalistic identification behind the transition from Er and Onan to Peretz. Rav Tzadok applies that identification to the pattern of darkness preceding light.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָךְ הוּא הַסֵּדֶר, וְ"הָעָם הַהֹלְכִים בַּחֹשֶׁךְ רָאוּ אוֹר גָּדוֹל" (יְשַׁעְיָה ט, א), מֻפְלָג מִמִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הוֹלֵךְ בַּחֹשֶׁךְ.
connections.quote: ‘The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; upon those dwelling in a land of death’s shadow, light has shone.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ דְּעֵשָׂו הָרָשָׁע שֶׁפָּגַע בְּכַף יֶרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “When he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was dislocated as he wrestled with him.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּהַהוּא דִּמְטָא זַרְזִיפָא דְּמַיָּא אַרֵישֵׁיהּ, אֲמַר וְכוּלֵי: "מֵאַשְׁפֹּת יָרִים אֶבְיוֹן" (יוֹמָא פז.):
connections.quote: ‘He raises the poor from the dust; He lifts the needy from the refuse heap.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּהַהוּא דִּמְטָא זַרְזִיפָא דְּמַיָּא אַרֵישֵׁיהּ, אֲמַר וְכוּלֵי: "מֵאַשְׁפֹּת יָרִים אֶבְיוֹן" (יוֹמָא פז.):
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Abba had a grievance against Rabbi Yirmeya. Rabbi Yirmeya went and sat at Rabbi Abba’s door. As Rabbi Abba’s maidservant poured out water, splashes of it reached his head. He said: ‘They have made me into a refuse heap.’ He applied to himself the verse: ‘He raises the needy from the refuse heaps.’ Rabbi Abba heard and came out to him. He said: ‘Now I need to appease you, as it is written: ‘Go, humble yourself, and plead with your fellow.’’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ח:) עַל "כָּל לֹחֲצָיו" – אֲפִילּוּ גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה.
connections.quote: “What authority is there in charity collection? Rav Nachman said in Rabba bar Avuha’s name: They take collateral for charity, even on the eve of Shabbat. Is that so? Is it not written, “I will punish all his oppressors,” and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta said in Rav’s name: Even charity collectors?”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ח:) עַל "כָּל לֹחֲצָיו" – אֲפִילּוּ גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה.
connections.quote: “It is not difficult: one case concerns someone assessed as wealthy, and the other someone who is not wealthy.”
connections.context: The Gemara distinguishes legitimate collection from pressing someone who cannot afford it. Rav Tzadok cites the warning about collectors as an example of responsibility for causing distress, even in an activity directed toward a mitzvah.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ח:) עַל "כָּל לֹחֲצָיו" – אֲפִילּוּ גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה.
connections.quote: ‘His children shall be as in former times, and his congregation shall be established before Me. I will call all his oppressors to account.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ח:) עַל "כָּל לֹחֲצָיו" – אֲפִילּוּ גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה.
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 7:11
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 7:11
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 7:11
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות מתנות עניים ז׳:י״א
connections.quote: “If a generous person gives more charity than is appropriate for him, or causes himself hardship and gives to the collectors so that he will not be embarrassed, it is forbidden to demand charity from him or collect it from him. A collector who humiliates him and asks him for it will eventually be punished, as it is said, “I will punish all who oppress him.””
connections.context: Rambam makes explicit that a donor’s shame-driven willingness does not permit collectors to press him beyond his means. This adds a concrete qualification to the existing Gemara and directly illustrates Rav Tzadok’s concern about causing pain in pursuit of a mitzvah.

connections.hePhrase: נֶעֱנַשׁ מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה: רָגְמוּ בוֹ אֶבֶן.
connections.quote: ‘King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was in charge of the levy, and all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam exerted himself to climb into his chariot and flee to Jerusalem.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (יא.) בַּאֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ: הַכֹּל נַעֲשׂוּ רָשִׁים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וַיָּשֶׂם מַס";
connections.quote: ‘Shmuel said: Because the faces of Israel were blackened—hushcheru—in his days like the bottom of a pot. Rabbi Yochanan said: Anyone who remembers him says, ‘Woe to his head’—ach le-rosho. Rabbi Chanina said: Because everyone became poor—rashim—in his days, as it is said: ‘King Achashverosh imposed a tax.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מִקְרָא דְּ"שָׂרֵי מִסִּים לְמַעַן עַנֹּתוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת א, יא), דְּהוֹרָאַת מַס הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּהַכְבָּדָה לְעַנּוֹת נֶפֶשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘They appointed taskmasters over them to afflict them with their burdens. They built store cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Raamses.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כד): אֲפִילּוּ אֶבֶן שֶׁנִּסְקַל וְעֵץ שֶׁנִּצְלַב עָתִיד לִיתֵּן הַדִּין.
connections.quote: see note 885 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The passage appears in a discussion of Amalek and responsibility for harm to Israel. Rav Tzadok extends the image of an accountable instrument to the agent of punishment. The source does not add the former footnote’s sentence about every instrument being purified.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הָיוּ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין מִתְעַנִּין אוֹתוֹ יוֹם (סַנְהֶדְרִין סג.) לְכַפֵּר עַל נַפְשׁוֹתָם,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Akiva says: From where do we know that a Sanhedrin that put a person to death may not taste anything for that entire day? Scripture says: ‘Do not eat over the blood.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הָיוּ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין מִתְעַנִּין אוֹתוֹ יוֹם (סַנְהֶדְרִין סג.) לְכַפֵּר עַל נַפְשׁוֹתָם,
connections.quote: “For even the tree on which a person was hanged and the stone with which he was stoned will eventually be called to account, as they said in Tanna Devei Eliyahu. Therefore the Sanhedrin fasted that day to atone for themselves and to clarify that their intention was for the sake of Heaven. The clarification came through the condemned person’s confession, for one mitzvah leads to another, and every holy matter and deed done for the sake of Heaven gives birth to holiness in the world. If an opening of repentance arose within him so that he confessed, their action was truly for life—eternal life—and not for death. Through this it became clear that their action was solely for the sake of Heaven, without any hatred or worldly motive.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s fuller explanation connects the judges’ fast with scrutiny of their own motives and with the condemned person’s repentance. It adds the inward reason for the fast to the existing Talmudic citation.

connections.hePhrase: וְסַנְהֶדְרִין הַהוֹרֶגֶת וְכוּלֵי נִקְרֵאת חָבְלָנִית (מַכּוֹת ז.),
connections.quote: ‘‘A Sanhedrin that executes,’ and so forth. They raised the following question: Is one that executes once in seventy years called destructive, or is that the ordinary course of things? The question remains unresolved.’

connections.hePhrase: וְסַנְהֶדְרִין הַהוֹרֶגֶת וְכוּלֵי נִקְרֵאת חָבְלָנִית (מַכּוֹת ז.),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: Had we been in the Sanhedrin, no person would ever have been executed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: They too would increase the number of murderers in Israel.”
connections.context: This is the continuation of the Mishnah after the statement quoted in the existing note. It preserves both the attempt to avoid executions and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s concern about its consequences, supplying the source’s own tension between restraint and the duty of judgment.

connections.hePhrase: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא בְּדִין נֶעֱנָשׁ, דְּגַם "כָּל שֶׁחֲבֵירוֹ נֶעֱנָשׁ עַל יָדוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (שַׁבָּת קמט:);
connections.quote: “Rather, it is derived from here: “Even to punish through a righteous person is not good.” “Not good” means evil, and it is written, “For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You”—You, Hashem, are righteous, and evil shall not dwell in Your abode.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s final proof for the statement that one through whom another is punished is not admitted to God’s presence. It completes the discussion begun in the existing note, which cites the dictum and an earlier proposed proof.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַהוֹרֵג שׁוֹגֵג חַיָּיב גָּלוּת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהַלָּה מְחוּיָּב מִיתָה כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מַכּוֹת י:) דִּמְגַלְגְּלִין וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: see note 491 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The story combines a providential outcome for the earlier intentional killer with continuing responsibility for the person whose accidental act brings it about. This is exactly the distinction Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מִצְוָה וּ"בִעַרְתָּ הָרָע", מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֲרֵי גּוֹרֵם צַעַר לְמַעְלָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם,
connections.quote: ‘The hand of the witnesses shall be against him first, to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. You shall remove the evil from your midst.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין מו.): שְׁכִינָה מָה אוֹמֶרֶת וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Meir said: When a person suffers, what expression does the Shekhinah utter? ‘My head is heavy upon Me; My arm is heavy upon Me.’ If, then, the Omnipresent suffers over the blood of the wicked that is shed, how much more so over the blood of the righteous.’

connections.hePhrase: [אַמְנָם מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הוּא דַּיְיקָא לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אַדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – יָדֶיךָ חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת בָּהֶן עוֹלָמִי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, “David, I know that your hands are sharp and resolute, and I wish to govern My world with them.” Another interpretation: “David, I need her for future generations. Your teacher Moshe already sought to contend with them, and I said to him, ‘Enough for you.’ Let the master command his disciples: ‘Go around this mountain.’””
connections.context: This is the Midrash behind the abbreviated description of David’s hands. Its setting concerns David’s desire to confront Rome/Edom, and the adjoining interpretation restraining such confrontation is retained; Rav Tzadok uses the first formulation to describe the severity attached to kingship.

connections.hePhrase: [אַמְנָם מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הוּא דַּיְיקָא לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אַדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – יָדֶיךָ חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת בָּהֶן עוֹלָמִי.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
connections.quote: ““Malki-Tzedek, king of Shalem, brought out bread and wine, and he was a priest.” The verse says, “Through Me kings reign.” In its plain word order it could have said, “Through Me reign kings.” Placing “kings” first hints that the Holy One appoints as king only someone able first to rule himself; such a person is then appointed over others, as in “Who is mighty? One who conquers his impulse.” Thus “through Me kings” means one who rules himself, whose mind governs his desire; then “they reign,” becoming king over all.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach interprets the same verse, “Through Me kings reign,” as self-rule preceding rule of others. This supplies a further condition beside the existing note on the Sanhedrin: the siman's royal exception is not an outlet for an uncontrolled impulse. The comparison describes a prerequisite of authority; self-confidence alone does not confer that office or its powers.
connections.headline: Rule over oneself precedes rule over others

connections.hePhrase: [אַמְנָם מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הוּא דַּיְיקָא לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אַדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – יָדֶיךָ חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת בָּהֶן עוֹלָמִי.
connections.quote: “And this is the high spiritual rung of King David, peace be upon him, as known in the mystical secret of “And I am prayer”, who is described as ruddy (admoni), paralleling the reddish power of Edom, whose hands are likewise sharp and zealous to conquer and dominate his world, except that David acts solely with the authorization of the Sanhedrin (Bereishit Rabbah 63), meaning: everything is conducted strictly according to Torah. And he merited that “Hashem was with him”— meaning the halachah is established in accordance with him everywhere (Sanhedrin 93b), because through heartfelt prayer one merits the wisdom of Torah in its ultimate wholeness.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla identifies David’s forceful royal role with action only under the direction of the Sanhedrin, and joins that role to prayer for the wisdom of Torah. This clarifies the boundary of the siman’s final exception. A private conviction that one is accomplishing a mitzvah is not the same thing as the accountable authority it describes.
connections.headline: The exception of authority remains governed by Torah

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "אַדְמוֹנִי" כִּבְעֵשָׂו, רַק "עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם" – מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סג), לְכָךְ זָכָה לְמַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: “The first came out ruddy (admoni), all of him like a hairy mantle, and they named him Esau.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "אַדְמוֹנִי" כִּבְעֵשָׂו, רַק "עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם" – מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סג), לְכָךְ זָכָה לְמַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: “He sent and brought him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a good appearance. The Lord said: Rise and anoint him, for this is he.”
connections.context: This is the biblical description of David on which the preceding Midrash builds. “Beautiful eyes” becomes the Midrash’s image of the Sanhedrin’s guidance; that interpretation is not a separate literal statement in the verse.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "אַדְמוֹנִי" כִּבְעֵשָׂו, רַק "עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם" – מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סג), לְכָךְ זָכָה לְמַלְכוּת.
connections.quote: ““Ruddy”—Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: As though a shedder of blood. When Samuel saw that David was ruddy, he feared and said: This one sheds blood like Esau. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “With beautiful eyes.” Esau kills on his own authority; this one kills on the authority of the Sanhedrin.”
connections.context: The Midrash reads the contrast between Esau and David through the qualification “beautiful eyes.” Rav Tzadok uses that distinction between unrestrained force and force governed by Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁאוּל נִסְתַּלֵּק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה רַחְמָן עַל הָאַכְזָרִים כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: see note 354 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Midrash interprets the specific biblical contrast between Shaul’s sparing Amalek and his violence against Nov, and records two conclusions. It supplies the background for Rav Tzadok’s reference to Shaul within his discussion of the responsibilities of biblical kingship.

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "בִּי מְלָכִים יִמְלֹכוּ", כִּי אוֹרַיְיתָא נָפְקָא מִגְּבוּרָה כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, פ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: ‘He said to him: ‘Fear of Hashem’ is written, not Torah. He said to him: That is certainly so, for Torah comes from the side of Gevurah. He said to him: Does it issue from there? It issues from here, for it is written: ‘The beginning of wisdom is fear of Hashem’ (Psalms 111:10), and it is written: ‘Fear of Hashem is pure.’ Torah is called holiness, as it is written: ‘For I, Hashem, am holy’; this is Torah, which is the supernal holy Name. Therefore, one who occupies himself with it is purified and afterward becomes holy, as it is written: ‘You shall be holy.’ It is not written ‘Be holy,’ but ‘You shall be’; you shall indeed be. He said to him: That is so, and Scripture says: ‘You shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation’ (Exodus 19:6), and it is written: ‘These are the words,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יָדוֹ זָכָה מֹשֶׁה לְמַלְכוּת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם, אָמַר לוֹ קֹרַח: "מַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ".
connections.quote: ‘They assembled against Moses and Aaron and said to them: ‘You have taken too much upon yourselves! The whole congregation is holy, every one of them, and Hashem is among them. Why, then, do you raise yourselves above Hashem’s assembly?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְנַשֵּׂא כְּשֶׁעוֹשֶׂה מִדַּת הַדִּין בָּרְשָׁעִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה]:
connections.quote: ““Speak to the children of Israel: You shall be holy.” This is what Scripture says: “Hashem of hosts is exalted through judgment.” When does the Holy One, blessed be He, become exalted in His world? When He executes judgment upon the nations, as it is said, “Hashem stands to contend, and stands to judge peoples.””
connections.context: The opening of Tanchuma Kedoshim supplies the precise Midrashic formulation invoked by Rav Tzadok’s closing sentence: divine exaltation through judgment.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין כ:): ג' מִצְווֹת נִצְטַוּוּ בִּכְנִיסָתָן וְכוּלֵי: מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק, וְאַחַר כָּךְ בִּנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosei says: Israel were commanded three commandments upon entering the land: to appoint a king, to cut off the descendants of Amalek, and to build the chosen House.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין כ:): ג' מִצְווֹת נִצְטַוּוּ בִּכְנִיסָתָן וְכוּלֵי: מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק, וְאַחַר כָּךְ בִּנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
connections.quote: “I still do not know whether building the chosen House comes first, or cutting off the descendants of Amalek comes first. When it says, “He will give you rest from all your enemies,” followed by, “Then the place that the Lord will choose,” it follows that cutting off the descendants of Amalek comes first.”
connections.context: The second passage supplies the order Rav Tzadok needs: the removal of opposition precedes the building of the Temple. A list of the three commandments alone did not establish that order.

connections.hePhrase: וַחֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): וְהֵיכָן מִתְרוֹמֶמֶת קַרְנָם? בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם;
connections.quote: “And where is their horn raised? In Jerusalem, as it says, “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem; those who love you shall prosper.””
connections.context: The Gemara is explaining the order of the Amidah’s blessings: the raising of the righteous is connected with Jerusalem. Rav Tzadok applies that link to the transition from defeating evil to establishing holiness.

connections.hePhrase: וּבָתֵּי כְּנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת הֵם קְדוּשַּׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּמְגִילָּה (כט.): דַּעֲתִידִים שֶׁיִּקָּבְעוּ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: “They told Rabbi Yochanan: “There are elderly people in Babylonia.” He was astonished and said: “It is written, ‘So that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied upon the land’—but not outside the Land?” When they told him that these people came early and stayed late at the synagogue, he said: “That is what has benefited them.””
connections.context: The Gemara connects the longevity promised in the Land with devotion to the synagogue in Babylonia. It supplies a distinct original source for the special quality of the synagogue outside the Land, alongside the existing source about its future relocation.

connections.hePhrase: וּבָתֵּי כְּנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת הֵם קְדוּשַּׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּמְגִילָּה (כט.): דַּעֲתִידִים שֶׁיִּקָּבְעוּ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: The synagogues and study houses in Babylonia will eventually be established in the Land of Israel, as it is said: ‘For like Tabor among the mountains, and like Carmel by the sea, he shall come.’ Is this not an inference from the lesser to the greater? Tabor and Carmel, which came only temporarily to learn Torah, became established in the Land of Israel. How much more so the synagogues and study houses in which people read and spread Torah!’

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בְּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת וּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ חָדָשׁ, שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא "מִקְדָּשׁ מְעַט" כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם), נִתְנַשֵּׂא גַּם כֵּן נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת נְשִׂיאוּת מְעַט עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַמְנָאַת מֶלֶךְ.
connections.quote: ““Yet I have been for them a small sanctuary”: Rabbi Yitzchak said: These are the synagogues and study houses in Babylonia. Rabbi Elazar said: This is the house of our master in Babylonia.”
connections.context: This is the precise source for the designation “small sanctuary.” Both interpretations are retained; the existing note elsewhere in the section quotes the separate teaching about future relocation to the Land of Israel.

connections.hePhrase: רַק בִּכְנִיסָה לָאָרֶץ הָיָה זֶה קוֹדֶם מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק.
connections.quote: “When it says, “For a hand is upon the throne of Yah: Hashem has war with Amalek,” you must say that appointing a king comes first. “Throne” means a king, as it is said, “Shlomo sat upon the throne of Hashem as king.””
connections.context: The existing quotation lists the three commands and proves that Amalek precedes the Temple. This intervening source unit supplies the omitted proof that appointing a king came first on Israel’s entry into the Land.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְעָתִיד לָבוֹא יִהְיֶה הַסֵּדֶר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (ה.) לִג' רִאשׁוֹן, וְחָשֵׁיב שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ בַּסּוֹף,
connections.quote: ‘For cutting off the descendants of Esau, as it is written: ‘The first came out ruddy, all over like a hairy cloak.’ And for the building of the Temple, as it is written: ‘A throne of glory, exalted from the first, is the place of our Sanctuary.’ And for the name of the Messiah, as it is written: ‘First to Zion: Behold, here they are.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְעָתִיד לָבוֹא יִהְיֶה הַסֵּדֶר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (ה.) לִג' רִאשׁוֹן, וְחָשֵׁיב שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ בַּסּוֹף,
connections.quote: ““As a reward for three instances of ‘first’”: The cessation of work on the festival of Pesach, the cessation of work on the festival of Sukkot, and the taking of the lulav, which were called “first”—through them they merited three things called “first.””
connections.context: Rashi identifies the three mitzvot behind the Gemara’s shorthand. This complements the existing note, which supplies the three future consequences and their verses.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא נֶגֶד רִאשׁוֹן דְּפֶסַח, דִּבְנִיסָן עֲתִידִין לִגָּאֵל.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua says: In Nisan the world was created; in Nisan the Patriarchs were born; in Nisan the Patriarchs died; on Pesach Yitzchak was born; on Rosh Hashanah Sarah, Rachel, and Channah were remembered; on Rosh Hashanah Yosef left prison; on Rosh Hashanah our ancestors’ labor in Egypt ceased; in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Nisan they are destined to be redeemed.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok invokes Rabbi Yehoshua’s position that future redemption will occur in Nisan. The immediately preceding baraita records Rabbi Eliezer’s different position, placing future redemption in Tishrei; the Nisan statement is attributed to its speaker.

connections.hePhrase: כְּרִיתַת זֶרַע עֲמָלֵק שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד לוּלָב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ל) דְּמוֹרֶה עַל נִצּוּחַ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Avin said: It is like two people who came before the judge, and we do not know which one won. When one takes palm branches in his hand, we know that he was victorious. So Israel and the nations of the world come before the Holy One, blessed be He, in judgment on Rosh Hashanah, and we do not know who won. When Israel comes out with palm branches and citrons in their hands, we know that Israel was victorious.”
connections.context: The lulav is the Midrash’s visible sign of victory in judgment. Rav Tzadok uses that symbolism when associating the lulav with overcoming opposition.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ דְּנִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן "סֻכַּת שָׁלֵם" (תְּהִלִּים עו, ג).
connections.quote: “His shelter was in Salem, and His dwelling in Zion.”
connections.context: The Hebrew word for “shelter” is sukkah. Rav Tzadok draws on that word to connect the Temple in Jerusalem, here called Salem, with Sukkot.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְעוֹלָם מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק קוֹדֶמֶת,
connections.quote: “As long as Amalek is in the world, the wing covers the face, and it is impossible to attain completely clarified knowledge. Therefore, when entering the land, Israel was commanded to cut off Amalek's seed. Clear knowledge would then follow, and they would attain a complete acquisition from the root according to the clarity of Israel's knowledge.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the order at entry to the land through the knowledge needed for a complete acquisition. Amalek covers the face; removing that concealment permits a clarified connection with the root. This develops why the siman connects the prior removal of the root of evil with the permanence of sacred place.
connections.headline: Clear knowledge and an acquisition from the root

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ קְדוּשַׁת הַמָּקוֹם לֹא פָּסְקָה, דִּקְדֻשָּׁה רִאשׁוֹנָה קִדְּשָׁה לִשְׁעָתָהּ וְקִדְּשָׁה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֵן שׁוֹמְמִין.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua said: I heard that sacrifices may be offered even though there is no Temple building; that the most sacred offerings may be eaten even though there are no enclosing curtains; and that offerings of lesser sanctity and the second tithe may be eaten even though there is no city wall, because the first sanctification sanctified the place for its own time and for the future.”
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s explicit formulation of the enduring sanctity of the Temple and Jerusalem despite the loss of their physical structures. It supplies the legal source abbreviated in the body.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ קְדוּשַׁת הַמָּקוֹם לֹא פָּסְקָה, דִּקְדֻשָּׁה רִאשׁוֹנָה קִדְּשָׁה לִשְׁעָתָהּ וְקִדְּשָׁה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֵן שׁוֹמְמִין.
connections.quote: “It is known that King Shlomo’s entire aim was to attain this light of Mashiach and that his building should be the final, hoped-for building. In truth, he achieved this spiritually, for we hold that the first sanctification sanctified for its own time and for the future; this is Shlomo’s sanctity. But he did not achieve it physically, in a form revealed to human eyes, for the building was destroyed. The destruction, however, is analogous to the shattering of the vessels, and in the future it will be revealed that even the substance of his building endures forever, as our Sages said.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok elsewhere distinguishes the enduring spiritual sanctity achieved by Shlomo from the visible destruction of the building. This develops the distinction used here between an interruption in outward form and an enduring sanctity.

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד פָּסְקָה לְפִי שָׁעָה, לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה אָז קוֹדֶמֶת לִמְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק.
connections.quote: “Shaul was the first king, and had he fulfilled the eradication of Amalek, the final repair would have occurred then. Concerning the Rosh Chodesh goat, the Zohar says that one goat draws the opposing power to its own place so that it separates from the moon; this is the eradication of Amalek commanded to Shaul. Although the principal kingship of David comes from Yehudah, Shaul was commanded concerning Amalek, who falls only through Rachel's descendants, as Bereshit Rabbah teaches. Amalek is the beginning of the impure shell, and the supernal crown is the crown of kingship; a king who embodies that quality can subdue it. “Mashiach” has the numerical value of “nachash,” as the holy books explain, and he will repair everything. Had Shaul fulfilled the command to erase Amalek's memory, he would have been Mashiach ben Yosef. As Rema MiPano wrote concerning Yonatan's words, “I shall be second to you,” he intended to be Mashiach ben Yosef; so too Shaul would have been Mashiach ben Yosef had he fulfilled Amalek's eradication. Shaul too is called “Hashem's anointed.””
connections.explanation: Kislev explains that Shaul, the first king, could have reached the completion associated with Mashiach ben Yosef by fulfilling the Amalek command. This supplies a concrete counterpart to the siman's distinction between the first, interrupted kingship and the later completion after the root of opposition is removed. The quotation addresses that national order; the siman itself makes the further, limited application to the leadership of a new mikdash me'at.
connections.headline: Shaul and the completion that did not yet occur

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד פָּסְקָה לְפִי שָׁעָה, לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה אָז קוֹדֶמֶת לִמְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק.
connections.quote: “So it will be in the future: Mashiach son of Yosef in Adar, and Mashiach son of David in Nissan, when the complete redemption will take place. Adar is the removal of Amalek, which falls only through Yosef's descendants, the flame consuming the house of Esav, preceding the completed divine name and throne disclosed in redemption. Mashiach son of Yosef will fight Amalek then. After its removal he will merit the complete name, the level of Judah, who is called by the Holy One's whole name, while Yosef has only three of its letters, corresponding to the time before the name is complete.”
connections.explanation: Divrei Chalomot develops the same future sequence through Adar and Nissan. The work associated with Yosef and Amalek precedes the full disclosure associated with Judah. This clarifies why the siman makes the order relevant to permanence. Its extension to a small sanctuary remains an analogy about preparing its foundations before personal elevation.
connections.headline: The two messianic stages have an order

connections.hePhrase: [קעז] בְּכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ פַּרְדֵּ"ס.
