connections.quote: “The Shechinah is also called the pardes of Torah because she comprises peshat, scriptural proof, derashah, and the secret of Torah. This is the mnemonic PaRDeS.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "חֵרֵשׁ רוֹמֵז וְנִרְמָז" (גִּטִּין נט.), שֶׁהָרֶמֶז הוּא רוֹמֵז עַל הַמְּכֻוָּון שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהוֹצִיאוֹ לַפּוֹעַל.
connections.quote: “MISHNAH: A deaf-mute may signal (his intent in a transaction), and others may signal to him. Ben Beteira says: He may move his lips, and others may move their lips to him, concerning movable property. Young children’s purchases are valid purchases, and their sales are valid sales, concerning movable property.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג שְׁלֹשָׁה אֵלּוּ – כְּלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גּוֹמְרִים, וְלֵב חוֹמֵד, וְעַיִן רוֹאֶה חָכְמַת הַדָּבָר – אָז זוֹכֶה לְסוֹד,
connections.quote: “What the Sages said (Yoma 75a), that the manna changed into every taste, refers to the actual manna that Israel ate. But when the Sages said (Mekhilta, Beshalach, Vayassa 5) that goats and gazelles ate from it and the nations of the world tasted manna in their flesh, what was perceptible there was only the essential taste of manna described in the Torah: “like a wafer with honey” (Exodus 16:31), and nothing more. The taste absorbed into their flesh no longer changed, and therefore the nations of the world could taste it too. This also resolves the statement that the mixed multitude could not taste the manna [meaning its changing tastes. This is the principal difference between manna and all other foods, revealing that it is bread from heaven rather than from earth, with no earthly counterpart at all. This belongs only to Israel, who could eat such bread. The mixed multitude, however, presumably were also nourished by manna in the wilderness; they were the ones who said, “Our soul loathes this insubstantial bread” (Numbers 21:5), since at least the beginning of all the complaints came from them, and most or all of them did. Because they sensed in it only one ordinary taste, they became weary of its sameness. See the holy Zohar, Ki Tissa 191b: Scripture proclaims, “The children of Israel ate the manna” (Exodus 16:35), excluding the mixed multitude. Nevertheless, it says there that they ate from its residue and from what Israel gave them; see there. This too can be explained as I have written].”
connections.explanation: Divrei Chalomot distinguishes the manna’s ordinary taste, which could be encountered indirectly, from its changing tastes experienced by Israel. This develops the present siman’s definition of sod as a taste that cannot simply be conveyed by description. The outward object may be shared while the inward reception differs. Tzidkat HaTzadik places that reception after action, desire of the heart, and understanding; the illustration therefore clarifies the meaning of taste without replacing those stages of avodah.
connections.headline: Sharing an outward food does not ensure sharing its inward taste

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא עִנְיַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.): לְאָדָם טוֹב מַטְעִימִין לוֹ מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: ““Say of the righteous that he is good, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.” Is there a righteous person who is good and one who is not good? Rather, one who is good toward Heaven and toward people is a good righteous person.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא עִנְיַן מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.): לְאָדָם טוֹב מַטְעִימִין לוֹ מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: “Merit has a principal and has fruits, as it says, “Say of the righteous that he is good.””
connections.context: These sayings distinguish the enduring principal from the fruits of good deeds. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the experiential “taste” of those fruits in this world.

connections.hePhrase: הַטַּעַם עַל דֶּרֶךְ "טַעֲמוּ וּרְאוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים לד, ט) נִקְרָא סוֹד,
connections.quote: ‘Taste and see that Hashem is good; fortunate is the man who takes refuge in Him.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַסְבִּיר לַחֲבֵירוֹ טַעַם שֶׁהוּא מַרְגִּישׁ בְּחִכּוֹ,
connections.heRef: יושר דברי אמת, קונטרס ראשון כ״ב:א׳
connections.quote: “This is called the hidden wisdom. I heard from the holy mouth of our teacher Rabbi Menachem Mendel, of blessed memory, that “hidden” means something a person cannot convey to another. It is like the taste of food: one cannot describe it to a person who has never tasted that flavor; one cannot explain in words how and what it is. This is called a hidden matter. So too with love and fear of the Creator, blessed be His name: one cannot explain to another what the love in the heart is like. This is called “hidden.” But as for what people call hidden—the wisdom of Kabbalah—how is it hidden? The book lies before anyone who wishes to study it. If he does not understand, he is unlearned, and for such a person Gemara and Tosafot are also called hidden. Rather, the hidden matters throughout the Zohar and the writings of the Ari are all founded on cleaving to the Creator, for one who merits to cleave to Him and behold the supernal Chariot, like the Ari, of blessed memory, to whom the paths of heaven were clear, and who constantly walked in them with the eyes of his intellect, like the four Sages who entered the pardes, as explained in Tosafot to Chagigah and in Hagahot Maimoniyot at the beginning of Sefer HaMadda, at the end of chapter four; see there.”
connections.context: Yosher Divrei Emet records Rabbi Menachem Mendel’s explanation of a secret as an inward experience that words cannot transmit, using the very analogy of taste. The selection retains the ensuing distinction between an unread or misunderstood book and the experience of attachment to God.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמְרוּ (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק לז): שְׁנַיִם אוֹכְלִין מִקְּעָרָה אַחַת, כָּל אֶחָד טוֹעֵם לְפִי מַעֲשָׂיו.
connections.quote: “Two people eat from one bowl: this one tastes according to his deeds, and that one tastes according to his deeds. Two dye in one vat: for one the color comes out beautiful, and for the other it comes out unattractive.”
connections.context: The common bowl illustrates different experiences of the same outward thing. Rav Tzadok uses this as an analogy for an inward taste of Torah that cannot be transferred merely by repeating words.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מַה שֶּׁאֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיד, הֲרֵי אַחַר שֶׁהִגִּיד שׁוּב נוֹדַע גַּם לְהָאַחֵר, וְאֵיךְ הוּא סוֹד וָסֵתֶר, וְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ: "סוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו" (תְּהִלִּים כה, יד) אוֹ "לִישָׁרִים סוֹדוֹ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, לב)?
connections.quote: “The secret counsel of the Lord is for those who fear Him, and His covenant is to make them know.”
connections.context: Sod can denote intimate counsel or a secret. Rav Tzadok asks what makes divine knowledge a true secret if it can simply be repeated to another person.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מַה שֶּׁאֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיד, הֲרֵי אַחַר שֶׁהִגִּיד שׁוּב נוֹדַע גַּם לְהָאַחֵר, וְאֵיךְ הוּא סוֹד וָסֵתֶר, וְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ: "סוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו" (תְּהִלִּים כה, יד) אוֹ "לִישָׁרִים סוֹדוֹ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, לב)?
connections.quote: “For the perverse person is an abomination to the Lord, but His secret counsel is with the upright.”
connections.context: This verse uses the same word sod as the preceding Psalm. It is the second stage, the upright, in the Midrashic progression quoted next.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה מט) וּבְתַנְחוּמָא (וַיֵּרָא ו): דִּבְסוֹף לִנְבִיאִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי אִם גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים" (עָמוֹס ג, ז);
connections.quote: “At first, “The secret of the Lord is for those who fear Him”; afterward, for the upright—“His secret is with the upright”; afterward, for the prophets—“The Lord God does nothing without revealing His secret to His servants the prophets.” The Holy One said: Abraham is God-fearing; Abraham is upright among the upright; Abraham is a prophet—and shall I not reveal it to him?”
connections.context: The Midrash applies all three descriptions to Abraham before the disclosure concerning Sodom. Rav Tzadok develops their sequence into his account of inward fear, upright action, and prophetic knowledge.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה מט) וּבְתַנְחוּמָא (וַיֵּרָא ו): דִּבְסוֹף לִנְבִיאִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי אִם גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים" (עָמוֹס ג, ז);
connections.quote: “Another explanation of Then he openeth the ears of men: This alludes to Abraham, for it is said: And God said: Shall I hide from Abraham?, and By their chastisement sealeth the decree (Job 33:16) refers to the Sodomites, against whom He sealed the decree when a single righteous man could not be found amongst them. Another comment on And the Lord said: Shall I hide from Abraham? Scripture states elsewhere in allusion to this verse: For the Lord will do nothing, but He revealeth His counsel unto His servants, the prophets (Amos 3:7). In the beginning the Holy One, blessed be He, used to reveal His secrets to those who feared Him, as it is said: The counsel of the Lord is with them that fear Him (Ps. 25:14). Then He made His secrets known to the righteous, as is said: In the council of the upright and in the congregation (Ps. 111:1); and finally He revealed it only to the prophets, as it is said: But He revealeth His counsel unto His servants, the prophets. After Israel transgressed at the time of Achan, the Holy One, blessed be He, informed Joshua, as it is said: Israel hath sinned (Josh. 7:11). When Eli’s sons sinned, the Holy One, blessed be He, disclosed it to Samuel, as is said: And the Lord called Samuel (I Sam. 3:4). When the Sodomites sinned, the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed it to Abraham, as is said: Shall I hide from Abraham?”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה מט) וּבְתַנְחוּמָא (וַיֵּרָא ו): דִּבְסוֹף לִנְבִיאִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי אִם גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ אֶל עֲבָדָיו הַנְּבִיאִים" (עָמוֹס ג, ז);
connections.quote: ‘For the Lord, Hashem, does nothing unless He has revealed His secret to His servants, the prophets.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה – עִיקָּר רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי, וּמִשֶּׁנִּתְּנָה תּוֹרָה נִתְחַדְּשׁוּ מַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת.
connections.quote: see note 1566 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rava’s comparison between his generation and Rav Yehudah’s concludes that inward devotion is decisive. It supplies the saying abbreviated here; Rav Tzadok’s application to the stages before and after the giving of the Torah is his own development.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בַּסּוֹף לִנְבִיאִים, דְּהַיְינוּ הַכּוֹלְלִים כָּל הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת צב.): אֵין הַשְּׁכִינָה שׁוֹרָה אֶלָּא עַל חָכָם בַּמּוֹחַ, גִּבּוֹר הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ בַּלֵּב, וְעָשִׁיר בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת
connections.quote: “Alternatively, it can be derived from the Ark. For the Master said: The Ark was nine handbreadths high and its cover one handbreadth, making ten. We have a received tradition that any load lifted by poles has one-third above the poles and two-thirds below; it follows that the Ark stood more than ten handbreadths above the ground. Why not derive it from Moshe? Perhaps Moshe was different, for the Master said: The Divine Presence rests only upon one who is wise, strong, wealthy, and tall.”
connections.context: The Gemara lists wisdom, strength, wealth, and stature as qualifications in its discussion of Moses. Rav Tzadok gives wisdom, strength, and wealth a spiritual application here: understanding, mastery of desire, and abundance of mitzvot. Those explanations are his interpretation of the list.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בַּסּוֹף לִנְבִיאִים, דְּהַיְינוּ הַכּוֹלְלִים כָּל הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת צב.): אֵין הַשְּׁכִינָה שׁוֹרָה אֶלָּא עַל חָכָם בַּמּוֹחַ, גִּבּוֹר הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ בַּלֵּב, וְעָשִׁיר בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת
connections.quote: “Know that no prophet prophesied until he possessed all the intellectual virtues and most of the moral virtues, including the strongest of them. This is their statement: “Prophecy rests only upon one who is wise, mighty, and wealthy.” “Wise” unquestionably includes all the intellectual virtues. “Wealthy” is one of the moral virtues, meaning contentment, for they call the contented person wealthy. Thus they define the wealthy person: “Who is wealthy? One who rejoices in his portion”—meaning that what his circumstances have provided suffices for him, and he does not grieve over what they have not provided. “Mighty” is likewise one of the moral virtues, meaning that he directs his powers according to understanding and counsel, as we explained in chapter five. This is their statement: “Who is mighty? One who masters his inclination.””
connections.context: Rambam interprets the prophetic qualities inwardly: wisdom, contentment, and self-mastery. The qualification “most” of the moral virtues is preserved. Rav Tzadok applies a related framework to the mind, heart, and performance of mitzvot.

connections.hePhrase: [וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד שְׁלֹשָׁה: קִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד; עָשִׁיר הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מְקַנֵּא, וְגִבּוֹר נֶגֶד הַתַּאֲוָה, וְכָבוֹד – חֲכָמִים יִנְחָלוּ]:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: Envy, desire, and honor remove a person from the world.”
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s threefold list behind the closing comparison. Rav Tzadok sets contentment, mastery of desire, and the honor associated with wisdom against these three destructive tendencies.

connections.hePhrase: [וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד שְׁלֹשָׁה: קִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד; עָשִׁיר הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מְקַנֵּא, וְגִבּוֹר נֶגֶד הַתַּאֲוָה, וְכָבוֹד – חֲכָמִים יִנְחָלוּ]:
connections.quote: “Ben Zoma says: … Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination… Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion…”

connections.hePhrase: [וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד שְׁלֹשָׁה: קִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד; עָשִׁיר הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מְקַנֵּא, וְגִבּוֹר נֶגֶד הַתַּאֲוָה, וְכָבוֹד – חֲכָמִים יִנְחָלוּ]:
connections.quote: “The wise shall inherit honor, but fools carry off disgrace.”

connections.hePhrase: [קעח] כָּל הִתְנַשְּׂאוּת הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בִּי מְלָכִים יִמְלֹכוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, טו);
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
connections.quote: “It is written (Proverbs 8:15), ‘By Me kings reign.’ In ordinary syntax it could have said, ‘By Me reign kings.’ This hints that the Holy One appoints as king only someone who can first rule over himself; him He appoints over others, as it says (Avot 4:1), ‘Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination.’ ‘By Me kings reign’ means: someone who rules himself, whose understanding governs his desire, will then reign—he will be king over all. He need not heed the person opposing him, since his entire intention is for Heaven.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach examines the word order in the same verse that opens this siman. A person must first govern his own desire before being entrusted with governing others. This gives a positive account of authority grounded in Torah alongside the siman's account of borrowed authority and words spoken without understanding.
connections.headline: Rule over oneself before rule over others

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת, הָאוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ תּוֹרָה בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים – אַל תַּאֲמֵן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה ב, ט), כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, כ).
connections.quote: “Her gates have sunk into the earth; He has destroyed and broken her bars. Her king and princes are among the nations; there is no Torah. Her prophets, too, have found no vision from the Lord.”
connections.context: The words “among the nations; there is no Torah” are the basis of the preceding Midrashic interpretation. The former quotation lost those words amid imported translation notes.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת, הָאוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ תּוֹרָה בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים – אַל תַּאֲמֵן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה ב, ט), כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, כ).
connections.quote: “If someone tells you there is wisdom among the nations, believe it, as it says, “I will destroy the wise from Edom.” If someone tells you there is Torah among the nations, do not believe it, as it says, “Her king and princes are among the nations; there is no Torah.””
connections.context: The Midrash explicitly distinguishes wisdom from Torah. Its comment is on Lamentations 2:9, but in the digital Midrash it is section 2:13; 2:9 of the Midrash itself contains a different passage.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת, הָאוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ תּוֹרָה בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים – אַל תַּאֲמֵן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה ב, ט), כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, כ).
connections.quote: ‘He has not done this for any other nation; they do not know His ordinances. Praise Hashem!’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת, הָאוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ תּוֹרָה בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים – אַל תַּאֲמֵן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה ב, ט), כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, כ).
connections.quote: “This occurred because the heart was diminished through the husk of Greek wisdom, which was without heart. As we explained concerning the Midrash, ‘If they say there is Torah among the nations, do not believe it,’ for ‘there is no Torah among the nations’: their wisdom is from the lips outward and does not instruct the heart. Torah’s wisdom is different; its essential acquisition is in the heart, as it says, ‘In the heart of every wise-hearted person I have placed wisdom.’ This is the meaning of the Sages’ statement that the Greeks defiled all the oils: the wisdom in the heart, for they darkened Israel’s eyes.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah contrasts wisdom remaining at the lips with Torah whose essential acquisition is in the heart. This clarifies the present siman’s otherwise surprising observation that wicked speakers can supply words later recorded in Torah. The speaker’s outward utterance and the prophet’s recognition of its Torah-content are different attainments. The siman’s claim about those words sustaining a temporary kingdom should therefore not be confused with its denial that the speaker has acquired Torah inwardly.
connections.headline: A statement recorded in Torah differs from Torah acquired in the heart

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, הֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב נִכְתַּב הַרְבֵּה דִּבְרֵי רִשְׁעֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וְהֵם מִכְּלַל הַתּוֹרָה, וְכֵן בִּנְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:5
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:5
connections.quote: “This explains why the words of Avimelech, Pharaoh, Bilam, and the like were written in the Torah: those utterances that expressed their entire vitality, reaching the holy spark within them, were taken into the words of Torah. Even Pharaoh’s words, “Who is Hashem, that I should listen to His voice?”—since they were written in the Torah—are words at the root of his vitality, where Hashem established this claim of “Who is Hashem?” For concealment too comes from Hashem, from His true will at the root of creation: that darkness should come first, and light afterward. “He forms light and creates darkness”: creation is a higher level, as is known, for darkness issues from a deeper will, since there is also a need for darkness. Thus Hashem established that the Egyptian exile would prepare for the giving of the Torah; the existence of Egypt and Pharaoh was therefore necessary, for Hashem willed the existence of these creatures who say, “Who is Hashem?””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s fuller exposition explains how the Torah can incorporate an opponent’s words, even Pharaoh’s denial. The claim concerns the divine purpose disclosed through the Torah’s account; the opposing speaker does not thereby consciously possess Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִיָּד שֶׁהוֹצִיאוּ בִּלְעָם מִפִּיהֶם, נִתְבַּטְּלָה מַלְכוּתָם.
connections.quote: “I will punish Bel in Babylon, and I will bring out of his mouth what he has swallowed; the nations shall no longer stream to him; the wall of Babylon too has fallen.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s words “הוֹצִיאוּ בִּלְעָם מִפִּיהֶם” echo this verse.

connections.hePhrase: וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל גְּזֵירוֹתָם הוּא "תָּא נֶהֱוֵי לְעַמָּא חַד", שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר בִּנְיַן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִימוֹת חוּרְבַּן רִאשׁוֹן וְאֵילָךְ: לַהֲפוֹךְ גַּם עַל כָּל עַמִּים שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה לִקְרוֹא בְּשֵׁם ה'.
connections.quote: “Caesar said to Rabbi Tanchum: “Come, let us all become one people.” He answered: “Certainly! We, who are circumcised, cannot become like you; you can be circumcised and become like us.” He said to him: “You have spoken well, but anyone who defeats the king in argument must be thrown into the enclosure of wild beasts.” They threw him into the enclosure, but the animals did not eat him. A certain sectarian said to Caesar: “They did not eat him because they are not hungry.” They threw that man himself in, and the animals ate him.”
connections.context: The complete aggadic episode supplies the demand “Let us become one people” and Rabbi Tanchum’s reversal of it. Rav Tzadok uses the demand as a model for the spiritual root he identifies beneath religious persecution; the subsequent interpretation is his own.

connections.hePhrase: וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל גְּזֵירוֹתָם הוּא "תָּא נֶהֱוֵי לְעַמָּא חַד", שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר בִּנְיַן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִימוֹת חוּרְבַּן רִאשׁוֹן וְאֵילָךְ: לַהֲפוֹךְ גַּם עַל כָּל עַמִּים שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה לִקְרוֹא בְּשֵׁם ה'.
connections.quote: ‘For then I will give the peoples a purified speech, so that all of them may call on the name of Hashem and serve Him with one shoulder, together.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן הַפְטָרָה שֶׁנִּתְקַן עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָה שֶׁלֹּא לִקְרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה, וְהֵבִינוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה דִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַדְּרַבָּה דְּקוֹרִין רַק מְעַט, וּדְצָרִיךְ לְהוֹסִיף עוֹד קְרִיאַת מַפְטִיר בַּנְּבִיאִים.
connections.quote: ““From the Prophets, etc.” The reason is that on one occasion a decree was imposed on Israel forbidding them to occupy themselves with Torah. Seven people read from the Prophets and recited blessings over them, corresponding to the seven who should have been called to read from the Torah. They did not read fewer than three verses with each person, making twenty-one verses altogether. Therefore, even though the decree was annulled, the practice was not annulled. For this reason they instituted that the maftir read no fewer than twenty-one verses from the Prophets, and that he first read from the Torah out of respect for the Torah, as explained in section 282, Mishnah Berurah 28. The maftir recites seven blessings—the two he recites over the Torah, before and after, one before the prophetic reading, and four afterward—corresponding to the seven who read from the Torah.”
connections.context: Mishnah Berurah records the traditional explanation of the haftarah’s institution under persecution and its continuation afterward. The passage also explains the twenty-one verses and seven blessings; Rav Tzadok develops the spiritual meaning of the additional reading.

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בַּאֲמִירַת "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" בִּקְדֻשַּׁת מוּסָף שֶׁנִּתְקַן בִּגְזֵירָה עַל יְדֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר הָאֶשְׁכּוֹל
connections.quote: “The author of HaEshkol wrote: In Musaf on Shabbat, festivals, and Yom Kippur, and at Ne’ilah, one says “Shema Yisrael” and “I am Hashem your God,” which are the beginning and end of the recitation of Shema. This is because a persecutory decree forbade the recitation of Shema altogether. They therefore instituted this Kedushah in every prayer service. After the persecution was annulled, they removed it from the other Kedushot, apart from these, so that Israel would retain a remembrance of the annulment of the persecution, since these services never otherwise include the recitation of Shema.”
connections.context: Kol Bo explicitly preserves this explanation in the name of the author of HaEshkol, the work cited in the body. The quotation retains both stages: insertion during persecution and selective retention afterward, including Ne’ilah.

connections.hePhrase: [וְכַיּוֹצֵא בָּזֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֶסְתֵּר פָּרָשָׁה ז) בְּהָמָן שֶׁלִּגְלֵג שֶׁהַיּוֹם פֶּסַח וְכוּלֵי: חַיֶּיךָ עוֹד מוֹסִיפִים מוֹעֵד עַל מַפַּלְתְּךָ].
connections.quote: “He said: They eat and drink and say, “The delight of Shabbat, the delight of the festivals.” … In Nisan, Passover; in Sivan, Shavuot; in Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah, the great fast, and the festival of Sukkot. … The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Wicked one! You cast aspersions on their festivals; I will bring you down before them, and they will add another festival over your downfall. These are the days of Purim.”
connections.context: Haman’s attack on the festivals becomes the occasion for an additional festival. Rav Tzadok uses that reversal as an example of opposition contributing to the growth of holiness.

connections.hePhrase: גַּם תְּקִיעוֹת בְּמוּסָף נִתְקַן עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לב:)
connections.quote: “The one who passes before the ark on the festival of Rosh Hashanah: the second leads the shofar sounding.”

connections.hePhrase: גַּם תְּקִיעוֹת בְּמוּסָף נִתְקַן עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לב:)
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: They taught this concerning a time of persecution.”
connections.context: “The second” means the leader of Musaf, after the morning service. The Gemara asks why the shofar was not sounded earlier and answers that the arrangement arose in a time of persecution.

connections.hePhrase: גַּם תְּקִיעוֹת בְּמוּסָף נִתְקַן עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לב:)
connections.heRef: רש"י על ראש השנה ל״ב ב:כ״א:א׳
connections.quote: ““They taught this during a decree of the government”: Enemies decreed that they must not sound the shofar, and lay in wait for them throughout the six hours until the end of the morning prayer. Therefore they transferred the sounding of the shofar to Musaf.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the practical explanation missing from the existing quotation of the Gemara: the watchers waited through the morning service, so sounding the shofar was moved to Musaf.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִמְצָא הֵם הֵבִיאוּ חִדּוּשׁ תּוֹרָה זֶה לָעוֹלָם;
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Shofar, chapter 3
connections.quote: “It appears to me that there are two shofarot: the small shofar of this world, in Tevunah, and the great shofar of the future, in the supernal Binah. It also seems to me that I heard from my master, of blessed memory, that the seated shofar blasts are in Tevunah, and those of Musaf are in Binah, for that is where they ascend during Musaf.”

connections.hePhrase: [קעט] "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו) מְפוֹרָשׁ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר קמד) דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁיֵּדַע בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא הוּא הַפּוֹעֵל כְּלָל, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “Of David. Blessed is the Lord, my Rock, who trains my hands for battle, my fingers for war.”
connections.context: This is the opening verse explained by Shocher Tov, quoted in the next footnote. David attributes even his acquired skill and success to divine teaching.

connections.hePhrase: [קעט] "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו) מְפוֹרָשׁ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר קמד) דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁיֵּדַע בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא הוּא הַפּוֹעֵל כְּלָל, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: ‘‘Of David. Blessed is Hashem, my Rock,’ and so on. Solomon said: ‘In all your ways know Him’ (Proverbs 3:6). What does ‘In all your ways know Him’ mean? Keep Him in your heart, before you, on every path you take, as David used to do. He was a king, yet said: ‘I am not king; He is King, and He made me king.’ Thus it says: ‘David knew that Hashem had established him as king over Israel’ (II Samuel 5:12). He was mighty, yet said: ‘I am not mighty.’ He was wealthy, yet said: ‘I am not wealthy.’ Thus he proclaimed: ‘Yours, Hashem, are greatness and might,’ and so on (I Chronicles 29:11). Thus it also says: ‘David administered justice and righteousness for all his people’ (II Samuel 8:15). He went down to battle and won, yet said: ‘I did not win through my own might. Rather, He helped me, He enabled me to win, and I won; He formed me to wage war.’ Thus it says: ‘The God who girds me with strength’ (Psalms 18:33). Therefore he said: ‘Blessed is Hashem, my Rock,’ and so on.’

connections.hePhrase: [קעט] "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו) מְפוֹרָשׁ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר קמד) דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁיֵּדַע בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא הוּא הַפּוֹעֵל כְּלָל, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
connections.quote: “"If he conquers it, well and good; and if not, let him recite the Shema": for within the study of Torah there is an element of spiritual self-elevation and vigor, so that through Torah study a person might feel emboldened in his soul and still fail to arrive at complete, humble clarity regarding his desire; therefore the third test is to recite the Shema ("Hashem is One"), for the essence of the Shema corresponds to what is explained in the Gemara (Ta'anit 31a), that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance (machol) for the righteous— meaning that all will see that everything is equally in the hand of Hashem, blessed be He, and no individual has any superiority or self-exaltation over his fellow, just like a circle which has no head or end; and the unification of the Shema alludes to this complete nullification of self.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the same counsel to recite Shema as the recognition that everything is in Hashem’s hand and no person possesses independent superiority. This clarifies the practical direction of “know Him” here. Recognizing the source of one’s power is meant to break the autonomous posture of the yetzer, rather than certify the act it is urging.
connections.headline: Shema removes the claim to independent power

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר אִיתָא: דַּע ה"וּ – גַּם כֵּן לְכָךְ נִתְכַּוֵּין,
connections.quote: “Therefore He said to them: “Let us make a human”—in partnership with Me. Neither Torah nor a mitzvah brings about an act or deed above or below apart from Me. Therefore: “In all your ways, know Him.””

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ דְּוָא"ו הֵ"א הוּא קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵיהּ, וְיִחוּדָם הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהוּא חַד עִם כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאֵין הֵם דָּבָר נִבְדָּל מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “Since Hashem wished to be called Lord and King, and there is no king without a people, He restricted the spread of His light so that the creatures could apprehend that light, which is their vitality and continued existence, as it is written, “You give life to them all.” This is the name Adnut, indicating that He is Lord of all and that they serve Him. This is called Shechinah: that which dwells within the children of Israel. Within a person, in the depth of the heart, dwell the light and apprehension of Hashem. By contrast, apprehending Hashem as infinite and without limit is called “the Holy One, blessed be He.” Holiness always means separation: this is removed from human apprehension, consecrated beyond it with ten sanctifications, and called holy, concealed by its abundant holiness. This is the meaning of the hidden name Havayah. Its revelation—that is, its spoken pronunciation—is through the name Adnut, which is what is revealed to human hearts.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes two aspects of apprehending the one divine light: its limitless character beyond human grasp and its presence that sustains creatures and is apprehended in the heart. This gives the terminology behind “the Holy One and His Shechinah” in the present paragraph.

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סג.): אֲפִילּוּ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה,
connections.quote: “Bar Kappara taught: What is a short passage upon which all the essentials of Torah depend? “In all your ways know Him, and He will make your paths straight.” Rava said: Even for a matter of transgression.”
connections.context: The short phrase “even for a matter of transgression” is the actual Talmudic wording; the former translation added an interpretive gloss inside the quotation. Rav Tzadok here distinguishes recognition after an act from the duty to resist wrongdoing before acting, and then interprets “He will make your paths straight” in relation to the past.

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּלֶכְתּוֹ לַעֲבֵירָה, אִם יָשִׂים אֶל לִבּוֹ דְּכֹחוֹ זֶה לָלֶכֶת לַהַמְרוֹת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי בִּלְתּוֹ מֵאַיִן לוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ כְּלָל – עַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵחָלֵשׁ כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר.
connections.quote: “The first quality: “Who is a God like You?” This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, is a King who bears insult, enduring an offense beyond what thought can encompass. Certainly nothing is hidden from His supervision. Moreover, there is no moment in which a person is not nourished and sustained by the supernal power flowing upon him. You will therefore find that no person has ever sinned against Him without His supplying, at that very moment, the flow of the person’s existence and the movement of his limbs. Although the person sins with that very power, He does not withhold it at all. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, bears such insult by continuing to supply the power that moves his limbs, while the person uses that power at that very moment for sin and iniquity, provoking Him—and the Holy One bears it. Do not say that He cannot withhold that good, Heaven forbid: He has the power in an instant to wither the person’s hands and feet, as He did to Yerovam. Yet, although He has the power to withdraw the power He supplies, and could say, “Since you sin against Me, sin with what is yours, not with what is Mine,” He does not on that account withhold His goodness from the person. He bears the insult, supplies the power, and bestows His goodness on the person. This is insult and forbearance beyond description. For this reason the ministering angels call the Holy One, blessed be He, the King who bears insult. This is the meaning of “Who is a God like You?” You are God, possessing kindness and bestowing good; God, possessing the power to exact retribution and reclaim what is Yours; yet You endure and bear insult until the person returns in repentance.”
connections.context: Tomer Devorah directly explains the premise that the power misused in sin still comes from God. It calls that misuse sin and concludes with the person’s return in repentance. Rav Tzadok here makes recognition of that dependence a means of weakening the impulse to transgress.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ (שָׁם ה.): לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז וְכוּלֵי, יִקְרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע – הַיְינוּ "דָּעֵהוּ".
connections.quote: see note 594 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the complete sequence abbreviated in the body. It retains Torah study before Shema and remembrance of death afterward; Rav Tzadok explains the particular role of Shema as recognition of God’s unity.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בֶּעָבָר, עַל יְדֵי זֶה: "וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו);
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yosef interprets the Talmudic saying through the continued availability of teshuvah

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בֶּעָבָר, עַל יְדֵי זֶה: "וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו);
connections.quote: “The Zohar in Shemini likewise teaches: when the Holy One wished to create the world, the Torah said before Him, “This person You are about to create is destined to sin before You.” He replied, “Is it for nothing that I am called patient?” The Midrash on Vaetchanan compares prayer to a mikveh and teshuvah to the sea. Just as a mikveh is sometimes open and sometimes closed, prayer is sometimes open and sometimes closed; but just as the sea is always open, so the Holy One's hand is always open to receive those who return. All this shows that even if a person has failed in a bad act, Heaven forbid, teshuvah is not withheld from him. This is the saying, “Know Him in all your ways,” upon which all the essentials of Torah depend, as Rava concludes, “Even concerning a transgression.” It means that a person must not despair after the failure of sin, for teshuvah is always available to him. This is a principle among the essentials of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef discusses the same Berakhot statement and explains its application after a failure: a person must not despair of return. The surrounding teaching explains why “Anochi” precedes “You shall have no other gods”: a person who is not yet free of wrongdoing must still have a place to do mitzvos. This complements the existing Shema note, which addresses temptation as it arises, with a source focused on the already-diverted path at the end of the siman.
connections.headline: The same verse as a refusal to despair after failure

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם בֶּעָבָר, עַל יְדֵי זֶה: "וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו);
connections.quote: “When a person does a transgressive act in the sense of “a time to act for Hashem” and “in all your ways know Him,” he nevertheless needs atonement for the act he did.”
connections.explanation: Siman 128 explicitly uses “In all your ways know Him” while retaining the need for atonement even for an act understood through a holy purpose. This is an important companion to the retrospective conclusion here. The knowledge that one's power came from Hashem is meant to weaken the urge to disobey and open return; it is not a self-issued exemption from the work of repair.
connections.headline: The same verse does not dispense with atonement

connections.hePhrase: "דֶּרֶךְ" נִקְרָא דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְ"אֹרַח" הוּא מִן הַצַּד,
connections.quote: “There is a difference between derekh and orach: derekh is the large, established road used by the public, while orach is the small path that branches off from the large road to the side and is less established.”
connections.context: Malbim explains this lexical distinction in his commentary on Sarah’s orach. Rav Tzadok applies the distinction to a person’s principal course and the side paths that can be made straight through renewed recognition of God.

connections.hePhrase: [קפ] אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (ט.): "לֹא זָכָה – מְרוּדִים", הַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם דִּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ לְכָךְ;
connections.quote: ‘(Mnemonic: Great; Temple; Moses.) Rabbi Elazar said: Greater is the one who induces others to give than the one who gives, as it says: ‘The work of righteousness will be peace, and the service of righteousness will be quiet and security forever.’ If he merits it: ‘Surely, share your bread with the hungry.’ If he does not merit it: ‘You shall bring the downtrodden poor into your house.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מֵהַזֹּהַר דְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ הוּא סוֹד הַמִּנְחָה שֶׁשָּׁלַח יַעֲקֹב לְעֵשָׂו.
connections.quote: see note 290 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Ramban makes the governing intention of the scapegoat explicit and explains it through the master’s feast. This qualifies the gift or “bribe” imagery: its religious meaning is obedience to the Creator’s command.

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ מֵהַזֹּהַר דְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ הוּא סוֹד הַמִּנְחָה שֶׁשָּׁלַח יַעֲקֹב לְעֵשָׂו.
connections.quote: “Further, “one male goat”: There are two goats, of which it is said, “He shall take the two goats,” and, “One lot for Hashem and one lot for Azazel.” The goat for Hashem is because of the diminution of the moon, and it is “one goat for Hashem as a sin offering.” “One” is from the side of unity. But concerning the goat for Azazel, neither “one,” “offering,” “fire offering,” nor “burnt offering” is written. Rather, “He shall send it by the hand of a designated man into the wilderness.” “He shall send”—as Yaakov said, “It is a gift sent to my lord, to Esav.” So too here, it is a bribe to break Samael’s anger, so that he will not approach the Sanctuary to accuse.”
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly links the scapegoat with Yaakov’s gift to Esav. Its own distinction between the goat for Hashem and the sent goat is retained. Rav Tzadok applies this image to the atoning dimension of painful compulsory payments.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דְּכָל מַה שֶּׁנּוֹתְנִים לְאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, הַכֹּל הוּא מִמַּעֲשֵׂה אָבוֹת בְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹרוֹן – סִימָן לַבָּנִים.
connections.quote: “He lodged there that night, and took from what he had with him a gift for Esau his brother… For he said: I will appease him with the gift that goes before me, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will accept me.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דְּכָל מַה שֶּׁנּוֹתְנִים לְאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, הַכֹּל הוּא מִמַּעֲשֵׂה אָבוֹת בְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹרוֹן – סִימָן לַבָּנִים.
connections.quote: ““Put a space between one drove and another”: to satisfy that wicked man’s eye and astonish him at the gift. In Bereshit Rabbah they understood this to contain an allusion: Yaakov said before the Holy One, blessed be He, “Master of the world, if troubles come upon my children, do not bring them one after another, but give them respite between their troubles.” He made this an allusion that the taxes and levies Esav’s descendants would exact from his offspring should come with respite and an interval between one and the next.”
connections.context: Ramban identifies the concrete “sign for the descendants” in Yaakov’s gift: intervals of relief between later taxes and levies. This supplies an original source for the historical analogy used in the body.

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי אֵין לְךָ בְּכָל הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת כַּפָּרָה גְּדוֹלָה כְּמוֹ שָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ, שֶׁהוּא מְכַפֵּר עַל כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “This is provided that he has repented. If he has not repented, the scapegoat atones for him only for the minor offenses. What are the minor offenses, and what are the grave ones? The grave offenses are those for which one incurs death by the court or excision. A vain oath and a false oath are also among the grave offenses, even though they do not carry excision. Other prohibitions and positive commands that do not carry excision are the minor offenses.”
connections.context: This is Rambam’s qualification immediately after his statement that the scapegoat atones for all transgressions. It preserves the role of repentance and the distinction between grave and minor offenses, clarifying the scope of the broad formulation quoted in the body.

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי אֵין לְךָ בְּכָל הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת כַּפָּרָה גְּדוֹלָה כְּמוֹ שָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ, שֶׁהוּא מְכַפֵּר עַל כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “For intentional impurity involving the Sanctuary and its sacred objects, the goat whose service is performed inside and Yom Kippur atone. For the other transgressions in the Torah—minor or grave, deliberate or inadvertent, whether one became aware of them or did not become aware, positive commands or prohibitions, offenses carrying excision or court-imposed death—the scapegoat atones.”
connections.context: The Mishnah states the comprehensive range of transgressions covered by the scapegoat and separately identifies the inner goat’s role concerning impurity of the Sanctuary. Rambam’s qualification concerning repentance is supplied in the adjoining source note.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל זֶה תֵּיכֶף בִּצְלִיעָתוֹ בְּרַגְלָיו, עַל יְדֵי נְתִינַת מָעוֹת לְנָכְרִי, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא "הַיְקוּם" שֶׁמַּעֲמִידוֹ עַל רַגְלָיו כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים קיט.).
connections.quote: “When he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh… The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, and he was limping on his thigh.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל זֶה תֵּיכֶף בִּצְלִיעָתוֹ בְּרַגְלָיו, עַל יְדֵי נְתִינַת מָעוֹת לְנָכְרִי, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא "הַיְקוּם" שֶׁמַּעֲמִידוֹ עַל רַגְלָיו כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים קיט.).
connections.quote: ‘‘Wealth kept for its owner to his harm.’ Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: This is Korach’s wealth. (As it is said:) ‘And all the substance that was at their feet.’ Rabbi Elazar said: This is a person’s money, which sets him on his feet. Rabbi Levi said: The keys to Korach’s treasuries were a load for three hundred white mules, and they were all keys and locks for leather sacks.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כְּשֶׁהֶאֱכִיל לוֹ עֲדָשִׁים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל קְנִיַּת הַבְּכוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ: "וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כו, א) – עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֶאֱכִיל לְנָכְרִי בָּא רְעָבוֹן לַצַּדִּיקִים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא לְצוֹרֶךְ.
connections.quote: “Jacob said: Swear to me this day; and he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. And Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew; he ate and drank, rose and went his way. So Esau despised the birthright.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כְּשֶׁהֶאֱכִיל לוֹ עֲדָשִׁים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל קְנִיַּת הַבְּכוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ: "וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כו, א) – עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֶאֱכִיל לְנָכְרִי בָּא רְעָבוֹן לַצַּדִּיקִים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא לְצוֹרֶךְ.
connections.quote: ‘There was a famine in the land, apart from the earlier famine in Abraham’s days. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וַיָּבֹא יַעֲקֹב שָׁלֵם" (שָׁם לג, יח), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת לג:): שָׁלֵם בְּגוּפוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Jacob arrived safe and sound at the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram, and he camped in front of the city.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וַיָּבֹא יַעֲקֹב שָׁלֵם" (שָׁם לג, יח), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת לג:): שָׁלֵם בְּגוּפוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ““Jacob came whole.” Rav said: Whole in his body, whole in his money, whole in his Torah. “He encamped before the city”: Rav said, he established a currency for them; Shmuel said, he established markets; Rabbi Yochanan said, he established bathhouses.”
connections.context: The three kinds of wholeness are the relevant part of the source. Rav Tzadok contrasts them with Jacob’s earlier injury and loss; the Gemara itself does not state that giving the gift caused that injury.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וַיָּבֹא יַעֲקֹב שָׁלֵם" (שָׁם לג, יח), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת לג:): שָׁלֵם בְּגוּפוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Yaakov was distressed over the gift he sent Esav: “the gift passed before him,” and he was in distress. He had already clarified his flocks: the Midrash says he had six hundred thousand flocks, corresponding to the number of the roots of Israel's souls, each root becoming a complete flock. Now that he had to send some to Esav, he feared that his property was not yet clarified. Later it became clear to him that he was complete in his property and nothing was lacking from that gift: the portion belonged to the relation with Esav, and through the gift he extracted the holy sparks from him.”
connections.explanation: Vayishlach explains that Yaakov's distress was not merely the loss of a quantity: he feared that his already clarified property was still not rightly sorted. The later completeness disclosed that the portion sent to Esav had a relation to the work of extracting the holy sparks. This develops the siman's final link between restored money and restored bodily wholeness through the spiritual relation of the property, rather than reducing the passage to a financial calculation.
connections.headline: What Yaakov's completeness clarified about the gift

connections.hePhrase: וּבְאוֹתוֹ דָבָר שֶׁחֶמְדָּתוֹ וְתַאֲוָתוֹ גּוֹבֶרֶת בְּיוֹתֵר, בְּדָבָר זֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא כְּלִי מוּכָן לְקַבֵּל בִּרְכַּת ה' אִם יָשׁוּב אֶל ה' בְּכָל לִבּוֹ,
connections.quote: “One who has a great yearning for bodily desires should not become sad about it, thinking how defective he must be to have such a yearning. On the contrary, he is a vessel prepared for a powerful love and yearning to seek the truth.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok states the underlying principle earlier: the intensity of a desire can become a capacity for seeking truth. Here he applies that principle to money and explicitly conditions its blessing on returning to God with the whole heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קי.) עַל פָּסוּק "וּשְׁבוּאֵל בֶּן גֵּרְשׁוֹם בֶּן מֹשֶׁה נָגִיד עַל הָאֹצָרוֹת" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כו, כד):
connections.quote: ‘When David saw that money was especially dear to him, he appointed him over the treasuries, as it is said: ‘Shevuel son of Gershom son of Moses was chief over the treasuries.’ Was his name Shevuel? Was his name not Jonathan? Rabbi Yochanan said: Because he returned to God—shav la-El—with all his heart.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קי.) עַל פָּסוּק "וּשְׁבוּאֵל בֶּן גֵּרְשׁוֹם בֶּן מֹשֶׁה נָגִיד עַל הָאֹצָרוֹת" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כו, כד):
connections.quote: ‘Shevuel son of Gershom son of Moses was the officer over the treasuries.’
connections.context: The verse in Chronicles reads “son of Moses.” The spelling “Manasseh” belongs to Judges 18:30, where the suspended letter nun is interpreted by the sages in relation to Jonathan’s conduct.

connections.hePhrase: כֵּיוָן שֶׁרָאָה דָוִד שֶׁמָּמוֹן חֲבִיבָה עָלָיו בְּיוֹתֵר, מִנָּהוּ עַל הָאוֹצָרוֹת וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “this occurred later, after the Philistines injected into her [Delilah] the lust for money, mirroring the primeval Serpent; and when they could not seduce her through food or promiscuity, they schemed to corrupt her through monetary greed, the root of all desires; wherefore silver (keseph) shares the root of kisufin, yearning and craving; being the all-inclusive desire through which all worldly acquisitions are obtained. Wherefore even one immersed in another desire is never free from this one; and those who are clean from all other bodily appetites are often not clean from monetary greed; for there are mortals who cherish their money more than their bodies [Berakhot 61b]; showing an obsession with money even when it satisfies no physical appetite and harms the body, loving wealth for its own sake; after the manner of "the mouse lying upon gold dinars" (Sanhedrin 29b); this being the root of the Serpent who bites without deriving any pleasure (Koheles Rabbah 10:11 on Koheles 10:11). And therefore through monetary greed comes the ultimate forgetting of Hashem more than through any other appetite;”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains why money can be desired for itself even when it no longer serves bodily enjoyment: it gathers many forms of longing into one apparently enduring possession. This makes David’s appointment intelligible. The repair is not simply giving Shevuel enough money to satisfy him, but turning a powerful attachment into responsible service of an entrusted store. The quoted discussion concerns Delilah. Citation correction: the teaching that some people value their money more than their bodies is in Berakhot 61b; the supplied Hebrew’s reference to Pesachim 105a has been corrected in square brackets.
connections.headline: Why a desire for money can be more than a desire for purchases

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְּשׁוּבָה הַיְינוּ שֶׁמֵּשִׁיב חֶמְדָּה זוֹ לִמְקוֹרָהּ, וּמַכִּיר שֶׁלּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ הַכֶּסֶף וְהַזָּהָב.
connections.quote: “Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, declares the Lord of hosts.”
connections.context: This is the biblical wording behind returning the desire for wealth to its source. Shevuel’s appointment becomes service of the One to whom the treasury belongs.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הוּא רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת עַל הָאוֹצָרוֹת דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁמַּלְכוּתוֹ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם,
connections.quote: “The Torah’s command concerning a king, that his awe should be upon you, does not mean fear of flesh and blood in its simple sense, for of that it is said, “Who are you that you fear a mortal man?” Rather, an Israelite king’s kingship is drawn from the kingship of Heaven. As is known, the spiritual level of King David, peace be upon him, is the attribute of kingship, for he was attached to God’s attribute of kingship, in the sense of “Solomon sat upon the throne of the Lord.””
connections.context: This explains why service in David’s treasury can redirect attachment to money toward Heaven: Rav Tzadok understands David’s kingship as an expression of divine kingship.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל מִינּוּיוֹ הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַמְמוּנֶּה עַל אוֹתוֹ הַדָּבָר הָיָה מַכִּיר וְיוֹדֵעַ לְהַקְנוֹת הַכֹּל לְעֶלְיוֹן קוֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ.
connections.quote: “Abram said to the king of Sodom: I have lifted up my hand to Hashem, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth.”

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם נֶאֱמַר: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט), וְהוּא הָיָה צַר עַיִן בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק הָרוֹאֶה הֲלָכָה ב),
connections.quote: “One of a good eye will be blessed, for he has given of his bread to the poor.”
connections.context: “A good eye” is the Hebrew expression for generosity. Rav Tzadok contrasts it with the begrudging or narrow eye and links the blessing specifically to giving bread.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם נֶאֱמַר: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט), וְהוּא הָיָה צַר עַיִן בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק הָרוֹאֶה הֲלָכָה ב),
connections.quote: “The colleagues asked Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: He was a priest for idolatry, yet he lived a long life? He said to them: Because his eye was begrudging toward his own idol. How so? A person would bring an ox, a sheep, or a kid for the idol, and he would tell him: What benefit does it give you? It does not see or hear, eat or drink, do good or harm, or speak.”
connections.context: The person is Jonathan, grandson of Moses. The story continues that he persuaded worshipers to substitute a small food offering, which he himself ate. This is the Jerusalem Talmud’s unusual use of a begrudging eye toward idolatry; it is unrelated to the Mishnah’s blessings on natural phenomena.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִמְקוֹם צָרוּת עַיִן הוּא טוֹבַת עַיִן כְּשֶׁשָּׁב כַּנּוֹדָע, לְכָךְ הַבְּרָכָה עַל יָדוֹ
connections.quote: “Song arises from longing, which is why there are “songs of desire.” When a person’s soul longs entirely for the blessed Lord and is sick with love for Him, his mouth opens to sing before Him. No songs awaken Israel’s love for their Father in Heaven and their union with Him like the Song of Songs. This love is the opposite of love for this world; therefore it is the holy of holies, belonging entirely to the blessed Lord and wholly separated from all the desires of this world, with no connection to them at all. This is the pattern: that same heart which tastes darkness to its furthest limit and seeks the Lord from there tastes light to its furthest limit, until it attains that there is no darkness—“even darkness does not darken,” and “night shines like day.” So it is with all the traits: in the place of a begrudging eye there is a generous eye, and in the place of an evil heart, a good heart.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּהוּא נָבִיא זָקֵן דְּבֵית אֵל,
connections.quote: “They challenged Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: Is it not written, “Until the day of the exile of the land”? He said to them: When David died, Solomon arose and replaced his officials, and he returned to his former corruption. This is what is written, “An old prophet was living in Bethel.” They said: It was he.”
connections.context: The identification with the old prophet of Bethel belongs to this rabbinic interpretation. The verse in I Kings 13:11 alone does not identify that prophet with Jonathan.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קד.) אָמְרוּ עָלָיו: גְּדוֹלָה לְגִימָה שֶׁמַּשְׁרָה וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘[Hospitality] also causes the Divine Presence to rest upon prophets of Baal, as we learn from the companion of Iddo the prophet. For it is written: ‘As they were sitting at the table, the word of Hashem came to the prophet who had brought him back.’’

connections.hePhrase: לְכָךְ אֶצְלוֹ הוּא רְבוּתָא גְּדוֹלָה, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דָּן כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּמִדּוֹתָיו]:
connections.quote: “The explanation is this: in actual conduct they were equally righteous. But one needed to labor and endure so that he could turn himself away from a bad trait, while the other did not need that labor. It is like two people: one is naturally, from birth, not prone to anger; the other is prone to anger, suffers from it and labors not to be angry. Hashem therefore gives him greater reward. Although his companion also has no anger, this person suffered and labored against it more than his companion; therefore Hashem gives him greater reward.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the Talmud's account of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva need not mean that their outward righteousness differed. One may need to labor against a trait that costs the other no struggle. This directly develops the siman's closing statement that Hashem judges each person according to his particular qualities.
connections.headline: The effort behind the same outward act

connections.hePhrase: [קפב] הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "שַׁוְעָה", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ג:) עַל פָּסוּק "קִדַּמְתִּי בַנֶּשֶׁף וָאֲשַׁוֵּעָה" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קמז): עַד חֲצוֹת הָיָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Rav Ashi said: Until midnight he occupied himself with words of Torah; from then onward, with songs and praises.”
connections.context: The Gemara is resolving the verses about David rising at night, including “I rose in the twilight and cried for help.” Rav Tzadok uses Rav Ashi’s answer to show that the cry described there can refer to Torah study.

connections.hePhrase: [קפב] הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "שַׁוְעָה", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ג:) עַל פָּסוּק "קִדַּמְתִּי בַנֶּשֶׁף וָאֲשַׁוֵּעָה" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קמז): עַד חֲצוֹת הָיָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘I rose before dawn and cried out for help; I placed my hope in Your word.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה קוֹרִין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי שֵׁם ה' אֶקְרָא" (דְּבָרִים לב, ג) – בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “For I will call the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה קוֹרִין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי שֵׁם ה' אֶקְרָא" (דְּבָרִים לב, ג) – בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “From where in the Torah do we know the blessing before Torah? As it is said, “For I will call the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God.””
connections.context: The Gemara reads calling God’s name as the setting for the blessing before Torah. Rav Tzadok develops that association into an account of Torah as calling upon God.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ שְׁמוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי, כִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא הַמִּדּוֹת, וְאֵין סוֹף עַצְמוֹ אֵין לוֹ שֵׁם כְּלָל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר;
connections.heRef: רמב"ן על בראשית, פתיחה לפירוש התורה י״ד
connections.quote: “We also possess a true tradition that the entire Torah consists of the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, its words being divided into names in another manner. For example, imagine the verse beginning “Bereshit” divided into different words, such as “be-rosh yitbara Elohim”; so it is with the entire Torah, apart from the permutations and numerical values of the names.”
connections.context: Ramban explicitly presents this as an esoteric tradition about the Torah’s letters and their divisions. It supplies the background to Rav Tzadok’s statement that the whole Torah is God’s names; it does not replace the ordinary reading of its narratives and commandments.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ שְׁמוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי, כִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא הַמִּדּוֹת, וְאֵין סוֹף עַצְמוֹ אֵין לוֹ שֵׁם כְּלָל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר;
connections.quote: “Before the Holy One, blessed be He, created any image in the world and fashioned any form, He was alone, without form or likeness. … But after He made this image of the chariot of the supernal Man, He descended there and was called by that image YHVH, so that He would be known through His attributes, through each and every attribute; and He was called El, Elohim, Shaddai, Tzevaot, Ehyeh.”
connections.context: In itself the Infinite has no name or image; the Names belong to His attributes, through which He is known.

connections.hePhrase: רַק מִדּוֹתָיו, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר רְצוֹנוֹ הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט בַּבְּרוּאִים, וְהַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ הִיא כְּלָלוּת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “In truth, at their root all is one, singular and united, just as before the world was created. Only in the created being's perception is there a perception of different powers, and according to each power He is named. Therefore the entire Torah, which includes the order of all the powers found in creation, consists of the names of Hashem, the source of life and existence for all these powers. Within every power we recognize that Hashem is the master of that power; He is therefore named for us as the master of that power, and so with every particular. These are deep matters, clear to one who understands.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains the premise behind calling through Torah: a name makes a particular revealed power recognizable, and Torah orders the powers present in creation. The multiplicity belongs to the recipient's apprehension, while the source remains one. This gives content to the siman's distinction between the infinite source beyond names and the divine will expressed in the Torah and its commandments.
connections.headline: Different names describe revelation from one source

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שֶׁהוּא דְּפוּס מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, וּלְכָךְ הִיא שְׁמוֹתָיו, וְלִמּוּדָיו, דְּהַיְינוּ יְדִיעַת זֶה
connections.quote: see note 869 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The opening midrash supplies the architectural comparison behind “the pattern of Creation.” Rav Tzadok uses it to connect the Torah with the divine will expressed throughout the created world.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, וּכְמוֹ הַקּוֹרֵא לַחֲבֵירוֹ בִּשְׁמוֹ, כְּשֶׁצּוֹוֵחַ שְׁמוֹ נִקְרָא שֶׁקּוֹרֵא, שֶׁרוֹצֶה שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶצְלוֹ וְיִפְנֶה לוֹ.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ל״ז:כ״ח-כ״ט
connections.quote: “Now, this drawing down and illumination that a person draws and causes to shine from the radiance of the blessed Infinite Light upon his soul and upon the souls of all Israel—which is the Shekhinah, the congregation of Israel, the source of all Israel’s souls, as will be explained below—through the study of Torah is called “calling”: “one who reads in the Torah.” This means that through studying Torah he calls the Holy One, blessed be He, to come to him, as it were, like a person calling his friend to come to him, and like a small child calling his father to come to him, to be together with him and not to separate from him and leave him alone, God forbid. This is the meaning of the verse, “The Lord is close to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth,” and “there is no truth but Torah.” That is, one calls the Holy One, blessed be He, specifically through Torah. This excludes someone who calls Him without studying Torah, but merely cries, “Father! Father!” As the prophet complains about him, “There is no one who calls upon Your name,” as explained elsewhere. From this, the discerning person should reflect so as to draw great awe upon himself while studying Torah, as explained above in chapter 23.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן תּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת, הַיְינוּ: "הִדָּבֵק בְּמִדּוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי", הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶצְלוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ח), שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “One who learns in order to teach is given the means to learn and to teach; and one who learns in order to practice is given the means to learn and to teach, to keep and to practice.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן תּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת, הַיְינוּ: "הִדָּבֵק בְּמִדּוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי", הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶצְלוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ח), שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “Abba Shaul says: “And I will glorify Him”—be like Him: just as He is gracious and compassionate, so you should be gracious and compassionate.”
connections.context: The cited ideal of attachment to God’s attributes has a concrete ethical meaning: becoming gracious and compassionate. Rav Tzadok identifies Torah studied in order to act with bringing that divine will into one’s life.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן תּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת, הַיְינוּ: "הִדָּבֵק בְּמִדּוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי", הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶצְלוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ח), שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: ‘They shall make a Sanctuary for Me, and I will dwell among them.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא "שַׁוְעָה", דְּהוּא מֵעֲשָׂרָה לְשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁל תְּפִלָּה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וָאֶתְחַנַּן),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Prayer is called by ten expressions, and these are: an outcry, a cry, a groan, a ringing call, an entreaty, distress, a calling, falling down, intercession, and supplication. An outcry and a cry are indicated by the verse, “The children of Israel groaned from the labor and cried out.””
connections.context: The midrash explicitly includes shavah, an outcry, among the names of prayer, and grounds it in the cry from Egyptian bondage. This connects the paragraph’s opening description of Torah with its later interpretation of Israel’s cry in Egypt.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר (שְׁמוֹת יט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אֵין לְךָ שַׁוְעָה אֶלָּא בִּתְפִלָּה וְכוּלֵי, וּבַכָּתוּב דְּמַיְיתֵי נִזְכַּר תְּפִלָּה וְשַׁוְעָה.
connections.quote: “How are tze’akah and shav’ah distinguished? Rabbi Yitzchak said: There is no shav’ah except in prayer. … Tze’akah is when one cries and says nothing. Rabbi Yehudah said: Therefore tze’akah is greater than all of them, for tze’akah is in the heart.”
connections.context: Shav’ah is articulated prayer in this distinction, while tze’akah is the heart’s wordless cry. Rav Tzadok is examining how Torah can itself be called shav’ah despite that association with prayer.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר (שְׁמוֹת יט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אֵין לְךָ שַׁוְעָה אֶלָּא בִּתְפִלָּה וְכוּלֵי, וּבַכָּתוּב דְּמַיְיתֵי נִזְכַּר תְּפִלָּה וְשַׁוְעָה.
connections.quote: ““Hear my prayer, Hashem, and give ear to my shav’ah” (Psalms 39:13); “To You, Lord, I have cried”; “I cried to You, and You healed me.””
connections.context: These are the Zohar’s verse proofs. The first explicitly places “prayer” and “shav’ah” together, which is the detail Rav Tzadok singles out immediately after his quotation.

connections.hePhrase: [שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן מִלְּשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁל תְּפִלָּה; וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מוּרְגָּל "הַקּוֹרֵא בַּתּוֹרָה" וְלֹא בִּתְפִלָּה, כִּדְאָמְרוּ (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נח:): לְשׁוֹן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים לְחוּד;
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Assi asked Rabbi Yochanan: What is the law of wine that a non-Jew has diluted (mesakho)? He replied: Say ‘mezago’! Rabbi Assi answered: I am speaking as Scripture does: ‘She has slaughtered her animals; she has mixed (masekhah) her wine.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: The language of Torah is its own, and the language of the Sages is its own.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּהַיְינוּ הַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה בַּלֵּב, כְּמוֹ בְּקַבָּלַת הַקָּרְבָּן שֶׁהוּא הַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה נֶאֱמַר בְּקַיִן שֶׁלֹּא קִבֵּל לְשׁוֹן "לֹא שָׁעָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ד, ה).
connections.quote: ‘But to Cain and his offering He did not turn. Cain became very angry, and his face fell.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב אֵין וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא בִּתְפִלָּה, הַיְינוּ כַּנּוֹדָע דְּאֵין תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא בִּמְקוֹם תְּפִלָּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (כט.).
connections.quote: “Rava expounded: “Lord, You have been our dwelling”—these are synagogues and study halls. Abaye said: At first I studied at home and prayed in the synagogue. When I heard David’s saying, “Lord, I love the dwelling of Your house,” I began studying in the synagogue.”
connections.context: Abaye’s change brings his study into the place of prayer. Rav Tzadok cites this as the practical expression of the inner connection he is making between Torah and prayer.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי תְּפִלָּה נִקְרָא יִרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ט:) עַל פָּסוּק "יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים עב, ה);
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Zeira said: What verse supports this? ‘They shall fear You with the sun, and before the moon, through all generations.’ Rabbi Yosei ben Elyakim testified in the name of the holy congregation in Jerusalem: Anyone who places the blessing of redemption immediately before prayer will not be harmed throughout that entire day.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי תְּפִלָּה נִקְרָא יִרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ט:) עַל פָּסוּק "יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים עב, ה);
connections.quote: ‘They shall fear You with the sun, and before the moon, throughout all generations.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ יַחַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): אֲנִי יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: see note 1236 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rav Tzadok brings David’s combined fear and joy as the model for joining prayer’s awe with Torah’s joy.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן י) דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא בְּלָא דְחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ לָא פָּרְחַת לְעֵילָא,
connections.quote: “Torah without fear and love does not fly upward.”
connections.context: The ascent of Torah requires the inward qualities of fear and love. Rav Tzadok connects this requirement with the preceding discussion of Torah accompanied by prayer and awe.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "וַתַּעַל שַׁוְעָתָם אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים מִן הָעֲבֹדָה" (שְׁמוֹת ב, כג),
connections.quote: ‘During those long days the king of Egypt died. The children of Israel groaned because of the labor and cried out, and their cry rose to God because of the labor.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, כז עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "בְּחֹמֶר" – דָּא קַל וָחֹמֶר, "וּבִלְבֵנִים" – בְּלִבּוּן הִלְכְתָא, שֶׁכָּל עֲבוֹדָתָם בְּמִצְרַיִם הָיָה לִמּוּד תּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “The masters of the Mishnah explained: “They embittered their lives with hard labor”—with difficulty in argument; “with clay”—with an a fortiori argument; “with bricks”—with clarification of halakhah; “with every labor in the field”—this is baraita; “all their labor”—this is Mishnah.”
connections.context: The interpretation plays on the Hebrew and Aramaic words: chomer, clay, and kal va-chomer; levenim, bricks, and libbun, clarification. This is the passage Rav Tzadok invokes when reading the Egyptian labor through the experience of Torah study.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, כז עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "בְּחֹמֶר" – דָּא קַל וָחֹמֶר, "וּבִלְבֵנִים" – בְּלִבּוּן הִלְכְתָא, שֶׁכָּל עֲבוֹדָתָם בְּמִצְרַיִם הָיָה לִמּוּד תּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “And they made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר" (שָׁם כד, י), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כג): הִיא וְכָל אַרְגַּלְיָא שֶׁלָּהּ,
connections.quote: “They saw the God of Israel; under His feet was something like the work of a sapphire brick, and like the very heavens in purity.”
connections.context: The Hebrew livnat is read as a brick in the Midrash quoted next, recalling Israel’s brickmaking in Egypt. That particular word is needed for Rav Tzadok’s connection with the preceding Zohar.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר" (שָׁם כד, י), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כג): הִיא וְכָל אַרְגַּלְיָא שֶׁלָּהּ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Berekhya said: It does not say, “the work of a sapphire brick,” but “like the work”—it and all its equipment were there: it, its basket, and its trowel. Bar Kappara said: Before Israel was redeemed from Egypt, its imprint was in the heavens; after they were redeemed, it was no longer seen there.”
connections.context: The Midrash includes the brickmaking implements in the heavenly image, making the suffering of the work itself present above. Rav Tzadok uses that full image, “it and all its equipment,” in his interpretation of the labor.

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ שֶׁכָּל פְּרָט מֵעֲבוֹדָתָם הָיָה מֵאֲמִיתַּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:11
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:11
connections.quote: “Everything comes from the true will of God; therefore Nebuchadnezzar is called “My servant,” and Assyria “the rod of My anger.” Yet “liability is brought about through one who is liable”: he thinks that he himself is the doer, so that he receives his punishment afterward. Otherwise, he would not deserve punishment, since it is God’s will—as Rambam asks concerning Egypt, when “they will enslave them” had been said beforehand. But because they said, “Who is the Lord?” they themselves were the enslavers, and therefore they were punished.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel treatment preserves the distinction essential here: recognizing divine providence in the exile does not absolve the Egyptians of their chosen oppression. He places their responsibility alongside his interpretation of the exile as an expression of divine will.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הָיוּ מַכִּירִים זֶה, "וַיֵּאָנְחוּ... וַיִּזְעָקוּ" לִהְיוֹת בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת, כִּי אֲנִי ה' שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: “You shall not defile the land which you inhabit, in the midst of which I dwell; for I, Hashem, dwell in the midst of the children of Israel.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קָרוֹב ה' לְכָל קֹרְאָיו לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יח), וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ה:): אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא קְרִיאָה.
connections.quote: “The Lord is near to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok connects the word “truth,” emet, with the Talmudic identification of truth as Torah in the next note.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קָרוֹב ה' לְכָל קֹרְאָיו לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יח), וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ה:): אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא קְרִיאָה.
connections.quote: ““Through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned.” “Kindness” means acts of kindness, as it says, “One who pursues righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.” “Truth” means Torah, as it says, “Acquire truth and do not sell it.””
connections.context: This is the specific identification of truth with Torah needed for “calling upon Him in truth.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קָרוֹב ה' לְכָל קֹרְאָיו לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת" (תְּהִלִּים קמה, יח), וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ה:): אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא קְרִיאָה.
connections.quote: “It uses the expression ‘he entreated,’ which the Sages explained in Sukkah 14a as turning judgment to mercy like a pitchfork. Every prayer needs a favorable time, as it says (Psalms 69:14), ‘My prayer to You, Hashem, is at a favorable time,’ and as the Sages said (Berakhot 8a), there are appointed times for prayer. At a time of judgment, which is not favorable, he is not answered. Torah, however, is above the sun and time. Of this it says (Psalms 145:18), ‘Hashem is near to all who call Him, to all who call Him in truth,’ and truth means Torah (Berakhot 5b). Through calling Him by means of Torah, He is close always, to every soul and at every time, for this is attachment to the living God, with nothing intervening.”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz uses the same verse and the same identification of truth with Torah. It distinguishes prayer's favorable time from the connection through Torah described as having no barrier. This explains why the siman calls Torah joined with prayer a cry that rises beyond prayer alone, while preserving the surrounding requirement of awe and actual inward connection.
connections.headline: Calling in truth through Torah

connections.hePhrase: [קפג] "שִׂיחָה" נִקְרָא מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְכוּלֵי, וּבְעֵירוּבִין (נד:) עַל פָּסוּק "עַל דֶּרֶךְ שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon said: From Rabban Gamliel’s conversation we learned two things: slaves are exempt from sukkah, and one who sleeps under a bed has not fulfilled the obligation.”

connections.hePhrase: [קפג] "שִׂיחָה" נִקְרָא מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְכוּלֵי, וּבְעֵירוּבִין (נד:) עַל פָּסוּק "עַל דֶּרֶךְ שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Why not say, “From Rabban Gamliel’s words”? It teaches us incidentally that even the conversation of Torah scholars requires study, as it says, “His leaf does not wither.””
connections.context: The Gemara itself notices the choice of the word “conversation.” This is why it supports Rav Tzadok’s distinction between a formal teaching and ordinary speech that nevertheless contains Torah.

connections.hePhrase: [קפג] "שִׂיחָה" נִקְרָא מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְכוּלֵי, וּבְעֵירוּבִין (נד:) עַל פָּסוּק "עַל דֶּרֶךְ שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘You who ride white donkeys, you who sit in judgment, and you who walk along the road—speak of it.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל "דִּבּוּר" הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (י:) עַל פָּסוּק "הָלוֹךְ וְדַבֵּר", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ‘Is that so? Did Rabbi Ilai bar Berechyah not say: Two Torah scholars who walk along the road without words of Torah between them deserve to be burned, as it is said: ‘As they continued walking and speaking, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them’? The reason is that there was speech; had there been no speech, they would have deserved to be burned!’
