connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל "דִּבּוּר" הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (י:) עַל פָּסוּק "הָלוֹךְ וְדַבֵּר", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “And it came to pass, as they still went on and talked, that behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire parted the two of them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּנָה גְּמוּרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יג:) עַל פָּסוּק "לְדַבֵּר בָּם" – כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיגְרְסוּ.
connections.quote: “It is written concerning words of Torah, and this is what the Merciful One says: Teach your children Torah so that they will recite them.”
connections.context: This answer treats “to speak of them” as Torah learning and recitation rather than as a rule about concentrating during the Shema. Rav Tzadok uses the term girsa, recitation, for a stage of learning that can precede full understanding.

connections.hePhrase: רַק רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּנָה גְּמוּרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יג:) עַל פָּסוּק "לְדַבֵּר בָּם" – כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיגְרְסוּ.
connections.quote: “And you shall teach them to your children, to speak of them, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise up.”

connections.hePhrase: וְגִירְסָא הַיְינוּ הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.) עַל פָּסוּק "גָּרְסָה נַפְשִׁי" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, כ).
connections.quote: ‘Rava also said: A person should always recite what he learns, even though he forgets it and even though he does not understand what he is saying, as it is said: ‘My soul is crushed with longing.’ Garsa, ‘crushed coarsely,’ is written; tachana, ‘ground finely,’ is not written.’

connections.hePhrase: וְגִירְסָא הַיְינוּ הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.) עַל פָּסוּק "גָּרְסָה נַפְשִׁי" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, כ).
connections.quote: ‘My soul is worn away with longing for Your ordinances at all times.’

connections.hePhrase: וְגִירְסָא הַיְינוּ הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.) עַל פָּסוּק "גָּרְסָה נַפְשִׁי" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, כ).
connections.quote: “It appears, however, that their language and their reading are included in the commandment of Torah study, like one studying Ezekiel’s passage of the Chariot: he is certainly called one who studies Torah, although he understands only the plain narrative. We read the Chariot as the haftarah on Shavuot; although none of us knows the extent of its mysteries, the reader is considered to be studying the words of the Prophets. In the first chapter of Avodah Zarah, concerning the revealed parts of Torah as well, they said: “Let a person recite, even though he does not know what he is saying.” The same applies to its hidden parts: since they are actual words of Torah, even though he does not understand, he has studied Torah. The Ari, our honored teacher Rabbi Yitzḥak of blessed memory, said that the language of the holy Zohar is beneficial to the soul. It seems that the intention is that familiarity with its language helps one arrive at true understanding.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the value of reading Torah from having already attained its inner meaning. The continuation does not make reading esoteric books obligatory and rejects adopting mystical prayer intentions without understanding them. The positive point relevant here is that faithful recitation can prepare the way for genuine understanding.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִמַּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: אַגְמִירוּ וְכוּלֵי כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיגְרְסוּ, נִרְאֶה דִּבְהַתְחָלָה צָרִיךְ לְיַגֵּעַ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ דְּבָרִים הַיּוֹצְאִים מִן הַלֵּב;
connections.quote: “It further says: because Moses said, “I am heavy of mouth,” and “I am not a man of words,” he merited the Holy One’s saying to him, “Mouth to mouth I speak with him,” and merited saying, “These are the words.” This is as stated in Tanchuma, Devarim 2, and in the Midrash Rabbah there: “Yesterday you said, ‘I am not a man of words,’ and now you speak so much,” and so forth; “Study the Torah and be healed,” and so forth. As it says, “A healing tongue is a tree of life.” The book of Deuteronomy is the root of the whole Oral Torah, as stated in Zohar III, 261a: “The Written Torah and the Oral Torah,” and “it is called Torah and Mishneh Torah.” Moses our teacher said this on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, as it says, “In the eleventh month, on the first of the month, Moses spoke,” and so forth—the month formed with the letter tzadi.”
connections.explanation: The Shvat passage presents Moshe’s later speech as the result of an earlier encounter with Torah that transformed his capacity to speak. This helps explain the order emphasized in the present siman: inward Torah comes first; only afterward can speech emerging readily from the person be called his own Torah. ‘From his own mouth’ thus describes an attained expression of Torah, not an independence from its divine source or a claim that every unprepared utterance has the same standing.
connections.headline: Moshe’s healed speech illustrates Torah becoming the speaker’s own

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לְדִבּוּר וְגִירְסָא הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא פִּטְטַיָּא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, גַּם כֵּן הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה גָּמוּר.
connections.quote: see note 478 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Yerushalmi provides the expression pittatya de-oraita. Rav Tzadok applies it to Torah words that have become natural speech after a person has first labored to bring them into the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (שָׁם): בַּתְּחִלָּה תּוֹרַת ה', וְאַחַר כָּךְ תּוֹרָתוֹ;
connections.quote: “Rava also said: At first it is called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and in the end it is called by the learner’s name, as it says, “His desire is in the Torah of the Lord,” and then, “In his Torah he meditates day and night.””
connections.context: The change from “the Torah of the Lord” to “his Torah” supplies Rav Tzadok’s language for Torah becoming internal to the learner, so that even apparently effortless speech can express it.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (שָׁם): בַּתְּחִלָּה תּוֹרַת ה', וְאַחַר כָּךְ תּוֹרָתוֹ;
connections.quote: “But his delight is in the Torah of Hashem, and in his Torah he meditates day and night.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה דְּהוּא תּוֹרָתוֹ, דּוּגְמַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נַעֲשׂוּ שְׁתֵּי כִּלְיוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא), גַּם דִּבּוּר שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “I bless the Lord who has counseled me; even at night my inward parts instruct me.”
connections.context: The Hebrew for “inward parts” is literally “my kidneys,” kilyotai. Bereshit Rabbah 61:1 cites this verse as its proof for Abraham’s two kidneys teaching him Torah; it supplies the textual basis for the preceding Midrash.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה דְּהוּא תּוֹרָתוֹ, דּוּגְמַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נַעֲשׂוּ שְׁתֵּי כִּלְיוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא), גַּם דִּבּוּר שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon said: He had no father to teach him and no teacher; from where did he learn Torah? Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, made his two kidneys like two teachers, and they flowed forth and taught him Torah and wisdom.”
connections.context: The Midrash portrays Abraham’s Torah as welling up from within. Rav Tzadok uses that image for Torah that has become so much a person’s own that even spontaneous speech expresses it.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּדוֹאֵג בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קו:) שֶׁכָּל תּוֹרָתוֹ וְכוּלֵי מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ, הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ הַהַתְחָלָה;
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 6
connections.quote: “‘The whole earth had one speech and common words.’ It does not say one tongue. The principal tongue is the holy tongue, which is implanted deep in the heart and flows from the root of life. Other tongues are called a stammering tongue, as it says (Isaiah 33:19), ‘A stammering tongue without understanding’: it has no root of life in the heart, for understanding is in the heart. Although the generation of the dispersion spoke the holy tongue, it had no root of life in them; they spoke it only from the lips outward, like the chatter and chirping of birds and other creatures. So too concerning the serpent: the commentators ask why its curse does not mention taking away its tongue. In truth it had no tongue at the root, since it spoke slander against its Creator. Understand this.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach contrasts holy language rooted in the heart with outward use of the same words by the generation of the dispersion. Its final harmful-speech example also matches the siman's qualification concerning Doeg. This helps distinguish superficial recitation without an inward beginning from the speech that remains Torah after such a beginning has been acquired.
connections.headline: Holy words and a living root in the heart

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם כִּי עַל יְדֵי לָשׁוֹן הָרָע נִתְקַלְקֵל הַדִּבּוּר שֶׁמֵּהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ.
connections.quote: “When Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said to him: David has come to the house of Ahimelech. Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? … Your tongue devises destruction, like a sharpened razor, working deceit.”
connections.context: The psalm is David’s rebuke of Doeg for the report that led to the slaughter of the priests of Nob (I Samuel 22:9–19).

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁפָּתַח בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה בְּפָסוּק "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, ד) עַיֵּין שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רסא עַמּוּד א): מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ אֲמָרָן.
connections.quote: see note 1370 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the opening of Devarim Rabbah to which Rav Tzadok directs the reader. It connects Torah’s “tree of life” with the healing of Moses’ speech and the opening of Deuteronomy.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁפָּתַח בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה בְּפָסוּק "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, ד) עַיֵּין שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רסא עַמּוּד א): מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ אֲמָרָן.
connections.quote: ‘What is called Mishneh Torah—Moses spoke these words from his own mouth. We have already explained the matter. Why is this so? Rather, supernal Wisdom is called the totality of Torah, and everything emerges from it through that inner voice. Afterward everything settles and is united in the place called the Tree of Life. Upon it depend the general and the particular, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah; it is called Torah and Mishneh Torah. At first there was unceasing Gevurah, and now everything is together. Therefore here, in these Ten Commandments, everything is marked with a vav: ‘And you shall not commit adultery,’ ‘And you shall not steal,’ ‘And you shall not bear witness,’ ‘And you shall not covet,’ ‘And you shall not desire.’ They have already explained this.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה הַיְינוּ שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת מִתּוֹךְ גְּרוֹנוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא דְּבָרִים הַיּוֹצְאִים מִן הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק "וְלִבִּי עֵר" – שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: see note 363 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The midrash’s identification of God as Israel’s heart explains Rav Tzadok’s association of speech “from the heart” with the Divine Presence speaking through Moses.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן "אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים א, א) מַשְׁמָע מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ, דְּלֹא יָדַע וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness, in the Aravah, opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Di-zahab.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר "לֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים", כִּי הוּא מַדְרֵגַת בַּעְלָהּ דְּמַטְרוֹנִיתָא שֶׁכָּל דְּבָרָיו נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה', וּמִלָּתוֹ לְבַד עַל לְשׁוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Moses said to Hashem: ‘Please, my Lord, I am no man of words—neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since You began speaking to Your servant—for my mouth is heavy and my tongue is heavy.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר "לֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים", כִּי הוּא מַדְרֵגַת בַּעְלָהּ דְּמַטְרוֹנִיתָא שֶׁכָּל דְּבָרָיו נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה', וּמִלָּתוֹ לְבַד עַל לְשׁוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: “The spirit of Hashem spoke through me, and His word was upon my tongue.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא "עֵץ חַיִּים" כַּאֲשֶׁר יוֹצֵא מִן הַלֵּב שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים.
connections.quote: “Above all that you guard, guard your heart, for from it are the sources of life.”
connections.context: The explicit word “heart” links the proverb to Rav Tzadok’s account of words emerging from the heart as a tree of life.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַעֲלֵי תַלְמוּד הוּא שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לְמַדְרֵגַת הַשִּׂיחָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ בַּעֲלֵי תַלְמוּד, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן וְכוּלֵי:
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:7
connections.linkedRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11 7
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:7
connections.heRef: ספר ליקוטי מאמרים, חודשים ומועדים י״א:ז׳
connections.quote: “Therefore they said (Eruvin 54b): “Converse”—these are masters of Torah, whose every conversation is Torah. Conversation means speech that is outward, from the lips, as when someone speaks innocently and unreflectively. Thus, at the end of the chapter HaYashen they said: “From Rabban Gamliel’s conversation we learned” (Sukkah 21b). Rabban Gamliel possessed this power in particular, as they said (Eruvin 64b): “From here we learned that Rabban Gamliel discerned correctly through the holy spirit.” The holy spirit means that the speech flows from the supernal holiness mentioned above. There he was merely speaking, calling the gentile by name, so deliberate intention was entirely inapplicable. Rather, every word and conversation of a master of Talmud is spontaneously Torah, flowing from the higher wisdom at the root of his life; he has no idle speech.”

connections.hePhrase: [קפד] הַהַתְחָלָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא הַחֵשֶׁק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי אִם בְּתוֹרַת ה' חֶפְצוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים א, ב), וְאָז נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.),
connections.quote: “Rather, his desire is in the Torah of the Lord, and in his Torah he meditates day and night.”
connections.context: The change from “the Torah of the Lord” to “his Torah” is the wording interpreted by the Gemara in the next note. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the initial desire from the later inward acquisition.

connections.hePhrase: [קפד] הַהַתְחָלָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא הַחֵשֶׁק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי אִם בְּתוֹרַת ה' חֶפְצוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים א, ב), וְאָז נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.),
connections.quote: see note 2454.
connections.context: The second “his” is read as the learner’s own. This is the specific teaching Rav Tzadok uses; the neighboring statement about studying what the heart desires did not establish that transition.

connections.hePhrase: [קפד] הַהַתְחָלָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא הַחֵשֶׁק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי אִם בְּתוֹרַת ה' חֶפְצוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים א, ב), וְאָז נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.),
connections.quote: “Chanukah means a beginning, when a person begins to educate himself. Through this something remains fixed for all time, as he accustoms himself through the desire and will of his youthful days, as it says: ‘Educate the youth according to his way; even when he grows old, he will not depart from it.’”
connections.explanation: Chanukah connects the beginning of self-education with habit formed through youthful desire. This helps resolve the present siman’s praise of both youth and old age. Desire has a distinctive greatness as the person’s awakening, while its lasting fruit appears in a learned way that continues into mature understanding and teaching. The cooling of the first excitement need not mean the loss of what that desire established.
connections.headline: The desire of youth endures by becoming a practiced way of learning

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, א) וְעַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ז:).
connections.quote: ‘A good name is better than fine oil, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, א) וְעַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ז:).
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Five Scrolls, Ecclesiastes 5
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Five Scrolls, Ecclesiastes 5
connections.quote: ““A good name is better than good oil.” A name alludes to desire, as explained in many places in the first volume. Thus “David made a name” means diligence and exertion in serving God, as stated in the holy Zohar, Vayera 116b. Good oil signifies clarity and wisdom in Torah. “A good name” thus means that desire and diligence are better than knowledge and wisdom. Just as someone satisfied with one loaf should not envy someone who needs many loaves, a person who studies one chapter all day should not envy a person of broad understanding who studies several chapters. The essential thing is diligence and desire: this is precious before God. How long a person takes to grasp a matter makes no difference to this value. This is “a good name is better than good oil.””
connections.context: Mei HaShiloach records the teaching alluded to here and gives its practical illustration: the measure of devotion is the learner’s diligence and desire, rather than the number of chapters understood.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, א) וְעַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ז:).
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan also said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: Attending a Torah teacher is greater than studying Torah, as it is said: ‘Here is Elisha son of Shaphat, who poured water over Elijah’s hands.’ It does not say ‘learned,’ but ‘poured.’ This teaches that attending is greater than studying.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, א) וְעַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ז:).
connections.quote: “Our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berakhot 7b, end): “Serving Torah is greater than studying it.” I heard that study has a limit: how much a person comprehends. Service, however, is the longing and love of the one who serves, which move him to serve and to strive to raise the banner of Torah; this has no limit. He does not comprehend the substance of the Torah revealed to the sages, but only desires and yearns for Torah—that is, for the root of the whole Torah. Thus, service also encompasses the power of the hidden fiftieth gate.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, א) וְעַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ז:).
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 15
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 15
connections.quote: “‘This is the book of Adam's generations; in God's likeness He made him.’ The secret of image and likeness is this: image is the substance of life without expansion, like a newborn infant at its first instant. Afterward it begins to expand through its desires, such as the desire to eat. Through that desire it eats, and its life grows continually until it matures in breadth and height. That expansion is called likeness. So too in the soul: the first drop of Torah entering a person is called image; the yearning for Torah is called likeness. Through that yearning more Torah is continually added. This is ‘On the day God created Adam, in God's likeness…’: the principal purpose of man's creation was to desire continually the increase of Torah. This is the meaning of the saying (Berakhot 7b), ‘Serving Torah is greater than its study’: serving Torah is called the yearning. ‘This is the book of Adam's generations’ means that if a person merits image and likeness as explained, he will continually see new Torah, count his years and generations, and lengthen his days.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the same saying about serving Torah being greater than its study through the image of a living body growing by desire. The first point of Torah is the image; longing brings its expansion. This adds a mechanism for the siman's valuation of early desire while its later discussion preserves the value of mature attainment.
connections.headline: Desire as the growth of the first point

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ בַּהַתְחָלָה וּבְיַלְדוּת שֶׁאָז הַחֵשֶׁק גּוֹבֵר, וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ שִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת (קנב.): יַנְקוּתָא כְּלִילָא דְּוַרְדָּא וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם שְׁבַח הַיַּלְדוּת וּגְנוּת הַזִּקְנָה שֶׁאָז הַחֵשֶׁק כָּבָה.
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma says: Two [legs] are better than three [with a staff]. Woe for the one thing that goes and does not return. What is it? Rav Chisda said: Youth. When Rav Dimi came, he said: Youth is a wreath of roses; old age is a wreath of nettles. It was taught in Rabbi Meir’s name: Chew with your teeth, and you will find the benefit in your steps, as it is said: ‘We had our fill of bread and were well, and we saw no harm.’ Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda: ‘Sharp one, open your sack [your mouth] and let in your bread. Until forty years, eating is beneficial; from then on, drinking is beneficial.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וְכוּלֵי, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת נִשְׁתַּבְּחוּ זְקֵנִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה) וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יא),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei says: As Torah scholars grow older, wisdom is added to them, as it says, “With the aged is wisdom, and length of days is understanding.””

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וְכוּלֵי, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת נִשְׁתַּבְּחוּ זְקֵנִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה) וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יא),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Akiva said: Why are Israel compared to a bird? Just as a bird flies only with wings, so Israel can stand only through its elders. Great is old age: when they are elders they are beloved before the Holy One, blessed be He; when they are young, youthfulness clings to them.”
connections.context: These are the two supports for Rav Tzadok’s contrast with declining youthful desire: wisdom may increase with age, and the elders sustain the community.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וְכוּלֵי, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת נִשְׁתַּבְּחוּ זְקֵנִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה) וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יא),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai taught: Not in one place or two have we found that the Holy One, blessed be He, honored the elders, but in many places: at the bush, “Go and gather the elders of Israel”; in Egypt, “You and the elders of Israel shall come”; at Sinai, “Ascend to the Lord, you, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel.” … In the future too He honors the elders, as it says, “Before His elders, glory.””
connections.context: This is the passage at the end of Vayikra Rabbah chapter 11 that Rav Tzadok cites. It supplies a sequence of divine honors to elders, distinct from the earlier description of youthful energy.

connections.hePhrase: דְּבֶאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ז.): הַרְבֵּה לָמַדְתִּי מֵרַבּוֹתַי וְכוּלֵי וּמִתַּלְמִידַי יוֹתֵר וְכוּלֵי, וּמֵרַבּוֹתַי הַיְינוּ הַהַתְחָלָה וְהַחֵשֶׁק.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Why are words of Torah compared to wood, as it is said: ‘It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it’? This tells you: Just as a small piece of wood kindles a large one, so lesser Torah scholars sharpen greater ones. This is what Rabbi Chanina said: ‘I learned much from my teachers, from my colleagues more than from my teachers, and from my students more than from them all.’’

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁהַהַשָּׂגָה הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי "ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה", וְהַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הַנּוּקְבָא וְהָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא בְּחֵשֶׁק וְרָצוֹן כַּנּוֹדָע, זֶהוּ בִּידֵי אָדָם, לְכָךְ זֶהוּ טוֹב וְגָדוֹל.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥanina also said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven, as it says, “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except to fear?””
connections.context: The Talmudic statement locates the demand for reverence in the human response. Rav Tzadok uses it to distinguish the desire and initiative for learning from the understanding received from God.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה כְּעִנְיַן: עֲתִידִים צַדִּיקִים שֶׁיִּקָּרְאוּ בִּשְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא עה:);
connections.quote: ‘Rabba also said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: In the future the righteous will be called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said: ‘Everyone called by My name, whom I created for My glory, whom I formed and indeed made.’ Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani also said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: Three are called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He. These are they: the righteous, the Messiah, and Jerusalem.’

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם שְׁמוֹתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּנּוֹדָע דְּיֵשׁ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא אוֹתִיּוֹת לַתּוֹרָה – וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד תּוֹרָתוֹ.
connections.quote: see note 873 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly acknowledges that six hundred thousand is not the ordinary count of written letters. His explanation is a spiritual correspondence between souls, letters, and the sparks within letters; this qualification clarifies the expression used here.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ פְּתִיחַת סֵפֶר שְׁמוֹת שֶׁהוּא סֵפֶר מַתַּן תּוֹרָה בְּ"וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" (שְׁמוֹת א, א).
connections.quote: ‘These are the names of the children of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob; each man came with his household.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קָרָא שֵׁמוֹת וְהַמַּלְאָכִים לֹא יָדְעוּ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יז),
connections.quote: “He brought the animals, beasts, and birds before the angels and said to them: What is this one’s name? They did not know. He passed them before Adam and asked: What is this one’s name? He said: This is an ox, this a donkey, this a horse, this a camel. … And what is My name? He said: It is fitting to call You Adonai, for You are the master of all Your creatures.”
connections.context: Naming expresses Adam’s understanding of the creatures and their relation to their Creator. Rav Tzadok develops this as a distinct human capacity in contrast with the angels.

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַלְאָכִים אֵין לָהֶם שֵׁם, דִּלְפִי שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ נִקְרָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם פָּרָשָׁה עח).
connections.quote: ““Jacob asked and said: Tell me your name.” Rav said in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Dostai: One verse says, “He counts the number of the stars; He calls them names,” and another says, “He brings out their host by number; He calls them all by name.” This teaches that the name changes: the name by which one is called now is not the name by which one is called later, as it says, “The angel of the Lord said to him: Why do you ask my name, since it is wondrous?” He does not know to which name he will change.”
connections.context: The midrash explicitly describes changing names. Rav Tzadok reads this change in relation to an angel’s changing mission, contrasting that dependence with the human experience of a stable identity and choice.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים, כִּי מִנְהַג מִצְרַיִם גַּם כֵּן וְאֶרֶץ הַקֶּדֶם שֶׁהָאֲדוֹנִים יִקְרְאוּ לְעַבְדֵיהֶם שֵׁמוֹת כִּרְצוֹנָם, לְהוֹרוֹת כִּי אֵינוֹ רְשׁוּת וּבַעַל בְּחִירָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ כְּלָל.
connections.heRef: רש"י על דברי הימים ב ל״ו:ד׳:א׳
connections.quote: ““He changed his name to Jehoiakim.” Such is the way of kings and rulers: they give their servants whatever name they wish. Examples are “Pharaoh called Joseph’s name,” “Moses called Hoshea son of Nun Joshua,” and “The chief of the eunuchs gave them names.” All this is to show that he rules over him, naming him as he wishes.”
connections.context: Rashi’s commentary supplies the explicit explanation of imposed names as a sign of a ruler’s authority. Rav Tzadok uses that relationship as an analogy for creatures whose agency is wholly dependent on their sender.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְפִי הַשָּׂגַת הַמַּלְאָכִים שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם בְּחִירָה, כָּךְ תְּפִיסָתָם בְּכָל הַנִּבְרָאִים, וּמִי שֶׁאָמַר לַשֶּׁמֶן וְיִדְלַק יֹאמַר לַחֹמֶץ וְיִדְלַק, אִם כֵּן אֵין לְשׁוּם דָּבָר שֵׁם מְיוּחָד.
connections.quote: “One Sabbath eve he saw his daughter looking sad. He said to her: “My daughter, why are you sad?” She replied: “I confused a container of vinegar with a container of oil and lit the Sabbath lamp from it.” He said: “My daughter, why should that trouble you? The One who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” It was taught: It continued burning all that day, until they took from it a flame for Havdalah.”
connections.context: The story concerns Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa. Its saying supplies Rav Tzadok’s example of seeing a thing’s activity as dependent on God’s command, even when ordinary natural distinctions appear decisive.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַהַתְחָלָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא מִצַּד הַבְּחִירָה, זֶה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהַסִּיּוּם – שְׁמוֹת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
connections.quote: “For the cloud of Hashem was upon the Tabernacle by day, and there was fire in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel, throughout all their journeys.”
connections.context: These are the closing words of the book of Shemot, which opens with “These are the names of the children of Israel” (Exodus 1:1).

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה.): "לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ" (תְּהִלִּים כד, א) קוֹדֶם בְּרָכָה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Levi raised a contradiction: It is written, “The earth and its fullness are the Lord’s,” and it is written, “The heavens are the Lord’s heavens, but the earth He gave to human beings.” It is not difficult: here it is before the blessing—”

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה.): "לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ" (תְּהִלִּים כד, א) קוֹדֶם בְּרָכָה,
connections.quote: “—there it is after the blessing.”
connections.context: The answer crosses the page boundary. Recognition of divine ownership through the blessing precedes the permission to enjoy, which is the pattern Rav Tzadok applies to Torah becoming the learner’s own.

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה.): "לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ" (תְּהִלִּים כד, א) קוֹדֶם בְּרָכָה,
connections.quote: ‘Of David, a psalm. The earth and all that fills it belong to Hashem, the world and those who dwell in it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר הַבְּרָכָה שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ, אָז "הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִבְנֵי אָדָם" (שָׁם קטו, טז).
connections.quote: ‘The heavens are the heavens of Hashem, but the earth He gave to human beings.’

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁתֵּי רִאשׁוֹנוֹת הֵם בְּיָדוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק א דְּאָבוֹת: "עֲשֵׂה וְכוּלֵי וּקְנֵה וְכוּלֵי", מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תַּלְמִיד, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם טוֹב.
connections.quote: “Yehoshua ben Perachya says: Make for yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person favorably.”

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁתֵּי רִאשׁוֹנוֹת הֵם בְּיָדוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק א דְּאָבוֹת: "עֲשֵׂה וְכוּלֵי וּקְנֵה וְכוּלֵי", מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תַּלְמִיד, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם טוֹב.
connections.displayRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:6:1
connections.linkedRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:6:1
connections.canonicalRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:6:1
connections.heRef: תוספות יום טוב על משנה אבות א׳:ו׳:א׳
connections.quote: “Midrash Shmuel writes in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Lerma that he asked why it did not instruct one to take students, since they said, “From my students more than from all.” He explained that students wish only to learn, and therefore learn where their heart desires or from someone from whom they think they will learn more. Since a person may not find someone willing to be his student, the tanna did not instruct him about them.”
connections.context: Tosafot Yom Tov records several answers and finally notes the earlier instruction to raise many disciples, which itself presumes willing students and a qualified teacher. Rav Tzadok takes up the contrast between choosing a teacher or friend and attracting students.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הַסִּיּוּם "וֶהֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי", נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ כְּלַפֵּי הַתַּלְמִידִים, לֹא כְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל שֶׁאָמַר בִּבְרָכוֹת (כח.): כָּל תַּלְמִיד שֶׁאֵין תּוֹכוֹ כְּבָרוֹ וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: On that day they removed the doorkeeper and gave the students permission to enter. For Rabban Gamliel had proclaimed: Any student whose inside does not match his outside may not enter the study hall.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּעַל תַּלְמִיד שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּיָדוֹ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ אַזְהָרָה, רַק שֶׁהוּא מִמֵּילָא, מִי שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים הַקּוֹדְמִים זוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ גַּם כֵּן לְתַלְמִידִים.
connections.quote: “This applies only to a person judging himself. If he sees a deficiency in another, he is not entitled to attribute the deficiency to that person; he must judge him favorably, holding that the person is surely inwardly clear of the bad traits that appear in him and that the failing is like an error proceeding from the ruler. This was the matter here: Rabbi Elazar saw bad traits in a person and judged that the person himself was not refined and possessed those traits. The person answered him: Although I myself must attribute the deficiency to myself, even when it seems to me that I am clear of those bad traits, it is otherwise with you. You are not entitled to attribute the deficiency to me; you must judge me favorably. Go to the Craftsman who made me and say to Him, ‘How ugly is this vessel You made.’”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the encounter with the apparently ugly person as a warning about interpreting another's character. The person must examine himself; the observer must allow for what he cannot see. This clarifies why the present siman places favorable judgment beside the work of finding friends and raising students. The discipline that makes a person demanding of himself need not become suspicion that closes the door to another's Torah growth.
connections.headline: Self-scrutiny is not the measure for judging another

connections.hePhrase: וּכְלַפֵּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה: "הַעֲמִידוּ תַלְמִידִים הַרְבֵּה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק א, א), אָמַר הוּא בְּלָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: "הֱוֵי וְכוּלֵי", דְּגַם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִהְיוּ הַרְבֵּה.
connections.quote: ‘Moses received Torah from Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua; Joshua to the elders; the elders to the prophets; and the prophets transmitted it to the Men of the Great Assembly. They said three things: Be deliberate in judgment, raise up many students, and make a fence for the Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִי שֶׁרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה הָיָה יוֹצֵאת בִּרְחוֹבוֹתָיו מֵאוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד (בְּרָכוֹת יז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב), וְהָיָה סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַרְבּוֹת תַּלְמִידִים, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה: לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין לָחוּשׁ לְכָךְ, וְאַתְּ הֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי, כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו סְתוּמִים, וּבַהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ.
connections.quote: see note 1097 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Sanhedrin 107b:8 explicitly names Yehoshua ben Perachya in the teaching “Let the left hand push away and the right draw near,” contrasting this with pushing a student away with both hands. That is the rabbinic background to the teacher-and-student allusion here; Rav Tzadok uses it to argue for judging an ambiguous student favorably.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִי שֶׁרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה הָיָה יוֹצֵאת בִּרְחוֹבוֹתָיו מֵאוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד (בְּרָכוֹת יז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב), וְהָיָה סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַרְבּוֹת תַּלְמִידִים, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה: לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין לָחוּשׁ לְכָךְ, וְאַתְּ הֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי, כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו סְתוּמִים, וּבַהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ.
connections.quote: “Hezekiah said to him: “Why so severe a judgment?” Isaiah said: “Because you did not engage in procreation.” Hezekiah replied: “Because I saw through the holy spirit that unworthy children would come from me.” Isaiah said: “What have you to do with the Merciful One’s hidden matters? You must do what you were commanded, and let the Holy One, blessed be He, do what is pleasing to Him.””
connections.context: The phrase about God’s hidden matters originally concerns Hezekiah’s refusal to have children because he foresaw their wrongdoing. Rav Tzadok applies the same distinction to teaching: an uncertain future outcome does not cancel the present duty to teach and to judge unknown conduct favorably.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַלִּמּוּד מֵרַב הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו.): אֶחָד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁשְּׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ מִקְּרָא דְּ"אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי" (שְׁמוֹת כ, כא), דְּהַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא שֵׁם ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.), וְ"אַזְכִּיר" הַיְינוּ דְּהוּא תּוֹרַת ה' כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ד, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר וּמְלַמֵּד.
connections.quote: ‘From where do we know that even when one person sits and occupies himself with Torah, the Shekhinah is with him? For it is said: ‘In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַלִּמּוּד מֵרַב הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו.): אֶחָד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁשְּׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ מִקְּרָא דְּ"אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי" (שְׁמוֹת כ, כא), דְּהַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא שֵׁם ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.), וְ"אַזְכִּיר" הַיְינוּ דְּהוּא תּוֹרַת ה' כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ד, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר וּמְלַמֵּד.
connections.quote: “Make for Me an altar of earth, and sacrifice upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your cattle. In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok focuses on the active wording “I cause My name to be mentioned,” reading the learner’s first acquisition of Torah as divine teaching.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַלִּמּוּד מֵרַב הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו.): אֶחָד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁשְּׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ מִקְּרָא דְּ"אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי" (שְׁמוֹת כ, כא), דְּהַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא שֵׁם ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.), וְ"אַזְכִּיר" הַיְינוּ דְּהוּא תּוֹרַת ה' כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ד, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר וּמְלַמֵּד.
connections.quote: “From where in the Torah do we know the blessing before Torah? As it says, “For I will call the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God.””
connections.context: This is the passage connecting Torah to calling God’s name. The neighboring argument about blessings before and after food did not contain the cited identification.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ בְּיָחִיד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (פא.): מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִים לִהְיוֹת בְּנֵיהֶם וְכוּלֵי? שֶׁלֹּא בֵּרְכוּ וְכוּלֵי, כִּי בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ "הַמְלַמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְעַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל", וּמַכִּיר שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְלַמֵּד וְהִיא תּוֹרַת ה', אָז נַעֲשֵׂית תּוֹרָתוֹ לְאַחַר בְּרָכָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל בְּאוֹת קפ"ד.
connections.quote: “Why is it not common for Torah scholars to have Torah scholars emerge from their children?”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ בְּיָחִיד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (פא.): מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִים לִהְיוֹת בְּנֵיהֶם וְכוּלֵי? שֶׁלֹּא בֵּרְכוּ וְכוּלֵי, כִּי בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ "הַמְלַמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְעַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל", וּמַכִּיר שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְלַמֵּד וְהִיא תּוֹרַת ה', אָז נַעֲשֵׂית תּוֹרָתוֹ לְאַחַר בְּרָכָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל בְּאוֹת קפ"ד.
connections.quote: “Ravina says: Because they do not bless over the Torah first.”
connections.context: Ravina’s answer is one of several explanations offered in the Gemara. Rav Tzadok is developing this particular answer: blessing expresses recognition of God as the teacher before Torah becomes the learner’s own.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת "אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (מַלְאָכִי ג, טז), מַדְרֵיגַת הַדִּבּוּר שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ג שֶׁהוּא מַקְבִּיל לָזֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר].
connections.quote: ‘Then those who feared Hashem spoke with one another. Hashem listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear Hashem and give thought to His name.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְחָלַת הַחֵשֶׁק לִלְמוֹד מֵרַב הוּא הַבְּחִירָה עַצְמָהּ, וְהוּא בְּסוֹד נָעוּץ סוֹפָן בִּתְחִלָּתָן שֶׁזֶּה גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת, וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה'.
connections.quote: see note 1617 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The image explains the return of the end to the beginning. Rav Tzadok applies it to the discovery that even the learner’s initial desire and power of choice were given by God.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר פְּטִירַת הָרַב, וְאָבְדוּ עֶשְׁתּוֹנוֹתָיו כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אַל תִּבְטְחוּ בִנְדִיבִים וְגוֹמֵר, בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אָבְדוּ עֶשְׁתֹּנֹתָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמו, ג–ד) [וְקָאֵי אַעֶשְׁתּוֹנוֹת הַבּוֹטֵחַ],
connections.quote: “Do not trust in nobles, in a human being who has no power to save.”
connections.context: This warning supplies the premise for the next verse about a mortal’s death and the loss of plans. These are verses in Psalms; the main text’s expanded reference to “Shammai” is not their attribution.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר פְּטִירַת הָרַב, וְאָבְדוּ עֶשְׁתּוֹנוֹתָיו כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אַל תִּבְטְחוּ בִנְדִיבִים וְגוֹמֵר, בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אָבְדוּ עֶשְׁתֹּנֹתָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמו, ג–ד) [וְקָאֵי אַעֶשְׁתּוֹנוֹת הַבּוֹטֵחַ],
connections.quote: “His breath goes out; he returns to his earth; on that day his plans perish.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok applies the loss of plans to the one who relies on a mortal patron or teacher, so that the death of the person relied upon unsettles the dependent person. That application extends the verse’s ordinary reference to the mortal whose life ends.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַתְחִיל לְהַכִּיר כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְלַמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְעַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְ"אַשְׁרֵי... שִׁבְרוֹ עַל ה' אֱלֹהָיו" (שָׁם, ה) – הַכָּרָה זוֹ נִקְרָא יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם, וְאָז "נִדְבְּרוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “Happy is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God.”
connections.context: The complete verse joins help with hope. Rav Tzadok reads this blessing, following the warning against relying on mortal patrons, as the learner’s recognition that God supplies the help through which Torah endures.

connections.hePhrase: וּמְבַקֵּשׁ לִקְנוֹת חֲבֵירִים כְּעִנְיַן שֶׁחֲבֵירֶיךָ יְקַיְּמוּהָ בְּיָדְךָ (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, יד), שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד יִרְאָה שֶׁמָּא יִשְׁכַּח חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כְּדֶרֶךְ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲרָךְ (שַׁבָּת קמז:), וְזֶהוּ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh went there, was drawn after those pleasures, and his learning was uprooted. When he returned, he rose to read from the scroll. He intended to read “This month is for you,” but read “Their heart was deaf.” The sages prayed for mercy for him, and his learning returned.”
connections.context: The following paragraph connects the incident with “Exile yourself to a place of Torah” and the role of companions in preserving one’s learning. The story supplies the concrete example of forgetting mentioned by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה תְּחִלָּה שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לְבָנִים תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי כֵן יְבֹרַךְ גֶּבֶר יְרֵא ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קכח, ד).
connections.quote: see note 1785 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The preceding verse makes the family blessing explicit. Rav Tzadok connects it with the preceding Nedarim discussion of children who become Torah scholars.

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה נִקְרָא "לְאוֹקְמֵי גִּירְסָא" שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (ו:) דְּהוּא סַיַּעְתָּא מִן שְׁמַיָּא
connections.quote: ‘This applies to words of Torah. In business, however, success is assistance from Heaven. Even concerning words of Torah, we said this only about sharpening one’s understanding; retaining one’s learning depends on assistance from Heaven.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "מִכְתְּבַן מִילַּיְיהוּ", פֵּירוּשׁ סֵפֶר הַזִּכְרוֹנוֹת הֵם נַפְשׁוֹתָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים עַל סִפְרָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים וְשֶׁל רְשָׁעִים דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, וּ"מִכְתְּבַן" הַיְינוּ שֶׁנֶּחְקַק לְזִכָּרוֹן וּלְאוֹקְמֵי גִּירְסָא שֶׁלֹּא יֵעָתֵק מֵהֶם עוֹד;
connections.quote: “Since this is true even of one person, is it necessary to say it of two? The words of two are written in the book of remembrance; the words of one are not written in the book of remembrance.”
connections.context: The preceding discussion affirms the Divine Presence even with one person studying. This passage adds the particular distinction of two learners, “their words are written,” which Rav Tzadok interprets as Torah becoming durably impressed upon their souls.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "מִכְתְּבַן מִילַּיְיהוּ", פֵּירוּשׁ סֵפֶר הַזִּכְרוֹנוֹת הֵם נַפְשׁוֹתָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים עַל סִפְרָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים וְשֶׁל רְשָׁעִים דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, וּ"מִכְתְּבַן" הַיְינוּ שֶׁנֶּחְקַק לְזִכָּרוֹן וּלְאוֹקְמֵי גִּירְסָא שֶׁלֹּא יֵעָתֵק מֵהֶם עוֹד;
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 8:2
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 8:2
connections.quote: “Just as, when a person engages in Torah through speech, the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and engages in it opposite him, as the Sages say in Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu Rabbah 18, so when he writes words of Torah, the Holy One writes them as well. God’s writing means the coming into being of souls—for example, the Written Torah, whose letters are the roots of the souls of Israel, as is known. So too all writing of the Oral Torah reveals what is concealed in the Written Torah. All souls consist of letters, and a person’s deeds, in commandments and transgressions, change their combination, as explained in Raavad’s commentary to Sefer Yetzirah at the beginning of chapter 3, concerning the three books of the wholly righteous and the others; see there. Through those letters written by the hand of the Holy One, souls are formed.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the mystical meaning of a heavenly book as the souls themselves. It is quoted as Rav Tzadok’s explanation in Likkutei Maamarim, including his attribution to the commentary on Sefer Yetzirah, rather than as an independently verified quotation from that commentary.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "מִכְתְּבַן מִילַּיְיהוּ", פֵּירוּשׁ סֵפֶר הַזִּכְרוֹנוֹת הֵם נַפְשׁוֹתָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים עַל סִפְרָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים וְשֶׁל רְשָׁעִים דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, וּ"מִכְתְּבַן" הַיְינוּ שֶׁנֶּחְקַק לְזִכָּרוֹן וּלְאוֹקְמֵי גִּירְסָא שֶׁלֹּא יֵעָתֵק מֵהֶם עוֹד;
connections.quote: “The explanation is that it is written (Numbers 10:9), ‘You shall be remembered before Hashem your God.’ What can remembrance mean for Hashem? For a person, who sometimes forgets, remembrance has a place. But before Hashem there is no forgetting before the throne of His glory, and nothing is hidden from His sight: what does remembrance mean? All this remembrance is on the human side. Where a person establishes continual remembrance of Hashem, Hashem fixes it within him permanently, so that he does not forget Hashem for even a moment. This is called remembrance with Hashem. As it says (Malachi 3:16), ‘Then those who fear Hashem spoke to one another; Hashem attended and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him.’ My holy grandfather explained in Mei HaShiloach that Hashem's book of remembrance means His establishing words of Torah permanently within the person.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks how remembrance can apply to Hashem, before Whom nothing is forgotten. It explicitly interprets the same book of remembrance as Hashem establishing Torah permanently within the person. This directly explains the siman's account of the writing as an engraving in the souls that preserves their learning.
connections.headline: The remembrance is fixed in the learner

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּיָחִיד שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (ז.) דְּמִטַּפְּשָׁן.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said: What is meant by “A sword upon the isolated, and they become foolish”? A sword upon Torah scholars who occupy themselves with Torah in isolation. Moreover, they become foolish, as it says, “They become foolish.””
connections.context: The rebuke concerns isolated study that lacks the correction and sharpening of fellow learners. Rav Tzadok contrasts it with the stable learning achieved through companionship.

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּגְמִילוּת חֲסָדִים בְּסֻכָּה (מט:): "מַה יָּקָר וְגוֹמֵר", וְהַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם שֶׁאָמַר בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (טז:): הַכְשִׁילֵם בְּשֶׁאֵינָם מְהֻגָּנִים.
connections.quote: see note 1472 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The teaching is attributed to Rabbi Elazar in the Gemara, not Shammai. It contrasts the rarity of successfully directed kindness with the enduring kindness available to those who fear God; Rav Tzadok applies that pattern to finding suitable students.

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּגְמִילוּת חֲסָדִים בְּסֻכָּה (מט:): "מַה יָּקָר וְגוֹמֵר", וְהַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם שֶׁאָמַר בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (טז:): הַכְשִׁילֵם בְּשֶׁאֵינָם מְהֻגָּנִים.
connections.quote: “How precious is Your lovingkindness, O God! The children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְכָךְ סִיֵּים רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה: "וֶהֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי", דְּאֵין לוֹ לָחוּשׁ לְכָךְ, דְּהֲגַם דִּבְרַב נֶאֱמַר "עֲשֵׂה" אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם שָׁם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים (פה עַמּוּד ב) דְּאִית לְמֵילַף מִכָּל בַּר נָשׁ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ““Make yourself a teacher.” This means: even if he is not fit to be your teacher, appoint him as your teacher until you regard him as one who teaches, and through this you will gain the study of wisdom. A person’s learning alone is not like learning from another. Learning alone is good, but learning from another remains with him more firmly and is clearer, even if the other is equal to him in wisdom or below him. This is how they explained this instruction.”
connections.context: Rambam makes the intended limitation explicit: the person may be equal or inferior in learning and still help one learn. “Not fit to be your teacher” here concerns scholarly rank; this passage does not authorize choosing a morally corrupt teacher.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְכָךְ סִיֵּים רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה: "וֶהֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי", דְּאֵין לוֹ לָחוּשׁ לְכָךְ, דְּהֲגַם דִּבְרַב נֶאֱמַר "עֲשֵׂה" אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם שָׁם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים (פה עַמּוּד ב) דְּאִית לְמֵילַף מִכָּל בַּר נָשׁ וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “Even so, a person should learn words of Torah from every person, even from one who does not know, for through this he will be roused to Torah and will come to learn from one who knows; and afterward he will be found walking in the Torah on a true path.”

connections.hePhrase: וּפָרָשַׁת "אַל תִּבְטְחוּ בִנְדִיבִים וְגוֹמֵר" מְסַיֶּימֶת: "הַשֹּׁמֵר אֱמֶת לְעוֹלָם" (תְּהִלִּים קמו, ו) – הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׁוֹמֵר הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁיִּתְקַיְּמוּ בְּיָדוֹ לְעוֹלָם, "עֹשֶׂה מִשְׁפָּט וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, ז),
connections.quote: “Maker of heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever.”
connections.context: The Hebrew emet, truth, allows Rav Tzadok to connect the verse with Torah as truth and with its enduring preservation in the learner.

connections.hePhrase: דְּרַק לְצוֹרֶךְ דִּינָא וּשְׁלָמָא בְּעָלְמָא, פֵּירוּשׁ שָׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם, כְּעִנְיַן "תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מַרְבִּים שָׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם" (בְּרָכוֹת סד.), וְהַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה, צָרִיךְ שְׁלֹשָׁה, כִּלְשׁוֹן "שֶׁחֲבֵירֶיךָ יְקַיְּמוּהָ" לְשׁוֹן רַבִּים.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said in Rabbi Chanina’s name: Torah scholars increase peace in the world, as it says: ‘All your children will be taught by Hashem, and great will be the peace of your children.’ Do not read ‘your children (banayikh),’ but ‘your builders (bonayikh).’ ‘Great peace belongs to those who love Your Torah, and there is no stumbling block for them.’ ‘May there be peace within your ramparts, tranquility within your palaces.’ ‘For the sake of my brothers and companions, I will speak of peace within you. For the sake of the House of Hashem our God, I will seek your good.’ ‘Hashem will give strength to His people; Hashem will bless His people with peace.’”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עֲשָׂרָה – זֶהוּ אַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁמַּרְבִּיץ תּוֹרָה בְּתַלְמִידִים, שֶׁהַשַּׂר הַיּוֹתֵר פָּחוּת בַּכָּתוּב הוּא שָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרוֹת, וְאֵין נִקְרָא רַב לְתַלְמִידִים בְּפָחוֹת מֵעֲשָׂרָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יב:),
connections.quote: “And you shall choose out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain, and place them over them as officers of thousands, officers of hundreds, officers of fifties and officers of tens.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עֲשָׂרָה – זֶהוּ אַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁמַּרְבִּיץ תּוֹרָה בְּתַלְמִידִים, שֶׁהַשַּׂר הַיּוֹתֵר פָּחוּת בַּכָּתוּב הוּא שָׂרֵי עֲשָׂרוֹת, וְאֵין נִקְרָא רַב לְתַלְמִידִים בְּפָחוֹת מֵעֲשָׂרָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יב:),
connections.quote: “They sent a pair of sages to consult with him, and he detained them. They sent another pair, and he detained them, until there were ten. Once there were ten, he opened, taught, and expounded, for one does not open a kallah lecture with fewer than ten.”
connections.context: The story concerns Mar bar Rav Ashi and a formal kallah teaching assembly. Rav Tzadok uses the group of ten as the pattern for the stage of teaching disciples.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז קָדְמָה שְׁכִינָה וְאָתְיָא, שֶׁכְּבָר נַעֲשָׂה גוּפוֹ מֶרְכָּבָה לִשְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ אַף קוֹדֶם שֶׁעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה, כְּטַעַם מַדְרֵגַת "שִׂיחוּ" שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתוֹ תּוֹרָה הַמְּבוֹאָר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ג:
connections.quote: “Since this is true even of two, is it necessary to say it of three? One might have thought that judgment merely makes peace and that the Divine Presence does not come; this teaches that judgment too is Torah. Since this is true even of three, is it necessary to say it of ten? With ten, the Divine Presence arrives beforehand; with three, only once they sit.”
connections.context: The Talmud distinguishes two learners, a court of three, and a gathering of ten. Rav Tzadok develops a spiritual sequence from these distinctions, culminating in the Presence preceding the group. The Talmud’s immediate discussion of ten concerns communal prayer; applying its pattern to a teacher and disciples is his interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: [קפו] עִיקַּר הַהִתְחַבְּרוּת הוּא לִירֵאִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "חָבֵר אָנִי לְכָל אֲשֶׁר יְרֵאוּךָ" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, סג), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי ה' אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ" (מַלְאָכִי ג, טז).
connections.quote: ‘I am a companion to all who fear You and to those who keep Your precepts.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי שָׁלֹשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת חָכְמָה, בִּינָה, דַּעַת: חָכְמָה – מַה שֶּׁמְּקַבֵּל מֵאֲחֵרִים, זֶהוּ מַה שֶּׁקִּבֵּל מֵרַבּוֹ;
connections.quote: ““The beginning of wisdom: acquire wisdom.” At the beginning of your wisdom, learn from others; acquire a teaching from the mouth of a teacher. Afterward, “with all your acquisitions, acquire understanding”: consider it on your own, to understand the reasons, deriving one matter from another.”
connections.context: Rashi distinguishes received teaching from the understanding developed through reflection. This supplies the distinction between chochmah and binah that Rav Tzadok applies to learning from a teacher and learning with companions.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְהָבִין דָּבָר מִתּוֹךְ דָּבָר – זֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי הִתְחַבְּרוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ז.): "בַּרְזֶל בְּבַרְזֶל יַחַד וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יז).
connections.quote: see note 2480.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְהָבִין דָּבָר מִתּוֹךְ דָּבָר – זֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי הִתְחַבְּרוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ז.): "בַּרְזֶל בְּבַרְזֶל יַחַד וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יז).
connections.quote: ‘Iron sharpens iron, and a person sharpens the face of his fellow.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַחֶבְרָה: לְחַדֵּד זֶה אֶת זֶה שֶׁיִּתְחַדְּשׁוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל יָדָם, דִּלְכָךְ מִצְטָרְפִין לְזִמּוּן כִּדְאִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (מז:) וְלֹא פָּרִיךְ "וְחִידּוּד גַּבְרָא",
connections.quote: ‘Rav Ami said: Two people and Shabbat combine [for a zimmun]. Rav Nachman said to him: Is Shabbat a person? Rather, Rabbi Ami said: Two Torah scholars who sharpen one another in halakhah combine. Rav Chisda indicated: Such as Rav Sheshet and I. Rav Sheshet indicated: Such as Rav Chisda and I.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַחֶבְרָה: לְחַדֵּד זֶה אֶת זֶה שֶׁיִּתְחַדְּשׁוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל יָדָם, דִּלְכָךְ מִצְטָרְפִין לְזִמּוּן כִּדְאִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (מז:) וְלֹא פָּרִיךְ "וְחִידּוּד גַּבְרָא",
connections.quote: “The halakhah does not follow any of these teachings, but rather this statement of Rav Naḥman: A minor who knows to whom the blessing is addressed may be included in a zimmun.”
connections.context: This is the conclusion of the discussion that includes the proposal to count two scholars who sharpen one another as three. Rav Tzadok develops the spiritual meaning of that proposal; the Talmud does not accept it as the practical rule for a two-person zimmun. Its concluding statement turns instead to the qualified case of a minor.

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַה שֶּׁצָּרִיךְ שְׁלֹשָׁה הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין חַבְרוּתָא בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (טז:) לְעִנְיַן שַׁיָּירָא, וּבְסֻכָּה (יג.) לְעִנְיַן אֲגֻדָּה וַחֲבִילָה עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת, וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח) עַל פָּסוּק "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ" – אֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
connections.quote: ‘Did Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehudah really say this? Was it not taught: Both an individual and a caravan may use ropes (as partitions). What is the difference between an individual and a caravan? An individual is allowed land that can be sown with two se’ah of seed; two people are allowed the same area of two se’ah; three form a caravan and are allowed an area of six se’ah. These are Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehudah’s words.’
connections.context: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes a single person, two people, and three people: three constitute a caravan. The attribution in this passage is to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda; the reader’s expanded phrase “Shammai” is not the speaker here. Rav Tzadok uses the distinction to explain why three create a collective unit.

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַה שֶּׁצָּרִיךְ שְׁלֹשָׁה הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין חַבְרוּתָא בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (טז:) לְעִנְיַן שַׁיָּירָא, וּבְסֻכָּה (יג.) לְעִנְיַן אֲגֻדָּה וַחֲבִילָה עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת, וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח) עַל פָּסוּק "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ" – אֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
connections.quote: “Rav Chisda said: Binding one object is not called a bundle; three is called a bundle; two is disputed by Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַה שֶּׁצָּרִיךְ שְׁלֹשָׁה הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין חַבְרוּתָא בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (טז:) לְעִנְיַן שַׁיָּירָא, וּבְסֻכָּה (יג.) לְעִנְיַן אֲגֻדָּה וַחֲבִילָה עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת, וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח) עַל פָּסוּק "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ" – אֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
connections.quote: “Perhaps, although generally three count as a group, this verse, “His group He founded upon the earth,” must refer to five, because it says, “My hand founded the earth,” and a hand has five fingers.”
connections.context: The Talmud supplies the general rule that three form an agudah. Tosafot, explicitly mentioned by Rav Tzadok, recognizes that general rule while explaining why a particular scriptural exposition requires five.

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַה שֶּׁצָּרִיךְ שְׁלֹשָׁה הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין חַבְרוּתָא בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (טז:) לְעִנְיַן שַׁיָּירָא, וּבְסֻכָּה (יג.) לְעִנְיַן אֲגֻדָּה וַחֲבִילָה עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת, וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח) עַל פָּסוּק "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ" – אֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
connections.quote: “For Hashem’s portion is His people; Jacob is the lot (chevel) of His inheritance.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּמַה שֶּׁצָּרִיךְ שְׁלֹשָׁה הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין חַבְרוּתָא בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (טז:) לְעִנְיַן שַׁיָּירָא, וּבְסֻכָּה (יג.) לְעִנְיַן אֲגֻדָּה וַחֲבִילָה עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת, וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח) עַל פָּסוּק "יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ" – אֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע בְּפָחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in Rabbi Levi’s name: You are the third leg. This accords with his teaching: “For the Lord’s portion is His people, Jacob the rope of His inheritance.” Just as this rope is not braided from fewer than three, so the patriarchs are no fewer than three.”
connections.context: Jacob completes the patriarchal triad, just as a rope is made from three strands. The Midrash’s verb refers to making or braiding the rope; its point is the threefold structure.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה הוּא חִבּוּר שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת וְאֶמְצָעִי הַמְחַבֵּר, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מה:): אִיכָּא דֵּעוֹת, דְּהָעִיקָּר שָׁלֹשׁ דֵּעוֹת הַנִּפְרָדוֹת שֶׁמִּתְחַבְּרִים יַחַד עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה יַחַד, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): אֵין הֲסָתָה בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Take two opposite things, such as black and white, and introduce a third color, such as red. This color is intermediate: it is neither black nor white, but stands between them. Through it the two opposites are joined, because it is between them. Thus, through the third, they have a connection.”
connections.context: Maharal’s example makes the threefold structure explicit: the third supplies a middle that connects the two extremes. Rav Tzadok applies this pattern to distinct minds joining in study and at a meal.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה הוּא חִבּוּר שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת וְאֶמְצָעִי הַמְחַבֵּר, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מה:): אִיכָּא דֵּעוֹת, דְּהָעִיקָּר שָׁלֹשׁ דֵּעוֹת הַנִּפְרָדוֹת שֶׁמִּתְחַבְּרִים יַחַד עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה יַחַד, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): אֵין הֲסָתָה בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “It is different there, because there are distinct minds.”
connections.context: The Gemara is discussing women forming their own zimmun. Although it compares their status to two men for another part of the argument, three women still constitute three distinct participants. Rav Tzadok cites “distinct minds” to explain the significance of three individual perspectives.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה הוּא חִבּוּר שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת וְאֶמְצָעִי הַמְחַבֵּר, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מה:): אִיכָּא דֵּעוֹת, דְּהָעִיקָּר שָׁלֹשׁ דֵּעוֹת הַנִּפְרָדוֹת שֶׁמִּתְחַבְּרִים יַחַד עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה יַחַד, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): אֵין הֲסָתָה בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Perhaps he slaughtered, but Jehoshaphat did not eat? It is written, “He persuaded him.” Perhaps with words? There is no such persuasion merely with words.”
connections.context: The discussion concerns Ahab’s feast for Jehoshaphat before persuading him to join a campaign. The Gemara takes the persuasion as evidence that Jehoshaphat ate. Rav Tzadok uses this to illustrate the attachment produced by shared food. This is an anonymous Talmudic argument, not a saying of Shammai.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה הוּא חִבּוּר שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת וְאֶמְצָעִי הַמְחַבֵּר, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מה:): אִיכָּא דֵּעוֹת, דְּהָעִיקָּר שָׁלֹשׁ דֵּעוֹת הַנִּפְרָדוֹת שֶׁמִּתְחַבְּרִים יַחַד עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה יַחַד, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): אֵין הֲסָתָה בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Therefore the Maharil explains that the intention concerns the tzitzit thread in the middle. A thread of tzitzit serves to recall all the mitzvot, and joining the two mitzvot of Chanukah and mezuzah helps that thread become strengthened like the threefold cord. Through this it becomes “Jacob, the rope of His inheritance,” tripled from the holiness of all three patriarchs, like a rope that is not plaited from fewer than three strands, as Bereishit Rabbah says. Through the Chanukah lamp this power was established and completed within the totality of Israel’s souls.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah applies the threefold cord to mitzvot joined at the doorway and to Yaakov’s inheritance from the three Avos. This gives a concrete image for the present siman’s distinction between separate minds and a bond that can hold them together. Here the third, connecting dimension is da’at: fellowship reaches beyond the mere presence of several people when their distinct powers are brought into a shared service of Hashem.
connections.headline: A threefold bond joins distinct powers without erasing them

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן פִּתָּן וְיֵינָן מִשּׁוּם בְּנוֹתֵיהֶם, שֶׁעִיקַּר הִתְחַבְּרוּת עַל יְדֵי אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה.
connections.quote: “Rather, they decreed concerning their bread and oil because of their wine, concerning their wine because of their daughters, concerning their daughters because of another matter, and concerning that other matter because of another matter.”
connections.context: The sequence of restrictions is explained through the social intimacy that food and wine can produce, ultimately leading to forbidden relationships and idolatry. This is the answer to the Gemara’s question, and supplies Rav Tzadok’s point about eating creating connection.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַזִּמּוּן דִּבְרָכָה לְפָנֶיהָ כְּשֶׁרָעֵב דּוּגְמַת שָׁבוּעוֹת [וּפֶסַח בְּחֹדֶשׁ הָאָבִיב], וּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ כְּשֶׁהוּא שָׂבֵעַ דּוּגְמַת סֻכּוֹת חַג הָאָסִיף שֶׁהוּא זְמַן שִׂמְחָתֵנוּ
connections.quote: “You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread; seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time in the month of Aviv, for in it you came out of Egypt.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַזִּמּוּן דִּבְרָכָה לְפָנֶיהָ כְּשֶׁרָעֵב דּוּגְמַת שָׁבוּעוֹת [וּפֶסַח בְּחֹדֶשׁ הָאָבִיב], וּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ כְּשֶׁהוּא שָׂבֵעַ דּוּגְמַת סֻכּוֹת חַג הָאָסִיף שֶׁהוּא זְמַן שִׂמְחָתֵנוּ
connections.quote: “And you shall observe the Feast of Weeks, the first fruits of the wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the turn of the year.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּבְמוֹעֵד קָטָן (ט.): אֵין שִׂמְחָה בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וְכוּלֵי],
connections.quote: “Let them celebrate, but not eat or drink! There is no joy without eating and drinking.”
connections.context: The Gemara is discussing the celebration of the Temple’s inauguration. Its answer supplies the specific connection between eating, drinking, and joy used here.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִשָּׁם שׁוֹאֲבִין רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה פֶּרֶק ה הֲלָכָה א), דְּדַעַת הַיְינוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י פָּרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Why is it called the House of Drawing? Because from there they draw the Holy Spirit, as it says, “You shall draw water with joy from the springs of salvation.””

connections.hePhrase: וּמִשָּׁם שׁוֹאֲבִין רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּהֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה פֶּרֶק ה הֲלָכָה א), דְּדַעַת הַיְינוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י פָּרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא.
connections.quote: “Knowledge: the Holy Spirit.”
connections.context: The Jerusalem Talmud explains the spiritual significance of the joyful Water-Drawing celebration, and later in the same passage says that the Holy Spirit rests only upon a joyful heart. Rashi supplies Rav Tzadok’s second link: da’at, knowledge, can denote the Holy Spirit.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה אָז צָרִיךְ זִמּוּן, דִּמְפוֹרָשׁ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מה.) דְּהַיְינוּ "גַּדְּלוּ לַה' אִתִּי וּנְרוֹמְמָה שְׁמוֹ יַחְדָּו" (תְּהִלִּים לד, ד), שֶׁלָּזֶה צָרִיךְ הֲכָנָה וְזִמּוּן לְהִתְכַּלֵּל יַחַד הַנְּפָשׁוֹת.
connections.quote: ‘Gemara: From where are these matters derived? Rav Assi said: Scripture says, ‘Magnify Hashem with me, and let us exalt His name together.’ Rabbi Abbahu said: From here: ‘When I proclaim the name of Hashem, ascribe greatness to our God.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה אָז צָרִיךְ זִמּוּן, דִּמְפוֹרָשׁ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מה.) דְּהַיְינוּ "גַּדְּלוּ לַה' אִתִּי וּנְרוֹמְמָה שְׁמוֹ יַחְדָּו" (תְּהִלִּים לד, ד), שֶׁלָּזֶה צָרִיךְ הֲכָנָה וְזִמּוּן לְהִתְכַּלֵּל יַחַד הַנְּפָשׁוֹת.
connections.quote: ‘Magnify Hashem with me, and let us exalt His name together.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בִּזְמַן, שׁוֹפָר דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שֶׁקּוֹדֶם סֻכּוֹת הוּא הַזִּמּוּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים דְּרוֹמֵז: עוּרוּ יְשֵׁנִים וְכוּלֵי, וַהֲכָנָה לְחִבּוּר וְיִחוּד הַקְּצוֹת עַל יְדֵי חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת.
connections.quote: “Although sounding the shofar on Rosh Hashanah is a decree of Scripture, it contains an allusion: Awake, sleepers, from your sleep; slumberers, arise from your slumber. Examine your deeds, return in repentance, and remember your Creator. You who forget the truth amid the vanities of the times and wander all year in emptiness that neither benefits nor saves: look to your souls, improve your ways and deeds, and let each of you abandon his evil path and his thought that is not good.”
connections.context: Rambam first preserves the shofar’s status as a scriptural command and then explains its call to awakening. Rav Tzadok uses that call as the preparation preceding the unity and joy of Sukkot.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַחִידּוּד מְחַבֵּר דּוּגְמַת הָעֲקֵידָה, דְּאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קיט עַמּוּד ב) דְּאָז נִתְכַּלְּלוּ יַחַד אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כב, יב);
connections.quote: ‘Come and see the mystery of the matter: Although we have said that Abraham is written and not Isaac, Isaac is also included in this verse. This is the mystery of what is written: ‘God tested Abraham.’ It does not say nissah le-Avraham, but et Avraham—et specifically; this is Isaac. For at that moment he was situated in the lower Gevurah. Once he was bound and properly prepared for judgment through Abraham, he was crowned in his place together with Abraham. Fire was included in water, and they ascended above. Then a fitting dispute came into being: water with fire.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַחִידּוּד מְחַבֵּר דּוּגְמַת הָעֲקֵידָה, דְּאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קיט עַמּוּד ב) דְּאָז נִתְכַּלְּלוּ יַחַד אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כב, יב);
connections.quote: ‘He said: ‘Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, and do not do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God: you have not withheld your son, your only one, from Me.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ דְּמַחֲוֵי רַב חִסְדָּא כְּגוֹן אֲנָא וְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת וְכוּלֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (סז.), דְּהֵם שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים: רַב חִסְדָּא חָרִיף וְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת סִינַי, וְכָל חַד מְרַתֵּת מֵחַבְרֵיהּ – זֶהוּ הַיִּרְאָה,
connections.quote: “When Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet met, Rav Chisda’s lips trembled at Rav Sheshet’s mastery of traditions, and Rav Sheshet’s entire body trembled at Rav Chisda’s analytical sharpness.”
connections.context: Each sage possessed a strength that the other revered. Their complementary forms of Torah knowledge illustrate why connection with another person can complete what one lacks.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ דִּלְכָךְ צָרִיךְ יִרְאָה, וְכִידוּעַ דְּבִינָה מִינַּהּ דִּינִין מִתְעָרִין, כִּי כָּל חִדּוּשׁ יֵשׁ יִרְאָה שֶׁמָּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם הוּא שָׁוְא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּהַקְדָּמַת הַזֹּהַר (ה עַמּוּד א) דְּלָכֵן אֵין לְחַדֵּשׁ דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא שָׁמַע מֵרַבּוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon said to the companions: I beg you not to bring from your mouths a word of Torah that you do not know and have not properly heard from a great tree, so that you do not cause that sinner to kill multitudes of people for nothing. They all began and said: May the Merciful One save us; may the Merciful One save us.”
connections.context: The great tree is the image of an authoritative teacher. The warning follows the Zohar’s symbolic account of someone unfamiliar with Torah’s mysteries inventing teachings without properly understanding them. It supplies the reverent caution required alongside the creativity that Rav Tzadok praises.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכִי הִתְנוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.) בִּמְחַדְּדִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִשְׁמָהּ וּבַעֲנָוָה, אָז מַצְלִיחִין, דְּגַם בְּמַחֲלוֹקְתָּן אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yirmeya said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: ‘When two Torah scholars sharpen one another in halakha, the Holy One, blessed be He, grants them success, as it is stated: ‘And in your splendor, succeed.’ Read it not as ‘your splendor,’ but as ‘your sharpening.’ Furthermore, they rise to greatness, as it is stated: ‘Succeed; ride forth.’ Could this apply even when they do not act for its own sake? The verse says: ‘For the sake of truth.’ Could it apply when one grows proud? The verse says: ‘And humility and righteousness.’ If they act in this way, they merit the Torah that was given with the right hand, as it is stated: ‘Your right hand will teach you awesome things.’’”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכִי הִתְנוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.) בִּמְחַדְּדִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִשְׁמָהּ וּבַעֲנָוָה, אָז מַצְלִיחִין, דְּגַם בְּמַחֲלוֹקְתָּן אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abba said in the name of Shmuel: For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed; these said, ‘The halakhah is as we say,’ and those said, ‘The halakhah is as we say.’ A heavenly voice went forth and said: These and those are the words of the living God, and the halakhah follows Beit Hillel.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא יִחוּד כְּמַחֲלוֹקֶת שַׁמַּאי וְהִלֵּל סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּים, שֶׁאֵינוֹ כָּזָב וְדָבָר הַפּוֹסֵק כְּכָל רִיב וּמְדָנִים יַפְרִיד אַחִים.
connections.quote: “Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven will endure; one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not endure. What is a dispute for the sake of Heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. What is one that is not for the sake of Heaven? The dispute of Korah and his entire company.”
connections.context: The Mishnah supplies both the positive example and its contrasting case. Rav Tzadok’s praise concerns disagreement directed toward Heaven, with the humility and sincerity specified immediately before it.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ "בִּינָה לִבָּא" שֶׁשָּׁם הַיִּרְאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (עב:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְלֶב אָיִן", וְעוֹשֶׂה חֲדָשׁוֹת בַּעַל מִלְחָמוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Chokhmah is the brain, which is thought within; Binah is the heart, and through it the heart understands.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ "בִּינָה לִבָּא" שֶׁשָּׁם הַיִּרְאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (עב:) עַל פָּסוּק "וְלֶב אָיִן", וְעוֹשֶׂה חֲדָשׁוֹת בַּעַל מִלְחָמוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.linkedRef: Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Blessings of the Shema, First Blessing before Shema 8
connections.canonicalRef: Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Blessings of the Shema, First Blessing before Shema 8
connections.heRef: סידור אשכנז, ימי חול, תפילת שחרית, ברכות קריאת שמע, יוצר אור ח׳
connections.quote: “For He alone performs mighty deeds, makes new things, is master of battles, sows righteousness, makes salvations sprout …”

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן שַׁבָּת הוּא מְנוּחָה, דְּזֶהוּ כְּשֶׁעוֹשִׂין לִשְׁמָהּ אָז "אֶת וָהֵב בְּסוּפָה" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כא, יד), וּמִתְיַיחֲדִין יַחַד וּמְזַמְּנִין, וְאָז עוֹלִין לִגְדוּלָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת שָׁם), דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁזּוֹכִין לְתַלְמִידִים שֶׁזֶּהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הַדַּעַת הַמְחַבֵּר, כְּמוֹ יִצְחָק עַל יְדֵי הָעֲקֵידָה נִזְדַּמְּנָה לוֹ רִבְקָה לְהוֹלִיד יַעֲקֹב הַמְחַבֵּר
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said: Even a father and his son, a teacher and his student, who study Torah at one gate become enemies of one another. They do not move from there until they become lovers of one another, as it says, “Et Vahev beSufah”: do not read “beSufah,” but “at its end.””
connections.context: The Gemara reads the place name in Numbers 21:14 as an allusion to love at the end of Torah debate. The argument can sharpen opposing positions and still culminate in affection; the biblical verse alone does not state this exposition.

connections.hePhrase: [עַיֵּין זֹהַר שְׁמוֹת יד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב דַּאֲבוֹת הֵם חָכְמָה, בִּינָה, דַּעַת]:
connections.quote: “Concerning this it is written, “Through knowledge rooms are filled.” At that time the entire world was completed. When Jacob’s twelve tribes were born, everything was completed in the likeness of what is above.”
connections.context: This continues the same Zohar passage quoted in the preceding note. Jacob’s da’at brings the structure to completion, and the twelve tribes complete its expression below. The two notes concern different clauses of one passage.

connections.hePhrase: [עַיֵּין זֹהַר שְׁמוֹת יד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב דַּאֲבוֹת הֵם חָכְמָה, בִּינָה, דַּעַת]:
connections.quote: “When He wished to establish the world, He made Abraham in the mystery of wisdom, Isaac in the mystery of understanding, and Jacob in the mystery of knowledge.”
connections.context: The Zohar maps the three patriarchs to chochmah, tevunah, and da’at. This is the specific threefold correspondence invoked here.
