connections.hePhrase: [קפז] הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֵם עֹז לָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְהַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז [לֶחָכָם]" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט), וְ"אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר? הַכּוֹבֵשׁ [אֶת יִצְרוֹ]" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, א), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין ל:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its seasoning. If you occupy yourselves with Torah, you are not handed over into its power.”

connections.hePhrase: [קפז] הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֵם עֹז לָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְהַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז [לֶחָכָם]" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט), וְ"אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר? הַכּוֹבֵשׁ [אֶת יִצְרוֹ]" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, א), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין ל:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: My son, if this wretched one encounters you, draw him to the study hall. If he is stone, he will dissolve; if he is iron, he will shatter.”
connections.context: These are two adjoining formulations of Torah’s power against the evil inclination. The first is the “seasoning” formulation explicitly used by Rav Tzadok; the second describes bringing the struggle into the study hall.

connections.hePhrase: [קפז] הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֵם עֹז לָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְהַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז [לֶחָכָם]" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט), וְ"אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר? הַכּוֹבֵשׁ [אֶת יִצְרוֹ]" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, א), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין ל:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “There is Amalek, the evil inclination, the accusing prosecutor continually present within a person, as the holy Zohar says. It is written, “Who cooled you on the way”: Amalek, the first of the nations, occupies himself with cooling a person and casting laziness and sadness upon him. This rules even among the great. Jabez spread Torah in Israel and restored through his reasoning the laws forgotten during the mourning for Moses. Nevertheless he asked, “That it not sadden me”—that the evil inclination not overpower him and prevent him from studying. A person cannot escape this shell through choice alone. Of this they said, “Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him, he could not overcome it,” and “The greater a person is than his fellow, the greater his inclination.” This is “Your miracles that are with us every day”: God’s help is a miracle beyond the regular order of governance through choice. It occurs every day, because the inclination grows stronger and renews itself every day. “The greater a person is than his fellow, the greater his inclination”—this explains its daily renewal.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah develops the daily renewal of the inclination through Yaavetz, whose great work in restoring Torah did not remove his need to ask for protection from discouragement and interruption of study. This gives the present siman’s ‘help’ a continuing character. Torah’s illuminating strength is not simply an achievement stored from an earlier victory; it is the form in which Hashem sustains the learner through the renewed struggle.
connections.headline: Renewed Torah strength answers an inclination that renews itself daily

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּהוּ "אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (סֻכָּה נב:), וְהָעֵזֶר וְהַסַּיַּעְתָּא הוּא עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁמֵּאִיר לוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yitzchak said: A person’s inclination grows stronger against him every day, as it is said: ‘Only evil all the day.’ Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: A person’s inclination grows stronger against him every day and seeks to kill him, as it is said: ‘The wicked watches the righteous and seeks to kill him.’ Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not helping him, he could not overcome it, as it is said: ‘Hashem will not abandon him into his hand, nor condemn him when he is judged.’’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּהוּ "אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (סֻכָּה נב:), וְהָעֵזֶר וְהַסַּיַּעְתָּא הוּא עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁמֵּאִיר לוֹ.
connections.quote: “The chief support for those who fall from their spiritual level is through words of Torah, which give strength and sound wisdom. This occurs through truthful speech recognizing God’s greatness, even when a person is utterly distant from Him. Such is Torah study: it is not like standing before the King. It is therefore possible even at a time of falling and distance, and through it the person is supported.”
connections.context: In his later explanation Rav Tzadok describes Torah as a source of strength even when one cannot feel close to God. This develops the meaning of the divine help identified here with the Torah that illuminates the learner.

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא) בְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: רַב לֹא הָיָה לוֹ וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה, מִפִּיו דַּעַת וּתְבוּנָה" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ו).
connections.quote: see note 2457.
connections.context: The subject is Abraham. Rabbi Shimon depicts his knowledge as arising from the inner teachers placed within him. This is the Midrash’s statement; it is not attributed to Shammai.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִיא תִּהְיֶה הָרַב וְהֶחָבֵר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י אָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק א מִשְׁנָה ו) עַל "קְנֵה לְךָ חָבֵר": יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים סְפָרִים.
connections.quote: ““Acquire a companion”: Some say books; some say an actual companion, because two are better than one. Thus it also says, “A sword against those who are alone, and they become foolish.””
connections.context: The commentary attributed to Rashi gives “books” as one interpretation alongside an actual study companion. This supplies the interpretation Rav Tzadok explicitly cites; the Mishnah’s bare instruction does not itself mention books.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הַסְּפָרִים הֵם רַבּוֹתָיו, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּשְׁבוּת יַעֲקֹב (חֵלֶק ב) מֵהַאי טַעְמָא לִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹרֶה בִּפְנֵי רַבּוֹ כְּשֶׁיָּכוֹל לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בַּסֵּפֶר.
connections.quote: “The Sages have already said that a student may not issue a ruling in his teacher’s place unless he is three parasangs away. All the more so, since our teachers are the books that have spread among Israel, it is fitting for everyone qualified to issue rulings not to give any ruling without first consulting a book.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ג): לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "בִּתִּי" וְכוּלֵי, "אֲחוֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי, "אִמִּי" וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: see note 1746 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Midrash immediately applies the parable to God’s love for Israel and supplies verses for daughter, sister, and mother. These names express increasingly intimate relationships, the progression Rav Tzadok applies to Torah.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל, עַל יְדֵי פֵּירוּשׁ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בַּכְּתוּבִים, וַדַּאי הֵם נִקְרָאִים בּוֹנֶיהָ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה, וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי סְפָרִים שֶׁחִבְּרוּ הֵם לְלַמֵּד חֲדָשׁוֹת לַאֲחֵרִים;
connections.quote: ““In His goodness He continually renews the work of creation every day.” This occurs through the new halakhic teaching that the Holy One, blessed be He, brings forth each day in the heavenly court (as stated in Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 49). The Torah scholars, to whom the task of bringing forth new teaching in the Oral Torah has been entrusted, are called builders of the world, as it says: “Great shall be the peace of your children”—read not “your children” but “your builders.” And the Gemara asks (Shabbat 114a): Who are the “builders”? These are Torah scholars, who engage in building the world. This is the meaning of “the statutes with which I engraved,” and so forth: that you should toil in Torah, for these are My statutes with which I engraved all of creation.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, לְכָךְ לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "אִמִּי", שֶׁהֵם הוֹלִידוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה וְהַחָכְמָה בָּעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “The Torah is entirely His very Name, hidden and revealed, in the mystery of His Name. … For we have learned: there are three levels bound to one another—the Holy One, blessed be He, the Torah, and Israel.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, לְכָךְ לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "אִמִּי", שֶׁהֵם הוֹלִידוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה וְהַחָכְמָה בָּעוֹלָם.
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות יסודי התורה ב׳:י׳
connections.quote: see note 285 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rambam supplies a related account of divine knowledge as inseparable from God, while explicitly acknowledging the limits of human understanding. This helps explain the premise behind Rav Tzadok’s language of Torah and God as one; it is not a claim that human knowledge has the same kind of unity.

connections.hePhrase: וְאוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, לְכָךְ לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "אִמִּי", שֶׁהֵם הוֹלִידוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה וְהַחָכְמָה בָּעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “Israel's beginning is Hashem: ‘For You are our Father.’ Yet the Sages said (Shemot Rabbah 52) that He did not cease cherishing her until He called her ‘My mother.’ This is the sense of ‘Give strength to God’ (Psalms 68:35): Hashem willed that a person's awakening below should bring forth an awakening above, as though the person were the beginning and the mother who afterward brings forth that awakening above. Above, the awakening corresponds to the person's awakening.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla directly explains the mother image and the same verse ‘Give strength to God.’ Hashem wills that human awakening bring forth an answering awakening above, so the person is spoken of as its beginning and mother. This clarifies the siman's claim about bringing new Torah into the world without positing an independent source outside Hashem.
connections.headline: The awakening that is called a mother

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא בְּחֵשֶׁק עָצוּם הַקּוֹדֵם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ד – נִקְרָא "בִּתִּי".
connections.quote: “At first, the five occurrences of “light” in the utterance “Let there be light” corresponded to the five books of the Torah, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. Afterward the first light was hidden away for those who labor in Oral Torah, as is taught in the Tanchuma in Noach. Concerning Oral Torah it is said, “May my utterance flow like dew.” As we have explained, Oral Torah is compared to dew: when dew descends, its descent from heaven is not visible; one understands that it fell only upon seeing the earth wet. Similarly, it appears to the sages that they are originating insights in their hearts, but in truth these are the word of God—“My words that I have placed in your mouth”—and they come from the dew of Atika. Abraham our father attained this: his two kidneys poured forth wisdom that God had prepared for him, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This is what was said to him, “Yours is the dew of your youth.” Shabbat too is the seventh quality, Malkhut: “the mouth, which we call Oral Torah.” It is the time to merit Torah, particularly at the meal of Atika.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik provides a concrete image for the movement described through “daughter,” “sister,” and “mother”: dew is known from its effect although its descent was not observed. In the same way, an insight can appear as the scholar’s innovation while being a Divine gift. The image clarifies the recognition on which Tzidkat HaTzadik makes the scholar’s subsequent attainment depend.
connections.headline: Receiving new Torah through longing and humility

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁבָּא אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא לְסִיּוּעַ וְנִתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ חִדּוּשִׁין וְנוֹלַד הַיִּרְאָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, אָז נִקְרָא "אֲחוֹתִי", וְאָז הֵם מִתְיַיחֲדִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר עַל פָּסוּק "אָמְנָה אֲחֹתִי וְגוֹמֵר וַתְּהִי לִי לְאִשָּׁה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כ, יב).
connections.quote: “Rather, everything was said concerning the Shekhinah. At first, “She is my sister,” as it is written, “Say to wisdom: You are my sister.””

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁבָּא אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא לְסִיּוּעַ וְנִתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ חִדּוּשִׁין וְנוֹלַד הַיִּרְאָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, אָז נִקְרָא "אֲחוֹתִי", וְאָז הֵם מִתְיַיחֲדִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר עַל פָּסוּק "אָמְנָה אֲחֹתִי וְגוֹמֵר וַתְּהִי לִי לְאִשָּׁה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כ, יב).
connections.quote: “Therefore, “She became my wife,” in brotherhood and love, as it is written, “His right hand embraces me”; all this is a mystery of wisdom.”
connections.context: The Zohar gives Abraham’s description of Sarah a symbolic reading concerning the Shekhinah and wisdom. Its sister-to-wife language supplies the mystical correspondence cited by Rav Tzadok; Genesis 20:12 alone does not state that correspondence.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהַחִדּוּשִׁין הֵם מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עֲנָוָה וְלִשְׁמָהּ, שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ מִגַּרְמֵיהּ כְּלוּם, אָז מַצְלִיחִין וְעוֹלֶה לִגְדוּלָּה לִהְיוֹת נִקְרָא "אִמִּי",
connections.quote: “The Chanukah lamp alludes to the illumination of Oral Torah. This is the menorah’s meaning when the Midrash relates that the Holy One, blessed be He, says, “Come and give Me light.” It is the light of Oral Torah, what the sages discover anew; “It is not in Heaven.” Thus the Talmud relates that God said, “My children have defeated Me.” It also says that He was repeating teachings from the mouths of all the sages, but not from Rabbi Meir, and then, “Now He says: My son Meir says,” and so forth.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah joins the menorah’s light with the sages’ innovations and ‘It is not in heaven.’ This illuminates the culmination of the present siman: the learner recognizes that the illumination comes from Hashem, yet Hashem attributes the resulting Torah to the learner. Humility and the standing of one’s own Torah therefore support each other. The gift becomes a real contribution precisely through the learner’s awakening, labor, and faithful reception.
connections.headline: Recognizing Torah as a gift does not erase the learner’s true innovation

connections.hePhrase: כְּמִשְׁפַּט אַחַר הַבְּרָכָה וְהַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹמֵר שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ, גַּם הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא הוּא מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, כְּטַעַם: תְּנוּ עֹז [הַיְינוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל] לֵאלֹהִים (תְּהִלִּים סח, לה), כִּי עַל יְדֵי אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא שֶׁנּוֹלַד זֶה:
connections.quote: ‘Ascribe strength to God. His majesty is over Israel, and His strength is in the skies.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמִשְׁפַּט אַחַר הַבְּרָכָה וְהַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹמֵר שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ, גַּם הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא הוּא מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, כְּטַעַם: תְּנוּ עֹז [הַיְינוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל] לֵאלֹהִים (תְּהִלִּים סח, לה), כִּי עַל יְדֵי אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא שֶׁנּוֹלַד זֶה:
connections.quote: see note 2582.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok directly connects the name “My mother” with “Ascribe strength to God.” The maternal image describes the human initiative that, by God’s own will, calls forth a response from above.

connections.hePhrase: [קפח] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּחֲבֵרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.): מְחַדְּדִים, וְנוֹחִים, וּמַקְשִׁיבִים, וּמַדְגִּילִים;
connections.quote: “Two Torah scholars who sharpen one another in halakhah: the Holy One, blessed be He, grants them success. ... Might this apply even when it is not for its own sake? Scripture says, “For the sake of truth.” Might it apply when one is arrogant? Scripture says, “And humble righteousness.””

connections.hePhrase: [קפח] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּחֲבֵרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.): מְחַדְּדִים, וְנוֹחִים, וּמַקְשִׁיבִים, וּמַדְגִּילִים;
connections.quote: “Two Torah scholars who are agreeable to one another in halakhah: the Holy One, blessed be He, attends to them.”

connections.hePhrase: [קפח] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּחֲבֵרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.): מְחַדְּדִים, וְנוֹחִים, וּמַקְשִׁיבִים, וּמַדְגִּילִים;
connections.quote: “Two Torah scholars who listen to one another in halakhah: the Holy One, blessed be He, hears their voice.”

connections.hePhrase: [קפח] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּחֲבֵרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.): מְחַדְּדִים, וְנוֹחִים, וּמַקְשִׁיבִים, וּמַדְגִּילִים;
connections.quote: “Two Torah scholars who are madgilin with one another in halakhah: the Holy One, blessed be He, loves them, as it says, “His banner over me is love.” Rava said: Provided that they know the basic form of the teaching, and that they have no master in town from whom to learn.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes all four teachings in this sequence, so all four are needed here. Madgilin is left transliterated because its interpretation is disputed: the following discussion contrasts Rashi’s public gathering with Tosafot’s explanation. The final teaching has Rava’s stated qualifications.

connections.hePhrase: [קפח] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּחֲבֵרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת סג.): מְחַדְּדִים, וְנוֹחִים, וּמַקְשִׁיבִים, וּמַדְגִּילִים;
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:31
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:31
connections.quote: “The matter is that Avraham's level was like the Sages' teaching: ‘The reward of the gathering is for the crowding; the reward of the discourse is for hurrying.’ What is chiefly precious in this world is longing and willingness to serve Hashem. It is precious beyond the action itself, even when the action is small. As King Shlomo said, ‘Vanity of vanities, Kohelet said’; yet this breath sustains and establishes the world. The Zohar says that this book was established upon seven breaths, and the world stands upon them. Hashem's principal concern with created beings in this world is their longing, willingness, and effort.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov uses the same sayings about the reward for hurrying and crowding to learn. It locates their preciousness in the longing and effort of the person, even when the immediate attainment is small. This explains why the siman's least advanced gathering is still beloved, while leaving intact its distinctions among the understanding, responsibilities, and creative work of the four kinds of companions.
connections.headline: Why the effort to gather has value of its own

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא "מַדְגִּילִים" לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י, שֶׁאֵין בְּיָדָם אֶלָּא הָאֲסִיפָה לְבַד,
connections.quote: ““Madgilin”: They gather one another and say, “Come, let us learn and understand between the two of us, since we have no teacher to teach us.” “The form”: They have learned a little of the root of the matter from their teacher.”
connections.context: Rashi’s own comments in Shabbat explain both the gathering and the prerequisite of knowing the basic teaching. This adds the direct wording alongside the existing Tosafot discussion of Rashi’s interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "אֲגָרָא דְּפִרְקָא – רִיהֲטָא, וּדְכַלָּה – דּוּחְקָא", שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו:) לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מְבִינִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Zeira said: The reward of attending the discourse is for running.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "אֲגָרָא דְּפִרְקָא – רִיהֲטָא, וּדְכַלָּה – דּוּחְקָא", שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו:) לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מְבִינִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Abaye said: The reward of the kallah gathering is for enduring the crowding.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "אֲגָרָא דְּפִרְקָא – רִיהֲטָא, וּדְכַלָּה – דּוּחְקָא", שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו:) לְפִי שֶׁאֵין מְבִינִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “The principal reward received by the people who run to hear a sage’s discourse is the reward for running, since most of them do not understand well enough to retain the lesson and repeat their teacher’s teaching afterward, so as to receive the reward of learning.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the first saying in terms of listeners who cannot retain and later repeat the teaching. Rav Tzadok draws on that explanation when discussing the value of the public gathering and the desire to hear Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּכַלָּה, מִפְּנֵי רִבּוּי הָעָם אֵין עוֹמְדִים עַל בּוּרְיוֹ, וְלֹא קַשְׁיָא קֻשְׁיַת תּוֹסָפוֹת דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כב:) עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.heRef: תוספות על עבודה זרה כ״ב ב:ו׳:א׳
connections.quote: “But Rashi interpreted madgilin as an expression of a banner: they gather public assemblies. This is difficult, for if so, what proof is needed? Surely it is obvious that they are loved before God.”
connections.context: Tosafot comments on the term madgilin in Shabbat 63a while discussing its linguistic parallel in Avodah Zarah. Rav Tzadok is answering this specific objection: the worth of a gathering is not obvious when many listeners cannot fully absorb the teaching.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, "צוּרָה" הוּא הַחֲשִׁיבוּת, כְּמוֹ "אֲנָשִׁים הַלָּלוּ בַּעֲלֵי צוּרָה" בְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן (ט.),
connections.quote: “He said to his son: These people are men of stature; go to them so that they may bless you.”
connections.context: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says this of Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim. “Men of stature” renders anshei tzurah, literally “men of form,” the expression Rav Tzadok uses for a distinguished Torah personality.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְאֵלּוּ לֹא אָמַר "אִם אֵין עוֹשִׂין כֵּן וְכוּלֵי" שֶׁיֵּעָנְשׁוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין יוֹדְעִין כָּל כָּךְ, רַק אֲסִיפָתָן הוּא נְדִיבוּת יוֹתֵר מִן הָרָאוּי, וְזֶה מוֹלִיד אַהֲבָה [כַּמַּיִם הַפָּנִים וְגוֹמֵר].
connections.quote: “As water reflects face to face, so the human heart reflects one person to another.”
connections.context: The verse supplies the image of reciprocal response. Rav Tzadok uses it to explain why the learners’ generous effort to gather, despite their limitations, calls forth love.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אֵין חִדּוּשִׁין, דְּהַיְינוּ בִּינָה, נוֹלָד בֵּינֵיהֶם, רַק עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פה:): עָבֵידְנָא דְּלָא תִּשְׁתַּכַּח וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יִגְמוֹר לַחֲבֵירוֹ סִדְרוֹ;
connections.quote: “I go to a town and teach five children the five books of the Torah, and teach six children the six orders of Mishnah. I tell them: Until I return, teach one another Scripture and teach one another Mishnah. Thus I make it so that Torah will not be forgotten from Israel.”
connections.context: Rabbi Chiyya first describes preparing the materials for teaching, including parchment for Torah scrolls. The quoted continuation is the educational method Rav Tzadok needs: different pupils learn different portions and then teach one another.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ זְמַן לוֹמַר שֶׁאָז שָׁמַע וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִסְתַּלְּקָה הַשְּׁמִיעָה, רַק שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹמֵעַ לְעוֹלָם;
connections.quote: “The Holy One’s knowing encompasses a thing from its beginning to its ultimate end, as it is written: “For I have known him, so that he will command his children,” and so forth. Thus, because the righteousness of our father Abraham, of blessed memory, would endure in his descendants, the Omnipresent knew him. Of something that does not endure forever, the expression “the Omnipresent’s knowing” is inapplicable, as it is written: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous,” and so forth, “but the way of the wicked shall perish”—for it is not something that endures, as explained above.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי קוֹלָן קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּימָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קסח עַמּוּד ב) דְּקָלִין דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וּצְלוֹתָא לָא אִתְאֲבִידוּ לְעָלְמִין, וְהַיְינוּ דְּלָא תִּשְׁתַּכַּח.
connections.quote: “Come and see: There are three voices that are never lost, apart from the voices of Torah and prayer, which ascend above and pierce the firmaments. There are other voices that do not ascend and are not lost.”
connections.context: The passage distinguishes the ascending voices of Torah and prayer from three other enduring voices, identified immediately afterward. Rav Tzadok applies its language of enduring voices to the lasting effect of Torah heard by a listener. The passage does not say that these voices are engraved in the firmament or that they awaken mercy for descendants.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְאֵלּוּ "אִם אֵין עוֹשִׂין וְכוּלֵי", שֶׁמְּחוּיָּיבִין בְּכָךְ מֵאַחַר שֶׁבְּיָדָן לְקַיֵּים הַשְּׁכִינָה, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא תִּשְׁתַּכַּח אוֹתוֹ קוֹל שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׁוֹמְעוֹ תָּמִיד, וְחַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְהֵיפֶךְ גּוֹרֵם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “If they do not do so, they cause the Divine Presence to depart from Israel, as it says, “Flee, my beloved, and be like…””
connections.context: This is the continuation of the preceding teaching about two scholars who listen to one another. It supplies the negative clause alluded to here, while the existing note quotes the positive promise that God hears their voice.

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁנֵי הָאֲחֵרִים הֵם כְּשֶׁמְּחַדְּשִׁין דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְאָז נִקְרָא "יִרְאֵי ה'", וְהֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת דְּנֹעַם וְחוֹבְלִים הַנִּדְרָשׁ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.) עַל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבָבֶל.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Oshaya said: What is the meaning of ‘I took for Myself two staffs; one I called Noam, and the other I called Chovlim’? ‘Noam,’ pleasantness, refers to the Torah scholars in the Land of Israel, who treat one another pleasantly in halakhic discussion. ‘Chovlim,’ those who injure, refers to the Torah scholars in Babylonia, who wound one another in halakhic discussion.’

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁנֵי הָאֲחֵרִים הֵם כְּשֶׁמְּחַדְּשִׁין דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְאָז נִקְרָא "יִרְאֵי ה'", וְהֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת דְּנֹעַם וְחוֹבְלִים הַנִּדְרָשׁ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.) עַל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבָבֶל.
connections.quote: “Homiletically, the passage is expounded as referring to the Oral Torah. These are “the wars of Hashem” conducted through a book of Torah. As the Sages said (Kiddushin 30b), even a father and son, or a teacher and student, studying Torah at one gate become enemies of one another, yet they do not leave until they love one another, as it says, “Et Vahev in Suphah,” and so forth. Afterward they sang concerning the well, which alludes to the Oral Torah.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah describes father and son, or rebbe and talmid, becoming opponents in Torah and remaining together until love emerges. This clarifies the connecting da’at required in the present siman’s account of sharpened disagreement. The disagreement can move each beyond his original limit, but its fruit is not the perpetuation of hostility. The siman’s requirements of truth, humility, and righteousness preserve the conditions in which such a dispute builds Torah and raises students.
connections.headline: A Torah dispute reaches its purpose in a renewed bond of love

connections.hePhrase: וְעִיקַּר הַרְבָּצַת תּוֹרָה הָיְתָה בְּבָבֶל כִּדְאִיתָא בִּכְתוּבּוֹת (קו.), כִּי רִבּוּי הַתַּלְמִידִים הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַפִּלְפּוּל וְהַחִידּוּד שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת וְהַהֲפָכִין, וְזֶהוּ הַמְּחַדְּדִין, עַל יְדֵי זֶה עוֹלִין לִגְדוּלָּה דְּהַיְינוּ הַעֲמָדַת תַּלְמִידִים.
connections.quote: “When the sages departed from Rav’s academy, twelve hundred sages remained; from Rav Huna’s academy, eight hundred remained. Rav Huna taught through thirteen interpreters. When the sages rose from Rav Huna’s academy and shook out their cloaks, dust rose and covered the daylight. In the West they said: They have risen from the academy of Rav Huna the Babylonian.”
connections.context: These figures concern the sages remaining after others departed, and the thirteen interpreters show how a large gathering heard a teacher’s words. This is the description of the academy’s scale invoked here.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים עַל כָּרְחֲךָ צְרִיכִין לְאֶמְצָעִי וְדַעַת הַמְחַבֵּר, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "וַהֲדָרְךָ", וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קמה:) שֶׁתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל עוֹשִׂין צִיצִין וּפְרָחִים לַתּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: ““Those who come shall cause Jacob to take root; Israel shall bud and blossom.” Rav Yosef taught: These are the Torah scholars of Babylonia, who make buds and blossoms for the Torah.”
connections.context: Rav Yosef applies Isaiah 27:6 to the development of Torah in Babylonia. The attribution is to Rav Yosef, not Shammai.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר נִקְרָא פִּלְפּוּל הַתַּלְמוּד קִשּׁוּטֵי כַּלָּה שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַהֶדֶר בֶּאֱמֶת, וּלְכָךְ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל מְצוּיָּינִין כִּדְאִיתָא (שָׁם), וּפֵירוּשׁ שֶׁאֵינָן בְּנֵי מְקוֹמָן, שֶׁהַחִידּוּד מוֹצִיאוֹ מִמְּקוֹמוֹ.
connections.quote: “They made many fences for her and cut many garments for her, garments of gold, through many rulings. They disputed and raised objections about these rulings, to prepare her through many resolutions and adorn her with many kinds of ornaments for Sabbaths and festivals, so that she would be adorned for you when you come to her at the final redemption.”
connections.context: The bride in this passage represents Torah, particularly its oral development through halakhic rulings. Questions, objections, and their resolutions become her garments and ornaments. This is the Zohar’s image behind Rav Tzadok’s description of Talmudic analysis as bridal adornment.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר נִקְרָא פִּלְפּוּל הַתַּלְמוּד קִשּׁוּטֵי כַּלָּה שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַהֶדֶר בֶּאֱמֶת, וּלְכָךְ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל מְצוּיָּינִין כִּדְאִיתָא (שָׁם), וּפֵירוּשׁ שֶׁאֵינָן בְּנֵי מְקוֹמָן, שֶׁהַחִידּוּד מוֹצִיאוֹ מִמְּקוֹמוֹ.
connections.quote: “Why are the Torah scholars of Babylonia distinguished by their appearance? Because they are not in their home place. As people say: In my town, my name identifies me; outside my town, my clothing does.”
connections.context: This is Rabbi Yoḥanan’s answer in the discussion, replacing the earlier suggestion that disparaged their learning. The immediate explanation concerns recognition away from home; Rav Tzadok interprets being taken beyond one’s place as a quality of analytical study.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי נוֹחִין בְּיִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת הֲרֵי זֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מְגִילָּה יב:): "שַׁאֲנַן מוֹאָב וְגוֹמֵר" (יִרְמְיָה מח, יא), וּבַגּוֹלָה וְגוֹמֵר דְּיָתְבֵי בְּדוּכְתַּיְיהוּ;
connections.quote: “They told him: Since the day the Temple was destroyed and we were exiled from our land, counsel has been taken from us, and we do not know how to judge capital cases. Go to Ammon and Moab, who remain in their own place like wine resting on its lees.”
connections.context: The Jewish sages answer Ahasuerus while avoiding a dangerous judgment about Vashti. The expression Rav Tzadok cites describes the settled circumstances of Ammon and Moab, contrasted with the dislocation of exile; the next verse comparison develops the image of undisturbed wine.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי נוֹחִין בְּיִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת הֲרֵי זֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מְגִילָּה יב:): "שַׁאֲנַן מוֹאָב וְגוֹמֵר" (יִרְמְיָה מח, יא), וּבַגּוֹלָה וְגוֹמֵר דְּיָתְבֵי בְּדוּכְתַּיְיהוּ;
connections.quote: ‘Moab has been undisturbed from his youth and has rested on his lees. He has not been poured from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile. Therefore his flavor has remained in him, and his scent has not changed.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה גּוֹרֵם לְגַסּוּת הָרוּחַ וּלְשֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ, דְּהַיְינוּ עַל מְנָת שֶׁיִּקְרָאוּהוּ רַבִּי כִּדְאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים (סב.),
connections.quote: “A person should not say: I will read Scripture so that they call me a sage; I will study Mishnah so that they call me Rabbi; I will repeat my learning so that I become an elder and sit in the academy.”
connections.context: The teaching interprets serving God out of love as excluding the pursuit of learned titles and status. Rav Tzadok invokes it when separating Torah’s value from the honor attached to a scholar.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:) דְּגַסּוּת לְבָבֶל נָחִית, לָכֵן הִתְנוּ בָּזֶה "עַל דְּבַר אֱמֶת וְעַנְוָה צֶדֶק" (תְּהִלִּים מה, ה).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: These are flattery and arrogance, which descended to Babylonia.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:) דְּגַסּוּת לְבָבֶל נָחִית, לָכֵן הִתְנוּ בָּזֶה "עַל דְּבַר אֱמֶת וְעַנְוָה צֶדֶק" (תְּהִלִּים מה, ה).
connections.quote: “Yes, it descended here, and then spread there. This is also indicated by the wording “to build her a house.” Learn from this.”
connections.context: The question asks how the preceding assignment of arrogance to Elam agrees with Rabbi Yochanan’s statement about Babylonia. The answer distinguishes descent to Babylonia from its later establishment in Elam. Rav Tzadok cites the initial descent.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מט:) דְּגַסּוּת לְבָבֶל נָחִית, לָכֵן הִתְנוּ בָּזֶה "עַל דְּבַר אֱמֶת וְעַנְוָה צֶדֶק" (תְּהִלִּים מה, ה).
connections.quote: ‘In your splendor, advance and ride forth for the cause of truth and righteous humility; may your right hand teach you awesome deeds.’

connections.hePhrase: [קפט] שְׁנֵי מִינֵי הַשָּׂגוֹת אֱלֹהוּת יֵשׁ:
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
connections.quote: “"And Hashem said to Avram: Go for yourself from your land, etc." (Genesis 12:1). It is written (Isaiah 44:3): "For I will pour water upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land"; when Avraham our Father, peace be upon him, began to seek and search after the root of his true life, after he understood that all delights of this world cannot be termed authentic life, for all worldly delight serves merely to remove afflictions and impediments; and after all anxieties are eliminated, what is the very substance of life for which the world was created? Concerning this Hashem, blessed be He, said to him: "Go for yourself"—meaning, unto your very self, for in truth, all mundane matters of this world cannot be termed life, and the core of life you will find within yourself: (Isaiah 41:16) "And you shall rejoice in Hashem, and shall glory in the Holy One of Israel"—this is the essence of life.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Avraham discovering the insufficiency of worldly satisfactions and then receiving the personal call “Go to yourself.” This gives a concrete movement between the two kinds of recognition discussed here: the question arises within reflection on the world, while the answer directs a particular person toward the life Hashem asks of him.
connections.headline: From asking about life to being addressed by Hashem

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת דִּרְאִיָּה וִידִיעָה שֶׁל אָבוֹת וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַנִּזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר וָאֵרָא (כג עַמּוּד א, עַיֵּין שָׁם),
connections.quote: “The higher colors are concealed and are not seen; no one attained them except Moses. Therefore it is written, “By My name, the Lord, I was not known to them”: I was not revealed to them in the higher colors. And if you say that the patriarchs did not know of them—the patriarchs did know of them, through those that were revealed.”
connections.context: The Zohar distinguishes direct attainment of the concealed level from knowing it through what is revealed. Its final qualification is essential: the patriarchs were not ignorant of the higher level. Rav Tzadok develops this into his distinction between seeing through creation and the knowledge associated with Moses.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהָאָבוֹת הִשִּׂיגוּ מִצַּד הַבְּרוּאִים, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה לט) בְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: רָאָה בִּירָה דּוֹלֶקֶת וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘‘Hashem said to Avram: Go forth from your land,’ and so forth (Genesis 12:1). Rabbi Yitzchak opened: ‘Listen, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house’ (Psalms 45:11). Rabbi Yitzchak said: This is a parable of someone traveling from place to place who saw a palace alight. He said: ‘Can it be that this palace has no one directing it?’ The owner of the palace looked out at him and said: ‘I am the owner of the palace.’ So, because our father Abraham was saying, ‘Can it be that this world has no one directing it?’ the Holy One, blessed be He, looked out at him and said: ‘I am the owner of the world.’ ‘The king will desire your beauty, for he is your master’ (Psalms 45:12). ‘The king will desire your beauty’—to make you beautiful in the world. ‘Bow down to him’ (Psalms 45:12). Thus: ‘Hashem said to Avram.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נִזְכַּר אוֹתוֹ שֵׁם אֶצְלָם שָׁם בַּכָּתוּב, הַמּוֹרֶה שֶׁאָמַר לְעוֹלָמוֹ "דַּי" כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֲגִיגָה יב.),
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, it kept expanding like two balls of warp thread unwinding, until the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked it and brought it to a halt, as it is said: ‘The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at His rebuke.’ This is what Reish Lakish said: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘I am El Shaddai’? I am the One who said to the world: ‘Enough’—dai. Reish Lakish said: When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the sea, it kept expanding until the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked it and dried it up, as it is said: ‘He rebukes the sea and dries it up, and He makes all the rivers dry.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּפֵירֵשׁ הָרַבִּי רַבִּי בּוּנִים זְצוֹקַ"ל: שֶׁיֵּשׁ דַּי בִּבְרִיאָה זוֹ לְהַכִּיר אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יָדוֹ
connections.quote: “It is said in the name of our master Rabbi Bunim, of blessed memory, that he explained “He said to His world: Enough” to mean that this would suffice for the creature to recognize His blessed kingship. The intended purpose of creation is that a person should recognize His kingship, and one can learn from everything that was created. As stated in Eruvin 100b: Had Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, the avoidance of theft from the ant, and sexual fidelity from the dove, and so forth. The world continued expanding so that people could recognize His kingship more fully, until the Holy One, blessed be He, told it that no further expansion was needed: the creation already made was sufficient to recognize the glory of His blessed kingship.”
connections.context: Peri Tzadik records Rabbi Bunim’s teaching explicitly and explains its purpose through learning from the creatures. This supplies the fuller account behind the brief attribution here.

connections.hePhrase: [וְאוֹתוֹ שֵׁם מוֹעִיל גַּם כֵּן לְבָנִים כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי זֶה מִצַּד הַבְּרִיאָה, כִּי לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ.
connections.quote: “‘And He said to him: I am El Shaddai.’ … After they are circumcised … the yod, the holy sign, is revealed in them, Shaddai is inscribed upon them, and they are made whole in the complete covenant. … And one who bears this sign is fit to be blessed by this Name, as it is written: ‘And El Shaddai bless you’ (Genesis 28:3).”
connections.context: The verse continues: “and make you fruitful and multiply you.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְאוֹתוֹ שֵׁם מוֹעִיל גַּם כֵּן לְבָנִים כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי זֶה מִצַּד הַבְּרִיאָה, כִּי לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ.
connections.quote: “For thus says the Lord, Creator of the heavens—He is God—who formed the earth and made it, who established it: He did not create it as emptiness; He formed it to be inhabited. I am the Lord, and there is no other.”
connections.context: The second half of the phrase, “He formed it to be inhabited,” completes the verse alluded to by “He did not create it as emptiness.” It explains the connection Rav Tzadok draws between creation, continuity, and children.

connections.hePhrase: וִידִיעָה הוּא בַּהַנְהָגָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הוֹדִעֵנִי נָא אֶת דְּרָכֶךָ" (שְׁמוֹת לג, יג), וְלֹא אִתְגַּלְיָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" וְגוֹמֵר (שָׁם, יט),
connections.quote: “Now, if I have found favor in Your eyes, make known to me Your ways, so that I may know You and find favor in Your eyes; and see that this nation is Your people.”

connections.hePhrase: וִידִיעָה הוּא בַּהַנְהָגָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הוֹדִעֵנִי נָא אֶת דְּרָכֶךָ" (שְׁמוֹת לג, יג), וְלֹא אִתְגַּלְיָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" וְגוֹמֵר (שָׁם, יט),
connections.quote: “I will cause all My goodness to pass before you, and proclaim the name of the Lord before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and show compassion to whom I will show compassion.”
connections.context: Verse 13 supplies Moses’ request to know God’s ways; verse 19 supplies the answer about divine grace and compassion invoked in the following argument. Rav Tzadok draws his distinction between disclosed ways and the depth of divine will from this exchange.

connections.hePhrase: וְלֹא הוֹדִיעוֹ, רַק יָדַע דִּשְׁמוֹ הֲוָיָ"ה – הוֹוֶה וּמְהַוֶּוה הַכֹּל, וְהָיָה הוֹוֶה וְיִהְיֶה,
connections.displayRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 19:1
connections.linkedRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 19 1
connections.canonicalRef: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 19:1
connections.heRef: פרי צדיק, וילך ושבת תשובה י״ט:א׳
connections.quote: “For this is the essence and foundation of everything: that the belief that Havayah, blessed be He, is Elohim should become firmly established in the soul. The name Elohim means that He is mighty and possesses power; this is easy for the human heart to apprehend and believe. But the aspect of the name Havayah—that He brings everything into being, possesses all powers, and that no power exists apart from Him; that He was, is, and will be; and that “You are He before the world was created, and You are He after the world was created”—is difficult to establish firmly in the human heart, because outward appearances show the opposite.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַדַּעַת מַדְרֵגַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשָּׂגָה זוֹ אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁהוּא תַּלְמִיד חָכָם.
connections.quote: see note 2012 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel explanation connects the continuing presence of Moses with the Torah sage who leads a later generation. It makes explicit the inheritance of Moses’ light that underlies the statement here.

connections.hePhrase: [וְדוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר שֶׁנִּקְרָא דּוֹר דֵּעָה: "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה עַל הַיָּם מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל",
connections.quote: “‘And Darda’ (I Chronicles 2:6)—this is the generation of the wilderness, which was entirely knowledge (dor de’ah).”

connections.hePhrase: [וְדוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר שֶׁנִּקְרָא דּוֹר דֵּעָה: "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה עַל הַיָּם מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל",
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְשִׁירָה ג׳:י׳
connections.quote: see note 2235.
connections.context: The Mekhilta continues with a parable contrasting uncertainty about a mortal king with Israel’s immediate recognition of God at the sea. The saying concerns the exceptional clarity of that revelation, which Rav Tzadok relates to the whole generation’s readiness for the knowledge of Moses.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ב): כֵּיצַד הִיא הַדֶּרֶךְ לְאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה? כְּשֶׁיָּשִׂים הָאָדָם אֶל לִבּוֹ וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם:
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות יסודי התורה ב׳:ב׳
connections.quote: see note 210 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Maimonides describes contemplation of God’s works as leading first to love and longing, and then to humility and awe. This is the teaching of Rambam, Maimonides; the reader’s expansion mentioning Shammai is not an attribution found in the source.

connections.hePhrase: [קצ] הָעַיִן וְהַלֵּב הֵם סַרְסוּרֵי הָעֲבֵירָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ה), וְכֵן סַרְסוּרִים לְטוֹב,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Levi said: The heart and the eye are two brokers of sin. It is written, “My son, give Me your heart, and let your eyes keep My ways.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you give Me your heart and your eye, I know that you are Mine.”
connections.context: The first sentence describes the heart and eye in relation to sin; the continuation describes giving these same powers to God. Both sides are needed for Rav Tzadok’s distinction between their evil and good uses.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: אִם אַתְּ יָהֵיב עֵינָא וְלִבָּא לִי, אֲנָא וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““My son, give Me your heart, and let your eyes keep My ways.” “To Me”: to fear and love Me. The heart is desire and longing. He therefore warns a person to give the whole heart to Him, blessed be He, for one is obliged to long and desire only for the service of God, and to make one’s worldly desires solely means of serving God. “Let your eyes keep My ways”: the commandments and good deeds.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "שְׁלַח אוֹרְךָ וַאֲמִתְּךָ הֵמָּה יַנְחוּנִי" (תְּהִלִּים מג, ג), דְּעִיקַּר הָרְאִיָּה הוּא הָאוֹר.
connections.quote: ‘Send Your light and Your truth; let them guide me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to Your dwelling places.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם מַדְרֵגַת יַעֲקֹב וְיוֹסֵף: "תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב" (מִיכָה ז, כ), וְ"אוֹר זָרֻעַ לַצַּדִּיק" (תְּהִלִּים צז, יא);
connections.quote: “You will give truth to Jacob and kindness to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers from days of old.”
connections.context: The Hebrew associates Jacob with emet, truth, and Abraham with chesed, kindness. These specific terms supply Rav Tzadok’s correspondence between the patriarchs and their qualities.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּיוֹסֵף (בְּרָכוֹת כ.): עַיִן שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי, אֵין עַיִן הָרָע וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘Alternatively, you may say: An eye that did not wish to feed upon what was not its own—the evil eye has no power over it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא אָמַר בַּשְּׁבָטִים "נוֹתְנִין עֵינֵיהֶם וְכוּלֵי", וְסָבוּר דְּשׁוּרְיָינָא דְּעֵינָא בְּלִבָּא תַּלְיָא כִּדְאִיתָא (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כח:),
connections.quote: “An inflamed eye may be treated with eye salve on Shabbat. Why? Because the vessels of the eye depend upon the chambers of the heart.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא אָמַר בַּשְּׁבָטִים "נוֹתְנִין עֵינֵיהֶם וְכוּלֵי", וְסָבוּר דְּשׁוּרְיָינָא דְּעֵינָא בְּלִבָּא תַּלְיָא כִּדְאִיתָא (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כח:),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon says: They set their eyes upon the daughters of the land.”
connections.context: The Talmudic sentence supplies the eye–heart connection that Rav Tzadok uses symbolically. The Midrash’s sentence describes what Joseph reported about his brothers; it is one interpretation of his adverse report, not an independent endorsement of the accusation. The Midrash goes on to connect that report to Joseph’s own test involving his master’s wife.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כד.): כַּלָּה שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ וְכוּלֵי כָּל גּוּפָהּ וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘It is like a bride in her father’s house: As long as her eyes are beautiful, the rest of her body does not need examination. If her eyes are weak, her entire body needs examination.’

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת הָעִיקָּר הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מִכָּל מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי ד, כג), שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַחַיּוּת וְהַדְּבֵיקוּת בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים,
connections.quote: see note 2467.
connections.context: “Heart” is the explicit Hebrew term, lev. It is the feature Rav Tzadok is contrasting with the eye, so it must not disappear into the broader translation “mind.”

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת הָעִיקָּר הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מִכָּל מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים" (מִשְׁלֵי ד, כג), שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַחַיּוּת וְהַדְּבֵיקוּת בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים,
connections.quote: “This is what is hinted at by placing “but there were snakes and scorpions in it” next to the first teaching about the Chanukah lamp. The essential point of the commandment is seeing, through which one merits the quality of “light sown for the righteous,” repairing the blemish of the covenant as mentioned above. This statement follows it so that a person will not rely upon the thought that everything has already been repaired. Rather, one should know that Chanukah is a preparation and initiation into the “light sown for the righteous,” through which one may merit the completeness of the repair during the days of Shovavim. The essential thing is to guard oneself in thought and sight. This is indicated by this month’s being created with the letter ayin: the preparation for repair through guarding the eyes. As it says, “Do not stray … after your eyes,” which Berakhot 12b explains as thoughts of transgression. Guarding the eyes saves one from such thoughts, as Avodah Zarah 28b says, “The vessels of the eye are attached to the chambers of the heart.” Every year, in these seasons, repair and clarification are brought about in the souls of Israel, with God’s help. When a person takes repair to heart, let him place his trust in God that he will be completely repaired, as is said of Joseph in Genesis Rabbah 89: “‘Happy is the man who makes the Lord his trust’—this is Joseph.””
connections.explanation: Chanukah uses the same connection between the eye and the heart, but stresses that a first illumination is preparation rather than proof that the entire task is finished. This develops the opening of the present siman, where both powers can become brokers for good. It also helps preserve the siman’s broader demand: guarding sight is essential, while a good eye ultimately includes a generous heart free of envy. The bodily guard and the heart’s positive direction belong together.
connections.headline: Guarding the eyes begins a repair that must also reach the heart

connections.hePhrase: וּבָזֶה יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה וְכֻלּוֹ זֶרַע אֱמֶת.
connections.quote: “Yet I had planted you a noble vine, wholly a seed of truth; how then have you turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine to Me?”

connections.hePhrase: וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים: "עַיִן יָפָה" וְ"עַיִן טוֹבָה" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר נְדִיבוּת הַלֵּב וְשֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַנֵּא,
connections.quote: “He said to them: Go out and see which is the upright path to which a person should adhere. Rabbi Eliezer said: A good eye. Rabbi Yehoshua said: A good companion. Rabbi Yose said: A good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon said: Seeing what is to come. Rabbi Elazar said: A good heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arakh to yours, for your words are included in his.”
connections.context: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai’s response includes the good eye within the good heart. The Mishnah provides the rabbinic terminology behind Rav Tzadok’s explanation of a generous, unenvious disposition.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ כִּי נָתַן מִלַּחְמוֹ לַדָּל" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט).
connections.quote: see note 2400.
connections.context: “Good eye” is the verse’s literal expression for generosity. Rav Tzadok depends on the eye-language itself when describing the good use of this faculty.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ כִּי נָתַן מִלַּחְמוֹ לַדָּל" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט).
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 2
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 2
connections.quote: “For this reason these two tribes oppose one another. Concerning the future it says, ‘Ephraim will not envy, and Yehudah will not harass.’ Ephraim will have no complaint against Yehudah concerning his going beyond the halakhic line, and will not distress him over it, because Hashem will show Ephraim that Yehudah's intention is directed toward Heaven rather than his own pleasure. Peace will consequently be between them.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the very promise about Ephraim cited here through the different roots of Ephraim and Yehudah. Its conclusion places reconciliation in a future clarification of intent: the other is serving Heaven rather than seeking personal pleasure. This develops the siman's demand that the repair of the eye reach the generous heart as well. The source describes that final disclosure; it does not authorize an observer now to presume the inward standing that only Hashem reveals.
connections.headline: Reconciliation requires seeing the other's intention

connections.hePhrase: וְהַהִיפּוּךְ: עַיִן רָעָה, וּבִלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב "רַע עַיִן" (שָׁם כג, ו).
connections.quote: “Do not eat the bread of one with an evil eye, and do not desire his delicacies. For as he reckons within himself, so he is. “Eat and drink,” he says to you, but his heart is not with you.”
connections.context: The verses describe a host whose outward invitation conceals inward reluctance to give. Here the evil eye denotes stinginess and begrudging another’s enjoyment, the opposite of the generosity discussed in the preceding sentence.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ יוֹסֵף יְרֵא חֵטְא, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁמִירַת הָעַיִן, וְהוּא אוֹתִיּוֹת רְאִיָּ"ה, כְּטַעַם: מַחֲוֵי לְהוּ יִצְחָק הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ (שַׁבָּת פט:), שֶׁזֶּה מִכֹּחַ יִצְחָק וּמִמִּדָּתוֹ.
connections.quote: see note 125 (Vol. I).
connections.context: After Isaac pleads for Israel, he directs their praise toward God. The repeated language of eyes is the particular detail invoked by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַנְּדִיבוּת הוּא מִמִּדַּת הָאַהֲבָה: "חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם" (מִיכָה ז, כ), שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ הַהֵיפֶךְ,
connections.quote: “This is what they said in Bava Kamma 97a: The coin of Abraham our patriarch had an old man and an old woman on one side, and a young man and a maiden on the other. A coin is something with which one acquires all necessities. Likewise, love and fear are the parents that bring forth all holy qualities, corresponding to jealousy and desire on the side of impurity. Love is familiar in youth, unlike old age: “Desire fails.” As is known, Solomon said the Song of Songs in his youth—the intensity of love—and Ecclesiastes in his old age—the intensity of fear. But Abraham introduced and established this as a current coin: on one coin there should be an old man and an old woman on one side, and a young man and a maiden on the other, all united in complete unity—love and fear.”
connections.context: This parallel explains why the contrast between the qualities of Joseph and his brothers is not the final ideal. Rav Tzadok describes completeness as bringing love and fear together, so that restraint and generosity become parts of one service of God.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין לא.): כֵּיוָן שֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ "כַּבֵּד", הוֹדוּ אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לַדִּבְּרוֹת;
connections.quote: “When the Holy One, blessed be He, said “I am” and “You shall have no other,” the nations of the world said: He seeks His own honor. Once He said “Honor your father and your mother,” they returned and acknowledged the earlier utterances. Rava said: From the end of Your word it becomes evident that the beginning of Your word is true.”
connections.context: The nations’ initial objection and subsequent acknowledgment explain why honoring parents reveals the truth of the earlier commandments. The command to honor parents is Exodus 20:12 in the linked numbering.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין לא.): כֵּיוָן שֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ "כַּבֵּד", הוֹדוּ אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לַדִּבְּרוֹת;
connections.quote: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long upon the land which Hashem your God gives you.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סה) דְּעֵשָׂו נִזְהָר בּוֹ הַרְבֵּה, וְאָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: אֲנִי וְכוּלֵי וְלֹא הִגַּעְתִּי וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““Rebecca took the fine garments of Esau, her elder son, that were with her in the house, and she dressed Jacob her younger son” (Genesis 27:15). “Rebecca took the fine [haḥamudot] garments of Esau, her elder son” – what he had coveted [sheḥamad] from Nimrod, and he killed him and took them. That is what is written: “The wicked covets the prey of the evil” (Proverbs 12:12). “That were with her in the house” – in them he would attend his father. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: I attended my father all my days, and I did not attend him one one-hundredth of what Esau attended his father. When I would attend my father, I attended him with dirty garments, but when I would go out on the road, I would go out with clean garments. But Esau, when he would attend his father, he would attend him only with royal garments. He said: ‘It is not in keeping with Father’s honor to attend him in anything other than royal garments.’ That is what is written: “That were with her in the house.” How many wives did he [Esau] have, and you say: “That were with her in the house”? It is because he [Esau] knew what their [his wives’] actions were. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: There was an incident involving a group of scoundrels in that Kefar Ḥatya, who were accustomed to eat and drink in the synagogue every Shabbat eve. When they finished eating they would take the bones and cast them on the scribe. One of them was dying; they said to him: ‘To whom do you wish to entrust your son?’ He said to them: ‘To the scribe.’ But, how many friends did he have, but he said: ‘To the scribe’? It is, rather, that he knew what their actions were, and that the scribe was much better than they were. So, how many wives did he have, and the verse says: “That were with her in the house”? It is because he knew what their actions were.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב.) עַל בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן: עֲשָׂאָן רַבִּי יְהוּדָה כְּהִלְכוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן הַיְינוּ הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵכִין מָזוֹן לְכָל חָי.
connections.quote: see note 1403 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב.) עַל בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן: עֲשָׂאָן רַבִּי יְהוּדָה כְּהִלְכוֹת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן הַיְינוּ הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵכִין מָזוֹן לְכָל חָי.
connections.quote: “Up to “He gives bread to all flesh” is the completion of the proper worldly conduct that preceded Torah: one recognizes the Giver. This is the blessing that comes first, through which “He gave the earth to human beings,” as explained at the beginning of the chapter How Do We Bless—that is, to engage in proper worldly conduct.”
connections.context: In explaining the concluding verses of Psalm 136, Rav Tzadok identifies the completion of derekh eretz with recognizing who provides one’s food. This supplies his fuller explanation of the connection between blessing, ordinary worldly activity, and recognition of God.

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בוּר" הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שָׂדֶה בּוּרָה, וְלֹא "שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרֲכוֹ ה'" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז) דְּהַיְינוּ חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין קַדִּישִׁין, דְּהוּא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ זְרִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבָּהּ מְלֵאִים מִצְווֹת וְהַכָּרָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על פרקי אבות ב׳:ה׳:א׳
connections.quote: “He used to say: A boor does not fear sin, and an unlearned person is not pious. A boor is empty: he has neither Torah nor commandments nor proper conduct expressed in good character. In the Targum, “Let it not become desolate” is rendered “Let it not lie fallow.” It was unnecessary to say that a boor is not pious, since he does not even fear sin: because of his emptiness, he does not know how to guard against transgressions. But an unlearned person participates in society with worthy qualities and has some sound views. He knows how to take care, guards himself against wrongdoing, and can be righteous, doing and fulfilling what he is told he has been commanded.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah distinguishes the person lacking both learning and cultivated conduct from the unlearned person who has worthy character and can obey the commandments. His explanation supplies the fallow-field image behind Rav Tzadok’s use of the word bor.

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בוּר" הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שָׂדֶה בּוּרָה, וְלֹא "שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרֲכוֹ ה'" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז) דְּהַיְינוּ חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין קַדִּישִׁין, דְּהוּא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ זְרִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבָּהּ מְלֵאִים מִצְווֹת וְהַכָּרָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
connections.quote: ‘He approached and kissed him. He smelled the scent of his garments, blessed him, and said: ‘See, the scent of my son is like the scent of a field that Hashem has blessed.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בוּר" הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שָׂדֶה בּוּרָה, וְלֹא "שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרֲכוֹ ה'" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז) דְּהַיְינוּ חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין קַדִּישִׁין, דְּהוּא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ זְרִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבָּהּ מְלֵאִים מִצְווֹת וְהַכָּרָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
connections.quote: “Derech eretz is what is needed for the settlement of the land and the world, for ‘He did not create it for emptiness, but formed it to be inhabited’ (Isaiah 45:18). Through it a person's household is settled. This is the meaning of derech eretz everywhere: engaging in the world's settlement, as Berakhot 35b says, ‘Conduct them according to derech eretz,’ and Kiddushin 40b says, ‘Someone who is not involved in derech eretz is not part of the settled world.’ Immersion in desires unnecessary for the world's settlement is the opposite of derech eretz. Avraham our father therefore chose the land of Israel: he saw them weeding and working, unlike those eating, drinking and behaving frivolously, as Bereishit Rabbah 39:8 says. He saw that they had the derech eretz preceding Torah (Vayikra Rabbah 9:3), and understood that this was the land prepared for Torah, for ‘Without derech eretz there is no Torah’ (Avot 3:17).”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim defines derech eretz through the settlement of the world, distinguishing necessary activity from immersion in surplus desire. It explains the barren-field image and why this conduct can prepare a person for Torah. The siman adds the decisive inward qualification: recognizing Hashem as the source of earthly life.
connections.headline: Derech eretz as sustaining an inhabited world

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בוּר" הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שָׂדֶה בּוּרָה, וְלֹא "שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרֲכוֹ ה'" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז) דְּהַיְינוּ חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין קַדִּישִׁין, דְּהוּא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ זְרִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבָּהּ מְלֵאִים מִצְווֹת וְהַכָּרָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
connections.quote: see note 1409 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the encounter between Rabbi Yannai and an unlearned guest into a responsibility of the scholar. The guest's lack of textual knowledge did not erase the Torah point expressed in his conduct. This clarifies why the present siman distinguishes an am haaretz belonging to the cultivated land from a barren field: the positive inward root must be recognized even where the person cannot himself name it.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְכָךְ בְּמַכַּת עָרוֹב נֶאֱמַר: "וְהִפְלֵיתִי" (שְׁמוֹת ח, יח), וְכֵן בְּדֶבֶר: "וְהִפְלָה" (שָׁם ט, ד), וּבִשְׁאָר מַכּוֹת לֹא נִזְכַּר כְּלָל, וּבְבָרָד נֶאֱמַר סְתָם שֶׁבְּגֹשֶׁן לֹא הָיָה, בְּלֹא "וְהִפְלָה".
connections.quote: ‘On that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where My people dwell, so that there will be no swarms of wild beasts there, in order that you may know that I am Hashem in the midst of the earth.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְכָךְ בְּמַכַּת עָרוֹב נֶאֱמַר: "וְהִפְלֵיתִי" (שְׁמוֹת ח, יח), וְכֵן בְּדֶבֶר: "וְהִפְלָה" (שָׁם ט, ד), וּבִשְׁאָר מַכּוֹת לֹא נִזְכַּר כְּלָל, וּבְבָרָד נֶאֱמַר סְתָם שֶׁבְּגֹשֶׁן לֹא הָיָה, בְּלֹא "וְהִפְלָה".
connections.quote: “The Lord will distinguish between Israel’s livestock and Egypt’s livestock, and nothing belonging to the children of Israel will die.”
connections.context: The verb vehiflah explicitly describes a distinction in the livestock plague. Rav Tzadok compares this wording with the already quoted verse about the swarms and with the differently worded account of the hail.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְכָךְ בְּמַכַּת עָרוֹב נֶאֱמַר: "וְהִפְלֵיתִי" (שְׁמוֹת ח, יח), וְכֵן בְּדֶבֶר: "וְהִפְלָה" (שָׁם ט, ד), וּבִשְׁאָר מַכּוֹת לֹא נִזְכַּר כְּלָל, וּבְבָרָד נֶאֱמַר סְתָם שֶׁבְּגֹשֶׁן לֹא הָיָה, בְּלֹא "וְהִפְלָה".
connections.quote: “Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail.”
connections.context: The verse states the exception for Goshen without using the verb “distinguish.” This is the textual difference on which Rav Tzadok’s comparison of the plagues depends.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קנא:): אֵין חַיָּה רָעָה וְכוּלֵי עַד שֶׁנִּדְמֶה כִּבְהֵמָה;
connections.quote: ‘Rav Pappa said: We have a received tradition that a lion does not attack two people. But we see that it does attack them! That is explained by Rami bar Abba’s teaching, for Rami bar Abba said: A wild animal has no power over a person until the person appears to it like an animal, as it is said: ‘A person does not remain in honor; he is compared to the animals, which perish.’ Rabbi Chanina said: It is forbidden to sleep alone in a house, and Lilith seizes anyone who sleeps alone in a house.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר "בְּקֶרֶב", כִּי בַּקְּרָבַיִם הוּא הַנְהָגַת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ; וְעוֹד, דְּעַל יְדֵי מַאֲכָלוֹת אֲסוּרוֹת נִדְמֶה לִבְהֵמָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קכה עַמּוּד ב) עַל נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר, וְדָנִיֵּאל שֶׁלֹּא נִתְגָּאַל בְּפַת בַּג וְגוֹמֵר נִיצּוֹל מֵאֲרָיוֹת].
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Through what merit were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah saved from those trials? It was because they did not defile themselves with their food. Rabbi Yehuda said: It is written, ‘Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s food,’ and so forth (Daniel 1:8). It was taught in the concealed teaching of the Mishnah: That wicked man’s food was meat with milk and cheese with meat, besides other foods; this was brought to his table every day.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר "בְּקֶרֶב", כִּי בַּקְּרָבַיִם הוּא הַנְהָגַת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ; וְעוֹד, דְּעַל יְדֵי מַאֲכָלוֹת אֲסוּרוֹת נִדְמֶה לִבְהֵמָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קכה עַמּוּד ב) עַל נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר, וְדָנִיֵּאל שֶׁלֹּא נִתְגָּאַל בְּפַת בַּג וְגוֹמֵר נִיצּוֹל מֵאֲרָיוֹת].
connections.quote: “But Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s food, nor with the wine that he drank.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר "בְּקֶרֶב", כִּי בַּקְּרָבַיִם הוּא הַנְהָגַת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ; וְעוֹד, דְּעַל יְדֵי מַאֲכָלוֹת אֲסוּרוֹת נִדְמֶה לִבְהֵמָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קכה עַמּוּד ב) עַל נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר, וְדָנִיֵּאל שֶׁלֹּא נִתְגָּאַל בְּפַת בַּג וְגוֹמֵר נִיצּוֹל מֵאֲרָיוֹת].
connections.quote: “The principal preservation of the divine image lies in guarding against forbidden food. Therefore Daniel, who separated himself from their royal food and the wine they drank, was saved from the lions’ den; as stated in the Zohar, “Your fear,” and so forth, was fulfilled in him. For no wild beast rules over a person unless he appears to it as an animal, as stated in Shabbat 151b. This comes about through eating the food of an animal—that is, when one does not recognize that the blessed God feeds and sustains him. Without Him, where would physical food obtain the vitality with which to sustain the soul?”

connections.hePhrase: [וּשְׁחִין נֶגֶד "לֹא תִנְאָף", לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ מְיַפִּין עַצְמָן, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְשִׂפַּח וְגוֹמֵר"].
connections.quote: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with outstretched necks and wanton eyes … therefore Hashem will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּשְׁחִין נֶגֶד "לֹא תִנְאָף", לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ מְיַפִּין עַצְמָן, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְשִׂפַּח וְגוֹמֵר"].
connections.quote: ““The Lord will afflict the scalp of the daughters of Zion.” Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Ḥanina said: This teaches that tzaraat broke out upon them. Here it is written vesippaḥ, “He will afflict,” and there it is written, “For a swelling or a scab.””
connections.context: The discussion concerns the ostentatious behavior described in Isaiah 3 and interprets Isaiah 3:17 through the vocabulary of skin afflictions in Leviticus 14:56. This is the passage behind the brief allusion here; the statement is attributed in the Talmud to Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Ḥanina.

connections.hePhrase: [קצב] עַל יְדֵי הַתַּאֲוָה מִסְתַּלֵּק הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּטְבִילַת בַּעַל קֶרִי בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב.): מִשּׁוּם דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה צָרִיךְ בְּאֵימָה, בְּיִרְאָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “It is taught: “Make them known to your children and your children’s children,” and afterward it is written, “The day you stood before the Lord your God at Horeb.” Just as there it was with awe, fear, trembling, and shaking, so here it is with awe, fear, trembling, and shaking.”
connections.context: The discussion compares learning Torah with standing at Sinai and then considers the condition of a person who has experienced a seminal emission. It is the requirement of awe, rather than the technical quantity of immersion water, that Rav Tzadok cites.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתִּיקּוּן לָזֶה – טְבִילָה בְּמַיִם, שֶׁרוֹמְזִים לְמִדַּת הַחֶסֶד וְאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת מַהוּ תַּאֲוָתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל? הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: Just as this date palm has a longing, so Israel’s longing is for the Holy One, blessed be He. Our Rabbis said: There was a date palm in Ḥamtan that they would pollinate, yet it bore no fruit. A palm grower said to them: This palm sees a palm from Jericho and longs for it. They went and brought from that palm; immediately it bore fruit. So is Israel’s longing for the Holy One, blessed be He.”
connections.context: The Midrash uses the date palm and a story of its longing as a parable for Israel’s desire for God. Rav Tzadok draws on this image when explaining how immersion can redirect desire toward divine love.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם): גָּדֵר גָּדוֹל וְכוּלֵי, רֵיקָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁזֶּה גִּדֵּר בִּפְנֵי הַתַּאֲווֹת שֶׁעוֹצֵר תַּאֲוָתוֹ כְּשֶׁאֵין לוֹ מַיִם לִטְבּוֹל, וְנִמְצָא תַּאֲוָתוֹ רַק כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאָז הוּא אֶחָד עִם הַיִּרְאָה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥanina said: They established a great fence through it. For it was taught: A man once solicited a woman for a transgression. She said to him: Empty fellow! Do you have forty seah in which to immerse? He immediately withdrew.”
connections.context: The story explains how the immersion requirement could restrain a person before acting on desire. Rav Tzadok then interprets that restraint as bringing desire into agreement with the fear of God. The later annulment discussed in the same chapter is quoted separately below.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם): גָּדֵר גָּדוֹל וְכוּלֵי, רֵיקָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁזֶּה גִּדֵּר בִּפְנֵי הַתַּאֲווֹת שֶׁעוֹצֵר תַּאֲוָתוֹ כְּשֶׁאֵין לוֹ מַיִם לִטְבּוֹל, וְנִמְצָא תַּאֲוָתוֹ רַק כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאָז הוּא אֶחָד עִם הַיִּרְאָה.
connections.quote: “This is surrendering all desires to Hashem: even at the utmost force of desire, a person is ready to refrain if it is not according to Hashem's will. As the Midrash says (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7; Midrash Tehillim 2) concerning ‘fenced with roses’: after incurring many expenses and approaching his wife, she says, ‘I saw [blood] red as a rose’; he turns aside. What thorn pricked him? Only words of Torah, soft as a rose. This is the meaning of Shavuot's two loaves being leavened: offering to Hashem the leaven in the dough that holds one back, as Berakhot 17a says. Through this one merits receiving Torah, the seasoning for the inclination (Kiddushin 30b)—using it only according to Hashem's will. Then it is ‘very good,’ as Bereishit Rabbah teaches; and as Berakhot 34a says of leaven, a little is beneficial, while much is harmful.”
connections.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains what it means to hand desire back to Hashem: even at its strongest, the person is willing to refrain when it conflicts with His will. Torah then directs the use of that power. This develops the siman's claim that desire ordered to Hashem's will can be united with awe rather than simply opposed to it.
connections.headline: Desire used according to Hashem's will

connections.hePhrase: וַחֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה סִדְּרוּ דִּינֵי טְבִילַת קֶרִי לְעִנְיַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּתְפִלָּה בְּיִחוּד, שֶׁבָּהֶם עִיקָּרֵי הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ט:) עַל פָּסוּק "יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים עב, ה).
connections.quote: see note 2425.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צָרִיךְ אַרְבָּעִים סְאָה מַיִם שֶׁכָּל גּוּפוֹ עוֹלֶה, כִּי הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב מְעוֹרֵר כָּל הַגּוּף עַד שֶׁכְּלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גּוֹמְרִין.
connections.quote: “And if a man’s seed goes out from him, he shall bathe all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the evening.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צָרִיךְ אַרְבָּעִים סְאָה מַיִם שֶׁכָּל גּוּפוֹ עוֹלֶה, כִּי הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב מְעוֹרֵר כָּל הַגּוּף עַד שֶׁכְּלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גּוֹמְרִין.
connections.quote: ““All his flesh”: water in which his whole body can be immersed. How much is that? A cubit by a cubit, with a height of three cubits. The Sages measured the water of a ritual bath as forty seah.”
connections.context: The Talmud connects forty seah with water sufficient for immersion of the entire body. Rav Tzadok interprets that bodily completeness as corresponding to desire that has stirred the whole body into action.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיְעוּיַּן שָׁם חִלּוּק בֵּין חוֹלֶה לְבָרִיא, דְּהַיְינוּ בֵּין תַּלְמִיד חָכָם לְעַם הָאָרֶץ, וּמִשָּׁם בְּאֵרָהּ דְּאֵין לְאֹנְסוֹ אֶלָּא בְּעַם הָאָרֶץ וְלֹא בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם לִמְסַקְנָא דְּרָבָא].
connections.quote: ““It is possible by pouring”: nine kav. Although below this was taught only concerning an ill person, Torah scholars are generally considered ill, as stated in tractate Nedarim: According to whom do we pray for ketzirei and meri’ei? According to Rabbi Yose. Ketzirei are the ill; meri’ei are the Rabbis.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the comparison between Torah scholars and the ill that Rav Tzadok invokes. His comment concerns the immersion discussion’s treatment of scholars whose strength has been diminished by study. It explains the textual basis for the comparison without turning every distinction here into an independent practical ruling.

connections.hePhrase: [וְיְעוּיַּן שָׁם חִלּוּק בֵּין חוֹלֶה לְבָרִיא, דְּהַיְינוּ בֵּין תַּלְמִיד חָכָם לְעַם הָאָרֶץ, וּמִשָּׁם בְּאֵרָהּ דְּאֵין לְאֹנְסוֹ אֶלָּא בְּעַם הָאָרֶץ וְלֹא בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם לִמְסַקְנָא דְּרָבָא].
connections.quote: “Rava said: The rule is that a healthy person who brings about the emission and an ill person who brings it about require forty seah. A healthy person whose emission occurs involuntarily requires nine kav. But an ill person whose emission occurs involuntarily is exempt from everything.”
connections.context: Rava distinguishes intentional from involuntary emission and health from illness. Rav Tzadok interprets these categories spiritually; the qualification exempting the ill person in the involuntary case is part of the Talmud’s actual wording.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִטְּלוּהָ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא דְּאָמַר: "הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ וְכוּלֵי" (יִרְמְיָה כג, כט), פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שׂוֹרְפִין כָּל תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת.
connections.quote: “It was taught: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira used to say that words of Torah do not contract impurity. A student was once reciting hesitantly before Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. He said to him: My son, open your mouth and let your words shine, for words of Torah do not contract impurity, as it says, “Is not My word like fire, declares the Lord?” Just as fire does not contract impurity, so words of Torah do not contract impurity.”
connections.context: Later on the same page, the Talmud explains the annulment of the immersion requirement by reference to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. His teaching and the encouragement to the hesitant student make clear why Torah study itself remains available. Rav Tzadok then gives the fire image its spiritual interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א): מַקִּישׁ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים וְכוּלֵי, וְהֵם עַצְמָן דּוּגְמַת טְבִילָה:
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chama bar Chanina said: Why were tents placed beside streams, as it is written, “Like streams stretched out, like gardens beside a river, like aloes planted”? To tell you: Just as streams raise a person from impurity to purity, so tents raise a person from the scale of guilt to the scale of merit.”
connections.context: The exposition reads ohalim, tents, alongside the verse’s ahalim, aloes. It compares Torah’s purification with immersion in water, which is the analogy Rav Tzadok invokes. The introductory question begins at the end of 15b and its answer is at the beginning of 16a.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א): מַקִּישׁ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים וְכוּלֵי, וְהֵם עַצְמָן דּוּגְמַת טְבִילָה:
connections.quote: “How goodly are your tents, O Jacob, your dwellings, O Israel! Like streams stretched out, like gardens by the riverside, like aloes which Hashem has planted, like cedars beside the waters.”

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א): מַקִּישׁ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים וְכוּלֵי, וְהֵם עַצְמָן דּוּגְמַת טְבִילָה:
connections.quote: see note 41 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rambam first states that ritual impurity and immersion are scriptural decrees: impurity is not physical dirt washed away by water. He then offers this analogy of inward purification through knowledge. The distinction illuminates Rav Tzadok’s comparison of Torah study with immersion.

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (טז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א): מַקִּישׁ אֹהָלִים לִנְחָלִים וְכוּלֵי, וְהֵם עַצְמָן דּוּגְמַת טְבִילָה:
connections.quote: “For this reason the tents of Torah were compared to streams that raise a person from impurity to purity.
