Just as one immerses in water covering the whole body, so words of Torah become permanently established in heart and mind until the person's whole stature is immersed in the waters of knowledge, as the Rambam describes at the end of the laws of immersion pools. This is what the Zohar indicates by purification from the spring of the deep stream. Through the understanding of the heart, in which Torah becomes established, the source from the breadth of the river opens for the purification of the soul.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik develops the tents-and-streams teaching with which this siman concludes. The water surrounds the whole body; correspondingly, Torah becomes continuously established in the heart and mind. This explains the positive content of Torah as purification and connects the outward immersion image to a sustained inward formation. It does not collapse the distinct practical categories discussed earlier in the siman.
connections.headline: Torah purifies by encompassing the person

connections.hePhrase: [קצג] גַּם בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שׁוֹמֵעַ כְּעוֹנֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת בִּבְרָכוֹת (כ:) גַּבֵּי: כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּסִינַי
connections.quote: ““As we find at Sinai”: Although thought is like speech for discharging the obligation, it is not like speech so as to forbid a person who has experienced a seminal emission to think. At Sinai there was speech and they needed to immerse; even though they were silent, one who hears is like one who answers.”
connections.context: Tosafot distinguishes thought from hearing words spoken aloud. Its final clause explicitly establishes the principle Rav Tzadok invokes: listening to Torah can count as speaking it.

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִיהוּ אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי דִּבְסִינַי הָיָה דִּבּוּר מַמָּשׁ, דְּ"וַיְדַבֵּר ה' וְגוֹמֵר" הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי ה' מוֹצָאוֹת הַפֶּה דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
connections.quote: “And God spoke all these words, saying.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִיהוּ אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי דִּבְסִינַי הָיָה דִּבּוּר מַמָּשׁ, דְּ"וַיְדַבֵּר ה' וְגוֹמֵר" הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי ה' מוֹצָאוֹת הַפֶּה דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
connections.quote: “And Hashem spoke to you out of the midst of the fire; you heard the sound of words, but you saw no form, only a voice.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמִיהוּ אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי דִּבְסִינַי הָיָה דִּבּוּר מַמָּשׁ, דְּ"וַיְדַבֵּר ה' וְגוֹמֵר" הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי ה' מוֹצָאוֹת הַפֶּה דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
connections.quote: “I heard that the voices at the giving of Torah came from the mouths of the children of Israel, for there is no voice in the world except through the five organs of speech. It says, “My soul went out when He spoke”: they then united all the parts of their souls with God. From each power of the soul came a cry particular to that power, recognizing the truth of God and uniting with Him; this is the purpose of the entire giving of Torah.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok repeats the teaching later and explains its inward meaning: each power of the soul responds to revelation with its own voice. This is his fuller account of the teaching reported briefly here.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה בָּרוּר וֶאֱמֶת דְּכָל נְבוּאָה הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי קוֹל הַנָּבִיא עַצְמוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם מה.) בְּקוֹלוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said: From where do we know that the interpreter may not raise his voice above that of the reader? For it is said: ‘Moses would speak, and God would answer him with a voice.’ There is no need for Scripture to say ‘with a voice.’ What, then, does ‘with a voice’ teach? At the level of Moses’ voice.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה בָּרוּר וֶאֱמֶת דְּכָל נְבוּאָה הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי קוֹל הַנָּבִיא עַצְמוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם מה.) בְּקוֹלוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה,
connections.quote: ““Malchut of Atzilut” means the “word of God” that gives life and existence to the great souls that belong to the level of Atzilut, such as the soul of Adam the first man, of whom it is said, “He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life,” and so forth; and such as the souls of the Patriarchs, the prophets, and others like them. They were truly a chariot for God, and their very existence was truly nullified before Him, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said: “The Divine Presence speaks from within the throat of Moses.” Likewise, with all the prophets and those endowed with the holy spirit, the supernal voice and speech were actually clothed in their own voice and speech, as the Ari, of blessed memory, said.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ דְּהַיִּרְאָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הַיְינוּ שֶׁמָּא הוּא מְדַבֵּר מַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ רָאוּי, וּבַלֵּב מוּתָּר הַכֹּל.
connections.quote: “The meaning is this: Even matters that are clear in thought should be held in doubt when they come to expression through the tongue, which brings into actuality what is latent in the heart, for a person is liable to error. Therefore all the outward manifestations of one’s actions must be matters clear to everyone, rather than what is clear only to oneself in thought. In one’s thoughts, however, one may consider even matters clear only to oneself. Concerning such a case: The heart does not disclose it to the mouth.”
connections.context: This earlier passage explains the caution required when private understanding becomes outward speech or action. It concerns ideas that a person finds clear inwardly, while acknowledging human susceptibility to error; it helps delimit the freedom of inward thought described here.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי תִּבְחַר וּתְקָרֵב יִשְׁכֹּן חֲצֵרֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים סה, ה) עַל אַהֲרֹן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג), וְהָיָה חוֹמֵד וּמִתְאַוֶּוה לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֱמַר: "וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת" (בַּמִּדְבָּר א, נא)
connections.quote: ‘Fortunate is the one You choose and draw near, who will dwell in Your courts. May we be satisfied with the goodness of Your house and the holiness of Your palace.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי תִּבְחַר וּתְקָרֵב יִשְׁכֹּן חֲצֵרֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים סה, ה) עַל אַהֲרֹן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג), וְהָיָה חוֹמֵד וּמִתְאַוֶּוה לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֱמַר: "וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת" (בַּמִּדְבָּר א, נא)
connections.quote: “David said: Happy is one whom the Holy One, blessed be He, has chosen, and happy is one whom He has brought near. Who is doubly happy? One whom the Holy One has chosen and brought near. Who is that? Aaron and Levi. … Concerning them Scripture says, “Happy is the one You choose and bring near, to dwell in Your courts.””
connections.context: The Midrash explicitly applies David’s verse to Aaron and Levi. Rav Tzadok uses that identification when describing David’s desire for the priestly service, despite the distinction between the royal and priestly roles.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי תִּבְחַר וּתְקָרֵב יִשְׁכֹּן חֲצֵרֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים סה, ה) עַל אַהֲרֹן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג), וְהָיָה חוֹמֵד וּמִתְאַוֶּוה לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֱמַר: "וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת" (בַּמִּדְבָּר א, נא)
connections.quote: ‘When the Mishkan travels, the Levites shall take it down; when the Mishkan encamps, the Levites shall erect it. An outsider who approaches shall be put to death.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי תִּבְחַר וּתְקָרֵב יִשְׁכֹּן חֲצֵרֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים סה, ה) עַל אַהֲרֹן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג), וְהָיָה חוֹמֵד וּמִתְאַוֶּוה לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֱמַר: "וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת" (בַּמִּדְבָּר א, נא)
connections.quote: “You and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood in every matter of the altar and within the curtain, and you shall serve. I give your priesthood to you as a service of gift; the outsider who approaches shall be put to death.”
connections.context: Numbers 18:7 applies the warning about an outsider specifically to priestly service at the altar and within the curtain. The verse already quoted in the reader, Numbers 1:51, concerns the Levites’ responsibility for dismantling and erecting the Tabernacle. This additional verse supplies the priestly setting relevant to David’s desire.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי תִּבְחַר וּתְקָרֵב יִשְׁכֹּן חֲצֵרֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים סה, ה) עַל אַהֲרֹן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ג), וְהָיָה חוֹמֵד וּמִתְאַוֶּוה לְהַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֱמַר: "וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת" (בַּמִּדְבָּר א, נא)
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 4:8
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 4:8
connections.quote: “Therefore the midwives, because they feared God, merited this status of an enduring dynasty ("house"). And being part of the House of Israel, they were granted the additional houses of Priesthood and Royalty, which pass by inborn heredity: even a day-old infant of Aaron's seed is a Kohen, and even an unlearned priest stands and offers sacrifices upon the altar, while choice cannot grant this to the greatest non-priest: "and the common man that draws near shall be put to death" Numbers 1:51.”
connections.explanation: Ohr Zarua stresses that priestly service is determined by the particular covenant of the priesthood, even where another person is greater in learning. This clarifies why David’s longing for Aharon’s avodah does not by itself authorize performing it. The siman’s freedom of inner yearning must be held together with the actual boundaries of the action desired.
connections.headline: A longing for avodah does not itself confer its office

connections.hePhrase: [וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּזָכָה לְמִלּוּי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ בַּאֲכִילַת לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים שֶׁאָכַל לְפִקּוּחַ נֶפֶשׁ,
connections.quote: “So the priest gave him holy bread, for there was no bread there but the showbread, which had been taken from before Hashem, to put hot bread in its place on the day it was taken away.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּזָכָה לְמִלּוּי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ בַּאֲכִילַת לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים שֶׁאָכַל לְפִקּוּחַ נֶפֶשׁ,
connections.quote: “Since he found there only the showbread, David said to him: Give it to me so that we do not die of hunger, for even a possible danger to life overrides Shabbat. How much did David eat at that time? Rav Huna said: David ate nearly seven seah because of his hunger, for he had been seized by ravenous hunger.”
connections.context: The Midrash explicitly presents David’s eating as a response to danger to life, describing an acute attack of hunger. This is the essential qualification in Rav Tzadok’s statement: the eating fulfilled his longing within the law governing the preservation of life.

connections.hePhrase: וּדְבֵירוּרִין שֶׁלּוֹ הָיָה עֻזִיָּה שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ לְהַקְטִיר, כִּי הַמְּלָכִים מֵעֻזִיָּה וְאֵילָךְ הֵם הַבֵּירוּרִים שֶׁל הַמְּלָכִים מִדָּוִד וְאֵילָךְ, כָּל אֶחָד מְבָרֵר הַמַּעֲלָלִים שֶׁל זֶה מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה שֶׁלֹּא בְּמִתְכַּוֵּין.
connections.quote: “When he became strong, his heart grew proud to the point of corruption. He trespassed against the Lord his God and entered the Temple of the Lord to burn incense on the incense altar. Azariah the priest entered after him, with eighty valiant priests of the Lord. They confronted King Uzziah and said to him: It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron who have been consecrated to burn incense. Leave the sanctuary, for you have trespassed, and this will bring you no honor from the Lord God. Uzziah became angry, holding a censer to burn incense; while he raged against the priests, tzaraat broke out on his forehead before the priests in the house of the Lord, beside the incense altar.”
connections.context: Chronicles explicitly describes Uzziah’s action as trespass and records the priests’ warning before the affliction appears. Rav Tzadok contrasts an inward longing for sacred service with an unauthorized outward act, and interprets Uzziah’s episode in relation to David.

connections.hePhrase: וְיוֹתָם שֶׁהָיָה בֵּירוּר שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶאֱמַר: "רַק לֹא בָא אֶל הֵיכַל ה'" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב כז, ב), שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם חִסָּרוֹן, כִּי כָּל מַעֲלָלֵי שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים, וְזֶה עַצְמוֹ חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חִסָּרוֹן, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ];
connections.quote: ‘He did what was upright in Hashem’s eyes, just as his father Uzziah had done, except that he did not enter Hashem’s sanctuary. The people, however, still acted corruptly.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיוֹתָם שֶׁהָיָה בֵּירוּר שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶאֱמַר: "רַק לֹא בָא אֶל הֵיכַל ה'" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב כז, ב), שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם חִסָּרוֹן, כִּי כָּל מַעֲלָלֵי שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים, וְזֶה עַצְמוֹ חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חִסָּרוֹן, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ];
connections.quote: “They said: “Leaven in excess is harmful, but a little is beneficial.” Likewise, I heard concerning Jotham, of whom it says, “Only he did not enter the Temple of the Lord,” that this was said as a deficiency in him: he had no deficiency at all. In truth it says, “A little folly is more precious than wisdom and honor,” for everyone must have at least a little folly, and this is completeness. Yet it is good for a person that this folly be as small as possible.”
connections.context: This later passage supplies the explanation postponed here. Rav Tzadok reads Jotham’s absence of deficiency as itself lacking something human; he immediately limits the “little folly” to the smallest possible measure. This is his homiletical reading, alongside the plain biblical account already quoted in the reader.

connections.hePhrase: וְדַוְקָא בְּדָבָר שֶׁהַצִּבּוּר עֲסוּקִין, כִּי יֵשׁ לְמַחְשְׁבוֹתָיו וְהִרְהוּרָיו חִבּוּר עִם הַצִּבּוּר,
connections.quote: “But if thought is not like speech, why does he think the words? Rabbi Elazar said: So that everyone should not be occupied with them while he sits idle. Then let him study another chapter! Rav Adda bar Ahava said: He should think about the matter with which the congregation is occupied.”
connections.context: The exchange explains silent participation according to the view that thought does not itself count as speech for fulfilling the obligation. It still requires engagement with the congregation’s subject. Rav Tzadok develops that shared attention into a connection between the individual’s thoughts and the congregation’s Torah.

connections.hePhrase: [קצד] אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת בְּיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם כַּנִּזְכָּר בִּבְרָכוֹת (כב.) לְעִנְיַן טְבִילַת קֶרִי: אֵימָה, וְיִרְאָה, וּרְתֶת, וְזֵיעָה.
connections.quote: “It is taught: “Make them known to your children and your children’s children,” and afterward it is written, “The day you stood before the Lord your God at Horeb.” Just as there it was with awe, fear, trembling, and shaking, so here it is with awe, fear, trembling, and shaking.”
connections.context: The four Hebrew expressions are eimah, yirah, retet, and zeiah. Rav Tzadok interprets the last through its association with sweating and unfolds the four as successive degrees of fear. That account is his explanation of the baraita’s terms.

connections.hePhrase: שְׁתֵּי הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת בַּלֵּב: אֵימָה בַּהַתְחָלָה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: עוֹנִים בְּאֵימָה וְאוֹמְרִים בְּיִרְאָה;
connections.linkedRef: Siddur Sefard, Weekday Shacharit, The Shema 10
connections.canonicalRef: Siddur Sefard, Weekday Shacharit, The Shema 10
connections.heRef: סידור ספרד, שחרית לימות החול, ק"ש וברכותיה י׳
connections.quote: “And all of them accept upon themselves the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven from one another … in clear speech and with sweetness; all of them as one answer with dread and say with awe: ‘Holy, holy, holy is Hashem of hosts.’”

connections.hePhrase: עֲנִיָּה בְּכָל מָקוֹם בְּקוֹל, וַאֲמִירָה בִּלְחִישָׁה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, פח עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: ““You shall answer”: in a raised voice.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the verb aniyah in the declaration over first fruits as speaking aloud. This supplies a direct example for Rav Tzadok’s distinction between answering aloud and the quiet amirah described in the existing Zohar note.

connections.hePhrase: עֲנִיָּה בְּכָל מָקוֹם בְּקוֹל, וַאֲמִירָה בִּלְחִישָׁה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, פח עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: “Say to the priests”—quietly. Just as all the priests’ service is performed quietly, so their saying is quiet.”
connections.context: The Zohar connects the word amirah, saying, with quietness. Rav Tzadok sets this beside aniyah, answering aloud, in explaining the difference between voiced speech and inward, quiet speech.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַתְּפִלָּה בִּלְחִישָׁה שֶׁהוּא כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 4:16
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 4:16
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 4:16
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות תפילה וברכת כהנים ד׳:ט״ז
connections.quote: “What is concentration? One should clear one’s heart of all thoughts and see oneself as though standing before the Divine Presence. Therefore one must sit a little before prayer to direct the heart, and afterward pray calmly and pleadingly. One should not make prayer like someone carrying a burden, throwing it down, and going away. Therefore one must sit a little after prayer and then depart. The early pious ones would wait an hour before prayer and an hour after prayer, and extend their prayer for an hour.”
connections.context: Rambam explains the inward preparation appropriate to standing before God, together with its expression in calm, pleading prayer. This develops the distinction that Rav Tzadok makes between the first cry of fear and the quieter prayer that follows.

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם נִקְרָא יִרְאָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קצ"ב, וְהַתְּפִלָּה בְּיוֹתֵר כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י בִּבְרָכוֹת (כה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א).
connections.quote: see note 45 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rashi explains the additional requirement of covering the upper body for prayer. Rav Tzadok cites his distinction between addressing the King in prayer and accepting Heaven’s kingship in Shema.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁמִּתְבּוֹנֵן יוֹתֵר, אָז זֵיעַ, שֶׁהוּא מֵזִיעַ מֵרוֹב הַפַּחַד, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה יג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): מִזֵּיעָתָן שֶׁל חַיּוֹת נְהַר דִּינוּר יוֹצֵא עַל רֹאשׁ רְשָׁעִים בְּגֵיהִנָּם, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “From where does [the River of Fire] issue? From the perspiration of the living creatures. Where does it flow? Rav Zutra bar Toviah said in the name of Rav: Upon the heads of the wicked in Gehenna, as it says, “Behold, the storm of the Lord has gone forth in wrath; a whirling storm shall whirl upon the heads of the wicked.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok connects the creatures’ perspiration with the final degree of awe he is describing. The quotation ends at the relevant explanation; the continuation about uncreated generations is a separate interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁמִּתְבּוֹנֵן יוֹתֵר, אָז זֵיעַ, שֶׁהוּא מֵזִיעַ מֵרוֹב הַפַּחַד, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה יג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): מִזֵּיעָתָן שֶׁל חַיּוֹת נְהַר דִּינוּר יוֹצֵא עַל רֹאשׁ רְשָׁעִים בְּגֵיהִנָּם, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “A river of fire issued and came forth from before Him; thousands upon thousands ministered to Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא "רֹאשׁ רְשָׁעִים בְּגֵיהִנָּם", דְּעִיקָּרוֹ בַּתַּאֲווֹת כִּדְאִיתָא בְּעֵירוּבִין (יט.) שֶׁהַכֹּל יוֹרְדִין עַל עִסְקֵי הִנָּם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: see note 994 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Eruvin 19a plays on Gehenna and the valley of Hinnom. Rashi identifies the relevant “hinnam” matters with sexual wrongdoing, supplying the connection with desire that Rav Tzadok needs here.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמַר הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל כִּי הַזֵּיעָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי עִסְקֵי הַמִּצְווֹת הוּא תִּיקּוּן לַקֶּרִי.
connections.displayRef: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 460:2
connections.linkedRef: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 460:2
connections.canonicalRef: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 460:2
connections.heRef: טורי זהב על שולחן ערוך אורח חיים ת״ס:ב׳
connections.quote: “In the book of the Ari’s intentions it is written that a person should exert himself over the matzah of the commandment until he becomes warm and sweats; through this he breaks the husks that were produced by semen emitted in vain.”
connections.context: Turei Zahav records this teaching in the Ari’s name specifically about the effort involved in preparing the matzah used for the commandment. Rav Tzadok relates that particular example to his broader account of exertion in mitzvot and returns to matzah below.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁזֶּה יָקָר וְקָשֶׁה, וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים קַל הוּא עַל יְדֵי פְּעֻלַּת אָדָם בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת בְּאֵבָרָיו.
connections.quote: “Regarding the study of halakhah in depth with companions: I saw my master, of blessed memory, exert himself with the strength of a lion while studying halakhah, until he was weary and perspired greatly. I asked him why he exerted himself so much. He answered me that in-depth study serves to break the husks, which are the difficulties in that halakhah that prevent a person from understanding it. A person therefore must exert himself and expend his strength then. For this reason Torah is called tushiyah: it weakens the strength of the one who studies it. Therefore it is fitting to exert oneself and expend one’s strength while engaged in Torah.”
connections.context: Rabbi Ḥayyim Vital describes the Ari’s exertion while learning with companions and records his explanation of intellectual difficulties as husks to be broken. This is a concrete parallel to Rav Tzadok’s account of bodily effort in sacred work.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְיוֹתֵר בְּמִצְוַת מַצָּה, שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה וְהַתַּאֲוָה.
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 27:3
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 27:3
connections.quote: “‘This matzah that we eat—why? Because our ancestors' dough did not have time to become leavened.’ Matzah indicates a small degree of human action, through which it is still easy to recognize the source. Chametz indicates more human action, which can conceal the source, as when the mixing of a person's own understanding obscures recognition. At the beginning Israel were therefore commanded concerning matzah to establish recognition of the source in their hearts. The Zohar says that when Israel left Egypt they did not know the root and secret of faith. Hashem said: Let Israel taste this medicine; while they eat it, no other food should be shown to them. Once they ate matzah, the medicine for entering and knowing the secret of faith, Hashem said: From now on chametz is fitting for them and cannot harm them. This resembles the command to return every first portion to Hashem, such as terumah, tithes and challah. When a person recognizes the source at the beginning and accepts Hashem's kingship at the start of an outpouring, Hashem grants him the remainder to receive from the divine table. So Israel must clarify their recognition of the source during these first seven days through eating matzah. Through this they can recognize His light in every gift throughout the year, even when eating chametz.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same Zohar description of matzah as medicine. The smaller human intervention makes the source easier to recognize, and the first seven days establish a recognition meant to continue when chametz returns. This clarifies the siman's account of matzah opposing the heart's leaven: the aim is an enduring direction within human activity, not simply the disappearance of activity or appetite.
connections.headline: Matzah establishes recognition before expansion

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל מִצְוָה נוֹתֶנֶת קְדוּשָּׁה בָּאָדָם כְּפִי עִנְיָנָהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמְּבָרְכִין "אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ".
connections.quote: “All the commandments bring holiness into the heart of a Jew, as it says: “So that you remember and perform all My commandments, and be holy to your God.” Likewise we say, “Sanctify us through Your commandments,” and bless over them, “Who has sanctified us through His commandments and commanded us.” It appears that this is the intended purpose of all the commandments: to become holy through them.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok opens Yisrael Kedoshim by explaining the sanctifying effect of mitzvot through the same wording of the blessing cited here. This supplies his general statement behind the particular holiness he associates with matzah.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַצָּה קְדוּשָׁה לְסִלּוּק הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה מֵהַלֵּב, דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפג עַמּוּד ב): מֵיכְלָא דְּאַסְוָותָא, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי שַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק יד הֲלָכָה ג): כָּל חוֹלִי – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע.
connections.quote: “Thus, when Israel left Egypt, they did not know the foundation and mystery of faith. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let Israel taste the remedy; until they eat this remedy, no other food shall be shown to them. Once they ate matzah, which is the remedy for entering and knowing the mystery of faith, the Holy One, blessed be He, said: From now on, leaven may be shown to them and they may eat it, for it cannot harm them. All the more so on Shavuot, when the higher bread is prepared, which is a remedy in every respect.”
connections.context: Matzah is explicitly identified as the remedy that introduces Israel to faith. Rav Tzadok applies that healing to removing the “leaven in the dough,” the inclination within the heart. The separate discussion of Rosh Hashanah on the same page assumes this explanation but does not itself supply it.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַצָּה קְדוּשָׁה לְסִלּוּק הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה מֵהַלֵּב, דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפג עַמּוּד ב): מֵיכְלָא דְּאַסְוָותָא, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי שַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק יד הֲלָכָה ג): כָּל חוֹלִי – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Avun said: This is the evil inclination, whose beginning is sweet and whose end is bitter.”
connections.context: The Yerushalmi interprets “all illness” in Deuteronomy 7:15 as the evil inclination. That identification, rather than the Mishnah’s rules about medicine on Shabbat, is the basis of Rav Tzadok’s use of healing language.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַצָּה קְדוּשָׁה לְסִלּוּק הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה מֵהַלֵּב, דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפג עַמּוּד ב): מֵיכְלָא דְּאַסְוָותָא, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי שַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק יד הֲלָכָה ג): כָּל חוֹלִי – זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע.
connections.quote: “And Hashem will remove from you all sickness, and He will put none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you know, upon you.”

connections.hePhrase: [קצה] יִרְאָה הִיא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהַיְינוּ כִּי כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּעֲלֵי יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם וְאַף עַם הָאָרֶץ.
connections.quote: “The lower heh represents the revelation of the kingship of Heaven in the souls of Israel, and from this fear shines into their souls, as it says, “If I am a master, where is the fear of Me?” As stated at the beginning of Oraḥ Ḥayyim: When a person takes to heart that the King of kings stands over him, fear and shame immediately come upon him.”
connections.context: Peri Tzadik explains how the attribute of divine kingship awakens fear within Israel. The lower heh refers to the final letter of the divine name, associated here with that revealed kingship.

connections.hePhrase: רַק הַבּוּר אֵין יְרֵא חֵטְא, שֶׁהוּא אֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, וְדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הַיְינוּ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם.
connections.quote: “He used to say: A boor does not fear sin, and an unlearned person is not pious.”
connections.context: The Mishnah uses different descriptions: the boor lacks fear of sin, while the unlearned person is denied the higher description of piety. Rav Tzadok builds on that distinction to explain how an unlearned person can nevertheless possess fear of Heaven.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yishmael bar Rav Nachman said: Derekh eretz preceded the Torah by twenty-six generations, as it is written: ‘to guard the way to the tree of life’ (Genesis 3:24). ‘The way’—this is derekh eretz; and afterward ‘the tree of life’—this is the Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa says: Anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom—his wisdom endures. Anyone whose wisdom precedes his fear of sin—his wisdom does not endure. He used to say: Anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom—his wisdom endures. Anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds—his wisdom does not endure.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ.
connections.quote: “At first there must be “fear and love”; afterward the order is reversed: “love and fear,” with love first. For proper worldly conduct precedes Torah. The world was created with the letter bet, which represents fear and constriction, as though there were two: Creator and creature. At first the world was created with the attribute of judgment, and afterward He joined to it the attribute of mercy. Therefore the order of proper worldly conduct is fear and love. This precedes Torah, which is a Torah of kindness and opens with alef, representing love and attachment, as though everything were one. When one reaches Torah, love comes first.”

connections.hePhrase: וְתוֹרָה הִיא מִדַּת "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב" (מִיכָה ז, כ) – אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ח).
connections.quote: see note 2630.
connections.context: The word emet, truth, is essential here: Rav Tzadok associates Jacob with Torah through the Yerushalmi’s teaching that “truth” denotes Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְתוֹרָה הִיא מִדַּת "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב" (מִיכָה ז, כ) – אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ח).
connections.quote: “Shmuel said: “It cast truth to the ground.” Truth means Torah, as you say, “Acquire truth and do not sell it.””
connections.context: The Yerushalmi joins Daniel 8:12 with Proverbs 23:23 to identify truth with Torah. Rav Tzadok uses precisely that identification in linking Torah to Jacob’s attribute of truth.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, כִּי יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב" (דְּבָרִים לג, ד), אֲפִילּוּ עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ.
connections.quote: ‘Moses commanded us the Torah, an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, כִּי יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב" (דְּבָרִים לג, ד), אֲפִילּוּ עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ.
connections.quote: “He rose, seized him, and said: My inheritance is with you, and you are withholding it from me! He said: What inheritance of yours is with me? He answered: Once I passed a school and heard the children saying, “Moses commanded us Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob.” It does not say “the congregation of Yanai,” but “the congregation of Jacob.” Rabbi Yanai said to him: What merit enabled you to eat at my table? He answered: In all my days I have never heard an evil report and repeated it to the person concerned; and whenever I saw two people quarreling, I made peace between them. Rabbi Yanai said: You possess all this proper conduct, and I called you a dog!”
connections.context: Rabbi Yanai had welcomed a guest, found him lacking in Torah learning, and insulted him. The guest’s reply establishes Torah as the inheritance of the entire congregation, and his conduct leads Rabbi Yanai to acknowledge his error. The Midrash joins precisely the two themes discussed here: unlearned people’s share in Torah and the worth of derekh eretz.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּלָאו הָכִי, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה.
connections.quote: see note 1878 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Mishnah states the relationship in both directions. Rav Tzadok uses this reciprocity to explain why fear presupposes some share in Torah, even where that share is concealed, and why Torah learning includes fear.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּלָאו הָכִי, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה.
connections.quote: “A person's principal power is the desire and yearning within him and his preparing himself to receive and fulfill the whole Torah. The rest comes from Hashem, Who completes it for him and gives wisdom. But He ‘gives only to the wise’: those who possess the beginning of wisdom, awe of Hashem, which is itself also called wisdom, as it says, ‘Behold, awe of Hashem is wisdom.’ This is preparing the heart not to do anything against Hashem's will. Then all Torah and wisdom is entrusted to him, to know Hashem's will and to have all his deeds and thoughts conform to Hashem's wisdom within him.”
connections.explanation: Divrei Soferim identifies the first wisdom as awe itself: preparing the heart not to act against Hashem's will. Received Torah then tells the person how to direct deeds and thoughts. This explains the siman's reciprocal relation of awe and wisdom without treating either as a dispensable addition to the other.
connections.headline: The awe that is itself called wisdom

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁתּוֹרָתָן אֻמָּנוּתָן, אָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים (שַׁבָּת יא.) שֶׁאֵין מַפְסִיקִין לִתְפִלָּה;
connections.quote: “‘If they have begun, they need not interrupt; they must interrupt for the recitation of Shema.’ But did he not teach in the first clause that they need not interrupt? In the latter clause we have come to the subject of Torah study. For it was taught: ‘Scholars engaged in Torah study interrupt for the recitation of Shema, but do not interrupt for prayer.’ Rabbi Yohanan said: ‘This was taught only of people such as Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and his companions, whose Torah is their occupation. But people such as ourselves interrupt both for the recitation of Shema and for prayer.’”

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם דְּאִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה, רַק יָדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, לט עַמּוּד ב) דִּבְמָקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ דְּכַר וְנוּקְבָא לֵית שְׁבָחָא אֶלָּא לִדְכוּרָא, וְגַם הַנּוּקְבָא נִקְרֵאת עַל שְׁמוֹ.
connections.quote: “There is no difficulty in Scripture not saying “this” in the feminine form, “this month” in the feminine, for “this” masculine and “this” feminine are bound together. Where male and female are joined as one, the praise is directed only to the male.”
connections.context: The Zohar explains masculine wording as encompassing the joined masculine and feminine aspects. Rav Tzadok applies this to wisdom and fear: the designation of wisdom can include the fear joined with it.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אֵצֶל הַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם הַיִּרְאָה נִכְלֶלֶת בְּהַתּוֹרָה, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרַבִּי בִּבְרָכוֹת (יג:) שֶׁבְּעֵת לִמּוּדוֹ מַעֲבִיר יָדָיו עַל עֵינָיו
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: ‘Hear, Israel: Hashem is our God; Hashem is one’ was Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi’s recitation of the Shema. Rav said to Rabbi Chiyya: ‘I have not seen Rabbi accept Heaven’s kingship upon himself.’ He answered: ‘Son of nobles, when he passes his hands over his face, he accepts upon himself the yoke of Heaven’s kingship.’’

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי עִיקַּר הַיִּרְאָה בַּעֲצִימַת הָעֵינַיִם מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע; וְלָכֵן מַדְרֵגַת יִצְחָק הוּא דְּמַחֲוֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:), וּמִשּׁוּם "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי וְגוֹמֵר" בְּעֵינֵי בָּשָׂר רַק בְּעֵינֵי הַשֵּׂכֶל, לְכָךְ מַעֲבִיר וְכוּלֵי],
connections.quote: “He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly … who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed, and shuts his eyes from looking upon evil.”

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי עִיקַּר הַיִּרְאָה בַּעֲצִימַת הָעֵינַיִם מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע; וְלָכֵן מַדְרֵגַת יִצְחָק הוּא דְּמַחֲוֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:), וּמִשּׁוּם "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי וְגוֹמֵר" בְּעֵינֵי בָּשָׂר רַק בְּעֵינֵי הַשֵּׂכֶל, לְכָךְ מַעֲבִיר וְכוּלֵי],
connections.quote: see note 125 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the conclusion of Isaac’s defense of Israel. Rav Tzadok develops the wording about their eyes as inward perception of God; the earlier note had quoted a different speech on the same page.

connections.hePhrase: [כִּי עִיקַּר הַיִּרְאָה בַּעֲצִימַת הָעֵינַיִם מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע; וְלָכֵן מַדְרֵגַת יִצְחָק הוּא דְּמַחֲוֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:), וּמִשּׁוּם "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי וְגוֹמֵר" בְּעֵינֵי בָּשָׂר רַק בְּעֵינֵי הַשֵּׂכֶל, לְכָךְ מַעֲבִיר וְכוּלֵי],
connections.quote: “And He said: You cannot see My face, for man shall not see Me and live.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן רַשְׁבִּ"י וַדַּאי הֲוָה מְהַדַּר אַשְׁמַעְתָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וַעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
connections.quote: “Does he return and complete it, or does he not return and complete it? Bar Kappara says: He does not return and complete it. Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi says: He returns and completes it. Bar Kappara said to Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi: According to me, who say that he does not return and complete it, this explains why Rabbi seeks a teaching that contains the Exodus from Egypt. But according to you, who say that he returns and completes it, why must he seek such a teaching? So that he mentions the Exodus from Egypt at its proper time.”
connections.context: This follows the account of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reciting the first verse of Shema while teaching. Both opinions recognize his effort to teach about the Exodus; they differ over whether he later completes the rest of Shema. Rav Tzadok uses this practice as an analogy for Torah study that includes the content of the service otherwise expressed through prayer.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הַכֹּל כָּלוּל בַּתּוֹרָה, כְּטַעַם "אֲנִי בִינָה" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, יד), שֶׁהוּא תְּשׁוּבָה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְזוֹ עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הַיּוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה, דְּבִינָה לִבָּא כַּנּוֹדָע;
connections.quote: ‘Counsel and sound wisdom are mine; I am understanding, and strength is mine.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הַכֹּל כָּלוּל בַּתּוֹרָה, כְּטַעַם "אֲנִי בִינָה" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, יד), שֶׁהוּא תְּשׁוּבָה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְזוֹ עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הַיּוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה, דְּבִינָה לִבָּא כַּנּוֹדָע;
connections.quote: “Chokhmah is the brain, which is thought within; Binah is the heart, and through it the heart understands.”

connections.hePhrase: [קצו] שָׁלֹשׁ אַהֲבוֹת יֵשׁ: אַהֲבַת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וְהַתּוֹרָה, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל; וְכֻלָּם חַד כִּידוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר, דְּהָא בְּלָא הָא לָא סַגִּי.
connections.quote: see note 2065 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly joins God, Torah, and Israel, and distinguishes the hidden and revealed aspect of each. This is the source behind the opening statement that the three loves belong together.

connections.hePhrase: [קצו] שָׁלֹשׁ אַהֲבוֹת יֵשׁ: אַהֲבַת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וְהַתּוֹרָה, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל; וְכֻלָּם חַד כִּידוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר, דְּהָא בְּלָא הָא לָא סַגִּי.
connections.quote: “as it is said: "but Esau I hated" (Malachi 1:3), being the polar opposite of the three aforementioned loves; as the Sages expounded on "since you have not hated blood" (Yechezkel 35:6): the blood of the Passover, the blood of circumcision, and the blood of man within his body. And the blood of the Paschal lamb awakens the love of the Blessed Name within the hearts of Israel like water reflecting face to face (Mishlei 27:19); because Hashem passed over and had compassion upon us, Pesach being the festival of love; and the blood of circumcision is the boundary separating Israel from the nations, all gentiles being uncircumcised (Nedarim 31b); this representing the love of Torah in the hearts of Israel who desired it and accepted it; whereas all the nations unto whom Hashem offered it refused to receive it (Avodah Zarah 2b);”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz explicitly returns to three loves and associates the blood of Pesach with Hashem’s compassion, and the covenant of milah with Israel’s willing reception of Torah. These concrete bonds help explain why the siman refuses to reduce love of Torah to intellectual taste or love of Israel to enjoyment of company. Their direction is toward the relationship Hashem establishes and the response it calls forth.
connections.headline: The three loves expressed through concrete bonds

connections.hePhrase: [וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּעַל זֶה תִּיקֵּן בֹּעַז שְׁאִילַת שָׁלוֹם בַּשֵּׁם, שֶׁהוּא אָהַב צַוְותָּא מְאֹד וּפָחַד שֶׁמָּא הוּא אַהֲבַת צַוְותָּא בְּזוּלַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “They instituted that a person should greet his fellow using God’s name, as it says: “Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers, ‘The Lord be with you’; and they said to him, ‘The Lord bless you.’” It also says: “The Lord is with you, mighty man of valor”; and: “Do not despise your mother when she is old”; and: “It is time to act for the Lord; they have violated Your Torah.” Rabbi Natan says: “They have violated Your Torah”—because it is time to act for the Lord.”
connections.context: This is the original enactment cited here. The following Mei HaShiloach passage explains the spiritual purpose Rav Tzadok finds in Boaz’s greeting.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הָיָה פְּתִיחַת צַוְותָּא שֶׁלּוֹ וּשְׁאִילַת שָׁלוֹם שֶׁלּוֹ בַּשֵּׁם, לוֹמַר שֶׁרוֹצֶה רַק צַוְותָּא לִכְבוֹד שָׁמַיִם].
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 54a:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 54a:1
connections.quote: “This was the matter with Boaz: by nature Boaz loved companionship, and he feared for himself that this might not be clarified as being for the sake of Heaven. He therefore instituted a restraint for himself: immediately upon seeing his fellow, his first words would be to inquire in God’s name—that they should mention and ask whether he had now, God forbid, departed from God’s name through any forgetfulness. This was to clarify his character, so that his companionship would be clearly intended for the sake of Heaven. After he devised this counsel, “they instituted” it: the Holy One, blessed be He, bestowed it and engraved it in the hearts of the children of Israel. This is why “they instituted” is plural.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer explains both Boaz’s personal concern and the Mishnah’s plural wording. Rav Tzadok’s report of what he heard has this direct parallel in Mei HaShiloach.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַהֲבַת תּוֹרָה בְּלֹא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ – הַיְינוּ אַהֲבַת הַחָכְמָה בִּלְבַד, זֶהוּ דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רטז עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁהָיָה רָאוּי אָז מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, דְּהֵמָּה אָהֲבוּ תּוֹרָה וְחָכְמָה מְאֹד
connections.quote: see note 683 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Zohar states the missed possibility of receiving Torah in the generation of the Flood and its obstruction through wickedness. The further description of that generation as loving wisdom without loving Hashem is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation here; it should not be presented as a quotation from this Zohar passage.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה טַעַם "בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים אֶל בְּנוֹת הָאָדָם", דִּידוּעַ נוּקְבָא הוּא הַחֵשֶׁק וּדְכוּרָא הַמִּלּוּי,
connections.quote: “The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of men, and they bore children to them; these were the mighty men of old, the men of renown.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַלְאָכִים יֵשׁ לָהֶם חָכְמָה וְהַשָּׂגָה רַק שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע וּתְשׁוּקָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קלח עַמּוּד א) דְּגַם חֵשֶׁק לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה צָרִיךְ יֵצֶר הָרָע,
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the statement that the righteous are greater than the ministering angels. We also find the reverse stated many times, as Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra wrote: the angels’ apprehension is certainly greater, as Rabbi Moses ben Maimon wrote. Yet they have no delight, as it was said, “Is there an evil inclination among you?” For delight proceeds only from its opposite.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the measure of intellectual apprehension from the delight born of overcoming concealment. This explains how he can grant the angels wisdom while locating the human contribution in desire.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַלְאָכִים יֵשׁ לָהֶם חָכְמָה וְהַשָּׂגָה רַק שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע וּתְשׁוּקָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קלח עַמּוּד א) דְּגַם חֵשֶׁק לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה צָרִיךְ יֵצֶר הָרָע,
connections.quote: see note 1592 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This passage in Midrash HaNe’elam, traditionally cited at Zohar I 138a, connects the power of desire to the delight of Torah. Its description of the future expressly preserves the removal of the inclination’s former power to cause sin.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אוֹהֲבִי, כְּבָר מִלֵּידָה מִבֶּטֶן קָבוּעַ בָּהֶם אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ, נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַכֶּתֶר שֶׁאֵינוֹ בִּתְפִיסַת אָדָם.
connections.quote: “But you, Israel, My servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham who loved Me.”

connections.hePhrase: וְחָכְמָה וּבִינָה הֵם אַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּבִינָה לִבָּא, וְשָׁם עִיקַּר אַהֲבַת חֲבֵירִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כֵּן לֵב הָאָדָם לָאָדָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יט)
connections.quote: “Chokhmah is the brain, which is thought within; Binah is the heart, and through it the heart understands.”

connections.hePhrase: וְחָכְמָה וּבִינָה הֵם אַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּבִינָה לִבָּא, וְשָׁם עִיקַּר אַהֲבַת חֲבֵירִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כֵּן לֵב הָאָדָם לָאָדָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יט)
connections.quote: see note 2596.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה", דְּשָׁם אֵין שַׁיָּיךְ קִלְקוּל, כִּי הוּא חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ.
connections.quote: “When he wakes, he says: My God, the soul which You placed within me is pure. You created it within me, You breathed it into me, You guard it within me, and You will one day take it from me and restore it to me in the time to come.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה", דְּשָׁם אֵין שַׁיָּיךְ קִלְקוּל, כִּי הוּא חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ב׳:א׳
connections.quote: “The second soul in Israel is truly a portion of God above, as it is written, “He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life,” and, “You breathed it into me.” As it is written in the Zohar, one who breathes blows from within himself: that is, from his inwardness and interior, for in forceful breathing a person brings forth the inward and interior vitality within him.”
connections.context: Tanya reads the soul’s origin through the image of divine breathing. Rav Tzadok invokes the same origin when explaining the soul’s purity at its root.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵין נִיזֶזֶת כְּלָל, וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה רֵישׁ פְּתִיחָתָא): "הַלְוַאי אוֹתִי עָזָבוּ וְאֶת תּוֹרָתִי וְכוּלֵי", דְּאוֹתוֹ כִּבְיָכוֹל אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לַעֲזוֹב, כְּעִנְיַן "בְּחֵמָה שְׁפוּכָה אֶמְלוֹךְ עֲלֵיכֶם" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כ, לג).
connections.quote: see note 74 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Midrash supplies both the striking formulation “If only they had forsaken Me” and the explanation that Torah’s light brings a person back. Rav Tzadok develops this as the revelation of an underlying love that has not been severed.

connections.hePhrase: וְחוּרְבָּן רִאשׁוֹן הָיָה עַל "עָזְבָם אֶת תּוֹרָתִי" (יִרְמְיָה ט, יב); אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה, הַמָּאוֹר שֶׁבָּהּ וְכוּלֵי מֵבִיא לְאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַנֶּעְלֶמֶת שֶׁתָּבוֹא לִידֵי גִּלּוּי.
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said: Because they abandoned My Torah, which I placed before them, did not listen to My voice, and did not walk in it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְחוּרְבָּן רִאשׁוֹן הָיָה עַל "עָזְבָם אֶת תּוֹרָתִי" (יִרְמְיָה ט, יב); אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה, הַמָּאוֹר שֶׁבָּהּ וְכוּלֵי מֵבִיא לְאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַנֶּעְלֶמֶת שֶׁתָּבוֹא לִידֵי גִּלּוּי.
connections.displayRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.linkedRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.canonicalRef: Derekh Hashem, Part Four, On Torah Study 6
connections.heRef: דרך ה', חלק רביעי, בתלמוד תורה ו׳
connections.quote: see note 925 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Ramḥal explains the gradual action of Torah’s light even where the ordinary conditions for drawing its spiritual influence are lacking. The closing restrictions on mockery and distorted interpretation are essential to that explanation.

connections.hePhrase: וְחוּרְבָּן שֵׁנִי הָיָה עַל יְדֵי שִׂנְאַת חִנָּם (יוֹמָא ט:), דְּהַיְינוּ הֶעְדֵּר אַהֲבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: ‘But why was the Second Temple destroyed, when they were occupied with Torah, mitzvot, and acts of kindness? Because there was groundless hatred in it. This teaches you that groundless hatred weighs as much as three transgressions: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה יד): דַּרְכָּן שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם לוֹמַר: אַהֲבַת תּוֹרָה קוֹדֶמֶת וְכוּלֵי, וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר: אַהֲבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל קוֹדֶמֶת.
connections.quote: “He said to me: There are two things in the world that I love in my heart with complete love: Torah and Israel. But I do not know which precedes the other. I said to him: My son, people commonly say that Torah preceded, as it says, “The Lord acquired me at the beginning of His way.” But I say that Israel preceded, as it says, “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first of His produce.””
connections.context: The speaker asks about Torah and Israel, both of which he loves. The answer gives Israel precedence. Rav Tzadok applies that order to the relation between love of Torah and love of Israel; the source does not contain the invented concluding explanation formerly added to the quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מַכּוֹת כב:): כַּמָּה טִפְּשָׁאֵי אִינָשֵׁי דְּקָיְימֵי מִקַּמֵּי סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה וְלֹא מִקַּמֵּי גַּבְרָא רַבָּא,
connections.quote: ‘Gemara: What is the reason? If it were written ‘forty in number,’ I would say: A count of forty. Now that it is written ‘by the number, forty,’ it means a number that leads up to forty [thirty-nine]. Rava said: How foolish are other people, who stand before a Torah scroll but do not stand before a great man! For in a Torah scroll ‘forty’ is written, yet the Rabbis came and reduced it by one.’

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "רֵאשִׁית תְּבוּאָתֹה" (יִרְמְיָה ב, ג) – הַיְינוּ הַפְּרִי וְהַתְּבוּאָה שֶׁרָצָה לְהַכְנִיס בִּזְרִיעַת הָעוֹלָם הֵם נַפְשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהֵם כּוֹלְלִים כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ,
connections.quote: ‘Israel is holy to Hashem, the first of His harvest. All who devour him will incur guilt; calamity will come upon them, declares Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁאֶצְלָם הוּא סָתוּם וְהַתּוֹרָה הוּא פֵּירוּשׁ עַל זֶה.
connections.quote: see note 1145 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Section 90 gives the fuller relationship between Torah, the souls of a generation, and the world they inhabit. It explains why the Torah can function here as an exposition of what is hidden within the souls. The six hundred thousand letters express a spiritual correspondence between Torah and souls.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא הַתּוֹרָה, לְפָרֵשׁ וּלְהָבִין הַמַּעֲמַקִּים הַגְּנוּזִים בְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ פְּרָטִי מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל:
connections.quote: “The wisdom of all the sages of Israel is a portion of His wisdom, blessed be He, as the blessing over the sages of Israel says: “Who has apportioned of His wisdom to those who fear Him.” These are the sages of Israel, in whom wisdom is revealed. Every other individual of Israel has some secret of His wisdom hidden at the root of his soul, of which he himself is unaware; this is the root of his vitality, as it is written, “Wisdom gives life to its possessors.” Through this, each person has an elevation above all Israel on account of the divine portion above at the root of his soul, containing a mystery and a secret concealed from all Israel.”
connections.context: The contrast is between wisdom already revealed in scholars and wisdom still concealed in every other soul. This directly explains the final statement about Torah disclosing the depths hidden within each individual.

connections.hePhrase: [קצז] שָׁלֹשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת בְּאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ" (דְּבָרִים ו, ה) – הַיְינוּ כָּל הַתְּשׁוּקוֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת שֶׁבַּלֵּב,
connections.quote: ‘You shall love Hashem your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נד.): בִּשְׁנֵי יְצָרֶיךָ, פֵּירוּשׁ: בֵּין בְּצָרְכֵי הַגּוּף בֵּין לְעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַבָּא, הַכֹּל לֹא יִהְיֶה לְאַהֲבַת עַצְמוֹ רַק לְאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “It is known that the correction of the character traits is to raise them to their source. Then the correction of the severity of the husk is through holy severity, being zealous against those who transgress His will; and the correction of the husk’s desire is through holy desire, longing for God. Victory, however, comes through the opposite; this transformation is for someone who has already won. Tanya, chapter 27, likewise says that this is only for a completely righteous person, whose alien thoughts come to him from others; see there. One engaged in battle opposes his adversary: if the adversary sets fire against him, he applies water and extinguishes it. But one who has already won and taken possession repairs everything the enemy prepared against him for battle, so that it serves the same function for his own use. Thus it was said: those bedclothes she prepared for him in prohibition she prepared for him in permission and for the sake of a commandment. And this is “with all your heart”—with both your inclinations: with the good inclination in subjugation and battle, and with the evil inclination after defeating it, when one uses its powers for good.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes resisting an inclination while the struggle continues from redirecting its powers after victory. This qualification governs his reading of “with both your inclinations.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן "נַפְשִׁי יָצְאָה בְדַבְּרוֹ" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ה, ו) מִפְּנֵי גּוֹדֶל קִשּׁוּר הַתְּשׁוּקָה הַמַּגִּיעַ עַד כְּלוֹת הַנֶּפֶשׁ מַמָּשׁ.
connections.quote: “I opened for my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul went out when he spoke. I sought him but did not find him; I called him but he did not answer me.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reads “my soul went out” as the intensity of longing reaching the point of the soul’s departure. A translation merely describing faintness would hide the wording on which his explanation rests.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּקְרָא ה) עַל פָּסוּק "וְנֶפֶשׁ כִּי תַקְרִיב" (וַיִּקְרָא ב, א): דְּעָנִי – נַפְשׁוֹ הוּא מַקְרִיב, שֶׁנַּפְשׁוֹ מְקֻשֶּׁרֶת בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר מוּעָט.
connections.quote: ““When a soul offers”: The word soul is not used of the other offerings, but of the poor person’s meal offering. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I account it to him as though he offered his own soul.”
connections.context: The Midrash explains the Torah’s choice of “soul” for the modest meal offering. Rav Tzadok develops the poor person’s attachment to that small possession as the reason it represents his life.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּקְרָא ה) עַל פָּסוּק "וְנֶפֶשׁ כִּי תַקְרִיב" (וַיִּקְרָא ב, א): דְּעָנִי – נַפְשׁוֹ הוּא מַקְרִיב, שֶׁנַּפְשׁוֹ מְקֻשֶּׁרֶת בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר מוּעָט.
connections.quote: “When a soul offers a meal offering to the Lord, his offering shall be fine flour; he shall pour oil upon it and put frankincense upon it.”
connections.context: “Soul” ordinarily means a person here. The Midrash quoted in the neighboring note gives that unusual designation its fuller force: the poor person who brings the offering is regarded as offering his own soul.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן נִקְרָא תְּפִלַּת הֶעָנִי "נֶפֶשׁ", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּחַנָּה: "וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי ה'" (שְׁמוּאֵל א א, טו), שֶׁתְּשׁוּקָתָהּ לְבֵן הָיָה כָּל נַפְשָׁהּ קְשׁוּרָה בִּתְשׁוּקָה זוֹ.
connections.quote: “Hannah answered: No, my lord. I am a woman of troubled spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink; I have poured out my soul before the Lord.”
connections.context: Hannah is answering Eli’s suspicion that she is drunk. “Poured out my soul” supplies Rav Tzadok’s language for prayer in which the person’s whole life is bound to the request.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן נִקְרָא תְּפִלַּת הֶעָנִי "נֶפֶשׁ", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּחַנָּה: "וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי ה'" (שְׁמוּאֵל א א, טו), שֶׁתְּשׁוּקָתָהּ לְבֵן הָיָה כָּל נַפְשָׁהּ קְשׁוּרָה בִּתְשׁוּקָה זוֹ.
connections.quote: “For this there is the eating of the bread of affliction, in the sense of “A prayer of the poor when he is overwhelmed,” which envelops all prayers and breaks through the heavens. Because of the magnitude of his want, the poor person pours out his plea with an outpouring of his soul, like Hannah’s pouring out her soul. He cannot contain it in his heart until he speaks with his mouth and cries aloud.”
connections.context: Et HaOchel describes prayer arising from a need felt with one’s whole life. It connects the poor person’s prayer directly to Hannah, as Rav Tzadok does here.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ תְּפִלִּין, שֶׁפֵּירוּשׁ דְּבֵקוּת, וְנִקְרָא חַיּוּתוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כד.) עַל פָּסוּק "וְהָיוּ חַיֶּיךָ תְּלֻאִים לְךָ מִנֶּגֶד" (דְּבָרִים כח, סו);
connections.quote: “This is what is written: “All the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall fear you.” Rabbi Eliezer said: these are the tefillin on the head. The explanation is that tefillin show that Israel is set apart for the unique Name, since the tefillin mention the exodus from Egypt, when He brought them out through miracles; the unique Name specifically performs wonders. Therefore “they shall fear you,” because of His mighty and awesome deeds. Rabbi Eliezer specified the tefillin on the head because the tefillin on the arm express Israel’s attachment to the Holy One, blessed be He; therefore it says of them, “You shall bind them.” This is the difference between the tefillin of the hand and the head. Those of the hand express the connection and attachment Israel has to the Holy One, blessed be He. From this aspect there is no fear, but connection and attachment to Him, for where there is connection there is no fear. With those of the head, however, there is no binding of that kind; rather, His name is called upon them. In having His name called upon them He is distinct from them, being called “the God of Israel.” As their God He is distinct from them, and from this aspect there is fear, for it is fitting to fear the God of Israel, to whom might belongs. Understand this.”
connections.context: Maharal distinguishes the attachment symbolized by the arm-tefillin from the awe associated with the divine name on the head-tefillin. His explanation gives a precise source for the link between tefillin and attachment.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ תְּפִלִּין, שֶׁפֵּירוּשׁ דְּבֵקוּת, וְנִקְרָא חַיּוּתוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כד.) עַל פָּסוּק "וְהָיוּ חַיֶּיךָ תְּלֻאִים לְךָ מִנֶּגֶד" (דְּבָרִים כח, סו);
connections.quote: ‘Those who expound difficult passages said: ‘Your life shall hang before you’—this is one who hangs up his tefillin.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ תְּפִלִּין, שֶׁפֵּירוּשׁ דְּבֵקוּת, וְנִקְרָא חַיּוּתוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כד.) עַל פָּסוּק "וְהָיוּ חַיֶּיךָ תְּלֻאִים לְךָ מִנֶּגֶד" (דְּבָרִים כח, סו);
connections.quote: see note 2207 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The verse describes insecurity in the passage of rebuke. Berakhot 24a applies its phrase “your life shall hang” to hanging up tefillin; Rav Tzadok draws attention to the identification of tefillin with a person’s life.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בְּפָרָשַׁת "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ" (דְּבָרִים יא, יג) שֶׁאָמַר "וּלְעָבְדוֹ", נִזְכַּר רַק שְׁנֵי אֵלֶּה,
connections.quote: ‘And it shall be, if you listen attentively to My commandments that I command you today, to love Hashem your God and to serve Him with all your heart and all your soul…’

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ כִּי הָרְכוּשׁ שַׁיָּיךְ לָאָדָם, וְכָל כָּךְ יִהְיֶה הָאָדָם כֻּלּוֹ מְמוּלָּא מֵאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּכָל מַעֲמַקָּיו, עַד שֶׁמִּמֵּילָא גַּם בְּכָל קִנְיָנָיו שֶׁהֵם הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁלּוֹ, יִהְיוּ גַּם כֵּן מְמוּלָּאִים מֵאַהֲבָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “Possessions belong to a person: even after they are lost they must be returned when he has an identifying mark or recognition, indicating a relation, recognition and testimony that they are his. Everything exists through the word of Hashem that gives it life, and a person's life must have a relation to that life. There are four levels in the lower world—inanimate, growing, living and speaking—and the fifth is the higher beings. Correspondingly there are four elements—fire, air, water and earth—with heaven as the fifth substance; and four soul levels—nefesh, ruach, neshamah and the soul of the soul, chayah—with yechidah as the fifth. The human being includes the inanimate, growing, living and speaking levels, and the inanimate power corresponds to nefesh. Certainly there is a difference between the inanimate power in an inanimate object and that power within a person; nevertheless they have a connection and relation.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains the premise behind holiness extending into possessions: the divine word sustains both the person and the object, and the powers within the person correspond to levels of created life. It explicitly preserves the difference between them. This helps the reader understand the present siman's extension of love into possessions without mistaking that relation for an assertion that every object is already a human soul or that every owner has reached this exceptional degree of holiness.
connections.headline: Related life does not erase the difference between person and object

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ כִּי הָרְכוּשׁ שַׁיָּיךְ לָאָדָם, וְכָל כָּךְ יִהְיֶה הָאָדָם כֻּלּוֹ מְמוּלָּא מֵאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּכָל מַעֲמַקָּיו, עַד שֶׁמִּמֵּילָא גַּם בְּכָל קִנְיָנָיו שֶׁהֵם הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁלּוֹ, יִהְיוּ גַּם כֵּן מְמוּלָּאִים מֵאַהֲבָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 18:3
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 18:3
connections.quote: “Even when a person is born, all the possessions and expansions are already included in him. But because his life is then constricted in the smallness of the point, the possessions stand at a distance. After the person grows, Hashem gives desire and yearning within that point to draw in, gather and bring close all the possessions belonging to the point and included in it. Then the person and all his possessions are joined together, and he is called ‘a new creature.’”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov describes possessions as included in the person's original point of life and later gathered into its expansion. This explains why the siman distinguishes a desire for property from holiness reaching the property itself. Its final degree of love still remains, as the siman expressly says, a gift requiring help from Heaven.
connections.headline: Possessions as an expansion of the person's point

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן חֲמוֹרוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי פִּינְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר דִּמְחַמְּרָא אַנַּפְשַׁהּ לֶאֱכוֹל אִיסּוּר (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ס).
connections.quote: “They gave [Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair’s donkey] barley, but she would not taste it. They told him: Rabbi, we gave her barley and she did not taste it. He said to them: Did you prepare it properly? They said: Yes. Did you separate demai?”
connections.context: The donkey refuses the food despite hunger, prompting the question whether its tithes were separated. Rav Tzadok treats the animal’s refusal as an example of holiness extending to a righteous person’s possessions.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן חֲמוֹרוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי פִּינְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר דִּמְחַמְּרָא אַנַּפְשַׁהּ לֶאֱכוֹל אִיסּוּר (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ס).
connections.quote: “They said: Did you not teach us, Rabbi, that one who buys seed for an animal, flour for hides, oil for a lamp, or oil for coating utensils is exempt from demai? He said to them: What can we do for her? She is stringent with herself.”
connections.context: This completes the episode: the donkey’s refusal goes beyond what the stated rule required for animal feed. It explains Rav Tzadok’s precise phrase “she is stringent with herself.” The passage is 60:8, rather than the unrelated opening of chapter 60.

connections.hePhrase: וְזוֹ בְּבַעֲלֵי חַיִּים, וּמִסְּתָמָא הוּא הַדִּין בְּדוֹמְמִים, כְּעִנְיַן "אֶבֶן מִקִּיר תִּזְעָק" (חֲבַקּוּק ב, יא) לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא כְּשֶׁיִּרְצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת אִיסּוּר, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים מִזְמוֹר עג).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Shimon the Pious: In this world a person goes to gather figs on Shabbat, and the fig tree says nothing. In the future, if a person goes to pick a fig on Shabbat, it cries out and says: Today is Shabbat.”
connections.context: The Midrash imagines created things themselves preventing a transgression. This is part of Midrash Tehillim on Psalm 73.

connections.hePhrase: וְזוֹ בְּבַעֲלֵי חַיִּים, וּמִסְּתָמָא הוּא הַדִּין בְּדוֹמְמִים, כְּעִנְיַן "אֶבֶן מִקִּיר תִּזְעָק" (חֲבַקּוּק ב, יא) לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא כְּשֶׁיִּרְצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת אִיסּוּר, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים מִזְמוֹר עג).
connections.quote: ‘For a stone will cry out from the wall, and a wooden beam will answer it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזוֹ בְּבַעֲלֵי חַיִּים, וּמִסְּתָמָא הוּא הַדִּין בְּדוֹמְמִים, כְּעִנְיַן "אֶבֶן מִקִּיר תִּזְעָק" (חֲבַקּוּק ב, יא) לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא כְּשֶׁיִּרְצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת אִיסּוּר, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים מִזְמוֹר עג).
connections.quote: “In this world a person goes to have relations with his wife while she is a niddah, and no one stops him. In the future, if he wishes to do it, the stone cries out from its place and says: She is a niddah, as it says, “For a stone shall cry out from the wall.””
connections.context: This is the continuation of the fig-tree example and the exact source for the stone in Rav Tzadok’s words. It extends the image from plants to inanimate objects.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן שְׁבִיתַת כֵּלָיו בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁאָז כֻּלּוֹ לַה' גַּם כָּל קִנְיָנָיו.
connections.quote: “Now that Rav Oshaya said in Rav Asi’s name: Who is the tanna who holds that the Sabbath rest of utensils is required by Torah law? It is Beit Shammai, and not Beit Hillel. According to Beit Shammai, whether the utensil performs an action or performs no action, it is forbidden. According to Beit Hillel, even if it performs an action, it is permitted.”
connections.context: The discussion concerns work set in motion before Shabbat. The legal doctrine of utensil-rest is identified here as Beit Shammai’s position. Rav Tzadok uses its spiritual meaning in describing the extension of Sabbath holiness into possessions; the source must not be read as an undisputed practical prohibition.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן צֹאן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה עג) שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא עֲדָרִים, דְּמִן הַשְׁתָּוַת הַמִּסְפָּר מְבוֹאָר דְּהֵן עַצְמָן שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: see note 893 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Midrash counts guarding dogs and specifies the number per flock. Six hundred thousand flocks follows from that calculation; it is not the wording of the separate count given earlier by Rabbi Abba bar Kahana. The passage is 73:11.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן צֹאן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה עג) שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא עֲדָרִים, דְּמִן הַשְׁתָּוַת הַמִּסְפָּר מְבוֹאָר דְּהֵן עַצְמָן שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: “This is the secret of what is stated in Bereshit Rabbah, section 73, that Jacob had six hundred thousand flocks of sheep. His soul comprised the six hundred thousand souls of Israel, each comprising its particular generations. Portions of the light of his soul then spread into the sheep, a pure animal, for at that time he was still called Jacob, the level of an unlearned person, as stated at the end of the chapter “Elu Metziot.” Israel is also compared to sheep. They were his possession, from which he earned his livelihood, for a person’s principal vitality is hidden in that which sustains him: livelihood is the principal support of his life. This is why it was said, “Do not throw a clod into the well from which you drank”—one must not treat it contemptuously. This is not the place to elaborate.”
connections.context: This earlier section explains the correspondence between Jacob’s flocks and Israel’s souls, and why a person’s means of livelihood bears a particular connection to his vitality.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קסב סוֹף עַמּוּד א) דְּכַוָּנַת יַעֲקֹב בַּמַּקְלוֹת הוּא עִנְיַן הַתְּפִלִּין, דְּהַיְינוּ הִתְקַשְּׁרוּת וּדְבֵיקוּת מְצוּי נַפְשׁוֹ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
connections.quote: “When their desire turns toward the supernal radiance above, the middle column, Jacob the complete one, takes those rods—the tefillin of the head—into the channels, the place and location where the tefillin dwell. From here all the supernal forces and camps receive light and radiance, those bound above and those bound below. Once they receive from the channels, the watering troughs, they become sources and springs to descend below and give to all.”
connections.context: The rods are expressly identified with head-tefillin. Rav Tzadok draws from this identification the attachment and devotion to Hashem achieved through Jacob’s intention; the general discussion of union elsewhere in the passage is insufficient without this sentence.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב הוּא נֶגֶד "בְּכָל מְאֹדְךָ": לְקַשֵּׁר כָּל כָּךְ כָּל מְצוּי וְנַפְשׁוֹ עַד שֶׁגַּם הַקִּנְיָנִים הַשַּׁיָּיכִים לוֹ כֻּלָּן יִהְיוּ בִּכְלַל הַהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת זֶה;
connections.quote: “Likewise, “with all your might” is our father Jacob, of whom they said that he remained behind for small vessels, because his money was dearer to him than his body. In him there was the generosity of “all your might,” and in him this trait was clarified—not in someone who is naturally lavish and to whom money has no importance at all. Nevertheless, they said, “I praise the lazy,” for it is certainly still good, and such a person is called “idle and rewarded”; but he is not on the level of “with all.” “All” denotes that to which one’s soul is naturally bound, and which one subordinates to the love and service of the blessed God.”
connections.context: The later section explains why Jacob’s valuing his possessions matters: devotion is tested in precisely what a person naturally holds dear. It retains the qualification that an easier good action is still good and rewarded.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אִי אֶפְשָׁר מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ לָרַבִּים, אֶלָּא לֶעָתִיד כְּשֶׁיִּשְׁפּוֹךְ רוּחוֹ עַל כָּל בָּשָׂר,
connections.quote: ‘Afterward, I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh. Your sons and daughters will prophesy; your elders will dream dreams; your young men will see visions.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁלֹּא שָׁלְטוּ שׂוֹנְאִים בְּמַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו, כִּי קִנְיָנָיו וּפְעֻלּוֹתָיו הַשַּׁיָּיכִים לוֹ, אֲפִילּוּ בְּדוֹמְמִים, קְבוּעָה בָּהֶם קְדוּשָּׁה דִּקְבִיעָא וְקַיָּימָא שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִינָּתֵק כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “Rav Ḥinena bar Pappa expounded: What is the meaning of “Sing joyfully, righteous ones, in the Lord; praise is fitting for the upright”? Read not “praise is fitting,” but “a dwelling of praise.” This refers to Moses and David, whose enemies did not gain control of their handiwork. Of David it is written, “Her gates have sunk into the earth.” Of Moses, the Master said: When the First Temple was built, the Tent of Meeting was hidden away—its boards, clasps, bars, pillars, and sockets. Where? Rav Ḥisda said in Avimi’s name: in the subterranean passages of the Sanctuary.”
connections.context: The Gemara supplies the concrete example behind the claim: Moses’ Tabernacle and its components were hidden rather than captured. Rav Tzadok reads their preservation as holiness enduring in a person’s work.

connections.hePhrase: וְרַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (צח:): אֵיתִיב בְּטוּלָּא דְּכוֹפִיתָא דַּחֲמָרֵיהּ.
connections.quote: “Ulla said: “Let him come, but may I not see him.” Rabba likewise said: “Let him come, but may I not see him.” Rav Yosef said: “Let him come, and may I merit to sit in the shadow of his donkey’s dung.””
connections.context: Rav Yosef accepts even the humiliation associated with the Messiah’s arrival. The Talmud attributes this particular statement to Rav Yosef; Rabbi Yochanan is mentioned separately in the surrounding discussion. Rav Tzadok uses the donkey image in his account of the material realm’s attachment to holiness.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ בְּכוֹרוֹת (ב.) דְּמוֹצִיא מִקְּדֻשָּׁתוֹ כְּשֶׁמּוֹכֵר הַחֲמוֹר לְעוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת לְחַד פֵּירוּשׁ בְּזוּלַת הַמְּלָאכָה דְּשַׁבָּת.
connections.quote: “The cases are necessary. Had the Mishnah taught only a purchaser, I might have said that this is because he brings it into sanctity. But a seller, who removes it from sanctity, perhaps should be penalized. Therefore it teaches otherwise.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ בְּכוֹרוֹת (ב.) דְּמוֹצִיא מִקְּדֻשָּׁתוֹ כְּשֶׁמּוֹכֵר הַחֲמוֹר לְעוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת לְחַד פֵּירוּשׁ בְּזוּלַת הַמְּלָאכָה דְּשַׁבָּת.
connections.quote: ““He brings it into sanctity”: Rashi explains that it will rest on Shabbat. Likewise, “he removes it from sanctity” means that the gentile will work it on Shabbat. But the expression “sanctity” does not suggest this; rather, it means the sanctity of the firstborn, like the case of Rav Mari bar Rachel, whose animals perished because he removed them from sanctity by transferring their ears to a gentile.”
connections.context: The opening passage is Bekhorot 2a. Tosafot explicitly contrasts Rashi’s Shabbat explanation with the firstborn’s sanctity, which explains Rav Tzadok’s qualification “according to one interpretation, apart from labor on Shabbat.” The related Rav Mari episode appears on 3b; it is an illustration cited by Tosafot, rather than the opening discussion itself.

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, כא עַמּוּד א) דְּהַר סִינַי דָּלֵיג לְמֹשֶׁה כְּמַחַט לְאֶבֶן הַשּׁוֹאֶבֶת:
connections.quote: ““He came to the mountain of God, to Horeb”—he alone, without the flock. Rabbi Yosei said: This stone that attracts iron—when [the needle] sees it, it leaps toward it. So it was with Moses and Mount Sinai: when they saw one another, it leaped toward him. Thus it is written, “He came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.” Rabbi Abba said: They had been prepared for one another from the six days of creation. On that day the mountain stirred toward Moses; when it saw him enter it and leap upon it, the mountain stood still. This teaches that they rejoiced in one another.”
connections.context: The magnet and needle are the actual comparison in the source, followed by the mountain’s movement toward Moses. Rav Tzadok uses that attraction as an image of the affinity between holiness and the material thing prepared to receive it.

connections.hePhrase: [קצח] מִי שֶׁאוֹהֵב אֶת הַתּוֹרָה, הַתּוֹרָה אוֹהַבְתּוֹ גַּם כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפָרָשַׁת "הֲלֹא חָכְמָה תִקְרָא" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, א): "אֲנִי אֹהֲבַי אֵהָב וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, יז),
connections.quote: “Does not wisdom call, and understanding raise her voice?”

connections.hePhrase: [קצח] מִי שֶׁאוֹהֵב אֶת הַתּוֹרָה, הַתּוֹרָה אוֹהַבְתּוֹ גַּם כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפָרָשַׁת "הֲלֹא חָכְמָה תִקְרָא" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, א): "אֲנִי אֹהֲבַי אֵהָב וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, יז),
connections.quote: “I love those who love me, and those who seek me shall find me.”
connections.context: Wisdom speaks as a person throughout this chapter. Verse 17 supplies the reciprocal love on which Rav Tzadok bases his opening statement about the Torah loving those who love it.

connections.hePhrase: וּמְגַלַּת לוֹ כָּל סְתָרֶיהָ וְרָזֵי הַתּוֹרָה כְּמוֹ הֶחָשׁוּק לַחֲשׁוּקוֹ.
connections.quote: ““His Torah labors for him”—it goes about on his behalf and asks its Maker to entrust him with the reasons and ordered principles of Torah. Why all this? Because he pressed and bent his mouth to the words of Torah.”
connections.context: The Gemara says that while a person labors in one place, his Torah labors for him elsewhere. Rashi explains that reciprocity as Torah’s petition that its student receive its reasons and principles.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הָאוֹהֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל, הֵן אוֹהֲבִין אוֹתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאַהֲרֹן בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק א, יב): "אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת", וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיִּבְכּוּ אֹתוֹ... כֹּל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ, כט) כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק יב, הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כַּמַּיִם הַפָּנִים לַפָּנִים כֵּן לֵב הָאָדָם לָאָדָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יט),
connections.quote: ‘Hillel and Shammai received the tradition from them. Hillel says: Be among the disciples of Aaron: love peace and pursue peace, love other people and bring them close to Torah.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הָאוֹהֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל, הֵן אוֹהֲבִין אוֹתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאַהֲרֹן בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק א, יב): "אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת", וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיִּבְכּוּ אֹתוֹ... כֹּל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ, כט) כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק יב, הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כַּמַּיִם הַפָּנִים לַפָּנִים כֵּן לֵב הָאָדָם לָאָדָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יט),
connections.quote: ‘The entire congregation saw that Aaron had died, and the whole house of Israel wept for Aaron for thirty days.’
