connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הָאוֹהֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל, הֵן אוֹהֲבִין אוֹתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאַהֲרֹן בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק א, יב): "אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת", וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיִּבְכּוּ אֹתוֹ... כֹּל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ, כט) כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק יב, הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כַּמַּיִם הַפָּנִים לַפָּנִים כֵּן לֵב הָאָדָם לָאָדָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, יט),
connections.quote: “LOVING PEACE. What does this mean? It teaches that a man should love [to foster] peace in Israel between man and man, just as Aaron loved [to foster] peace in Israel between man and man, as it is stated, The law of truth was in his mouth, and unrighteousness was not found in his lips; he walked with Me in peace and uprightness, and did turn many away from iniquity. R. Meir said: What is meant by and did turn many away from iniquity? Whenever Aaron walked along the road and met a wicked man, he would offer him greetings. On the following day when that man was about to commit a transgression, he would say, ‘Woe is me! How can I raise my eyes after doing that and look Aaron in the face? I should be ashamed before him, since he greeted me’. Consequently that man withholds himself from transgression. Similarly, when two men had quarrelled one with the other, Aaron would go and sit with one of them and say, ‘My son, see what your companion is doing! He beats his breast and tears his clothes, exclaiming, “Woe is me! how can I raise my eyes and look my companion in the face? I am ashamed before him since it is I who offended him” ’. Aaron would sit with him until he had removed all enmity from his heart. Then Aaron would go and sit with the other and say likewise, ‘My son, see what your companion is doing! He beats his breast and tears his clothes, exclaiming, “Woe is me! how can I raise my eyes and look my companion in the face? I am ashamed before him since it was I who offended him” ’. Aaron would sit with him until he had removed all enmity from his heart. Later when the two met, they embraced and kissed each other. Therefore it is stated, They wept for Aaron thirty days, even all the house of Israel.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם: "וְנָשָׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת כח, כט), כִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ כֹּחַ חַיּוּת נַפְשׁוֹ בִּמְקוֹרָהּ וּמְקוֹם אֲצִילוּתָהּ לְמַעְלָה מַּעְלָה.
connections.quote: ‘Aaron shall carry the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart when he enters the sanctuary, as a remembrance before Hashem always.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּלִּין לוֹ כָּל חֲלָלֵי עָלְמָא שֶׁהָיוּ שׁוֹאֲלִין בְּאוּרִים וְתֻמִּים, וְהָאוֹתִיּוֹת בּוֹלְטִין,
connections.quote: ““Protrude”—the letters protrude; for example, the ayin from Shimon, the lamed from Levi, and the heh from Yehuda, to say “Go up.” Each letter does not move from its place; rather, it protrudes in its place, and he combines them.”
connections.context: Rashi explains Rabbi Yoḥanan’s account of the Urim and Tummim. The letters become prominent in their own locations, and the priest combines them; Rav Tzadok develops that prominence as something recognized within the loving heart.

connections.hePhrase: [הַכְּלוּלִין בִּמְקוֹרָן שְׁמוֹת הָאָבוֹת וּשְׁבָטִים הַחֲקוּקִים בְּצֵירוּף תֵּיבוֹת "שִׁבְטֵי יְשֻׁרוּן" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יוֹמָא עג:),
connections.quote: ‘But the letter tzadi is not written on them! Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak said: ‘Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov’ is written there. But the letter tet is not written! Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: ‘Shivtei Yeshurun’—‘the tribes of Yeshurun’—is written there.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעִיקַּר הַהַמְשָׁכָה עַל יְדֵי אוֹת הַטֵּי"ת כְּטַעַם "אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב" שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא בְּכֻלָּן;
connections.quote: “Say of the righteous that it shall be well with him (ki tov), for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעִיקַּר הַהַמְשָׁכָה עַל יְדֵי אוֹת הַטֵּי"ת כְּטַעַם "אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב" שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא בְּכֻלָּן;
connections.quote: “It is in the month of Shevat, which was formed with the letter tzadi, as stated in Sefer Yetzirah [and tet frequently interchanges with tzadi in Aramaic, as stated in the glosses to the Arukh. This accords with “Say of the righteous that he is good,” for one who damages the covenant is called evil, as stated in the Zohar].”
connections.context: In its discussion of repairing the covenant, section 174 explicitly links tet with tzadi and with “the righteous is good.” This is the author’s own parallel for the letter symbolism used here.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא לִמּוּד דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל, אֲבָל בִּפְרָט בְּעִתּוֹ בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן וְנֶפֶשׁ וּמָקוֹם – זֶהוּ בִּבְנֵי יִשָּׂשכָר "יוֹדְעֵי בִינָה לַעִתִּים" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א יב, לג),
connections.quote: ‘Of the descendants of Issachar, who understood the times and knew what Israel should do: their heads numbered two hundred, and all their brothers followed their direction.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא לִמּוּד דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל, אֲבָל בִּפְרָט בְּעִתּוֹ בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן וְנֶפֶשׁ וּמָקוֹם – זֶהוּ בִּבְנֵי יִשָּׂשכָר "יוֹדְעֵי בִינָה לַעִתִּים" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א יב, לג),
connections.quote: “In this the children of Issachar were praised: “Those who understood the times, to know what Israel should do.” They know at each time what is suitable for that time and the remedy beneficial to the dispositions of that generation; therefore they are fit to instruct Israel what to do. The tribe of Levi is likewise suited and chosen to know the action appropriate to each particular soul and generation. This comes through complete attachment to the blessed God, as stated in Sanhedrin: “The Lord was with him”—the law followed him everywhere. Reaching the practical legal conclusion, as stated there in Yoma, comes through God’s being with him continually, as it is written, “I have set the Lord before me always.” His heart’s entire purpose is only to be an agent of the Merciful One in His service, drawn after no worldly concern. Of this it is said, “He guards the feet of His faithful ones.” A ḥasid is one separated from every kind of worldly craving, as the Sages explained in Berakhot: the term denotes separation from the three principal worldly desires—envy, appetite, and honor—as the discerning reader will see there. Therefore the holy Zohar says that a ḥasid is called an angel of the Lord, and Torah is to be sought from his mouth: he is guarded from stumbling in practice and directed toward the truth.”
connections.context: The parallel states both the need to discern the person and generation and the conditions of selfless attachment under which that discernment becomes trustworthy. It concerns practical Torah instruction, not private preference.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנִּמְשָׁךְ מִן הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב שֶׁשָּׁם הוּא הָרַחֲמָנוּת וְהָאַהֲבָה לַבְּרִיּוֹת.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ל״ב:ה׳-ז׳
connections.quote: “But regarding one who is not his companion and is not close to him, Hillel the Elder said: “Be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace … loving creatures and bringing them close to Torah.” That is, even those distant from God’s Torah and service, and therefore described simply as “creatures,” must be drawn with thick cords of love. With all this, perhaps one may bring them close to Torah and God’s service; if not, one has still not lost the reward of the commandment to love one’s fellows. Even those close to him whom he rebuked and who did not return from their sins, whom it is a commandment to hate, must also be loved. Both are true: hatred on account of the evil within them, and love on account of the hidden good within them—the divine spark within them that gives life to their divine soul. One must also awaken compassion in one’s heart for that soul, for it is in exile within the evil of the other side that overpowers it in the wicked. Compassion cancels hatred and awakens love, as is known from “Jacob, who redeemed Abraham.” [King David’s statement “I hate them with utmost hatred” referred only to the sectarians and heretics who have no portion in the God of Israel, as stated at the beginning of chapter 16 of Shabbat.]”
connections.context: Tanya explicitly connects compassion with awakened love, distinguishing the soul’s hidden good from wrongdoing and explaining the scope of its cited rebuke and hatred passages. The complete qualifications belong with the statement about compassion.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִכְלָל הַכֹּהֲנִים וְהַלְוִיִּם הֵם הַשּׁוֹפְטִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּבָאתָ אֶל הַכֹּהֲנִים הַלְוִיִּם וְאֶל הַשֹּׁפֵט" (דְּבָרִים יז, ט) וּבְכָל מָקוֹם.
connections.quote: “You shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who shall be in those days; you shall inquire, and they shall tell you the matter of judgment.”
connections.context: The verse names the priestly authorities alongside the judge. Rav Tzadok cites that association in explaining the relation between the Levitical service and the authority to give practical rulings.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (כו.): צוּרְבָא מֵרַבָּנָן דְּמוֹרֵי – מִלֵּוִי אוֹ מִיִּשָּׂשכָר;
connections.quote: “Rava said: You will not find a Torah scholar who issues rulings unless he comes from the tribe of Levi or the tribe of Issachar. Levi, as it is written: ‘They shall teach Your judgments to Jacob.’ Issachar, as it is written: ‘The children of Issachar, who understood the times, to know what Israel should do.’ But say that Judah is included too, as it is written: ‘Judah is My lawgiver’! I am speaking of bringing a discussion to its conclusion in accordance with the halakhah.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה עב): "רָאשֵׁיהֶם מָאתַיִם" – רָאשֵׁי סַנְהֶדְרָאוֹת;
connections.quote: ““Leah went out to meet him” – it teaches that she did not allow him to wash his feet. “And said: You will consort with me” – Rabbi Abahu said: The Holy One blessed be He saw that her intention was exclusively for the sake of Heaven, to produce tribes. That is why it was necessary for the verse to say: “God heeded Leah” (Genesis 30:17). “And said: You will consort with me” – Rabbi Levi said: Come and see how pleasing the mediation of mandrakes was before the One who spoke and the world came into being, as, by means of the mandrakes, two great tribes in Israel were produced – Issachar and Zebulun. Issachar sits and engages in Torah study, Zebulun sets out to the seas and comes and provides for Issachar’s mouth, and the Torah proliferates in Israel – “the mandrakes emitted fragrance” (Song of Songs 7:14). “Leah said: God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband. She called his name Issachar” (Genesis 30:18). “Leah said: God has given me my reward [sekhari]…She called his name Issachar.” Issachar was the ninth of the tribes, but he brought his offering second to the king. That is what is written: “On the second day, Netanel ben Tzuar, prince of Issachar, presented his offering” (Numbers 7:18). Why was that? It is because he was a Torah personality. That is what is written: “From the children of Issachar, possessors of understanding of the times” (I Chronicles 12:33). What is “of the times”? Rabbi Tanḥuma said: Of the propitious time for everything. Rabbi Tanḥuma said: Of intercalations. “Their leaders were two hundred, and all their brethren at their command” (I Chronicles 12:33) – Issachar would produce two hundred heads of the Sanhedrin, and all their brethren in accordance with them, and they all agreed to rule halakha in accordance with them, and he would answer them with halakha like a halakha transmitted to Moses at Sinai. From where did Issachar come to all this prominence? It was from Zebulun, who would engage in his commerce, and would feed Issachar, who was a Torah personality. That is what is written: “Zebulun will dwell at the shore of seas” (Genesis 49:13). When Moses came to bless the tribes, he had the blessing of Zebulun precede the blessing of Issachar: “Of Zebulun he said: Rejoice, Zebulun, in your departure, and, Issachar, in your tents” (Deuteronomy 33:18) – Rejoice, Zebulun, in your departure from the fact that Issachar is in your tents. Some say: There is reward [yesh sakhar] in the tents of Zebulun.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֵין מְמַנִּין בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין זָקֵן וְסָרִיס וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין לו:), דְּצָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן אַהֲבַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת כְּדֵי לֵידַע הַדָּבָר בְּעִתּוֹ,
connections.quote: ‘But there is another difference, for it was taught: An old man, a eunuch, or a man without children may not be seated on the Sanhedrin. Rabbi Yehudah adds: Nor may a cruel person. The opposite applies in the case of one who incites others to idolatry, for the Merciful One said: ‘Do not have compassion and do not cover for him.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה זָכָה יִשָּׂשכָר עַל יְדֵי דִּמְרַצְיָא אַרְצוֹיֵי כִּדְאִיתָא בְּעֵירוּבִין (ק:), שֶׁזֶּהוּ תֹּקֶף הָאַהֲבָה לַבְּרִיּוֹת, וּבְכֹחַ זֶה נוֹלָד.
connections.quote: “And Jacob came from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him and said: You must come in to me, for I have surely hired you with my son’s mandrakes. And he lay with her that night.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה זָכָה יִשָּׂשכָר עַל יְדֵי דִּמְרַצְיָא אַרְצוֹיֵי כִּדְאִיתָא בְּעֵירוּבִין (ק:), שֶׁזֶּהוּ תֹּקֶף הָאַהֲבָה לַבְּרִיּוֹת, וּבְכֹחַ זֶה נוֹלָד.
connections.quote: ‘What we were speaking of is a woman showing him signs of affection.’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יְהוּדָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (י:), כִּי אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קָבוּעַ בּוֹ
connections.quote: ‘Judah, who sanctified the name of Heaven in public, merited having the entire name of the Holy One, blessed be He, included in his name. When he admitted and said, ‘She is more righteous than I,’ a heavenly voice came forth and said: ‘You saved Tamar and her two sons from the fire. By your life, in your merit I will save three of your descendants from the fire.’ Who were they? Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.’

connections.hePhrase: [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי: כִּי מִי שֶׁשּׂוֹנֵא הַנִּבְחָר מִשֵּׁבֶט יְהוּדָה נִקְרָא "שׂוֹנֵא ה'", וְכֵן נִקְרְאוּ שׂוֹנְאֵי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם;
connections.quote: “Do I not hate those who hate You, Hashem? And do I not strive with those who rise up against You?”

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּשְׁאָר שְׁבָטִים, כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַעֲלָתוֹ: מִשֵּׁבֶט יוֹסֵף, הַשּׂוֹנְאוֹ נִקְרָא "שׂוֹנֵא צַדִּיק", וּמִגָּד – "שׂוֹנֵא תָּם", וּמִלֵּוִי – "שׂוֹנֵא יִשְׂרָאֵל", כָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי],
connections.quote: “Evil shall slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous shall be condemned.”

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּשְׁאָר שְׁבָטִים, כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַעֲלָתוֹ: מִשֵּׁבֶט יוֹסֵף, הַשּׂוֹנְאוֹ נִקְרָא "שׂוֹנֵא צַדִּיק", וּמִגָּד – "שׂוֹנֵא תָּם", וּמִלֵּוִי – "שׂוֹנֵא יִשְׂרָאֵל", כָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי],
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:12
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:12
connections.quote: “I also heard that the root of the name “Israel” is in the tribe of Levi. One who hates the chosen righteous person of Levi is called “one who hates Israel”; of Judah, “one who hates the Lord”; of Joseph, “one who hates the righteous”; and of Gad, “one who hates the blameless,” as it is written, “Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless.” Thus I heard; this is not the place to discuss it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok records the same received teaching in Likkutei Maamarim, preserving the distinct designation for each tribe. This is a direct authorial parallel to the report “thus I heard” here.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נִקְרְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל שְׁמוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה צח).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said: All your brothers shall be called by your name. A person does not say, “I am a Reubenite” or “I am a Simeonite,” but “I am a Jew.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains Jacob’s blessing to Judah. The name Yehudi derives from Judah and becomes the shared designation that Rav Tzadok uses here; the former quotation concerned Reuben instead.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (יג.): כָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא "יְהוּדִי",
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: He was indeed descended from Benjamin. Why, then, is he called a ‘Yehudi’? Because he rejected idolatry. Anyone who rejects idolatry is called a ‘Yehudi,’ as it is written: ‘There are Jewish men,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (יג.): כָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא "יְהוּדִי",
connections.quote: “The first banner, that of the camp of Judah, is the root of Oral Torah, as it says, “Judah is My lawgiver.” Although they said that he does not bring the discussion to its halakhic conclusion, the principal root of Oral Torah nevertheless comes from the tribe of Judah. His not bringing the discussion to its halakhic conclusion is because of its great depth, which others cannot fully fathom, as they said concerning Rabbi Meir. Nevertheless, an anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, and he is called Rabbi Meir because he illuminates the sages’ eyes in halakhah.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah compares Yehudah’s depth to Rabbi Meir: the inability to determine the final ruling from his discussion does not mean his Torah lacks illumination for the sages. This clarifies the distinction the present siman draws between an insight into divine decrees and the practical ‘way in which to walk.’ Both can be Torah, but they play different roles. Revealed depth does not dispense with the processes through which a ruling becomes authoritative in practice.
connections.headline: A teaching can illuminate halakhah without itself settling the ruling

connections.hePhrase: לָכֵן אָמְרוּ שָׁם בְּיוֹמָא דְּגַם בּוֹ נֶאֱמַר: "יְהוּדָה מְחֹקְקִי" (תְּהִלִּים ס, ט), רַק דְּלָא מַסִּיק וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is the stronghold of My head, Judah is My lawgiver.”
connections.context: The word mechokeki can be rendered scepter or lawgiver. The latter meaning makes visible the connection to legal teaching that Yoma 26a and Rav Tzadok draw from it.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ לְשׁוֹן "הֲלָכָה" הַיְינוּ מִלְּשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב "זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ לְכוּ בוֹ" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כא).
connections.quote: see note 1662 (Vol. I).
connections.context: “Walk,” lekhu, is the word Rav Tzadok associates with halakhah. His explanation concerns a way of proceeding in actual conduct, rather than abstract knowledge alone.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְעִנְיַן הַנְהָגַת הָעוֹלָם אָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (נט:): "לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִוא", וְאֵין מַשְׁגִּיחִין בְּבַת קוֹל;
connections.quote: see note 2090 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: (וְשָׁם פו.) נֶחְלְקוּ בִּמְתִיבְתָּא דִּרְקִיעָא: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אוֹמֵר וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: “They were debating in the heavenly academy: If a bright skin lesion preceded the white hair, it is impure; if the white hair preceded the lesion, it is pure. In a doubtful case, the Holy One, blessed be He, says: Pure; and the entire heavenly academy says: Impure. They said: Who will decide? Rabbah bar Naḥmani will decide, for Rabbah bar Naḥmani said: I am singular in the laws of skin lesions and singular in the laws of tent-impurity. They sent a messenger after him. The angel of death could not approach him because his mouth did not cease from study. Meanwhile a wind blew and rustled among the reeds. He thought it was a troop of horsemen, and said: Let that man’s soul rest, rather than be delivered into the hands of the government. As his soul departed, he said: Pure, pure. A heavenly voice proclaimed: Fortunate are you, Rabbah bar Naḥmani, for your body is pure and your soul departed with “pure.””
connections.context: This is the heavenly dispute Rav Tzadok mentions. The narrative identifies the exact uncertainty, the opposing opinions, and Rabbah’s concluding declaration; it belongs beside the preceding discussion of heavenly knowledge and legal decision.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם נִקְרָא: חֻקָּה חָקַקְתִּי, גְּזֵירָה גָּזַרְתִּי וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I have enacted a statute, I have decreed a decree; you are not permitted to transgress My decree.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַבְּרִיאָה דְּהוּא מַעֲשֵׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִקְרָא "חֻקּוֹת שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ",
connections.quote: “Thus says Hashem: If My covenant be not with day and night, if I have not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth …”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּתּוֹסֶפְתָּא, הוּבָא בְּתוֹסָפוֹת חֲגִיגָה (ב:) עַל דָּוִד וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: אֵין לְמֵדִין מִתְּקוֹעַ,
connections.quote: “In the Tosefta of Kilayim it is taught: Rabbi Issi ben Yehuda said that it is forbidden to ride a mule. … They said to him: But it is written, “Have Solomon my son ride upon the mule”! He replied: One does not learn Torah from the Tekoa case. They said to him: But it is written, “He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord.””
connections.context: Tosafot quotes a dispute about whether royal conduct supplies a legal precedent for riding a mule. The reply invoking Tekoa belongs to that dispute, and the final objection must also be retained. Rav Tzadok develops the relation between the king’s inward will and ordinary legal inference; this is not the Gemara’s discussion of freeing a half-slave.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם טַעַם, כִּי אֵין טַעַם לָרָצוֹן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר שָׁאֲלוּ עֵינַי לֹא אָצַלְתִּי מֵהֶם" (קֹהֶלֶת ב, י),
connections.quote: ‘Whatever my eyes desired, I did not withhold from them. I did not keep my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced in all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.’

connections.hePhrase: אַף לְהָפֵר תּוֹרָה, הֲגַם שֶׁלֹּא יָדַע טַעַם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה'", רַק חֻקָּה,
connections.quote: “And it says: ‘It is a time to act for Hashem; they have made void Your Torah’ (Psalms 119:126). Rabbi Natan says: ‘They have made void Your Torah’ because ‘it is a time to act for Hashem.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): בִּקֵּשׁ שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לָדוּן בְּלֹא עֵדִים וְהַתְרָאָה,
connections.quote: ‘One said: Among prophets none like him arose, but among kings one did arise. How, then, do I interpret ‘Kohelet sought to find words of delight’? Kohelet sought to judge cases through his inner discernment, without witnesses and without prior warning. A heavenly voice came forth and said to him: ‘What is written uprightly: words of truth’—‘On the testimony of two witnesses,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְטַעַם "וַיֵּשֶׁב שְׁלֹמֹה עַל כִּסֵּא ה'" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, כג), וַהֲרֵי עַל כִּסֵּא ה' יוֹשֵׁב הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא!
connections.quote: “Solomon sat upon the throne of the Lord as king in place of David his father; he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.”
connections.context: The striking wording is that Solomon “sat upon the throne of the Lord.” Rav Tzadok builds his explanation on that formulation, rather than merely on Solomon succeeding David.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִי שֶׁאוֹהֵב הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁעַל זֶה יִסַּד שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כָּל סֵפֶר שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים, הֲרֵי דָּבוּק בּוֹ עַד כִּבְיָכוֹל "וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד":
connections.quote: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִי שֶׁאוֹהֵב הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שֶׁעַל זֶה יִסַּד שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כָּל סֵפֶר שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים, הֲרֵי דָּבוּק בּוֹ עַד כִּבְיָכוֹל "וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד":
connections.quote: “In every generation, no one tasted all the attractions of this world as King Solomon did, as stated in Ecclesiastes: “I made for myself … and whatever my eyes asked for,” as is known. Nor is there a heart clean of all kinds of desire like his, as the Sages said of the Song of Songs: it is the Holy of Holies. Wherever you find a boundary against forbidden sexuality and desire, there you find holiness. For holiness means separation from desires, being devoted only to the blessed God; these are opposites. Of one immersed in desires it is said, “One who separates himself seeks desire”—he is separated from the blessed God. In holiness, however, one is consecrated to Heaven, as the Sages explain betrothal as a term of consecration, whereby a woman belongs to her husband. Song comes from longing, hence the name “songs of love.” When his soul yearns for the blessed God and is lovesick for Him, his mouth opens to sing before Him. No songs awaken Israel’s love for their Father in Heaven and their union with Him as does the Song of Songs. This love is the opposite of love of this world. Therefore it is the Holy of Holies: wholly belonging to the blessed God, entirely separated from all worldly desires and having no connection with them at all. Such is the measure: the very heart that tastes darkness to its furthest limit and seeks God from there tastes light to its furthest limit, until it apprehends that there is no darkness, and “darkness does not darken … night shines as day.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains Solomon’s Song of Songs through consecrated longing and separation from worldly desire. The final condition—seeking God from within the darkness—is retained in the account of how darkness leads to light.

connections.hePhrase: [קצט] הַכָּרַת הָאַהֲבָה הוּא בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין סה:) שֶׁאָדָם נִיכָּר.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Ilai said: A person can be recognized through three things: his cup, his purse, and his anger. Some say: also through his laughter.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת סא:): יֵשׁ לְךָ אָדָם שֶׁמָּמוֹנוֹ וְכוּלֵי, לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר: "בְּכָל מְאֹדְךָ".
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer says: If a person’s body is dearer to him than his property, therefore it says “with all your soul”; and if a person’s property is dearer to him than his body, therefore it says “with all your might.” Rabbi Akiva says: “With all your soul”—even if He takes your soul.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok applies the second clause to the test of one’s purse.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְחֻלִּין (צא.) לָמְדוּ מִיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּמָמוֹנוֹ חָבִיב מִגּוּפוֹ
connections.quote: ‘‘Jacob remained alone.’ Rabbi Elazar said: He remained behind for some small jars. From here we learn that the righteous cherish their property more than their bodies. Why so much? Because they do not stretch out their hands to robbery.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְחֻלִּין (צא.) לָמְדוּ מִיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּמָמוֹנוֹ חָבִיב מִגּוּפוֹ
connections.quote: “But our Sages of blessed memory said that they rise in their garments. Those garments, which will be created anew after decay, will certainly endure forever like the bodies. They surpass even the garments in the wilderness, of which the Sages said that they grew with the wearers, and of which it is written, “Your garment did not wear out upon you.” Thus some of one’s possessions also endure forever, as they become clothing for the body. This is through the Torah and its commandments, for many commandments—almost most of them—depend on a person’s money and possessions; through this, eternal life and permanence extend into them too. The body is the garment of the soul, and possessions are the garment of the body. The righteous, whose bodies have already been refined, cherish the garment, namely money: the coarser and more outward the garment, the more effort it needs. This is therefore more precious and beautiful to them, for there the effort is greater, and therefore the longing is greater.”
connections.context: Machshavot Charutz explains why care for possessions need not express materialism: property can bear the lasting effect of the commandments performed with it. The argument concerns possessions sanctified through Torah and mitzvot.

connections.hePhrase: [וְזֶה נֶגֶד אַהֲבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא בְּמָמוֹנוֹ, וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אוֹהֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל].
connections.quote: “Israel is likewise compared, in the chapter “Gid HaNasheh” in Ḥullin, to silver: “Silver—these are Israel.” They said of Jacob that his money was dearer to him than his body, for he remained behind for small vessels. These are the small souls of Israel, as I wrote elsewhere.”
connections.context: The “small vessels” receive a symbolic reading as souls that might otherwise be overlooked. This directly connects Jacob’s care for property with his love of Israel.

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בְכוֹסוֹ" – נֶגֶד "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יַיִן וְתִירוֹשׁ יִקַּח לֵב" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ד, יא).
connections.quote: “Promiscuity, wine, and new wine take away the heart.”
connections.context: “Heart” is the Hebrew wording, encompassing judgment and inward disposition. It is essential to Rav Tzadok’s alignment of a person’s conduct with his cup and the demand to serve God “with all your heart.”

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בְכוֹסוֹ" – נֶגֶד "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יַיִן וְתִירוֹשׁ יִקַּח לֵב" (הוֹשֵׁעַ ד, יא).
connections.quote: “Likewise, “They drank and became intoxicated with him” took place at a Shabbat meal. Bereishit Rabbah expounds “and prepare”: “Preparation” refers to Shabbat. On Shabbat the will of Atika, the Ancient One, is revealed: by day is the meal of Atika, and at the Friday-night meal the Holy Ancient One comes to dine with her [the Shekhinah]. Knowledge, which is the inwardness of the supernal crown, is revealed, and for this reason drinking is permitted then. This is why Joseph’s brothers drank at that time, although they had not drunk throughout the preceding twenty-two years, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah and the Talmud. Joseph shone the holiness of Shabbat into them; they felt the holiness of the Shabbat meal and drank. Joseph’s intention in giving them wine was to learn the depths of their hearts: were they bound to the root? This resembles the saying in Sanhedrin, “Increase their wine ... wine enters, the secret comes out.””
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik applies the general test of the cup to Joseph and his brothers. Joseph first brings them to experience Shabbat holiness and then seeks to know whether their hearts are bound to the root. This narrative illustrates why Tzidkat HaTzadik makes the heart’s prior content decisive for the secret wine reveals.
connections.headline: The cup as a test of love that fills the heart

connections.hePhrase: וְאִם כְּבָר מְמוּלָּא כָּל חֲלָלוֹ מֵעֵבֶר לְעֵבֶר בְּאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת, גַּם כְּשֶׁנִּכְנַס יַיִן יָצָא סוֹד ה' הַגָּנוּז בּוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥiyya said: One who remains composed in his wine has the understanding of seventy elders. “Wine” has the numerical value seventy, and “secret” has the numerical value seventy. Wine enters; the secret comes out.”
connections.context: The source praises remaining composed while drinking. Rav Tzadok applies its image of the emerging secret to a heart already filled with love of God.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל עִנְיַן הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת הוּא עַל יְדֵי קִיחַת הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי מֵעִנְיַן אֲמַצְיָהוּ, וְכֵן מֵחִזְקִיָּהוּ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ: "עֲזָבוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים לְנַסּוֹתוֹ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב לב, לא).
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Vayikra 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Vayikra 6
connections.quote: “To this matter also belongs the case of Amaziah king of Judah. He struck ten thousand of Edom and hurled ten thousand from the top of the rock, so that they were shattered. Afterward he worshipped the gods of Edom and sent to Joash king of Israel: “Come, let us face one another.” The meaning is that Edom is the foremost husk, the most important of all the nations, as stated in Avodah Zarah: Edom enters immediately after Israel because of its importance. Immediately beyond this husk begins the name Israel. At present Israel has not been granted authority over them; that is only for the future, as explained in its place. Amaziah’s killing of the twenty thousand corresponds to the ten levels of the husk, for “God made this opposite that”: twenty thousand alludes to all ten levels from below upward and from above downward. He thought that since his power over them had become so great, whatever he now did would surely not turn his heart from God, nor would any evil have power to prevail over him, as will be in the future. He therefore tried worshipping the gods of Edom and sent Joash, “Come, let us face one another,” meaning: Although I have done something that appears evil, I am still more attached to the blessed God than you. But this was not the blessed God’s will. Therefore he was punished, and Joash king of Israel captured him. Nevertheless, it says there that Amaziah lived fifteen years after Joash’s death, hinting that in all fifteen levels found in Israel, Amaziah was greater than Joash, and his sin was only relative to the limits of human apprehension.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer explicitly says that Amaziah’s attempted test was not God’s will and that he was punished. His subsequent spiritual interpretation does not remove that statement. Both parts are retained in this direct parallel to what Rav Tzadok heard.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל עִנְיַן הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת הוּא עַל יְדֵי קִיחַת הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי מֵעִנְיַן אֲמַצְיָהוּ, וְכֵן מֵחִזְקִיָּהוּ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ: "עֲזָבוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים לְנַסּוֹתוֹ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב לב, לא).
connections.quote: ‘So too, in the matter of the envoys of the rulers of Babylon, who were sent to him to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land, God left him, to test him and to know everything in his heart.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל עִנְיַן הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת הוּא עַל יְדֵי קִיחַת הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי מֵעִנְיַן אֲמַצְיָהוּ, וְכֵן מֵחִזְקִיָּהוּ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ: "עֲזָבוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים לְנַסּוֹתוֹ" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב לב, לא).
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Shabbat 138b:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Shabbat 138b:1
connections.quote: ““The deep” signifies the things a person does in concealment while directing himself to the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, because in the depths of his heart he is attached to Him, even where his intellect and awareness do not reach. This is “By His knowledge the depths were split”: from the depths of the human heart, the Holy One, blessed be He, builds within a person’s heart the fulfillment of His will even in concealment, thereby clarifying that he is wholly attached to Him. This is the meaning of “by His knowledge”—not by human knowledge. Thus we find of Hezekiah king of Judah: “And so with the envoys of the princes of Babylon … God left him, to test him, to know all that was in his heart.” He concealed Himself from him and tested whether he would direct himself to God’s will even in concealment, as it is written, “I will surely hide My face on that day.””
connections.context: This is the received teaching’s direct parallel for Hezekiah. It explains the trial as the concealment of felt divine guidance, exposing what is present in the depths of the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ" נִתְנַסָּה בְּנִסְיוֹנוֹת;
connections.quote: “With ten trials was our father Abraham, peace be upon him, tried, and he withstood them all, to make known how great was the love of our father Abraham, peace be upon him.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא עִיקָּרוֹ בְּאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ", כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:): רַחֲמָנָא לִבָּא בָּעֵי.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yehudah would remove his shoes, and rain would come; we cry out, and no one pays attention to us. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the heart, as it is written: ‘Hashem sees into the heart.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בְכַעֲסוֹ" – זֶה נוֹגֵעַ עַד הַנֶּפֶשׁ, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "טֹרֵף נַפְשׁוֹ בְּאַפּוֹ" (אִיּוֹב יח, ד), הוּא נֶגֶד "בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ" – אֲפִילּוּ נוֹטֵל נַפְשְׁךָ,
connections.quote: ‘You who tear yourself apart in your anger—should the earth be abandoned for your sake, or a rock be moved from its place?’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי כָּל הַמְצָאוֹת וְחִדּוּשִׁין שֶׁל חָכְמָה מִסִּטְרָא דְּיִצְחָק.
connections.quote: “The Torah comes from the side of might, which is the mystery of restraint: one’s conduct is bounded by “Do this and do not do that.” Yet this restraint of Torah is entirely an expansion, for it is the root of Jacob’s inheritance without boundaries. Through this temporary restraint in this world, one grasps the tree of life and merits the abundance of Torah, whose measure is “longer than the earth and broader than the sea.” The restraint applies only to bodily activities and deeds. In apprehension, however—the principal wisdom of Torah, through contemplation in the mind and heart—one may expand without boundaries. “From the narrow place I called to God; He answered me with spaciousness”: the calling is the beginning of entry into Torah, which needs restraint and a narrow passage. Afterward, when the blessed God answers and helps him, he is in spaciousness.”
connections.context: The author explains how the discipline associated with Isaac and gevurah can produce intellectual breadth. The limits on bodily conduct remain in place while understanding opens beyond them.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַתּוֹרָה נֶאֱמַר: "כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יט, יד) – שֶׁמֵּמִית עַצְמוֹ, וְהַיְינוּ "בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ".
connections.quote: “Another interpretation of “Be silent and listen, Israel”: crush yourselves over words of Torah. This is as Reish Lakish said: From where do we know that words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself as dead over them? For it is written, “This is the Torah: when a person dies in a tent.””
connections.context: The Gemara supplies the homiletic reading of the verse cited in the body. Rav Tzadok uses it for wholehearted devotion to Torah under the heading “with all your soul.”

connections.hePhrase: וְרוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן טָב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפב עַמּוּד ב), וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (ד.): דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא דְּקָא מְרַתְּחָא,
connections.quote: ‘If you say: But what about the anger of the Sages? The anger of the Sages is good from every side, for we have learned that Torah is fire, and it is Torah that makes him boil, as it is written: ‘Is not My word like fire, declares Hashem?’ (Jeremiah 23:29). The anger of the Sages concerns words of Torah. The anger of the Sages is to give honor to Torah, and all of it is for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He. Therefore it is said: ‘For Hashem your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God’ (Deuteronomy 4:24).’

connections.hePhrase: וְרוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן טָב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפב עַמּוּד ב), וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (ד.): דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא דְּקָא מְרַתְּחָא,
connections.quote: “The root of the evil inclination is the fire of anger, as in “His fury burned within him”; it wishes to burn and consume everything. Corresponding to this in holiness is Oral Torah: much wisdom to repair much anger. It too is fire, as the Gemara says: “When a Torah scholar grows heated, Torah is what heats him, as it is written, ‘Are not My words like fire?’” It is a fire consuming the fire of the evil inclination, burning and consuming that inclination. This is why the Zohar says, “The anger of the sages is good on every side.””
connections.explanation: The Kislev passage explains what distinguishes two outwardly similar intensities: the inclination’s fire consumes indiscriminately, while Torah’s fire is directed against the inclination itself. This sharpens the test given here for the anger of a talmid chacham. The Sanhedrin’s search for merit and continuing compassion are not exceptions to holy zeal; they show that the heat remains governed by Torah rather than by personal aggression. Self-restraint therefore expresses love ‘with all your soul.’
connections.headline: The test of Torah’s fire is that it consumes the inclination’s destructive anger

connections.hePhrase: זֶה נִקְרָא רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן, הָאוֹהֲבֵי הַתּוֹרָה בֶּאֱמֶת, שֶׁגַּם בְּעֵת כַּעֲסוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַתּוֹרָה וְזוֹכֵר וּמִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּרַחֲמִים.
connections.quote: “Ravina said: Even so, a person must train himself to act gently, as it is written, “Remove anger from your heart.””
connections.context: This qualification follows the Gemara’s description of a scholar whose Torah makes him heated. It adds the requirement of gentleness, complementing the already-present quotation about Torah’s fire and Rav Tzadok’s insistence that compassion remain active.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָעֲצִירָה בְּעֵת הַכַּעַס הוּא אַהֲבָה "בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ", כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה, קָשָׁה כִשְׁאוֹל קִנְאָה" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ח, ו),
connections.quote: ‘Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy as unyielding as Sheol. Its flashes are flashes of fire, a flame of Yah.’

connections.hePhrase: [ר] יֵשׁ שְׁלֹשָׁה מִינִים בְּאַהֲבָה: אַהֲבָה זוּטָא וְאַהֲבָה רַבָּה נִזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר פְּקוּדֵי (רנד עַמּוּד ב), וְאַהֲבָה רַבָּה וְאַהֲבַת עוֹלָם נִזְכָּר בְּנוּסַח בִּרְכַּת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא:).
connections.quote: “When he reached that place called the Palace of Love, he attached himself to it with the will of his heart. He said: This palace must be joined to the palace above, in great love. Then he was perfected in the mystery of faith, and he ascended and completed lesser love with greater love, as was fitting. Therefore he died in love, and his soul departed with this verse, “You shall love.” Fortunate is his portion.”
connections.context: In its account of Rabbi Akiva’s ascent, the Zohar describes completing “lesser love” with “greater love.” This supplies the Zohar passage cited in the opening sentence, alongside the already-present discussion of the prayer wording in Berakhot.

connections.hePhrase: [ר] יֵשׁ שְׁלֹשָׁה מִינִים בְּאַהֲבָה: אַהֲבָה זוּטָא וְאַהֲבָה רַבָּה נִזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר פְּקוּדֵי (רנד עַמּוּד ב), וְאַהֲבָה רַבָּה וְאַהֲבַת עוֹלָם נִזְכָּר בְּנוּסַח בִּרְכַּת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא:).
connections.quote: ‘It was likewise taught: One does not say ‘Ahavat Olam (everlasting love),’ but ‘Ahavah Rabbah (great love).’ The Sages, however, say ‘Ahavat Olam,’ as Scripture says: ‘I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with kindness.’ Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name: One who rises early to study before reciting Shema must recite a blessing. After he has recited Shema, he need not recite a blessing, for he has already fulfilled his obligation through ‘Ahavah Rabbah.’’

connections.hePhrase: [ר] יֵשׁ שְׁלֹשָׁה מִינִים בְּאַהֲבָה: אַהֲבָה זוּטָא וְאַהֲבָה רַבָּה נִזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר פְּקוּדֵי (רנד עַמּוּד ב), וְאַהֲבָה רַבָּה וְאַהֲבַת עוֹלָם נִזְכָּר בְּנוּסַח בִּרְכַּת קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא:).
connections.quote: “There, at the upper root, it is called great love; all the levels and garments are called everlasting love, which is small love. Through their service in small love, Israel breaks through all the veils and recognizes His unity, saying, ‘Hear, Israel… Hashem is one.’ Israel therefore has a place in the light of His unity, so that even this verse, ‘Hear, Israel… Hashem is one,’ is called kingship on Israel's side. This is Rabbi Yose's reasoning in saying that ‘Hear, Israel…’ counts as kingship.”
connections.explanation: The terms need to be read in context. This siman distinguishes hidden love, revealed intensity and love's endurance through changing conditions. Sod Yesharim instead calls the revealed upper root great love and the clothed levels everlasting love or small love. Its measure is concealment and revelation. The shared names therefore do not justify treating the two classifications as an identical fixed hierarchy.
connections.headline: The same love terms in a different classification

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ: "אַהֲבָה זוּטָא" הִיא הַנִּקְרֵאת בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב "אַהֲבָה מְסֻתָּרֶת" (מִשְׁלֵי כז, ה), שֶׁאֵינָהּ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת בְּלִבּוֹ לִהְיוֹת בּוֹעֵר כְּרִשְׁפֵּי אֵשׁ,
connections.quote: ‘Open rebuke is better than concealed love.’

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא שֶׁזֶּה רַק מַתְּנַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵינוֹ בְּיַד הָאָדָם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ, כְּמוֹ הַיִּרְאָה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁיָּכוֹל לָבוֹא עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹכַחַת לְלִבּוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם לג:): הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים י״ד:ב׳
connections.quote: “By contrast, in a matter entrusted to the heart—that evil should truly be repulsive to one’s heart and hated with utter hatred, or even without utter hatred—this cannot be fully true except through the greatness and intensity of love of God, in the form of “love in delights”: delighting in God with a foretaste of the World to Come. Of this our Sages said, “May you see your world in your lifetime.” Not everyone merits this, for it is like receiving a reward, as it is written, “I grant your priesthood as a service of gift,” as explained elsewhere.”
connections.context: Tanya identifies the inward delight that transforms one’s relation to evil as a gift not attained by everyone. Rav Tzadok similarly distinguishes great love from the fear cultivated through deliberate effort.

connections.hePhrase: אֶלָּא שֶׁזֶּה רַק מַתְּנַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵינוֹ בְּיַד הָאָדָם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ, כְּמוֹ הַיִּרְאָה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁיָּכוֹל לָבוֹא עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹכַחַת לְלִבּוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם לג:): הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Chanina said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven, as it says: ‘And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, except to fear?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם רֹאשׁ הַמִּשְׁתַּדְּלִים זָכָה לְמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה שֶׁהוּא מַתְּנַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת;
connections.quote: “For Abraham is called “the first of the converts”: he is the first of those who exert themselves. Of him it is said, “Walk before Me”—walking signifies effort, the level of “when you walk.” This is called the convert, of whom the Sages said in Kiddushin that first comes “You shall be My people”; he merits only through his own effort.”
connections.context: Resisei Layla names Abraham as the beginning of self-initiated service. Rav Tzadok’s point here is the reversal: this patriarch of effort ultimately receives love as a divine gift.

connections.hePhrase: וְיִצְחָק, רֹאשׁ הַנּוֹלָדִים מְקוּדָּשִׁים מִלֵּידָה מִבֶּטֶן וְהֻבְטַח טֶרֶם לֵידָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶרַע ה', זָכָה לְמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁהוּא בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם.
connections.quote: “And God said to Abraham: … in all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for in Isaac shall seed be called to you.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיִצְחָק, רֹאשׁ הַנּוֹלָדִים מְקוּדָּשִׁים מִלֵּידָה מִבֶּטֶן וְהֻבְטַח טֶרֶם לֵידָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶרַע ה', זָכָה לְמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁהוּא בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם.
connections.quote: “And God said: Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish My covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, for his seed after him.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיִצְחָק, רֹאשׁ הַנּוֹלָדִים מְקוּדָּשִׁים מִלֵּידָה מִבֶּטֶן וְהֻבְטַח טֶרֶם לֵידָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶרַע ה', זָכָה לְמִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁהוּא בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם.
connections.quote: “Fear is the root of the prohibitions, the level of Isaac, the mighty one who conquers his inclination. This is the whole root of his effort: to clarify “You shall have no other gods”—every kind of dross and the separation of evil from good, the outer boundary of the world that distinguishes it from what lies beyond. This is possible only for one whose conception and birth are in holiness, and in whose heart the root of “I am the Lord your God” is already fixed and enduring, a peg that cannot move. Nevertheless, afterward he still needs the warning “You shall have no other gods.” Even one who is an Israelite from birth, a believer descended from believers, can have evil prevail within him, God forbid, so strongly that it says to him, “Go, worship,” until it can even sever his root, God forbid—as with Esau, who is called an apostate Israelite in Kiddushin, yet became a nation of his own. All the effort of our father Isaac was directed toward this: to beget Jacob, whose offspring are complete, whose root cannot be severed in any way, for “even though he sinned, he is Israel.””
connections.context: The parallel explains why inherited holiness does not eliminate Isaac’s task of resisting evil. Its qualification about the continuing need for vigilance, and its distinction between Esau and Jacob, are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִיא מִדַּת "אַהֲבַת עוֹלָם", שֶׁהוּא הַמַּבְרִיחַ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה, וּמִדַּת הָאֱמֶת וְקַיָּים לָעַד שֶׁאֵין לוֹ בִּיטּוּל וְהֶפְסֵק, כְּטַעַם (תַּעֲנִית ה:): יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לֹא מֵת.
connections.quote: ‘After he had eaten, he said to him: Thus said Rabbi Yochanan: Our father Jacob did not die. He said to him: ‘Then did the eulogizers eulogize, the embalmers embalm, and the buriers bury for nothing?’ He answered: ‘I am expounding a verse, for it is said: ‘But you, do not fear, My servant Jacob, declares Hashem, and do not be dismayed, Israel, for behold, I am saving you from afar and your descendants from the land of their captivity.’ It compares him to his descendants: just as his descendants are alive, so he too is alive.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְגַם יֵשׁ חִלּוּק לָאָדָם: כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּשִׂמְחָה וְנִיחָא אָז גּוֹבֵר מִדַּת אַהֲבָה, וּבְצַעַר וְצָרָה – מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה;
connections.quote: “Love is characteristic of youth, unlike old age, when ‘desire fails.’ As is known, Shlomo in his youth composed Shir HaShirim, the intensity of love, and in his old age Kohelet, the intensity of awe. Avraham, however, established something new in the circulating coin: on one coin, an old man and woman on one side, and a young man and maiden on the other, all united in a complete union—love and awe.”
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah uses Avraham's coin to describe love and awe existing within one whole. The image helps explain the present siman's demand for love that remains even in darkness and distress: the purpose is not to eliminate awe, but to prevent either condition from excluding the other. It also preserves the distinction between a passing intensity of love and the union that continues through changing circumstances.
connections.headline: One coin holds love and awe together

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת צָרִיךְ לְאַהֲבָה בֵּין בְּטִיבוּ בֵּין בְּעָקוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּהַקְדָּמַת הַזֹּהַר (יב עַמּוּד א).
connections.quote: “Therefore we learned: love, the love of the Holy One, blessed be He, is distinguished on two sides. There is one who loves Him because he has wealth, length of days, children around him, mastery over his enemies, and success in his ways; because of this he loves Him. If these circumstances were reversed and the Holy One, blessed be He, brought upon him a turn of harsh judgment, he would hate Him and not love Him at all. Therefore this love is not a love with a root. Love called complete is that which exists on both sides, in judgment as in goodness. His ways are set right so that he loves his Master, as we learned, even if He takes your soul from you. This is complete love on both sides. Thus the light of Creation came forth and afterward was hidden. When it was hidden, harsh judgment emerged, and both sides were included together, so that this love would be properly complete.”
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly contrasts love dependent on favorable circumstances with love sustained through both goodness and adversity. This is the passage cited at the introduction to the Zohar, 12a.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִדְרַשׁ בִּבְרָכוֹת (נד.) מִ"בְּכָל מְאֹדְךָ", שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה כּוֹלֵל שְׁתֵּי הַמִּדּוֹת בְּכָל זְמַן, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): אֲנִי יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי.
connections.quote: see note 1236 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The source places these words in David’s mouth. Rav Tzadok invokes their mutual inclusion of joy and fear to explain the enduring love associated here with Jacob.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אוֹמְרִים בְּעַרְבִית "אַהֲבַת עוֹלָם" נֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁתִּיקֵּן תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית, וְהוּא מִדָּתוֹ: לִהְיוֹת גַּם בָּעֶרֶב וְעֵת חֶשְׁכַּת הַצָּרוֹת הָאַהֲבָה בִּלְתִּי נִיתֶּקֶת.
connections.quote: “A baraita was taught in support of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina, and a baraita was taught in support of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. The baraita supporting Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina teaches: Abraham instituted the morning prayer, as it is written, “Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood.” Standing means prayer, as it is written, “Pinehas stood and prayed.” Isaac instituted the afternoon prayer, as it is written, “Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening.” Meditation means prayer, as it is written, “A prayer of the poor when he is overwhelmed and pours out his plea before the Lord.” Jacob instituted the evening prayer, as it is written, “He encountered the place and spent the night there.” Encounter means prayer, as it is written, “Do not pray for this people, do not raise a cry or prayer for them, and do not entreat Me.””
connections.context: This baraita connects each patriarch with a daily prayer. It provides the source for the attribution of evening to Jacob and morning to Abraham in this and the next sentence.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לִפְעָמִים, אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא דִּמְיוֹן וּבְהִתְגַּלּוּת הַלֵּב וְלֹא בְּמַעֲמַקָּיו.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים י״ג:י״א-י״ד
connections.quote: “This love described in intermediate people during prayer, through the strengthening of the divine soul, is not called “service in truth” at all in comparison with the level of the righteous who serve God in His fullest truth, since it passes and departs after prayer; and it is written, “A truthful lip endures forever, but a lying tongue is only for a moment.” Nevertheless, in relation to the level of intermediate people it is called complete service in their fullest truth, each according to his own level among them. I also apply “A truthful lip endures forever” to their love during prayer, since their divine soul has the power to awaken this love again always, through its strengthening during prayer day after day, with the preparation suited to each soul’s standing and level. For truth is the attribute of Jacob, called “the middle bar that extends from end to end”—from the height of levels to the end of all ranks. Within every level it runs through the middle point, which is that level’s point and quality of truth. Truth is “an inheritance without boundaries,” without an upward limit, to the highest levels. All lower levels are as nothing compared with those above them [as is known to those versed in the hidden wisdom: the head and intellect of lower levels are below the heels and feet of higher ones, as our Sages said, “The feet of the living creatures correspond to them all”].”
connections.context: Tanya distinguishes the enduring truth of a higher spiritual level from the recurring truth of an intermediate person’s prayer. Its explicit affirmation that such prayer is true at that person’s level qualifies the comparison and must accompany it.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל "לֹא בָאֵשׁ ה'" (מְלָכִים א יט, יב), כִּי צָרִיךְ לָזֶה מִבְחָן וּבֵירוּר עֲדַיִן אִם הוּא אֱמֶת גָּמוּר שֶׁאַהֲבָתוֹ עַזָּה כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגַת הַדְּבֵיקוּת, וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה ה' בְּקִרְבּוֹ מַמָּשׁ כְּמִשְׁפַּט הָאַהֲבָה בַּחֲשׁוּקִים:
connections.quote: see note 588 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל "לֹא בָאֵשׁ ה'" (מְלָכִים א יט, יב), כִּי צָרִיךְ לָזֶה מִבְחָן וּבֵירוּר עֲדַיִן אִם הוּא אֱמֶת גָּמוּר שֶׁאַהֲבָתוֹ עַזָּה כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגַת הַדְּבֵיקוּת, וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה ה' בְּקִרְבּוֹ מַמָּשׁ כְּמִשְׁפַּט הָאַהֲבָה בַּחֲשׁוּקִים:
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Numbers, Korach 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Numbers, Korach 1
connections.quote: “All this is not yet completely clarified, as we find written: “The Lord was not in the wind … the Lord was not in the earthquake.” Wind corresponds to the will found in a person of good deeds; earthquake is the fear within Torah, corresponding to the righteous person; and fire corresponds to the priest, whose service is in mighty love. Therefore it was first written, “The God who answers by fire—He is God; and all the people answered, ‘The proposal is good.’” They all agreed that the one able to act before the blessed God through service in mighty love is the one God chose. Yet afterward the blessed God showed Elijah the prophet that after all these things a person still needs God to agree and set His seal upon all of them. Thus it says, “After the fire, a still, thin voice”: voice is God’s seal upon wind, the will of one who performs good deeds—when they come from God, they are good; stillness is God’s seal upon earthquake; thinness is God’s seal upon fire. When God seals these things, so that the person does not incline in them toward his own interest, they are completely clarified. For even in such matters, when a person longs for love and fear, he may covet them as he covets worldly things. He needs the blessed God to affirm that his intention is truly for the sake of Heaven.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer’s teaching explains why spiritual intensity alone still needs examination: even love and fear can become objects of self-interested desire. This is the direct parallel to the closing report “as I heard.”

connections.hePhrase: [רא] מְסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת ה' אֵינוֹ הַנֶּפֶשׁ לְבַד כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ, אֶלָּא גַּם הַנְּשָׁמָה,
connections.quote: “He did not look to any of this, but cast his life aside for love of Hashem. He surrendered himself in both worlds, agreeing that no continuation of himself should remain, solely for love of Hashem. His reward is therefore doubled and multiplied.”
connections.explanation: In the preceding paragraph Beit Yaakov explains that Avraham's readiness to offer his only son seemed to leave him without reward or enduring continuation. The quoted conclusion therefore describes self-giving in two worlds, not bodily courage alone. This makes the opening of the present siman concrete: the attachment being yielded can include one's expectation of spiritual attainment and legacy. The illustration remains Avraham's response to a divine command.
connections.headline: Surrender can reach even one's expected spiritual legacy

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר תְּרוּמָה (קסג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א) דְּ"בְכָל נַפְשְׁךָ" הַיְינוּ נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה
connections.quote: ““And with all your soul”: it could have said “with your soul.” What is “with all your soul”—why this “all”? Rather, it includes nefesh, ruaḥ, and neshamah. This is “with all your soul”: with everything bound to this soul. “And with all your might” is similar: there are several kinds of possessions, all differing from one another, and therefore it says “all.” Love of the Holy One, blessed be He, means handing all of this over to Him, loving Him with each and every one.”
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly includes all three levels of soul and all varieties of possessions. The latter part also supplies the source Rav Tzadok cites a few phrases later.

connections.hePhrase: [דִּלְשׁוֹן "כָּל" מַשְׁמָע לְפָחוֹת עַל שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת כְּתוּבּוֹת (ח.).
connections.quote: “Afterward we read, “Therefore let us say both of them,” and we do not read “all of them,” for that would imply that there are three blessings.”
connections.context: Tosafot is discussing the wording of the conclusion about the blessings over Torah in Berakhot 11b. Rav Tzadok borrows its linguistic distinction between “both” and “all” for the three dimensions he includes in “all your soul.”

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בְכָל מְאֹדְךָ" אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר שָׁם דְּכַמָּה זִינִין אִינּוּן בְּמָמוֹן, פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי תְּרוּמוֹת סוֹף פֶּרֶק ח): לִבָּא בְּכִיסָא תַּלְיָא;
connections.quote: “All the limbs depend upon the heart, and the heart depends upon the purse.”
connections.context: Rabbi Yoḥanan says this after being robbed, when his distress prevents him from answering Resh Lakish’s questions. Rav Tzadok applies the dependence of the heart upon possessions to the different desires that money can serve.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ אֲשֶׁר כָּתָבְתָּ" (שְׁמוֹת לב, לב) בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
connections.quote: ‘And now, if You will forgive their sin… But if not, please erase me from Your book that You have written.’

connections.hePhrase: וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּקֵּשׁ לַעֲבוֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קז.) כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִתְחַלֵּל וְכוּלֵי, דְּהַיְינוּ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name: Even during David’s illness, he fulfilled eighteen conjugal obligations, as it says: ‘I am weary with my sighing; every night I make my bed swim; with my tears I dissolve my couch.’ Rav Yehudah also said in Rav’s name: David sought to practice idolatry, as it says: ‘David came to the summit (rosh), where he would bow down to God.’ Here ‘head (rosh)’ means idolatry, as it says: ‘That statue—its head was of fine gold.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּמְקוֹשֵׁשׁ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם נִתְכַּוֵּין, הַיְינוּ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה הֲלָכָה זוֹ בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁל חִיּוּב מִיתָה לִמְחַלֵּל שַׁבָּת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קיט: בְּשֵׁם מִדְרָשׁ), הֲגַם דְּהוּא יֵעָנֵשׁ;
connections.quote: “While the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. … And they put him in custody, for it had not been declared what should be done to him. And Hashem said to Moses: The man shall surely be put to death …”

connections.hePhrase: וּמְקוֹשֵׁשׁ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם נִתְכַּוֵּין, הַיְינוּ בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה הֲלָכָה זוֹ בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁל חִיּוּב מִיתָה לִמְחַלֵּל שַׁבָּת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קיט: בְּשֵׁם מִדְרָשׁ), הֲגַם דְּהוּא יֵעָנֵשׁ;
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא בתרא קי״ט ב:י״א:ב׳
connections.quote: “The Midrash says that he intended it for the sake of Heaven. Israel were saying: Since it was decreed after the incident of the spies that they would not enter the land, they were no longer obligated in the commandments. He arose and desecrated Shabbat so that he would be put to death and others would see.”
connections.context: Tosafot reports this explanation of the wood-gatherer’s intention while identifying him with Zelophehad. Rav Tzadok stresses the stated intention to make the continuing force of the commandment known, without denying the act’s punishment.

connections.hePhrase: וְזָכָה גַּם כֵּן לְבָנוֹת שֶׁנִּתְלִין בּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ נִדָּה לא סוֹף עַמּוּד א): חַכְמָנִיּוֹת, דַּרְשָׁנִיּוֹת, וְנִתְגַּלָּה גַּם כֵּן עַל יָדָם פָּרָשָׁה מְחוּדֶּשֶׁת מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בִּנְחָלוֹת.
connections.quote: “It was taught: Zelophehad’s daughters were wise, skilled in interpretation, and righteous. They were wise because they spoke at the appropriate moment. Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak said: This teaches that Moses our teacher was sitting and expounding the passage about levirate marriage, as it says, “When brothers dwell together.” They said to him: If we count as a son, give us an inheritance as a son; if not, let our mother enter levirate marriage! Immediately, “Moses brought their case before the Lord.” They were skilled in interpretation because they said: Had he had a son, we would not have spoken. But was it not taught, “a daughter”? Rabbi Yirmeya said: Remove “a daughter” from here. Abaye said: Even had the son had a daughter, we would not have spoken. They were righteous because they married only men worthy of them. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov taught: Even the youngest of them did not marry before the age of forty.”
connections.context: The existing Niddah note explains the relationship of daughters to their father. This passage is the separate source for their wisdom and interpretive ability, and preserves the Gemara’s third description, their righteousness.

connections.hePhrase: וְזָכָה גַּם כֵּן לְבָנוֹת שֶׁנִּתְלִין בּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ נִדָּה לא סוֹף עַמּוּד א): חַכְמָנִיּוֹת, דַּרְשָׁנִיּוֹת, וְנִתְגַּלָּה גַּם כֵּן עַל יָדָם פָּרָשָׁה מְחוּדֶּשֶׁת מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בִּנְחָלוֹת.
connections.quote: ““Moses brought their case”: The law escaped him; here he was repaid for taking a crown for himself when he said, “The matter that is too difficult for you, bring to me.” Another interpretation: This passage was fit to be written through Moses, but Zelophehad’s daughters merited that it be written through them.”
connections.context: Rashi’s second interpretation supplies the claim that the daughters brought a new Torah passage into revelation. The first interpretation is retained as Rashi’s distinct explanation of why Moses brought the question before God.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי: עִנְיַן הַיְרֻשָּׁה עִיקָּרוֹ יְרֻשַּׁת הַכֹּחוֹת שֶׁל הָאָב לַבֵּן.
connections.quote: “Whether a person is rich or poor depends on his mazal—that is, on the receptivity of his mazal and hidden root. How, then, does a poor son inherit a rich father when the father dies, if the son lacks the capacity to receive so much wealth? In truth, the father’s hevel de-garmei, the power of his mazal and hidden root, extends into the son himself, and the son becomes a vessel able to receive it. Therefore, in the chapter “HaPoalim,” concerning Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, they said, “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life”: every son can attain his father’s level after his death if he wishes. This concerns the level of a righteous person; concerning the level of a Torah scholar, however, they said in Nedarim that scholars do not commonly bequeath it to their sons, for the three kinds of gifts correspond to the three hidden powers mentioned above.”
connections.context: This parallel explains inheritance as a transmission of spiritual capacity. It expressly distinguishes inheriting a righteous father’s level from the different case of scholarly attainment, and conditions attainment on the son’s will.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחֵר לֹא הָיָה שָׁלֵם בְּ"בְכָל לְבָבְךָ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה טו: רַשִּׁ"י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "נוֹשְׁרִין"): טִינָא הָיְתָה בְּלִבּוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה נֶגֶד אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קצ"ט – יָצָא לְתַרְבּוּת רָעָה.
connections.quote: “They said of Acher: When he rose from the study hall, many books of heretics would fall from his lap.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחֵר לֹא הָיָה שָׁלֵם בְּ"בְכָל לְבָבְךָ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה טו: רַשִּׁ"י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "נוֹשְׁרִין"): טִינָא הָיְתָה בְּלִבּוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה נֶגֶד אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קצ"ט – יָצָא לְתַרְבּוּת רָעָה.
connections.quote: ““Falling from his lap”: Before he abandoned himself to an evil course. It follows that there was already corruption in his heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly cites Rashi’s comment beginning “falling.” It explains the earlier inward defect in Acher; the general Gemara statement about corruption in the hearts of Doeg and Ahithophel is a different passage.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶן עַזַּאי נַפְשׁוֹ חָשְׁקָה בַּתּוֹרָה, זֶהוּ נֶגֶד "בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ" וְאַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה, רַק שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה נָאֶה מְקַיֵּים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (סג:);
connections.quote: ‘They said to Ben Azzai: ‘Some expound well and fulfill well; some fulfill well but do not expound well. But you expound well and do not fulfill well.’ Ben Azzai said to them: ‘What can I do? My soul longs for Torah. The world can be sustained through others.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (שָׁם קט.): כָּל הָאוֹמֵר אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה, אַף תּוֹרָה אֵין לוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה חִסָּרוֹן בְּאַהֲבַת הַתּוֹרָה כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַיֵּים, וְהוּא חִסָּרוֹן בְּאַהֲבָה דְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ, לָכֵן עָנְשׁוֹ בַּנֶּפֶשׁ וּבְמִיתָה.
connections.quote: “One who fixes himself in a matter of halakhah: it was taught that Rabbi Yosei says, “Whoever says that he has no Torah has no Torah.” That is obvious! Rather: “Whoever says that he has only Torah has only Torah.” This too is obvious! Rather, he does not have even Torah. Why? Rav Pappa said: Scripture says, “You shall learn and you shall do”—whoever participates in doing participates in learning; whoever does not participate in doing does not participate in learning. Alternatively, it is as you said at first: whoever says that he has only Torah has only Torah. This is needed where he teaches others and they go and act. One might have thought that he receives their reward; it teaches us otherwise.”
connections.context: The Gemara’s principal reading makes action integral to learning. It also records a second reading, concerning a teacher who does not himself act and cannot claim the reward for his pupils’ actions; both readings are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָצִינוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (י.) בְּחִזְקִיָּהוּ גַּם כֵּן: "מֵת תָּמוּת" עַל שֶׁלֹּא קִיֵּים פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה.
connections.quote: ‘He said to him: ‘Why such severity?’ He answered: ‘Because you did not engage in procreation.’ He said to him: ‘That is because I saw through the holy spirit that unworthy children would descend from me.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר פְּקוּדֵי (רנד עַמּוּד ב) דְּהוּא אִדְבַּק בְּעָפָר, וְיָדוּעַ דְּרַע שֶׁבִּיסוֹד הֶעָפָר הוּא הָעַצְלוּת בְּקִיּוּם הַמִּצְווֹת.
connections.quote: “In this manner we learned: Four entered Pardes, and all were tested at this place, in these four elements. Each became attached to his place: one to the side of fire, one to water, one to air, and one to earth. All sank in their element as they entered, except for that perfect, pious one, who came from the right side, clung to the right, and ascended above. When he reached the place called the Palace of Love, he clung to it with the will of his heart. He said: This palace must be joined to the palace above through great love. Then he became complete in the mystery of faith; he ascended and properly completed lesser love with great love. Therefore he died in love, and his soul departed with the verse “You shall love.” Happy is his portion! All the others descended below, each one, and were punished in the element into which they descended. Elisha descended on the left side, which is fire; he descended into it and did not ascend, encountering the other side called “another god.” Repentance was withheld from him, and he was expelled because he clung to it; therefore he is called Aḥer, as we have explained. Ben Azzai descended into the element of earth; before reaching the burning of earth that extends to the other side, he sank in that earth and died. Of this it is written, “Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones.” Ben Zoma descended into the element of air and encountered another spirit reaching the side of impurity, called an evil affliction. It therefore struck him, and he did not become settled. None of them escaped punishment. Of this Solomon said, “There is a vanity that occurs upon the earth: there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked,” because these descended into these levels and were punished.”
connections.context: The Zohar assigns the three unsuccessful entrants to distinct elements and contrasts them with Rabbi Akiva’s ascent through love. Its account of his later death in love is distinct from his safe departure from Pardes.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחֵר אִדְבַּק בְּאֵשׁ, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ הַכַּעַס נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב אֵשׁ, וְכֵן הַתַּאֲוָה בְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (קִדּוּשִׁין פא.): חֲזֵי דְּאַתְּ נוּרָא.
connections.quote: ‘When he reached halfway up the ladder, he braced himself with his legs spread and cried out: ‘Fire in Amram’s house!’ The Rabbis came and said to him: ‘You have embarrassed us.’ He answered: ‘Better that you should be ashamed of Amram’s house in this world than be ashamed on his account in the World to Come.’ He adjured [the evil inclination] to leave him. It came out of him like a pillar of fire. He said to it: ‘See, you are fire and I am flesh, yet I am stronger than you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶן זוֹמָא בְּרוּחַ, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ בָּא לֵיצָנוּת וְהִתְפָּאֲרוּת.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים א׳:ט״ו
connections.quote: “The explanation is based on what Rabbi Ḥayyim Vital wrote in Shaar HaKedushah, and in Etz Ḥayyim, gate 50, chapter 2: every person of Israel, righteous or wicked, has two souls, as it is written, “Souls I have made.” These are two animating souls. One is from the kelippah and the other side; it clothes itself in a person’s blood to give life to the body, as it is written, “The life of the flesh is in the blood.” From it come all the bad traits, from the four bad elements within it: anger and pride from fire, which rises upward; desire for pleasures from water, for water causes every kind of pleasure to grow; frivolity, mockery, self-glorification, and idle talk from air; and laziness and sadness from earth.”
connections.context: Tanya provides the explicit correspondence between elements and character traits that Rav Tzadok invokes here. It speaks of the negative traits of the animal soul, rather than defining every use of these elements as evil.

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲגַם דְּאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה הַכֹּל קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר בִּבְרָכוֹת (נח.): וּבָרָא כָּל אֵלּוּ לְשַׁמְּשֵׁנִי, וְהוּא לְשִׁיטָתוֹ (שָׁם ו:): כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ לְצַוֶּות לָזֶה, וְכָךְ הוּא הָאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai, and some say Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma, says: The whole world was created only to be a companion to this one.”
connections.context: “This one” is the person described in Ecclesiastes 12:13, who fears God and keeps His commandments.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּחֲגִיגָה (יד:): שָׁאֲלוּ אֶת בֶּן זוֹמָא: מַהוּ לְסָרוֹסֵי כַּלְבָּא, שֶׁהוּא אִם לֹא נִתְלוֹצֵץ מִבְּרִיָּה הַיּוֹתֵר פְּחוּתָה שֶׁבַּבְּרִיּוֹת, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
connections.quote: “They asked Ben Zoma: ‘What is the law concerning castrating a dog?’ He said to them: ‘‘In your land you shall not do this’—do not do this to any creature in your land.’ They asked Ben Zoma: ‘A virgin who became pregnant—what is her status regarding the High Priest? Do we take account of Shmuel’s statement, for Shmuel said, ‘I can have intercourse several times without blood’? Or is Shmuel’s case uncommon?’ He said to them: ‘Shmuel’s case is uncommon, and we take account of the possibility that she became pregnant in a bath.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּחֲגִיגָה (יד:): שָׁאֲלוּ אֶת בֶּן זוֹמָא: מַהוּ לְסָרוֹסֵי כַּלְבָּא, שֶׁהוּא אִם לֹא נִתְלוֹצֵץ מִבְּרִיָּה הַיּוֹתֵר פְּחוּתָה שֶׁבַּבְּרִיּוֹת, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Emor 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Emor 4
connections.quote: ““In your land you shall not do this”: this means not to mock the creatures of the Holy One, blessed be He. The Gemara in Ḥagigah derives from this that castration is forbidden, and this signifies the prohibition against mockery. As stated there, they asked Ben Zoma: May one castrate a dog? He answered: “In your land you shall not do this”—do not do this to anything in your land. They also asked whether a virgin who became pregnant was permitted to a High Priest: should one be concerned about Shmuel’s case? He answered that Shmuel’s case was uncommon. They asked these questions because they saw that he had not descended in peace—as the Gemara says, he looked and was stricken—and understood that his apprehension was incomplete and that he had erred in something. Their first question tested whether he lightly regarded mocking God’s creatures. They asked about castrating a dog, the lowliest creature, to see whether nullifying its existence seemed trivial to him. He answered that it was forbidden: one must not mock it, for it is a creature of the blessed God. Then they asked whether his error lay in the opposite direction, attributing to created beings more power than they possess. This was the question about a pregnant virgin and the High Priest: the High Priest is the greatest of created beings, and perhaps he had overestimated the power of his existence. He answered that Shmuel’s case was uncommon: one should not ascribe to him greater existence than he possesses, or impose more stringency upon him than is fitting; since Shmuel’s case is uncommon, she is permitted to him. In truth, his principal error was apprehending a great distinction between the lower and upper waters, although only a hair’s breadth—the separating firmament—stands between them. Both are God’s creations, and one must receive them according to His will. This was the meaning of the lamb accompanying the omer, whose meal offering was doubled to two tenths, corresponding to the upper and lower waters, while the lamb alludes to the separating firmament. [Supplement:] As the Gemara says, he stated that only three fingerbreadths separate the lower and upper waters, and they said, “Ben Zoma is still outside.” This means that he apprehended a great separation between evil desire and good desire.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer reads the questions as tests of Ben Zoma’s attitude toward creation. The complete passage preserves both tests and his actual error; it does not say that his answer about the dog was mistaken.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ עָלָיו: "פֶּן תִּשְׂבָּעֶנּוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי כה, טז), שֶׁקִּבֵּל יוֹתֵר מֵהָרָאוּי.
connections.quote: ‘If you find honey, eat just enough, lest you gorge on it and vomit it up.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ עָלָיו: "פֶּן תִּשְׂבָּעֶנּוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי כה, טז), שֶׁקִּבֵּל יוֹתֵר מֵהָרָאוּי.
connections.quote: “"His cup" corresponds to the perfection of Wisdom, for drunkenness removes Da'at, rendering a person like a simpleton (Eruvin 65a). Matching Avot (3:17): "Anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds... is uprooted," for excessive theory is not true wisdom, matching Proverbs (25:16): "If you find honey, eat only what is sufficient, lest you become sated and vomit it."
