For excess regurgitates even what was previously internalized, matching: "Give me neither poverty nor riches" (Proverbs 30:8)—meaning excessive intellectual wealth that detaches from reality uproots everything. So too with wine in Berakhot (57a): "There is one who drinks it and it is good for him, and one who drinks it and it is bad for him," for Torah is likened to wine (life for those on the right, poison for those on the left). In moderation, "wine and fragrance sharpen the mind" (Yoma 76b), adding wisdom; but in excess, it removes wisdom and uproots a person entirely. And perfection in Wisdom is that one does not become intoxicated, matching: "Who is wise? He who knows his place" and his true spiritual stature, never overreaching beyond his bounds.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek uses the same warning about eating too much honey to explain wisdom pursued beyond one’s proper measure. It defines the wise person here as one who knows his place and level. This adds a needed distinction to the present siman: intensity of love is not the whole of spiritual readiness; wisdom also includes receiving an attainment in a form that one can sustain.
connections.headline: Receiving wisdom in the measure one can sustain

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת חָכְמָתוֹ מֻפְלֶגֶת מִכָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, שֶׁמִּצַּד זֶה נִמְשַׁךְ הִתְפָּאֲרוּת נֶגֶד הַכֹּל כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּזְכַרְיָה: רָאָה עַצְמוֹ לְמַעְלָה וְכוּלֵי (קֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה י), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (נז:): בֶּן זוֹמָא יְצַפֶּה לְחָכְמָה, וּלְכָךְ עָנְשׁוֹ "נִפְגַּע", שֶׁהוּא הֶעְדֵּר הַחָכְמָה.
connections.quote: ““If the spirit of the ruler comes upon you, do not forsake your place, as in its abating he will pardon great sins” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). “If the spirit of the ruler comes upon you, do not forsake your place” – when dominion comes to you, do not forsake your attribute of humility, to teach you that anyone who forsakes his humility causes death to his world and sin to his generation. From whom do you learn this? From Zekharia, as it is stated: “The spirit of God clothed Zekharia….and he stood above the people” (II Chronicles 24:20). Did he, in fact, walk above the people? It is, rather, that he considered himself greater than all the people; son-in-law of the king, priest, prophet, and judge. He began speaking arrogantly to the people, and saying to them: “Why are you violating the mitzvot of the Lord so that you will not succeed?” (II Chronicles 24:20). Immediately, “they conspired against him and stoned him with stones at the command of the king [in the courtyard of the house of the Lord]” (II Chronicles 24:21). Rabbi Yudan asked Rabbi Aḥa: Where did they kill Zekharia, in the Israelite Courtyard or in the Women’s Courtyard? [Rabbi Aḥa] said to him: Neither in the Israelite Courtyard nor in the Women’s Courtyard, but rather in the Priests’ Courtyard. They did not treat his blood like the blood of a gazelle or the blood of a deer. Regarding the blood of a gazelle and a deer whose blood has been spilled, it is written: “You shall spill its blood and cover it with dirt” (Leviticus 17:13), but this righteous one [Zekharia], they did not treat his blood like the blood of a gazelle and not like the blood of a deer. Why [did God allow them to be wicked] to such an extent? It was “to arouse fury and to take vengeance” (Ezekiel 24:8). You find that when Nevuzaradan ascended to destroy Jerusalem, the Holy One blessed be He indicated to that blood that it should seethe. He said to it: This is the time that you will collect your debt. [Nevuzaradan] said to them: ‘What is the nature of this blood?’ They said to him: ‘It is the blood of bulls, rams, and sheep that we were sacrificing to the Holy One blessed be He.’ Immediately, he brought bulls, rams, and sheep and slaughtered many of them onto it, but it did not stop. He said to them: ‘If you tell me, fine. But if not, I will comb the flesh of these people with a comb of iron,’ but [at first] they did not say. Once he [again] said to them that [their explanation] was not [true], they said to him: ‘Why should we conceal it from you? We had a prophet, a priest, who would reprimand us in the name of Heaven. [He said to us]: Accept it, but we did not accept it from him. Rather, we rose against him and killed him.’ [Nevuzaradan] said to them: ‘I will assuage it.’ He then brought the Great Sanhedrin and slaughtered them onto it, but it did not rest. He slaughtered the lesser Sanhedrin onto it, but it did not rest. He brought young priests and slaughtered them onto it, but it did not rest. He slaughtered schoolchildren onto it, but it did not rest. He said to [the seething blood]: ‘Zekharia, I have eliminated the best of your people. Would you like all of them to be eliminated?’ Immediately, it rested. That wicked one contemplated repentance, and said: ‘One who eliminates a single Israelite soul, it is written in his regard: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, his blood will be spilled by man” (Genesis 9:6); this man who eliminated many souls, all the more so.’ At that moment, the Holy One blessed be He became filled with mercy, and He intimated to the blood, and it was absorbed in its place. Rabbi Yudan said: [The Israelites] performed seven transgressions [via one act] on that day: They killed a priest, a prophet, and a judge, they spilled innocent blood, they impurified the Temple Courtyard, and it was Shabbat and Yom Kippur. But Yaḥaziyel did not do so; rather, “Yaḥaziyel, son of Zekharia, son of Benaya, son of Yaḥaziyel, son of Matanya the Levite, from the sons of Asaf, the spirit of the Lord was upon him in the midst of the assembly” (II Chronicles 20:14). What is “in the midst of the assembly”? It is that he likened himself to the assembly. Another matter: “If the spirit of the ruler comes upon you,” is speaking of Noah. He entered the ark with permission and he emerged with permission. From where [is it derived] that he entered with permission? [It is from the verse:] “Come you and all your household to the ark” (Genesis 7:1). From where [is it derived] that he emerged with permission? [It is from the verse:] “Go out of the ark, you …” (Genesis 8:16). Another matter: “If the spirit of the ruler comes upon you,” is speaking of Joshua. Just as the Israelites crossed the Jordan with permission, so too they emerged only with permission. From where [is it derived that] they crossed with permission? As it is stated: “Pass through the midst of the camp…[in another three days you are crossing this Jordan]” (Joshua 1:11). They emerged with permission, as it is stated: “Joshua commanded the priests saying: Emerge from the Jordan” (Joshua 4:17). Another matter: “If the spirit of the ruler…” is speaking of David. Before he reigned, “David is the youngest” (I Samuel 17:14). When he reigned, “King David stood on his feet [and said: Hear me my brethren]” (I Chronicles 28:2). Another matter: “If the spirit of the ruler…” is speaking of Mordekhai. Before prominence came to him, “Mordekhai was sitting at the king’s gate” (Esther 2:19). When prominence came to him, “Mordekhai returned to the king’s gate” (Esther 6:12).”

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת חָכְמָתוֹ מֻפְלֶגֶת מִכָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, שֶׁמִּצַּד זֶה נִמְשַׁךְ הִתְפָּאֲרוּת נֶגֶד הַכֹּל כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּזְכַרְיָה: רָאָה עַצְמוֹ לְמַעְלָה וְכוּלֵי (קֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה י), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (נז:): בֶּן זוֹמָא יְצַפֶּה לְחָכְמָה, וּלְכָךְ עָנְשׁוֹ "נִפְגַּע", שֶׁהוּא הֶעְדֵּר הַחָכְמָה.
connections.quote: ‘Three Torah scholars: One who sees Ben Azzai in a dream should expect piety; Ben Zoma, he should expect wisdom; Acher, he should fear calamity.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִי שֶׁהַפְּגָם בְּאַהֲבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַנִּפְגָּע וְיוֹצֵא מִדַּעַת הוּא מוּבְדָּל מֵאַהֲבַת רֵעִים, וְאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא קַמָּא פז.): חֵרֵשׁ, שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן פְּגִיעָתָן רָעָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘An encounter involving a person who is deaf and unable to speak, a person of unsound mind, or a minor can be harmful: someone who injures them is liable, but if they injure others, they are exempt.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר בְּיַלְדוּתוֹ שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, לט עַמּוּד א).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yonatan said: He wrote Song of Songs first, then Proverbs, and afterward Ecclesiastes. Rabbi Yonatan brought a proof from ordinary life: When a person is young, he speaks words of song; when he matures, words of parables; when he grows old, words of futility.”
connections.context: The Midrash records several opinions about the order of Solomon’s books. Rav Tzadok adopts Rabbi Yonatan’s account, which places Song of Songs in youth; it should not be presented as the only opinion in the passage.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר בְּיַלְדוּתוֹ שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, לט עַמּוּד א).
connections.quote: “It was taught: His names are called according to wisdom, and therefore he composed three books—Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, and Proverbs—all to complete wisdom. Song of Songs corresponds to Chesed; Ecclesiastes corresponds to judgment; Proverbs corresponds to mercy.”
connections.context: This Zohar passage supplies the spiritual association of Song of Songs with Chesed, love and kindness. The claim that Solomon composed it in his youth is Rabbi Yonatan’s interpretation in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:1:10, quoted in the neighboring note. The two sources illuminate different parts of Rav Tzadok’s discussion; this Zohar passage does not itself state Solomon’s age.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אַבְרָהָם שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:): "לֹא בְּסָבָא טַעְמָא וְלֹא בְּדַרְדְּקֵי עֵצָה"
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘For You are our Father, for Abraham does not know us and Israel does not recognize us; You, Hashem, are our Father; Our Redeemer from everlasting is Your name’? In the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will say to Abraham: ‘Your children have sinned against Me.’ He will say before Him: ‘Master of the universe, let them be blotted out for the sanctification of Your name.’ He will say: ‘I will tell Jacob, who suffered the hardship of raising children; perhaps he will plead for mercy for them.’ He will say to him: ‘Your children have sinned.’ He will say before Him: ‘Master of the universe, let them be blotted out for the sanctification of Your name.’ He will say: ‘There is no discernment among the elders and no counsel among the young.’ He will say to Isaac: ‘Your children have sinned against Me.’ He will say before Him: ‘Master of the universe, are they my children and not Your children? When they put ‘We will do’ before ‘We will hear’ before You, You called them ‘My son, My firstborn.’ Now are they my children and not Your children?’”

connections.hePhrase: "דַּרְדְּקֵי" הוּא אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ שֶׁהָיָה הַהַתְחָלָה וְהַיַּלְדוּת, וְ"סָבָא" – יַעֲקֹב.
connections.quote: “This was the root of our father Abraham’s soul: the first beginning of holiness, the aspect of loving kindness. As we heard from the holy master, of blessed memory, in his explanation of “There is no understanding among the elders, and no counsel among the children”: the elder is our father Jacob, in whom holiness had already matured and become threefold; “the children” refers to our father Abraham, who was the beginning of holiness, as in the days of youth.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok records the same teaching elsewhere, explicitly identifying Abraham with the beginning of holiness and Jacob with its mature, threefold development.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹהֵב הָאָדָם בַּיַּלְדוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי נַעַר יִשְׂרָאֵל וָאֹהֲבֵהוּ" (הוֹשֵׁעַ יא, א).
connections.quote: ‘When Israel was a child, I loved him, and from Egypt I called My son.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ סֵדֶר שֶׁל שְׁלֹשָׁה אָבוֹת וְכֵן שְׁלֹשָׁה רְגָלִים כְּסִדְרָן.
connections.quote: “I heard a reason for this from my brother Rabbi Yehudah: the festivals were established corresponding to the patriarchs. Passover corresponds to Abraham, as it says, “Knead and make cakes,” and it was Passover. Shavuot corresponds to Isaac, for the shofar blast at the giving of the Torah was with the horn of Isaac’s ram. Sukkot corresponds to Jacob, as it says, “For his livestock he made booths.””
connections.context: The Tur supplies the precise sequence of the three festivals and patriarchs used here. His larger discussion concerns the festivals and Rosh Ḥodesh; this is the complete unit concerning the three pilgrimage festivals.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּהוּא כְּמוֹ פֵּירוּשׁ עַל הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁכָּל הַתַּרְיַ"ג מִצְווֹת מַעֲשִׂיּוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה – טַעְמָן וּרְמִיזָתָן בַּלֵּב כְּלָלָן שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁלֵי.

connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 6
connections.quote: “Moses our teacher embodied the wisdom of all Israel, and all his power lay in this: the mind and thought, with the blessed God always before him. Therefore the Torah speaks chiefly of actual deeds, so that action too should be as purified as thought. For this Moses made the Tabernacle, whose place was in the human form, in the depth of the heart, and which could be dismantled and carried elsewhere. Solomon’s wisdom, however, lay in actions; therefore he built the chosen House in a fixed place. The book of Proverbs that he composed speaks chiefly of the uprightness of the heart and thought, that they should be established as firmly as action.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer contrasts the Torah’s direction of practical action with Proverbs’ direction of the heart. This is the parallel behind Rav Tzadok’s report that Proverbs unfolds the inner meaning of the commandments.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּלָכֵן קוֹרִין אוֹתוֹ בְּסֻכּוֹת, לֹא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמַּהְבִּיל שִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִקַּח תֹּקֶף וְעִיקַּר הַשִּׂמְחָה הָאֲמִיתִּית עַל יְדֵי הַהַבְלָת כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה: "רַק זֶה חֶלְקִי וְכוּלֵי", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
connections.quote: see note 2825.
connections.context: The wording “this was my portion” is in 2:10. Ecclesiastes 3:22 offers a related teaching but says “that is his portion.” Rav Tzadok invokes the surviving portion of joy while considering the book’s dismissal of worldly pursuits.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּלָכֵן קוֹרִין אוֹתוֹ בְּסֻכּוֹת, לֹא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמַּהְבִּיל שִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִקַּח תֹּקֶף וְעִיקַּר הַשִּׂמְחָה הָאֲמִיתִּית עַל יְדֵי הַהַבְלָת כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה: "רַק זֶה חֶלְקִי וְכוּלֵי", וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.

connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ספר בראשית, חיי שרה ג׳
connections.quote: ““Abraham was old, advanced in days, and God had blessed Abraham in everything.” It is written (Ecclesiastes 2:10), “This was my portion from all my labor.” The Gemara states (Sanhedrin 20b): Rav and Shmuel—one said, his staff; the other said, his pitcher. Certainly King Solomon, peace be upon him, was not lamenting, Heaven forbid, the loss of this world’s pleasures, for all of these counted as nothing to him. Rather, he took pride in himself and said that although it appeared that everything had been taken from him, the essence of all the life of this world nevertheless remained with him. These two things contain the essence of all the life of this world. This is what he meant by “This was my portion from all my labor.” One said, his staff: a staff alludes to life, meaning that the power of life remained with him. We find that a staff alludes to life, as it is written (Zechariah 8:4), “Each man with his staff in his hand.” The other said, his pitcher: his pitcher is a vessel for receiving, meaning that he was still ready and yearning for more. This was his delight, for this is the essential thing in the life of this world. This is the meaning of the verse, “Abraham was old, advanced in days”: he had reached the roots of life, and he was a vessel ready to receive and yearning for ever greater additions of life from God.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַסֵּדֶר הַזֶּה הוּא מִצַּד הַשְּׁלֵימוּת הָרָאוּי, אֲבָל מִצַּד הַחֹמֶר וְשֶׁהָאָדָם בַּעַל חִסָּרוֹן וְצָרִיךְ לְהַגְדָּרָה – הַיִּרְאָה קוֹדֶמֶת, כַּיָּדוּעַ בְּכָל מָקוֹם הַסֵּדֶר "דְּחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ", דְּ"סוּר מֵרָע" וְאַחַר כָּךְ "עֲשֵׂה טוֹב" (תְּהִלִּים לד, טו).
connections.quote: ‘Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַסֵּדֶר הַזֶּה הוּא מִצַּד הַשְּׁלֵימוּת הָרָאוּי, אֲבָל מִצַּד הַחֹמֶר וְשֶׁהָאָדָם בַּעַל חִסָּרוֹן וְצָרִיךְ לְהַגְדָּרָה – הַיִּרְאָה קוֹדֶמֶת, כַּיָּדוּעַ בְּכָל מָקוֹם הַסֵּדֶר "דְּחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ", דְּ"סוּר מֵרָע" וְאַחַר כָּךְ "עֲשֵׂה טוֹב" (תְּהִלִּים לד, טו).
connections.quote: “Therefore, from the standpoint of Israel’s service, which is an awakening from below, fear comes first. From the standpoint of His attributes, however, love is known to come first, as it says, “Yours, Lord, are greatness and might”—greatness precedes. Likewise with the patriarchs, who are the divine chariot: “Abraham fathered Isaac.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly distinguishes the order of individual service from the order of divine initiative. That distinction explains why this section first presents love before fear and then requires fear before love.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הֵם כְּלוּלִים זֶה בָּזֶה, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֵינָם שְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם עֲדַיִן, כִּי אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָא "גַּדְפִין" בַּזֹּהַר, כִּי יַעֲקֹב גּוּפָא וְאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה דְּרוֹעִין.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים מ׳:י״ב-י״ד
connections.quote: “Just as a bird’s wings are not its essence, and its life does not depend on them at all—as we learned, “If its wings were removed, it is kosher”—its head and entire body are the principal thing, and its wings only serve the head and body by enabling flight. So, by analogy, Torah and commandments are the essence of the supernal union, through the revelation of the higher will disclosed by them; fear and love raise them to the place where the will, the blessed Infinite Light, and the union are revealed, namely Yetzirah and Beriah. [Gloss:] Or even into the ten holy sefirot of Asiyah, the place of practical commandments, and likewise Scripture. In Mishnah, however, the union and the blessed Infinite Light are revealed in Yetzirah, and in Talmud in Beriah. Through studying Scripture, the union and the Infinite Light extend from Atzilut to Asiyah; through Mishnah, only to Yetzirah; and through Talmud, only to Beriah—for all are in Atzilut. Kabbalah, however, does not extend from Atzilut into Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah at all, as stated in Peri Etz Ḥayyim. Although fear and love themselves are among the 613 commandments, they are nevertheless called “wings,” because the purpose of love is service from love. Love without service is “love in delights,” delighting in God as a foretaste of the World to Come and the receiving of reward; but it is written, “Today, to perform them,” and tomorrow to receive their reward.”
connections.context: Tanya explains why love and fear serve the fuller life of Torah and action as wings serve a bird. The concluding qualification is essential: love and fear are themselves commandments, even while they function as means of ascent.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הֵם כְּלוּלִים זֶה בָּזֶה, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֵינָם שְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם עֲדַיִן, כִּי אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָא "גַּדְפִין" בַּזֹּהַר, כִּי יַעֲקֹב גּוּפָא וְאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה דְּרוֹעִין.
connections.quote: “He said to him: Certainly, the body and the two arms correspond to the patriarchs. The head corresponds to the first Adam; the right arm to Abraham; the left arm to Isaac; and the body to Jacob.”
connections.context: This passage in Raaya Meheimna supplies the explicit bodily arrangement. Rav Tzadok uses Abraham’s love and Isaac’s fear as the arms serving the whole represented by Jacob.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הֵם כְּלוּלִים זֶה בָּזֶה, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֵינָם שְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם עֲדַיִן, כִּי אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָא "גַּדְפִין" בַּזֹּהַר, כִּי יַעֲקֹב גּוּפָא וְאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה דְּרוֹעִין.
connections.quote: “Mikdash means a place of holiness: it is the opposite of Mishkan, for holiness means distinction and separation, while dwelling means being present and joined, without separation, as it says, ‘Who dwells with them amid their impurities’ (Yoma 56b). Holiness, by contrast, separates from impurity. Yet we find Mishkan called Mikdash and Mikdash called Mishkan (beginning of Eruvin): all is one, and both are true together. The Holy One dwells within Israel and is also distinct from them. As Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah says (beginning of chapter 3), ‘I feared from within my joy and rejoiced from within my fear.’ Joy between companions proceeds from love and connection; awe proceeds from respect for someone greater and distinct. With Hashem both are together, and neither suffices without the other. Awe alone brings folly, as in ‘Is not your fear your folly?’ Joy alone brings levity. Of this the Sages said (Shabbat 31a), ‘Better that you had not brought it up,’ for Torah is called ‘rejoicing the heart,’ and through it one connects with Hashem.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla interprets Mishkan and Mikdash as connection and separation, two aspects that remain true together. It uses the same combination of joy and awe and warns against either isolated extreme. This develops the siman's distinction between an ideal order and the practical balancing required by a person's present deficiencies.
connections.headline: Connection together with awe

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עִיקַּר צוּרַת הָאָדָם הִיא הַדֵּעָה שְׁלֵימָה וְקַו הָאֶמְצָעִי, וְהוּא לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ בְּלֵבָב שָׁלֵם הָאָמוּר אַחַר אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה.

connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 4:8

connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות יסודי התורה ד׳:ח׳
connections.quote: “The soul of every living body is the form that God gave it. The additional knowledge found in the human soul is the form of a human being perfected in knowledge. Concerning this form the Torah says, “Let us make a human in Our image, according to Our likeness”: that he should possess a form that knows and apprehends intelligible things without material substance, like the angels, who are form without matter, so that he resembles them. This does not refer to the form visible to the eyes—the mouth, nose, jaws, and the other bodily features—which is called physical appearance. Nor is it the soul found in every living being, through which it eats, drinks, reproduces, perceives, and thinks. Rather, it is the knowledge that is the form of the soul; concerning the form of the soul Scripture says, “In Our image, according to Our likeness.” This form is often called nefesh or ruaḥ. Therefore one must be careful with these names to avoid error; each term must be understood from its context.”
connections.context: Maimonides supplies the philosophical meaning of human “form” as knowledge, while distinguishing it from bodily shape and from the ordinary life powers of a living creature.

connections.quote: “May He open our heart to His Torah, and set in our heart love of Him and fear of Him, to do His will and to serve Him with a whole heart.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צוּרַת יַעֲקֹב חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “It was taught: They ascend and gaze at his image above, and descend and gaze at his image below.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צוּרַת יַעֲקֹב חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “‘Israel, in whom I will be glorified’ (Isaiah 49:3)—you are the one whose image is engraved above.”
connections.context: The angels of Jacob’s ladder are meant. Rashi on Chullin explains that the image above is the human face among the four living creatures of the Chariot, in the likeness of Jacob.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צוּרַת יַעֲקֹב חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Our father Jacob is the ultimate perfection of the human form that the blessed God fashioned in His world. Therefore his form is engraved on the Throne of Glory: it is the “likeness with the appearance of a human” upon the throne, for he is the Lord’s portion and is attached to the name Havayah, blessed be His name, as is known.”
connections.context: This exact parallel links Jacob’s complete human form, its engraving on the throne, and his attachment to the divine name.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ צוּרַת יַעֲקֹב חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “The third stage is named when a person returns through his service to the first kindness. Although the Zohar says that Torah issues from the side of severity, this concerns the stage before he breaks through the concealment. Then Hashem's light and the concealment appear to him as opposites. Afterward he truly sees that all is through His kindness: the concealment too exists because Hashem abounds in kindness and wanted the person to have a share in the service he performs. He therefore concealed that kindness so there would be room for service. This is then called threefold Torah.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the third dimension as a return, through one's work, to the first kindness. The intervening severity had seemed to oppose the light, but the completed understanding sees why concealment allowed meaningful service. This clarifies the siman's final distinction: love and awe are necessary powers of service, while the complete human form is a settled direction toward Hashem's will that can hold them together.
connections.headline: The third stage discloses the unity of the earlier stages

connections.hePhrase: כִּי זֶה כָּל הָאָדָם: לִהְיוֹת נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר אֲמִיתַּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּלִי שׁוּם מָסָךְ וּמוֹנֵעַ;
connections.quote: “The end of the matter, when all has been heard: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ: יוֹשֵׁב בָּטֵל כְּיָשֵׁן דָּמֵי, שֶׁהוּא אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בְּמִיתָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:) בְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת, דְּמִיתָה הַיְינוּ מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם יח:): רְשָׁעִים בְּחַיֵּיהֶם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: see note 136 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This comment is about the custom of sleeping on Rosh HaShanah. Its final comparison supplies a precise parallel for Rav Tzadok’s analogy between waking idleness and sleep; its qualifications concerning actual sleep are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ: יוֹשֵׁב בָּטֵל כְּיָשֵׁן דָּמֵי, שֶׁהוּא אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בְּמִיתָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:) בְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת, דְּמִיתָה הַיְינוּ מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם יח:): רְשָׁעִים בְּחַיֵּיהֶם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘‘Five, six, and ten’ is a mnemonic. Five things are one sixtieth of something else. These are they: fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and a dream. Fire is one sixtieth of Gehinnom. Honey is one sixtieth of the manna. Shabbat is one sixtieth of the World to Come. Sleep is one sixtieth of death. A dream is one sixtieth of prophecy.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ: יוֹשֵׁב בָּטֵל כְּיָשֵׁן דָּמֵי, שֶׁהוּא אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בְּמִיתָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:) בְּאוֹתוֹ עֵת, דְּמִיתָה הַיְינוּ מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם יח:): רְשָׁעִים בְּחַיֵּיהֶם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““The dead know nothing”: these are the wicked, who are called dead during their lives, as it says, “And you, slain wicked prince of Israel.” Alternatively, it is from here: “By the testimony of two witnesses or three witnesses the dead one shall be put to death.” But he is alive! Rather, he is already called dead.”
connections.context: This is the original aggadic description cited alongside the saying that sleep is one sixtieth of death. The two sayings are distinct sources.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ: חֲלוֹם אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בִּנְבוּאָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:), כִּי בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם, יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב, הַנִּסְתָּרוֹת שֶׁהֵם חַבַּ"ד בְּהֶעְלֵמָן, לֹא מִצַּד גִּלּוּיָן לַפּוֹעַל, הֵם לַה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ עַל יְדֵי מוֹרָשָׁה מֵהָאָבוֹת שֶׁזִּכְּכוּם שְׁתֵּי כֹּחוֹת אֵלּוּ.
connections.quote: “You already know the actions of this imaginative faculty: recalling objects perceived by the senses, combining them, and the imitation natural to it. Its greatest and noblest activity occurs when the senses rest and cease their operations; then a measure of influence flows upon it in accordance with its preparedness. This is the cause of true dreams, and it is itself the cause of prophecy: the difference is one of more or less, not of kind. You know their statement that a dream is one sixtieth of prophecy. A numerical ratio does not apply to things differing in kind: it would be inappropriate to say that human perfection is so many times the perfection of a horse. They repeated this matter in Bereshit Rabbah, saying, “The fallen fruit of prophecy is a dream”—a marvelous comparison. Fallen fruit is the fruit itself, but it fell before attaining perfection and ripening. Likewise, the imaginative faculty’s action during sleep is its action during prophecy, though deficient and not brought to its full extent.”
connections.context: In Ibn Tibbon’s translation, Maimonides explains the shared faculty behind true dreams and prophecy. “One sixtieth” describes a relation in degree; it does not make every ordinary dream a reliable revelation.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ: חֲלוֹם אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בִּנְבוּאָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:), כִּי בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם, יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב, הַנִּסְתָּרוֹת שֶׁהֵם חַבַּ"ד בְּהֶעְלֵמָן, לֹא מִצַּד גִּלּוּיָן לַפּוֹעַל, הֵם לַה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ עַל יְדֵי מוֹרָשָׁה מֵהָאָבוֹת שֶׁזִּכְּכוּם שְׁתֵּי כֹּחוֹת אֵלּוּ.
connections.quote: see note 1687 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The final comparison, a dream as one-sixtieth of prophecy, is the exact statement Rav Tzadok uses in his account of concealed spiritual faculties.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ: חֲלוֹם אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בִּנְבוּאָה (בְּרָכוֹת נז:), כִּי בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם, יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב, הַנִּסְתָּרוֹת שֶׁהֵם חַבַּ"ד בְּהֶעְלֵמָן, לֹא מִצַּד גִּלּוּיָן לַפּוֹעַל, הֵם לַה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ עַל יְדֵי מוֹרָשָׁה מֵהָאָבוֹת שֶׁזִּכְּכוּם שְׁתֵּי כֹּחוֹת אֵלּוּ.
connections.quote: “The hidden things belong to Hashem our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת בְּטֵלִים דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, מֵאַחַר שֶׁנּוֹבְעִים מֵחַבַּ"ד שֶׁבּוֹ, הֲרֵי יֵשׁ לָהֶם פִּתְרוֹן מַמָּשִׁי וַאֲמִיתִּי עַל הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁהֵן נוֹבְעִים, אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּתְלַבְּשׁוּ בְּדִבְרֵי בַּטָּלָה.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
connections.quote: see note 1689 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach extends the dream image to ordinary experience, using bread as its concrete example. Recognizing the divine word within it reveals a deeper life than the surface impression. This illustrates the siman's distinction between an image and the truth concealed within it. The siman's restrictions concerning who can discern such mixtures remain essential.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ פִּרְקֵי דִּשְׁטוּתָא הַנִּזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, מז עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁמֵּהֶם יְכוֹלִים לַעֲמוֹד עַל דִּבְרֵי חָכְמָה.
connections.quote: ‘This is what Rav Hamnuna the Elder would do: When the companions learned the mysteries of wisdom from him, he would set before them a chapter of foolish sayings, so that wisdom would benefit through it. This is what is written: ‘A little folly is more precious than wisdom and honor’ (Ecclesiastes 10:1), because it is the adornment of wisdom and the honor of wisdom. Therefore it is written: ‘My heart guiding itself with wisdom, and to take hold of folly.’ Rabbi Yosei said: ‘More precious than wisdom and honor’—that is, what brings splendor and beauty to wisdom and splendor to the honor above? ‘A little folly.’ A little foolishness displays and reveals the splendor of wisdom and the honor above more than all the ways of the world.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל עִיקָּרָהּ שֶׁל נְבוּאָה מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי, וְכֵן הוּא בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, כִּי הַנְּבוּאָה חָלוּק מֵהַחָכְמָה וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.), וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַמְדַמֶּה, וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן ו' מַדְרֵגוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר, וּבִכְלָלוּתָן ס'.
connections.quote: “Know that the truth and essence of prophecy is an influence flowing from God, blessed and exalted, through the Active Intellect, first upon the rational faculty and afterward upon the imaginative faculty. This is the highest of human levels and the ultimate perfection possible for the human species. It is the ultimate perfection of the imaginative faculty. It is in no way possible for every individual, nor is it attained through perfection in theoretical sciences and the improvement of character—even when both reach the highest possible goodness and excellence—unless these are joined by the greatest possible perfection of the imaginative faculty in one’s original constitution.”
connections.context: This is the chapter Rav Tzadok expressly cites. Maimonides makes imagination part of prophetic reception while retaining the requirements of intellectual, moral, and innate imaginative preparedness.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל עִיקָּרָהּ שֶׁל נְבוּאָה מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי, וְכֵן הוּא בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, כִּי הַנְּבוּאָה חָלוּק מֵהַחָכְמָה וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.), וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַמְדַמֶּה, וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן ו' מַדְרֵגוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר, וּבִכְלָלוּתָן ס'.
connections.heRef: חידושי רמב"ן על בבא בתרא י״ב א:א׳
connections.quote: see note 929 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Ramban distinguishes visionary prophecy from the sages’ apprehension through wisdom and holy inspiration. His explanation is more specific than the bare statement that a sage is superior to a prophet.

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל עִיקָּרָהּ שֶׁל נְבוּאָה מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי, וְכֵן הוּא בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, כִּי הַנְּבוּאָה חָלוּק מֵהַחָכְמָה וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.), וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַמְדַמֶּה, וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן ו' מַדְרֵגוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר, וּבִכְלָלוּתָן ס'.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa said: From the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to the Sages. Is a sage not also a prophet? This is what he meant: Although it was taken from the prophets, it was not taken from the Sages.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֲלוֹם שֶׁבְּעֵת הַשֵּׁינָה שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּיָדוֹ וּבְחִירָתוֹ לְנַקּוֹת הִרְהוּרָיו, וְכֵן הִרְהוּרֵי וְדִמְיוֹנוֹת כָּל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל זְמַן שֶׁהֵם דּוּגְמַת חֲלוֹם, הֵם אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים מֵאֲמִיתַּת הַמְדַמֶּה שֶׁהִיא נְבוּאָה.
connections.quote: “Sleep, which is one-sixtieth of death, can serve the same purpose: a person can attain in sleep what he could not possibly attain while awake. Thus it is written of the Ari that on one occasion he said he had received and attained in his sleep on Shabbat, concerning the portion of Balak, what he could not expound in eighty years. This accords with the Talmud’s saying that a dream is one-sixtieth of prophecy, and the Midrash’s saying that a dream is an offshoot of prophecy.”
connections.explanation: The report about the Ari illustrates why sleep need not be spiritual emptiness. Read with this siman, however, the possibility of hidden wisdom does not certify every dream or passing image. Tzidkat HaTzadik explicitly retains the mixture of idle material and explains the purity from personal desires required for interpretation. The two passages distinguish the presence of a hidden content from a person’s ability to identify that content faithfully.
connections.headline: An inward insight during sleep still requires discernment of its mixture

connections.hePhrase: כִּי גַּם בָּהֶם מְלוּבָּשׁ פִּתְרוֹן הָאֲמִיתִּי וּמְרוּמָּז חָכְמַת אֱמֶת הַנִּמְשָׁכוֹת מֵחַבַּ"ד שֶׁבְּמוֹחוֹ, אֶלָּא שֶׁמְּעוּרְבָּב בְּבַטָּלָה הַרְבֵּה, כְּעִנְיַן "אֵין חֲלוֹם בְּלֹא דְּבָרִים בְּטֵלִים" (בְּרָכוֹת נה.).
connections.quote: ‘‘The prophet who has a dream should tell a dream, and the one who has My word should speak My word truthfully. What has straw to do with grain, declares Hashem?’ What do grain and straw have to do with a dream? Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s name: Just as grain cannot be without straw, so a dream cannot be without meaningless details.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְלִקּוּטֵי תּוֹרָה פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב בֵּיאֵר עִנְיַן הַחֲלוֹם: מוֹחִין דְּגַדְלוּת שֶׁבְּתוֹךְ מוֹחִין דְּקַטְנוּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “We shall now explain the dreams of Pharaoh, the chief cupbearer, and the chief baker. You know the Sages’ statement that Joseph rejoiced in these dreams because they pointed to him; their entire meaning concerns Joseph’s exile and the redemption from Egypt. Understand this as follows: the mystery of the dream is the three expanded intellectual powers, represented by three names Havayah, whose numerical value equals ḥet-lamed-mem, “dream.” This is when they descend within the three names Elohim in the throat, represented by the three officials. You know that sleep occurs entirely in a state of diminished consciousness. The dream then comes from the expanded consciousness remaining within the diminished consciousness, where it is concealed. Therefore the dream is concealed and is explained only through the interpreter—Joseph, who is the Yesod of Zeir Anpin. All the higher lights gather there.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַמֵּבִין עַל זֶה לָדַעַת הַתּוֹכִיּוּת שֶׁבְּכָל הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת הוּא מִי שֶׁנָּקִי מִתַּאֲווֹת, כְּיוֹסֵף בְּתַאֲוַת נָשִׁים וְדָנִיֵּאל בְּתַאֲוַת אֲכִילָה – הֵם הָיוּ פּוֹתְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת;
connections.quote: “But Daniel resolved in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s food, nor with the wine that he drank.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה סוֹד הַעֲלָאַת מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת שֶׁבִּתְפִלָּה הַיָּדוּעַ בַּסְּפָרִים שֶׁאָמוּר לִגְדוֹלִים, הַיְינוּ לְשֶׁאֵין שְׁקוּעִים בְּתַאֲוָה, הֵם יְכוֹלִים לַעֲמוֹד עַל הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וּמוֹחִין דְּגַדְלוּת הַגְּנוּזִים בְּתוֹךְ מַחְשְׁבוֹת הֶבֶל שֶׁלּוֹ.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים כ״ח:א׳-ו׳
connections.quote: “Even if thoughts of desire or other alien thoughts fall upon a person while serving through Torah or attentive prayer, he should pay no attention to them, but immediately turn his attention away from them. Nor should he foolishly engage in elevating the traits within the alien thought. Those teachings were said only of righteous people, whose alien thoughts are not their own but come from others. But someone whose thoughts arise from his own evil, in the left chamber of his heart—how can he raise them above when he himself is bound below? Nevertheless, he should not become dejected and downcast during his service, which requires great joy. On the contrary, he should strengthen himself and add all his energy to the concentration of prayer with greater gladness and joy, considering that the alien thought comes from the kelippah in the left chamber, which struggles in the intermediate person against his divine soul. As is known of those who fight or wrestle, when one grows stronger the other strives with all his strength to prevail as well. Therefore, when the divine soul strengthens itself to pray, the kelippah also rises against it, to confuse it and cast it down with its alien thought. This is contrary to the common error of inferring from the arrival of an alien thought that one’s prayer is worthless, since proper prayer would supposedly exclude such thoughts. That would be true if one soul alone both prayed and produced the alien thoughts. In truth, however, there are two souls struggling in a person’s mind, each wishing to rule and fill the mind alone. Thoughts of Torah and fear of Heaven come from the divine soul, while worldly thoughts come from the animal soul, within which the divine soul is clothed.”
connections.context: The limitation to exceptional righteous people is explicit. The same passage also rejects discouragement and the inference that an unwanted thought proves the prayer worthless; these qualifications are part of the source’s meaning.

connections.hePhrase: [רד] הַנּוֹתֵן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל לִבּוֹ – מְבַטְּלִין מִמֶּנּוּ כָּל מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים, וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: כְּשֶׁאֵין נוֹתֵן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל לִבּוֹ – נוֹתְנִין לוֹ כָּל מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כ
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chananyah, deputy of the priests, says: Whoever places words of Torah upon his heart has thoughts of the sword, hunger, foolishness, sexual misconduct, the evil inclination, adultery, idle matters, and human burdens removed from him. For it is written through David king of Israel, “The precepts of Hashem are upright, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of Hashem is clear, enlightening the eyes.” Whoever does not place words of Torah upon his heart is given thoughts of the sword, hunger, foolishness, sexual misconduct, the evil inclination, adultery, idle matters, and human burdens. For it is written through Moses our teacher: “They shall be upon you as a sign and wonder, and upon your descendants forever, because you did not serve Hashem your God with joy and gladness of heart from abundance; you shall serve your enemies whom Hashem sends against you in hunger, thirst, nakedness, and lack of everything.””
connections.context: Both halves of the teaching are necessary: Torah placed upon the heart displaces distracting thoughts, while its absence leaves room for them. Rav Tzadok develops the phrase “upon his heart” into the difference between inwardly received Torah and merely external knowledge.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם חָשַׁב ח' מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים, וְהֵם נֶגֶד ח' מַדְרֵגוֹת מִבִּינָה עַד מַלְכוּת, דְּהַתְחָלַת הִרְהוּרִים זָרִים נוֹבְעִים מֵהַלֵּב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סא.) דְּיוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִכְנָס לַמּוֹחַ.
connections.quote: “As stated in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 20: whoever places words of Torah upon his heart has the various thoughts removed from him. It counts eight kinds of thoughts and concludes with the verse in Psalms: “The precepts of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.” Rescue from these eight thoughts alludes to Torah entering the innermost point of the heart, the aspect of Binah, “the heart, the eighth level.” All eight traits in the heart are purified, from Malkhut, the lower heh and the heart’s exterior, through Binah, the upper heh and its interior. This is alluded to in “gladdening the heart” and “enlightening the eyes.” Concerning contrary thoughts it says, “Do not stray after your heart and after your eyes,” and the Sages interpret the heart as thoughts of heresy and the eyes as thoughts of transgression: the eye sees and the heart desires. When Torah enters the depth of the heart, joy is born in it, and the eyes are illuminated to see His providence in everything: “Raise your eyes on high and see who created these.” Conversely, one who does not place Torah upon his heart receives all eight thoughts; the teaching concludes with “Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and a good heart.” The central aim is service in the innermost point of the heart, from which joy arises, redeeming one from all the thoughts that constrict and burden the soul. One reaches this particularly through the holiness of Shabbat, which commemorates the exodus from Egypt.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok gives a full parallel to the eightfold structure, including the link between Torah, the inner heart, the eyes, and joy. The source interprets the list spiritually rather than merely repeating it.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם חָשַׁב ח' מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים, וְהֵם נֶגֶד ח' מַדְרֵגוֹת מִבִּינָה עַד מַלְכוּת, דְּהַתְחָלַת הִרְהוּרִים זָרִים נוֹבְעִים מֵהַלֵּב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סא.) דְּיוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִכְנָס לַמּוֹחַ.
connections.quote: “And Hashem said in His heart: I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake, for the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם חָשַׁב ח' מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים, וְהֵם נֶגֶד ח' מַדְרֵגוֹת מִבִּינָה עַד מַלְכוּת, דְּהַתְחָלַת הִרְהוּרִים זָרִים נוֹבְעִים מֵהַלֵּב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סא.) דְּיוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִכְנָס לַמּוֹחַ.
connections.quote: ‘Rav said: The evil inclination resembles a fly and sits between the two entrances of the heart, as it is said: ‘Dead flies make a perfumer’s oil stink and bubble.’ Shmuel said: It resembles a grain of wheat, chittah, as it is said: ‘Sin, chatta’t, crouches at the entrance.’’

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם חָשַׁב ח' מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים, וְהֵם נֶגֶד ח' מַדְרֵגוֹת מִבִּינָה עַד מַלְכוּת, דְּהַתְחָלַת הִרְהוּרִים זָרִים נוֹבְעִים מֵהַלֵּב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סא.) דְּיוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִכְנָס לַמּוֹחַ.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ט׳:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: see note 216 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Tanya supplies the account of emotion arising in the heart and recruiting thought in the mind. Its description is the historical spiritual physiology used by the passage.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ עַצְמוֹ אֵין מָקוֹם לְרָע כְּטַעַם "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה הִיא" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר מִצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא חֵלֶק ה' מַמָּשׁ],
connections.quote: “When he wakes, he says: My God, the soul which You placed within me is pure. You created it within me, You breathed it into me, You guard it within me, and You will one day take it from me and restore it to me in the time to come.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהֲגַם דְּכָל אֶחָד יֵשׁ זְמַן שֶׁהוּא בְּקַטְנוּת וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת לְעוֹלָם בְּגַדְלוּת וּדְבֵיקוּת הָרָאוּי,
connections.quote: “In Bereshit Rabbah it is taught: ‘Behold, it was very good’—this is sleep. They ask: is sleep very good? Rather, through sleeping a little, a person rises and labors greatly in Torah. In this way one repairs the fall itself: it becomes an aid to divine service, and one draws service from it. This is in the following month, Kislev, whose letter is samekh and whose attribute is sleep.”
connections.explanation: Cheshvan makes the usefulness of rest explicit: a little sleep enables greater labor afterward, and the apparent descent itself becomes an aid to avodah. This clarifies the present siman’s permission for an interval of diminished consciousness. The continuity lies in the Torah already placed upon the heart and in the renewed life the rest makes possible. It is a purposeful rhythm of service, rather than a demand that one sustain the same intensity at every moment.
connections.headline: Rest becomes part of Torah when it restores the capacity to learn

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּבְרֵאת הַשֵּׁינָה וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ט) שֶׁהוּא "טוֹב מְאֹד", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִינּוֹחַ וְחוֹזֵר לְקַבֵּל חַיּוּת חָדָשׁ,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said: “Behold, it was very good”—behold, sleep is good. Is sleep very good? Have we not learned that wine and sleep are fitting for the wicked and fitting for the world? Rather, by sleeping a little, a person rises and toils much in Torah.”
connections.context: The good of sleep is its renewal of the ability to study. Rav Tzadok applies this to the need for measured rest and the return of fresh vitality.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּבְרֵאת הַשֵּׁינָה וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ט) שֶׁהוּא "טוֹב מְאֹד", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִינּוֹחַ וְחוֹזֵר לְקַבֵּל חַיּוּת חָדָשׁ,
connections.quote: “They likewise expounded “very good” as referring to sleep, because through it one gains strength afterward. This is a descent for the sake of ascent. Only when a person sinks into sleep and fails to awaken in fear of the blessed God and for His service does the evil inclination awaken him to worldly desires, and it may, God forbid, bring him down to the pit. This no longer proceeds from the blessed God, who made him upright and created him. He created sleep only to rest and pause briefly from work and exertion, so that one could serve afterward with greater strength and immediately rise like a lion to the service of one’s Creator.”
connections.context: This parallel preserves the distinction between restorative rest and remaining sunk in inactivity. The goodness of sleep is explained through the renewed service it makes possible.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן צָרִיךְ לִינּוֹחַ מְעַט מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִפְעָמִים, וּ"בִיטּוּלָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה זֶהוּ יְסוּדָהּ" (מְנָחוֹת צט:),
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Sometimes the suspension of Torah is its foundation, as it is written, “Which you broke.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: Well done for breaking them.”
connections.context: The immediate example is Moses breaking the tablets. Rav Tzadok applies the broader principle to a temporary rest that enables renewed Torah study. That application should be distinguished from the example explicitly given by the Talmud.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן צָרִיךְ לִינּוֹחַ מְעַט מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִפְעָמִים, וּ"בִיטּוּלָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה זֶהוּ יְסוּדָהּ" (מְנָחוֹת צט:),
connections.quote: ““Its interruption is its foundation”: for example, interrupting Torah for accompanying the dead or bringing a bride to her wedding. “This is its foundation” means that one receives reward as though sitting, establishing Torah, and studying it. For it says, “Which you broke,” and He did not speak to Moses angrily. We learn that the divine Presence agreed with him when he interrupted Torah and broke the tablets, since he intended it for the good.”
connections.context: Rashi illustrates the Talmudic saying with concrete obligations and Moses’ breaking of the tablets. Rav Tzadok applies its larger principle to necessary rest; the original examples remain visible.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, חֲלוֹמוֹ שֶׁהוּא הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ בְּעֵת הַקַּטְנוּת הוּא גַּם כֵּן: "וְהִנֵּה ה' נִצָּב עָלָיו" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, יג), וְכֵן כָּל אֶחָד לְפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Behold, Hashem was standing over him and said: I am Hashem, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land on which you are lying, I will give to you and to your descendants.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, חֲלוֹמוֹ שֶׁהוּא הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ בְּעֵת הַקַּטְנוּת הוּא גַּם כֵּן: "וְהִנֵּה ה' נִצָּב עָלָיו" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, יג), וְכֵן כָּל אֶחָד לְפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 4
connections.quote: ““And behold, the Lord was stationed over him”: this verse itself is a blessing. Its explanation is like the holiness of Shabbat, which is fixed and enduring without any sanctification or awakening from Israel, but is holy from the blessed God Himself, unlike festivals, which Israel sanctifies. So is our father Jacob’s holiness like the holiness of Shabbat: holy from the blessed God, requiring no awakening. Therefore it does not say “standing over him,” but “stationed”: “standing” would imply that He is standing over him now and not previously, through Jacob’s own awakening, whereas “stationed” means that He is always attached to him.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer interprets the wording within Jacob’s dream as constant attachment. This supports Rav Tzadok’s distinction between Jacob’s sleeping consciousness and the lower state of others.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁאֵצֶל אֶחָד הוּא מַחְשֶׁבֶת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, הוּא אֵצֶל אַחֵר מַחְשֶׁבֶת הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת, כִּי הוּא מַעֲמִיק יוֹתֵר בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְהַגִּיעַ אֶל הָאֱמֶת הַבָּרוּר הַנִּיכָּר לָעַיִן שֶׁהוּא כֵּן, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא אֱמֶת שֶׁהוּא מְבוֹרָר בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ וְעֵינֵי שִׂכְלוֹ,
connections.quote: “Nevertheless, it was still imagination, and the brothers' thought was not false either, for there truly are degrees. Although it was not an entirely false imagining, since it was fulfilled, it was still not complete truth that would endure forever, in the manner of ‘A truthful lip is established forever’ (Proverbs 12:19). Yosef's kingship lasted only for a time and in this world. The enduring kingship belongs to King David, from Yehudah's seed.”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz preserves both sides of Yosef's dreams: they truly came about, yet the kingship they depicted was temporary. This provides a concrete comparison for the siman's claim that what counts as Torah thought at one level may still be called imagination from a deeper one. Calling it imagination does not mean every part of it was simply false.
connections.headline: Fulfilled truth and a deeper enduring truth

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ כֵּן נִקְרָא דִּמְיוֹן, כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רפ עַמּוּד ב) עַל "וּבְיַד הַנְּבִיאִים אֲדַמֶּה" (הוֹשֵׁעַ יב, יא), דְּדִמְיוֹן הוּא אַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא דְּלָא נָהֲרָא הַנִּקְרָא אֱמוּנָה וּמִדַּת לַיְלָה, דְּהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁהוּא בַּחֲשֵׁיכוּת וְהֶעְלֵם מוֹחִין דְּגַדְלוּת.
connections.quote: “She has many visions, images, and appearances, and all are known through the intellectual eye of the heart, of which it is said: The heart knows; the heart understands. As for “Through the prophets I shall present images,” this image is in the understanding of the heart, not an image seen by the eye. Thus it is written, “To whom will you compare Me, that I should be equal?” and “To whom will you compare God?” There are visions such as those of the astrologers, but prophetic vision is like a vision of the night.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ כֵּן נִקְרָא דִּמְיוֹן, כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רפ עַמּוּד ב) עַל "וּבְיַד הַנְּבִיאִים אֲדַמֶּה" (הוֹשֵׁעַ יב, יא), דְּדִמְיוֹן הוּא אַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא דְּלָא נָהֲרָא הַנִּקְרָא אֱמוּנָה וּמִדַּת לַיְלָה, דְּהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁהוּא בַּחֲשֵׁיכוּת וְהֶעְלֵם מוֹחִין דְּגַדְלוּת.
connections.quote: “A dream occurs with the eyes closed; therefore she is called the mirror that does not shine.”
connections.context: The passage distinguishes inward apprehension from an ordinary visible likeness and associates dreaming with the mirror that does not shine. Rav Tzadok develops this into his distinction between direct, clear recognition and the level of faith during concealment. His explanatory language about faith and expanded consciousness should not be inserted into the Zohar’s quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ כֵּן נִקְרָא דִּמְיוֹן, כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רפ עַמּוּד ב) עַל "וּבְיַד הַנְּבִיאִים אֲדַמֶּה" (הוֹשֵׁעַ יב, יא), דְּדִמְיוֹן הוּא אַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא דְּלָא נָהֲרָא הַנִּקְרָא אֱמוּנָה וּמִדַּת לַיְלָה, דְּהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁהוּא בַּחֲשֵׁיכוּת וְהֶעְלֵם מוֹחִין דְּגַדְלוּת.
connections.quote: ‘I spoke to the prophets, and I multiplied visions; through the prophets I conveyed likenesses.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת הַדַּעַת, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ דִּמְיוֹן כְּלָל, רַק כְּדֶרֶךְ "זֶה הַדָּבָר" (סִפְרֵי רֵישׁ מַטּוֹת), הַגַּדְלוּת לְבַדּוֹ מְגוּלֶּה,
connections.quote: “When all the prophets receive their prophecy, it is not fully explicit, but has a likeness and a relation to the recipient’s disposition. Therefore the prophet has the ability to express the words according to that disposition. As the Sages said, Josiah sent to Huldah because women are compassionate. Moses adds to this by prophesying “This is the word”: he received this very word from the blessed God as it is in itself.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the contrast in the Sifrei through the prophetic recipient’s contribution to expression, and Moses’ distinctive reception of the word itself.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת הַדַּעַת, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ דִּמְיוֹן כְּלָל, רַק כְּדֶרֶךְ "זֶה הַדָּבָר" (סִפְרֵי רֵישׁ מַטּוֹת), הַגַּדְלוּת לְבַדּוֹ מְגוּלֶּה,
connections.quote: ““This is the word”: this teaches that just as Moses prophesied with “Thus says,” so the prophets prophesied with “Thus says”; Moses adds beyond them, “This is the word.””
connections.context: The Sifrei preserves both parts: Moses also used “Thus says,” but uniquely adds “This is the word.” Rav Tzadok explains the latter as direct clarity rather than an image resembling the matter.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי לֹא הָיָה דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל לִבּוֹ לְבַד, רַק בְּלִבּוֹ, דְּמֹשֶׁה מִלְּגָאו, וְכָל פְּנִימִיּוּתוֹ מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְאֵין בּוֹ דִּמְיוֹן וְכֹחַ הַמְדַמֶּה שֶׁחוּץ לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “Jacob is surely the image of the Central Pillar from the outside; and Moses was there too, but he was from the inside—this one from the body and that one from the soul.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לַדּוֹרוֹת נֶאֱמַר: "וְהָיוּ וְגוֹמֵר עַל לְבָבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ו, ו), וְלֹא "בִּלְבָבְךָ", שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר, וְ"לֹא קָם נָבִיא וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם לד, י) שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עֶצֶם לִבּוֹ וְנַפְשׁוֹ רַק דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁלָּכֵן נִקְרֵאת הַתּוֹרָה עַל שְׁמוֹ כִּי הוּא מַמָּשׁ כֻּלּוֹ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “These words that I command you today shall be upon your heart.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok expressly distinguishes “upon your heart” from “in your heart.” Retaining the preposition makes his distinction between receiving Torah and having one’s very being constituted by Torah intelligible.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לַדּוֹרוֹת נֶאֱמַר: "וְהָיוּ וְגוֹמֵר עַל לְבָבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ו, ו), וְלֹא "בִּלְבָבְךָ", שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר, וְ"לֹא קָם נָבִיא וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם לד, י) שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עֶצֶם לִבּוֹ וְנַפְשׁוֹ רַק דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁלָּכֵן נִקְרֵאת הַתּוֹרָה עַל שְׁמוֹ כִּי הוּא מַמָּשׁ כֻּלּוֹ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “Remember the Torah of Moses My servant, which I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel, statutes and ordinances.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל לַדּוֹרוֹת נֶאֱמַר: "וְהָיוּ וְגוֹמֵר עַל לְבָבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ו, ו), וְלֹא "בִּלְבָבְךָ", שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר, וְ"לֹא קָם נָבִיא וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם לד, י) שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עֶצֶם לִבּוֹ וְנַפְשׁוֹ רַק דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁלָּכֵן נִקְרֵאת הַתּוֹרָה עַל שְׁמוֹ כִּי הוּא מַמָּשׁ כֻּלּוֹ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: Since you made yourself small, it shall be called by your name, as it is said: ‘Remember the Torah of Moses My servant.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַחָכְמָה חֲלוּקָה מִן הַדִּמְיוֹן, וּמַה שֶּׁמְּחַדְּשִׁים בְּחָכְמָתָן אֵינוֹ דְּבַר ה' רַק חָכְמַת עַצְמָן, כִּי דְּבַר ה' הוּא מַה שֶּׁמַּגִּיעַ אֵלָיו בְּכֹחַ הַמְדַמֶּה בְּלֹא תּוֹסֶפֶת הַעֲמָקַת חָכְמָה מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ מִתְיַיחֲדִים אֶצְלָם כְּאֵצֶל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם:
connections.quote: “From the incident involving the spies until the entire generation of the wilderness had died, Moses, peace be upon him, did not receive prophecy as he had previously, because he grew weary of bearing them through their many complaints. This was so even though the imaginative faculty had no part in his prophecy: the intellect flowed upon him without its mediation, as we have mentioned several times, for he did not prophesy in parables like the other prophets. This will be explained, but it is not the subject of the present chapter.”
connections.context: The Guide expressly excludes imaginative mediation from Moses’ prophecy. Rav Tzadok develops his own description of Moses’ unity of Torah, wisdom, and prophetic apprehension; the distinction from other prophets is explicit in this earlier source.

connections.hePhrase: [רה] הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת כֻּלָּם נוֹלָדִים מִן הַלֵּב שֶׁבּוֹ הֵם הַהִרְהוּרִים וְנִמְשָׁכִים מִמֶּנּוּ לַמּוֹחַ, וּמִן הָעַיִן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה נִכְנָסִים הַהִרְהוּרִים לַלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כ:).
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: “Do not stray after your heart” teaches that the eyes follow the heart. Or does the heart follow the eyes? You must ask: Is there not a blind person who commits all the abominations in the world? What, then, does “Do not stray after your heart” teach? That the eyes follow the heart.”
connections.context: The Sifrei discusses the direction from the heart to the eyes, complementing the existing Talmudic source about what sight can awaken in the heart. The two directions are both part of Rav Tzadok’s account.

connections.hePhrase: [רה] הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת כֻּלָּם נוֹלָדִים מִן הַלֵּב שֶׁבּוֹ הֵם הַהִרְהוּרִים וְנִמְשָׁכִים מִמֶּנּוּ לַמּוֹחַ, וּמִן הָעַיִן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה נִכְנָסִים הַהִרְהוּרִים לַלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כ:).
connections.quote: “The matter of blotting out Amalek, which we were commanded with "do not forget" (Deuteronomy 25:19), we learn from this that the matter is prone to easily slip into forgetfulness. For this is the very essence of Amalek, who attacks due to the slackening of hands from words of Torah, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sanhedrin 106a) concerning Rephidim (from rifui yadayim), and as it is written: "all that were feeble behind you, etc., faint and weary, etc."— meaning lacking the strength to exert oneself vigorously in words of Torah. When one falls into laxity, then immediately the power of Amalek overpowers within the heart, which is the force that causes forgetfulness of the truth of Hashem, blessed be He, and inflates all manner of vain fantasies and illusory musings that run directly contrary to Truth. And this phenomenon is perceived empirically through the senses: that immediately upon slackening from words of Torah, illusion surges in the heart, and we deduce from this that such is the quintessential root of Amalek, whose modus operandi is to strike instantaneously upon the slackening from words of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla identifies a linked sequence: weakening engagement with Torah, forgetting the truth of Hashem, and the strengthening of empty imaginings. This explains why the remedy described here is not merely substituting a pleasant image for an unpleasant one. Renewed Torah and remembrance address the loss of orientation that allows the imagination to govern the heart.
connections.headline: The loss of remembrance makes room for illusion

connections.hePhrase: וְאָסְרוּ (מְגִילָּה כח.) לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בִּפְנֵי אָדָם רָשָׁע, כִּי בַּפָּנִים בּוֹלְטִין כָּל מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים שֶׁבַּלֵּב לַמְּבִינִים, כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קצ עַמּוּד א) דְּהִכִּירוּ בְּאֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מַחֲשֶׁבֶת עֲבֵירָה שֶׁפָּנָיו מוֹרִיקוֹת
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah: ‘By what merit have you lived so long?’ He answered: ‘Have you grown tired of my life?’ Rabbi said: ‘My teacher, this is Torah, and I need to learn.’ He replied: ‘In all my days I have never gazed at the likeness of a wicked person.’ For Rabbi Yochanan said: A person may not gaze at the image of a wicked person, as it says: ‘Were it not that I show regard for Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָסְרוּ (מְגִילָּה כח.) לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בִּפְנֵי אָדָם רָשָׁע, כִּי בַּפָּנִים בּוֹלְטִין כָּל מִינֵי הִרְהוּרִים שֶׁבַּלֵּב לַמְּבִינִים, כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קצ עַמּוּד א) דְּהִכִּירוּ בְּאֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מַחֲשֶׁבֶת עֲבֵירָה שֶׁפָּנָיו מוֹרִיקוֹת
connections.quote: ‘One day he saw a student occupied with Torah whose face had turned pale. He said: Surely this one is contemplating sin. He brought him before him and drew him along with words of Torah until his spirit settled within him. From that day onward, he resolved not to pursue those evil thoughts, but to occupy himself with Torah for its own sake.’

connections.hePhrase: [וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּסוֹטָה (כ.) פָּנֶיהָ מוֹרִיקוֹת, כִּי עֲבֵירָה הוּא מִיתָה לַנֶּפֶשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ בְּמֵת (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם) מִמֶּנָּה פָּנָיו מוֹרִיקוֹת],
connections.quote: “Before she has finished drinking, her face turns greenish, her eyes bulge, and veins stand out all over her. They say, ‘Take her out, take her out, so that she does not render the Temple courtyard impure.’ If she has merit, it suspends the punishment for her. Some merit suspends it for one year, some for two years, and some for three years. From this Ben Azzai says: A person is obligated to teach his daughter Torah, so that if she drinks, she will know that merit can suspend her punishment. Rabbi Eliezer says: Whoever teaches his daughter Torah is as though he were teaching her lewdness.”

connections.hePhrase: [וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּסוֹטָה (כ.) פָּנֶיהָ מוֹרִיקוֹת, כִּי עֲבֵירָה הוּא מִיתָה לַנֶּפֶשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ בְּמֵת (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם) מִמֶּנָּה פָּנָיו מוֹרִיקוֹת],
connections.quote: “Nor may one gaze at a woman’s colored garments, nor at a male or female donkey, a male or female pig, or birds when they are mating, even if one is as full of eyes as the Angel of Death. They said of the Angel of Death that he is entirely full of eyes. When a sick person is about to die, he stands above the person’s head with his drawn sword in his hand and a drop of gall hanging from it. When the sick person sees him, he trembles and opens his mouth, and the angel throws the drop into his mouth. From it he dies, from it his body gives off a foul odor, and from it his face turns greenish.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הַכָּרַת פְּנֵיהֶם עָנְתָה בָּם" (יְשַׁעְיָה ג, ט).
connections.quote: “The appearance of their faces testifies against them; they declare their sin like Sodom and do not conceal it. Woe to their soul, for they have brought evil upon themselves.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok takes the opening words as visible recognition in a person’s face. The note preserves that reading of the Hebrew expression rather than translating it as judicial favoritism.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה נִכְנָסִין הַהִרְהוּרִים בּוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בִּרְאִיַּת תַּלְמִיד חָכָם כִּדְאִיתָא (עֵירוּבִין יג:) דַּחֲזִיתֵיהּ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר מֵאֲחוֹרֵיהּ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi said: The reason I am sharper than my colleagues is that I saw Rabbi Meir from behind. Had I seen him from the front, I would have been sharper still, as it is written: ‘Your eyes shall see your teachers.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה נִכְנָסִין הַהִרְהוּרִים בּוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בִּרְאִיַּת תַּלְמִיד חָכָם כִּדְאִיתָא (עֵירוּבִין יג:) דַּחֲזִיתֵיהּ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר מֵאֲחוֹרֵיהּ.
connections.quote: “For this reason Rabbi said: “The reason I surpass my colleagues is that I saw Rabbi Meir from behind. Had I seen him from the front, I would have surpassed them still more, as it is said: ‘Your eyes shall see your teacher’” (Isaiah 30). For in proportion to the influence bestowed upon the teacher, which is visible in his face—as Scripture says, “A person’s wisdom illuminates his face” (Ecclesiastes 8)—that influence will flow more abundantly upon the student when he receives it.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כַּמָּה תִּיקּוּנִים עָשׂוּ שֶׁלֹּא יָדוּר עִם עוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (לו:) וּבְעֵירוּבִין (סב.), כִּי בְּדִירָתוֹ וּמִשְׁכָּנוֹ הַמְּיוּחָד לוֹ יֵשׁ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִכֹּחוֹתָיו כַּנּוֹדָע מֵהַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב זַ"ל דִּבְקִנְיָנֵי הָאָדָם מִתְפַּשְּׁטִין כֹּחוֹת נַפְשׁוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Geneiva said in Rav’s name: They decreed all these prohibitions because of idolatry. For when Rav Acha bar Adda came, he said in Rabbi Yitzchak’s name: They decreed against their bread because of their oil. In what way is oil more serious than bread?’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כַּמָּה תִּיקּוּנִים עָשׂוּ שֶׁלֹּא יָדוּר עִם עוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (לו:) וּבְעֵירוּבִין (סב.), כִּי בְּדִירָתוֹ וּמִשְׁכָּנוֹ הַמְּיוּחָד לוֹ יֵשׁ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִכֹּחוֹתָיו כַּנּוֹדָע מֵהַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב זַ"ל דִּבְקִנְיָנֵי הָאָדָם מִתְפַּשְּׁטִין כֹּחוֹת נַפְשׁוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Meir holds that sometimes a person happens to live there. The Sages therefore said: An eruv is ineffective where a non-Jew lives, and relinquishing rights to the domain is ineffective where a non-Jew lives, until he rents out his rights. But a non-Jew will not rent them out.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כַּמָּה תִּיקּוּנִים עָשׂוּ שֶׁלֹּא יָדוּר עִם עוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (לו:) וּבְעֵירוּבִין (סב.), כִּי בְּדִירָתוֹ וּמִשְׁכָּנוֹ הַמְּיוּחָד לוֹ יֵשׁ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִכֹּחוֹתָיו כַּנּוֹדָע מֵהַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב זַ"ל דִּבְקִנְיָנֵי הָאָדָם מִתְפַּשְּׁטִין כֹּחוֹת נַפְשׁוֹ.
connections.heRef: דגל מחנה אפרים, לך לך י״ב
connections.quote: “I heard this introduction from my grandfather, whose soul rests in Eden, of blessed memory: every righteous person has holy sparks belonging to the root of his soul that he must repair and raise. Even his servants, animals, and utensils all contain holy sparks, and he must repair them and raise them to their root.”
connections.context: The Baal Shem Tov’s grandson records the teaching directly in his name. It explains the spiritual connection between a person and the objects surrounding him.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי דַּאֲוִירָא דְּאֶרֶץ הָעַמִּים הוּא מַכְנִיס לַלֵּב כֹּחוֹת הַזָּדוֹן שֶׁל הָאֻמּוֹת, וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּאֲוִירָא מַחְכִּים (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קנח:).
connections.quote: ‘Gemara: In whose presumed possession? Rabbi Ila said: In the presumed possession of the mother’s heirs. Rabbi Zeira said: In the presumed possession of the son’s heirs. When Rabbi Zeira went up [to the Land of Israel], he adopted Rabbi Ila’s position. Rabbah adopted Rabbi Zeira’s [former] position. Rabbi Zeira said: Learn from this that the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּרִית חָלוּק לַאֲוִירוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה לד), וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִסַּד גְּבוּלוֹת עַמִּים לְכָל אוּמָּה שֶׁהִיא כֹּחַ מְיוּחָד, מָקוֹם מְיוּחָד, וַאֲוִיר הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁאוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה דָּרָה שָׁם וּקְנוּיָה לָהֶם יוּכַל לְהַכְנִיס מֵאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ גַּם בְּלֵב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
connections.quote: “The world corresponds to the soul, as written in Sefer Yetzirah. As the Midrash says, a covenant was apportioned to the different airs: one atmosphere makes wise, another enriches, and so forth. Every atmosphere has a particular power, corresponding to the different powers of the soul. The Land of Israel, “a land that the Lord your God seeks,” alludes to the power in the soul that God seeks, namely fear, as it says, “What does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear?” This is the meaning of “The air of the Land of Israel makes wise,” as it says, “Fear of the Lord is wisdom.” Likewise, “One who lives in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God”: as is known, Elohim signifies judgment, which is fear.”
connections.context: This parallel makes explicit the correspondence between places in the world and powers in the soul. It interprets the wisdom associated with the Land of Israel as recognition and fear of God.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּרִית חָלוּק לַאֲוִירוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה לד), וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִסַּד גְּבוּלוֹת עַמִּים לְכָל אוּמָּה שֶׁהִיא כֹּחַ מְיוּחָד, מָקוֹם מְיוּחָד, וַאֲוִיר הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁאוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה דָּרָה שָׁם וּקְנוּיָה לָהֶם יוּכַל לְהַכְנִיס מֵאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ גַּם בְּלֵב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
connections.quote: “Resh Lakish said: A covenant has been apportioned to the climates. … He said: Blessed is He who gives a place favor in the eyes of its inhabitants.”
connections.context: The examples concern people’s attachment to their own locality and its climate. Rav Tzadok extends the association between place and its inhabitants to the spiritual influence of a nation’s environment. The source is 34:15, not the discussion of Noah’s altar in 34:9.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּרִית חָלוּק לַאֲוִירוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה לד), וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִסַּד גְּבוּלוֹת עַמִּים לְכָל אוּמָּה שֶׁהִיא כֹּחַ מְיוּחָד, מָקוֹם מְיוּחָד, וַאֲוִיר הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁאוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה דָּרָה שָׁם וּקְנוּיָה לָהֶם יוּכַל לְהַכְנִיס מֵאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ גַּם בְּלֵב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
connections.quote: “When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when He separated the children of man, He set the borders of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן מַיְיתֵי בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן שָׁם אַהַכְנָסַת הִרְהוּרִים בְּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה קְרָא דְּ"תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר לֹא עָבַדְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר וְעָבַדְתָּ אֶת אֹיְבֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים כח, מז–מח), פֵּירוּשׁ כִּי הֵם הַמַּכְנִיסִים הַהִרְהוּרִים בְּלֵב הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "וְעָבַדְתָּ".
connections.quote: “Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and a good heart, amid an abundance of everything.”
connections.context: This is the first half of the contrast quoted through Avot DeRabbi Natan: neglect of joyful divine service leads to the service described in the next verse.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן מַיְיתֵי בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן שָׁם אַהַכְנָסַת הִרְהוּרִים בְּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה קְרָא דְּ"תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר לֹא עָבַדְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר וְעָבַדְתָּ אֶת אֹיְבֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים כח, מז–מח), פֵּירוּשׁ כִּי הֵם הַמַּכְנִיסִים הַהִרְהוּרִים בְּלֵב הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "וְעָבַדְתָּ".
connections.quote: “You shall serve your enemies whom the Lord sends against you, in hunger, thirst, nakedness, and want of everything; He shall put an iron yoke upon your neck until He destroys you.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok applies the verse’s “you shall serve” to subjection to alien thoughts. That is his explanation of the cited teaching; the verse itself speaks of service to enemies.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁמּוֹצִיאִים הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הַגָּנוּז בּוֹ וּמוֹצִיא בִּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו, מִמֵּילָא מִתְבַּטֵּל הַדִּמְיוֹן וְהוּא נִצּוּחַ לְאוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה.
connections.quote: “And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he has swallowed, and the nations shall no longer flow to him.”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּמִצְרַיִם רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דִּמְיוֹן, וְיַצִּיבָא מִילְּתָא מִטַּעַם הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּלִקּוּטֵי תּוֹרָה פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שֶׁהוּא הַגָּרוֹן וּמוֹחִין דְּקַטְנוּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 12b:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 12b:1
connections.quote: “The meaning of a thought of idolatry is that a person’s heart contains fear and submission to emptiness and imagination, something he need not fear. Opposite this stands the exodus from Egypt, as it says, “Who brings you up from the land of Egypt”: that you should always be above all matters of this world. Egypt alludes to worldly matters in their entirety, as we say, “He brought His people Israel out to eternal freedom.” Why, then, should you contain submission and fear toward vanity and imagination? Yet against this a person must guard against heretical thinking, lest he reject submission where it is needed—accepting the yoke of Heaven. Opposite this stands the yoke of the commandments: where it is needed, be like an ox under its yoke. Here too one must guard against thoughts of transgression, so that God’s commandments do not appear a burden, and one does not serve merely from fear but serves from love. This is called a thought of transgression: even if one commits no transgression in deed, thoughts in the heart that prevent love of the Holy One, blessed be He, are called thoughts of transgression.”
connections.context: The Ishbitzer explicitly interprets Egypt through imagined fear. The passage preserves its balancing conditions: freedom from misplaced fear must not become rejection of the divine yoke, and that service should develop into love.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּמִצְרַיִם רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דִּמְיוֹן, וְיַצִּיבָא מִילְּתָא מִטַּעַם הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּלִקּוּטֵי תּוֹרָה פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שֶׁהוּא הַגָּרוֹן וּמוֹחִין דְּקַטְנוּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “The king answered and said: The thing is certain, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which may not be revoked.”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּמִצְרַיִם רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דִּמְיוֹן, וְיַצִּיבָא מִילְּתָא מִטַּעַם הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּלִקּוּטֵי תּוֹרָה פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שֶׁהוּא הַגָּרוֹן וּמוֹחִין דְּקַטְנוּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Know that the throat is called the land of Egypt, because it is the narrowest place in the human form. When the three intellectual powers descend and spread below into the body, they spread across its breadth in three lines. Above, at their root in the head, their place is narrower than the body. But when they descend into the throat, it is extremely narrow: how can three intellectual powers gather in a place as narrow as the throat? They are therefore delayed there, and this is the mystery of Egypt. This, however, is only from the aspect of the rear, for the external forces have no hold from within. As I have explained, “God made this corresponding to that,” and the external forces have a hold throughout Zeir Anpin. The kingdom of Egypt corresponds to the throat but draws nourishment from the rear, the back of the throat. In that constriction the three higher intellectual powers extend; therefore Egypt’s wisdom is greater than that of the other nations, since it takes all the intellectual powers in a single constriction and receives an illumination at the furthest limit.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְמַכָּה י' אָמַר לוֹ: "לֹא תֹסֶף רְאוֹת פָּנַי וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת י, כח), וְאָמַר לוֹ: "כֵּן דִּבַּרְתָּ" (שָׁם, כט) בִּזְמַנּוֹ, כִּי מֵעַתָּה אֵין לוֹ מַה לִּקְלוֹט מִמֶּנּוּ.
connections.quote: ‘Pharaoh said to him: ‘Leave me! Take care not to see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְמַכָּה י' אָמַר לוֹ: "לֹא תֹסֶף רְאוֹת פָּנַי וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת י, כח), וְאָמַר לוֹ: "כֵּן דִּבַּרְתָּ" (שָׁם, כט) בִּזְמַנּוֹ, כִּי מֵעַתָּה אֵין לוֹ מַה לִּקְלוֹט מִמֶּנּוּ.
connections.quote: ““You have spoken correctly”: You have spoken well and at the proper time. It is true that I shall no longer see your face.”
connections.context: Rashi supplies the wording “at the proper time,” which Rav Tzadok develops as the completion of what Moses had to draw out of Egypt.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, הֲגַם שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ עֲדַיִן בְּמַדְרֵגַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, רַק בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף שֶׁרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי, אָז אָמַר לָהֶם: "לֹא תוֹסִפוּ לִרְאֹתָם עוֹד עַד עוֹלָם" (שָׁם יד, יג).
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְשִׁירָה ג׳:י׳
connections.quote: see note 2235.
