connections.context: The complete parable explains the exceptional directness of recognition at the sea, which Rav Tzadok contrasts with ordinary imaginative apprehension.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, הֲגַם שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ עֲדַיִן בְּמַדְרֵגַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, רַק בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף שֶׁרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי, אָז אָמַר לָהֶם: "לֹא תוֹסִפוּ לִרְאֹתָם עוֹד עַד עוֹלָם" (שָׁם יד, יג).
connections.quote: “And Moses said to the people: Do not fear; stand still and see the salvation of Hashem, which He will work for you today; for as you have seen the Egyptians today, you shall see them again no more, forever.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁעַל יְדֵי כָּל מַכָּה לְפַרְעֹה נִתְבָּרֵר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא נָקִי מִדִּמְיוֹן עַד מַדְרֵגָה י', שֶׁהוּא בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁנֶּגֶד זֶה מַכַּת בְּכוֹרוֹת שֶׁהוּא הָעֹמֶק רֵאשִׁית, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁגַּם שָׁם נָקִי, עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִצְּחוֹ.
connections.quote: “Therefore, in the plague of the firstborn, “from Pharaoh’s firstborn” and so forth—firstborn means beginning, and it is the tenth plague, for the plagues correspond to the ten sefirot from below upward, uprooting the beginning of evil—Moses was afraid, and it could not be done through him, but only by “I, the Lord” Himself. “I” signifies the attribute of His kingship, from which the root of evil is drawn. When it is revealed, as in His passing through Egypt, the yoke of His kingship over creatures is revealed and illuminated before all; the root of utter evil is taken from its evil place and sweetened, and all the bodies that served as vessels for that light of the root of evil are nullified. Pharaoh alone remained, as the Sages said, so that he would see further. Had there been a complete revelation, leaving not even Pharaoh, it would also have been a complete revelation for Israel and the final end would have arrived. Not only the firstborn but the entirety of evil would then have had to be removed. But the time had not yet come, because this did not arise through Israel’s own effort; Israel still had to wait until they attained it through their effort. Therefore Pharaoh remained, and all the unfolding of evil apart from the firstborn remained as well. Nevertheless, it was then clarified that “Every firstborn is Mine,” and that Israel’s root clings to the good. The judgment therefore arrived for the exodus from Egypt: their root, for whose clarification the exile had existed, was already clarified, and they could consequently depart.”
connections.context: This fuller parallel connects the firstborn, the tenth plague, and the hidden beginning. It also distinguishes that clarification from the complete future removal of evil; Pharaoh’s remaining and the continuing need for Israel’s effort are essential qualifications.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַבֵּירוּר בְּי' מַדְרֵגוֹת הוּא בֵּירוּר גָּמוּר, וְכֵן אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אַחַר נִסָּיוֹן עֲשִׂירִי נִתְבָּרֵר לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.quote: “All the trials correspond to the attributes from below upward, up to the ninth trial, corresponding to Ḥokhmah—the first revelation from creation out of nothing that human apprehension can reach, the first attribute of which there is some grasp. Abraham was then perfected in everything that could be clarified from his own side. Afterward came the trial of the binding of Isaac, corresponding to the supernal Keter, concealed from every thought. This was clarification from the blessed God’s side, clarifying him in everything down to the root, so that he attained the aspect of “elder.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explains why the tenth trial completes the series while distinguishing what Abraham can clarify through his own powers from the divine clarification at the hidden root.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא, וּבְיוֹם הַמִּיתָה מִתְגַּבֵּר קִטְרוּג אוֹתוֹ חֵטְא לוֹמַר שֶׁצָּרִיךְ בֵּירוּרִין אֲחֵרִים, וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר עוֹד בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְבָּרֵר וּמַה יוֹסִיף, וְצָרִיךְ לְהַכְנִיסוֹ לְעוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים.
connections.quote: “Rav Ami said: There is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity. There is no death without sin, as it is written: ‘The soul that sins, it shall die’ (Ezekiel 18:20).”
connections.context: On 55b the Gemara challenges Rav Ami from the four who died only through the serpent’s counsel, and concludes that there is death without sin.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אִיתָא (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת וָאֶתְחַנַּן) בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנִּסְתַּמּוּ מִמֶּנּוּ מַעַיְנוֹת הַחָכְמָה בְּאוֹתוֹ יוֹם.
connections.quote: see note 751 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Midrash narrates the transfer of teaching authority and wisdom to Joshua immediately before Moses’ death. This is the narrative source behind the statement that Moses’ fountains of wisdom closed on that day.

connections.hePhrase: [רו] כְּלַל הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת וְהַהִרְהוּרִים שֶׁבָּאָדָם הֵם קְבוּעִים בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה שָׁרָשִׁים דְּקִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, שֶׁהֵם שָׁרְשֵׁי הַמִּדּוֹת רָעוֹת.
connections.quote: see note 2347.
connections.context: This is the Mishnah’s triad that Rav Tzadok identifies as the roots of the harmful traits and thoughts discussed here.

connections.hePhrase: וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַשָּׁרָשִׁים הוּא הַגַּאֲוָה, כַּנּוֹדָע דְּשׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרַע הוּא מֵעוֹלַם הַתֹּהוּ וּשְׁבִירַת הַכֵּלִים הַבָּא עַל יְדֵי מַחֲשֶׁבֶת "אֲנָא אֶמְלוֹךְ" כַּיָּדוּעַ;
connections.quote: “Pride is the root of many transgressions, whether between a person and God or between one person and another. It causes a person to harm his fellow, hate him, speak slander about him, and do many similar things. As for relations with God, Scripture says: “Your heart will become haughty, and you will forget the Lord your God.””
connections.context: Rabbi Ḥayyim Vital explains the two directions in which pride generates wrongdoing: injury to other people and forgetfulness of God.

connections.hePhrase: וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַשָּׁרָשִׁים הוּא הַגַּאֲוָה, כַּנּוֹדָע דְּשׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרַע הוּא מֵעוֹלַם הַתֹּהוּ וּשְׁבִירַת הַכֵּלִים הַבָּא עַל יְדֵי מַחֲשֶׁבֶת "אֲנָא אֶמְלוֹךְ" כַּיָּדוּעַ;
connections.quote: “As is known, the breaking of the vessels began through the thought “I shall reign” and through their presumption in receiving an influx greater than was fitting for them. This brought about the breaking of the vessels, which is their death (Bava Kamma 54a).”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִזֶּה נוֹלָד יֵצֶר, דְּפֵירוּשׁ "יֵצֶר" – מַחֲשָׁבָה וְהִרְהוּר בַּלֵּב, דְּשָׁם הוּא הַתְחָלַת הָרַע בַּלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת סא.): יוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב.
connections.heRef: רד"ק על דברי הימים א׳ כ״ח:ט׳:ב׳
connections.quote: ““And understands every formation of thoughts”: The activity of the heart is called yetzer, because the heart acts and forms matters in thought, whether for good or for evil.”
connections.context: Radak supplies the lexical explanation of yetzer as the heart’s forming activity. His wording includes both good and evil thoughts.

connections.hePhrase: [וּמַה שֶּׁהֵם ז' מְלָכִים, דְּנֶצַח וָהוֹד תְּרֵי פַּלְגֵי גּוּפָא, וְכֵן שָׁם בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן יֵשׁ שְׁנַיִם הַדּוֹמִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם].
connections.quote: “Netzach and Hod are two halves of the body, like two twins; therefore they are called shechakim. The two of them together are one vav.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמַה שֶּׁהֵם ז' מְלָכִים, דְּנֶצַח וָהוֹד תְּרֵי פַּלְגֵי גּוּפָא, וְכֵן שָׁם בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן יֵשׁ שְׁנַיִם הַדּוֹמִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם].
connections.quote: “We shall therefore first explain the order of these seven kings. They are from Daat downward: Daat is one; Ḥesed, two; Gevurah, three; Tiferet, four; Netzaḥ and Hod are two halves of one body and are five; Yesod, six; and Malkhut, seven. For Netzaḥ and Hod are each regarded as half a body, and together they are only one.”
connections.context: Etz Ḥayyim explicitly begins with Daat and explains why the eight named powers are counted as seven kings: Netzaḥ and Hod are counted together.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רַשִּׁ"י פָּרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא פֵּירֵשׁ: דַּעַת הַיְינוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא מִצַּד חָכְמָה רַק מִצַּד הַמְדַמֶּה.
connections.quote: ““Wisdom”: What a person hears from others and learns. “Understanding”: He understands something from his own heart out of the things he has learned. “Knowledge”: The holy spirit.”
connections.context: Rashi distinguishes the three terms in the description of Bezalel. The last gloss is the precise source for Rav Tzadok’s identification of daat with ruaḥ ha-kodesh.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי רַשִּׁ"י פָּרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא פֵּירֵשׁ: דַּעַת הַיְינוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא מִצַּד חָכְמָה רַק מִצַּד הַמְדַמֶּה.
connections.quote: “As is known from Ramban on Bava Batra 12a, the holy spirit is an apprehension of wisdom that enters a person’s heart beyond what his intellect can attain. Higher wisdom lies beyond the human intellect’s apprehension in this world. This apprehension does not come to a person through the wisdom in his brain at all, but through the understanding in the heart—that is, through feeling, for the power of feeling is in the heart.”
connections.context: This parallel explains Rav Tzadok’s distinction between ordinary intellectual attainment and the heart’s reception of an apprehension beyond it.

connections.hePhrase: [וְגוֹרֵם גַּם כֵּן קְצָת קִלְקוּל בְּחָכְמָתוֹ כַּנּוֹדָע, דְּגַם אֲחוֹרַיִים דְּאַבָּא וְאִמָּא נָפְלוּ, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁאֲמִיתַּת הַחָכְמָה דְּגַדְלוּת וַדַּאי שָׁם אֵין הַדִּמְיוֹן שַׁלִּיט, רַק הָאֲחוֹרַיִים דְּהַיְינוּ הַהֶעְלֵם, כִּי מִצַּד הַזֶּה יֵשׁ לוֹ הִתְחַבְּרוּת עִם הַדִּמְיוֹן].
connections.quote: “The matter is that aspects certainly fell from all ten points, and all experienced some annulment. Yet Zeir Anpin and the feminine aspect fell entirely, both in their back-to-back and their face-to-face states. This is called death, because everything descended completely. But Abba and Imma, of which only the rear aspects descended, are described as undergoing annulment, not death. From Keter, only its Netzaḥ, Hod, and Yesod fell, which had entered as the intellectual powers of Abba and Imma, as explained above. Since this aspect is not even classed as rear aspects, Keter is not described as undergoing annulment, but only a blemish. There is another reason: only one who passes from one world to another and is separated from his world is called dead. Therefore the seven kings, which were in Atzilut and descended to Beriah, are called truly dead. As the Idra says: Do not say that they died; rather, whoever descends from the former level at which he stood is described as dead, as in “The king of Egypt died.” But although the rear aspects of Abba and Imma fell, they did not descend into Beriah; they remained in the world of Atzilut itself. Because they were displaced from their proper place, this is called annulment, but not death.”
connections.context: The original passage distinguishes the limited fall of the rear aspects of Abba and Imma from the complete descent of the lower vessels. That distinction is essential to Rav Tzadok’s qualification that the truth of mature wisdom itself is beyond the rule of imagination.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִידוּעַ דְּעוֹלַם הַתִּיקּוּן נִבְנֶה עַל יְדֵי שֵׁם מַ"ה הֶחָדָשׁ; פֵּירוּשׁ "מָה" כְּמוֹ "וְנַחְנוּ מָה" (שְׁמוֹת טז, ח) מוֹרֶה עֲנָוָה,
connections.quote: “When it arose in the Emanator’s will to revive the dead and repair these kings that had broken and fallen into the world of Beriah, He decreed and raised the feminine waters from below upward. Through this there was a supernal union of the inner Ḥokhmah and Binah of Adam Kadmon; it brought forth the new Name MaH, and the kings were repaired.”
connections.context: This is Etz Ḥayyim’s explicit account of repair through the new Name MaH. Rav Tzadok applies that account to humility and the restoration of the person’s capacity to receive.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִידוּעַ דְּעוֹלַם הַתִּיקּוּן נִבְנֶה עַל יְדֵי שֵׁם מַ"ה הֶחָדָשׁ; פֵּירוּשׁ "מָה" כְּמוֹ "וְנַחְנוּ מָה" (שְׁמוֹת טז, ח) מוֹרֶה עֲנָוָה,
connections.quote: “Moses said: When the Lord gives you meat to eat in the evening and bread to satisfy you in the morning, it is because the Lord has heard the complaints you direct against Him. And what are we? Your complaints are not against us, but against the Lord.”
connections.context: “What are we?” is Moses and Aaron’s expression of self-effacement. Rav Tzadok connects the word mah, “what,” with the divine Name designated MaH and the humility associated with repair.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִידוּעַ דְּעוֹלַם הַתִּיקּוּן נִבְנֶה עַל יְדֵי שֵׁם מַ"ה הֶחָדָשׁ; פֵּירוּשׁ "מָה" כְּמוֹ "וְנַחְנוּ מָה" (שְׁמוֹת טז, ח) מוֹרֶה עֲנָוָה,
connections.quote: “Rava said, and some say Rabbi Yochanan: Greater is what is said of Moses and Aaron than what is said of Abraham. Of Abraham it is written, ‘I am but dust and ashes’ (Genesis 18:27), while of Moses and Aaron it is written, ‘And what are we?’”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם הוּא בְּסוֹד הַדַּעַת דִּקְדוּשָׁה שֶׁהוּא תִּיקּוּן כָּל הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת ר"ד,
connections.quote: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than any man on the face of the earth.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנַעֲשָׂה בֶּאֱמֶת מֶלֶךְ בִּישֻׁרוּן כִּי אַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן נִתְרַחֲבוּ כָּל הַכֵּלִים כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “When a person despairs of himself and imagines that repentance has been withheld from him, this harms him most of all. The Sages alluded to this when they said that everything depends on the wind: were it not for the wind, they could make a remedy and live. This final stage too is called masculine, and Amalek again stands to accuse. ‘The first of nations is Amalek’ means that the beginning is drawn from him. ‘Its end is destruction’ means that at the conclusion Amalek again stands to introduce slackness and anxious suspicions into a person's heart, as though repentance had been withheld from him, Heaven forbid.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes the temptation toward an act from the later temptation to despair after its pleasure has ended. This adds an essential qualification to the siman's sequence of a broken vessel, recognized smallness, and a renewed cry. Humility makes room for help and repair; it is not the judgment that further return is impossible.
connections.headline: The cry of humility differs from giving up

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ דְּהַגַּאֲוָה הוּא שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְקַבֵּל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לִיכָּנֵס בַּכְּלִי שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ כְּלִי קִבּוּל כָּל כָּךְ טוֹבָה וְשֶׁפַע, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִשְׁבָּר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
connections.quote: “This is the imagining the serpent introduced by saying, ‘You shall be like God…’: it is the root of the empty thoughts, vanities and imaginings within a person—picturing himself at a level or condition above him, which is not fitting for him, each person according to his understanding.”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz identifies the serpent's promise as the model for imagining oneself at a level that is not one's own. This explains the siman's relation between pride, illusion and receiving more light than the vessel can contain. The subsequent humility is therefore a correction of the person's claim and capacity, not merely a change in outward status.
connections.headline: Imagining an unearned higher station

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי הַשְּׁבִירָה מַכִּיר שִׁפְלוּתוֹ אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם מִן הָאוֹר וְנֶעְלַם מִמֶּנּוּ, עַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לַעֲנָוָה גְּדוֹלָה וְנוֹלָד שֵׁם מַ"ה הֶחָדָשׁ הַמְּתַקֵּן הַכֵּלִים וּמַרְחִיבָן לְקַבֵּל בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל כָּךְ.
connections.quote: “This is what was said: “Just as water leaves a high place and goes to a low place.” The explanation is that water continually spreads in every direction and has no fixed boundary or limit. It is unlike a solid body that extends only according to its size; water continues spreading without a boundary. Water therefore leaves a high place and goes to a low place: the high place has a boundary, being limited by its surface, and water leaves that bounded place for the low place, where it will not be confined. Likewise, Torah is intellectual and has no limit. It therefore leaves the high place—the proud person who bounds himself by saying how great he is—and goes to the low place: the lowly of spirit, those who are humble, who do not delimit themselves or consider themselves anything, as though they were not a bounded thing. Torah is therefore found with them. See our explanation of “Not everyone who engages extensively in commerce becomes wise.” We have already explained in the Path of Humility that humility has the quality of simplicity, for a person does not regard himself as something; this is the essence of humility. One who considers himself something and is important in his own eyes does not possess that simplicity. Therefore Torah, which is a simple intellect, is fit to dwell only in one who is simple and does not consider himself something. This is the definition of the simplicity that is fit for intellect.”
connections.context: Maharal explains how humility enlarges receptivity: the proud person imposes a fixed measure upon himself, whereas humility leaves room for Torah beyond that measure. “Simple” here means free of the self-imposed boundedness described in the passage.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ: "לִפְנֵי שֶׁבֶר גָּאוֹן, וְלִפְנֵי כָבוֹד עֲנָוָה" (מִשְׁלֵי טז, יח; יח, יב).
connections.quote: ‘Pride comes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before stumbling.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ: "לִפְנֵי שֶׁבֶר גָּאוֹן, וְלִפְנֵי כָבוֹד עֲנָוָה" (מִשְׁלֵי טז, יח; יח, יב).
connections.quote: “Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honor comes humility.”
connections.context: The words “before honor comes humility” appear also in Proverbs 15:33; here they are joined to the breaking that follows haughtiness.

connections.hePhrase: בַּהַתְחָלָה כְּשֶׁמַּתְחִיל לִכְנוֹס בַּעֲבוֹדַת ה', שֶׁאָז הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה עַל הַיָּם מַה וְכוּלֵי" כַּנּוֹדָע, נִכְנָס בּוֹ גַּאֲוָה,
connections.quote: “On the seventh day of Passover, at the splitting of the sea, a maidservant saw what Ezekiel did not see, as stated in the Mekhilta and elsewhere. Our holy master of Ishbitz said that this was the kind of vision shown to a person at his beginning. This accords with what is said in the Baal Shem Tov’s name: that he envied the strength of the awakening of youth when entering the gates of piety. As the Rokeaḥ writes, there is no strength like piety at its beginning. Our teacher Rabbi Bunim said that this is the meaning of “Do not say that the former days were better than these,” when the awakening was very strong: “For it is not from wisdom that you have asked this”—it was not from your own wisdom, but was lent to you by the blessed God. The principal thing is what a person afterward acquires through his own effort. Our holy master of Ishbitz said that everything a person has the capacity afterward to attain as his own acquisition is shown to him by the blessed God at the beginning as a vision. It is only a loan; afterward it departs so that he will labor to attain it as his own acquisition.”
connections.context: This fuller parallel explains the initial illumination, its departure, and the task of acquiring it through effort. It supplies the background for Rav Tzadok’s comparison with the vision at the sea without treating the initial experience as a permanent achievement.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ מִתְעוֹרֵר וּמַכִּיר שִׁפְלוּתוֹ, וְצוֹעֵק "הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא" מֵעוּמְקָא וּתְבִירוּ דְּלִבָּא – אָז הוּא זוֹכֶה לְעוֹלַם הַתִּיקּוּן וְרוֹאֶה עוֹלָם חָדָשׁ:
connections.quote: “Please, Hashem, save now! Please, Hashem, grant success now!”

connections.hePhrase: [רז] דִּמְיוֹנוֹת שָׁוְא הֵם חוֹצְצִים בִּפְנֵי יְדִיעַת אֱלֹהוּת וְהַכָּרָתוֹ מִלְּהִכָּנֵס בַּלֵּב.
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:7
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:7
connections.quote: “‘Go forth’ corresponds to ‘I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’ The Exodus meant that Israel should no longer be sunk in any one thing. Sometimes a person is immersed in small pleasures and desires and cannot separate from them because they appear to him to be his life; so Israel were immersed in Egypt. The Sages teach that no slave could escape Egypt: it seemed better to him to serve Egypt than to be a ruler elsewhere. Similarly, a person can be immersed in one conception or opinion and unable to move from it. This was the principal Egyptian exile: they were content to be slaves and imagined they had always been slaves. Hence, ‘who brought you out of the house of slaves.’ Hashem does not desire a person to be bent beneath one opinion, stubbornly refusing to move from it. He desires the person to be ready at every moment to follow only His will.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why leaving Egypt is more than receiving an argument about the Creator. A person can feel unable to leave an enjoyment or a fixed conception because it seems to constitute his life. Freedom makes him ready to follow Hashem's will afresh. This gives a concrete meaning to the present siman's contrast between constricting imagination and the enduring recognition established through the Exodus.
connections.headline: A fixed view can become a house of slavery

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמַר פַּרְעֹה, שֶׁהוּא מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם וּבוֹ תֹּקֶף הַשְּׁקִיעוּת בַּדִּמְיוֹן: "לֹא יָדַעְתִּי אֶת ה'" (שְׁמוֹת ה, ב).
connections.quote: ‘Pharaoh said: ‘Who is Hashem, that I should obey His voice and release Israel? I do not know Hashem, nor will I release Israel.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְחָלַת "אָנֹכִי [ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ] אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ [מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם]" (שָׁם כ, ב), וְאֵין זֶה טַעַם אוֹ מוֹפֵת, דְּאִם כֵּן הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר: אֲשֶׁר בָּרָאתִי שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ אוֹ בְּרָאתִיךָ.
connections.quote: ‘I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק כִּי "אָנֹכִי" אֵין מַתְחִיל בִּלְשׁוֹן מִצְוָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, דְּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְצַוּוֹת וּלְהַזְהִיר, כִּי מִי שֶׁאֵין מַאֲמִין כְּלָל מַה יּוֹעִיל הַצִּוּוּי;
connections.quote: “Moreover, the utterance “I am the Lord your God,” which is their acceptance of His divinity and kingship, cannot take the form of a command or decree. If He is not their King and God, a decree upon them is inapplicable, for one issues a decree over them only after already being king. But if He is already King over them, there is no need to say, “Accept My kingship,” since He is already King. A king therefore cannot say, “I decree upon the people that you accept me as king”: if he is not their king, a decree that he issues is inapplicable; and if he is already king, there is no need to decree that they accept his kingship. Rather, he says, “You know that I am your king; therefore act accordingly, accepting my kingship.” Thus the first utterance takes this form: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”; since I brought you out of Egypt, accept My kingship.”
connections.context: Maharal explains the same logical difficulty: a command presupposes the authority of the one commanding. His explanation retains the positive demand to accept divine kingship, rather than removing the first utterance from the Decalogue.

connections.hePhrase: רַק כִּי "אָנֹכִי" אֵין מַתְחִיל בִּלְשׁוֹן מִצְוָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, דְּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְצַוּוֹת וּלְהַזְהִיר, כִּי מִי שֶׁאֵין מַאֲמִין כְּלָל מַה יּוֹעִיל הַצִּוּוּי;
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:3
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:3
connections.quote: “The first utterance, “I am,” does not begin in the form of a command, “Know that I am,” or “Believe,” and the like. A command is altogether inapplicable here. Rather, for one who belongs from the outset to Israel’s holy root, this becomes established and confirmed in his heart of itself: “I am,” and so forth. For one who does not believe this, all commands and warnings will be of no help; this is a root bearing poison, and his essential being is not of Israel’s holiness at all, whose principal source and root of life is the utterance “I am,” and so forth. Therefore this is not a command that depends on an awakening from below. It is a gift from above without any awakening from below, as explained earlier; this is simply the nature of their root.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s parallel explains why the first utterance is expressed as a declaration. Within his account of Israel’s spiritual root, the capacity for recognizing the divine Commander precedes the response to a command.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן פַּרְעֹה שֶׁאָמַר "לֹא יָדַעְתִּי", אָמְרוּ עָלָיו (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ג): בִּדְבָרִים לֹא יִוָּסֶר עָבֶד, רַק שֵׁבֶט וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ““Take this staff in your hand”: You said, “I am not a man of words,” and “A servant is not corrected by words.” What does one do to a servant? One chastises him with a stick. So take the staff, with which you will chastise him.”
connections.context: The Midrash applies the proverb to Pharaoh and explains the staff given to Moses. The relevant lines occur at the end of the section; its earlier discussion of anger at Moses does not explain Rav Tzadok’s citation.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן פַּרְעֹה שֶׁאָמַר "לֹא יָדַעְתִּי", אָמְרוּ עָלָיו (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ג): בִּדְבָרִים לֹא יִוָּסֶר עָבֶד, רַק שֵׁבֶט וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘A servant will not be disciplined by words, for even when he understands, he does not respond.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן פַּרְעֹה שֶׁאָמַר "לֹא יָדַעְתִּי", אָמְרוּ עָלָיו (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ג): בִּדְבָרִים לֹא יִוָּסֶר עָבֶד, רַק שֵׁבֶט וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.”

connections.hePhrase: וְחֵרֵשׁ, שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן, דְּלָאו בְּנֵי דֵּעָה נִינְהוּ וְאֵין לָהֶם אֶלָּא מוֹחִין דְּקַטְנוּת – פְּטוּרִים מִכָּל הַמִּצְווֹת.
connections.quote: ““Except a deaf person, a person without legal mental competence, and a minor,” and so forth. It teaches “deaf person” alongside the person without legal mental competence and the minor: just as those two lack legal understanding, so the deaf person meant here lacks legal understanding. It teaches what we learned: The deaf person of whom the Sages speak everywhere is one who neither hears nor speaks. Thus one who speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, is obligated. We learned support for this, as the Sages taught: One who speaks but does not hear is deaf; one who hears but does not speak is mute; both are regarded as legally competent in all respects. From where is it known that one who speaks but does not hear is deaf and one who hears but does not speak is mute? For it is written, “I am like a deaf person who does not hear, and like a mute person who does not open his mouth.” Alternatively, as people say, his speech has been removed. But it was taught that one who speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, is exempt! Ravina—or, some say, Rava—said: The text is incomplete and should read: Everyone is obligated in appearance at the Temple and festival rejoicing, except one who speaks but does not hear or hears but does not speak, who is exempt from appearance. Although exempt from appearance, he is obligated in rejoicing. One who neither hears nor speaks, a person without legal mental competence, and a minor are exempt even from rejoicing, since they are exempt from all the commandments stated in the Torah.”
connections.context: The Gemara defines the classical legal category used in this exemption and expressly distinguishes people who can either hear or speak. It also distinguishes the particular obligation of appearance at the Temple from festival rejoicing; those qualifications are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, כז עַמּוּד א) אָמַר: "בְּחֹמֶר" – דָּא קַל וָחֹמֶר וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי עֲבוֹדָתָם בִּלְבֵנִים הוֹצִיאוּ מִדּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה.
connections.quote: see note 2432.
connections.context: The Zohar reads the words of the Egyptian servitude as forms of Torah study: chomer becomes kal vachomer, and levenim becomes libbun halakhah. Those wordplays are the basis of Rav Tzadok’s statement that the labor with bricks brought forth the methods of Torah.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁבְּמוֹת יוֹסֵף וְכָל הַדּוֹר הַהוּא, וְהָיָה אֶפְשָׁר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁיֻּשְׁקְעוּ בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת מִצְרַיִם, אָז נִגְזַר הַשִּׁעְבּוּד וְהַיְגִיעָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ גַּם כֵּן שֶׁהִיא שִׁכְחַת עָוֹן.
connections.quote: see note 1439 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the Mishnah behind the phrase that exertion in derekh eretz makes sin forgotten. Its statement concerns the combination of Torah and work; Rav Tzadok applies the role of necessary work to Israel’s situation before receiving the Torah.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁבְּמוֹת יוֹסֵף וְכָל הַדּוֹר הַהוּא, וְהָיָה אֶפְשָׁר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁיֻּשְׁקְעוּ בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת מִצְרַיִם, אָז נִגְזַר הַשִּׁעְבּוּד וְהַיְגִיעָה בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ גַּם כֵּן שֶׁהִיא שִׁכְחַת עָוֹן.
connections.quote: ““Worldly occupation”: A craft or commerce. “For the exertion of both makes sin forgotten”: Torah weakens a person’s strength, and work strains and wears down the body; through this the evil inclination becomes inactive within him. “Any Torah study unaccompanied by work”: If you ask, let him labor continually in Torah and let its exertion make sin forgotten—why is work needed? It was therefore necessary to say that Torah unaccompanied by work will ultimately cease, for a person cannot do without sustenance; he will rob others and forget his learning.”
connections.context: Bartenura explains both the effect of exertion and the practical need for a livelihood. His complete explanation prevents the first sentence from being read as a recommendation simply to increase exhaustion.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עִיקַּר הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת מִצַּד הַבַּטָּלָה שֶׁמְּבִיאָה וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer says: Even if she brought him a hundred maidservants, he may require her to work in wool, because idleness leads to sexual immorality. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Even one who vows that his wife may do no work must divorce her and give her the marriage settlement, because idleness leads to mental disturbance.”
connections.context: The Mishnah discusses work within marriage and gives these two formulations of the harmful effects of idleness. Rav Tzadok invokes that underlying concern in his account of distracting thoughts.

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם שֶׁבַע עֲבוֹדוֹת בַּכָּתוּב, נֶגֶד שִׁבְעָה מְלָכִין דְּמִיתוּ, שֶׁהֵם שִׁבְעָה כֹּחוֹת שֶׁל דִּמְיוֹנוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים שֶׁעוֹלִים בְּלֵב הָאָדָם כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּקַטְנוּת, וְעַל יָדָם נִיצּוֹלוּ.
connections.quote: “It was taught: When the Holy One, blessed be He, handed Israel over to the prince of Egypt, He decreed seven decrees upon them by which the Egyptians would enslave them. This is what is written: “They embittered their lives with hard labor, with mortar and bricks,” and so forth. Corresponding to them were seven for good: “The children of Israel were fruitful,” “swarmed,” “multiplied,” “grew strong,” “very,” “very,” and “the land was filled with them.””
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly counts seven aspects of the Egyptian oppression and places seven expressions of blessing opposite them. Rav Tzadok connects the sevenfold labor with the sevenfold repair of thought.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכוּ נֶגְדָּם לְשֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת לְדִבְרֵי הִלֵּל (רֵישׁ תּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים), וְכֵן הֵם שִׁבְעָה סִפְרֵי תּוֹרָה לְמַאן דְּאָמַר כֵּן בְּשַׁבָּת (קטז.), כִּי כָּל דָּבָר חָלוּק לְשִׁבְעָה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Hillel the Elder expounded seven methods before the elders of Beteira: inference from minor to major, verbal analogy, two verses, general and particular, the like of it elsewhere, and a matter learned from its context. These are the seven methods that Hillel the Elder expounded before the elders of Beteira.”
connections.context: The parallel in Tosefta Sanhedrin 7:5 counts the seven by listing a general principle drawn from one passage and one drawn from two passages separately.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכוּ נֶגְדָּם לְשֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת לְדִבְרֵי הִלֵּל (רֵישׁ תּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים), וְכֵן הֵם שִׁבְעָה סִפְרֵי תּוֹרָה לְמַאן דְּאָמַר כֵּן בְּשַׁבָּת (קטז.), כִּי כָּל דָּבָר חָלוּק לְשִׁבְעָה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: ‘With whose view does this statement of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in Rabbi Yonatan’s name agree: ‘She has hewn her seven pillars’—these are the seven books of Torah? With whose view? With Rabbi’s.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכוּ נֶגְדָּם לְשֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת לְדִבְרֵי הִלֵּל (רֵישׁ תּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים), וְכֵן הֵם שִׁבְעָה סִפְרֵי תּוֹרָה לְמַאן דְּאָמַר כֵּן בְּשַׁבָּת (קטז.), כִּי כָּל דָּבָר חָלוּק לְשִׁבְעָה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “Everything that comes into actuality has three initial powers that generate it potentially, from which proceed seven lower powers—the attributes that build its actual expression. Every bounded thing must be divided into three parts and boundaries: beginning, middle, and end; these are the first three. [From them actual expression is built through extension in space: three dimensions—length, breadth, and height or depth—within which are the six extremities of every thing, while the seventh is the whole extent, as is known.]”
connections.context: This parallel explains Rav Tzadok’s general sevenfold scheme through three dimensions, six extremities, and their whole. It is his account of the structure of manifestation.

connections.hePhrase: כָּךְ הוּא מִדָּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ: בְּעֵת שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְהוֹשִׁיעַ, אָז נוֹתֵן בְּלֵב אוֹתוֹ אָדָם לִצְעוֹק לוֹ.
connections.quote: see note 2181 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The existing Peri Tzadik note explains shegurah as “sent.” This fuller parallel adds compassion for another’s suffering and expressly urges prayer before distress is needed to awaken it.

connections.hePhrase: כָּךְ הוּא מִדָּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ: בְּעֵת שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְהוֹשִׁיעַ, אָז נוֹתֵן בְּלֵב אוֹתוֹ אָדָם לִצְעוֹק לוֹ.
connections.quote: “Since Israel is truly free at the root and is considered children of Hashem, as it says (Exodus 4), ‘Israel is My firstborn son,’ Hashem awakened from His side a cry in Israel's heart that He should redeem and rescue them from Egypt. As it says, ‘The children of Israel groaned from the labor and cried out.’ After Israel also awakened, from their side, to recognize that they lacked redemption—because they are free at the root—as soon as they cried to Hashem and felt their distress, it immediately says (Exodus 2:23–24), ‘Their cry rose to God from the labor, and God heard their groaning.’”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef develops the same cry in Egypt. Because Israel is free at the root, Hashem awakens the awareness that bondage is a lack; the cry can then rise. This explains the siman's statement that when Hashem wishes to rescue, He puts the cry into the person's heart. The later source context distinguishes freedom of understanding from continuing bodily exile.
connections.headline: The Giver awakens the cry for freedom

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם (בְּרָכוֹת לד:): אִם שְׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתִי בְּפִי וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר הִיא פּוֹעֶלֶת, אָז הִיא שְׁגוּרָה וּשְׁלוּחָה הַתְּפִלָּה לְפִיו מֵאֵת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Rabban Gamliel’s son once fell ill. He sent two Torah scholars to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa to ask for mercy on his behalf. When Rabbi Chanina saw them, he went up to the upper room and asked for mercy for him. When he came down, he told them: ‘Go, for his fever has left him.’ They said to him: ‘Are you a prophet?’ He answered: ‘I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, but this is the tradition I have received: If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know that he is accepted; if not, I know that he is rejected.’ They sat down, wrote it down, and recorded the exact time. When they came to Rabban Gamliel, he said to them: ‘By the Temple service! You have neither subtracted nor added anything. This is exactly what happened: At that hour his fever left him, and he asked us for water to drink.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם (בְּרָכוֹת לד:): אִם שְׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתִי בְּפִי וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר הִיא פּוֹעֶלֶת, אָז הִיא שְׁגוּרָה וּשְׁלוּחָה הַתְּפִלָּה לְפִיו מֵאֵת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: ““If it is fluent”: If my prayer is ordered swiftly in my mouth, without my stumbling, and my supplication flows from my heart to my mouth for as long as I wish to continue pleading. “That he is rejected”: The sick person. Another interpretation: It is an expression of casting his prayer back in his face; that is, the prayer offered for him is cast away and driven from him, and is not accepted.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the fluency described in the Mishnah as the unimpeded flow of supplication from the heart. Both interpretations of the contrasting term metoraf are retained.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם (בְּרָכוֹת לד:): אִם שְׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתִי בְּפִי וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר הִיא פּוֹעֶלֶת, אָז הִיא שְׁגוּרָה וּשְׁלוּחָה הַתְּפִלָּה לְפִיו מֵאֵת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “What is said in the name of our teacher Rabbi Elimelekh, of blessed memory, concerns the Mishnah’s statement: “If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know that he has been accepted.” “Fluent” has the sense of being sent: the blessed God sends the prayer into his mouth and takes pride in him, for he is His servant, as explained above. Through this, “I know that he has been accepted.””

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קוֹדֵם לַתּוֹרָה בְּהֶכְרֵחַ, דַּי בְּדָבָר מוּעָט הָאֶפְשָׁרִי וְתַכְלִית יִסּוּרִין:
connections.quote: see note 1408 (Vol. I).
connections.context: In its original setting, the teaching follows an account of a guest who avoids slander and makes peace between people; derekh eretz there includes proper conduct. Rav Tzadok applies the precedence of derekh eretz here to necessary worldly occupation.

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ קוֹדֵם לַתּוֹרָה בְּהֶכְרֵחַ, דַּי בְּדָבָר מוּעָט הָאֶפְשָׁרִי וְתַכְלִית יִסּוּרִין:
connections.quote: “What is the smallest measure of suffering? Rabbi Elazar said: When a garment is woven for a person to wear and it does not please him. Rava Zeira—or, some say, Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani—objected: They said something still less: even when people intended to mix a drink with hot water and mixed it with cold, or with cold and mixed it with hot; and you require so much? Mar son of Ravina said: Even if his garment turns inside out. Rava—or, some say, Rav Ḥisda; some say Rabbi Yitzḥak; and some say it was taught in a baraita—said: Even if he puts his hand into his purse to take out three coins and two come up in his hand. Specifically, when he wanted three and two came up; but if he wanted two and three came up, that does not count, since there is no trouble in throwing the extra one back.”
connections.context: The Gemara is identifying how small an inconvenience can count as suffering. Its final distinction is retained: retrieving an additional missing coin entails trouble, while simply returning an extra one does not.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (סוֹף תִּיקּוּן יג וְרֵישׁ תִּיקּוּן כא): מַאן דְּנָצַח בִּקְרָבָא יְהִיבִין לֵיהּ בְּרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא – דָּא צְלוֹתָא.
connections.quote: “Therefore a proclamation goes out every day: Whoever kills that serpent nesting in the great mountains will be given the king’s daughter, who is prayer, seated upon the tower of which it says, “The name of Hashem is a tower of strength; the righteous runs into it and is exalted.””
connections.context: At the end of Tikkun 13, the king’s daughter is explicitly identified as prayer. Rav Tzadok uses victory over the serpent as the image for overcoming the inclination and attaining wholehearted prayer.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (סוֹף תִּיקּוּן יג וְרֵישׁ תִּיקּוּן כא): מַאן דְּנָצַח בִּקְרָבָא יְהִיבִין לֵיהּ בְּרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא – דָּא צְלוֹתָא.
connections.quote: “The daughter is upon the tower that flies in the air. Every day they proclaim in the firmament that whoever kills this serpent will be given her as a wife: “The king’s daughter within; her garment is of settings of gold.””
connections.context: This parallel at the beginning of Tikkun 21 supplies the second source named by Rav Tzadok. The identification of the daughter as prayer is explicit in the companion passage at the end of Tikkun 13, quoted in the neighboring note.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה הוּא הַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח וּכְעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (סד.),
connections.quote: ‘One of them began and said: What defines someone who has been drinking, and what defines someone who is drunk? Someone who has been drinking is anyone who can speak before the king. Someone who is drunk is anyone who cannot speak before the king.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה הוּא הַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח וּכְעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (סד.),
connections.quote: see note 45 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rashi explains the Gemara’s distinction between the dress required for Shema and for prayer. His explanation supplies the specific meaning of prayer as an address before the King.

connections.hePhrase: דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב, וְאִם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יֶאֱרַע לוֹ אֵיזֶה מַחֲשָׁבָה זָרָה וְהִרְהוּר חִיצוֹנִי, הֲרֵי אֵינוֹ עוֹמֵד בְּאוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.quote: “For it is not as man sees: man looks at the outward appearance, but Hashem looks at the heart.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, דִּגְאֻלַּת מִצְרַיִם הַיְינוּ יְצִיאָה מִדִּמְיוֹן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
connections.quote: “In the Zohar, Vaera, it says that in Egypt speech was in exile. This means that they were good in their hearts, but not so in bringing this into actual deeds. It is like what I heard concerning “a foolish speaker will stumble”: he cannot bring potential into actuality, as the Sages said in Sotah concerning “a people without understanding will stumble,” referring to the loss of the sotah waters’ power to produce their effect. Speech is the explicit disclosure of what is in the heart. For this reason they established the joining of redemption to prayer: a person may cry to God in his heart but be unable to express this with his mouth so purely, without any alien thought, and truly from the heart. This is the redemption from Egypt: their redemption was the redemption of that faculty. Through recalling it, the same is brought about within him, so that he can speak words of prayer with all his heart.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the relation between redemption from Egypt and prayer through the restoration of speech’s ability to express the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ד:): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְכוּלֵי, וּבִתְהִלָּה לְדָוִד מוּבְטָח לוֹ שֶׁהוּא בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא.
connections.quote: “The master said: He recites Shema and prays. This supports Rabbi Yoḥanan, for Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Who belongs to the World to Come? One who joins redemption to the evening prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: The prayers were instituted in the middle.”
connections.context: Rabbi Yoḥanan’s formulation is the first statement in Rav Tzadok’s comparison. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s differing order places the prayers between the morning and evening recitations of Shema; that disagreement is retained. The existing notes supply the separate promise concerning Ashrei.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ד:): אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְכוּלֵי, וּבִתְהִלָּה לְדָוִד מוּבְטָח לוֹ שֶׁהוּא בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Avina: Whoever recites ‘A praise of David’ three times each day is assured that he belongs to the World to Come.”
connections.context: “A praise of David” is Psalm 145. The promise Rav Tzadok discusses is the Gemara’s teaching about its recitation, not a sentence in the psalm itself.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְסֵדֶר אָלֶ"ף-בֵּי"ת שֶׁהוּא סֵדֶר הַבְּרִיאָה כֻּלָּהּ, שֶׁהַכֹּל מְסוּדָּר מֵאֵת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “What is the reason? If it is because the psalm follows the alphabet, let him say “Happy are those whose way is blameless,” which follows it eightfold. If it is because it contains “You open Your hand,” let him say the Great Hallel, in which it is written, “Who gives bread to all flesh.” Rather, it is because it contains both.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s explanation of the distinctiveness of Psalm 145: its alphabetical structure together with its praise of God’s provision of sustenance. It supplements the existing quotation about the reward for reciting it.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל מִי שֶׁיָּצָא מִדִּמְיוֹן – זֶהוּ מִדַּת אֱמֶת, וּמַסְמִיךְ גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, שֶׁזּוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי כֵן לְהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, שֶׁהוּא יִחוּד אֱמֶת וֶאֱמוּנָה – קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵיהּ;
connections.quote: “For this reason the masters of the Mishnah established: Study is not the principal thing, but action. For the Holy One, blessed be He, is concealed in the secrets of Torah. Through what is He known? Through the commandments, which are His Shekhinah, His likeness. Just as He is humble, His Shekhinah is humility. He is pious, and she is pious. He is mighty, and she rules over all the nations of the world. He is truth, and she is faith. He is a prophet, and she is a prophetess. He is righteous, and she is righteous. He is king, and she is kingship. He is wise, and she is wisdom. He understands, and she is His understanding. He is a crown, and she is His diadem, a diadem of splendor. For this reason the Sages established: Whoever is not inwardly as he is outwardly should not enter the house of study. This follows the likeness of the Holy One, blessed be He: He is its inner aspect and the Shekhinah its outer aspect; He is inward within, and she outward without. That which is outward does not differ from that which is inward, so that it may be known that she is His emanation and that there is no separation there at all: “Within and without you shall overlay it.””
connections.context: The original passage explicitly pairs truth with the Holy One and faith with the Shekhinah. Its conclusion that there is no separation is retained, along with the passage’s connection between inward reality and outward action.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אֱמוּנָה פֵּירוּשׁ בְּטוּחוֹת, שֶׁמַּאֲמִין בְּחֵי עוֹלָמִים, אֲבָל אֱמֶת הוּא שֶׁמְּבוֹרָר לָעַיִן וְאֵין צָרִיךְ בְּטוּחוֹת;
connections.quote: ““Faithfulness”—this is the Order of Seeds: The Jerusalem Talmud explains that he trusts in the Life of the Worlds and sows.”
connections.context: Tosafot’s gloss is the source for the expression “trusts in the Life of the Worlds.” Its concrete example is the trust involved in sowing.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי נִצּוּחַ אֵינוֹ קָרוּי נִצּוּחַ לְשָׁעָה, רַק כְּעִנְיַן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁאָמַר: "וְלִבִּי חָלַל בְּקִרְבִּי" (תְּהִלִּים קט, כב), שֶׁכְּבָר הֲרָגוֹ לְיֵצֶר הָרָע (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: see note 596 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The preceding sentence distinguishes Abraham, who transformed his evil inclination into good. David’s different path is described here through the verse about the hollow heart. This adds the Yerushalmi’s distinction to the existing Avodah Zarah quotation.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁגַּם "חֲצוֹת לַיְלָה" – פֵּירוּשׁ בְּתַכְלִית הַחַשְׁכוּת וְהֶעְדֵּר הַיִּשּׁוּב וְהַיְגִיעָה לְכַוֵּין הַלֵּב – כִּנּוֹרוֹ מְנַגֵּן מֵאֵלָיו לָקוּם לְהוֹדוֹת וְכוּלֵי, כִּי אֵין לוֹ מַחֲשָׁבָה וְרָצוֹן אַחֵר כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “David had a sign, for Rav Acha bar Bizna said in the name of Rabbi Shimon the Pious: A lyre hung above David’s bed. When midnight arrived, a north wind would blow upon it, and it would play by itself. He would immediately rise and occupy himself with Torah until dawn. When dawn came, the sages of Israel entered and said to him, ‘Our master the king, your people Israel need sustenance.’ He told them, ‘Go and support one another.’ They replied, ‘A handful cannot satisfy a lion, and a pit cannot be filled with its own excavated earth.’ He told them, ‘Go and send out your forces on a military expedition.’”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁגַּם "חֲצוֹת לַיְלָה" – פֵּירוּשׁ בְּתַכְלִית הַחַשְׁכוּת וְהֶעְדֵּר הַיִּשּׁוּב וְהַיְגִיעָה לְכַוֵּין הַלֵּב – כִּנּוֹרוֹ מְנַגֵּן מֵאֵלָיו לָקוּם לְהוֹדוֹת וְכוּלֵי, כִּי אֵין לוֹ מַחֲשָׁבָה וְרָצוֹן אַחֵר כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “At midnight I rise to give thanks to You for Your righteous judgments.”

connections.hePhrase: הוּא זָכָה לִבְרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא כְּטַעַם "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה" (תְּהִלִּים קט, ד), שֶׁהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: see note 1732 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The ordinary sense is that David responds with prayer. Rav Tzadok relies on the verse’s compressed wording, “I am prayer,” to describe prayer as David’s own spiritual quality.

connections.hePhrase: הוּא זָכָה לִבְרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא כְּטַעַם "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה" (תְּהִלִּים קט, ד), שֶׁהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “‘Who hears prayer’ (Psalms 65:3) … Prayer—this is Knesset Yisrael, who is prayer, as it is written: ‘And I am prayer’ (Psalms 109:4); David said this for the sake of Knesset Yisrael.”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּק"נ מִקְוֵה טָהֳרָה דְּיָם שֶׁל שְׁלֹמֹה הֵם נֶגֶד ק"נ מִזְמוֹרֵי תְּהִלִּים, וְנִרְאֶה דְּק"נ מִינֵי טְהָרוֹת בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה יֵשׁ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥiyya taught: The sea that Solomon made could hold one hundred and fifty ritual baths for purification.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s explicit capacity statement concerning Solomon’s sea. Rav Tzadok then connects that number with the psalms and the purification of thought.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּק"נ מִקְוֵה טָהֳרָה דְּיָם שֶׁל שְׁלֹמֹה הֵם נֶגֶד ק"נ מִזְמוֹרֵי תְּהִלִּים, וְנִרְאֶה דְּק"נ מִינֵי טְהָרוֹת בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה יֵשׁ.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Prophets, I Samuel 20:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Prophets, I Samuel 20:1
connections.quote: “The stone of Judah set in the breastplate was called nofekh, whose numerical value is one hundred and fifty. King David, peace be upon him, composed one hundred and fifty sections in Psalms, for fifty signifies purification, and three times fifty signifies the completeness of true purification. King Solomon, peace be upon him, made the bronze sea, which held one hundred and fifty ritual baths for purification. He also composed Proverbs, Song of Songs, and Ecclesiastes, which comprise fifty chapters, apart from the final chapter of Proverbs, the section “A woman of valor.””
connections.context: This is the Ishbitz parallel to the teaching Rav Tzadok says he heard: the shared number of David’s psalms and the purification capacity of Solomon’s sea. It develops the association with Judah and three times fifty.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ דְּיָדוּעַ דְּיֵשׁ נ' שַׁעֲרֵי טֻמְאָה, הַיְינוּ שְׁעָרִים בַּדִּמְיוֹן שֶׁהָיוּ מְשׁוּקָּעִים בְּמִצְרַיִם בְּמ"ט מֵהֶם כַּנּוֹדָע, וְכָל אֶחָד כָּלוּל מִג' – קִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ר"ו – הֲרֵי ק"נ מִינֵי טְהָרוֹת וְנִצּוּחַ בִּקְרָבָא.
connections.quote: “He said to him: Come and see, my son. The Holy One, blessed be He, covenanted with Abraham only to bring Israel out of the exile of Egypt, not from under the bondage of another object of worship. For when Israel were in Egypt, they certainly defiled and sullied themselves with every kind of impurity, until they were under forty-nine powers of impurity. The Holy One, blessed be He, brought them out from the service of all those other powers. Moreover, He brought them into forty-nine gates of understanding corresponding to them. He had covenanted with Abraham only to bring them out of Egypt, but He acted toward them with His goodness and kindness. Therefore you will find the exodus from Egypt fifty times in the Torah, to show everyone the kindness that the Holy One, blessed be He, did for Israel: He brought them out of those powers of impurity and into the powers of purity, which are the fifty gates of understanding. These are what we count from the festival day of Passover. We count days and weeks, as the companions have explained: It is a commandment to count days, and a commandment to count weeks. For each day He brought us out of a power of impurity and into a power of purity.”
connections.context: The Zohar Chadash gives the forty-nine powers of impurity in Egypt, their corresponding gates of understanding, and the larger fiftyfold account of the exodus. It connects that movement with counting the Omer.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל כָּל נִצּוּחַ יִסַּד מִזְמוֹר אֶחָד, וּבְוַדַּאי בְּכֹחַ אוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר לְזַמֵּר עָרִיצִים, הַיְינוּ מַחֲשָׁבוֹת וְדִמְיוֹנוֹת מֵאוֹתוֹ שַׁעַר.
connections.quote: “Likewise King David, peace be upon him, was chosen; it is written of him, “He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes,” and he is called “the sweet singer of Israel.” For it says in Shir HaShirim Rabbah: Ten people uttered the Book of Psalms; the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “You are all pleasing,” but let David, whose voice is sweet, say it. Zemirot means cutting, from “You shall not prune,” as we say in the prayer before Psalms: to cut down the violent and cut away all the thorns and briars surrounding the supernal rose. He therefore established the yoke of repentance, which removes the evil in the fool’s heart on the left and brings all the souls of Israel near to the Holy One, blessed be He, because he is the aspect of the heart of all Israel. As we have said many times, the king is Israel’s heart and introduces the power of repentance into all the hearts of the children of Israel. Through Torah and prayer they uproot the evil inclination from their hearts, purify their hearts from every abomination and defilement, and repair all the damage.”
connections.context: This parallel explains the wordplay between zemirot, songs, and pruning. It connects David’s psalms with repentance and the removal of harmful forces from the heart.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר א) דְּבִקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כִּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת,
connections.quote: “Let them not read them as one reads other books; rather, let them read them and receive reward for them as for Nega’im and Ohalot.” This is David’s request on “May the words of my mouth be acceptable” (Psalms 19:15), which the Midrash also expounds: “Let the words of my mouth be made, written and engraved for generations.”
connections.context: Nega’im and Ohalot are difficult areas of Torah study; Rav Tzadok explains the requested equivalence through Torah’s power to overcome the evil inclination.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ דְּעִיקַּר נִצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת הֵם הַיְקָרִים מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (נ.) עַל פָּסוּק "יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן" (זְכַרְיָה יד, ו) – שֶׁיְּקָרִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: ‘The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: If this vile one confronts you, drag him to the study house. If he is stone, he will dissolve; if he is iron, he will shatter. If he is stone, he will dissolve, as it is written: ‘Ho, everyone who is thirsty, go to the water,’ and it is written: ‘Water wears away stones.’ If he is iron, he will shatter, as it is written: ‘Is not My word like fire, declares Hashem, and like a hammer that shatters rock?’’

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ דְּעִיקַּר נִצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת הֵם הַיְקָרִים מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (נ.) עַל פָּסוּק "יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן" (זְכַרְיָה יד, ו) – שֶׁיְּקָרִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: These are Nega’im and Ohalot, which are weighty in this world and light in the World to Come. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: These are people who are highly esteemed in this world but of little account in the World to Come. This is like the case of Rav Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who fell ill and his soul departed. When he returned, his father asked, ‘What did you see?’ He answered, ‘I saw an upside-down world: those above were below, and those below were above.’ He said to him, ‘My son, you saw a world in its true order. And how are we regarded there?’ ‘As we are regarded here, so are we regarded there.’”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ דְּעִיקַּר נִצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת הֵם הַיְקָרִים מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (נ.) עַל פָּסוּק "יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן" (זְכַרְיָה יד, ו) – שֶׁיְּקָרִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: “On that day there shall be no light—precious things and congelation.”
connections.context: This deliberately close rendering preserves yekarot, “precious things,” and kippaon, “congelation.” Pesachim 50a reads them homiletically: teachings considered weighty or difficult in this world will be easy in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok is invoking that derash, rather than a description of weather.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ דְּעִיקַּר נִצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת הֵם הַיְקָרִים מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (נ.) עַל פָּסוּק "יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן" (זְכַרְיָה יד, ו) – שֶׁיְּקָרִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:9
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:9
connections.quote: “for his [David’s] intrinsic rung was transient life in the union of soul and body, centered in the heart whence issue the forces of life to the limbs, wherein lies moral exertion; for the evil inclination sits at the two gates of the heart (Berakhot 61a), and only "he who conquers in battle is given the daughter of the King—which is prayer" (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13); whereas the eternal life of Torah, residing in the brain independent of bodily limitations, is open to all; and on the contrary: "if this repulsive one encounters you, drag him to the study hall" (Sukkah 52b), Torah acting as the antidote to conquer the inclination, studied prior to victory rather than only after it.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim quotes the same image of the victor receiving prayer, then explicitly contrasts Torah, which is available before victory as the remedy against the yetzer. This keeps the siman’s description of an attained level from closing the path to someone who still experiences distraction. The remedy is already available within the struggle, rather than only after one has overcome it.
connections.headline: Torah is also the means of winning the struggle

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי טֻמְאַת צָרַעַת וְטֻמְאַת מֵת הֵם נֶגֶד קִנְאָה וְכָבוֹד, וּדְבָרִים אֵלּוּ קָשִׁים מְאֹד הַלִּמּוּדִים אֵיךְ לְהִנָּצֵל.
connections.quote: “There are three impurities corresponding to the three kelipot of envy, desire, and honor. The impurity of tzaraat comes through slander, which arises from hatred of other people and the kelipah of anger and envy; this is the kelipah of Esau. The impurity of a bodily discharge comes through desire, the kelipah of Ishmael, which is alien cravings and loves. The impurity of the dead corresponds to the kelipah of pride and honor, which is the root of the serpent’s enticement, “You shall be like God.” This was explained in teaching 6. From these three kelipot branch the three grave transgressions: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed. The culmination of pride reaches the declaration, “I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall resemble the Most High.” Forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed correspond to desire and envy.”
connections.context: This parallel makes explicit Rav Tzadok’s symbolic association of tzaraat with envy and corpse impurity with honor, placing them alongside the third member, desire. These are his spiritual correspondences, distinct from the legal definitions of ritual impurity.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא נט.) בְּדוֹאֵג וַאֲחִיתֹפֶל: וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁהָיוּ עוֹסְקִים בִּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת אָמְרוּ: דָּוִד וְכוּלֵי,
connections.quote: ‘Moreover, even when they are occupied with Nega’im and Ohalot, they say to me: ‘David, what is the death penalty for one who has intercourse with a married woman?’ I tell them: ‘His death penalty is strangulation, and he has a share in the World to Come. But one who humiliates his fellow in public has no share in the World to Come.’’

connections.hePhrase: [רט] בְּעֵת הַתְּפִלָּה בְּיוֹתֵר הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת גּוֹבְרִים בָּאָדָם, וְזֶהוּ עִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה שֶׁאֵין אָדָם נִיצּוֹל בְּכָל יוֹם (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קסד:).
connections.quote: “Rav Amram said in the name of Rav: There are three transgressions that a person does not escape each day: thoughts of transgression, iyun tefillah, and lashon hara.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reads iyun tefillah here, with Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot and the Ran (notes 3081, 3083), as failing to concentrate in prayer.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת וְהָרַ"ן בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (טז:) הֵבִיאוּ עַל זֶה הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּפֶרֶק הָיָה קוֹרֵא: "אֲנָא מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוְּונִית וְכוּלֵי" כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ.
connections.heRef: תוספות על ראש השנה ט״ז ב:ה׳:א׳
connections.quote: “Rabbeinu Tam says that “examination of prayer” here is like that in “Get Pashut,” where it is counted among three things from which a person is not saved each day: namely, that he does not direct his heart in prayer. As the Jerusalem Talmud says: Rabbi Chiyya the Great said, “All my days I have not concentrated. Once I sought to concentrate, and I thought in my heart: Who enters before the king first, the chief officer or the exilarch?””
connections.context: Tosafot records this explanation and the Yerushalmi passage, but then rejects it as the meaning of the particular warning in Rosh Hashanah, interpreting that warning as confident expectation of an answer. The lack-of-concentration explanation applies to the daily failing in Bava Batra. Rav Tzadok is examining the Yerushalmi’s account of the sages’ concentration.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת וְהָרַ"ן בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (טז:) הֵבִיאוּ עַל זֶה הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּפֶרֶק הָיָה קוֹרֵא: "אֲנָא מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוְּונִית וְכוּלֵי" כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Chiyya the Great said: In all my days I never concentrated. Once I sought to concentrate, and I thought in my heart: Who goes in first before the king, the chief officer or the exilarch? Shmuel said: I counted fledglings. Rabbi Bun bar Chiyya said: I counted rows of stones.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת וְהָרַ"ן בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (טז:) הֵבִיאוּ עַל זֶה הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּפֶרֶק הָיָה קוֹרֵא: "אֲנָא מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוְּונִית וְכוּלֵי" כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ.
connections.heRef: ר"ן על ראש השנה ג׳ ב:ד׳
connections.quote: ““Examination of prayer”: He relies on his prayer and is confident that it will be heard. As for what we say in the chapter Get Pashut, that there are three transgressions from which no person is free each day, one of which is examination of prayer—the examination of prayer there is not the same as here. Were it the same, how could it say that no one is free of it each day? There are many people who do not rely on their prayer every day. Rather, examination of prayer there means that he does not attend to his prayer. It therefore says that no one is free of it, for no one directs his attention as he should. As we read in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot: Rabbi Ḥiyya said, “All my days I have not concentrated. Once I came to concentrate, and I thought in my heart: Who enters before the king first, the chief official or the exilarch?” Shmuel said, “I counted chicks.” Rabbi Bun, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya, said, “I counted rows of masonry.” Rabbi Matanya said, “I am grateful to my head, for when it reached Modim it bowed of itself.” This is what is meant in the chapter Kol Kitvei HaKodesh: “May I be rewarded for having fulfilled examination of prayer.” It is also what is meant in the chapter Mefannin: There are six things whose fruits a person enjoys in this world, one of which is examination of prayer—that is, he attends to it and directs his intention in it.”
connections.context: Ran distinguishes presumptuous reliance on an answer from insufficient attention in prayer, and then explains positive uses of the same expression. His complete discussion includes all four statements from the Yerushalmi. Rav Tzadok offers a further interpretation of those statements here.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת עַל אֲנָשִׁים גְּדוֹלִים כָּאֵלֶּה רָחוֹק מִלִּשְׁמוֹעַ זֶה, בִּפְרָט רַבִּי חִיָּיא דְּאָמְרוּ עָלָיו בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פה:) שֶׁאָמַר: מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ – נָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: ‘He asked him: ‘Is there anyone like them in this world?’ He answered: ‘There are Rabbi Chiyya and his sons.’ Rabbi decreed a fast and brought Rabbi Chiyya and his sons down [to lead the prayers]. He said, ‘Who makes the wind blow,’ and the wind blew. He said, ‘Who brings down rain,’ and rain came. As he reached ‘Who revives the dead,’ the world trembled.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ: "לָא כַּוְּונִית" – לֹא הוּצְרַךְ;
connections.quote: “One may explain that this is what Rabbi Ḥiyya the Great meant by “All my days I have not concentrated”: he did not need to straighten his heart and direct it to his Father in Heaven through preparation in Torah or fear, by waiting before prayer. Rather, he would rise and find his heart hoping toward love and fear, as in Rabbi Elazar’s prayer, “May we rise,” and so forth. “Once I wished to concentrate”: on that occasion he needed to prepare for prayer and wait an hour beforehand, and he was unsure which preparation to make—according to the Mishnah or according to the baraita. This is what he meant by “I thought in my heart: Who enters before the king first, the chief official or the exilarch?” The chief official signifies a Torah scholar, as we find in Zevaḥim: “The chief official took my hand, and his scent reached my hand”—because you went before Rav Sheshet, have you become like Rav Sheshet? Rav Sheshet was a Sinai, as it says in Eruvin: “Rav Ḥisda’s lips trembled before the teachings of Rav Sheshet.” This is the meaning of the chief official. The expression concerning the grasp and the scent follows what is said in the Zohar: They caused Issachar to come into the world, because the scent of Torah rose before the Holy One, blessed be He; this is “the mandrakes gave forth their scent.” It also follows the teaching that with each utterance the whole world filled with fragrance. The exilarch, however, is a ruling scepter, as it says in Sanhedrin: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah”—these are the exilarchs in Babylonia, who rule Israel with a rod. We also find in Ḥullin: “For you have striven with divine beings and men”—He alluded to the exilarchs in Babylonia and the patriarch in the Land of Israel. The patriarch’s role is in Torah, as Rashi explains that those ordained are called elohim; the exilarchs are the “men,” the ruling scepter. We find in Berakhot that once a king bows, he does not straighten up, for he is full of fear, submission, and dread. Rabbi Ḥiyya was therefore unsure which preparation to make in order to direct and straighten his heart to his Father in Heaven: through gravity, submission, and fear, signified by the exilarch’s level and corresponding to the Mishnah; or through a conclusive halakhah, corresponding to the baraita and signified by the chief official. This is what he meant: Who enters before the King first—the chief official, signifying Torah, or the exilarch, signifying fear? In truth, both are one, as it says in Avot: “If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom.” Rabbi Ḥiyya was unsure only where the awakening should begin: with Torah, or with fear and submission. “Who enters before the King first” means which should come first.”
connections.context: This parallel supplies a further reading of the particular thought about precedence before a king: it becomes a question about preparing for prayer through Torah or through fear. The conclusion preserves the unity of both approaches; the question concerns their order.

connections.hePhrase: דְּכַוָּנַת הַלֵּב שַׁיָּיךְ בְּבַעַל דִּמְיוֹן וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת, שֶׁהַלָּשׁוֹן מְשׁוּלָּח לְדַבֵּר אַף שֶׁלִּבּוֹ בַּל עִמּוֹ, וְצָרִיךְ לְכַוֵּין לִבּוֹ.
