connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות תפילה וברכת כהנים ד׳:ט״ז
connections.quote: see note 2703.
connections.context: Maimonides describes the ordinary practice of directing the heart: preparation, awareness of standing before the Shekhinah, and unhurried supplication. This provides the practical meaning of the concentration whose necessity Rav Tzadok discusses.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא לֹא הוּצְרַךְ מֵעוֹלָם לָזֶה, שֶׁמֵּעוֹלָם לֹא הָיָה בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹכַח עֵינָיו, וְלֹא הָיָה מְדַבֵּר אֶלָּא כִּמְדַבֵּר לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים לְעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: “Isaac came and added that even prayer without deliberate concentration is prayer. This was his level: he would show them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their very eyes (Shabbat 89b)—how the whole earth is filled with His glory, literally present before the eye. With such clear recognition, deliberate concentration of the heart no longer makes a difference, as it says (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 2:4): “All my days I did not concentrate,” and so forth. For when a person has such clear recognition, this itself is a comprehensive intention encompassing all his thoughts, words, and deeds. Even his ordinary conversation is entirely from the blessed God alone, and there is none besides Him. There is no difference between concentrating this way or that, for which he must make an effort; instead he should leave everything to the blessed God and exert himself only in the fundamental intention, “I have set the Lord before me always”—literally before me. Then, of itself, when he fulfills “Commit,” and so forth, “they shall be established,” and so forth. This is called an unintended act, rather than mere unawareness, for a comprehensive intention is nevertheless required, as explained above, and he must know that he is going to pray.”

connections.hePhrase: וְ"יוֹמָא חַד בָּעֵי כַּוְּונִית וְכוּלֵי" – פֵּירוּשׁ הוּצְרַךְ לְכָךְ, שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מַחֲשָׁבוֹת מַטְרִידִים, וְאוּלַי הַיְינוּ עוּבָדָא דְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (שָׁם) דְּאֵלִיָּהוּ טַרְדִינְהוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “They said in Heaven: Who revealed the secrets in the world? They said: Elijah. They brought Elijah and struck him with sixty lashes of fire. He came, appeared to them like a bear of fire, entered among them, and disturbed them.”
connections.context: The preceding passage describes Rabbi Chiyya and his sons’ effective prayer and the danger of prematurely awakening resurrection. Rav Tzadok suggests that this divinely caused disturbance may explain the exceptional interruption of Rabbi Chiyya’s concentration; he presents the identification as a possibility.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל תָּמִיד לָא צְרִיכֵי כַּוָּנָה כְּלָל, דְּמִמֵּילָא צָעַק לִבָּם אֶל ה' בְּעֵת הַתְּפִלָּה בְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל דִּמְיוֹן.
connections.quote: see note 1733 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah connects David's ‘I am prayer’ to the request ‘Adonai, open my lips.’ Accepting divine lordship allows speech to become an expression of that relation. This illuminates the siman's distinction between a mouth moving on its own and speech opened from the heart. The full attained condition is a model toward which the ordinary opening request turns, rather than something proved merely by pronouncing its words.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בְּכָל אָדָם כִּמְעַט אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּצֵל כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
connections.quote: “To be saved all day from alien thoughts and thoughts outside the will of the blessed God is possible only for one entirely free of personal self-interest. This is when he has already killed the evil inclination, as did King David, peace be upon him; “whoever wins the battle is given” prayer, as stated at the end of Tikkun 13. Whoever is not free of alien thoughts all day will not escape alien thoughts in prayer either. Thus Bava Batra says that no one is free of examination of prayer, apparently speaking of every person. The words of the Yerushalmi cited by Tosafot, “All my days I have not concentrated,” then retain their plain meaning: he could not escape every flash of an alien thought throughout the entire prayer. The thought “Who enters before the king?” concerns honor. Because of an attachment to honor, this thought entered on the day he wished to concentrate, when he prepared himself like the early pious ones who waited in order to direct their hearts—that is, to straighten the heart so that it would contain no self-interest or desire apart from the will of the blessed God. Perhaps at that moment the blessed God would help him win the battle and remove the inclination from within him. The thoughts “I counted chicks” and “rows of masonry,” concerning possessions, arise from an attachment to the desire for money. “I am grateful to my head” means that envy brings an alien thought at Modim, the thanksgiving for God’s kindnesses: the envious person feels deprived and does not thank the blessed God for His benefits, but instead complains that He gives benefit to another. This is the meaning of Bava Kamma’s teaching about a person’s spine, applying it to one who did not bow at Modim, for “envy rots the bones.” The serpent’s root is envy, as the Sages said: he saw and became envious. Eve likewise fed Adam because of envy. It is known that almost no one is entirely free of these three—envy, desire, and honor. As I wrote above, “Who can stand before envy?” Concerning desire, the Sages said, “Even the most pious of the pious,” and so forth. All the more so honor, which includes both, as is known. Therefore no one escapes alien thoughts.”
connections.context: Later in the same work, Rav Tzadok explicitly develops the Yerushalmi’s plain reading as an alternative to the interpretation offered here. This passage preserves that difference and traces the distracting thoughts to the three traits, rather than presenting one interpretation as his only explanation.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה תִּקְּנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יז), שֶׁהַשֵּׁם אֲדֹנָ"י מוֹרֶה עַל שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבְּקֶרֶב לִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: At the beginning one says, ‘Hashem, open my lips’ (Psalms 51:17), and at the end one says, ‘May the words of my mouth be acceptable’ (Psalms 19:15).”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה תִּקְּנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יז), שֶׁהַשֵּׁם אֲדֹנָ"י מוֹרֶה עַל שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבְּקֶרֶב לִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: ‘Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה), וְהַיְינוּ מִדַּת הַשֵּׁם הַנִּזְכָּר כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “My flesh and my heart fail, but God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה), וְהַיְינוּ מִדַּת הַשֵּׁם הַנִּזְכָּר כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: see note 363 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וּבַסּוֹף: "יִהְיוּ לְרָצוֹן וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים יט, טו), שֶׁעַל הֶעָבָר מְבַקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הֶגְיוֹן הַלֵּב לְרָצוֹן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה מְעוֹרָב בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת,
connections.quote: “May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, Lord, my rock and my redeemer.”
connections.context: At the close of prayer, this asks that both spoken words and inward meditation be accepted. Rav Tzadok applies the request to prayer that has already been offered despite intrusive thoughts.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַסּוֹף: "יִהְיוּ לְרָצוֹן וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים יט, טו), שֶׁעַל הֶעָבָר מְבַקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הֶגְיוֹן הַלֵּב לְרָצוֹן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה מְעוֹרָב בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת,
connections.quote: “It is written (Psalms 19:15), ‘May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You…’ The Zohar says (Vayishlach 169a): King David said, ‘The words of my mouth’—these are expressed words; ‘the meditation of my heart’—these are hidden words that a person cannot express with his mouth, the meditation in the heart. One corresponds to the lower level and one to the upper level; expressed speech corresponds to the lower level. My holy grandfather explained that a person has actions in which he does not recognize Heaven's honor, to the point that he himself doubts whether his intention was clearly for Hashem's will. Actual mitzvot give him great assurance, for he knows that he fulfilled Hashem's will through them, as the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Ki Tavo): see what assurance and room to speak those who perform mitzvot have. But in ordinary optional matters he may doubt whether his intention was expressly to fulfill Hashem's will. This gives rise to accusations that perhaps this was not his intention. The counsel is to remove, from his side, every private interest, so that he has no worldly stake in these matters; then all the accusing powers will fall away.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same closing prayer verse through the Zohar's distinction between expressed words and inward matters that cannot be articulated. It then requires the person to remove private worldly interests. This gives a complementary account of asking that both mouth and heart be accepted, while preserving the siman's acknowledgment that the actual prayer may still contain distracting thoughts.
connections.headline: The spoken words and the hidden heart

connections.hePhrase: וְטַעַם: מַצְלֵי הֵיכָא דְּגָרְסֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ח.) גַּם כֵּן, כִּי הַתּוֹרָה מוֹצִיאָה דִּמְיוֹן שֶׁהוּא הֶפְכּוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
connections.quote: ‘Abaye said: At first I would study in the house and pray in the synagogue. Once I heard Rabbi Chiya bar Ami’s statement in Ulla’s name—that from the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has only the four cubits of halakhah in His world—I would pray only where I studied.’

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה יֵשׁ לוֹ קְדוּשַּׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאִם כֵּן אֲוִירָהּ מַחְכִּים כְּמוֹ אֲוִיר אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְחָכְמָה הוּא הִיפּוּךְ דִּמְיוֹן, כְּשֶׁזֶּה קָם זֶה נוֹפֵל.
connections.quote: “As I heard, the four cubits of halakhah are holy with the holiness of the Land of Israel. The air of the lands of the nations is expelled from them entirely on every side by the double-edged sword, and the holy air of words of Torah enters. This is the air of the Land of Israel, which therefore imparts wisdom, like Torah’s quality of making the simple wise. But the synagogue and prayer do not help when a person has already encountered and become entangled in alien thoughts, for his entire prayer will likewise be full of alien thoughts. Rather, he must direct his heart to distance himself from alien thoughts; then through prayer he can bring holy thoughts into the depth of the heart and kill the evil from afar, as in “their tongue is a sharpened arrow.” The tongue is like an arrow that kills from a distance, and this is through prayer, as stated in the Tikkunim, at the end of Tikkun 13 and elsewhere: he shoots arrow after arrow at it.”
connections.context: This parallel repeats the teaching about the four cubits of halakhah and then preserves the complementary power of prayer. Torah clears the immediate surrounding thoughts; properly directed prayer works upon the heart’s deeper interior.

connections.hePhrase: וּ"מֵסִיר אָזְנוֹ מִשְּׁמֹעַ תּוֹרָה, גַּם תְּפִלָּתוֹ תוֹעֵבָה" (מִשְׁלֵי כח, ט; שַׁבָּת י.) – פֵּירוּשׁ: "תּוֹעֵבָה" נִקְרָא כְּשֶׁמְּלֵאָה מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְדִמְיוֹנוֹת;
connections.quote: ‘One who turns away his ear from hearing Torah—even his prayer is an abomination.’

connections.hePhrase: וּ"מֵסִיר אָזְנוֹ מִשְּׁמֹעַ תּוֹרָה, גַּם תְּפִלָּתוֹ תוֹעֵבָה" (מִשְׁלֵי כח, ט; שַׁבָּת י.) – פֵּירוּשׁ: "תּוֹעֵבָה" נִקְרָא כְּשֶׁמְּלֵאָה מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְדִמְיוֹנוֹת;
connections.quote: ““People like us interrupt both for Shema and for prayer”: As for Rabbi Zeira’s saying to Rabbi Yirmeya, “One who turns his ear from hearing Torah,” and so forth, one may answer that Torah was his occupation, or that the time for prayer was not yet about to pass.”
connections.context: Tosafot explains the episode cited in the existing Shabbat note with two alternatives. Its distinction concerning a prayer time that is not yet passing is retained, so the verse is not presented as an unrestricted refusal to interrupt study.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְּפִלָּה הוּא עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַלֵּב מָלֵא מַחְשֶׁבֶת פִּגּוּל, הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כְּמוֹ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְתוֹעֵבָה, רַק דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צוּרוֹ וְגוֹאֲלוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
connections.quote: “As it was taught: ‘To love Hashem your God and to serve Him with all your heart’ (Deuteronomy 11:13). What is the service that is in the heart? You must say: this is prayer.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אִידַךְ סָבַר זְמַן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד, וְתַלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (לא.): אִם עוֹמְדִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל מִתּוֹךְ הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה שֶׁהִיא הַמְזַכֶּכֶת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, אוֹ מִתּוֹךְ כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: One should not stand to pray straight from a court case or a halakhic discussion, but from a settled halakhic ruling.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אִידַךְ סָבַר זְמַן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד, וְתַלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (לא.): אִם עוֹמְדִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל מִתּוֹךְ הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה שֶׁהִיא הַמְזַכֶּכֶת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, אוֹ מִתּוֹךְ כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ
connections.quote: “The Sages acted according to the Mishnah; Rav Ashi acted according to the baraita. The Sages taught: One should not stand to pray from sadness, idleness, laughter, conversation, levity, or idle matters, but from the joy of a commandment.”
connections.context: The preceding Mishnah requires gravity, while the preceding baraita requires a conclusive halakhah. The Gemara names the practices followed by the Sages and Rav Ashi, then adds the requirement of the joy of a commandment. This completes the discussion cited in the existing note.

connections.hePhrase: זֶהוּ כְּדִבְרֵי הָאוֹמֵר זְמַן תְּפִלָּה לְחוּד שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חִבּוּר עִם תּוֹרָה, רַק עַל יְדֵי כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ יוֹצִיא הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְהַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת מֵהַלֵּב:
connections.quote: ““One does not stand to pray except with gravity,” and so forth: Gravity means standing with intention and fear, as it says, “Serve the Lord with fear.” “They would wait” means that they delayed for one hour before prayer in order to settle their minds and quiet their thoughts, and only then would they begin prayer.”
connections.context: Maimonides explains the Mishnah’s gravity as intention and fear, and its waiting as the settling of the mind. This directly supplies the meaning of the alternative preparation at the close of Rav Tzadok’s discussion.

connections.hePhrase: [רי] כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְכַוֵּין, כָּתַב תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ה, כה עַמּוּד ב) בְּשֵׁם הַקַּדְמוֹנִים: שֶׁיִּפְשׁוֹט גּוּפוֹ מִנִּשְׁמָתוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, פֵּירוּשׁ כֵּן: לִבּוֹ לְמַעְלָה (יְבָמוֹת קה:).
connections.heRef: רבינו יונה על ברכות כ״ב ב:ג׳
connections.quote: ““He must direct his eyes downward and his heart upward”: This means that he should think in his heart as though he were standing in heaven, and remove from his heart all the pleasures of this world and all bodily enjoyments, as the ancients said: “When you wish to concentrate, strip your body away from your soul.” After reaching this thought, he should also imagine himself standing in the Temple below, for through this his prayer will be more acceptable before the Omnipresent.”

connections.hePhrase: [רי] כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְכַוֵּין, כָּתַב תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ה, כה עַמּוּד ב) בְּשֵׁם הַקַּדְמוֹנִים: שֶׁיִּפְשׁוֹט גּוּפוֹ מִנִּשְׁמָתוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, פֵּירוּשׁ כֵּן: לִבּוֹ לְמַעְלָה (יְבָמוֹת קה:).
connections.quote: “He said to them: Thus my father said: One who prays must direct his eyes downward and his heart upward, so that both these verses may be fulfilled.”
connections.context: Rabbeinu Yonah supplies the actual wording about stripping the body away from the soul; Yevamot supplies “his heart upward.” In the Vilna Rif this is on 22b; Rav Tzadok’s 25b follows an older printing. Rav Tzadok explains these expressions as inward concentration beyond bodily sensation, not a physical act.

connections.hePhrase: [רי] כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְכַוֵּין, כָּתַב תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ה, כה עַמּוּד ב) בְּשֵׁם הַקַּדְמוֹנִים: שֶׁיִּפְשׁוֹט גּוּפוֹ מִנִּשְׁמָתוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, פֵּירוּשׁ כֵּן: לִבּוֹ לְמַעְלָה (יְבָמוֹת קה:).
connections.quote: “And these two sublime faculties are spiritual states operating beyond the physical limbs; unlike mental thought which remains linked to the brain as a physical bodily organ; for these two higher levels transcend the body, termed in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 98:1) "the stripping away of corporeality" (hitpashtut hagashmiyut); wherein reaching these rungs one loses all physical awareness of the body, as recorded of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Eruvin 54b) who embodied "be you ravished always with her love" Proverbs 5:19.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet uses the same Shulchan Aruch reference and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat’s immersion in Torah to explain this language. In its preceding paragraph, the two powers are identified as chayah and yechidah, modes of the soul’s attachment to its source. This clarifies that the discussion concerns the direction and absorption of awareness, rather than a physical separation that one attempts to perform.
connections.headline: Absorption in Torah and the language of leaving bodily awareness

connections.hePhrase: וּבְטוּר וְשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ סִימָן צ"ח נִקְרָא זֶה "הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת", וְשֶׁהוּא קָרוֹב לִנְבוּאָה.
connections.quote: “Thus would the pious and the men of practice act: they would seclude themselves and concentrate in prayer until they reached a divestment of corporeality and a strengthening of the intellectual faculty, until they came close to the level of prophecy.”
connections.context: This is the precise description Rav Tzadok calls “divestment of corporeality.” The passage describes absorbed concentration in prayer; its comparison to prophecy explains the next sentence in this section.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הַנְּבִיאִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשָׁאוּל שֶׁהָלַךְ וּמִתְנַבֵּא עָרוֹם (שְׁמוּאֵל א יט, כד), פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהַגּוּף הוּא לְבוּשׁ לַנֶּפֶשׁ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ נִקְרָא עָרוֹם;
connections.quote: “It is known that in the three matters we have included—the perfection of the rational faculty through learning, the perfection of the imaginative faculty in its original constitution, and the perfection of character through withdrawing thought from all bodily pleasures and removing the desire for the foolish and harmful kinds of self-aggrandizement—those who are perfected differ greatly from one another. According to the degree of difference in each of these three matters, the ranks of all the prophets differ from one another.”
connections.context: Maimonides summarizes the intellectual, natural, and ethical conditions in his account of prophecy. The withdrawal from bodily desire belongs to this larger set of conditions; the passage does not describe it as a sufficient condition by itself.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הַנְּבִיאִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשָׁאוּל שֶׁהָלַךְ וּמִתְנַבֵּא עָרוֹם (שְׁמוּאֵל א יט, כד), פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהַגּוּף הוּא לְבוּשׁ לַנֶּפֶשׁ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ נִקְרָא עָרוֹם;
connections.quote: ““He too stripped off his clothes”: This teaches that the other prophets stripped off their clothes, for “he too” includes them. The matter is that when prophecy comes upon a person, his senses cease to function and he falls, as it says of Balaam, “fallen, with eyes uncovered,” and as Daniel says, “I was in a deep sleep on my face, with my face to the ground.” Sometimes he strips off his clothes because of the great cessation of his sensory and psychic activities, and he remains with the intellectual faculty alone.”
connections.context: Radak explains the bodily behavior described in the narrative through the suspension of ordinary sensory activity. Rav Tzadok uses the narrative to explain the spiritual meaning of divestment.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הַנְּבִיאִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשָׁאוּל שֶׁהָלַךְ וּמִתְנַבֵּא עָרוֹם (שְׁמוּאֵל א יט, כד), פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהַגּוּף הוּא לְבוּשׁ לַנֶּפֶשׁ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ נִקְרָא עָרוֹם;
connections.quote: ‘He too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel. He lay naked all that day and all that night. Therefore people say: Is Saul also among the prophets?’

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הַנְּבִיאִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשָׁאוּל שֶׁהָלַךְ וּמִתְנַבֵּא עָרוֹם (שְׁמוּאֵל א יט, כד), פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהַגּוּף הוּא לְבוּשׁ לַנֶּפֶשׁ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ נִקְרָא עָרוֹם;
connections.quote: see note 1741 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rabbi Ḥayyim Vital states the soul-and-garment analogy invoked here. His description includes both life in the body and the different garment after death.

connections.hePhrase: וְתַרְגּוּם יוֹנָתָן שָׁם: "בַּרְשָׁן", פֵּירוּשׁ מְשֻׁגָּע, שֶׁאֵינוֹ פּוֹנֶה כְּלָל לְגוּפוֹ, וּפְעֻלַּת הַגּוּף הֵם כִּמְעַט בְּלֹא יְדִיעָתוֹ כְּלָל וּכְמוֹ מְשֻׁגָּע.
connections.quote: ““And he fell naked”: “And he fell barshan.” Jonathan rendered it, “And he fell naked.” In the name of Rabbi Menaḥem, who heard it from an Arab: barshan in Arabic means mad.”
connections.context: Rashi records both the rendering as naked and the explanation of barshan as mad. The latter is the lexical interpretation Rav Tzadok adopts in explaining the prophet’s lack of attention to bodily activity.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן קָרְאוּ לַנָּבִיא גַּבֵּי יֵהוּא (מְלָכִים ב ט, יא): "הַמְשֻׁגָּע".
connections.quote: ‘Jehu went out to his master’s servants. One of them said to him: ‘Is all well? Why did this madman come to you?’ He answered them: ‘You know the man and his talk.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן קָרְאוּ לַנָּבִיא גַּבֵּי יֵהוּא (מְלָכִים ב ט, יא): "הַמְשֻׁגָּע".
connections.quote: ““This madman”: They called the prophet mad because at times during prophecy his behavior was like that of a madman who had lost his reason, as it says, “He too stripped off his clothes,” because their senses and psychic faculties cease their ordinary activity. The wicked Israelites, whose minds and hearts followed Baal, called the prophet of the Lord mad as an expression of contempt.”
connections.context: Radak distinguishes the prophet’s unusual behavior from the contemptuous way the followers of Baal spoke of him. Both parts of his explanation are retained.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה גַּם כֵּן נֶאֱמַר: "בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה [תָמִיד]" (מִשְׁלֵי ה, יט), וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:) עַל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פְּדָת שֶׁשּׁוֹכֵחַ עִנְיְנֵי הַגּוּף, וְהוּא בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּתוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה, זֶה אֶפְשָׁר גַּם בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: ‘‘Be absorbed in her love always’—like Rabbi (Eliezer) ben Pedat. They said of Rabbi (Eliezer) that he would sit and occupy himself with Torah in the lower market of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper market of Tzippori. (It was taught:) Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar said: Once someone came to take it and found a fiery serpent in it.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַדְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (כְּתוּבּוֹת קיא:): וְכִי אֶפְשָׁר לִדְבַּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ? אֶלָּא הַמַּשִּׂיא וְכוּלֵי, וְזֶהוּ בְּעַם הָאָרֶץ כְּשֶׁנִּדְבָּק לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם.
connections.quote: ‘Similarly, concerning ‘To love Hashem your God and to cling to Him’: Can a person cling to the Shechinah? Rather, anyone who marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, conducts business on behalf of Torah scholars, or enables Torah scholars to benefit from his property is credited by Scripture as though he clung to the Shechinah.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם כְּשֶׁדָּבוּק בַּתּוֹרָה הוּא דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי אוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא וְחָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ אֶחָד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה (פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה י), וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא חָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְהַדָּבוּק בָּהּ דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבְאוֹתוֹ עֵת הוּא בְּמַדְרֵגַת נְבוּאָה, רַק חָכָם עָדִיף.
connections.quote: “We have learned that three levels are bound to one another: the Holy One, blessed be He, the Torah, and Israel; and each of them is level upon level, hidden and revealed.”
connections.context: This passage (Zohar III:73a) is the source of the saying that the Torah and the Holy One, blessed be He, are one.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם כְּשֶׁדָּבוּק בַּתּוֹרָה הוּא דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי אוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא וְחָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ אֶחָד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה (פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה י), וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא חָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְהַדָּבוּק בָּהּ דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבְאוֹתוֹ עֵת הוּא בְּמַדְרֵגַת נְבוּאָה, רַק חָכָם עָדִיף.

connections.quote: see note 285 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Maimonides’ statement of divine unity includes its essential qualification: human language and understanding cannot fully comprehend this identity. His conclusion explains that God’s knowledge of creation is through His own reality.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם כְּשֶׁדָּבוּק בַּתּוֹרָה הוּא דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי אוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא וְחָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ אֶחָד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה (פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה י), וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא חָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְהַדָּבוּק בָּהּ דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבְאוֹתוֹ עֵת הוּא בְּמַדְרֵגַת נְבוּאָה, רַק חָכָם עָדִיף.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ה׳:ב׳-ו׳
connections.quote: “When any intellect understands and apprehends an intelligible matter, the intellect grasps and encompasses it in the mind, and the intelligible matter is grasped, encompassed, and clothed within the intellect that has apprehended and understood it. The intellect is also clothed in that intelligible matter while apprehending and grasping it. For example, when a person correctly and thoroughly understands a halakhah in the Mishnah or Gemara, his intellect grasps and encompasses it, while his intellect is also clothed in it at that time. This halakhah is the wisdom and will of the Holy One, blessed be He: it arose in His will that if, for example, Reuven makes one claim and Shimon another, the ruling between them shall be such and such. Even if such a case never has and never will come to judgment with these claims and demands, nevertheless, since it arose in the will and wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He, that if one makes this claim and the other that claim, the ruling shall be so, when a person knows and intellectually apprehends that ruling as set out in the Mishnah, Gemara, or legal authorities, he thereby apprehends, grasps, and encompasses in his intellect the will and wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He. No thought can grasp Him, His will, or His wisdom except as they are clothed in the halakhot set before us; his intellect is also clothed in them. This is a wondrous union, with no comparable union or equivalent anywhere in physical existence: they become actually one and united in every respect.”
connections.context: Tanya explains how understanding Torah is described as attachment to divine wisdom and will. The qualification that this apprehension is through their clothing in the laws of Torah is retained.

connections.hePhrase: וּבַזֹּהַר שְׁמוֹת (ו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) הַטַּעַם דִּלְנָבִיא הוּא רַק לְזִמְנִין וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “The sages are greater than prophets at all times, for the holy spirit rests upon prophets at some times and at other times does not; but the holy spirit does not leave the sages even for a single moment. They know what is above and below, but do not wish to reveal it. Rabbi Yose—another reading has Rabbi Yehudah—said: It is all wisdom, and Rabbi Elazar’s wisdom exceeds them all. Rabbi Abba said: Were it not for the sages, people would not know what Torah is or what the commandments of the Master of the world are, and the human spirit would not be distinguished from the spirit of an animal.”
connections.context: This is the Zohar’s explicit contrast between the occasional prophetic experience and the sage’s continuing attainment. Its account also ties the sages’ wisdom to understanding Torah and the commandments.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח – זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת בִּתְמִידוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לא.): יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל כָּל הַיּוֹם כֻּלּוֹ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: וְזִמְנִין וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת כָּל הַיּוֹם בִּתְפִלָּה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאֵינוֹ בְּכֹחַ אָדָם שֶׁבַּגּוּף כְּלָל, וַאֲפִילּוּ הֶאָרַת פָּנִים לַמַּלְאָכִים אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּמַרְאֵה הַבָּזָק כְּרֶגַע וּמִיָּד נִתְעַלֵּם.
connections.quote: ‘Could a person pray throughout the entire day? It has already been made explicit through Daniel: ‘Three times,’ and so forth. Could this practice have begun only when he came into exile? It has already been said: ‘As he had been doing before this.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח – זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת בִּתְמִידוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לא.): יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל כָּל הַיּוֹם כֻּלּוֹ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: וְזִמְנִין וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת כָּל הַיּוֹם בִּתְפִלָּה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאֵינוֹ בְּכֹחַ אָדָם שֶׁבַּגּוּף כְּלָל, וַאֲפִילּוּ הֶאָרַת פָּנִים לַמַּלְאָכִים אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּמַרְאֵה הַבָּזָק כְּרֶגַע וּמִיָּד נִתְעַלֵּם.
connections.quote: ““Running and returning, like the appearance of a flash”: Our Sages explained: Running and returning like the flame of a furnace, which continually comes out of the furnace’s opening and quickly returns inside. So, when they put their heads out from beneath the firmament stretched above them, as the passage explains, they recoil before the Shekhinah above the firmament and hasten to draw their heads back.”
connections.context: Rashi explains the living creatures’ movement in Ezekiel’s vision through their immediate recoil before the Shekhinah. This supplies the image behind Rav Tzadok’s description of a momentary illumination.

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.) הִרְבָּה בִּתְפִלָּה עַד שֶׁיָּצְתָה נִשְׁמָתוֹ – הַיְינוּ מִכֹּחַ רִבּוּי הַתְּפִלָּה, כִּי אֵין בְּכֹחַ אָדָם לִסְבּוֹל, כִּי זֶה נִקְרָא עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב וּמְיַגַּעַת הָאָדָם.
connections.quote: ‘He said: ‘The matter depends only on me.’ He placed his head between his knees and sobbed until his soul departed. A heavenly voice came forth and said: ‘Rabbi Elazar ben Durdayya is destined for life in the World to Come!’ (Yet here he had committed a transgression and died!) In that case too, since he was deeply attached to it, it was like heresy.’

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא לֶחֶם וּמָזוֹן וְעֵץ חַיִּים שֶׁהִיא הַנּוֹתֶנֶת קִיּוּם לָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי שִׂמְחָתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתוֹ,
connections.quote: “Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled.”

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא לֶחֶם וּמָזוֹן וְעֵץ חַיִּים שֶׁהִיא הַנּוֹתֶנֶת קִיּוּם לָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי שִׂמְחָתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתוֹ,
connections.quote: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, and happy is every one who holds her fast.”

connections.hePhrase: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא לֶחֶם וּמָזוֹן וְעֵץ חַיִּים שֶׁהִיא הַנּוֹתֶנֶת קִיּוּם לָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי שִׂמְחָתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתוֹ,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ה׳:ט׳-י״ג
connections.quote: “Because, through knowing Torah, Torah is clothed in the person’s soul and intellect and encompassed within them, it is called “bread” and “food for the soul.” Just as physical bread nourishes the body when brought inside it and becomes blood and flesh like its own flesh, enabling it to live and endure, so through knowing and apprehending Torah in the soul—learning it thoroughly through intellectual examination until it is grasped by the intellect and united with it—it becomes food for the soul and life within it, from the Life of life, the blessed Infinite, clothed in His wisdom and Torah within it. This is the meaning of “Your Torah is within my inward parts.” As Etz Ḥayyim, Gate 44, chapter 3, explains, the soul’s garments in the Garden of Eden are the commandments, while Torah is the food of the souls that engaged in Torah for its own sake in this world, as also stated in Zohar, Vayakhel 210. “For its own sake” means in order to bind one’s soul to God through understanding Torah, each according to his intellect, as explained in Peri Etz Ḥayyim. [The food is inward light, while the garments are surrounding lights. Therefore our Sages said that Torah study is equivalent to all the commandments, for the commandments are garments alone, while Torah is both food and a garment for the understanding soul, which clothes itself in Torah through its examination and study. All the more so when one expresses it aloud, for the breath of speech becomes surrounding light, as explained in Peri Etz Ḥayyim.]”
connections.context: Tanya explains the nourishment metaphor through Torah being understood and inwardly absorbed. The discussion retains both the requirement of thorough understanding and its definition of study for its own sake.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בָּהּ: "לֹא יָמוּשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ א, ח), שֶׁיָּכוֹל לִהְיוֹת דָּבוּק בָּהּ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְבַּטֵּל אֲפִילּוּ רֶגַע אֶחָד.
connections.quote: ‘This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth. You shall meditate on it day and night, so that you take care to do everything written in it; then you will make your way prosper, and then you will act with understanding.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם עֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וְשַׂר לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לד:) לוּלֵי פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י, רַק הַשַּׂר הוּא תָּמִיד בְּבֵית הַמֶּלֶךְ, אֲבָל הָעֶבֶד רַק בְּעֵת שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְשִׁימּוּשׁוֹ.
connections.quote: “His wife said to him: Is Chanina greater than you? He said to her: No; rather, he resembles a servant before the king, and I resemble a minister before the king.”
connections.context: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai says this after Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa’s prayer heals his son. Rav Tzadok explicitly offers an interpretation different from Rashi’s: he associates the minister’s continuing place in the palace with Torah, and the servant’s particular service with prayer. Those explanations should not be inserted into the Gemara’s own words.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם עֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וְשַׂר לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לד:) לוּלֵי פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י, רַק הַשַּׂר הוּא תָּמִיד בְּבֵית הַמֶּלֶךְ, אֲבָל הָעֶבֶד רַק בְּעֵת שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְשִׁימּוּשׁוֹ.
connections.quote: ““Like a servant”: A member of the household who enters and leaves without permission. “Like a minister before the king”: One who is not accustomed to come before him.”
connections.context: This is the interpretation from which Rav Tzadok expressly distinguishes his own. Rashi associates the servant with familiar access and the minister with less frequent access; Rav Tzadok then develops a different account through prayer and Torah.

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי דָּבוּק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא דְּבֵיקוּת תְּמִידִי נִקְרָא "שַׂר", וְלוֹ נִפְתָּחִין כָּל סוֹדוֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ, וּבְוַדַּאי כָּל דְּעָבֵיד רַחֲמָנָא לְטָב, וּמְגַלֶּה לוֹ הַטּוֹבָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ כְּשֶׁלֹּא יִפְעַל בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ, וּלְכָךְ אֵין מַשְׁגִּיחִין עָלָיו [לִפְעוֹל בְּנֵס בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ].
connections.quote: “Rav Huna said in the name of Rav, citing Rabbi Meir, and so it was taught in the name of Rabbi Akiva: A person should always be accustomed to say, ‘Whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good.’”

connections.hePhrase: [ריא] תּוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה צְרִיכִים שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַחַד לָאָדָם, וְלֹא גָּרְסֵי אֶלָּא הֵיכָא דִּמְצַלֵּי (מְגִילָּה כט.) וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ (בְּרָכוֹת ח.);
connections.quote: see note 2424.
connections.context: Abaye brings his Torah study into the place of prayer. This supplies the direction of the connection stated here; Berakhot 8a, cited next, supplies the complementary connection of prayer with the place of study.

connections.hePhrase: [ריא] תּוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה צְרִיכִים שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַחַד לָאָדָם, וְלֹא גָּרְסֵי אֶלָּא הֵיכָא דִּמְצַלֵּי (מְגִילָּה כט.) וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ (בְּרָכוֹת ח.);
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Miketz 6
connections.quote: see note 1689 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach uses bread to distinguish receiving worldly sustenance from recognizing the divine utterance that gives it life. This sheds light on the siman’s comparison to the manna: a reliable source of nourishment need not produce spiritual self-sufficiency. Recognition of the Giver belongs within the act of receiving and enjoying it.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (קט:): כָּל הָאוֹמֵר אֵין לִי אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יָבוֹא לִשְׁכּוֹחַ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִנְיַן הַתְּפִלָּה – הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיְּמַלְּאֶנּוּ.
connections.quote: “One who says, “I have only Torah”—he does not have even Torah. What is the reason? Rav Pappa said: Scripture says, “You shall learn and perform”: whoever is included in performing is included in learning; whoever is not included in performing is not included in learning.”
connections.context: This is the explanation Rav Tzadok invokes. The next paragraph offers a different interpretation about teaching others who act; quoting that alone omitted the precise statement “not even Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (קט:): כָּל הָאוֹמֵר אֵין לִי אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יָבוֹא לִשְׁכּוֹחַ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִנְיַן הַתְּפִלָּה – הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיְּמַלְּאֶנּוּ.
connections.quote: “In Torah, the levels are determined by excellence: whoever exceeds his fellow in wisdom is the greater. In prayer, however, the reverse is true: the levels are determined by lack, as stated in the Zohar (I, 23b), “A prayer of the poor,” which envelops all prayers, and as in Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai’s analogy of a servant and a minister (Berakhot 34b). For the more a person lacks and the more he needs, the more he can accomplish through his prayer, because his prayer comes from a deeper place in the heart. The essence of prayer arises from lack, as one asks the blessed God to supply what is missing; before the blessed God there is no distinction between the great and the small.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא לַחֲסֵרִים וּמַכִּירִים חֶסְרוֹנָם וּמְבַקְּשִׁים לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיּוֹשִׁיעֵם,
connections.quote: “A person must recognize his own deficiency, since the decisive reason for giving him the Torah is to complete what he lacks. If he imagines that he is complete and has no deficiency, completion does not apply to him at all. Therefore Moshe himself had to answer them, so that he would know and recognize his deficiency.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הָעֲנִיִּים וְהָאֶבְיוֹנִים מְבַקְשִׁים מַיִם וָאַיִן לְשׁוֹנָם בַּצָּמָא נָשָׁתָּה" (יְשַׁעְיָה מא, יז), וְאֵין מַיִם אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה (בָּבָא קַמָּא יז.).
connections.quote: ‘The poor and needy seek water, but there is none; their tongue is parched with thirst. I, Hashem, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הָעֲנִיִּים וְהָאֶבְיוֹנִים מְבַקְשִׁים מַיִם וָאַיִן לְשׁוֹנָם בַּצָּמָא נָשָׁתָּה" (יְשַׁעְיָה מא, יז), וְאֵין מַיִם אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה (בָּבָא קַמָּא יז.).
connections.quote: ““Seeking water”: The prophet prophesied about the end of days: “Not a hunger for bread and not a thirst for water, but to hear the word of Hashem”; “they will wander to seek the word of Hashem and will not find it.” When His anger subsides, He will prepare bread and water for them and cause His Presence and spirit to dwell in the mouths of their prophets.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הָעֲנִיִּים וְהָאֶבְיוֹנִים מְבַקְשִׁים מַיִם וָאַיִן לְשׁוֹנָם בַּצָּמָא נָשָׁתָּה" (יְשַׁעְיָה מא, יז), וְאֵין מַיִם אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה (בָּבָא קַמָּא יז.).
connections.quote: ‘For it is said: ‘Fortunate are you who sow.’ ‘Sowing’ means charity, as it is said: ‘Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and reap according to kindness.’ ‘Water’ means Torah, as it is said: ‘Ho, everyone who is thirsty, come to the water.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעִיקַּר רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה רַק לִכְבוֹדוֹ וּלְקִילּוּסוֹ וְשֶׁיְּצַפּוּ לוֹ;
connections.quote: “When the Sages heard of the matter, they said: Whatever the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created for His glory, as it is said: ‘Every one that is called by My name, and whom I have created for My glory’ (Isaiah 43:7).”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת סד.): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְאַוֶּוה לִתְפִלָּתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים.
connections.quote: see note 2190 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The passage presents lack as calling forth prayer and describes prayer’s effect through the image of turning grain. The following, incomplete sentence about Abraham and Sarah is a new teaching and is not part of this quotation.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (נִצָּבִים): שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר לְרָעַתְכֶם נָתַתִּי הַתּוֹרָה? לֹא נִיתְּנָה אֶלָּא לְטוֹבַתְכֶם וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: The Sages said that the Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you bless the Torah, you bless yourself. From where is this known? It is said, “For through me your days will increase, and years of life will be added to you.” If you should say, “Perhaps I gave you the Torah to your detriment,” I gave it to you only for your benefit. The ministering angels desired it, but it was concealed from them, as it is said, “It is hidden from the eyes of every living being”—these are the heavenly living creatures—“and concealed from the birds of heaven”—these are the angels. From where is this known? It is said, “One of the seraphim flew to me.” He said to them: My children, it is beyond the ministering angels, but it is not beyond you. From where is this known? From what we read in this passage: “For this commandment that I command you today is not beyond you.””

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא לְטוֹבָתְךָ, שֶׁזֶּה אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר וּמַבְהִיק שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהִשָּׁעֵן עָלָיו, וּבְלֹא הַתּוֹרָה הָיָה עוֹמֵד בְּיִרְאָה בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁמָּא טוֹעֶה וְאֵין רָצוֹן אֲמִיתִּי דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כֵּן.
connections.quote: “In truth, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal oppressively with His creatures, imposing decrees on them in order to punish them if they transgress. Concerning this they said in the Midrash: “Do not say that I gave the Torah to your detriment; it was given only for your benefit.” “To your detriment” cannot mean this literally, for such a thought cannot arise, Heaven forbid. Rather, it means that the Torah is not merely an arbitrary decree. If it were, it would be detrimental to those who transgress, who are the majority, for “there is no righteous person on earth,” and so forth, and Bava Batra says, “Most succumb to robbery, a minority to forbidden relations, and everyone to the dust of evil speech.” It would then have been better not to decree and not to punish. In truth, however, the Torah is the pattern of the work of Creation, as they said in Bereshit Rabbah. According to the laws of Creation, keeping the Torah’s laws is necessary to sustain the world. “Evil pursues sinners”—the transgression itself pursues them. One should complain only about oneself, not about the Life of the worlds. God did us a great good in giving the Torah: He made known the things a person should do and live, and repeatedly urged choosing life, for they are intrinsically our life.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "מִשְׁעָן", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (יד.), וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כא): "עַמּוּד בַּרְזֶל – מִשְׁנָה";
connections.quote: “‘Support’—these are the masters of Scripture. ‘Staff’—these are the masters of Mishnah, such as Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima and his companions. … ‘Every support of bread’—these are the masters of Talmud, as it is said: ‘Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed’ (Proverbs 9:5). ‘Every support of water’—these are the masters of aggadah, who draw a person’s heart like water through aggadah.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "מִשְׁעָן", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (יד.), וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כא): "עַמּוּד בַּרְזֶל – מִשְׁנָה";
connections.quote: see note 383 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּמוֹ אֲכִילַת מָן, שֶׁהָיוּ מְצַפִּים בְּכָל עֵת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם חַיּוּתָם, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ח, ג), שֶׁזֶּה עִנּוּי נֶפֶשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא עד:): רֶמֶז לַסוּמִין וְכוּלֵי שֶׁגַּם הֵם לֹא רָאוּ.
connections.quote: ‘He afflicted you and made you hungry, then fed you the manna, which you had not known and your fathers had not known, in order to make you know that a person does not live on bread alone: a person lives on everything that issues from the mouth of Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּמוֹ אֲכִילַת מָן, שֶׁהָיוּ מְצַפִּים בְּכָל עֵת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם חַיּוּתָם, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ח, ג), שֶׁזֶּה עִנּוּי נֶפֶשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא עד:): רֶמֶז לַסוּמִין וְכוּלֵי שֶׁגַּם הֵם לֹא רָאוּ.
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yosef said: From here there is an indication concerning blind people: they eat but are not satisfied. Abaye said: Therefore, someone who has a meal should eat it only by daylight. Rabbi Zeira said: What is the verse? ‘Better is what the eyes see than the wandering of desire.’ Reish Lakish said: The sight of a woman gives more pleasure than the act itself, as it is said: ‘Better is what the eyes see than the wandering of desire.’’

connections.hePhrase: וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּמוֹ אֲכִילַת מָן, שֶׁהָיוּ מְצַפִּים בְּכָל עֵת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם חַיּוּתָם, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ח, ג), שֶׁזֶּה עִנּוּי נֶפֶשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא עד:): רֶמֶז לַסוּמִין וְכוּלֵי שֶׁגַּם הֵם לֹא רָאוּ.
connections.quote: ““Who fed you manna in the wilderness…in order to afflict you”: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi disagreed. One said: Someone who has bread in his basket is not like someone who has no bread in his basket. The other said: Someone who sees what he eats is not like someone who does not see what he eats.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): הַמַּאֲרִיךְ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ וּמְעַיֵּין בָּהּ וְכוּלֵי, וּמַאי תַּקַּנְתֵּיהּ? יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: “Is that so? But Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan: ‘Anyone who prolongs his prayer and looks expectantly for its fulfillment will ultimately suffer heartache, as it is stated: ‘Prolonged expectation makes the heart sick.’ What is his remedy? Let him engage in Torah, as it is stated: ‘A desire fulfilled is a tree of life.’ And ‘a tree of life’ means none other than Torah, as it is stated: ‘It is a tree of life to those who grasp it.’’ There is no difficulty: one case concerns someone who prolongs his prayer and looks expectantly for its fulfillment; the other concerns someone who prolongs his prayer without looking expectantly for its fulfillment.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה נִקְרָא "תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמֻשָּׁכָה" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, יב), שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּטִיחוּת גָּמוּר;
connections.quote: ‘Hope drawn out makes the heart sick; a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר שֶׁפָּעַל מַה שֶּׁהִתְפַּלֵּל, זֶהוּ מִשְׁעָן חָזָק, וְ"תַאֲוָה בָאָה" כְּאִלּוּ כְּבָר בָּאָה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא בָּאָה, אֵינוֹ תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמֻשָּׁכָה, מֵאַחַר שֶׁרוֹאֶה בְּבֵירוּר וְנָכוֹן לִבּוֹ בָּטוּחַ בַּה' שֶׁיּוֹשִׁיעוֹ.
connections.quote: “He shall not be afraid of evil tidings; his heart is steadfast, trusting in Hashem.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְכִילְתָּא רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח): לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא לְאוֹכְלֵי מָן, שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת גַּם בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה צְרִיכִים לְהִתְנַהֵג כְּאוֹכְלֵי מָן: לְצַפּוֹת בְּכָל רֶגַע לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיָּאִיר לוֹ אוֹרוֹת מְחוּדָּשׁוֹת בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְלֹא שֶׁיִּסְמוֹךְ עַל מַה דִּכְתִיבָא וּמַנְחָא וְהַמְּפוֹרָשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.displayRef: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayehi Beshalach 1:4
connections.linkedRef: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayehi Beshalach 1:4
connections.canonicalRef: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayehi Beshalach 1:4
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דְוַיְהִי בְּשַׁלַּח א׳:ד׳
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: All the more, God did not bring them by the direct route. Rather, God said: If I bring Israel into the Land now, they will immediately take possession—one of his field and another of his vineyard—and will neglect Torah. Instead, I shall lead them around in the wilderness for forty years, so that they will eat manna and drink water from the well, and the Torah will become absorbed into their bodies. From here Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai would say: The Torah was given for exposition only to those who eat manna; next to them are those who eat terumah.”

connections.hePhrase: דִּבֶּאֱמֶת גַּם אַחַר שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר בְּכָל רֶגַע לִמְבַקְשָׁיו זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ בִּפְרָטוּת אֵיךְ לְהִתְנַהֵג.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 19
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 19
connections.quote: “The revelation of secrets hidden from those who receive them is what is called the Oral Torah. This is “His secrets are concealed”: they are not revealed to everyone, but only to the person to whom God reveals them. A person cannot know this independently, or even through learning from another, except through recognizing that it is impossible without God. If one could learn it from another or from what is written in books, it too would be called “written and already laid down,” as though one did not need God. In truth, however, to know the depth of wisdom, the secret hidden in Torah, is impossible unless a person recognizes that God teaches him. Then God reveals His secret to him and opens the gates of his heart. As stated in Shocher Tov on Psalm 119: “Do not say: Here is the book, come and learn,” and so forth; then he knows. Thus one cannot reveal this and teach it to someone who does not recognize and know this, and whom God is not teaching. In knowing the hidden things of Torah—the Oral Torah concealed in the Written Torah—there is no other teacher: God alone is called “the One who teaches Torah to His people Israel.” As it is said, “For Hashem gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.””

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה בִּקֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הֲבִינֵנִי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קכה), וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה פְּעָמִים נִדְרָשִׁים בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב שֶׁאֵין לוֹ נִיחָא בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה רַק מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר וּמְלַמֵּד לוֹ:
connections.quote: “I am Your servant; give me understanding, that I may know Your testimonies.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה בִּקֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הֲבִינֵנִי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קכה), וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה פְּעָמִים נִדְרָשִׁים בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב שֶׁאֵין לוֹ נִיחָא בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה רַק מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר וּמְלַמֵּד לוֹ:
connections.quote: ““I am Your servant; give me understanding.” What does “I am Your servant; give me understanding” mean? Do not say: The book is before you; read, and you will find and know. Likewise it is said, “The book is given to one who does not know writing,” and so forth, “and he says: I do not know writing.” Therefore David said: “I am Your servant; give me understanding.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט.): כְּלוּם יֵצֶר הָרָע יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם? וְלָמָּה לָכֶם אוֹרָהּ.
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: ‘Give them an answer.’ He said before Him: ‘Master of the universe, I fear that they may burn me with the breath of their mouths.’ He said to him: ‘Take hold of My Throne of Glory and give them an answer,’ as it is stated: ‘He takes hold of the face of the throne; He spreads His cloud over him.’ Rabbi Nahum said: ‘This teaches that Shaddai spread some of the radiance of His Shekhinah and His cloud over him.’ Moses said before Him: ‘Master of the universe, what is written in the Torah that You are giving me? ‘I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’’ He said to them: ‘Did you descend to Egypt? Were you enslaved to Pharaoh? Why should the Torah be yours? Again, what is written in it? ‘You shall have no other gods.’ Do you dwell among nations that worship idols? Again, what is written in it? ‘Remember the Shabbat day to sanctify it.’ Do you perform work, so that you need to rest? Again, what is written in it? ‘You shall not take’—are there commercial dealings among you? Again, what is written in it? ‘Honor your father and your mother’—do you have a father and mother? Again, what is written in it? ‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not steal.’ Is there jealousy among you? Is there an evil inclination among you?’ Immediately they conceded to the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is stated: ‘Hashem, our Master, how mighty is Your Name,’ and so on; whereas ‘Set Your splendor upon the heavens’ is not written.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן תְּחִלַּת שְׁנֵיהֶם הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי: כִּי עִיקַּר יִרְאָה פֵּירוּשׁ הַכָּרַת הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁמִּפְּנֵי זֶה הוּא מִתְיָירֵא;
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 9
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 9
connections.quote: ““Now I know that you fear God.” The distinction between fear of Hashem and fear of Elohim is as follows. Fear of Elohim is a person’s restraining himself from doing something, such as eating and the like, because he is not yet complete and still has a deficiency. He limits himself according to his understanding; this is called fear of Elohim. Fear of Hashem, however, means that even when a person understands that he could do this thing because his soul has been purified of that deficiency, it remains forbidden to him by God. For God commanded upright precepts for every soul. Since there is someone who has not yet been purified in this respect, God did not permit the thing, because it is not equally suitable for everyone. A person is obligated to bear a prohibition on account of his fellow. This is called fear of Hashem.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכִידוּעַ דְּיִרְאָה נִקְרָא נוּקְבָא, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהִיא חֲסֵרָה וּמְבַקֶּשֶׁת הַשְׁלָמָה.
connections.quote: “Therefore one must give precedence to reverence from the side of the Shechinah, both in Torah and in the commandments. But from the side of the Holy One, blessed be He, one must give precedence to Torah before reverence in all the commandments. For there is a reverence belonging to Torah that is called the feminine, the Oral Torah, concerning which it is said there, “Then the trees of the forest shall sing.””

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה מִיָּד הוּא הַשְׁלָמַת הַחִסָּרוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פִּקּוּדֵי [ה' יְשָׁרִים] מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (תְּהִלִּים יט, ט), וְשִׂמְחָה הוּא הִיפּוּךְ הַיִּרְאָה.
connections.displayRef: Tiferet Yisrael, Introduction to Tiferet Yisrael 20
connections.linkedRef: Tiferet Yisrael, Introduction to Tiferet Yisrael 20
connections.canonicalRef: Tiferet Yisrael, Introduction to Tiferet Yisrael 20
connections.quote: “The meaning is that, through Torah, a person is considered a complete being, and therefore it gladdens his heart. When a person is in a state of completion, he is joyful. The opposite occurs when he is in a state of deficiency: he is in mourning. Therefore, when death occurs among his close relatives, he is in mourning.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה מִיָּד הוּא הַשְׁלָמַת הַחִסָּרוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פִּקּוּדֵי [ה' יְשָׁרִים] מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (תְּהִלִּים יט, ט), וְשִׂמְחָה הוּא הִיפּוּךְ הַיִּרְאָה.
connections.quote: “In truth, from Hashem's side there is no change, as it says, ‘I, Hashem, have not changed.’ All the change is on the recipient's side. Hashem's outpouring never ceases. Only from the recipient's side does it sometimes appear to have ceased; through his prayer he attains that outpouring.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks how the Sages can describe righteous prayer as changing the divine measure when Hashem does not change. Its answer locates the change in the recipient's attainment of the gift. This illuminates the present siman's language that Hashem Himself desires the requested fulfillment and waits for prayer. The petition opens a relation of reception; it is not portrayed as persuading an unwilling giver to acquire a new disposition.
connections.headline: The change is in receiving the gift

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, אִם הוּא כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אָמַר מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ – נָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי, עַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" (יְשַׁעְיָה נו, ז), שֶׁמִּיָּד מַגִּיעַ הַמִּלּוּי;
connections.quote: “According to Shmuel HaKatan, what would constitute the praise of the community? He says “Who makes the wind blow,” and the wind blows; he says “Who causes rain to fall,” and rain comes.”
connections.context: Shmuel HaKatan distinguishes this immediate correspondence between prayer and response from rain arriving before the prayer or only after a delay. This is the model of effective prayer that Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, אִם הוּא כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אָמַר מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ – נָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי, עַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" (יְשַׁעְיָה נו, ז), שֶׁמִּיָּד מַגִּיעַ הַמִּלּוּי;
connections.quote: “I shall bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in the house of My prayer. Their burnt offerings and sacrifices shall be accepted upon My altar, for My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
connections.context: The first clause literally says “the house of My prayer.” Rav Tzadok connects its promised joy with prayer whose request receives an immediate answer.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ז.): "תְּפִלָּתָם" לֹא נֶאֱמַר וְכוּלֵי, כִּי גַּם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל, פֵּירוּשׁ מִתְאַוֶּוה וְרוֹצֶה לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר,
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Yosei’s name: From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays? It says: ‘I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them rejoice in My house of prayer.’ It does not say ‘their prayer,’ but ‘My prayer.’ From here we learn that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ז.): "תְּפִלָּתָם" לֹא נֶאֱמַר וְכוּלֵי, כִּי גַּם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל, פֵּירוּשׁ מִתְאַוֶּוה וְרוֹצֶה לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר,
connections.quote: “This is what they meant by “From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays?” Because He is the true good and abundant in kindness, He is called “desiring kindness” and seeks the good. His praying means seeking the good. Prayer means a request; this is the essential meaning of the word everywhere. In a human being, however, the request is directed to God—otherwise, what would his request accomplish? Nevertheless, prayer means a request. The teaching says that God desires and seeks this: that it be His will for His mercy to overcome His anger, for Him to conduct Himself toward His children with the attribute of mercy, and to go beyond the strict measure of judgment.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): כָּל הַמְעַיֵּין בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁאֵין לָאָדָם לִבְטוֹחַ כָּל כָּךְ בְּבֵירוּר עַל הַתְּפִלָּה, רַק: "קַוֵּה אֶל ה' חֲזַק [וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ] וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה'" (תְּהִלִּים כז, יד).
connections.quote: “One who prolongs his prayer and examines it ultimately comes to heartache, as it says, “Hope deferred makes the heart sick.” What is his remedy? Let him occupy himself with Torah. … This refers to one who prolongs prayer and examines it; [the favorable teaching] concerns one who prolongs prayer without examining it. Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said: If a person prayed and was not answered, let him pray again, as it says, “Hope to the Lord; be strong and let your heart take courage, and hope to the Lord.””
connections.context: The contrast is between sustained prayer and relying on one’s prayer as a guarantee that the requested outcome must follow. Rav Tzadok needs both the warning and the instruction to continue hoping and praying.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר: "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּיִרְאָה" (שָׁם ב, יא), שֶׁהָעֲבוֹדָה דִּתְפִלָּה הִיא בְּיִרְאָה וְלֹא בְּשִׂמְחָה, כִּי אֵינוֹ בָּטוּחַ כָּל כָּךְ, אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן כְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא כְּשֶׁשְּׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתוֹ.
connections.quote: “Serve Hashem with fear, and rejoice with trembling.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק בְּמִזְמוֹר לְתוֹדָה נֶאֱמַר: "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּשִׂמְחָה" (שָׁם ק, ב), כִּי בְּכָל תְּפִלָּה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת הוֹדָאָה עַל הֶעָבָר וּצְעָקָה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא.
connections.quote: “Serve Hashem with gladness; come before His presence with singing.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק בְּמִזְמוֹר לְתוֹדָה נֶאֱמַר: "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּשִׂמְחָה" (שָׁם ק, ב), כִּי בְּכָל תְּפִלָּה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת הוֹדָאָה עַל הֶעָבָר וּצְעָקָה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא.
connections.quote: “One entering a fortified town prays twice: once upon entering and once upon leaving. Ben Azzai says: Four times—twice upon entering and twice upon leaving. He gives thanks for what has passed and cries out concerning what is to come.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל קְצִיבַת עֵץ דֶּאֱלִישָׁע, שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהַרְאוֹת דָּבָר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה כַּהַאי גַּוְונָא שֶׁהָעֵץ צָף, וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן יָכוֹל לְבַקֵּשׁ בְּחֹזֶק שֶׁגַּם הַבַּרְזֶל יָצִיף, כִּי מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֵּין עֵץ לְבַרְזֶל.
connections.quote: ‘The man of God said: ‘Where did it fall?’ He showed him the place. He cut a piece of wood, threw it there, and made the iron float.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל קְצִיבַת עֵץ דֶּאֱלִישָׁע, שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהַרְאוֹת דָּבָר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה כַּהַאי גַּוְונָא שֶׁהָעֵץ צָף, וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן יָכוֹל לְבַקֵּשׁ בְּחֹזֶק שֶׁגַּם הַבַּרְזֶל יָצִיף, כִּי מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֵּין עֵץ לְבַרְזֶל.
connections.quote: “As we find with Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who said, “He who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” Why did he mention “He who told oil to burn”? One must recall that God implanted in the nature of oil that it should burn, and through this one can draw forth His saying that vinegar should burn. This accords with what I heard from the holy master, of blessed memory, concerning Elisha: “He cut a piece of wood, threw it there, and the iron floated.” Why did he need to cut and throw wood? He wished to recall that God implanted in wood the nature of floating on water, and through this he threw it so that God would give the iron this nature as well. Elisha did this through an action, whereas Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa recalled it verbally: “He who told oil to burn,” and so forth. For him, this was not an act of miracles, since otherwise he would certainly not have wished to benefit from a miracle. Rather, it was completely clear before his eyes that there is no independent nature or habit, only what God gives the thing as its nature. The burning of oil was like the burning of vinegar to him. By recalling aloud, “He who told oil to burn,” that it comes only from God’s utterance, he drew forth the influence that would make the vinegar burn. Thus “He made a memorial for His wonders” is explained by “Hashem is gracious and compassionate”: through remembrance they can draw forth the influence from Atika, which is wonder.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תְּכוּפָה לָהּ וּמְחוּבָּר וּמְיוּחֶדֶת לָהּ, אָז גַּם בִּתְפִלָּה יֵעָנֶה, וְהוּא בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא;
connections.quote: ““For what great nation,” and so forth. A legal question: May a person of Israel who has recited Shema wait after Shema and then pray? The Sages taught: There are three immediate successions—slaughter immediately after laying hands on the offering; a blessing immediately after washing the hands; and prayer immediately after redemption. What is the reward of one who does this? Rabbah bar Abbahu said: If he lays hands and slaughters, he may be assured that his offering has been accepted. If he washes his hands and immediately blesses, he may be assured that no accuser will prosecute during his meal. If he recites Shema and immediately prays, he may be assured that his prayer is heard.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "בְּרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא דָּא צְלוֹתָא" הִיא מִדַּת אֶרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק עַל עוֹלָם הַבָּא מִקְּרָא דִּ"לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (יְשַׁעְיָה ס, כא).
connections.quote: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever—the shoot of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to be glorified.””
connections.context: The opening Mishnah of Perek Chelek cites inheriting the “land forever” as the proof of the World to Come. This is the textual basis for Rav Tzadok’s identification of the higher land with that world.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן תִּקְּנוּ שָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת בְּשֶׁבַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לַטַּעַם הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל: מֵאַחַר שֶׁאַתָּה יָכוֹל עַל הַכֹּל, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מְבַקְּשִׁים י"ב אֶמְצָעִיּוֹת, וְאַחַר כָּךְ שָׁלֹשׁ אַחֲרוֹנוֹת כְּעֶבֶד הַנּוֹטֵל פְּרָס שֶׁבָּטוּחַ עַל הַמִּלּוּי.
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda said: A person should never ask for his needs in the first three blessings or in the last three, but in the middle ones. For Rabbi Chanina said: The first blessings resemble a servant arranging praise before his master; the middle ones resemble a servant asking his master for a gift; the last ones resemble a servant who has received a gift from his master and takes leave.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת יֵשׁ לִבְטוֹחַ בַּה' שֶׁיַּעֲנֵהוּ וִיקַבֵּל תְּפִלָּתוֹ, רַק שֶׁלֹּא יְעַיֵּין בָּהּ, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יִבְטַח בְּשֵׁם ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה נ, י).
connections.quote: ‘Who among you fears Hashem and listens to the voice of His servant? One who has walked in darkness and has no light should trust in the name of Hashem and lean upon his God.’

connections.hePhrase: וּתְחִלָּתוֹ: "מִי בָכֶם יְרֵא ה' וְגוֹמֵר" – פֵּירוּשׁ, הֶחָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ הַשְׁלָמָה עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו:) עַל זֶה דְּרָגִיל לָבוֹא לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת.
connections.quote: ‘Ravin bar Rav Adda said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak: If someone regularly comes to the synagogue and fails to come one day, the Holy One, blessed be He, inquires about him, as it is said: ‘Who among you fears Hashem and listens to the voice of His servant, yet has walked in darkness and has no light?’’

connections.hePhrase: "הָלַךְ חֲשֵׁכִים", וּפֵירְשׁוּ שָׁם: לִדְבַר הָרְשׁוּת;
connections.quote: “If he went for a mitzvah, he has brightness; if he went for an optional matter, he has no brightness. “Let him trust in the name of Hashem”—what is the reason? Because he should have trusted in the name of Hashem, but did not.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ רַק בִּטָּחוֹן, אֲבָל "יִשָּׁעֵן" – מִשְׁעָן הוּא יוֹתֵר, וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּיָדוֹ וְנִשְׁעָן עָלָיו, זֶהוּ "בֵּאלֹהָיו",
connections.quote: “At least an awakening from below in prayer is also needed: to ask His help against the inclination that seeks to kill him, which he cannot overcome. God then helps through an awakening from above. Samekh indicates “The Lord supports all who fall,” and the fallen sukkah of David: it surrounds like a sukkah, protecting those who seek His help. From the person’s side, the work of this month is to stir the good inclination against the bad with all his strength, until he cannot overcome it from his own side.”
connections.explanation: Kislev joins full effort against the inclination with the prayer that calls forth assistance from above. This explains the present siman’s distinction between leaning on the powers Hashem has already given and trusting in salvation beyond them. Neither side cancels the other: existing wisdom and ability are themselves gifts to be used, while their limitation gives prayer its honest sense of need. Support is received by the person who turns toward Hashem from within that work.
connections.headline: Using one’s given powers and praying beyond them belong to the same reliance

connections.hePhrase: כִּידוּעַ דְּשֵׁם זֶה מוֹרֶה עַל כֹּחוֹת הַמּוּטְבָּעִים בַּבְּרוּאִים, וֶ"אֱלֹהָיו" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כֹּחוֹתָיו שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שֶׁנָּתַן לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְכַלְכֵּל עַצְמוֹ עַל יָדוֹ בְּכָל צְרָכָיו בְּעֵצוֹת מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְחָכְמָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – בָּזֶה הוּא עִיקַּר הַשְּׁעִינָה.
connections.displayRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 6:1-2
connections.linkedRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 6:1-2
connections.canonicalRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 6:1-2
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שני; שער היחוד והאמונה ו׳:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: “The name Elohim is the name of the attribute of strength and contraction. Therefore it also has the numerical value of hateva, “nature,” because it conceals the supernal light that brings the world into being and gives it life, so that the world appears to stand and operate by nature. This name Elohim is a shield and covering for the name Havayah, concealing the light and vitality that flow from Havayah and bring something into being from nothing, lest they be revealed to the creatures and the creatures lose their independent existence. This strength and contraction are themselves also a form of kindness through which the world is built. This is strength included within kindness.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יִבְטַח בִּישׁוּעָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִכֹּחוֹ גַּם כֵּן, כִּי אֵין מַעְצוֹר לַה', וְהֵן לֹא קָצְרָה יָדוֹ מֵהוֹשִׁיעַ:
connections.quote: “For there is no restraint to Hashem to save by many or by few.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יִבְטַח בִּישׁוּעָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִכֹּחוֹ גַּם כֵּן, כִּי אֵין מַעְצוֹר לַה', וְהֵן לֹא קָצְרָה יָדוֹ מֵהוֹשִׁיעַ:
connections.quote: “Behold, Hashem’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, neither is His ear heavy, that it cannot hear.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קצה עַמּוּד א) דִּתְפִלָּה דְּעָנִי כְּלַל כָּל צְלוֹתִין וּבָקְעֵי רְקִיעִין.
connections.quote: “Why? Because the poor person is brokenhearted, and it is written, “Hashem is close to the brokenhearted.” The poor person constantly disputes with the Holy One, blessed be He, and He attends and hears his words. When he prays, He opens all the windows of the heavens, and that brokenhearted poor person pushes aside all the other prayers ascending above. It is written, “A prayer of the poor when he wraps”: it should have said “when he wraps himself.” Rather, he wraps up all the prayers of the world, and they do not enter until his prayer enters. The Holy One, blessed be He, says: Let all the prayers be wrapped up, and let this prayer come to Me. I do not want a court here to judge between us. Let his complaints be before Me, and let him and Me be alone. The Holy One, blessed be He, communes alone with those complaints, with that prayer, as it says, “Before Hashem he pours out his speech”—before Hashem indeed.”
connections.context: The quotation “Hashem is close to the brokenhearted” is Psalms 34:19. The passage explains the priority and direct access of the poor person’s prayer; Rav Tzadok uses this to describe prayer from a broken heart.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קצה עַמּוּד א) דִּתְפִלָּה דְּעָנִי כְּלַל כָּל צְלוֹתִין וּבָקְעֵי רְקִיעִין.
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of eating the bread of poverty, like ‘A prayer of the poor person when he is overwhelmed,’ which envelops all prayers and breaks through the heavens. Because of his great lack, the poor person pours out his speech as the pouring out of his soul, like Channah pouring out her soul. He cannot contain it within his heart, until he speaks with his mouth and raises his voice. That eating has the power to bring forth speech that issues from the heart; the principal vitality is in proportion to the depth of the poverty and the felt need.”
connections.explanation: Et HaOchel develops the same Psalm and the comparison to Channah. Its larger context defines the soul's poverty as acknowledging that it has nothing independently and lives through heavenly mercy. The quoted passage explains why such a prayer can emerge as poured-out speech rather than a polished arrangement. This supports the siman's emphasis on the heart's reality, without making disorder of words a substitute for that reality.
connections.headline: The poor person's speech overflows from felt need

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין עָנִי אֶלָּא בְּדַעַת (נְדָרִים מא.), אֲפִילּוּ אֵין יוֹדֵעַ אֵיךְ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וּלְרַצּוֹת לְקוֹנוֹ,
connections.quote: ‘Abaye said: We have a received tradition: Poverty is only in understanding. In the West they say: One who has this has everything; one who lacks this, what does he have? If he has acquired this, what does he lack? If he has not acquired this, what has he acquired?’

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין עָנִי אֶלָּא בְּדַעַת (נְדָרִים מא.), אֲפִילּוּ אֵין יוֹדֵעַ אֵיךְ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וּלְרַצּוֹת לְקוֹנוֹ,
connections.quote: “We have learned concerning all languages other than the sacred language alone, in which the world was created, that they are not worthy to be bound into the crown of the Life of the worlds—unless the person praying is poor in understanding and does not understand the sacred language. Then “before Hashem,” specifically, he pours out his speech, before the One who examines the inner parts and the heart. Prayer in a foreign language with a broken and contrite heart gives Him greater satisfaction than prayer without intention, even in the sacred language. This is plain, for intention cannot exist without the heart understanding what a person brings forth from his mouth.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וְלִפְנֵי ה' יִשְׁפֹּךְ שִׂיחוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים קב, א), וְ"שִׂיחָה" פֵּירוּשׁ מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא וְלֹא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
connections.quote: “A prayer of the afflicted one when he grows faint and pours out his speech before the Lord.”
connections.context: Sicho can denote his complaint, meditation, or speech. Rav Tzadok emphasizes its relationship to ordinary conversation: the poor person pours the concerns of daily life into prayer.

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וְלִפְנֵי ה' יִשְׁפֹּךְ שִׂיחוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים קב, א), וְ"שִׂיחָה" פֵּירוּשׁ מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא וְלֹא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
connections.quote: “From where is it derived that even the conversation (sichat) of Torah scholars requires study? As it is stated: ‘And whose leaf does not wither’ (Psalms 1:3).”
connections.context: The Gemara asks why the baraita says “from the conversation of Rabban Gamliel” rather than “from his words”: sichah is casual, everyday talk, as distinct from formal teaching.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבְיִצְחָק נֶאֱמַר גַּם כֵּן "לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כד, סג), כִּידוּעַ דְּהוּא עַמּוּד הַתּוֹרָה, וְ"שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ בַּעֲלֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:), שַׁיָּיךְ שַׁפִּיר "שִׂיחוֹ"],
connections.quote: “Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening; he lifted his eyes and saw that camels were coming.”
connections.context: The verb lasuach shares its root with the “speech” discussed in the preceding note. Rav Tzadok explains how that term applies to Isaac, whose conversation itself is associated here with Torah.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבְיִצְחָק נֶאֱמַר גַּם כֵּן "לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כד, סג), כִּידוּעַ דְּהוּא עַמּוּד הַתּוֹרָה, וְ"שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ בַּעֲלֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:), שַׁיָּיךְ שַׁפִּיר "שִׂיחוֹ"],
connections.quote: “This matter of conversation—meaning prayer—is alluded to in Isaac. From the perspective of his attribute, prayer exists only when his entire being is this way, like David’s “I am prayer,” as is known, until he does not need to direct his intention at all. As the Jerusalem Talmud says: “In all my days I never directed my intention,” and so forth. That is, directing intention is not applicable as a separate act, because his entire being is this way, and all his words, even without deliberate intention, are prayer.”

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ שֶׁמְּדַבֵּר בְּלֹא דַעַת, וְ"יִשְׁפֹּךְ" – וְלֹא בְּמָתוֹן וּבְסֵדֶר, רַק שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שְׁבִירוּת לִבּוֹ שׁוֹפֵךְ נַפְשׁוֹ לַה' וּדְבָרִים בִּלְתִּי מְסוּדָּרִים וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּדַעַת, וְזוֹ מְקוּבֶּלֶת יוֹתֵר.
connections.quote: “Certainly, in ordinary prayer to the blessed God one should not raise one’s voice; doing so is a sign of little faith. But sometimes a person is in very great distress and can no longer contain within himself the anguish over some matter for which he needs deliverance. Then he cries out from the depth of his heart. He does not intend to raise his voice before the blessed God; rather, the cry comes from the walls of his heart because he has no recourse. As the Sages said concerning “They cried out in a loud voice”: they said, “Woe, woe”—in another language, “Gevalt, gevalt”—because they were greatly distressed by the evil inclination that surrounded them, and there was no way to escape. Prayer with such a cry is accepted before Him, blessed be He, and does not return empty.”

connections.hePhrase: וּתְפִלָּה בִּמְקוֹם קָרְבָּנוֹת, וּדְעָנִי נִקְרָא "מִנְחָה", שֶׁחָשׁוּב לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַתָּנָה וּמִנְחָה, וְגַם הוּא לְשׁוֹן נִיחָא, כִּי הוּא מְקַבֵּל תֵּיכֶף הַנִּיחָא.
