connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ספר במדבר, נשא ד׳
connections.quote: “‘And they shall send out of the camp every leper, and every zav, and whoever is impure through a corpse’ (Numbers 5:2). The leper is anger, for tzara’at comes for the sin of evil speech (Arakhin 15b); the zav is the man of desire; and one impure through a corpse is sadness. Therefore the leper is sent out of all three camps, for the trait of anger has no share in Israel; and the zav is sent only from the camp of the Levites and the camp of the Shechinah, for the trait of desire does not befit Torah scholars.”
connections.context: This is the teaching of Rav Tzadok’s master, the Rebbe of Izhbitz, that he says he “heard”: desire (the zav) is not sent out of the camp of Israel, while anger (the leper) has no place in Israel at all.

connections.hePhrase: "וּמִשְּׂמֹאלוֹ" – דְּהַיְינוּ גְּבוּרָה רָעָה בְּכַעַס וְקִנְאָה וְנִיצּוּחַ וַאֲבִיזְרַיְיהוּ, "אַלְפָּא" הוּא הַמִּסְפָּר הַיּוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ן עַל פָּסוּק "נָתַתִּי אֶלֶף כֶּסֶף" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כ, טז).
connections.quote: “It is possible that “a thousand silver” means thousands of silver—a great sum, as befits a king. Likewise, “the smallest shall become a thousand” means a numerous people.”
connections.context: Ramban allows “a thousand” to denote a very great amount rather than a precise total. Rav Tzadok develops that usage into his contrast between an intense but bounded quantity and the more indefinite multiplicity of “myriads”; the whole numerical distinction is not a verbatim statement of Ramban.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, דְּלָכֵן שָׂרִים עַד אֶלֶף, וְעַל הָרִבּוֹא הוּא מַדְרֵגַת מֶלֶךְ.
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 4:14
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 4:14
connections.quote: “Elsewhere we explained in this connection the matter of Israel’s officers, whose ranks extend only as far as officers of thousands and no further. We do not find officers of myriads, for what is beyond a thousand is the level of the king. This is why Saul was angered when they assigned the thousands to him and the myriads to David: “What more can he have but the kingship?” Likewise, they told David that he was worth ten thousand; see there. For the king includes all the complete created bodies. This too is a collective number, and such a complete structure is ten; this is not the place for it.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְפִי שֶׁיֵּצֶר הָרָע דְּתַאֲוָה הוּא "טוֹב מְאֹד", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעֱלָם (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קלח עַמּוּד א) שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר גַּם לֶעָתִיד רַק דְּאִתְלַבַּן, דְּלוּלֵי כֵן לָא אִשְׁתֲּכַח חֲמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, וּמִצַּד זֶה הוּא בִּלְתִּי גְּבוּל, לְכָךְ גַּם הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ לְרַע הוּא בְּרִבּוּי.
connections.quote: see note 358 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Bereishit Rabbah supplies the expression “very good.” Midrash HaNe’elam, Zohar I 137b–138a, then describes the future purification of the inclination and the continuing need for its energy in the joy of Torah learning. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the underlying force of desire from its present misuse for evil. The comparison to Lavan is an allegory of whitening and purification; the quotation does not praise the historical Lavan’s conduct.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"אֵלֶיךָ" – פֵּירוּשׁ אֶל פְּנִימִיּוּתְךָ וּמַעֲמַקֵּי שָׁרְשְׁךָ – "לֹא יִגָּשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צא, ז), דְּהַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁאָר, וְ"אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא – יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד.), רַק לָבוּשׁ תּוֹךְ הָאָדָם רָע.
connections.quote: ‘A thousand may fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand; it will not approach you.’

connections.hePhrase: וְ"אֵלֶיךָ" – פֵּירוּשׁ אֶל פְּנִימִיּוּתְךָ וּמַעֲמַקֵּי שָׁרְשְׁךָ – "לֹא יִגָּשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צא, ז), דְּהַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁאָר, וְ"אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא – יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד.), רַק לָבוּשׁ תּוֹךְ הָאָדָם רָע.
connections.quote: “In the case of Achan, why were they punished? Because his wife and children knew about it. ‘Israel has sinned.’ Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said: ‘Even though he has sinned, he is still Israel.’ Rabbi Abba said: ‘This is what people say: A myrtle standing among nettles is named myrtle, and myrtle is what they call it.’ ‘They have also transgressed My covenant that I commanded them; they have also taken from what was under the ban, also stolen, also denied it, and also put it among their belongings.’ Rabbi Ilaa said in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta: ‘This teaches that Achan transgressed the five books of the Torah, for ‘also’ is said five times.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "אִישׁ חֲמָסִים", שֶׁהוּא בָּא לַעֲשׁוֹק הַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁכְּבָר נֶחֶלְצָה מִמֶּנָּה כְּשֶׁרוֹאֶה שֶׁהִיא חֲלוּשָׁה, כְּטַעַם: אֵיזֶהוּ גִּבּוֹר הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ, וּכְשֶׁאֵין בּוֹ כֹּחַ לִכְבּוֹשׁ הוּא חוֹמְסוֹ;
connections.quote: “Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination, as it is said: ‘He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה כֹּחַ הָאִישׁ, וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַכַּעַס כַּיָּדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל עַל פָּסוּק "טֹרֵף נַפְשׁוֹ בְּאַפּוֹ" (אִיּוֹב יח, ד), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַכַּעַס הַנֶּפֶשׁ נִטְרֶפֶת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, שֶׁהָאִישׁ חֲמָסִים הַמַּכְנִיס הַכַּעַס חוֹמְסָהּ,
connections.quote: see note 2844.
connections.context: Bildad addresses Job. Rav Tzadok, invoking the Ari, gives “tear your soul in your anger” a spiritual application: anger damages the soul. The biblical quotation supplies the wording; that account of the soul is the interpretation cited by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה כֹּחַ הָאִישׁ, וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַכַּעַס כַּיָּדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל עַל פָּסוּק "טֹרֵף נַפְשׁוֹ בְּאַפּוֹ" (אִיּוֹב יח, ד), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַכַּעַס הַנֶּפֶשׁ נִטְרֶפֶת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, שֶׁהָאִישׁ חֲמָסִים הַמַּכְנִיס הַכַּעַס חוֹמְסָהּ,
connections.quote: “My teacher, of blessed memory, was more stringent about anger than about all the other transgressions, even when a person becomes angry for the sake of a mitzvah, as in the case of Moshe mentioned above. He gave this reason: all the other transgressions cause damage only in the particular limb affected by each transgression, but the trait of anger damages the entire soul and completely exchanges it. The matter is that when a person becomes angry, the holy soul departs from him entirely, and a soul from the side of the husk enters in its place. This is the secret of Scripture’s words, “He tears his soul in his anger,” and so forth: he actually tears his holy soul, makes it torn and unfit, and kills it at the time of his wrath and anger. This is explained in the Zohar, Tetzaveh, page 182b; see there how severely it describes anger, to the point of saying that one who speaks with an angry person is as though he speaks with idolatry itself; see there.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁמֵּאַחַר שֶׁכָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹתָיו שְׁקוּעִים בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֵין שְׁלִיטָה לְהִרְהוּרֵי תַּאֲווֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם (סוֹף הִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִיאָה) דְּאֵין הִרְהוּרִין שׁוֹלְטִים אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִן הַתּוֹרָה.
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות איסורי ביאה כ״ב:כ״א
connections.quote: “Greater than all this, they said: let a person turn himself and his thoughts to words of Torah and broaden his mind in wisdom, for thoughts of forbidden relations prevail only in a heart empty of wisdom.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם: אִם אַתְּ יָהֵיב עֵינָא וְלִבָּא לִי – אֲנָא יָדַע דְּאַתְּ דִּילִי (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ה), שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר הָאָדָם;
connections.quote: see note 2627.
connections.context: The Jerusalem Talmud names the heart and eye as the channels of sin and, when given to Hashem, of belonging to Him. It is this passage, rather than the Mishnah about mentioning the Exodus at night, that Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵצֶר דִּרְצִיחָה נוֹלָד מִכֹּחַ הַתַּאֲוָה וְנִתְחַדֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם עַל יְדֵי קַיִן הַנּוֹלָד מֵהֶם, וּבָא לוֹ מִכֹּחַ חֶמְדָּתוֹ וְתַאֲוָתוֹ לִירַשׁ כָּל הָעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: ““Cain said to Abel his brother, and when they were,” and so forth: What were they disputing? They said: Let us divide the world. One took the land and the other took the movable property. One said: The land on which you stand is mine. The other said: What you are wearing is mine. One said: Take it off! The other said: Fly away! As a result, “Cain rose against Abel his brother and killed him.” Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in Rabbi Levi’s name: Both took land and both took movable property. What, then, were they disputing? One said: The Temple will be built in my territory; the other said: The Temple will be built in my territory. For it is said, “When they were in the field,” and “field” means the Temple, as you would say, “Zion shall be plowed as a field.” As a result, “Cain rose against Abel his brother,” and so forth. Yehuda bar Ami said: They were disputing over the first Eve. Rabbi Aivu said: The first Eve had returned to the dust. What were they disputing? Rav Huna said: An additional twin sister was born with Abel. One said: I shall take her, for I am the firstborn; the other said: I shall take her, for she was born with me. As a result, “Cain rose.””

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בְּרִיאַת הַיֵּצֶר בָּאָדָם הוּא בְּתַאֲוָה, שֶׁזֶּה יֵשׁ בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן טוֹב בַּחֲמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:6
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:6
connections.quote: “It is known that there are two kinds of evil inclination: the power of anger and the power of desire. Desire is rooted in holiness; therefore a person with a discharge is permitted within the Israelite camp. A person afflicted with tzaraat, which comes through anger and evil speech, is sent outside the Israelite camp, for this, which is called “evil,” has no root in holiness. Before the sin, holy powers of severity consisted only of the power of restraint, preventing an expansion beyond what is appropriate that would cause destruction. As it is said, “From the mouth of the Most High evils do not come,” and “Evil does not dwell with You.” The trait of anger did not become actual until existence was given to sin, for through sin “Hashem’s anger will flare,” and so forth. The same applies to judging cases in the Sanhedrin, to zealots striking sinners, and to taking vengeance upon idolaters: before sin there was no occasion for these. Therefore Adam’s initial sin was through desire, and afterward Cain’s sin of murder followed.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי תוֹרָה תַּבְלִין" (קִדּוּשִׁין ל:), שֶׁהִיא מְתַבַּלְתּוֹ וְעוֹשָׂה אוֹתוֹ מַאֲכָל רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת בְּמַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל;
connections.quote: see note 2569.
connections.context: The word tavlin means seasoning; the Talmud uses it here for Torah’s remedy against the inclination. Rav Tzadok develops the culinary meaning: Torah seasons and transforms the inclination into something fit to be brought within Israel’s camp. Rendering the word only as “antidote” would conceal the wordplay on which his explanation depends.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִמֵּילָא מִתְפּוֹצֵץ גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִצְרָא דְּכַעַס וּרְצִיחָה, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם תַּאֲוָה וְחֵשֶׁק רַק לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 4
connections.quote: see note 844 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach gives an exact example of the problem: a heart emptied of a lustful thought can next fill with anger. When turning away is directed by love of Hashem, that love remains within the heart. This helps explain why the present siman places the chief work in drawing desire into Torah rather than trusting anger to defeat anger. The sources describe related forms of positive direction, while the siman retains its demanding conditions for any use of anger.

connections.hePhrase: אֵינוֹ כּוֹעֵס אֶלָּא בִּמְקוֹם דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא מְרַתְּחָא לֵיהּ (תַּעֲנִית ד.), כְּעִנְיַן "מְשַׂנְאֶיךָ ה' אֶשְׂנָא" (תְּהִלִּים קלט, כא).
connections.quote: ‘Do I not hate those who hate You, Hashem, and contend with those who rise against You?’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף, שֶׁהוּא טְבִיעַת מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהֵם כֹּחוֹת הַדִּמְיוֹן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת ר"ה, נֶאֱמַר: "וְהַמַּיִם לָהֶם חוֹמָה מִימִינָם וּמִשְּׂמֹאלָם" (שְׁמוֹת יד, כב),
connections.quote: ‘The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry land, with the waters forming a wall for them on their right and on their left.’

connections.hePhrase: וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח לְגִרְסַת יַלְקוּט שִׁמְעוֹנִי) עַל תּוֹרָה וּתְפִלִּין,
connections.quote: ““The children of Israel walked on dry land in the midst of the sea.” The ministering angels were astonished, saying: Human beings who worship idols are walking on dry land! From where is it known that the sea too was filled with wrath against them? Earlier it says, “The waters were a wall for them”; the word is written ḥemah, “wrath.” What caused them to be saved? “On their right and on their left.” “On their right”—through the merit of the Torah they would receive, as it is said, “From His right hand, a fiery law for them.” “On their left”—this is tefillin.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַנִּצּוּחַ בִּתְפִלִּין, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ו.): "וְיָרְאוּ מִמֶּךָּ" (דְּבָרִים כח, י) – אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם): "וּבִזְרוֹעַ עֻזּוֹ" (יְשַׁעְיָה סב, ח) – זֶה תְּפִלִּין,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda said in Rabbi Yitzchak’s name: From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, puts on tefillin? It says, “Hashem swore by His right hand and by the arm of His strength.” “His right hand” is Torah, as it says, “From His right hand, a fiery law for them.” “The arm of His strength” is tefillin, as it says, “Hashem will give strength to His people.” And from where do we know that tefillin are strength for Israel? It says, “All the peoples of the earth shall see that Hashem’s name is called upon you, and they shall fear you.” Rabbi Eliezer the Great taught: These are the tefillin of the head.”
connections.context: The source supplies both parts of Rav Tzadok’s sentence: the nations’ fear and the arm of divine strength. The first concerns Israel’s head-tefillin; the second arises in the discussion of Hashem’s tefillin. Both support his association of tefillin with victory and strength.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַנִּצּוּחַ בִּתְפִלִּין, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ו.): "וְיָרְאוּ מִמֶּךָּ" (דְּבָרִים כח, י) – אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם): "וּבִזְרוֹעַ עֻזּוֹ" (יְשַׁעְיָה סב, ח) – זֶה תְּפִלִּין,
connections.quote: ‘All the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of Hashem is called upon you, and they shall fear you.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַנִּצּוּחַ בִּתְפִלִּין, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ו.): "וְיָרְאוּ מִמֶּךָּ" (דְּבָרִים כח, י) – אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם): "וּבִזְרוֹעַ עֻזּוֹ" (יְשַׁעְיָה סב, ח) – זֶה תְּפִלִּין,
connections.quote: ‘Hashem has sworn by His right hand and by His mighty arm: I will no longer give your grain as food to your enemies, nor will foreigners drink the wine for which you have labored.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁזֶּה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קל.) דְּמִצְוַת תְּפִלִּין מְרוּפָּה בְּיָדֵינוּ, דִּצְרִיכִין גּוּף נָקִי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar taught: Every commandment for which Israel gave themselves over to death during a royal decree, such as rejecting idolatry and circumcision, remains firmly held by them. Every commandment for which they did not give themselves over to death during a royal decree, such as tefillin, remains loosely held by them. For Rabbi Yannai said: Tefillin require a clean body like Elisha, Man of Wings. What does this mean? Abaye said: Not to pass wind while wearing them. Rava said: Not to sleep while wearing them.”
connections.context: Both clauses are needed here: observance of tefillin remains “loosely held,” and wearing them requires bodily cleanliness. Rav Tzadok interprets these requirements within his account of the struggle against the evil inclination.

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁזֶּה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קל.) דְּמִצְוַת תְּפִלִּין מְרוּפָּה בְּיָדֵינוּ, דִּצְרִיכִין גּוּף נָקִי,
connections.quote: “‘Like Elisha, Man of Wings’: It mentions Elisha because, presumably, since a miracle was done for him through tefillin, he was careful with them and had a clean body. … And it is no wonder that this mitzvah is loosely held by us, for in the days of the Sages too it was loosely held.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן אֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹף סַנְהֶדְרִין קיג:) דְּקַפְּדָן הֲוָה, כִּי הָיָה מְרוּחָק מִתַּאֲווֹת גּוּפוֹ לְגַמְרֵי,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosei expounded in Tzippori: ‘Father Elijah was quick to take offense.’ Elijah used to visit him. He concealed himself from him for three days and did not come. When he came, Rabbi Yosei said to him: ‘Why did the Master not come?’ He said to him: ‘You called me quick to take offense!’ He replied: ‘Here we have it—the Master is taking offense!’”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כז): הֲרֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא [הַיְינוּ בְּחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּתַאֲוָה] וְחַי לְעוֹלָם.
connections.quote: see note 1954 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא יָבוֹא לִפְנֵי בִּיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה כֹּחוֹ בְּלִבּוֹת כָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִהְיוֹת נְקִיִּים מִנְּגִיעָה לַגּוּף לְגַמְרֵי, וּלְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּמִדַּת הַכַּעַס וְהַנְּקָמָה נֶגֶד הָעַכּוּ"ם בִּזְרוֹעַ עֹז, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נוֹלָד בְּלִבָּם הִתְעוֹרְרוּת – זֶה נִקְרָא בִּיאַת אֵלִיָּהוּ.
connections.quote: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome day of Hashem.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַסַּנְהֶדְרִין הָיוּ דָּנִין דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת וְלֹא הָיוּ אוֹכְלִין כָּל אוֹתוֹ יוֹם (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין סג.), שֶׁהָיוּ צְרִיכִין לִהְיוֹת גּוּף נָקִי מִכָּל חֶמְדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
connections.quote: see note 2293.

connections.hePhrase: "רַק בְּעֵינֶיךָ תַבִּיט [וְשִׁלֻּמַת רְשָׁעִים תִּרְאֶה]" (תְּהִלִּים צא, ח) הוּא כְּעִנְיַן "דּוֹם לַה' [וְהִתְחוֹלֵל לוֹ]" (שָׁם לז, ז) דְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּגִטִּין (ז.),
connections.quote: ‘You will only look on with your eyes and see the repayment of the wicked.’

connections.hePhrase: "רַק בְּעֵינֶיךָ תַבִּיט [וְשִׁלֻּמַת רְשָׁעִים תִּרְאֶה]" (תְּהִלִּים צא, ח) הוּא כְּעִנְיַן "דּוֹם לַה' [וְהִתְחוֹלֵל לוֹ]" (שָׁם לז, ז) דְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּגִטִּין (ז.),
connections.quote: ‘He sent to him: ‘They are causing me great distress, and I cannot stand up to them.’ He sent back: ‘Be still before Hashem and wait for Him’—be still before Hashem, and He will cause them to fall before you, slain one after another. Go early and late to the study hall on their account, and they will come to an end by themselves. The words left Rabbi Elazar’s mouth, and Geneiva was put in a prisoner’s collar.’

connections.hePhrase: "רַק בְּעֵינֶיךָ תַבִּיט [וְשִׁלֻּמַת רְשָׁעִים תִּרְאֶה]" (תְּהִלִּים צא, ח) הוּא כְּעִנְיַן "דּוֹם לַה' [וְהִתְחוֹלֵל לוֹ]" (שָׁם לז, ז) דְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּגִטִּין (ז.),
connections.quote: “Although many words of Torah can be attained only through toil, patience and preceding failure—as Gittin 43a says, a person does not stand upon words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them—my holy grandfather explained that this too is only from the person's concealment. Because he distances himself from them, he needs toil, patience and a preceding failure. In truth, even the teachings reached only through failure do not require that he himself fail. By seeing others who wish to distance themselves from Torah fail, one can likewise reach and understand those teachings. He need not fail personally; seeing another's failure suffices, as it says (Psalms 91:8), ‘You shall see the recompense of the wicked.’”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef directly explains the siman's closing verse about seeing the recompense of the wicked. A person can learn from another's failure instead of undergoing or choosing it himself. This supports the siman's ordinary instruction to remain in Torah and refrain from anger, while the earlier discussion of exceptional purity remains qualified.
connections.headline: Learning through seeing another's failure

connections.hePhrase: [ריט] כְּפִי יִתְרוֹן הַדַּעַת וְהַחָכְמָה שֶׁבָּאָדָם, כָּךְ מִתְגַּבְּרִים לְעֻמָּתָן הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת בְּמוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן: "יוֹסִיף דַּעַת [יוֹסִיף מַכְאוֹב]" (קֹהֶלֶת א, יח).
connections.quote: ‘For with much wisdom comes much vexation, and one who increases knowledge increases pain.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע: עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנִּכְנַס בּוֹ דַּעַת טוֹב נִכְנַס גַּם כֵּן הַהֵיפֶךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה כא:): נִכְנְסָה חָכְמָה – נִכְנְסָה עַרְמוּמִיּוּת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲנִי [חָכְמָה שָׁכַנְתִּי] עָרְמָה" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, יב).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Abbahu said: What is Rabbi Eliezer’s reason? It is written, “I, wisdom, dwell with cunning”: once wisdom enters a person, cunning enters with it.”
connections.context: This explanation is given in the discussion of Rabbi Eliezer’s position on teaching Torah to a daughter. Rav Tzadok takes its general formulation about wisdom and cunning as the basis for the danger that can accompany increased understanding.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע: עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנִּכְנַס בּוֹ דַּעַת טוֹב נִכְנַס גַּם כֵּן הַהֵיפֶךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה כא:): נִכְנְסָה חָכְמָה – נִכְנְסָה עַרְמוּמִיּוּת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲנִי [חָכְמָה שָׁכַנְתִּי] עָרְמָה" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, יב).
connections.quote: ‘I, Wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge of thoughtful planning.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (ע:): אֵין הַתִּינוֹק יוֹדֵעַ לִקְרוֹת "אַבָּא" וְ"אִמָּא" עַד שֶׁטּוֹעֵם דָּגָן, וְנִמְצָא אָז נִכְנַס בּוֹ דַּעַת וְחָכְמָה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah says: It was wheat, for an infant does not know to call “Father” and “Mother” until it tastes grain.”
connections.context: Rabbi Yehudah is identifying the Tree of Knowledge as wheat. The infant’s new ability to name father and mother is his evidence for grain’s connection with knowledge; this is the connection Rav Tzadok develops.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז מַרְחִיקִין מִצּוֹאָתוֹ (סֻכָּה מב:), וּמְפוֹרָשׁ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ה) הַטַּעַם: שֶׁמַּחְשְׁבוֹתָיו רָעוֹת.
connections.quote: “If a child can eat an olive’s bulk of grain, one must keep four cubits away from his feces and urine. Rav Chisda said: This applies if he can eat it within the time it takes to eat a half loaf. Rav Chiyya son of Rav Yeiva said: For an adult, this applies even if he cannot eat it within the time it takes to eat a half loaf, as it is written: ‘One who increases knowledge increases pain.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָז מַרְחִיקִין מִצּוֹאָתוֹ (סֻכָּה מב:), וּמְפוֹרָשׁ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ה) הַטַּעַם: שֶׁמַּחְשְׁבוֹתָיו רָעוֹת.
connections.quote: “It was taught: From the feces and urine of a child able to eat an olive’s volume of grain, one withdraws four cubits; if he cannot eat an olive’s volume of grain, one does not withdraw four cubits from either. They asked Rabbi Abbahu: Why does one withdraw from his feces and urine? He said: Because his thoughts are evil. They said to him: But is he not a child? He replied: Is it not written, “The inclination of the human heart is evil from youth”? Rabbi Yudan said: It is written in a form that can be read “from his stirring”—from the time he stirs and emerges into the world.”
connections.context: This is the Jerusalem Talmud’s explanation quoted by Rav Tzadok. It expressly connects the child’s excrement with his thoughts; the similarly numbered Mishnah does not contain that explanation. Rav Tzadok develops the connection between food, bodily residue, and foreign thoughts.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי, כִּי בִּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה שֶׁנִּכְנַס יֵצֶר טוֹב, שֶׁאָז הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מִתְגַּבֵּר, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב.): "כָּל הַגָּדוֹל מֵחֲבֵירוֹ [יִצְרוֹ גָּדוֹל הֵימֶנּוּ]".
connections.quote: ““Better a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king.” “A poor and wise child”—this is the good inclination. Why is it called a child? Because it does not join a person until the age of thirteen and onward. Why is it called poor? Because not everyone listens to it. Why is it called wise? Because it teaches people the upright path. “Than an old and foolish king”—this is the evil inclination. Why is it called a king? Because everyone listens to it. Why is it called old? Because it joins a person from childhood through old age. Why is it called foolish? Because it teaches a person an evil path. “Who no longer knows to take warning”: it does not know how much pain and suffering come upon it, and it does not guard against them.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִי שֶׁמִּתְגַּבֵּר וְכוֹבֵשׁ יִצְרוֹ לְגַמְרֵי, עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "אֹיְבֵי אִישׁ אַנְשֵׁי בֵיתוֹ" (מִיכָה ז, ו).
connections.quote: ‘For a son dishonors his father, a daughter rises against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the members of his own household.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע נִקְרָא "שׂוֹנֵא", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם) [וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נד) נִדְרַשׁ מִקְרָא זֶה אַיֵּצֶר],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: This is the evil inclination. … Solomon said, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread; if he is thirsty, give him water”—from the bread of Torah, as it says, “Come, eat of my bread,” and from the water of Torah, as it says, “All who are thirsty, come to the water.””
connections.context: The Midrash interprets the enemy as the evil inclination and its food and drink as Torah. “Come, eat of my bread” is Proverbs 9:5; the former quotation’s embedded reference to 9:4 was incorrect.

connections.hePhrase: וּמֶלֶךְ, שֶׁכָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲבָדָיו, וְכָל מִינֵי יְצָרִים שֶׁבְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל הֵם מוֹלִידִים דִּמְיוֹנוֹת בּוֹ, וְהוּא צָרִיךְ לְחַלְּצָם הַטּוֹב מֵהָרָע, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְקָנִים מִמֵּילָא אוֹתָם הָאֲנָשִׁים גַּם כֵּן.
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות מלכים ומלחמות ג׳:ו׳
connections.quote: “The Torah was concerned about his heart being turned aside, as it is said, “His heart shall not turn aside.” For his heart is the heart of the entire congregation of Israel. Therefore Scripture attached him to Torah more than the rest of the people, as it is said, “All the days of his life.””

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה בִּקֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "מֵאֹיְבַי תְּחַכְּמֵנִי מִצְוֹתֶךָ [כִּי לְעוֹלָם הִיא לִי]" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, צח),
connections.quote: ‘Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is mine forever.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי לַעֲמוֹד עַל חָכְמַת הַמִּצְווֹת אִי אֶפְשָׁר רַק עַל יְדֵי הַתַּחְבּוּלוֹת אֵיךְ לְהִנָּצֵל מִיֵּצֶר מַחְשְׁבוֹת לִבּוֹ.
connections.quote: “And Hashem saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the day.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהַתַּרְיַ"ג מִצְווֹת הֵם תַּרְיַ"ג עֵיטִין לָזֶה (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, פב עַמּוּד ב), וְלָכֵן אָמַר לְמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת: יֵצֶר הָרָע יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם וְכוּלֵי (שַׁבָּת פט.),
connections.quote: see note 586 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Zohar explicitly calls the 613 commandments kinds of counsel for attaining completeness with Hashem. This is the precise formulation behind Rav Tzadok’s explanation; the preceding paragraph also includes the counsel of repentance.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֹהֲנִים רִבָּה בָּהֶן הַכָּתוּב מִצְווֹת יְתֵירוֹת, לְפִי שֶׁנִּבְדַּל אַהֲרֹן לְהַקְדִּישׁוֹ קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים, לְעֻמָּתוֹ גַּם כֵּן הַיֵּצֶר מוּבְדָּל מִיֵּצֶר מַחְשְׁבוֹת אֲחֵרִים, וְצָרִיךְ עֵצוֹת יְתֵירוֹת לְהִשָּׁמֵר מִמֶּנּוּ.
connections.quote: “The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses; and Aaron was set apart, to sanctify him as most holy, he and his sons forever, to offer before Hashem, to minister to Him, and to bless in His name forever.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִצְווֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ הֵם לְהִנָּצֵל מִיֵּצֶר הַכְּלָלִי דִּכְלָלוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ הַסֵּפֶר תּוֹרָה עַל לִבּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין כא: וְעַיֵּין כֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג מֵהִלְכוֹת מְלָכִים),
connections.quote: “The scroll that goes out and comes in with him is made like an amulet and hung upon his arm, as it says, “I have set Hashem before me always; because He is at my right hand, I shall not falter.” He does not enter with it into a bathhouse or privy, as it says, “It shall be with him, and he shall read in it”—in a place fit for reading.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִצְווֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ הֵם לְהִנָּצֵל מִיֵּצֶר הַכְּלָלִי דִּכְלָלוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ הַסֵּפֶר תּוֹרָה עַל לִבּוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין כא: וְעַיֵּין כֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג מֵהִלְכוֹת מְלָכִים),
connections.displayRef: Kessef Mishneh on Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 3:1
connections.linkedRef: Kessef Mishneh on Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 3:1
connections.canonicalRef: Kessef Mishneh on Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 3:1
connections.heRef: כסף משנה על משנה תורה, הלכות מלכים ומלחמות ג׳:א׳
connections.quote: “It requires examination why our master did not write that the scroll which goes out and comes in with him is made like an amulet and hung upon his arm, as appears in the baraita that I have quoted.”
connections.context: The Talmud places the king’s portable Torah scroll on his arm. Kesef Mishneh asks why Rambam omitted this detail. Rav Tzadok describes its spiritual relation to the king’s heart; the source quotation itself says “arm,” not “heart.” His citation is to the specific carrying requirement, beyond the general command to write a scroll.

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין לְעֵיל אוֹת צ"ח, וְשָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי כָּל פְּעֻלָּתָן עִנְיָנָם עַל דֶּרֶךְ קְצִיבַת הָעֵץ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת רי"ב;
connections.quote: “Every verse of Torah contains the power and vitality of the matter stated in it. You can see this from tefillin, concerning which it is said, “It shall be a sign,” and so forth, without specifying which passage of Torah must serve as the sign. The halakhah is to write those passages in which this is stated. Presumably, the very passage in which “It shall be a sign,” and so forth, is stated contains that matter’s power and special efficacy, so that it will be a sign. Much of this kind is known to those versed in the divine names and in practical Kabbalah: from each verse there emerges a name effective for the matter mentioned in that verse. Likewise, the verse “Hear, Israel” contains the power of establishing hearing within the heart; therefore one must also say the words “Hear, Israel.” This is also the secret of what I heard concerning “The lips of the righteous know favor”: the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote that a remedy for someone whose inclination entices him toward a particular transgression is to speak aloud several times the verse prohibiting that transgression; through this the desire will change. The same applies to a mitzvah and a good matter.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁמְּשַׁנִּים סֵדֶר צֵירוּף הָאוֹתִיּוֹת, בַּפָּשׁוּט הַטַּעַם מִשּׁוּם דְּאָסוּר לְהִתְרַפּאוֹת בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְגַם כְּדֵי לְהַעֲלִים כִּי דֶּרֶךְ הַנֵּס לָבוֹא בַּחֲשַׁאי],
connections.displayRef: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 11:12
connections.linkedRef: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 11:12
connections.canonicalRef: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 11:12
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות עבודה זרה וחוקות הגויים י״א:י״ב
connections.quote: “One who whispers over a wound and recites a verse of Torah; likewise, one who recites over an infant so that it will not be frightened, or places a Torah scroll or tefillin upon a child so that it will sleep—not only are these people included among diviners and charmers, but they are also included among those who deny the Torah, for they make words of Torah a remedy for the body, whereas they are only a remedy for souls, as it is said, “They shall be life for your soul.” But a healthy person who recites verses and a psalm so that the merit of their recitation may protect him and save him from troubles and injuries is permitted to do so.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַה שֶּׁמְּשַׁנִּים סֵדֶר צֵירוּף הָאוֹתִיּוֹת, בַּפָּשׁוּט הַטַּעַם מִשּׁוּם דְּאָסוּר לְהִתְרַפּאוֹת בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְגַם כְּדֵי לְהַעֲלִים כִּי דֶּרֶךְ הַנֵּס לָבוֹא בַּחֲשַׁאי],
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: Blessing is found only in something concealed from the eye, as it is said, “Hashem shall command the blessing for you in your storehouses.” The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: Blessing is found only in something over which the eye has no mastery, as it is said, “Hashem shall command the blessing for you in your storehouses.” The Sages taught: One who enters to measure his grain says: “May it be Your will, Hashem our God, that You send blessing upon the work of our hands.” When he begins measuring, he says: “Blessed is the One who sends blessing upon this heap.” If he measured and then blessed, this is a vain prayer, because blessing is found neither in something weighed, nor in something measured, nor in something counted, but in something concealed from the eye.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (יז.): הַנָּחַת סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה – לוֹמַר: קִיֵּים זֶה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.quote: ‘Rather, they placed a Torah scroll upon his bier and said: ‘This man fulfilled what is written in this scroll.’ But we do this nowadays as well! We bring out a scroll, but we do not place it on the bier. Alternatively, you may say: We also place it there, but we do not say, ‘He fulfilled it.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא קַמָּא (יז.): הַנָּחַת סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה – לוֹמַר: קִיֵּים זֶה וְכוּלֵי;
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:4
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:4
connections.quote: “When he is not engaged in it, the body's share in the mitzvah's holiness does not remain, because the body does not understand its root. But with a mitzvah related to a person—especially when he increases his care for its details and his understanding—Hashem illuminates for him an understanding of the mitzvah in Torah's light. The mitzvah's very substance becomes Torah for him; he understands its intention and sees that the garment and action of the mitzvah belong to this world. This is our prayer, ‘May He open our heart in His Torah’: it alludes to the Torah teachings and mitzvot particularly related to each person's essential root.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov develops the same distinction from Sotah with which this siman concludes. The person does not only perform a momentary act; attention to its particulars and meaning allows its Torah light to be grasped within him. This explains why the siman connects wisdom in the mitzvah with something that remains his beyond the moment of performance. The particular root described by Beit Yaakov deepens general observance rather than exempting the person from other mitzvot.
connections.headline: Understanding makes a mitzvah a lasting Torah acquisition

connections.hePhrase: וְסִיֵּים: "כִּי לְעוֹלָם הִיא לִי", לְפִי שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (כא. לְרַב יוֹסֵף) דְּרַק בְּעִידָּנָא דְּעָסֵיק בְּמִצְוָה מַצְּלָא;
connections.quote: ‘Rav Yosef said: A mitzvah, while one is engaged in it, protects (from suffering) and rescues (from sin). When one is not engaged in it, it protects but does not rescue. Torah, whether one is engaged in it or not, protects and rescues.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק כְּשֶׁעוֹמֵד עַל הַחָכְמָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בַּמִּצְוָה, אָז נַעֲשָׂה מִן הַמִּצְוָה גַּם כֵּן תּוֹרָה, כִּי עִיקַּר הַתּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת הַיְינוּ הַלִּמּוּד לְהָבִין חָכְמַת הַמִּצְווֹת,
connections.quote: “Although we do not have an actual offering, nevertheless we have the Torah light within the performance of the commandment of offerings. This is as we said concerning the teaching, “A mitzvah is a lamp”: just as a lamp illuminates for a time, so does a mitzvah, and so forth. It appears that the Gemara understands “a mitzvah is a lamp” as a lamp while it is burning. In the holy Zohar, however, the mitzvah is only the lamp—that is, the lamp, wick, and oil without a flame. We said that every mitzvah has a light: its intended purpose for the sake of Heaven. This is called Torah light, for the essence of Torah is the fulfillment of the commandments. What difference is there between studying the passage and directing oneself to the mitzvah’s intended meaning? Yet the Torah light within the mitzvah illuminates only for a time, whereas the Torah light in fulfilling the positive commandment of Torah study illuminates forever. Of this it is said, “Torah is light” (as explained in discourse 2).”

connections.hePhrase: רַק כְּשֶׁעוֹמֵד עַל הַחָכְמָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בַּמִּצְוָה, אָז נַעֲשָׂה מִן הַמִּצְוָה גַּם כֵּן תּוֹרָה, כִּי עִיקַּר הַתּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת הַיְינוּ הַלִּמּוּד לְהָבִין חָכְמַת הַמִּצְווֹת,
connections.quote: “As the Talmud says (Sotah 21a), a mitzvah protects and rescues at the time one is occupied with it; Torah does so both while one is occupied with it and while one is not. A mitzvah means that at the time of doing it one sees Hashem's light. Torah means the holiness established permanently within oneself through the mitzvot; this established presence remains always. Although Torah too is described (Proverbs 23:5), ‘You cast your eyes upon it and it is gone,’ suggesting that Torah can sometimes cease from the person, this is when he turns his attention away and proceeds presumptuously: because he already had this recognition called Torah, he thinks that he needs no further work. Then it says, ‘You cast your eyes upon it and it is gone.’ But when he does not turn his attention away, it remains established in him both while he is occupied with it and while he is not.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same difference between the time of a mitzvah's performance and the lasting effect of Torah. It then expressly warns against assuming that the acquired recognition makes further work unnecessary. This clarifies the siman's concluding claim that understanding and embodying a mitzvah's wisdom gives it an enduring presence.
connections.headline: Lasting Torah requires continuing attention

connections.hePhrase: [רכ] הָעֵצוֹת לְמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים הוּא מִצְוַת צִיצִית וּתְפִלִּין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה יז.): בִּשְׂכַר "אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יד, כג), זָכוּ בָנָיו לְחוּט שֶׁל תְּכֵלֶת וּרְצוּעָה שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין.
connections.quote: ‘Rava expounded: As a reward for our father Abraham’s saying, ‘Not so much as a thread or a sandal strap,’ his descendants merited two mitzvot: the thread of techelet and the strap of tefillin. The strap of tefillin is understandable, for it is written: ‘All the peoples of the earth will see that Hashem’s name is called upon you.’ It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says: These are the tefillin worn on the head.’

connections.hePhrase: [רכ] הָעֵצוֹת לְמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים הוּא מִצְוַת צִיצִית וּתְפִלִּין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה יז.): בִּשְׂכַר "אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יד, כג), זָכוּ בָנָיו לְחוּט שֶׁל תְּכֵלֶת וּרְצוּעָה שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין.
connections.quote: ‘I will take neither a thread nor a sandal strap, nor anything that belongs to you, so that you will not say: ‘I made Abram wealthy.’’

connections.hePhrase: [רכ] הָעֵצוֹת לְמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים הוּא מִצְוַת צִיצִית וּתְפִלִּין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה יז.): בִּשְׂכַר "אִם מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יד, כג), זָכוּ בָנָיו לְחוּט שֶׁל תְּכֵלֶת וּרְצוּעָה שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין.
connections.quote: see note 440 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains Korach’s all-blue garment as a mistaken inference from the soul’s holy root: if one is already surrounded by divine light, why need the mitzvah? His answer gives substance to the siman’s distinction between erasing every thought and having the power to reject it. The commanded reminder makes return and responsible human effort possible within concealment.

connections.hePhrase: בְּצִיצִית מְפוֹרָשׁ: "וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וְגוֹמֵר וְלֹא תָתוּרוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (בַּמִּדְבָּר טו, לט).
connections.quote: ‘It shall be a tzitzit for you, and you shall look at it and remember all Hashem’s commandments and fulfill them. You shall not wander after your hearts and after your eyes, after which you stray unfaithfully.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְשׁוֹן "וְלֹא תָתוּרוּ" מַשְׁמָע לֹא שֶׁיֵּעָקֵר הַהִרְהוּר מִלֵּב לְגַמְרֵי, רַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּכֹחוֹ לִדְחוֹתוֹ.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים כ״ז:א׳-ד׳
connections.quote: “If the sadness does not arise from concern about sins but from evil thoughts and desires that enter his mind, then, if these occur outside the time of divine service, while he is occupied with his business and worldly affairs or the like, he should instead rejoice in his portion. For although they enter his mind, he turns his attention away from them, fulfilling the words, “You shall not stray after your hearts and after your eyes, after which you go astray.” Scripture is not speaking of righteous people, calling them those who go astray, Heaven forbid. It speaks of intermediate people like him, into whose minds thoughts of illicit relations arise, even concerning what is permitted, and so forth. When he turns his attention away, he fulfills this prohibition. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: “If a person sits and does not commit a transgression, he is given a reward as though he performed a mitzvah.” Therefore he should rejoice in fulfilling the prohibition just as in fulfilling a positive commandment. Indeed, the sadness comes from arrogance: he does not recognize his place, and therefore feels bad that he is not on the level of a righteous person. Such foolish thoughts certainly do not enter righteous people. If he recognized his place—that he is very far from the level of a righteous person, and would that he were an intermediate person and not wicked throughout his life, even for one hour—he would recognize that this is the quality and service of intermediate people: to subdue the inclination and the thought rising from the heart to the mind, turn his attention entirely away from it, and reject it with both hands, as explained above. With every act of rejection by which he removes it from his thought, the other side is subdued below. Through this awakening below comes an awakening above, and the other side above, which raises itself like an eagle, is subdued, fulfilling the words, “Though you rise like the eagle,” and so forth, “from there I shall bring you down, says Hashem.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים לב:): דִּבִשְׁעַת יֵצֶר רָע לֵית דְּמַדְכַּר לְיֵצֶר טוֹב, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְאָדָם לֹא זָכַר וְגוֹמֵר" (קֹהֶלֶת ט, טו),
connections.quote: ‘‘And there was found in it a poor, wise man’—this is the good inclination. ‘He saved the city through his wisdom’—this is repentance and good deeds. ‘Yet no one remembered that poor man’—when the evil inclination holds sway, no one remembers the good inclination.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים לב:): דִּבִשְׁעַת יֵצֶר רָע לֵית דְּמַדְכַּר לְיֵצֶר טוֹב, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְאָדָם לֹא זָכַר וְגוֹמֵר" (קֹהֶלֶת ט, טו),
connections.quote: ‘A poor, wise man was found in it, and he delivered the city through his wisdom, yet no one remembered that poor man.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה הוּא מִצְוַת צִיצִית לְהַזְכִּירוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת שְׁלַח שֶׁהוּא הָרְצוּעָה לְאַלְקָאָה בִישַׁיָּא וּמְעוֹרֶרֶת הַיִּרְאָה עַל הָאָדָם,
connections.quote: “It is written, “From the corner of the earth we have heard songs: glory to the righteous; and I said, My secret is mine,” and so forth. “From the corner of the earth”—this is the corner of tzitzit, which is the corner of the earth. “We have heard songs”—these are the other threads, which emerge and hang from a higher place, among those higher paths that emerge from supernal wisdom. “Glory to the righteous”—this is the Righteous One, the Life of the worlds; those threads are His beauty, for they emerge from Him, and each thread includes two sides. When I looked, I said, “My secret is mine, my secret is mine,” for they emerge from the supernal mystery of all faith. When I looked at the blue thread and saw a strap for punishment, a place of awe to be feared, I said, “Woe to me,” for people do not know to attend and consider what brings punishment upon them for falsehood. In this, “traitors have betrayed”: they recite Shema without tzitzit and bear false testimony. These are the traitors who have betrayed, deceiving themselves. “And with the betrayal of traitors they have betrayed”: their garment without tzitzit is called a garment of traitors—the garment of those traitors who have betrayed, who lie and bear false testimony each day. Woe to them; woe to their souls, which ascend to that throne of blue to be judged. Of them it is written, “One who speaks falsehood shall not stand before My eyes.” Their garment is recognized by all the masters of judgment. Woe to them, for they have no portion in the World to Come. Fortunate are the righteous, whose garments and adornments are recognized above, to do good to them in this world and in the World to Come. (End here; Exodus 43a: “It shall be a sign,” and so forth.) This commandment, the mitzvah of tzitzit, includes blue and white—judgment and mercy within fire. White fire does not consume; blue consumes and destroys. “It consumed the burnt offering”: white is on the right, blue on the left. The middle column, green, unites them both. Therefore the masters of the Mishnah established: From when is Shema recited in the morning? From when one can distinguish between blue and white. Therefore they instituted reading the passage of tzitzit as part of the declaration of divine unity.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מְנָחוֹת מג:): וּזְכוֹר מִצְוָה אַחֶרֶת הַתְּלוּיָה בָּהּ, וְאֵיזוֹ זוֹ? קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע,
connections.quote: ‘And the Rabbis—what do they do with ‘You shall look at it’? They need it for what was taught: ‘You shall look at it and remember’—look at this mitzvah and remember another mitzvah that depends on it. Which one is that? The recitation of Shema, as we learned: From when may one recite Shema in the morning? From when one can distinguish between techelet and white.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה הוּא מְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְזוֹכֶה לְאַהֲבָה דְּ"וְאָהַבְתָּ", וְאַחַר כָּךְ לְ"וּקְשַׁרְתָּם" דִּתְפִלִּין.
connections.quote: “And you shall love Hashem your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה הוּא מְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְזוֹכֶה לְאַהֲבָה דְּ"וְאָהַבְתָּ", וְאַחַר כָּךְ לְ"וּקְשַׁרְתָּם" דִּתְפִלִּין.
connections.quote: “And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי צִיצִית אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְבוּשׁ שֶׁמִּתְעַטֵּף בּוֹ רוֹב גּוּפוֹ, דְּהַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ לֹא נִתְנַקָּה עֲדַיִן, רַק שֶׁמְּעוּטָּף בִּלְבוּשׁ שֶׁל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הַמַּזְכִּירוֹ בְּכָל עֵת לְבִלְתִּי לָתוּר אַחַר הִרְהוּרִים זָרִים.
connections.quote: “The commandment of tzitzit on one’s garments clothes and covers all the blemishes of the body. The greater part counts as the whole, and therefore wrapping the head and most of the body is sufficient: through this, the whole person is completely covered, so that no creature recognizes what is in his heart—only the blessed God alone—and there is no place for accusation.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַתְּפִלִּין, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן לְבוּשׁ וְאוֹר מַקִּיף, רַק שֶׁהוּא בִּקְשִׁירָה וּדְבֵיקוּת לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Fringes 1:13
connections.linkedRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Fringes 1:13
connections.canonicalRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Fringes 1:13
connections.heRef: פרי עץ חיים, שער הציצית א׳:י״ג
connections.quote: “The matter is as follows. The tallit is always the encompassing light of Binah surrounding Zeir Anpin. It has two aspects. The first is during Zeir’s smallness, when he is in the state of gestation within her: then he is in the state of three included within three, and she surrounds him while he is within her in gestation. This is called the small tzitzit, for she surrounds him during his smallness. At that time he corresponds to Asiyah, for Zeir then has only the aspect of Asiyah. Thus the small tallit is in Yetzirah, but during its smallness, in the aspect of Asiyah alone. The second aspect is the large tallit, when he is in the actual state of maturity in Yetzirah. Tefillin, however, encompass the faculties of consciousness. The tallit encompasses that which encompasses Zeir’s faculties of consciousness—namely, tefillin.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעִיקָּר מַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא "מַחֲנֶיךָ קָדוֹשׁ" בְּהַרְחָקַת הַצּוֹאָה הוּא מִפְּנֵי הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְרָעוֹת שֶׁבָּאוֹת מִשָּׁם, שֶׁהַקְּדוּשָּׁה הִפּוּכוֹ;
connections.quote: “For Hashem your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you; therefore your camp shall be holy, that He see no unseemly thing in you and turn away from you.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת טו.): יִפָּנֶה וְיִטּוֹל וְכוּלֵי, זֶהוּ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שְׁלֵימָה, גַּם "יִפָּנֶה" מִכְּלַל הַקַּבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם].
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: One who wishes to accept upon himself the complete yoke of the kingdom of Heaven should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, recite Shema, and pray. This is the complete kingdom of Heaven.”
connections.context: The bodily preparation is expressly included in the sequence for complete acceptance of Heaven’s rule. Rav Tzadok emphasizes that even relieving oneself belongs to this preparation, following his explanation of the body’s purification.

connections.hePhrase: [רכא] הַשִּׁכְחָה הוּא הַתְחָלַת הָרָע, שֶׁהַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת מַשְׁכִּיחִים מִן הַמּוֹחַ וָלֵב מַחְשְׁבוֹת אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְתוֹרָתוֹ וְאַהֲבָתוֹ וְיִרְאָתוֹ,
connections.quote: “Forgetting comes from the absence of awe, and it is the beginning of every evil, as it says, ‘If you forget… and follow other gods.’ Awe is the gate to the righteous person's courtyard. Through awe comes remembrance, for something a person regards with awe is fixed in the heart. Therefore Yoma 72b interprets ‘without a heart’ as the absence of awe. Something continually present in the heart cannot be forgotten.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin uses the same forgetting verse and calls forgetting the beginning of evil. It then supplies the positive mechanism: awe establishes the matter in the heart, where it remains present. This explains why the siman later requires awe for hearing and developing the continuing voice of Torah.
connections.headline: Awe fixes remembrance in the heart

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (פָּרָשַׁת עֵקֶב): "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁכֹחַ תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת ה' [אֱלֹהֶיךָ]", תֵּיכֶף "וְהָלַכְתָּ אַחֲרֵי [אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים]" (דְּבָרִים ח, יט) – פֵּירוּשׁ: בְּתַאֲוָה וְרָצוֹן אַחַר כֹּחוֹת זָרִים, וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וַעֲבַדְתָּם" בְּמַעֲשֶׂה;
connections.quote: ‘If you do forget Hashem your God, follow other gods, serve them, and bow down to them, I bear witness against you this day that you will certainly perish.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל דָּבָר כָּלוּל מֵעֶשֶׂר כַּנּוֹדָע, וְכֶתֶר דְּרָע, דְּהַיְינוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם, זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל, שֶׁלְּעוֹלָם שָׁרְשָׁם דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְחֵלֶק ה' עַמּוֹ וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִינָּתֵק כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “For Hashem’s portion is His people; Jacob is the lot of His inheritance.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמְסַיֵּים: "עֵקֶב לֹא תִשְׁמְעוּן בְּקוֹל [ה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם]" (דְּבָרִים ח, כ), וְקוֹל ה' הַיְינוּ קוֹלוֹת דְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “Like the nations whom the Lord causes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord your God.”
connections.context: The literal word “voice” matters: Rav Tzadok connects it with the voices of the giving of the Torah and the inward reception of God’s teaching.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, נ עַמּוּד ב וּשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת) דְּקוֹל דָּא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, כִּי קוֹלוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הֵם חַיִּים וְקַיָּימִים לָעַד וּלְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים.
connections.quote: “From here comes forth Torah, which is the voice of Jacob. This audible voice issues from that which is not heard. Afterward speech joins it and comes forth through its power and strength. The voice of Jacob, which is Torah, holds between the two feminine aspects: it holds to the inner one that is not heard and to the outer one that is heard.”
connections.context: The passage expressly identifies Torah as the voice of Jacob and distinguishes voice from the speech that joins it. Rav Tzadok applies this distinction to the Written Torah and its lasting divine voice. The earlier sentence about the hidden “great voice” alone would not supply the identification he cites.

connections.hePhrase: וְאוֹתָם קוֹלוֹת גַּם הַיּוֹם מְצוּיִים לְמִי שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְהַאֲזִין, וְהֵן הֵם הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת הָעוֹלִים בְּלֵב כָּל אֶחָד בְּכָל פַּעַם לָשׁוּב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלָדַעַת כִּי "אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: “You shall have no other gods before Me.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאוֹתָם קוֹלוֹת גַּם הַיּוֹם מְצוּיִים לְמִי שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְהַאֲזִין, וְהֵן הֵם הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת הָעוֹלִים בְּלֵב כָּל אֶחָד בְּכָל פַּעַם לָשׁוּב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלָדַעַת כִּי "אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ““And you shall listen to His voice” accords with what we said in the preceding portion: this is why it says everywhere, “If you shall surely listen to the voice of the Lord your God,” although the voices sounded only at the giving of the Torah. Rather, this refers to what is said in the sixth chapter of Avot: Every day a heavenly voice goes forth from Mount Chorev and proclaims, “Woe to the creatures because of the Torah’s humiliation.” This remains from the voices at the giving of the Torah, concerning which it says there, “All the people see the voices”—“see” in the present tense. The heavenly voice is the awakening that comes into the heart of every Jew, as is reported in the name of the Baal Shem Tov, of blessed memory.”

connections.hePhrase: וְקוֹל הוּא כְּלָל וְדִבּוּר פְּרָט, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר רֵישׁ שְׁמוֹת;
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon said: This verse, ‘With me from Lebanon, O bride’ (Song of Songs 4:8), is said of the mystery of the unity of faith. Voice says to Speech, ‘With me,’ for Voice comes to Speech and speaks with her, so that they are one without any separation. For Voice is the general and Speech is the particular; the general needs the particular and the particular needs the general, for there is no voice without speech and no speech without voice.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב נִקְרָא "קוֹל" וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה "דִּבּוּר",
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:11
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:11
connections.quote: “Because he was pressed for livelihood, he had the understanding to devise a means of livelihood. Similarly, if a person needs words of Torah, seeks them and searches for them like hidden treasures, he will attain them, as it says, ‘If you seek it like silver.’ This was certainly a great person, since Eliyahu appeared to him. Yet Eliyahu taught him that he must seek Torah not like someone who wants to gain a great fortune—that is, luxuries—but by recognizing his lack: without Torah he is lacking life. He must seek it as his livelihood, and then he will find it.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains Eliyahu's challenge to a fisherman who said he lacked the understanding for Torah. The intelligence he found for necessary livelihood illustrated what a search driven by actual need could accomplish. This develops the present siman's quotation from Proverbs: hearing the general call leads to a search through the heart's particulars when Torah is recognized as needed life, not merely added information.
connections.headline: The search becomes different when Torah is needed as life

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַהַשְׁמָעָה לַלֵּב הוּא רַק בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל לָדַעַת אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּלְחַפֵּשׂ אַחֲרָיו: "אִם [תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכוּלֵי] תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה, אָז תָּבִין יִרְאַת ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ד–ה) בַּבִּינָה שֶׁבְּלֵב הָאָדָם בְּפִרְטֵי פְּרָטוֹת כְּפִי הַצָּרִיךְ לוֹ.
connections.quote: “If you seek it like silver and search for it like hidden treasures.”
connections.context: The search is the condition stated before the promise of understanding in the next verse. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the initial call to seek from the detailed understanding that follows.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַהַשְׁמָעָה לַלֵּב הוּא רַק בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל לָדַעַת אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּלְחַפֵּשׂ אַחֲרָיו: "אִם [תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכוּלֵי] תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה, אָז תָּבִין יִרְאַת ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ד–ה) בַּבִּינָה שֶׁבְּלֵב הָאָדָם בְּפִרְטֵי פְּרָטוֹת כְּפִי הַצָּרִיךְ לוֹ.
connections.quote: “Then you will understand the fear of the Lord, and you will find the knowledge of God.”
connections.context: This gives the result of the search described in the preceding verse. “Understand” is the word Rav Tzadok relates to the individual person’s inward discernment.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הַמַּלְאָכִים מַשְׁמִיעִים בְּיִרְאָה יַחַד בְּקוֹל דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים וְכוּלֵי.
connections.displayRef: Siddur, weekday Shacharit, blessing Yotzer Or
connections.linkedRef: Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Blessings of the Shema, First Blessing before Shema 3
connections.canonicalRef: Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Blessings of the Shema, First Blessing before Shema 3
connections.heRef: סידור אשכנז, ימי חול, תפילת שחרית, ברכות קריאת שמע, יוצר אור ג׳
connections.quote: “And His ministers all stand in the heights of the universe and proclaim with awe, together, aloud, the words of the living God and eternal King.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא בְּוַדַּאי נִשְׁמָע לְכָל אִישׁ יִשְׂרְאֵלִי אֲשֶׁר מֵכִין אָזְנֵי לְבָבוֹ לְכָךְ בְּיִרְאָה, אָז שׁוֹמֵעַ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, וְהַיְינוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא כֵּן בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֵירוּבִין יג:): אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Abba said in the name of Shmuel: For three years, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed. These said, ‘The halakhah follows us,’ and those said, ‘The halakhah follows us.’ A heavenly voice went forth and said: ‘Both these and those are the words of the living God, and the halakhah follows Beit Hillel.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל "מֵבִין וְלֹא בְּבִינָה יְדוּעָה", שֶׁהַמַּלְאָכִים אֵין לָהֶם בִּינָה דְּהַיְינוּ הַרְגָּשָׁה בַּלֵּב, שֶׁזֶּהוּ רַק לִבְנֵי אָדָם שֶׁהֵם חֲסֵרִים וּצְרִיכִים לָזֶה;
connections.quote: “You are wise, but not with a known wisdom; You understand, but not with a known understanding. You have no known place, except to make Your power and might known to mankind.”
connections.context: From Elijah’s prayer “Patach Eliyahu” in the introduction to the Tikkunim.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵבִין, כְּמוֹ הַבְּנֵי אָדָם הוּא מַרְגִּישׁ, אֲבָל לֹא בְּבִינָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵינוֹ חָסֵר.
connections.quote: “As I heard concerning the wording of the Tikkunim, “You are wise, but not with a known wisdom; You understand, but not with a known understanding”: wisdom is the intellect’s knowledge in the brain, whereas understanding is the heart’s feeling. Angels possess knowledge through the wisdom God imparts to them, but they do not possess the heart’s feeling. (This is as I wrote: nothing can be felt in the heart unless its opposite also exists in the heart. Angels do not possess free choice, and therefore they are called “the enduring ones,” for they are fixed and enduring as God created them, without change. Their wisdom, too, is fixed and enduring, each according to what God imparted to it at its creation. This is called knowledge and wisdom, rather than understanding and feeling in the heart.) Israel possesses (only) understanding, which is the feeling in the heart. (All their wisdom is drawn from the feeling of their heart. Therefore the Talmud commonly says, “According to the heart of Rabbi so-and-so”; I heard that this is an expression of “heart,” for each sage stated every legal teaching only according to the feeling of his heart. Likewise, Sanhedrin 35b says, “People’s hearts forget.” This is the lower wisdom, the wisdom of King Solomon, of blessed memory: the wisdom of the Oral Torah flowing from the hearts of Israel’s sages. Concerning this, Bava Batra 12a says that a sage is superior to a prophet, from the verse, “And we shall bring a heart of wisdom.” Through the wisdom within their hearts, where feeling is found and from which their wisdom flows, it is superior to prophecy, which is through sight. Likewise, concerning wisdom in the heart it says, “My heart has seen much wisdom,” for what a person feels in the heart is as though he sees it with his eyes. At the giving of the Written Torah, too, although it was given from Heaven, it says, “All the people see the voices”: they saw what was heard. Hearing is the brain’s knowledge of what one hears, but seeing comes through the heart’s feeling. This is the essential purpose of giving the Torah to Israel: that it be absorbed into their hearts, as it says, “Write them upon the tablet of your heart,” and concerning the future, “Upon their heart I shall write it.” It says, “If only this heart of theirs would remain theirs,” for “the Merciful One desires the heart,” as Sanhedrin 106b says. The Torah was given principally to the hearts of Israel, as Devarim Rabbah, the portion Berakhah, says: Whoever has fear of Heaven has all the Torah and all wisdom placed within his heart. Fear of Heaven is principally the heart’s feeling, as Yoma 72b says concerning the verse, “But there is no heart.” Therefore it is called “the Torah of Moses,” for in relation to him fear is a small matter, as Berakhot 33b says. He embodies the mystery of knowledge, which, as is known, joins wisdom and understanding. Although the Torah is the wisdom of God, its giver, Israel nevertheless apprehends it only through the heart’s feeling, the understanding by which one understands on one’s own. This is what Rashi writes in the portion Ki Tissa: knowledge is the holy spirit. This is the prophecy of the sages, as Ramban writes in Bava Batra there: what one grasps truthfully through the wisdom of the heart is an influx of the holy spirit flowing from the supernal holiness and wisdom. Therefore Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 17, says, “The fallen fruit of the supernal wisdom is Torah.” This is not the place to elaborate further.) The Holy One, blessed be He, includes both. Yet His wisdom is not a known wisdom: unlike every wise person who knows through wisdom, for whom wisdom is something distinct from the person apprehending it, with God all is one, for He is the knower, and so forth, as Rambam writes in Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 2:10. This is “wise, but not through wisdom,” and likewise “understanding, but not through understanding.” He has feeling, as human beings do, but not through understanding in the manner of someone who understands: that person’s feeling comes from the prior concealment and opposite state, and now he understands, and from this comes feeling. This does not apply at all to the Holy One, blessed be He, but only to separate beings. With Him everything is in unity and essential being. Therefore His understanding is not through understanding, nor in the manner of human feeling through the understanding of the heart. Thus far is the substance of what I heard, with added explanation and elaboration as it appeared to me.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל "חַכִּים וְלֹא בְּחָכְמָה יְדוּעָה", דְּמַלְאָכִים יֵשׁ לָהֶם חָכְמָה (וּפֵירוּשׁ: כֹּחַ הַשְּׁמִיעָה לְקוֹל דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים), מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּנֵי אָדָם;
connections.quote: “You are wise, but not with a known wisdom.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי בִּינָה וְהַרְגָּשָׁה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הוּא עוֹמֵד עַל הַפְּרָטִים שֶׁבְּדִבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, כָּל אֶחָד לְפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ, וְאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחֲלוּקִים בִּפְרָטִים בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
connections.quote: “In every new Torah teaching, a matter cannot be so fully determined that there is no inclination in either direction, as it says (Ḥagigah 3b): “These declare impure,” and so forth; and “these and those are the words of the living God” (Eruvin 13b). Elohim means the Possessor of all the distinct powers in the world, and therefore it is a plural expression. “Living,” too, is plural, for words of Torah are the life of the whole creation, and life has different divisions. Of this it is said: “Like streams of water, a king’s heart is in the hand,” and so forth. Who are the kings? The rabbis (Gittin 62a); and water means Torah (Bava Kamma 17a). They divide into different springs, to prohibit and to permit. We think that this depends upon the sage’s own mind, but it is not so: this too is in the hand of the Lord, who illuminates his eyes and inclines his heart solely according to the divine desire and will.”

connections.hePhrase: וְדָבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ לְיִרְאָה, כִּי פֵּירוּשׁ "מַלְאָכִים" – כָּל מִינֵי כֹּחוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם בִּהְיוֹתָם מוּפְשָׁטִים מִלְּבוּשׁ הַחָמְרִי שֶׁבְּעוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה, רַק בִּהְיוֹתָם בְּמַדְרֵגַת בְּרִיאָה וִיצִירָה, דְּהַיְינוּ רוּחָנִיּוּת אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ מִבְּלִי הַרְכָּבָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ כֹּחַ הַבְּחִירָה, וְכָל מִינֵי כֹּחוֹת כְּלוּלִים בָּאָדָם.
connections.quote: “The truth of the matter is that an angel is the power within each thing: the power that strikes is the angel appointed over striking, and the power that saves is the angel appointed over saving. Every spiritual power created at the creation of the world to serve in the world is what is called an angel—that is, a power sent by God.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּמֵאוֹתָן קוֹלוֹת הוּא הַבַּת קוֹל שֶׁיּוֹצֵא בְּכָל יוֹם מֵהַר חוֹרֵב: אוֹי לַבְּרִיּוֹת מֵעֶלְבּוֹנָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Every single day a heavenly voice goes forth from Mount Horeb, proclaiming and saying: Woe to the creatures for the insult to the Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר דְּבַת קוֹל הוּא אֲחוֹרַיִים שֶׁל קוֹל וְקָלָא דְּהָדְרָא, דְּמִתּוֹךְ שֶׁאוֹתָן קוֹלוֹת דְּקַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה נִשְׁמָעִין לְהַשּׁוֹמְעִים, הַקָּלָא דְּהָדְרָא מֵאוֹתָן הַשּׁוֹמְעִים הוּא "אוֹי וְכוּלֵי" לְשֶׁאֵין שׁוֹמְעִין,
connections.quote: “The phenomenon of a reverberating sound is what our Sages call a “bat kol,” a daughter of a voice. The Midrash, at the end of Shemot Rabbah, chapter 29, says: A person’s voice has an echo. See Tosafot in the first chapter of Sanhedrin, 11a, concerning the statement that when the last prophets died, prophecy departed, yet they still made use of a heavenly voice. Tosafot explains that a bat kol is a reverberation of the voice of God; see there.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִשְׁמָע לְכָל אֶחָד הַמְקוֹרָב לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אֹזֶן שֹׁמַעַת תּוֹכַחַת חַיִּים בְּקֶרֶב חֲכָמִים תָּלִין" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, לא)].
connections.quote: ‘An ear that listens to life-giving rebuke will dwell among the wise.’

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּאָמַר גַּם עַל הַשִּׁכְחָה "וְהָיָה", שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן שִׂמְחָה כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה מב),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman came and made a distinction: Wherever vayhi is said, it serves for distress; vehayah, for joy.”
connections.context: The Midrash discusses and tests this distinction through many examples. Rav Tzadok invokes the particular reading of vehayah as joy, applying it to eventual repair of a condition that is presently harmful.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הֲגַם דִּבְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא מוֹשֵׁךְ חֲטָאִים וְנֶעֱנָשִׁים עַל זֶה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם בֶּאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ מִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ שִׂמְחָה גְּדוֹלָה לֶעָתִיד כְּשֶׁיְּתוּקַּן הַכֹּל, אָז יְבוֹרַר זֶה:
connections.quote: “For this purpose God created the evil inclination, as they said, “I created the evil inclination; I created Torah as its remedy”: so that there would be a power of concealment through which renewal would become recognizable. This is the sense of “And it shall be, if you indeed forget,” where “and it shall be” signifies joy everywhere, as our Sages said in Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 42. For through this comes the intensity of joy when remembrance awakens out of forgetfulness. This is like the familiar parable of a king’s son returning to the king from the land of his captivity—even when he is not actually in a land of captivity, but merely lives in another city, or even in another house, or even in another room. For constant pleasure is no pleasure. Likewise, our Sages, Niddah 31b, explain the reason for the days of menstrual separation: to make her beloved to her husband.”

connections.hePhrase: [רכב] הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קוֹרֵא לָאָדָם בְּכָל יוֹם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "יַעַן קָרָאתִי וַתְּמָאֵנוּ, נָטִיתִי יָדִי [וְאֵין מַקְשִׁיב]" (מִשְׁלֵי א, כד).
connections.quote: ‘Because I called and you refused, I stretched out my hand and no one paid attention…’

connections.hePhrase: הַקְּרִיאָה הוּא הִרְהוּרֵי הַלֵּב הַבָּאִים מֵעַצְמָן בִּתְשׁוּקָה לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי קְרִיאַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לוֹ, כְּ"מַיִם הַפָּנִים [לַפָּנִים]" וְכוּלֵי.
connections.quote: “As in water face answers to face, so the heart of man to man.”

connections.hePhrase: וּנְטִיַּת הַיָּד הוּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא יְמִינוֹ (בְּרָכוֹת ו.), אוֹ לְעַם הָאָרֶץ עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלִּין שֶׁהוּא שְׂמֹאלוֹ.
connections.quote: ‘‘By His right hand’—this is Torah, as it says: ‘From His right hand came a fiery law for them.’ ‘And by His mighty arm’—these are tefillin, as it says: ‘Hashem will give strength to His people.’ From where do we know that tefillin are strength for Israel? It is written: ‘All the peoples of the earth will see that Hashem’s name is called upon you, and they will fear you.’ It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says: These are the tefillin worn on the head.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ צְלוֹתָא דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנִּקְרָא "עֲמִידָה" לְבַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק תְּפִלַּת הַשַּׁחַר (בְּרָכוֹת כו:) עַל פָּסוּק "אֶל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר עָמַד שָׁם" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יט, כז) – מִשָּׁם נִלְמַד תְּפִלַּת שַׁחֲרִית.
connections.quote: “A baraita supports Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina, and a baraita supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. The baraita supporting Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina teaches: Abraham instituted the morning prayer, as it is said, ‘Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood.’ ‘Standing’ here means prayer, as it is said, ‘Pinchas stood and prayed.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ צְלוֹתָא דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנִּקְרָא "עֲמִידָה" לְבַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק תְּפִלַּת הַשַּׁחַר (בְּרָכוֹת כו:) עַל פָּסוּק "אֶל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר עָמַד שָׁם" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יט, כז) – מִשָּׁם נִלְמַד תְּפִלַּת שַׁחֲרִית.
connections.quote: ‘Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before Hashem.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בַּבֹּקֶר כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מִתְעוֹרֵר מִשְּׁנָתוֹ, אָז צָרִיךְ הוּא הַתְּשׁוּקָה בָּאָדָם מַה לַּעֲשׂוֹת בְּיוֹם זֶה דָּבָר שֶׁחָפֵץ, וְצָרִיךְ לְיַחֵד כָּל חֲשָׁקוֹתָיו וְתַאֲווֹתָיו לְאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ – מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – וִיקַוֶּוה לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי יַשְׁפִּיעַ אֵלָיו שִׁפְעוֹ;
connections.quote: “Afterward it is written, “Journeying onward toward the south.” Abraham our father’s level was love, and his attribute was kindness. All his work was to refine his love so that it would be pure, directed to God alone, with no worldly desire entering his heart. This is what “Journeying onward toward the south” means, in the manner of their exposition in Temurah 16a: “‘For you have given me a dry land’—a house dried of all goodness.” This is Abraham’s level: he refined his attribute, kindness, so that it would be pure for God, with no worldly desire mixed into it. Concerning Isaac, whose attribute was “the fear of Isaac” and restraint, it is written, “He was dwelling in the land of the south.” He was at ease with this attribute, having become refined in the attribute of restraint, fear, and awe.”

connections.hePhrase: אָז בָּא לְמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בֶּאֱמֶת וֶאֱמוּנָה, שֶׁמִּתְחַזֵּק בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁוַּדַּאי יוֹשִׁיעַ וְהַכֹּל לְטוֹבָה, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָאֱמֶת הַגָּמוּר.
connections.quote: “Although Hashem knew that his prayer would not save Sodom, since even ten righteous people would not be found there, his prayer nevertheless availed to save Lot.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik discusses the very morning prayer at the place of Avraham's earlier standing. It points out that the prayer's result was not exhausted by the failure to save Sodom: it rescued Lot, from whom David's root of prayer would emerge. The example gives substance to continued prayer when the visible outcome remains dark. It illustrates a real effect without identifying that partial result with the complete salvation for which this siman continues to ask.
connections.headline: An effect of prayer may emerge through another path

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא חִבּוּר שְׁתֵּי מִדּוֹת דְּאַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, דְּהַיְינוּ הַיִּרְאָה בַּהֹוֶה וְהַבְּטִיחוּת וְהַשִּׂמְחָה בֶּעָתִיד, וּתְפִלָּתוֹ אָז נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן "פְּגִיעָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, יא; בְּרָכוֹת כו:).
connections.quote: ‘He came upon the place and spent the night there because the sun had set. He took some of the stones of the place and put them at his head, and he lay down in that place.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא חִבּוּר שְׁתֵּי מִדּוֹת דְּאַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, דְּהַיְינוּ הַיִּרְאָה בַּהֹוֶה וְהַבְּטִיחוּת וְהַשִּׂמְחָה בֶּעָתִיד, וּתְפִלָּתוֹ אָז נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן "פְּגִיעָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, יא; בְּרָכוֹת כו:).
connections.quote: “Jacob instituted the evening prayer, as it says, “He encountered the place and lodged there.” “Encounter” means prayer, as it says, “Do not pray for this people, do not raise a cry or prayer for them, and do not entreat Me.””
connections.context: The passage interprets Jacob’s vayifga as prayer. This is the source for the term pegiah used here, following Rav Tzadok’s description of Jacob as joining the qualities of Abraham and Isaac.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא חִבּוּר שְׁתֵּי מִדּוֹת דְּאַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, דְּהַיְינוּ הַיִּרְאָה בַּהֹוֶה וְהַבְּטִיחוּת וְהַשִּׂמְחָה בֶּעָתִיד, וּתְפִלָּתוֹ אָז נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן "פְּגִיעָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, יא; בְּרָכוֹת כו:).
connections.quote: “The patriarchs established the prayers, as the Gemara and Midrash Rabbah say. Abraham established the morning prayer, as it is said, “To the place where he had stood,” and standing means prayer. His prayer is in the morning, in the light of day, alluding to the absence of any darkness before him in the light of God’s holiness; he was as one actually standing before the King. Likewise Isaac established the afternoon prayer, which is also still in daytime. They learned this from “Isaac went out to converse in the field,” and conversation means prayer. For him too, the light of God’s holiness was clear, and he poured out his conversation before Him, as one tells the King his situation and speaks before Him all that is in his heart. Jacob our father, however, saw that he was the purpose of creation in the world and the root of the entire divine chariot. This was when he heard the angels calling him “sun”: “The sun has come.” His name was like that of the Holy One, blessed be He, who is called sun, as it says, “For the Lord God is a sun and shield,” as Sotah 10a says. Likewise, Megillah 18a says that the Holy One, blessed be He, called Jacob “El”: “He called Jacob El.” Thus he too is called sun, illuminating the holy moon so that it will shine even in the darkness of night. Therefore he lodged there and established the evening prayer, as they expounded from “He encountered the place.” That is, even when a person is in darkness and cannot see the light of His holiness because of the great darkness surrounding him, repentance and prayer can still help him merit seeing light out of darkness. This is “He encountered the place,” for encounter signifies actual attachment, as the word itself indicates. Through attaching himself to the Holy One, blessed be He, he becomes, as it were, the very light of the Holy One. This is “He lodged there”: he established the evening prayer to illuminate the moon, “for the sun had come,” for the angels called him sun, saying, “The sun has come,” as the Midrash concludes, “Who revealed to him that my name is sun?” This is also what it says afterward, “They said: We are from Charan,” which Midrash Rabbah, chapter 70, expounds: We are fleeing from the wrath of the Holy One, blessed be He. “He said to them: Do you know Laban?” Midrash Rabbah says: Do you know the One who will whiten your sins like snow? That is, it is possible to remove the darkness and merit a great light.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל לְשׁוֹן "מַפְגִּיעַ בִּתְפִלּוֹת", וּ"מַפְגִּיעַ אֵין בְּיָדֵינוּ", וּבְפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּתַעֲנִית (ח.) עַל פָּסוּק "וַיְצַו עָלָיו כִּמְפַגִּיעַ" (אִיּוֹב לו, לב), דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּמוֹ פָּגַע, שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב וְלָלֶכֶת מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשׁוּם אֹפֶן רַק שֶׁיַּעֲנֵהוּ, וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּאוֹחֵז בִּבְגָדוֹ וְאוֹמֵר: אֵינִי מַנִּיחֲךָ.

connections.quote: “Mighty Redeemer, redeem us for Your sake; see that our strength is gone; behold that our pious ones are lost, and there is none to intercede (mafgia) for us.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל לְשׁוֹן "מַפְגִּיעַ בִּתְפִלּוֹת", וּ"מַפְגִּיעַ אֵין בְּיָדֵינוּ", וּבְפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּתַעֲנִית (ח.) עַל פָּסוּק "וַיְצַו עָלָיו כִּמְפַגִּיעַ" (אִיּוֹב לו, לב), דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּמוֹ פָּגַע, שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב וְלָלֶכֶת מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשׁוּם אֹפֶן רַק שֶׁיַּעֲנֵהוּ, וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּאוֹחֵז בִּבְגָדוֹ וְאוֹמֵר: אֵינִי מַנִּיחֲךָ.
connections.quote: ‘If he whispered a prayer and was not answered, what remedy is available to him? Let him go to a pious person of the generation, who should pray at length on his behalf, as it says: ‘He commands it through an intercessor.’ Intercession means prayer, as it says: ‘As for you, do not pray for this people; do not raise a cry or prayer for them, and do not entreat Me.’’
