In the seventh he shall go free without payment’: they went free from all four exiles.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim reads ‘in the seventh he shall go free’ through the same inner point that cannot be enslaved. It distinguishes that point from the outward concealment in which servitude appears. This develops the siman's seventh-day and seventh-year correspondence; the source's Pesach setting is preserved rather than being presented as an identical account of every detail of Shabbat.
connections.headline: The seventh and the inward point of freedom

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא שְׁבִיעִית, שֶׁהוּא הַמֶּרְכָּז מֵהָעֲגֻלָּה,
connections.quote: “The number seven signifies the level at which the physical and the nonphysical are joined. It is known that seven corresponds to the six extremities and the center, which is called the “Holy Palace” among them. This is known to those who understand: seven corresponds to the six extremities and the Holy Palace among them. The six extremities are especially related to the physical, for they possess extension, and extension belongs to a body. The center, however, has no extension at all, for extension does not apply to the center; it is therefore related to the nonphysical. This is why they called the center the “Holy Palace” within the six extremities: it is separate from the physical, and this is its holiness.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא שְׁבִיעִית, שֶׁהוּא הַמֶּרְכָּז מֵהָעֲגֻלָּה,
connections.quote: “The seven double letters—bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, pe, resh, and tav—correspond to seven extremities. Six of them are the extremities above and below, east and west, north and south; the Holy Palace is aligned in the center and sustains them all.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי מְכִירַת פֵּירוֹת שְׁבִיעִית כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִידּוּשִׁין (כ.),
connections.quote: “If a person trades in produce of the Sabbatical year, he will eventually sell his movable possessions, as it says, “In this Jubilee year each of you shall return to his holding,” and next to it, “When you sell something to your fellow or buy from your fellow’s hand”—something acquired from hand to hand.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי מְכִירַת פֵּירוֹת שְׁבִיעִית כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִידּוּשִׁין (כ.),
connections.quote: “He does not come to his senses until he borrows at interest, as it says, “If your brother becomes poor and his hand falters beside you,” and next to it, “Do not take from him interest.” He does not come to his senses until he sells himself, as it says, “If your brother becomes poor beside you and is sold to you.””
connections.context: The Talmud traces a progression of losses from trading in Sabbatical produce to selling oneself into servitude. The intervening stages include selling land, a house, and a daughter. The endpoint is necessary for Rav Tzadok’s explanation of how the Hebrew servant comes to his condition.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (שָׁם): "הַקּוֹנֶה עֶבֶד עִבְרִי כְּקוֹנֶה אָדוֹן לְעַצְמוֹ",
connections.quote: “It was taught: “For it is good for him with you”—with you in food and with you in drink. You must not eat fine bread while he eats coarse bread, drink old wine while he drinks new wine, or sleep on soft bedding while he sleeps on straw. From here they said: Whoever acquires a Hebrew servant is as though he acquires a master for himself.”
connections.context: The saying follows the master’s obligation to provide comparable food, drink, and lodging. This context explains why Rav Tzadok calls the servant’s redemption and support a divine gift rather than unrestricted domination by the purchaser.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא עג:):
connections.quote: ‘Rav Se’oram, Rava’s brother, would compel unworthy men and press them into service for Rava’s carriage. Rava said to him: ‘You are acting properly, for we learned: If you see that someone does not behave properly, from where do we know that you may make him serve you? Scripture says: ‘You shall make them serve forever, and your brothers.’ Could this apply even to someone who behaves properly? Scripture says: ‘But over your brothers, the children of Israel, one over his brother,’ and so forth.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה:) עַל "וְאָסַפְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר":
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says: Can a person plow in the plowing season, sow in the sowing season, reap at harvest time, thresh at threshing time, and winnow when the wind blows? What will become of the Torah? Rather, when Israel do the will of the Omnipresent, their work is done by others, as it is said, ‘Strangers shall stand and tend your flocks,’ and so on. When Israel do not do the will of the Omnipresent, they must do their work themselves, as it is said, ‘You shall gather your grain.’ Not only that: they also have to do the work of others, as it is said, ‘You shall serve your enemy,’ and so on.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְרָרְשׁוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): "הָא לִדְבַר אֱמֶת כָּל מְשָׁרְתָיו וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘You cannot suppose this, for it says: ‘When a ruler listens to falsehood, all his attendants are wicked.’ It follows that when he listens to truth, his attendants are righteous.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן הוּא יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי נֶגֶד שֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 16:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 16:1
connections.quote: “Hashem established this order: according to the person's work and self-limitation from below to above through six levels, Hashem illuminates corresponding levels from above to below, until ‘in the seventh he goes free, without payment.’ Further constriction is no longer needed. The person had limited himself at the last point, where there are no eyes and the world appears merely to follow its course, and introduced eyes there to recognize the governance of Heaven. Correspondingly, Hashem shows that this last and lowest point is the chief purpose and original intention of His will. This illumination is called ‘in the seventh he goes free, without payment.’”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same verse about the Hebrew servant's release. The movement through six stages culminates in recognizing divine kingship precisely where it had seemed absent. This explains the present siman's use of the seventh point as a return to freedom and Torah. The source's discussion of optional matzah after the first night is an analogy for that freedom; it does not make Shabbat observance optional.
connections.headline: The last point can disclose the purpose of the whole work

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "תִּתְעַנַּג עַל ה'" (יְשַׁעְיָה נח, יד).
connections.quote: “Then you shall delight in the Lord; I shall make you ride upon the heights of the earth and feed you the inheritance of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”
connections.context: The context is honoring Shabbat. Rav Tzadok needs the explicit promise of delight, which is concealed by a translation such as “seek the Lord’s favor.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְדִבְּרוֹת רִאשׁוֹנוֹת נֶאֱמַר "זָכוֹר",
connections.quote: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”

connections.hePhrase: וְדִבְּרוֹת אַחֲרוֹנוֹת שֶׁאַחַר הַחֵטְא נֶאֱמַר "שָׁמוֹר",
connections.quote: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Hashem your God commanded you.”

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם בְּדִבּוּר אֶחָד נֶאֶמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כז.),
connections.quote: “Was it not taught: “Remember” and “Guard” were said in a single utterance—something the mouth cannot speak and the ear cannot hear?”
connections.context: These are the two formulations of the Shabbat commandment in Exodus 20:8 and Deuteronomy 5:12. Their unity in a single divine utterance is the detail Rav Tzadok invokes. Shabbat is the fourth of the Ten Commandments in the traditional Jewish enumeration.

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם בְּדִבּוּר אֶחָד נֶאֶמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כז.),
connections.quote: “The explanation is that in the first tablets it is written, “Remember.” The Zohar describes a place where there is no forgetting and forgetting does not abide. As the Midrash says, when Israel heard “I am,” Torah study became fixed in their hearts, and when they heard “You shall have no other,” the evil inclination was uprooted from their hearts. It was enough to remember verbally at the beginning of Shabbat, and throughout Shabbat one would be guarded by the holiness of Shabbat, which is fixed and established by the blessed God. In the second tablets, after the damage, it is written, “Guard”: guarding is required all day so that one does not cause damage, God forbid. As the Midrash on Psalms says: “What was created on the seventh day? Shabbat,” and so forth; “He found it entirely holiness and rest,” and so forth. “Afterward He saw that a person sins on it and incurs guilt against his life, and said, ‘This too is vanity.’” Since Scripture speaks of “those who desecrate it,” the evil inclination can enter and cause someone to desecrate Shabbat, God forbid. “Guard” is therefore required through awe, which involves human effort.”

connections.hePhrase: [רלח] הַשֵּׁינָה גַּם הִיא טוֹבָה לַחֲזוֹר וּלְהִתְעוֹרֵר
connections.quote: “During sleep, it is possible for the soul to be exchanged, for our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded in Shocher Tov (Psalm 25) on the verse 'They are new every morning, etc.,' that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not exchange souls, inferring from this that an exchange is indeed possible, only that the Holy One, blessed be He, is trustworthy and does not switch deposits entrusted to Him. This applies to one who commits his soul into the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, saying 'Into Your hand I commit, etc.,' but for one who regards everything as chance and nature running its course, it can be exchanged. And they taught (Berakhot 57b): 'Sleep is one-sixtieth of death,' just as after death we maintain (Chagigah 15a): 'If a righteous person merits, he receives his portion and the portion of his peer in Gan Eden; if a wicked person is found guilty, etc.,' so too can it happen during sleep that an exchange occurs where the spark of goodness in the soul of the wicked is transferred to another who merits it, while the wicked person absorbs the evil in his counterpart. Concerning this they described the ways of the wicked who would arise early in the morning to pursue evil, etc., whereas conversely it is stated (Berakhot 16b): 'May we awaken and find the yearning of our heart directed toward You, etc.' And this explains what they stated (Sanhedrin 71b): 'Sleep for the wicked is beneficial for them in their way, and beneficial for the world.' The reverse is true for the righteous, for even though he absorbs that good, it is nonetheless deeply entwined with much evil from its original source and requires refinement and rectification; hence it is detrimental for them and detrimental for the world, since he absorbs that good from the creatures of the world during sleep. The remedy for both is the Bedtime Shema and one verse of divine mercy, 'Into Your hand I commit, etc.' (Berakhot 5a), for no evil emanates from Before Him, blessed be He, to any creature in the world, and therefore all will be for the good.”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla uses the same Midrash about Hashem faithfully returning the soul and the same prayer to awaken with a heart turned toward Him. It places the night within an act of entrusting oneself to Hashem. This helps explain the siman’s “finding” a new heart: the beginning is received as help, and is then a basis for renewed effort rather than a claim to permanent attainment.
connections.headline: Entrusting the night and receiving a renewed morning

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים רֵישׁ מִזְמוֹר כה):
connections.quote: “Rabbi Alexandri said: A human receives new things in trust and returns them worn and frayed. The Holy One, blessed be He, receives them worn and frayed and returns them new. A worker labors all day, and his soul becomes tired and worn. When he sleeps, he entrusts his soul to the Holy One; in the morning it returns to his body as a new creation, as it says, “New every morning; great is Your faithfulness.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains sleep as the return of a tired soul renewed. That is the source for Rav Tzadok’s account of recovering from confused thoughts and beginning again; the former note quoted an unrelated verse of Psalm 25.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה הוּא הַבַּקָּשָׁה דִּבְרָכוֹת (טז:):
connections.quote: ‘After Rabbi Elazar finished his prayer, he would say: ‘May it be Your will, Hashem our God, to make love, brotherhood, peace, and friendship dwell in our lot. Increase our territory with students, and let our end prosper with a future and hope. Set our portion in Gan Eden, and equip us with a good companion and a good inclination in Your world. May we rise early and find our hearts’ yearning directed toward fearing Your name, and may the contentment of our souls come before You for good.’’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה תִּקְּנוּ נְטִילַת יָדַיִם שַׁחֲרִית וּבִרְכַּת אֱלֹהַי נְשָׁמָה כַּמּוּבָא בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף.
connections.quote: “If you ask: Why is the morning prayer different from the afternoon and evening prayers? It may be answered: Because in the morning we become like a new creation, as it is written, “New every morning; great is Your faithfulness.” We must thank Him, blessed be He, for creating us for His glory, to serve Him and bless His name. For this reason they instituted in the morning all those blessings that we recite each and every morning. We must therefore sanctify ourselves with His holiness and wash our hands from a vessel, like a priest who sanctifies his hands from the basin before his service. This concludes his words.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: "הַמְחַדֵּשׁ בְּכָל יוֹם תָּמִיד מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית",
connections.displayRef: Siddur, weekday Shacharit, blessing Yotzer Or
connections.linkedRef: Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Blessings of the Shema, First Blessing before Shema 8
connections.canonicalRef: Siddur Ashkenaz, Weekday, Shacharit, Blessings of the Shema, First Blessing before Shema 8
connections.heRef: סידור אשכנז, ימי חול, תפילת שחרית, ברכות קריאת שמע, יוצר אור ח׳
connections.quote: “For He alone performs mighty deeds and makes new things … who in His goodness renews each day, continually, the work of Creation.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם (מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין עא:) "שֵׁינָה לִרְשָׁעִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘Wine and sleep for the wicked are a benefit to them and a benefit to the world; for the righteous, they are harmful to them and harmful to the world.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה אָמַר דְּזֶהוּ רַק בִּשְׁינַת הַיּוֹם, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Recitation of the Shema Before Retiring 1:3
connections.linkedRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Recitation of the Shema Before Retiring 1:3
connections.canonicalRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Recitation of the Shema Before Retiring 1:3
connections.heRef: פרי עץ חיים, שער קריאת שמע שעל המיטה א׳:ג׳
connections.quote: “Sleep during the day is harmful for the righteous and beneficial for the wicked. This is what our Sages said: “Sleep for the wicked is beneficial to them and beneficial to the world.” The explanation is that, through his deeds, a righteous person may receive the souls of the righteous in ibbur when he sleeps at night. His soul returns to him and draws with it the souls of the righteous to assist him. When he sleeps during the day, those souls return and separate from him. In particular, at night a person deposits his soul in the care of Malkhut, and it returns pure, clear, and complete. During the day, however, the soul finds no resting place in which to be deposited, and therefore loses what it received at night. With the wicked, the opposite occurs: at night they are not taken into safekeeping beneath the wings of the Shekhinah, and their souls wander through the world and draw out souls of the wicked, which come with them in ibbur. If they sleep during the day, it is possible that, through a good deed those wicked people performed that day, these souls will separate from them when they sleep. Thus there are righteous people to whom the lot of the wicked comes, and wicked people to whom the lot of the righteous comes. However, for a person of great standing, like the earlier sages, it is possible that even if he sleeps during the day, he will gain as he does at night.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כָּרִמּוֹן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סוֹף חֲגִיגָה)
connections.quote: ‘Reish Lakish said: The fire of Gehinnom has no power over the transgressors of Israel, as may be inferred from the golden altar. The golden altar had only a coating as thick as a gold dinar, yet for so many years the fire had no power over it. How much more so the transgressors of Israel, who are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate! For it is written: ‘Your temple (rakkatekh) is like a slice of pomegranate.’ Do not read ‘rakkatekh,’ but ‘the empty ones among you’—all the more so.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמְלֵאִים חֲרָטָה בַּלֵּב גַּם כֵּן.
connections.quote: “For the wicked person’s corrupt thoughts sadden their owner’s soul and continually cause it pain, because it was hewn from an exalted place. Even though it consents to evil deeds, it becomes distressed after doing them or when contemplating them. The philosopher wrote this in chapter five of the ninth book of the Ethics: “The wicked are full of regrets,” and so forth. They also tend to be continually distressed by fear of the punishments that will overtake them, as the wise man said: “What the wicked person fears will come upon him,” as explained in the discussion of Shemini, gate sixty.”

connections.hePhrase: הַגַּם דְּהַדּוֹרוֹת מִתְקַטְּנִים כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: “As is known, whenever one person has experienced the clear illumination of a matter in its fullness, the gate of that light has already been opened in the world. It remains open afterward to everyone. This is the whole purpose of the succession of generations established by the blessed God, even though they become progressively smaller. For all the lights opened in each generation by outstanding individuals among the sages of Israel are never closed again. They remain open forever and become established teachings for all Israel. Therefore, although the later generations are smaller, they nevertheless possess the advantage of a dwarf upon a giant: all the gates opened by earlier generations already stand open before them, and they continue to bring forth new teaching and open other gates. Although they are very small, they nevertheless reach deeper places, for their souls have already passed through the gate that was opened for the earlier generations.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְוַדַּאי גַּם כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּלְּמוּ, קְדוּשָּׁתָם כְּבָר גְּלוּיָה בָּעוֹלָם,
connections.quote: “For every generation that passes, its Torah and commandments remain and become fixed in the hearts of the children of Israel in the next generation. Were it otherwise, what purpose would the length of the exile serve, while the generations grow ever smaller? Where would there be hope of meriting the coming of the Messiah, speedily in our days, when the earlier generations, greater and better than these, did not merit it? Although the generations themselves grow smaller and are called the “footsteps of the Messiah,” because their souls are from the heels, nevertheless all the merits of all the earlier generations, and all the Torah and commandments they acquired in this world, remain fixed and firmly planted in the depths of the hearts of the last generation. From this perspective, each later generation possesses an advantage of preparedness and standing. The familiar comparison made concerning wisdom—a dwarf atop a giant—also applies to service, Torah, and commandments. From this perspective the generations continually ascend from level to level, through the additional merits and attainments renewed in every generation, which remain forever. Sins and deficiencies, however, are cleansed by death; they gradually pass away, and nothing of them remains. Only the good remains and becomes fixed in all hearts.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם: "מֹשֵׁל מַקְשִׁיב עַל דְּבַר אֱמֶת, כָּל מְשָׁרְתָיו צַדִּיקִים" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ חֻלִּין ד:).
connections.quote: “A ruler who listens to a false word—all his servants are wicked.”
connections.context: The positive wording in Rav Tzadok, a ruler listening to truth and righteous servants, is the inference made in Chullin 4b, quoted in the following note. It is not the literal wording of this verse.

connections.hePhrase: דְּ"מָצָא מִין אֶת מִינוֹ וְנִיעוֹר" (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה עג.),
connections.quote: ‘When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came, he reported that Rabbi Yochanan said: They taught this only when a jug of water fell in first. But if a jug of water did not fall in first, one kind has found its own kind and is reawakened.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּ"מָצָא מִין אֶת מִינוֹ וְנִיעוֹר" (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה עג.),
connections.quote: “What helps one attain this quality (holiness) is solitude and extensive withdrawal, so that, in the absence of distractions, one’s soul can strengthen itself more fully and cleave to the Creator. What damages this quality is a lack of true knowledge and excessive association with people, for materiality finds its own kind, awakens, and gains strength. The soul then remains trapped within it and cannot leave its imprisonment.”

connections.hePhrase: יַשְׁכִּים וְיִמְצָא עַצְמוֹ בְּרַע בֶּאֱמֶת,
connections.quote: ““Even a convert”: This means that he should say, “Who made me a convert,” for this is called making, as it is written, “The souls that they made in Haran.” (Darkhei Moshe.) Shelah and Bach wrote that it is inappropriate to say this, because becoming a convert resulted from his own choice to choose the religion of Israel. He should therefore not recite this blessing, but only the two concerning a slave and a woman. This concludes their words. According to their view, one must say that “Who did not make me a slave” refers to his original creation. Although at his original creation his status was inferior to that of a slave, nevertheless, if he had been a slave he could not have converted unless his master freed him. But according to what the kabbalists wrote, these blessings are recited concerning the soul’s departure at night—that the soul of a gentile or a slave did not attach itself to it. If so, a convert, too, can recite them in this form.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ וְכוּלֵי וְאַחַר כָּךְ נַעֲשָׂה וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת כט.)
connections.quote: “Does one not change? Have we not learned: Do not trust yourself until the day of your death, for Yochanan the High Priest served in the high priesthood for eighty years and finally became a Sadducee? Abaye said: Yannai and Yochanan are the same person. Rava said: Yannai is one and Yochanan is another; Yannai was wicked from the outset, while Yochanan was righteous from the outset. This is satisfactory according to Abaye, but difficult according to Rava.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ וְכוּלֵי וְאַחַר כָּךְ נַעֲשָׂה וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת כט.)
connections.quote: “Rava could answer you: Even one righteous from the outset may turn back.”
connections.context: The discussion acknowledges the possibility of a later fall even after many years of service. Abaye’s words identify Yannai and Yochanan; they do not state a general theory about the whole Hasmonean dynasty. Rava distinguishes the two and allows that someone initially righteous can change.

connections.hePhrase: עַל יְדֵי עִיבּוּר נִשְׁמַת רָשָׁע.
connections.displayRef: Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on the Falling on the Face Prayer 2:4
connections.linkedRef: Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on the Falling on the Face Prayer 2:4
connections.canonicalRef: Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on the Falling on the Face Prayer 2:4
connections.heRef: שער הכוונות, דרושי נפילת אפים ב׳:ד׳
connections.quote: “Through this you will understand a great mystery. We have observed a puzzling matter: sometimes a person is completely righteous and afterward becomes another person and turns completely wicked, as we find with Yochanan the High Priest, who served in the priesthood for eighty years and ultimately became a Sadducee. The explanation is that when a person surrenders his soul to death during the falling-on-the-face prayer, down to the place of the shell, some sin he has committed may prevent his soul from ascending from there. The shells seize it, and it remains there forever; they then give him another, evil soul from the side of the shells. This is what our Sages meant when they said that the wicked are called dead even during their lifetimes: during the falling-on-the-face prayer they descend to the place of death and remain there, their souls do not emerge, and an evil soul is given them in exchange. They do not perceive this within themselves, and then become completely wicked, may the Merciful One save us. Therefore I warn you very strongly about this: a person directing his intention during the falling-on-the-face prayer in the manner described must be completely righteous, or at least direct his intention throughout that prayer from beginning to end, as explained above.”

connections.hePhrase: אִם אֵינוֹ נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי כְּעִנְיַן "לִבִּי חָלָל",
connections.quote: see note 595 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Chalal can describe one pierced or slain. Rav Tzadok invokes the rabbinic reading of David’s slain heart as the removal of his evil inclination, hence a person’s complete inward cleansing. The ordinary image of a wounded heart alone does not convey that application.

connections.hePhrase: [רמ] הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין לַיֵּצֶר כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה,
connections.quote: “Solomon said that in Torah the counsel is: “Feed him bread,” and it will not harm you. When a person desires Torah in order to escape the evil inclination, the Torah will help for the good: “You are heaping coals upon his head.” The Torah will not give strength to the husk, God forbid.”
connections.explanation: The Kislev passage answers the difficulty implicit in the opening of this siman: how can Torah help someone whose heart is not yet clean? Its stated direction matters—the person wants Torah in order to escape the inclination. Torah then acts as the seasoning Rav Tzadok describes, making the existing power fit for good. Perfect purity is not a prerequisite for beginning this work; seeking Torah’s correction is part of the work itself.
connections.headline: A sincere turn to Torah can begin before the heart is fully purified

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים מט:):
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabbi says: An unlearned person may not eat meat (of an animal), as it says: ‘This is the Torah of the animal and the bird.’ Anyone who engages in Torah may eat the meat of animals and birds; anyone who does not engage in Torah may not eat the meat of animals and birds.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ מִטַּעַם הָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה מִצַּד הַנְּפָשׁוֹת הַמְּגוּלְגָּלוֹת.
connections.quote: “The matter of eating has thus been explained in its two aspects. The first is to repair and separate out the dross in that food, and the second is to repair the souls reincarnated in that food. A person must therefore exercise the greatest care while eating and not eat like cattle and other living creatures that do not distinguish good from evil. Our Sages accordingly spoke at length about this, saying that a table resembles an altar, because the altar accomplished these two things. They also said that the table atones for a person’s sins, and made many similar statements. Since some souls reincarnated because of the transgressions they committed may be present in that food—or even in the water one drinks—or even if no reincarnated soul is present and there are only the dross and shells within the food, which is the first aspect: if the person eating is righteous and a Torah scholar, not only will these not become mixed into his soul, but, on the contrary, he will repair them, separate the food from the waste, and repair those reincarnated souls, as will be explained. But if the person is wicked or unlearned, not only does he fail to repair them; through his deeds he may actually damage and spoil the souls reincarnated there, or that food, beyond their existing damage. There is a third possibility as well: they may instead overpower him, cause him to sin, and lead him along an evil path, until they bring his soul harm from which he cannot be healed. This is the mystery of those people upon whom a harsh and evil occurrence sometimes suddenly comes, who change their religion, God forbid, and leave the faith, as in the case of Yochanan the High Priest who became a Sadducee, and similar cases. Everything depends on the character of the reincarnated soul that became mixed with him—whether it was completely wicked or not. Know that an unlearned person does not repair any level at all, even a soul reincarnated in an animal. If he eats that animal’s meat, he cannot repair it, and certainly cannot repair what is reincarnated in a plant, and still less in the inanimate. For someone reincarnated in the inanimate must rise through three levels. Even if he rises through them together, as explained above—for example, when a person eats a little earth—he still requires a far greater repair than one who rises through only two levels, and greater power is needed to repair him. Likewise, one lacking only one level is repaired much more easily than one needing two levels. An unlearned person lacks the power to separate, repair, and raise even one level. It would follow that he should be forbidden even inanimate and plant food. However, because he is not to be penalized for failing to repair two or three levels together, he is permitted inanimate and plant food. Animal flesh, however, is forbidden to him, because he lacks the power to repair even one level, from animal to human.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֹחַ נוֹסָף עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשָׂיו אֵיזֶה דָּבָר טוֹב.
connections.quote: “Ibbur takes place during life, as explained above. That is, sometimes a person encounters a particular commandment and performs it properly. A soul of an earlier righteous person who performed that same commandment properly then becomes available to him. Since they resemble one another in this commandment, that righteous person’s soul enters him in ibbur. Moreover, it is also possible for this to happen while that righteous person is living at the same time as he is. When this person performs a commandment, or commandments related to that righteous person, which the righteous person also performed properly in the same way, that righteous person’s soul enters him in ibbur even while both are alive. This is the mystery of the verse, “David’s soul became attached to Jonathan”: while both were alive together, David’s soul entered Jonathan in ibbur.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ה דִּבְרָכוֹת סוֹף הֲלָכָה ב): "אִם אֵין דֵּעָה, הַבְדָּלָה מִנַּיִן?".
connections.quote: “This accords with Rabbi, for Rabbi said: I wonder how they omitted “Who grants knowledge” on Shabbat. If there is no knowledge, from where can prayer come? And here: If there is no knowledge, from where can distinction come?”
connections.context: The Jerusalem Talmud explains the relation between knowledge and havdalah, the discernment that distinguishes categories. The Mishnah states where havdalah is inserted; this discussion supplies the actual question quoted by Rav Tzadok.

connections.hePhrase: אִם לְטוֹבָה נוֹצָר בַּעַל חַי טָהוֹר, וּלְרַע – בַּעַל חַי טָמֵא.
connections.quote: “All a person’s possessions are portions of his vitality extending into created things, as it is written: “In the beginning”—for the sake of Israel, and so forth. We say that He continually renews the work of creation in His goodness every day, and each day the renewal is for Israel’s sake. Every part of the world belongs to a particular Israelite soul; that is, the light of its vitality sustains those creatures. Good deeds sustain good and pure creatures (while thoughts and desires produce angels and spiritual beings); evil deeds produce evil creatures (in the manner of the saying in Eruvin that the emission of seed in vain produces spirits, demons, and night spirits): harmful animals, and likewise murderous idolaters. Among inanimate things, this includes a stone used for stoning and wood on which someone was hanged (this is the mystery of the saying in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu that the Holy One, blessed be He, will exact payment from everything, even from a stone, and so forth. This is “Evil pursues sinners,” as well as “I created the destroyer to ruin,” and the teaching in Bereshit Rabbah that fire goes forth from the bodies of the wicked and burns them). Among growing things, it includes a deadly poison, may the Merciful One save us, and the like.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לב.): "מְלֵי כְּרֵיסֵיהּ זְנֵי בִּישֵׁי",
connections.quote: “Rav Acha son of Rav Huna said in Rav Sheshet’s name: This is what people say: A full belly brings evil kinds of conduct, as it says, “When they were pastured, they became full; they were full, and their heart grew haughty; therefore they forgot Me.” Rav Nachman said: It is derived from here: “Your heart grows haughty and you forget Hashem.” The Sages said: From here: “He will eat, be satisfied, grow fat, and turn aside.””
connections.context: The saying links satiety with the danger of pride and wrongdoing. It does not define the act of filling the stomach itself as a sin. Rav Tzadok uses this tendency in explaining the bodily source of the inclination.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַם הָאָרֶץ אָסוּר,
connections.quote: “In truth, concerning meat too we find: “There is no joy except with meat.” This means meriting straightness of heart, as it is said, “Joy for the upright of heart.” After the damage, meat is needed because there are more holy sparks to bring out from meat than from plants. Thus the Ari explains Rav Chisda’s statement in Shabbat: “In my wealth I did not eat vegetables, for I said: where vegetables would enter, let meat and fish enter.” God forbid that his meaning was to choose meat and fish for pleasure. Rather, “in my wealth” means when he became a Torah scholar and meat was permitted to him, since an unlearned person is forbidden to eat meat, as stated in Pesachim. He then did not eat vegetables because there are more holy sparks to bring out from animals than from plants; therefore he said, “Where vegetables would enter, let meat and fish enter.” This is the end of that explanation. This is also the meaning of their saying in Berakhot: “Every living thing restores the soul, and whatever is near the soul restores the soul”: it too means that there are more holy sparks in it.”
connections.explanation: Lech Lecha applies the same account of holy sparks to a particular sage’s conduct and expressly rejects pleasure as its intended explanation. This helps make the present siman’s transformation of animal vitality into human vitality intelligible. The physical nourishment is real, but its spiritual elevation depends on the Torah that directs the life it sustains. Merely choosing a richer food does not by itself establish the clarification described here.
connections.headline: Elevating a bodily power requires a purpose beyond its enjoyment

connections.hePhrase: וְעַם הָאָרֶץ אָסוּר,
connections.quote: “Raising all foods that come from plants is accomplished through faith in the blessed God alone, and through the blessing beforehand, by which one believes that “the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord.” Therefore “faith” refers to the order Zeraim, and tractate Berakhot was placed at its beginning. This is the order of raising all kinds of seeds to the blessed God through the fulfillment of their prescribed commandments and the blessing beforehand: the faith that everything belongs to the blessed God. This simple faith is fixed in the heart of every Israelite, as the Sages said in Shabbat that they are “believers, children of believers.” Such food was therefore permitted even to an unlearned person. Eating meat, however, is forbidden except to a Torah scholar. Tractate Chullin was therefore placed in the order Kodashim: it was permitted only to someone who eats ordinary food in the purity of holiness, whose table resembles an altar and whose meat is like an offering and sacred meat. This comes only through words of Torah, as it is written: “Since the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has only the four cubits of halakhah.” When one’s table becomes four cubits of halakhah, it resembles the Temple and altar, and what one eats resembles the priests’ eating: “When they receive their share, they receive it from the table of the Most High.” The fat and blood—that is, the principal vitality within the food and the person’s desire for it—have been raised to the blessed God through words of Torah, which are compared to fire, the fire of the altar’s arrangement. Through them one recognizes that the blessed God gives vitality to the food and gives the person desire and longing for this food to sustain his soul.”
connections.explanation: Et HaOchel supplies the liturgical and institutional structure for these two routes: faith and blessing at the beginning of Zeraim, and the Torah table as an altar in the account of Chullin and Kodashim. Its explicit inclusion of both the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire clarifies what must be directed toward holiness.
connections.headline: Torah’s wisdom can transform the power received from food

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר: "בְּחָכְמָה אִתְבְּרִירוּ",
connections.quote: “The essential refinement of the shattered vessels cannot take place if a person is attached to, desires, and delights in physical pleasure, God forbid. How could he separate out what is pure if he willingly desires the waste? Rather, refinement takes place through cleaving to the blessed God with love and awe, and bringing everything through awe to “nothing,” which is wisdom. This means understanding that physical pleasure is vanity and comes to be despised in his eyes. Of his own will he would not enjoy such physical pleasures as eating, drinking, and sexual relations, except because of the Creator’s commandment and because they also contain a spark of the Creator’s love and delight. Through this, the delight separates itself from the waste, and desire for the waste becomes repugnant to him through wisdom. It is like a wise person who is brought an inferior object—a coin or a garment—covered with a very fine color. A fool imagines that it is entirely good, but the wise person understands that only the color is good. This is what the Zohar says: “Everything is refined through wisdom.””

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר: "בְּחָכְמָה אִתְבְּרִירוּ",
connections.quote: “Come and see: At the head, the beginning of faith, within thought, the lamp of impenetrable darkness struck and rose within thought—another reading: and brought forth—sparks. It cast glimmering sparks (Vayikra 292b) in three hundred and twenty directions, separated dross from within thought, and was refined.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הַבַּעַל חַי יֵשׁ לוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סא.),
connections.quote: “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objected: If so, an animal, for which “He formed” is not written with the doubled letter, has no inclination? Yet we see that it injures, bites, and kicks!”
connections.context: The objection assumes that animals also have an inclination, as shown by their aggressive actions. This is the precise basis for Rav Tzadok’s statement about living creatures, distinct from the later comparison of the human inclination to a fly.

connections.hePhrase: וּבָזֶה "רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כֵּן מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כָּרִמּוֹן" (כִּמְאַמְרָם שָׁם נז.) בְּמַעֲשֶׂה,
connections.quote: “If he is an ignoramus, he should look forward to mitzvot, as it says, ‘Your temple (rakatekh) is like a slice of pomegranate.’ What is rakatekh? Even the empty ones (reikanin) among you are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate.”

connections.hePhrase: [רמא] הַמִּצְוֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים שֶׁל הָאָדָם,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 8:3
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 8:3
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of resurrection: a breath remains in the bones, as the Zohar teaches. It comes from the true Torah established within a person's body, each according to his own root, which he acquired through his labor, service and endurance. Through this power Hashem will awaken him to resurrection. Every good action, will and thought is stored and hidden with Hashem, and not the smallest part is lost. As the Zohar teaches, no good will is lost before the holy King; even the breath of the mouth has its particular place.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains the lasting trace of good service through the account of resurrection: the person rises with the Torah truly acquired through his own work. Its explicit statement that no good action, will or thought is lost gives depth to the siman's assertion that a deed generates a continuing spiritual power. This complements the present distinction between the influence of an angel and the felt contribution of a soul, without collapsing those two descriptions.
connections.headline: A good act leaves more than a passing moment

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מִכָּל מִצְוָה נִבְרָא מַלְאָךְ,
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:16
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:16
connections.quote: see note 140 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek explicitly defines the angel born from a mitzvah as the spiritual power of that human service. Its explanation of the angels' dependence on Israel's service clarifies the siman's account of an acquired power encouraging further good; it is more specific than simply repeating that one mitzvah leads to another.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, ק עַמּוּד ב; נט עַמּוּד א):
connections.quote: ‘These are the supernal powers of the holy, supernal King, and nothing is lost. Even the breath of the mouth has a place and a location, and the Holy One, blessed be He, makes from it what He makes. Even a person’s word, and even a sound, is not in vain; everything has its place and location.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִתְרַבִּים הַמַּלְאָכִים הַמַּזְכִּירִים לְמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ: "אַל דֳּמִי לָךְ".
connections.quote: “O God, do not keep silent; do not hold Your peace, and do not be still, O God.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ בְּטוֹבָה: דְּמַחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ קִידּוּשִׁין מ.).
connections.quote: “A good intention is joined to an action, as it is said: “Then those who feared the Lord spoke to one another … and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the Lord and think upon His name.” What does “think upon His name” mean? Rav Asi said: Even if someone intended to perform a mitzvah but was prevented and did not perform it, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it.”
connections.context: This is the positive intention that Rav Tzadok is discussing here. He explains that its spiritual effect can already be present in the heart, even when circumstances prevent the intended mitzvah from becoming an outward act.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם אֵשׁ זָרָה דְּנָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא
connections.quote: “Nadav and Avihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his fire pan, put fire in it and laid incense on it, and offered before Hashem a strange fire, which He had not commanded them.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "אֲנִי וְאַתָּה נַנְהִיג וְכוּלֵי" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין נב.).
connections.quote: ‘Once Moses and Aaron were walking along the road, with Nadav and Avihu walking behind them and all Israel behind them. Nadav said to Avihu: ‘When will these two old men die, so that you and I can lead the generation?’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: ‘We shall see who buries whom.’ Rav Pappa said: This is what people say: Many old camels carry the hides of young camels.’

connections.hePhrase: (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֵּאָה פֶּרֶק א סוֹף הֲלָכָה א),
connections.quote: “The Omnipresent joins a good intention to an action; He does not join an evil intention to an action. … “If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear.” This statement applies to Israel; concerning the nations the converse applies: the Holy One does not join a good intention, but He does join an evil intention. … “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob.” Did he actually kill him? Rather, this teaches that he planned to kill him, and Scripture credited it to him as though he had killed him.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok cites the Yerushalmi’s distinction while contrasting the roots and spiritual consequences of good and evil thought. The psalm quoted in the passage is Psalms 66:18; the former English excerpt incorrectly labeled it 66:12. The final example concerns Esau’s intention against Jacob.

connections.hePhrase: דְּהוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז.),
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: Satan, the evil inclination, and the angel of death are one and the same. He is Satan, as it is written, ‘Satan went out from Hashem’s presence.’ He is the evil inclination: there it is written, ‘Only evil all day,’ and here it is written, ‘Only do not stretch out your hand against him.’ He is the angel of death, as it is written, ‘But spare his life,’ showing that his life is in Satan’s power.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּ"חַרְבָּם תָּבוֹא בְלִבָּם".
connections.quote: ‘Their sword will enter their own heart, and their bows will be broken.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּיָדוּעַ דְּהוּא נֶגֶד מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:4
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:4
connections.quote: “Balaam stood at the head of this, as is known. Therefore the Sages of blessed memory said (Sifrei Deuteronomy 357): “But among the nations one did arise. Who was it? Balaam.” He was the counterpart of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him: just as Moses was the essence and source of all the Torah’s wisdom, so Balaam was the essence and source of all Egypt’s wisdom.”

connections.hePhrase: דִּלְמֶעְבַּד עַל חַרְשִׁין דִּילֵיהּ הוּא עַל יְדֵי הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote:
“We found in the book of Ashmedai, which he gave to King Solomon, that anyone who wished to perform powerful sorceries hidden from the eye, if he knew the rock where Balaam fell, would find there some of the serpents that came from that wicked man's bones. If he killed one of them, he could use its head to perform higher sorceries, its body for other sorceries, and its tail for other sorceries. Each one contains three kinds of sorcery.

When the Queen of Sheba came to Solomon, among the things she asked him was: “The bone of a serpent containing three kinds of sorcery—by what is it captured?” Immediately, “There was nothing hidden from the king that he did not explain to her.” She asked about this because she needed those serpents and could not take even one of them. What did he answer her? The things that were in her heart. Thus he made them known to her, as it is written: “Solomon told her all her matters.” No one in the entire world can overcome those serpents except by one secret thing. What is it? Hot semen.

If you ask who can do this: when a person emits that semen while filled with desire, he emits it in the name of that serpent, with the will of desire. When it comes out hot, they immediately receive it in a garment and throw that garment toward the serpent. At once it lowers its head, and they capture it as one captures a domestic chicken. If they attacked even one of them with all the weapons of war in the world, they could not overcome it. With this, however, a person needs neither weapons of war nor anything else, and need not guard against them, for they are all subdued before him. These things then became fixed in her heart, and she desired this.

From then on, Elazar my son, the Holy One, blessed be He, did what He did to that wicked man. These hidden secrets ought not to be revealed, but I have revealed them to you so that the companions here may know the hidden ways of the world. For there are many hidden laws in the world that people do not know, wondrous and concealed, great and exalted. Concerning him and those like him, we proclaim: “The name of the wicked will rot.” Happy are the truly righteous, of whom it is written: “Surely the righteous will give thanks to Your name,” and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי לֹא עִנָּה מִלִּבּוֹ כְּלָל.
connections.quote: “For He does not afflict from His heart, nor grieve the children of men.”
connections.context: The verse speaks of God; Rav Tzadok borrows its words for a person whose wrongdoing did not come from his heart.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעוֹקֵר הַדָּבָר לְמַפְרֵעַ,
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: If she went to a sage and he released her from her vow, she is betrothed. If she went to a physician and he healed her, she is not betrothed. What distinguishes a sage from a physician? A sage uproots the vow from its very beginning, whereas a physician heals only from now onward.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמֵאַהֲבָה – שֶׁנַּעֲשִׂין כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
connections.quote: “And in this exist two modes of victory: either subjugation (itkafya), like Elijah and Mashiach ben Yosef; or transformation (ithapcha), like Mashiach ben David, through whom all is whitened following the slaying of the impulse by Mashiach ben Yosef. And Saul, whose kingship was borrowed, not being his essential rung but David's, attempted to utilize borrowed spiritual tools; for his personal attribute as a consummate tzaddik without sin was suited strictly for subjugation (itkafya); while the attribute of King David, who raised the yoke of repentance, was suited for transformation (ithapcha); and likewise Mashiach ben David who will rectify the wicked of all generations, turning scarlet sins white as snow when the impulse is slaughtered and drained of its fiery redness, leaving pure lovingkindness for Israel, for "the desire of a man is his kindness" Proverbs 19:22. And Saul sought to elevate the attribute of holy Chesed, drawing desire to its holy source: dragging the impulse to the study hall (Kiddushin 30b) for the love of Torah; but through this he misapplied Chesed into unholy pity upon the cruel, sparing Agag I Samuel 15:9. And Saul stumbled in this single matter and lost his throne, proving kingship was only borrowed by him, for "the king by justice establishes the land" Proverbs 29:4. And King David was likewise ruddy, yet stern to execute justice upon those deserving it, "with beautiful eyes" acting solely with the sanction of the Sanhedrin, synthesizing both opposites, wielding the power of transformation (ithapcha).”
connections.explanation: Poked Akarim develops the distinction between subduing and transforming through Shaul and David. David’s capacity includes both opposites, while Shaul’s attempted kindness toward Agag illustrates the danger of placing a real power of kindness where it does not belong. This helps explain why transformation here is more demanding than removing restraints: the recovered power must be directed rightly, with the siman itself retaining a distinction between the prohibited act and the desire that can be returned to holiness.
connections.headline: Transformation includes discernment and restraint

connections.hePhrase: זֶהוּ ב' דַּרְגִּין דִּ"לְאִתְהַפְּכָא" וְ"לְאִכַּפְיָא".
connections.quote: “Overcoming the evil inclination takes two forms: subduing and transforming. Subduing means mastering one’s inclination and separating oneself entirely. Transforming means turning everything toward holiness. The transformative repair of Adam’s eating comes through eating in holiness: although a person eats, he does not eat for bodily enjoyment, as Adam did because the food was good and desirable and because of the inclination, but only for holiness. Thus it says, “A righteous person eats to satisfy his soul”: his eating is solely to sustain his soul. We find this with our holy Rabbi, who ate all the world’s delicacies and whose table was a royal table, yet said of himself that he had not taken pleasure even with his little finger. Hillel the Elder likewise said that he was going to perform kindness for a guest within his home, meaning himself. Transformation of this kind is a higher level than subduing, because he brings his inclination into complete holiness.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קלח א) דַּחֲמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא עַל יָדוֹ.
connections.quote: see note 1592 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This passage is in Midrash HaNe’elam, Zohar I 138a, whose paragraph numbering is distinct from the ordinary Zohar text on that folio. Rav Tzadok cites the positive energy within desire: its force can become delight in Torah when its sinful expression is removed.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִמְּךָ הַכֹּל, כִּי לְעוֹלָם לֹא זָזָה אַהֲבָתְךָ מֵעִמָּנוּ,
connections.quote: “But who am I, and who are my people, that we should have the strength to give so freely as this? For all things come from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, ריד ב)
connections.quote: “These words apply when he has not undertaken complete repentance—a repentance fit to cover all his deeds. Even so, it is better for him not to enter a coffin, for as long as the body endures, the soul is judged and does not enter its place, except for those supreme holy pious ones who are worthy to ascend with their bodies. Happy is their portion in this world and in the world to come.”
connections.context: Zohar II 214b has just described the judgment of one who damaged the covenant. This paragraph expressly qualifies that warning by making room for complete repentance. Rav Tzadok cites that qualification and explains the depth of repentance needed to transform the desire involved. “Coffin” here is the burial context of the Aramaic arona.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָז עוֹנַת תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים (כְּתוּבּוֹת סב:),
connections.quote: ‘When is the marital obligation of Torah scholars? Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel: From one Friday night to the next. ‘Who gives his fruit in its season’: Rav Yehudah said—and some say Rav Huna, while others say Rav Nachman—this refers to someone who has marital relations from one Friday night to the next.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נה:).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: A person is shown only the thoughts of his heart, as it is said: “You, O king, your thoughts arose upon your bed”; or, from here: “that you may know the thoughts of your heart.” Rava said: Know that this is so, for a person is shown neither a golden palm tree nor an elephant entering the eye of a needle.”
connections.context: The statement concerns what a person is shown in a dream. It supplies Rav Tzadok’s premise that the images and impulses appearing in sleep draw on the thoughts cultivated while awake.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִקְרָא אֵצֶל רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה "רוּחַ הַטֻּמְאָה" הַשּׁוֹכֵן בַּשֵּׁינָה
connections.quote:
“It has been said that when a person is dreaming and does not control his body, and his body is at rest, an impure spirit comes and rests upon him. Sometimes impure female spirits come and draw near to him, draw him to themselves, and become heated from him. Afterward they give birth to spirits and harmful beings (“the plagues of human beings”; another reading: “in the likeness of human beings”). Sometimes they appear in human form, except that they have no hair on their heads.

In all circumstances, a person must guard himself against them, so that he walks in the ways of Torah and does not become defiled through them. For no one sleeps in his bed at night without tasting the taste of death and having his soul depart from him. Once the body remains without its holy soul, an impure spirit is at hand and rests upon it, and it becomes defiled. We have explained the matter: a person must not pass his hands over his eyes in the morning, because the impure spirit rests upon them, and so forth, as has been said.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְוַדַּאי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 1
connections.quote: “When Yaakov our father dreamed his dream on the way to Lavan, he began examining it and taught all the tribes the depth found in it. They studied it, and new teachings of Torah emerged for them each time, for many depths of Torah were found in this dream.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Yaakov examining his dream and teaching its depths to the tribes, who continued finding new Torah in it. This develops the siman's contrast between distracting dreams and Yaakov's dream. The surrounding passage reports the brothers' accusation concerning Yosef; that accusation is not presented here as an established judgment on his dreams.
connections.headline: Yaakov's dream as a source of Torah

connections.hePhrase: דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה מַזִּיקִין בְּדֵילִין (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם ה.),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: Harmful spirits keep away from anyone who recites the Shema upon his bed, as it is said: ‘The sons of reshef soar high in flight.’ ‘Flight’—uf—refers to Torah, as it is said: ‘Will you close your eyes to it? It will be gone’—hata’if einekha bo ve’einennu. ‘Reshef’ refers to harmful spirits, as it is said: ‘Wasted by hunger, consumed by burning—reshef—and bitter destruction.’”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע הוּא קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹל מִצְווֹת,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥah said: Why does “Shema” precede “And it shall be, if you listen”? So that one first accepts the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, and afterward accepts the yoke of the commandments. Why does “And it shall be, if you listen” precede “And He said”? Because “And it shall be, if you listen” applies by day and by night, whereas “And He said” applies only by day.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "טוֹב וְגוֹמֵר עוֹל בִּנְעוּרָיו",
connections.quote: ‘It is good for a man to bear a yoke in his youth.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה שְׁכִיחַ בְּתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים בְּיוֹתֵר כְּטַעַם "כִּי הִגְדִּיל לַעֲשׂוֹת" בְּסֻכָּה (נב.),
connections.quote: “I will remove the northern one far from you and drive him into a land barren and desolate … his stench shall rise and his foul smell shall go up, for he has done great things.”
connections.context: Sukkah 52a reads “the northern one” as the evil inclination, and “for he has done great things” as its special strength against Torah scholars.

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר פָּסוּק: "בְּיָדְךָ אַפְקִיד וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Into Your hand I entrust my spirit; You have redeemed me, Hashem, God of truth.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ, הוּבָא בְּתוֹסָפוֹת בְּרָכוֹת יב. דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל 'לְהַגִּיד').
connections.quote: “Alternatively, this follows the Midrash on “They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness”: a person has faith and deposits his spirit in His hand, and He returns it without weariness.”
connections.context: This is the alternative explanation in Tosafot, s.v. “Lehagid baboker ḥasdekha.” It connects nighttime faith with entrusting the soul to God and receiving it back in the morning. Rav Tzadok uses that image to explain the bedtime declaration “Into Your hand I entrust my spirit.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם "פּוֹדֶה ה' וְגוֹמֵר"
connections.quote: ‘Hashem redeems the lives of His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be held guilty.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָמָּה נִבְרָא זֶה,
connections.quote: “Another interpretation of “He made everything beautiful in its time”: everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, made in His world, He made well. David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “Everything You made is beautiful, and wisdom is the most beautiful of all.” Thus he says, “How many are Your works, Hashem! You made them all with wisdom.” “Everything You made, You made well. But what pleasure do You have in the folly You created? A person walks in the market tearing his clothes, children run after him, and people laugh at him—is this pleasing before You?” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “David, you challenge folly? By your life, you will need it.” Thus Solomon said, “One who despises a thing will be bound to it.” What does “will be bound to it” mean? He will be held as a pledge for it, as in “If you take a pledge.” Another interpretation: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, “David, you challenge folly? By your life, you will suffer and pray for it until I give it to you.” ”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט:):
connections.quote: “One of the Sages said to Rav Kahana, ‘Have you heard why it is called Mount Sinai?’ He answered, ‘The mountain on which miracles were performed for Israel.’ ‘Then it should be called Mount Nissai!’ ‘Rather, the mountain on which a favorable sign was given to Israel.’ ‘Then it should be called Mount Simanai!’ He said to him, ‘Why do you not spend time with Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, who investigate aggadah? For Rav Chisda and Rabbah, son of Rav Huna, both said: Why is it called Mount Sinai? It is the mountain on which hatred toward the nations of the world descended.’ This is what Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Chanina, said: It has five names. The wilderness of Tzin, because Israel were commanded there; the wilderness of Kadesh, because Israel were sanctified there; the wilderness of Kedemot, because the primordial Torah was given there; the wilderness of Paran, because Israel were fruitful and multiplied there; and the wilderness of Sinai, because hatred toward the nations of the world descended upon it. What, then, is its name? Its name is Chorev. This disagrees with Rabbi Abbahu, for Rabbi Abbahu said: Its name is Mount Sinai. Why is it called Mount Chorev? Because devastation for the nations of the world descended upon it.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ה.):
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yitzḥak said: Anyone who recites Shema upon his bed is as though he holds a double-edged sword in his hand, as it is said: “The exaltations of God are in their throats, and a double-edged sword is in their hand.” How does this refer to bedtime? Mar Zutra, or some say Rav Ashi, said: From the beginning of the passage, “Let the faithful rejoice in glory; let them sing upon their beds,” followed by “The exaltations of God are in their throats, and a double-edged sword is in their hand.””
connections.context: Rav Tzadok is explaining this sword image. He then connects it with the following verse, “to execute vengeance upon the nations,” and with his account of the spiritual effects of bedtime Shema.

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת הַמִּקְרָא מְסַיֵּים: "לַעֲשׂוֹת נְקָמָה בַגּוֹיִם וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘To carry out vengeance among the nations, and punishments among the peoples.’

connections.hePhrase: [רמד] עַל יְדֵי הַשֵּׁינָה הָרְאוּיָה בְּלֹא חֲלוֹמוֹת וְהִרְהוּרִים רָעִים וְזָרִים,
connections.quote: “They therefore established the blessing over sleep to begin, “Who casts the bonds of sleep upon my eyes…”—He casts sleep so that one cannot see at all—and to conclude, “Who illuminates the entire world with His glory.” On the contrary, God illuminates a person through sleep, by surrounding one with an encompassing light and guarding one, as it is said, “For the Lord will be your confidence, and will guard your foot [from being caught].””
connections.explanation: Kislev comments on the same transition in HaMapil that this siman explains: the eyes cease seeing, yet the blessing concludes with illumination. This clarifies why the siman prays for sleep that will make the morning’s recognition of Heaven easier. The desired light is not ordinary sight continuing uninterrupted through the night; it is the guarding and inward renewal received while conscious control is set aside.
connections.headline: HaMapil joins the closing of the eyes to a request for illumination

connections.hePhrase: וּמְסַיֵּים: "הַמֵּאִיר לָעוֹלָם וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “One who goes to sleep on his bed says from “Hear, Israel” until “And it shall be, if you listen,” and says: “Blessed … who casts the bonds of sleep upon my eyes and slumber upon my eyelids, and gives light to the pupil of the eye. May it be Your will, Hashem my God, to lay me down in peace. Grant me my portion in Your Torah; accustom me to a mitzvah, and do not accustom me to a transgression. Do not bring me to sin, iniquity, trial, or disgrace. Let the good inclination rule over me, and do not let the evil inclination rule over me. Save me from an evil occurrence and from evil illnesses. Let neither evil dreams nor evil thoughts terrify me. May my bed be whole before You. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death. Blessed are You, Hashem, who illuminates the entire world with His glory.””

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם "כָּל פָּעַל לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ" – לְקִילּוּסוֹ (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים מִזְמוֹר קמח).
connections.quote: see note 2258.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok cites Shoḥer Tov, the Midrash on Psalms 148, explaining Proverbs 16:4. Its interpretation of “for His purpose” as “for His praise” explains how the light of morning can reveal divine glory.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם: "וְהָאֵרָה עֵינַי פֶּן אִישַׁן הַמָּוֶת" (תְּהִלִּים יג, ד),
connections.quote: ‘Look, answer me, Hashem my God; give light to my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "שׁוּרְיָינָא דְּעֵינָא בְּלִבָּא תַּלְיָא" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כח:).
connections.quote: ‘Is this my own teaching? It is Mar Shmuel’s! A maidservant in Mar Shmuel’s house developed a burning inflammation in her eye on Shabbat. She cried out, but no one attended to her, and her eye burst. The next day Mar Shmuel went out and taught: An eye that has become inflamed may be treated with eye salve on Shabbat. Why? Because the vessels of the eye are connected to the membranes of the heart.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַשֵּׁינָה "טוֹב מְאֹד" כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט).
connections.quote:
“Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said: “And behold it was very good” – and behold sleep is good. Is sleep, then, very good? This is a rhetorical question. Did we not learn: Wine and sleep are beneficial for them [the wicked] and beneficial for the whole world? However, as a result of a person sleeping a bit, he can get up and toil extensively in the Torah.

Rabbi Naḥman bar Shmuel bar Naḥman said in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Naḥman: “Behold it was very good” – this is the good inclination; “and behold it was very good” – this is the evil inclination. Is the evil inclination, then, very good? This is a rhetorical question. Rather, were it not for the evil inclination, a man would never build a house, would never marry a wife, would never beget children, and would never engage in commerce. Likewise, Solomon says: “[And I have considered all toil and all excelling in work,] that it is each man’s envy of his counterpart” (Ecclesiastes 4:4).”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה הָיָה טַעַם דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁלֹּא יָשַׁן שִׁשִּׁים נְשִׁימוֹת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סֻכָּה כו:),
connections.quote: see note 182 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר וָאֵרָא (כז א);
connections.quote: ““You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.” … “With all your heart”—this is the right and the left, called the good inclination and the evil inclination. “With all your soul”—this is the nefesh of David, placed between them. “With all your might”—to include them above, in a place without measure. Here is complete unification, to love the Holy One, blessed be He, fittingly.”
connections.context: The relevant words on Zohar II 27a are “the nefesh of David.” Rav Tzadok draws on that designation in relating David to the nefesh, the soul’s level associated with bodily action. The old quotation about Reuben and the tribal camps did not explain this point.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַחֵטְא כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא",
connections.quote: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying: If a soul (nefesh) shall sin through error against any of the commandments of Hashem concerning things that ought not to be done, and shall do any one of them.”

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בְּרֵישׁ כָּל מַרְעִין אֲנָא דָּם" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא נח:),
connections.quote: “He saw that it was written: ‘At the head of all death am I, blood; at the head of all life am I, wine.’ But if so, when someone falls from a roof and dies, or falls from a palm tree and dies, was it blood that killed him? Moreover, if someone is about to die, can one give him wine to drink and he will live? Rather, this is what should be written: ‘At the head of all illnesses am I, blood; at the head of all remedies am I, wine.’ They wrote this: ‘However, the Jewish elders say: At the head of all illnesses am I, blood; at the head of all remedies am I, wine. Where there is no wine, medicines are needed.’”

connections.hePhrase: לִמְצוֹא מָקוֹם לַה' שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה אוֹרָה יוֹצֵאת לָעוֹלָם (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ד דִּבְרָכוֹת הֲלָכָה ה),
connections.quote: see note 1619 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the Yerushalmi’s explanation of the Ark’s name, aron, following its discussion of prayer directed toward the Holy of Holies. Rav Tzadok uses its image of light going out to the world when describing the Temple as a permanent dwelling of divine holiness.

connections.hePhrase: עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ מִפִּי ה' (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כב, ח): "לֹא תִבְנֶה וְגוֹמֵר כִּי דָמִים רַבִּים וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: ‘The word of Hashem came to me, saying: ‘You have shed much blood and fought great wars. You shall not build a house for My name, because you have shed much blood upon the earth before Me.’’

connections.hePhrase: מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּיוֹמָא (סט:)
connections.quote: “He said to them: ‘Take care: if you kill that inclination, the world will come to an end.’ They imprisoned it for three days. They searched throughout the Land of Israel for an egg laid that day, and none could be found. They said: ‘What should we do? If we kill it, the world will come to an end. Shall we plead for mercy to take away half of it? Heaven does not grant things by halves.’ They blinded its eyes and let it go. This helped in that it no longer incites a person toward his close female relatives.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם (תּוֹלְדוֹת קלח א) אָמַר דְּצָרִיךְ לַחֲמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא.
connections.quote: see note 1592 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The continuation in Midrash HaNe’elam, Zohar I 138a, distinguishes the force needed for Torah delight from its corruption into sin. This is why Rav Tzadok can speak of preserving the force of desire while transforming it into good.

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בִּימֵי שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "שָׁלוֹם יִהְיֶה לוֹ",
connections.quote: “Behold, a son shall be born to you; he shall be a man of rest, and I will give him rest from all his enemies round about. For Solomon (Shlomo) shall be his name, and I will give peace (shalom) and quiet to Israel in his days.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.
connections.quote: “(7) This is what they said (Shabbat 30a): “In the lifetime of your son Solomon I shall make it known,” and so forth. The clarification of King David’s excellence came through the opening of the gates, for that is David’s level (fear), as stated. Yet this announcement, which clarifies the repair of what came before (as I wrote above in section 1), occurred only in Solomon’s lifetime. Through his repentance, Solomon reached the Throne of Glory, for he sat upon Hashem’s throne. There there is no sin at all, in the sense of “Even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for You are with me.” “You” is the recognition of the blessed God as present before oneself; “with me” means actually with me in the world of the Throne, called “et Hashem your God,” as stated. Then, even “when I walk” and do whatever I may do, Heaven forbid, there is no fear of evil, for it is written, “Evil shall not dwell with You,” and no evil thing descends from Heaven. Recognizing His presence means recognizing that “the whole earth is full of His glory”; consequently evil has no existence at all. This explains Solomon’s marrying foreign women, and also the expression applied to him in the Jerusalem Talmud (cited in Tosafot to the first chapter of Ḥagigah), “One does not learn from the one who fixed himself”: he fixed himself upon a matter of Torah, entering matters that appear like walking in the valley of the shadow of death. They even sought to count him among those who have no share in the World to Come (in the chapter Ḥelek). They were answered, “Should He repay it according to you?” This means: You suppose that he is with you, a human being of your measure. In fact he is “with Me” and upon My throne, and therefore he fears no evil at all. King Solomon was the first to attain this level of “for You are with me”; down to the lowest of all levels, whoever holds fast to it will fear no evil. Consequently, what came before is also repaired retroactively.”

connections.hePhrase: וְנִקְרָא "חֲנֻכַּת הַבַּיִת לְדָוִד",
connections.quote: ‘A psalm, a song for the dedication of the House, by David.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ז, הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י רֵישׁ מְלָכִים א),
connections.quote: “An aggadic Midrash: Rav Shmuel bar Naḥmani said: When David saw the angel standing in Jerusalem with his sword in his hand, his blood grew cold from fear.”
connections.context: This is the explanation Rav Tzadok explicitly cites as preserved in Rashi at the opening of I Kings. The verse itself only reports that David could not get warm; the commentary supplies the encounter with the angel and the chilling of his blood.

connections.hePhrase: וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אַדְּרַבָּה יָשַׁן הַרְבֵּה,
connections.quote: “King Solomon attained all the wisdom of Solomon, lower wisdom, through one dream. “He was wiser than all men.” There is no way to attain this wisdom while awake. Such sleep is very good: it is the deep sleep of prophecy, in which he attains much in Torah and thereby rises and labors greatly in Torah.”
connections.explanation: Kislev identifies Shlomo’s dream as the setting in which his distinctive wisdom was received, and relates that sleep to renewed labor in Torah. This develops the present siman’s contrast between David’s struggle and Shlomo’s settled stage. The sleep is valuable through what it receives and what it enables afterward. The example therefore explains a particular completed stage; it does not make every sleep equivalent to Shlomo’s prophetic reception.
connections.headline: Shlomo’s sleep represents receiving wisdom after the stage of struggle

connections.hePhrase: וְעָלָיו נֶאֱמַר: "כֵּן יִתֵּן לִידִידוֹ שֵׁנָא" (תְּהִלִּים קכז, ב),
connections.quote: “It is vain for you to rise early, to sit up late, eating the bread of toil; so He gives His beloved sleep.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok follows the reading of the final words as God giving sleep to His beloved, and applies it here to Solomon. This wording makes the verse’s connection with Solomon’s sleep explicit; some English translations instead render it as provision given during sleep.

connections.hePhrase: וְכִמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב)
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yudan said: During all the seven years that Solomon built the Temple, he did not drink wine. Once he had built it and married Bitya daughter of Pharaoh, that night he drank wine. There were two dances there, one a celebration for the building of the Temple and one a celebration for the daughter of Pharaoh. The Holy One blessed be He said: ‘Whose [dance] shall I accept, of these or of those?’ At that moment, it entered His mind to destroy Jerusalem. That is what is written: “For this city has been a cause of My wrath [api] and of My anger [from the day that they built it until this day, to remove it from My presence]” (Jeremiah 32:31). Rabbi Hillel bar Hileni said: This is like one who passes a filthy place and wrinkles his nose. Rabbi Ḥonya said: Pharaoh’s daughter danced eighty kinds of dances that night. Solomon slept until four hours of the day, and the keys to the Temple were under his head. That is what we learned regarding the daily morning offering, that it was sacrificed at four hours. His mother entered and rebuked him. Some say that Yerovam ben Nevat entered and rebuked him. How was he able to do so? Rabbi Ḥagai in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak: He stood and assembled one thousand from his tribe and entered and rebuked him. That is what is written: “As Ephraim spoke there was trembling [retet]” (Hosea 13:1); as Yerovam spoke [he aroused] the trembling of Solomon. The Holy One blessed be He said to him: ‘Why are you rebuking him? He is a prince in Israel! As you live, I will give you a taste of his authority and you will be unable to bear it.’ Immediately, when he entered the kingship, “he became guilty through the Baal and he died” (Hosea 13:1). The Rabbis say: Certainly, his mother rebuked him. She took her shoes and was slapping him with them this way and that, and she said to him: “What, my son [beri], and what, son of my womb?” (Proverbs 31:2). Rabbi Hoshaya said: “What, my son [beni]” is not written here, but rather, “what beri.” These are the commands and the prohibitions of the Torah, which is called bar, just as it says: “Yearn for bar” (Psalms 2:12), because all its matters are clear [barim]. “And what, son of my vows” (Proverbs 31:2) – she said to him: ‘My son, your father married many wives. When Natan the prophet came and said to him: “Behold, a son is born to you…for Solomon will be his name” (I Chronicles 22:9), each of them would say: ‘If I produce Solomon, I will sacrifice all the offerings in the Torah.’ Now, I have stood and my offerings are with me, and you are sleeping? “Do not give your strength to women, or your ways to that which destroys kings”’ (Proverbs 31:3).
