She said to him: ‘My son, the generation of the Flood was erased from the world because they were steeped in licentiousness.’ “It is not for kings, Lemoel” (Proverbs 31:4). Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Kingdom is not given to one who distances himself from the words of the Lord, but one who performs the word of God, he will be installed as king. “It is not for kings to drink wine” (Proverbs 31:4); let kings not drink wine, lest they forget and say like the one who said: “Who is God, that I should heed his voice?” (Exodus 5:2). “Or for princes: Where is [ei] strong drink?” (Proverbs 31:4). “O” is written; woe [oi], because of wine. “Lest he drink and forget what was legislated” (Proverbs 31:5). Anyone who drinks much wine will ultimately forget the two hundred and forty-eight limbs that are in him. That is what is written: “Lest he drink and forget what was legislated [meḥukak].” Meḥukak is written [without a vav], and they are two hundred and forty-eight. Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa said: The Holy One blessed be He said: ‘I had a great House and I destroyed it only due to wine.’ The Rabbis say: I had two princes and they died only due to wine, as Rabbi Yishmael taught: The two sons of Aaron died only because they entered intoxicated with wine…The Holy One blessed be He said: ‘Because in this world, wine is trouble for the world; in the future I will render it joy.’ That is what is written: “It will be on that day the mountains will drip with wine” (Joel 4:18).”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר וָאֵרָא (כד ב) שֶׁהוּא מֵעָפָר
connections.quote: “As for the earth we mentioned, when it is by itself, in its dryness and coldness, iron comes forth. Its sign is: “If the iron is blunt.””
connections.context: Zohar II 24b is describing the elements and the metals that arise from their combinations. The relevant point is the association of earth by itself with iron. Rav Tzadok connects that symbolism with David and then develops the image of iron refined into steel.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סב:): "שֵׁינָה בְּעַמּוּד הַשַּׁחַר כְּאִסְטְמָא לְפַרְזְלָא".
connections.quote: “Shmuel said: Sleep at dawn is like istama for iron. Relieving oneself at dawn is like istama for iron.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סב:): "שֵׁינָה בְּעַמּוּד הַשַּׁחַר כְּאִסְטְמָא לְפַרְזְלָא".
connections.quote: ““Like istama for iron”—steel in the vernacular. As it benefits iron, so it benefits the body. “Relieving oneself” means going to the privy.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok explicitly adopts the beneficial explanation of the comparison: dawn sleep perfects the body as steel strengthens or refines iron. The point is the beneficial image, which he relates to Solomon and the completion of the night’s spiritual work.

connections.hePhrase: רַק מַחֲשָׁבָה זָרָה וּבְטֵילָה לְגַמְרֵי
connections.quote: “Even if a person has damaged and corrupted his three levels—mind, heart and organs of action, corresponding to nefesh, ruach and neshamah—within all seven holy qualities, the forty-nine gates in each, he still has hope of purification through repentance from the depth of the heart, the fiftieth gate within each. The Sages alluded to this in the disciple of Rabbi Meir who could purify the creeping creature: it symbolizes the three impure shells together. Even if a person has become impure through them all, Heaven forbid, he can nevertheless be purified through the fiftieth gate within each. This explains the hundred and fifty reasons: the three fiftieth gates, through which there is hope of purification from all three shells.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik states the distinction between the three impure shells and mixed nogah, then expressly preserves hope for the person who has damaged mind, heart and action. This helps the reader follow the present siman's several levels of repair without treating a limitation on one form of restoration as the end of all purification. The source reads the teaching about purifying a creeping creature allegorically; it does not alter that creature's halakhic status.
connections.headline: Deep damage does not exhaust the possibility of purification

connections.hePhrase: כַּיָּדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה בִּפְרִי עֵץ חַיִּים שַׁעַר קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע שֶׁעַל הַמִּטָּה.
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Bedtime Shema, chapter 5
connections.quote: “Concerning lying down with the recitation of Shema: Know that no transgressions in the entire Torah generate destructive beings as does the wasting of semen. The reason is that when someone commits other transgressions, destructive beings clothe themselves in them and become accusers; but the punishment of one who wastes semen is great. We shall explain a great, hidden, and exceedingly wondrous mystery for repairing a person’s soul, so that he may emerge clean and pure from this sin. Know that one who wastes semen impairs thought, since he makes use of no vessel; his punishment reaches the supernal da’at of Abba and Imma. Just as he acts as a male without a female, so too, as it were, above: the drop of that soul is drawn from the male but is not imparted into Malkhut. Instead, it goes outside into kelipat nogah. This is the scale that seizes souls, mentioned in the Elder’s discourse in Mishpatim. The lower “woman of harlotry” entices Eve through kelipat nogah; that soul is drawn to her, and the power of a destructive being from the woman of harlotry clothes itself in it, becoming a body for that soul. Thus the person who wastes semen causes the drops of his children’s souls to be clothed in bodies made from the woman of harlotry: he has turned holiness and goodness toward evil. The repair of this sin is to put to death those bodies made for the souls, so that the souls may escape to their place and ascend with him each night. These are the destructive beings that a person puts to death through the Shema he recites upon his bed. Understand this great mystery.”

connections.hePhrase: הַנִּזְכָּר בְּזֹהַר מִשְׁפָּטִים (צה ב)
connections.quote: ‘There is a secret here: how souls are taken captive. This entire world is governed through the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. When the people of the world conduct themselves on the side of good, the balance stands and tips toward the side of good. When they conduct themselves on the side of evil, it tips toward that side. All the souls that were in the balance at that hour are seized and taken by it. But this is ‘to its own harm,’ for those souls subdue (another reading: ‘cover over’) everything they find from the evil side, and they destroy it. An illustration is the holy Ark, which was captured among the Philistines. They gained power over it—to their own harm. So too, these souls are taken captive by the Other Side to its own harm.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (נט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב) דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה.
connections.quote: see note 1447 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Tosafot is asking why procreation is absent from the seven Noahide commandments and explains that the command also contains a prohibitive aspect. Rav Tzadok cites precisely this linkage between procreation and the prohibition on destroying seed.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים (סִימָן קעו) דְּמוּטָב לְהוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה וְלֹא לַחְטוֹא בַּעֲרָיוֹת,
connections.quote: ‘There was a person who asked: ‘If someone’s inclination overpowers him and he fears that he may sin by lying with a married woman, with his wife while she is a niddah, or in another sexual relationship forbidden to him, may he emit his semen so that he will not sin?’ He was answered: ‘At that moment he should emit it, for if it is impossible (to resist otherwise), it is better for him to emit his semen and not sin with a woman. But he requires atonement: let him sit in ice during the winter, or fast for forty days during the summer.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְרַק בְּהוֹלִיד מַמְזֵר אָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (ט.) דְּלֹא יָכוֹל לְתַקֵּן.
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says: What is the crooked thing that cannot be set right? One who has intercourse with a woman forbidden to him and fathers a mamzer by her. If you say it refers to one who steals or robs, he can return what he took and set it right.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת זֶה יִסַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה בִּרְאִיַּת קֶרִי בַּלַּיְלָה,
connections.quote: “During those 130 years [Adam] spent fasting to return from his sin, he also produced spirits, demons and lilin through an involuntary seminal emission, as stated in Eruvin 18b. There he is called ‘a great pious person.’ Nevertheless, ‘even the most pious of the pious…’: his heart was not yet purified of bodily desire so as not to produce flesh, and through this he experienced impurity at night involuntarily. Although it was involuntary, he nevertheless produced spirits, demons and lilin and increased the power of the impure side, may the Merciful One protect us. Certainly it was not because he had entertained thoughts by day and violated ‘Guard yourself from every evil thing’—that one should not entertain thoughts, and so forth. Although the Torah had not yet been given to warn of this, they would not otherwise have called him ‘a great pious person.’ Nor would this have been called involuntary if he had brought it upon himself through his thoughts. Therefore he certainly guarded himself completely from every trace of such thought.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin discusses Adam's penitential years and insists that his involuntary occurrence did not follow a deliberate prior thought; otherwise the text would not call him a great pious person or describe it as involuntary. This is a necessary qualification when reading the siman's distinction between an occurrence built into bodily life and chosen wrongdoing. It does not erase the source's separate symbolic account of refinement.
connections.headline: An involuntary occurrence does not prove a chosen thought

connections.hePhrase: עַיֵּין רַמְבַּ״ם הִלְכוֹת מְלָכִים;
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות מלכים ומלחמות ח׳:י״א
connections.quote: “Anyone who accepts the seven commandments and is careful to observe them is one of the righteous of the nations of the world and has a share in the World to Come. This is provided that he accepts and performs them because the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded them in the Torah and informed us through Moses our teacher that the descendants of Noah had previously been commanded concerning them.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵין גֵּר תּוֹשָׁב נוֹהֵג אֶלָּא בִּזְמַן שֶׁהַיּוֹבֵל נוֹהֵג (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֲרָכִין כט.),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says: The law of fields devoted as cherem applies only when the Jubilee is observed, as it is said: ‘When the field goes out at the Jubilee, it shall be holy to Hashem, like a field devoted as cherem.’ Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: The status of ger toshav, a resident alien, applies only when the Jubilee is observed.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁכָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּאָרֶץ,
connections.quote: “Impurity at the fiftieth gate would mean that one could no longer return to one’s root, like a branch severed from the root. Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, feared this: perhaps they had sunk so deeply that they would not even believe, meaning that, Heaven forbid, they had been entirely uprooted from the good root inherited from their ancestors. For this the blessed God was angry with him: that he should suspect Israel’s offspring of such a thing—that the blessed God would allow them to sink so deeply. They are His portion and inheritance, believers descended from believers, and in this respect they cannot sink so far. Although “the wicked watches for the righteous and seeks to put him to death” completely, Heaven forbid, “Hashem will not abandon him into his hand.” The blessed God showed that, although they were immersed in such darkness, faith had nevertheless not perished or been cut off from their mouths and hearts. The essence of faith is to believe precisely this: wherever a person may be, the blessed God is nevertheless with him, for “I am Hashem who dwells with them amid their impurities.” Through this he can emerge from darkness and impurity, since, with the blessed God beside him, there is no evil at all. Rather, the blessed God wished that darkness should come first, and light afterward (Shabbat 77b).”

connections.hePhrase: וּבִזְמַן הַזֶּה: "חֶסֶד לְאֻמִּים חַטָּאת" (מִשְׁלֵי יד, לד),
connections.quote: see note 1633 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The first quotation follows the homiletic reading used in the Talmud and by Rav Tzadok, reading ḥesed as kindness. Other translations render that word as reproach. This reading explains Rav Tzadok’s discussion of the spiritual benefit that sustains the nations even when an act serves their own interest.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (י:) עַל פָּסוּק "בִּיבֹשׁ קְצִירָהּ".
connections.quote: ‘Ifra Hormiz, the mother of King Shapur, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, but he did not accept them. She sent them to Rava, and he accepted them for the sake of peace with the government. Rabbi Ami heard and was displeased. He said: ‘Does he not accept the verse, “When its branches dry out, they will be broken; women come and set them alight”?’ And Rava? He acted for the sake of peace with the government.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יח:),
connections.quote: see note 884 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Gemara’s clarification follows its account of Adam’s years of abstinence. These are the spirits, demons, and lilin to which Rav Tzadok refers, before explaining their place in his account of bedtime Shema and the recovery of the holy spark.

connections.hePhrase: רַק עוֹמֵד בְּנוֹגַהּ לוֹ סָבִיב
connections.quote: ‘I saw something like the appearance of chashmal, with the appearance of fire inside it all around, from what looked like his waist upward. From what looked like his waist downward I saw the appearance of fire, with radiance all around it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ: "מִשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁנִּטְמְעָה – נִטְמְעָה" (קִדּוּשִׁין עא.),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘By the Temple! We have the information in our hands. But what can I do? The great men of the generation have already become intermingled in it.’ He follows Rabbi Yitzchak, for Rabbi Yitzchak said: A family that has become intermingled remains intermingled.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל כָּל חֲלוּקַּת כָּבוֹד לְאָדָם בִּבְרָכוֹת (יד.)
connections.quote: ‘Shmuel said: What regard have you shown this person that you have not shown God? Rav Sheshet objected: At the breaks between passages, one may offer a greeting out of respect, and may respond!’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן יָדוּעַ מֵהַזֹּהַר גִּלְגּוּלֵי עֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שֶׁהֵם שׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּקִנְאָה וְתַאֲוָה,
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of The New Month, Chanukah, and Purim 3:29-30
connections.linkedRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of The New Month, Chanukah, and Purim 3:29-30
connections.canonicalRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of The New Month, Chanukah, and Purim 3:29-30
connections.heRef: פרי עץ חיים, שער ר"ח חנוכה ופורים ג׳:כ״ט-ל׳
connections.quote:
“Esau came from the side of judgment, as the son of Isaac, but he drew sustenance from the first three sefirot. Therefore it is written: “Isaac loved Esau, for game was in his mouth.” This means that a holy spark was within him, in the first three sefirot. Because of that game, Isaac loved him, in the hope that he might be rectified through it.

Elsewhere, the name is written עשיו, because he was reincarnated as Yeshua, the disciple of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachiah; and because they pushed him away with both hands and punished him, as stated. For this reason Chushim son of Dan killed Esau: he cut off his head, and the head fell inside the cave and was buried there with Jacob. Because the holiness within him was in his head alone, he was therefore buried there.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כה):
connections.quote: “Blessed is the Omnipresent, blessed is He, who chose Israel from all His handiwork, acquired them as a complete possession, and called them children and servants to His name. Sometimes He speaks with them as one speaks with many, and sometimes He speaks with them as one speaks with an individual. Why all this? Because of the love with which He loves them and the joy He takes in them, He therefore speaks with them in the singular and the plural. Accordingly I would say: every individual in Israel is obligated to say, “When will my deeds reach the deeds of my ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?” For the ancestors acquired this world, the World to Come, and the days of the son of David only through their good deeds and Torah study.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר בִּיהוֹשָׁפָט: "וַיִּגְבַּהּ לִבּוֹ בְּדַרְכֵי ה'" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב יז, ו),
connections.quote: ‘His heart was uplifted in Hashem’s ways. He also removed the high places and the asherah trees from Judah.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עָלָיו אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (כְּתוּבּוֹת קג:): "'יְרֵאֵי ה' יְכַבֵּד' –
connections.quote: ‘Is that so? Is it not written: ‘He honors those who fear Hashem’? The Master said: This refers to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Whenever he saw a Torah scholar, he would rise from his throne, embrace him, kiss him, and call him: ‘My teacher, my teacher! My master, my master!’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עָלָיו אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (כְּתוּבּוֹת קג:): "'יְרֵאֵי ה' יְכַבֵּד' –
connections.quote: “In whose eyes a vile person is despised, but he honors those who fear Hashem; he swears to his own hurt and does not change.”

connections.hePhrase: הֲרֵי זֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה כז:): "מְשַׁבֵּחַ אֲנִי אֶת הָעַצְלָנִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elai went to greet his teacher Rabbi Eliezer in Lod during the festival. He said to him: Elai, you are not among those who rest at home on the festival. Rabbi Eliezer used to say: I praise the lazy who do not leave their houses on the festival, as it is written: “You shall rejoice, you and your household.””
connections.context: The praise concerns the result of staying home to rejoice with one’s household. Rav Tzadok uses it as an example of an ordinarily flawed trait producing a good action, just as concern for one’s dignity can prevent an offense.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַלְבּוּשֵׁי גֵּיאוּת דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "ה' מָלָךְ גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צג, א).
connections.quote: ‘Hashem reigns, clothed in majesty. Hashem is clothed in strength and has girded Himself. The world too is firmly established; it will not be shaken.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַלְבּוּשֵׁי גֵּיאוּת דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "ה' מָלָךְ גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צג, א).
connections.quote: “and 'before honor comes humility' (Proverbs 15:33), for the ultimate strength of Israel's light is designated as humility. Reflecting the nature of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who is the greatest in Israel, whose greatness lay in: 'And the man Moses was exceedingly humble, etc.' (Numbers 12:3). For exalted majesty (ge'ut) is the outward garment of Hashem, blessed be He, as it is written: 'Hashem reigns, He is robed in majesty' (Psalms 93:1); meaning: the World of Action and what is visible to the eyes of flesh and blood, this is termed the garment of Hashem, blessed be He, like a garment that conceals and shrouds the body. And from the perspective of this outer vestment, Hashem is described as 'exceedingly exalted,' for in this physical world, sovereignty and ruling power are termed grandeur, since being sovereign over all is viewed as lofty majesty and greatness. Yet according to ultimate truth, this is nothing other than lowliness, in the spirit of (Horayot 10b): 'Servitude am I conferring upon you,' for one who descends to exercise dominion over lowly, base subjects experiences lowering, becoming a head to foxes. And for the children of Israel, who recognize the inner truth (Megillah 31a): "Wherever you find His greatness, there you find His humility," "I dwell with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit, etc." (Isaiah 57:15). And so they cling unto Him; the supreme force of their light is humility,”
connections.explanation: Resisei Layla explains the image of greatness as a garment, with leadership understood inwardly as service. This supplies a criterion for the difficult distinction in this siman. The useful outward bearing is a means of responsibility and service, while the inner recognition remains humble; self-exaltation that becomes an independent inner claim reproduces the very root of distraction the siman warns against.
connections.headline: Outward strength with inward humility

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר שָׁם (קה ב) דְּנָחִית לְעָלְמָא דְּנוּקְבָא
connections.quote:
“That old man began and said: “When you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh,” and so forth. This verse demonstrates all that has been said. Come and see: every male stands in his corresponding form in the male world, and every female stands in her corresponding form in the female world. As long as he is a servant of the Holy One, blessed be He, he cleaves to Him in those six primordial years. But if he uproots himself from His service, the Holy One, blessed be He, uproots him from those six years of the male world and hands him over to a human being, who is of six sides. He serves him for six years and is uprooted from the six years above (another reading adds: “primordial”).

Afterward he descends from there and is handed over to the female world. He did not wish to remain in the male; he descends and remains in the female. The female, which is the seventh, comes and takes him. From this point onward, he belongs to the female world.

If he does not wish to remain in her and in her redemption, he descends below, attaches himself below, and takes hold of the other side. From this point onward, he is uprooted from the male world and from the female world. He has taken hold among those servants who belong to the other side.

Now, since this is so, a blemish is required, and a mark of blemish must be made upon him, for every blemish belongs to the other side. From the Jubilee onward, he returns to reincarnation and comes back to the world as before (another reading: “If he becomes worthy and rectifies himself, he is broken”), and attaches himself to that female world, but no further. If he becomes worthy, he produces offspring in the female world. All this is the mystery of what is written: “Virgins after her, her companions, are brought to You.” Happy is he when he is rectified and becomes worthy of this.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי "וְהוּא יִמְשָׁל בָּךְ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ג, טז);
connections.quote: ‘To the woman He said: ‘I will greatly increase your suffering and your pregnancy pains. In pain you will give birth to children. Your yearning will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.’’

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל אִם אָמַר "אָהַבְתִּי וְכוּלֵי"
connections.quote: “But if the servant shall plainly say, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (קִידּוּשִׁין כב:):
connections.quote: ‘Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai used to expound this verse with an interpretation like a jewel: Why was the ear singled out from all the body’s limbs? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: The ear that heard My voice at Mount Sinai when I said, ‘For the children of Israel are My servants’—not servants of servants—and yet this person went and acquired a master for himself: let it be pierced.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת קמו.),
connections.quote: “Why are the nations contaminated? Because they did not stand at Mount Sinai. For when the serpent had intercourse with Chavah, it implanted contamination in her. Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai, had their contamination cease; the nations, who did not stand at Mount Sinai, did not have their contamination cease. Rav Acha, son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi, ‘What about converts?’ He answered, ‘Although they themselves were not there, their heavenly counterparts were there, as it is written: “With whoever is here with us, standing today before Hashem our God, and with whoever is not here,” and so forth.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ אֵלּוּ סוּרָן רַע (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא מְצִיעָא נט:)
connections.quote: “It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says: Why did the Torah warn concerning the convert in thirty-six places—or, according to some, forty-six? Because his inclination may turn toward evil.”
connections.context: This warning is given in the discussion prohibiting mistreatment of converts; the concern is that mistreatment may drive a convert back toward his former ways. Rav Tzadok cites the phrase “suro ra” within his explanation of differing spiritual receptivity.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהֲרֵי מִטַּעַם זֶה יְכוֹלִים לַחֲזוֹר בַּחֲצִי הַיּוֹם,
connections.quote: “But Rav said: A worker may withdraw even in the middle of the day! He answered him: As long as he has not withdrawn, his hand is like his employer’s hand. When he withdraws, the reason is different, for it is written, “For the children of Israel are servants to Me; they are My servants”—and not servants to servants.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן עַבְדוּת בְּשִׁילְהֵי הוֹרָיוֹת (י רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: “When he came ashore, he sent for them, but they did not come. He sent again, and they came. He said to them: Do you imagine that I am granting you rulership?”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן עַבְדוּת בְּשִׁילְהֵי הוֹרָיוֹת (י רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: “I am granting you servitude, as it is said: “They spoke to him, saying: If today you will be a servant to this people.””
connections.context: Rabban Gamliel is appointing scholars to public responsibility. The sentence crosses the page boundary and reaches “servitude” at the beginning of Horayot 10b, exactly as Rav Tzadok indicates. He applies this model of service to leadership of the generation.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנִּקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לד:): "עֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ";
connections.quote: see note 3133.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא מִשְׁפָּטִים (קטז ב) דָּרְשׁוּ "עֶבֶד עִבְרִי" עַל תְּפִלָּה.
connections.quote: “For in prayer a person is like a servant, of whom it is said: “He shall serve six years.” Service means prayer. “He shall serve six years”: the first three blessings and the last three blessings, in which the prayer leader discharges a person's obligation for one who does not know how to pray them. For in them the Righteous One, the life of the world, is called by these names: Boaz, Righteous, Redeemer, Near, and Faithful.”

connections.hePhrase: (תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר סוֹף תִּקּוּן יג וְשִׁיּוּרֵי מִדְרָשִׁים).
connections.quote: see note 3051.
connections.context: This is the passage at the end of Tikkun 13. Rav Tzadok identifies victory in this spiritual battle with overcoming evil through the “double-edged sword” of Shema; the resulting gift is the ability to pray.

connections.hePhrase: אֵיךְ הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת "מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ"
connections.quote: ‘One called to another and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy is Hashem of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory.’’

connections.hePhrase: זֶה הוּא כְּבָר נוֹשָׁע בִּישׁוּעָה שְׁלֵימָה,
connections.quote: “Once, on the first festival day of Pesach, I dreamed an explanation of the Haggadah's words, ‘I am He and no other.’ The level called ‘I’ is the lowest level, the secret of the Shechinah dwelling within Israel's hearts. It is itself the level called ‘He,’ the highest hidden level, the secret of the supernal crown. The Zohar calls ‘He’ Atika, beyond the human stature and intellectual grasp. It is not another thing; all is one.”
connections.explanation: Divrei Chalomot interprets ‘I am He and no other’ through the same vocabulary of the lowest indwelling disclosure and the highest hidden root. Its conclusion guards the present hierarchy from being mistaken for separate divine sources. The difference belongs to how the person apprehends the presence, while the reality recognized at the root remains one.
connections.headline: The lower disclosure and the hidden root are not separate

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ וְנִוָּשֵׁעָה" (תְּהִלִּים פ, ד).
connections.quote: see note 1876 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rav Tzadok reads the shining of God’s face as inward illumination: recognition of God’s presence itself dispels the darkness and constitutes salvation.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי מְעַט מִן הָאוֹר דּוֹחֶה הַרְבֵּה מִן הַחֹשֶׁךְ,
connections.displayRef: Duties of the Heart, Fifth Treatise on Devotion 5:13-14
connections.linkedRef: Duties of the Heart, Fifth Treatise on Devotion 5:13-14
connections.canonicalRef: Duties of the Heart, Fifth Treatise on Devotion 5:13-14
connections.heRef: חובות הלבבות, שער חמישי - שער ייחוד המעשה ה׳:י״ג-י״ד
connections.quote: “For a little truth will overcome much falsehood, just as a little light drives away much darkness. This calls our attention to the battles against desires and to standing against the inclination with effort and diligence. For its weakness in standing before reason, and how quickly it is defeated by it, have already become clear, as Scripture says: ‘The wicked bow before the good’ (Proverbs 14:19).”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר פ'
connections.quote: ““O God, restore us; make Your face shine, and we shall be saved.” Rabbi said: We have nothing but the shining of Your face.”
connections.context: Shoḥer Tov is Midrash Tehillim, not the biblical psalm itself. This is its explicit comment on Psalms 80:4, the statement Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וּבְשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר פ'
connections.quote: ““O Lord God of hosts, restore us.” Rabbi Yoḥanan said: We have nothing but the shining of Your face; save us, and we shall be saved.”
connections.context: The Midrash repeats the same point at its conclusion. This supplies the actual wording behind Rav Tzadok’s “we have nothing but the shining of Your face”; the former tuple-like note and its rose imagery were not a quotation of this statement.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ נֶאֱמַר: "יֵרָאֶה וְגוֹמֵר פְּנֵי הָאָדֹן"
connections.quote: “The place of the tower causes forgetting, as the Sages said (Sanhedrin 109a), the opposite of the Temple's air, which increased the power of remembrance. For ascent to the Temple is called in Scripture seeing ‘the face of the Master, Hashem’ (Exodus 23:17). Concerning seeing King David, the Sages said (Eruvin 64b) on ‘goodly to look upon’ (I Samuel 16:12): whoever saw him remembered his learning. All the more so the Master's face. The holy Zohar (II 163b) says: who is ‘the face of the Master, Hashem’? Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, for in truth it is the same matter. In particular this is King David, whose quality is known to be called by the name Adnut [the sefirah of kingship]. As I have also written elsewhere, the Temple's holiness in the dimension of world corresponds exactly to King David's holiness in the dimension of souls. Seeing him and his atmosphere likewise brought remembrance, the opposite of seeing the tower.”
connections.explanation: Sichat Shedim uses the same verse about seeing the Master's face and explains the Temple as a place that strengthens remembrance. Its comparison with David's presence develops the siman's relation between recognition and revealed presence without making its three degrees of apprehension interchangeable.
connections.headline: The Temple's face-to-face vision and remembrance

connections.hePhrase: וְהַגַּם דִּבְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶאֱמַר: "וּפָנַי לֹא יֵרָאוּ" (שְׁמוֹת לג, כג),
connections.quote: ‘I will remove My palm, and you will see My back, but My face will not be seen.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי דִּלְכָךְ בִּרְכַּת הַזָּן שֶׁתִּיקֵּן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (מח:),
connections.quote: “Rav Nahman said: ‘Moses instituted the blessing ‘Who sustains’ for Israel when the manna descended for them. Joshua instituted the blessing over the land for them when they entered the land. David and Solomon instituted ‘Who builds Jerusalem.’ David instituted ‘For Israel Your people and for Jerusalem Your city,’ and Solomon instituted ‘For the great and holy House.’ ‘Who is good and does good’ was instituted at Yavneh on account of those slain at Betar. For Rav Matna said: ‘On the day when those slain at Betar were permitted burial, they instituted ‘Who is good and does good’ at Yavneh: ‘Who is good,’ because they had not putrefied; ‘and does good,’ because they were permitted burial.’’”

connections.hePhrase: לְפִי שֶׁ"הַדָּר בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ דּוֹמֶה כְּמִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ אֱלוֹהַּ" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ כְּתוּבּוֹת קי:)
connections.quote: ‘The Sages taught: A person should always live in the Land of Israel, even in a city whose majority are gentiles, and should not live outside the Land, even in a city whose majority are Israelites. For anyone who lives in the Land of Israel resembles someone who has a God, and anyone who lives outside the Land resembles someone who has no God, as it is said: ‘To give you the land of Canaan, to be your God.’’

connections.hePhrase: [וְעַיֵּין כֵּן בַּזֹּהַר],
connections.quote: “Moses remained outside and did not enter there, neither his body nor his bones; rather, the Shechinah entered the Land … Moses merited in his lifetime what Jacob did not merit … And if you say that this was a deficiency in Moses, it is not so. Rather, when Israel went out of Egypt, it was from the side of the Jubilee.”
connections.context: This passage is on Zohar I 21b–22a.

connections.hePhrase: כַּיָּדוּעַ מִג' מַדְרֵגוֹת אֲנִ"י, אַתָּ"ה, הוּ"א,
connections.quote: “This is why he blessed him “on that day,” which alludes to Atika. We refer to the blessed God in three modes: He, You, and I. “He” alludes to Atika, language of hiddenness and concealment—the intellect hidden from every thought. “You” alludes to Ze’ir Anpin, the name Havayah, through which we speak directly: “You, Hashem,” as is known (Zohar III 290a). “I” alludes to the Divine Presence, the field of apple trees, the souls of Israel, as it says, “I am Hashem who dwells among the children of Israel” (ibid. 223a). These are the three names Ehyeh, Havayah, and Adonai. Ehyeh means what is not present now but will be in the future, when this will be revealed.”

connections.hePhrase: אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ז:):
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: From the day the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, no person called the Holy One, blessed be He, ‘Master’ until Abraham came and called Him Master, as it is said: ‘He said: My Lord God, how shall I know that I will inherit it?’’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ל.):
connections.quote: see note 759 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר: "שְׁלַח אוֹרְךָ וַאֲמִתְּךָ הֵמָּה יַנְחוּנִי, יְבִיאוּנִי אֶל הַר קָדְשְׁךָ וְאֶל מִשְׁכְּנוֹתֶיךָ; וְאָבוֹאָה אֶל מִזְבַּח אֱלֹהִים" (תְּהִלִּים מג, ג–ד),
connections.quote: “Send Your light and Your truth; let them lead me, let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to Your dwelling places. Then I shall come to the altar of God, to God, the joy of my rejoicing, and thank You with the lyre, O God, my God.”
connections.context: Both verses are cited. Their sequence moves from light that guides the person to arrival at God’s dwelling and altar, matching Rav Tzadok’s description of illumination as an entrance to fuller closeness.

connections.hePhrase: הוּא "הַשַּׁעַר לַה', צַדִּיקִים יָבֹאוּ בוֹ" עַל יָדוֹ לְמַדְרֵגָה עֶלְיוֹנָה.
connections.quote: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok uses this gate as an image of the first illumination through which the righteous enter a higher level of closeness. Here tzaddikim is rendered “the righteous,” the sense used in his explanation.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם הַפַּיְיטָן שֶׁיָּסַד לְפָרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים "אוֹר פָּנֶיךָ וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ““Lift the light of Your face upon us, Master” is said in the Musaf prayer, in the liturgical poem within each blessing. Since these poems have been accepted throughout Israel, their words deserve interpretation. Even if their author and arranger did not intend a particular interpretation, it may still be true, as the Urim VeTummim writes concerning the Shulḥan Arukh and similar works accepted throughout Israel: their words may be interpreted even beyond their authors’ intention, because the spirit of Hashem spoke through them. “The light of Your face” indicates the light of Atika. At the Shabbat meal we say, “May its light rest within her,” and at the third meal there is the revelation of the forehead of Atika, as stated in the Idra. It is taught (Shabbat 151b), “‘The sun and the light’—the forehead and the nose.” Thus “the light of Your face” is Atika’s light “upon us,” above us like a crown upon the head. Each blessing likewise ends, “God, high and exalted,” indicating Atika, the intellect hidden from every thought. “High and exalted,” when applied to the blessed God, indicates what is without measure, beyond the grasp of all created beings, as explained many times.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הַנִּקְרָא יֵצֶר: יֵצֶר טוֹב וְיֵצֶר רָע;
connections.quote: “Afterward the Men of the Great Assembly said: “On the contrary, this is the might of His might: He masters His inclination,” and so forth. The marginal gloss changes this to “His anger,” in accordance with the Ein Yaakov’s reading, because the phrase “masters His inclination” seemed difficult when applied to the blessed God. In truth, however, yetzer means desire, as it says, “Preserve this forever for the inclination of the thoughts of Your people’s heart.” He prayed that the desire with which they had offered willingly, wholeheartedly, should endure forever. When desire is directed toward good it is called the good inclination, and when directed oppositely it is called the evil inclination. Thus “masters His inclination” can apply to the blessed God: He has a desire to take vengeance and restrains that desire. Nevertheless, the expression “the might of His might” suggests that He restrains even His might, supporting the Ein Yaakov’s reading, “masters His anger.””

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְנָחוֹת כט:):
connections.quote: “Why was this world created with the letter he? Because it resembles an open portico, so that whoever wishes to leave may leave. And why is its leg suspended? So that if a person returns in repentance, they bring him in.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְנָחוֹת כט:):
connections.quote: “Why was the world to come created with the letter yod? Because the righteous in it are few. And why is its head bent? Because the righteous in it bow their heads on account of their deeds, which are not alike.”
connections.context: Both halves of the contrast are needed: he for this world and yod for the world to come. Rav Tzadok then relates those letters to heart and mind, distinguishing the work of desire and choice now from the future attainment of understanding.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָאָבוֹת נִקְרְאוּ "אֵיתָנִים" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יא.),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer says: How do we know that the patriarchs were born in Tishrei? “All the men of Israel gathered to King Solomon in the month of the mighty ones, at the festival”—the month in which the mighty ones of the world were born. How does eitan mean strength? As it is written: “Strong is your dwelling place,” and “Hear, mountains, the Lord’s contention, and you mighty foundations of the earth.””
connections.context: The relevant point is the designation eitanim, “mighty” or “steadfast ones,” for the patriarchs. Rav Tzadok reports an interpretation of that strength as the unyielding desire to reach their spiritual goal; that further explanation is his teaching here.

connections.hePhrase: וְהָאָבוֹת נִקְרְאוּ "אֵיתָנִים" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יא.),
connections.quote: “For the three Patriarchs are the living root of these three holinesses: Abraham our father, the first of converts (Chagigah 3a), is the inception of holiness from below, fencing all his organs to be holy; having to draw himself near, converts being accepted initially through human initiative; tested with Ten Trials (Avos 5:3) to refine the ten rungs of human stature through his war against the yetzer. For every trial requires an inciting yetzer whom man must conquer, for if the yetzer is already tamed, no trial exists;”
connections.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim describes Avraham’s tests as the clarification of the full range of his powers, and states that an actual test requires an opposing impulse to overcome. This clarifies the present siman’s claim about the human advantage over angels. The power that makes willing service possible also makes struggle possible; what determines its direction is the work of bringing it into kedushah.
connections.headline: The presence of struggle is not the absence of a holy task

connections.hePhrase: וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּיִחוּד נִקְרָא "אֵיתָן" בִּתְהִלִּים (פט, א וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טו.),
connections.quote: “A maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite.”
connections.context: The psalm’s heading supplies the name Ethan. The following note on Bava Batra 15a supplies the rabbinic identification of Ethan with Abraham, which Rav Tzadok uses to develop the theme of steadfast desire.

connections.hePhrase: וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּיִחוּד נִקְרָא "אֵיתָן" בִּתְהִלִּים (פט, א וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טו.),
connections.quote: ‘David wrote the book of Psalms through ten elders. But let him also count Ethan the Ezrahite! Rav said: Ethan the Ezrahite is Abraham. Here it is written, ‘Ethan the Ezrahite,’ haEzrachi, and there it is written, ‘Who aroused righteousness from the east,’ mimizrach, and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: כָּל הַמִּתְפַּתֶּה בְּיֵינוֹ יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִדַּעַת קוֹנוֹ.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥanina said: Anyone who is readily appeased over his wine has something of his Creator’s disposition, as it says, “Hashem smelled the pleasing fragrance,” and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, דִּבְיָמָיו סִיהֲרָא בְּאַשְׁלָמוּתָא וְלֹא הָיָה שׁוּם מוֹנֵעַ,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
connections.quote: see note 481 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach first describes silver as longing that acquires the gold of Torah. Its later reversal explains why the acquired Torah must itself kindle further longing as the person's natural energy changes. This develops the siman's account of a power impressed on possessions into a reciprocal process: the desire seeks wisdom, and the wisdom received can renew that desire. The siman's opening condition concerning divine judgment remains in force.

connections.hePhrase: נֶאֱמַר: "כִּכְלוֹת וְגוֹמֵר כָּל חֵשֶׁק שְׁלֹמֹה וְגוֹמֵר" (מְלָכִים א ט, א),
connections.quote: ‘It happened when Solomon had finished building the House of Hashem, the king’s house, and everything Solomon had desired to make…’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁכָּל חֶשְׁקוֹ הָיָה נִשְׁלָם וּמוּבָא לוֹ.
connections.quote: “All wisdom on the human side, called “lower wisdom,” consists only in the desire to acquire wisdom. The blessed God “gives wisdom to the wise” (Daniel 2:21)—to someone who possesses the beginning of wisdom, which is desire. King Solomon’s great wisdom corresponded to his great desire, for in desire he attained the utmost perfection possible for the human species. Thus it says in I Kings (9:19), “And all Solomon’s desire that he wished (to build),” and so forth. This is Solomon’s essential quality: desire and seeking, which remain forever, as explained (and all his wisdom remains forever in the three books he composed). This is the beginning of wisdom in the heart, as stated in Berakhot 55a from the verse, “In the heart of every wise-hearted person I have placed wisdom” (Exodus 31:6). Wisdom itself is chiefly in the brain, but in the heart there is desire. Lower wisdom chiefly comes from the heart’s desire—that is, a heart possessing fear of Heaven, which is the essence of the Israelite heart. When fear of Heaven is absent, however, it says, “Why is there a price in a fool’s hand to acquire wisdom, when there is no heart?” (Proverbs 17:16). The Sages of blessed memory in Yoma 72b apply this even to those who engage in Torah without fear of Heaven, meaning within Israel.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל שִׁישַׁק מֶלֶךְ מִצְרַיִם
connections.quote: “In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the House of Hashem and the treasures of the king’s house; he took away everything, and he took all the shields of gold that Solomon had made.”

connections.hePhrase: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (פְּסָחִים פז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב):
connections.quote: “This accords with Rabbi Alexandri, who said: ‘Three returned to their place of origin: Israel, Egypt’s money, and the writing on the tablets. Israel—as we have said. Egypt’s money, as it is written: ‘In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt went up against Jerusalem,’ and so on. The writing on the tablets, as it is written: ‘I broke them before your eyes.’ It was taught: The tablets broke, and the letters flew away.’”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, קכה סוֹף עַמּוּד א בְּמִדְרַשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם)
connections.quote: “With every drop that goes forth from Eden, a spirit of wisdom goes forth. Therefore it was taught: Some waters nurture wise people and some waters nurture fools; the waters that nurture the wise come from the drops of Eden. Rabbi Yosei said: The waters containing more of these drops are those of the first of the four rivers, as it is written: “The name of the first is Pishon.” The one distinguished above them all is Pishon, which flows into the land of Egypt; therefore Egypt’s wisdom exceeded that of the whole world.”
connections.context: This is Midrash HaNe’elam on Zohar I 125a. It supplies the specific description of Egypt’s exceptional wisdom. Rav Tzadok’s further explanation concerns Egypt’s intense desire for wisdom and the spiritual quality associated with its wealth.

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן עֲבָדִים כְּנָשִׁים וַאֲסוּרִין בְּתַלְמוּד תּוֹרָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ כְּתוּבּוֹת כח.).
connections.quote: ““So-and-so would leave the school to immerse and eat terumah.” But perhaps he was a priest’s slave? This supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said: It is forbidden for a person to teach his slave Torah.”
connections.context: The Gemara uses attendance at Torah school to distinguish a priest from the priest’s slave, since both could eat terumah. The restriction on teaching the slave is the point Rav Tzadok invokes in describing servitude as subjection of the head to another’s authority.

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים קיב.):
connections.quote: ‘Rav Pappa said: Not buying from him or selling to him, but entering a partnership with him. Now that Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak has said, ‘What is meant by “You have blessed the work of his hands”? Anyone who receives a perutah from Job is blessed,’ even buying from him and selling to him is appropriate.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם שֶׁקִּבֵּל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מַתָּנוֹת מִמִּצְרַיִם,
connections.quote: “This is why he was informed here of the Egyptian exile and, at its end, “Afterward they will go out with great possessions.” “Great” indicates the qualities of Atika: being bound to the root. These are the great possessions they brought out of Egypt. Through the ten plagues they were clarified there in all ten qualities: in each plague Israel left one quality on the impure side, which also has ten corresponding qualities, and entered one quality in holiness. This resembles the holy Zohar’s expression, “Striking Egypt and healing Israel.””
connections.explanation: Lech Lecha explains the promised possessions through Israel’s movement from each impure quality into its holy counterpart. This develops the present siman’s claim that a people’s intense desire can become impressed upon its wealth. The possessions matter through the powers carried and redirected with them, especially the desire that becomes preparation for Torah’s wisdom. Their value cannot be reduced to an increase of property without that clarification.
connections.headline: The great possessions of Egypt include powers redirected into holiness

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה לִשְׁתֵּי כִלְיוֹתָיו כִּשְׁנֵי רַבָּנִים וְהָיוּ מְלַמְּדִין אוֹתוֹ חָכְמָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא),
connections.quote: see note 2457.

connections.hePhrase: [וְכָךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קִבֵּל רוּחַ חָכְמָה וּבִינָה מִמִּצְרַיִם,
connections.displayRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:3
connections.canonicalRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:3
connections.quote: “This is the meaning of the Torah’s descent into Egypt through the sins of the generations of the Flood and the dispersion, as is known from the writers of ancient history. The beginnings of all the sciences were in Egypt, through the ancient Egyptian sages; afterward (during the Babylonian exile and somewhat earlier) they were in the land of the Chaldeans, and then in Greece (in the days of Shimon the Righteous and the Oral Torah, as I wrote above in section 5). In the nation in which wisdom abounded, a great measure of the wisdom that the blessed God created and gave to humanity had spread. Only, because of their bad disposition, it turned toward evil for them. They were exceedingly wise in worldly sciences and also in the art of sorcery. The character of wisdom among the nations corresponds to the character of the wisdom the blessed God grants at that time to the one who imparts it within this world. Among Israel, they perceive in that wisdom its true point, which is called “Torah.” ”

connections.hePhrase: וְשֶׁזֶּה טַעַם שֶׁאָמְרוּ: מֵאֲבִימֶלֶךְ נִתְעַבְּרָה שָׂרָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תּוֹלְדוֹת),
connections.quote: “This follows what I heard concerning “Sarah conceived from Abimelech”: From where did Abraham obtain the strength to father a son? Only through Abimelech’s being restrained. At the very moment the power was taken from Abimelech, it was given to him, for sometimes this is the measure and judgment: one cannot receive an influence unless it is taken from another. Our father Abraham received the spirit of wisdom and understanding from Pharaoh, and the spirit of counsel and strength from Abimelech; but in him they operated through the spirit of knowledge and fear of Hashem, and he fathered Isaac. Likewise, from where did King David obtain strength? Only from overcoming Goliath. Then that strength was, of itself, joined to fear of Hashem in him, and he attained his own hidden root. But because he took it from the Philistine, he is called “Philistia.” (Nevertheless, this is a disparaging name, in the sense of “Through you he was driven out,” and so forth: punishment arises for this when accusation is made. He is therefore called this, because the power was not originally his but came from the Philistine, and from this side accusation could arise. For the same reason Isaac fathered Esau, from the side of Abimelech’s evil fear, as I wrote elsewhere.)”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן הַבְטָחַת: "יֵצְאוּ בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל" (בְּרֵאשִׁית טו, יד) וּבִזַּת הַיָּם,
connections.quote: ‘But I will also judge the nation whom they serve, and afterward they will go out with great possessions.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶאֱמַר: "וַתֵּרֶב חָכְמַת וְגוֹמֵר וּמִכָּל חָכְמַת מִצְרָיִם" (מְלָכִים א ה, י),
connections.quote: ‘Solomon’s wisdom exceeded the wisdom of all the people of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר: "וְכִי יָזִד אִישׁ עַל רֵעֵהוּ לְהָרְגוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת כא, יד),
connections.quote: ‘If a man acts deliberately against his fellow to kill him by cunning, you shall take him even from My altar to be put to death.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק פֵּירוּשׁ "יָזִיד" מִן "וַיָּזֶד יַעֲקֹב" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כה, כט),
connections.quote: ‘Jacob was cooking a stew, and Esau came in from the field, exhausted.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן "בַּדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם" (שְׁמוֹת יח, יא)
connections.quote: ‘Now I know that Hashem is greater than all the gods, for (He judged them) through the very matter in which they acted arrogantly against (Israel).’

connections.hePhrase: אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה יא.):
connections.quote: “Alternatively, He does not bring it upon them; they come and fall into it themselves. Thus it says, ‘The Egyptians were fleeing toward it.’ This is what Rabbi Elazar said: What is the meaning of ‘For in the matter in which they acted arrogantly against them’? In the very pot in which they cooked, they themselves were cooked. How do we know that zadu is an expression connected with cooking in a pot? It is written, ‘Yaakov cooked a stew (vayazed).’”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב):
connections.quote: ““If it please the king, let it be written to destroy them, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver.” Resh Lakish said: It was revealed and known before Him who spoke and the world came into being that Haman would weigh out shekels against Israel. Therefore He caused their shekels to precede his shekels.”
connections.context: The statement contrasts Israel’s shekel contributions with Haman’s proposed payment to destroy them. Rav Tzadok uses expenditure as an expression of desire and explains that Israel’s corresponding devotion had already preceded Haman’s.

connections.hePhrase: וּמָה טַעַם יֵשׁ בִּשְׁקָלָיו שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ אֵיזֶה טַעֲנָה לְשֶׁיִּזְכֶּה
connections.quote: “On the side of wisdom, he certainly recognized that the world cannot exist without Israel. Therefore, in his wickedness he devised the statement, “I shall weigh ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who perform the work, to bring into the king’s treasuries” (Esther 3:9). This too means the King of kings. He was saying: Israel’s entire preciousness lies in their ability to surrender all their longings and desires to the blessed God; he too could do this, and could take their place. He was the first to think that he was Israel, as the Sages of blessed memory said (Numbers Rabbah 14:10), that the nations will eventually say, “We are Israel.” This began with him, as it says, “Whom would the king wish to honor (more than me)?” (Esther 6:6), meaning the King of kings. In his wisdom he recognized that his success came from the blessed God, who wished to exalt him and had agreed with him about destroying Israel, Heaven forbid. Since he knew that the whole world had been created only for their sake, he thought that the blessed God had certainly chosen him in their place—until he saw that “it was reversed” (Esther 9:1), and our handful of barley came and displaced his ten thousand talents of silver (Megillah 16a). The omer offering is called an “offering of jealousy,” like the offering of the suspected adulteress, as is known from the Zohar (II 148b): it tests the “woman of valor,” distinguishing her from the “woman of harlotry” who imitates the woman of valor. This follows “Better a meal of vegetables (with love there) than a fattened ox (with hatred in it)” (Proverbs 15:17), which the Sages expounded concerning Balaam’s offerings and his seven altars (Numbers 23:1). He too thought to build altars corresponding to all the righteous and the patriarchs who had built them, like Haman with his shekels, claiming the ability to offer and serve in place of them all, and still more. Thus Tanchuma at the beginning of Tzav (1) says that they would offer “thousands of rams … myriads of streams of oil” (Micah 6:7). But the distinction is that the righteous offered a pleasing fragrance, to bring satisfaction before Him, whereas Balaam offered in order thereby to create hatred between Israel and their Father in Heaven. His intent was only to harm. So too, Haman’s shekels were only a means of enabling him to destroy Israel, Heaven forbid.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּטַעַם (חֲגִיגָה טו.):
connections.quote: ‘He said to him: Your teacher Rabbi Akiva did not say that. Rather: He created righteous people and He created wicked people; He created Gan Eden and He created Gehinnom. Each person has two shares, one in Gan Eden and one in Gehinnom. If a righteous person merits, he takes his own share and his fellow’s share in Gan Eden. If a wicked person incurs guilt, he takes his own share and his fellow’s share in Gehinnom.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְשֶׁרָאָהוּ יַעֲקֹב עָיֵיף מֵרְצִיחָה,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: That wicked one committed five transgressions on that day … He killed a person: it is written here, ‘and he was weary’ (Genesis 25:29), and it is written there, ‘Woe is me now, for my soul is weary because of the killers’ (Jeremiah 4:31).”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מַכּוֹת י רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א):
connections.quote: see note 1339 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Gemara explains the placement of cities of refuge by the prevalence of killers in Gilead and Shechem. Both places appear in Rav Tzadok’s sentence. His further account of the spiritual force involved and its redirection toward holiness develops this reference.

connections.hePhrase: וְשֶׁזֶּה טַעַם: "הַיְדַעְתֶּם כִּי לָנוּ רָמֹת גִּלְעָד" (מְלָכִים א כב, ג) דְּאַחְאָב,
connections.quote: see note 733 (Vol. I).
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik distinguishes Moshe's slight lapse into anger from the particular zeal fitting to Pinchas. This is an important qualification beside the present account of Gilead and Ahab's attempt to vindicate his use of force: recognizing that severity can have a holy root does not by itself establish that a given act expresses it. The distinction is consistent with the siman's opening condition that desire's force remains subject to judgment.

connections.hePhrase: וְשֶׁזֶּה טַעַם: "הַיְדַעְתֶּם כִּי לָנוּ רָמֹת גִּלְעָד" (מְלָכִים א כב, ג) דְּאַחְאָב,
connections.quote: “[As I heard concerning the verse, ‘Do you know that Ramot Gilad belongs to us?’ (I Kings 22:3), and as it says, ‘Your hair is like a flock [of goats streaming] from Mount Gilad’: the hairs are judgments, indicating anger and killing, as is known, but from Mount Gilad it is the good form of killing, in accord with Hashem's will. Achav therefore sought to conquer Ramot Gilad, so that through this he would know that his killing of the prophets would be atoned for, as though it too had been killing in accord with Hashem's will. Therefore he did not succeed there.]”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek repeats this interpretation of Achav's proposed battle and adds its decisive outcome: he did not succeed. This keeps the siman's report of what Achav wanted to prove from being mistaken for approval of his claim that killing the prophets was righteous. The passage's own attribution of that attempted argument remains clear.
connections.headline: Achav's attempted claim was not vindicated

connections.hePhrase: (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פְּסִיקְתָּא רַבָּתִי פָּרָשָׁה יג),
connections.quote: see note 605 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The passage identifies the descendants of Rachel as those who overcome Amalek: Joshua comes from Ephraim, descended from Joseph, while the continuation also names Benjamin. This is the precise tradition Rav Tzadok uses in explaining why Amalek falls before Rachel’s descendants.

connections.hePhrase: מִיָּד "וַיָּבֹא עֲמָלֵק" (שְׁמוֹת יז, ח):
connections.quote: ‘Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם: "אִם יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶת כָּל הוֹן בֵּיתוֹ בָּאַהֲבָה וְגוֹמֵר" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ח, ז),
connections.quote: see note 673 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The biblical verse supplies the wording. The Midrash cited in Rav Tzadok’s continuation applies it to the nations’ inability to extinguish God’s love for Israel or purchase atonement with their wealth. Rav Tzadok contrasts material payment with a love that cannot be bought.

connections.hePhrase: [רנא] עַל יְדֵי הַחֵשֶׁק הוּא כְּלִי קִבּוּל
connections.quote: “On Chanukah we light eight lamps. The eighth alludes to understanding in the heart, the source of the seven lights mentioned above: the heart’s longing and will to reach the illumination of Torah so that it spreads within the heart. The deepest yearning to attain Torah’s light was revealed in the days of the Greek decree, which sought to abolish Torah and commandments. Their hearts were greatly broken by this: it seemed that Heaven was preventing them because their Torah and commandments were not accepted before God, like a servant whose pitcher is poured back into his face. Through this they grew bitter and their hearts’ longing to study Torah in secret increased. Even those who could not hide themselves and study had an even greater cry and longing within their hearts to attain Torah’s light. Through this they merited the miracle of finding iron spits to make the menorah, the vessel receiving the light of the seven lamps. It corresponds to the will in the heart, through which a vessel is made to receive Torah’s illumination.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah describes both those able to learn in secret and those prevented from doing so, whose yearning nevertheless deepened. It relates the resulting menorah to the heart made ready to receive illumination. This gives a concrete example of the present siman’s opening: the willing heart is itself part of building a dwelling for the Shechinah. The siman then distinguishes this varied measure of positive reception from the equal foundation shared by all Israel.
connections.headline: Longing for Torah can prepare a vessel even when its outward expression is obstructed

connections.hePhrase: [רנא] עַל יְדֵי הַחֵשֶׁק הוּא כְּלִי קִבּוּל
connections.quote: “The chief purpose in creating the world was that the Shekhinah should dwell primarily in the lower realm. On Shabbat He rose and sat upon His throne of glory: that is, He established His presence in the lower realm, and then held its dedication. The same applies to the dedication of the Mishkan and the Temple. Likewise, in the Hasmonean dedication they instituted that every Jew should dedicate a dwelling, for God dwells in the hearts of the children of Israel. This can be done “in those days, at this time.” It endures forever, even in exile and outside the Land of Israel. It commemorates the Mishkan’s dedication, which likewise took place in the wilderness, outside the Land. The Mishkan was not fixed in one location; wherever Israel encamped, they established its place, and there the divine presence dwelled.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah explains how the dwelling described in this siman is relevant beyond the original building of the Mishkan. Each person’s dedication of a house expresses the Shechinah’s dwelling in Jewish hearts, and this remains possible outside Eretz Yisrael and in exile. This preserves both dimensions of the siman: the divine purpose of dwelling below is shared, while the willing heart gives each person’s reception its particular measure and expression.
connections.headline: The dedication of a dwelling in the heart remains possible in exile

connections.hePhrase: "מֵאֵת כָּל אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִדְּבֶנּוּ לִבּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ב),
connections.quote: ‘Speak to the children of Israel, and let them take a contribution for Me. From every person whose heart moves him willingly, you shall take My contribution.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבָזֶה הוּא כָּל חַד לְפוּם מַה דִּמְשַׁעֵר בְּלִבֵּיהּ,
connections.quote: “Rather, ‘Her husband is known in the gates (bishe’arim)’: this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is known and cleaved to according to what each one measures (meshaer) in his heart, as far as he is able to cleave to the spirit of wisdom; and as he measures in his heart, so He is known in his heart. … But to know Him as He truly is, there has never been anyone able to cleave to Him and know Him.”
connections.context: The passage is on Zohar I 103b and expounds Proverbs 31:23.

connections.hePhrase: וְיֵשׁ עוֹד תְּרוּמַת הָאֲדָנִים וּדְקָרְבָּנוֹת,
connections.quote: “The contribution for the sockets indicates what we find: all Israel have a share in the World to Come. After the clarification, all Israel will be equal, so this contribution was equal; no one has an advantage over another in this. The altar contribution indicates that Israel arose first in divine thought; there too all are equal. The Mishkan contribution indicates how each person breaks through concealment so that Hashem dwells with him. Between the first choice of Israel and their share in the World to Come, a person must clarify why Hashem chose him before his service and why He establishes Torah with him permanently. Therefore this contribution is according to the willing heart: according to the effort is the reward. To the extent that a person breaks through concealment, Hashem dwells with him permanently.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef distinguishes the same three contributions. The sockets signify the equality reached after clarification, and the public offerings the common root before individual service. The freely given Mishkan contribution concerns the intervening work of breaking through concealment. This makes the siman's contrast precise: different intensity of longing describes the person's present reception without cancelling Israel's shared foundation or eventual equality.
connections.headline: Equal belonging and different measures of striving

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהּ: "הֶעָשִׁיר לֹא יַרְבֶּה וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת ל, טו),
connections.quote: ‘The wealthy shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than half a shekel when giving Hashem’s contribution to atone for your souls.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי דִּשְׁקָלִים (פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ד):
connections.quote: “It is written: “This they shall give, everyone who passes among those counted.” Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Neḥemya: one said, Because they sinned at midday, they shall give half a shekel. The other said, Because they sinned at the sixth hour, they shall give half a shekel, which amounts to six gramisin. Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Neḥemya said in the name of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai: Because they transgressed the Ten Commandments, each person shall give ten gerah.”
connections.context: This is the Yerushalmi’s explanation of the half-shekel as atonement for the sin of the golden calf. Rav Tzadok cites the passage as chapter 2, halakhah 4; the linked digital edition locates it at 2:3:5. His point is the common obligation of atonement, contrasted with the varying amounts of voluntary gifts for the Mishkan.

connections.hePhrase: "תָּמִיד שֶׁל שַׁחַר מְכַפֵּר וְכוּלֵי";
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon said: No person in Jerusalem ever had a sin remaining in his hand. How so? The morning daily offering atoned for the transgressions of the night, and the afternoon daily offering atoned for the transgressions committed during the day. In any event, no one spent the night in Jerusalem with a sin remaining in his hand, as it says, “Righteousness lodged in her,” and so forth (Isaiah 1:21).”

connections.hePhrase: אָז "תִּשְׂמַח בְּתוּלָה בְּמָחוֹל" (יִרְמְיָה לא, יב),
connections.quote: “Then the maiden shall rejoice in the dance, and young men and old men together; I shall turn their mourning into joy, comfort them, and gladden them after their sorrow.”
connections.context: The Hebrew verse numbered Jeremiah 31:12 in Rav Tzadok’s citation corresponds to 31:13 in the linked digital edition. The shared future dance introduces his comparison with the circle of the righteous in the next source.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא הַמָּחוֹל לַצַּדִּיקִים מִצַּד הָעִגּוּלִים,
connections.quote: ‘Ulla Bira’a said in Rabbi Elazar’s name: In the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will arrange a circle dance for the righteous, and He will sit among them in Gan Eden. Each one will point with his finger, as it is said: ‘It will be said on that day: Behold, this is our God; we have waited for Him, that He might save us. This is Hashem; we have waited for Him. Let us rejoice and be glad in His salvation.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיָן בַּמָּן גַּם כֵּן: "לֹא הֶעְדִּיף הַמַּרְבֶּה וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוֹת טז, יח),
connections.quote: ‘They measured with the omer, and the one who had gathered much had no excess, while the one who had gathered little had no shortage. Each had gathered according to what he would eat.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד הָיָה טוֹעֵם כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁרוֹצֶה, כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא עה.),
connections.quote: ‘‘Its taste was like the taste of the richness of oil—leshad hashamen.’ Rabbi Abbahu said: Just as a baby tastes many flavors at this breast, shad, so whenever Israel ate the manna they found many flavors in it. Some say: It refers to a shed, a demon, literally. Just as a demon changes into many forms, so the manna changes into many flavors.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר לֶעָתִיד: "וְלֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד וְגוֹמֵר" (יִרְמְיָה לא, לג),
connections.quote: see note 562 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Rav Tzadok’s Hebrew numbering, Jeremiah 31:33, corresponds to 31:34 in the linked edition. He cites “they shall all know Me” to describe a future shared knowledge of God, after distinguishing the varying degrees of Torah apprehension in this world.

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א, ג):
connections.quote: see note 1882 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: [רנב] הָאָדָם צָרִיךְ לְהַכִּיר כִּי הַחֵשֶׁק וּנְדִיבוּת לֵב שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.quote: “A person has the clearest recognition in the first produce, for there he recognizes explicitly that the entire power of growth comes from Hashem. The Torah therefore commanded, “You shall take from the first of all the fruit of the ground”: in the place where a person recognizes that Hashem has left him an opening to recognize “everything comes from You,” there he must return it to Hashem.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef applies the same verse “everything comes from You” to the first fruits, before possession and habit obscure the source of their growth. The gift is returned at the moment its dependence is clearest. This illuminates why the present siman begins by returning even the generous impulse to Hashem: that recognition is part of acquiring a lasting relation to the good, rather than merely surrendering ownership of it.
connections.headline: Returning the gift at the point of first recognition

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): "הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל",
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 14:1
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 14:1
connections.quote: “That is, there are two kinds of awakening of a person's intellect. One is the wisdom and intellect in the mind. This intellect belongs to him because he is human, for the nations, too, have intellect. There is also an awakening that comes from the understanding in the heart. This belongs to him specifically because he is a descendant of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for the blessed God dwells within the hearts of the children of Israel. Among the nations of the world, by contrast, this heart is absent. Therefore, among the nations of the world an evil thought is joined to an action, but not among Israel. Between a thought in the mind and its actual realization in action stands the heart, where a person may reconsider. Among the nations of the world, however, the heart is filled with evil, and he will certainly not reconsider. Concerning this they said: “If there is Torah among the nations, do not believe it.” For the essence of Torah is in the heart, as in the words of our Sages: “I cannot learn the Torah in another person's heart.” Thus all the Torah is held in his heart. Similarly, our Sages say: “According to the heart of Rabbi so-and-so,” and many other such expressions. “He has not done so for any nation,” but only for the children of Israel, of whom it is said: “The Rock of my heart and my portion—God forever.” As our Sages said concerning the verse “My heart is awake,” the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel. Therefore they possess an awakening understanding in the heart. This, too, offers assurance: that he will awaken through the wisdom and understanding the blessed God has bestowed upon him. But “it is better to take refuge in the blessed God.””

connections.hePhrase: "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ וְגוֹמֵר", "וּלְךָ הַכֹּל" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יד).
connections.quote: “Who am I, and who are my people, that we should have the strength to offer freely in this way? For everything is from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.”

connections.hePhrase: "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ וְגוֹמֵר", "וּלְךָ הַכֹּל" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יד).
connections.quote: “Lord our God, all this abundance that we have prepared to build You a house for Your holy name is from Your hand, and everything is Yours.”

connections.hePhrase: "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ וְגוֹמֵר", "וּלְךָ הַכֹּל" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יד).
connections.quote: “Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel our fathers, preserve this forever in the formation of the thoughts of Your people’s heart, and direct their heart toward You.”
connections.context: David’s prayer over the gifts for the Temple contains all three expressions used here. “Everything is from You” is in verse 14; “everything is Yours” is in verse 16; and the request to preserve this disposition forever is in verse 18. Rav Tzadok connects recognition of the divine source of generosity with its becoming enduring.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ: "שָׁמְרָה זֹּאת לְעוֹלָם וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, יח),
connections.quote: “King David likewise said, “With an upright heart I have willingly offered all these things; and now Your people,” and so forth, “joyfully offer willingly to You.” As stated earlier, “The people rejoiced over their willing offering, for with a whole heart they offered willingly,” and so forth. Afterward he prayed, “Preserve this forever for the inclination of the thoughts of Your people’s heart,” and so forth: that this desire should remain forever in Israel’s heart, with love and generosity for the blessed God’s honor, so that He should dwell continually among Israel. This means that there should be holiness in Israel’s bodies—the holiness of the actual performance of mitzvot, which requires the price of fear and love.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם "וְיִקְחוּ לִי תְּרוּמָה" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ב),
connections.quote: see note 4021.
connections.context: The wording matters to Rav Tzadok’s argument: “take” becomes an image of acquiring a lasting disposition; “for Me” connects the contribution with its divine source; and “My contribution” supports his explanation of the union of human desire with God’s will.

connections.hePhrase: דְּפֵירֵשׁ בַּזֹּהַר (תְּרוּמָה קלד ב, קמ ב) דְּהוּא יִחוּד, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ““They shall take for Me a contribution.” Here is union in one whole, above and below. It does not say, “They shall take a contribution,” but “They shall take for Me a contribution”: above and below in one whole, without any separation.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּפֵירֵשׁ בַּזֹּהַר (תְּרוּמָה קלד ב, קמ ב) דְּהוּא יִחוּד, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ““From every man whose heart moves him willingly, you shall take My contribution.” Why “from every man”? Here is a mystery for those who know. Happy are the righteous, who know how to direct their heart’s desire toward the holy supernal King. Their desire is not for this world and its empty longing; they strive to attach themselves above, to draw their Master’s will toward them from above to below.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּפֵירֵשׁ בַּזֹּהַר (תְּרוּמָה קלד ב, קמ ב) דְּהוּא יִחוּד, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: ““And this is the contribution”—this is the Congregation of Israel. Although all her love is toward Him and His love toward her, they take her from Him to dwell among them. … “From there you shall take My contribution.” Happy is the portion of Israel, and happy are all who merit this.”
connections.context: These passages on Terumah 134b–135a explain the union and the wording “from every man” and “My contribution,” to which Rav Tzadok returns later in the section. He develops their account of desire above and below as recognition that even the heart’s generosity comes from God.

connections.hePhrase: דְּפֵירֵשׁ בַּזֹּהַר (תְּרוּמָה קלד ב, קמ ב) דְּהוּא יִחוּד, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Therefore, “They shall take for Me a contribution.” It does not say, “They shall take Me and a contribution,” but “They shall take for Me a contribution,” to show that all is one without separation. The work of the Mishkan corresponds to that above, this opposite that, so that the Shekhinah is included from every side, above and below. Its work in this world is like a body that contains a spirit: this is the Shekhinah, which includes above and below and is the holy spirit.”
connections.context: This is the relevant explanation on Terumah 140b. The absence of “and” between “Me” and “a contribution” expresses the unity that Rav Tzadok invokes. The former note quoted only an earlier question about Moses and did not reach this explanation.

connections.hePhrase: עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מוֹעֵד קָטָן טז:): "הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא גּוֹזֵר וְצַדִּיק מְבַטֵּל",
connections.quote: ‘‘Tachkemoni’: Rav said: The Holy One, blessed be He, told him: Since you have humbled yourself, you shall be like Me, for I issue a decree and you annul it.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה סוֹד יִחוּדָא עִילָּאָה וְיִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה הַנִּזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם (קלד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: “They said: Just as there is only One in your heart—you belong to the mystery of the upper world, and it is one—so with us, who belong to the mystery of the lower world, it is one. Thus they mentioned two hearts: the mystery of the upper world, the heart of Jacob; and the mystery of the lower world, the heart of his sons. … Just as they unified the upper world in oneness and the lower world in oneness, so must we unify the upper world and the lower world.
