This has six sides and that has six sides; therefore there are six words here and six words there: “The Lord is one and His name is one.””
connections.context: This is the passage on Terumah 134b about the heart of Jacob and the hearts of his sons. The two sets of six words are Shema Yisrael and Barukh shem. It directly supports Rav Tzadok’s following explanation of the higher and lower unifications.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה סוֹד יִחוּדָא עִילָּאָה וְיִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה הַנִּזְכָּר בַּזֹּהַר, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם (קלד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב).
connections.quote: “These are the two unifications, upper and lower, of ‘Shema’ and ‘Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever.’ The Zohar explains that Shema is actual unity: the whole earth is filled with His glory, and no place in any bodies or creatures is empty of Him. This is upper unity. ‘Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever’ is lower unity, at the level of His kingship: there is no king without a people, and there are distinct powers, but He is the master of them all, as the name Elokim indicates, and He is their lord and king.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek supplies a complementary definition of the terms used here. Upper unity recognizes that no place is empty of the divine presence; lower unity recognizes His kingship through the powers that appear distinct. The present siman applies these recognitions to the movement between received wisdom and the willing heart. Its later insistence on the actual limits of bodily action remains part of that account.
connections.headline: The two unifications describe two recognitions

connections.hePhrase: דְּזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֵין בְּלִבְּךָ אֶלָּא אֶחָד וְכוּלֵי" (פְּסָחִים נו.),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: ‘Yaakov called to his sons and said: Gather together, and I will tell you.’ Yaakov wished to reveal the end of days to his sons, but the Divine Presence withdrew from him. He said, ‘Perhaps, Heaven forbid, there is a flaw among my offspring, as with Avraham, from whom Yishmael emerged, and my father Yitzchak, from whom Esav emerged?’ His sons said to him, ‘Hear, Israel: Hashem is our God, Hashem is one.’ They said, ‘Just as there is only One in your heart, so there is only One in our hearts.’ At that moment Yaakov our father began to say, ‘Blessed is the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever.’”

connections.hePhrase: הוּא כְּטַעַם אָמְרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לה:):
connections.quote: see note 2491.
connections.context: The sentence begins at the end of 35a and concludes at the beginning of 35b, the folio cited by Rav Tzadok. Blessing recognizes God as the source, after which a person may receive the benefit as a gift. Rav Tzadok uses this as a parallel to Torah becoming “his Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּלֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "אִמּוֹ" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב).
connections.quote: “Another matter, “they brought the Tabernacle” – that is what is written: “Emerge, daughters of Zion, and look at King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, and on the day of the rejoicing of his heart” (Song of Songs 3:11). When was this verse stated? On the day that the Tabernacle was set up, when there was great celebration in Israel because the Holy One blessed be He rested amongst them. “Daughters of Zion [tziyon]” – the children who are conspicuously [hametzuyanim] Mine, as acknowledged by the idolaters. Just as a signpost is pointed at with a finger, so, too, Israel is pointed at with a finger. That is, “the daughters of Zion.” “[Look] at King Solomon [Shlomo],” at the King of Whom [it may be said] that peace [hashalom] is His; that is the King of kings the Holy One blessed be He. “With the crown with which his mother crowned him,” this is the Tabernacle. Why did he call it a crown? Because just as a crown is beautifully designed, so, too, the Tabernacle was beautifully designed, as it is stated: “And the embroiderer in sky blue, purple, and scarlet wool, and in linen, and of the weaver, performers of all craftsmanship and devisers of designs” (Exodus 35:35). That is, “with the crown with which his mother crowned him.” Rabbi Yitzḥak said: I reviewed the entire Bible and I did not find that Batsheva crafted a crown for Solomon. Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai asked Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei: ‘Did you, perhaps, hear from your father what is meant by [the phrase]: “With the crown with which his mother crowned him”?’ He said to him: ‘Yes; it is analogous to a king who had an only daughter and he loved her exceedingly. He called her: My daughter. He did not cease increasing his love for her until he called her: My sister, and until he called her: My mother. So, initially, the Holy One blessed be He called Israel a daughter, as it is stated: “Listen, daughter, and take note; incline your ear. Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalms 45:11). He did not cease increasing His love for them until he called them: My sister, as it is stated: “Open for me, my sister, my love, my faultless dove, for my head is filled with dew, my locks, with drops of night” (Song of Songs 5:2). He did not cease increasing His love for them until he called them: My mother, as it is stated: “Pay attention to Me, My people, and listen to Me, My nation [uleumi]; for Torah will emerge from Me and My judgment I will lay down as a light for peoples”’ (Isaiah 51:4). Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai stood and kissed him on the head. “On the day of his wedding,” at Sinai; “and on the day of the rejoicing of his heart,” in Jerusalem. Alternatively, “on the day of his wedding,” at the sea; “and on the day of the rejoicing of his heart,” in the Tent of Meeting. Alternatively, “on the day of his wedding,” in the Tabernacle; “and on the day of the rejoicing of his heart,” in the Temple. Likewise, David said: “Beautiful in its view, joy of the entire world, is Mount Zion, the northern summit, the city of the great King.” (Psalms 48:3). “Beautiful in its view, joy of the entire world.” Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar said: There was an incident involving a certain merchant who went to Jerusalem to sell his merchandise. He went and sat there but did not sell [anything]. He said: ‘Is this [the city] of which they say it is the “joy of the entire world”?’ A short time later he sold all his merchandise. He said: “Beautiful in its view, joy of the entire world.” Rabbi Yoḥanan said: There was a dome of accounting outside of Jerusalem, and anyone who sought to take an accounting would go and take an accounting there, so that he would not take an accounting in Jerusalem and be distressed, for it is called “joy of the entire world.” Why is it the object of all this praise? Because it is “the city of the great King.” But when it was destroyed: “All joy is negated [arva], gladness of the land is exiled” (Isaiah 24:11). What is arva? It grew dark, just as it says: “It was evening [erev] and it was morning, one day” (Genesis 1:5). In this world, “the joy of the entire world” is suspended. But when the Holy One blessed be He will rebuild Jerusalem, He will restore all the joy to its midst, as it is stated: “For the Lord will comfort Zion; He will comfort all its ruins; He will render its wilderness like Eden and its desert like a garden of the Lord. Gladness and joy will be found in it, thanksgiving and the sound of music” (Isaiah 51:3).”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב אַחַר כָּךְ: "וְזֹאת הַתְּרוּמָה אֲשֶׁר תִּקְחוּ מֵאִתָּם" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ג) בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבִּים,
connections.quote: “And this is the contribution that you shall take from them: gold, silver, and copper.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok emphasizes “this” as something that can be pointed to: the contribution has reached actual performance. He also attends to the plural “you shall take” and “from them,” which he connects with a capacity shared by Israel.

connections.hePhrase: וְאָסוּר לְבַזְבֵּז כָּל מָמוֹנוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ כְּתוּבּוֹת נ.),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Ila said: In Usha they enacted that one who gives generously should not give away more than a fifth. It was likewise taught: One who gives generously should not give away more than a fifth, lest he come to depend on other people. An incident occurred in which someone wished to give away more than a fifth, but his companion did not allow him. Who was that companion? Rabbi Yeshevav. Some say that Rabbi Yeshevav was the one who wished to give, and his companion did not allow him. Who was that companion? Rabbi Akiva.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְמִצְוֹת "עַד שְׁלִישׁ בְּמִצְוָה" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא קַמָּא ט:),
connections.quote: ‘Rather, Rabbi Zeira said: To enhance a mitzvah, one adds up to a third of its price. Rav Ashi asked: A third of the original price, or a third of the total price including the addition? The question stands unresolved.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהַחֲטָאִים מְסוּדָּרִים וּבָאִים מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית (שַׁבָּת פט:),
connections.quote: see note 1017 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Gemara reads the word kashanim, “like scarlet,” also as “like years.” Its comparison is to the ordered years since Creation. Rav Tzadok develops that language into his account of the place of human failures within God’s encompassing purpose; the Gemara’s quoted wording should be distinguished from that further explanation.

connections.hePhrase: דִּגְמִירֵי דְּלָא כָּלֶה שִׁבְטָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קטו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: ‘How, then, does it work? The inheritance keeps tracing its way through the family line, all the way back to Reuben. Why not say all the way back to Jacob? Abaye said: We have a tradition that a tribe does not cease to exist.’

connections.hePhrase: הֲרֵי קַיְימָא לַן (בְּרָכוֹת יג.): "הַקּוֹרֵא אֶת שְׁמַע וְלֹא הִשְׁמִיעַ לְאָזְנוֹ – יָצָא",
connections.quote: ‘And the Rabbis? They hold like the one who says: If he did not make the words audible to his own ear, he has fulfilled his obligation. But according to the Rabbis too, is it not written, ‘And they shall be’? They need that to teach that one must not recite the passage out of order.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.): "מִי שֶׁטָּרַח בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת יֹאכַל בְּשַׁבָּת".
connections.quote: ‘They said before Him: ‘Master of the world, give it to us afresh, and we will fulfill it.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: ‘Fools of the world! One who labored on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat. One who did not labor on the eve of Shabbat—from where will he eat on Shabbat? Nevertheless, I have an easy mitzvah, called sukkah. Go and fulfill it.’’

connections.hePhrase: כָּךְ יֵשׁ נֶפֶשׁ נִבְחָר,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 3
connections.quote: ““And behold, Hashem was stationed over him.” It is known that the blessed God’s principal revelation within the world comes through three: world, year, and soul. “World” is the place of the Temple, where His divinity is revealed. “Year” is the choicest of times, Shabbat, in which His divinity is revealed. “Soul” means that He reveals His Divine Presence upon souls from Israel. Here all three were complete: the place of the Temple, as it says, “This is none other than the house of God”; the choicest time, for this revelation certainly occurred on the holy Shabbat; and the soul, our father Jacob, the choicest of souls, in whom all the souls of Israel were included, as it says (Isaiah 29:23), “They shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob.””

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם (סַנְהֶדְרִין סה:): "מַה יּוֹם מִיּוֹמַיִם? מַה גְּבַר מִגֻּבְרִין?".
connections.quote: ‘The wicked Turnus Rufus also asked Rabbi Akiva this question: ‘What makes one day different from the other days?’ Rabbi Akiva replied: ‘What makes one man different from other men?’ He answered: ‘My master wishes it so.’ ‘Shabbat too—its Master wishes it so.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַמָּקוֹם: עֶשֶׂר קְדוּשּׁוֹת (כֵּלִים פֶּרֶק א),
connections.quote: ‘There are ten degrees of holiness. The Land of Israel is holier than all other lands. What is its holiness? That the omer, the first fruits, and the two loaves are brought from it, whereas these are not brought from any of the other lands.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבַמָּקוֹם: יְרוּשָׁלַיִם הוּא קְדוּשַּׁת הַמָּקוֹם;
connections.quote: “The prayer that the rule of authority not depart from the house of Judah has this same intention. My holy father explained that he prayed to Hashem to attend continually and especially to the root. The tribe of Judah is the root of the life of all Israel; when the root is blessed, blessing will consequently not be lacking for the branches either.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the precise prayer quoted here: Judah is the common root, so blessing the root sustains the branches. The surrounding discussion says that the Kohen Gadol's inward service must be followed by prayer that the light become perceptible in ordinary human life. This clarifies why the siman places the Kohen Gadol and the prayer for kingship together within the sanctity of a particular soul, whose service bears upon the whole people.
connections.headline: Why the Kohen Gadol prays for Judah

connections.hePhrase: וּמְבַקֵּשׁ: "לָא יַעֲדֵי עָבֵיד שׁוּלְטָן מִדְּבֵית יְהוּדָה" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ יוֹמָא נג:) גַּם כֵּן קְדוּשַּׁת נֶפֶשׁ,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Acha son of Rava would conclude it in Rav Yehudah’s name: ‘May one who exercises rule never depart from the house of Judah. May Your people Israel not need one another for their sustenance. And may the prayer of travelers not enter before You.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכַוָּנַת הַלֵּב הוּא "בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ", שֶׁזֶּהוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל דִּמְקַדְּשֵׁי.
connections.quote: “‘Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons’—that is, Israel, who sanctify the seasons. ‘Who sanctifies Israel and the New Moons’—Israel, who sanctify the New Moons.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבַנְּפָשׁוֹת יֵשׁ מֶלֶךְ, וְהוּא נֶגֶד הַלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה,
connections.quote: “The teli in the world is like a king upon his throne. The sphere in the year is like a king in his province. The heart in the soul is like a king in battle. God also made every matter, one opposite the other: good opposite evil, good from good and evil from evil. Good makes evil discernible, and evil makes good discernible. Good is reserved for the good, and evil is reserved for the wicked.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ (יוֹמָא יח.): "גַּדְּלֵהוּ מִשֶּׁל אֶחָיו" בְּעוֹשֶׁר,
connections.quote: ‘But it was taught: ‘The priest who is greater than his brothers’—he must be greater than his brothers in strength, beauty, wisdom, and wealth. Others say: From where do we know that, if he lacks wealth, his fellow priests must make him great? Scripture says: ‘The priest who is made great through his brothers’—make him great from his brothers’ resources.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי שִׂפְתֵי כֹהֵן יִשְׁמְרוּ דַעַת וְתוֹרָה יְבַקְשׁוּ מִפִּיהוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (מַלְאָכִי ב, ז).
connections.quote: ‘For a priest’s lips should guard knowledge, and people should seek Torah from his mouth, for he is a messenger of Hashem of hosts.’

connections.hePhrase: לֹא מִי שֶׁמְּקוֹרָר בְּטִבְעוֹ וְאֵינוֹ בַּעַל תַּאֲוָה,
connections.quote: “The distinction is this: the evils that the philosophers call evils, concerning which they say that one who does not desire them is superior to one who desires them but restrains his inclination, are matters recognized by all people as evil: bloodshed, theft, robbery, fraud, harming someone who has done one no harm, repaying a benefactor with evil, dishonoring father and mother, and similar things. These are the commandments of which the Sages of blessed memory said, “Had they not been written, they would have deserved to be written” (Yoma 67b). Some of our later scholars, afflicted by the sickness of the theologians, call them “rational commandments.” There is no doubt that a soul that longs for any of these things and desires it is deficient. An excellent soul does not desire any of these evils at all, and is not distressed by refraining from them. The matters concerning which the Sages said that one who restrains his inclination is superior and receives a greater reward, however, are the laws received through revelation. This is true, because without the Torah they would not have been evils at all. Therefore they said that a person should allow his soul to desire them, with only the Torah preventing him from them. Consider their wisdom, peace be upon them, and the examples they gave. They did not say: “A person should not say, ‘I do not wish to kill a person; I do not wish to steal; I do not wish to lie,’ but rather, ‘I wish to, yet what can I do? My Father in Heaven has decreed against it.’” Instead, all their examples were revealed laws: meat with milk, wearing wool and linen together, and forbidden sexual unions. These commandments, and others like them, are what the blessed God calls “statutes.””

connections.hePhrase: לֹא מִי שֶׁמְּקוֹרָר בְּטִבְעוֹ וְאֵינוֹ בַּעַל תַּאֲוָה,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ט״ו:ד׳-ח׳
connections.quote: “Among the intermediate people there are also two levels: “one who serves God” and “one who has not served Him.” Nevertheless, the latter is not wicked: he has never committed even a minor transgression, has fulfilled every mitzvah he could fulfill, and has engaged in Torah study, which is equal to them all, without ceasing his review. Yet he does not wage any battle to overcome the inclination through Hashem’s light illuminating the divine soul in the brain, which rules the heart, as explained above. His inclination does not oppose him at all to distract him from Torah and service, and he has no need to fight it. For example, he may be diligent in study by his inborn nature, because of a predominance of “black bile”; he may have no struggle with desire for women because he is naturally cold, and likewise may naturally lack a feeling of pleasure in other worldly enjoyments. He therefore need not contemplate Hashem’s greatness so extensively in order to generate from his understanding a spirit of knowledge and fear of Hashem in his brain, to guard against violating prohibitions, and love of Hashem in his heart, to cling to Him through performing the mitzvot and Torah study, which is equal to them all. The hidden love in the heart of Israel as a whole, called “those who love His name,” is sufficient for him. He is therefore not called “one who serves” at all, for this hidden love is not his own action or labor, but our inheritance from our ancestors for all Israel, as will be explained below. Likewise, even someone who is not naturally diligent in study, but has trained himself to study with great diligence until habit becomes second nature, can suffice with this hidden love—unless he wishes to study beyond his usual measure.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה כז:): "מְשַׁבֵּחַ אֲנִי אֶת הָעַצְלָנִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: see note 3937.
connections.context: Remaining at home can serve the mitzvah of rejoicing with one’s household, even when the immediate motive is laziness. Rav Tzadok distinguishes this beneficial result from the greater achievement of overcoming a strong opposing inclination.

connections.hePhrase: וְ"עָצֵל וְנִשְׂכָּר" קָרֵינַן לֵיהּ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פְּסָחִים נ:);
connections.quote: “The Sages taught: Some are diligent and rewarded, and some are diligent and lose out. Some are idle and rewarded, and some are idle and lose out. Diligent and rewarded: one who works all week but does not work on Shabbat eve. Diligent and losing out: one who works all week and also works on Shabbat eve. Idle and rewarded: one who does not work all week and does not work on Shabbat eve. Idle and losing out: one who does not work all week but works on Shabbat eve. Rava said: Although the women of Mechoza do not work on Shabbat eve, it is because they are accustomed to luxury, for they do not work on the other days either. Nevertheless, we call them ‘idle and rewarded.’”

connections.hePhrase: בָּזֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְנַסּוֹ "לָדַעַת אֵת אֲשֶׁר בִּלְבָבוֹ".
connections.quote: ‘Remember the entire road on which Hashem your God led you these forty years in the wilderness, to humble you and test you, to know what was in your heart: whether you would keep His commandments or not.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנִסָּיוֹן יִצְחָק – בְּמַאֲמַר "גּוּר בָּאָרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כו, ג),
connections.quote: ‘Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and bless you. For I will give all these lands to you and to your descendants, and I will uphold the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיִּזְרַע יִצְחָק וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם, יב) – עֵסֶק הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
connections.quote: “Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in that year a hundredfold, and Hashem blessed him.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאִם לֹא עָמַד בּוֹ כְּאִלּוּ לֹא עָמַד בְּכֻלָּם (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נו),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Ḥanin said: “Because you have done this thing”—it was the tenth trial, yet you say, “Because you have done this thing”? Rather, this final trial weighed as much as all the others; had he not accepted it upon himself, he would have lost everything.”
connections.context: The Midrash speaks of Abraham’s acceptance of the binding of Isaac as the decisive completion of his trials. Rav Tzadok uses this to explain why the final trial can represent a whole sequence of spiritual clarification.

connections.hePhrase: וְנִסָּיוֹן הָעֲשִׂירִי שֶׁלּוֹ הָיָה בְּלָבָן: "דְּמָה מַשְׂכֻּרְתֶּךָ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כט, טו),
connections.quote: ‘Laban said to Jacob: ‘Because you are my kinsman, should you serve me for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בִּקְנִיַּת הַמְּעָרָה כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה לא),
connections.quote: “When Isaac died, Jacob and Esau came and divided everything. Jacob said: This wicked man and his sons will enter the Cave of Machpelah and have a share and a dwelling with the righteous buried there. At once he took all the money in his possession, made it into a heap, and said to Esau: My brother, would you prefer your share in this cave, or this silver and gold? … Esau took all that money and gave him his share. This is what Jacob said to Joseph: “In my grave that I dug for myself”—it does not say “purchased” but “dug”: I gave Esau a heap of dinars.”
connections.context: The play on kariti, “I dug,” and keri, “a heap,” explains Jacob’s purchase of Esau’s share in the burial cave. Although possessions were precious to Jacob, he gave them up for this holy acquisition. This is the portion of the long Midrash needed for Rav Tzadok’s argument.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בְּנוּקְבָא תּוֹקֶף הַחֵשֶׁק שֶׁאֵין לוֹ מִלּוּי וּשְׂבִיעָה,
connections.quote: “The fundamental power of deficiency in the world is called “woman” and “female,” as is known. The essence of deficiency seeks completion; only the power of completion’s hidden root descends into the world, and it seeks to be completed in perfection. This is called desire, the inclination of the human heart that longs for that one measure. Concerning this it says, “Three are never satisfied,” because that measure of the hidden root is expansive, and what is deficient wishes to be completed so that it too will be expansive like that measure. In truth this is impossible, because the nine measures that are existence from nothing are bounded and contracted, and from this comes their existence. Infinite expansion is nothingness, not a distinct existent, for a distinct existent is what is bounded. Nevertheless, it has no satiety, wishing to resemble its cause and source of influence. These are “the grave and the closed womb,” in the sense of “One who loves silver (will not be satisfied with silver).” The Sages of blessed memory expounded this in Leviticus Rabbah: “One who loves mitzvot (will not be satisfied with mitzvot).” It also bears its plain meaning regarding worldly desire, which is the grave.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ד) עַל פָּסוּק "שְׁאוֹל וְעֹצֶר רָחַם" (מִשְׁלֵי ל, טז).
connections.quote: “Because the soul knows that all its exertion is for itself, it is never satisfied with mitzvot and good deeds. Rabbi Levi said: It is like a villager married to a king’s daughter: even if he feeds her all the delicacies in the world, he does not discharge his obligation, because she is a king’s daughter. So, whatever a person does for his soul does not discharge his obligation, because it comes from above. Three are ungrateful: the earth, the woman, and the soul. … Concerning the soul: “The soul is also not filled.””
connections.context: The Midrash connects the soul’s inability to be filled with its origin above, and places earth, woman, and soul together in a discussion of insatiability. Rav Tzadok develops the aspect of unending desire and its redirection toward God. The biblical phrase “Sheol and the closed womb” is quoted separately in the following note.

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ד) עַל פָּסוּק "שְׁאוֹל וְעֹצֶר רָחַם" (מִשְׁלֵי ל, טז).
connections.quote: ‘Sheol, the barren womb, the earth that is not sated with water, and fire that never says, ‘Enough.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא לֹא עָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן,
connections.quote: “Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: A person should never bring himself into a trial, for David king of Israel brought himself into a trial and failed. He said before Him: Master of the universe, why do they say “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob,” but not “God of David”? He said: They were tried before Me, but you were not tried before Me. He said: Master of the universe, examine me and try me.”
connections.context: This is the direct source for the statement at this marker that David did not withstand the trial. His later explanation of “that You may be justified in Your word” belongs at the separate citation near the end of the section.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט) עָלָיו.
connections.quote: see note 358 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Midrash identifies the driving force of ordinary human activity with the inclination that can become destructive. Rav Tzadok focuses on that force at its strongest and explains how unending desire can be drawn toward God.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְחָלָה זוֹ הוּא גֶּדֶר "טוֹב מְאֹד"
connections.displayRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:27
connections.canonicalRef: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:27
connections.quote: ““Am I not devoted?” A devoted person is separated from envy, desire and honor, which take a person out of the world. Corresponding to them are the three things on which the world stands. Torah repairs desire, as in “a tree of life is a desire fulfilled.” Desire—the condition of always wanting more than one has—was principally created for Torah, as the Sages interpreted “one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver.” When a person places his desire in Torah, he is saved from worldly desires. Rambam writes that desire is found only in a heart empty of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Dover Tzedek identifies the proper use of a desire that is never satisfied: increasing in Torah. This helps explain why the siman relates endless longing to teshuvah and to never considering oneself complete. The constructive direction is renewed attachment and growth; the cited paragraph does not make committing a transgression a method of acquiring that growth.
connections.headline: A desire whose proper object has no end

connections.hePhrase: מַדְרֵגַת: "אוֹהֵב כֶּסֶף לֹא יִשְׂבַּע כֶּסֶף" (מַכּוֹת י.).
connections.quote: ‘One who loves money is not satisfied with money; one who loves a multitude [of attendants] has no yield. This too is futility.’

connections.hePhrase: מַדְרֵגַת: "אוֹהֵב כֶּסֶף לֹא יִשְׂבַּע כֶּסֶף" (מַכּוֹת י.).
connections.quote: “Rabbi Simai taught: “One who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver”—this is Moses our teacher. He knew that the three cities across the Jordan would not admit fugitives until the three cities in the land of Canaan had been designated, yet he said: A mitzvah that has come into my hand, I shall fulfill.”
connections.context: The rabbinic reading turns unsatisfied love of silver into an image of unsatisfied love of mitzvot. This is the positive form of unending desire that Rav Tzadok invokes.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם טַעֲנָתוֹ: "לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ו),
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 1
connections.quote: “Judah corresponds to the cupbearer, for David is called the King's entertainer, and David's songs are heard over the wine libation. In Judah's act with Tamar and the similar acts of his tribe, Hashem placed in them such a power of desire that they were unable to overcome it, as the Midrash explains that the angel appointed over desire compelled him. He is therefore not held guilty for what he could not overcome. This is the meaning of the King's entertainer: he allows himself to be overcome by Hashem. As David said, “So that You be justified in Your words”: whom does it befit to be justified, me or You?”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach discusses the same words, “so that You be justified,” through the contrast between Yosef and Judah. It first stresses that Yosef was given the power to overcome his desire and was therefore judged with exceptional rigor; only then does it discuss the distinct account of Judah. This provides context for Rav Tzadok's difficult conclusion about David. Both are particular expositions of these figures and their divine clarification, rather than a general instruction to choose sin or dispense with the restraint demanded at the siman's opening.
connections.headline: A particular account of Judah and David

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְאַמַּר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קז.),
connections.quote: see note 1023 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the explanation of David’s plea that Rav Tzadok develops here. He interprets it in terms of David’s continuing dependence on God and refusal to regard himself as spiritually complete. The Gemara’s wording is attributed to Rava.

connections.hePhrase: [רנה] בְּדָבָר שֶׁהָאָדָם חָסֵר בּוֹ וְצָרִיךְ תִּיקּוּן עַל יְדֵי הִתְנַהֲגוּת בַּהֵיפֶךְ,
connections.quote: “What is their cure? A person prone to anger is told to train himself so that even if he is struck and cursed, he takes no notice at all. He should follow this course for a long time, until anger is uprooted from his heart. If he is haughty, he should conduct himself with great self-abasement: sit below everyone, wear worn-out rags that bring their wearer into contempt, and do similar things, until haughtiness is uprooted from him and he returns to the middle way, which is the good way. Once he returns to the middle way, he should follow it all his days. He should proceed along these lines with all the other character traits: if he has gone far toward one extreme, he should move far toward the other extreme and conduct himself that way for a long time, until he returns to the good way, which is the intermediate measure in every character trait.”

connections.hePhrase: [רנה] בְּדָבָר שֶׁהָאָדָם חָסֵר בּוֹ וְצָרִיךְ תִּיקּוּן עַל יְדֵי הִתְנַהֲגוּת בַּהֵיפֶךְ,
connections.quote: “Protective repentance, although he does not cite it from the Gemara, is explained in “This One Selects”: dice players do not play even without stakes; an interest lender does not lend even to a non-Jew; and pigeon racers do not do it even in the wilderness. See there.”
connections.explanation: Takanat HaShavin names the precise category used here: teshuvat ha-geder, repentance through a protective boundary, with the same examples of gambling and lending. This explains why the siman distinguishes this person from someone else for whom the act could be a mitzvah. Its explicit condition remains essential: the proposed abstention must not itself involve a transgression. The note concerns the extra boundary needed for repair, rather than a general cancellation of obligations.
connections.headline: Protective repentance concerns the person needing repair

connections.hePhrase: כִּדְשָׁמְעִינַן (סַנְהֶדְרִין כה:) בְּמַלְוֶה בְּרִבִּית
connections.quote: “The rule concerning a lender at interest applies to both the lender and the borrower. When is their repentance recognized? When they tear up their loan documents and make a complete withdrawal from this practice, so that they no longer lend at interest even to a gentile. Those who fly pigeons are those who incite pigeons to fight one another. This was said not only of pigeons, but even of domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds. When is their repentance recognized? When they break the boards with which they urge the animals on and make a complete withdrawal from this practice, so that they do not do it even in the wilderness.”

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם שֶׁיֵּשׁ מִצְוָה דְּ"לַנָּכְרִי תַשִּׁיךְ",
connections.quote: “To the foreigner you shall lend at interest, but to your brother you shall not lend at interest, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all that you undertake in the land that you are entering to possess.”

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם שֶׁיֵּשׁ מִצְוָה דְּ"לַנָּכְרִי תַשִּׁיךְ",
connections.heRef: משנה תורה, הלכות מלווה ולווה ה׳:א׳
connections.quote: “It is a positive commandment to lend to a non-Jew at interest, as it is said: “To the foreigner you shall lend at interest.” By received tradition they learned that this is a positive commandment.”
connections.context: The second source explains the commandment reading assumed by Rav Tzadok; the verse alone, rendered as permission, did not explain his wording. He is discussing the special corrective discipline of a person who had sinned through forbidden interest, whose complete repentance requires avoiding even the otherwise permitted activity.

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי סַנְהֶדְרִין פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ג)
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehuda bar Pazi said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: This teaches that David would have their hair braided, adorn them, and bring them before him every day. He would say to his evil inclination: You desired what was forbidden to you; by your life, I shall make you desire what is permitted to you.”
connections.context: The passage discusses David’s concubines after Absalom’s rebellion. On Rabbi Yoḥanan’s account, David deliberately refrained from a permitted relationship as discipline for his inclination; the sages of Caesarea give a different explanation, that the women were actually forbidden to him. Rav Tzadok is developing the first account. The speaker addressing his inclination is David.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן הַקְדָּמַת רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה דְּמָרְדֳּכַי בְּבִגְתָן וָתֶרֶשׁ (בִּמְגִילָּה יג:),
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Bigthan and Teresh were two Tarsians who spoke in the Tarsian language. They said: Since this woman came, we have seen no sleep. Let us put poison in the cup so that he will die. They did not know that Mordecai was among those who sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone and knew seventy languages.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן הַקְדָּמַת רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה דְּמָרְדֳּכַי בְּבִגְתָן וָתֶרֶשׁ (בִּמְגִילָּה יג:),
connections.quote: ““After these events”—Rava said: After the Holy One, blessed be He, had created a remedy for the blow. For Resh Lakish said: The Holy One, blessed be He, does not strike Israel unless He has first created a remedy for them, as it is said: “When I would heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim is revealed.””
connections.context: Mordecai’s discovery of the plot precedes Haman’s promotion and becomes the means of the later reversal. Rav Tzadok examines the inward character correction corresponding to that outward remedy. The added quotation supplies the actual “remedy before the blow” statement, which the old note omitted.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה עִנְיַן הַקְדָּמַת רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה דְּמָרְדֳּכַי בְּבִגְתָן וָתֶרֶשׁ (בִּמְגִילָּה יג:),
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 5:2
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 5:2
connections.quote: “This is the reason for Mordechai's intention in rescuing him from Bigtan and Teresh (Esther 2:21–23). Even during this intense darkness of slumber he understood ‘all that had happened’ (4:1), the purpose of it all, and knew the matter through the holy spirit. He apprehended that Esther's root was the root of the congregation of Israel, and that her being seized by Achashverosh was no accident. It would have seemed more fitting to rescue her and seek Achashverosh's death. He did not do so because he understood that everything was truly under Hashem's providence.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim asks the same question: why rescue Achashverosh when Esther needed deliverance? Here the answer emphasizes Mordechai's recognition that her situation belonged to divine providence even during concealment. This adds another aspect to the siman's analysis of correcting a personal motive; the two explanations are not presented as identical.
connections.headline: Recognizing providence in Mordechai's rescue

connections.hePhrase: וְדִלְכָכָן תִּקְּנוּ מִשְׁלוֹחַ מָנוֹת בְּפוּרִים
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Megillah 7a:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Megillah 7a:1
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yosef taught: “Sending portions, one to another”—two gifts to one person; “and gifts to the poor”—two gifts to two people. The distinction between sending portions and gifts to the poor is this. The Men of the Great Assembly established these two enactments after the miracle because Shushan the capital was in the province of Elam. Elam merited learning but did not merit teaching, as stated in Pesaḥim 87a: “We have a little sister, and she has no breasts”—this is Elam, which merited learning but not teaching, and so forth. This is because the root of the Persian kingdom and that nation’s character is narrowness of spirit, as explained in its place; therefore it did not merit teaching. But when the Men of the Great Assembly investigated where the decree had arisen at its root and recognized that it arose from narrowness of spirit, immediately upon their discovering the truth, salvation came and the decree was annulled. They therefore afterward instituted these two mitzvot, whose root is generosity. The mitzvah was divided in two. “Sending portions, one to another” means to righteous and upright people: two gifts, meaning that one should expand in generosity to give with both hands. For the poor and needy, however, one must give to anyone who extends a hand; the group includes people of different levels. Here one gift signifies the obligation, without that expansive giving. This also explains what is taught in Peah 4:1: even if ninety-nine say to distribute and one says to let them gather for themselves, one listens to the one who speaks according to the law. Since among the poor there are also those unworthy to receive directly from one’s hand, the mitzvah is to leave it for them to gather. The Men of the Great Assembly thus enacted this because they understood that the decree had grown from the beginning of narrowness of spirit. They recognized this, and immediately when it became clear to them the decree was annulled; afterward they established this enactment. Likewise, the root of the growth of evil decrees—may they not come upon Israel—is only the deficiency present in their hearts at that time. If we can reach its root, it can be annulled immediately, as it was in the days of the Men of the Great Assembly.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן נִרְאֶה מִמַּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.):
connections.quote: ‘But the Master said: A sign of arrogance is poverty, and poverty descended to Babylonia! What poverty is meant? Poverty of Torah, as it is written: ‘We have a little sister, and she has no breasts.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: This is Elam, which merited learning but did not merit teaching.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן נִרְאֶה מִמַּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כד.):
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Night of Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach 16:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Night of Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach 16:1
connections.quote: ““Your name is oil poured out”: words of Torah are always greatly generous and seek to give themselves to Israel's pure heart, as in “wine and milk without price.” This is the opposite of the other side, which is extremely narrow of eye. Though it too is called “free,” as the Zohar interprets the fish eaten in Egypt without blessing or the higher yoke, its wish to hide the light and leave creation in darkness is the greatest narrowness of eye. Torah, however, continually shines its light with great generosity.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes giving light from withholding it, even when both may outwardly be called “free.” This illuminates the siman's explanation of the request “to learn and teach”: the desired good is that another receive what one knows and be able to stand equally. It is this generosity, rather than the pursuit of the status of a teacher, that reverses narrowness of eye.
connections.headline: Teaching as generosity of eye

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל "לִלְמוֹד וּלְלַמֵּד",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Tetzaveh 3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Tetzaveh 3
connections.quote: ““And to teach” corresponds to the forehead plate. Concerning the forehead plate it says, “It shall be upon his forehead continually, for acceptance”: this means that a person should have a generous eye in teaching his fellow.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ד:): "אֵין הַסָּתָה בְּלֹא אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה",
connections.quote: ‘But perhaps he slaughtered the animals and did not eat! It is written, ‘He enticed him.’ But perhaps it was with words? Enticement is not through words [alone].’

connections.hePhrase: [וְכִדְשָׁמְעִינַן בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ח.):
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael says: Israelites outside the Land are worshippers of idolatry in purity. How so? A gentile held a feast for his son and invited all the Jews in his city. Even though they eat their own food and drink their own drink, and their own attendant stands before them, Scripture accounts it to them as though they ate sacrifices to the dead, as it is said: ‘He will invite you, and you will eat of his sacrifice.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְתוֹקֶף כֹּחַ הָאוּמָּה בְּיוֹתֵר הוּא בַּמֶּלֶךְ,
connections.quote: “Every king is the root of his entire nation. Therefore a king in the world is likened to the heart in the body: it is the body’s root, and from it life proceeds to all the limbs. When Israel is under their rule (that of the nations), this is the exile of the Divine Presence, which is the kingdom of Heaven clothing itself in them in order to impart influence to Israel through them.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יב סוֹף עַמּוּד א):
connections.quote: “‘There was no compulsion’: Rabbi Elazar said that this teaches that each person was served wine from his own country. ‘To do according to the wish of each and every man’: Rava said, ‘To do according to the wishes of Mordechai and Haman.’ Mordechai is called ‘a Jewish man,’ and Haman is called ‘a man who is an adversary and an enemy.’”

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֶסְתֵּר, הוּבָא בְּתוֹסָפוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין סא:)
connections.quote: “If you ask: According to Rava, why did Mordecai not bow to Haman? One may answer as it says in the Midrash: There were images upon his chest. Alternatively, it was for the sanctification of God’s name.”
connections.context: Tosafot discusses the status of bowing from love or fear and gives two explanations of Mordecai’s refusal. Rav Tzadok invokes the first: Haman bore idolatrous images, so refusing him also corrected the earlier bowing to an image. This is the Tosafot passage cited in the body, rather than the Gemara’s general formulation of Abaye’s position.

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם", דִּלְוּלֵי כֵן כְּלֹא הָיָה.
connections.quote: ‘You alone are Hashem. You made the heavens, the heavens of heavens and all their host, the earth and everything upon it, the seas and everything in them. You give life to them all, and the host of heaven bows down to You.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם", דִּלְוּלֵי כֵן כְּלֹא הָיָה.
connections.displayRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 2:1-7
connections.linkedRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 2:1-7
connections.canonicalRef: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 2:1-7
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שני; שער היחוד והאמונה ב׳:א׳-ז׳
connections.quote:
“Here is the answer to the heretics, and the exposure of the root of the error of those who deny individual providence and the signs and wonders of the Torah. In their false imagination they mistakenly compare Hashem’s work—‘the Maker of heaven and earth’—to human work and craftsmanship. Once a vessel has left the craftsman’s hands, it no longer needs him: even when his hands have withdrawn from it and he goes away to the market, the vessel remains in precisely the form and shape it had when it left his hands. These foolish people imagine the making of heaven and earth in the same way.

But ‘their eyes are shut against seeing’ the great difference between human work and craftsmanship, which make something from something already existing—merely changing its form and shape from a piece of silver into a vessel—and the making of heaven and earth, which brings something into being from nothing.

This is a greater wonder than, for example, the splitting of the Red Sea. ‘Hashem drove the sea back with a strong east wind all that night, and the waters were divided’; they ‘stood like a heap’ and like a wall. Had Hashem stopped the wind for a moment, the water would have returned and flowed downward in its usual, natural way, and would certainly not have remained standing like a wall. This is so even though this nature of water was itself created and brought into being from nothing: a stone wall stands by itself without wind, but the nature of water is different.

All the more so with creation from nothing, which transcends nature and is an even greater wonder than the splitting of the Red Sea. If the Creator’s power were to withdraw from the created being, Heaven forbid, the created being would return to actual nothingness and nonexistence. Rather, the power of the maker must remain continually within what is made, giving it life and sustaining it. These are the letters of speech of the ten utterances through which the created beings were made.

Of this it is said, ‘You give life to them all.’ Read not merely ‘give life’ but ‘bring into being’—that is, bring something into being from nothing. ‘You’—atah—signifies the letters from alef to tav, while the hei signifies the five organs of speech, the source of the letters. These are the letters of speech of the ten utterances through which the created beings were made.

Although He has no bodily likeness, Scripture states explicitly, ‘Hashem spoke’ and ‘Hashem said.’ This is the revelation of the twenty-two supernal letters to the prophets. They are clothed in the prophets’ intellect and comprehension in the prophetic vision, and also in their thought and speech, as it is written: ‘The spirit of Hashem spoke through me, and His word was upon my tongue,’ and as the Ari, of blessed memory, explained in the Gate of Prophecy.

The letters are similarly clothed in created beings, as it is written: ‘By the word of Hashem the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their host.’ This, however, takes place through numerous and immense stages of descent, until the letters descend into physical action. By contrast, the prophets’ apprehension is in Atzilut as it is clothed in the World of Beriah.”

connections.hePhrase: דִּבְגָלוּת הַשֶּׁפַע הוֹלֵךְ לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְיִשְׂרָאֵל קוֹלְטִין תַּמְצִית.
connections.quote: “When Israel were in the Holy Land, sustenance descended to them from a supernal place, and they gave a share of the remainder to the idol-worshipping nations; all the nations were nourished only from the remainder. Now that Israel are in exile, the arrangement has been reversed. It is like a king who prepared a meal for his household. As long as they carry out his will, they eat the meal with the king and give the dogs a portion of bones to gnaw. When his household do not carry out the king’s will, the king gives the whole meal to the dogs and sets aside bones for them. So too, as long as Israel carry out their Master’s will, they eat at the King’s table and the whole meal is prepared for them. Out of their joy, they give the bones—the remainder—to the idol-worshippers. When Israel do not carry out their Master’s will, they go into exile; the meal goes to the dogs, and the remainder is set aside for them: “Thus shall the children of Israel eat their bread impure among the nations,” for they eat the remainder of their defilement. Woe to the king’s son who sits waiting at the servant’s table and eats what is left over from that table.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהָיְתָה צַדֶּקֶת גְּמוּרָה וּבַעֲלַת רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כִּדְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יד:),
connections.quote: ‘Esther, as it is written: ‘On the third day, Esther clothed herself in royalty.’ It should have said ‘royal garments’! Rather, the holy spirit clothed her. Here it is written, ‘She clothed herself,’ and there it is written, ‘A spirit clothed Amasai,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי עִיקַּר רָזֵי תּוֹרָה לֹא נִגְלָה אֶלָּא בְּבַיִת שֵׁנִי,
connections.heRef: אוצר מדרשים, היכלות, היכלות רבתי קמ״ד
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yishmael said: Thus Rabbi Akiva said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: From the day the Torah was given until the later Temple was built, the Torah was given, but its splendor was not given. Its honor, greatness and beauty; its awe, dread and fear; the crown of its majesty and exaltation; its radiance and brilliance; its strength and might, dominion and power—these were not given until the later Temple was built and the Divine Presence dwelled in it.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת "חָכָם עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא",
connections.quote: ‘Ameimar said: A sage is greater than a prophet, as it says: ‘And a prophet has a heart of wisdom.’ Who is compared to whom? You must say: The lesser is compared to the greater.’

connections.hePhrase: עַיֵּין בָּרַמְבַּ״ן פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.) הַטַּעַם, דְּנוֹבֵעַ מִמָּקוֹם יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל,
connections.heRef: חידושי רמב"ן על בבא בתרא י״ב א:א׳
connections.quote: see note 929 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Ramban distinguishes a prophet’s explicit vision from the inward apprehension of a sage. Rav Tzadok uses that distinction to explain how wisdom can reach beyond prophecy while remaining concealed rather than appearing as an openly heard divine statement.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם בִּנְיַן בַּיִת שֵׁנִי עַל יְדֵי מַלְכֵי פָּרַס,
connections.quote: “This is also the hint in what is said in Berakhot 8b: “In three matters I love the Persians: they are modest in their eating, modest in the privy, and modest in another matter.” For this is the root of modesty. Yet close to it the Sages said, “‘I have commanded My consecrated ones’—these are the Persians, who are consecrated and prepared for Gehinnom.” Among Israel, this matter is holiness—restraining oneself in modesty—whereas among them it is only the outward appearance, and they are consecrated for Gehinnom. This was explained in discourse 14.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah places the praise of Persian modesty beside its criticism and distinguishes the outward form from its inward purpose. This clarifies the precise extraction described in the present siman: Esther receives the holy quality of concealed service, rather than adopting the intention in which that quality had been clothed. The siman’s later discussion of her concealed holiness depends on this distinction between the appearance of an act and the direction of the heart within it.
connections.headline: The holiness of modesty depends on what its concealment serves

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ח:): "בְּשַׁבָּת הַפַּרְסִיִּים צְנוּעִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘It was taught: Rabban Gamliel said: I love the Persians for three things: They are modest in their eating, modest in the privy, and modest in another matter (sexual relations). ‘I have commanded My consecrated ones’—Rav Yosef taught: These are the Persians, who are set apart and destined for Gehinnom.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק דְּמַיְיתֵי עֲלָהּ תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ: "אֵלּוּ פַּרְסִיִּים הַמְקוּדָּשִׁים לְגֵיהִנָּם",
connections.quote: ““I have commanded My consecrated ones.” Rav Yosef taught: These are the Persians, who are consecrated and designated for Gehinnom.”
connections.context: This is the statement immediately following Rabban Gamliel’s praise of three forms of Persian modesty in Berakhot 8b. Its juxtaposition is central to Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the positive quality itself and the purpose for which it is used.

connections.hePhrase: דְּאָסוּר לְסַפֵּר בְּשֶׁבַח עַכּוּ״ם (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ.).
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: “Lo teḥonnem”—do not grant them favor. This supports Rav, for Rav said: A person may not say, “How beautiful is this gentile woman.””
connections.context: The Gemara derives a restriction on bestowing admiring praise from lo teḥonnem. Rav Tzadok invokes this in explaining the immediate qualification that follows the praise of Persian modesty in Berakhot.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בַּאֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, שֶׁהַמֶּלֶךְ כֹּחוֹ יוֹתֵר שֶׁכּוֹלֵל כָּל הָאוּמָּה (מְגִילָּה יג.):
connections.quote: “‘In the evening she would come, and in the morning she would return.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: From this disgraceful account of that wicked man, we learn something to his credit: he did not have sexual relations during the day. ‘Esther won favor.’ Rabbi Elazar said: This teaches that each person thought she belonged to his own nation. ‘Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, to his royal house, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tevet’—the month when one body takes pleasure in another’s warmth.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזָכְתָה אֶסְתֵּר, כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם עַמּוּד ב): "בִּשְׂכַר צְנִיעוּת שֶׁהָיְתָה וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ““He does not withdraw His eyes from the righteous”: In reward for the modesty that Rachel possessed, she merited that Shaul descended from her; and in reward for the modesty that Shaul possessed, he merited that Esther descended from him.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהִיא קָלְטָה מִדַּת הַצְּנִיעוּת הַטּוֹבָה "הַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת עִם אֱלֹהֶיךָ",
connections.quote: ‘He has told you, human being, what is good. What does Hashem seek from you but to act justly, love kindness, and walk modestly with your God?’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן אַחַר הַחֵטְא "נֶחְבָּאוּ",
connections.quote: ‘They heard the sound of Hashem God moving about in the garden in the breeze of the day. The man and his wife hid from Hashem God among the trees of the garden.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא תִּשָּׂא לא) בְּלוּחוֹת שְׁנִיּוֹת:
connections.quote: ““Hew for yourself … and be ready in the morning.” At the first giving it was, “On the third day, when it was morning”; here it is, “Let no man be seen.” Because the first tablets were given publicly, the evil eye prevailed over them and they were broken. Here the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Nothing is more beautiful than modesty, as it is said, “What does the Lord require of you? Only to do justice, love kindness, and walk modestly.””
connections.context: The Midrash contrasts the publicity of the first tablets with the privacy of the second. The Hebrew says ayin hara, “the evil eye.” Rav Tzadok applies the model of the second tablets, given after the sin, to the concealed holiness of the Second Temple period.

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יא.):
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yoḥanan introduced this passage with: “He remembered His kindness and faithfulness to the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God.” When did “all the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God”? In the days of Mordecai and Esther.”
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s application of Psalms 98:3 to the Purim deliverance. Rav Tzadok explains how recognizing divine direction within apparently natural events can become a revelation reaching “all the ends of the earth.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי אָז הָיָה יְשׁוּעָה בְּדֶרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע וְנִגְלָה לַכֹּל דְּהוּא מִפְּעוּלוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Megillah 11a:1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Megillah 11a:1
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan opened his exposition of this passage with “He remembered His kindness,” and “All the ends of the earth have seen.” When did all the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God? In the days of Mordechai and Esther. It is written, “You are the God who works wonders; You made Your might known among the peoples.” All the miracles the Holy One, blessed be He, performed for Israel—such as the exodus from Egypt, the splitting of the sea, and all the wars that departed from the natural order—are called wonders. The language of seeing does not apply to them, because after the miracle the world remains as it was before. The language of hearing applies: what remains is the report heard by the ears that a wonder occurred in the world at that time. But in the miracle of Mordechai and Esther, the Holy One, blessed be He, showed that even all the natural processes operating in the world serve Israel’s good. This miracle appeared to follow the natural order, through his taking Esther, and the events involving Mordechai likewise appeared natural. Here the language of seeing applies, for this can be recognized by the eye at every time and moment.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן חָכְמָה, הֲגַם דְּהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם, הוּא הַשָּׂגָה גְּדוֹלָה מִנְּבוּאָה.
connections.displayRef: Gevurot Hashem, Introduction to Gevurot Hashem 4-6
connections.linkedRef: Gevurot Hashem, Introduction to Gevurot Hashem 4-6
connections.canonicalRef: Gevurot Hashem, Introduction to Gevurot Hashem 4-6
connections.quote:
“There is a difference between wisdom and prophecy. The sage apprehends through his intellect, and because he apprehends through his intellect, he can apprehend the most hidden and concealed things. The prophet, however, is called a ‘visionary’ or a ‘seer’: seeing applies when someone sees a thing from outside. Every prophet must therefore have a connection to the matter concerning which he prophesies. He connects himself to those things and knows them through his prophecy.

The Sages therefore said, ‘A sage is greater than a prophet.’ The explanation is that prophecy resembles the sense of sight, which perceives its object from outside. Although prophecy does not come through the perception of a physical sense, nevertheless, just as a sense connects with its object, so the prophet’s power of prophecy—the imaginative faculty, or whatever faculty receives prophecy—connects with the thing about which he prophesies. For this reason the sage is greater: he apprehends and knows hidden matters and brings them forth from his own intellect. Because of this difference, the prophet is called a ‘visionary’ or a ‘seer,’ whereas the sage is not. It is therefore impossible for the matter of the World to Come and the soul’s continued existence to enter prophecy at all, since ‘seeing’ or ‘vision’ does not apply to them. This matter is separate from the human being; because it is completely separate from him, prophecy does not apply to it. We have already explained that prophecy requires an external connection with that about which one prophesies. The World to Come and the soul’s continued existence are therefore explained more fully through wisdom—for the sage apprehends hidden matters—than through prophecy. Thus ‘a sage is greater than a prophet,’ because he can apprehend something that cannot be apprehended through prophecy. The power of prophecy resembles the sense of sight, which receives its objects from outside. How, then, could the matter of the World to Come be written in the Torah, when it does not belong to the domain of prophecy? Anyone who knows the distinction between the sage and the prophet knows that this is impossible, for the prophets connected themselves with the things about which they prophesied.

The Sages therefore said: ‘All the prophets prophesied only concerning the days of the Messiah; but concerning the World to Come, “No eye has seen, O God, except You.”’ The explanation is that since prophecy requires seeing—an external connection with what is known through prophecy—the prophets could prophesy only concerning the days of the Messiah. The matter of the Messiah belongs to this world and is not completely separate from the human being, for it is in this world. But there is no prophecy concerning the World to Come, which is separate from this world, for no eye has seen it. The prophet prophesies only through seeing, as has been explained.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק עֵילָם זָכְתָה לִלְמוֹד וְלֹא לְלַמֵּד (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פְּסָחִים פז.),
connections.quote: ‘‘We have a little sister, and she has no breasts.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: This is Elam, which merited learning but did not merit teaching.’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא "וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ".
connections.quote: “The two of them were naked, the man and his wife, and they were not ashamed.”
connections.context: The verse describes the condition before the sin. Rav Tzadok contrasts it with the subsequent need for modesty and shame, and with Amalek’s attempt to retain shamelessness after wrongdoing.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא מַבִּיט רַק עַל הַנִּגְלֶה,
connections.quote: “The clarification that they had acted only outwardly became known to them after Hashem opened the deliverance. Before the deliverance, it seemed to them that they had become entirely estranged, Heaven forbid; such a clarification is possible only after the deliverance.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim places an explicit limit on retrospective recognition: only after Hashem opened the deliverance did they know clearly that their outward act had not severed the inward bond. Beforehand, they feared that they had become estranged. This sharpens the siman's movement from hidden loyalty to visible rescue and guards against treating a person's advance assertion of a hidden good intention as the same thing as that later clarification.
connections.headline: The timing of the inner clarification matters

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵשָׂו (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה סה): "פּוֹשֵׁט טְלָפָיו וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Why is it compared to a pig? Just as the pig, when it lies down, extends its hooves as if to say, “I am pure,” so this wicked kingdom robs and takes by force while appearing to establish a court of justice. So Esau, throughout forty years, would seize married women and violate them; when he reached forty, he likened himself to his father and said: Just as my father married at forty, I too shall marry at forty.”
connections.context: The exposed split hooves display an outward sign of purity while concealing the animal’s disqualification. The Midrash uses the image for Esau and the kingdom associated with him; Rav Tzadok invokes it to distinguish outward appearance from inward character.

connections.hePhrase: אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת "אִם יִסָּתֵר וְגוֹמֵר וַאֲנִי לֹא אֶרְאֶנּוּ",
connections.quote: ‘Can a person hide in concealed places without My seeing him, declares Hashem? Do I not fill the heavens and the earth, declares Hashem?’

connections.hePhrase: וְכִמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים מִזְמוֹר כב) דְּכָעַס עַל זֶה אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ.
connections.quote: “When did Esther say, “Do not be far from me, for trouble is near”? When Ahasuerus decreed destruction and killing, and Esther entered without permission. … When she entered the fourth enclosure, he began grinding and gnashing his teeth. He said: Alas for those who are lost and cannot be found! How much I desired and asked Vashti to enter before me, and she would not; yet this woman has entered like a harlot, without permission. … At that time Esther said, “Do not be far from me, for trouble is near.””
connections.context: Shoḥer Tov is Midrash Tehillim, and the relevant passage comments on Psalm 22. It describes the king’s anger at Esther’s uninvited entrance. Rav Tzadok contrasts its outward appearance with her concealed holy purpose in risking herself to save Israel.

connections.hePhrase: [וּבְוַדַּאי אָז נִתְעַבְּרָה מִדָּרְיָוֶשׁ שֶׁבָּנָה הַבַּיִת].
connections.quote: “Israel remained inactive and did not build the Temple throughout the reigns of Cyrus and of Achashverosh, who reigned after him, until the second year of the reign of Darius son of Achashverosh, king of Persia—Darius son of Esther. In the second year of his reign they began building the Temple, until the building was completed.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי הִיא אוֹת קוֹ״ף וְאֵשֶׁת חַיִל אוֹת הֵ״א, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “We have learned: Everywhere this serpent follows the mystery of the woman of valor, and the woman of harlotry seeks to fashion herself in her likeness, but cannot. The mark and letter of the woman of valor is the letter heh, as befits her. The mark and letter of the woman of harlotry is in that likeness [another reading: in the required likeness], but she cannot become so; her letter is qof. Her letter is fashioned in the shape of heh [another reading likewise describes qof as resembling heh without being able to become it], like an ape beside human beings: it follows human beings but cannot accomplish what they do.”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁם (קנב עַמּוּד א) דְּאוֹת קוֹ״ף שַׁרְיָא עַל גֵּיהִנָּם,
connections.quote: “Just as this letter rules in this place, so another letter rules in the place of Gehinnom. Which is it? The letter qof.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם (קנ עַמּוּד ב) דְּאֵשׁ דְּגֵיהִנָּם הוּא אֵשׁ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְהוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehuda said: We have learned about the judgment of the punishments of Gehinnom, where the wicked are judged. Why are they judged in the fire of Gehinnom? Gehinnom is a fire burning day and night, corresponding to the way the wicked become heated by the fire of the evil inclination in order to transgress the words of Torah. With every surge of heat with which they inflame themselves through the evil inclination, the fire of Gehinnom is kindled. Once the evil inclination was absent from the world, for they placed it in an iron container in the opening of the great abyss. Throughout that time the fire of Gehinnom was extinguished and did not burn at all. When the evil inclination returned to its place, the wicked of the world began to inflame themselves through it, and the fire of Gehinnom began to burn. For Gehinnom burns only through the heat of the force of the wicked people’s evil inclination. Through that heat, the fire of Gehinnom burns day and night without resting.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְהַקְדָּמַת הַזֹּהַר דְּקוֹ״ף רֵי״שׁ אַתְוָון דְּשִׁקְרָא,
connections.quote: “The letter shin entered before Him and said: Master of the worlds, may it please You to create the world through me, for through me Your name Shaddai is pronounced, and it is fitting to create the world through the holy name. He said to it: You are fitting, good, and true. But because the letters of falsehood take you to be with them, I do not wish to create the world through you, for falsehood cannot endure unless qof and resh take you. From here we learn that one who wishes to tell a falsehood takes a foundation of truth first and afterward establishes the falsehood upon it, for you are a letter of truth, the true letter of the patriarchs who are united in it. Qof and resh are letters that appear on the evil side; to endure, they take the letter shin among them and form qesher, a bond. When shin saw this, it departed from before Him.”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קעח עַמּוּד ב) דְּהֵ״א דָּלֶ״ת הֲוַות,
connections.quote: “Yod alone is male; he is female. He was at first dalet, and when she became pregnant with vav within her, she brought forth vav.”
connections.context: The letter imagery treats he as a dalet receiving an additional inner stroke. Rav Tzadok uses that image of reception and completion to explain the move from lack to fullness, and then contrasts its upright form with the corresponding forms of resh and qof.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קעח עַמּוּד ב) דְּהֵ״א דָּלֶ״ת הֲוַות,
connections.quote: “Twenty-two concealed letters, twenty-two revealed letters; yod concealed, yod revealed.”

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קעח עַמּוּד ב) דְּהֵ״א דָּלֶ״ת הֲוַות,
connections.quote: “From yod emerge male and female, vav and dalet; in this place vav is male and dalet is female. … He was at first dalet, and when she became pregnant with vav within her, she brought forth vav.”
connections.context: This gives the immediate setting of the letter transformation: concealed and revealed letters, and masculine and feminine aspects. The following clause about dalet and he is the specific image Rav Tzadok draws on. His comparison with resh and qof develops the corresponding forms of lack and reception.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִפְרִי עֵץ חַיִּים רֵישׁ שַׁעַר הַשַּׁבָּת דְּכֵן גַּם כֵּן אוֹת קוֹ״ף רֵי״שׁ הֲוַות וְכוּלֵי,
connections.displayRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Sabbath, Introduction 1:15
connections.linkedRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Sabbath, Introduction 1:15
connections.canonicalRef: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Sabbath, Introduction 1:15
connections.heRef: פרי עץ חיים, שער השבת, הקדמה א׳:ט״ו
connections.quote: “We have explained that, through our sins, the shell rules over Netzach, Hod, and Yesod; this is the shin of sheqer. What does the shell do afterward? It takes for itself the embryo of Malkhut, the vav within the holy heh. When the adulterous woman takes it, she becomes pregnant through it. At first she is in the mystery of resh, as is known: dalet belongs to holiness and resh to the shell. This resh takes the letter vav, the embryo within the heh of Malkhut, and joins it to her resh. Moreover, she extends it in the mystery of the leg of qof, so that it joins her in the mystery of the shell, a serpent coiled about the heel. She then becomes qof, for the shell is called an ape beside a human being. These are the letters shin and qof of sheqer. Afterward the Holy One, blessed be He, in His mercy takes it back from her, and she returns to being resh as at first and diminishes, as explained above.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ "רָשׁ הוֹלֵךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ",
connections.quote: ‘Better is a poor person who walks with integrity than someone whose lips are crooked and who is a fool.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה עא): "כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר רָשׁ וָדַל וְכוּלֵי – בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְדַבֵּר",
connections.quote: ““The Lord saw that Leah was unloved, and He opened her womb, and Rachel was barren” (Genesis 29:31). “The Lord saw that Leah was unloved…” “For the Lord hears the impoverished and does not despise His prisoners” (Psalms 69:34) – Rabbi Binyamin ben Levi said: The beginning of this verse does not correspond with its end, nor does its end correspond to its beginning. The verse should have said only: “For the Lord hears the impoverished and does not despise the prisoners” or: “For the Lord hears His impoverished and…His prisoners.” Rather: “For the Lord hears the impoverished” – this is Israel, as Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Every place that impoverished [dal], poor [ani], and indigent [evyon] is stated, the verse is speaking of Israel. “And does not despise His prisoners” – these are the barren women, who are prisoners in their homes, and forlorn. But when the Holy One blessed be He remembers them with children, they stand erect. Know that Leah was the unloved one of the household, but when the Holy One blessed be He remembered her, she stood erect. That is what is written: “The Lord saw that Leah was unloved.””

connections.hePhrase: כִּי שֶׁקֶר נִקְרָא דָּבָר לְפִי שָׁעָה כִּלְשׁוֹן כְּזָב, דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דָּבָר הַפּוֹסֵק.
connections.quote: “The explanation is that this world is called the world of falsehood, and the World to Come the world of truth. Falsehood is something that ceases, as in “its waters fail,” something without permanence. These are all the matters of this world, which appear in the imagination to endure, but do not truly do so, for they will pass away. The World to Come means stripping each thing of imagination to reach that thing’s truth: the underlying power of that power, which endures forever. This is eternal.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן כָּל חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְשָׁעָה, וְ"לֹא בְמוֹתוֹ יִקַּח הַכֹּל".
connections.quote: ‘For when he dies he will take none of it; his glory will not descend after him.’

connections.hePhrase: וְעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת בְּאוֹת רֵי״שׁ,
connections.quote: “Seven double letters, bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, peh, resh, and tav: He engraved them, hewed them, combined them, and formed through them planets in the world, days in the year, and gates in the living being. From them He engraved seven heavens, seven lands, and seven sabbaths; therefore He cherished the seventh beneath all the heavens. How? He made bet king over life, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Saturn in the world, the first day in the year, and the right eye in the living being. He made gimel king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Jupiter in the world, the second day in the year, and the left eye in the living being. He made dalet king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Mars in the world, the third day in the year, and the right ear in the living being. He made kaf king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it the sun in the world, the fourth day in the year, and the left ear in the living being. He made peh king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Venus in the world, the fifth day in the year, and the right nostril in the living being. He made resh king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it Mercury in the world, the sixth day in the year, and the left nostril in the living being. He made tav king, bound a crown to it, and formed through it the moon in the world, Shabbat in the year, and the mouth in the living being.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת (קנו.): "מַאן דִּבְעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת – חַזְרָן בְּמִצְווֹת".
connections.quote: ‘One born on the fifth day of the week will be a person who performs acts of kindness. Why? Because fish and birds were created on that day. One born on the eve of Shabbat will be a person who seeks things out. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: He seeks out mitzvot. One born on Shabbat will die on Shabbat, because the great day of Shabbat was desecrated on his behalf. Rava bar Rav Sheila said: And he will be called a greatly holy person.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן יֵשׁ פְּעָמִים ב' אֲדָרִים כְּמוֹ פְּעָמִים שֵׁבֶט יוֹסֵף נֶחְלָק לִבְנַיִם.
connections.quote: “The month of Adar corresponds to Joseph, from whom two tribes emerged, Ephraim and Manasseh. Therefore Adar is the month that is intercalated, and there are sometimes two months of Adar. This is also why Adar’s sign is Pisces, the fish, which is the aspect of Joseph, as it is written: ‘May they multiply like fish in the midst of the earth’ (Genesis 48:16). It is known that Joseph’s descendants are compared to fish: just as the fish in the sea are covered, so are Joseph’s descendants—‘Joseph is a fruitful son, a fruitful son above the eye’ (Genesis 49:22).”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַזָּלוֹ דָּגִים שֶׁכֵּן נִתְבָּרַךְ "וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב",
connections.quote: “May the angel who redeemed me from all evil bless the lads; may my name be called upon them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they multiply like fish in the midst of the earth.”
connections.context: Jacob blesses Joseph’s sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. The verb veyidgu evokes dagim, “fish,” which is the link Rav Tzadok makes between Joseph, his two tribes, and the sign of Adar.

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא נִבְרָא בְּאוֹת קוֹ״ף כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה,
connections.quote: see note 2268.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד חוֹדֶשׁ נִיסָן, שֶׁהוּא רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לַמְּלָכִים,
connections.quote: see note 2268.

connections.hePhrase: רַק בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם הַקּוֹ״ף מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:38
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:38
connections.quote: “Within holiness this corresponds to Naftali, who joins all Israel, and Adar stands beside Nissan. In Israel, qof hints at “holy”: the body too has holiness through its connection with the soul, whose principal power is wisdom. Israel's souls derive from the letters of Torah. These are the six hundred thousand souls of the wilderness generation; the souls of other generations derive from the renewed Oral Torah of their own generation. The true reception of new life on the soul's side is therefore in the he of Nissan. The qof of bodily reception exists also among the nations, but Israel receives from Hashem, and bodily reception is never without spiritual reception. Both need one another, as the Sages' parable of body and soul explains regarding judgment, and likewise reward. The soul is the body's life, while the soul's manifestation in this world is through the body. So too Nissan comes in the spring through Adar's intercalation.”
connections.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim develops the same contrast between the letters qof and he through bodily and spiritual reception. It explains that the body can share in holiness through its bond with the soul, while the soul becomes manifest in this world through the body. This helps explain why the siman proceeds from suppressing desire to transforming permissible enjoyment for holiness. The two passages use different tribal associations in developing their particular arguments; the comparison concerns the reception and body/soul structure.
connections.headline: Bodily reception can join spiritual reception
