connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם הַכְלָלַת קְלִיפַּת נוֹגַהּ בִּקְדוּשָׁה לִפְעָמִים כַּיָּדוּעַ,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ז׳:ב׳-ז׳
connections.quote: “It is an intermediate level between the three entirely impure shells and the level of holiness. Therefore it is sometimes included in the three impure shells, as stated in Etz Chaim in the name of the Zohar; at other times it is included and rises into the level of holiness, when the good mixed within it is separated from the evil, prevails, rises, and is included in holiness. For example, someone eats rich ox meat and drinks fragrant wine to broaden his mind for God and His Torah—as Rava said, “Wine and fragrance,” and so forth—or to fulfill the mitzvah of delighting in Shabbat and the festivals. Then the vitality of the meat and wine that flowed from nogah is refined and rises to God like a burnt offering and a sacrifice. Likewise, someone says something humorous to clear his mind and gladden his heart for God, His Torah, and His service, which require joy, as Rava did for his students when he began with a humorous remark and the Sages became cheerful. But someone who gluttonously eats meat and drinks wine to satisfy the desire of his body and animal soul—the element of water among its four evil elements, from which desire comes—causes the vitality of the meat and wine within him to descend and become temporarily included in the complete evil of the three impure shells. His body temporarily becomes their garment and vehicle, until he repents and returns to serving God and studying His Torah. Since the meat was permitted and the wine kosher, they can return and rise with him when he returns to God’s service. This is the meaning of heter and mutar, “permitted”: it is not bound and held by the external forces so that it cannot return and rise to God. Nevertheless, a trace of it remains in the body, and therefore the body requires the affliction of the grave, as will be explained later.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק לֵידָתוֹ מֵעַמְרָם, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת נה:) שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ,
connections.quote: ‘They raised an objection: Four died through the serpent’s counsel. These are they: Benjamin son of Jacob, Amram the father of Moses, Jesse the father of David, and Chileab son of David. All these are known through tradition except Jesse the father of David, concerning whom Scripture speaks explicitly, for it is written: ‘Absalom appointed Amasa over the army in Joab’s place. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had intercourse with Abigail daughter of Nachash, the sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.’’

connections.hePhrase: (מִדְרָשׁ, הוּבָא בְּעַשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת, מַאֲמַר חֲקוֹר דִּין חֵלֶק ג פֶּרֶק י),
connections.quote: “The aggadah relates that Jesse, his father, withdrew from his wife in his old age. We have no doubt that this was an act of piety: perhaps the Torah’s statement “An Ammonite and a Moabite shall not enter” means a male Moabite and even a female Moabite. For this law was uncertain in that generation until Yitra the Ishmaelite, Jesse’s son-in-law, sharpened and girded his sword like an Ishmaelite and planted it in the study hall to establish the law, “A male Moabite, but not a female Moabite,” from the court of Shmuel of Ramah. Jesse the righteous, to remove himself from doubt and fulfill “In the evening do not let your hand rest,” sought to come to his maidservant. It seems plausible to us that this was after he had freed her conditionally: If the Torah said a male Moabite but not a female Moabite, you are free; but if it meant a male Moabite and even a female Moabite, my words have no effect, for those of definite disqualified status are permitted to one another, as taught in the chapter Asarah Yuchasin. Although a mamzer may marry a female convert or freed maidservant, and the same applies to a male Moabite, since the community of converts and freed slaves is not called the congregation, he preferred that his children should be slaves whom he could immediately free, so that they would not inherit his disqualification. If their mother had been freed, the children would follow his disqualified status and be prohibited from entering the congregation forever. The faithful maidservant, knowing that the established law permits women from Ammon and Moab to enter the congregation, gave the identifying signs to Jesse’s wife, who was then hated by her husband because of her exalted level, as will be explained concerning Leah in chapter eighteen. From that event David was born.”

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ עִנְיַן תַּזְרִיעַ).
connections.quote: see note 1258 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the Midrash at the opening of Tazria that Rav Tzadok cites. Its interpretation concerns the element of personal enjoyment in conception, even in a righteous person. Rav Tzadok relates that residual element of desire to his explanation of “the serpent’s counsel.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן עַמְרָם חֲזָרַת לִיקּוּחִין ב',
connections.quote: “It was taught: Amram was the leader of the generation. When he saw that Pharaoh the wicked had said, “Every son born you shall cast into the Nile,” he said: We are laboring in vain. He arose and divorced his wife, and everyone arose and divorced their wives. His daughter said to him: Father, your decree is harsher than Pharaoh’s. Pharaoh decreed only against the males, while you have decreed against both males and females. Pharaoh decreed only concerning this world, while you have decreed concerning both this world and the World to Come. Pharaoh is wicked, and it is uncertain whether his decree will be fulfilled; you are righteous, and your decree will certainly be fulfilled, as it is said, “You shall decree a matter and it shall be established for you.” He arose and took his wife back, and everyone arose and took their wives back. “He took”: should it not say “he took back”? Rav Yehuda bar Zevina said: He performed a marriage ceremony for her. He seated her in a bridal litter, Aaron and Miriam danced before her, and the ministering angels said, “The happy mother of children.””

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם "וְנַהֲפוֹךְ הוּא",
connections.quote: ‘In the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on its thirteenth day, when the king’s word and decree were due to be carried out—on the day the Jews’ enemies had hoped to rule over them—the reverse occurred: the Jews themselves ruled over those who hated them.’

connections.hePhrase: וּ"לְאִתְהַפְּכָא", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְרַבִּים מֵעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ מִתְיַהֲדִים וְגוֹמֵר".
connections.quote: “In every province and every city, wherever the king’s word and decree arrived, there was joy and gladness for the Jews, a feast and a holiday. Many of the peoples of the land became Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok cites the final clause as the example of transformation, it’hapkha, after distinguishing it from subduing opposition, itkafya. The marker therefore belongs with the quotation about the people becoming Jews.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה ו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): "מִסְמַךְ גְּאוּלָּה לִגְאוּלָּה עָדִיף",
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Tavi said: Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel’s reason is that placing one redemption next to the other is preferable. Rabbi Elazar said: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s reason is derived from here, as it is written: ‘To confirm this second letter of Purim.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל תַּעֲנִית שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מִפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ תַּעֲנִית כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (כְּרֵיתוֹת ו:) מֵחֶלְבְּנָה,
connections.quote: ‘Rav Chana bar Bizna said in Rabbi Shimon Chasida’s name: Any fast that does not include some of the transgressors of Israel is not a fast, for galbanum has a bad odor, yet Scripture counted it among the ingredients of the incense. Abaye said: The source is here: ‘He founded His gathered band upon the earth.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ז): "כְּשֵׁם שֶׁקִּילוּסוֹ עוֹלֶה מִן הַצַּדִּיקִים, כָּךְ עוֹלֶה מִן הָרְשָׁעִים".
connections.quote: “Another interpretation: “Concerning Pharaoh king of Egypt” – Rabbi Levi said: This is analogous to a king who had an orchard and he planted non-fruit-bearing trees and fruit trees in it. His servants said to him: ‘What pleasure do you get from these non-fruit-bearing trees?’ He said to them: ‘Just as I need fruit trees, so too I need the non-fruit-bearing trees, as were it not for the non-fruit-bearing trees, with what would I make bathhouses and furnaces?’ That is why it says: “Concerning the children of Israel and concerning Pharaoh” – just as the praise of the Holy One blessed be He rises to Him from the Garden of Eden from the mouths of the righteous, so too it rises from Gehenna from the mouths of the wicked, as it is stated: “They pass through a valley of tears, they render it a place of springs” (Psalms 84:7). What is “they render it a place of springs”? They shed tears like springs until they cool Gehenna with their tears. The praise rises from there, as it is stated: “Blessings cover the early rain [moreh]” (Psalms 84:7). What do they say? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: You have said well, You have judged well, You have purified well, You have impurified well, You have condemned well, You have taught well, and You have ruled well. The Garden of Eden is destined to shout and say: Give me the righteous, I have no interest in the wicked, as it is stated: “I hate those who regard empty folly” (Psalms 31:7). Whom do I seek? Those who trusted in Your name, as it is stated: “But I trust in the Lord” (Psalms 31:7). Gehenna is destined to shout and say: I have no interest in the righteous. Whom do I seek? The wicked: “Empty folly,” those who engage in folly. The Holy One blessed be He says: ‘Give this one the righteous and this one the wicked,’ as it is stated: “The leech has two daughters” (Proverbs 30:15).”

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם כְּעִנְיַן (מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרָכוֹת סג.): "גַּנָּבָא אַפּוּם מַחְתַּרְתָּא רַחֲמָנָא קָרֵי".
connections.quote: “Rav Pappa said: This is what people say: A thief at the mouth of the tunnel calls upon the Merciful One.”
connections.context: Ein Yaakov preserves this reading of Berakhot 63a after the teaching “In all your ways acknowledge Him.” It supplies the proverb Rav Tzadok quotes: a person can still recognize and appeal to God even while acting wrongly. His point concerns that surviving recognition within the person.

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם כְּעִנְיַן (מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרָכוֹת סג.): "גַּנָּבָא אַפּוּם מַחְתַּרְתָּא רַחֲמָנָא קָרֵי".
connections.quote: ““Even when I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for You are with me.” The matter follows what they said in Berakhot 63a concerning “Know Him in all your ways, and He will straighten your paths”: Rava said, “Even in a matter of transgression.” The reading in Ein Yaakov adds: Rav Pappa said, “This is what people say: A thief at the mouth of the tunnel calls upon the Merciful One.” That is, although he commits an explicit transgression, violating “You shall not steal,” nevertheless, since he does not forget the blessed God and believes in Him at the time of the deed, calling upon the Merciful One, concerning this it is said, “He will straighten your paths”: God will straighten his paths, no outcast will remain cast out, and he will have a correction.”

connections.hePhrase: וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם כְּעִנְיַן (מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרָכוֹת סג.): "גַּנָּבָא אַפּוּם מַחְתַּרְתָּא רַחֲמָנָא קָרֵי".
connections.quote: “After commanding the poor person, Scripture says, “You shall keep the commandments,” and so forth, to warn about observing the commandments as a whole. For one who trusts in the Lord must join his trust with keeping His commandments, rather than act wickedly and trust that God will nevertheless treat him well. As Shmuel says in the chapter HaRo’eh, according to the reading of Ein Yaakov: “A thief at the mouth of the tunnel calls upon the Merciful One.” And in the first chapter of Yoma: “They were wicked, but they placed their trust in the Holy One, blessed be He.” This is not the quality of trust—to trust that, although one has sinned, the Holy One is with him—for this causes heedlessness about sinning. Even if he sees fortune smiling upon him, they said in Bava Kamma: “Whoever says that the Holy One, blessed be He, waives wrongdoing,” and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּ"אוֹדֶה בְּכָל לֵבָב" – הַיְינוּ גַּם בְּיֵצֶר הָרָע,
connections.quote: ‘Hallelujah! I will thank Hashem with all my heart, in the company of the upright and in the congregation.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "בְּסוֹד יְשָׁרִים וְעֵדָה",
connections.quote: ““I shall thank the Lord with all my heart”: with the good inclination and with the evil inclination that dwells within him. For one must thank the Holy One, blessed be He, for everything, with the good inclination and the evil inclination. From the side of the good inclination, good comes to a person, and one must bless the Holy One as “the Good who does good.” From the side of the evil inclination, accusation comes upon a person, and one must thank the Holy One [with the good inclination and the evil inclination] for whatever comes upon him, from this side and from that side. “In the council of the upright and the congregation”: “in the council of the upright” means those who know the mystery of the Holy One [another reading: the supernal holy angels], for they know all His mysteries and are His council. “And the congregation” means Israel when they gather in ten to thank the Holy One. Therefore one must thank the Holy One for good and for bad, and make it known before everyone. If you say: He already knows, so why must one publicize it? Through publicizing the miracle, the Holy One is honored in the world. Therefore it is written of the Holy One, “I shall be magnified and sanctified,” and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת לד.): "שְׂאוֹר, רוּבּוֹ קָשֶׁה וּמִיעוּטוֹ יָפֶה",
connections.quote: ‘The Rabbis taught: Three things are harmful in excess but good in small measure: leaven, salt, and reluctance to accept an invitation.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת לד.): "שְׂאוֹר, רוּבּוֹ קָשֶׁה וּמִיעוּטוֹ יָפֶה",
connections.quote: “Therefore they said it quietly and compared it to a king's daughter who smelled a dish's seasoning and would feel ashamed to ask for it. It is a disgrace to the congregation of Israel when its heart is not completely pure. Yet “a little foolishness is more precious than wisdom and honor,” and a little leaven is beneficial: His praise and the glory of His kingship rise still more when an impulse remains in the heart and, despite it, the heart recognizes His unity and that there is none besides Him.”
connections.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains the same images of a little leaven and a little foolishness through the quietly spoken declaration of lower unity. The added praise comes from recognizing Hashem while an opposing impulse remains, rather than from expanding that impulse. This fits the siman's own qualification that the remaining foolishness should be as little as possible, and its turn toward blessing over permissible enjoyment.
connections.headline: The remaining impulse can deepen the praise

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁזֶּה נֶאֱמַר לְחִסָּרוֹן עָלָיו, לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם חִסָּרוֹן כְּלָל.
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 30:3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 30:3
connections.quote: ““The semamit is grasped by the hands, yet it is in kings’ palaces.” Semamit signifies anger and sadness, from the word shemamah, desolation. “It is grasped by the hands” means that this deficiency can grow even in very great people, for “Who are the kings? The sages.” The sages, heads of Israel’s thousands, labor over this to perfect themselves so that no root of it remains in their hearts. This was the matter with Uzziah, who entered the innermost place to burn incense because he wished to perfect himself in this respect. As long as he knew that he had not attained completion in this, he understood that he had not attained completion in everything. Incense gladdens a person’s heart, as it is written, “Oil and incense gladden the heart.” This is what is said: “As he raged against the priests, the leprosy shone upon his forehead.” Because he recognized that he was not free of this fault, he judged himself to be in mortal danger and permitted himself to burn incense to attain the completion of his soul, for nothing stands in the way of saving life. Indeed, he truly succeeded, for afterward he attained completion. Scripture says of him, “The leprosy shone,” using the language of shining: only in outward appearance did it seem that he had acted improperly; in depth he attained completion through it. It is said of him, “He dwelt in the house of freedom”: he became free, for he was in a state of completion. But because he was among the priests, and the depth of his intention was hidden from them, he appeared to them as one profaning God’s name; according to their apprehension, he was afflicted with leprosy. This is what is said of his son Jotham: “He did what was upright in the eyes of the Lord, like everything his father Uzziah had done; only he did not enter the Lord’s sanctuary.” The word “only” limits, like all occurrences of akh and rak in the Torah: he did not reach that level. Had Uzziah burned the incense, he would immediately have entered the life of the World to Come.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבֶאֱמֶת נֶאֱמַר: "יָקָר מֵחָכְמָה מִכָּבוֹד סִכְלוּת מְעָט",
connections.quote: see note 1081 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The verse’s ordinary comparison describes the disproportionate effect of a little folly. Rav Tzadok reads yakar homiletically as “precious”: the minimum element of ordinary human desire can itself have a necessary role, just as a little leaven is useful. This explains his positive use of the phrase “a little folly.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּצָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּכָל אֶחָד סִכְלוּת מְעַט עַל כָּל פָּנִים, וְזֶהוּ הַשְּׁלֵימוּת.
connections.quote: “This is the matter of the two loaves of Shavuot, which are brought as leaven: it is offering to the blessed God the obstructing leaven in the dough, as stated in Berakhot 17a. Through this one merits receiving the giving of the Torah, which is the remedy for the inclination—that is, using it only according to God’s will. Then it is “very good,” as our Sages say in Bereshit Rabbah, and as stated in Berakhot 34a concerning leaven: a little is beneficial, but much is harmful. This is the little folly that is more precious than wisdom and honor. Wisdom is apprehending the words of Torah themselves, while honor is what ultimately follows from it, for “the wise inherit honor.” The little folly brings all this through the feeling of deficiency: through it a person longs, desires, and waits for words of Torah to fill his lack. This is the principal human power: the yearning and longing one has, and the preparation to receive and do all the Torah. Everything else comes from God, who completes it for him. He gives wisdom, but “gives only to the wise”—those who have the beginning of wisdom, the fear of God, which is itself called wisdom, as it is written, “Behold, the fear of God is wisdom.” This is preparing the heart to do nothing contrary to God’s will. Then the whole Torah and wisdom are entrusted to him, to know God’s will and to make all his deeds and thoughts accord with the divine wisdom within him.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק שֶׁזֶּה טוֹב לָאָדָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אוֹתוֹ הַסִּכְלוּת כַּמִּיעוּט הַיּוֹתֵר אֶפְשָׁרִי.
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 4:6
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 4:6
connections.quote: “Mar Zutra said: ‘At a time of finding’ means finding a privy. In the West they said that Mar Zutra's interpretation is preferable to all the others: every pious person should pray for this. A privy indicates shame, meaning that a person should pray not to be put to shame. At the root, a deficiency is found in every person from birth. Hashem therefore created openings and cavities in a person, so that he should not become proud and imagine himself perfect in every respect. As the Talmud states (Bava Batra 75a), the Holy One said to Chiram king of Tyre, ‘I looked at you and created openings in the human person.’ This was said because he made himself a god. A person's openings indicate his lack of perfection: no person can be without deficiency, as it says (Ecclesiastes 7:20), ‘There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.’ This indicates deficiency at the root of each person's life. Therefore every person has surplus that is completely rejected and discharged: the excess of food and drink is not absorbed in his 248 limbs but is lost and rendered unfit. This indicates a deficiency present from birth; if there were only good in a person, from where would waste and surplus come? Every pious person should pray that this inherited deficiency be exceedingly fine and slight.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov also discusses ‘a little folly,’ but first insists that a person pray for the inherited deficiency to be as fine as possible. Its later examples concern carefully guarded people whose unintended speech is clarified. This supports the siman's express ‘smallest possible’ qualification, rather than suggesting that one should deliberately create a fault.
connections.headline: Praying for the smallest possible deficiency

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "יִתְרוֹן אֶרֶץ בַּכֹּל הוּא", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "אֲפִילּוּ וְכוּלֵי" (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כב).
connections.quote: “The benefit of the land is for all; even a king is served by the field.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok follows the Midrash’s reading of bakkol, “in everything”: even something apparently unnecessary can contribute to the world’s benefit. The following note supplies that Midrash and its examples.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "יִתְרוֹן אֶרֶץ בַּכֹּל הוּא", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "אֲפִילּוּ וְכוּלֵי" (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כב).
connections.quote: ““Any man from the house of Israel who will slaughter a bull, or a sheep, or a goat, in the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp” (Leviticus 17:3). “Any man from the house of Israel who will slaughter a bull, or a sheep, or a goat” – that is what is written: “The advantage of land is in every way” (Ecclesiastes 5:8). Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Neḥemya, Rabbi Yehuda said: Even matters that you consider to be superfluous for the world are beneficial for the world; palm fiber to make rope; a thorn bush to fence a garden, “A king is subservient to a field” (Ecclesiastes 5:8); even if he is king and he rules from one end of the world to the other, “he is subservient to the field.” If the field produces, he will be successful; if the field does not produce, there is nothing. Therefore, “one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver” (Ecclesiastes 5:9); one who loves money will not be satisfied with money, “nor one who loves abundance, with produce…” (Ecclesiastes 5:9), as anyone who avidly pursues money, but has no land, what benefit does he have? Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Tanḥum and Rabbi Ḥanin son of Rabbi in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya: It is written: “They will disembark from their ships…they will stand on the ground” (Ezekiel 27:29). Do we not know that they would stand on the ground? Rather, one whose ship sinks at sea and he has land on the shore, he will recover. If he does not have land, you do not have any greater futility. Rabbi Neḥemya said: “The advantage of land is in every way” – even matters that you consider superfluous to the giving of the Torah, e.g., the halakhot of ritual fringes, phylacteries, and mezuza; they, too, are included in the giving of the Torah, as it is stated: “The Lord gave me the two tablets of stone inscribed with the finger of God and on them were all the matters [kekhol hadevarim]” (Deuteronomy 9:10). And it is written: “All the mitzva [hamitzva] that I [command you this day you shall take care to perform]” (Deuteronomy 8:1). Kol, kekhol; devarim, hadevarim; mitzva, hamitzva – [to teach that] Bible, Mishna, halakha, Talmud, addenda, aggadot, and even what a distinguished disciple is destined to say before his teacher, all these were stated to Moses from Sinai, as it is stated: “There is a matter regarding which one would say: See, this is new” (Ecclesiastes 1:10), his counterpart responds to him: “It has already been, in the ages [that were before us]” (Ecclesiastes 1:10). “A king is subservient to a field,” Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Neḥemya, Rabbi Yehuda says: “King,” this is an expert in Talmud; “is subservient to a field,” this is an expert in Mishna, as he arranges the halakha before him. Rabbi Neḥemya says: “King,” this is an expert in Mishna; “is subservient to a field,” this is an expert in Talmud, as he receives the halakha before him. Therefore, “one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver,” – one who loves Torah will not be satisfied with Torah. “Nor one who loves abundance, [with produce]” as anyone who avidly pursues Torah, but does not have Talmud, what benefit does he have? Rabbi Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Aḥa: One who studied but does not teach, you have no greater futility than this.”

connections.hePhrase: וְ"כָל עַצְמוֹתַי תֹּאמַרְנָה ה' וְגוֹמֵר", בָּזֶה נִתְעַלֶּה הַכֹּל.
connections.quote: ‘All my bones shall say: Hashem, who is like You, rescuing the poor from one stronger than he, and the poor and needy from the one who robs him?’

connections.hePhrase: וּב' יְצָרִים הֵם: תַּאֲוָה, וְכַעַס דִּרְצִיחָה,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Nasso 4
connections.linkedRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Nasso 4
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Nasso 4
connections.heRef: מי השלוח, חלק א, ספר במדבר, נשא ד׳
connections.quote: “‘They shall send from the camp every person afflicted with tzaraat, every person with a discharge, and everyone impure through contact with a corpse.’ A person afflicted with tzaraat represents anger, for tzaraat comes as punishment for evil speech. A person with a discharge represents one ruled by desire, and impurity through a corpse represents sadness. Therefore the person afflicted with tzaraat is sent out of all three camps, for the trait of anger has no share in Israel. The person with a discharge is sent out only from the Levite camp and the camp of the Divine Presence, for the trait of desire is unfitting for Torah scholars. The person impure through a corpse is sent out only from the camp of the Divine Presence, for the trait of sadness is sometimes found even among Torah scholars, as the Gemara says: ‘It is the Torah that makes him seethe’; this seething is sadness. He is therefore sent out only from the camp of the Divine Presence, for ‘strength and joy are in His place.’”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי "שָׁלֹשׁ הֵנָּה לֹא תִשְׂבַּעְנָה וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘The leech has two daughters: ‘Give! Give!’ Three things are never sated; four never say, ‘Enough.’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סֻכָּה נב:) בְּיִצְרָא דְּתַאֲוָה: "מַשְׂבִּיעוֹ רָעֵב".
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: A man has a small organ: if he starves it, it is sated; if he sates it, it is hungry, as it is said: ‘As they grazed, they became sated,’ and so forth.’

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה מז.) עַל זֶה: "יֵצֶר שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה וְיָמִין מְקָרֶבֶת".
connections.quote: “Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: With regard to the inclination, a child, and a woman, let the left hand push away and the right hand draw near.”
connections.context: The relevant item here is the inclination itself. Rav Tzadok uses the balance of restraining and drawing near to explain why desire must be governed without being abolished entirely; the world also needs it.

connections.hePhrase: [וְהֶבֶל בְּהֵ״א, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
connections.quote: “The same pattern applies below. What is written below? “Adam knew his wife Eve, and she conceived and bore Cain.” Qof began to give birth within her, through Adam’s strength and assistance, after she had received impurity from that qof. Therefore it does not say here “he begot,” but “he knew,” “she conceived,” and “she bore,” and dross emerged within the female. “She continued to bear his brother Abel”: here too it does not say “he begot,” although he came from the male side. But the accuser grew weak and its strength was broken, for the letters had begun giving birth with qof. Once the dross was separated, the letters began to give birth through the mystery of the letters shin-tav: the rectification of male and female in agreement together. Then it is written, “He begot in his likeness, according to his image, and he called his name Seth”; it does not say “she called.” He called, not she: he called his name Seth, the rectification of male and female together in one accord. The letters then revolved again, returning to bring forth the alef of Adam and the letters at the place where his name ends. Which is it? Nun; afterward vav, not heh, for heh had already become pregnant with Abel [another reading: had already been born in Abel]. Therefore it took the following letter, vav, and concluded with the initial of Seth, shin, and he was called Enosh.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר שָׁם (קס עַמּוּד א) דִּבְאוֹת הַקּוֹ״ף הָיוּ יְרִיעוֹת עִזִּים בַּמִּשְׁכָּן,
connections.quote: “Qof remained alone, ascending and descending, standing within the opening of the great abyss. The Holy One, blessed be He, saw it in confusion, without a body or form, and it did not enter the Tabernacle. He made it a covering for the Tabernacle. What was it? Curtains of goats’ hair for a tent over the Tabernacle, as it is said, “You shall make curtains of goats’ hair for a tent over the Tabernacle”: for a tent, and not the tent itself; qof, and not a human being.”

connections.hePhrase: בְּסוֹד "וְאֵת עֹרֹת גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים הִלְבִּישָׁה וְגוֹמֵר", עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: ‘She put the skins of the young goats upon his hands and upon the smooth part of his neck.’

connections.hePhrase: בְּסוֹד "וְאֵת עֹרֹת גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים הִלְבִּישָׁה וְגוֹמֵר", עַיֵּין שָׁם,
connections.quote: “This is the mystery of “She clothed his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the skins of the young goats.” In the same manner, “You shall make curtains of goats’ hair for a tent over the Tabernacle.” This portion must be shown outside in order to guard what is within; through this mystery she clothed Jacob on the outside. Satan-qera are letters marked on the outside for guarding the Tabernacle, which is the mystery of the holy covenant, and afterward the foreskin is uncovered with this covering.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סג) בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "אַדְמוֹנִי עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם – מִדַּעַת סַנְהֶדְרִין".
connections.quote: see note 2308.
connections.context: The Midrash distinguishes a violent impulse acting on its own from force governed by lawful judgment. Rav Tzadok draws a corresponding distinction within the individual, where the force of anger can be directed toward restraining one’s evil inclination.

connections.hePhrase: בְּרוֹגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן דְּטָב.
connections.quote: “If you say: What of the anger of the sages? The anger of the sages is good in every respect, for we have learned that Torah is fire, and Torah heats him, as it is written, “Is not My word like fire, declares the Lord?” The anger of the sages is in matters of Torah; the anger of the sages is to give honor to Torah, and it is all for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He. Therefore it is said, “For the Lord your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.” But if it concerns other matters, this is not service of the Holy One. Among all the sins a person commits, none is actual idolatry like this, and one may not approach such a person. If you say: It was only momentary, and after it passed he returned—this is not so. Once he uprooted the holiness of his soul from himself and its place, that foreign god seizes the place, grows strong in him, and does not leave him, unless he purifies himself completely, uproots it forever, and afterward strives to sanctify himself and draw holiness upon himself. Then, if only he becomes sanctified! Rabbi Yosei said to him: He does indeed become sanctified. [Another reading: “Why? Has the foreign power not been expelled and the person sanctified?”]”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ אַבַּיֵּי דִּמְכַפֵּין נַפְשֵׁיהּ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שַׁבָּת לג סוֹף עַמּוּד א)
connections.quote: “Shmuel HaKatan suffered from it. He said, ‘Master of the universe, who can distinguish?’ He was healed. Abaye suffered from it. Rava said, ‘I know that Nachmani deprives himself of food.’ Rava suffered from it. But was it not Rava who said, ‘More are killed by the cooking pot than by the swelling of hunger’? Rava was different: the Sages kept him occupied at his mealtime against his will.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית בִּדְמָצֵי לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ (תַּעֲנִית יא רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב),
connections.quote: “…as though holiness dwells within his bowels, as it is said, “The Holy One is in your midst, and I will not come into the city.” There is no difficulty: this case is where he is able to afflict himself, and that case is where he is unable to afflict himself.”
connections.context: The discussion begins on 11a and asks how Rabbi Elazar can praise fasting while also insisting on care for one’s own body. The distinction turns on the person’s capacity to bear the deprivation. Rav Tzadok cites that qualification when describing fasting as a means of restraining desire.

connections.hePhrase: זֶהוּ כִּרְצִיחָה וְאֵינוֹ "גּוֹמֵל נַפְשׁוֹ אִישׁ חָסֶד".
connections.quote: ‘A person of kindness treats his own self well, while a cruel person afflicts his own flesh.’

connections.hePhrase: [רנט] כְּמוֹ שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל דָּבָר טוֹב הוּא הָאֱמוּנָה, שֶׁבּוֹ פָּתְחָה הַתּוֹרָה "אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר" שֶׁלֹּא בִּלְשׁוֹן צִיוּוּי,
connections.quote: “All the nations heard, ‘Peoples tremble’: after seeing open, explicit miracles they could not deny them. But Amalek, through mockery, dismissed everything and denied it. This comes from pride: in his eyes it is impossible that anything should be hidden from his intellect and above his apprehension. Through this he becomes a scoffer and denies everything by mockery. This is ‘Amalek is the first of the nations,’ the beginning of the husk, for the root of the serpent’s enticement was ‘You will be like God.’ This is the utmost pride, as said concerning Nebuchadnezzar and Hiram, and it is the root of the evil inclination.”
connections.explanation: The Chanukah passage explains the inward mechanism of the mockery called a root of evil here: it refuses the possibility that something can be true while exceeding the observer’s comprehension. This sharpens the siman’s distinction between Yisro’s misdirected readiness to believe and Amalek’s rejection of belief itself. The former can be corrected toward truth; the latter first blocks the receptivity through which correction could enter. Faith here is therefore joined to humility, rather than to indiscriminate acceptance.
connections.headline: Mockery can close the very willingness to receive what exceeds one’s grasp

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ גַּם כֵּן בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ז עַמּוּד ב; יא עַמּוּד ב) עַל פָּסוּק "זֶה הַשַּׁעַר לַה' צַדִּיקִים יָבֹאוּ בוֹ",
connections.quote: “Thus it is written: “Open for me the gates of righteousness.” This is certainly “the gate of the LORD”: if one does not enter through this gate, one will never enter.”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ גַּם כֵּן בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ז עַמּוּד ב; יא עַמּוּד ב) עַל פָּסוּק "זֶה הַשַּׁעַר לַה' צַדִּיקִים יָבֹאוּ בוֹ",
connections.quote: ““In the beginning God created”: this is the first commandment of all, called fear of the LORD, which is called “beginning.” For it is written: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the LORD,” and “Fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.” This matter is called beginning, and it is the gate through which to enter faith. On this commandment the whole world stands.”
connections.context: These are the relevant passages at Zohar I 7b and I 11b. The first explains the Psalm’s gate as reverence leading inward to divine wisdom; the second explicitly calls it the entrance to faith. Rav Tzadok uses this language to explain why faith is the root and entry point of holiness.

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ גַּם כֵּן בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ז עַמּוּד ב; יא עַמּוּד ב) עַל פָּסוּק "זֶה הַשַּׁעַר לַה' צַדִּיקִים יָבֹאוּ בוֹ",
connections.quote: see note 3971.
connections.context: The verse names the gate through which the righteous enter. The Zohar passages cited beside it describe reverence as the entrance to higher wisdom and to faith; Rav Tzadok develops faith as the point of entry to holiness.

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם "רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם עֲמָלֵק",
connections.quote: “As the Midrash says: “Strike a scoffer, and the simple person becomes discerning.” The scoffer is Amalek, and the simple person is Yisro. After the Exodus and the splitting of the sea, evil was separated from good: Amalek became separated entirely toward evil, while Yisro became included within Israel.”
connections.explanation: Tiferet Yosef places the same verse about Amalek and Yisro within an account of separating the good from the evil mixed with it. This clarifies why the siman can distinguish the simple person's misdirected belief from the scoffer's obstruction of belief: openness has something that can be redirected, but it still needs clarification toward truth. The surrounding incense discussion preserves the good capable of giving fragrance rather than identifying every existing mixture with its final condition.
connections.headline: Receptivity is clarified toward the good

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כז) עַל פָּסוּק "לֵץ תַּכֶּה" – זֶה עֲמָלֵק, "וּפֶתִי יַעְרִם" – זֶה יִתְרוֹ.
connections.quote: “Another matter, “Yitro…heard,” that is what is written: “Strike the cynic, and the naïf will become clever” (Proverbs 19:25). Likewise, it says: “With the punishment of a cynic, the naïf becomes wise” (Proverbs 21:11). Amalek and Yitro were consulted by Pharaoh. When Yitro saw that the Holy One blessed be He eliminated Amalek from this world and from the World to Come, he reconsidered and repented, as it is written above: “For I will expunge the memory of Amalek” (Exodus 17:14) and afterward: “Yitro heard.” He said: ‘I must go only to the God of Israel.’ From where do you derive that Amalek and the Midianites were enemies of Israel? As it is stated: The elders of Moav and the elders of Midian went” (Numbers 22:7). Likewise, “[Whenever Israel would sow,] the Midianites, Amalekites, and the people of the east [would come up against them. They would encamp against them and destroy the produce of the earth]” (Judges 6:3–4), and likewise, the wicked Bilam says: “He saw Amalek” (Numbers 24:20); that it did not change its ways. But when he saw that Yitro had repented, what did he say? “He saw the Kenite” (Numbers 24:21); this is analogous to a hunter who would hunt birds. He trapped the first. He came to trap the second. It went and sat on the statue of the king. The hunter stood bewildered by it. He said to it: ‘If I throw a rock at you, I will be liable to be executed. If I extend the reed, I am afraid that it might touch the king’s statue. I do not know what to say to you; rather, you fled to a fine place and were spared.’ So too, Bilam saw Yitro and Amalek in counsel. He stood [and looked] at Amalek and eradicated its name. He came to look at Yitro and found that he repented. He said to him: ‘You fled well.’ That is, “Mighty is your dwelling” (Numbers 24:21), like Abraham. That is, “strike the cynic,” this is Amalek; “and the naïf will become clever,” this is Yitro. “Rebuke the discerning” (Proverbs 19:25), this is Moses, whom Yitro admonished when he saw him sitting and judging Israel all day. He said to him: “Why are you sitting alone?” (Exodus 18:14). “You will wear away” (Exodus 18:18). He said to him: ‘Do not do it because it is my opinion, but rather, consult with the Holy One blessed be He,’ as it is stated: “Heed my voice, I will counsel you [and may God be with you]” (Exodus 18:19). What is written thereafter? “Moses heeded his father-in-law, and he performed everything that he had said” (Exodus 18:24).”

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כז) עַל פָּסוּק "לֵץ תַּכֶּה" – זֶה עֲמָלֵק, "וּפֶתִי יַעְרִם" – זֶה יִתְרוֹ.
connections.quote: “Strike a scoffer, and the simple person will become prudent; rebuke a discerning person, and he will understand knowledge.”
connections.context: Shemot Rabbah 27:6 applies the first half of this verse to Amalek being struck and Jethro learning from the event. This supplies the contrast between the hardened scoffer and a simple person capable of being instructed.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּפֶתִי הוּא הַמַּאֲמִין בַּכֹּל, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "פֶּתִי יַאֲמִין לְכָל דָּבָר",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Exodus, Yitro 3
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Exodus, Yitro 3
connections.quote: ““Jethro heard.” In the Midrash: This is what is written, “Strike a scoffer and the naive person becomes discerning.” “Strike a scoffer”—this is Amalek; “the naive person becomes discerning”—this is Jethro. A scoffer is one who mocks something true, whereas a naive person believes everything. In truth, neither is good. Yet of the scoffer it says, “Strike,” because he will not come to recognize his deficiency and correct it, since he mocks every true matter and does not listen at all. The naive person, however, who is persuaded by anything, can receive the truth and come to correct the root of his deficiency. Therefore we were commanded to erase Amalek, for no good will emerge from him. Jethro, however, sought to know the ultimate good, but at first believed in the worship of stars and constellations and in vanities. Afterward, when he saw the exaltedness of God, he said, “Now I know that the Lord is great,” and converted.”

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּפֶתִי הוּא הַמַּאֲמִין בַּכֹּל, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "פֶּתִי יַאֲמִין לְכָל דָּבָר",
connections.quote: ‘The simpleton believes every word, but the discerning person considers his steps.’

connections.hePhrase: וְיִתְרוֹ לֹא הִנִּיחַ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמְּכִילְתָּא) שֶׁהֶאֱמִין בַּכֹּל;
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דַעֲמָלֵק ג׳:מ״ב
connections.quote: “What does “above all gods” teach? They said: Jethro left no form of idolatry in the entire world without pursuing and worshipping it, as it says, “above all gods.” Naaman acknowledged more than he did, as it says, “Now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” Likewise, Rahab the harlot says, “The Lord your God—He is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.””

connections.hePhrase: וּכְטַעַם "שְׂחוֹק וְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ מַרְגִּילִין לְעֶרְוָה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג).
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Akiva says: Laughter and frivolity lead a person toward sexual transgression. The transmitted textual tradition is a fence for Torah. Tithes are a fence for wealth. Vows are a fence for abstinence. A fence for wisdom is silence.’

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן נִקְבַּע בַּשַּׁ״ס בִּתְחִלַּת סֵדֶר אֱמוּנוֹת,
connections.quote: “Reish Lakish said: What is meant by the verse, “The faithfulness of your times shall be a store of salvation, wisdom and knowledge”? “Faithfulness”—this is the Order of Seeds. “Your times”—this is the Order of Festivals. “A store”—this is the Order of Women. “Salvation”—this is the Order of Damages. “Wisdom”—this is the Order of Sacred Things. “And knowledge”—this is the Order of Purities. Even so, “Fear of the Lord is its treasure.””

connections.hePhrase: וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (יח.): "כֵּיוָן שֶׁבָּא דָּוִד בָּאת תְּפִלָּה",
connections.quote: ‘‘Afterward, the children of Israel will return and seek Hashem their God and David their king.’ Once David comes, prayer comes, as it is said: ‘I will bring them to My holy mountain and gladden them in My house of prayer.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִדָּתוֹ גַּם כֵּן מִדַּת הָאֱמוּנָה כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: ““I have sworn to David My servant”—this is the mystery of faith, which is constantly established through this righteous one, the sustaining foundation of the world, so that they should never be separated. The exception is the time of exile, when the flow of blessings is withheld, the mystery of faith is not complete, and all joys are withheld. When night enters, from that time joys do not enter before the King.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלָכֵן אָמַר: "אֲנִי אַרְבֶּה וְלֹא אָסוּר וְכוּלֵי" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין כא:).
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yitzchak said: Why were the reasons for the Torah’s laws not revealed? The reasons for two verses were revealed, and the greatest man in the world stumbled through them. It is written: ‘He shall not multiply wives for himself.’ Solomon said: ‘I will multiply wives and will not turn aside.’ But it is written: ‘When Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart astray.’’

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ: "כְּמִתְלַהְלֵהַּ וְגוֹמֵר הֲלֹא מְשַׂחֵק אָנִי" (מִשְׁלֵי כו, יח-יט),
connections.quote: “Like a madman who shoots firebrands, arrows, and death, so is a man who deceives his fellow and says, “Am I not only playing?””
connections.context: The second verse contains the word mesachek, “playing,” on which Rav Tzadok’s comparison depends. Its setting is a harmful deed excused as a joke, an example of folly enacted outwardly.

connections.hePhrase: "יוֹשֵׁב בַּשָּׁמַיִם יִשְׂחָק, ה' יִלְעַג לָמוֹ".
connections.quote: ‘He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord mocks them.’

connections.hePhrase: וְנֶאֱמַר בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם "מְשַׂחֲקִים וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “David and all the house of Israel were playing before the LORD with all manner of cypress-wood instruments, with lyres, harps, drums, rattles, and cymbals.”
connections.context: The Hebrew mesachakim, “playing” or “making merry,” describes David’s celebration as the Ark is brought up. Rav Tzadok compares the outward activity denoted by this word with other uses of “playing”; here its setting is sacred rejoicing.

connections.hePhrase: וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים: "מְשַׂחֵק בְּקֻבְיָא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין כד:) וּ"מְשַׂחֵק בַּתִּינֹקֶת" (נִדָּה יג:),
connections.quote: ‘Gemara: What wrong does a dice player commit? Rami bar Chama said: His wager is an asmakhta [a conditional commitment made without full resolve], and an asmakhta does not effect an acquisition.’

connections.hePhrase: וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים: "מְשַׂחֵק בְּקֻבְיָא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין כד:) וּ"מְשַׂחֵק בַּתִּינֹקֶת" (נִדָּה יג:),
connections.quote: see note 1485 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The discussion ultimately identifies the expression with marriages that delay childbearing. Rav Tzadok cites its wording as an example of an act described as “playing” because it does not achieve its procreative end. The previous excerpt about a deaf woman belonged to a different discussion on the page.

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵיפֶךְ זֶה חָכְמַת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁאָמַר: "לִשְׂחוֹק אָמַרְתִּי מְהוֹלָל וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Of laughter I said: ‘It is madness’; and of joy: ‘What does it accomplish?’’

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל חָכְמָתוֹ הוּא לְחַבֵּר אֱמֶת וֶאֱמוּנָה בְּיַחַד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר תְּרוּמָה (קמה עַמּוּד א),
connections.quote: “Moses rose upward in his praise. His praise was to give praises and thanks to the supernal King, who rescued Israel and performed miracles and mighty deeds for them in Egypt and at the sea. But King David and Solomon his son sang in another manner. David labored to prepare the maidens and adorn them together with the Queen, so that the Queen and her maidens would appear in beauty. He therefore labored in their songs and praises until he had prepared and adorned all the maidens and the Queen. When Solomon came, he found the Queen adorned and her maidens in beauty. He labored to bring her to the bridegroom, brought the bridegroom into the bridal canopy with the Queen, and introduced words of love between them, to join them as one and bring both into one completeness, in complete affection. Thus Solomon rose in supernal praise above all people. Moses united the Queen in this world below, so that she would be in this world in complete union among those below. Solomon united the Queen in complete union above: first he brought the bridegroom into the bridal canopy; afterward he brought them both into this world and welcomed them in joy in the Temple he built. If you ask how Moses brought the Queen alone into this world, which appears to be separation: come and see. The Holy One, blessed be He, first united her with Moses, and she was Moses’ bride, as has been said. Once she was united with Moses, she descended into this world in its union and was established here as she had not been before. She was never in separation. But from the day Adam was created, no person introduced love, affection, and words of union above except King Solomon, who first established the union above and afterward welcomed them together into the house he prepared for them. Fortunate are David and Solomon his son, who established the union above. From the day the Holy One, blessed be He, told the moon, “Go and diminish yourself,” she was not united with the sun in complete union until King Solomon came.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבָחַר בְּחוֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר שֶׁנֶּגֶד הַקּוֹ״ף שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הַשְּׂחוֹק כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה;
connections.quote: “In Sefer Yetzirah, the expression for every month is “He made such-and-such a letter reign over such-and-such a power.” The intention is that the power should operate in its good direction, since every power exists in good and, God forbid, in its opposite. Likewise, concerning Adar it says, “He made the letter qof reign over laughter…Adar in the year.” There is joy and laughter of which it is written, “Of laughter I said, ‘It is madness,’ and of joy, ‘What does it accomplish?’” He made the letter qof reign so that the joy and laughter should be good.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבָחַר בְּחוֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר שֶׁנֶּגֶד הַקּוֹ״ף שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הַשְּׂחוֹק כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה;
connections.quote: “He made the letter qof reign over laughter, bound a crown to it, combined them with one another, and through them formed Pisces in the world, Adar in the year, and the spleen in the person, male and female.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מְגִילָּה יג:): "וְלֹא יָדַע כִּי בְּז' בַּאֲדָר מֵת וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: ‘‘He cast pur, that is, the lot.’ It was taught: When the lot fell in the month of Adar, he rejoiced greatly. He said: ‘The lot has fallen for me in the month in which Moses died.’ But he did not know that Moses died on the seventh of Adar and was born on the seventh of Adar.’

connections.hePhrase: רַק "יָדוֹ אֹחֶזֶת בַּעֲקֵב" וּבְסוֹף הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
connections.quote: “Afterward his brother emerged, his hand grasping Esau’s heel, and he called his name Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.”
connections.context: Jacob’s hand grasps the heel, the lower extremity. Rav Tzadok uses that image to describe Jacob’s hold on the lowest, outward point of the opposing power.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַתְחָלַת זֶה בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִתְחִיל גַּם כֵּן בְּיִחוּד אֱמֶת וֶאֱמוּנָה,
connections.quote: “Come and see: Solomon could not have established the union above unless the union below had already existed. What was it? The union of Moses. Had that union not existed, the union above would not have been established. All this is a supernal mystery for the wise of heart.”

connections.hePhrase: כַּנּוֹדָע דְּ"מֹשֶׁה מִלְּגָאו, יַעֲקֹב מִלְּבָר" (תִּיקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּיקּוּן יג).
connections.quote: “Therefore they said, “Jacob outwardly, Moses inwardly.” Jacob’s soul includes all the souls of Israel, since they are all his descendants and part of his soul; the totality of their souls is included in him. Moses our teacher belongs to the mystery of knowledge—as is known, this is why the wilderness generation is called the generation of knowledge, as the Midrash on Hukkat explains concerning Darda—for he includes all the souls in respect of knowledge, the inward dimension of the soul. As is known, when the ten sefirot are considered in their outward aspect, knowledge is not counted among them. It is counted only in their inward aspect, where the crown is not counted, since it is called “nothingness”: the skull and the place of the head-tefillin, above the brain and wisdom, the beginning of emergence from nothing into something. Inwardly, in what is accessible to a person, knowledge therefore fills the place of the crown. Rashi explains “and with knowledge” in Ki Tisa as divine inspiration: an apprehension above the wisdom in the brain and beyond its bounds. Thus Moses our teacher is the inward dimension of all the souls of Israel: the apprehension of knowledge that comes from the soul’s root and source in the letters of Torah. It is the knowledge within the souls of Israel in every generation.”

connections.hePhrase: כַּנּוֹדָע דְּ"מֹשֶׁה מִלְּגָאו, יַעֲקֹב מִלְּבָר" (תִּיקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּיקּוּן יג).
connections.quote: “When the sukkah is completed in its thigh, it is said of Jacob, “Jacob came whole.” Jacob is certainly the image of the middle pillar from its outward side. Moses was there as well, but from its inward side: this one from the body, and that one from the soul. Therefore the two thighs of the complete middle pillar are Netzach and Hod.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁחָשַׁב כִּי הַתְחָלַת כֹּחוֹ וְהַשְׁלָמַת כָּל דָּבָר בְּז' יָמִים שֶׁהֵם ז' יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: “The seven double letters are the seven sefirot of building. They are doubled, composed of judgment and mercy. The letters bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, peh, resh, and tav allude to them: these letters receive a hard pronunciation, signifying judgment, and a soft pronunciation, signifying mercy.”

connections.hePhrase: אַחַר כָּךְ הוּא פּוּרִים דְּ"חַיָּיב לִבְסוֹמֵי",
connections.quote: “Rava said: A person is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know the difference between “Cursed is Haman” and “Blessed is Mordecai.” Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira held their Purim feast together. They became intoxicated. Rabbah arose and slaughtered Rabbi Zeira. The next day he prayed for mercy and revived him. The following year he said to him, “Let the master come, and let us hold the Purim feast together.” He replied, “A miracle does not occur on every occasion.””

connections.hePhrase: דַּרְגָּא דִּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "תַּרְתִּי בְלִבִּי וְגוֹמֵר בַּיַּיִן וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘I explored in my heart how to indulge my body with wine, while my heart guided me with wisdom, and how to take hold of folly, until I could see what is good for human beings to do under the heavens during the numbered days of their lives.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה רִידְּתוֹ אִמּוֹ כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין ע:).
connections.quote: ‘‘The words of Lemuel the king, the admonition with which his mother disciplined him.’ Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s name: This teaches that his mother bound him to the post and said to him: ‘What, my son? What, son of my womb? What, son of my vows?’ ‘What, my son?’—everyone knows that your father feared Heaven. Now they will say that his mother brought this upon him.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה רִידְּתוֹ אִמּוֹ כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין ע:).
connections.quote: ““It is not for kings, Lemuel; it is not for kings to drink wine.” “It is not for kings”: She said to him, “What have you to do with kings who drink wine, become intoxicated, and say, ‘Why do we need God?’” “And for princes, where is strong drink?” Should one to whom all the secrets of the world are revealed drink wine and become intoxicated? Some say: Should one to whose door all the princes of the world come early drink wine and become intoxicated?”

connections.hePhrase: וְ"עַד דְּלָא יָדַע" – הַיְינוּ הֶעְדֵּר הַדַּעַת דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
connections.quote: “This holiness is revealed in its full strength on Purim, concerning which they said, “One is obligated to become intoxicated until he does not know.” Its plain meaning is the revelation that the hearts of Israel are truly attached to God even when they do not know their right from their left. A person is recognized through three things; through his cup and his intoxication, he no longer has complete awareness with which to conceal and hide the depths of his heart. What lies within the depths of the heart is then revealed, as they said, “Wine enters; the secret emerges.” It is revealed that the depths of Israel’s heart are attached to God without deliberate calculation or coercing the heart’s desire. Rather, the true point of desire is, of itself, truly attached to God.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל חָכְמָתוֹ הִשִּׂיג בַּחֲלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא בְּעֵת הִסְתַּלְּקוּת הַדַּעַת לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.quote: “At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream at night. God said: “Ask what I shall give you.””

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל חָכְמָתוֹ הִשִּׂיג בַּחֲלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא בְּעֵת הִסְתַּלְּקוּת הַדַּעַת לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.quote: “Behold, I have done according to your words: I have given you a wise and discerning heart, so that none like you has been before you, and none like you shall arise after you.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל חָכְמָתוֹ הִשִּׂיג בַּחֲלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא בְּעֵת הִסְתַּלְּקוּת הַדַּעַת לְגַמְרֵי.
connections.quote: “Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream.”
connections.context: Verse 5 supplies the dream setting; verse 12 records the gift of wisdom; verse 15 confirms that Solomon receives this revelation while dreaming. Together they explain Rav Tzadok’s statement that Solomon attained wisdom when ordinary waking awareness was absent.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "שְׂחֹק לְרֵעֵהוּ אֶהְיֶה", וְזֶהוּ לֵיצָנוּת.
connections.quote: ‘I am a laughingstock to my companion—I, who call to God and am answered. A righteous, blameless man is a laughingstock.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה נִזְכַּר בְּמַסֶּכֶת מְגִילָּה (כה:)
connections.quote: ‘Rav Nachman said: All mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, which is permitted. For it is written: ‘Bel bends down; Nebo crouches,’ and it is written: ‘They crouched and bent down together; they could not escape the burden,’ and so forth. Rabbi Yannai said: The source is here: ‘The inhabitants of Samaria fear for the calves of Beth Aven, for its people mourn over it, and its priests who rejoiced over it mourn its glory, because it has departed from it.’ Do not read kevodo, ‘its glory,’ but keveido, ‘its heavy load’ [of excrement].’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁלָּכֵן מִנְהַג יִשְׂרָאֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת בּוֹ מִינֵי שְׂחוֹק וְלֵיצָנוּת מֵהָמָן,
connections.quote: “The month of Adar was formed through the letter qof, as Sefer Yetzirah says: “He made the letter qof reign over laughter…and through it formed fish in the world.” It appears to me that this means, “This Leviathan You formed to play with,” from which comes laughter above, as stated at the beginning of Avodah Zarah and in the chapter HaSefinah. Certainly the constellation Pisces in the heavens corresponds to Leviathan, chief of the fish of the sea. Adar in the year is the time when “we increase joy,” and laughter comes from it, for laughter is the opposite of weeping, as stated among the twenty-eight times in Ecclesiastes: one comes from sadness and mourning, and the other from abundant gladness and joy. It is an ancient custom to practice all kinds of play on Purim; see Sanhedrin concerning “like the Purim jumping” and Rashi there. The spleen in the person is the source of laughter, as stated in the chapter HaRo’eh. Both [laughter “with His creatures” and laughter “at His creatures”] are included, for these are two kinds of laughter: “with His creatures”—this is the play with Leviathan; and “at His creatures,” as stated in Avodah Zarah—this is the laughter of Purim at Haman’s downfall.”

connections.hePhrase: כִּי כָּל השס"ה לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה הֵם עֲנָפִים מִ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ",
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים כ׳:א׳
connections.quote: “It is known to all that the commandment and prohibition concerning idolatry—the first two commandments, “I am” and “You shall have no other”—include the whole Torah. The declaration “I am” includes all 248 positive commandments, and “You shall have no other” includes all 365 prohibitions. Therefore we heard only “I am” and “You shall have no other” directly from the Almighty, as our Sages said, because they include the whole Torah.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכָל מִינֵי רַע נִקְרָא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים כ״ד:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: ““God made one corresponding to the other”: these are the 365 Torah prohibitions and all rabbinic prohibitions. Since they oppose His blessed will and wisdom and are their very opposite, they are utterly separated from His blessed unity and oneness, like the other side and the shell called “idolatry” and “other gods,” because the face of the supernal will is concealed, as explained above. Likewise, the three garments of the soul in Israel that derives from the shell of nogah—thought, speech, and action—when clothed in the 365 prohibitions of the Torah or the rabbinic prohibitions, and likewise the soul’s own essence clothed in those garments, are all truly united with this other side and shell called “idolatry.””

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין פא.):
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Meir used to mock those who committed transgressions. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the other side of the river. There was no ferry, so he grasped a rope and began to cross. When he reached the middle of the rope, the temptation left him. Satan said: Had they not proclaimed in Heaven, ‘Take care with Rabbi Meir and his Torah,’ I would have reduced your worth to two ma’ah coins.’

connections.hePhrase: אֵין לוֹ לְהִתְלוֹצֵץ מִן הָאַחֵר,
connections.quote: “For someone who has no trace of a deficiency cannot suspect his fellow of that deficiency either: he does not sense the existence of the deficiency and judges everyone favorably. Therefore our Sages said, “Whoever disqualifies another does so through his own blemish.” A person does not disqualify his fellow for something absent from himself, unless there is some trace of it in his own soul. He then sees in his fellow that same deficiency which is in himself, for souls are like mirrors, as is known.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ג:)
connections.quote: “Immediately the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and laughs at them, as it is stated: “He who sits in heaven laughs.” Rabbi Yitzchak said: There is no laughter before the Holy One, blessed be He, except on that day alone.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ג:)
connections.quote: “In the fourth period He sits and plays with Leviathan, as it is stated: “This Leviathan You formed to play with.” Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: He plays with His creatures; He does not laugh at His creatures except on that day alone.”
connections.context: The distinction between playing with a creature and laughing at it is explicit in the Gemara. Rav Tzadok uses it to distinguish divine participation in creation from ridicule that accompanies the final removal of evil.

connections.hePhrase: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ג:)
connections.quote: “According to the Geonim’s reading, “the letter ayin with laughter”: our Sages indeed said that a person may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world. Rather, “with laughter” has the meaning we explained in the teaching, “He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice.” Although God does not rejoice in the downfall of the wicked—He would have wanted them not to perish, and their suffering to help them improve their ways—it nevertheless benefits Israel, whose blood was shed, by bringing them to joy. They attain this only when they attain an upright heart, without any inclination toward evil, as it says, “The upright, for joy.” At Chanukah they attained the light of Oral Torah; likewise, every Chanukah is a time to attain the shining of Oral Torah’s light in the heart. It is written, “The Lord’s precepts are upright, rejoicing the heart”: through the light of Oral Torah, one attains an upright heart and joy.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah develops the same distinction used in this siman—‘He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice’—by specifying the preferred outcome: that suffering lead to improved conduct rather than destruction. This explains why the siman bases Hashem’s relation to the wicked on His continuing creation and sustenance of them. Israel’s permitted joy is related to deliverance and an upright heart, not to a simple adoption of contempt for another created being.
connections.headline: Joy in deliverance differs from taking pleasure in a creature’s destruction

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (י:) דְּאָמַר: "מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי טוֹבְעִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yochanan said: What is meant by “one did not draw near the other all night”? The ministering angels wished to sing. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: “The work of My hands is drowning in the sea, and you are singing?””

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (י:) דְּאָמַר: "מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי טוֹבְעִים וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Rabbi Elazar said: He Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice. This is also precise in the verse, which says yasis, “He will cause to rejoice,” and not yasus, “He will rejoice.” Learn from this.”
connections.context: The continuation supplies Rav Tzadok’s explicit phrase “He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice.” He explains this through God’s continuing relationship to the creatures He sustains.

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם לֹא יַרְגִּישׁוּ בָּזֶה, "וְיֶהְגּוּ רִיק וְגוֹמֵר" –
connections.quote: “Why are the nations in an uproar, and why do the peoples meditate a vain thing?”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "יָקוּמוּ נָא הַנְּעָרִים וִישַׂחֲקוּ לְפָנֵינוּ".
connections.quote: ‘Abner said to Joab: ‘Let the young men rise and sport before us.’ Joab said: ‘Let them rise.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְעִנְיַן (שַׁבָּת ל:) "מִילְּתָא דִּבְדִיחוּתָא" וּבְדָחֵי רַבָּנָן קוֹדֶם הַלִּימּוּד,
connections.quote: “Is that so? Rav Giddel said in Rav’s name: Any Torah scholar who sits before his teacher without his lips dripping bitterness deserves to have them burned, as it is said, ‘His lips are lilies, dripping flowing myrrh.’ Read mor over, ‘flowing myrrh,’ as mar over, ‘flowing bitterness’; read shoshanim, ‘lilies,’ as sheshonim, ‘those who study.’ There is no difficulty: one statement concerns the teacher, the other the student. Alternatively, both concern the teacher, and there is still no difficulty: one concerns the time before he begins, the other the time after he has begun. Thus, before Rabbah began teaching the scholars, he would say something humorous, and they would laugh. Then he would sit in awe and begin the teaching.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהָיָה מֵשִׂים לְפָנָיו תֵּל דִּנְרֵי זָהָב בְּעֵת לִימּוּד סוּגְיָא עֲמוּקָה לְהַרְחָבַת הַדַּעַת.
connections.displayRef: Shem HaGedolim, Maarekhet Sefarim, Letter Tav 20:7
connections.linkedRef: Shem HaGedolim, Maarekhet Sefarim, Letter Tav 20:7
connections.canonicalRef: Shem HaGedolim, Maarekhet Sefarim, Letter Tav 20:7
connections.heRef: שם הגדולים, מערכת ספרים, מערכת ת כ׳:ז׳
connections.quote: “The sun shone, a star went forth from Jacob: Rabbenu Tam, possessing Torah and greatness. As Maharil wrote, he would place a heap of gold coins before him to broaden his heart in the depths of halakhic study—he, his brother, and his students.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה פב) דְּאַבְנֵר מִקְרָא דָּרַשׁ דְּ"מְלָכִים מֵחֲלָצֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר" וְהִמְלִיךְ אִישׁ בֹּשֶׁת,
connections.quote: ““God said to him: I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply; a nation and an assembly of nations will be from you, and kings will emerge from your loins” (Genesis 35:11). “God said to him: I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply” – Rabbi Yudan said in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak: I used to say: Reuben was already out. Simeon was already out. Benjamin had already emerged from his loins and was still in his mother’s womb. Then I said: “A nation” – this is Benjamin; “and an assembly of nations” – this is Manasseh and Ephraim, as it is written: “His descendants will be a plenitude of the nations” (Genesis 48:19). Rabbi Berekhya, Rabbi Ḥelbo, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman: “And kings will emerge from your loins” – this is Yerovam and Yehu. The Rabbis say: Is it possible that Avner was a righteous man and he disputed that the kingdom [belonged to] the house of David? It is that he expounded a midrash, and crowned Ish Boshet. That is what is written: “And kings will emerge from your loins” – this is Saul and Ish Boshet. What did they see that led them to draw near and ostracize in the case of the concubine in Giva? It is, rather, that they read a verse and ostracized them, and read a verse and immediately welcomed them. They read a verse and ostracized them: “Ephraim and Manasseh will be like Reuben and Simeon for me” (Genesis 48:5). They read a verse and welcomed them: “A nation and an assembly of nations will be from you.””

connections.hePhrase: וְכִדְשָׁמְעִינַן (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי שַׁבָּת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ד) בְּי״ח דָּבָר,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Yehoshua of Ono taught: The disciples of the House of Shammai stood below and were killing disciples of the House of Hillel. It was taught: Six of them went up, while the rest stood over them with swords and spears.”
connections.context: This is the Jerusalem Talmud’s account connected with the eighteen decrees. Rav Tzadok cites its description of violence surrounding a Torah dispute when explaining the fighting between Abner’s and Joab’s men. The Mishnah records the vote and decrees but not this account.

connections.hePhrase: דְּתַלְמִידֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי הָיוּ הוֹרְגִים מִבֵּית הִלֵּל שֶׁהָיוּ נִלְחָמִים עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
connections.displayRef: Korban HaEdah on Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 1:4:3:1-3
connections.linkedRef: Korban HaEdah on Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 1:4:3:1-3
connections.canonicalRef: Korban HaEdah on Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 1:4:3:1-3
connections.heRef: קרבן העדה על תלמוד ירושלמי שבת א׳:ד׳:ג׳:א׳-ג׳
connections.quote: ““They were killing the disciples of Hillel”: Had they wished to go up—but, Heaven forbid, they did not actually kill them; so it appears to me. “Six”: Of Hillel’s disciples went up to the study hall. “And the rest stood”: The disciples of the House of Shammai stood below with swords and spears and did not allow them to go up, so that they themselves would form the majority.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֵּאָה פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה א וּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת אֱמוֹר)
connections.quote: “Why is it called “triple?” Because it kills three: The one who says it, the one who accepts it, and the one calumniated. And in the days of Saul, four were killed: Doeg who said it, Saul who accepted it, Aḥimelekh who was calumniated, and Abner. Why was Abner killed? Rebbi Joshua ben Levi, Rebbi Simeon ben Laqish, and the rabbis. Rebbi Joshua ben Levi said, because he made fun of the lives of his squires as it is said (2Sam. 2:14): “Let the squires get up and play before us, and Joab said, let them get up.” R. Simeon ben Laqish, because he prefaced his name before that of David; that is what is written (2Sam. 3:12) “Abner sent messengers to David the underling, saying: Whose is the land?” He wrote: From Abner to David. The rabbis say, because he did not let Shaul make peace with David. That is what is written (1Sam. 24:5): “My father, see, but see the corner of your coat in my hand!” He said to him, what do you want from the prattling of this one, it was torn off by thorns. But when they came to the circle, he said to him (1Sam. 26:14): “Can you answer, Abner?” About the corner, you said it was torn off by a thorn; were spear and pitcher cut off by a thorn? But some say, because he had it in his power to intervene for Nob, the city of priests, and he did not intervene.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאֵצֶל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נֶאֱמַר גַּם כֵּן: "וְרָגַז וְשָׂחַק וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘When a wise person argues with a fool, whether he shows anger or laughter, he finds no satisfaction.’

connections.hePhrase: וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קג.): "שָׂחַקְתִּי עִם אֲמַצְיָה",
connections.quote: ‘I smiled on Amaziah and delivered the kings of Edom into his hand. He brought their gods and bowed down to them, as it is said: ‘After Amaziah came back from striking the Edomites, he brought the gods of the people of Seir and set them up as gods for himself. He bowed down before them and burned incense to them.’ Rav Pappa said: This is what people say: ‘They weep for a man, and he does not understand; they laugh with him, and he does not understand. Woe to a man who does not know the difference between good and bad.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ: "יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יָעַץ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘As he was speaking to him, the king said to him: ‘Have we appointed you as an adviser to the king? Stop! Why should they strike you?’ The prophet stopped and said: ‘I know that God has resolved to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel.’’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁיִּשְׁחָטֵם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:7
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:7
connections.quote: “These two inclinations are opposites, and each, when directed toward holiness, nullifies the other. In the chapter HaSefinah it says that this hunt of Leviathan is carried out through Gabriel, who represents holy powers of severity. For the inclination to bloodshed and anger will be nullified entirely, whereas the inclination of desire is also needed for the service of God. The Zohar says that it is called Laban because it will be whitened, and it will not be nullified. As our Sages said, “I will give you a heart of flesh”—a heart to produce flesh, rather than for one’s own pleasure. Its hunt will therefore be through the holy powers of severity, and the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, as stated there: without this, even the most pious of the pious…and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: וְלִוְיָתָן הוּא הַטִּיקְלָא הַנִּזְכָּר בְּסָבָא דְּמִשְׁפָּטִים (צה עַמּוּד ב; צו עַמּוּד ב)
connections.quote: “This is a supernal mystery beyond all others. At the beam on which the balances stand, within the blowing air, there is one scale on this side and another scale on that side. On this side are scales of justice, and on that side scales of deceit. This balance never rests: souls rise and descend, enter and return. Some souls are oppressed when one person rules over another, as it is written, “At a time when one person rules over another, to his harm”—certainly to his harm. But this soul, which came to the other side, to a stranger, and was oppressed by him, is “to his harm”: his—the stranger’s. She may not eat of the sacred offering until the Holy One, blessed be He, does with her what He does. Scripture therefore says, “If a priest’s daughter becomes married to a stranger”—so it is. Here is the mystery of how souls are oppressed. This world is entirely governed through the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. When the people of the world conduct themselves on the side of good, the balance stands and inclines toward good; when they conduct themselves on the side of evil, it inclines toward that side. All the souls that were in the balance at that time are oppressed and taken by it.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁחוֹטֶפֶת הַנְּפָשׁוֹת וְחָיְיכָא עִם יְנוֹקָא,
connections.quote: “If you say that this side brought her into that child, it is not so. Rather, it took her and rejoiced in her; she flew from its hands and entered that place. It visits that child, rejoices in him, laughs with him, and desires that flesh, until afterward the Holy One, blessed be He, takes his soul, and it takes the body. Afterward, everything is under the authority of the Holy One, blessed be He.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם עַל פָּסוּק "שָׁלַט הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ" דַּיְיקָא.
connections.quote: see note 3297.
connections.context: The Hebrew le-ra lo means “to his harm.” Rav Tzadok, following the Zohar passage he cites, reads the harm as ultimately rebounding upon the dominating power itself. A translation that fixes the pronoun only on the oppressed person obscures that interpretation.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם עַל פָּסוּק "שָׁלַט הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ" דַּיְיקָא.
connections.quote: “But it is “to his harm,” for those souls subdue [another reading: cover] whatever they find of the evil side, and destroy it. A sign of this is the holy Ark, which was seized among the Philistines: they ruled over it to their own harm. So too, these souls are seized by the other side to its harm. What became of those souls? We have seen in the books of the ancients that from them came the righteous among the nations, and those Torah scholars who are mamzerim and take precedence over an ignorant high priest, esteemed in the world though he enters the innermost sanctuary. The elder wept for a moment. The companions were astonished and said nothing.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ מִשֶּׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ דְּאֵין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שְׂחוֹק (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם),
connections.quote: “Rav Acha said to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: From the day the Temple was destroyed, there is no laughter for the Holy One, blessed be He.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ מִשֶּׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ דְּאֵין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שְׂחוֹק (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם),
connections.quote: “What does He do during the fourth period? He sits and teaches Torah to schoolchildren, as it is stated: “To whom shall He teach knowledge, and to whom shall He explain the message? Those weaned from milk, those removed from the breasts.” To whom shall He teach knowledge and explain the message? To those weaned from milk and removed from the breasts.”
