connections.context: The discussion replaces the previously described time of play with Leviathan with the teaching of children after the Temple’s destruction. Rav Tzadok develops the inner connection between these two activities in the following paragraphs.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי שְׁכִינָה בַּגָּלוּת וִינִיקָתָן מִצַּד רַע דִּבְנֵי אָדָם.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק שלישי; אגרת התשובה ו׳:ז׳-י״א
connections.quote:
“It is written, ‘Jacob is the cord of His inheritance.’ By way of analogy, a cord has one end above and its other end below. If a person pulls the lower end, he also moves and draws the upper end after it, as far as it can be drawn.

Exactly so with the root and source of a person’s soul in the lower hei mentioned above: through his evil deeds and thoughts, he draws its influence down, as it were, into the chambers of the other side, from which his thoughts and deeds derive. Since he is the one who draws this influence to them, he takes the first share; this is sufficient for one who understands.

This is what our Sages, of blessed memory, meant by saying, ‘Neither the tranquility of the wicked, and so forth, is in our hands.’ ‘In our hands’ is precise: it means during the exile after the destruction of the Temple. This is the exile of the Divine Presence, as it were: to bestow influence upon the chambers of the other side, which His blessed soul abhors.

When a person repents properly, he removes from them the influence that he drew down through his deeds and thoughts, for through his repentance he restores the influence of the Divine Presence to its proper place.

This is the return of the lower hei from exile. As it is written, ‘Hashem your God will return with your captivity’—that is, together with your captivity. As our Sages, of blessed memory, said: ‘It does not say, “He will bring back,”’ and so forth.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "מְשַׂחֲקִין בַּתִּינֹקֶת" בְּנִדָּה (יג:),
connections.quote: see note 1485 (Vol. I).
connections.context: This is the Gemara’s explanation of the expression. Rav Tzadok uses its association with immaturity as an analogy within his discussion of yesod in a state of katnut, limited development; the earlier excerpt about arousing improper thoughts did not contain the phrase he cites.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד יְסוֹד דְּקַטְנוּת הַיָּדוּעַ שֶׁנִּקְרָא נָחָשׁ דִּקְדוּשָׁה.
connections.quote: “However, since all the mental powers have not yet been repaired, this is not a complete and exalted union. Rather, it is called a union of smallness, because Zeir Anpin has not yet grown.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהָא וְהָא עָבֵיד – דִּמְלַמֵּד גַּם כֵּן לְתִינוֹקוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית רַבָּן,
connections.quote: “And previously, who used to teach them? If you wish, say: Metatron. And if you wish, say: He would do both.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁנּוֹתְנִין לוֹ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר אוֹ מְפַתִּין לוֹ בְּאֵיזֶה דְּבַר כָּבוֹד וְחֶמְדָּה וְכַיּוֹצֵא.
connections.quote: “Imagine a young child brought to a teacher to learn Torah. This is a great good for him because of the perfection he will attain through it. Yet because of his few years and the weakness of his intellect, he does not understand the excellence of that good or the perfection he will attain through it. The teacher, whose understanding is more complete, must therefore encourage him to learn through things he loves at his young age. He says: “Read, and I will give you nuts or figs, or a little honey.” The child reads and makes an effort, not for the reading itself, whose excellence he does not know, but so that he will receive that food. Eating those delicacies is more precious in his eyes than reading, and undoubtedly much better. He therefore regards learning as toil and exertion, and works at it so that through this effort he will attain the goal he loves: a nut or a piece of honey.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי כֵּן לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא מִפְּעוּלַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת.
connections.quote: “Anyone who occupies himself with Torah in order to receive reward or to avoid punishment occupies himself with it not for its own sake. Anyone who occupies himself with it neither from fear nor to receive reward, but because of love for the Master of all the earth who commanded it, occupies himself with it for its own sake. The Sages said: A person should always occupy himself with Torah, even not for its own sake, because through doing so he comes to do so for its own sake. Therefore, when teaching children, women, and the unlearned generally, they are taught only to serve from fear and in order to receive reward, until their knowledge increases and they gain greater wisdom. Then this secret is revealed to them little by little, and they are gently accustomed to it until they grasp and understand it and serve Him from love.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא.):
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: A person is forbidden to fill his mouth with laughter in this world, as it is said: ‘Then our mouths will be filled with laughter, and our tongues with joyous song.’ When? At the time when ‘they will say among the nations: Hashem has done great things with these people.’ They said of Reish Lakish that he never filled his mouth with laughter in this world from the time he heard this teaching from Rabbi Yochanan, his teacher.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "יִמָּלֵא פִי תְּהִלָּתֶךָ", שֶׁלָּמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נא.)
connections.quote: “Let my mouth be filled with Your praise, with Your glory all day long.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok compares a mouth completely filled with praise with a mouth completely filled with laughter. The following Berakhot passage applies this verse to keeping food out of the mouth while reciting a blessing.

connections.hePhrase: כְּעִנְיַן "יִמָּלֵא פִי תְּהִלָּתֶךָ", שֶׁלָּמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם נא.)
connections.quote: ‘Even with something that does not become repulsive, why should he not move it to one side and recite the blessing? Rav Yitzchak Kaskesa’a explained before Rabbi Yosei bar Avin in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: Because it is said, ‘Let my mouth be filled with Your praise.’’

connections.hePhrase: כָּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּאֵיזֶה כַּוָּנָה לְמִצְוָה וְהַרְחָבַת לֵב דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.displayRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 11:1
connections.canonicalRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 11:1
connections.quote: “Through Israel's not relying on the assurance of the holiness fixed within them, but instead restraining themselves in the work of this world within the cycle of seven and submitting to Hashem like a horse to its rider, they will merit the day when even the horse's bells will be holy to Hashem. Hashem will then illuminate that Israel is kodesh to Hashem, without the letter vav.”
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same promise that even the horse's bells will be holy by first insisting that Israel not rely on an already fixed holiness. Present restraint and work prepare its disclosure. This makes the siman's concluding boundary precise: its future account of everything becoming holy is not a reason to erase the intention and discipline it requires of laughter in this world.
connections.headline: The future disclosure follows present restraint

connections.hePhrase: רַק "אָז יִמָּלֵא שְׂחוֹק וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “Then our mouths will be filled with laughter and our tongues with song; then they will say among the nations: “The LORD has done great things with these.””
connections.context: The opening “then” is essential: Berakhot 31a contrasts future complete joy with the present restriction on filling one’s mouth with laughter. Rav Tzadok explains why that future laughter will have no element of spiritual emptiness.

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "מְצִלּוֹת הַסּוּס וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘On that day, upon the bells of the horses will be ‘Holy to Hashem.’ The pots in the House of Hashem will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar.’

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא הָאוֹהֵב זִמָּה כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים קיג:) גַּם כֵּן קֹדֶשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘Six things are said of a horse: It loves sexual promiscuity, loves war, is proud, loathes sleep, eats much, and produces little dung. Some say: It also seeks to kill its owner in battle.’

connections.hePhrase: וְלֵית אֲתַר פָּנוּי מִינֵּיהּ,
connections.quote: “There is no angel in whom the name YHWH is not found, for it is found everywhere, just as the soul is found in each and every limb. Therefore a person must acknowledge YHWH as King in all the sefirot, in all the thrones, in all the angels, and in every limb of the human being, for no place is empty of Him, neither in the upper realms nor in the lower realms.”

connections.hePhrase: זֶה נִקְרָא "הוֹצִיאָנוּ מֵאֲפֵלָה לְאוֹר גָּדוֹל" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים בַּהַגָּדָה.
connections.quote: “In every generation a person must see himself as though he had gone out from Egypt, as it is said: “You shall tell your son on that day, saying: It is because of what the Lord did for me when I went out from Egypt.” Therefore we are obliged to thank, praise, extol, glorify, exalt, honor, bless, raise on high, and laud the One who performed all these miracles for our ancestors and for us. He brought us out from slavery to freedom, from sorrow to joy, from mourning to a festival, from darkness to great light, and from bondage to redemption. Let us say before Him: Hallelujah!”

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ל):
connections.quote: ““Noah walked with God.” Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Neḥemya, Rabbi Yehuda said: This is analogous to a prince who had two sons, one older and one younger. He said to the younger, ‘Walk with me,’ and he said to the elder, ‘Come and walk before me.’ So too, of Abraham, whose strength was great, [God said,] “Walk before Me and be faultless” (Genesis 17:1). But Noah, whose strength was lesser, “Noah walked with God.” Rabbi Neḥemya said: This is analogous to a friend of the king who was sinking in thick mud. The king looked and saw him. He said to him: ‘Rather than sink in the mud, walk along with me.’ That is what is written: “Noah walked with God.” To what is Abraham comparable? To a friend of the king who saw the king walking in dark alleys. His friend peered and began illuminating for him through the window. The king peered and saw him. He said to him: ‘Rather than illuminating for me through the window, come and illuminate before me.’ So too, the Holy One blessed be He said to Abraham: ‘Rather than illuminating for Me from Mesopotamia and its environs, come and illuminate before Me in the Land of Israel!’ That is what is written: “He blessed Joseph, and said: The God before whom my fathers, [Abraham and Isaac], walked…” (Genesis 48:15). Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: It is analogous to a shepherd who is standing and looking at his flock. Reish Lakish said: It is analogous to a prince who is walking with the elders going before him. According to the opinion of Rabbi Yoḥanan, we are in need of His glory. According to the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, He is in need of our glory.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לֶךְ לְךָ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘Hashem said to Abram: Go forth from your land, from your native place, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you.’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לֶךְ לְךָ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
connections.quote: “The Midrash says, “Who is the owner of the palace? The owner of the palace looked upon him.” It might have said “looked toward him.” Avraham saw the activity of the generation of dispersion as a burning palace; he wondered greatly and his soul cried, “Who created these?” The Holy One answered him: see for yourself that this does not trouble the rest of the world and none of them asks who made it, while you find it astonishing. From the stirring of your heart you can discern that there is certainly a Creator who surrounds and fills all worlds, and that He awakened your heart and soul to this. “Upon him” refers to his question: the question itself is a sufficient answer for him.”
connections.explanation: Mei HaShiloach offers a related reading of the same Midrash: Hashem answers Avraham through the very fact that his heart asks what the surrounding world does not. This illuminates the siman's question about why the light burns in this particular heart. The readings differ in how they describe the burning palace, but both move from a general observation of the world to recognition of the Creator's particular awakening of the person.
connections.headline: The question within Avraham's heart

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמַר "דּוֹלֶקֶת", כִּי "נֵר מִצְוָה וְתוֹרָה אוֹר"
connections.quote: see note 2264.
connections.context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the practical commandment as a vessel that holds light from Torah as the light perceived inwardly in the heart.

connections.hePhrase: פֵּירוּשׁ: הַמִּצְוָה מַעֲשִׂית הוּא הַנֵּר, שֶׁהוּא הַכְּלִי קִבּוּל שֶׁבּוֹ נִתְפָּס הָאוֹר,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ל״ה:ד׳
connections.quote: “The explanation of this analogy—which compares the light of the Divine Presence to a lamp’s light, which neither shines nor takes hold of the wick without oil—is clear and understandable to every discerning person. Similarly, the Divine Presence rests upon the human body, which is compared to a wick, specifically through good deeds. The soul, although it is a portion of God above, does not by itself suffice to serve as oil for the wick. Even the soul of a completely righteous person, who serves Hashem with awe and a love of delights, is not wholly nullified out of existence so as to be nullified and incorporated within the actual light of Hashem, becoming one with it in complete unity. Rather, he remains a distinct being who fears Hashem and loves Him. This is unlike the commandments and good deeds, which are His blessed will. His blessed will is the source of life for all worlds and created beings; it descends to them through many contractions, through concealment of the countenance of the supernal will, blessed be He, and through successive levels of descent, until they can come into being and be created from nothing as separate entities, without being nullified out of existence, as explained above. The commandments, however, are the inner dimension of His blessed will, where there is no concealment of the countenance at all. Their life-force is therefore not a separate entity at all, but is united with and incorporated within His blessed will, becoming truly one with it in complete unity.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם שֶׁמֶן לַמָּאוֹר, כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה א, ג)
connections.quote: “The Sages say: These are two Torahs, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. Rabbi Yudan said: “Your name is poured oil”—oil increases upon everyone who occupies himself with the rich substance of Torah. ... Just as oil brings light to the world, so Israel is a light to the world, as it is stated: “Nations shall walk by your light.””
connections.context: The Midrash explains the verse’s oils through Torah and then through illumination. This is the relevant passage behind Rav Tzadok’s statement that oil alludes to wisdom and that wisdom supplies light; the first paragraph previously quoted did not present these comparisons.

connections.hePhrase: דְּשֶׁמֶן רוֹמֵז לְחָכְמָה, וְהַחָכְמָה הִיא הַמְּאִירָה.
connections.quote: “Gemara: “Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman.” Why specifically Tekoa? Rabbi Yohanan said: Because they are accustomed to olive oil, wisdom is found among them.”

connections.hePhrase: רַק "דּוֹלֶקֶת", שֶׁמִּצַּד זֶה מָסַר עַצְמוֹ לְאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים מִצַּד גּוֹדֶל הַתַּבְעֵרָה שֶׁהָיָה בְּלִבּוֹ,
connections.quote: “Some say that Gabriel said, “The truth of the Lord endures forever.” When the wicked Nimrod cast our father Abraham into the fiery furnace, Gabriel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: “Master of the world, I will descend, cool it, and save the righteous man from the fiery furnace.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “I am unique in My world, and he is unique in his world; it is fitting for the Unique One to rescue the unique one.” Since the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any creature, He said: “You will merit to rescue three of his descendants.””

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם "תַּבְעֵרָה", כִּי "בָעֲרָה בָם אֵשׁ ה'",
connections.quote: “He called the name of that place Taverah, because the fire of the LORD had burned among them.”
connections.context: Taverah is associated with burning through the verb ba’ar. Rav Tzadok reads this fire as an overwhelming spiritual illumination and develops that interpretation in the following sentences.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הַמִּתְאוֹנְנִים שָׁמַעְתִּי דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁהָיוּ בְּעַצְבוּת וּמָרָה שְׁחוֹרָה,
connections.displayRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Numbers, Beha'alotcha 5
connections.canonicalRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Numbers, Beha'alotcha 5
connections.quote: ““The people were like complainers, evil in the ears of the Lord; the Lord heard and His anger burned,” and so forth. “The rabble among them craved a craving,” and so forth; “the Lord’s anger burned greatly, and it was evil in Moses’ eyes.” We must understand why, concerning the sin of the complainers, it does not say, “It was evil in Moses’ eyes.” The sin of the complainers consisted only of sadness, as explained in the first volume. No person can regard his fellow with displeasure for sadness, because this world gives cause for sadness. It says only, “The Lord heard and His anger burned,” because strength and joy are in His place. But in the sin of craving it was evil even in Moses’ eyes, because a person can object to his fellow’s craving. In the matter of the sin of craving, God shows that He punishes a person only for his intention. In truth, God’s will was that they should desire only in accordance with the depth of His will. They desired according to their own intention, and therefore were punished for it.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בְּמַחֲנֵה לְוִיָּה אַף בִּמְקוֹם מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מוּתָּר, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵין יָכוֹל לְסָבְלוֹ.
connections.quote: “Someone rendered impure through a corpse may enter the Levite camp. They said this not only of someone rendered impure through a corpse, but even of the corpse itself, as it is said: “Moses took Joseph’s bones with him”—“with him,” within his own precinct.”

connections.hePhrase: עַד שֶׁצָּעֲקוּ הָעָם, הַיְינוּ כְּטַעַם "אַל יְדַבֵּר עִמָּנוּ אֱלֹהִים פֶּן נָמוּת", וַתִּשְׁקַע הָאֵשׁ.
connections.quote: ‘They said to Moses: You speak with us, and we will listen; let God not speak with us, lest we die.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכַאֲשֶׁר נִשְׁקַע הָאֵשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּסִפְרֵי הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ״י) דְּשָׁקְעָה בִּמְקוֹמָהּ,
connections.quote: ““The fire sank”: It sank in its own place, for had it turned toward any direction, it would have advanced, consuming everything in that direction. (Sifrei.)”

connections.hePhrase: וְיָדוּעַ דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם הָרְשִׁימוּ נִשְׁאָר, וְנִשְׁאַר בָּהֶם מִדַּת אַהֲבָה.
connections.quote: “It is known that when the supernal light spreads and then withdraws and becomes concealed, it necessarily leaves a trace, an imprint, below. That light is the impression that remains below: when the supernal light departs and becomes concealed in its source, the light of that impression remains below without the supernal light that has departed.”

connections.hePhrase: [וּבֶאֱמֶת גַּם תַּאֲוָה דְּשָׁם הָיָה הַכֹּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר].
connections.quote: “Their craving for meat was presumably for the sake of Heaven, in honor of Shabbat. Likewise, “We remember the fish” refers to a Shabbat food, as Shabbat states: “With what does one delight in it? With large fish.” Even concerning something small, they said: “What is it? A dish of small fish,” which is a food made from fish. It is known from the Ari, of blessed memory, that there is no waste in Shabbat eating: even what a person eats to satisfy his appetite is entirely in holiness. As is known, Shabbat eating has the holiness of the manna, bread from heaven that was absorbed into the 248 limbs and had no waste at all. But manna, being from heaven, contains no earthliness, physicality, or sensation of bodily appetite at all; on Shabbat it is a commandment to delight the body, which also ascends then. Through the serpent’s influence in Adam’s sin of desire for food, an impression remained, so that the body enjoys food and meat desired for pleasure. Through this they “craved a craving”—that is, food involving physical appetite. Israel’s intention was also to elevate and repair bodily appetite, for on Shabbat everything enters holiness. Throughout the days of this world, God desires this: to elevate physical things too. But in the wilderness generation, at the beginning of the formation of the holy nation, God wished to establish words of Torah in their hearts through another way of life: that they should eat only bread from heaven, free of all bodily appetite. Through this their limbs and the depths of their hearts would become sanctified to God, until afterward they could also eat bread from the earth with greater holiness.”

connections.hePhrase: וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, לִהְיוֹתוֹ אָב כּוֹלֵל כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת
connections.quote: “The Hasmonean priests followed this same path. A small number risked their lives against the great multitude and sanctified His name. We say, “For Yourself You made a great and holy name in Your world”: the name of Heaven was sanctified then. We recognize that this power too came from God, yet the principal awakening came from them. Thus we say, “What You did for our ancestors ... through Your holy priests.” This is exceedingly dear and pleasing before Him, for He desires that we give light before Him from the human side. Therefore the Midrash interprets “the locks of your head are like purple” to mean that even the poor and lowly Israelite can be as dear as Daniel, called “a man greatly desired,” and told explicitly, “You are greatly desired.” Even the lowest person, if he awakens on his own to sanctify God’s name, becomes desired and pleasing before Him. The end of the verse, “A king is bound in the tresses,” is therefore interpreted concerning Moses, “And you shall command.” The power to fulfill all the mitzvot properly comes from God’s utterance commanding them in the Torah: “My word that leaves My mouth will not return empty, but will accomplish what I desire.” Here, however, the lighting of the lamps is specifically expressed as “You shall command,” so that the command too comes from Moses himself, from the human side. This is the very meaning of lighting the lamps: that we give light before Him ourselves, which is exceedingly dear before Him.”
connections.explanation: Chanukah explains the human side of the lamp imagery through the Hasmoneans’ initiative and extends its value even to the lowliest Jew who awakens to sanctify Hashem’s Name. This develops the conclusion of the present siman, where the divine light in the heart is attributed to the people who kindle before Him. Receiving the power from Hashem does not make their awakening unreal. The deed gives the received light an enduring form within the commandments.
connections.headline: Hashem cherishes the human awakening even though its power comes from Him

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא תְּצַוֶּה ב):
connections.quote: see note 308 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא כְּטַעַם "לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד וְכוּלֵי" (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה נב),
connections.quote: see note 4051.
connections.context: The Midrash immediately applies these three names to God’s relationship with Israel. “My mother” expresses, within the parable, the extraordinary role God grants Israel in sustaining and manifesting His presence. Rav Tzadok cites it after explaining that the light awakened in Israel is reckoned as light they provide before God.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְטַעַם "תְּנוּ עֹז לֵאלֹהִים".
connections.quote: “Come and see: Of all the peoples in the world, they stand to scrutinize the deeds of Israel alone, because these are children of the Holy One, blessed be He. When Israel’s deeds are not as they should be, those appointed messengers, as it were, when they seek to stand against those deeds of Israel, stand against the Lord Himself. For when Israel performs unworthy deeds, they weaken the strength of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it were. When they perform worthy deeds, they give might and strength to the Holy One, blessed be He. Of this it is written: “Give strength to God.” How? Through worthy deeds. Therefore on that day all the great appointed ones assembled against the Lord—against the Lord indeed, for since they assembled against Israel, they assembled against Him.”

connections.hePhrase: וּמַחֲשָׁבָה דִּבּוּר וּמַעֲשֶׂה הֵם לְבוּשֵׁי הַנֶּפֶשׁ,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ד׳:א׳-ב׳
connections.quote: “Every divine soul also has three garments: thought, speech, and action in the Torah’s 613 commandments. When a person fulfills all the practical commandments in action, engages in explaining all 613 commandments and their laws in speech, and comprehends in thought all that he can comprehend in the Torah’s plain meaning, allusion, exposition, and mystery, the whole of his soul’s 613 limbs is clothed in the Torah’s 613 commandments. More particularly, the aspects of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in his soul are clothed in his understanding of Torah through its plain meaning, allusion, exposition, and mystery, according to his capacity and the root of his soul above. The emotions—fear and love, with their branches and offspring—are clothed in fulfilling the commandments in action and speech, the latter being Torah study, which is equivalent to them all.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל עֶצֶם הַנֶּפֶשׁ הוּא חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ב׳:א׳
connections.quote: see note 2747.

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא נֶאֱמַר "וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל ה'" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שַׁבָּת קיח:).
connections.quote: “Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak said: ‘He is saved from the subjugation of exile.’ It is written here: ‘I will have you ride upon the heights of the earth,’ and it is written there: ‘You will tread upon their heights.’ Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: ‘Anyone who makes Shabbat a delight is granted the requests of his heart, as it is stated: ‘Delight in Hashem, and He will grant you the requests of your heart.’ I do not know what this delight is. When it says, ‘You shall call Shabbat a delight,’ you must say that this is the delight of Shabbat.’ With what does one delight in it? Rav Yehuda, the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, said in the name of Rav: ‘With a dish of beet greens, large fish, and heads of garlic.’ Rav Hiyya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav: ‘Even a small thing, if one made it in honor of Shabbat, is a delight.’ What is it? Rav Pappa said: ‘A dish of small fish.’”

connections.hePhrase: רַק הַתּוֹרָה – מִזֶּה הָאָדָם מְקַבֵּל עוֹנֶג עָצוּם בַּנֶּפֶשׁ,
connections.quote: “‘All [a person's] toil is for his mouth’ (Ecclesiastes 6:7): its plain meaning concerns eating, for the mouth receives food to sustain his life. This is the purpose of all human service: sustaining his life and the life of the entire world. The whole world was created only for him and to accompany him, and he is equal to them all, as stated in Berakhot 6b, for they all depend on him. The Sages interpreted it in the chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 99b) as toil in Torah. For ‘a person does not live by bread alone, but by everything proceeding from Hashem's mouth [does a person live]’ (Deuteronomy 8:3), which is within the bread, as is known. Concerning Torah it says, ‘Come, eat of My bread’ (Proverbs 9:5): it is the principal bread sustaining human life, as it says, ‘For it is your life’ (Deuteronomy 32:47). In Adam's curse it says, ‘By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread’ (Genesis 3:19), and toil in Torah was then decreed as well. As the Sages said (Berakhot 63b) on the verse, ‘Pressing milk brings forth butter, and pressing the nose [brings forth blood, and pressing anger brings forth strife]’ (Proverbs 30:33): this refers to the butter of Torah.”
connections.explanation: Kedushat Shabbat explicitly reads bread as Torah's sustenance and then connects the labor of bread with the toil of Torah. This explains the siman's description of Torah as actual nourishment for the soul. Its later account of purifying toil concerns devotion of one's vitality to learning, within the same nourishment metaphor.
connections.headline: Torah as sustaining bread

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל מִצְוָה פְּרָטִית הִיא עוֹנֶג פְּרָטִי,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:4
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:4
connections.quote: “For in this world Hashem, blessed be He, concealed the depth of intention hidden in the performance of the commandments. If a commandment consisted solely of its intention, why, then, did Hashem, blessed be He, command its actual performance? This shows that a person does not know the Torah concealed and hidden in the performance of the commandments in this world. As stated in the Talmud (Sotah 21a): Rav Yosef said: “A commandment, while one engages in it, protects and saves; when one is not engaging in it, it protects, but does not save.” That is, when he is no longer engaged in it, none of the commandment’s holiness remains in his body, because the body does not understand its root. But regarding a commandment belonging to a person, especially if he devotes himself extensively to its details and understanding, Hashem, blessed be He, will illuminate it for him, so that he understands the commandment through the light of Torah, such that the commandment’s entire essence becomes words of Torah. He will understand its intention, and see that the commandment’s outward form and action belong only to this world.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov likewise explains why the deed of a mitzvah cannot be replaced by its presently understood intention: its inner Torah is still concealed. When that inner meaning is illuminated, the mitzvah can be apprehended as Torah. This clarifies the siman’s distinction between a general joy in fulfilling Hashem’s will and the particular delight disclosed through a mitzvah’s inner meaning.
connections.headline: The act can contain more than the doer presently understands

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל" שֶׁיִּסְּדוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים לְבַעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.displayRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Rosh HaShanah, Derekh Chayim 40
connections.linkedRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Rosh HaShanah, Derekh Chayim 40
connections.canonicalRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Rosh HaShanah, Derekh Chayim 40
connections.heRef: שני לוחות הברית, עשרת הדברות, מסכת ראש השנה, דרך חיים מ׳
connections.quote: “Eighth, one should know what the Rokeach wrote in the Laws of Repentance: there are four kinds of repentance. Kol Bo, section 67, brings them, and one of them is repentance by balance. He explains: repentance by balance means that a person must weigh his suffering against his enjoyment. One who sinned with a woman—as much as he enjoyed kissing, touching her, and initial penetration, so must he experience distress through sorrow of heart and fasting. End of quotation.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁפּוֹשֵׁט בְּגָדִים הַצּוֹאִים וְלוֹבֵשׁ מַחֲלָצוֹת דְּתוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת.
connections.quote: ““Fine garments”: Changes of beautiful clothing—that is, merits. Since he compared sin to filthy garments, he compared merits to changes of beautiful, white garments.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן בְּכֹחוֹ לְלַבֵּן הַנֶּפֶשׁ וּלְהוֹצִיא מִמֶּנָּה חֶלְאָתָהּ הַבְּלוּעַ,
connections.quote: “So too is the fire of Gehinnom: it resembles heating iron utensils until they glow, which expels the absorbed tastes while the substance of the utensil remains. It burns only the evil that a person absorbed in this world. In a Torah scholar, the fire of Torah burns these things away in this world.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "מִיץ חָלָב יוֹצִיא וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: ‘For pressing milk produces butter, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.’

connections.hePhrase: וְאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁילְהֵי בְּרָכוֹת (סג:) שֶׁמֵּקִיא חָלָב שֶׁיָּנַק מִשְּׁדֵי אִמּוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
connections.quote: ‘In whom do you find the butter of Torah? In one who, for its sake, vomits up the milk he nursed from his mother’s breasts. ‘Pressing the nose brings out blood’—any student whose teacher becomes angry with him the first time and who remains silent merits distinguishing impure blood from pure blood.’

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל" – שֶׁמֵּמִית וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם),
connections.quote: see note 1434 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Gemara rereads the law of corpse impurity as an image of complete dedication to Torah. Rav Tzadok immediately explains the image as putting all one’s vitality into study, through which previously absorbed worldly pleasures are expelled.

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַבְּרָכָה יִהְיֶה נִזְכָּר לָדַעַת לְקַבֵּל עוֹנֶג זֶה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלֹא עוֹנֶג גּוּפָנִי,
connections.quote: “For this the Sages instituted blessings over enjoyment. Before becoming immersed in the pleasure, a person says the blessing, “Blessed are You,” and so forth, addressing God directly and recognizing that all his pleasures come from the blessed God. This is the meaning of “‘Faithfulness’ refers to the order Zeraim”: he has faith in the Life of the worlds and sows, as Tosafot cites from the Jerusalem Talmud, and as appears in Shoher Tov on Psalm 19. He receives his pleasures from the blessed God even though his activity takes place in darkness. Of this they said, “The righteous person shall live by his faith.” Habakkuk said this, for he belongs to the feminine side, as is known from the Zohar. This is the counsel for a person immersed in this world: at least the simple faith that everything comes from the blessed God, and that there is none besides Him, must not leave him.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נִגְזְרָה הַמִּיתָה וְחִבּוּט הַקֶּבֶר כַּנּוֹדָע, שֶׁהוּא עַל כָּל עִינּוּגֵי הָרְשׁוּת.
connections.quote: “Through this you can understand the beating of the grave. Its matter is as follows. After a person dies and is buried in the earth, four angels immediately come, lower the floor of the grave, and deepen it below, leaving a space the height of the person buried there, as mentioned in the tractate Perek Hibbut HaKever; see there. Then they return his soul to his body as during his life. The reason is that the kelipah is still attached and bound to the soul and the body and has not separated from them; therefore his soul and body must be reunited. The angels each hold him at one end, shake him, and strike him with rods of fire, as one holds a garment by its two ends and shakes off the dust clinging to it, until that kelipah is entirely separated from them. It is therefore called the beating of the grave, like a person beating and shaking out his garment. The grave must consequently be deepened to provide room to shake and strike him. However, not all people are equal. The righteous, who during their lives kept away from the evil inclination and humbled and afflicted themselves through the sufferings that came upon them, and also through Torah and commandments, which weaken a person’s strength, do not need great suffering when their time comes to leave the world and receive the beating of the grave: even a small beating suffices to separate it from them. This is not so with the wicked; through their pleasures in this world they bind and strengthen the kelipah still further in their bodies and souls. This is the secret of the statement that no person escapes the beating of the grave, as mentioned in Perek Hibbut HaKever. As we explained above concerning those who died through the serpent’s influence, there is no remedy for separating it except through death and the beating of the grave, apart from those mentioned there in Perek Hibbut HaKever because of a particular commandment especially effective for this. All other people require the beating of the grave, though there is a difference between much and little beating, as stated. Each person bears his punishment according to the degree of his kelipah and the strength of its attachment. Even for those who are spared the beating of the grave, those specially effective commandments separate the kelipot from them after death without suffering. But they must still die, as explained concerning those who died through the serpent’s influence.”

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁעַל זֶה נִגְזְרָה הַמִּיתָה וְחִבּוּט הַקֶּבֶר כַּנּוֹדָע, שֶׁהוּא עַל כָּל עִינּוּגֵי הָרְשׁוּת.
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ח׳:ג׳-ד׳
connections.quote: “By contrast, the evil inclination and the power that desires permitted things in order to satisfy its craving are a demon of the Jewish demons, because they can return to holiness, as explained above. Nevertheless, before returning to holiness, they belong to the other side and to kelipah. Even afterward, their impression remains attached to the body, because every food and drink immediately becomes blood and flesh of its flesh. Therefore the body requires the beating of the grave to cleanse and purify it from the impurity it received through the enjoyment and pleasures of this world, from the impurity of kelipat nogah and the Jewish demons. The exception is someone who never took enjoyment from this world throughout his life, like our holy Rabbi.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת קג סוֹף עַמּוּד א) בְּיָעֵל "דְּלָא מִתְהַנְיָא מֵעֲבֵירָה, דְּכָל טוֹבָתָן וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “But does she not derive pleasure from the transgression? Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: All the benefits of the wicked—”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת קג סוֹף עַמּוּד א) בְּיָעֵל "דְּלָא מִתְהַנְיָא מֵעֲבֵירָה, דְּכָל טוֹבָתָן וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “—are harmful to the righteous, as it is stated: “Take care not to speak to Jacob, either good or bad.” Granted, bad is understandable; but why not good? Rather, learn from this that the benefits of the wicked are harmful to the righteous.”

connections.hePhrase: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת קג סוֹף עַמּוּד א) בְּיָעֵל "דְּלָא מִתְהַנְיָא מֵעֲבֵירָה, דְּכָל טוֹבָתָן וְכוּלֵי".
connections.quote: “Because he introduces defilement into her.”
connections.context: The question concerns Yael and Sisera. The answer begins at the end of 103a and is completed on 103b: what might ordinarily be pleasure is repellent to her because of the defilement involved. Rav Tzadok invokes precisely this answer in describing the absence of bodily enjoyment.

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (כְּתוּבּוֹת קד.) בְּרַבִּי שֶׁאָמַר: "דְּלֹא נֶהֱנָה מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּאֶצְבַּע קְטַנָּה",
connections.quote: ‘As Rabbi was dying, he raised his ten fingers upward and said: ‘Master of the world! It is revealed and known before You that I labored in Torah with my ten fingers, and I took no pleasure even with my little finger. May it be Your will that there be peace in my rest.’ A heavenly voice came forth and said: ‘He will enter peace; they will rest upon their beds.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּכְקוּשְׁיַת תּוֹסָפוֹת (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יא.) מִ"לֹא פָּסְקוּ צְנוֹן וַחֲזֶרֶת",
connections.quote: “These are Antoninus and Rabbi: lettuce, cucumbers, and radishes never ceased from their table, either in summer or in the rainy season.”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְקוּשְׁיַת תּוֹסָפוֹת (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יא.) מִ"לֹא פָּסְקוּ צְנוֹן וַחֲזֶרֶת",
connections.heRef: תוספות על עבודה זרה י״א א:ו׳:א׳
connections.quote: “Even though we say that Rabbi did not derive enjoyment from the world even with his little finger, nevertheless many people ate at his table.”
connections.context: Tosafot explicitly raises the apparent contradiction between Rabbi’s lavish table and his statement at death that he had derived no worldly enjoyment. Tosafot answers that many others ate at his table. Rav Tzadok uses the same difficulty to explain that Rabbi employed worldly necessities without experiencing the bodily enjoyment associated with the serpent’s influence.

connections.hePhrase: וְעַל רַבִּי נוֹדַע מִטַּעַם הַמְּקוּבָּלִים דְּבֶאֱמֶת לֹא מֵת,
connections.quote: “Our holy Rabbi used to appear in the fine garments he wore on Shabbat, rather than in burial shrouds, to make known that he still retained his strength. He would discharge the many from their obligation of the day’s Kiddush. He was not like other dead people, who are free of the commandments, but like a living person in the clothes he wore during his life. The righteous are called living even in their death, and he would discharge the members of his household through Kiddush.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קיג.): "דְּמָאנֵי מְכַבְּדוּתָא".
connections.quote: see note 1930 (Vol. I).
connections.context: Both sayings expressly cited in the opening are about the honor conveyed by clothing. Rav Tzadok applies them to the soul’s garments of thought, speech, and action: at its root the soul is known in itself, while elsewhere its acquired garments reveal its standing.

connections.hePhrase: וּ"בְּמָתַאי שְׁמַאי" (שָׁם קמה:) –
connections.quote: “Why are the Torah scholars in Babylonia distinguished by their clothing? Because they are not in their native place. As people say: ‘In my own town, my name; outside my town, my clothing.’”

connections.hePhrase: וְעִיקַּר הַכָּבוֹד מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה לח) מִיַּעְבֵּץ,
connections.quote: “Another matter: “This is the matter” – that is what is written: “The wise will inherit honor” (Proverbs 3:35). Honor is nothing other than Torah. Know [this to be true]: What is said at the beginning of Chronicles? “Adam, Seth, Enosh” (Chronicles 1:1), and likewise all of them; you do not find honor written regarding any of them until you reach Yabetz, as it is stated: “Yabetz was honored more than his brethren” (I Chronicles 4:9). Why is honor written in his regard? It is because he toiled in Torah. That is, “the wise will inherit honor.” Likewise you find regarding Aaron. What is written? “The Torah of truth was in his mouth” (Malachi 2:6). What did the Holy One blessed be He say to Moses? “You shall make holy vestments for Aaron your brother, for honor and for splendor” (Exodus 28:2). All this was due to the Torah in which he toiled. That is, “the wise will inherit honor.””

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסָחִים (קיא:): "סוּדָרֵיהּ דְּמָר כִּי צוּרְבָא מֵרַבָּנַן",
connections.quote: ‘There was a town watchman who went and stood beside a zardeta tree near the town. Sixty demons entered him, and he became dangerously ill. He came to a scholar who did not know that the zardeta was a tree of sixty demons; the scholar wrote him an amulet for one demon. He heard them holding a celebration inside him and chanting: ‘The master’s headscarf looks like a Torah scholar’s. We have tested the master: he does not know ‘Barukh’ [the blessing for his headscarf].’ A scholar who knew that the zardeta had sixty demons came and wrote him an amulet for sixty demons. He heard them saying: ‘Clear your belongings out of here.’’

connections.hePhrase: וּבְשַׁבָּת (עז:): "סוּדְרָא – סוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו",
connections.quote: “‘Levusha’ (a garment): ‘lo busha’—no shame. ‘Gelima’ (a cloak): because in it one becomes like a golem, an unformed mass. ‘Gulta’ (a fine cloak): ‘galli ve-ittiv’—uncover and sit down. ‘Purya’ (a bed): because one is fruitful and multiplies—parin ve-ravin—upon it. ‘Bor zinka’ (a dried-out cistern): ‘bor zeh naki’—this cistern is empty. ‘Sudara’ (a scarf): ‘The secret of Hashem is for those who fear Him’—sod Hashem lire’av. ‘Apadna’ (a palace): ‘a-pitha dein’—at this entrance. The Sages taught: Three grow stronger as they grow older: the fish, the snake, and the pig.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבְשַׁבָּת (עז:): "סוּדְרָא – סוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו",
connections.quote: see note 2338.
connections.context: The word sod can mean intimate counsel or secret. Rav Tzadok emphasizes its inward sense: Torah reveals divine truth to those whose reverence makes them receptive to it. Shabbat 77b uses this verse to explain the scholar’s sudara, or head covering.

connections.hePhrase: רַק כַּאֲשֶׁר הָעוֹנֶג מִצַּד שֶׁהִיא תּוֹרַת ה' וְשֶׁדָּבוּק עַל יָדָהּ בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
connections.displayRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 46:6
connections.canonicalRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 46:6
connections.quote: “When Avraham had reached the age of ninety-nine, having served Hashem throughout his life, the time came for the services he had performed to begin to become established within him. Hashem then revealed this secret to him, as it says, “The secret of Hashem is for those who fear Him, and His covenant is to make it known to them.” The Midrash [Genesis Rabbah 49:2] interprets this verse concerning circumcision. This word remained secret until ninety-nine, throughout the years in which he still had strength to acquire holiness through his service.”
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov interprets the same verse, “The secret of Hashem is for those who fear Him,” through the revelation of the covenant to Avraham after years of service. The secret is received when that service begins to become settled within him. This provides a concrete counterpart to the siman's distinction between enjoying Torah as an intellectual subject and receiving it as the completion of a felt lack before Hashem. Citation correction: the circumcision interpretation is in Genesis Rabbah 49:2; the supplied Hebrew’s Vayikra Rabbah 49 is mistaken.
connections.headline: Fear prepares the vessel for the secret

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ "יִרְאַת ה' אוֹצָרוֹ",
connections.quote: ‘The faithfulness of your times shall be a store of deliverance, wisdom, and knowledge; fear of Hashem is his treasure.’

connections.hePhrase: כְּטַעַם "וְהַלְבֵּשׁ אֹתְךָ מַחֲלָצוֹת" (זְכַרְיָה ג, ד),
connections.quote: ‘He answered and said to those standing before him: ‘Remove the filthy clothes from him.’ He said to him: ‘See, I have removed your guilt from you, and I will clothe you in fine garments.’’

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁרָאִיתִי מִכְּתַב יָד: פֵּירוּשׁ, מַלְבּוּשׁ הַמַּחֲלִיץ וּמֵסִיר הַלְּבוּשׁ,
connections.quote: ““And garments” alludes to the performance of the commandments, for, as is known, these become the soul’s garment in Gan Eden, as it says, “Remove the soiled garments, and I shall clothe you in machalatzot.” As has been said in the name of the holy Rabbi Mendel of Lubavitch, of blessed memory, the garment of a commandment is called machalatzot because it removes and strips the garments of this world from the soul; these are the soiled garments.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ הַיִּתְרוֹן שֶׁל לְבוּשֵׁי מַחֲשָׁבָה דִּבּוּר וּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּתוֹרָה
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ל״ז:ו׳-ח׳
connections.quote:
“Likewise, the power of the vital, animal soul in the bodily limbs of the person performing the commandment is clothed in this action. It rises out of the kelipah, is incorporated within the holiness of the commandment, which is His blessed will, and is nullified within the light of the blessed Infinite.

Even with the commandments of Torah study, reciting the Shema, prayer, and the like, although they do not involve actual physical action under the dominion of kelipat nogah, we nevertheless hold that thought is not equivalent to speech: a person does not discharge his obligation until he expresses the words with his lips. We also hold that moving one’s lips counts as an action. For the divine soul cannot express itself through the physical lips, mouth, tongue, and teeth except by means of the vital, animal soul that is actually clothed in the bodily limbs. The more forcefully a person speaks, the more powers of the vital soul he invests and clothes in these words.

This is what Scripture means by, ‘All my bones shall say,’ and so forth. It is also what our Sages, of blessed memory, meant: ‘If it is ordered in all 248 limbs, it is retained; if not, it is not retained.’ Forgetfulness comes from the kelipah of the body and the vital, animal soul, which derive from kelipat nogah. They are sometimes incorporated within holiness: this happens when a person exhausts their power and invests all their strength in the holiness of Torah or prayer.”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י:): "וַאֲנַן הֵיכִי אִיתִינַן הָתָם וְכוּלֵי",
connections.quote: “Yosef, the son of Rabbi Yehoshua, became ill and lost consciousness. His father asked him: “What did you see?” He said: “I saw an inverted world: those above were below, and those below were above.” His father said: “You saw a clear world. And how did you see us there?” He answered: “As we are esteemed here, so we are esteemed there.””

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶה טַעַם שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י:): "וַאֲנַן הֵיכִי אִיתִינַן הָתָם וְכוּלֵי",
connections.heRef: תוספות על בבא בתרא י׳ ב:ה׳:א׳
connections.quote: “Rabbeinu Chananel explained that the Geonim had a tradition, teacher from teacher: the inverted world means that he saw Shmuel sitting before his disciple Rav Yehudah, because Rav Yehudah had protested to Shmuel in the chapter Bammeh Behemah. A woman came and cried before Shmuel, and he paid no attention to her. Rav Yehudah said to him: “Does the Master not accept, ‘One who closes his ear to the cry of the poor,’ and so forth?””
connections.context: Tosafot supplies the concrete example invoked later in this paragraph: the disciple’s response to a person in distress elevated him above his teacher. The standard Tosafot text names Rav Yehudah, although the reader’s body says Rav Yosef. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the standing revealed by Torah from the deeper value of practical deeds.

connections.hePhrase: אֵין נִגְלֶה, "וְנָעוּ מַעְגְּלֹתֶיהָ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “Her paths wander; you cannot know.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok applies the wording about paths that cannot be known to the hidden inward value of deeds. Their appearance in this world does not disclose the measure of their reward. This is his homiletic application of the verse, whose plain setting concerns the dangerous woman described in Proverbs 5.

connections.hePhrase: אֵין נִגְלֶה, "וְנָעוּ מַעְגְּלֹתֶיהָ וְגוֹמֵר",
connections.quote: “This is what Scripture says: “Lest you weigh the path of life; her courses shift, and you cannot know.” What does “Lest you weigh the path of life” mean? Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Do not sit and weigh the commandments of the Torah, in the sense of “He weighed the mountains in a balance.” Do not say: Since this commandment is great, I shall perform it, for its reward is abundant; since this is a light commandment, I shall not perform it. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He did not reveal to people the reward of each and every commandment, so that they would perform all the commandments wholeheartedly. From where is this learned? “Her courses shift, and you cannot know.” To what is this comparable? To a king who hired workers and brought them into his orchard. He concealed from them and did not reveal the payment for work in the orchard, so that they would not leave work whose payment was small and go do work whose payment was great. In the evening he called each one and asked: “Under which tree did you work?” He answered: “Under this one.” The king said: “It is a pepper tree; its payment is one gold coin.” He called another and asked: “Under which tree did you work?” He answered: “Under this one.” The king said: “Its payment is half a gold coin; it is a white-flowered tree.” He called another and asked: “Under which tree did you work?” He answered: “Under this one.” The king said: “It is an olive tree; its payment is two hundred zuz.” They said to him: “Should you not have told us which tree brought greater payment, so that we could work under it?” The king answered: “Had I told you, how would my entire orchard have been tended?” So the Holy One, blessed be He, did not reveal the reward of the commandments, except for two: the weightiest of the weighty and the lightest of the light. Honoring father and mother is the weightiest of the weighty, and its reward is length of days, as it says, “Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be lengthened.” The lightest is sending away the mother bird. What is its reward? Length of days, as it says, “You shall surely send away the mother,” and, “you shall lengthen your days.” Thus: “If a bird’s nest happens before you.””

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זְבָחִים פח:) שֶׁגַּם כֵּן מְכַפְּרִים.
connections.quote: “Rabbi Inyani bar Sason said: Why is the passage about sacrifices placed beside the passage about priestly garments? To tell you: just as sacrifices atone, so priestly garments atone.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זְבָחִים פח:) שֶׁגַּם כֵּן מְכַפְּרִים.
connections.quote: “The tunic atones for bloodshed. ... The trousers atone for forbidden sexual relations. ... The turban atones for arrogance: let something worn high come and atone for haughtiness. The sash atones for the thoughts of the heart, at the place where it is worn. The breastplate atones for judgments. ... The ephod atones for idolatry. ... The robe atones for harmful speech: let something that makes a sound come and atone for an evil sound. The forehead plate atones for brazenness.”
connections.context: These are the eight garments and corresponding faults that Rav Tzadok interprets in the remainder of this section. His explanation connects the four ordinary priestly garments and the four additional high-priestly garments with the soul’s activities and their hidden source.

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זְבָחִים פח:) שֶׁגַּם כֵּן מְכַפְּרִים.
connections.quote: “The explanation is that a person’s sins are also considered a garment, for a person clothes himself in sins, and they are called soiled garments. You will find in many places that sins are called a garment. The commandments and good character traits are likewise a person’s garment, and they are a garment of honor. When the High Priest wears garments of holiness, this removes the garment of sins, especially when the sins are the opposite of them. When a person clothes himself in this sin, making his tongue heard in evil speech, he clothes himself in these inferior garments. When the High Priest, who is High Priest for all Israel, clothes himself in a holy garment that makes a holy sound, this atones for Israel’s evil speech. Likewise, the other garments atone for Israel and remove sin from Israel in the matter related to each garment, as explained there. Therefore the robe with bells, which makes a holy sound, removes the soiled garments of evil speech.”

connections.hePhrase: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל קִנְאָה תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד מוֹחַ לֵב כָּבֵד.
connections.quote: “Corresponding to them in the divine image within a person is wisdom in the brain, opposite honor, as our Sages said in Eruvin 55a: Torah is not found among the haughty; and at the end of the chapter “Bameh Ishah”: “The bush, the bush,” and so forth. Throughout the Sages’ words, its dwelling is with the lowly in spirit, and therefore honor pursues them, as it is written, “The wise shall inherit honor”; as explained above, this applies only to a Torah scholar. Wisdom is the camp of the Divine Presence, as it is written in the Zohar that the Torah and the Holy One, blessed be He, are one, and at the beginning of Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 1, that Torah was with Him as an amon, within His camp. (Elsewhere we explained this at length concerning “My God, the soul You placed within me is pure”: the neshamah is in the brain and is entirely pure. It is the assistance of God mentioned by our Sages in Sukkah 52b: “Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him, he could not overcome it.” Yoma 38b says that he is assisted. This is through “Who dwells with them amid their impurity”—the camp of the Divine Presence. This is not the place to elaborate.) Understanding in the heart corresponds to desire, which comes from the heart, as it is written, “His heart’s desire,” and as they said, “The heart desires.” Awe saves from it, as stated at the beginning of the chapter “Kol HaYad”; see there. Its dwelling is in the camp of the Levites, who perform God’s service, as it is written, “If I am a master, where is My fear?”—the fear a servant has of his master, whose dread rests upon him. By contrast, one who grasps Torah is as though he grasps the Holy One, blessed be He, and is on the level of a son. This accords with what Rabban Gamliel said about Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa in Berakhot 34b: he is like a servant, and so forth. As is known, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa was devoted to the service of the heart, which is prayer, and few legal teachings in the Gemara are found in his name; Rabban Gamliel was the nasi and head of the academy, whose principal occupation was Torah. The final emergence into actuality through the organs of action corresponds to envy, which applies only when something emerges into actuality and is recognizable to another. This is the root of envy in relations between one person and another: matters of damages, which are the activity of evil in deed, and opposite them in goodness, the activity of good. This belongs to the camp of Israel, as our Sages said in Eruvin 19a and elsewhere: even the sinners of Israel are full of commandments like a pomegranate. (An unspecified “commandment” in the Sages’ words means charity—see Rashi, Shabbat 156a—as is known; it is doing good to another. They said in Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 8: “Kindness says: Let him be created, for he is entirely acts of kindness.” (These are the three levels of “One who wishes to be pious” in the Sages’ words, Bava Kamma 30a; this is not the place to elaborate.))”

connections.hePhrase: וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר עֲבֵירוֹת,
connections.quote: “Concerning the statement that anyone who possesses brazenness will ultimately stumble in transgression: the explanation is that “transgression” here means a forbidden sexual relationship. Everywhere, too, the Sages call a forbidden sexual relationship “transgression” without qualification, unlike any other sin, as is evident in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah, 3a, and in many places. The reason is that concerning forbidden relationships it is written, “You shall keep My statutes,” and the Sages called forbidden relationships a statute. Thus they expounded in the Mekhilta, Mishpatim: “There He established for him a statute and an ordinance”—“a statute” refers to forbidden relationships. God gave a person a boundary, that he should not approach a forbidden relationship, as it is written, “You shall not approach to uncover nakedness.” All this is because of the boundary governing forbidden relationships. One who has a forbidden relationship crosses the boundary stated concerning it. It has already been explained that the trait of brazenness means departing from the boundary and measure through excessive boldness. This is why it says that he will ultimately stumble in transgression: when a brazen person begins to depart from measure through the force of his brazenness, he ultimately departs entirely from the fixed boundary, until he stumbles in transgression, as it is written concerning forbidden relationships, “You shall keep My statutes.””

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן קוֹרִין בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים פָּרָשַׁת עֲרָיוֹת כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה לא. וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ״י).
connections.quote: “On Yom Kippur they read “After the death,” and read as the prophetic portion “Thus says the High and Exalted One.” In the afternoon they read the forbidden sexual relations, and read Jonah as the prophetic portion.”

connections.hePhrase: דְּלָכֵן קוֹרִין בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים פָּרָשַׁת עֲרָיוֹת כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה לא. וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ״י).
connections.quote: ““They read the forbidden sexual relations”—so that someone who has such transgressions will withdraw from them, for forbidden sexual relations are a common transgression: a person’s soul desires them and his inclination overpowers him.”
connections.context: Rav Tzadok expressly cites both the Gemara and Rashi. Rashi’s explanation supplies the reason for this reading that is relevant to the discussion of the trousers and the correction of wrongful action.

connections.hePhrase: וְהַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁנִּכְנָס לְקָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים,
connections.quote: see note 3515.
connections.explanation: Sod Yesharim contrasts the golden garments that reveal divine light throughout the forms of worldly service with the linen garments of the inward Yom Kippur entry. This clarifies the register of the siman’s symbolism: its account of the eight garments is not a statement that all eight are worn in the innermost entry. The contrast also explains how a garment can reveal inward meaning while a further stage expresses the surrender of the receiving vessel itself.

connections.hePhrase: הוּא כְּטַעַם מַאֲמַר זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה טו:): "לְרוּחַ מִשְׁפָּט – זֶה הַדָּן אֶת יִצְרוֹ",
connections.quote: ““And for a spirit of judgment”—this is one who judges his inclination. “And for one who sits in judgment”—this is one who judges a true judgment in its truth. “And for strength”—this is one who overcomes his inclination. “Those who turn back the battle”—those who debate in the battle of Torah. “To the gate”—the Torah scholars who come early and stay late in synagogues and study halls.”
connections.context: The words about judging one’s inclination occur on Megillah 15b. They connect judgment to the inner struggle of the heart, which is why Rav Tzadok cites them in explaining the breastplate of judgment.

connections.hePhrase: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת "יֵצֶר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר", וְ"אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סֻכָּה נב:),
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים י״ג:א׳-ד׳
connections.quote: “Through this one can understand the Sages’ wording: “Intermediate people are judged by both this and that” (meaning the good inclination and the evil inclination), as it is written, “For He stands at the right of the needy, to save him from the judges of his soul.” They did not say that both rule, Heaven forbid: when the evil inclination has any control or rule over the “small city,” even for a brief moment, the person is called wicked at that moment. Rather, the evil inclination is only like a judge who expresses his opinion in a judgment. Nevertheless, the practical ruling need not follow that opinion, because there is another judge who disagrees with him; a decision between them is necessary, and the law follows the deciding judge. So the evil inclination expresses its opinion in the left chamber of the heart, and from the heart it rises to the brain to be considered. Immediately the second judge disagrees with it: the divine soul in the brain, which extends into the right chamber of the heart, the dwelling of the good inclination. The law follows the deciding judge—the Holy One, blessed be He, who assists the good inclination, as our Sages said: “Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him, he could not overcome it.” This assistance is the illumination with which the light of God shines upon the divine soul, giving it advantage and mastery over the fool’s folly and the evil inclination, as light has an advantage over darkness, as explained above.”

connections.hePhrase: וּבַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרֵף מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה לְמַעֲשֶׂה כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.).
connections.quote: “The Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to an act, as it is stated: “If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear.””

connections.hePhrase: וּבַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרֵף מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה לְמַעֲשֶׂה כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.).
connections.quote: “But what of the verse, “In order to seize the house of Israel in their heart”? Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: That verse is written about idolatry. For the Master said: Idolatry is severe, since whoever rejects it is as one who acknowledges the entire Torah.”
connections.context: The second passage states the exception about idolatry that Rav Tzadok needs here. The previous excerpt gave only the general rule about evil thoughts and therefore omitted the point attached to this footnote.

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ דְּבֶאֱמֶת "הַנִּסְתָּרֹת לַה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ" וְ"חֵלֶק ה' עַמּוֹ",
connections.quote: “But all this has no bearing on the thought that is the essence of the person: the wisdom within the brain, which is “the soul You placed within me is pure.” As is known concerning nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, the neshamah is in the brain and comes from God, as it is written, “He breathed into his nostrils,” and so forth. One who breathes forth does so from within: it is a portion of God, and therefore it is pure. Concerning this they said in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2 that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel, as it is written, “The rock of my heart and my portion,” and so forth. For the brain and heart are two companions, as explained; since He dwells within a person’s brain, which is called “my portion,” He is consequently also in his heart.”

connections.hePhrase: הַיְינוּ דְּבֶאֱמֶת "הַנִּסְתָּרֹת לַה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ" וְ"חֵלֶק ה' עַמּוֹ",
connections.quote: see note 623 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יז.): "גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ וְכוּלֵי וּמִי מְעַכֵּב וְכוּלֵי";
connections.quote: ‘After his prayer, Rabbi Alexandri would say: ‘May it be Your will, Hashem our God, that You place us in a corner of light and not in a corner of darkness. May our heart not ache, and may our eyes not grow dark.’ Some say that Rav Hamnuna prayed this, while Rabbi Alexandri, after praying, would say: ‘Master of the worlds, it is revealed and known before You that our desire is to do Your will. What prevents us? The leaven in the dough and subjection to kingdoms. May it be Your will to save us from their hands, so that we may return to carrying out the statutes of Your will with a whole heart.’’

connections.hePhrase: זוּלַת מַעֲשֵׂה הַכְּתָב דְּהֻותַּר בַּדּוֹרוֹת אַחֲרוֹנִים מִשּׁוּם "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת וְגוֹמֵר" כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: see note 1048 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The Talmud uses this verse in explaining why oral teachings could be committed to writing to prevent their loss. Rav Tzadok develops writing as a practical deed through which Torah enters the realm of action.

connections.hePhrase: רַק דְּזֶה כְּבָר כְּרָתָן דָּוִד בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרָכִין (טו:),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Acha, son of Rabbi Chanina, says: If he has already spoken harmful speech, he has no remedy, for David has already cut him off through the holy spirit, as it is said: ‘May Hashem cut off all smooth lips, the tongue that speaks boastfully.’ Rather, what is his remedy so that he will not come to harmful speech? If he is a Torah scholar, let him occupy himself with Torah. If he is unlearned, let him humble his mind, as it is said: ‘Perverseness in it brings a breaking of the spirit.’’

connections.hePhrase: וְצָרִיךְ לְדוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת דְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קה.) שֶׁגַּם לָהֶן יֵשׁ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
connections.quote: see note 664 (Vol. I).

connections.hePhrase: וּפֵירוּשׁ "רְשׁוּמוֹת" הוּא הָרְשִׁימוּ דְּנֶפֶשׁ עַצְמָהּ הַנִּגְלֶה מִכֹּחַ הַפּוֹעֵל שֶׁבַּנִּפְעָל,
connections.displayRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:41
connections.canonicalRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:41
connections.quote: “The meaning of “those who expound traces” is that they can apprehend what has no full manifestation, only some trace. The teaching that certain people have no share in the World to Come concerns the revealed apprehension that the Sages of Israel had of the World to Come. In truth, however, its essence is something “no eye has seen.” What is attained is only an apprehension through wisdom, while it contains depths that none of the Sages of Israel in this world can apprehend at all. Concerning this it says, “No eye has seen, O God, besides You,” as stated in Berakhot 34b. From those depths, too, there are some traces revealed to those who truly seek them, enabling them to apprehend a hint, as one apprehends a trace of the thing itself. By apprehending this trace they said that these people, too, have a share in the World to Come, for in truth Israel’s root is never lost. All corruption comes from this world; even corruption affecting the World to Come occurs through this world, as in the analogy of the eve of Shabbat and Shabbat, or dry land and the sea, in Avodah Zarah 3a; see there. This is the entire apprehension of the World to Come available in this world: it is apprehended only through this world, insofar as this world prepares for it. In truth, however, there are further matters in the World to Come entirely concealed in this world, because there is no preparation for them except through a trace. That is, the preparation consists only of the holiness of the root, which existed in this world in utter concealment, like a trace alone. Those who expound traces apprehend the trace of holiness present even in the lowest person of Israel. Through this they apprehend the trace of a share in the World to Come belonging even to these people, because of some trace of holiness found in their root. As is known, every light and holiness that departs leaves a trace in its place, which the masters of Kabbalah call a reshimu. Likewise, Jewish holiness is present from birth, from the womb. Even if a person subsequently corrupts his deeds until, Heaven forbid, he is utterly rejected and the light departs entirely, so that he has no share in the World to Come, the trace nevertheless remains. Because of this trace, some holiness still remains within him, although it is not revealed; those who expound traces recognize it through their exposition.”

connections.hePhrase: [רסד] הַכְּנִיסָה לָרַע הוּא עַל יְדֵי לֵיצָנוּת,
connections.quote: “but external wisdom found among the nations of the world, and there is that which is genuinely termed "wisdom" even in the language of Scripture, yet they absorb the dross from it, such being their root, and its dross is mockery of true sacred wisdom; and in all pagan idolatries that misled the masses, they demonstrated through their corrupted intellect that it supposedly held substance, yet all of it derived from cynicism toward the truth, forging a falsehood that mimics the truth. And this is likewise the nature of the idolatry of Ba'al Pe'or (Bamidbar 25:3); directly opposite which Moshe Rabbeinu was buried, he being the root of the Torah called by his name (Malachi 3:22), which is the exact antithesis of mockery, as written: "when a word of Torah enters, a word of scoffing departs" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2);”
connections.explanation: Machshavot Charutz describes the progression from mocking true wisdom to constructing a false appearance of truth. This explains why the present siman gives leitzanus a foundational role, rather than counting it as just another isolated bad habit. Once the mind dismisses the very standard by which it could be corrected, it becomes able to justify a substitute on its own terms.
connections.headline: Mockery can manufacture a false substitute for truth

connections.hePhrase: כִּמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּיוֹמָא (לח:):
connections.quote: see note 264 (Vol. I).
connections.context: The continuation across the page break distinguishes merely allowing someone to proceed from actively assisting him. Rav Tzadok concentrates on “giving an opening” and connects it to the apparent opening that the scoffer is shown for further mockery.

connections.hePhrase: "הַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא פּוֹתְחִין [לוֹ]", מִקְּרָא דְּ"אִם לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, לד);
connections.quote: ‘He scoffs at scoffers, but gives favor to the humble.’

connections.hePhrase: וְ"הוּא יָלִיץ" פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קפד עַמּוּד ב; וְחֵלֶק ג, צב עַמּוּד ב)
connections.quote: ‘When Israel arouses itself below with the shofar, the sound that comes from the shofar strikes the air and splits the heavens, until it rises to that mighty rock (another reading: ‘the Other Side’) that covers the moon. The one covering the moon looks and finds an awakening of mercy; then the one that rose and stands above is confounded. That sound then stands firm and removes that judgment. Since mercy has been awakened below, another, upper shofar is likewise awakened above. It produces a sound that is mercy, and sound meets sound, mercy meets mercy. Through the awakening below, there is likewise an awakening above.’

connections.hePhrase: דִּכְמוֹ שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר לְמַטָּה כָּךְ לְעוּמָּתוֹ לְמַעְלָה.
connections.quote: “We have learned: an act below awakens an act above. If a person acts properly below, he correspondingly awakens a power above in a proper manner. If a person performs kindness in the world, kindness is awakened above, rests upon that day, and crowns it on his account. If a person conducts himself mercifully below, mercy is awakened upon that day, and it is crowned with mercy on his account. Then that day stands over him as a guardian when he needs it. The same applies in the opposite direction. (And concerning everything:) if a person performs an act of cruelty, he awakens the same quality upon that day and damages it; afterward it stands over him cruelly, to remove him from the world. With the measure that a person measures, he is measured.”

connections.hePhrase: וְהֵם מִד' כִּתּוֹת שֶׁאֵין מְקַבְּלִים פְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סוֹטָה מב.),
connections.quote: ‘Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said: Four groups do not receive the presence of the Shekhinah: the group of scoffers, the group of flatterers, the group of liars, and the group of those who speak lashon hara.’

connections.hePhrase: וּלְכָךְ בּוֹ "תִּמְחֶה",
connections.quote: ‘When Hashem your God gives you rest from all your enemies around you, in the land that Hashem your God gives you as an inheritance to possess, you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from beneath the heavens. Do not forget.’

connections.hePhrase: וּמִצַּד הַטּוֹב הֵם חֲסִידֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer says: All the wicked among the nations have no share in the World to Come, as it is said, “The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God.” “The wicked shall return to Sheol”—these are the wicked of Israel; “all the nations that forget God”—these are the wicked among the nations. Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: Had Scripture said, “The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations,” and stopped there, it would say as you do: the wicked of Israel and the wicked among the nations. But now that Scripture says, “that forget God,” it follows that there are righteous people among the nations who have a share in the World to Come.”

connections.hePhrase: הֲגַם דְּ"בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח",
connections.quote: ‘He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord, Hashem, will wipe tears from every face. He will remove His people’s disgrace from all the earth, for Hashem has spoken.’

connections.hePhrase: וְכִמְשֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים סח.): "דְּהַנַּעַר בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה יָמוּת"
connections.quote: “Ulla raised a contradiction: It is written, ‘He will swallow up death forever,’ yet it is written, ‘The youth will die at a hundred years old.’ There is no difficulty: the first concerns Israel; the second concerns the nations. But what are the nations doing there? As it is written, ‘Strangers shall stand and tend your flocks, and foreigners shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.’”

connections.hePhrase: וּכְמַאֲמַר זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְכִילְתָּא סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח) דְּאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּר מֵעֲמָלֵק.
connections.heRef: מכילתא דרבי ישמעאל, מַסֶּכְתָּא דַעֲמָלֵק ב׳:נ׳
connections.quote: “Rabbi Eliezer says: The Omnipresent swore by the Throne: If someone from any of the nations comes to convert, Israel shall accept him; but someone from the house of Amalek they shall not accept, as it is said, “David said to the young man who told him: Where are you from? He said: I am the son of an Amalekite convert.” At that moment David recalled what had been said to Moses: If someone from any of the nations comes to convert, Israel shall accept him; but someone from the house of Amalek they shall not accept, as it is said, “David said to him: Your blood is upon your own head, for your mouth has testified against you.””

connections.hePhrase: שֶׁהוּא הַמּוּרְגָּשׁ וְנִקְרָא "יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן", וְהוּא הַנִּקְרָא אַבָּא כַּנּוֹדָע.
connections.quote: “As is known, “ayin,” nothingness, is the name of Keter, which is already included among God’s attributes that extend through the mystery of contraction to become revealed and apprehensible to a person. But this attribute is their root, and therefore it is called “ayin.” For the beginning of apprehension’s revelation to the brain is called “yesh me-ayin,” existence from nothingness: this is the apprehension of wisdom in the brain, which is already something existent.”

connections.hePhrase: אֲבָל כֶּתֶר הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם וּכְמוֹ מַקִּיף כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.quote: see note 3559.
connections.explanation: Beit Yaakov identifies kelipas nogah with permitted matters that nevertheless require clarification, through the example of Lot’s rescue for Avraham’s sake. This helps explain why the final siman still speaks of repair after discussing the rejection of open evil. The remaining task concerns the direction and use of permitted powers, not a claim that everything permitted is already a transgression.

connections.hePhrase: וְשָׁרְשָׁן מִקְּלִיפַּת נוֹגַהּ שֶׁמִּכֹּחוֹ כָּל דִּבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת כַּנּוֹדָע,
connections.heRef: תניא, חלק ראשון; ליקוטי אמרים ז׳:א׳-ה׳
connections.quote:
